papers.node_id: 37setonhalllrev67!!Article: "You don't have to be Ludwig Wittgenstein": How Llewellyn's Concept of Agreement Should Change the Law of Open-quantity Contracts
papers.title: Article: "You don't have to be Ludwig Wittgenstein": How Llewellyn's Concept of Agreement Should Change the Law of Open-quantity Contracts
papers.abstract:
"The real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new landscapes but in having new eyes."
In all of the hubbub over the recent revisions to Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code ("UCC" or "Code"),a seemingly innocuouschange to Official Comment 1 to section 2-201,the statute of frauds provision of the UCC,has escaped critical attention. Thischange, however, warrants a closer look.With the change, Official Comment 1 to amended section 2-201 now acknowledges, albeit somewhat covertly, the existence and potential enforceability of a category of contracts that most courts and commentators have declared unenforceable: non-exclusive open-quantity contracts.
New Official Comment 1 provides that "a term indicating that the quantity is based on the output of the seller or the requirements of the buyer satisfies [the quantity requirement of section 2-201]."To this point, the Comment merely recognizes a growing trend among courts.The new Comment goes on, however, to add that "the same reasoning can be extended to a term that indicates that the contract is similar to, but does not qualify as, an output or requirement contract."This reference to quasi-requirement or output contracts is puzzling. What exactly would a contract that is similar to, but not qualifying as, a requirement or output contract look like?
A lone citation to PMC Corp. v. Houston Wire & Cable Co.,which follows this oblique reference, provides the answer. Like the new Official Comment 1 to section 2-201 of the UCC, however, PMC Corp. has received little critical attention. The fact that PMC Corp. has not been, to date, cited by other courts and has only been generally cited by a few commentatorsis not too surprising if one merely skims the opinion of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. Indeed, the court's discussion of the statute of frauds appears, on the surface, to be rather pedestrian, merely recapping a well-developed body of scholarship and case law on what constitutes a sufficient quantity term to satisfy section 2-201.But PMC Corp. is not being cited in new Official Comment 1 for its analysis of the statute of frauds. New Official Comment 1 instead cites PMC Corp. as an example of a case about a contract resembling, but not quite qualifying as, a requirement or output contract. The quasi-requirement contract at issue in PMC Corp. is a non-exclusive open-quantity contract.
The decision in PMC Corp. is remarkable (and thus its citation in new Official Comment to section 2-201 is remarkable) because the New Hampshire Supreme Court enforced a non-exclusive open-quantity contract when a vast majority of courts and commentators would not.Grounded on pre-Code case law, the general rule espoused by courts and commentators requires that open-quantity contracts be "exclusive."In other words, to be enforceable, open-quantity contracts must, according to the general rule, obligate the party with discretion over quantity - the quantity-determining party - to deal in the goods that are the subject of the contract exclusively with the other contracting party.
Given the prominence of this generally-accepted rule, it is a fair question to ask whether the favorable citation to PMC Corp. in new commentary to Article 2 has, or should have, any significance to the law of open-quantity agreements. This Article endeavors to answerthat question. I contend that the result in PMC Corp. (though not the entirety of the court's reasoning) is completely appropriate and, in fact, comports with the underlying jurisprudence of the UCC.Rather than working a revolutionary change in the law of open-quantity agreements, the court in PMC Corp. merely recognized and enforced the serious business commitments of two sophisticated commercial parties and thus did precisely what the Code was meant to do.That a majority of courts and commentators would find the outcome in PMC Corp. unorthodox means only that the time has come to take a fresh look at the UCC's full potential to validate open-quantity contracts.The majority rule requiring exclusivity as a prerequisite to the enforceability of open-quantity contracts not only stands at odds to the UCC's fundamental goal of respecting actualcommercial practices, but it overlooks Karl Llewellyn's concept of agreement,a concept at the core of the UCC.
This Article is divided into three parts. Part I begins by tracing the legal history of open-quantity agreements. It starts by considering some of the earliest cases recognizing the commercial utility of such agreements but struggling with how to validate them. Part I shows that courts initially refused to enforce open-quantity agreements, hewing closely to strict classic contract theory. Eventually, however, consistent with the realist turn in American jurisprudence taking place at the end of the nineteenth century,courts began acknowledging that businesses had legitimate reasons for entering open-quantity agreements, and courts thus strove to fashion an exception to the dictates of classic contract doctrine. Ultimately, that exception took the form of the exclusivity requirement. After tracing this pre-Code history, Part I then briefly discusses the UCC's provisions governing open-quantity agreements, highlighting the fact that no provision in the Code conditions enforceability of open-quantity agreements on exclusivity. Part I closes with an analysis of several post-Code cases, exposing the jurisprudential underpinnings of the modern rule requiring that open-quantity agreements be exclusive.
Part II starts a critique of the majority rule governing open-quantity agreements. It demonstrates some of the theoretical and practical weaknesses with the majority rule. Part II then looks at the seminal work of Professor Caroline Brown, who is one of the few scholars that has advocated for validation of open-quantity contracts.Part II surveys the key arguments Professor Brown advances to support her claims, but discusses why these arguments fall short of providing a complete basis for validation of open-quantity contracts. Part II closes with a brief evaluation of PMC Corp., which serves as an example of decisions rendered by a small minority of courts either rejecting the majority rule of exclusivity outright or radically expanding exceptions to the majority rule. Part II concludes that the small, but potentially growing, number of courts challenging the rule that open-quantity agreements must be exclusive are on the right track but have not yet articulated a rationale that fully comports with the underlying jurisprudence of the UCC.
Building on the work started by Professor Brown and embraced by courts like the New Hampshire Supreme Court in PMC Corp., Part III provides a theoretical basis for validating all open-quantity agreements. Part III starts by recalling the legal-realist foundations of the UCC, with the aim of showing how the UCC was intended by its drafters to accommodate, flexibly and liberally, the actual practices of commercial parties, displacing the rigid formalities that were hallmarks of classic contract law. Part III then discusses the fundamental mechanism through which this flexibility is realized: Karl Llewellyn's concept of agreement. Part III contends that Llewellyn believed that the Code's concept of agreement would replace the common law's rigid offer-consideration-acceptance model of contracting with a pragmatic approach to commercial deal making. The Code concept of agreement looks to the understanding, in fact, between the parties, which is discovered through consideration of not only the language of the parties' contract but also the circumstances surrounding their encounter. In so doing, the Code concept of agreement eschews rigid formalities, focusing instead on evaluation of the aggregate relations and commercially reasonable expectations of contracting parties. Full recognition by courts of the flexible character of agreements under the Code leads inexorably to the conclusion that the serious commercial undertakings of sophisticated business entities should be enforced, even if the parties have entered into a nonexclusive open-quantity agreement.

questions.question: Whether non-exclusive open-quantity contracts should be legally enforceable.
Whether a flexible, contextual conception of agreement-one that looks to parties' commercial expectations and surrounding circumstances-justifies enforcing non-exclusive open-quantity contracts.

Whether the traditional requirement that the party with discretion over quantity deal exclusively with its counterparty is supported by commercial practice or is inconsistent with the goal of respecting real-world commercial arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of recent Article 2 revisions and Official Comments in light of commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the amendment to Official Comment 1 to section 2-201 and argues it signals (and should signal) a shift toward enforcing non-exclusive open-quantity agreements; Paper B situates section 2-207 within ongoing Article 2 revision efforts and uses empirical interviews to assess how proposed changes would affect real-world contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role and scope of the UCC gap-fillers when parties leave terms open or conflict
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on the UCC's flexible approach (and Llewellyn's idea of agreement) to justify enforcing deals despite indeterminate quantity language rather than imposing formal requirements, while Paper B repeatedly identifies reliance on UCC gap-fillers as the practical and doctrinal backstop that governs terms when the exchange-of-forms yields no bargain in fact.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal doctrinal rules (mirror-image/last-shot; exclusivity requirement) and pragmatic, fact-sensitive standards for finding agreement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the majority exclusivity rule for open-quantity contracts as anachronistic formalism and urges a pragmatic Llewellynian approach, and Paper B critiques the mirror-image/last-shot common-law rules and shows how section 2-207 was designed to replace them with a more practice-oriented regime.

shared_topics.topic: standards for enforceability of contracts with indeterminate or conflicting terms (open-quantity vs. battle-of-the-forms scenarios)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when a non-exclusive output/requirement-like clause satisfies the quantity requirement of section 2-201 and should be enforced, while Paper B analyzes when exchange-of-forms transactions form contracts under section 2-207 and which conflicting terms (if any) will be enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrine should respond to, and be informed by, actual commercial behavior and business practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should honor the serious commitments of sophisticated parties and adapt doctrine accordingly (invoking commercial realities and Llewellyn's concept), and Paper B reports empirical interviews showing how businesses actually draft and respond to forms, using that evidence to recommend modest statutory and doctrinal adjustments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34tourolrev83!!SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment of contracts with missing or open terms (indefiniteness/gap-filling)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Cardozo's Sun Printing refusal to enforce a contract for leaving price and duration terms open and situates it within the indefiniteness doctrine; Paper B examines courts' enforcement (or refusal) of open-quantity contracts and whether non-exclusive quantity terms satisfy UCC requirements, both engaging the question of when courts should fill gaps or decline enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the UCC/Restatement versus common-law formalism in validating commercial agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the UCC and Restatement (Second) encourage gap-filling in contrast to Cardozo's Sun Printing approach, while Paper B centers on Article 2, Official Comment 1, and Llewellyn's UCC-based concept of agreement as a basis for validating open-quantity contracts, comparing Code flexibility to older common-law rules.

shared_topics.topic: historical and contextual critique of key judicial decisions to reassess doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts a historical and economic investigation of Sun Printing and surrounding circumstances to critique Cardozo's reasoning and effects, and Paper B traces pre-Code and post-Code case law (including PMC Corp.) to reassess the origins and appropriateness of the exclusivity rule for open-quantity agreements.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal certainty and commercial realism (respecting business practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Cardozo's prioritization of certainty in contracts versus the commercial need for adaptable arrangements and the courts' gap-filling, while Paper B argues that the UCC's realist, flexible approach (via Llewellyn's concept of agreement) better respects commercial practices like open-quantity deals.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrines shaping enforceability affect market behavior and business arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A suggests Sun Printing's dismissal of the agreement may have increased uncertainty and facilitated anticompetitive conduct in the newsprint industry, and Paper B argues that the majority exclusivity rule (and its rejection in cases like PMC Corp.) has real consequences for how businesses structure and rely on open-quantity contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43iowajcorpl1!!ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of existing contract doctrine to novel or nontraditional contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that self-driving contracts expose deficiencies in traditional contract vocabulary (rules vs standards, complete vs incomplete) and urges development of new doctrinal language; Paper B similarly interrogates whether UCC doctrine and Llewellyn's concept of agreement properly accommodate non‑traditional open‑quantity contracts and calls for doctrinal recalibration.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of agreements containing open, indeterminate, or gap‑filling terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contracts that intentionally leave broad ex ante objectives to be specified later by algorithms and asks how doctrines like definiteness and agreements to agree apply; Paper B analyzes the statutory and common‑law treatment of open‑quantity (indeterminate‑quantity) contracts and whether such open terms can be enforced under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' sophistication and commercial context in judicial treatment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a key distinction between consumer transactions and sophisticated commercial parties when assessing how law should treat self‑driving contracts and their providers; Paper B emphasizes enforcing serious commitments of sophisticated commercial parties and argues the UCC (via Llewellyn's realist approach) should give weight to commercial practices and party sophistication.

shared_topics.topic: relying on commercial practices and external mechanisms to validate or supply contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights markets for third‑party providers, platform vendors, arbitration and insurance as mechanisms that will supply or govern the computational terms that fill contractual gaps; Paper B likewise invokes commercial practices, precedent (e.g., PMC Corp.), and the UCC's realist orientation as the appropriate external bases for validating open‑quantity agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62amjcompl687!!ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+

shared_topics.topic: flexible versus formalistic contract doctrines in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the UCC (via Llewellyn's concept of agreement) should be read flexibly to enforce non‑exclusive open‑quantity bargains rather than adhere to rigid common‑law formalities; Paper B analyzes the broader policy tradeoff between flexible private ordering (defaults) and rigid mandatory terms when designing contract regulation.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional allocation of authority to shape contract rules (courts vs legislatures/regulators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the role of courts in interpreting the UCC and urges judicial recognition of commercial realities to validate novel contract forms, while Paper B explicitly compares courts, legislatures, and executive agencies—evaluating which institutions are best placed to create interpretive defaults or mandatory contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: grounding doctrinal rules in actual commercial practices and parties' expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes respecting the real commercial undertakings and expectations of sophisticated parties as the normative basis for enforcing open‑quantity agreements, and Paper B treats states' preference for 'reasonableness' and information costs/mobility as reasons to shape whether rules should reflect prevailing market practices.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between private ordering and public intervention in contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends enforcement of commercial parties' private agreements under the UCC, challenging doctrinal barriers that impede private ordering, whereas Paper B examines when default rules (preserving private ordering) are preferable to mandatory regulation and how political‑economic factors affect that choice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 37jlegalstud503!!ARTICLE: Completing Contracts in the Shadow of Costly Verification
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Completing Contracts in the Shadow of Costly Verification

shared_topics.topic: how courts' capacity and costs of fact‑finding shape which commercial contract terms parties include and rely on
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how costly judicial verification and litigation influence parties to include imperfect, costly signals and standards (and sometimes prefer facing litigation costs) to secure incentives; Paper B analyzes how courts' willingness to enforce nonstandard quantity terms (via UCC interpretation and case law) determines whether businesses can rely on open‑quantity clauses in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the use and enforceability of indeterminate or standard‑based contract terms (e.g., 'best efforts', confidentiality, non‑exclusive quantity) that require judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies covenants like confidentiality and 'best efforts' as costly‑to‑verify standards that invite litigation and affect contracting choices, while Paper B focuses on non‑exclusive open‑quantity clauses—another form of indeterminate term—and whether doctrinal interpretation should validate such commercially used standards.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal legal doctrine and actual commercial practices in validating incomplete or nontraditional contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the binary verifiability assumption of contract theory and shows how real contracts incorporate imperfect signals despite enforcement frictions; Paper B argues that the UCC (and Llewellyn's concept of agreement) should be read flexibly to respect actual commercial open‑quantity practices rather than strict exclusivity rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of doctrinal interpretation (statutory comments, case law) in expanding or restricting the set of enforceable commercial agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how the court's fact‑finding and the enforceability of certain signals affect contractual completeness and incentives, implying that doctrinal stances on verifiability matter; Paper B performs a doctrinal history and critique of UCC commentary and cases (like PMC Corp.) to show how judicial and statutory interpretation can validate previously unenforceable open‑quantity contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: whether mutually-intended meaning (a 'meeting of the minds') can be ascertained or should govern ex post contract disputes

papers.node_id: 55umiamilrev369!!ARTICLE: 2-207 and Company (For Richard A. Hausler)
papers.title: ARTICLE: 2-207 and Company (For Richard A. Hausler)
papers.abstract:
Richard Hausler possessed--or was possessed by--a distinctive intelligence. He was often characterized as theatrical (the recessional at his funeral was "There's No Business Like Show Business"). But this label is too straightforward. Hausler's mind worked with extraordinary facility within conventions, within overtly artificial points of view. His thought pushed quickly and elaborately to the limit of his chosen conceit or stance, and demanded that those who would engage him proceed likewise. Hausler knew as well--seemed to grasp immediately in any particular setting--the power that conventions confer on transitions. Moving outside until-then confining formulas imparts a force, an urgency, a sense of the real and the authentic, to what is said next. Richard Hausler was able--remarkably often--to conjoin the theatrical and the moral (a distinctive accomplishment).
will try to write for Richard Hausler. My subject (his, not ordinarily mine) will be contracts and the Uniform Commercial Code. My point of departure will be an essay by Richard Hyland, at one time also a member of the University of Miami faculty. (Familiar Miami figures stir in the background--Soia Mentschikoff and Daniel Murray.) In particular, I will discuss section 2-207 and associated sections of the proposed revisions of Articles 1 and 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code. It is not clear, at this point, that revised Articles 1 and 2 will clear all the necessary hurdles. The provisions that I read are not much in controversy--or so I understand. They are, however, jurisprudentially provocative--or so I will argue.

questions.question: How should the law determine whether a binding contract exists and which terms govern when parties exchange standardized pre-printed commercial forms that contain additional or conflicting terms?

What are the jurisprudential and normative effects of revising foundational commercial contract rules-do the proposed changes improve doctrinal clarity, commercial predictability, and fairness, and what tradeoffs do they create?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates a growing ‘new formalism’ in contract law and analyzes how courts invoke party sophistication to reintroduce contextual concerns into otherwise literal enforcement; Paper B treats UCC section 2-207 and proposed revisions—doctrines governing the "battle of the forms"—which raise the same jurisprudential question of how much weight to give written/formal terms versus commercial practice and context.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party status (sophistication / merchant) in determining which rules apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts rely on a status-based dichotomy (sophisticated vs unsophisticated) to decide interpretive and remedial questions and calls for a clearer definition; Paper B centrally engages the merchant/non-merchant distinction baked into UCC 2-207, which similarly conditions when extra or conflicting terms become part of a contract.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules and defaults allocate risk and enforce standardized terms in commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that labeling a party sophisticated shifts the legal regime toward freedom of contract and forces risk-bearing on that party, while Paper B analyzes 2-207 and proposed UCC revisions that operate as default rules determining whether additional/form boilerplate terms are incorporated, thereby allocating contractual risks between parties.

shared_topics.topic: the need for clearer, fact-driven doctrinal standards rather than rhetorical labels or conventions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' slipshod use of the 'sophistication' label and urges an exacting, evidence-based standard; Paper B engages proposed statutory revisions and jurisprudential debate over 2-207 and related conventions, reflecting concern with whether existing categories and rules give sufficiently clear guidance to courts and commercial actors.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: the role of customs/conventions/norms in shaping commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how conventions and formal stances govern contract practice and how moving outside those conventions has force in interpretation (discussing the conventions surrounding UCC Article 2 and 2-207), while Paper B centrally argues that market customs and norms—more than welfare calculus—drive how bait-and-switch tactics are regulated and enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretation and scope of statutory/regulatory provisions for commercial conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes section 2-207 and proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the UCC, raising jurisprudential questions about the provision's reach and application; Paper B examines the FTC Act's section 5, statutory and regulatory definitions of 'bait-and-switch,' and how legal definitions do or do not capture a range of marketplace behaviors.

shared_topics.topic: the legal treatment of standardized market practices and forms (boilerplate, ads, promotions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the 'battle of the forms' under 2-207—how standardized contractual forms and their differing terms are reconciled—while Paper B analyzes standardized commercial tactics such as advertised specials, free offers, and teaser rates and how law treats these common promotional forms.

shared_topics.topic: how legal change or reform alters market behavior and reflects normative aims (fairness vs welfare)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the UCC and the jurisprudential and moral implications of changing contract rules, and Paper B studies regulatory interventions (e.g., the CARD Act, FTC rules) showing how shifts in law can change entrenched business practices and reflect tradeoffs between reinforcing norms/fairness and promoting welfare.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2011utahlrev1461!!ARTICLE: Confronting the Certainty Imperative in Corporate Finance Jurisprudence
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Confronting the Certainty Imperative in Corporate Finance Jurisprudence

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation of commercial contracts and statutory provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the jurisprudential implications of UCC section 2-207 and proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2—raising questions about how courts will construe 'battle of the forms' issues—while Paper B analyzes the interpretive stance courts adopt in corporate finance cases and critiques the prevailing judicial methodologies that shape contractual outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: role of statutory reform and rules (e.g., UCC revisions or regulatory change) in shaping commercial/financial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on proposed revisions to the Uniform Commercial Code and how those changes would affect contract law in commercial transactions, and Paper B discusses ongoing legal reform debates in financial markets and how statutory characterization and reclassification of instruments influence market practice and judicial reach.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A's treatment of section 2-207 implicates which contractual terms govern and thus which parties obtain what remedies when forms conflict, and Paper B explicitly argues that courts should allocate rights and remedies in finance cases according to the economic substance of arrangements rather than rigid doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between legal certainty/stability and doctrinal flexibility in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops the notion of a 'Certainty Imperative' that drives judicial restraint to preserve market stability, while Paper A raises jurisprudentially provocative questions about disrupting conventional doctrinal formulas (via UCC revisions), thereby engaging the same tradeoff between predictable rules and the need for doctrinal adaptation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: the problem of inferring mutual intent (the 'meeting of the minds') in contract formation and later interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally argues that in complex commercial contracts mutual intent often does not exist or cannot be recovered ex ante, making searches for a historical 'meeting of the minds' futile; Paper B engages the same problem via the Uniform Commercial Code (notably §2-207 and related revisions), which addresses when parties' forms and conduct evidence an intent to be bound and thus how courts should infer assent.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal textual rules and pragmatic/contextual interpretation for resolving contractual gaps and ambiguities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts formalist approaches (inducing a rule from text or prior law) with pragmatic, language-game and rule-skeptical accounts that treat meaning as arising when applied; Paper B debates proposed UCC provisions that function as formal default rules but are jurisprudentially provocative because they interact with commercial practices and contextual conventions, raising the same formalism-versus-pragmatism questions.

shared_topics.topic: limitations of negotiated or standardized documentation (including the 'battle of the forms') to control opportunism or determine ex post outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that ex post disputes reveal that contractual language often does not prevent opportunistic reinterpretation because meaning is imputed only when a dispute arises; Paper B directly addresses the mechanics and doctrinal consequences of standardized commercial paperwork (and §2-207's treatment of additional/contradictory terms), showing how the law attempts — and sometimes fails — to allocate risk and curb opportunism in form-based contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal doctrine and judicial rule‑induction in shaping commercial contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links contract interpretation to broader debates about rule‑induction, judicial creativity, and the limits of deriving principles from prior decisions; Paper B examines proposed statutory revisions to the UCC and their jurisprudential implications, engaging how doctrinal choices (legislative or judicial) create or modify the rules that govern commercial practice.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how contract form (e.g., OEM-drafted SFKs, unanimity clauses) reflects bargaining positions and is used to centralize control over quality and planning; Paper B analyzes statutory rules (2-207 and proposed revisions) that determine which party's terms govern when merchants exchange competing forms, thereby effecting doctrinal allocation of contractual power.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: AN EMPIRICAL VIEW OF CONTRACT.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents—empirically—that academic doctrine does not descriptively capture how parties actually make deals and resolve disputes, while Paper B interrogates how statutory formulations (e.g., UCC provisions) map onto real transactional conventions, highlighting tensions between doctrine and practice.

shared_topics.topic: the consequences of legal change and statutory revision for contracting behavior over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reflects on developments across decades and what new empirical realities would alter in earlier accounts of contracting, while Paper B focuses on proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the UCC and considers how those changes would affect jurisprudence and commercial practice.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the limited practical role of academic contract law creates important theoretical problems for scholars, and Paper B describes certain UCC provisions and revisions as 'jurisprudentially provocative,' engaging similar concerns about legal theory and interpretive consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal conventions, images, and background rules versus party autonomy in shaping contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how inherited images from goods commerce and the need for background legal rules influence outcomes and party planning, and Paper B interrogates the conventions and jurisprudential stances embedded in UCC revisions (and how moving outside formulas affects doctrinal force), implicating the balance between background norms and contractual freedom.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes interpretive rules from reconstruction and argues courts should resort to reconstruction in a 'twilight zone' of unexpected events, while Paper B focuses on 2-207 and associated revisions that supply default rules for additional or different terms and thus perform gap‑filling and interpretive functions in commercial transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract/party autonomy and intervention for fairness or commercial efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly addresses and seeks to rebut freedom‑of‑contract and efficiency objections to judicial modification of contracts by grounding certain doctrines in fairness-based principles; Paper B raises jurisprudentially provocative questions about UCC revisions that alter default bargaining allocations, thereby implicating how much law should defer to commercial parties' form bargains versus enforce normative defaults.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends contextual standards (good faith, best efforts) as appropriate tools for regulating staged negotiations despite verification costs, while Paper B engages jurisprudentially with the conventions and doctrinal choices embodied in 2-207 and the UCC revisions—i.e., whether to rely on formalized rules or more flexible, convention-sensitive approaches to govern commercial contracting.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how preliminary agreements allocate exogenous risks (e.g., interest-rate risk), protect reliance investments, and justify remedies (including expectation damages) for breaches of negotiation duties; Paper B’s focus on 2-207 implicates how divergent form terms (warranties, disclaimers, limitation of liability) allocate commercial risk and what remedies attach when parties’ forms conflict.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts new formalist calls for clear remedial rules with a 'new legal realism' emphasis on empirical law-in-action and negotiated process rationality, arguing that rules interact with informal networks and settlements; Paper B raises jurisprudential questions about UCC revisions and relies on commercial conventions, prompting a similar debate over whether bright-line statutory provisions or attention to commercial practice should govern contract disputes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the proper judicial stance—whether courts should rigidly enforce promises or craft rules that facilitate efficient renegotiation and protect vulnerable parties—and notes the crowding-out/paternalism concerns; Paper B's examination of revised Article 2 and section 2-207 likewise implicates how much gatekeeping and interpretation courts should perform in deciding which terms survive and how disputes between standard forms are resolved.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and reform of UCC Article 2's section 2-207 (the 'battle of the forms')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly takes section 2-207 and associated proposed revisions of Articles 1 and 2 as its subject matter and probes the jurisprudential implications of those revisions; Paper B treats Article 2 of the UCC as a central object of study, diagnosing how its rules (including the sales-law frameworks that govern form-exchange disputes) have aged and why revision or reinterpretation may be necessary.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of private lawmaking bodies (ALI, ULC) and the UCC revision process in producing commercial contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its discussion in the context of proposed UCC revisions and the institutional actors who draft and push those changes, while Paper B analyzes at length how private bodies like the ALI and ULC created major instruments (the UCC and Restatements), the institutional constraints that make their outputs sticky or obsolete, and the political/economic forces shaping revision outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: default contract rules (their creation, persistence, and parties' ability or inability to contract around them)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this theme through its focus on 2-207 and related default allocations in sales law that govern how terms become part of contracts, and Paper B develops a sustained theoretical and empirical account of how default and quasi-mandatory rules are produced, persist despite changed commercial circumstances, and prompt parties to contract around or adopt second‑best solutions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (including section 2-207) as a form of statutory governance of commercial exchanges, while Paper B studies the Dojima futures exchange as a historical private-ordering governance system and directly compares private versus public enforcement regimes.

shared_topics.topic: the role and treatment of contractual conventions and merchant-written terms in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how conventions and the 'battle of the forms' (UCC §2-207) govern which contract terms control, and Paper B interrogates whether private ordering systems prioritize merchant-written contracts and trading rules over state law, treating merchant norms as binding legal content.

shared_topics.topic: normative and empirical assessment of legal rules' effects on market efficiency and distributional outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises jurisprudential (normative) questions about the implications of revised commercial-law provisions, and Paper B empirically evaluates claims that private ordering produced efficient market outcomes—ultimately offering a public-choice/rent-seeking critique that challenges efficiency-based justifications.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the role of commercial conventions (and their force in transitions) when interpreting and reforming UCC section 2-207, while Paper B systematically traces the shift from non‑state commercial customs to state law and analyzes how private rules interact with statutory regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how codification / revision of commercial law (e.g., the UCC) reshapes commercial practice and raises jurisprudential questions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the UCC and treats those changes as jurisprudentially provocative, and Paper B situates codification within a historical and functional account of why states replace or supplement private ordering in trade.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of private rule‑making (non‑state law) for commerce and when it can or should supplant state regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the potency of conventions and private practices in guiding contractual outcomes (illustrated by section 2-207 disputes), while Paper B investigates the varieties, functions, and conditions that favor the emergence of private rules instead of, or alongside, state law.

papers.node_id: 68amulrev1621!!ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: A BARGAINING LENS THAT EXPLAINS THE RISE OF THE LTA AND THE PERSISTENCE OF ALTERNATIVES AS A COST MINIMIZING STRATEGY
Long-term agreements ("LTAs") in the supply chain, with their information sharing provisions, have been heralded as a new way of doing business.Recent scholars examining how these LTAs are structured explain their emergence as a byproduct of a new deverticalized production economy and the increased uncertainty in an innovation economy.
Much of the literature examining LTAs in the manufacturing and innovation context have conceptualized these agreements as a blend of formalprovisions that enable informal enforcementin a variety ofways. Recent scholars have studied LTAs in two primary contexts: the innovation economy and the standard form contract LTA in a manufacturing context between Original Equipment Manufacturers ("OEMs") and automobile suppliers.These scholars have treated these LTAs as a new phenomenon, and a new way of doing business that departs from the vertically integrated firm.Instead ofmakingparts, companies nowbuyexternally and enter contracts to govern their purchases.
Scholars of LTAs begin with the premise the premise that these LTAs are all necessarily incomplete. In the context of innovation of a new product that is yet undiscovered, the contract cannot specify performance obligations because of the uncertainty about the final product. In the manufacturing context, the uncertainty is different: it concerns whether the supplier will effectively collaborate with the buyer to produce high quality goods by participating in a process of learning by monitoring that will improve both the quality and timeliness of production.
One response to this uncertainty in each setting is to provide formal contract provisions that obligate the supplier or the innovator to share information.Innovation scholars posit that although these information sharing provisions are "formal," they facilitate informal enforcement that results in a "braiding" of formal contract provisions and informal norms for enforcement.Some argue that such settings call for "low-powered sanctions."Others, such as Professor Matthew Jennejohn, argue that braiding theory does not fully explain the diversity of arrangements that include unanimity requirements for decision making.He explains unanimity requirements as a specific response to threats the parties face, such as entropy and spillover.
This Article takes a different approach, while still drawing on the literature of these scholars. The arrangements parties enter into in a variety of settings--to purchase or sell goods or to innovate on a product--can best be understood in terms of a bargaining dynamic that looks at how the private interests of the parties are turned into joint interests in the agreement reached.
It is a mistake to talk about the form of a contract without first understanding the bargaining needs and positions of the parties, and how those needs get reflected in the form of the agreement, given the options each party has. The form of the contract is not an end in itself. As a result, to analyze the form that contracting takes, one must understand the function that each party needs the contract to perform, as well as the kinds of transaction costs that each party must minimize if they want to go forward with their projects. These costs include opportunism, asymmetric information, uncertainty, and other frictions, such as entropy and spillover highlighted by Jennejohn.Each party approaches the bargaining with its own private goals and will reach a bargain only if the benefits of achieving those goals--through a particular contract type or form--outweigh the costs. This means firms are constantly looking for a contract form that will minimize their costs while maximizing contractual benefits.
This Article examines the choice of contractual form through this lens of bargaining theory. The choice of contractual form depends on how each of the parties defines its individual interests and its willingness to sacrifice some of its interests in order to get a deal that advances other interests--all in a cost minimizing way.
Explaining the choice of contractual form must also include one factor that has previously been ignored in the literature: the need for a document that functions as a planning tool for the transaction.This Article will also examine a range of reasons why parties would enter written LTAs, including the benefits they offer of facilitating planning while minimizing misunderstandings.The planning needs of parties will be greater in some settings than others.
Another purpose that may underlie the use of LTAs that take the form of standard form contracts (SFKs) is centralizing the processes and standards governing the sale of goods in a uniform document, whose costs can be recouped by repeated use over multiple transactions.The Article will suggest that certain types of LTAs that take the form of SFKs drafted by OEMs offer other advantages such as "centraliz[ing] decision-making." SFKs by OEMs centralize "control over terms that need to be standardized for various reasons."
Using the bargaining lens, this Article will seek to identify explanations first for why parties to a transaction use a particular form, such as a purchase order or an LTA, and second, whether they use an LTA that is a bespoke contract or a SFK LTA. This Article offers a transaction cost minimizing explanation to rationalize the choice of form and particular provisions in terms of how the LTA or other formal arrangement responds to problems that parties face when significant obstacles hinder complete contractual solutions. The Article also explores other functions of LTAs, such as planning and centralization of uniform terms. The transaction cost minimizing explanation for the choice of form that is tied to the lens of bargaining theory.
Although LTAs were initially thought to offer some security for buyers for future business, LTAs now place more requirements on suppliers than on buyers. Because buyers have been demanding more from suppliers in return for less than a binding commitment, some suppliers view the LTA as undesirable, prompting them to opt out of signing one or to use different arrangements in certain settings.
This Article will also consider alternatives to using LTAs and will suggest that parties deliberately choose among several options for selling goods, including avoiding an LTA altogether, and it offers some tentative explanations for why and when parties opt for alternatives to the LTA paradigm with its information sharing protocols. Further, the Article suggests that parties can rely on informal enforcement mechanisms regardless of whether they opt for an LTA or another means of exchanging goods such as a purchase order; therefore, there must be other reasons to adopt an LTA. It will examine whether some of the benefits offered by LTAs drafted by OEMs, such as centralized control and planning and control of opportunism under conditions ofuncertainty, can be achieved by other written agreements such as purchase orders, at least when those agreements reference elaborate documents such as quality control manuals available on the internet.
This Article seeks to explain the "alliance diversity"arrangements in the supply chain context as different means for controlling contractual hazards while minimizing costs. The total cost minimization may explain why, in some contexts, "formal" LTA contracts may be cost justified.Both automobile suppliers to OEMs and parties involved in joint innovation use formal contracts that take the form of LTAs.Although the context of these agreements differs, what may have tied them together is that they both involve large sunk costs, which means parties cannot exit easily. These costs arise from the demand of OEMs for informational disclosures on cost and quality, as well as large investments in parts for automobile manufacturers as well as innovation funding partners in the biotech and pharmaceutical arena demanding information on research progress and investment. Where, however, the product is fungible and can be easily resold, parties may avoid the cost of LTAs and operate purchase order by purchase order.Uncertainties exist in all three contexts concerning product quality and reliability of the counterparty (and, in theinnovation context, reliability of the product itself). There are ways of achieving planning benefits without an LTA and ways of achieving standardization through incorporating quality standards of excellence available online. Thus, sunk costs may be the differentiating factor that helps explain why automobile suppliers rely on LTAs, while makers of other products (some fungible, some not) often do not.
The Article also suggests that using the bargaining dynamic to understand the parties' individual interests and their joint desire to minimize transaction costs to maximize value can illuminate differences in agreements on such matters as the structure for resolving disputes. In the innovation context, unanimity is often required for decisions made during the collaboration. Why would such unanimity be required in such contexts? And why would many agreements not require such unanimity?And why, despite the presence of LTAs in the automotive setting, would a leading researcher suggest that LTAs are not elaborate contractual mechanisms, but instead, a structure for learning by doing and monitoring that revolves around information sharing and benchmarking?Why would that less contractual, more pragmatic approach that is premised on a way of operating, be a win-win approach for OEMs but not for innovation collaborators? Jennejohn suggests one answer to this conundrum based on the need to exclude a counterparty from appropriating property.This Article suggests that a bargaining theory lens transaction cost minimizing explanation that builds on the need to protect property and sunk costs in situations where the uncertainty about continuing relationships makes a long-term agreement without veto provisions less satisfactory for controlling appropriation at the least cost.
The Article also explores why these frameworks break down, and it ties both the diversity of arrangements and their possible breakdown to legal enforcement issues. It addresses whether, when, and why, as the contract innovation theorists suggest, legal remedies should berestricted to "low-powered sanctions."The bargaining dynamic lens may also illuminate which enforcement mechanism would be consistent with a transaction cost-value maximizing outcome for the parties. To resolve that issue of enforcement and to resolve what enforcement approach would be cost minimizing and value maximizing, this Article engages literature on the role of law intersecting with the informal enforcement of norms and analyzes both the experimental literature on crowding out,the law and economics of norms,and the purpose behind normsto ascertain the proper role for law when informal enforcement exists in a contract with some formal terms. It suggests that the bargaining lens may also offer insights into what level of enforcement would be warranted in different settings.
Part I will analyze the origins of LTAs in the new industrial economy. Part II will address the contracting obstacles parties face in allexchanges and the risks of opportunism in the supply chain that parties want to control. Part III will examine the legal issues surrounding these structures. Then Part IV will detail the distinctive features of the information sharing and supplier excellence training programs in many LTAs, examine whether these information sharing protocols have always existed, and analyze if and why they were part of the formal agreement. Next, Part V will examine alternative ways of exchanging goods and suggest reasons why parties opt out of an LTA but still achieve their long-term goals. Part VI will explore relational contracts and parties' positions in a network as mechanisms for informal enforcement. Further, Part VI will consider how informal enforcement can facilitate the transfer of information used to sanction counterparties, regardless of whether the parties opt for an LTA or another mode of exchanging goods. Part VII looks at network governance as an alternative or supplement to relational contracts, LTAs, and other supply chain relationships. Part VIII considers how networks fail, the consequences of network failures, and potential solutions for network failures. Part IX examines what the role of legal enforcement should be when parties are using agreements that are partially enforced by informal sanctions. Part X offers advice to lawyers negotiating agreements concerning the supply of goods. Part XI concludes that various types of arrangements will allow for informal enforcement and can be beneficial for parties in the supply chain, where informal enforcement breaks down, legal enforcement is appropriate if cost minimizing.

questions.question: When and why do firms choose long-term framework agreements (LTAs) instead of repeated spot contracts or other alternatives, and why do they choose bespoke LTAs versus standardized form LTAs?

How do bargaining positions and transaction costs (e.g., opportunism, asymmetric information, sunk costs, risk of appropriation) shape the specific contractual features parties include in supply agreements-such as information-sharing protocols, centralized standard terms, or unanimity decision rules?

Under what circumstances is it cost-minimizing for parties to rely on informal enforcement and norms versus formal legal remedies (including ''low-powered'' sanctions), given the parties' incentives, sunk investments, and risks of contractual breakdown?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49ucdavislrev1097!!ARTICLE: Contract Meta-Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Meta-Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: parties' preferences as the appropriate basis for selecting contractual rules or forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the choice of an interpretive regime should mirror the parties' preferences (or what reasonable parties would have preferred) and urges courts to determine that choice contextually; Paper B analyzes how bargaining positions and private interests shape the parties' selection of contract form (LTA, purchase order, SFK, bespoke) as a deliberate, negotiated outcome.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and cost‑minimization as explanatory grounds for doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages law‑and‑economics arguments (e.g., Schwartz & Scott) that posit litigation and evidentiary costs make textualism attractive and critiques those models; Paper B builds a transaction‑cost/bargaining account explaining why parties choose LTAs, standard forms, or alternatives in order to minimize costs like opportunism, uncertainty, and sunk investments.

shared_topics.topic: information, uncertainty, and the admissible evidentiary base
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether courts should admit broader contextual or post‑formation information (a larger evidentiary base) when construing contracts and questions parties' epistemic limits; Paper B treats uncertainty about products and processes as central and studies formal information‑sharing provisions in LTAs and how those provisions function to reduce uncertainty and support planning.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal legal enforcement and informal norms (low‑powered sanctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts interpretive regimes by their influence on administrability and litigation (textualism tending to limit evidence and litigation costs versus contextualism allowing broader inquiry), implicating when formal legal enforcement will be invoked; Paper B directly examines how LTAs braid formal provisions with informal enforcement, asks when legal remedies should be limited to low‑powered sanctions, and analyzes the cost‑minimizing role of law versus norms.

shared_topics.topic: standardization/centralization (standard form contracts) versus tailored, context‑sensitive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends pluralism in interpretive methodologies and notes institutional differences (e.g., merchant law vs common law) that permit varying approaches across contexts; Paper B analyzes why OEMs use standard form LTAs to centralize terms and when parties instead opt for bespoke agreements or purchase‑by‑purchase arrangements based on context and costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev170!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS

shared_topics.topic: contracting under uncertainty and innovation-driven changes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how parties design new or modified contractual forms in response to uncertainty created by innovation or changing economic conditions—Paper A maps how private actors stabilize emergent practices before courts see them, and Paper B explains why parties use LTAs or other forms when product, process, or relationship uncertainty prevents complete specification.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay of formal contract terms and informal enforcement ('braiding')
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the theme that formal provisions are often supplemented by informal norms and enforcement mechanisms—Paper B develops the 'braiding' account for LTAs and alternatives, while Paper A emphasizes that contextualizing regimes created by parties (including informal practices) shape interpretation prior to judicial involvement.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, opportunism, and bargaining as determinants of contract form
shared_topics.justification: Both adopt a transaction-cost/bargaining perspective to explain why particular contractual forms arise: Paper B explicitly models how bargaining over transaction costs (opportunism, information asymmetry, sunk costs) selects LTAs or alternatives, and Paper A argues parties (not courts) craft regimes to minimize such risks before litigation.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of courts and legal enforcement versus party-designed regimes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question when courts should intervene versus defer to party-created arrangements—Paper A calls for generalist courts to respect contextualizing regimes and practice 'passive virtues,' while Paper B examines when legal remedies (including low-powered sanctions) are warranted if informal enforcement fails.

shared_topics.topic: how market structure, scale (thickness), and institutional context shape contract choice
shared_topics.justification: Both investigate how features of the market and institutional environment determine contract form: Paper A uses a taxonomy based on market thickness and uncertainty to predict which contextualizing regimes arise, and Paper B ties LTA adoption (vs purchase‑orders or other alternatives) to industry structure, sunk costs, fungibility, and centralized OEM practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103columlrev1641!!ARTICLE:A THEORY OF SELF-ENFORCING INDEFINITE AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A THEORY OF SELF-ENFORCING INDEFINITE AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: deliberate contractual incompleteness as a design choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats LTAs and related long‑form agreements as necessarily incomplete and asks why parties choose particular incomplete forms (bespoke LTA vs standard form) given bargaining positions and sunk costs; Paper B focuses on deliberately indefinite agreements and develops why parties intentionally leave verifiable terms unspecified rather than drafting fully enforceable contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of informal enforcement and norms (including reciprocity) in sustaining agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how formal provisions are braided with informal enforcement, relational contracts, and network norms to achieve cooperation; Paper B advances a theory of reciprocal fairness and self‑enforcement to explain why parties rely on informal mechanisms instead of legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: coping with asymmetric information, hidden action, and monitoring through contract design or self‑enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies information‑sharing, monitoring, and benchmarking provisions in LTAs as responses to uncertainty and supplier opportunism; Paper B addresses hidden action/hidden information problems and argues reciprocity can substitute for legally specified, verifiable performance measures.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between legal enforcement and nonlegal (self‑help) mechanisms, including the effects of legal remedies on behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks when legal enforcement should step in versus relying on informal sanctions and examines crowding‑out literature; Paper B explains the persistence of the indefiniteness doctrine by arguing that imposing legal liability can crowd out efficient reciprocal self‑enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑cost and bargaining explanations for choice of contractual form and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly uses a bargaining dynamic and transaction‑cost minimization to explain why firms choose LTAs, purchase orders, or standardized forms; Paper B provides an efficiency rationale (lower enforcement and contracting costs through reciprocity) for why parties might optimally choose indefinite, self‑enforcing agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1998wislrev463!!ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.topic: the role of standard-form and industry model contracts in governing repeated commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how construction relies on extensively integrated, standard industry contract models and asks whether those models should be supplemented or replaced by codification; Paper B studies why firms adopt standard-form LTAs or bespoke agreements (SFKs) and how SFKs drafted by OEMs centralize terms and reduce costs across repeated supply-chain transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between formal legal rules and private ordering/informal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes private orderings (industry norms, internal organizations, mediated conflict management) operating alongside public law and asks when external law should act as a safety net; Paper B examines how LTAs braid formal provisions with informal norms, when low-powered (informal) sanctions suffice, and when legal enforcement is warranted to backstop informal mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form functions as a planning and transaction-cost minimizing tool
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames construction contracting as a transactional system where contract form and reform can reduce recurring conflicts and transaction frictions; Paper B develops a bargaining/transaction-cost account showing that parties choose LTAs, purchase orders, or other forms to minimize opportunism, uncertainty, and other transaction costs while serving planning needs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry governance structures and professional institutions in managing conflict and shaping contractual behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights implementing structures — the legal profession, industry organizations, educational and research institutions, and conflict-management mechanisms — as central to improving practice and lawmaking; Paper B considers network governance, relational contracting, and supplier-buyer practices (information sharing, benchmarking, training) as institutional alternatives or complements that govern behavior and resolve disputes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of codification and the prospects for legal reform versus private solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically assesses the possibility and limits of codifying construction transactions (even proposing a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts) while stressing bottom-up reform; Paper B questions whether formal LTA provisions or legal remedies should be expanded or restrained given informal enforcement and suggests when legal enforcement is cost-minimizing versus when private arrangements suffice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36houslrev1!!ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION

shared_topics.topic: need to adapt contract law and doctrine to new economic forms (innovation/information economies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates long-term agreements and supply‑chain contracting within a deverticalized, innovation‑driven economy and argues for analyzing contract form through transaction costs and bargaining in that new context; Paper B argues the shift from a goods‑based to an information/services economy requires retooling contract law (and the UCC) because old categories and images misfit modern information transactions.

shared_topics.topic: information as distinct contract subject matter and the role of information‑sharing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes LTAs' formal information‑sharing provisions (and their role in monitoring, learning, and protecting sunk investments), while Paper B focuses on transactions where the commodity is digital information or access and asks what accuracy, quality, and control obligations should govern those exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: incompleteness, uncertainty, and how contracts respond to them (bargaining and planning under uncertainty)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats LTAs as necessarily incomplete in innovation and manufacturing settings and explains contract forms as bargains that allocate risks and planning needs under uncertainty; Paper B highlights how information transactions resist neat categorization under existing doctrines, producing uncertainty about parties' obligations that the law must better accommodate.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal legal rules and informal enforcement/norms (appropriate level of legal enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly examines when informal enforcement and 'low‑powered' sanctions suffice versus when legal remedies are warranted in supply‑chain LTAs, drawing on law‑and‑norms literature; Paper B similarly emphasizes that contract rules should serve as a background to commercial practice and facilitate party reliance, implicating choices about how much law should govern information transactions.

shared_topics.topic: use of standardized contractual forms (SFKs, licenses) as governance and control devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes OEM‑drafted standard form LTAs as tools to centralize terms, planning, and control opportunism across repeated transactions; Paper B identifies licenses and limited grants as the dominant contractual form in information markets and examines how those forms differ functionally from goods sales and how doctrine should treat them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: the role of standard-form contracts and purchase orders in allocating contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how exchanged boilerplate forms (purchase orders and acknowledgments) trigger section 2-207 rules and determine which party's standard terms govern, while Paper B analyzes SFK LTAs and OEM-drafted standard forms (and purchase orders) as a deliberate form choice that centralizes and standardizes terms across transactions.

shared_topics.topic: how incomplete contracts get resolved (legal gap-fillers versus negotiated or implicit solutions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on U.C.C. gap-fillers and section 2-207's mechanisms for supplying missing or conflicting terms when parties' forms do not produce a bargain-in-fact, and Paper B treats LTAs and purchase orders as necessarily incomplete and analyzes how parties use contractual design, bargaining, or alternative mechanisms to fill or live with those gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal contractual language and informal commercial practices or enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports empirical findings about firms' real-world practices (reading forms, tailoring boilerplate, opting out) and how those behaviors interact with section 2-207, while Paper B studies 'braiding' of formal provisions and informal norms, exploring when formal clauses are backed by informal enforcement and when law should supplement or defer to norms.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of bargaining power and market structure (e.g., OEMs, mega-retailers) on contract form and content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how market power (mega-retailers, buyer/seller positions) and business realities affect which terms prevail and how firms draft forms, and Paper B explains why buyers like OEMs use SFKs and LTAs to centralize control and impose terms on suppliers, showing how relative leverage shapes contractual form.

shared_topics.topic: transaction-cost considerations (including planning, sunk costs, and negotiation costs) driving choice of contractual form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes firms' cost-driven tradeoffs between negotiating complete bilateral contracts versus relying on forms and U.C.C. gap-fillers (including costs of refusing performance), and Paper B offers a transaction-cost/minimizing bargaining-account for why parties choose LTAs, SFKs, purchase orders, or alternatives given sunk costs, uncertainty, and planning needs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 121columlrev1659!!ARTICLE: OBSOLESCENCE: THE INTRACTABLE PRODUCTION PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: OBSOLESCENCE: THE INTRACTABLE PRODUCTION PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: how parties and institutions fill gaps in incomplete contracts (default rules and gap‑filling)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how common law courts, statutes, and private lawmaking supply default rules to fill contractual gaps and how those defaults become obsolete; Paper B starts from the premise that LTAs and framework contracts are necessarily incomplete and examines how formal provisions and other mechanisms are used to fill gaps in practice.

shared_topics.topic: private versus public production of contract rules (who supplies standardized terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies (ALI/ULC/UCC) and private market actors as sources of contract rules and critiques their ability to update; Paper B examines how firms (OEMs, suppliers) create LTAs and standard form Ks as privately produced, centralized rule-sets and when parties rely instead on alternatives or legal intervention.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑cost and bargaining dynamics as explanations for contract form choice and persistence of alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers an economic theory showing why parties avoid or fail to replace obsolete state‑supplied terms because of the costs and coordination problems involved; Paper B advances a bargaining/dynamic transaction‑cost account explaining why firms choose LTAs, purchase orders, or other arrangements and why alternative forms persist as cost‑minimizing strategies.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between informal enforcement (relational norms) and formal legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how parties may contract around or exploit obsolete rules and how courts play a role in updating and enforcement, implying reliance on informal practices when law is mismatched; Paper B studies the ‘braiding’ of formal information‑sharing provisions with informal enforcement, asks when low‑powered or legal remedies are appropriate, and analyzes the law’s role where norms already govern behavior.

shared_topics.topic: standard‑form contracting, centralization, and coordination problems in multilateral markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights coordination failures that prevent revision of standardized, interdependent contract terms and the stickiness of such standards in large markets; Paper B focuses on SFK LTAs drafted by OEMs that centralize decision‑making and standardize terms across many suppliers, and explores when that centralization succeeds or when coordination leads parties to choose alternatives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2011utahlrev1461!!ARTICLE: Confronting the Certainty Imperative in Corporate Finance Jurisprudence

papers.node_id: 56scallrev573!!ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.
papers.title: ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.
papers.abstract:
Contract law is characterized by a comforting symmetry.  Minds must meet, consideration must be reciprocal, and remedies are designed to protect the expectancies of both parties.  Most contractual problems can be analyzed in terms of this balance; those that cannot are particularly troublesome.  One especially perplexing and discomforting problem is how to allocate reliance losses when performance is excused because of impossibility, frustration of purpose, or commercial impracticability.The appropriate allocation of reliance losses in these cases is difficult to determine because pure losses are involved.  Pure losses are expenditures by one party that do not result in commensurate gain to the other party.  In these instances, remedies based upon theories of desert and unjust enrichmentfail to indicate clearly who should bear the loss.
The competing views divide between those who would assign the losses to encourage economic efficiency or wealth maximizationand those who seek an arguably higher, though less well-defined, goal of"fairness" or "justice."The primary distinction between these views is that an efficient allocation of reliance losses places the entire loss on one of the two parties -- specifically, the party in the best position to avoid or insure against the loss.Fairness, on the other hand, usually requires the parties to share the loss.Furthermore, the wealth maximizing approach is characterized by its simplicity and its firm support in economic theory.  Fairness approaches, however, are typically quiteamorphous and without strong theoretical bases.
This Article presents a theoretical justification for evenly dividing losses associated with excused performance.The argument uses the notion of a contract as a moral partnership or "common enterprise"to reject the "all-or-nothing" solution.  Since partnerships and contracts have fundamentally similar purposes,the reliance losses associated with contracts should be treated like unanticipated partnership losses.  There is also a moral basis for dividing contractual losses evenly; individuals who are unable to take advantage of each other are likely to view loss sharing as a just result.
Before proceeding to the argument itself, Section I of this Article discusses in some detail the problem of frustrated contracts and reviews the current treatment of reliance losses.  Section II discusses and critiques the wealth maximizing approach.  Finally, Section III presents a partial ignorance model designed to minimize the prospect of one party taking advantage of the other and a justice-based argument for equal sharing of reliance losses.

questions.question: Whether reliance losses incurred when contractual performance is excused because of unforeseen events should be divided equally between the parties rather than borne entirely by one party.
Whether conceiving contracts as a moral partnership or common enterprise provides a defensible theoretical or moral justification for equal sharing of those reliance losses.
Whether a decision rule based on partial ignorance (designed to limit one party taking advantage of the other) supports equal loss-sharing as the preferred allocation to minimize opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: how to allocate risk and determine outcomes when standard contract doctrines break down
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses allocation of reliance losses when performance is excused for impossibility/frustration/impracticability (situations where ordinary expectations fail), while Paper B addresses how to determine governing terms and allocate contractual obligations when counterpart forms conflict (battle of the forms), so both grapple with doctrinal gaps in resolving atypical contract problems.

shared_topics.topic: critique of doctrinal reform and defense of alternative decision processes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the prevailing, economically framed approach to reliance losses and proposes a normative model (partial ignorance/common enterprise) as an alternative; Paper B critiques the proposed UCC revision to 2-207 and recommends abandoning the codified fix in favor of judicially driven resolution, making both papers interventions in debates over contract law reform.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and responsibility for unanticipated contractual losses

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW
