shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that American contract law should prioritize ex ante personal sovereignty and enforce the parties' agreed terms rather than allowing courts to invoke vestigial ex post equitable doctrines; Paper B examines whether courts (or parties) should reallocate losses after unforeseen events and weighs fairness-based sharing against economically efficient reallocations, engaging the same debate over honoring ex ante bargains versus correcting perceived ex post injustice.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability and desirability of contract terms that allocate risk or prescribe non‑compensatory outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the enforceability of liquidated damages and other ex ante risk allocations (including supra‑compensatory terms) as expressions of party sovereignty, criticizing courts that override them; Paper B proposes and normatively defends an ex ante or default rule of loss‑sharing (modeled on partnership norms), treating contractual design of risk allocation as central and debating whether courts should impose or respect such allocations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts (in Frigaliment) use extrinsic sources—trade usage, parties' communications, and course of dealing—to ascertain the meaning of contract terms; Paper B also relies on background facts and the idea of a contractual 'common enterprise' to argue that context and parties' shared expectations should shape how losses and obligations are allocated.

shared_topics.topic: normative frameworks guiding contract rules (efficiency vs fairness/justice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly contrasts wealth-maximizing (efficiency) and fairness-based approaches to allocating reliance losses and advocates a justice-based, equal-sharing rule; Paper A, in assessing judicial interpretation methods, engages with the normative question of which principles (textual certainty, commercial expectations, fairness to parties) should guide courts in resolving contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing contracts as relational agreements (partnership/common enterprise) rather than purely textual bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper B advances a model treating contracts like moral partnerships to justify loss-sharing; Paper A, through detailed discussion of extrinsic evidence and parties' shared understandings in Frigaliment, likewise treats contracting as a relational practice where meaning and obligations arise from the parties' interaction and commercial context rather than from text alone.

papers.node_id: 67arklrev873!!ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts
papers.abstract:
Technology is redefining relationships. And in long-term commercial transactions, where relationship is the coin of the realm, emerging technologies often foster intense collaborations. Thus may commence a new era for relational contract.
This article explores how collaborative technologies may be expanding opportunities for relational contract in commercialtransactions, especially in the form of what may be called the intentionally relational contract. That is, a flexible, negotiated agreement designed essentially for the management, preservation, and success of an interdependent relationship that the parties establish for a common goal in a context of uncertainty and change over time.In this regard, the digital world sometimes plays a key role by fostering and rewarding interdependence, adaptability, and reciprocity among otherwise autonomous, self-interested actors in the marketplace.
Unlike traditional legal doctrine, relational contract comfortably accommodates arrangements in which the parties to a commercial exchange aspire to rise above individual opportunism to manage an endeavor collectively and to share the risks and rewards of the venture.The intentionally relational contract stands in contrast to the more conventional notion of a commercial agreement, which intends, as much as possible, to allocate risks associated with a discrete transaction between the parties through contractual terms that attempt to anticipate and govern all reasonably foreseeable contingencies. As an example, the joint venture or strategic alliance formed for a specific endeavor is one of the most highly relational contracting structures widely in use today, while a simple purchase order from a buyer to a seller often exists at the discrete end of the spectrum.
This article presents a case study involving the most important technology affecting contractual relations in the construction industry. In brief, building information modeling ("BIM") is reshaping contractual relationships in the industry by facilitating and encouraging a previously unimagined degree of collaboration among design professionals, builders, specialty trade subcontractors, suppliers, manufacturers, and owners and operators.The result could be a truly transformative shift toward the intentionally relational contract in the building sector.
Part II of this article explores BIM, primarily from a construction law perspective rather than from a technical one.Then, Part III develops the thesis that as BIM becomes prevalent in the construction industry, project participants will pursue a more highly collaborative project delivery system that could foster a truly relational contract framework throughout the industry based on principles of integrated project delivery.But first, these introductory comments pause to suggest the potentially broader influence of the underlying phenomenon by which collaborative technology can lean toward relational contract.
The essential inquiry is not simply whether new technologies promote collaboration in the construction industry and other areas of commerce; rather, it is whether their effects on contracting practices might be transformative. Does an intentionally relational contract structure offer any compelling advantages for digitally based collaborations, and are collaborative technologies therefore producing more highly relational commercial exchanges? Given that the relational construct offers a dynamic understanding of interdependent exchanges, might not the proliferation of technologies that facilitate commercial teamwork and strategic alliances therefore support the broader hypothesis of a reciprocal association between collaborative technologies and relational contract?
The remainder of this introduction briefly discusses a few examples that seem to support this hypothesis. Whether the collaborative aspects of the technologies involved in any of these situations are in fact leading toward relational contracting practices in a significant way is a matter for much further analysis at a later date. For the modest purposes of setting the stage for the featured case study, it is enough at this point to mention a few illustrations that suggest the possibility.
A simple example appears in the pharmaceutical industry, where technology sharing plays a major role in the development and distribution of new products.Today, the field of biotechnology sometimes creates firms with narrow, unique expertise that can benefit from the efficiencies of strategic alliances.Relational contract often facilitates the integration of the distinct strengths of a biotech firm's research innovationsand intellectual property with a major pharmaceutical company's financial, marketing, and product development capacities.This is true because "biotechnology companies rely heavily on strategic alliances with pharmaceutical companies to finance their research and development (R&D) expenditures."Cooperation between pharmaceutical and biotech companies increasingly involves alliances that introduce governing structures allowing for shared risk and shared decision making.Unquestionably, these features are intentionally relational.
Technological advances are also presenting more opportunities for relational contracting structures between commercial buyers and their suppliers. For example, with the assistance of scanner technology, a retailer and its supplier can make joint decisions by analyzing real-time, in-store sales data.In a similar way, developments in data interchange can create "reciprocal interdependency" between a buyer and a supplier leading to "higher incentives for both parties to safeguard the relationship."One attribute of relational contracts particularly relevant to this context is that they help the parties cope with uncertainty by allowing some critical terms of the exchange to be determined during the course of the ongoing relationship without the need to amend written contracts.Technology motivates a retailer and its supplier to behave in this way, for example, when the parties allow the nature and quantityof product shipments to be determined based on a computerized analysis of changing sales data.
While these two indications of the relational influences of technology lend some support to the hypothesis, the manufacturing industry provides a much closer analogy to developments in the construction sector. The "formalized production network" represents a technologically advanced approach to manufacturing collaborations.Manufacturers of heavy equipment, together with their key component suppliers, frequently use three-dimensional computer modeling to help coordinate and manage the design and manufacturing process.The technology can result in a "digital prototype" of the product.An example is Boeing's much-studied 787 project, in which suppliers participated in an integrated design and manufacturing process.Indeed, modeling technology used in sophisticated equipment manufacturing is an antecedent to the BIM process, and it fosters and facilitates interdependent collaborations in much the same way.Reportedly, the commercial arrangements between the manufacturer and the suppliers in such situations manifest many relational contract characteristics.Due to the nature of the manufacturing industry, "companies must increasingly look outside their organization for new ideas and technologies… . Spurred by the rapid pace of technological innovation, research partnerships and joint ventures have consequently flourished."Industry literature highlights this movement by references to "ad hocpartnerships," "strategic partners," and "long-term, collaborative supplier relationships" that are "closely managed" and designed to align the incentives of multiple participants.As the discussion of integrated project delivery in Part III illustrates, the intentionally relational contract provides a structure for lawyers to translate these business concepts into contractual terms.
Software projects provide another especially apt example of collaborative technologies having the potential to draw commercial parties into highly relational exchanges. Often, heavily interdependent relationships contribute to the design and marketing of a program or application.Indeed, computer game developers have been known, contrary to standard firm behavior in the marketplace, to "open[] a portion of their proprietary digital content for transformation by the public," thereby "allowing digital consumer networks to generate new derivatives that can possibly be reintegrated into the firms' innovation process."This is an intentionally relational arrangement.
For me, however, the story that best evokes the relational alchemy of digital technology comes from the world of computer animation. Walter Isaacson's biography of the computer industry's most volatile creative genius, Steve Jobs, describes the business relationship behind Toy Story, the blockbuster film that revolutionized the animated movie genre.According to this account, after a successful preliminary contract in which Jobs's Pixar licensed its innovative animation system to Disney, Jobs wanted to produce a film in partnership with Disney.Reportedly, the negotiations were extended, tough, and contentious.In the language of contract theory, the process yielded an exchange far more transactional and discretethan relational. Pixar was financially unstable, while Disney was the industry giant.In keeping with the rational self-interest model of transactional contracting, the result was predictable. "Disney would own the picture and its characters outright, have creative control," and simply pay a percentage of ticket revenues to Pixar.Other deal points were equally protective of Disney, who "had the option (but not the obligation) to do Pixar's next two films and the right to make (with or without Pixar) sequels using the characters in the film."Disney even had the right to "kill the film at any time with only a small penalty."
Viewed through a lens of contract theory, the initial arrangement was static and tightly controlled by a set of discrete and comprehensive terms mostly designed to maintain Disney's dominance and to manage the company's risks. All Pixar had to offer was imagination and its whiz-bang animation technology. But as the relationship evolved after Toy Story's spectacular success, the terms of the written agreement became less significant and relational norms took hold.In particular, leaders at Disney apparently came to believe that achieving the full creative potential of Pixar's animation required an intimate understanding of the technology. As a result, a reincarnated deal implemented such values as pervasive cooperation, the flexibility to respond to unanticipated developments, reciprocity, strategies to deter opportunistic behavior, and a commitment to preserve the relationship.Pointing to these features, a relational theorist might readily conclude that the real contract between Pixar and Disney was governed by relational factors rather than by the written agreement fashioned at the beginning of the exchange. Relational theory emphasizes that contracts "grow and change as the parties perform over time."
And the contractual relationship between Pixar and Disney did indeed grow and change.Eventually, and with a considerable boost from Pixar's successful IPO, the result was a completely restructured deal that reflected how the working arrangement had matured.Although Disney already had a binding, and highly favorable, contractual right to make two sequels, the new commercial structure essentially reflected an equal partnership, with each company providing half of the financing and each taking half of the profits.Perhaps even more amazing, and much to Pixar's advantage, Disney agreed to co-branding so that the resulting films no longer seemed to be Disney movies made with the help of a creative outside contractor.
Anecdotal? Certainly. Apocryphal? Perhaps. But if the Toy Story enterprise could have achieved equal success without these relational contract enhancements, Disney should have been eager to maximize its profits by exploiting this fantastic technology within the original contract structure. But as things turned out, the animation process was not simply a marvelous tool for a film producer to use, but the medium that gave life to an interdependent and dynamic commercial exchange.
To summarize, in limited ways such as in the situations just discussed, collaborative technologies sometimes seem to go hand-in-hand with intentionally relational contract norms. These narrow examples, of course, cannot show that collaborative technologies will transform contracting practices for entire classes of exchanges or throughout any particular industry. But they can suggest that when a collaborative technology becomes powerful enough to reshape a commercial exchange, it may also move traditional contracting structures toward the more highly relational end of the spectrum.
The task at hand is to explore, in much greater detail, how a highly collaborative and powerful technology might promote a transformative shift toward relational contracting practices in the construction industry. The peculiar significance of BIM lies in the unique benefits that digital simulation offers in the context of the built environment. Achieving the full capacity of the technology requires intensive teamwork involving a diverse group of designers, technical experts, specialty consultants, trades, and project managers, each serving limited and highly specialized functions critical to achieving the project owner's objectives. While the remainder of this article concerns the construction industry alone, the issue lying just beneath the surface continues to be whether emerging collaborative technologies may be similarly poised to transform contracting practices in other segments of the economy.

questions.question: Do collaborative digital technologies lead commercial parties to adopt more intentionally relational contracting structures for interdependent, long-term exchanges?

Does the use of Building Information Modeling (BIM) in construction projects promote a shift from discrete, transaction-focused contracts toward more highly collaborative, relational contracting practices among project participants?
Do intentionally relational contracts offer measurable advantages for managing uncertainty, interdependence, and adaptability in digitally enabled commercial collaborations?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj103!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Desperately Seeking Consideration: The Unfortunate Impact of U.C.C. Section 2-306 on Contract Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Desperately Seeking Consideration: The Unfortunate Impact of U.C.C. Section 2-306 on Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: designing contracts to manage long‑term interdependence and uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties to long‑term variable‑quantity or exclusive‑dealing contracts structure terms (capacity limits, minimums, pricing schemes) to allocate risk and enable adaptation; Paper B examines the ‘intentionally relational’ contract as a negotiated, flexible agreement (often supported by BIM) specifically intended to manage interdependent commercial relationships over time under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: who controls discretionary decision rights and how those rights are constrained
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on buyer/seller discretion in output/requirements contracts and critiques courts’ use of implied ‘good faith’ to reshape those discretionary boundaries; Paper B addresses how collaborative technologies and relational contracts reallocate decision‑making (shared decisions, integrated delivery) and thus alter or limit unilateral discretion within projects.

shared_topics.topic: contractual mechanisms to protect reliance and deter opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A catalogs tools (take‑or‑pay, minimum quantities, standby charges, performance bonds, price‑indexing) parties use to protect relation‑specific investments and shape incentives; Paper B discusses contractual and normative strategies (reciprocity, shared risk/reward, integrated governance) that parties use in technologically enabled collaborations to deter opportunistic behavior and protect investments.

shared_topics.topic: the role of law, doctrine, and drafting in shaping commercial practices versus informal relational norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques judicial intervention (e.g., courts reading in ‘good faith’/‘best efforts’) as potentially undermining parties’ negotiated allocations; Paper B explores how lawyers translate business relational practices into formal contract terms but also acknowledges that relational norms and technology‑enabled practices can supersede or supplement written doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of contractual flexibility and adaptive terms for efficient performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that fine‑tuned contractual provisions (pricing adjustments, quantity caps, contingency devices) better serve adaptation than after‑the‑fact judicial standards; Paper B argues that intentionally relational contracts, enabled by collaborative technologies like BIM, permit terms and performance to be adjusted during the relationship to cope with change and complexity.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68stanlrev281!!ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting in collaborative commercial exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the idea of an "intentionally relational contract," arguing that collaborative technologies like BIM push construction projects toward negotiated, flexible agreements that manage long-term interdependence; Paper B situates its analysis in the relational contracting literature (Macaulay/Macneil) and evaluates how relational norms and theories explain governance in innovation networks and alliances.

shared_topics.topic: design and governance of interfirm alliances under uncertainty and interdependence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes integrated project delivery and joint-venture-like arrangements in construction where many specialized actors must coordinate under uncertainty; Paper B studies alliance contracts across high-technology industries, examining governance mechanisms (e.g., management committees, vetoes) used to coordinate partners and manage interdependent innovation tasks.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal contracts and the role of informal/adaptive governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that BIM-enabled projects often rely on relational norms and in-performance adjustment rather than exhaustive written terms to cope with unforeseeable contingencies; Paper B critiques relying solely on formal contract doctrine, develops braiding/multivalent contracting to explain how formal provisions and informal constraints jointly govern collaborations, and questions minimalistic judicial enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of collaborative technologies and digital modeling on contractual practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally argues that BIM and related collaborative technologies can transform contracting in construction by fostering tighter cooperation and new contracting forms; Paper B draws on technology-driven examples (e.g., digital prototyping, Boeing 787) to show how technological coordination challenges reshape alliance design and reveal contract governance problems.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk, incentives, decision rights, and ownership in collaborative projects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how intentionally relational contracts reallocate risk and reward, align incentives, and enable shared decision-making among designers, builders, and suppliers; Paper B analyzes how alliance contracts allocate veto rights, IP ownership, and payment/incentive structures and how those allocations create tradeoffs that influence governance choices.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: relational contract theory as the appropriate legal framework for multi‑party, interdependent endeavors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the idea of an 'intentionally relational contract' to capture how BIM-driven construction projects require flexible, relationship‑centred agreements, while Paper B explicitly grounds collective impact initiatives in relational contract theory and argues that such a framework better explains and supports cross‑sector social collaborations.

shared_topics.topic: designing contractual forms (term sheets/standard agreements) for collaborative, multi‑stakeholder projects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines integrated project delivery and other contract structures that lawyers can use to translate highly collaborative BIM projects into enforceable arrangements, and Paper B proposes drafting principles and a standard form collective impact term sheet to memorialize and sustain public‑interest coalitions.

shared_topics.topic: how collaborative processes or technologies create incentives for parties to move from discrete transactions toward ongoing, adaptive agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how collaborative technologies (e.g., BIM, digital modeling, shared data systems) foster interdependence, reciprocity, and adaptability that push parties toward relational contracting, while Paper B analyzes collective impact as a structured collaborative process that similarly produces 'agree to agree' dynamics requiring relational agreements.

shared_topics.topic: using contract design to manage uncertainty, align incentives, and allocate shared risk/reward over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that intentionally relational contracts accommodate uncertainty and enable shared decision‑making, risk sharing, and adaptability in construction projects using BIM, and Paper B argues that collective impact agreements can clarify authority, accountability, and resource commitments to align incentives and sustain long‑term social initiatives.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transactional lawyers in enabling and structuring collaborative public‑private ventures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights lawyers' work in translating integrated, technology‑driven business practices into contractual terms for construction projects, and Paper B advocates a new mode of 'impact transaction' lawyering where transactional attorneys draft relational contracts to effectuate large‑scale collective impact efforts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62amjcompl687!!ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+

shared_topics.topic: how exogenous changes (mobility or collaborative technology) drive shifts in contract form and regulatory choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how population and firm mobility reshape demand for and feasibility of mandatory contract terms across jurisdictions, while Paper B examines how collaborative technologies (e.g., BIM) can transform commercial exchanges toward intentionally relational contracts, with both treating external change as a causal driver of contract form.

shared_topics.topic: information frictions and uncertainty as determinants of contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that mobility and cross-border contracting raise information costs for consumers and employees and thus affect the value of default versus mandatory rules, whereas Paper B shows that relational contracting and collaborative technologies reduce informational barriers and permit ex post determination of terms to manage uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: industry- or sector-specific forces shaping contracting regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that a country’s sectoral composition (e.g., export-oriented manufacturing) conditions the desirability and feasibility of standardized mandatory terms, and Paper B demonstrates the same idea at the firm/industry level by showing how construction (and analogous sectors like manufacturing and pharma) produce incentives for relational, integrative contracting when particular technologies are present.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between private ordering (flexible negotiated arrangements) and formal legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a core debate between default rules that preserve private ordering and mandatory statutory terms, while Paper B explores private ordering through intentionally relational contracts as an alternative to comprehensive, transaction-focused legal drafting, with both assessing when private ordering should be relied upon.

shared_topics.topic: how firm bargaining power, exit threats, and coalition dynamics shape contract norms and regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights firms’ credible threats of exit and their disproportionate influence on policymakers (and the need for coalitions to pass mandatory rules), and Paper B illustrates how asymmetric firm power and strategic alliances (e.g., Disney–Pixar) determine whether relationships evolve toward relational norms or remain transactionally captive to stronger parties.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Desperately Seeking Consideration: The Unfortunate Impact of U.C.C. Section 2-306 on Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: managing long-term commercial relationships under uncertainty and the need for contractual adaptability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how variable-quantity and output/requirements contracts allocate decision-making discretion over time and how courts' good-faith readings affect parties' ability to adapt to changed circumstances; Paper B studies intentionally relational contracts (especially in construction BIM projects) that are designed to allow ongoing adjustment of critical terms and collaborative decisionmaking in the face of uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: protection of reliance and relation-specific investments in interdependent exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how sellers' or buyers' relation-specific investments (e.g., plant capacity, a toaster oven) create reliance interests and how contractual devices or judicial doctrines protect them; Paper B emphasizes relational structures that share risk and reward and preserve investment-backed cooperation among parties (designers, builders, suppliers) enabled by collaborative technologies.

shared_topics.topic: the proper allocation of risk and mechanisms for fine-tuning contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses concrete contractual tools (minimums, take-or-pay, standby charges, price adjustments, liquidated damages) parties can use to calibrate protection for counterparties' reliance and marginal prices; Paper B examines how intentionally relational contracts and integrated project delivery allocate risks and use governance and cooperative mechanisms to fine-tune responsibilities as a project evolves.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy versus judicial (or doctrinal) intervention in shaping what is enforced
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' use of an open-ended good-faith/best-efforts gloss under UCC §2-306 that can override parties' negotiated allocations, arguing parties are better positioned to tailor terms; Paper B contrasts negotiated, flexible relational contracting (often enabled by technology) with traditional transactional contracts and raises questions about how legal doctrine should recognize and enforce such intentionally relational arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1591!!ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults

shared_topics.topic: how contracts cope with incompleteness and uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that relational (intentionally relational) contracts offer a flexible governance mechanism that lets parties determine key terms through ongoing interaction to cope with project uncertainty, while Paper B analyzes why contracts are incomplete (transaction costs, private information) and how default rules (majoritarian or penalty) should be chosen to fill those gaps efficiently.

shared_topics.topic: the role of incentives and information asymmetry in shaping contractual form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes designing contractual regimes and relational norms (reciprocity, deterrence of opportunism) to align incentives in highly interdependent, technology-enabled collaborations, and Paper B studies how default rules create incentives (or fail to) for parties to reveal private information and avoid opportunistic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: static written terms versus dynamic, relationship-based governance

papers.node_id: 36geojintll1145!!ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China
papers.abstract:
Thanks to Dean Zhu Suli of Beijing University Law School, the works of Richard A. Posner were translated into Chinese in the new millennium, making law and economics a popular topic among graduate students in this top Chinese law school.During an interview in 2003, a young judge from the famous higher-education and high-tech district of Haidian in Beijing told me with pride that he was intrigued by Posner's ideas and was even trying to apply some of the principles in his adjudication practice.To be sure, the passion for law and economics is perhaps too new to conquer the long established and well-entrenched mainstream scholarship of the civil law tradition. But will it grow and eventually pave the way for law and economics to enter the minds of lawmakers and adjudicators sometime in the future? Although it is probably too early to make any prediction at this point, I will try to place one law and economics doctrine--efficient breach--in the context of China, and examine how far China is from realizing the spirit of law and economics.
The idea of efficient breachhas been celebrated as a milestone of the law and economics movement. It suggests that when it is more efficient for a party to breach rather than perform a contract, contractual remedies and other legal rules should give the party an incentive to do so. A standard illustration is the situation where a second buyerapproaches the seller to the original contract offering a higher price. The efficient breach theory relies on the fact that if the second buyer can buy off both parties to the original contract so that even the buyer under the original contract will be adequately compensated, it is Pareto-efficient for the seller to breach because no one is left worse off and both the seller and the second buyer are better off.It holds that an optimal remedy for breach of contract is a remedy that is able to induce both efficient performance and efficient breach. Starting from this idea, one line of literature argues that the award of expectation damages, the dominant default remedy for breach of contract in the common law world, which seeks to put the aggrieved party in the position he would have been in had the contract been performed, does a better job of regulating breach-or-perform incentives than its leading competitor, specific performance.Another line of literature argues that efficient breach does not necessarily suggest expectation damages as the optimal remedy, as efficiency will be better served with the general availability of specific performance.
Reflecting the Chinese traditional value of promise-keeping, the civilian tradition ofpacta sunt servanda(i.e., agreements must be kept), and the planned-economy tenet of inviolability of state plans, a breach of contract in China has never been an act free from moral and legal condemnation unless no fault is found on the breaching party's side. Specific performance has been the dominant contractual remedy in China since the reconstruction of the legal system after the Cultural Revolution, and remains a generally available contractual remedy under the current law.Recently however, the rigidity of the rules favoring specific performance has been reduced while the importance of compensatory damages has been increasingly stressed.Enacted in 1986, the General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL) stipulates that in thecase of breach, the aggrieved party has the "right" to specific performance or remedial measures.By contrast, China's first unified contract law (UCL), enacted in 1999,does not specify a priority in the first article of the remedy chapter among "continuing to perform the obligations, taking remedial measures, or compensating for losses,"which arguably leaves the remedial measure a choice to be made by the plaintiff.It also avoids using the word "right" and only states that the aggrieved party "may demand" that the breaching party "discharge non-pecuniary debt as contracted" except when "(1) legally or practically the discharge is impossible; (2) the targeted matter of the debt is unsuitable for a compulsory discharge or too expensive for the discharge; or (3) the creditor does not demand the discharge within a reasonable period of time."
Some writers suggest that Article 110(2) of the UCL partially allows efficient breach in China because it frees a breaching party fromspecific performance when costs of performance are "too expensive." The problem is that great ambiguity surrounds the words "too expensive," which leaves too much to judges' discretion. Furthermore, Article 110(2) seems more concerned with equity than with efficiency, as it arguably shares much similarity with Article 114(2):If the stipulated penalty for breach of contract is lower than the loss caused by the breach, the party concerned may apply to a people's court or an arbitration institution for an increase. If the stipulated penalty for breach of contract is excessively higher than the loss caused by the breach, the party concerned may apply to a people's curt or an arbitration institution for an appropriate reduction.More explicit efforts to introduce the idea of efficient breach into the UCL were made during its drafting stages. The official draft of the UCLcontained one more exception to the aforementioned Article 110: "the aggrieved party may not demand specific performance in a situation where 'the subject matter of the debt is not difficult to obtain from the market.'"This provision would have given commercial players a great deal of flexibility, and arguably would have moved China much closer to endorsing, at least implicitly, the idea of efficient breach.However, this exception was deleted from the final version of the UCL.
If the stipulated penalty for breach of contract is lower than the loss caused by the breach, the party concerned may apply to a people's court or an arbitration institution for an increase. If the stipulated penalty for breach of contract is excessively higher than the loss caused by the breach, the party concerned may apply to a people's curt or an arbitration institution for an appropriate reduction.
Since the public has no access to records of legislative debates and discussions, we do not know exactly what kind of concerns the lawmakers had in mind at the time of this deletion. A statement concerning this deletion appeared in a 1999 annotation of the UCL of which Vice President of the Supreme People's Court Li Guoguang is the chief editor:As to [this deletion], most scholars believe that the establishment of the market economy and the formation of the buyers' market should not constitute reasons for giving up the remedy of specific performance; specific performance should not be abandoned no matter under what kind of economic conditions, while whether it becomes the priority of remedies for breach of contract depends on the will of the non-breaching party.This passage suggests that the concern of the lawmakers was geared exactly towards utilitarian breaches of contract.
As to [this deletion], most scholars believe that the establishment of the market economy and the formation of the buyers' market should not constitute reasons for giving up the remedy of specific performance; specific performance should not be abandoned no matter under what kind of economic conditions, while whether it becomes the priority of remedies for breach of contract depends on the will of the non-breaching party.
This Article does not purport to examine the merits of the idea of efficient breach in itself; neither will it take part in the debate on whether expectation damages or specific performance regulate breach or perform incentives more efficiently. Taking into account the rapid change of rules in contemporary China, the Article assumes that the Chinese lawmakers accept the idea of efficient breachand are willing to change the laws accordingly to carry out the idea. It also will not directly ask whether efficient breach should be transplanted to China or how the law is to be designed in accordance with the idea of efficientbreach. Rather, it examines factors that may influence the viability of efficient breach as a legal transplant in China, and thereby identifies issues that must be taken into account when asking whether efficient breach is desirable in China. And because of the assumption that any change in the law on the books is possible, discussions on past and current legal rules will only serve as evidence for identifying relevant social contexts that are persistent and unlikely to change together with any official change of law.
This Article starts by discussing one social attitude required by the efficient breach theory, that is, the willingness of contracting parties to go to court. Part I suggests that efficient breach presumes that contracting parties are always willing to go to court, while parties in China are less willing to resort to litigation than those in the West.
Part II focuses on the fact that even if a contracting party is willing to breach a contract based on efficiency concerns, an efficient breach decision cannot be made without a great deal of information. Through a survey of theoretical literature, Part II suggests that such a requirement is already problematic in a developed market. A presentation of the difference between a close-knit community and a full-fledged market suggests that the information problem is even more severe in a developing country with a transitional market such as China.
The remaining two parts deal with certain aspects of Chinese legal culture that are essential to the realization of the idea of efficient breach. Part III demonstrates that, unlike the all-or-nothing approach of Western courts in granting remedies, the flexible way in which Chinese courts grant contractual remedies makes it difficult for a breaching party to predict the outcome of a potential lawsuit. Part IV focuses on the practical concern that Chinese courts typically grant inaccurate compensation, suggesting that a lack of sufficient legal expertise is an issue that must be considered when transplanting a complex legal design. The conclusion connects the Chinese case study with the broader issue of legal transplantation in developing countries.

questions.question: Whether adopting a legal framework that permits parties to breach contracts when doing so increases overall economic efficiency would be viable in China given its social, cultural, and institutional context.
Whether contracting parties in China are willing to resort to litigation with the frequency and predictability required for such an efficiency-oriented contract regime to function.

Whether Chinese courts and legal institutions can provide the information, predictable remedies, and accurate compensation necessary for economically efficient breach decisions to be implemented effectively.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nyulrev487!!ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS

shared_topics.topic: the proper boundary between default and mandatory rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether Chinese law should move away from a mandatory-specific-performance regime toward remedies (like expectation damages) that allow efficient breach, while Paper B debates whether rules governing contract modifications (anti-modification clauses) should be treated as default (freely contractible) or as mandatory limits on private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: judicial enforcement, discretion, and predictability of contractual remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how Chinese courts' flexible, unpredictable allocation of remedies and inaccurate compensation undermine the feasibility of doctrines like efficient breach, and Paper B analyzes Anglo‑American courts' blanket refusal to enforce anti-modification clauses as a key enforcement rule and considers legal objections that shape predictability of outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and informational constraints as limits on contractual strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the informational demands and litigation/willingness-to-sue costs that make efficient-breach calculations impractical in China, while Paper B studies the transaction costs of implementing anti-modification devices (multi-party schemes, trustee techniques) and how those costs limit demand for immutable contracts.

shared_topics.topic: whether changing formal law is necessary versus relying on private ordering or other legal institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the issue as a question of legal transplantation—whether doctrinal change (to permit efficient breach) would succeed given social/legal context—whereas Paper B shows how parties can sometimes achieve similar ends through private-ordering techniques (trusts, organizational forms, MFN clauses) without altering contract law.

shared_topics.topic: normative trade-offs between efficiency and commitments/promise‑keeping
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law-and-economics' efficiency rationale for allowing breach with China's cultural and doctrinal commitment to pacta sunt servanda and equitable concerns, and Paper B weighs efficiency gains from freedom to contract against the social value of immutable commitments and mandatory protections when assessing anti-modification rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80tullrev1109!!AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Experiment in the Optimal Precision of Contract Default Rules
compared_to.partner_title: AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Experiment in the Optimal Precision of Contract Default Rules

shared_topics.topic: judicial predictability and institutional capacity for applying contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats judges' ability to identify and apply more granular default rules as a constraint on how precise defaults should be, while Paper B emphasizes Chinese courts' flexible and sometimes unpredictable remedial practices and limited expertise as a barrier to implementing doctrines like efficient breach.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between simple, uniform defaults and more tailored (complex) defaults given transaction, drafting, and administration costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an empirical/analytic investigation of when simple one-size-fits-all defaults outperform segmented, complex defaults due to administrative and transaction costs, and Paper B discusses how shifting from specific performance to breach-friendly remedies (a change in default) may be impractical given the costs and frictions of China's institutional context.

shared_topics.topic: information and litigation costs as prerequisites for contract-law designs that rely on private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether parties will recognize and opt out of defaults and uses marketing data to model information frictions, while Paper B argues that efficient breach presumes parties have access to sufficient information and willingness to litigate—both identify information and dispute-cost barriers to achieving efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the design and choice of default remedies (damages vs specific performance) and their incentive effects on breach or performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the Hadley rule and consequential-damages defaults as its empirical testing ground for optimal default precision, and Paper B centrally analyzes expectation damages versus specific performance in the context of efficient breach and how default remedies shape breach-or-perform incentives.

shared_topics.topic: market heterogeneity and the suitability of segmented legal rules or transplants across different markets/contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether lawmakers should segment default rules across markets or parties to improve fit, and Paper B studies how China's particular market structure, social norms, and transitional economy affect the viability of transplanting a law-and-economics doctrine like efficient breach into that different market context.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99michlrev1724!!ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS

shared_topics.topic: role and viability of private dispute-resolution and non-state enforcement mechanisms in contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the cotton industry's long-standing private commercial law system (private default rules, merchant tribunals, arbitration) and how it substitutes for public courts to resolve disputes efficiently; Paper B examines China's mix of courts and arbitration (and parties' reluctance to litigate), assessing whether non-judicial resolution and institutional design can support doctrines like efficient breach in a transitional market.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules (specific performance vs expectation damages) shape contracting incentives and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares the substantive rules and adjudicative approaches of the industry's private law to public default rules, arguing that rule design influences parties' behavior and transaction costs; Paper B engages directly with the efficient-breach debate—whether specific performance or expectation damages better induce efficient breach/performance—and analyzes how remedy choice affects incentives in China.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of reputation, social norms, and extralegal sanctions for sustaining cooperation in markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes reputation-based nonlegal sanctions and norms as central to making the cotton industry's PLS effective and to restoring cooperative contracting; Paper B explores Chinese cultural norms (promise-keeping, pacta sunt servanda), parties' social attitudes toward litigation, and how those norms affect willingness to breach or enforce contracts.

shared_topics.topic: information availability and transaction costs as constraints on contract governance and efficient breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how the cotton institutions build social and informational infrastructures to lower transaction and error costs and thereby support complex private contracting; Paper B argues that efficient breach requires substantial information and that information problems and transaction-cost constraints in China make implementing such a doctrine difficult.

shared_topics.topic: conditions and limits of transplanting legal or institutional designs across contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A suggests lessons from the cotton industry's PLS for identifying other industries/contexts where private institutions can support trade, while Paper B studies the feasibility of transplanting the efficient-breach doctrine into China, identifying social, informational, and institutional constraints that affect such legal transplantation.

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: role of adjudicators (who decides) in shaping contract outcomes and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Chinese judges' discretionary practices and courts' flexible remedial approaches affect whether efficient-breach incentives can operate in practice, while Paper B analyzes the impact of juries (versus judges) and the fact/law distinction on how written contracts are interpreted and thus how contract disputes are resolved.

shared_topics.topic: predictability and uncertainty of contract remedies and rulings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that unpredictability in Chinese courts' remedial decisions and inaccurate compensation undermine the information and incentive structure needed for efficient breach, and Paper B argues that confusion and inconsistency in interpretation doctrines (and efforts to avoid jury decision-making) produce legal uncertainty in contract litigation.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules of interpretation affect enforcement and remedy allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how statutory wording and remedial doctrines (priority of specific performance vs damages, ambiguous exceptions like 'too expensive') influence whether efficient breach is feasible, while Paper B focuses on interpretive doctrines (plain meaning, parol evidence) that determine contractual obligations and therefore which remedies become available or appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and procedural constraints on the practical operation of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates institutional factors in China—litigation willingness, courts' expertise, market information—that limit transplanting efficiency-oriented remedies, and Paper B addresses procedural design choices (jury trial, fact/law distinction, appellate review) that constrain how contract law develops and is applied in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis383!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT

shared_topics.topic: doctrines for excusing performance versus compelling performance (specific performance, expectation damages, impossibility/impracticability/frustration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the legal regime in China that favors specific performance and the move toward compensatory damages in light of the law-and-economics idea of efficient breach; Paper B defends the shared-assumption test for excusing performance (impossibility/impracticability/frustration) and debates when courts should relieve parties from contractual obligations rather than enforce them.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' tacit assumptions and foreseeability in assessing contractual obligations or excuses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops and defends the shared-assumption test—asking whether parties tacitly assumed a circumstance was 'certain' or 'problematic'—while Paper A emphasizes how information gaps and differing market contexts affect parties' expectations and the feasibility of making efficient breach decisions.

shared_topics.topic: judicial factfinding, predictability, and the information problems courts face in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that Chinese courts' flexible remedies and inexperienced adjudicators create unpredictability and inaccurate compensation, undermining efficient-breach-style rules, whereas Paper B engages the objection that courts cannot reliably determine parties' tacit assumptions and responds that courts routinely make similar inferential judgments.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between efficiency (law-and-economics) and promise-keeping / cultural or equitable values in remedy selection

papers.node_id: 75notredamelrev1681!!ARTICLE: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF HOLMES'S THEORY OF CONTRACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF HOLMES'S THEORY OF CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
A scholar, like everyone else, needs heroes - those whose lives show the possibilities and the glory of a life devoted to discovering and reporting the truth about important things.
One of my scholar-heroes is John Finnis. I first read his Natural Law and Natural Rightsin 1982. That brilliant synthesis of the natural law tradition with the positivism of H.L.A. Hart was an inspiring example of methodical, painstaking, and scrupulously honest scholarship. Moreover, his reformulation of a natural law social science methodology provided a fruitful methodology to use in my own legal theory.I first met John Finnis on a visit to Notre Dame in 1984. Since then, he has generously supported, encouraged, and, at times, edited my work. I am deeply grateful for his inspiring example, his foundational thought, and his friendly help.
It is an honor for me to dedicate this Article, heavily influenced by his work,to my friend John Finnis.

questions.question: Whether Holmes's theory of contract accurately describes and predicts when courts will enforce or refuse to enforce promises (i.e., its descriptive/explanatory power for judicial behavior).
Whether Holmes's theory supplies a defensible normative justification for existing or proposed contract rules (i.e., whether it should guide how contract law ought to be structured).
Whether Holmes's theory adequately accounts for non-legal factors (moral, social, or economic) that influence contractual obligations and outcomes compared with alternative theoretical accounts.

papers.node_id: 71indlj45!!ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts
papers.abstract:
The doctrines on impracticability, mistake, penalties, forfeiture, and good faith share a feature that is unusual in contract law. They give courts the power to excuse or modify terms in contracts between sophisticated parties who bargained over the terms of the contract with equal power and information. Such judicial modification of contracts seemingly violates the basic principle of freedom of contract in a context where the interference cannot be justified on the ground that it protects the weak or the ignorant from exploitation.Judicial interference is also subject to strong criticism on economic grounds since sophisticated parties who bargain as equals might be expected to do a better job than courts in designing contracts to serve their interests.
This Article argues that some aspects of these doctrines and related parts of contract law may be restated around two principles in a way that makes at least these aspects of the law defensible against the freedom of contract and efficiency objections.I call thetwo principles "unselfish performance" and "loss alignment." The principle of unselfish performance overrides contract terms that would permit a party to profit from acting or threatening to act in a way that would impose a significant joint net loss on the parties. The principle echoes a familiar justification for the doctrine on penalties, which is said to eliminate the incentive a promisor might have to perform inefficiently or that a promisee might have to induce or falsely claim breach if the promisor had to pay damages on breach that greatly exceeded the promisee's loss on breach.
The principle of loss alignment relieves a party from a significant and unexpected loss under a contract when such relief would leave the other party in a position no worse than she would have been in had the contract not been made. While the principle of loss alignment is novel,it is similar to other positions with deep roots in contract law. For example, it is consistent with the position that a promise should not be enforced absent detrimental reliance or unjust enrichment.The principle of loss alignment excuses a promisor from an obligation only if excuse neither leaves him enriched, nor leaves the promisee at a reliance loss. Usually obligation in contract is grounded on consentrather than on reliance or enrichment, but it is not surprising to find that when unexpected events alter the terms of performance in a way that makes consent a tenuous basis for enforcement of a contract, the absence of reliance and enrichment may justify nonenforcement of a contract. The principle of loss alignment also is akin to Charles Fried's principle of sharing.And, part of my argument supporting the principle of loss alignment builds on the work of others who have argued that courts often invoke the impracticability doctrine to save a promisor from an unexpected loss when doing so only deprives the promisee of a windfall.However, as will become apparent, the principle of loss alignment accounts for the law better than either Fried's principle of sharing or the anti-windfall principle.
The principles help to explain and justify what courts do in cases that fall in a twilight zone of contract where terms malfunction because of the unexpected. In this twilight zone, courts do not interpret contracts in the usual way because a contract can no longer be construed by reference to the parties' likely expectations. Perhaps it is this inability to ground construction on the parties' likely expectations that justifies the resort to principles of unselfish performance and loss alignment, which derive their force frombeliefs about what is fair and efficient. Of course the line between interpretation and reconstruction of a contract is hazy, for interpretation is influenced by norms of human behavior, including beliefs about what is fair and efficient.
Unexpectedness is not an explicit element of the principle of unselfish performance because the fact that a contract makes it possible for a party to enrich himself by acting or threatening to act in a way that would result in a significant joint net loss to the parties is itself evidence that a contract is not functioning as expected. Rational people do not expose themselves to such behavior. Unexpectedness is an explicit element of the principle of loss alignment because people do enter into contracts that are zero-sum games, where one party's loss is the other's gain. That is the nature of gambling and insurance. The strongest case for reconstruction is when both principles apply, as they sometimes do in the penalty and forfeiture cases, for rational people try not to provide insurance for or gamble on events that the other party might practicably cause to happen in order to collect on the contract.
propose that we reorder the way we think about the doctrines on impracticability, mistake, penalties, forfeiture, and good faith not just by recasting them around the principles of unselfish performance and loss alignment, but also by fragmenting each doctrine into parts. Only some aspects of each doctrine ground on these two principles. Thus, the law of impracticability and mistake is best understood if cases that are governed by a few well-settled rules allocating riskare separated from those involving unexpected events for which there is no such rule.The principle of loss alignment applies in this second category of cases, and as we will see, cases in the second category pose fundamentally different problems from cases in the first.
The doctrine of good faith is best understood as serving two different goals. Usually courts invoke the doctrine to protect expectations based on the contract itself or on trade norms from over-literal interpretations of a contract.This aspect of the good faith doctrine is essentially interpretive. But courts sometimes use the doctrine to prevent a party from selfishly injuring the other party in circumstances the parties did not anticipate in contracting.My most novel claim concerns the prohibition on penal damage clauses. I claim that often when courts invalidate stipulated damage clauses it is because an unexpected event causes a clause to overcompensate or because the promisee behaves opportunistically.If I am right, then this use of the doctrine is more akin to the mistake and good faith doctrines than it is to the unconscionability doctrine (which polices terms that are unfair from the inception).My restatement of the law leads straightforwardly to its defense against the freedom of contract objection. The freedom of contract objection cannot stand if, as I claim, these doctrines serve as tools of contract construction that are employed when events occur that the parties did not anticipate in contracting. Such tools, if properly used, do not interfere with the freedom of contract since contract terms are respected so long as they serve their intended purpose. Any strength left to the freedom of contract objection depends on the contestable claim that judges and juries cannot determine whether the parties accounted for an event when they contracted.
A response to the economic objection to these doctrines is developed at length in Part II. I show that the possibility of judicial reconstruction of contracts under the two principles has no demonstrable harmful effect and may even have a beneficial effect on behavior in contract formation, performance, and modification or settlement. Overriding terms that permit a party to profit from an action that imposes a significant joint net loss on the parties has obvious positive economic value to the extent that it prevents a party from engaging in harmful behavior.Of course, we might expect parties to negotiate to avoid such an outcome once its possibility arises even without judicial reconstruction of a contract. The real value of these doctrines often lies in the way they reduce incentives for strategic bargaining.The possibility of judicial reconstruction of a contract to align losses should not have a harmful effect and may even have a beneficial effect on the precautions parties take in contract formation because it reduces the pressure on parties to account for risks that probably are not worth accounting for in a contract--that is, risks of low probability that even if they occur will not leave the parties in a worse position than they would have been in without the contract.
By defending these doctrines from the economic objection I do not mean to claim an economic justification for them. The economic analysis is inconclusive, and it rests on problematic assumptions about human behavior. Probably the best justification for these doctrines is on fairness grounds. I think the principle of unselfish performance may ground on a belief that it is not right to profit by inflicting, or threatening to inflict, a much greater loss on another. Loss alignment may ground on a belief that (gambling aside) it is not right to profit from another person's accidental loss. The strength of such a justification depends significantly on the fit between the asserted norms and the law, for if the norms did not fit closely with the law we would question their validity or relevance. This approach to justification is open to the same criticism that Richard Craswell levies at Charles Fried's theory of contract.Fried bases most of contract law on a principle of individual autonomy, but he invokes principles of fault and altruism to explain rules like impracticability that do not derive from the parties' agreement.Craswell complains that Fried does not identify the source of these values or provide "any explicit theory explaining when each of these different values is an appropriate guide."Without such a theory, Craswell concludes, Fried's argument "looks more like anex postrationalization of the rules of contract law than a philosophical justification of thoserules."An answer to Craswell's objection is that a philosophical justification of contract may proceed from the bottom up by formulating principles that best fit the law and commercial practice, for these are good evidence of the principles to which we are committed. Those principles may then be tested against intuitions about fairness or the more rigorous calculus of efficiency. Some, including Fried presumably, might object to the principle of loss alignment on the very different ground that it is too parsimonious since it does not allow for sharing of unexpected losses.An answer to this objection is that a principle of loss sharing fits neither the law nor commercial practice, whatever its intuitive appeal. Courts rarely override contracts that provide for sharing of unexpected losses, and people often contract to bear losses asymmetrically.
My defense of these doctrines extends only to those aspects that are consistent with the principles of unselfish performance and loss alignment. This is not to say that the other aspects of these doctrines are indefensible from the freedom of contract or efficiency objections. Rather, for many of the doctrines the other aspects are uncontroversial. The other aspects of the impracticability doctrine--the traditional rules of excuse--may be justified either by the parties' actual expectations, precedent, or even efficiency. The other aspects of the doctrine of good faith consist of interpretive rules that allow courts to protect expectations grounded on contract terms or practice from overly formal interpretations of a contract. The other aspect of the rule on penalties--the actual prohibition of clauses that parties intend to serve as penalties--is the most difficult to justify. Perhaps this aspect of the rule on penalties should be abolished. Its abolition may have less effect than one might suppose, for, as I will demonstrate, only a few cases that void liquidated damage clauses seem to involve genuine penalties.

questions.question: Whether courts may justifiably modify or excuse contractual terms between sophisticated, equally informed parties when unexpected events make performance inefficient, impose significant joint losses, or otherwise frustrate the parties' original bargain.

Whether normative principles that (a) prevent a party from profiting by inflicting or threatening to inflict a significant joint loss and (b) realign unexpected losses so no party is unjustly enriched can provide a defensible legal and economic foundation for judicial reconstruction of contracts.

What effect does the prospect of judicial reconstruction have on parties' contracting, bargaining, performance, and risk-allocation incentives (i.e., whether it harms or improves ex ante efficiency and strategic behavior)?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: doctrines that excuse, modify, or police contractual terms in response to unexpected events
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on specific doctrines (impracticability, mistake, good faith, penalties, forfeiture) that permit courts to excuse or modify terms when events frustrate contractual expectations; Paper A likewise examines how high uncertainty and unforeseen contingencies undermine expectation-based remedies and create situations where courts or alternative regimes must fill gaps or reframe remedies (including when expectation damages are inappropriate).

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the role of specialized interpretive regimes versus generalist courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts are often institutionaly ill-suited to combine text and context and shows why contracting parties create specialized or private interpretive regimes; Paper B engages the competence of judges and juries to determine whether parties anticipated events and whether judicial reconstruction will produce better or fairer outcomes, weighing judicial capacity and incentives.

shared_topics.topic: economic and fairness justifications for limiting freedom of contract through judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses efficiency and protection rationales (especially for unsophisticated parties and thick markets) for limiting pure textualist enforcement and for deploying regulatory or collective interpretive responses; Paper B explicitly defends judicial modification doctrines against freedom-of-contract and economic-efficiency objections, invoking fairness (unselfish performance, loss alignment) and possible efficiency benefits.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: how contracts should respond to contingency and unexpected events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops doctrinal principles (unselfish performance and loss alignment) to justify judicial excuse or modification of contract terms when unexpected events render contractual terms malfunctioning, while Paper B philosophically analyzes contingency in complex business transactions and how lawyers and contracts attempt (and sometimes fail) to manage uncertain future events.

shared_topics.topic: when judicial or lawyerly intervention should override explicit contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends limited judicial reconstruction of contracts against freedom-of-contract and efficiency objections, specifying conditions for override; Paper B critiques reliance on formal models and argues for a practical, philosophically informed role for lawyers to step in where written terms and economic models do not suffice in getting deals done.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-economic normative values (fairness, honor, good faith) in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its defense of certain doctrines primarily on fairness-based principles (unselfish performance, loss alignment) rather than pure efficiency, and Paper B argues that moral philosophy, honor, obligation, and pragmatic idealism regularly influence dealmaking alongside rational self-interest.

shared_topics.topic: risk allocation and the limits of purely economic models in complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes rules that allocate predictable risks from doctrines used when events are unforeseen, arguing judicial reconstruction can reduce inefficient bargaining over low-probability risks; Paper B critiques economic theories (e.g., Coasean optimal risk allocation and strategic models) as inadequate for many complex deals and urges broader philosophical and practical approaches.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract interpretation and reconstruction (and the practical role of lawyers/judges)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts should interpret versus reconstruct contracts, arguing reconstruction is justified in a 'twilight zone' of unexpected events; Paper B examines the complementary practical role of lawyers in resolving ambiguity and filling gaps in contracts outside of formal adjudication, emphasizing pragmatic problem-solving over strict doctrinalism.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between ex ante private ordering and ex post judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on parties' ability and incentives to design procedural governance before disputes arise as a preferred way to manage risks; Paper B defends courts' power to reconstruct or excuse contract terms after unforeseen events, explaining when and why judicial adjustment is appropriate despite concerns about freedom of contract.

shared_topics.topic: the role of interpretive regimes versus reconstruction in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contract designers choose interpretation regimes and procedural rules that shape how disputes will be decided (rules vs standards, who decides, what evidence counts); Paper B distinguishes ordinary contract interpretation from judicial reconstruction, identifying conditions (unexpected events, malfunctioning terms) that justify moving beyond interpretation to modifying obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how uncertainty and transaction attributes shape governance choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a framework tying environmental/behavioral uncertainty and scale/frequency of transactions to the desirability and form of procedural customization; Paper B centers on 'unexpectedness' (unanticipated events) as the key trigger for applying doctrines that reallocate losses or excuse performance, and analyzes how these features affect contracting behavior and judicial roles.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant

shared_topics.topic: critique of the private‑ordering narrative and the empirical basis for legal doctrines favoring nonstate solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with economic and freedom‑of‑contract objections to judicial intervention and reassesses empirical/economic arguments about whether courts’ gap‑filling harms private ordering, whereas Paper B explicitly challenges the historical myth that merchants established a uniform private lex mercatoria and questions the empirical foundations of modern advocacy for private, judge‑free commercial order.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
