papers.node_id: 20utahlrev1121!!ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication
papers.abstract:
Formalism "has a bad name."The label invites associations with the exploitation of the weak by powerful commercial interests,as well as with a naive and mythological view of legal institutions.In contract law, specifically, formalism has been commonly seen as a set of "ivory tower abstractions"and "mystical absolutes."Its defenders feel compelled to explain why it is not a "stupid thing."
Thus, labeling something - a form of legal reasoning, a theory of adjudication, an approach to statutory interpretation, or an interpretive account of the law - as formalistic is a dismissive gesture, a warning sign that tells us we are better off not wasting our time. As the saying goes, at least in American legal academia, "we are all realists now,"and an important part of being a realist is thinking that legal materials do not determine case outcomes. The actual work, or so we are told, is always done by policy.
This Article defies this trend and marks a departure from the conventional wisdom. It argues for formalism as the best normative theory of contract law adjudication.It attempts to show, in other words, that things go better if we actuallyask judges not to resort to policy when deciding contractual disputes, but to insteadapply the law. Given formalism's disrepute in American legal culture,as well as how little has been done to identify the precise target of the criticisms, a fully articulated description and a robust defense of formalism are crucial. This Article attempts to be a contribution, focused specifically on contract law, in both of these respects: it sets out the specific features of a formalist theory of adjudication and offers a normative argument for its implementation in contractual disputes.
As will become clear below, formalism has a certain resemblance,in its operation, to the non-instrumental views of private law theorists like Ernest Weinriband Peter Benson.However, unlike Weinrib and Benson, in this Article I start from a thoroughlyinstrumentalistjustification of contract law. Thus, the Article assumes a very different view about contract law's foundations and their relationship to contract law adjudication.Moreover, formalism is not based on philosophically thick commitments. It does not rest on a Kantian reconstruction of private rights or on an elucidation of the conditions that allow for the reciprocal freedom of purposive agents. Instead, it coheres with the more traditional, bread-and-butter approach of the doctrinal lawyer, who aspires to achieve systematicity and coherence at a much lower level of abstraction, and whose tools are not found in the philosophy of Kant or Hegel, but in the precedents, doctrines, and treatises of the law of contracts. The question, then, is whether this less philosophically ambitious theory of adjudication is normatively desirable. Thus, while the completeclarification of formalism as an approach and the normative argument for it will rest on philosophical considerations, the approach itself is not philosophically ambitious. This, as will become clearer below, is a feature, not a deficit.
Precisely because formalism is unashamedly doctrinal, it is also distinct from the interpretive textualism of Scaliaand its staunch preference for rules as opposed to standards.While formalism is sympathetic to the value of rules in the cost-effective resolution of easy cases and recommends limiting attention to semantic (as opposed to pragmatic) considerations in adjudication, it also acknowledges the need for adjudicating hard cases and for the incremental development of law beyond the pure semantic meaning of legal materials. In this aspect, the notion oflegal principles, as I will explain below,plays a crucial role.
Formalism is thus neither metaphysical nor textualist. And it rests on a normative argument about what approach to contract law adjudication would make things go best. Because of this, the question this Article asks is the following: If contract law is morally valuable and politically justified because of its good social effects, such as its contribution to market exchange and economic efficiency, how should judges decide contractual disputes? The answer is that they should follow a formalist theory of adjudication such as the one presented in this Article. Thus, this Article describes formalism as a theory of adjudication, setting out its main features, and offers a normative argument in favor of its use as the appropriate approach to contract law adjudication.
I will begin by clarifying the precise meaning of formalism and setting out its specific features - for now, a concise idea will suffice: formalism recommends applying the limitedly enriched literal meaning of the legal rules and doctrines of contract law and their settled doctrinal construction, without directly considering the instrumental purposes of contract law. Thereafter, I will argue that instrumentalists - those who, like law and economics scholars, believe that contract law's value derives from its contribution to social welfare- should see formalism as the appropriate approach to the adjudication of contractual disputes. Indeed, formalism is a decision procedure that, in the long run, and given the current state of the law of contracts, maximizes the instrumental efficacy of contract law.The reasons underlying this claim, as I will explain, are connected to several of formalism's advantages, including that it contributes to simple, generalizable, and cost-effective decision-making; it is consistent with the institutional competence of courts; it reduces the risks and overall costs of legal mistakes; and it increases predictability, protecting contractual parties' legitimate expectations. Moreover, formalism is an adequate means to deal with value pluralism and is consistent withthe main values plausibly served by the law of contracts, such as autonomy and efficiency. Thus, we are notallrealists now; nor should we be.
Part II of the Article describes the instrumentalist starting point of my argument, as well as some of the argument's additional assumptions. Part III states and describes the main structural features of formalism as a theory of adjudication, focusing particularly on its operation in routine or easy cases. Because questions about the right normative theory of adjudication are comparative, Part IV offers a brief sketch of some possible alternative theories. Part V moves on to describe formalism's operation in hard cases, and how a formalist theory of adjudication can make sense of the idea of adjudication as application of pre-existing law even in such cases. Part VI supplements the description of formalism with actual examples from contract law. Part VII contains the normative argument for formalism and offers a series of instrumentalist considerations in favor of its use as the best approach towards the adjudication of contractual disputes. Finally, the conclusion refers to the comparative advantages of formalism over other theories of adjudication, and argues that, because of these advantages, instrumentalist and non-instrumentalist scholars could agree at the level of adjudication about the value of a formalist approach, despite their deeper disagreements about contract law's normative foundations.

questions.question: Should judges decide contractual disputes by following a formalist adjudication procedure (applying the limitedly enriched literal meaning of legal materials and settled doctrinal constructions) rather than by directly relying on policy or instrumental considerations?

Does a formalist approach to contract-law adjudication better promote the instrumental aims ascribed to contract law (such as economic efficiency, predictability, reduced error costs, and protection of parties' expectations) compared with alternative adjudicative approaches?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: whether legal decisionmakers should prioritize instrumental (welfare/economic) aims versus established norms or customs

shared_topics.topic: the importance of rule stability and predictability for protecting parties' legitimate expectations in commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends formalism in adjudication partly on the ground that it increases predictability and protects contracting parties' expectations, and Paper B analyzes how regulatory tolerance of customary sales tactics (teasers, free offers) affects consumer expectations and market trust.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and their enforcement shape commercial practices and market behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims that an adjudicative method (formalism) will produce clearer, generalizable rules that influence market exchange and efficiency over time, while Paper B traces how regulatory design and enforcement (or lack thereof) incentivize or deter bait-and-switch practices and other commercial strategies.

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the proper roles of courts, regulators, and legislatures in addressing commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should constrain policy-driven decisionmaking and stick to doctrinal application consistent with judicial institutional competence, whereas Paper B examines how agencies like the FTC, statutes (e.g., the CARD Act), and political processes respond to or reshape commercial norms, highlighting practical institutional limits on reform.

shared_topics.topic: the definitional and doctrinal boundaries of legal categories and their normative consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A specifies the contours of a formalist adjudicative doctrine and distinguishes it from textualism and other theories, and Paper B expands and critiques legal definitions of 'bait-and-switch,' exploring how different doctrinal definitions map onto regulatory outcomes and normative judgments about deception and fairness.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the role of enforcement (formal and informal) in producing contractual compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates adjudication strategies by considering how judicial enforcement (and predictable application of law) influences parties' behavior, and Paper B investigates why parties comply with non‑binding 'faux contracts' by relying on alternative motivators like reputational pressure, trust, and deal‑process incentives when formal enforcement is absent.

shared_topics.topic: instrumentalist/efficiency justifications for contract law and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A adopts an instrumentalist starting point and argues that formalist adjudication best advances contract law's social and efficiency goals, while Paper B analyzes non‑binding agreements through a transaction‑cost/efficiency lens, asking how such design choices facilitate dealmaking and lower coordination costs.

shared_topics.topic: how ex ante contractual forms and drafting choices shape parties' expectations and subsequent behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that predictable doctrines and clear adjudicative rules protect parties' legitimate expectations and reduce legal mistakes, whereas Paper B studies how term sheets and other preliminary, formal‑looking documents (even when non‑enforceable) create expectations, 'nudge' behavior, and structure the subsequent formation of binding deals.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional limits and costs of litigation or adjudication and their implications for legal practice and contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its advocacy for a formalist approach partly in courts' institutional competence and the costs of legal error, and Paper B documents how high litigation/discovery costs and arbitration expenses lead sophisticated parties to design non‑enforceable mechanisms and rely on non‑judicial means to govern transactions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party intent and economic efficiency in resolving contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes courts' use of default rules that either track parties' ex ante intentions or impose penalty defaults to promote efficient contracting, while Paper B directly addresses whether judges should consider instrumental (efficiency) reasons in adjudication and argues that a formalist application of doctrinal meaning better secures long‑run instrumental aims.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial rule‑selection or interpretation structures parties' expectations and background entitlements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that default rules (the background legal framework) instantiate particular distributive arrangements that parties implicitly accept or contract around, and Paper B stresses that formalist adjudication increases predictability and protects contractual parties' legitimate expectations by adhering to settled rules and doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations of contract adjudication (instrumentalism versus other justificatory frameworks)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates debates over default rules within competing normative commitments (libertarian freedom of contract, distributive justice, efficiency) and uses Hohfeldian analysis to show judges inevitably choose distributive positions, whereas Paper B starts from an instrumentalist justification of contract law and defends a formalist adjudicative method as normatively superior given those instrumental ends.

shared_topics.topic: the proper judicial methodology in contract disputes — applying preexisting law versus deciding by policy or creating new terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the role courts play when supplying default contract terms and questions whether courts should design rules with distributional or policy aims, while Paper B presses for a formalist methodology that limits reliance on policy in favor of applying established legal meanings, arguing this better serves institutional competence and rule‑of‑law values.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Impracticability as Risk Allocation: The Effect of Changed Circumstances Upon Contract Obligations for the Sale of Goods

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for changed circumstances (impracticability/frustration) in contracts for the sale of goods

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in applying doctrinal rules versus policy when resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques judicial decision‑making in impracticability cases—arguing courts often fail to follow Code drafters' intent and commercial realities—while Paper B develops a normative defense of judges applying established rules and doctrines (formalism) rather than ad hoc policy reasoning in contract adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contract doctrine (including UCC provisions and precedent) and commercial/efficiency considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the drafting history and purposes of relevant UCC sections and urges aligning impracticability law with commercial realities; Paper B argues that a formalist approach to applying established doctrinal materials best serves instrumental goals like efficiency, predictability, and market exchange.

shared_topics.topic: predictability and protection of contracting parties' legitimate expectations through doctrinal adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes risk allocation and the consequences of excusing performance for sellers and buyers—concerns tied to protecting expectations in commercial transactions—while Paper B emphasizes that formalist adjudication enhances predictability and protects contractual expectations as a normative good.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: how verifiability, litigation/enforcement costs, and renegotiation shape contract design and judicial review

shared_topics.topic: the importance of predictability, reliance, and investment incentives in choosing interpretive or doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes predictability and protection of parties' legitimate expectations as instrumental benefits of formalist adjudication that promote market exchange; Paper B focuses on how different judicial rules and contract designs affect ex ante investment, reliance incentives, and transactional value in the face of incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: private drafting and doctrinal/delegation devices as tools to manage incompleteness and influence judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the role of settled doctrines, precedents, and doctrinal tools in a formalist adjudicative regime, while Paper B catalogs party-side strategies (parol evidence rules, liquidated damages, delegation clauses, litigation strategies) that transactors use to mitigate incompleteness and to signal or shape the interpretive regime courts should apply.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: how courts should resolve conflicts among competing normative values (efficiency, autonomy, equality) in contract law

shared_topics.topic: different adjudicative treatment of easy/routine cases versus hard/corner cases
shared_topics.justification: Both articles distinguish adjudicative methods across case types: Paper B details how formalism operates efficiently in routine cases and how it should be adapted for hard cases (via principles and incremental development), while Paper A describes how judges apply pluralist reasoning and rank values differently across ordinary and difficult factual or structural contexts when forming contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Incomplete Contracts and the Theory of Contract Design

papers.node_id: 54ambuslj519!!ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts
papers.abstract:
In recent years, a fierce debate has reemerged in legal opinions over the essence of contract interpretation. The controversy has major implications for lawyers, businesses, and judges, as contract interpretation is among the most frequently litigated civil issues, and is the largest cause of litigation between business entities.This article brings a novel perspective to contract interpretation by drawing on hermeneutics andmodern contract theory to develop a more precise taxonomy of interpretive challenges, and to offer an innovative normative model of contract interpretation.
Two approaches dominate the debate over contract interpretation: the textualist and the contextualist.The textualist approach focuses primarily on the plain meaning of the language contained within the four corners of the contract.In contrast, the contextualist approach allows courts to consider a wider array of information outside the text of the agreement in order to comply with the parties' intended purpose.Doctrines inspired by the contextualist approach also include equitable rules of interpretation aimed at achieving fair results through the interpretive process.
The two poles of this debate are often understood to represent New York, embracing the textualist view,and California, adopting the contextualist approach.However, a closer look at legal opinions from courts throughout the United States reveals a great deal of inconsistency regarding how to approach contract interpretation, even within states that putatively fit into either the textualist or contextualist camp.The emergence of contract interpretation as a dynamic and controversial subject in recent decades is not limited to the United States.Other common law countries, including England,Canada,and Israel,have witnessed a similar debate.
The debate has also been revived within legal scholarship. Until recently, it appeared that the contextualist approach had won the academic debate, a point that was supported and reinforced by the development of relational contract theory by scholars such as Stewart McCauleyand Ian McNeil.Relational contract theory emphasizes the richness of the contractual relationship beyond the text of the contract, with the underlying assumption that contract law should abandon the formalism of traditional textualist doctrines. Recently, however, the normative argument has been rekindled, as a cadre of scholars known as neoformalists,such as Lisa Bernstein,Alan Schwartz,and Robert E. Scott,have breathed new life into the textualist approach by emphasizing its institutional, economic, and behavioral advantages.
This article seeks to contribute to this discussion by integrating two bodies of knowledge: hermeneutics, the theory and methodology of textual interpretation, and modern contract theory. By applying hermeneutic theories,the article offers a more precise taxonomy of contractual interpretation than the conventional debate between textualists and contextualists allows, enriching the interpreter's range of analytic and conceptual possibilities. By integrating the discussion of modern contract theory with the innovative taxonomy, this article reveals the normative relevance of an entire variety of interpretive possibilities that the present scholarly discussion tends to disregard and provides normative criteria for choosing between them.
Using the precise taxonomy of hermeneutics, this article demonstrates that there are three distinct interpretive debates beneath the surface of the controversy between textualists and contextualists. The first debate concerns the precise goal of the interpretive process, as expressed in the tension between theauthorialand thetextualapproaches: should contract interpretation identify the shared intention or the meaning contained within the four corners of contractual text? The second debate addresses the ideal interpretive approach toward the text, as reflected in the tension between thelinguisticand metalinguistic orpurposivemethods: should interpreters focus primarily on the plain meaning of the language, or seek the deeper meaning or purpose that the text embodies? The final debate is about the hermeneutic theory known as theinterpreter as an authorapproach: should the interpreter play an active role by incorporating equitable considerations into the contractual interpretation process?
By introducing hermeneutics into the discussion of contract interpretation, this article challenges the conventional premise under which all interpretive approaches share the common goal of identifying theparties' intent.The only difference between the textualist and contextualist approaches is how to best achieve that goal. The hermeneutic framework shows that the debate over contract interpretation is not limited to the best way to identify the parties' intent. Rather, this article shows that, even in the context of contractual interpretation, disputes over interpretive techniques may reflect underlying disagreements about the fundamental goals of interpretation.
However, hermeneutic methods, do not and cannot claim to answer the normative question of which interpretive method should be adopted in any given legal context. After all, as a philosophy of interpretation, hermeneutics functions on a fundamentally different plane from legal interpretation. Legal interpretation, as expressed in judicial opinions, involves the use of government authority and the power of enforcement. This use of government authority raises a variety of normative considerations regarding the appropriate method of interpretation that should override the normative influence of hermeneutics.The discussion of hermeneutics, therefore, merely offers an analytical, conceptual, and ontological display of existing interpretive possibilities. The normative question of which approach is preferable must remain the purview of contract theory.
This is where the debate between the two dominant approaches to modern contract theory, neoformalism and relational contract theory, becomes pertinent. Modern theories of contract law, especially the normative discussion in recent years, tend to focus on economic, institutional, and behavioral aspects of contract law.By reframing thediscussion of modern contract theory into three distinct interpretive debates (authorial versus textual, linguistic versus metalinguistic or purposive, and interpreter as an author), this article sheds new light on the debate, revealing that neoformalists support a combination of the textual and linguistic approaches, whereas relational contract theory combines the authorial and purposive approaches with that of the interpreter as an author.
This article goes beyond reframing the debate between relational contract theory and neoformalism, and offers an innovative framework for contract interpretation. First, it proposes a context-dependent model, in which the characteristics of the contract and the nature of the relationship between the contracting parties are used to determine the relative weight ascribed to the intent of the parties, as it arises from the text, as opposed to their intent arising from sources external to the text. Second, in contrast to the conventional "coalition" between the authorial and the purposive approaches, this article develops an authorial-linguistic coalition, according to which, although the interpretation of a contract goes beyond the mere text and includes external circumstances and purposive analysis, the linguistic meaning of the word limits the interpretation. Third, this article generally rejects the interpreter as an author approach, which seeks to interpret the contract in light of equitable values that are not grounded in the contractual text or in the parties' intent. Despite this rejection, this article cites three types of contractual contexts in which it is possible to consider equitable considerations during the stage of interpretation.
This article contains three parts. Part I briefly sets out the fundamental hermeneutic principles that bear on the interpretation of contracts and relies on them to identify three of the core tensions that animate the debate over contract interpretation. Part II explores the ways in which hermeneutic analysis can be integrated into modern theories of contract law. It then translates existing controversies in contract interpretation into hermeneutic language, and subsequently identifies a conflict in the theoretical discussion of contract law between two coalitions of interpretive theories, one side adhering to a hermeneutic approach of the textual-linguistic coalition, coupled with an objection to the interpreter as an author approach, the other side supporting the authorial-purposive coalition, in conjunction with the interpreter as an author approach. Part III offers an innovative model of contract interpretation that integrates the strengths of both the textualist and contextualistapproaches by making available a broader variety of interpretive possibilities as well as criteria for adapting them to different contractual contexts.

questions.question: Whether contract interpretation should aim to identify the parties' shared intention or instead determine the meaning contained within the contractual text.
Whether interpreters should prioritize the plain linguistic meaning of contract language or seek a purposive/metalinguistic understanding that looks beyond the words.
Whether and in what contractual contexts judges should incorporate equitable considerations not grounded in the text or parties' intent into the interpretive process.

papers.node_id: 88indlj339!!ARTICLE: A Lesson on Some Limits of Economic Analysis: Schwartz and Scott on Contract Interpretation
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Lesson on Some Limits of Economic Analysis: Schwartz and Scott on Contract Interpretation
papers.abstract:
Judging by the huge number of reported cases raising contract interpretation issues, parties often manifest their intention in unclear language. Words may be vague or ambiguous, pronouns and syntactical errors may create indefinite referents, and two or more clauses may have incompatible implications for resolving a dispute.When a party contends that contract language thus fails, as relevant to a dispute, interpretation is needed and litigation may ensue.In a litigation context, a court may find that the language is "unambiguous" and enter judgment accordingly as a matter of law.Or the court may find that the language isambiguous and proceed to resolve the ambiguity itself or charge a jury with doing so. There is a near-consensus that the interpreter's job is to ascertain the meaning(s) of the relevant language when the contract was made, if possible.
After decades of relative neglect, contract interpretation became a hot topic of scholarly debate after 2003.In that year, Professors Alan Schwartz of Yale and Robert E. Scott of Columbia published Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law,much of which presents and defends a novel theory of contract interpretation.The article provoked much commentary, including the present author's passing critique in his 2009 book, Elements of Contract Interpretation.In 2010, Schwartz and Scott reacted by publishing Contract Interpretation Redux,a restatement and clarification of their theory, as well as a reply to critics.

questions.question: Whether economic-theory-based approaches can identify parties' intentions and prescribe how courts should interpret ambiguous contractual language.
What the conceptual and practical limits are of using economic analysis to explain or guide judicial decisions in contract interpretation disputes.
When contract-interpretation disputes should be resolved as questions of law by judges versus treated as factual matters for fact-finders (e.g., juries).

papers.node_id: 98geolj77!!ARTICLE: A Pragmatic Defense of Contract Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: A Pragmatic Defense of Contract Law
papers.abstract:
Contract law is such a fixed part of our legal practice that it may seem odd to suggest that it requires a defense, except perhaps among utopians or anarchists.To be sure, one might believe that this or that rule of contract law ought to be altered. Perhaps the parol evidence rule should be given greater force,or perhaps courts should be more generous with the doctrines of duress and unconscionability,but surely no one objects to the idea of having at least some sort of law of contracts? The answer depends on what one means by contract law. If one means rules governing disputes of the kind generally discussed in a first-year law school course on contracts, it would likely be difficult to find someone opposed to the existence of contract law. Even with its command-and-control economy, for example, the Soviet Union had a body of rules that purported to govern contracts.On the other hand, if one means by contract law a single set of legal principles that purports to govern liability for basically all voluntary transactions, call it "General Contract Law," then the question becomes much more controversial. Indeed, since the early twentieth century, successive generations of critics have argued that General Contract Law in this sense is a mistake and that in many--perhaps most--cases we would be better off fragmenting the field into distinctive bodies of law for different sorts of transactions.The hostility continues in present contracts scholarship. For example,Roy Kreitner has suggested contract law should be thought of not as a of abstract rules governing a wide variety of cases, but rather as a "set of relationships whose terms are potentially regulated by the state."On this view, General Contract Law ought to be replaced by labor law,employment law,landlord-and-tenant law,insurance law,lending law,and the like. According to Kreitner, specialized bodies of regulations would improve the law "by ridding it of those commitments that have the effect of limiting contract's fairness-promoting, or redistributive potential."As the list above suggests, on at least some fronts the critics of General Contract Law can claim victory; in many areas we already have specialized bodies of law governing particular kinds of transactions.
The strongest case for skepticism about the value of a General Contract Law rests on three related intellectual moves. The first part of the argument is to delegitimize the drive for generality and abstraction in contract law by giving it a disreputable intellectual pedigree. Historically, so the argument goes, General Contract Law grew out of the formalism of Christopher Columbus Langdell, which was ultimately based on a set of aesthetic rather than functionalist commitments.The second move is to associate General Contract Law with an unworkable attempt to derive the whole body of law from a single normative theory. The final move is to argue that the application of a General Contract Law to certain kinds of cases results in undesirable outcomes. Notice how in this indictment of General Contract Law, generality serves no practical purpose. It is simply the vestigial result of a particular historical moment in the development of the common law or the hypothesis of an untenable theoretical ambition. It is not something that serves any concrete, practical purpose--or at least any concrete practical purpose of great worth--and accordingly, when faced with unpleasant results there is no normative basis for maintaining the generality ofcontract law.
While at some level I am sympathetic to the arguments put forward against General Contract Law, I think that the indictment fails to appreciate the virtues of generality. What I hope to show in this Article is that the abstraction of contract law serves important practical purposes in its own right. In particular, it guards against the capture of the law by special interests that seek to manipulate legal rules for their own benefit, and it allows contracts to serve as "laboratories of democracy"--ways of searching for solutions to collective problems. My argument makes an essentially pragmatic case for General Contract Law, one that can be thrown into our normative calculus against the pragmatic arguments that can be made in favor of dissolving it into particular fields.
Part I of this Article takes up the case against General Contract Law, outlining the arguments that can be made in favor of dividing it into specialized bodies of law. Part II argues that the generality of contract law serves as a check on the power of factions to manipulate the law. Part III argues that the generality of contract law facilitates the decentralized and experimental search for solutions to collective problems, a virtue that is sacrificed by specialized bodies of law. Because the arguments put forward in this Article in favor of General Contract Law are ultimately pragmatic, I do not purport to offer an Archimedean criterion for choosing between generality and specificity in every case. In place of such a theory, however, in Part IV, I offer an analysis of one particular area of contract law--the assignment of contract rights and the rise of so-called asset securitization transactions--to show both how the generality of contract law creates problems that justify more specialized bodies of law and how that specialization can give rise to pathologies that generality can guard against. In place of a simple policy algorithm for avoiding such apparent circularity, this account shows how to recognize the pragmatic tensions on both sides of the issue. At best what emerges is a useful rule of thumb: the problems giving rise to the urge for specialized law are often best dealt with at the highest level of generality possible.

papers.node_id: 27cornelljlpubpoly553!!ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW
papers.abstract:
The market organizes human activity by allocating goods in ways that can support efficient production, investment, and consumption. Market allocation is the result of individual exchanges, rather than the outcome of collective decision-making processes or the exercise of bureaucratic expertise. In this Article, I seek to debunk the conventional wisdom about the characteristic relations that generate such exchanges: that they are impersonal. The conventional wisdom casts characteristically market relations in terms of a detached form of social coordination. By implication, market relations can or should bracket out, and to this extent depersonalize, any and all information about the parties to the interaction that is not necessary to get their transaction going. Some take this wisdom to reflect the nature of market relations.Others proceed by supposing that it is the inevitable outcome of the internal workings of the market under conditions of modernity.And yet others take the conventional wisdom to be a normative judgment concerning the desirable form of interaction for market participants.
I devote the first half of these pages to showing that the conventional wisdom is indefensible. I make this showing in two steps. Concerning the phenomenology of market relations, I argue that the connection between impersonality and market relations is highly contingent. Concerning the desirability of impersonal market relations, I argue that the normative arguments in its favor suffer from certain structural and substantive deficiencies.
The conventional wisdom, on its different versions, carries any number of implications. I am currently interested in considering just one: that of insulating market participants from the responsibility to realize the demands of morality and justice (and, in particular, respect for the rights and well-being of others). In debunking the thought that market relations are characteristically impersonal, I seek to show that the familiar case for driving a wedge between doing well in the market sphere by satisfying one's preferences and doing right fails.
Apart from criticizing the conventional wisdom on both phenomenological and normative grounds, the latter half of these pages identifies two key aspects that support a better understanding of market relations. The first aspect is law and, in particular, its role in the market. The conventional wisdom concerning the impersonality of market relations contains an implicit or explicit view about the normative status of law in market orderings: that law enforces and facilitates commercial transactions. By contrast, I argue that the law governing market relations assumes a qualitatively different role - it forms, rather than merely facilitates or enforces, certain market relations. The formative role of law suggests that law partially constructs the moral landscape and the moral demands that apply to market participants by virtue of participating in market transactions that take the legal forms associated with contract and property (et alia). The second aspect takes up the notion of personal responsibility in the market sphere. If market relations do not and should not insulate people from the demands of right reason, it becomes necessary to delineate the limits of the responsibility participants should assume in their market engagements. Let me emphasize that the responsibility at the center of my analysis is strictly moral, not legal. It means that there can be a gap between the moral and legal requirements that apply to people by virtue of participating in market transactions: on the one hand, legal permissions (say, to engage in certain forms of trade that are rightly viewed as immoral) cannot crowd out or override thedemands of morality; on the other hand, moral duties are not automatically incorporated into legal prescriptions.

questions.question: Are market transactions characteristically impersonal-that is, do typical market relations legitimately bracket out personal information and moral considerations between parties?
Does the conventional view of market impersonality justify insulating market participants from moral responsibility for the harms or injustices connected to their market conduct?
Does the legal ordering of market transactions play a formative role in shaping market relations and the moral obligations of participants, rather than merely facilitating or enforcing exchanges?

papers.title: ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?
papers.abstract: In Jacksonville, Florida, a city official complains that contractors "low bid contracts only to pile up thousands of dollars in change orders later."In Honolulu, Hawaii, a city council member grills a city planner as to how a fixed-price contract for simple renovations to a Waikiki fountain doubled from the original award.The planner sheepishly explains the water table was higher than expected, and the council member throws up her hands in exasperation.In Buffalo, New York, a public works commissioner reports that overall, road projects average fourteen percent over budget and "questions whether low bidders deliver the most inexpensive work."There is no disputing that fixed-price government construction contracts frequently run well over budget.A mischievous clause, found in most government contracts, called the differing site condition provision, is a principal reason behind the additional costs. This clause undermines the concept of a fixed-price contract. It leaves a jaded, cynical public shaking its head as government owners pay for costs associated with unforeseen conditions discovered during contract

questions.question: How should the risk of unforeseen subsurface and latent site conditions be allocated between owners and contractors in fixed-price construction contracts to minimize cost overruns and change orders?

Can judge-made rules (rather than explicit contractual provisions) effectively allocate the risk of unforeseen site conditions, and what are the effects of each approach on contract pricing and project performance?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes differing site condition clauses in fixed-price government construction contracts and how they shift costs for unforeseen subsurface or latent conditions; Paper B analyzes the broader choice between default rules and mandatory terms in contract law and when states are likely to impose mandatory allocations of risk rather than relying on private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: the political and institutional determinants of contract design in public procurement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the prevalence and fiscal/political consequences of particular contractual clauses (e.g., differing site conditions) in government construction procurement, while Paper B develops a political-economy account (mobility, sectoral composition, institutional capacity) explaining why jurisdictions adopt particular regulatory strategies that shape the substance of public contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information problems and unforeseen contingencies in producing cost overruns and shaping optimal regulatory or contractual responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on informational gaps about subsurface conditions that produce change orders and budget overruns in construction contracts; Paper B examines how information costs (e.g., matching, cross-border information asymmetries) affect the relative value and likelihood of default rules versus mandatory contract terms as policy responses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: post-contractual price increases and who bears the risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how fixed-price government construction contracts are routinely subject to unexpected cost increases (change orders) when differing site conditions or latent subsurface facts are discovered and asks how risk should be allocated; Paper B analyzes 'teasers' and bait-and-switch tactics where consumers are lured by low initial prices but later face higher costs, and considers who ultimately bears those added costs and how law should respond.

shared_topics.topic: the role of customs/norms versus formal legal rules in governing market behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether common law principles have a continuing role alongside contract clauses and statutory provisions in allocating risk for unforeseen site conditions in public works procurement, while Paper B argues that market customs and norms often drive when and how formal regulation (FTC rules, CARD Act, etc.) is applied to bait-and-switch practices rather than pure welfare-maximizing logic.

shared_topics.topic: limits of legal definitions and doctrines to capture problematic commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how contractual clauses (the differing site condition provision) and existing legal doctrines may fail to address or properly allocate liability for unforeseen conditions, and Paper B critiques the narrow legal definitions of bait-and-switch (and the need to expand or reinterpret them) to encompass a wider set of deceptive or misleading pricing tactics.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:Language and Formalities in Commercial Contracts: A Defense of Custom and Conduct

shared_topics.topic: the role of extrinsic evidence, trade usage, and parties' conduct in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how government construction contracts and differing site condition clauses produce disputes over what risks were allocated and whether contractors can recover for unforeseen site conditions—questions that turn on how contract terms are read in context—while Paper B defends treating usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance as legitimate interpretive evidence of the parties' assent under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of unforeseen or latent risks between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses how differing site condition provisions and fixed-price government contracts allocate (or fail to allocate) the risk of unforeseen subsurface and latent conditions, and Paper B examines how recognizing custom, conduct, and performance as part of contractual language affects which party bears various commercial risks.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of strict formalism (written terms) versus contextual, relational approaches to contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes the notion that a fixed-price written award captures the full bargain when latent conditions arise, suggesting a need to look beyond the paper contract, while Paper B critiques neoformalism and argues for incorporating nonverbal conduct and industry context so that judges do not rigidly enforce written terms divorced from the parties' manifested assent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107geolj1277!!ARTICLE: Contract Creep
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Creep

shared_topics.topic: portability of standardized/boilerplate risk‑allocation clauses across contract types
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how a widely used differing‑site‑condition clause in government fixed‑price construction contracts shifts unforeseen subsurface risk and produces widespread cost overruns, while Paper B analyzes more generally how modular contract terms and the ease of copying clauses cause doctrinal and practical migration of provisions across transactional contexts, producing mismatches between clause design and the environments into which they are transplanted.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of general/common‑law doctrines versus specialized regimes for resolving specialized contracting problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether the common law has a meaningful role in allocating risk of unforeseen, subsurface and latent conditions in government construction contracts (versus statutory or express contractual regimes), and Paper B interrogates the broader project of having tracked or fragmented contract law—showing how doctrinal migration complicates efforts to tailor distinct legal regimes for different transaction types.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial interpretation and doctrinal rules shape allocation of unforeseen costs and contractual risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how clauses and their application (e.g., differing site conditions, change orders) determine who bears surprise costs in fixed‑price construction work, and Paper B studies doctrinal tools (like contra proferentem, arbitration enforceability, and analogical reasoning) and how their movement between tracks affects which parties bear risk and how courts resolve ambiguities.
