shared_topics.topic: when formal legal enforcement is necessary versus reliance on self-enforcement and market norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies self-enforcing contracts and market reputation as substitutes for legal enforcement and pinpoints when courts are needed (volatile markets, relation-specific investments); Paper B similarly shows how frequency and scale (and industry norms or trade associations) reduce reliance on formal adjudication and explain when parties adopt formal procedural safeguards instead.

shared_topics.topic: contract design to manage transaction-specific risks under incomplete contracting (relation‑specific investment, hold-up, and litigation opportunism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its normative theory in the need to facilitate efficient trade and ex ante investment, stressing enforcement to protect relation-specific investments and prevent hold-up; Paper B situates procedural customization as a tool to address shading and litigation opportunism arising from incomplete contracts and uncertain future states, and analyzes how parties trade off ex ante and ex post governance.

shared_topics.topic: choice of interpretation and adjudication regimes (who decides, evidentiary scope, standards) as part of contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a textualist default, narrow evidentiary rules, and party-tailorable interpretation regimes for business contracts; Paper B treats selection of decision‑makers, adjudicative fora, evidentiary and decision standards (e.g., arbitral authority, standards of decision) as deliberate procedural design choices that parties use to shape dispute outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev681!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.

shared_topics.topic: use of arbitration as a contractual dispute-resolution forum and its procedural consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on arbitration as a central mechanism for resolving contract disputes—Paper A studies how parties choose and customize arbitration (forum selection, arbitrator qualifications, and bespoke procedures) as part of contract design, while Paper B examines how arbitration decisions (particularly in labor contracts) turn on interpretive practices applied by arbitrators.

shared_topics.topic: standards of contract interpretation applied in arbitration (plain meaning vs. extrinsic/intention-focused approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of which interpretive regime governs contractual language in arbitration—Paper B analyzes the plain meaning rule and its exclusion of extrinsic evidence in labor arbitration and courts' rejection of that rule, while Paper A notes parties sometimes authorize arbitrators to use non-legal or alternative standards of decision and discusses how interpretive regimes can be selected ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: the extent to which procedural/default rules are mandatory versus subject to private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address whether procedural norms are immutable defaults or can be opted out of: Paper A debates commentators' claim that parties rarely customize litigation procedures and shows pockets of ex ante procedural contracting, while Paper B documents an anomaly where courts reject the plain meaning default yet arbitrators continue to apply it, raising questions about deference to procedural norms in private dispute resolution.

shared_topics.topic: how ex ante procedural design affects substantive enforcement and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how pre-dispute procedural choices shape post-dispute outcomes and strategic behavior—Paper A argues procedural customization can mitigate litigation opportunism and shading by allocating decisionmakers and standards, and Paper B shows that arbitrators' interpretive practices (e.g., invoking plain meaning) can produce outcomes at odds with parties' intentions, with implications for opportunism and enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev936!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Everywhere a Cluck-Cluck: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. Int'l Sales Corp. *
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Everywhere a Cluck-Cluck: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. Int'l Sales Corp. *

shared_topics.topic: contract interpretation regimes and the use of extrinsic evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Frigaliment as a paradigmatic discussion of how courts use extrinsic sources (trade usage, parties' communications, course of dealing) to interpret ambiguous terms; Paper B treats interpretation regimes as a design choice, arguing that transaction type helps determine which interpretive regime (and evidentiary/decision standard) should govern a contract.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between precise (complete) drafting and vague/open-ended terms (ex ante vs ex post specification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A illustrates the practical consequences of ambiguous wording by showing how courts resolve disputes over a vague term, while Paper B analyzes the economic and strategic tradeoffs of drafting precise obligations versus leaving vagueness for ex post interpretation or adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: who decides disputes and the standard of decision (procedural allocation of interpretive authority)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A showcases judicial interpretive practices and the implications of a judge's approach to evidence and meaning, and Paper B explores parties' ability to choose adjudicators (courts, arbitrators), limit decisionmaker authority, or specify nonlegal decision standards that will determine how contractual meaning is resolved.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry norms, trade usage, and informal governance in resolving contractual meaning and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses trade usage and industry context as central extrinsic aids to construe contract terms, and Paper B emphasizes that parties often rely on industry-provided norms, trade associations, and specialized tribunals as governance alternatives that shape how disputes are interpreted and enforced.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54smulrev617!!SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:Language and Formalities in Commercial Contracts: A Defense of Custom and Conduct
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:Language and Formalities in Commercial Contracts: A Defense of Custom and Conduct

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and interpretive role of non-textual elements (custom, course of dealing/performance, and procedural terms) in defining contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats procedural customization as a form of private ordering that shapes how disputes will be adjudicated and thereby affects substantive outcomes; Paper B defends usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance as part of the parties' language and essential evidence of assent and contract meaning.

shared_topics.topic: parties' autonomy to design governance mechanisms (including procedural regimes) and the limits of formal written terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the extent to which commercial parties can and do author procedural rules ex ante (arbitration clauses, bespoke procedures) to govern the back-end of contracting; Paper B argues against neoformalism by defending parties' ability to rely on custom and conduct rather than only on papered terms, emphasizing that nonverbal/formalities matter to assent.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between ex ante specification (writing more detailed terms) and reliance on informal norms or post‑formation behavior to manage uncertainty and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates procedural customization within the literature on balancing front‑end drafting costs and back‑end enforcement costs, arguing parties may deliberately leave procedures open or tailor processes to address opportunism; Paper B highlights the costs of attempting to capture all terms in writing and endorses using industry custom and parties' conduct as cheaper, informative substitutes.

shared_topics.topic: mitigating opportunism and uncertainty through contractual design (procedural or customary mechanisms) rather than purely substantive clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers procedural customization as a tool to offset litigation opportunism and shading under uncertainty; Paper B presents custom and course of performance as mechanisms that reveal assent and constrain opportunistic reinterpretation, resisting a move to restrict courts from considering those mechanisms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 19upajbusl809!!ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: limits on parties' ability to opt out of legal or procedural rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether statutes are automatically incorporated into contracts and whether parties may waive or opt out of those statutory protections, concluding implied incorporation is often treated as mandatory; Paper B examines when contracting parties can and do opt out of default procedural rules (e.g., forum, arbitration, jury, class actions) and shows both the scope and perceived limits of procedural autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual gaps get filled ex ante and ex post (implied terms vs deliberate procedural design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes courts' use of the implied incorporation doctrine as a judicial gap‑filling technique that imports laws into contracts, while Paper B treats procedural customization as an intentional, ex ante method for parties to fill gaps in incomplete contracts by tailoring dispute-resolution processes.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between private ordering and public law constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the tension between private contracting and public statutes (including police-power constraints) when courts import laws into private agreements, and Paper B considers when parties rely on private procedural ordering versus industry norms, public tribunals, or statutory processes—both interrogate when public law should constrain or yield to private contract design.

shared_topics.topic: the classification of rules as mandatory versus default and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes contract construction from interpretation to argue that implied incorporation behaves as an immutable (mandatory) rule rather than a removable default, and Paper B documents that many procedural rules are treated in practice as mandatory defaults (limiting fine-grained customization), exploring the implications for contract design and enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev675!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting and the centrality of relationships/norms to understanding contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an explicit defense and historical account of relational contract theory (arguing that contracts are best understood as embedded in ongoing relationships and normative frameworks), and Paper B invokes relational norms (particularly the cooperative, pre-dispute bargaining ethos) to explain why parties can and do design bespoke procedural regimes.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracting and contract design under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats relational contracting as a response to the limits of discrete, fully specified bargains over time, and Paper B frames procedural customization as a tool transaction-cost-conscious contract designers use to manage contractual incompleteness and environmental/behavioral uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay and 'braiding' of formal legal rules with informal norms, industry practices, and alternative governance mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contractual obligations are embedded in broader relational and normative contexts beyond formal doctrine, while Paper B surveys how parties mix formal procedures (arbitration, forum selection, adjudicatory rules) with industry norms, trade associations, and private dispute systems to create hybrid governance arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42sandiegolrev533!!EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts

shared_topics.topic: choice of interpretive regime for contracts (authorial intent vs pluralist/multi-factor approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the transactional context to which interpretation regime (rules vs standards, ex ante specificity vs ex post interpretation) should govern a contract, arguing parties design procedure with an eye to how texts will be read; Paper B directly debates single-inquiry (author's intent) versus pluralist, multifactor accounts of interpretation and defends a pluralist approach for wills and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between ex ante contract design and ex post adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties allocate costs between front-end specification and back-end processes by drafting procedural terms to shape future adjudication, while Paper B examines whether meaning is fixed at the text's origin or can be altered by later judicial interpretation, framing a similar tension between pre-commitment and later decision-making.

shared_topics.topic: procedural and interpretive mechanisms as governance tools to manage opportunism and incentives in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that procedural customization (forum choice, arbitration rules, tailored adjudicatory systems) mitigates litigation 'shading' and opportunism; Paper B shows that different interpretive doctrines (and the extent to which judges may 'displace' apparent meaning) affect incentives for drafting, litigation, and judicial creativity, thereby functioning as governance mechanisms that shape parties' strategic behavior.

papers.node_id: 135upalrev1123!!ARTICLE: APPLICATION OF THE DOCTRINE OF COMMERCIAL IMPRACTICABILITY: SEARCHING FOR "THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON".
papers.title: ARTICLE: APPLICATION OF THE DOCTRINE OF COMMERCIAL IMPRACTICABILITY: SEARCHING FOR "THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON".
papers.abstract:
Important shifts in contract doctrine may be traced to certain decisions.  Judge Traynor's opinion inDrennan v. Star Paving Co.gave new, different, and permanent life to the principle of reliance as a formative device.  Judge Cardozo's words inWood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordonhave indelibly colored application of judicial interpolation of good faith obligations into contractual relationships.  These, and other such opinions, were the means by which the law of contracts expanded.  They were not necessarily "right" compared to the possible doctrinal alternatives,but they moved the law to new and perhaps higher ground.
Similarly, inAluminum Company of America v. Essex Group, Inc. ("ALCOA"),Judge Teitelbaum attempted to fashion a new, expansive approach to the doctrine of "excuse"to determine whethercertain supervening eventsrelieved Alcoa from performing its contractual obligations.The exercise, a determination whether the events fit under the "traditional" excuse rubrics of mistake, impossibility, impracticability, or frustration of purpose was not a novel one.  Courts had resolved such questions on a case-by-case basis long beforeALCOA.What was different inALCOAwas Judge Teitelbaum's readiness, with little, if any, supporting authority, to take an expansive view of these rubrics in finding that Alcoa was entitled to relief.
Had Judge Teitelbaum confined his analysis to broadening the traditional excuse doctrine,ALCOAmight have served as the cornerstone of a more expansive, or at least more fully integrated, doctrine of excuse that avoids the anomaly of a doctrine that is hardly ever applied.Even a concerted effort to reconcile or reverse his untraditional findings of mistake, impracticability, and frustration might have produced a unitary approach to excuse built around the single concept of fundamental fairness.
Judge Teitelbaum, however, was not content to stop with an expanded concept of relief-supporting events.  He took the more radical step of holding that the supervening events served not to provide an "excuse" relieving performance, but rather to justify modification of the performance obligation through the imposition of loss- and risk-sharing: the judicial interpolation of new pricing terms to ameliorate the perceived hardship caused by the putatively excusing events.Here wasa radical departure that overshadowed the more subtle, but no less radical departure embodied in the underlying determination that Alcoa was not to be held strictly to its voluntarily-assumed contractual obligations.
Although Judge Teitelbaum's loss-sharing methodology evoked a flurryof both positiveand negativecommentary, it is perhaps also responsible for the fact that, in the seven years since the case was decided,ALCOAhas had little impact on judicial thought.  The judicial sands seem to have shifted more to cover over the decision than to expand upon it.One might then wonder why a decision apparently asportentous asALCOAhas virtually faded into obscurity.  The answer lies in an analysis of both the doctrine of excuseand the often unarticulated relationship between that doctrine and more fundamental contract doctrine.
It has been suggested that "[i]mpossibility cases are a special breed of contract law."I believe, however, that the judicial approach to impossibility is consistent with the development of contract law and not significantly different from the general approach to matters of interpretation and inference in the context of a contractual omission.The fictions that the courts employ and the reliance on presumptions of intent are essentially the same tools that are applied to other questions of contract interpretation and enforcement.For example, the contractual fiction of presumed intent allows one to assume that the excuse arises from the terms of the contract itself rather than from extrinsic standards.Adorned with the talisman of intent, the contract is subject tojudicial interpretation rather than judicial legislation,and the search for objective, presumed intent, instead of subjective, actual intent.  Absent an express indication, the fiction creates the presumption that the parties intended what theyreasonablywould have articulated expressly had they been required to deal with the matter at the time of contracting.Whatever its failings, judicial implication tends toward the fostering of justice and fairness, even if at the expense of the application of firm rules.  It is perhaps the special genius of the law to temper the absolute with reasoned flexibility, even if application is difficult.  As Judge Cardozo stated: "Those who think more of symmetry and logic in the development of legal rules than of practical adaptation to the attainment of a just result will be troubled by a classification where the lines of division are so wavering and blurred."
The relationship between the doctrine of excuse and contract doctrine works at an even more fundamental level.  The "excuse" issue arises only if there is preceding consensus that contractual obligations are to be performed, that non-performance will give rise to the law's enforcement or remedial sanctions.Under an approach to contract focusing on the centrality of the norm of enforcement of the parties' express agreements, one seeking discharge from a contractual undertaking must demonstrate either (1) that the promise, by its very terms or from the circumstances of its making, is excepted from the norm, or (2) that circumstances exist that give rise to another, excusing norm.  Excuse becomes a stark "either/or" issue that precludes the middle ground ofcontract modification:either the defense is allowed and performance is discharged, or the defense is disallowed and performance is directed or performance damages are awarded.
If, however, one is more concerned with the relationship that the contract has established, one might easily define the primary role of contract doctrine in terms of nurturing, fostering, and perpetuating that relationship.The parties themselves should cope with disruptive events not expressly provided for in the contract while they go about the rest of their business together.The contract is a skeleton-like structure upon which the relationship is built, designed to do little more than describe the general policy governing the relationship.Under this view, when a supervening event renders a party's performance impracticable, fairness within the context of the relationship may require a sharing of the consequential losses between the parties.It is not unreasonable to posit an unarticulated "duty to adjust," an obligation on the part of one party not only to act in good faith, but also to agree to an adjustment of the contract terms in order to avoid any fortuitous advantage at the expense of the other party.
Inevitably, then, to define a doctrine of excuse is to define a doctrineof contract.Any examination of the doctrine of excuse must consider the doctrine as it has evolved, always understanding that it is a manifestation of an overall theory of contract.  Radical departure from the way in which the doctrine of excuse is articulated and applied can be meaningful only if there is consensus for a radical departure from the way in which we look at contractual relationships.  To the extent that change is advocated in the doctrine of excuse, it must be recognized that change can follow meaningfully only from more fundamental change in the reality of contract.  It is this reality, as we understand it through the assimilation of experience, that must inform doctrine.  Ultimately, theALCOAdecision has been ineffectual in the development of a modern approach to excuse because there is no consensus about contract doctrine that can serve as the basis for Judge Teitelbaum's vision.
What follows is an attempt to examine the excuse of commercial impracticabilityin terms of what parties to agreements need and what kind of "glue"contracts can provide for complex relationships.What is ultimately required is a base from which to look at future events that provides some certainty in planning.  A cohesive understanding of the major contractual disruptions of the recent past from which such a base can emerge has not yet developed.  What is needed for the present are flexible and workable tools rather than all-embracing theories, and a continuing effort to keep emerging doctrine consonant with commercial reality.

questions.question: Should unforeseen, disruptive events excuse a party from performing its contractual obligations entirely, or should they justify judicially imposed renegotiation and loss- and risk-sharing between the parties?

Should contract law prioritize strict enforcement of the parties' express agreements, or should it prioritize sustaining the ongoing commercial relationship by imposing duties to adjust terms in good faith when disruptions occur?
What practical legal standards or tools best balance commercial certainty for planning with flexible, fair responses to major unforeseen disruptions of contractual performance?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43flastulrev1265!!ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: judicially supplied default terms / implied contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts fill contractual gaps through presumptions of objective intent and judicial interpolation (e.g., ALCOA's imposition of new pricing/loss-sharing terms), while Paper B analyzes the broader phenomenon of courts choosing default rules to supply missing terms and the methods used to select those defaults.

shared_topics.topic: the weight of presumed party intent versus other justificatory criteria in gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the fiction of presumed intent as the justificatory basis for judicial implication of terms, and Paper B contrasts that party‑intent approach with alternative justifications (economic efficiency and distributive aims) for choosing default rules.

shared_topics.topic: use of equitable / fairness considerations (good faith, duty to adjust) instead of strict enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates a relational view that endorses good‑faith duties and an implied 'duty to adjust' or loss‑sharing when supervening events occur, while Paper B treats courts' consideration of distributive justice as a form of choosing fair or redistributive default rules rather than mechanically enforcing express terms.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of losses and the distributive consequences of judicial gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly discusses judicial imposition of loss‑ and risk‑sharing (ALCOA) and its distributive effects between contracting parties, and Paper B argues that every choice of default rule embodies a distributive preference, so gap‑filling necessarily allocates gains and losses between parties.

shared_topics.topic: relationship between contract doctrine and broader normative theories (how doctrinal choices reflect theory)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the doctrine of excuse within competing overarching theories of contract (enforcement‑centered vs relationship‑centered) and argues doctrine must align with commercial reality, while Paper B locates default rules within background regulatory and distributive schemes and uses Hohfeldian tools to show doctrinal choices embody normative commitments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment of impossibility/impracticability (excuse doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively engage with the doctrines of impossibility and commercial impracticability: Paper A analyzes how courts have applied and reshaped excuse doctrines (and critiques ALCOA's expansive approach), while Paper B treats impossibility/impracticability as a legal mechanism courts use to fill obligational gaps (e.g., awarding zero damages) and thereby influence contracting outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: courts as gap-fillers/default-rule makers versus strict enforcers
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine the role of courts in filling contractual gaps — Paper A discusses judicial implication of terms, modification, and loss‑sharing as alternatives to strict enforcement, and Paper B models how default rules and judicially-imposed damage measures fill obligational incompleteness and alter parties' incentives.

shared_topics.topic: state-contingent obligations and the desirability of contractual flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on whether and how contracts (or judicial responses) should be made contingent on unforeseen states of the world: Paper A argues for a pragmatic, relationship‑oriented duty to adjust and flexible tools to handle supervening events, while Paper B analyzes how making default rules more state‑contingent can (or cannot) correct contingency incompleteness and affect efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: judicial modification/allocation of losses and risk-sharing
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of when courts should reallocate losses or impose risk‑sharing: Paper A critiques judicial interpolation of new pricing and loss‑sharing in ALCOA, and Paper B shows how default damage rules and court gap‑filling can reallocate obligations and influence whether parties renegotiate or breach.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between doctrinal choice and commercial/efficiency consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers link doctrinal choices to commercial realities and efficiency: Paper A argues that excuse doctrine must be grounded in an agreed vision of contract to be practically useful for commerce, while Paper B models how the choice of defaults, transaction costs, and market structure affect contractual efficiency and the feasibility of contracting around rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43hastingslj1!!ARTICLE: Mistake, Frustration, and the Windfall Principle of Contract Remedies.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mistake, Frustration, and the Windfall Principle of Contract Remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal relationship among mistake, frustration, impossibility, and commercial impracticability
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat these doctrines not as isolated categories but as overlapping responses to supervening events; Paper A proposes a unified model tying mistake and frustration together, while Paper B seeks a coherent account of commercial impracticability within the broader ‘excuse’ family and calls for integration of these doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling versus leaving contracting parties to their bargain
shared_topics.justification: Both authors debate whether courts should 'fill gaps' in incomplete contracts or refrain from intervention; Paper A argues courts often properly leave parties alone (the windfall principle), whereas Paper B critiques cases that judicially interpolate new terms (e.g., ALCOA) and examines the legitimacy of court-imposed adjustments.

shared_topics.topic: whether relief should be denial of enforcement (excuse) or modification/loss‑sharing
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question the proper remedy when performance is disrupted: Paper A emphasizes that findings of mistake or frustration typically result in denying relief and letting consequences stand, while Paper B analyzes the alternative of judicially imposed modifications or loss‑sharing and critiques that shift from discharge to reallocation of contractual burdens.

shared_topics.topic: the use of interpretive fictions and presumed intent in excuse cases
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with the courts' reliance on presumptions of parties' presumed intent and other interpretive tools when addressing contractual omissions or excuses; Paper A examines case law patterns supporting nonintervention, and Paper B defends the judicial implication of terms as a means to approximate what contracting parties would have agreed to.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs among fairness, efficiency, and commercial reality in shaping excuse doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers weigh normative consequences of different doctrinal choices—interventionist versus hands‑off approaches—including impacts on efficiency, fairness between parties, and commercial certainty; Paper A asks whether nonintervention can achieve equal or greater efficiency, and Paper B urges flexible, practicable tools that reflect commercial realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23fordhamurblj69!!ARTICLE: THE WARNING FROM PITTSBURGH'S GOLDEN TRIANGLE: HOME OF THE STEELERS, THE PIRATES AND THE AMORPHOUS FAVORED NATION CLAUSE IN THE COMMERCIAL LEASE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE WARNING FROM PITTSBURGH'S GOLDEN TRIANGLE: HOME OF THE STEELERS, THE PIRATES AND THE AMORPHOUS FAVORED NATION CLAUSE IN THE COMMERCIAL LEASE

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation of ambiguous contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts use presumptions of intent and judicial implication to supply terms or excuses (e.g., impracticability, mistake) when contracts omit contingencies, and Paper B (on the amorphous 'most favored nation' clause in commercial leases) examines how courts must construe vague MFN clauses and resolve their indeterminacy in lease disputes.

shared_topics.topic: judicial modification or interpolation of contract obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques ALCOA's judicially imposed loss- and risk-sharing (new pricing terms) as a form of court-ordered modification, and Paper B addresses how MFN clauses and their enforcement can lead courts to interpolate pricing or parity obligations across separate agreements.

shared_topics.topic: pricing and allocation of commercial risk in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how supervening events raise questions of who bears consequential losses and whether courts should reallocate risk (e.g., duty to adjust, loss-sharing), while Paper B concerns clauses (MFN/pricing parity in leases) that directly govern how price concessions and benefits are allocated among contracting parties and third-party comparators.

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal rules and commercial realities requiring flexible remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that excuse doctrine must remain consonant with commercial reality and call for flexible, workable tools rather than rigid theory, and Paper B similarly highlights practical problems created by amorphous MFN lease clauses and the need for doctrines that produce predictable, commercially sensible outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev170!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS

shared_topics.topic: proper judicial role in adapting contract law to novel commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether generalist courts should actively extend existing doctrine to emergent contractual forms or instead defer to parties and other institutions, arguing for a largely passive role; Paper B critiques cases that have either expanded or interpolated doctrines (e.g., ALCOA) and asks whether judges should reshape obligations or stick to traditional enforcement norms.

shared_topics.topic: the primacy of party autonomy and contextualizing regimes versus judicial reinterpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that private parties and multilateral contextualizing regimes (trade associations, party-crafted regimes, specialized tribunals) typically create the interpretive context for innovations and courts should respect those allocations; Paper B likewise foregrounds the idea that parties and their ongoing relationships should drive adjustments (duty to adjust, relationship-focused contracting) and questions judicial substitution of terms for parties' own arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal responses to exogenous shocks and commercial uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps how courts should respond to contract innovations driven by market shocks along axes of market thickness and uncertainty, arguing different interpretive regimes are appropriate; Paper B examines commercial impracticability and other excuse doctrines as the contract-law tools for addressing supervening events and argues doctrine should be consonant with commercial reality and provide flexible, workable responses to shocks.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and limits of judicially imposed contract modification (implied duties, loss‑sharing, and incorporation of practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses risks that courts will incorporate informal practices or apply default rules contrary to party arrangements (e.g., via UCC-style incorporation) and how that can facilitate or frustrate innovation; Paper B analyzes judicial efforts to impose loss‑ and risk‑sharing (as in ALCOA), the interpolation of new pricing terms, and the normative bounds on courts imposing modifications versus enforcing or excusing performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev31!!ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and loss‑sharing in commercial contracts when unforeseen events occur
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes commercial impracticability and the possibility of judicially imposed loss‑ and risk‑sharing (modification vs excuse) when supervening events disrupt performance; Paper B studies how transactional lawyers allocate contingent risks contractually (including latent rights/hostages) to deter opportunism and shape who bears loss in adverse scenarios.

shared_topics.topic: role and limits of implied duties, good faith, and judicial interpolation versus explicit contractual modification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the judicial implication of a 'duty to adjust' or good‑faith modification as an alternative to strict excuse or enforcement; Paper B considers how explicit versus hidden contractual provisions (and doctrines that construe them) affect the ability of parties (and their lawyers) to create obligations that discipline future behavior.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior, sunk costs, and bounded rationality as justificatory concerns for intervention or adjustment

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpolation of contract terms versus default rules

shared_topics.topic: the need for doctrinal rules to reflect commercial reality and practical efficiency

shared_topics.topic: critical reappraisal of landmark contract doctrines/cases as foundations for doctrine

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and arbitration as alternatives to public-court enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the industry's extensive use of privately drafted default rules and merchant tribunals instead of the Uniform Commercial Code or courts; Paper B engages with the limits of judicially created excuse doctrines and emphasizes the role of parties and their relationships (and by implication nonjudicial solutions) in coping with disruptions to contractual performance.

shared_topics.topic: relational governance, norms, and reputation as mechanisms for sustaining contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes reputation-based nonlegal sanctions, norms, and institutional supports that create and restore cooperative contracting relationships; Paper B advances a relationship-centered view of contract law (including a 'duty to adjust') that privileges ongoing norms of cooperation and fairness within contractual relationships over strict judicial enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and modification of obligations after unforeseen events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how private contract rules and governance structures in the cotton trade allocate risks and enable cooperative responses to market shocks through rules, adjudication, and reputation; Paper B directly analyzes doctrines (impossibility, impracticability, frustration, and judicially imposed loss-sharing) and debates when and how contractual obligations should be excused, modified, or shared following supervening events.

shared_topics.topic: judicial implication, presumptions of intent, and the legitimacy/limits of courts filling contractual gaps (including appropriate remedies)

papers.node_id: 100geolj5!!ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
papers.title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
papers.abstract:
Contractual obligations are mere options. That is one of the basic assumptions of the economic analysis of contract law regarding the behavior of contracting parties.In other words, parties are assumed to perform their contractual duties if, and only if, doing so enhances their personal welfare. In cases in which the legal price of breach is lower than the cost of performance,the promisor will choose to breach and pay that price (that is, damages).Thus, as a positive matter, contractual obligations are viewed as if they lack any noninstrumental dimension that may affect the behavior of contracting parties.
In a recent study, we introduced an empirical framework that could be used to measure the noninstrumental power associated with legal obligations.This framework was based on an experimental design which compared the effect of two types of uncertainty that are associated with legal liability. The first type, legal uncertainty, relates to uncertainty regarding the content of an obligation. In many cases, legal obligations are vague, and therefore, parties may not be sure, ex ante, whether liability will be attached to a certain type of behavior. The second type, enforcement uncertainty, relates to uncertainty regarding implementation of the legal norm. Violations of legal norms often do not entail any consequences due to problems such as lack of detection. Thus, parties again cannot be sure, ex ante, what will actually be the cost of violating the norm.
To the extent that legal compliance is driven by purely instrumental motivations, legal uncertainty and enforcement uncertainty are expected to affect behavior in a similar fashion. Whether the source of uncertainty stems from the content of an obligation or from its enforcement, potential violators will simply discount legal liability by the probability that it will actually be applied to them. To the extent legal obligations carry an expressive force that drives people to conform, however, the two types of uncertainty are expected to affect behavior distinctly. Specifically, legal uncertainty is expected to have a greater effect on the behavior of people than enforcement uncertainty because its introduction not only reduces the expected cost of noncompliance but also dilutes the expressive power of the legal norm. Thus, by comparing the effect of the two types of uncertainty on the way people treat different types of legal norms, we can ascertain the degree to which each type of norm carries an expressive power that brings about compliance that is not tied to instrumental calculations.
In our previous study, we focused on a regulatory--criminal setting in which the source of the legal norm was the state.We demonstrated that legislation carries an expressive power that induces compliance.Moreover, we showed that this power is sensitive to the type of legislation applicable and is stronger inthe context of criminal prohibitions.In this study, we wish to extend this analysis to obligations created by individuals rather than by the state. We explore whether contracts hold an expressive power that induces people to fulfill their promises irrespective of consequential considerations. In addition, we examine whether this power depends on different characteristics of the contractual obligation.
In order to answer these questions, we designed a series of between-subject experimental surveys that measured and compared participants' attitudes toward contractual performance under conditions of uncertainty. In the scenarios given to participants, their chances of facing contractual liability were identical; we manipulated whether the source of uncertainty stemmed from the ambiguity of the contract or from the ability of the promisee to detect the breach. Overall, these studies confirmed our central hypothesis that people are less committed to complying with the terms of a contract when the source of uncertainty is in the contract itself versus when the source of uncertainty is in the enforcement of the contract (holding the expected liability constant in all cases). Thus, the findings indicate that contractual obligations carry an expressive power above and beyond their instrumental power. Furthermore, the results suggest that this power depends on the characteristics of the contractual obligation. For example, they demonstrate that negotiated contracts carry greater expressive power than standard-form contracts accepted on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.
This project is part of a growing body of literature that has turned to using empirical methods to deepen our understanding of contractual behavior.These studies include both qualitative projects that document contractual behavior in the fieldas well as experimental projects that study such behavior in stylized settings.Viewed as a whole, these studies have added richness and complexity to the way in which we model the behavior of contracting parties. Morespecifically, it has demonstrated that forces such as the moral commitment to promise keeping, cognitive biases, and reputational concerns may affect contractual relationships.This Article builds on these findings and adds to them along two different dimensions. First, it employs a novel methodology that permits measurement of noninstrumental motivations in a subtle and indirect way. This methodology enables us to distinguish between different types of contractual obligations and to compare their relative expressive power. Second, our focus on uncertainty brings the study closer to real-world settings that are inherently probabilistic. This focus allows us to evaluate different aspects of contract law that deal with uncertain contractual obligations such as the doctrines governing contract interpretation.
The Article is organized as follows: in Part I, we describe the background of the study. We review the traditional law and economics literature modeling the incentives of contracting parties. We then present several bodies of literature that suggest that parties may treat their contractual obligations in a noninstrumental fashion. Part II describes the design of the experiments and their results. Finally, in Part III, we explore potential implications of our results for policymakers as well as contracting parties and address the limitations of our study.

questions.question: Whether contractual obligations produce noninstrumental (expressive or moral) motivations that cause people to perform promises beyond what monetary incentives and expected liability predict.
Whether uncertainty about the content/terms of a contract (ambiguity) reduces compliance more than uncertainty about enforcement/detection, when the expected legal liability is held constant.
Whether the expressive power of contractual obligations differs across contract types (for example, negotiated agreements versus standard-form/take-it-or-leave-it contracts).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: the role of contractual ambiguity in shaping outcomes and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes that many hard interpretive disputes arise because contract language lacks a determinate ex ante meaning and only acquires application ex post, while Paper B experimentally manipulates contractual vagueness (legal uncertainty) to show that ambiguity in contract content alters parties' willingness to perform.

shared_topics.topic: noninstrumental/expressive forces versus opportunistic breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that what looks like opportunism in ex post disputes may be an artifact of the absence of shared ex ante intention and that moral norms lie outside what contract language can control, and Paper B empirically measures an expressive (noninstrumental) power of contractual obligations—showing that promise-keeping motivations affect performance beyond instrumental incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the behavioral effects of different kinds of uncertainty (content vs enforcement) on compliance and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how parties, courts, and scholars attempt to infer meaning after the fact when uncertainty exists about what was intended, and Paper B directly compares legal-content uncertainty (ambiguity) to enforcement uncertainty to demonstrate they have distinct behavioral effects on compliance.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract doctrine and the judicial role in resolving disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates reorienting courts toward pragmatic resolution instead of searching for elusive ex ante mutual intent, using rule-induction and philosophy of language, while Paper B connects its experimental findings to doctrines governing uncertain obligations and discusses policy consequences for how the law should treat ambiguous or probabilistic contractual duties.

shared_topics.topic: how formation mode (negotiated complex contracts versus standard-form drafting) influences meaning and compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on complex, long-term negotiated agreements drafted by lawyers and argues that much drafting does not fix ex ante meanings, and Paper B shows experimentally that negotiated contracts carry greater expressive power (and thus different compliance dynamics) than take-it-or-leave-it standard-form contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev1443!!ARTICLE:WHY CONTRACTS SCHOLARS SHOULD READ LEGAL PHILOSOPHY: POSITIVISM, FORMALISM, AND THE SPECIFICATION OF RULES IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:WHY CONTRACTS SCHOLARS SHOULD READ LEGAL PHILOSOPHY: POSITIVISM, FORMALISM, AND THE SPECIFICATION OF RULES IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: expressive (noninstrumental) force of contractual obligations and promise-keeping
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally tests whether contracts motivate performance beyond instrumental (cost/benefit) incentives, showing an expressive/moral commitment effect; Paper B engages this theme theoretically by debating the promise theory of contract and whether moral norms can or should be incorporated into legal rules to guide behavior.

shared_topics.topic: effects of vagueness/legal uncertainty versus enforcement uncertainty on compliance and guidance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally contrasts legal- content uncertainty (vague obligations) with enforcement/detection uncertainty to see differential effects on compliance, while Paper B analyzes the problems posed by vague, norm-laden or context-dependent rules (and their inability to guide conduct unless specified), treating ambiguity as central to debates over rule design.

shared_topics.topic: role of contract form and bargaining structure (negotiated vs standard-form, formal rules vs defaults) in shaping obligations and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds negotiated contracts carry greater expressive power than standard-form take-it-or-leave-it contracts, linking contract form to compliance; Paper B examines the move between classical formal rules and U.C.C. default/standard-form-friendly regimes, arguing formality versus flexibility affects certainty, fairness, and who bears the burden of specification.

shared_topics.topic: contract interpretation, gap-filling, and who/specification procedures for partial rules (e.g., parol evidence, defaults)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A ties its uncertainty findings to real-world doctrines governing contract interpretation and how ambiguous terms are resolved, whereas Paper B theorizes at length about the need for procedures to specify initially partial or vague legal rules (discussing parol evidence, default rules, and the common-law specification process) and the consequences of different specification choices for guidance and dispute resolution.

shared_topics.topic: how rule-design (rules vs standards) affects litigation, guidance, and compliance costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses policy implications of uncertainty and expressive effects for policymakers and contracting parties (including litigation and enforcement consequences), and Paper B grounds a normative argument about returning to more formal rules in concerns that standards and context-dependence increase uncertainty, litigation costs, and reduce the law's capacity to guide behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev170!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS

shared_topics.topic: how different kinds of uncertainty (content/ambiguity vs enforcement/market uncertainty) affect behavior and institutional response
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally contrasts legal-content uncertainty (ambiguous contract terms) with enforcement uncertainty (detection/enforcement probability) and shows ambiguity more strongly reduces compliance; Paper B treats uncertainty about market activities as a central variable determining whether private parties or courts will shape and stabilize novel contractual forms, and how courts should respond to innovation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract interpretation and ambiguity in determining compliance and the stability of agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how vagueness in contractual language dilutes the expressive power of obligations and lowers performance, while Paper B analyzes how courts and other contextualizing regimes interpret novel or ambiguous agreements and whether judicial interpretation should extend, reshape, or defer to parties' understandings.

shared_topics.topic: the allocation between judicial enforcement and private ordering/party autonomy in sustaining contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares the behavioral effects of enforcement mechanisms versus the non‑instrumental (expressive) power of promises, suggesting commitments can matter independently of formal enforcement; Paper B argues that contractual innovation is usually driven and stabilized by parties and private institutions, and that generalist courts should often defer to those party-created regimes rather than proactively reshape agreements.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form and party sophistication (negotiated vs standard-form; trade/regulatory regimes) shape the normative force and treatment of obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds negotiated contracts carry greater expressive power and elicit more compliance than standard-form take‑it‑or‑leave‑it contracts; Paper B emphasizes that sophisticated parties, trade associations, and multilateral regimes better contextualize and discipline novel contractual practices and that courts should recognize differences in form and the parties' chosen regimes when resolving disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90minnlrev1664!!ARTICLE: An Embedded Options Theory of Indefinite Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: An Embedded Options Theory of Indefinite Contracts

shared_topics.topic: effects of contractual vagueness/ambiguity on parties' performance and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally compares 'legal uncertainty' (ambiguity of contract content) to enforcement uncertainty and finds ambiguity reduces contractual compliance and expressive commitment; Paper B theorizes that vague or indefinite terms create economic effects (embedded interpretive options) that change parties' incentives to perform, invest, or breach.

shared_topics.topic: implications for doctrines of contract interpretation and gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links its findings about uncertainty and expressive power to real-world doctrines governing contract interpretation and highlights policy implications; Paper B develops an account of the indefiniteness doctrine and argues for tailored gap‑filling rules (e.g., pro‑defendant fillers) based on the economic costs of embedded options.

shared_topics.topic: behavioral foundations of contract law — departures from standard instrumental models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides experimental evidence that noninstrumental motives (expressive force, moral commitment) influence compliance beyond simple cost–benefit calculations; Paper B challenges standard transaction‑cost explanations and emphasizes cognitive limitations, mispricing of implicit options, and informational asymmetries that alter contracting outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of distinct forms of uncertainty (content vs enforcement vs market volatility) in shaping contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between uncertainty about a contract's content and uncertainty about enforcement and shows they have different behavioral effects; Paper B emphasizes uncertainty in future valuations and interpretation (volatility, contract length) as key determinants of embedded option value and parties' ex ante contract design choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53wakeforestlrev1!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE

shared_topics.topic: expressive or noninstrumental force of contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether contractual duties induce compliance for reasons beyond expected legal sanctions (the 'expressive' power of contract), and Paper B theorizes the normative power of promise and contract as practices that bind agents for reasons internal to agency rather than mere deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between commitment and ongoing agency (autonomy/fickleness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cites moral commitment and promise-keeping as motives that affect contractual performance and explores when those motives weaken, while Paper B centrally analyzes how binding commitments constrain persistent agency and the moral value of revising commitments (the problem of 'fickle' people).

shared_topics.topic: how features of contracts and their formation affect bindingness and compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares negotiated versus standard-form contracts to show variation in expressive power and compliance, and Paper B contrasts promise and contract institutions and discusses doctrinal choices that reflect different assumptions about who is being bound and how much flexibility should be permitted.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of ambiguity, uncertainty, or indeterminacy on obligations and legal responses

papers.node_id: 43lawsocinquiry1427!!ARTICLE: Authoritarianism and the Internet
papers.title: ARTICLE: Authoritarianism and the Internet
papers.abstract:
Control over the flow of information is critical to authoritarian rule. In the Information Age, command of online communication has become indispensable for dictatorial regimes to realize this goal. It is thus no surprise that the contemporary repression apparatus devotes considerable energy and resources to snuffing out online dissent. Modern strategies of cyber censorship have been largely successful. However, we argue that Internet censorship is in fact more fragile than it appears. Cyber censorship, this article posits, is structurally circumscribed. The sheer volume of electronic communications that proliferate in present-day, wired societies represents a serious challenge to the successful control of information. In reality, effective surveillance of only a fraction of online communications is ever possible the quantity and rapidity of online behavior renders it logistically impossible to police every post and every page on the Internet. To achieve large-scale suppression of online dissent, therefore, authoritarian and semi-authoritarian governments are forced to rely substantially on Internet users to police themselves in the form of self-censorship (Herold and Marolt 2011, 55).
This strategy gets results--fear of government scrutiny discourages the open expression of dissent (Deibert et al. 2008, 180, 197-98, 211, 216, 260-61, 325; Hachigian 2001; Yu 2009, 115; Hayhtio and Jarmo 2008, 196).However, this reliance on self-censorship, we argue, renders cyber censorship implicitly susceptible to abrupt collapse. It is constructed upon the shaky edifice of collective paranoia--a fragile foundation that can crumble as the result of small, individual acts of defiance observed sequentially by other Internet users until a point is reached where the norms that underpin self-censorship suddenly collapse. Utilizing the theory ofinformational cascadesin the economics literature, and the related concepts ofavailabilityandnorm cascadesin the legal academic literature, this article advances a model that explains sudden spontaneous collapses in censorial control unique to online communication. We refer to this phenomenon as acyberspeech cascade.
To encourage Internet users to self-censor, authoritarian governments deliberately thrust their populations into a state of informational uncertainty regarding the precise boundaries of permissible speech. Because the legal boundaries of officially tolerated speech are left unclear, even modest, unintentional expressions of contentious online speech can trigger small shifts in perception regarding the acceptable limits of public expression that may then grow into larger ones. The basic model is as such: because the precise line between permissible and impermissible expression is unclear, small acts of uncensored online speech slightly alter collective perceptions of what constitutes acceptable public expression. With the perceived boundaries of permissible online speech slightly expanded, the process repeats itself: building on what they mistakenly believe are the new expanded limits of acceptable speech, fresh waves of Internet users engage in slightly more contentious speech, further pushing back the perceived boundaries of tolerated expression.
With sufficient iterations, this process creates a snowball effect as mass perceptions regarding the acceptable limits of public expression shift significantly. Reputational concerns will also arise, powerfully strengthening this process--a desire for social approval and a wish to avoid disapproval will further incentivize people, intentionally or not, to push the boundaries of public expression. Thus, trickles of progressively more brazen speech can proliferate into large-scale torrents of uncensored expression, triggering the temporary (or permanent) collapse of self-censorship norms.
This process is, we argue, facilitated by the unique character of online interaction--constraints on information, a linear sequentiality, the hyper-connectivity and speed of online communication, and, to the degree that it is present, anonymity between users--render such explosions of expression more likely to occur online than in the offline world. A cyberspeech cascade may vary in terms of initial speed and scale. However, the highly networked character and exponential potential of Internet communication allows collective shifts in perceptions as to the permissible boundaries of public expression to gain momentum and eventually to reach a tipping point. At that juncture, previously stable norms of self-censorship give way as online discourse is overwhelmed by the sheer enormity and widespread presence of uncensored speech. While informational cascades represent the focus of our model,availability and norm cascades, which incorporate reputational considerations, play a decisive role in producing cyberspeech cascades and, as such, form an integral part of our model.
The usefulness of the model we propose is in explaining initial breakdowns in online censorship that often precede eruptions of offline social dissent (existing cascade models already capture quite well the growth of political protest offline). The model is both descriptive and predictive. It describes the sudden collapses in Internet censorship that have been observed across the world in recent years. The model is predictive as it suggests that as Internet usage grows in repressive societies, governments will likely need to rely increasingly on self-censorship, rendering such systems of control even more vulnerable to outbreaks of cyberspeech cascades with potentially massive sociopolitical consequences. We present our argument not as established fact, but as a hypothesis that, ultimately, can be tested only by the unfolding of real-world events as we progress further into the Internet age. We are currently experiencing "the greatest information and communications revolution in human history" (World Bank 2016, xxi) and the full political impact of this transformation remains to be seen. It may be that future events will prove our model extraordinarily accurate, extraordinarily inaccurate, or somewhere in between.
In any event, this article provides a much-needed update to cascade theory in light of the transformative effect of twenty-first-century Internet technology. In an age in which a single individual can upload a video of a panda sneezing that is then viewed by a quarter of a billion people across the planet (Oloffson 2010), the concept of cascades needs to be reexamined. The Internet has become an essential form of communication for billions of people, performed with stunning rapidity. It is a medium for transmitting information at speeds and on a scale unprecedented in human history that has transformed the conduits of social connection upon which cascade theory was first understood. The world has changed, and we need to understand this change. Historically, strongmen have been able to dismantle printing presses with hammers or silence political opponents in prison cells. Internet communication, however, has created new opportunities to disrupt authoritarian control. This article seeks to expose that new reality.

questions.question: Whether authoritarian and semi-authoritarian regimes' reliance on user self-censorship makes online censorship structurally fragile and prone to sudden collapse via information cascades (i.e., cyberspeech cascades).

Whether intrinsic features of online communication (high volume, rapid sequential posting, hyper-connectivity, and anonymity) increase the likelihood and speed of such cascades compared with offline communication.

Whether greater Internet penetration and usage in repressive societies increases the risk that self-censorship norms will break down and produce large-scale, uncensored online expression with political consequences.
