papers.node_id: 85neblrev875!!ARTICLE: Avoiding Economic Waste in Contract Damages: Myths, Misunderstanding, and Malcontent
papers.title: ARTICLE: Avoiding Economic Waste in Contract Damages: Myths, Misunderstanding, and Malcontent
papers.authors: Juanda Lowder Daniel; Kevin Scott Marshall
papers.abstract:
In the realm of contractual remedies, there are two axioms upon which legal scholars and jurists have come to rely, to wit, the court will not make for the parties a better contract than they made for themselves,and the goal of awarding contract damages is to put the aggrieved party in as good of a position as he would have enjoyed upon full performance.These two basic principles were etched into contractjurisprudence with the tools of justice and retribution in order to assure that contracting parties remain in complete control of their relations and that judicial involvement in contractual disputes is limited to fulfilling the intent of the parties.Thus, whenever a doctrine appears to run afoul of the underpinnings of contractual intent, it stands to reason that its veracity is called into question.
This Article calls into question one such doctrine, the doctrine of economic waste. As applied in the context of contractual rights and remedies, the doctrine of economic waste exemplifies the difficulties of utilizing a robust but misunderstood theoretical construct. While such a doctrine is best understood from an economic perspective, such a perspective has been virtually ignored in the doctrine's jurisprudential application in contract law. Theoretical ignorance and a cavalier application of the economic waste doctrine is particularly problematic when it leads to confounding and incoherent remedial outcomes that defy the primary goal of contract damages - that is, to award the nonbreaching party his expectation interests.
"Economic waste" is the label that courts have adopted as justification for not awarding an aggrieved party the cost of performanceas damages for breach of a construction contract.Although it is widely accepted that cost of performance is generally the proper measure of damages to compensate for deficient performance under a construction contract, it is also widely regarded that such damages may be inappropriate when the increase in objective value to be achieved by finishing the task is grossly disproportionate to the cost involved.This gross disparity is commonly referred to as economic waste, which is frowned upon by the majority of courts, causing them to opt for an alternative measure of the loss of value in terms of the diminution in value - the difference in value with and without completion of the contract.Moreover, concerns about creating a windfall for the aggrieved party are used to bolster adoption of the alternative measure of damages because the court generally does not believe the aggrieved partywill, in fact, use the damages awarded to finish a task that would result in little or no increase in market value.
However, it is difficult, if not impossible, to reconcile the justification for the use of this alternative measure of damages with the basic notions of economics and contractual intent. This difficulty stems from the misunderstanding of the economics of a bargained-for exchange, whereby both parties have weighed the pros and cons of entering into the transaction beforehand and have decided they are better off entering into the deal than not.The bargain between the parties is supposed to reflect their assessment of the costs and benefits of doing exactly what they agreed to do. Thus, when a court upsets this bargain after the fact by unilaterally deciding the parties' exchange is not worth what the parties agreed to pay or do, the court then creates a situation whereby the aggrieved party is not given the equivalent of the benefit of her bargain, and the breaching party is in a better position than he would have been had he fully performed. Thus, the windfall inures to the benefit of the breaching party. The result is an economically inefficient transaction, the very thing that the court ostensibly sought to prevent by resort to this alternative, albeit less desirable, measure of damages.
This Article explores the myths, misunderstanding, and malcontent generated by the judicial application of the economic waste doctrine. It specifically examines the doctrine of economic waste as it is commonly invoked as a justification for awarding diminution-in-value damages, ultimately revealing that the very condition (i.e., economic waste) the court seeks to avoid, ironically, is created when the court strays from its role of fulfilling the intent of the parties, alas the myth. This reverse phenomenon occurs because of a failure to understand the basic premise of economic waste from a microeconomics perspective, thus the misunderstanding. Given the myth and misunderstanding of the economic waste doctrine as applied in contract cases, as well as the litany of inconsistent and incoherent remedial outcomes revealed by a review of its judicial application, it can be of no surprise that the propriety of the current state of the law is suspect and in need of change, hence the malcontent.
Part II commences the following analysis with a discussion of the origin and development of the economic waste doctrine, as well as its modern application in renowned cases widely cited for discussion of the diminution-in-value alternative measure of damages. Part III explains economic waste from an economic perspective. Its discussion of the perfectly competitive model of microeconomics provides a backdropfor a proper understanding of the economic waste doctrine. Part IV analyzes the expected strategic behavior of contracting parties utilizing conventional theoretical game models to further demonstrate problems with the courts' present application of the economic waste doctrine. Part V highlights the fallacies in the general assumption that this alternative measure of damages is needed to prevent economic waste, it explains how this alternative measure actually creates economic waste, and it suggests a simplified default rule for determining the proper measure of damages. Finally, Part VI concludes with a few thoughts about how the policies and premises discussed in this Article hold true in evaluating the propriety of other types of contractual remedies, thereby raising issues deserving of additional exploration.

questions.question: Whether awarding damages that enable the nonbreaching party to finish performance (cost-to-complete) rather than awarding the loss in market value better protects the parties' expectation interests and yields economically efficient outcomes.

Whether courts' substitution of an alternative damages measure to avoid perceived 'economic waste' is justified by basic microeconomic and bargaining principles, or whether that substitution itself creates inefficiency and unjust windfalls.
What simplified default rule for measuring contract damages would most reliably minimize economic inefficiency while respecting the parties' agreed-upon bargain.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16tourolrev1037!!COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?
compared_to.partner_title: COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?

shared_topics.topic: critique of law-and-economics reasoning in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers scrutinize courts' reliance on economic reasoning—Paper A critiques the Seventh Circuit's use of a neoclassical 'rational person'/efficiency model to infer assent in Hill v. Gateway, while Paper B criticizes judges' theoretical ignorance and misapplication of microeconomic concepts in the 'economic waste' doctrine governing contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: conflict between actual party assent/intent and judicially imposed economic norms
shared_topics.justification: Both works address situations where courts substitute efficiency-driven norms for the parties' manifested bargains—Paper A shows courts treating efficiency as evidence of assent (rather than relying on actual manifestations), and Paper B shows courts upsetting contracted-for expectation interests by refusing cost-of-performance damages to avoid perceived economic waste.

shared_topics.topic: need for richer behavioral and economic models to guide doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both call for better modeling of contracting behavior—Paper A urges incorporation of empirical, interdisciplinary (behavioral) insights beyond simplistic rational-agent assumptions, and Paper B applies microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to demonstrate how courts should more accurately predict parties' strategic behavior and remedial incentives.

shared_topics.topic: judicial application of doctrine producing perverse or inefficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers document that current judicial doctrines can generate undesirable results—Paper A argues that invoking 'common sense'/efficiency can legitimise normative biases and misallocate risks, while Paper B argues that using diminution-in-value to avoid 'economic waste' often creates the very inefficiency and windfall the courts seek to prevent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68stanlrev281!!ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks

shared_topics.topic: appropriate scope of judicial intervention and remedial design in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts should (or should not) intervene when collaborative innovation alliances fail, arguing that tribunals must balance multiple doctrines (contract, patent, property) rather than adopt a purely minimalistic enforcement stance; Paper B critiques courts' use of the economic-waste rationale in awarding damages, showing that judicial reallocation of remedies can subvert parties' bargains and produce inefficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic theory to evaluate contract doctrine and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds on contract economics to explain alliance governance (opportunism, transaction costs, spillovers, coordination entropy) and proposes multivalent contracting as an economic-informed framework; Paper B deploys microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to expose misunderstandings in the economic-waste doctrine and to recommend an economically coherent default rule for damages.

shared_topics.topic: protection of expectation and reliance interests as incentives for relationship-specific investment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that formal contract terms foster informal governance and lock parties into relationship-specific investments (reliance), raising questions about courts’ role in vindicating those expectations; Paper B centers the expectation interest as the proper objective of contract damages and argues that doctrines like economic waste often deny the nonbreaching party the benefit of the bargain, undermining incentives to perform or invest.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules interact with multiple contractual hazards and produce tradeoffs/unintended consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A introduces multivalent contracting to show that particular provisions can address some hazards (e.g., opportunism) while exacerbating others (e.g., coordination entropy or spillovers), shaping alliance design; Paper B demonstrates that judicial adjustments to remedies (invoking economic waste) can unintentionally create the very inefficiencies they aim to prevent, highlighting doctrinal tradeoffs and perverse incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55umiamilrev369!!ARTICLE: 2-207 and Company (For Richard A. Hausler)
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: 2-207 and Company (For Richard A. Hausler)

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should enforce the parties' bargain or reshape it through doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates proposed revisions to UCC §2-207 and related provisions that determine when form exchanges become binding agreements, raising questions about how much courts should intervene in the parties' chosen conventions; Paper B argues that the economic waste doctrine improperly alters the bargained-for exchange by substituting a court-determined damages measure for the parties' agreed expectations.

shared_topics.topic: design and reform of default rules/statutory provisions in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on proposed revisions to Articles 1 and 2 of the UCC (including §2-207), engaging the normative and doctrinal choices embodied in statutory default rules; Paper B proposes a simplified default rule for measuring damages and critiques the existing judicially-applied default (diminution-in-value) as economically and doctrinally misguided.

shared_topics.topic: the conflict between doctrinal conventions/formalism and economic/theoretical analysis as bases for resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the power of legal conventions, formal stances, and jurisprudential framing in shaping outcomes under the UCC provisions it examines; Paper B explicitly brings microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to bear, criticizing courts' doctrinal applications for ignoring economic theory and producing inefficient results.

shared_topics.topic: concerns about doctrinal incoherence and the need for doctrinal or jurisprudential clarification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the UCC provisions it treats as 'jurisprudentially provocative,' signaling potential incoherence or contestable interpretation under the current regime; Paper B catalogs inconsistent and incoherent remedial outcomes produced by the economic waste doctrine and argues the law is in need of change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98iowalrev535!!ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory role of economic efficiency in contract law and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically examines courts' invocation of 'economic waste' and economic reasoning to deny cost-of-performance expectation damages, arguing that the courts misapply efficiency arguments; Paper B analyzes economic efficiency as a prominent monist normative theory for contract law and evaluates its adequacy compared to pluralist approaches.

shared_topics.topic: judicial deference to parties' contractual intent versus judicial substitution of value judgments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts improperly remake parties' bargains when they substitute diminution-in-value for cost of performance, undermining the parties' expectation interests; Paper B considers how normative theories should guide judges and warns against legal theories that would permit courts to impose a single overriding value rather than respect competing considerations like contractual security and administrability.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal decisionmaking should balance multiple values or rely on a single governing value (pluralism vs monism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the problem of courts privileging a single concern (avoiding 'windfalls' or perceived economic waste) at the expense of other contract-law values, while Paper B directly argues for pluralism and balancing over monist single-value theories such as efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: use of microeconomic and strategic (game-theoretic) analysis to evaluate contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops microeconomic models and conventional game-theoretic analysis to demonstrate the consequences of judicially imposed damage rules, and Paper B engages economic reasoning (notably efficiency) as a central theoretical lens when assessing competing normative accounts of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98iowalrev535!!ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of economic efficiency as a sole normative standard in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques monist theories that take a single value (especially efficiency) as the lone basis for doctrinal recommendations and argues they cannot achieve the all-things-considered justificatory goal; Paper B targets judicial uses of an ostensibly economic doctrine (economic waste) and shows that relying on economic judgments (as courts have done) produces incoherent, inefficient outcomes, undermining the view that efficiency alone should govern remedy choices.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification and legitimacy of contract doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the project of normative legal theory as producing justified final recommendations about what the law should be and uses contract examples to illustrate this task; Paper B interrogates whether the economic-waste doctrine and diminution-in-value remedies legitimately fulfill the core remedial purpose of contract law (protecting expectation interests), thereby assessing the justificatory quality of current doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: need to balance multiple values (pluralism) rather than applying single-value rules in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for pluralist theories that balance competing values (e.g., autonomy, fairness, administrability, Rule of Law) instead of adopting monist rules; Paper B reveals how courts' unilateral economic judgments upset parties' bargains and create inefficiencies, illustrating the practical importance of weighing contractual intent, fairness, and economic effects rather than defaulting to a single corrective metric.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation and misuse of economic analysis in doctrinal decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the proliferation of economically framed monist theories in legal scholarship and worries about their normative limits; Paper B provides a microeconomic analysis of the economic waste doctrine, diagnosing theoretical misunderstandings and strategic behavior consequences when courts attempt to apply economic concepts without proper economic or doctrinal grounding.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev1437!!ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis (microeconomics/game theory) to evaluate contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly applies microeconomic models and game-theoretic reasoning to critique the judicial application of the economic-waste doctrine and to predict parties' strategic behavior; Paper B likewise treats parties' intent and enforcement rules as a design problem evaluated with economic logic about incentives, defaults, and transaction costs.

shared_topics.topic: choice of default rules and opt-out mechanisms in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a simplified default rule for determining the proper measure of damages when courts confront economic-waste questions, while Paper B develops an analytic framework comparing enforcement versus nonenforcement interpretive defaults and opt-out regimes for determining whether parties intended legal liability.

shared_topics.topic: respecting parties' expectations/intent when determining remedies or enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should honor the parties' bargained-for expectation (cost of performance) rather than substituting diminution-in-value measures, and Paper B analyzes when legal enforcement should track parties' manifested intent to be bound and how that affects appropriate remedies and reliance/expectation tradeoffs.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between judicial intervention and party autonomy (when courts should alter bargains)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes judicial refusal to enforce the parties' agreement (via invoking economic waste) as creating inefficiency and a windfall for breachers, and Paper B examines when courts should or should not infer an intent to create legal consequences, weighing the social role of courts against parties' freedom to structure relationships without legal enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113nwulrev279!!ARTICLE: DEAL STRUCTURE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DEAL STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: courts' role in honoring the parties' bargain versus reshaping agreements through interpretation or remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how judicial interpretation of interlinked provisions can alter deal outcomes depending on contract structure (potentially producing results different from parties' expectations), while Paper B argues courts violate contractual intent when they substitute diminution-in-value remedies for agreed-upon measures (thereby reshaping the bargain and producing windfalls).

shared_topics.topic: how contract design or structure affects enforcement outcomes and dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory of contractual structuralism showing that modular versus integrated drafting materially changes design, performance, and adjudication, and Paper B analyzes how the chosen contract terms and the expectation of cost-of-performance versus diminution remedies shape parties' incentives and the practical results of breaches.

shared_topics.topic: application of economic analysis and efficiency reasoning to doctrinal choices in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links structural drafting choices to economic and adjudicative goals and cites literature on complexity and private ordering, while Paper B applies microeconomic models and game theory to critique the economic waste doctrine and to recommend efficiency-improving default rules for damages.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between rules and standards (or default doctrines) and its implications for interpretation and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that rule-like versus standard-like terms interact with a contract's structural design to determine whether textualist or contextualist interpretation is feasible, and Paper B critiques courts' ad hoc invocation of the 'economic waste' standard, proposing a clearer default rule for measuring damages to avoid inconsistent remedial outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev99!!ARTICLE: THE SPACE BETWEEN MARKETS AND HIERARCHIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SPACE BETWEEN MARKETS AND HIERARCHIES

shared_topics.topic: economic analysis of contractual design and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers apply economic theory to evaluate contractual institutions: Paper A uses transaction-cost and property-rights arguments to analyze hybrid outsourcing contracts as governance mechanisms between markets and hierarchies, while Paper B uses microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to critique the judicial application of the economic-waste doctrine and to recommend economically sound default rules for damages.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and judicial doctrines shape parties' incentives and contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how legal allocation of ownership and bespoke contractual control rights (e.g., in hybrid outsourcing) affects firms' organizational choices and incentives, and Paper B shows how courts' remedial choices (cost of performance versus diminution-in-value) alter contracting parties' ex post incentives and can produce inefficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: hold-up, relation-specific investment, and strategic behavior surrounding performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies hold-up risk from relation-specific investments as a central concern motivating hybrid contracts that carve out control rights, and Paper B models contracting parties' strategic behavior in response to remedial doctrines—arguing that mistaken judicial interventions can create perverse incentives analogous to hold-up and generate economic waste.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of control/ownership rights and their impact on completion and performance decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on carving out control rights and legal ownership in outsourcing deals to manage who bears operational risk and who controls critical inputs, while Paper B analyzes how the chosen damage measure (awarding cost of performance versus diminution-in-value) effectively reallocates the power and incentives to complete performance, influencing whether and how contracts are carried out.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22galrev503!!ARTICLE: Impracticability as Risk Allocation: The Effect of Changed Circumstances Upon Contract Obligations for the Sale of Goods
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Impracticability as Risk Allocation: The Effect of Changed Circumstances Upon Contract Obligations for the Sale of Goods

shared_topics.topic: proper measurement of contractual remedies to protect expectation interests (cost of performance vs diminution in value; when to award damages versus excuse performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether courts should award cost of performance or instead limit recovery to diminution in value in construction breaches, focusing on preserving the nonbreaching party's expectation; Paper B addresses whether changed circumstances should lead to excuse (impracticability) or to damages, examining how the law determines the appropriate remedial response for sales contracts.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unforeseen or changed circumstances (who bears the risk of increased cost or decreased value)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly analyzes risk allocation under impracticability doctrines and the UCC when conditions change after contract formation; Paper A treats judicial refusal to award full performance costs as a de facto reallocation of the risk of costly performance and critiques that reallocation as contrary to the parties' bargain.

shared_topics.topic: application of economic and microeconomic analysis to contract doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses microeconomics and game-theoretic models to show how the economic waste doctrine is misunderstood and leads to inefficient outcomes; Paper B likewise grounds its critique in commercial realities and economic reasoning about how risk should be allocated under the Code and by courts.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between judicial intervention and enforcement of parties' bargains (courts substituting their judgment and creating inefficiencies or windfalls)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for upsetting negotiated exchanges by substituting diminution measures and thereby creating windfalls and inefficiency; Paper B criticizes judicial handling of impracticability cases for failing to align with the parties' expectations and the Code's aim of reflecting commercial practice, implicating the proper limits of judicial modification of contractual obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46sandiegolrev595!!Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should alter the parties' bargain or enforce expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes judicial departures from the bargained-for contract (e.g., substituting diminution-in-value for cost of performance) as undermining contractual intent and creating inefficiency; Paper B directly debates the propriety of judicial adjustment of contracts, arguing there are limited circumstances in which courts altering contract terms may be justified.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/efficiency reasoning to justify or condemn remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the economic waste doctrine through microeconomic and game-theoretic lenses and faults courts for misunderstanding efficiency implications; Paper B evaluates Speidel's court-adjustment proposal largely as a policy/efficiency question, asking whether judicial intervention can produce better economic outcomes in disrupted long-term contracts.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies when performance completion is costly or circumstances change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on construction and similar cases where cost of completion may far exceed value added and examines choice between cost-of-performance and diminution measures; Paper B deals with disrupted long-term contracts (ALCOA and successors) and whether courts should adjust contractual obligations or remedies when changed circumstances make original terms problematic.

shared_topics.topic: importance of context, uncertainty, and strategic behavior in choosing doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses game models to show parties' strategic responses and how a one-size-fits-all judicial rule can produce perverse results; Paper B emphasizes that too many variables and unknowns surround long-term contract disruption, making simple universal rules about court adjustment inappropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75molrev493!!Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism

shared_topics.topic: judicial deference to party autonomy versus judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts in the recent ‘new formalism’ increasingly defer to the literal terms and autonomy of (so‑called) sophisticated parties, while Paper B criticizes courts that intervene in remedies (via the economic waste doctrine) by refusing to enforce the parties' bargained‑for expectation interests.

shared_topics.topic: need for clearer doctrinal standards and predictability in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the label 'sophistication' is used inconsistently and calls for a precise, fact‑driven standard to promote certainty; Paper B documents inconsistent and incoherent applications of the economic‑waste doctrine and proposes clearer, economically grounded rules to restore predictable remedial outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic reasoning and information/resource asymmetries in evaluating contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes assessing party sophistication by comparing parties' relative access to information, experience, and resources, while Paper B deploys microeconomic and game‑theoretic analysis to show how courts misunderstand economic incentives and information problems when applying the economic‑waste doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: how contextual/party characteristics affect remedial and substantive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts adjust a wide array of contract doctrines (e.g., enforceability, parol evidence, fraud, mistake) based on perceived party sophistication, and Paper B shows courts alter the measure of damages (cost of performance vs diminution in value) based on normative judgments about economic waste and parties' likely behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65uclalrev376!!ARTICLE: Deal Momentum
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Momentum

shared_topics.topic: judicial enforcement versus private ordering in contractual relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies why sophisticated parties use non-binding preliminary agreements and argues these documents function as private-ordering signposts rather than instruments meant for judicial enforcement; Paper B critiques courts' intervening remedial choices (like substituting diminution-in-value for cost of performance) and argues judicial alteration of parties' bargains undermines private ordering and contractual intent.

shared_topics.topic: when and whether courts should honor parties' expressed intentions about bindingness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes instances (e.g., SIGA) where courts nonetheless award damages despite explicit 'non-binding' language and asks whether courts need to enforce preliminary agreements at all; Paper B examines courts' refusals to award the measure of damages parties would expect, arguing that courts often improperly override the parties' agreed exchange.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis to evaluate contract doctrine and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs economic-informed notions (deal momentum, transaction costs, investment incentives) to explain why non-binding agreements facilitate efficient dealmaking without enforcement; Paper B deploys microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to show that invoking 'economic waste' and substituting remedies can create inefficiencies and strategic distortion.

shared_topics.topic: the proper measure of remedies and the choice between alternative damage doctrines (expectation vs reliance/cost vs diminution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the scholarly debate over whether preliminary agreements should trigger reliance or expectation damages and how enforcement choices affect deal behavior; Paper B focuses on the conflict between cost-of-performance (expectation) and diminution-in-value measures, arguing that courts' adoption of the latter often thwarts expectation interests and creates waste.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev1443!!ARTICLE:WHY CONTRACTS SCHOLARS SHOULD READ LEGAL PHILOSOPHY: POSITIVISM, FORMALISM, AND THE SPECIFICATION OF RULES IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:WHY CONTRACTS SCHOLARS SHOULD READ LEGAL PHILOSOPHY: POSITIVISM, FORMALISM, AND THE SPECIFICATION OF RULES IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: judicial deference to parties' bargains vs judicial modification of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for upsetting the parties' bargain by invoking the economic-waste doctrine to reduce expectation damages, arguing judges should honor the contracted-for exchange; Paper B evaluates formalism versus anti-formalism and argues about whether courts should rigidly apply rules that enforce bargains or instead modify outcomes in light of fairness, context, or norms.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic reasoning and efficiency as a justification for doctrinal choices

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FREEDOM FROM CONTRACT: SOLUTIONS IN SEARCH OF A PROBLEM?

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

papers.node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
papers.title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
papers.abstract:
Recent work in contract theory, epitomized by an influential article by Alan Schwartz and Robert Scott, suggests that business entities benefit from formal rather than contextual rules of contract law.Such firms are better off, according to this theory, when courts interpret contracts according to their terms and do not attempt to substitute the courts' own concepts of reasonableness or fair dealing for bargains actually struck.
This theoretical work challenges conventional views in contract scholarship that favor looser, more contextual approaches.But does it accurately describe the real world? Lisa Bernstein's important studies of internal industry dispute resolution practices find that private arbitration tribunals employ bright-line rules; these rules deviate, in some respects, from the more nuanced approach that would apply if the disputing parties brought their controversy before a court.Bernstein's work suggests that industry actors, when given the freedom to devise their own procedures, opt for a system of rules much like that predicted in Schwartz and Scott's theory.
This Article offers a more general test of the proposition that formal rules are efficient means for governing commercial contracts. It draws on Eisenberg and Miller's empirical study of dispute resolution clauses in major transactions.Nearly half of the contracts in Eisenberg and Miller's sample chose New York law to govern disputes, and nearly half of the contracts that contained forum selection clauses opted for New York state or federal courts.California, on the other hand, was distinctly unpopular with the parties represented in Eisenberg and Miller's study. Many fewer contracts opted for California law or a California forum than would be expected given the size and commercial importance of that state.
The contrast between California and New York law has implications for contract theory. Since choice-of-law and forum selection clauses are negotiated ex ante, they likely represent efforts by the contracting parties to maximize the joint value of the undertaking.And because the contracts in the Eisenberg-Miller study were, by definition, important to the financial results of large corporations,it can be presumed that they received scrutiny from well-qualified attorneys.Accordingly, compared with California, New York may provide the more efficient regime for interpreting and enforcing commercial agreements.Analysis of the relevant differences between the two states' contract law could then provide information on optimal contract rules.
This Article performs such an analysis. It compares New York and California across a range of contract law issues. As would be expected, the laws are similar in broad outline. Each state respects freedom of contract and each recognizes other social and moral objectives that occasionally trump private agreements. Each state's law grows out of a dialectic process in which competing values are reconciled in different settings. Yet a closer analysis reveals substantial differences in tone and substance. New York and California are close siblings - children of the common law and a shared legal and political tradition. But they are far from identical twins.
The differences between New York and California contract law turn out to align with the formalist-contextualist distinction in contract theory. New York judges are formalists. Especially in commercial cases, they have little tolerance for attempts to re-write contracts to make them fairer or more equitable, and they look to the written agreement as the definitive source of interpretation. California judges, on the other hand, more willingly reform or reject contracts in the service of morality or public policy; they place less emphasis on the written agreement of the parties and seek instead to identify the contours of their commercial relationship within a broader context framed by principles of reason, equity, and substantial justice.
Both approaches to contract law are commendable. Both serve important social goals and employ sophisticated and well-reasoned doctrines in the service of those ends. This article takes no position on whether one is better than the other. What is clear, however, is that contracting parties do take a position on this question. The testimony of the marketplace - the verdict of thousands of sophisticated parties whose incentives are to maximize the value of contract terms - is that New York's formalistic rules win out over California's contextualist approach. As predicted by theory, sophisticated parties prefer formalistic rules of contract law.

questions.question: Do sophisticated commercial contracting parties prefer and select jurisdictions that apply formal, bright-line rules for interpreting and enforcing contracts over jurisdictions that apply more contextual, fairness- or equity-oriented approaches?

Do contracting parties' ex ante choices of governing law and forum (in major commercial agreements) provide evidence that formal, predictable contract rules are the more efficient regime for governing commercial transactions?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105califlrev1725!!SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: formal versus contextual rules in legal governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether federal structures should be judged by doctrinal coherence or by their practical effects, implicitly weighing fixed constitutional doctrines against flexible, consequentialist approaches; Paper B directly compares formalist (New York) and contextualist (California) contract doctrines and evaluates which style parties prefer in commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante private ordering and choice of governing rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats federalism as a constitutional 'contract' that allocates rules and relationships among governmental units and emphasizes how decentralization allows subunits to craft different policy regimes, while Paper B analyzes how contracting parties and private tribunals deliberately choose governing law, forum, and bright-line procedures to shape dispute resolution ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between centralization (uniformity/predictability) and decentralization (local adaptation/information)

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical and social-science evidence to evaluate legal-institutional theories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates Gerken's claims by invoking social science to assess inherent tendencies of federalism and predict effects on people, whereas Paper B relies on empirical studies (Eisenberg & Miller, Bernstein) and marketplace behavior to test contract-theory predictions about rule choice and efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54ambuslj519!!ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the textualist/formalist versus contextualist/relational debate in contract interpretation

shared_topics.topic: the significance of jurisdictional choice (New York v. California) as empirical and doctrinal evidence about optimal interpretive regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses choice‑of‑law and forum selection practices (the market's preference for New York over California) to argue that sophisticated parties prefer formalist rules, and Paper B treats New York and California as paradigmatic examples in explaining variation in interpretive practice and doctrinal commitments across jurisdictions.

shared_topics.justification: Both articles grapple with which interpretive methods should be normatively preferred: Paper A emphasizes efficiency and predictability for commercial actors as support for formal rules, while Paper B develops hermeneutic distinctions but explicitly connects those analytical options to normative choices in contract theory and proposes criteria for selecting among them.

shared_topics.topic: context‑sensitive or contract‑specific models of interpretation (tailoring method to contractual characteristics)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper rejects a one‑size‑fits‑all rule: Paper A argues that sophisticated commercial parties choose rules suited to their transactional needs (favoring formalism for major commercial contracts), and Paper B formalizes a context‑dependent interpretive model that weights textual versus extratextual sources according to the contract's characteristics and relational context.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110nwulrev63!!Article: CUSTOM IN THE COURTS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: CUSTOM IN THE COURTS

shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally compare and evaluate the merits of a formalist, text‑centered approach (exemplified by New York law and courts that enforce the written bargain) against a contextual/usage‑based approach (exemplified by the UCC's incorporation of trade usages and California‑style contextualism), arguing about which should govern commercial disputes.

shared_topics.justification: Each paper subjects theoretical claims to empirical scrutiny — Paper A by analyzing reported trade‑usage cases (1970–2007) to test whether incorporation reduces specification costs without raising error costs, and Paper B by using contract choice and industry dispute‑resolution evidence to test the claim that sophisticated parties prefer and benefit from formal rules.

shared_topics.topic: parties' ex‑ante choices (choice‑of‑law, forum, or private rules) as revealing preferred legal regimes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the observable decisions of sophisticated commercial parties — e.g., choice of New York law or private industry tribunals with bright‑line rules — as informative about which legal/regulatory regimes firms find most valuable and efficient.

shared_topics.topic: the role and quality of evidence (proof standards) for importing industry practices/usages into contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how courts or private adjudicators rely on evidence of trade usages or industry norms — Paper A documents weak evidentiary practices in UCC trade‑usage rulings (party testimony, lack of statistical proof), while Paper B discusses how private fora and choice patterns reflect reliance on clearer bright‑line rules rather than nebulous contextual proof.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev128!!ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on empirical studies of forum/choice-of-law selection and industry arbitration practices to infer which doctrinal regimes commercial parties prefer, and Paper B analyzes contract clauses and judicial decisions (including patterns across jurisdictions) to infer when parties tacitly accept or reject default damage allocations and how defaults might be calibrated.

compared_to.partner_title: COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?

papers.node_id: 67dukeljonline102!!ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS
papers.abstract:
In their articleThe Black Hole Problem in Commercial Boilerplateand its companion pieces,Stephen Choi, Mitu Gulati, and Robert Scott [hereinafter "CG&S"] introduce and explore the concept of "contractual black holes," boilerplate contract provisions that have been "emptied of any recordable meaning"through rote repetition,the introduction of essentially "random variations in language,"and the absence of "any validation [of their meaning] from courts or industry institutions."The article presents a detailed case study of the sovereign debt market's slow response to the Second Circuit's errantinterpretation of thepari passuclause at issue inNML v. Argentina,a common clause in sovereign debt contracts that they view as the "prototypical exemplar"of a black hole. Noting that theNMLdecision put a multi-trillion dollar market at risk by making it more difficult to restructure sovereign debt,and that it took years for market transactors to draft clauses eliminating the problem,the authors conclude that changes in contract doctrine are needed to deal with the problems caused by black holes. As they explain, "while black holes often remain for many years as relatively harmless surplusage, they can [also] generate substantial social costs once litigation results in an interpretation that introduces inefficiencies into the market."
This Comment focuses on the authors' proposed doctrinal solution to the black hole problem, which seeks to eliminate any inquiry into "subjective intent" when courts are faced with the task of interpreting a black hole. It explores the conceptual and practical challenges of implementing the authors' proposal and then questions whether legal reform is really needed to deal with the black hole problem. Part I identifies several common ways that standardized contract provisions that are often indistinguishable from true black holes may arise.It suggests that any doctrinal solution to the black hole problem will have to either reliably distinguish real black holes from these relatively common "black hole apparitions," or be desirable when applied to both types of provisions. Part II describes the proposed reform and explores the practical barriers to implementingit. Along the way it also sketches out several alternative avenues for solving the problems evidenced in thepari passusaga. It suggests that these avenues, while more limited in scope than the authors' proposed reform, may turn out to be more feasible and less costly to implement. Part III questions whether any doctrinal or other solution to the socalled black hole problem can be justified on the basis of the lessons learned from thepari passusaga alone, given that other markets have been able to overcome collective action problems and adopt and amend standard-form contracts through processes that have tended to work more quickly and less contentiously over time. Finally, Part IV concludes by suggesting that the interpretive approach adopted by the Second Circuit inNMLmight be a passably good response to the black hole problem writ large.

questions.question: Should courts adopt a doctrinal rule that bars inquiry into parties' subjective intent when interpreting indeterminate or meaning-empty standardized contract clauses?

How can courts or market participants reliably distinguish genuinely indeterminate (meaning-empty) boilerplate clauses from superficially similar standardized provisions, and what are the practical consequences of different methods of distinction?

Can private ordering and market-based solutions (e.g., contract drafting practices, industry conventions) address the risks posed by indeterminate boilerplate clauses more effectively or feasibly than judicial doctrinal reform?

papers.node_id: 45iowajcorpl885!!ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory
papers.title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory
papers.abstract:
The corporate form is often viewed as one of the critical legal tools necessary to achieve the scale economies pursued across a number of markets during the Industrial Revolution.Mass production required the raising of dramatic amounts of capital, which the corporation facilitated through unique characteristics, such as delegated management, perpetual existence, readily alienable shares, and limited stockholder liability.Bycentralizing control, the corporate form was also a means for managing the increased complexity of producing at scale.
Pursuing economies of scale is not the only strategy in a company's playbook, however. Pressure to innovate new marketable technology has pushed companies to adopt more collaborative modes of production, where a significant amount of activity occurs across firm boundaries rather than solely within them.As a result, the corporate form is not the only primary tool of private law upon which modern capitalism relies. As production becomes more collaborative, the role of contracting becomes increasingly important.
The stakes for understanding this collaborative production model are high. When interfirm collaboration operates effectively, the gains can be dramatic. For instance, many of the medicinal breakthroughs of the 21st century have been achieved through collaboration between a promising biotechnology company and an established pharmaceutical company. At the same time, dysfunctional collaborations can have disastrous consequences, as commercial aerospace demonstrates. In the early 2000s, Boeing shifted to a collaborative design and production process in order to introduce carbon fiber technology in its 787 Dreamliner, hoping to incorporate the advanced material on a reduced timeframe and under budget.What resulted, however, were a series of quality problems and cost overlays that continue to dog the Dreamliner to this day.Another Boeing aircraft provides a far more troubling example: It appears that thesoftware solution to the 737 MAX 8's tendency to pitch up that Boeing developed with external engineers was ineffective and ultimately caused the deaths of over 300 people.
As a result, the increasing importance of contractual governance mechanisms in the modern economy has attracted a great deal of scholarly attention. The literature's foundation was laid in Macauley's landmark paper, which presented empirical evidence that flexibility in these contractual relationships is not achieved through formal legal doctrines but through informal norms.Research on relational contracting has since flourished. Debate has focused upon a positive question that has important normative implications: What is the relationship between formal and informal contracting? Understanding whether formal and informal contracts are substitutes or complements to one another matters because it steers how we think about court intervention. For instance, if informal governance is a substitute for formal contracting, then judicial involvement may "crowd out" efficient informal institutions. On the other hand, if informal contracts complement formal agreements, then judicial intervention may be beneficial, although that will depend on the specifics of exactly how formal and informal agreements work together.
Within this literature Gilson, Sabel & Scott's ("GSS") trilogy of relational contracting papers, of whichBraiding: The Interaction of Formal and Informal Contracting in Theory, Practice, and Doctrineis the core, stands out.Their theory of "braided" contracting is the most ambitious of recent relational contracting efforts, because it attempts to explain behavior in a wide range of modern markets, engaging directly with the large, dynamic industries of the 21st century economy, rather than focusing solely upon niche trading communities. Braiding also carefully engages with the complexity of modern transactions - attempting to explain in detail how the elements of formal agreements interact with informal governance. Finally, braiding theory is an important part of GSS's broader attempt to outline the positive foundations for a non-unitary theory of U.S. contract law.
The braiding thesis can be summarized as follows. GSS argue that collaborative innovation depends upon a unique blend of both formal contract provisions, enforceable in a court of law, and informal constraints, which rely upon extra-legal sanctions to police behavior.In a braided agreement, certain formal contract provisions create information sharing routines, which in turn foster informal governance by (1) making each collaborator's performance more transparent, (2) revealing whether the parties are proneto cheating, and (3) locking the parties into the partnership as they make mutual investments in relationship-specific learning. This "braid" of formal and informal contracting harnesses the opportunism problems GSS see plaguing interfirm collaborations.
This paper, prepared for a conference celebrating Ron Gilson's impressive oeuvre, attempts to do two things. First, it provides an assessment of the braiding thesis by analyzing a market that has not yet attracted scholarly scrutiny to determine whether braiding explains the behavior observed. Second, it introduces areas where further theoretical and empirical work are needed to advance our understanding of how relational contracting works, thereby providing a roadmap for future research. The treatment throughout the essay is light, in an attempt to cover ground rather than drill down into discrete issues.
To assess the braiding thesis, the paper undertakes a circumscribed but illuminating exploration of a market with immense untapped opportunity: U.S. defense contracting. The U.S. government's acquisition of weapon systems is not only heavily outsourced but also technologically ambitious - a perfect combination for studying relational contracting. In particular, the paper studies a variation of braided contracting: The use of preliminary agreements in complex negotiations, here in the context of negotiations for the acquisition of advanced weapon systems. The question is simple: Do preliminary negotiations in defense contracting reflect the braiding thesis?
To provide some perspective, the paper first examines the available historical record relating to the negotiations for the development of theUSS Monitorduring the U.S. Civil War. TheMonitorwas a highly novel design that entailed a great deal of risk and a significant upfront investment - exactly the type of situation where precisely delineating the supplier's performance obligations would be impossible, and relational contracting would be necessary. The historical record is not substantial, but the first-hand account of one of the partners developing theMonitoris revealing. Negotiations were entirely informal, and personal relationships among U.S. Navy command and the partners developing the new vessel were key to securing each side's commitment. The negotiations for theMonitorare an example of classic relational contracting.
The paper then presents a far different arrangement known within the Department of Defense as "alpha contracting," which was introduced at the close of the 20th century. Modern sourcing negotiations typically follow an iterated process of arm's-length negotiations between the government and a prime contractor. The government defines the scope of the acquisition project with a statement of work and then builds a request for proposals based upon that statement. It then shares that request with multiple potential suppliers, who then formulate proposals in response. The government scrutinizes the proposals and selects a supplier, or small subset of suppliers, for final negotiations, and eventually an agreement is reached. It is a back-and-forth process where each side works alone.
Alpha contracting differs from that standard process by blending what were once arm's-length negotiations into a collaborative effort to develop the terms of the project. At the start, the government approaches a key supplier for the project, rather than sending the work out to bid. The government and supplier then jointly design the statement of work, the request for proposals, and the proposal itself. No longer are those elements developed in isolation. The teams designing those preliminary documents then negotiatethe final agreement. Overseeing this entire process is a formal committee structure, jointly staffed with representatives from the government and the prime contractor. Major decisions and disputes are escalated to a management level committee, which also has visibility over the engineering teams cooperating on the technical development of the weapon system. Publicly available Department of Defense studies analyzing alpha contracting conclude that the process builds trust between the government and the prime contractor teams as the structure leads them through the process of joint learning. In short, alpha contracting is the Department of Defense's version of braided preliminary agreements.
Alpha contracting is a particularly interesting example of the braiding thesis, because traditional informal sanctions are presumably readily available, but they are not relied upon. Alpha contracting is undertaken usually when the government single-sources a system, and frequently the prime contractor approached is one with a longstanding relationship with the government. That type of situation, where the two parties have had prior deals and, as a result, also have a strong expectation of future deals, is the sort of scenario where bilateral informal sanctions, such as the threat to cut a party off from future transactions, should have significant bite. That is theMonitorexample in a nutshell. Yet, in alpha contracting the parties erect an elaborate formal structure for their preliminary negotiations, lending support to the braiding thesis's claim that formality complements informality, rather than substituting for it.
The paper then shifts to the new possible frontiers for relational contract scholarship. It uses the braiding thesis as a starting point, focusing upon a natural follow-on question to the analysis discussed above: What is the scope of the braiding thesis? When is braiding used, and when is it not? GSS take an important first step towards answering that scoping question in an important subsequent paper,Text and Context: Contract Interpretation as Contract Design, which situates braiding within a broader non-unitary theory of contract law.That paper argues that braiding is one approach among many, and that a market's level of uncertainty and "thickness" will determine whether braiding or different contractual tools are used.The final section of this paper builds upon theText and Contextargument by introducing additional possible determinants, not just market uncertainty and scale, that may provide a more nuanced understanding of when parties' use braiding mechanisms. Two possibilities are introduced: Alternative types of exchange hazards affecting transactions and the differing topologies of transactional networks in industries. Exploring how these considerations may affect governance decisions is an important task for future research.

questions.question: Whether preliminary negotiations in complex procurement (e.g., defense) contracts rely on a blend of enforceable formal provisions and informal norms (a "braid") to govern interfirm collaboration and manage opportunism.

When and why parties choose braided contracting versus other governance forms - i.e., whether factors such as transaction uncertainty, market thickness, types of exchange hazards, and the topology of industry networks determine the use of braided mechanisms.
