papers.node_id: 42jlegalstud1!!ARTICLE: Conceptualizing Contractual Interpretation
papers.title: ARTICLE: Conceptualizing Contractual Interpretation
papers.abstract:
Contract interpretation has been an important subject in the law-school world for decades. There have been few law and economics analyses and very few formal economic treatments, however.This paper doesthree things. First, it creates a model to show how contract interpretation works when an ideal enforcer does it. Second, it characterizes how the optimal interpretive rule trades off the costs and benefits of different sources of information, including the contract itself. This analysis serves as a premise for understanding parties' and decision makers' actual interpretive practices and for making policy suggestions as to how to improve those practices. Third, the paper compares the ideal enforcer to real courts, which we characterize as driven by an accuracy objective.
Our ideal enforcer is ideal in two senses. (1) Motivation: the enforcer's goal is to maximize welfare, which is the expected value of commercial transactions over the set of contractual relationships. (2) Expertise: the enforcer can make the cost/benefit calculations that this maximization exercise requires. In the model, a population of matched sellers and buyers choose their contracts, and then the sellers make private sunk-cost investments that stochastically increase the buyers' values for a product or a service. Hence, our ideal enforcer interprets contracts to induce sellers to invest efficiently.
The interpretive process requires two tasks: creating an interpretive rule and adjudicating interpretive disputes.An interpretive rule can be effective at motivating the seller to invest only if it induces the following accuracy condition to hold with high probability: the seller is paid if she renders a compliant performance and is not paid otherwise. The enforcer, we assume, observes the seller's performance. The interpretive issue for him thus is to decide whether the parties wanted the seller to tender exactly the observed performance.
The parties' goal is to maximize surplus; thus, they want to maximize the likelihood that the accuracy condition is satisfied. To do this requires the parties to make trade-offs among three sets of costs: (1) the cost of writing the contract, which conveys information about their intent, (2) the cost of investing in performance, which (a) increases its value to the buyer and (b) increases the likelihood that the seller will be found to comply,and (3) the cost of a possible trial, which also reveals intent. Unconstrained parties will make these trade-offs in privately, but notnecessarily socially, optimal ways. An efficient interpretive rule induces welfare-maximizing trade-offs on these three margins.
To make this view of the interpretive process a little more transparent, we begin with an example. In the example, and in the model below, each contracting relationship is a particular type. The concept of type captures an intention: the performance that the contracting relationship intended to trade. A typet[i]relationship intends to trade a different thing--different goods or services--than a typet[j]relationship does. We assume that the seller must expend effort to ensure that the performance is compliant (the good or service is the intended one).
For illustrative purposes, let there be three party types, each of which intends to trade a grade of raw cotton that the buyer will make into cloth. There are seven cotton grades, ranging from grade 1 (Egyptian superfine) to grade 7 (Bulgarian). A typet[1] relationship intends to trade grade 1 cotton; the buyer in this relationship produces high-quality fabric for clothes sold in boutique stores. A typet[2] relationship intends to trade either grade 2 or grade 3 cotton; here the buyer produces fabric for moderately priced clothing, and either of these grades will do. A typet[3] relationship intends to trade grade 7 cotton: this buyer is making fabric for work clothes.
The enforcer observes the grade of cotton that the seller tenders.Assume first that the enforcer can recover the relationship type, and let the tendered grade be 4. The enforcer would then find that the seller breached, since no type intended to trade grade 4 cotton. Next assume that the seller tendered grade 2 cotton. The enforcer would find that the seller's performance was compliant only if the relationship was determined to be typet[2].
Suppose next that the enforcer cannot recover type perfectly; he makes a determination of the type, which is likely to be accurate but with some probability is inaccurate. He then can make an interpretive error. For example, the enforcer could observe a tender of grade 2 cotton and believe that the relationship is typet[2], when in fact the type ist[1]. Because the performance appears to match the type, the enforcer would then mistakenly order the buyer to pay. If such an outcome would occur with significant probability, then the seller's incentive to invest in effort would diminish.
In the common view, there is one interpretive task: to assign meaning to a contract's words when there is an interpretive dispute. This exampleis meant to suggest that the common view is not so much incorrect as too narrow. The adjudicative task is to identify contracting relationship types, and the parties' contract constitutes only one category of relevant evidence. There are three more. The performance the seller tendered is probative, more or less, of the performance the parties intended the seller to tender. The litigation documents--the complaint and answer, the exhibits--provide narratives from which type information may be extracted. Finally, trial evidence (testimony, documents), when permitted, also is probative of party type to some degree. In the model below, evidence in the four evidentiary categories are signals of party type. The enforcer's adjudicative task is to infer the litigation parties' type from these signals and then order the buyer to pay only if he believes that the seller's performance is compliant. A compliant performance, in turn, is the performance that is consistent with the parties' type, as the enforcer finds it.
An innovation of this paper is to analyze the rule-creation process and to show how an interpretive rule influences the parties' earlier choices. The rule's goal is to induce parties optimally to identify their types. A feature of the cotton example is that cotton has a wide variety of uses. Consider a different case. Let a particular rare-earth metal have only two industrial applications: in jet engines and in catalytic converters. In this case, the seller's performance--the type of rare-earth metal tendered--is highly probative of the parties' type. Tendering anything other than the particular rare-earth metal would be a breach for either the engine maker or the converter maker; tendering that rare-earth metal would be a compliant performance for both. An optimal interpretive rule would induce types that intend to trade the rare-earth metal at issue to write short contracts: a contract can describe either intended use concisely. In contrast, the relationship between a physical performance and a party type is less direct for cotton traders or, for example, oil traders (who deal with many types of oil with different uses). Hence, the optimal rule would induce cotton and oil traders either to write longer contracts or to rely on trial evidence, depending on whether it is more efficient to convey type in the writing or at a trial.
To summarize, the interpretive process includes, but is not constituted by, the job of attributing meaning to a contract's words. Rather, the process's task ex post is to recover a contracting relationship's type from the contract and other signals, and the task ex ante is to induce parties to take optimal actions both to create value and to facilitate accurate type identification.
We use this understanding of the interpretive process to analyze some significant interpretive practices. As examples, there is a strong, though not complete, congruence between the ideal enforcer's goal and the parties' goals: the ideal enforcer and the parties both prefer to satisfy the accuracy condition efficiently. This congruence implies that parties seldom would want to tell an enforcer how to interpret their contract and how to utilize evidence. If actual parties often attempt to tell actual enforcers what to do, then real-world interpretation may deviate in material ways from the ideal. As a second example, enforcement institutions differ in the nature of the expertise they bring to bear. We analyze the nature of interpretive expertise to better understand how parties choose enforcement institutions.
We also want to provide a basis for making interpretive policy. To illustrate, let courts and parties actually differ regarding how much and what types of evidence courts should consider when making interpretations. An analysis of ideal interpretation may illuminate whose preferences should prevail. We generate the following results.
Inefficiency with the Ideal Enforcer.The accuracy condition cannot be perfectly satisfied: the costs of reducing uncertainty regarding the parties' intentions to zero exceed the incentive gains. Because efficiency requires absolutely correct interpretations, even an ideal enforcer cannot induce first-best investment incentives. The effect of residual uncertainty cannot be eliminated by punishing probabilistically noncompliant performances, if penalties are not permitted as aids to contract enforcement.
Optimal Contracting.As suggested above, an optimal interpretive rule induces parties to choose efficient contracts. If, say, a particular set of contracting relationships can best indicate their intentions by writing extensive contracts, the rule will induce them to write these contracts rather than simple contracts and a reliance on trials to reveal intent. It follows that, under some conditions, the enforcer optimally restricts trial evidence. In addition, an optimal interpretive rule correctly induces some potential relationships not to form. The cost of conveying intent, for them, would exceed the investment efficiency gain.
Forms of Expertise.Expertise in interpretation comes in three forms: expertise in extracting meaning from words, expertise in inferring party intentions by applying industry knowledge to evaluate a seller's performance, and expertise in evaluating trial evidence.
Relation between Parameters.Institutional changes that lower contract-writing costs and changes that increase expertise in evaluating a tendered performance are complements; in contrast, changes that lower contract-writing costs and trial costs are substitutes. Regarding complements, a more extensive contract description better permits an enforcer to match the actual performance to the intended performance. Regarding substitutes, an extensive trial can make up for a sketchy contract. Illumination regarding the relationships among these variables of interest may facilitate legislative or administrative interventions to improve the efficiency of the interpretive process.
Accuracy and Bias.When the enforcer maximizes accuracy in interpretation rather than welfare over the population of contractual relationships, welfare is lower; parties' contracting choices are biased, often unexpectedly in the direction of writing more complicated contracts; and some contracting relationships inefficiently fail to form.
Real Courts.Many courts do attempt to maximize accuracy (see Pos-ner 2004), and actual parties commonly send interpretive instructions to them.These instructions almost invariably attempt to reduce the probability and cost of trials.Party instructions, if followed, thus would make courts function more as the ideal enforcer functions; hence, courts should obey them. Many courts today do not.
We conclude this Introduction with two remarks and a brief description of the literature. Recall that, in the common view, the interpretive task is to minimize the distance between the intention the interpreted words support and the parties' true intent. In our model, we invert this process. The enforcer treats the words as one of several signals that together support his inference of intent, an inference that is summarized in the enforcer's identification of the parties' probable type. Further, in the usual view, interpreters are not tasked with considering the cost of interpretive accuracy. In contrast, the enforcer, in his rule-making mode, induces parties, when pursuing their goal of identifying type to a latter adjudicator, to take optimally into account the costs of adjudication, contract writing, and party investment. We take a different view of theinterpretive process because we assume that the interpretive goal is to maximize welfare over a relevant set of contractual relationships. An interpretive rule realizes that goal, in our analysis, when it functions not so much to facilitate the finding of meaning as to maximize the cost-justified probability that sellers are rewarded only for performances that are consistent with type.
Second, the subject of interpretation is important. Contract theory models exclude interpretive issues by assumption. In these models, the parties either describe the subject of trade perfectly or do not describe it at all. Perfect descriptions need not be interpreted, and null descriptions cannot be interpreted. In the usual case, however, the court can observe the performance the seller tendered, and the parties' contract describes the subject of sale imperfectly. In these contexts, the court is not asked to decide whether a party verified a payoff-relevant variable. The court instead must find what the parties intended that variable to be, which is an interpretive question. Judge Richard Posner thus estimated that 80 percent of the contract cases that come before the Seventh Circuit involve interpretive issues.
Regarding the literature, our paper utilizes the same foundation as Shavell's (2006) model, whereby there is a population of contractual relationships with different types, contracting is costly, and contract selection partitions the space of relationship types and thus provides coarse information about type to the interpreter.We are also similarly focused on optimal interpretation to maximize social welfare. However, there are major differences between Shavell (2006) and this paper. First, there is no investment in Shavell's model, so the interpreter there is concerned only with ex post efficiency. In contrast, we analyze how the choice of interpretive practices can induce efficient investment, in which there are trade-offs between costs realized at different stages of productive relationships. Second, Shavell assumes that all terms have an exogenously defined literal meaning, and his results focus on demonstrating that it is sometimes optimal for the enforcer to depart from literal interpretation.We argue, in contrast, that context commonly isindispensable to interpretation when the interpreter's task is to induce efficient party behavior, and we determine the optimal interpretive rule absent exogenous constraints on the meaning of contract terms. Doing this allows us to explore the implications of court bias toward accuracy. It also allows us to provide results on trade-offs in various dimensions of evidence and expertise and on the optimal use of multiple enforcers.
Listokin (2010) considers a problem related to ours. He shows how a court that wants to maximize accuracy in interpretation would use Bayesian analysis to interpret contract terms. The enforcer in our model also does Bayesian updating, but our model differs in at least three significant respects from Listokin's. First, our enforcer maximizes welfare, not accuracy. Second, our enforcer interprets contracts in the service of inducing investment; there is no investment in Listokin's model. Third, a court cannot be a good Bayesian unless it has an informed prior. Listokin assumes that courts have such priors. In our model, the informativeness of the enforcer's prior is a facet of his expertise. This permits us to model the parties' choice of an enforcer.
Finally, Kvaloy and Olsen (2009) analyze a model with investment in which parties can affect the verifiability of payoff-relevant variables by the contracts they write and the investments themselves. This paper is illuminating regarding contract choice, but it assumes that values are deterministic and, importantly, that litigation is costless. The last assumption is limiting because the common question for parties, and for our enforcer, is when is it efficient to reveal their initial intentions in a costly contract or in a costly trial or in some combination of these?
Section 2 sets out the model, which Section 3 solves. Section 4 is a conclusion. Some details of our analysis and proofs of our technical results are in Appendix A. Appendix B contains an extension of our analysis to the case of multiple enforcers, which we hope might usefully serve as a bridge between our theory and future empirical work. A pilot study may be found in the working paper version of this paper (Schwartz and Watson 2012).

questions.question: What interpretive rule should an enforcer adopt to maximize social welfare by inducing sellers to make efficient sunk-cost investments and parties to choose optimal contract detail and litigation strategies, given that the enforcer infers parties' intended 'type' from multiple imperfect signals?

How do trade-offs among contract-writing costs, performance-investment costs, and trial (litigation) costs determine whether parties should convey intent in the contract or rely on trial evidence, and how should an interpreter optimally weight those evidence sources?

How does the enforcer's objective (welfare-maximizing versus accuracy-maximizing) and the enforcer's expertise in different evidentiary modes affect welfare outcomes, contract complexity, and the endogenous formation or non-formation of contracting relationships?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Filling Gaps in Incomplete Contracts: An Economic Theory of Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules should be designed to induce efficient ex ante behavior (contracting and investment)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how legal-design (defaults in Paper A; interpretive/enforcement rules in Paper B) should be chosen to change parties' pre-dispute actions — Paper A via penalty, tailored and untailored defaults that push parties to contract around undesirable defaults, and Paper B via interpretive rules that induce optimal contract-writing and seller investment.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and informational frictions as drivers of contractual incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with the role of drafting costs and asymmetric information in producing gaps: Paper A distinguishes transaction-cost and strategic (information withholding) sources of incompleteness, while Paper B models costs of writing, trial, and noisy signals (performance) that make contracts imperfectly informative about parties' intended 'type.'

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between ex ante contracting and ex post adjudication (court evidence rules and reliance on courts)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study the welfare trade-offs of shifting informative effort between parties and courts — Paper A asks when defaults should encourage ex ante contracting versus leave gap-filling to courts, and Paper B analyzes when interpretive rules should restrict or permit trial evidence and how contract-writing and litigation substitute or complement each other.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms to elicit private information and the resulting separating vs pooling equilibria
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze how legal rules affect information revelation: Paper A shows defaults (including penalty defaults) can produce separating or pooling equilibria among types of parties, and Paper B models multiple evidentiary signals (contract, performance, trial) and how rules influence whether parties reveal type through writing, performance, or litigation.

shared_topics.topic: choice of normative objective for interpreters/legislators (welfare maximization versus accuracy/paternalism/externalities)
shared_topics.justification: Both confront the appropriate objective of legal actors — Paper A weighs immutability and default choice against parentalistic or externality-based justifications and efficiency, while Paper B contrasts an ideal enforcer who maximizes welfare with real courts that often maximize accuracy, analyzing the different policy implications of each objective.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPLIED WARRANTIES V. EXPRESS SPECIFICATIONS UNDER THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE

shared_topics.topic: when and how express contractual specifications displace default (implied) obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys UCC case law and doctrinal tests about whether express specifications override implied warranties of merchantability and fitness, recommending the 'precise-and-complete' approach; Paper B models how an interpretive rule should treat the contract text as one signal of parties' intent and when the writing should be decisive versus supplemented by other evidence.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules and doctrines shape parties' contract-drafting and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that whether specifications control affects parties' exposure to implied warranty liability and thus influences drafting and product-design choices in complex supply chains; Paper B formally analyzes how different interpretive rules induce efficient trade-offs among contract-writing costs, performance investment, and litigation costs.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary role of performance and extra-textual signals in resolving contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how courts consider different kinds of specifications and surrounding facts in deciding whether express terms govern implied warranties; Paper B treats performance, litigation documents, trial evidence, and the contract itself as complementary signals that an enforcer must weigh to infer the parties' intended 'type.'

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation and normative design of judicial/interpretive frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques competing judicial analytical frameworks (e.g., 'precise-and-complete' vs. 'requires defect') and recommends a doctrinal rule, while Paper B develops a welfare-maximizing model of optimal interpretive rules and compares that ideal to actual courts that prioritize accuracy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88michlrev489!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.

shared_topics.topic: normative criteria for choosing interpretive/default contractual rules (welfare/efficiency vs fidelity/autonomy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models an ideal enforcer who selects interpretive rules to maximize social welfare and contrasts that with courts that aim at accuracy; Paper B surveys philosophical accounts (fidelity, autonomy) and economic efficiency, arguing that fidelity/autonomy do not by themselves determine which background rules the law should adopt and that efficiency is a competing justificatory standard.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape parties' ex ante contract drafting and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how an interpretive rule alters parties' choices over contract length, reliance on trial evidence, and sellers' sunk investment, showing rule design changes investment and relationship formation; Paper B treats background/default rules and waivability as central determinants of what obligations parties face and therefore as shaping how parties draft agreements and what terms they will accept or attempt to vary.

shared_topics.topic: the relation between contract text and extrinsic/contextual evidence in fixing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models contract words as one of multiple signals (contract text, performance, pleadings, trial evidence) and studies how an enforcer should weigh them to infer parties' intended type; Paper B emphasizes that background rules fill in details beyond explicit promises and questions whether philosophical theories of promising can dictate which extrinsic facts or implied terms should constitute the promisor's obligation.

shared_topics.topic: the proper design and scope of background/default rules (mandatory vs waivable rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is centrally concerned with whether background rules should be mandatory or merely default and what principles should govern that choice; Paper A engages this issue functionally by showing when an optimal interpretive rule will induce parties to write detailed contracts or rely on trials and when the enforcer should limit evidence or thereby effectively mandate certain information-revealing practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36houslrev1!!ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION

shared_topics.topic: tailoring contract rules and interpretive doctrines to fit commercial context (including information/digital transactions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that goods-based contract concepts and images misfit transactions in the information economy and calls for new lexicon and rules (e.g., Article 2B) to align law with digital/licensing practices; Paper B provides a formal framework showing how interpretive rules should be designed to induce efficient ex ante contracting and investment across different market contexts, a framework that applies when courts must adapt rules to nontraditional transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the failure of traditional categories/images and the need for new categorizations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses harms from applying legacy 'goods' images (title, risk-of-loss) to information and service contracts and urges new categories; Paper B centers analysis on 'types' and shows how misclassification or coarse legal categories (and imperfect inference about type) produce interpretive errors and misaligned incentives.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs among contract-writing costs, investment incentives, and evidentiary/adjudicative rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that information transactions involve different obligations and contract forms, so legal rules must account for how parties bargain and draft to allocate risk and quality obligations; Paper B formally models the trade-offs between the cost of writing detailed contracts, the seller's investment incentives, and the cost/role of trial evidence and shows how interpretive rules shape those trade-offs.

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim of contract doctrine (facilitating commerce/welfare versus accuracy/formal fidelity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a regime where contract law serves as background rules to facilitate freedom of contract and commercial practice in new markets; Paper B contrasts an ideal welfare-maximizing enforcer with courts that pursue accuracy, showing that prioritizing accuracy can bias contracting and reduce social welfare.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45arizstlj925!!ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years

shared_topics.topic: use of extrinsic, parol, and performance evidence to infer parties' intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the interpretive process as an enforcer inferring a contracting 'type' from multiple signals (the written contract, the seller's performance, litigation documents, and trial evidence); Paper B analyzes the doctrinal distinction between 'extrinsic evidence' and 'parol evidence' under the UCC and common law and how courts actually use those categories when deciding what external materials may inform meaning.

shared_topics.topic: how evidentiary/admissibility rules affect parties' contracting and litigation incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows formally how an interpretive rule that admits or restricts types of evidence changes parties' choices about how much to spend on drafting contracts, investment in performance, and pursuing trials; Paper B demonstrates that uncertainty and doctrinal confusion about admissibility under UCC §2-202 and related provisions can alter parties' expectations about what evidence will be considered and thus their behavior in negotiating, documenting, and litigating sales contracts.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of ambiguous contractual terms and ambiguity doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the adjudicative task as recovering intended meaning when contract descriptions are imperfect and analyzes optimal rules for resolving ambiguity to induce efficient investment; Paper B focuses on classic ambiguity disputes (e.g., Frigaliment's 'chicken') and compares how the parol-evidence rule and UCC provisions govern the resolution of ambiguous or contested term meanings.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts' interpretive objectives and institutional expertise in shaping outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts an ideal, welfare-maximizing enforcer with courts that prioritize accuracy and highlights different forms of interpretive expertise (text, performance, trial evidence) and their welfare implications; Paper B critiques how actual courts and judges apply (or misapply) UCC terminology and rules, implicating judicial practices, expertise, and institutional choice in the resulting interpretive outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29urichlrev1471!!ARTICLE: QUANTIFYING LIABILITY UNDER THE ARCHITECT'S STANDARD OF CARE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: QUANTIFYING LIABILITY UNDER THE ARCHITECT'S STANDARD OF CARE

shared_topics.topic: how legal standards for assessing performance (interpretive rules vs professional standard of care) shape parties' contracting and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how an enforcer's interpretive rule influences parties' choices about contract detail and sunk investment to induce efficient performance, while Paper B criticizes how the architect's standard of care and resulting liability allocation distort the economic balance among contracting parties and the incentives borne by design professionals.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of litigation and litigation costs as information-revealing mechanisms that influence behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats trial costs and trial evidence as deliberate means for parties to reveal intent and as a factor in optimal contract design, and Paper B highlights the costs of defending claims and insurers absorbing errors/omissions liability, implying that litigation dynamics affect how claims are pursued and how parties bear risk.

shared_topics.topic: the role of domain expertise and fact-finding in assigning liability or meaning to performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes types of interpretive expertise (textual interpretation, industry knowledge applied to observed performance, and evaluation of trial evidence) as crucial to accurate and welfare-maximizing enforcement; Paper B centers on assessing architectural errors against a professional standard of care, which similarly requires industry-specific factual and technical judgment to allocate liability properly.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and welfare implications of legal rules governing liability and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a welfare-maximizing ideal enforcer with accuracy-focused courts and analyzes welfare losses from biased interpretive practices, while Paper B argues current treatment of design claims yields a distorted allocation of liability that is not justified by contractual arrangements or the economic balance of projects, suggesting inefficiencies in existing legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj335!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity

shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses UCC §2‑209 (modification and waiver) as a case study showing that vague statutory drafting produces judicial confusion, advisory difficulty, and commercial chaos; Paper B models how interpretive uncertainty reduces welfare by distorting parties' contracting and investment choices and raising adjudication costs.

shared_topics.topic: how rule design (statutory drafting or interpretive rules) should be structured to induce efficient contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the drafting strategy that produced §2‑209 and offers suggestions for how drafters should (or should not) draft to avoid obfuscation; Paper B formally characterizes optimal interpretive rules that induce parties to choose efficient contract length, investment, and reliance on trials.

shared_topics.topic: the role and objectives of enforcers/courts (accuracy versus welfare) in shaping incentives and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that judges' inability to apply an unclear provision undermines enforcement, while Paper B contrasts an ideal enforcer who maximizes welfare with real courts that often maximize accuracy, showing how those differing objectives bias parties' contract choices and affect social welfare.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs among contract-writing costs, performance/investment costs, and litigation costs as drivers of contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how an unclear legal provision drives practical trade-offs (e.g., when to rely on modifications, waivers, or litigation) in commercial practice; Paper B models these same margins formally, showing how interpretive rules alter the optimal balance between spending on detailed drafting, investing in performance, or revealing intent through trials.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: the normative tradeoff between formal/plain-meaning rules and contextual interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models an ideal enforcer who chooses interpretive rules to maximize welfare and contrasts that welfare-maximizing rule with courts that pursue accuracy, while Paper B analyzes and critiques recent neoformalist calls for sharper/plain-meaning rules and argues such formalism is empirically and normatively problematic in the real world of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: which evidentiary sources courts should consider (text, performance, trade usage/course of performance, trial evidence) and their relative weight
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the contract text, the seller's performance, litigation documents, and trial evidence as distinct probabilistic signals of parties' ‘type’ and studies how a rule should trade off those signals; Paper B focuses on debates over reducing or preserving the roles of trade usage and course of performance under Article 2 and the practical consequences of privileging or excluding certain evidence.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules shape parties' ex ante behavior — contract drafting, costly investments, and reliance on litigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models how interpretive rules induce parties to choose contract length, investment effort, and whether to rely on trials, showing welfare effects from those incentives; Paper B discusses how shifts toward formalism would change how real-world businesses and lawyers draft and use form contracts and the costs this would impose.

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the choice of enforcement mechanism (courts' expertise, legislative reform, and policy implications for the U.C.C.)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes different forms of interpretive expertise and how institutional features (expertise, trial costs) interact with optimal rules, while Paper B assesses the feasibility and likely adverse consequences of legislating greater formalism into Article 2 of the U.C.C., stressing institutional fit and empirical foundations for reform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69uchilrev917!!SYMPOSIUM: MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF THE MODERN BUSINESS CORPORATION: EXECUTIVE COMPENSATION & TAKEOVERS: Designing Mechanisms to Govern Takeover Defenses: Private Contracting, Legal Intervention, and Unforeseen Contingencies
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF THE MODERN BUSINESS CORPORATION: EXECUTIVE COMPENSATION & TAKEOVERS: Designing Mechanisms to Govern Takeover Defenses: Private Contracting, Legal Intervention, and Unforeseen Contingencies

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that shareholders cannot costlessly write contracts to forbid all possible antitakeover devices because of unforeseeable actions and unverifiability of what counts as an antitakeover measure; Paper B analyzes residual uncertainty and noisy signals of 'type' (unverifiability) and shows such informational limits prevent perfect ex ante contracting and optimal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how legal standards and interpretive doctrines affect welfare, transaction structure, and which relationships form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses whether Delaware's reduced scrutiny ('just say no') harms shareholder welfare and may prevent desirable contractual constraints on boards, while Paper B shows interpretive rules influence contract complexity, reliance on trials, investment incentives, and can cause some contracting relationships to form or fail—with direct welfare consequences.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the parol evidence rule and the doctrinal confusion over when and how courts may consider evidence beyond the written text; Paper B models contract interpretation as an inference problem in which the contract is one of several signals (performance, pleadings, trial evidence) and studies when an optimal rule should restrict or permit such evidence.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules alter parties' drafting and investment incentives and affect transactional efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that ambiguous or inconsistent interpretive doctrines impose drafting costs, increase litigation, and create inefficiencies for contracting parties; Paper B formalizes those incentives, showing how an interpretive rule trades off contract-writing costs, investment effort, and trial costs to induce efficient ex ante behavior.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps and critiques textualist and contextualist approaches—including the ambiguity-determination stage and how contextualism may eliminate it—while Paper B argues that words are only one signal among many and that contextual information is often indispensable for an optimal interpretive rule.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A constructs a taxonomy of interpretive disputes and analyzes which questions are proper law (judge) versus fact (jury), whereas Paper B compares an ideal welfare-maximizing enforcer to real courts (accuracy-maximizers), analyzes forms of interpretive expertise, and examines implications of different enforcement institutions.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: INTERPRETING STALE PREFERENTIAL RIGHTS TO ACQUIRE REAL ESTATE: BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT OF PROPERTY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models interpretation as an inferential task of recovering parties' 'type' when contractual descriptions are imperfect, while Paper B confronts long‑standing preferential purchase rights whose express terms fail to anticipate changed future circumstances and advocates judicial gap‑filling; both directly address how to resolve contractual incompleteness over time.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules shape parties' ex ante contracting and investment choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A formalizes how rules about admissible evidence and interpretation change parties' incentives to write detailed contracts, invest in performance, or rely on trials; Paper B examines the practical costs and risks of long‑term preferential rights and stresses that drafting choices (or lack thereof) determine future disputes, recommending structuring agreements and doctrines that influence parties' ex ante behavior.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats contracts, tendered performance, litigation documents, and trial evidence as multiple signals and emphasizes different kinds of interpretive expertise, while Paper B urges courts to weigh contextual factors (including passage of time and changed circumstances) rather than rely solely on formal property rules, so both engage with what evidence and expertise courts should use when interpreting contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that collaborative technologies like BIM push construction participants toward intentionally relational contracts and integrated project delivery instead of exhaustive, contingency-filled agreements; Paper B formally models the same trade-off by showing how contract-writing costs, investment incentives, and trial costs determine whether parties write long, precise contracts or rely on other mechanisms to handle uncertainty and induce effort.

shared_topics.topic: how information, observability, and shared data affect enforcement, interpretation, and the feasibility of collaborative contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that BIM's shared digital models and real‑time information make parties more interdependent and facilitate cooperative governance; Paper B analyzes how signals—contract language, the observed performance, litigation documents, and trial evidence—inform an enforcer's inference about parties' intent and thus affect interpretive accuracy and incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the design of rules, clauses, or interpretive regimes to induce efficient investment and cooperative behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how intentionally relational contracts and integrated delivery structures can align incentives, share risk, and encourage the specialized investments required by BIM collaborations; Paper B studies how an ideal interpretive rule (and the choice of admissible evidence) can be set to induce sellers to make welfare-maximizing sunk investments and to reveal their 'type' efficiently.

shared_topics.topic: the role of institutional choice and expertise (contract drafters, enforcers, dispute-resolution processes) in governing complex, interdependent projects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights new contractual forms and practitioner roles (e.g., lawyers translating business concepts into relational contract terms) and delivery models for BIM projects; Paper B examines how different forms of interpretive expertise and different enforcement institutions affect interpretive outcomes, parties' contracting choices, and overall welfare.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55wmmarylrev1869!!ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING

shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how parties choose among costly ex ante specification, relying on courts ex post, or using alternative mechanisms during performance — Paper A introduces and documents 'ex tempore' (dispute boards, ISDA committees) as a third option to complete incomplete contracts in real time, while Paper B models how an optimal interpretive rule shapes parties' decisions about how much to write versus rely on adjudication given costs of writing, trials, and investment.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and defends the use of non-judicial, industry-based decisionmakers (dispute boards, ISDA committees) to specify obligations in the moment, and Paper B analyzes how parties choose among enforcers with different expertise and objectives (ideal welfare-maximizer vs accuracy-driven courts), showing how institutional choice affects interpretive outcomes and welfare.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive regimes affect parties' investment and performance incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study how the way contracts will be interpreted changes parties' ex ante behavior: Paper B formally shows that interpretive rules must induce efficient seller investment by making compliance errors costly, and Paper A argues that ex tempore mechanisms provide timely clarity that improves performance incentives and reduces costly disputes in industries like construction and derivatives.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary bases and expertise required for accurate and efficient contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B models interpretation as inference from multiple signals (contract text, tendered performance, pleadings, trial evidence) and classifies forms of interpretive expertise, while Paper A highlights how ex tempore agents bring industry-specific expertise and how courts' misunderstandings of those evidentiary/expertise roles can undermine parties' chosen contracting mechanisms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93scallrev1323!!ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A formalizes an ideal enforcer who maximizes welfare across contractual relationships and contrasts that objective with real courts that pursue accuracy; Paper B critiques courts' reliance on ex post equitable doctrines and argues contract law should vindicate ex ante personal sovereignty rather than second-guess bargains for perceived fairness.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how interpretive rules influence parties' trade-offs among contract-writing costs, performance investments, and trial costs and thereby affect efficient investments; Paper B shows that penalty, forfeiture, and just-compensation doctrines distort parties' preferred contracting strategies (e.g., liquidated-damages clauses) and push them toward less effective means.

shared_topics.topic: the role and competence of institutional interpreters (courts or other enforcers) and historical/institutional explanations for doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes different forms of interpretive expertise (textual, industry-performance, trial-evidence) and how institutional characteristics affect optimal rules and enforcer choice; Paper B locates ex post equitable doctrines in the historical role of courts of equity and criticizes modern judicial practice for misapplying institutional history and judicial discretion.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules shape parties' ex ante contracting and investment choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how an interpretive rule influences parties' choices about contract length, reliance on trials, and sellers' sunk investments to induce efficient behavior; Paper B discusses how the UNIDROIT Principles and Danish doctrine (e.g., the General Clause) affect drafting of standard terms, incorporation practices, and parties' contractual strategies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models multiple evidentiary signals—written contract, the performance tendered, litigation documents, and trial evidence—and studies their relative informativeness; Paper B examines incorporation, trade usages/lex mercatoria, prior communications, and international restatements (UNIDROIT) as sources courts use to interpret, fill gaps, or reject surprising standard terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts an accuracy-focused court with an ideal enforcer who trades off accuracy against welfare and shows accuracy-driven interpretation can reduce welfare and distort contracting; Paper B explores limits on pacta sunt servanda (surprising terms, unfair exemptions, hardship) and Danish courts' use of reasonableness (General Clause) versus strict enforcement, including concerns about overuse of gap-filling rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF HOLMES'S THEORY OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A's critique of Holmes addresses how a theory of contract influences parties' expectations and the functioning of contract law, and Paper B analyzes how specific interpretive rules shape ex ante actions—contract drafting, investment in performance, and the decision whether a relationship forms—by altering parties' incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38sandiegolrev13!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Placid, Clear-Seeming Words: Some Realism About the New Formalism (with Particular Reference to Promissory Estoppel)

papers.title: ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages
papers.abstract: Bargains are central to the law of contracts, and the expectation measure is central to bargains. However, that measure, although apparently simple - put the promisee in the position he would have been in if the contract had been performed - raises a number of puzzles that have not been solved to the satisfaction of the profession.The expectation measure is seldom applied directly. Instead, a number of more specific formulas mediate between the expectation measure, on the one hand, and recurring scenarios of breach, such as breach by a buyer or a seller of goods, on the other. Often, two or even three different expectation-based formulas can be applied in a given type of case, and more often than not, these formulas produce drastically conflicting results. Moreover, there are no universally accepted principles that determine which formula to apply in the case of such conflicts. The purpose of this Article is to develop and clarify the various formulas that can be used to apply the expectation measure in recurring types of cases, and to develop the principles that should determine which formula should be applied when the formulas conflict. Part I introduces the basic building blocks of expectation-damages formulas. Parts II and III analyze the standard formulas that apply to breach of contracts for services and goods. Part IV considers two important scenarios of breach in which the standard formulas are inappropriate.

questions.question: Which of the competing expectation-based calculation formulas yields the appropriate measure of expectation damages in common types of contract breach?
What principles or criteria should determine which expectation-damages formula to apply when multiple expectation-based formulas conflict?
In which breach scenarios are the standard expectation-damages formulas inappropriate, and what alternative measures should be used instead?
