shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how courts invoke 'common sense' to smuggle normative expectations into doctrinal rules about formation and notice; Paper B interrogates the normative commitments (honor, obligation, moral philosophy) that actually guide dealmaking and criticizes pragmatic skepticism that excludes moral reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: whether formal assent and doctrinal rules adequately capture how parties manage uncertainty/contingency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions judicial reliance on presumptions about parties' assent (e.g., accept-or-return clauses) rather than investigating actual agreement or informational context; Paper B treats contracts as one of several real-world mechanisms (alongside trust, leadership, and norms) for coping with contingency and asks whether formal contract doctrine is adequate for that task.

shared_topics.topic: the need for interdisciplinary approaches to model and understand real-world contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges incorporation of nonlegal disciplines and empirical work to produce more accurate behavioral models for contract law; Paper B likewise advocates bringing philosophy (pragmatism, Kant, Hume) and empirical social science into legal thinking about contingency and complex commercial transactions.

papers.node_id: 113yalelj1417!!ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration
papers.abstract:
Promises lie at the center of persons' moral experience of one another, and contracts lie at the center of their legal experience of one another. Many of the most important relationships in our moral and legal culture characteristically arise in connection with promises and contracts of some form or other: Persons' families are connected to marriage promises, their work is connected to employment contracts, and even their citizenship is connected (albeit metaphorically) to the social contract. In all these cases, and in myriad others, promises and contracts establish relations among the persons who engage them.
But in spite of the obviously communal character of promise and contract, the most prominent accounts of these practices remain firmly individualistic, seeking to explain the obligations they involve in terms of one or another service that these practices render to the several parties who engage them. Some theories emphasize that promissory and contractual obligations increase the freedom of promisors, by enabling them to project their intentions into the future and rendering plans of action that require such precommitments available to them.Other theories emphasize that promissory and contractual obligations reflect concern for the reasonable expectations of promisees and the harms that promisees suffer when these expectations are disappointed.And, most prominently, yet other theories emphasize that promissory and contractual obligations promote the well-being of both promisees and promisors, by increasing the reliability of social coordination and promoting the efficient allocation of resources.These theories differ from one another in many ways, to be sure, and they often cast themselves as competitors. But they are of a piece insofar as they all seek the roots of the morality of promise and contract in properties of the several individual participants in such agreements.
do not doubt that the individualistic values from which these theories begin can give rise to reasons for action and indeed to moral obligations. I insist, however, that individualistic theories do not capture or reflect the distinctive moral center of promise and contract, which cannot be found inany properties of the parties taken severally but appears instead in the relations among persons that promises and contracts create. I develop the insight that promise and contract establish relations among the persons who engage them into a mature theory of promise and especially of contract, in which I describe the relations among persons that promises and especially contracts establish, and I characterize these relations in terms of familiar and attractive moral and political values. I claim that promises generally, and contracts in particular, establish a relation of recognition and respect - and indeed a kind of community - among those who participate in them, and I explain the reasons that exist for making and for keeping promises and contracts in terms of the value of this relation.
Moreover, I argue that contract participates in this ideal of respectful community even though contracts typically arise among self-interested parties who aim to appropriate as much of the value that contracts create as they can. Respectful community, as I understand it, is a capacious ideal, which encompasses many forms of joint endeavor, including contract. The centerpiece of my approach to the morality of contract is an argument that finds the value of community directly in the form of the contract relation rather than in any substantive ends that the parties to contracts pursue. I present a detailed account of the characteristic relations that this form of community, which I call collaboration, involves.
Finally, because my ultimate purpose is to develop a theory of contract law, I show that the contract relation as I characterize it is no mere academic conceit but is instead immanent in our legal practice. In particular, I consider two familiar doctrinal puzzles presented by the law of contracts - involving the consideration doctrine and the expectation remedy - in light of the values that I claim lie beneath the contract relation.I argue that the general theory of contractual obligation I am proposing underwrites a more satisfactory account of these doctrines than has so far been possible.
seek, then, to reclaim for practical philosophy the communal character that is the essence of both the obligations and the lived experience of promise and contract, and that the dominant, individualistic accounts obscure. Furthermore, instead of deriving the morality of promise and contract from more general and more fundamental moral principles (of freedom, harm, or welfare), I understand promise and contract as presenting distinctive and freestanding moral ideals. These ideals, moreover, radiate outwards from promise and contract, to illuminate aspects of practical life that lie beyond the narrow confines of these practices. I propose, at the end of the argument, that the collaborative ideal I find in the contract relation represents a crucial foundation stone for the authority of modern, pluralist economic and political institutions. In addition to developing a legal theory of contract, these pages therefore also contribute to the political theory of the market, and indeed of liberalism.
At the same time, the theory that I develop remains humble in other important ways, and it pays to identify these before commencing with the argument, in order to avoid appearing to claim more than I do. I do not deny that a wide array of moral obligations arise in and around promise and contract or that many of these obligations may be illuminated by reference to the ideas of freedom, harm, and welfare that figure so prominently in the familiar theories of contract that I seek to supplant.I deny only that these obligations are of a piece with promise and contract, and that these familiar explanations capture the characteristic moral and legal core of promise and contract. Moreover, I focus my attention on contracts among individual, natural persons. I take these cases to represent the core of contract and content myself to address contracts that involve organizations in a derivative fashion only.Each of these restrictions is intimately connected to my broader ambitions. A theory that understands contract as a distinctive and freestanding fount of moral obligation will naturally distinguish between contract proper and various associated forms of obligation; and a theory that seeks to connect contract to the basic structure of liberal political authority will naturally emphasize the individual persons to whom political justifications must be addressed.

questions.question: Are the moral and legal reasons to make and keep promises and contracts best explained by individual-centered goods (e.g., enhanced freedom, protection of expectations, or welfare/efficiency) or by a distinctive relational value-recognition, respect, and collaborative community-that the agreements create among the parties?
Does a relational/collaborative account of contract provide a better normative grounding and explanatory fit for contractual legal rules and remedies than competing individualistic accounts?
Can contractual relations legitimately instantiate a form of respectful community that grounds the authority of market and liberal political institutions even when the parties are self-interested?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of contract law — efficiency versus relational/communal values
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates legal rules (defaults vs immutables) primarily through an efficiency lens (gains from trade, transaction costs, bargaining inefficiencies) while Paper B develops a competing normative account that grounds contractual obligation in relations of recognition, respect, and collaboration; both thus engage the question of what values contract law should serve and how doctrinal design tracks those values.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules (defaults vs mandatory rules) shape private contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how the choice of default rules and the costs of contracting around them affect what contracts parties actually form and the resulting social welfare, and Paper B treats doctrines (like consideration requirements and remedies) as legal structures that instantiate and shape the contract relation; both analyze the law’s role in structuring the parties’ agreements rather than treating contracts as purely private.

shared_topics.topic: remedies and gap–filling (expectation damages, excuse doctrines, Hadley-type rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how courts fill obligational gaps via damage rules and excuse doctrines (e.g., awarding zero damages under impossibility) and analyzes Hadley v. Baxendale as a paradigmatic default; Paper B explicitly engages the expectation remedy (and consideration) as doctrinal puzzles and seeks to explain them in light of the contract relation, so both papers focus on why and how remedies and default gap‑filling doctrines operate.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as mechanisms of coordination/collaboration that enable gains from trade
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats contracts as tools to realize gains from trade and studies how contingent completeness and state‑contingent terms affect renegotiation and efficiency, while Paper B characterizes contracts as relations of collaboration and joint endeavor that create and sustain social coordination; both therefore analyze contracts’ role in enabling cooperative interaction among parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1joflegalanalysis207!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate remedy when a contract is disrupted (expectation vs reliance and modified damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly engages the expectation remedy as a doctrinal puzzle its relational theory must explain, while Paper B develops detailed rules about when promissors should be liable for expectation damages, reliance damages, or a modified expectation measure in unexpected-circumstances cases.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' expectations and tacit assumptions in determining contractual obligations and relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats reasonable expectations as a central theme of individualistic accounts of promise and contract, which it contrasts with a relational account, and Paper B builds its shared-assumption test around the idea that tacit (shared) assumptions at formation determine when judicial relief is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law should allocate or reallocate risk between parties when unforeseen events occur
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how parties to contracts pursue and appropriate value and how doctrines should reflect the contractual relation rather than solely individual interests, and Paper B confronts risk allocation directly (risk-shifting, bounded-risk test, rejection of 'cheapest insurer' rule) in prescribing when courts should excuse or adjust performance.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract doctrine should be grounded in narrow economic/individualistic principles or broader normative values
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contracts rest on a distinctive, relational ideal of recognition, respect, and collaboration rather than only freedom, harm, or welfare, and Paper B rejects single-stranded, purely ex ante/economic tests (like cheapest-insurer reasoning), arguing for a richer set of principles that include methodological, psychological, and equitable considerations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99yalelj87!!ARTICLE: Filling Gaps in Incomplete Contracts: An Economic Theory of Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Filling Gaps in Incomplete Contracts: An Economic Theory of Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: when and why the law should impose mandatory (immutable) contract rules rather than preserving freedom to contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic taxonomy (parentalism vs externalities) for when rules should be immutable and displace private ordering, and analyzes costs/benefits of immutability; Paper B offers a normative account (contracts as relations of recognition/respect) that can justify legal constraints on bargaining beyond individualistic efficiency reasons.

shared_topics.topic: design of default rules and courts' gap‑filling versus inferring parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with how courts and legislatures should fill gaps—tailored vs untailored defaults, penalty defaults to induce ex ante contracting, and what suffices to 'contract around' a default; Paper B engages the question of how legal doctrine should interpret incomplete agreements by arguing that contract law doctrines embody a relational ideal that should inform judicial gap‑filling and interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory grounding of specific contract doctrines (e.g., consideration and expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights doctrines like consideration as effectively immutable background rules and discusses remedial approaches (e.g., diminution in value) in gap contexts; Paper B analyzes the consideration doctrine and the expectation remedy through its relational/collaborative theory and argues that these doctrines are best understood against the moral value of the contract relation.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as mechanisms for coordination/collaboration and the implications for legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contracting as an activity shaped by transaction costs and information asymmetries, using default design to foster separating/pooling equilibria and efficient coordination; Paper B treats contracts as forms of collaboration and communal recognition, drawing implications for how law should regulate and support cooperative relations among parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53wakeforestlrev1!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE

shared_topics.topic: how promises and contracts shape individual agency and autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how promises and especially contracts reconfigure the moral positions of parties (enabling plans and self-binding) but locates the core value in the relations contracts create; Paper B treats promises and contracts as 'normative powers' that author our moral world, emphasizing both their autonomy-enhancing role and the need to accommodate persistent agency and revision.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of individualistic or instrumental explanations for contractual obligation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that familiar individualistic justifications (freedom/precommitment, expectation protection, welfare/efficiency) fail to capture the distinctive, relational moral core of contract; Paper B similarly questions the prevailing view that self-binding is unambiguously autonomy-enhancing, showing that instrumental accounts overlook the costs of constraining evolving agents.

shared_topics.topic: how moral theory about promise/contract should inform contract law doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses doctrinal puzzles (e.g., consideration, expectation remedy) to show that a relational/collaborative account better fits existing law; Paper B surveys and defends legal doctrines that treat contracts more leniently than moral promises, arguing law should accommodate change of mind and persistent agency.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between the value of commitment and the value of revising commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents contract as fostering a relation of respect and collaborative community that grounds reasons to commit and keep promises; Paper B foregrounds the moral importance of revision (fickleness/persistent agency) and explores how institutions (especially contract law) should balance commitment's stabilizing moral role against agents' legitimate reasons to change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81uchilrev53!!SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an account of why promises and contracts give rise to moral and legal obligations (arguing for a relational/communal grounding rather than individualistic accounts), and Paper B asks what normative foundations (efficiency/incentives versus alternatives like strict liability) justify tort rules such as negligence, treating competing justificatory frameworks explicitly.

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectations and information in assigning responsibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically engages with theories that ground promissory and contractual duties in the reasonable expectations of promisees, while Paper B analyzes how parties' information and expectations affect the efficiency and appropriateness of negligence versus strict liability rules and shows that incomplete information can undermine rules that work in other contexts.

shared_topics.topic: using theoretical frameworks to explain and evaluate specific legal doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a philosophical theory of the contract relation to illuminate doctrinal puzzles (e.g., consideration doctrine and expectation remedies), and Paper B develops a formal decision-theoretic/economic framework (Savage Tables and general equilibrium models) to explain and evaluate tort doctrines like the Hand negligence formula, strict liability, and causation.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape interpersonal behavior and coordination
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promises and contracts as practices that create relations of recognition, respect, and collaboration among participants, while Paper B studies how tort and liability rules create incentives that affect individuals' precautionary choices and the broader patterns of social coordination.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: what counts as 'contract' / the proper definition of the contractual domain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly debates rival canonical definitions (residualist vs imperialist) and proposes a working definition based on whether parties can privately reorder a substantial portion of their legal relations; Paper B likewise takes up the definitional question by rejecting individualistic accounts and offering a substantive, relational account of what contract is (a form of collaboration), thereby reshaping which practices should be treated as contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal significance of doctrines like consideration and expectation remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes traditional doctrinal markers (e.g., the consideration requirement) as part of discussions about whether an area is 'contractual' and how courts deploy such tests; Paper B directly analyzes the consideration doctrine and the expectation remedy, arguing these doctrines are best understood in light of the contract relation and its moral values.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for enforcing and structuring contract law (why and how to justify defaults or mandatory rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds consequentialist and policy questions—asking which rules should be mandatory vs. defaults, which defaults to choose, and when parties should be allowed to contract around rules; Paper B develops a moral-philosophical foundation (contract as recognition/collaboration) that bears on when promises and agreements ought to be enforceable and how law should treat contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between private ordering/autonomy and limits on contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its definition on parties' capacity to privately reorder legal relations and stresses evaluating the consequences of allowing such reordering; Paper B treats contracts as products of self-interested parties forming collaborative relations and addresses the justificatory limits of legal enforcement of those private bargains, engaging the same issue of how much freedom contracting parties should have.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 115yalelj814!!ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design

shared_topics.topic: normative grounding of contractual obligations beyond narrow individualistic accounts

papers.node_id: 88nyulrev170!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
papers.authors: Ronald J. Gilson; Charles F. Sabel; Robert E. Scott
papers.abstract:
Contract is broadly regarded as a cohesive body of law precise enough to facilitate transactions across very different domains, yet open and flexible enough to accommodate and eventually discipline substantial variations and changes in commercial practice without sacrificing its cohesion. There is disagreement as to whether contract achieves these ends best when judges most fully respect the autonomy of the parties and decide disputes principally by reference to the formal agreements that the parties enter, or when judges are instead free to go beyond the terms of the contract and inquire into the context of the parties' dealings, and decide disputes with reference to the parties' practices and informal understandings.But there is littledisagreement that contract law, as developed by generalist judges, approximates the ideal image of the common law as a highly decentralized and sensitive institution for responding incrementally to incipient changes in the parties' relations. Thus, common law courts are generally believed to be fully capable of extending the reach of existing legal principles to emergent forms of agreement without undermining the security of actors who continue to rely on traditional doctrine.
In our view, this familiar picture mischaracterizes the ways in which generalist courts do, and do not, effectively support innovation in contract law. The goal of this Article is to replace this common but erroneous picture with a more accurate one. We argue first and most fundamentally that contractual innovation does not come to courts incrementally - as where innovation is shaped gradually through iterative exchanges between contracting parties and the courts - but instead reaches the courts later in the innovation's evolution and more fully developed than the standard picture contemplates. Highly stylized, the trajectory of innovation in contract we find is this: Private actors respond to exogenous shocks in their economic environments by changing existing structures or procedures to make them efficient under the new circumstances. The innovating parties stabilize their newly emergent practices through a variety of regimes, both bilateral and multilateral, with the goal of establishing the context through which the innovation is implemented. It is only at this point, and when a dispute is presented to them, that courts step in.
As we develop here, the nature of these "contextualizing regimes,"and hence the courts' function and the allocation of responsibility between courts and alternative interpretive institutions, depends on two characteristics of the economic market in which the innovating parties participate: the thickness or scale of that market, as measured by the number of actors who understand themselves to be transacting under similar circumstances,and the uncertainty associated with that market.Across the four principal regions of space defined by these two dimensions - low and high levels both of scaleand uncertainty - courts must follow the instructions of the contracting parties as to how their contract is to be adapted to its particular context. In each case, the role of generalist courts - the nonspecialized workhorses of formal dispute resolution - is more restricted than in the standard account, as much of the interpretation of context will already have been established by other institutions including by the parties themselves. Thus, in responding to contract innovation driven by changes in the contracting parties' business environment, courts must practice the passive virtues: The parties, not the courts, drive innovation. Nonetheless, a court's approach to an innovative contract can support or undermine the innovation - the court can be either a friction or a facilitator.
In practice, the respect for party autonomy that we urge is under threat from two directions. First, courts can - through inertia or jurisprudential conviction - apply what they take to be standard default rules of the common law of contract in disregard of the parties' explicit understanding to the contrary (often elaborated jointly with trade associations and regulators).Second, contemporary courts can reinterpret or disregard the parties' agreement in favor of the judges' understanding of the context of their dealings. Common law courts were traditionally reluctant to incorporate informal understandings and practices in the course of resolving commercial disputes, relying instead on the maxim that "the courts do not make a contract for the parties."However, the adoption of the Uniform Commercial Code presaged the triumph in many areas of contract law of a new activist approach.The Code's incorporation doctrine is the standard bearer for the activist judicial role in the development of new forms of agreement; it explicitly commits the courts to aid in the continued expansion of commercial practices so that the law can be developed "by thecourts in the light of … new circumstances and practices."This commitment to the incorporation of inchoate contractual understandings through the agency of generalist courts is deeply embedded in contemporary contract law and forms the foundation for the standard account of the role of courts in the development of contract.
Our argument, in contrast, is that sophisticated parties better understand the subtleties of their context and better grasp the implications of the applicability vel non of the standard rules of contract law to the support of their dealings than do even the most acute generalist courts.Courts facilitate innovation in contract most directly by recognizing these limits and giving effect to the regimes that the parties have created to take account of their context and its interaction with the law of contract.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I frames the taxonomy of contract innovation: the multi-dimensional space on which we build our account of the relationship between generalist courts, contextualizing regimes, and contract innovation. Part II develops the general argument of the relation between contractual innovation and contextualizing regimes with regard to bilateral contracts and the role of uncertainty. We stress two exemplars: first, the emergence of collaborative contracting in global supply chains, platform production, and project development that has figured prominently in recent years, and second, the use of preliminary agreements as a means to investigate whether to pursue a business opportunity with a partner. Part III discusses multilateral contextualizing regimes involving institu-tions beyond the particular contracting parties, ranging from tradeassociations in the cotton industry to the Delaware Court of Chancery in complex corporate disputes. We situate these regimes by mapping them against the combination of the two central characteristics of the environment in which each arises: the level of uncertainty concerning the activities that are covered, and the thickness of the market for those activities - whether there are many or few participants facing similar circumstances.
We conclude by summarizing the relation between the character of the contextualizing regime and the uncertainty and scale associated with the relevant market. In the end, the message is straightforward: To facilitate innovation, courts must pay increased attention to the role the contracting parties have given them through the formation of contextualizing regimes. That role will only infrequently reflect the traditional assumption that courts appropriately respond to innovation by extending the reach of existing contract doctrine to emergent forms of agreement. Nonetheless, even in respecting these limits, generalist courts will retain an important, albeit less central, role than that accorded by the standard account. Common law contract doctrine and generalist courts are still needed to deter opportunistic efforts by contracting parties to exploit their counterparties. In this way, generalist courts will retain their historic role in policing efforts to game the system.

questions.question: Whether and when generalist courts should defer to contracting parties' own contextualizing regimes (including party-crafted bilateral or multilateral institutions) rather than extending or reinterpreting existing contract doctrine to novel contractual forms.

How market characteristics - specifically the scale (thickness) of the market and the level of uncertainty in the contracting environment - affect the appropriate allocation of interpretive and enforcement authority between generalist courts and alternative institutions in supporting contractual innovation.

Whether generalist courts remain necessary to deter opportunistic or gaming behavior in novel contractual arrangements even when most interpretive and normative work is performed by party-driven or specialized regimes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape private contracting behavior and the design of contractual arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how private actors respond to shocks by designing and stabilizing new contractual forms and contextualizing regimes that courts later must respect, while Paper B models how rules governing contractual liability change parties' strategic behavior (particularly information-revealing behavior) and thereby affect how contracts are structured.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role and limits of courts and other legal institutions versus private ordering in regulating contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts should defer to contextualizing regimes and party-driven solutions except to police opportunism, and Paper B engages with how legal rules (and their interpretation/enforcement) influence outcomes, treating the design of those institutional rules as central to incentives and information transmission between parties.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between contractual rules and informational uncertainty/asymmetries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A makes market uncertainty a core axis in its taxonomy—showing that uncertainty shapes which contextualizing regimes arise and how contracts evolve—while Paper B directly studies how limitations on liability affect the revelation of private information (valuations) and the welfare consequences of such information transfers.

shared_topics.topic: normative and economic evaluation of contract doctrines and rule design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses when courts should facilitate or refrain from reshaping contract doctrine to promote innovation and economic efficiency (while deterring opportunism), and Paper B evaluates when limiting contractual liability is socially desirable given its informational effects, treating rule design as a welfare-relevant decision.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev936!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Everywhere a Cluck-Cluck: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. Int'l Sales Corp. *
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Everywhere a Cluck-Cluck: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. Int'l Sales Corp. *

shared_topics.topic: use of extrinsic evidence, trade usage, and industry practice to determine contract meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Frigaliment as a paradigmatic opinion about using extrinsic sources (trade usage, course of dealing, parties' communications) to interpret ambiguous contract terms; Paper B analyzes the incorporation of informal understandings and trade/practice-based regimes into contractual interpretation and how those contextualizing regimes interact with courts.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate degree of judicial deference to parties' agreements versus judicial supplementation or activism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A showcases a judicial approach to deciding how much weight to give parties' stated meanings and extrinsic context, and Paper B directly debates whether generalist courts should defer to sophisticated parties and their contextual regimes or instead extend or modify contract doctrine in an activist fashion.

shared_topics.topic: how court decisions and interpretive doctrines influence the evolution and stability of commercial practices and novel contractual forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the Frigaliment decision as an influential guide shaping contract interpretation, while Paper B examines how courts can either facilitate or obstruct contractual innovation by the extent to which they respect party-created regimes or impose default/common-law rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of interpretive doctrines and precedent (including the UCC/incorporation principles) in allocating responsibility between parties and courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A implicitly illustrates how a leading opinion establishes interpretive norms for allocating meaning-making power, and Paper B explicitly contrasts the traditional common-law reluctance with the UCC's incorporation doctrine and assesses how these doctrinal regimes affect whether parties or courts bear primary responsibility for contextualizing agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1547!!ARTICLE: The Questionable Ascent of Hadley v. Baxendale
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Questionable Ascent of Hadley v. Baxendale

shared_topics.topic: the design and limits of default rules (information-forcing or penalty-defaults) in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques generalist courts' tendency to apply standard default rules rather than honoring parties' bespoke arrangements, while Paper B analyzes the theoretical limits of penalty-defaults (Hadley-derived information-forcing rules) and when such defaults fail to induce efficient opt-out or separation.

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence: when courts versus private or legislative institutions should fill contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should defer to contextualizing regimes created by parties, trade associations, or specialized tribunals, and Paper B questions judicial or legislative competence to set effective default rules, stressing difficulties lawmakers face in identifying efficient defaults.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and incentives to reveal or conceal private information in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that sophisticated contracting parties and industry regimes better understand contextual details than generalist judges and thus are better positioned to reveal and stabilize innovations, while Paper B models how asymmetric private information interacts with default rules and can produce pooling or concealment that undermines information-forcing mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of uncertainty or stochasticity in shaping appropriate legal responses to contract failures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the uncertainty of a market as a core axis determining which contextualizing regimes and judicial roles are appropriate, and Paper B shows that stochastic (uncertain) damages alter the incentives created by default rules and complicate the assessment of efficient default regimes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53santaclaralrev73!!ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: proper role of courts in interpreting and adapting contracts (party autonomy vs judicial intervention)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for limiting judicial inquiry to public, conventional meanings for negotiated commercial contracts and restricting intrusive inquiry into parties' subjective intent, while Paper B examines when generalist courts should defer to parties' contractual regimes versus actively reshaping agreements to accommodate or discipline novel forms of contracting.

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and utility of extrinsic or contextual evidence (trade usage, course of performance, negotiations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the plain meaning rule versus the context rule and proposes admitting only public/conventional evidence (e.g., trade usage) while excluding parties' course of performance except under equity, and Paper B analyzes the extent to which courts incorporate inchoate practices and informal understandings (through doctrines like incorporation) when resolving disputes over emergent contractual forms.

shared_topics.topic: tension between predictability/security of contracts and flexibility for commercial innovation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that interpretation rules should preserve predictability and mutual constraint by privileging public meanings, warning that contextual inquiry can undermine certainty, while Paper B studies how courts and contextualizing regimes should balance legal stability with the need to support or adapt to private innovation in contracting practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry norms and institutional regimes (trade associations, market practices, UCC incorporation) in supplying contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A endorses admitting trade usage and other shared linguistic conventions as evidence of public meaning, and Paper B maps how multilateral contextualizing regimes — from trade associations to specialized institutions and doctrines like the UCC's incorporation principle — establish practices that courts may recognize or defer to when adjudicating novel contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev527!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: PRICE ADJUSTMENT IN LONG-TERM CONTRACTS.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: PRICE ADJUSTMENT IN LONG-TERM CONTRACTS.

shared_topics.topic: judicial intervention versus party autonomy in adapting contracts to changed circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts should be largely deferential to the parties' own contextualizing regimes and warns that activist reinterpretation or application of default common-law rules can undermine contractual innovation; Paper B examines the concrete choices courts face when circumstances change in long-term contracts (e.g., excuse performance, revise price, impose a duty to renegotiate) and critiques judicial rewriting of contract terms (notably discussing Alcoa v. Essex).

shared_topics.topic: private contractual and non‑judicial mechanisms for handling contractual change (price‑adjustment clauses, force majeure, arbitration, contextualizing regimes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties and institutions (bilateral regimes, trade associations, specialist fora) create the interpretive frameworks that stabilize innovations; Paper B analyzes the substance and limits of private mechanisms—price adjustment provisions, force majeure, delegating decisionmaking to arbitrators or open‑ended drafting—as alternatives to leaving adjustment to courts.

shared_topics.topic: managing uncertainty in long‑term or evolving commercial relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a taxonomy where market uncertainty (and market thickness) shapes which contextualizing regimes arise and how courts should respond to innovations in contracting; Paper B develops a relational‑contract analysis of price adjustment, treating the problem as one of ongoing relational uncertainty in long‑term supply arrangements rather than mere risk allocation, and addresses how to determine when changed circumstances justify relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23fordhamurblj69!!ARTICLE: THE WARNING FROM PITTSBURGH'S GOLDEN TRIANGLE: HOME OF THE STEELERS, THE PIRATES AND THE AMORPHOUS FAVORED NATION CLAUSE IN THE COMMERCIAL LEASE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE WARNING FROM PITTSBURGH'S GOLDEN TRIANGLE: HOME OF THE STEELERS, THE PIRATES AND THE AMORPHOUS FAVORED NATION CLAUSE IN THE COMMERCIAL LEASE

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and enforceability of novel or ambiguous contractual clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how generalist courts confront emergent contractual forms and argues they often should defer to the parties' contextualizing regimes rather than reshape novel terms; Paper B centers on the interpretive problems posed by an 'amorphous' favored‑nation clause in commercial leases and the difficulties courts face in giving effect to such unclear contractual language.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy in contracting and judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that sophisticated parties and industry regimes often best determine how new contractual practices should operate and that courts should respect those allocations of interpretive authority; Paper B raises the practical problem of whether courts should enforce a tenant/landlord’s MFN clause as written or reinterpret it, illustrating the same conflict between honoring parties’ agreements and judicial correction.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual terms affect market relations among similarly situated market participants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames innovation in contract around the 'thickness' of markets and how private regimes coordinate many actors facing similar circumstances; Paper B examines a favored‑nation (MFN) clause — a device designed to align treatment across multiple tenants/transactions — and the implications of such clauses for parity and market relations in commercial leasing.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46sandiegolrev595!!Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment

shared_topics.topic: when and whether courts should adjust or rewrite contracts in response to changed circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should generally be passive and defer to the parties' own contextualizing regimes rather than extending common‑law doctrine to novel agreements, while Paper B surveys the debate (centered on ALCOA and Speidel) about judicial contract adjustment and contends that adjustment may be defensible in limited circumstances though many questions remain unresolved.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy and judicial activism in contract interpretation and innovation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes party-driven innovation and warns against courts overriding explicit party arrangements or imposing default rules, and Paper B engages the same tension by weighing Speidel's pro‑adjustment stance against arguments for judicial restraint and asking when intervention is permissible.

shared_topics.topic: the role of exogenous shocks, market uncertainty, and long‑term disruption in shaping contractual responses and appropriate legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract innovation as a response to exogenous economic shocks and analyzes how uncertainty and market thickness affect whether courts or other institutions should interpret new forms, while Paper B focuses on disrupted long‑term contracts and argues that the plurality of variables created by such shocks makes the proper judicial response indeterminate.

papers.node_id: 53wakeforestlrev1!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE
papers.abstract:
We often understand promise and contract as practices that promote autonomy.By making a promise or entering into a contract, we are able to alter our moral and legal position, respectively, merely by expressing an intention to do so. You are not obligated to pick up your friend from the airport on a given occasion until you promise to do so. You are not obligated to refrain from disparaging a company's products until you agree not to as its employee. Most of what we owe each other does not depend on our communicated intentions in this way. Similarly, most of our legal duties to others do not depend on a communicated intent to assume them. Obligations of our own deliberate making are unique.
Why recognize the power to bind ourselves in this way? The promise to help your friend advances your friendship and the promise not to disparage your employer makes it possible to access employment. More generally, David Owens has argued persuasively that "normative powers"like promise allow us to author our normative world, rendering it more of our making.When we actively shape our normative position, we exercise a distinctive dimension of our moral agency. The resulting responsibility for our moral position is important to our self-conception as agents. Whether we are responsible for what we owe others is not a metaphysical fact; it depends on whether we take each other to be responsible. By treatingpromises and other exercises of normative power as binding, we construct our own agency.
But the binding character of promise and contract is constrictive too. In fact, on their face, promise and contract reduce the choices available to us in the future.Because you promised to pick up your friend, you can no longer spend the afternoon reading, running, or staring at the wall, even if you later decide that one of those is a better way to spend the afternoon. Because you agreed not to disparage your employer, you may not share views that you come to hold deeply about the place where you spend most of your time. Scholars of promise and contract have tended to conclude that because we bind ourselves through those practices, the constrictive effect of promise and contract does not pose a threat to autonomy. Pursuant to the prevailing view, the power to put ourselves in a new moral position enhances our autonomy even if we find ourselves newly encumbered.
Such optimism about promise and contract is excessive. This Article does not set out to deny that the normative power to make promises and contracts enhances our moral agency. But that benefit comes at a cost. The same ideal of moral agency that makes promise valuable makes the power to revise and reject commitments that we have made valuable too. In fact, the power to revise and reject recognizes an important feature of our agency: it is persistent. That is, because we are persistent agents, we continuously revisit our values and ends. We can and should act in a manner that reflects our new assessments.
Of course, the human tendency to break promises and breach contracts reflects a variety of weaknesses, including the bare temptation of self-interest. We might fail to follow through on a promise because we have already obtained the advantage we sought in making the promise and see nothing to gain from performance. Or we might regret an agreement because we learn new facts that reveal it to have been a bad deal for us. Arguably, the assignment of risk in contract is intended precisely to deal with this sort of painful resolution to factual uncertainty. However, we also break promisesand breach contracts because we have changed our minds in a morally significant way.
We often change our minds about the commitments we have made because we reject some value on which the commitment was based - a life plan, a relationship - or because we reassess the balance of the same reasons we had previously considered.Even a decision to breach that appears at first blush to be a momentary failure of will likely reflects some underlying ambivalence in our reasoning about the agreement. At a critical moment, we might revive reasons that we earlier rejected or had previously judged to be outweighed by other reasons.Our tendency to change our minds is easily dismissed as fickleness because the internal processes that result in a change of mind are often opaque to others.All that others see is the same person doing something different.A change in behavior will appear sudden, even though the reasons for the change have been accumulating for an agent for some time before the reasons reached tipping weight. Of course, some people are more sympathetic to change in others and will project reasonable uncertainty that they cannot directly observe. Similarly, some cultures are more tolerant than others of such "multiplicity" within a single person and her life.
Regardless of our particular dispositions, we all know from subjective experience that we change our minds because we are still thinking. And, as agents, we aim to translate our new thoughts intonew action. The reasoning behind a change can be careless or careful, just as our initial commitments are sometimes careless and sometimes careful. Either case is an exercise of practical reason, the capacity for which defines us as moral agents.Persistent agency is thus a morally valuable capacity, and it deserves accommodation. I will argue below that the practice of promise cannot accommodate persistent agency within itself, but the institution of contract can. It should, and it does.
To be sure, contract law does not entitle us to impose losses on others so that we might indulge our fickleness. But in several respects, contract law is more lenient than its private counterpart - the morality of promise.Promise-making befits individuals who are committed to moral stability and prepared to undertake its weighty obligations. Many of us choose to exercise normative power over time at the expense of constricting our persistent agency - at least in some areas of our lives. Others might self-consciously take steps to avoid moral encumbrances. Because we are all equally entitled to the support that contract law provides in our daily lives, it is a more liberal institution than promise. Contract law facilitates commitment without endorsing any one conception of personal virtue over others.
Many scholarly discussions of promise and contract elaborate their relationships with the principle of autonomy. By contrast, this Article's focus is on the broader concept of agency. I should therefore specify how I use each concept. I take a moral agent to generate reasons for herself and others. She is an agent in that she is not merely responsive to external facts but processes facts in a way that makes her decision to act in one way rather than another her own.Because she is a moral agent, her choices reflect moral deliberation, or they should.And just as she ought to take into account the moral claims of others, her interests are of the sort that should be given special weight (as compared to other beings) by other moral agents.
I take autonomy to be a more robust principle: an autonomous person governs herself by reference to the right reasons.That is, a person can fail to act autonomously where she does not act on the moral reasons that apply to her. Although autonomy is often used more broadly to encompass what is here either agency or the capacity for autonomy, I am using a more restrictive conception of autonomy in order to be able to distinguish systematically between our moral interest in exercising agency and our interest in exercising it well. Nevertheless, both agency and autonomy drive at the idea of self-authorship, and such self-authorship is facilitated by promising. Only if we share a conception of the person that is well-served by the power to promise does the law of contract have noninstrumental reasons for helping to construct the normative power of promise in the context of legally binding exchange.
A few years ago, Dori Kimel wrote a book chapter wondering whether the autonomy-enhancing effects of promise have caused us to overlook or downplay (in theory, at least) the obvious downsides of commitment for autonomy.People can bind themselves until they are too bound up. Does autonomy not require that we retain the right to change our minds?
Kimel considers a number of problems that promise might pose for autonomy, but I will argue that he does not do the challenge justice. His account is thrown off by adopting the starting point of the literature on promise: only a morally continuous and unitary person can be autonomous.Starting there, Kimel misjudges the value of changing one's mind and its relation to a fragmented and discontinuous identity.
The idea of autonomy that Kimel employs presupposes a more basic moral agency. Because persistent agency is in basic tension with commitments across time, the implications of promising for autonomy are more ambiguous than Kimel allows. The power to promise is valuable, but normative powers outside promise have value too; the power to make a promise sits tightly against the power to revise that promise. The same ambition of agency that motivates the basic normative power of promise motivates us to revise our commitments in light of evolving values that may coexist in tensionwith each other. Revision and internal conflict are what we call fickleness. We may conceive ourselves as continuous persons, but we rightly accommodate our fickleness too.
Part II summarizes and suggests limitations in Kimel's arguments "in defense" of promise and contract in the face of the value of changing one's mind. In doing so, my aim is to show the scope of the challenge here, which applies not only to bad promises but also promises per se. Part III argues that agency under nonideal conditions, including limited cognitive faculties and limited knowledge, requires continuous revision of our basic moral commitments. Some degree of indecision is morally compulsory. Part IV suggests that people reasonably disagree about the value of stability and unity and makes sense of why promise and contract should diverge in their treatment of regret and reversal. Promise is properly associated with continuity of a singular identity and contract appropriately declines to presuppose such a conception of the person. This divergence is good, especially in a liberal state. Part V discusses several doctrines that accommodate fickleness.

questions.question: Whether the binding force of promises and contracts undermines or supports agents' moral agency by constraining their ability to revise commitments in light of changed values (i.e., does binding oneself reduce the morally valuable capacity to change one's mind?).

Whether legal institutions (contract law) should accommodate agents' persistent capacity to change their commitments more permissively than moral norms governing promises (i.e., should contract law permit or facilitate revision/rejection of obligations arising from agreements?).
Whether recognition of the moral value of changing one's mind (fickleness/persistent agency) requires treating promises and contracts differently in terms of enforceability and remedial response.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 129yalelj690!!ARTICLE: Paid on Both Sides: Quid Pro Quo Exchange and the Doctrine of Consideration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Paid on Both Sides: Quid Pro Quo Exchange and the Doctrine of Consideration

shared_topics.topic: distinction between moral promises and legally enforceable contracts and its implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how promises and contracts differently bind agents, contrasting the moral power of promise with the legal institution of contract and its effects on agency and autonomy; Paper B analyzes how the doctrine of consideration operates to demarcate which interpersonal commitments become legally enforceable contracts versus unenforced promises.

shared_topics.topic: role of social context (intimate/domestic vs commercial) in determining enforceability of commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how friendships, employment, and cultural attitudes shape expectations about promises and why contract law should not presume a single conception of the person; Paper B examines how family and friendship networks tend to avoid quid pro quo forms and argues the consideration doctrine (and related legal-intent rules) function to screen informal social/domestic commitments from legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how legal doctrine should accommodate change of mind, revisions, and contract modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that persistent agency and morally significant changes of mind (fickleness) should be accommodated by legal institutions and that contract law can and should allow revision in ways promise morality does not; Paper B critiques the modern consideration rule for producing counterintuitive results in contract modifications and preexisting-duty situations and offers an alternative formulation that preserves enforceability of genuine post-formation adjustments.

shared_topics.topic: the normative rationale for enforcing some commitments and exempting others (the screening function of contract law)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends contract law's relative leniency and its role in enabling plural approaches to commitment without imposing one moral ideal, suggesting legal enforcement serves distributive/liberal aims; Paper B develops a historical and functional rationale for the bargain/consideration requirement as a rough but serviceable mechanism to identify classes of promises the law has reason not to enforce (e.g., intimate/domestic agreements).

shared_topics.topic: the nature of obligations created by promises/contracts (binding power, responsibility, and debt-like relations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how promises and contracts generate binding obligations and personal responsibility that restructure an agent's normative position; Paper B provides a theoretical account of quid pro quo by analyzing obligations as debt and reciprocal remuneration, thereby exploring what it means for performances or promises to discharge obligations in exchange relations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100geolj5!!ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?

shared_topics.topic: expressive or noninstrumental force of contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether contractual duties induce compliance for reasons beyond expected legal sanctions (the 'expressive' power of contract), and Paper B theorizes the normative power of promise and contract as practices that bind agents for reasons internal to agency rather than mere deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between commitment and ongoing agency (autonomy/fickleness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cites moral commitment and promise-keeping as motives that affect contractual performance and explores when those motives weaken, while Paper B centrally analyzes how binding commitments constrain persistent agency and the moral value of revising commitments (the problem of 'fickle' people).

shared_topics.topic: how features of contracts and their formation affect bindingness and compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares negotiated versus standard-form contracts to show variation in expressive power and compliance, and Paper B contrasts promise and contract institutions and discusses doctrinal choices that reflect different assumptions about who is being bound and how much flexibility should be permitted.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of ambiguity, uncertainty, or indeterminacy on obligations and legal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally contrasts legal-content uncertainty and enforcement uncertainty to see how different uncertainties influence compliance, and Paper B addresses indeterminacy in agents' reasons and values over time and considers doctrinal accommodations for regret, revision, and limited knowledge.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38yalejonreg678!!ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract

shared_topics.topic: renegotiation, commitment devices, and ex post modification of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract law sometimes prohibits renegotiation‑proof schemes and how doctrines of contract modification and enforcement can undo ex ante commitment devices, while Paper B examines the moral and legal significance of revising commitments, surveying doctrines that accommodate or constrain agents who change their minds.

shared_topics.topic: how default, mandatory, and standard rules shape private autonomy and market completion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates default, mandatory and standard rules in a general‑equilibrium/market‑completion framework and emphasizes their distinct planning functions, and Paper B explores how contractual rules (as compared with moral promise) enable or limit individuals' self‑authorship and practical autonomy in choosing to bind themselves.

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in enforcement, interpretation, and communication (formalism vs contextualism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the adjudication system's capacity to implement planning (including advocacy for formalism, specialized courts, and the communication problem between parties and courts), while Paper B attends to how judicial doctrines and interpretive practices should treat regret, reversal, and the permissibility of breaking commitments.

shared_topics.topic: normative limits and justification for contractual freedom versus state intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the proper scope of freedom of contract versus state 'planning' to correct market incompleteness and externalities, and Paper B provides a normative account of why contract law in a liberal state should be more permissive than moral promise—both grapple with why and how law should enable or restrict parties' ability to bind themselves.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16tourolrev1037!!COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?
compared_to.partner_title: COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?

shared_topics.topic: how contract law infers or imputes assent when parties' actual intentions are unobserved or changing
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that agents persistently revise their intentions and that law should recognize the difference between exercised normative powers (promises) and later revisions, while Paper B critiques cases like Hill v. Gateway where courts impute assent from context or efficiency considerations rather than from actual manifested assent.

shared_topics.topic: the normative values that justify enforcing contracts (agency/autonomy versus efficiency/wealth maximization)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract and promise doctrines in terms of competing values—supporting agency, revision, and autonomy—whereas Paper B shows how courts rely on 'common sense' and economic efficiency as covert normative assumptions shaping contractual rules.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how the law should accommodate post-formation change of mind, regret, or consumer ignorance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally defends accommodating 'fickleness' and revision across time in contractual relations, and Paper B examines doctrinal outcomes (e.g., accept-or-return, arbitration-in-a-box) that enforce terms despite buyer ignorance or later regret, raising the same question of permissive versus strict enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal doctrines and institutions in mediating private commitments and public enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the moral practice of promising with the institutional role of contract law and surveys doctrines that can accommodate persistent agency, while Paper B analyzes how judicial doctrines and rhetorical invocations of 'common sense' operationalize particular models of contracting within the court system.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78valrev821!!ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory role of consent/manifested assent in enforcing contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a 'consent theory of contract' arguing that both a consent to be legally bound and more indirect forms of consent (e.g., silence vis-à-vis default rules) can justify enforcement; Paper B treats promise and contract as exercises of normative power that bind agents by their communicated intentions and examines when and why those communicative acts should be treated as creating legal/moral obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law should respond to changes in parties' preferences or 'fickleness' over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how incomplete contracting and the use of default rules address parties' inability to foresee or expressly bargain for future contingencies, including how silence may be interpreted across time; Paper B focuses on the moral and legal problem of agents changing their minds, arguing that contract law (unlike moral promise) should accommodate persistent agency and contains doctrines that permit or limit revision and breach.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between binding commitments and individual autonomy/agency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates consent and freedom of contract within liberal principles (freedom to and freedom from contract) and asks how default rules can respect individual self-governance, while Paper B analyzes how the power to bind oneself via promise or contract both advances and constrains agency and autonomy, asking how law should balance commitment value against the value of revisability.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional role of contract law (background rules/defaults/doctrines) in structuring private normative powers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes background legal mechanisms—default rules versus immutable gap-fillers—and how those institutional choices reflect or displace party consent; Paper B compares the institution of contract to the moral practice of promise, emphasizing how legal doctrines (as an institutional scaffold) differently enable, limit, or accommodate commitments and revisions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113yalelj1417!!ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: how promises and contracts shape individual agency and autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how promises and especially contracts reconfigure the moral positions of parties (enabling plans and self-binding) but locates the core value in the relations contracts create; Paper B treats promises and contracts as 'normative powers' that author our moral world, emphasizing both their autonomy-enhancing role and the need to accommodate persistent agency and revision.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of individualistic or instrumental explanations for contractual obligation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that familiar individualistic justifications (freedom/precommitment, expectation protection, welfare/efficiency) fail to capture the distinctive, relational moral core of contract; Paper B similarly questions the prevailing view that self-binding is unambiguously autonomy-enhancing, showing that instrumental accounts overlook the costs of constraining evolving agents.
