shared_topics.topic: the parol evidence rule and the status of extrinsic evidence
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the parol evidence rule and the admissibility/role of extrinsic evidence: Paper A critiques the term's multiple meanings and clarifies how parol-evidence doctrines interact with interpretation, and Paper B treats the parol-evidence principle as evidence of doctrinal plurality and as part of the ‘evidentiary base’ debate underlying textualist versus contextualist methods.

shared_topics.topic: who should determine the applicable interpretive regime (meta-interpretation) and the relevance of parties' preferences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider whether and how the parties' expectations or preferences should influence which interpretive approach governs: Paper B develops a meta-interpretive theory that the parties' (or reasonable parties') preferred regime should guide selection, and Paper A repeatedly links interpretive doctrine to parties' drafting incentives and the policy implications of choosing one regime over another.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary base and procedural stages (what evidence is used and when in litigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze the scope and timing of admissible evidence and how interpretive decisions map onto litigation phases: Paper B frames interpretation as varying by size of the evidentiary base (minimum vs broader evidence) and critiques cost/benefit models, while Paper A details the stages of interpretation, relates them to pleading/discovery/trial, and explains how different approaches admit and weigh evidence differently.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs between predictability/administrability and justice/efficiency in interpretive choice
shared_topics.justification: Both address normative tradeoffs driving interpretive doctrine: Paper A documents how competing policy arguments (predictability and administrability for textualism versus justice and accuracy for contextualism) create doctrinal incoherence, and Paper B evaluates those same efficiency and justice claims (including economic models like Schwartz & Scott) to argue for context-sensitive rule selection.

papers.node_id: 47hofstralrev1011!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION ENFORCEMENT COSTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY OF TEXTUALISM VERSUS CONTEXTUALISM CONDUCTED VIA THE WEST KEY NUMBER SYSTEM
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION ENFORCEMENT COSTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY OF TEXTUALISM VERSUS CONTEXTUALISM CONDUCTED VIA THE WEST KEY NUMBER SYSTEM
papers.abstract:
Contract interpretation is one of the most important topics in commercial law.It lies at the heart of contract doctrine, which contains numerous rules designed to address the construction of agreements.And interpretive disputes constitute the largest source of contract litigation.In fact, contractual meaning may be the most frequently contested issue in civil cases generally.The significance of contract interpretation explains why the field has received extensive academic attention since the turn of the century.And the subject is recognized as "the least settled, most contentious area of contemporary contract doctrine and scholarship."
The central policy issue in contract interpretation is the role of extrinsic evidence in the interpretive process.The rules regarding suchevidence can influence virtually every aspect of the parties' contractual relationship.As a result, numerous factors are relevant in deciding the optimal interpretive regime.It should thus not be surprising that there is fierce debate among courts and scholars over the proper approach to extrinsic evidence.
The disputants are organized into two basic camps. "Textualist" judges and commentators argue that the interpretation of contracts should focus primarily on the language contained within the four corners of written agreements. According to this view, extrinsic evidence - such as preliminary negotiations, the surrounding commercial circumstances, course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade - is of secondary importance, and many contracts can and should be interpreted without these materials. "Contextualists," in contrast, believe that courts generally ought to examine both the language of the parties' agreement and extrinsic evidence when determining contractual meaning.
The textualist/contextualist controversy cannot be resolved in the abstract. It raises dozens of questions about the real world that are answerable only via observation and statistical analysis.Unfortunately, empirical evidence bearing on this debate is sorely lacking.Data-driven research is beyond the province of the judicial process. The responsibility for completing such work thus falls principally to academics. But scholarship concerning contract interpretation is almostalways theoretical in nature. As a result, there are exceptionally few empirical studies of interpretive issues.This Article contains such a study. The Article is actually the second of two pieces setting forth empirical research regarding the textualist/contextualist debate.
Perhaps the signature claim advanced by textualists in defense of their position is that contextualism results in more litigation over the meaning of contracts than textualism. In other words, enforcement costs are higher in a contextualist regime. Many contextualists disagree; they maintain that enforcement costs are actually larger under textualism.My first article concerned this debate and it set forth an empirical study designed to test which side is correct.The study compared the level of interpretation litigation in a group of textualist states to the level in a group of contextualist states using fourteen distinct measures.Under one measure, there was more litigation in the textualist group by a statistically significant amount.But under the other thirteen measures, there was no statistically significant difference between the textualist and contextualist jurisdictions.I thus concluded that my study provided no support for the textualist hypothesis that enforcement costs are greater under contextualism, and very little support for the contextualist counter-hypothesis that textualism has higher enforcement costs.
This study was actually part of a broader project. The primary purpose of my first article (which I shall refer to as "Article One") was to explain how researchers can use the West Key Number System to dramatically streamline the process of data collection and coding that is central to most empirical work.Collecting and coding data is normally a resource-intensive process, requiring expenditures of time and money that go well beyond what is necessary for doctrinal and theoretical scholarship.Any tool capable of reducing these outlays holds considerable value. My principal goal in Article One was to set forth an argument that West's Key Number System is one such tool. Accordingly, a substantial portion of the paper focused on the methodological questions raised by employing the Key Number System as a data collection and coding device.The empirical study ofinterpretation enforcement costs was intended both to serve as a demonstration of the Key Number System in action and contribute to the empirical literature regarding contract law.
In the concluding section of Article One, I discussed four potential follow-up studies that would also utilize the Key Number System to compare litigation levels under textualism and contextualism.Each project had the potential to (1) add to the body of evidence regarding which approach to contract interpretation best minimizes enforcement costs, and (2) further illustrate how to use the Key Number System for empirical research.This Article concerns those four studies.
After considerable analysis, I determined that three of the proposed studies are subject to fatal feasibility issues. The decisive problem for two projects is that the contract interpretation caselaw appears too convoluted to classify the requisite number of states as either textualist or contextualist.A third project suffers from critical logistical and technical challenges - challenges that many researchers will face when attempting to conduct empirical research using the Key Number System.
I was able to complete the fourth study.In that project, there was no statistically significant difference between textualism and contextualism with respect to the quantity of contract interpretation litigation under any of the twelve measures employed.Therefore, the findings presented in this Article do not support either the textualist hypothesis or the contextualist counter-hypothesis.
As with the study in Article One, the protocol I used for the project in this paper has important methodological limitations.But the results of the study conducted here nonetheless constitute important evidence regarding the debate over the optimal method of contract interpretation. And the description below of the issues I faced in attempting to complete each of the four proposed studiesshould (1) provide important guidance to future researchers conducting empirical work, whether they choose to utilize the Key Number System for data collection and codingor deploy an alternative technique, such as manual coding, and (2) clarify several aspects of the contract interpretation caselaw.
Part II of this Article briefly describes the textualist and contextualist approaches to contract interpretation and summarizes the policy debate over which approach best minimizes enforcement costs.Part III reviews the advantages and disadvantages of using the Key Number System as a data collection and coding device that were discussed in Article One.Part IV contains a synopsis of the empirical study set forth in my prior article.Part V describes the four additional proposed studies and explains why I did not finish three of the projects.Part VI discusses the specific methodology and results of the completed study.Finally, Part VII contains some closing thoughts.

papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.
papers.abstract:
ARBITRATION decisions often turn on the interpretation of contract language, and numerous arbitrators base their awards on the plain meaning of collective bargaining agreements.Application of what has been characterized as the plain meaning ruleas a standard of contract interpretation requires that the meaning of contractual language be determined solely by attaching the plain or usual meaning to words that appear clear and unambiguous on the face of an agreement.Consequently,the plain meaning rule often operates to exclude extrinsic evidenceoffered to explain the intentions of the contracting parties.In many cases, evidence of a past practiceof the contracting parties at variance with express provisions of their agreement is disregarded when an arbitrator invokes the plain meaning rule.  As a result, the rule has produced arbitral opinions based on interpretations of collective bargaining agreements contrary to the intentions of either party.
Although favored a century ago, the plain meaning rule has been rejected by the Uniform Commercial Code (the U.C.C. or the Code)and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts (the Restatement),and condemned by treatise writers.In addition, the rule has been discredited by an increasing number of courts.Significantly, recent court decisions recognize that labor arbitrators have broad authority to consider extrinsic evidence in addition to the actual language of the agreement.Nevertheless,arbitrators continue to make frequent use of the plain meaning rule.
This Article analyzes the application of the plain meaning rule in labor arbitration awards in an attempt to reconcile the anomaly that exists: while courts are progressing toward rejection of the rule, arbitrators continue to rely on it.  Part I discusses the anatomy of the plain meaning rule.  Part II addresses its rejection by the courts.  Part III analyzes arbitration decisions in which the plain meaning rule has been invoked.  Part IV examines alternatives to the plain meaning approach.  Because the general aim of contractual interpretation is to effectuate the intention of the parties, this Article concludes with a formulation of an approach that embodies this objective.

questions.question: Whether a strictly text-based approach to interpreting collective bargaining agreements that excludes extrinsic evidence leads arbitrators to issue awards inconsistent with the contracting parties' actual intentions.

Why arbitrators continue to apply a strictly text-based, exclusionary approach to contract interpretation in labor arbitration despite broader legal and scholarly movement toward admitting extrinsic evidence.
What alternative interpretive approach would allow arbitrators to consider extrinsic evidence and better effectuate the contracting parties' intent, and how would that approach operate in practice?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev982!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Mitchill v. Lath and Masterson v. Sine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Mitchill v. Lath and Masterson v. Sine

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of extrinsic/parol evidence in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the plain meaning rule in labor arbitration excludes extrinsic evidence (including past practice) and the consequences of that exclusion, while Paper B centers on the parol evidence rule and the competing Williston/Corbin treatments of when and how extrinsic/parol evidence may be admitted to prove or interpret alleged side agreements.

shared_topics.topic: textualist (plain-meaning/Williston) versus contextualist (Corbin/intent-focused) interpretive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the plain-meaning/textualist rule and surveys alternatives that allow consideration of surrounding circumstances, and Paper B explicitly contrasts the Williston textualist approach with Corbin's contextualist approach and examines how each produces different results in practice.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract interpretation should prioritize parties' intent versus certainty/predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the general aim of interpretation is to effectuate the parties' intentions and proposes an approach reflecting that aim, while Paper B weighs the trade-offs between effectuating intent (avoiding unjust outcomes) and the benefits of certainty and efficiency that stricter textual rules can provide.

shared_topics.topic: practical consequences of rigid interpretive doctrines (justice, efficiency, and fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents cases where literal/plain-meaning application produced awards contrary to parties' intentions, and Paper B criticizes Mitchill and Masterson for yielding, respectively, unjust or wasteful outcomes when courts applied their favored parol-evidence approaches too rigidly.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of interpretive authority and doctrinal evolution (courts vs arbitrators/role of precedent)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights a divergence in doctrinal practice—courts rejecting the plain meaning rule while arbitrators continue to apply it—and Paper B examines how influential courts (and specific judges) adopt and entrench particular parol-evidence approaches, using decisions to signal norms to lower courts and practitioners.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53santaclaralrev73!!ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: criticisms of the plain meaning rule in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze and criticize the plain meaning rule — Paper A documents how arbitrators invoke the rule to exclude extrinsic evidence (often producing outcomes contrary to parties' intentions), while Paper B surveys doctrinal and theoretical objections to the rule and explains its practical shortcomings in commercial contracting.

shared_topics.topic: when and which extrinsic evidence should be admissible
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with the admissibility of extrinsic evidence (e.g., prior negotiations, course of performance, trade usage), with Paper A examining arbitrators' exclusion of such evidence and Paper B proposing principled limits on which categories of extrinsic evidence courts should consider.

shared_topics.topic: proposed alternatives to the plain meaning/context dichotomy
shared_topics.justification: Each paper evaluates alternatives to strict plain-meaning or full-context approaches — Paper A reviews and advocates for interpretive methods that better effectuate parties' intentions in arbitration, while Paper B develops and defends a specific 'public meaning' rule as a middle ground for negotiated commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between effectuating parties' intent and promoting predictability
shared_topics.justification: Both articles address the normative trade-off between discovering subjective party intent and preserving predictable, public meanings for contractual language — Paper A frames this in arbitration outcomes that may depart from parties' intentions, and Paper B argues the public meaning rule better preserves predictability while limiting unreliable subjective evidence.

shared_topics.topic: role of past practice, trade usage, and course of dealing/performance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with how courts and arbitrators should treat objective patterns like past practice and trade usage — Paper A criticizes arbitrators who ignore past practice under a plain meaning approach, and Paper B distinguishes admissible public/conventional usages from inadmissible evidence of subjective course of dealing or performance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres135!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence versus literal/plain-meaning interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes arbitrators' frequent invocation of the plain-meaning rule to exclude extrinsic evidence (past practice, party intent) and proposes alternatives that better effectuate parties' intentions; Paper B discusses parol-evidence devices and the choice between literalist/formalistic interpretation and contextual gap-filling when parties or courts must decide whether to rely on outside evidence.

shared_topics.topic: when and how tribunals should 'fill gaps' in incomplete contracts (gap‑filling and default rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques application of a strict plain-meaning approach that forecloses consideration of contextual practices and thereby produces awards contrary to parties' intentions, while Paper B is centrally concerned with the normative and doctrinal question of whether courts should fill contractual gaps (hypothetical bargain, default or penalty defaults) and how such gap‑filling affects incentives and efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' drafting choices and litigation strategies shape interpretation and enforcement costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how arbitration outcomes depend on interpretive doctrines and thus implicate how collective bargaining language and practices are drafted or presented, and Paper B analyzes specific private transactional devices (parol evidence clauses, liquidated damages, delegation) and litigation strategies that parties use to manage verifiability, lower enforcement costs, and influence how disputes will be interpreted or resolved.

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the proper role of courts versus arbitrators/tribunals in resolving interpretive or verifiability problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts courts' rejection of the plain-meaning rule with arbitrators' continued reliance on it and discusses arbitrators' authority to consider extrinsic evidence; Paper B examines courts' limited ability to verify facts (verifiability), the costs of judicial enforcement, and when judicial intervention or deference to private resolution/renegotiation is appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73molrev667!!Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs

shared_topics.topic: ensuring mutual assent / the 'meeting of the minds' requirement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how nondisclosure and unilateral mistake doctrines are used to police whether contracting parties shared a mutual understanding, while Paper B analyzes how interpretive doctrines (like the plain meaning rule) either advance or frustrate the goal of effectuating the parties' intentions and thus a meeting of the minds.

shared_topics.topic: treatment of extrinsic information and communicative acts (silence, past practice, signals) in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats silence and other non-verbal or non-textual information as communicative (examining when silence must be disclosed or can signal private information), and Paper B addresses whether arbitrators may or should admit extrinsic evidence (past practice, negotiations) when the contract text appears plain.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules allocate incentives to generate, reveal, or rely on information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly models how disclosure rules (Silence-is-Golden, Optimal Dishonesty, Word-to-the-Wise) affect a buyer's incentive to search for and exploit private information, while Paper B shows how interpretive rules (plain meaning versus contextual approaches) shape parties' drafting, bargaining, and reliance incentives in collective bargaining and arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: conflict between formalist/textualist rules and contextual/intent-focused approaches in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques treating silence as a unitary formal rule and favors a richer account of signaling and context, and Paper B critiques the plain meaning textualist rule and argues for alternatives that incorporate context and parties' intentions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev451!!Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem

shared_topics.topic: the tension between the plain-meaning rule and contextual/incorporationist approaches to contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the continued use of the plain meaning rule by labor arbitrators and contrasts it with courts' and commentators' rejection of that rule, while Paper B directly frames the debate as plain-meaning (anti-incorporation) versus norm-incorporation strategies (trade usages, course of dealing) under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: the legal treatment and evidentiary role of extrinsic sources (trade usages, past practice, course of performance) in construing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the plain meaning rule excludes extrinsic evidence such as past practices in arbitration, often producing outcomes at odds with parties' behavior, and Paper B examines judicial incorporation of trade usages, course of dealing, and course of performance as part of the contract and the costs/benefits of giving such practices legal effect.

shared_topics.topic: whether interpretive methods serve to effectuate the parties' intentions and deter opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the general aim of interpretation is to effectuate parties' intentions and proposes alternatives to better achieve that end, while Paper B argues that incorporation of trade usages should be evaluated functionally—by whether recognizing usages furthers parties' goals (e.g., controlling opportunistic behavior) and reduces transaction hazards.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of interpretive authority between courts and arbitrators (and the normative implications thereof)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights an apparent institutional divergence—courts moving away from plain meaning while arbitrators continue to apply it—and analyzes arbitral practice, whereas Paper B critiques judicial interpretive strategies (and the role of courts under the UCC) and engages with debates about how much courts should intervene to incorporate commercial norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: whether contract interpretation should prioritize the parties' actual intent (including extrinsic evidence) over a rigid textual/plain-meaning reading
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges focusing on the practical consequences of doctrinal labels and how rules affect parties' ability to order their relations, while Paper B analyzes the plain-meaning rule in arbitration and advocates for interpretive approaches that effectuate the parties' intentions, including consideration of extrinsic evidence and past practice.

shared_topics.topic: the degree of private autonomy to reshape legal relationships (contracting around defaults or by practice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defines the contractual domain by the parties' ability to privately reorder substantial portions of their legal relations and asks when defaults should be defeasible, and Paper B examines whether collective-bargaining parties' practices and agreements should be allowed to alter or displace textual provisions in arbitration outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between textualist/default rules and contextual/party-focused rules (and the normative consequences of that choice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames key normative questions as whether rules should be mandatory or defaults and which defaults to adopt, whereas Paper B confronts the practical effects of applying a textual default (the plain meaning rule) versus contextual alternatives favored by the UCC/Restatement and courts, emphasizing how that choice changes outcomes for contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: evaluating doctrinal rules by their real-world effects rather than by semantic labels
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes essentialist definitional disputes and urges assessment of which characterization matters for policy consequences, and Paper B documents how the plain-meaning rule can produce arbitral awards at odds with parties' expectations, using outcome-based critique to motivate a different interpretive approach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73molrev667!!Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs

shared_topics.topic: when decision-makers may consider extrinsic evidence to ascertain parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the plain-meaning rule's tendency to exclude extrinsic evidence (past practice, party intent) in labor arbitration and surveys alternatives that allow outside evidence; Paper B similarly grapples with whether and how courts should treat information revealed (or withheld) outside the contract text when assessing parties' understandings and obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the goal of contract doctrine to effectuate parties' mutual intent versus enforcing literal text
shared_topics.justification: Paper A expressly frames interpretation doctrines around the objective of effectuating parties' intentions and critiques literal plain-meaning outcomes that frustrate that aim; Paper B evaluates disclosure/mistake rules (e.g., Silence-is-Golden, Optimal Dishonesty, Word to the Wise) in terms of whether they produce agreements that reflect actual, enforceable bargains between parties.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between formal doctrinal rules and policy considerations (efficiency, fairness, incentives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts rigid textual rules with the U.C.C./Restatement and case law trends that favor contextual approaches, implicitly weighing doctrinal clarity against just results; Paper B explicitly models and compares rules on nondisclosure for their efficiency, fairness, and incentive effects, then brings non-efficiency values into rule choice.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicators should respond when contractual outcomes diverge from parties' expectations (mistake, past practice, rescission/remedy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents instances where arbitrators' literal interpretations produce outcomes at odds with parties' past practice or expectations and explores remedial interpretive approaches; Paper B studies doctrines of unilateral mistake and nondisclosure that allow avoidance or adjustment of contracts when one party enters under a misunderstanding, comparing which remedial rules best address such divergences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules shape parties' incentives to reveal private information during bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Hadley foreseeability default (treated as an information‑forcing or "penalty" default) interacts with strategic bargaining incentives and argues that such defaults may fail to induce truthful revelation; Paper B shows that the plain‑meaning rule's exclusion of extrinsic evidence affects parties' ability and incentives to present past practices or contextual facts that reveal their true intentions in disputes and during contract formation.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal/textual rules and effectuating the parties' intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the Coasean/default‑rule approach that treats doctrinal rules as neutral defaults and argues for rules that account for strategic behavior to better reflect parties' interests, while Paper B criticizes rigid invocation of the plain meaning rule and advocates interpretive methods that allow context and extrinsic evidence to ascertain and enforce the parties' actual intent.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal and empirical case analysis to evaluate interpretive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts an empirical survey of consequential‑damages cases over 120 years to test whether the information‑forcing hypothesis explains litigant behavior and doctrinal evolution, and Paper B analyzes arbitration awards and recent court decisions to assess whether the plain‑meaning doctrine aligns with arbitral practice and should be sustained or reformed.

shared_topics.topic: normative implications of interpretive doctrines for bargaining efficiency and contract performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Hadley and default rules within economic/game‑theoretic accounts of efficiency (arguing that strategic bargaining undermines some efficiency justifications), and Paper B examines how interpretive standards like plain meaning versus contextual approaches affect the likelihood that contracts will reflect true bargains and lead to efficient enforcement outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6dukejconstlawppsidebar126!!ARTICLE: LACKING SWISS PRECISION: THE FIRST-SALE DOCTRINE IN COSTCO V. OMEGA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LACKING SWISS PRECISION: THE FIRST-SALE DOCTRINE IN COSTCO V. OMEGA

shared_topics.topic: interpretive methodology (textual/plain-meaning versus contextual approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how different rules of interpretation — in Paper A the 'plain meaning' rule for contract language, and in Paper B statutory/doctrinal interpretation of the first-sale doctrine — determine legal outcomes and whether interpreters should rely solely on text or consider broader context.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence or purpose in construing legal rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes excluding extrinsic evidence (past practice, parties' intentions) when arbitrators apply the plain meaning rule, while Paper B engages the problem of whether extraterritorial context and legislative purpose should inform whether the first-sale doctrine applies to goods made and first sold abroad.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive choices affect allocation of commercial control and distribution rights
shared_topics.justification: Both articles show that interpretive doctrines have concrete commercial consequences: Paper A concerns how contract interpretation governs workplace rights and enforcement between employer and union, and Paper B concerns whether interpretation of the first-sale doctrine limits a copyright holder's control over importation and resale of goods.

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty produced by divergent authorities or unresolved precedent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a divergence between courts (increasingly rejecting the plain meaning rule) and arbitrators (continuing to apply it), while Paper B highlights the Supreme Court's equally divided, non-precedential decision leaving the key question about first-sale and imported goods unresolved.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46amjcompl485!!ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law

shared_topics.topic: arbitral authority to consider extrinsic evidence in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how labor arbitrators invoke the plain meaning rule to exclude extrinsic evidence (past practice, parties' intent) and critiques that practice; Paper B discusses how Danish courts and international arbitrators may apply UNIDROIT Principles and judge-made rules, highlighting the willingness (or limits) of arbitrators and courts to look beyond the written text and use external sources such as lex mercatoria.

shared_topics.topic: textual/plain-meaning versus contextual/purposive approaches to interpreting contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the debate over the plain meaning rule (textualism) and alternatives that promote effectuating parties' intentions, while Paper B contrasts literal incorporation/interpretation of standard clauses with purposive tools (contra proferentem, reasonableness tests, UNIDROIT gap-filling) to reach commercially reasonable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: policing and enforceability of standard-form or ‘surprising’ contract terms and limits on party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how strict textual application can uphold contract language even against contrary industry practice or intent in labor arbitration; Paper B engages in detailed comparison of UNIDROIT and Danish law on surprising standard terms, unfair exemption/penalty clauses, and the doctrinal mechanisms used to refuse enforcement or amend such terms.

shared_topics.topic: the influence and use of restatements/international principles as persuasive interpretive sources
shared_topics.justification: Paper A points to the Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the U.C.C. as rejecting strict plain-meaning and influencing courts, whereas Paper B treats the UNIDROIT Principles as an international 'Restatement' that national courts and arbitrators may invoke as persuasive gap-fillers and interpretive guidance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54smulrev867!!SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:The Statute of Frauds and the Parol Evidence Rule Under the NCCUSL 2000 Annual Meeting Proposed Revision of U.C.C. Article 2
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:The Statute of Frauds and the Parol Evidence Rule Under the NCCUSL 2000 Annual Meeting Proposed Revision of U.C.C. Article 2

shared_topics.topic: admissibility of extrinsic (parol) evidence to determine contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines proposed revisions to UCC Article 2's parol evidence rule and related provisions governing when and what outside evidence may be admitted to prove contract terms, while Paper B analyzes how the plain meaning rule operates to exclude extrinsic evidence in labor arbitration and surveys alternatives that allow such evidence.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalist interpretive rules and intent-focused approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether the statute of frauds and the parol evidence rule should be retained, liberalized, or clarified—i.e., whether formal requirements should govern enforceability—while Paper B critiques the plain meaning rule's formalism and advocates approaches aimed at effectuating the parties' intent.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal reform, rejection, and institutional responses to interpretive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes proposed legislative/revision activity by the NCCUSL and questions about adopting revised Article 2 provisions, whereas Paper B documents courts' rejection of the plain meaning rule and contrasts that trend with continued arbitrator reliance, highlighting differing institutional trajectories for change.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive rules affect enforcement outcomes and fidelity to parties' intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how revisions to the statute of frauds and parol evidence rule would change which agreements are enforceable and what evidence shapes terms, and Paper B shows that reliance on the plain meaning rule can produce arbitration awards contrary to the parties' past practices and actual intentions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68tennlrev73!!ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

shared_topics.topic: effectuating the parties' intent as the primary goal of contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the central objective of contract interpretation as giving effect to the parties' mutual intent — Paper A frames this as the rationale for rejecting or limiting the plain meaning rule in arbitration, while Paper B organizes Tennessee law around discovering and implementing that intent when resolving ambiguities.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence (past practice, parol evidence) in resolving meaning
shared_topics.justification: Both manuscripts engage the question whether and when tribunals may consider evidence beyond the four corners of the document — Paper A critiques the plain meaning rule's exclusion of extrinsic evidence (including past practice) in labor arbitration, and Paper B addresses use of extrinsic materials to resolve ambiguities and the evidentiary difficulties that arise.

shared_topics.topic: how to resolve ambiguities caused by imperfect drafting (including doctrines like contra proferentem)
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront interpretive problems arising from imprecise or faulty drafting: Paper B directly analyzes doctrines such as contra proferentem and offers solutions for Tennessee courts, while Paper A examines how reliance on literal/plain-meaning readings can misinterpret agreements when drafting fails and proposes alternative approaches.

shared_topics.topic: tension between rigid textual rules and more contextual/systematic interpretive frameworks (and recommending alternatives)
shared_topics.justification: Each article critiques rule‑laden or overly textualist approaches (Paper A criticizing continued arbitrator use of the plain meaning rule despite judicial rejection; Paper B noting the maze of conflicting canons) and both propose more systematic, flexible methods for resolving contract ambiguity.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70stjohnslrev239!!ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus intent‑oriented/contextual contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the plain meaning rule as a text‑centered interpretive approach and argues for alternatives that prioritize effectuating the parties' intentions; Paper B likewise contrasts formal doctrinal labels with whether the parties' underlying bargaining purpose should excuse performance, debating when courts should honor the parties' actual motivations rather than a literal reading of the contract.

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and weight of extrinsic evidence and supervening circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how the plain meaning rule excludes extrinsic evidence (past practices, parties' intent) and the implications of that exclusion in arbitration; Paper B examines whether courts will treat exceptional supervening events (which are extrinsic to the contract text) as a basis for discharge under frustration of purpose and how often such circumstances are actually credited.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between black‑letter authorities (Restatements/treatises) and adjudicative practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes the UCC and Restatement rejection of the plain meaning rule yet documents continued arbitrator reliance on it despite judicial movement away; Paper B shows that although treatises and the Restatements recognize frustration of purpose, courts rarely grant relief on that ground, highlighting a gap between doctrinal statements and case law.

shared_topics.topic: role of gap‑filler/default doctrines and judicial reluctance to apply them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys alternatives to strict plain‑meaning textualism (including doctrines that imply terms or consider context) as gap‑filling interpretive tools; Paper B interrogates the Second Restatement's treatment of frustration as a potential gap‑filler and analyzes policy and doctrinal reasons courts are reluctant to use such default doctrines to discharge contractual obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64dukelj605!!Article: HOLLYWOOD DEALS: SOFT CONTRACTS FOR HARD MARKETS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: HOLLYWOOD DEALS: SOFT CONTRACTS FOR HARD MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: how levels of contractual formalization and interpretive doctrine determine enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the plain meaning rule (an interpretive doctrine) can make ostensibly clear contract language decisive and exclude other evidence, affecting whether and how agreements are enforced in labor arbitration; Paper B studies how parties choose degrees of formalization (hard vs soft contracts) to calibrate legal enforceability in Hollywood transactions and how that choice affects expected enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence and past practice in resolving disputes over incomplete or ambiguous agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on arbitrators' exclusion or consideration of extrinsic evidence (including past practice) under the plain meaning rule and the consequences for discerning parties' intentions; Paper B documents how courts, industry practices, and reputational norms are used as evidentiary and enforcement mechanisms when unsigned or informal 'soft' agreements are disputed.

shared_topics.topic: the trade-off between contractual certainty and transactional flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques a rigid plain-meaning approach for producing results inconsistent with parties' intended bargains and therefore reducing the ability to effectuate negotiated expectations; Paper B models the choice of contract formality as a deliberate trade-off—less formal (soft) contracts sacrifice certainty to gain flexibility and lower transaction costs.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicators and dispute-resolution institutions shape commercial practice through interpretive choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines arbitrators' frequent reliance on the plain meaning rule despite courts and commentators rejecting it, showing how arbitral interpretation affects labor-contract outcomes; Paper B surveys court opinions and industry dispute histories to show how judicial treatment of informal/unsigned deals influences the prevalence and design of soft contracting in the film industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71indlj45!!ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: when literal contract language should yield to non-textual considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts may reconstruct or override contractual terms (through doctrines like impracticability, mistake, penalties, and good faith) rather than enforcing literal text, and Paper B examines arbitrators' invocation of the plain-meaning rule versus occasions when they should set aside literal wording to achieve parties' intended outcomes in collective bargaining agreements.

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence, past practice, and trade usage in ascertaining parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how interpretation relies on expectations, norms, and commercial practice and when courts move beyond those expectations to reconstruct contracts, while Paper B focuses on the plain-meaning rule's tendency to exclude extrinsic evidence (including past practice) and argues for allowing such evidence in labor arbitration to effectuate the parties' intent.

shared_topics.topic: criteria and standards for excusing, modifying, or interpreting contractual obligations (e.g., unexpectedness, ambiguity, opportunism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops specific principles (unselfish performance and loss alignment) and emphasizes unexpected events as a trigger for excuse or reconstruction, and Paper B engages with the standards arbitrators use (plain meaning versus contextual approaches) to decide when to interpret literally or allow deviation based on ambiguity, established practice, or equitable considerations.

shared_topics.topic: the normative justification for intervention in private agreements (freedom of contract vs fairness/efficiency concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends judicial reconstruction against freedom-of-contract and economic objections by appealing to fairness and strategic-behavior mitigation, and Paper B critiques the plain-meaning rule on doctrinal and pragmatic grounds, arguing for interpretive approaches that better serve the parties' intentions and fairness in labor relations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54depaullrev1077!!ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: limits of formalist/textualist contract interpretation in real-world practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the dominance of single-model legal and economic thinking (including strict rule application) in addressing complex deals, arguing that rigid models fail to capture how lawyers actually manage transactions; Paper B documents how the plain meaning/textualist rule in arbitration produces outcomes at odds with parties' real-world expectations and continues despite courts' rejection of the rule.

shared_topics.topic: the role of extrinsic evidence, past practice, and parties' intent in construing agreements

papers.node_id: 95indlj485!!ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias
papers.abstract:
Should contractual rights be transferable? It depends. Rights holders generally prefer to have the option to transfer their rights, whereas those subject to duties often have reasons to prefer rights to be nontransferable. If transferability were treated as an ordinary contract issue, the law would not exhibit a preference either for or against it. Contractual rights would be transferable where the parties agreed to make them transferable; likewise, they would be nontransferable where the parties agreed to make them nontransferable, unless there was some special reason to doubt that the term was the product of genuine agreement. Where the parties had not made an express provision either way, courts would apply a default rule crafted to maximize the joint value of the contract; the content of the rule would depend, for the most part, on whether transferability or non-transferability would maximize the parties' joint value.
But that is not contemporary contract law's approach. Instead, the law of assignment--the body of doctrine mostly responsible for governing transfers of contractual rights--is biased towards transferability. Consider these examples:
(i) "Grudge Assignee": Oliver hires Andrea to replace the floors in Oliver's home. The contract says nothing about whether Andrea's rights are assignable. After Andrea does the work, Oliver gets into financial difficulty and asks for more time to pay the debt. Tatiana, Oliver's neighbor, has held a long-standing grudge against Oliver and sees the chance to drive him into bankruptcy. She pays Andrea to assign the debt to her. In return, Tatiana agrees to transfer the proceeds of any successful legal action to Andrea; Tatiana's interest in suing Oliver is purely spiteful. A court is likely to allow Tatiana's suit against Oliver to proceed: contractual rights are generally assignable in the absence of agreement to the contrary and there is no exception for malicious transferees (or "assignees").
(ii) "Disputatious Developer": Ophelia Corp. is a construction company. It agrees to build an apartment block for Andrew, a property developer. Construction contracts are notoriously prone to disputes, so Ophelia Corp. wants to deal only with Andrew, with whom Ophelia has a long-term relationship. At Ophelia's insistence, the written contract contains nonassignment clauses. The contract states: "This contract is not assignable." For good measure, the contract also says that Andrew "shall not assign his rights under the contract." Later, however, Andrew suffers from a cash-flow problem, and so he purports to sell his contractual rights to Donald, a developer with a terrible reputation for litigiousness. A court is likely to recognize the assignment and to allow Donald to sue Ophelia in the event of a contractual dispute. Despite theapparently plain language of the clauses, most courts will construe them to preserve rather than deny the power to assign.
(iii) "Interloping Bank": Oscar's Bakery needs flour, so it enters into a year-long flour supply contract with Acme Flour Corp. Oscar wants to ensure that it is only obligated to Acme because assignment increases the risk of paying the wrong creditor due to administrative error. At the time of the contract, Acme does not see any particular reason it would want to transfer its rights to someone else, so Acme happily agrees to a contractual clause stating: "The parties hereby agree that any attempt by Acme to assign its rights under this contract is totally and absolutely invalid, void, and of no effect." Nevertheless, Acme later purports to assign its rights to payment under the contract to Terrestrial Bank as part of a refinancing transaction. Under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.), the nonassignment clause is void and Acme is liable to suit by Terrestrial Bank.
In each of these cases, the defendant may object that she did not expect this plaintiff, a stranger to the contract, to be able to sue her. She may say that she would never have dreamed of entering into a contract with this person (as in "Grudge Assignee"). She may complain that she sought to protect herself from exactly this contingency by negotiating a clause prohibiting it (as in "Disputatious Developer" and "Interloping Bank"). In each of the examples, however, the court is likely to reject these arguments and allow the suit to proceed. Contractual rights are generally assignable, subject only to narrow exceptions (such as in "Grudge Assignee"). Attempts to make them nonassignable will often be interpreted not to have this effect (as in "Disputatious Developer") unless the parties use a special form of words. Even where the parties choose the "magic words" that would be interpreted so as to render the assignment void (as in "Interloping Bank"), a court will often be required to disregard this aspect of the parties' agreement because of Article 9's mandatory assignability rule.
These examples illustrate what courts say explicitly: "the law looks 'with favor on the free assignability of rights and frowns on restrictions that would limit or preclude assignability.'"In this regard, the law treats contractual rights quite differently from contractual duties. Contractual duties may sometimes bedelegatedto, and vicariously performed by, someone else. But even then, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise, the original promisor remains subject to the duty she undertook and will be liable if it is not performed.For obvious reasons--trustworthiness, competence, creditworthiness--the law recognizes that the identity of the person subject to a contractual duty and amenable to suit for breach is typically crucial. But the law has a general tendency to treat the identity of a contractualrightholder as insignificant. In this regard, contract law has come a long way since medieval common law, which held that contractual rights were, by their nature, personal to the parties and hence nontransferable.A detailed examination of the law shows that contemporary contract law tends to hold that rights should be transferable, regardless of party intention.
Contract law's bias in favor of transferability, then, is not based on freedom of contract: indeed, it runs counter to contemporary contract law's general principle of party autonomy. If not freedom of contract, what explains the law's move to a pro-transferability policy? The shift to alienability appears to be a symptom of broader currents in economic thought.Scholars of economic history have analyzed capitalism's "tendency to detach economic action from social context[]."For Max Weber, the transferability of contractual rights is part of "that legal state of affairs which is required by advanced and completely commercial social intercourse" and "indispensable for a modern capitalistic society."Echoing Weber, John R. Commons claimed that "modern capitalism begins with the assignment and negotiability of contracts."The transferability of contractual rights is generally thought of as an essential component of the prevailing economic regime. In particular, permitting transferability allows the transferor to use its contractual rights as collateral and hence serves the transferor's interest by increasing its ability to access credit. According to a leading contracts treatise, if most contract rights were not assignable, our modern credit economy could not exist.The policy is felt most strongly in the case of debts--that is, contractual obligations to pay agreed sums of money.Contemporary market economies have long reached the stage where debt is conceptualized as a kind of asset.The commodification of debt is a centuries-old process, but it has reached new heights in recent years with the intense financialization of modern economies.Nor is the process limited to debts: other kinds of rights to sue for breach are also treated as marketable commodities.
Although making contractual promises transferable might be regarded by some as a symptom of moral decline,this Article does not seek to mount a general critique of the transferability of contractual rights. Rather, it contends that courts and legislatures have overestimated the arguments for transferability. While the economic arguments to allow parties toopt into assignability are powerful, the economic arguments forforcingassignability upon them appear to be weak. The law's pro-assignability policy seems to be based either on circular conceptual arguments that contractual rights are a form of property and must therefore be transferable, or on simplistic instrumental arguments that predate the emergence of sophisticated economic analysis of law. Grant Gilmore, a leading supporter of the policy, admitted that his belief in it was "instinctive and irrational, not logical and reasoned."This Article contends that none of the available arguments is sufficient to justify the law's pro-transferability bias. In particular, the social benefits of transferability are typically adequately factored into the initial contractual negotiation. If transferability serves social welfare, then we can expect parties to bargain for it or, at least, not to agree to a nonassignment clause.
Conversely, legal doctrine in its current form systematically underestimates the reasons for restricting transfers of contractual rights. Contractual exchange, even under capitalism, is very far from an impersonal affair. As the most sophisticated contract-law scholarship stresses, parties to contracts combine legally enforceable promises with nonlegal mechanisms based on trust, reciprocity, and social sanctions.Legally enforceable contracts are typically embedded in a broader set of relations between the parties. It is not feasible, or even possible, to make precise, legally enforceable provisions for all contingencies. Parties often expect that, in a spirit of give-and-take, the terms of their exchange will be adjusted and renegotiated during performance. They fear, however, that the other party will exploit changed circumstances. They know they cannot rely on courts to protect the full extent of their interests, so they want the other party to be disposed towards cooperative behavior.
As a result, the identity of one's contractual counterparty is often crucial. Parties choose their business partners based on prior experience with that party, on thatparty's reputation for trustworthy and reasonable behavior, and on that other party's need to maintain a good reputation in the marketplace. Assignment may render the duty holder liable to suit by someone with whom she has no experience and who has no reputation for trustworthiness and reasonableness. The transferee may also be free of reputational constraints that bound the transferor. The most extreme example is assignment to a "vulture fund," an entity with no incentive to be reasonable and with every incentive to play "hardball" to develop an aggressive and fearsome reputation. These considerations are essential to the way parties use contract law, and they cannot be brushed aside with assertions that disregarding them will make it easier for contractual right holders to obtain credit.
The main purpose of this Article is to challenge contract law's pro-assignability policy. As things stand, the best explanation of the law's transferability bias is that it makes life easier for banks and other financial industry players, who have long had an outsized influence on the making of American secured-transactions law.At the very least, the aim of the Article is to provoke other scholars to produce a more compelling justification for the policy than has previously been offered.For, despite the topic's obvious importance, the literature on the contemporary American law of assignment is surprisingly slim. The assignability of tort and copyright claims has attracted recent scholarly attention,and a few articles address assignability in particular contractual contexts.But very few discuss the topic as a whole.Theissue has attracted some attention among doctrinally oriented scholars of Anglo-Commonwealth commercial law in recent years,but this important aspect of contract law rarely features in larger debates about the nature and purpose of the institution.The few theoretical treatments of contract law to take notice of the assignability rules accept those rules as given. Thus, Curtis Bridgeman uses the law's attitude to the transferability of contractual rights to criticize interpretive theories that view contract law as a reflection of the moral obligation to keep one's promises."Allowing such transferability," Bridgeman points out, "is at the least not required by the moral obligation to keep one's promises, and in fact requiring the promisor to deliver performance to a stranger may go beyond what the morality of promising would even allow."Bridgeman does not question the justifiability of the assignability rules; rather, he contends that this feature shows that contract law, as it currently stands, is less concerned with promissory morality and more with protecting "property-like" rights to performance.Bridgeman is right to note a tension between certain conceptions of contract law and the assignability rules. Because his aim is to interpret rather than to evaluate contract law, however, he does not consider the possibility that the assignability rules might be rejected or changed.
In Part I, this Article explores the reasons that parties to contracts might want to make contractual rights transferable or nontransferable. Part II explains the current law of assignability and its pro-transferability bias. Part III considers possible justifications for this bias and finds none of them persuasive. Part IV explores what the law would look like if freed from the policy in favor of transferability.

questions.question: Should contractual rights be presumptively transferable when parties do not expressly address transferability, or should nontransferability be the default?

Do the economic and social benefits of legally forcing transferability (for example, easing access to credit and marketability of claims) outweigh the harms caused by undermining counterparty-specific reliance, trust, and reputational mechanisms?
To what extent do contracting parties internalize the social value of transferability in their bargaining (so that default legal rules imposing transferability are unnecessary)?

shared_topics.topic: the tension between background/default rules and party autonomy/express terms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze doctrines that allow background legal rules to displace or reinterpret parties' explicit agreements—Paper A shows how incorporation of trade usages can override express contract terms, and Paper B shows how default assignability rules (and courts' construction of nonassignment clauses) routinely undermine parties' attempts to make rights nontransferable.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules affect transaction costs and commercial efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with economic tradeoffs of legal rules for commerce—Paper A frames the incorporation approach in terms of specification costs and interpretive error costs, while Paper B evaluates the gains from transferability (credit access, marketability) against costs to reputation, trust, and cooperative contracting.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on UCC-driven regimes that shape contract outcomes—Paper A studies the Code's incorporation strategy (Articles 1 and 2 and proposed revisions) and its judicial application, and Paper B analyzes Article 9 and the UCC's role in rendering nonassignment clauses ineffective in many commercial contexts.

shared_topics.topic: questioning doctrinal justifications and the case for reform
shared_topics.justification: Each paper critiques dominant theoretical or policy rationales for entrenched doctrines and urges reconsideration—Paper A empirically challenges the assumptions underpinning incorporation of trade usages and recommends shifting toward a more formalist default for B2B deals, while Paper B argues that the pro-assignability bias lacks persuasive justification and should be rethought.

shared_topics.topic: litigation realities, evidentiary practices, and strategic behavior enabled by doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how doctrines interact with litigation dynamics—Paper A documents that trade usages are often proved by self-serving party testimony and affect summary judgment and strategic behavior, and Paper B highlights how assignability rules enable third-party plaintiffs (including hostile assignees or financiers) to litigate in ways that parties originally did not anticipate.
