papers.node_id: 88michlrev489!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.
papers.abstract:
Among the topics addressed by moral philosophy is the obligation to keep one's promises.  To many philosophers, there is something strange (or, at least, something calling for explanation) in the idea that moral obligations can be created simply by an individual's saying so -- yet this is what seems to happen when a person makes a promise.  Consequently, there is by now a large body of literature attempting to identify the exact source and nature of this moral obligation.
Contract law, too, has something to do with promises, so philosophers of law (and philosophically minded lawyers) often draw on philosophical theories about promising when writing about contract law.  For example, a recent book by Charles Fried purports "to show how a complex legal institution, contract, can be traced to and is determined by a small number of basic moral principles. . . ."In Fried's view, a recognition of the proper philosophical basis of contract law leads to conclusions profoundly different from those that would result from any attempt to rest contract law on other social policies, such as economic efficiency or the redistribution of wealth.
My thesis is that such claims on behalf of philosophical theories of promising are greatly exaggerated.  In particular, analyses such as Fried's have little or no relevance to those parts of contract law that govern the proper remedies for breach, the conditions under which the promisor is excused from her duty to perform, or the additional obligations (such as implied warranties) imputed to the promisor as an implicit part of her promise.  These doctrines, which serve to define the exact scope of contractual obligations, are often referred to as"background rules" or "default rules," although the term "default rules" more commonly refers only to those rules which the parties are free to vary by appropriate language in their contract.As not all contract rules can be varied in this way, I will use the term "background rules" to refer to both waivable and nonwaivable rules.
not asserting here that philosophical theories about promising can have no implications for any part of contract law.  Such theories may well have implications for questions about the proper scope of freedom of contract -- that is, questions about whether any given rule ought to be merely a default rule, or whether it ought to be mandatory for all parties.  In addition,certainphilosophical theories may have implications for the proper content of contract law's background rules.  For example, theories that justify the enforceability of promises on grounds of economic efficiency, or on the special value of certain kinds of relationships, may imply that the law should adopt those background rules that are most efficient or that best promote the most highly valued kinds of relationships.
Other philosophical theories, however -- including the one endorsed by Fried -- have no such implications for the content of the law's background rules.  These theories ground the enforceability of promises on considerations of individual freedom and autonomy, or on the principle of fidelity to one's prior statements or commitments.  In a nutshell, the fidelity principle is consistent with any set of background rules because those rules merely fill out the details of what it is a person has to remain faithful to, or what a person's prior commitment is deemed to be.  Thus, while fidelity may dictate that a promisor must live up to the obligations described by any set of background rules the law has adopted, it cannot guide the legal system in deciding which background rules to adopt in the first place.  The principle of individual freedom is equally unhelpful, for it implies only that individuals should be left free to change whatever default rule the law adopts as a starting point.  Once again, some other value must be invoked to explain why one starting point ought to be picked by the law in preference to another.
If I am right, this means that it is not enough to reject notions such as economic efficiency, or theories that value certain kinds of relationships more highly than others, as insufficient or incorrect justifications for the basic proposition that promises ought to be enforced.  Even ifthose theories are rejected at this most basic level, further argument is needed to explain why they are inadmissible bases for selecting the law's background rules or starting points, and, if so, to explain what other values ought to be used instead.  Unfortunately, current writings bringing philosophical analysis to bear on contract law have focused almost entirely on the more basic question of why promises ought to be enforced at all, and have tended to overlook this second level of analysis.  This frequently leads to careless or ad hoc statements concerning the proper content of contract law's background rules.
Part I of this article presents a more detailed survey of recent philosophical writings about promises, for the benefit of legal readers who may be unfamiliar with that literature.  Part II then discusses the role of background rules in contract law, and shows why the content of those rules cannot be derived from philosophical theories based on individual liberty, or on ideals such as fidelity or truthfulness.  Finally, Part III examines the writings of Charles Fried and Randy Barnett to illustrate the consequences of attempting to apply philosophy to contract law without addressing these problems.  These two authors have supplied the most comprehensive attempts to give contract law a philosophical grounding, yet each falls into exactly this error.

questions.question: Whether philosophical theories that justify the enforceability of promises (for example, theories grounded in fidelity or individual autonomy) can determine which default or background rules contract law should adopt to define the scope of contractual obligations.

Whether rejecting instrumental justifications for enforcing promises (for example, economic-efficiency or relationship-value arguments) is sufficient to exclude those justifications from selecting the content of contract-law default rules, or whether additional normative reasons are required.
What normative criteria or values should guide the choice among alternative default/background rules in contract law when philosophical accounts of promising underdetermine those choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42jlegalstud1!!ARTICLE: Conceptualizing Contractual Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conceptualizing Contractual Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: normative criteria for choosing interpretive/default contractual rules (welfare/efficiency vs fidelity/autonomy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models an ideal enforcer who selects interpretive rules to maximize social welfare and contrasts that with courts that aim at accuracy; Paper B surveys philosophical accounts (fidelity, autonomy) and economic efficiency, arguing that fidelity/autonomy do not by themselves determine which background rules the law should adopt and that efficiency is a competing justificatory standard.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape parties' ex ante contract drafting and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how an interpretive rule alters parties' choices over contract length, reliance on trial evidence, and sellers' sunk investment, showing rule design changes investment and relationship formation; Paper B treats background/default rules and waivability as central determinants of what obligations parties face and therefore as shaping how parties draft agreements and what terms they will accept or attempt to vary.

shared_topics.topic: the relation between contract text and extrinsic/contextual evidence in fixing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models contract words as one of multiple signals (contract text, performance, pleadings, trial evidence) and studies how an enforcer should weigh them to infer parties' intended type; Paper B emphasizes that background rules fill in details beyond explicit promises and questions whether philosophical theories of promising can dictate which extrinsic facts or implied terms should constitute the promisor's obligation.

shared_topics.topic: the proper design and scope of background/default rules (mandatory vs waivable rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is centrally concerned with whether background rules should be mandatory or merely default and what principles should govern that choice; Paper A engages this issue functionally by showing when an optimal interpretive rule will induce parties to write detailed contracts or rely on trials and when the enforcer should limit evidence or thereby effectively mandate certain information-revealing practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: role of background/default rules (U.C.C. gap-fillers) in resolving form conflicts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how section 2-207 pushes courts to rely on U.C.C. gap-fillers when forms conflict and reports practitioners' attitudes toward that fallback; Paper B analyzes the normative status of background/default rules in contract law and argues that philosophical theories of promising do not determine which default rules should be chosen.

shared_topics.topic: scope of contractual obligations (warranties and remedies) as background rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that battle-of-the-forms disputes frequently turn on unsettled nonimmediate terms like warranties and remedies and how those are supplied by the U.C.C.; Paper B treats implied warranties and remedial doctrines as examples of background rules whose content must be justified independently of broad philosophical accounts of promise enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: fit between formal doctrine and commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates how businesses actually behave under section 2-207 and whether doctrine reflects marketplace realities; Paper B critiques how abstract philosophical accounts of promising are often disconnected from the practical task of choosing and justifying the law's background rules and mandatory/default structure.

shared_topics.topic: principles of formation and consent (offer/acceptance, conditional acceptances)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrinal formation questions under the mirror-image rule, section 2-207(1)'s "definite and seasonable" acceptance and conditioning language, and their practical effects; Paper B engages with the underlying notions of consent, autonomy, and fidelity that are invoked to justify enforcing promises and the limits of those principles for settling formation and scope issues.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: how contract remedies and background/default rules shape incentives to breach, renegotiate, or settle (the economics of 'efficient breach')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines like expectation damages and mitigation create incentives for loss-sharing, renegotiation, and settlements in relational and market contracts and treats 'efficient breach' as an outcome of the law in action; Paper B treats remedies and background rules as the legal starting points whose selection (e.g., efficiency-oriented defaults) will materially affect parties' behavior, arguing that philosophical accounts of promising do not by themselves determine those defaults.

shared_topics.topic: whether moral/philosophical theories of promising (fidelity, autonomy) can determine the content of contract background rules and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly argues that fidelity- or autonomy-based philosophical theories cannot uniquely prescribe which background rules or remedial defaults the law should adopt; Paper A engages the same normative terrain by contrasting moral norms (a deal is a deal) with pragmatic legal rules and business norms that permit breach and adjustment, questioning the import of moralizing rhetoric in judicial and scholarly accounts.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal, predictable legal rules and the law-in-action of negotiated, informal adjustments (formal rules vs negotiated process rationality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes 'new legal realism' and 'negotiated process rationality,' showing how informal settlements and business practices often govern outcomes more than bright‑line rules; Paper B likewise interrogates whether rules should be mandatory or default (and thus alterable by parties through negotiation), engaging the question of how formal legal choices influence or should defer to private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: the role of specific doctrines (mitigation, foreseeability/Hadley v. Baxendale, and excuse doctrines like impossibility/frustration) in allocating risk and defining the scope of obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds much of its empirical and doctrinal analysis in mitigation, Hadley foreseeability, and excuse doctrines, showing how they limit damages and push parties toward adjustments; Paper B treats precisely these kinds of background rules—remedies and conditions for excuse—as the doctrinal loci whose selection cannot be settled merely by promise-based philosophical justification and must be evaluated on other grounds.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev379!!SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

shared_topics.topic: design and justification of background/default rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on the normative foundations for background or default rules (e.g., UCC defaults) — Paper A analyzes when law-imposed background rules or defaults should substitute for explicit contractual language in light of opportunism and transaction costs, while Paper B interrogates what values (efficiency, fidelity, autonomy) can or cannot legitimately determine the content of those background rules.

shared_topics.topic: when courts or the law should imply terms / intervene in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of legal intervention into incomplete agreements — Paper A develops criteria (bounded rationality, sunk costs, opportunism) for implying terms or creating defaults, and Paper B criticizes attempts to ground post-hoc doctrinal fillings (remedies, implied obligations) in philosophical accounts of promising, arguing that such theories do not by themselves tell courts which terms to imply.

shared_topics.topic: the role of promissory obligations and promissory estoppel in imposing duties beyond explicit consent
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine doctrines that create obligations beyond explicit promises — Paper A treats promissory estoppel as a complicating, fact-sensitive means by which liability can arise and affect freedom from contract, while Paper B surveys moral theories of promise and evaluates their relevance to legal doctrines (including estoppel and implied warranties) that impose or define promisor duties.

shared_topics.topic: consent, freedom-from-contract, and the problem of notice/uncertainty when legal standards impose liability
shared_topics.justification: Both express concern that vague or indeterminate legal standards (e.g., all-things-considered utilitarian tests or reasonableness inquiries in estoppel) can impose obligations contrary to parties' expectations; Paper A emphasizes freedom from contract and the need for clear notice of default rules, and Paper B discusses how autonomy/fidelity theories fail to resolve whether rules should be mandatory or opt-outable, thereby implicating consent and predictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 109columlrev431!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legally enforceable contract terms and informal/relational obligations as governance devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and theorizes a ‘‘braiding’’ of explicit (legally enforceable) clauses and implicit (relational, social) obligations that firms use to govern collaborative innovation; Paper B analyzes how moral theories of promising relate (or fail to determine) the law’s background rules and highlights the distinction between what parties morally commit to and what the legal system actually enforces.

shared_topics.topic: how contracts manage incompleteness and uncertainty in collaborative innovation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how parties facing unforeseeable technology and product specifications use iterative governance processes instead of fully specified ex ante contracts; Paper B examines how legal background/default rules operate to fill gaps in incomplete agreements and argues philosophical accounts do not determine which gap-filling rules the law should adopt.

shared_topics.topic: limits of existing theoretical frameworks to prescribe contract content or governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contemporary contract theory cannot generally solve the problem of ensuring efficient, transaction‑specific investment and post‑uncertainty adjustment in rapidly innovating industries; Paper B argues that prominent philosophical theories about promising (e.g., fidelity or autonomy) cannot by themselves justify or select the concrete background rules and remedies that contract law uses.

shared_topics.topic: the design and role of default/background rules and remedies in deterring opportunism and shaping investments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that governance structures (including non‑enforceable expectations) raise switching costs and constrain opportunism to protect relationship‑specific investments; Paper B focuses on the legal side — how background/default rules and remedies define the scope of obligations and thus affect incentives for performance and opportunistic breach, while disputing that moral theories uniquely determine those defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49akronlrev1!!ARTICLE: Liberty at the Borders of Private Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Liberty at the Borders of Private Law

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between individual liberty/autonomy and contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how specific contract doctrines (e.g., morals clauses, lifestyle covenants, unconscionability) can advance or intrude on individuals' spheres of personal autonomy and privacy; Paper B analyzes philosophical theories (fidelity, individual freedom) that ground the enforceability of promises and assesses their implications for autonomy-based justifications of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of state enforcement (courts) in making private promises coercive
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that judicial enforcement of private legal rights is an exercise of state coercion with direct consequences for liberty; Paper B focuses on the legal rules that define enforceable obligations, remedies, and excuses—i.e., what courts will enforce—and thus engages with the institutional effects of turning promises into legally backed duties.

shared_topics.topic: limits on freedom of contract and whether contractual terms should be waivable or mandatory
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally examines which rules should be default/waivable versus mandatory background rules and how freedom of contract figures into that choice; Paper A raises parallel concerns about whether the law should allow enforcement of certain private contractual terms (e.g., morals clauses, lifestyle covenants, private land-use restrictions) that can systematically undermine liberty, implying limits on enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for choosing contract doctrines (which values should guide background rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that philosophical accounts of promising (fidelity, autonomy) cannot by themselves determine the content of background rules and calls for explicit normative choices about which values should guide rule-selection; Paper A uses liberty as an explicit normative yardstick to evaluate and critique particular contract doctrines and to argue for constructing private law in ways that advance, rather than undermine, liberty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20ncjltechon267!!ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS

shared_topics.topic: whether private promises/terms should define legally enforceable rights in contexts of unequal bargaining power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how promises and contractual undertakings create moral and legal obligations and how background rules fill out the scope of those obligations; Paper B shows that DTC companies’ privacy policies function as consumer contracts that effectively allocate ownership and use of genetic information, raising the same question of whether private agreements should be dispositive when consumers lack meaningful bargaining power or understanding.

shared_topics.topic: when contract rules should be default (waivable) versus mandatory (nonwaivable)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A’s core argument centers on the distinction between background/default rules and the limits of philosophical theories in selecting which rules should be waivable, while Paper B advocates for an external federal statute to impose nonwaivable limits on how DTC firms collect, store, and use genetic data rather than leaving those choices to companies’ privacy terms.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of public policy and extra-contractual values in shaping the content of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that neither fidelity nor individual autonomy suffice to determine the content of background rules and that other values (e.g., efficiency or relational concerns) must be invoked to choose legal starting points; Paper B explicitly invokes public-policy concerns—consumer protection, privacy, and societal risks—to justify statutory limits on private contracting over genetic information.

shared_topics.topic: the sufficiency and quality of consent in consumer contracting (information asymmetry and disclosure failures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises issues about freedom of contract and the normative force of promises without resolving how consent defects should alter background rules; Paper B documents how consumers typically ignore or do not understand privacy policies for DTC tests, calling into question whether such consent legitimately authorizes the transfer and use of highly sensitive genetic data.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81uchilrev53!!SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that philosophical theories about promising (e.g., fidelity, autonomy) cannot by themselves determine the content of contract law's background or default rules, and Paper B shows that the economic 'precaution' model is only a special-case formalism and that rational-choice theory does not uniquely imply a single tort rule absent further restrictions — both thus critique relying solely on an abstract theory to pick concrete legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: how to choose the form of legal standards or default rules (negligence vs strict liability; waivable vs mandatory contract defaults)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether particular contract rules should be default/waivable or mandatory and criticizes philosophical accounts for failing to guide that choice, while Paper B analyzes the relationship between negligence and strict liability (showing strict liability as a special case) and demonstrates that which liability standard is efficient depends on informational and contextual factors.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency versus other justificatory values in shaping law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts arguments that enforce promises on grounds of economic efficiency or relational value with theories grounded in autonomy/fidelity and shows the former can have content implications for background rules, and Paper B explicitly uses law-and-economics models (and engages Posner/Epstein debates) to assess when efficiency-based rules like the Hand Rule or strict liability are appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: need for additional constraints, context, or empirical support beyond formal theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that rejecting efficiency-based justifications still leaves open why certain background rules should be chosen and calls for further argument about competing values, and Paper B emphasizes that models must be paired with empirical evidence and that different informational environments can make a rule efficient in one context but not another.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally argues that moral/philosophical theories about promising (e.g., fidelity or individual liberty) cannot by themselves determine which background/default rules contract law should adopt; Paper B confronts the normative implications of different doctrinal starting points (formal vs contextual rules) and thus implicates the question of what normative bases justify particular background rules.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency as a justificatory criterion for selecting background/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies economic efficiency as one candidate theory that could guide which background rules the law adopts and distinguishes it from fidelity/autonomy grounds; Paper B treats efficiency and private‑ordering benefits as central to explaining why formal, predictable rules (e.g., New York law) may be preferred by commercial actors.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Law and Economics and the Rule of Law The Sixteenth Annual National Student Federalist Society Symposium on Law and Public Policy -- 1997: PANEL IV: HOW SHOULD JUDGES USE ECONOMICS?: THREE PROPOSALS TO HARNESS PRIVATE INFORMATION IN CONTRACT

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Contractual Incompleteness: A Transactional Perspective

papers.node_id: 75molrev493!!Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism
papers.title: Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism
papers.abstract:
An ever growing body of case lawand scholarshiphas fashioned a rigid dichotomy between sophisticated and unsophisticated parties in a widearray of contract inquiries. Courts mention party sophistication in determining whether the parties intended to form a contractand what they meant by the terms they used.They determine the enforceability of reliance disclaimers,exculpatory clausesand liquidated damages provisionsbased, at least in part, on party sophistication. Courts also reference sophistication in determining whether a party can avoid a contract on the grounds of mistake or fraud.While consumers are commonly contrasted with sophisticated parties,the relevance of party sophistication is not limited to consumer transactions. Its relevance transcends any one area of substantive law - arising in commercial, business, employment, franchise, insurance, family and property disputes, among others.
For its ubiquity, party sophistication remains an unstudied and largely unaddressed question in contract law. Although they often mention sophistication, the extensive contract treatises of Williston, Corbin and Farnsworth do not dedicate a section to clarifying what is meant by the terminology.This Article begins the discussion.
It is not certain why the dichotomy between sophisticated and unsophisticated parties has grown in significance. To be sure, courts often use "sophistication" as code for socio-economic status - wealth and education arecommon attributes of individuals that are deemed sophisticated."Sophisticated" parties, whether individuals or business entities, are presumed to have access to information, resources to allocate risk and experience or predisposition to counteract cognitive bias.Often, a court's indication that a party is "sophisticated" is used to signal that, even though the result may seem harsh, it should be interpreted as fair. But none of these descriptions elucidates the trend of increased reference to sophistication. The trend appears to be best explained by examining what is happening in contract law on a theoretical level.
Scholars have observed that contract law is experiencing a period of renewed formalism - which has been variably described as "neoformalism" and "anti-anti-formalism."However, this new formalism, which values the literal content of a contract and the autonomy of the parties, has not completely abandoned the normative concerns characteristic of the realist period. At least nominally, through the dichotomy based on party sophistication, the law has attempted to preserve concern about the context of a transaction.
In the new formalism, sophisticated parties are held to a different set of rules,grounded in freedom of contract. It is presumed ex post that a sophisticated party was aware of what to bargain forand read (or should have read) and understood (or should have understood) the terms of a written agreement.Sophisticated parties are expected to negotiate ably and order contract risks sensibly. It is, therefore, now an accepted tenet of contract law that "freedom of contract prevails in an arm's-length transaction between sophisticated parties . . . and in the absence of countervailing public policy concerns there is no reason to relieve them of the consequences of their bargain."Courts frequently state that it is not their role to interfere with or "rewrite" the terms of a deal for sophisticated parties.
This Article does not advocate abandoning this status-based dichotomy; rather, it argues that courts need to define sophistication, which cannot be done with ready, bright lines. As currently used, "sophistication" is a slippery word. Courts have not established clear, meaningful criteria for sophistication and often presume without analysis that parties to a commercial transaction are sophisticated.In this regard, party sophistication has served as a pretense of concern for context that allows courts to avoid more difficult questions about the relative positions of the contracting parties. Often, labeling the parties "sophisticated" allows the court to avoid further discussion of any disparities in the parties' bargaining positions. However, the label should not lead; rather, the court should apply a rigorous fact-driven analysis to determine whether assignment of the sophistication label is appropriate.
Absent evidence of a deliberative approach to assessing sophistication, and for want of the guidance a definition would provide, some cases have been wrongly decided. It is evident that, in at least some instances, courts have erroneously deemed parties sophisticated and, in so doing, denied those parties the benefits of certain defenses or arguments.For example, where a party is not sophisticated, she will more likely be able to a establish mistake of fact or fraud in the inducement. Similarly, for unsophisticated parties, a relaxed parol evidence rule is often applied.
Of course, the meaning of party sophistication is of significance to the contracting parties when they find themselves litigating a dispute; it is important to them that the case is appropriately and fairly decided. Further, to theextent that sophistication is treated as a question of fact,the issue is conclusively decided in the trial court and is reversible only if "clearly erroneous."But the importance of defining sophistication is not limited to the handful of questionable cases where a trial court may have erred in rashly deeming a party sophisticated.
Party sophistication has even broader significance for contracting parties and for the goals of formalism - certainty and predictability in the law. A deliberative approach to sophistication would enable courts to reach fair decisions for just and identifiable reasons, which would develop the law in a way that enables parties to contract with more certainty about their obligations and better ability to predict whether their deals will be enforced as written.
Part II of this Article positions the discussion in a theoretical context and describes the significance of party sophistication as a compromise between formalist and realist concerns. Part III collects examples of settings in which courts have used party sophistication as a tool to organize the world of contracting parties and, with that, the applicable legal principles. For sophisticated parties, in answering a wide array of contract questions, courts employ a formalist approach. Part IV begins descriptively and addresses the general lack of meaningful assessment of party sophistication. Drawing upon the review of hundreds of cases, Part IV identifies what appears to be germane to courts as they apply the label of sophistication and details the attributes common among parties that courts have deemed sophisticated.
Finally, Part V presents the central normative claim of this Article: courts should undertake a more exacting, fact-driven approach in addressing party sophistication. Drawing upon the extensive review of case law, Part V provides a definition of sophistication that assesses information and resource asymmetries among the contracting parties. The proposed standard assesses whether a party, relative to the other parties to the contract, has sufficient experience and access to information and resources that the person or entity understands or should understand the intricacies, risks and consequences of the transaction. This standard takes into account the theoretical underpinnings of applying the sophistication label: for knowledgeable and experienced parties dealing in familiar industries, private autonomy should prevail over normative concerns. However, where a party lacks relative knowledge and experience, normative concerns may outbalance the literalism and private autonomy championed by formalism.
In the absence of a meaningful definition of sophistication, however, courts are not actually addressing the context of the deal. Rather, they are simply reciting well-worn cliches about "sophisticated parties dealing at arms' length."

Whether adopting a clear, relative standard of party sophistication (based on comparative information/resource/experience asymmetries) would improve the fairness, predictability, and doctrinal consistency of contract enforcement

shared_topics.topic: when courts should defer to literal contractual terms versus intervene

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between formalist freedom-of-contract and context-sensitive fairness

shared_topics.topic: party bargaining power/sophistication and remedies for unequal contracts

papers.node_id: 49ucdavislrev1097!!ARTICLE: Contract Meta-Interpretation
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contract Meta-Interpretation
papers.abstract:
Interpretive questions are the core questions of contract law. Problems of assent, unexpected circumstances, and remedies can all be conceived through an interpretive lens.In addition to their theoretical and structural significance, interpretive questions are also among the most frequently litigated matters in contract cases.
Still, there is little agreement on the right approach to interpreting contracts.The interpretive debate centers on the tension between the impulse to do justice in individual cases and the desire to impose rules of general scope and application; this tension leads some (the "contextualists") to favor a broad inquiry into the intent of contracting partiesand others (the "textualists") to favor a narrower, supposedly more predictable interpretive focus on the text of written contracts.The debate plays out along several dimensions: the contextualists focus more on the subjective intent of the parties, whereas the textualists objectivize "intent";the contextualists admit a larger base of evidence whereas the textualists prefer a smaller base;the contextualists consider post-formation information, whereas the textualists would require that courts adopt the epistemic limitations of the parties at the time of contract formation.
do not wish to hide my own biases: I think textualism, at least in its stronger forms, is a misguided approach to the interpretation of contracts, both on grounds of justice and grounds of efficiency.In my view, the commercial and juristic gains of enforcing the deal that parties actually made, when it is possible to discern that deal, clearly overwhelm the benefits that might derive from the purported regularity or reduced administrative costs of a textualist regime.Moreover, I dispute that textualist regimes even achieve the predictability they purport to achieve or that they are any more administrable than rules that pay more attention to what individual parties wanted (or what reasonable parties in their circumstances would have wanted).
To advance the debate, however, my initial goal in this Article is to attempt to convince the opposing sides that there need not be a single answer - a single regime for interpreting contracts.Instead,textualists should recognize that their stated goals can be realized only in some, not in all, cases; contextualists, for their part, should recognize that a commitment to context and to the intent of contracting parties compels the adoption of an approach that looks more like textualism in several important circumstances.
The thesis of this article is straightforward; it has two parts. Importantly, the article's central arguments do not concern contract interpretation itself; they concern meta-interpretation, or the selection of an interpretive regime to use when addressing interpretive questions.The article's first, most general argument is that contracts should be interpreted using the methodology that best suits their circumstances on grounds of morality and policy. Apart from limited exceptions,the methodology that satisfies this criterion will be the one that the parties preferred - or, failing that, the one that reasonable parties in their circumstances would have preferred.The determination of this preference mirrors the underlying interpretive inquiry in contract law.This part of my thesis is not itself original; it is often latent, and occasionally expressed, as a premise in argumentson both sides of the debate about contract interpretation.Usually this principle's role is simply to serve as one step in an argument that leads, monotonically or at least very generally, to a unitary interpretive regime that covers all or most cases.Instead, my argument is that this principle should provide the basis for the dynamic selection of an interpretive regime, a selection that may vary from situation to situation based on many relevant factors.
My second argument is that courts should adopt a contextualist mode of interpretation for determining the parties' choice of an interpretive regime, at least in those cases where the parties' choice of an interpretive regime matters. That is, courts should use all available information to determine the agreement that the parties had, or the agreement that reasonable parties would have had, about their preferred mode of interpretation, whether that mode ultimately be textualist, contextualist, or something else.
call the combination of these two principles meta-contextualism because it uses a contextualist mode of interpretation to answer the meta-interpretive question about what interpretive regime to apply.Though at one level of generality meta-contextualism is sensitive to the circumstances that surround a contract, it tolerates much or all of the principles of textualist interpretation where the circumstances call for it - particularly, although not exclusively,where the parties preferred or would prefer a textualist interpretive regime.
In showing how contract law should be pluralistic in the possibilities of interpretive regimes it considers, I also intend to show that contract law in fact already implements, somewhat covertly, the principles I suggest.For example, we can conceive the parol-evidence rule as an important, though admittedly confused, step toward the recognition that written text does not always carry the same importance in all contractual settings.Similarly, we can harmonize what some commentators have argued is a mandatorycontextualism in the law with the law's occasionally textualist tendencies. And the classic differences between the merchant law and the common law suggest that the regulation of private contracts is open to plurality in interpretive methodologies.
This article proceeds in two stages. First, in Part I, I critique a variety of what I consider to be problematic arguments in favor of the proposition that all parties, or a broad class of them, do or should prefer a single interpretive regime.I do this because the field is dominated by strong and often very sophisticated arguments for very particular rules of contract interpretation; I respect these analyses, but I believe they are ultimately mistaken. Having done this, I then in Part II affirmatively build up the more context-sensitive meta-interpretive principles that I have outlined above.In Part III, I briefly show how modern contract law already accommodates some of these principles.
. The Limits of Generalized Solutions to the Meta-Interpretive Problem
A chief contention of my "meta-contextualist" argument - that determining the parties' chosen interpretive regime requires sensitivity to context-specific information about the parties' preferences - relies on the more fundamental proposition that there is no general, context-insensitive way to select a universal interpretive regime (or even one of broad application). If it were possible to show that a single interpretive regime (either textualist or contextualist) were appropriate to all situations, then courts should simply apply that regime; there would be no further meta-interpretive question to decide.
Despite a variety of attempts to present a single interpretive regime as universally optimal - or even just as optimal in a large, very general class of cases- this Part contends that there has been no persuasive account of the reasons or scope for such a general interpretive regime. It does so first by critiquing the theoretical bases of such regimes - for example, the view that all parties, or at least all rational or reasonable parties, will prefer textualist modes of interpretation - and then by critiquing the empirical arguments in favor of such regimes.
To be clear, I define meta-interpretation as the legal determination of the appropriate interpretive regime to apply in a particular case.Determining the legal meaning of the parties' expressions is an interpretive question;determining the mechanism by which to determine that legal meaning is a meta-interpretive question. For example, if a written contract specifies that one of the parties must deliver "a dozen eggs," the meaning of the words "dozen" and "eggs" raise interpretive questions.The different possibilities that a court faces in selecting an interpretive regime for answering this question - for example, relying on a dictionary, or admitting trade usage or course of dealing - raise meta-interpretive questions.
A. Theoretical Derivations About Rational Contracting Parties: Schwartz and Scott on Contract Theory, Risk-Neutrality, and Textualism
In an extremely influential article, Professors Alan Schwartz and Robert Scott in 2003 offered a theoretical economic argument that rational parties - and thus, according to them, business firms - prefer textualism; indeed, I take their argument to be the leading modern statement of the law-and-economics movement's theoretically derived formalism.The argument is subtle, and I have critiqued some of its features in detail in prior work.After summarizing Schwartz and Scott's argument, this Section quickly outlines my prior critique and then offers a new general critique in view of their more recent formulations of the argument.
At the outset, it is important to clarify that I share several significant premises with Schwartz and Scott. In particular, as I have noted above, I endorse their view that a single interpretive regime need not be appropriate in all cases.Moreover, with limited exceptions that I describe in Part III.B, I agree with Schwartz and Scott that the parties' preferences should ordinarily dictate the choice of an interpretive regime.Moreover, even in specific cases where I do not think the parties' preferences should dictate the choice of an interpretive regime, I believe their preferences are relevant to the court's determination of the appropriate interpretive regime to use. With those agreements inmind, we differ only on the mechanism by which the interpretive regime should be chosen in individual cases.
Schwartz and Scott's approach to meta-interpretive questions in contract law is deductive and theoretical; that is, their method to address meta-interpretive questions is to deduce an answer based on the necessary behavior of rational parties, as modeled by formal economics. They do briefly survey empirical evidence that they believe supports their position,but their argument fundamentally attempts to demonstrate on theoretical grounds that rational parties, particularly business firms involving five or more people, are (1) necessarily risk-neutral and (2) as a result of that risk-neutrality, prefer a textualist mode of interpretation.My most practical disagreements with Schwartz and Scott are that I deny that business firms are necessarily risk-neutral and that risk-neutral firms necessarily prefer textualism.
To understand the debate, it will be helpful to elaborate Schwartz and Scott's deductive model in some detail. The essential insight of their model, which is quite intuitively appealing at first, is that a risk-neutral party will be a contract textualist because admitting more evidence increases the costs of litigation without changing the expected value of the court's interpretive result.This conclusion depends on a model of interpretive results as (1) reducible to scalar values that (2) have a mean value that is invariant to the amount of evidence used during the interpretive process.Moreover, their modelof the difference between textualism and contextualism - which I accept for the purposes of this discussion - is also essentially scalar; the different interpretive modes simply allow a court to use a larger or smaller "evidentiary base"to carry out its interpretive process. On one end of the spectrum, a court might flip a coin (using no evidence at all). On the other, a court might use all relevant evidence that the parties submit. Schwartz and Scott's argument for textualism is an argument for what they call the "minimum evidentiary base," which includes specifically "the parties' contract, a narrative concerning whether the parties performed the obligations that the contract appears to require, a standard English language dictionary, and the interpreter's experience and understanding of the world."
have previously given an example of how I understand the way in which Schwartz and Scott intend for their model to work:
Suppose my contracting partner and I agreed on the number fifty. Schwartz and Scott's central conclusion is that even if the larger base of information reduces my risk (say, makes it nearly certain that the court will decide on the number fifty, rather than something between thirty and seventy), using this larger base of information will not be worthwhile because of its costs: I'll have to introduce more evidence, contest more evidence, go through a longer trial, and pay my lawyers more. Given that I didn't care about the risk (formally, the variance) in the court's result in the first place, I would prefer not to pay to reduce it.
My earlier critique of this model was quite technical and drew a distinction between the lack of systematic bias and the affirmative assertion of a statistical mean; it thus depended on the differencebetween uncertainty and probability.But a response to Schwartz and Scott's argument need not be so technical; moreover, a technical response could conceivably fail to respond to a more general insight that their model suggests, which is simply that a contextualist interpretive regime has costs that a textualist interpretive regime might productively avoid.This Section develops a variety of more general responses to Schwartz and Scott's model.

questions.question: Whether courts should select a contract interpretive methodology on a case-by-case basis according to the parties' preferences and the contract's circumstances, rather than applying a single universal interpretive rule.

Whether courts should resolve the meta-question of which interpretive methodology to apply by using a broad, context-sensitive inquiry that considers all available evidence about what the parties wanted (including post-formation information).

Whether rational contracting parties, particularly businesses, prefer a narrow, text-focused interpretive regime because risk-neutrality and litigation-cost considerations make broader evidentiary inquiry unattractive.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev429!!SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism as competing interpretive regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly theorizes a meta-interpretive framework for choosing between textualist and contextualist methodologies and argues for 'meta-contextualism'; Paper B criticizes a rising formalist/textualist tendency in scholarship and defends contextual, practice-sensitive adjudication of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper weight of party consent and party preferences in interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the parties' preferences (or what reasonable parties would have preferred) as decisive in selecting an interpretive regime, while Paper B contests scholarship that overprotects explicit consent and instead defends an objective theory that permits obligations beyond strictly expressed consent.

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and role of extrinsic evidence (parol evidence and evidentiary base) in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the costs and benefits of expanding the evidentiary base (discussing the parol-evidence rule and minimum evidentiary base), and Paper B objects to calls to 'avoid contextual interpretation'—both engage the question of when courts should consider extrinsic facts, practices, or trade usage.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between predictability/administrability and justice or efficiency in interpretive choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques claims that textualism yields superior predictability/administrability and weighs those against justice and efficiency gains from contextualism, while Paper B diagnoses formalist appeals to limiting liability (often for predictability) as a 'fear of contract' and argues for the normative necessity of some contextual flexibility.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and institutional role of courts in shaping default rules and extending contractual obligations beyond explicit terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the court's choice of interpretive regime as a meta-legal decision with policy consequences (including how doctrines like parol evidence operate), and Paper B critiques efforts to constrain judicially-created default rules or limits on precontractual and relational obligations, engaging the same question of how active courts should be in structuring contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1621!!ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: parties' preferences as the appropriate basis for selecting contractual rules or forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the choice of an interpretive regime should mirror the parties' preferences (or what reasonable parties would have preferred) and urges courts to determine that choice contextually; Paper B analyzes how bargaining positions and private interests shape the parties' selection of contract form (LTA, purchase order, SFK, bespoke) as a deliberate, negotiated outcome.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and cost‑minimization as explanatory grounds for doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages law‑and‑economics arguments (e.g., Schwartz & Scott) that posit litigation and evidentiary costs make textualism attractive and critiques those models; Paper B builds a transaction‑cost/bargaining account explaining why parties choose LTAs, standard forms, or alternatives in order to minimize costs like opportunism, uncertainty, and sunk investments.

shared_topics.topic: information, uncertainty, and the admissible evidentiary base
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether courts should admit broader contextual or post‑formation information (a larger evidentiary base) when construing contracts and questions parties' epistemic limits; Paper B treats uncertainty about products and processes as central and studies formal information‑sharing provisions in LTAs and how those provisions function to reduce uncertainty and support planning.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal legal enforcement and informal norms (low‑powered sanctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts interpretive regimes by their influence on administrability and litigation (textualism tending to limit evidence and litigation costs versus contextualism allowing broader inquiry), implicating when formal legal enforcement will be invoked; Paper B directly examines how LTAs braid formal provisions with informal enforcement, asks when legal remedies should be limited to low‑powered sanctions, and analyzes the cost‑minimizing role of law versus norms.

shared_topics.topic: standardization/centralization (standard form contracts) versus tailored, context‑sensitive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends pluralism in interpretive methodologies and notes institutional differences (e.g., merchant law vs common law) that permit varying approaches across contexts; Paper B analyzes why OEMs use standard form LTAs to centralize terms and when parties instead opt for bespoke agreements or purchase‑by‑purchase arrangements based on context and costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24chaplrev89!!ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the textualist/contextualist divide: Paper A maps doctrinal variations, misapplications, and the multi-step structure of each approach, while Paper B critiques strong textualism, defends contextualist virtues, and argues for a pluralistic selection among regimes.

shared_topics.topic: the parol evidence rule and the status of extrinsic evidence
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the parol evidence rule and the admissibility/role of extrinsic evidence: Paper A critiques the term's multiple meanings and clarifies how parol-evidence doctrines interact with interpretation, and Paper B treats the parol-evidence principle as evidence of doctrinal plurality and as part of the ‘evidentiary base’ debate underlying textualist versus contextualist methods.

shared_topics.topic: who should determine the applicable interpretive regime (meta-interpretation) and the relevance of parties' preferences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider whether and how the parties' expectations or preferences should influence which interpretive approach governs: Paper B develops a meta-interpretive theory that the parties' (or reasonable parties') preferred regime should guide selection, and Paper A repeatedly links interpretive doctrine to parties' drafting incentives and the policy implications of choosing one regime over another.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary base and procedural stages (what evidence is used and when in litigation)
shared_topics.justification: Both analyze the scope and timing of admissible evidence and how interpretive decisions map onto litigation phases: Paper B frames interpretation as varying by size of the evidentiary base (minimum vs broader evidence) and critiques cost/benefit models, while Paper A details the stages of interpretation, relates them to pleading/discovery/trial, and explains how different approaches admit and weigh evidence differently.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs between predictability/administrability and justice/efficiency in interpretive choice
shared_topics.justification: Both address normative tradeoffs driving interpretive doctrine: Paper A documents how competing policy arguments (predictability and administrability for textualism versus justice and accuracy for contextualism) create doctrinal incoherence, and Paper B evaluates those same efficiency and justice claims (including economic models like Schwartz & Scott) to argue for context-sensitive rule selection.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71chikentlrev1181!!SYMPOSIUM ON DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL PRODUCTS: ISSUES PERTAINING TO DERIVATIVE MARKET PARTICIPANTS AND THEIR RELATIONSHIPS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL PRODUCTS: ISSUES PERTAINING TO DERIVATIVE MARKET PARTICIPANTS AND THEIR RELATIONSHIPS

shared_topics.topic: industry 'best practices' and standardized assumptions as gap-fillers in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how industry guidelines and the Principles supply standard assumptions and internal policies that may fill contractual gaps in derivatives transactions; Paper B treats external norms (e.g., merchant usage, parol evidence, and doctrinal rules) as mechanisms that courts use to supply meaning when contracts are silent, arguing for selecting interpretive methodologies that reflect parties' circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and evidentiary role of course of dealing, trade usage, and external practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the concern that documented assumptions or market practices could create a 'course of dealing' used against market participants in litigation; Paper B explicitly examines when courts should admit or exclude evidence like course of dealing and trade usage as part of choosing an interpretive regime.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between predictability (standard/textual approaches) and case-specific justice (contextual approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights debates over whether standardized Principles accurately reflect market standards or instead impose a dealer-favoring regime and create predictable but potentially biased rules; Paper B develops the textualist vs. contextualist debate and defends a pluralist/meta-contextualist approach that weighs predictability against the justice of fitting interpretation to circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: ascertaining parties' expectations or preferred interpretive regime when agreements are silent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that in the absence of express contractual terms, market assumptions or Principles may be treated as the parties' agreed expectations or default rules; Paper B argues that courts should determine which interpretive methodology parties preferred (or reasonable parties would have preferred) and use contextual tools to discover that preference when the contract is silent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21upajbusl142!!ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: plurality of legal regimes across industry sectors (sectoral fragmentation / legal pluralism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of 'sectoral fragmentation,' arguing transnational contract law will fragment into distinct, overlapping bodies of law organized by industry; Paper B endorses plural interpretive regimes and cites differences like merchant law vs common law as evidence that contract law already varies by context and sector.

shared_topics.topic: role of party preferences and private ordering in shaping formal contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that private contractual governance and industry practices are being incorporated into state lawmaking, reshaping public contract rules; Paper B argues that the parties' (or reasonable parties') choice of interpretive regime should guide courts' meta-interpretive selection, putting party autonomy at the center of which legal methodology applies.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between predictability/administrability and context-sensitive justice/efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs efficiency gains from specialized, sector-specific rules against complexity, barriers to entry, and threats to rule of law; Paper B analyzes the costs and benefits of textualist (predictable, administrable) versus contextualist (case-sensitive, potentially fairer) interpretive regimes and urges a context-dependent balance.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation and recognition of private standards, usages, and interpretive practices into public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that states increasingly validate, incorporate, and supplement privately-generated standards into formal contract law; Paper B points to doctrines like the parol-evidence rule, trade usages, and merchant law as mechanisms through which private practices and evidentiary bases are (covertly) recognized in courts' interpretive work.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43lawsocinquiry1427!!ARTICLE: Authoritarianism and the Internet
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Authoritarianism and the Internet

shared_topics.topic: limits of one-size-fits-all regulatory or interpretive regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that no single interpretive regime (textualism or contextualism) is optimal for all contracts and promotes dynamic, context-sensitive selection of interpretive methods; Paper B argues that authoritarian cyber-censorship—a uniform regime of control—is structurally fragile and that reliance on a single censorship strategy (self-policing backed by surveillance) can suddenly collapse.

shared_topics.topic: how information availability and evidentiary scope shape institutional outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the debate on the size of the evidentiary base (minimal textual evidence versus broader contextual evidence) and how that affects interpretive results, while Paper B analyzes how the volume, speed, and availability of online information produce informational and norm cascades that determine whether censorship holds or collapses.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between predictability/administrability and situational responsiveness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the claimed advantage of textualism in predictability and lower administrative costs versus contextualism's case-level justice, and Paper B examines authoritarian regimes' desire for predictable control versus the unpredictable, context-driven breakdowns of censorship when online dynamics shift.

shared_topics.topic: strategic behavior and incentives in response to institutional rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats parties as strategic actors whose preferences over interpretive regimes (influenced by risk attitudes and litigation costs) should guide meta-interpretation, whereas Paper B models internet users' strategic self-censorship and reputation-driven behavior that collectively produces or undermines censorial control.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 144upalrev1971!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT

shared_topics.topic: normative role of written formalities and the Statute of Frauds (UCC §2-201) in commercial contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly considers the normative defense of formal written requirements (the Statute of Frauds and UCC §2-201) and the role of formalities in contract law; Paper B engages the same terrain by assessing when courts should privilege written text (textualist tendencies), invoking doctrines like the parol-evidence rule and merchant law that operationalize the weight of writings in commerce.

shared_topics.topic: business firms' actual practices and preferences regarding written contracts and interpretive regimes

shared_topics.topic: the textualism vs. contextualism debate about contract interpretation and when each is appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's focus on formalities and a defense of UCC §2-201 intersects with the textualist impulse to give primacy to written evidence, while Paper B is centrally devoted to the tension between contextualist and textualist approaches and proposes a meta-contextualist framework for choosing between them in particular commercial contexts.

shared_topics.topic: methodological use of empirical and economic arguments to justify doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds methodological issues in using case reports to discover business norms and bases its positive and normative claims on that empirical evidence; Paper B critiques deductive law-and-economics models (e.g., Schwartz & Scott) and surveys empirical arguments about parties' preferences to support a pluralistic, context-sensitive doctrinal account.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: sectoral or industry-specific differentiation of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of "sectoral fragmentation," arguing that transnational contract rules will become distinct across industry sectors; Paper B likewise recognizes plurality in contractual regulation (e.g., merchant law vs common law) and argues that interpretive regimes should vary with the contract's context, including industry-specific practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private ordering and parties' preferences in shaping public contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that private contractual governance and industry standards are being incorporated into state lawmaking, remaking formal contract law in the shadow of private contracts; Paper B centers parties' preferences as the primary guide to choosing interpretive regimes and proposes courts infer those preferences when selecting how to interpret contracts.

shared_topics.topic: plurality of interpretive regimes (meta-interpretation) tied to context
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly theorizes meta-interpretation and defends a pluralist, context-sensitive method (meta-contextualism) for selecting interpretive regimes; Paper A likewise anticipates a legal landscape of multiple overlapping, sector-specific rules rather than a single universal regime, implying different interpretive approaches by sector.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between predictability/administrability and contextualized, efficient outcomes (transaction costs and justice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes the costs and benefits of textualist (predictable, administrable) versus contextualist (case-sensitive, justice-oriented) interpretation, emphasizing litigation and transaction costs; Paper A similarly weighs the efficiency gains of specialized sectoral rules against complexity, regulatory fragmentation, and potential transaction-cost/entry-barrier effects for firms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87tullrev1!!ARTICLE: The Financial Crisis and the Forgotten Law of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Financial Crisis and the Forgotten Law of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: choice of interpretive regime and its effects on enforcing or reforming mortgage contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts could and should deploy flexible interpretive and remedial contract doctrines to allow mortgage modifications and depart from strict enforcement in the securitization context; Paper B develops a theory (meta-contextualism) about selecting textualist or contextualist interpretive regimes based on parties' circumstances, which directly bears on whether courts will permit such departures in financial-contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law allocates and reallocates contractual risk (assignment, modification, excuse doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how securitization, assignment to trusts, and servicer incentives redistributed credit, collateral, modification, and legal risk and explores doctrines (assignment, unconscionability, mistake, impracticability, frustration) that could reallocate risk; Paper B shows that interpretive choices (textualist vs contextualist) materially affect who bears interpretive and litigation risk and ties those choices to party preferences and economic incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretive consequences of multi‑party/third‑party contract structures (assignments, trusts, servicers, representations and warranties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that pooling mortgages into trusts and creating servicer/investor structures transforms who makes decisions and what contractual terms mean in practice (e.g., representations and warranties, authority to modify); Paper B examines how different contractual settings and the presence of specialized commercial practices justify different evidentiary and interpretive approaches, implicating how courts should treat complex multi‑party instruments.

shared_topics.topic: the role and scope of extrinsic evidence/parol‑evidence in resolving disputes over complex financial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses litigation over alleged misrepresentations in origination and disclosure (and the factual context behind representations and warranties) which often requires courts to consider extrinsic facts, while Paper B directly addresses the parol‑evidence rule and the evidentiary base debate, arguing for context‑sensitive admission of external evidence when appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85brooklynlrev393!!ARTICLE: The Impossibility Doctrine in Commercial Contracts: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Impossibility Doctrine in Commercial Contracts: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: whether contracting parties prefer economic risk‑allocation rules versus traditional doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether sophisticated commercial parties adopt the law‑and‑economics 'superior risk bearer' model or prefer the traditional impossibility doctrine and finds most parties prefer the latter; Paper B engages this same normative axis by evaluating whether parties (and firms) actually favor particular interpretive or doctrinal rules, critiquing theoretical claims that parties necessarily prefer efficiency‑driven regimes.

shared_topics.topic: empirical testing of law‑and‑economics predictions about party behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A fills an empirical gap by systematically measuring contract language and parties' revealed preferences about the impossibility doctrine versus economic allocation; Paper B critiques deductive law‑and‑economics arguments (e.g., Schwartz & Scott) and emphasizes the need to assess empirical evidence rather than rely solely on formal models.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of parties' risk preferences (e.g., risk‑neutrality) on optimal contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on allocating losses to the party that can bear risk at least cost (the economic model of risk allocation), while Paper B directly interrogates the assumption that business firms are risk‑neutral and shows how different risk attitudes affect whether parties would favor textualist or contextualist interpretive regimes.

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should adopt default rules or interpretive regimes based on parties' ex ante preferences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats parties' contracting choices as evidence about the defaults they prefer and considers implications for judicial allocation of nonperformance risk; Paper B's thesis (meta‑contextualism) argues courts should determine and apply the interpretive methodology that parties preferred or reasonable parties would have preferred, using contextual inquiry to decide the meta‑rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95nwulrev91!!Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS

shared_topics.topic: using contract form (complexity vs simplicity) as a signal for judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the degree of contractual complexity reveals information about parties' negotiation process, informational constraints, and reliance on reputation, and therefore courts should factor complexity into how they interpret and enforce contracts; Paper B likewise treats contract features as relevant to selecting an interpretive regime, arguing that courts should choose textualist or contextualist methods based on the circumstances surrounding the contract.

shared_topics.topic: selecting an interpretive regime (textualism vs contextualism) based on parties' preferences and context
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a meta-interpretive framework (meta-contextualism) that says courts should apply the interpretive methodology parties would have preferred or that reasonable parties in their situation would have preferred; Paper A similarly contends that courts can learn from contract design (e.g., simplicity/complexity) about the parties' goals and thus about the appropriate interpretive posture to adopt.

shared_topics.topic: critique of economic models that assume idealized party behavior (e.g., risk-neutrality, full rationality) when prescribing interpretation or contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that many formal contract-theory models predict complex, fine-tuned contracts only under unrealistic assumptions about human behavior and the environment (bounded rationality, reputation, renegotiation), while Paper B criticizes deductive law-and-economics arguments (notably Schwartz & Scott) that assume risk-neutral, purely rational parties to claim universal preferences for textualism.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between contract design (completeness/complexity) and legal doctrines or rules (evidence, parol-evidence, enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the economics of contract design to legal interpretive practice and urges courts to incorporate insights from contract theory when applying doctrines, while Paper B surveys existing doctrines (parol-evidence rule, merchant law versus common law) to show that the law already variably accommodates different interpretive methodologies and that doctrine should respond to design features and parties' expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Law and Economics and the Rule of Law The Sixteenth Annual National Student Federalist Society Symposium on Law and Public Policy -- 1997: PANEL IV: HOW SHOULD JUDGES USE ECONOMICS?: THREE PROPOSALS TO HARNESS PRIVATE INFORMATION IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: judicial harnessing of parties' private information in contract disputes
