shared_topics.topic: law-and-economics evaluation of interpretive rules and litigation costs (Schwartz & Scott debate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically engages with the Schwartz & Scott economic argument that risk-neutral parties prefer minimal evidentiary (textualist) regimes because broader proofs raise litigation costs, and Paper B uses law-and-economics reasoning to design rules (damages doctrine, injunctive options) weighing error costs and incentives under judicial informational limits.

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of procedural and remedial rules on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different interpretive regimes and evidentiary rules affect parties' expectations and transactional choices (including concerns about predictability and administrability), while Paper B recommends altering remedial and procedural doctrines (extending Hadley, making injunctions inalienable) to change parties' incentives and the information revealed through litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev631!!SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM

shared_topics.topic: whether contracting parties prefer self-enforcing governance rather than coercive, legally enforceable mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this question by discussing Scott and Stephan's claim that states often avoid coercive enforcement in international agreements (treating WTO dispute settlement as effectively self-enforcing) and by questioning whether that preference generalizes to commercial parties; Paper B engages an analogous question about parties' preferences by evaluating the claim (from Schwartz & Scott) that rational contracting parties prefer a textualist interpretive regime (a narrower, lower-cost evidentiary/enforcement posture) and by arguing about when parties would actually choose different interpretive regimes.

shared_topics.topic: the use and limits of formal economic/contract-theoretic models to prescribe legal rules for contracts

shared_topics.topic: the importance of contextual differences (no one-size-fits-all) in selecting legal regimes or rules governing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that differences between international and commercial contracting (third-party impacts, political incentives, managerial preferences) counsel against straightforward analogies and universal prescriptions; Paper B develops a meta-contextualist thesis that the appropriate interpretive regime should be chosen based on the contract's circumstances and the parties' (or reasonable parties') likely preferences rather than a single universal interpretive rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97columlrev1343!!ARTICLE: DRAFT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DRAFT

shared_topics.topic: resolution of conflicting standardized contract terms (the "battle of the forms")
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes the UCC's treatment of battle-of-the-forms (proposing deletion of §2-207 and leaving term-determination to courts), while Paper B engages the same practical problem as part of its broader inquiry into how courts should interpret contracts (including how to treat form terms, merchant law, and differences between standardized commercial settings and ordinary contracts).

shared_topics.topic: the admissible evidentiary base for determining contractual meaning (parol evidence, trade usage, course of dealing, and related doctrinal tools)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes the evidentiary scope of textualist versus contextualist methodologies (the 'minimum evidentiary base' versus admitting broader contextual evidence, and treats the parol-evidence rule as part of this landscape), and Paper A—in its discussion of battle-of-the-forms and comparative commercial codes—engages the same doctrinal choices about when courts should consider extrinsic evidence like trade usage, course of dealing, or subsequent conduct to decide contract terms.

papers.node_id: 2012uilllrev89!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S CONSTITUTIVE CORE: SOLVING PROBLEMS BY MAKING DEALS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S CONSTITUTIVE CORE: SOLVING PROBLEMS BY MAKING DEALS
papers.abstract:
Problem solving - eliminating obstacles to progress - is central to human experience.It begins at the earliest stages of developmentand carries through to the end of one's days.Individuals solve many problems so automatically that they hardly notice, relying on combinations of mental shortcuts and rules of thumb.With respect to more deliberative problem solving, the human mind is capable of dealing with complex, novel situations, employing techniques that this Article will examine. Actors solve problems not only individually but also interactively. When two or more persons share the same objectives, they often collaborate in reaching mutually beneficial solutions. The primary glue that holds most of these informal private initiatives together is the bond of mutual trust. Law in general and contract law in particular are more likely to play a role in shaping behavior when actors lack common objectives and have no particular reason to trust each other. To be sure, strangers may cooperate with each other and make deals without help from the law.But such help is available when the parties need it. Thus, contract law consists of officially derived solutions to the persistent problem of coordinating human conduct; more particularly, the problem of how individualswho do not necessarily share common objectives can more effectively solve their individual problems by binding themselves to promises of mutual assistance.
Regarding the explanatory power of this Article's problem-solving perspective, the underlying logic is quite simple. Given that contracts involve promises of future performance, it is understandable that scholarly observers would begin with the notion that contract law is mainly about keeping promises.But the unenforceability of gift promises, even when earnestly and solemnly made, demands the qualification that only promises supported by consideration - bargains - are enforceable. But then the unenforceability of gambling contracts and clauses calling for breach-based penalties, both of which involve mutual consideration, embarrasses the bargain theory, which forces the conclusion, embraced by this analysis, that courts enforce only those categories of bargains that appear on their face, or may be presumed, to constitute solutions to preexisting problems. The outline of this Article's explanation of contract law is complete when one factors in the limits of the judicial contract-enforcement process as a problem-solving mechanism. A court, it turns out, does not so much solve the parties' problems when it litigates contract claims as it implements the solutions already reached by the parties when they made their deal.
Part II consists of a descriptive overview of the nature of contract law as a set of constitutive tools by which actors reach and implement solutions to both individual and shared problems. Part II also addresses the question of why the problem solving facilitated by deal making is sufficiently important to warrant encouragement by contract law and describes how this Article fits into the broader scheme of contracts scholarship. Part III lays out the conceptual framework of problem solving - what problems are, what solutions are, and why it is useful to distinguish between solving a problem and implementing a solution. Part IV describes the decision processes by which both individual and institutional actors solve problems and identifies limits on the capabilities of different governmental decision makers. Because courts play the major institutional roles in contract settings, the main focus will be on the limits of adjudication. Part V relies on the insights from Parts III and IV to explain U.S. contract law generally as well as a number of its specific features that other perspectives on contract have difficulty explaining. The Article concludes by considering future applications of the problem-solving perspective to other aspects of U.S. law.

questions.question: Whether and how private agreements are enforced to the extent that they function as solutions to preexisting problems faced by the parties (i.e., whether courts preferentially enforce bargains that appear to solve coordination, trust, or information problems).

How the adjudicative process shapes the role of contract law - specifically, whether courts primarily implement solutions the parties have already reached rather than creating novel solutions ex post.

When and why legal enforcement of private deals should be encouraged: under what conditions does intervention in support of party agreements improve parties' ability to solve individual or shared problems?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71fordhamlrev799!!SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrines shape the implementation and stability of agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the limits of adjudication and how courts do not so much create solutions as implement the bargains parties have reached, while Paper B studies how doctrines like the parol evidence rule and plain meaning determine when courts will treat a writing as the final deal and thereby stabilize or unsettle parties' expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the trade-off between formal certainty/predictability and fidelity to parties' actual intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes contract law's role in promoting coordination and reliable solutions when trust is absent (favoring predictability), and Paper B explicitly interrogates the tension between the psychic/instrumental comforts of rigid written rules and more liberal approaches that admit extrinsic evidence to vindicate parties' true intent.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of written integration for determining which bargains are enforceable and what they mean
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses why courts enforce only certain categories of bargains that appear to solve preexisting problems and how the form of agreement influences enforceability, while Paper B focuses on integration, the parol evidence rule, and plain meaning as mechanisms that decide whether prior or extrinsic terms can affect the meaning or scope of the written contract.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal rules as constitutive tools that facilitate or constrain private problem-solving and coordination
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract law as a set of constitutive tools that enable individuals to make deals and solve coordination problems, and Paper B treats interpretive rules (plain meaning, parol evidence) as instrumental doctrines that either facilitate contractual stability and predictability or constrain parties' ability to present evidence of their negotiated solutions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and choice of default rules (e.g., Hadley rule vs full expectation damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and theoretically evaluates whether the Hadley rule or a full-expectation damages default leads to more efficient outcomes under different distributions of buyer valuations; Paper B treats contract law as a set of constitutive tools and discusses how courts select and enforce categories of bargains that function as legal defaults to implement solutions reached by parties.

shared_topics.topic: contract law as a problem‑solving/coordination mechanism for parties without mutual trust
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly frames contract law as facilitating problem solving and enabling actors who do not share objectives to coordinate by making deals; Paper A analyzes how a particular default (Hadley) can serve that coordinating role by inducing information revelation and efficient precautions when parties lack common information or trust.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private information and asymmetric valuations in shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how private buyer valuations and their distribution affect which legal default is efficient and how defaults induce revelation of private information; Paper B examines limits of deal‑making and adjudication in contexts where parties have different objectives and information, explaining why law steps in to structure bargains under informational constraints.

shared_topics.topic: bargaining, transaction costs, and the legal enforcement environment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how defaults influence bargaining around contracts and how a Hadley default can minimize transaction costs by eliciting information; Paper B emphasizes that courts typically implement parties' negotiated solutions and analyzes how the institutional limits of adjudication interact with the costs and processes of private bargaining.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100cornelllrev23!!ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: limits of generalist courts in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the institutional limits of judicial adjudication: Paper A argues that generalist courts lack the epistemic capacity to combine text and context across varied commercial settings and thus cannot reliably determine when context matters, while Paper B treats courts as limited problem-solving actors that implement parties' solutions rather than create them, stressing the constraints of adjudication as an institutional means of resolving contractual problems.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive or decision rights between parties and courts (contract design vs adjudication)
shared_topics.justification: Both works focus on who should choose the mix of textual and contextual rules — Paper A frames this as an allocation problem in contract design (parties choosing interpretive regimes vs courts imposing context), and Paper B explains contract law as enabling parties to structure solutions and examines when the law (courts) should step in to implement or enforce those privately designed solutions.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as problem‑solving devices to enable cooperation under uncertainty and scale
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat contracting as a mechanism for coordinating action: Paper B develops a general problem‑solving account of why deals matter, and Paper A analyzes how different levels of uncertainty and market thickness produce distinct contracting practices and interpretive regimes that facilitate collaborative problem solving (e.g., information‑exchange regimes, trade association codes).

shared_topics.topic: role of party sophistication, trust, and need for legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both address how characteristics of parties shape reliance on private ordering versus legal protection: Paper A distinguishes legally sophisticated and unsophisticated actors (and the consequences for textualist versus contextualist regimes), while Paper B emphasizes how preexisting common objectives and mutual trust reduce the role of law, and lack of trust or divergent objectives makes contract law necessary to solve coordination problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev243!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:INTRODUCTION: THE HISTORICAL SETTING FOR HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:INTRODUCTION: THE HISTORICAL SETTING FOR HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: foreseeability and limits on recovery for consequential losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts Hadley v. Baxendale and the emergence of the foreseeability test that limits recoverable consequential damages to those losses the breaching party could reasonably contemplate; Paper B analyzes why courts restrict enforcement and remedies (by excluding certain bargains and limiting judicially-provided solutions), situating rules that curtail recovery within a broader theory of what contract law should and will enforce.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of parties' knowledge and communication in allocating risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows the outcome turned on what the carrier could reasonably have contemplated about the Hadleys' lost profits (the Hadleys had not communicated that risk), while Paper B emphasizes that bargains are solutions to preexisting problems and that enforceability depends on the parties' shared or ascertainable expectations and information when the deal was made.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial context and transactional practices shape contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides detailed background on the Gloucester docks, mill operations, and shipping practices to explain the factual matrix underlying the dispute and the judge's assessment of reasonable contemplation; Paper B argues that contract law operates as a constitutive tool rooted in real problem-solving among actors, so institutional enforcement must be read in light of the commercial and decision-making contexts in which deals are struck.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope and limits of judicial intervention in private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A illustrates a judicial decision that constrained damages to what was reasonable to expect from the parties' agreement (thereby refraining from fully compensating the Hadleys), and Paper B develops a theory of contract law that stresses courts do not create solutions ex post but implement or limit the solutions parties reached, highlighting institutional limits on adjudication as a means of solving parties' problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44lawsocyrev299!!ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how social norms and interpersonal trust shape everyday contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the emergence and persistence of a dollar-indexing norm in Israeli real estate driven by conformity and cognitive biases among ordinary market participants, while Paper B analyzes how mutual trust and private ordering enable parties to make deals outside of legal enforcement — both examine non-legal social forces that determine contract content in ordinary transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction and limits of legal intervention on private contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies Israeli legislative attempts to curb dollarization and the uneven effects of regulation on entrenched contracting practices, and Paper B theorizes the limits of adjudication by arguing that courts implement parties' bargains rather than remake them — both engage with how law succeeds or fails in altering private contracting norms.

shared_topics.topic: explanations for persistent or apparently suboptimal contract terms beyond standard bargain/economic models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that dollar-indexed leases persisted despite seeming inefficiencies because of social defaults and cognitive factors, while Paper B critiques pure bargain theory and explains contract enforcement in terms of problem-solving categories rather than mere surplus maximization — both seek behavioral and institutional explanations for why contracts look the way they do.

shared_topics.topic: the view of contracts as problem‑solving devices and private-ordering mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents dollarization as a market-wide coordination device that structured risk allocation and expectations among contracting parties, and Paper B develops a general theory of contract law as constitutive tools that help actors solve coordination problems — both treat contracts primarily as instruments for solving practical problems and coordinating conduct.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67emorylj1!!ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE

shared_topics.topic: contract law as a problem‑solving/coordination mechanism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an explicit theory that contract law exists to implement and encourage private problem‑solving and coordination among actors who lack shared objectives or trust; Paper B treats patient‑provider contracting as a failure of that coordinating function and evaluates how contract doctrine either enables or obstructs efficient, consumer‑protective outcomes in health care.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the treatment of incomplete contracts (including open‑price terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the limits and roles of adjudication in implementing parties' solutions and when courts should or should not supply terms, while Paper B focuses on the doctrinal practice of enforcing open price term contracts and proposes a specific doctrinal change (an information‑forcing penalty default) for courts to fill price gaps.

shared_topics.topic: use of defaults and doctrinal rules to incentivize contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contract law selects which bargains to enforce and thereby shapes private ordering, and Paper B operationalizes that idea by arguing for a penalty default (price = $0) to force providers to include price terms and change market behavior.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry, bargaining power, and the justificatory grounds for legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law plays a larger role where parties lack common objectives or trust (i.e., where private ordering is fragile), and Paper B documents and theorizes how stark information and power imbalances in health care make enforcement of incomplete price terms normatively and economically problematic.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59emorylj649!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS

shared_topics.topic: the relational nature of many contracts (long-term, interdependent agreements with open terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats contracting as a form of problem-solving among parties whose objectives may align over time and highlights collaborative, non-discrete deals; Paper B centers relational contracting and argues friendships more accurately model the long-term, interdependent, and open-ended character of many real-world agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms and private ordering (trust, friendship) versus legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that trust and informal cooperation often govern transactions and that law intervenes where trust and common objectives are absent, while Paper B analyzes how friendship-based social norms operate as a substrate for relational contracts and how legal norms interact with those informal governance mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: contract incompleteness and the courts' limited role in filling gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between solving problems by deal-making and courts' role in implementing party solutions, stressing limits on adjudication, and Paper B underscores that relational contracts (like friendships) leave many terms open and presuppose good faith, raising questions about how and when law should supply gaps or enforce expectations.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for enforceability and why some bargains are enforced while others are not
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes that courts enforce bargains that appear to constitute solutions to preexisting problems and analyzes doctrinal exclusions, whereas Paper B uses the friendship/relational lens to argue for recognizing and sometimes enforcing implicit agreements among friends, thereby rethinking the boundaries of enforceability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105valrev1025!!ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: contracts as tools for solving coordination and practical problems (not just promise enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a problem‑solving account of contract law, arguing contracts are constitutive tools parties use to reach and implement solutions to individual and shared problems; Paper B shows that parties use formal‑looking but non‑binding documents to achieve organizational and coordination goals in complex transactions, demonstrating contracts’ instrumental problem‑solving role beyond mere enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal legal enforcement and the importance of non‑judicial compliance mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the limits of adjudication and explains how courts often implement parties’ own solutions rather than create them, while Paper B investigates why sophisticated parties sign unenforceable ‘faux contracts’ and how compliance often occurs without formal judicial enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: ex ante contract design choices, including preliminary and non‑binding agreements, to shape deal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links legal doctrines and contract features to the ways parties design deals to solve problems and implement solutions, and Paper B empirically studies the use, timing, and structure of term sheets and other preliminary, non‑binding documents as deliberate design choices that guide later definitive agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the role of trust, reputational pressures, and social capital in enabling performance absent formal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes mutual trust as the glue for informal deals and a reason legal enforcement intervenes only when trust and common objectives are lacking, whereas Paper B shows that term sheets and non‑binding documents help build trust and rely on social capital and reputational incentives to secure adherence to agreed terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2014uilllrev1795!!LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
compared_to.partner_title: LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between trust and legal/regulatory mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally debates whether legal forms and mandatory regulation 'crowd out' personal or traditional trust and whether trust can be captured by economic models; Paper B examines how informal trust sustains private cooperation and positions contract law as the fallback when trust is lacking, thereby exploring when law supplements or substitutes for trust.

shared_topics.topic: contracts and business-organization forms as tools for managing future uncertainty and agency costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that uncorporate forms (partnerships, LLCs) function as long-term contractual devices to allocate decision rights and control agency problems; Paper B characterizes contract law as a constitutive set of tools that enables parties to make deals that solve preexisting coordination problems and bind future performance under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard economic/bargaining models and the search for alternative conceptual frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes transaction-cost and law-and-economics approaches as 'in a box' for failing to capture noncalculative trust and human virtues/vices; Paper B rejects a pure bargain/consideration account of contract enforcement and proposes a problem-solving perspective as a better explanatory framework.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role and limits of courts and legal enforcement versus private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends fiduciary duties and legal remedies have scope limits and that personal trust often operates outside legal enforcement, while Paper B explicates the limits of adjudication—arguing courts largely implement the parties' own solutions and that contract law is appropriately geared toward facilitating deals rather than substituting for all private problem solving.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95indlj485!!ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias

shared_topics.topic: how default rules interact with party autonomy in contracting (assignability and enforceability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how assignability doctrines function as default rules that often override or reinterpret parties' expressed intentions (producing a pro-transferability bias), while Paper B explains contract law as a set of constitutive tools and defaults that implement or enable the parties' problem-solving bargains and thus explores the boundary between judicially supplied defaults and party autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of counterparty identity, trust, and reputation for whether rights should be transferable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the identity of a rightholder or obligor and reputational constraints can justify restricting assignments, since parties rely on trust and relational expectations; Paper B likewise emphasizes that private trust and shared objectives allow parties to solve problems without law and that the presence or absence of trust drives whether legal enforcement (including rules about who may enforce) is necessary.

shared_topics.topic: economic/instrumental justifications for contract doctrines (efficiency, credit access, and problem solving)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A scrutinizes economic rationales for forced assignability—credit access, commodification of debt, and financial-market interests—and finds them insufficient to justify the bias toward transferability; Paper B situates contract law in an instrumental, problem‑solving framework, defending enforcement rules insofar as they facilitate efficient coordination and solution of preexisting problems.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of judicial enforcement versus private ordering in contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how parties rely on nonlegal mechanisms (renegotiation, reciprocity) and contends that courts' assignability rules can undermine those private-ordering practices; Paper B analyzes the limits of adjudication, arguing courts mainly implement parties' deals and that contract law should encourage private problem solving where possible rather than supplant it.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69minnlrev521!!ARTICLE: Commercial Rationality and the Duty to Adjust Long-Term Contracts.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commercial Rationality and the Duty to Adjust Long-Term Contracts.

shared_topics.topic: judicial reluctance to rewrite or adjust contracts after unforeseen events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes courts' resistance to imposing a duty to adjust long-term commercial contracts (under doctrines like frustration, impracticability, and UCC §2-615) and defends nonadjustment; Paper B explains the limited role of adjudication in contract law, arguing courts implement parties' solutions rather than rewrite deals, which likewise supports judicial restraint in post‑formation modification disputes.

shared_topics.topic: whether parties can and should bargain under uncertainty (commercial actors' decisionmaking capacity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a model arguing commercial actors are capable of rationally bargaining with uncertainty and so their original allocations should be respected; Paper B frames contracts as problem‑solving bargains reached by actors using decision processes, emphasizing the parties' capacity to design solutions to future contingencies.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unanticipated contingencies in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly engages with doctrines and the UCC provisions that allocate risk when unanticipated events occur and debates whether law should require reallocation; Paper B situates contract enforcement as selecting and upholding bargains that function as prechosen solutions to problems, including how parties allocate future risks, explaining why courts favor honoring those allocations.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of adjudication versus private ordering as the normative basis of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against a communitarian duty-to-adjust that would make courts impose sharing arrangements, favoring respect for private bargaining; Paper B develops a problem‑solving theory showing contract law's normative role is to facilitate private ordering and only minimally intervene, highlighting institutional limits on courts in crafting post hoc solutions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18geomasonlrev245!!ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY

shared_topics.topic: law as a tool to facilitate private transactions and coordinate parties' expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how commercial statutes (UCC, supplemental acts, international conventions) and reform efforts are designed to structure and simplify commercial transactions, while Paper B frames contract law as a constitutive set of tools that enables actors to solve coordination problems and implement mutually beneficial deals.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between bright‑line rules and flexible standards in legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether bright‑line rules or standards better reduce commercial‑law complexity and proposes strategies that may rely on standards, and Paper B examines how courts enforce only certain categories of bargains and the practical limits of adjudication—issues that turn on whether law adopts categorical rules or flexible, problem‑solving standards.

shared_topics.topic: legal complexity and uncertainty as costs for transactors and decisionmakers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the external and internal complexity of commercial law and the economic and doctrinal costs that complexity imposes on practitioners and markets, while Paper B explores how limits on judicial problem‑solving and the need for predictable, implementable solutions constrain when and how courts will enforce agreements, highlighting the transaction‑cost consequences of legal uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional allocation of responsibility between legislatures and courts in shaping commercial/contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys legislative responses (UCC revisions, new articles, model acts, international conventions) to commercial practice and technological change, and Paper B analyzes the role and limits of courts (and other institutional decision makers) in implementing parties' solutions, together addressing how statutory drafting and adjudication interact to produce the governing legal rules for deals.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: contract law as a tool for enabling coordination and problem-solving between parties

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrines (defaults) shape private bargaining and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that courts implement or enable the solutions parties reach and that the design of doctrines affects when law, rather than trust or private ordering, governs exchanges; Paper B analyzes the Hadley default specifically for how it influences bargaining around damages and the transaction costs of contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between adjudication and private ordering — limits of courts in resolving contractual problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly examines the limits of adjudication and argues courts often implement rather than create solutions, focusing on when legal intervention is warranted; Paper B treats Hadley as a judicially articulated default whose optimality depends on how it interacts with private information and downstream private arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: incentives, private information, and efficiency considerations in contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper B builds economic models showing how Hadley can efficiently reveal asymmetric information (buyer valuations) and induce precaution or bargaining; Paper A similarly grounds enforcement choices in a problem‑solving framework that evaluates which bargains courts will enforce based on their capacity to solve preexisting problems and promote effective outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith

shared_topics.topic: judicial limits and deference in contract interpretation and enforcement

shared_topics.topic: contracts as problem‑solving devices that allocate decision rights and manage uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats long‑term open‑quantity contracts as instruments that allocate discretion to respond to changing supply/demand and examines how that allocation should be respected; Paper B develops a general problem‑solving account of contracts, seeing deals as constitutive tools parties use to solve coordination and uncertainty problems.

shared_topics.topic: protection of reliance and parties' expectations versus opportunistic behavior and its costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on sellers' reliance interests (and the desire to price that protection) and analyzes when buyer discretion becomes opportunistic, while Paper B explains contract enforcement as protecting solutions to preexisting problems and thus vindicating reasonable expectations while acknowledging limits to judicial problem‑solving.

papers.node_id: 101valrev559!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S ROLE IN RELATIONAL CONTRACT
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S ROLE IN RELATIONAL CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
A long line of legal scholarship has emphasized the prevalence and importance of using nonlegal, informal sanctions to deter misbehavior and maintain cooperation among private entities. Celebrated examples include the ranchers in Shasta County, the whalers in New England, the cotton traders in the South, the diamond merchants in New York, and even sophisticated commercial entities.Particularly with respectto the last group, Professor Stuart Macaulay famously posed the questions: What good is contract law? Who uses it? When and how?Based on surveys of corporate executives, he found that commercial parties in long-term relationships rarely relied on, or even looked at, the written agreement.Instead, according to the survey respondents, they performed obligations out of the need to preserve a reputation as a good business partner, as someone who could be trusted with future deals.Inspired by such observations, research by several influential scholars led to the birth of what is known as the "relational contract" theory,which fundamentally questions what role, if any, contract law plays in promoting and maintaining trade.
While the relational contract theory has had much influence on the legal scholarship over the past fifty years, some important questions have remained unanswered: If the parties perform obligations, or fulfill their promises, out of the fear of reputational or relational sanctions, why do they bother to write enforceable formal contracts in the first place? Why do they often set up private dispute resolution mechanisms with bells and whistles that resemble those of court-based litigation? After all, writing a long-term commercial agreement or setting up a dispute resolutionsystem is not free. The parties haggle over terms and procedures, they hire lawyers, and they send multiple drafts back and forth. That is a lot of trouble if, in fact, the formal contract or the dispute resolution process will not be used or will be used rarely. What role does the formal contract and the accompanying dispute resolution mechanism play in an "informal" relationship? What is the relationship between the formal sanctions available under the contract and the informal sanctions that are utilized outside the dispute resolution system?
This Article will attempt to answer some of these puzzles with the help of a simple repeated game model. The basic problem is that contracting parties in a long-term arrangement need a mechanism to control opportunism. Imagine a buyer and a seller engaged in a sale of goods transaction. Both the buyer and the seller fear that the other will take the benefit of the exchange and then not live up to her end of the bargain. The seller might take the buyer's cash and provide a substandard product or service in return. The buyer might take delivery on credit and subsequently not pay on time, perhaps arguing opportunistically that the delivered good is nonconforming. To assuage these fears and thereby promote a mutually beneficial relationship in the long run, both the buyer and the seller must anticipate and suffer negative consequences for a decision not to honor commitments.
In a long-term relationship, these negative consequences could flow from (1) formal or legal sanctions, such as monetary damages imposed by a court or arbitrator following a lawsuit; (2) informal or relational sanctions, such as the suspension or termination of trade; or (3) a combination of the two. To make the analysis interesting and realistic, we consider settings where both legal and relational sanctions are costly to impose. Legal sanctions, on the one hand, require spending resources, including time, money, and opportunity cost on dispute resolution. Relational sanctions, on the other hand, involve failure or refusal to trade even when trade may be beneficial.Indeed, imposing relational sanctionsoften means switching contracting partners and incurring the startup costs of a new relationship. In theory, parties would desire a system that deters opportunistic conduct at the lowest possible cost, understanding that neither sanction is free. When both types of sanctions are costly, it is a priori unclear which sanctions the parties will rely on more heavily in a given relationship.
Notwithstanding the theoretical indeterminacy, this Article will show that legal sanctions have two benefits that relational sanctions often lack. First, parties can decouple the deterrence benefit of a legal sanction from its execution cost. Relational sanctions deter misconduct largely by taking away (or threatening to take away) the benefits or the surplus from future transactions: Parties behave because they do not want to lose future business. The larger the value of the future business, the more the threat to take it away will cause a party to think twice about reneging. At the same time, the larger the value of the future transactions between the two parties, the higher the cost the parties suffer if they have to actually execute the threat by stopping or suspending that relationship. In short, the deterrence benefit and the execution cost of informal sanctions are closely intertwined.
The story, however, differs for legal or formal sanctions. When the parties adopt monetary damages as formal sanctions, for instance, the amount of deterrence is largely dictated by the size of the damages that the losing party has to pay. At the same time, the dispute resolution cost incurred by the parties will often be smaller than the damages. This will be particularly true since litigation is usually brought when the size of the (expected) recovery is larger than the (expected) cost of litigation. Furthermore, parties in a long-term relationship can contain the cost of dispute resolution, for instance, by using arbitration and through tailoring of rules on procedure and evidence, while keeping the size of thepromised monetary damages sufficiently large. Through proper tailoring of monetary recovery (for example, liquidated damages) and successful control of dispute resolution cost (for example, arbitration), formal sanctions can, on occasion, deter contractual opportunism at a lower cost than informal sanctions.
Furthermore, through the dispute resolution process, legal sanctions allow the parties to uncover relevant information that enables them to better tailor relational sanctions. One reason that relational sanctions are costly is that they can misfire. In an ideal world, transacting parties would be fully aware of one another's behavior and the relational sanctions would get carried out only when one misbehaves. In fact, termination of the relationship would never happen since, with sufficient deterrence, no one would misbehave. Unfortunately, knowledge and monitoring are imperfect in reality. Parties have to rely on indicators - rather than perfect knowledge - of misbehavior in imposing relational sanctions, and with imperfect indicators, relational sanctions will sometimes misfire. Examples are easy to find. A shoddy product by a manufacturer or an unsatisfactory experience at a restaurant is not necessarily the result of negligence or lack of care, but can nevertheless lead to a decrease in demand or a cessation of customer traffic.
Given the tendency of relational sanctions to misfire, transacting parties will naturally want to increase the reliability of any indicators of poor performance. A formal dispute resolution helps by allowing parties to use the resolution process to uncover relevant evidence of true behavior and to then condition relational sanctions on the more accurate indicators.For instance, instead of using poor quality as the only signal of misbehavior, the parties or other market actors might impose relational sanctions upon observing both poor quality and a judicial or arbitrator's finding of insufficient effort or bad faith. To the extent that the adjudicator's finding is correlated with the true behavior, any relational sanctions that follow a judgment will misfire less frequently and become a more effective deterrent.In fact, parties can induce the judge or arbitrator tomake findings about behavior by conditioning liability on fault-based standards, such as "best efforts" and "good faith" in the performance of a contract. In a long-term relationship, such terms can improve the performance of relational sanctions.
Although we emphasize these two important benefits provided by legal sanctions, there are, of course, costs to harnessing these advantages. Larger damages will likely induce larger litigation expenditure, either due to more suits being filed or because parties will spend more in any given suit. It may very well be the case that providing $ 100 worth of deterrence through damages might actually require litigation expenditures of more than $ 100. In such cases, the parties are better off relying more on relational sanctions. Similarly, adopting a fault-based and open-ended standard, such as "best efforts," could lead to additional expenditure in dispute resolution, as parties will have to litigate over what the standard means and whether one or both parties have abided by that standard. This will cause the parties to think more carefully about the tradeoff between the informational benefit and the additional cost of dispute resolution, leading them, on occasion, to adopt a no-fault standard rather than a fault-based standard for determining breach.
This Article is organized as follows. Part I will review the existing scholarships on both relational contract theory and on nonlegal sanctions more generally. It also presents the unsolved puzzle over why formal sanctions and adjudication processes play an important part in many long-term relationships. Part II will present the main arguments of the Article in nontechnical language. It focuses on how formal sanctions operate differently from informal sanctions in terms of the deterrence cost-benefit calculus and various strategies that real-world parties have adopted to maximize the deterrence bang for the buck. This Part will also show the information benefits that using open-ended obligations, such as "best efforts," can achieve. That analysis, in turn, leads to implications about the proper judicial interpretation of "good faith" in contractual performance. Part III will present a more formal analysis based on a repeated game model. It stylizes a long-term relationship between a buyer and a seller. The example shows how relying solely on either formal or informal sanctions will be suboptimal and how, in many cases, parties will want to rely on a combination of both types of sanctions. Italso formally demonstrates the deterrence cost-benefit advantage and informational benefits of formal sanctions. The final Part will conclude.

questions.question: Whether and when parties in ongoing commercial relationships use enforceable written contracts and private dispute-resolution mechanisms, instead of or alongside informal reputational/relational sanctions, to deter opportunistic behavior.

Whether formal legal sanctions and adjudication can deter opportunism at lower expected cost than informal sanctions and/or produce informational benefits that make relational punishments more reliable, and how these effects determine the optimal mix of formal and informal enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69alalrev469!!ARTICLE: THE INTERPRETATION OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INTERPRETATION OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY

shared_topics.topic: why sophisticated commercial parties include specific interpretation/enforcement clauses (e.g., merger, no‑oral‑modification) to constrain behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents the widespread inclusion of textualist clauses (merger, no‑oral‑modification, notices) in SEC‑filed commercial contracts, interpreting these as deliberate drafting choices; Paper B theoretically explains why parties invest in formal contractual terms and procedures—including tailored sanctions—to deter opportunism and control the costs of enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between textual certainty and contextual/flexible enforcement in long‑term relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central debate as textualist versus contextualist approaches to contract interpretation and asks which parties prefer; Paper B analyzes an analogous tradeoff between relying on formal (legal, rule‑based) sanctions versus informal (relational, context‑dependent) sanctions and when parties will favor one approach over the other.

shared_topics.topic: the role of procedural clauses and dispute‑resolution design (notice rules, modification rules, arbitration/litigation procedures) in managing enforcement costs and information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the prevalence of clauses like notice and no‑oral‑modification that structure post‑contract procedures and limit evidentiary scope; Paper B focuses on why parties create and tailor dispute‑resolution systems (arbitration, procedural rules, damages schedules) to lower deterrence and adjudication costs and to generate better information for relational enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how contract wording and open‑ended standards (e.g., 'best efforts', 'good faith') shape monitoring, evidence, and the effectiveness of relational sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how contractual text and interpretation clauses determine the meaning and scope of obligations; Paper B shows that fault‑based, open‑ended standards can be used strategically in adjudication to produce informative findings that improve the accuracy and effectiveness of subsequent relational sanctions.

shared_topics.topic: using observed contract terms to infer parties' revealed preferences and implications for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses empirical analysis of contract texts to infer that sophisticated parties predominantly adopt textualist clauses and draws normative implications; Paper B offers a theoretical account of why rational parties would include formal terms and adjudicative mechanisms, using that rationale to inform how courts should interpret standards like good faith.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68stanlrev281!!ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks

shared_topics.topic: why parties draft detailed formal contracts and dispute-resolution procedures despite reliance on reputation and informal sanctions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the puzzle of why firms expend resources drafting enforceable contracts and dispute-resolution mechanisms when relational sanctions and reputation can sustain cooperation; Paper B empirically and theoretically examines why complex alliance agreements are commonly used in innovation networks even though informal governance plays a major role.

shared_topics.topic: how formal/legal mechanisms interact with and strengthen (or substitute for) informal/relational sanctions via information generation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that adjudication and monetary remedies can decouple deterrence from execution cost and produce informational findings that make relational sanctions more reliable; Paper B's 'braiding' (and its extension to multivalent contracting) likewise argues that formal contract provisions create information-sharing routines that enable informal governance among collaborators.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs in governance design between deterrence strength, enforcement/transaction costs, and misfire or coordination risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the cost–benefit tradeoffs of larger damages, litigation expense, and fault-based standards versus no-fault rules in sustaining cooperation; Paper B develops a multivalent framework showing how contracts must balance opportunism deterrence against spillovers and coordination entropy, explaining diverse governance choices in alliances.

shared_topics.topic: the structuring of dispute-resolution and governance mechanisms (arbitration, management committees, veto rights) and their effects on coordination and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses tailoring dispute-resolution (e.g., arbitration, procedural rules, liquidated damages) to contain adjudication costs and to condition relational sanctions on judicial findings; Paper B studies specific governance devices—management committees, veto rights, and bifurcated private adjudication—and how their design affects coordination, incentives, and alliance success.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrinal interpretation (e.g., good faith, best efforts, interplay with IP) when collaborative contracts break down
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws implications about how courts should interpret open-ended standards like 'good faith' to preserve informational benefits and manage dispute costs; Paper B examines how courts and multiple legal doctrines (contract, patent, property) must be balanced when resolving alliance disputes and how case law (e.g., Eli Lilly) bears on enforcement approaches.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105califlrev1725!!SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: the interplay of formal legal institutions and informal mechanisms in sustaining cooperation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats federalism as a legal-institutional framework that prescribes how states and the national government cooperate (or come into conflict) and considers how doctrine shapes real-world intergovernmental practices; Paper B models how written contracts and adjudicatory procedures interact with reputational and relational sanctions to sustain long-term commercial cooperation.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between decentralized versus centralized provision/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies a fundamental trade-off—decentralized provision creates collective-action problems while centralized provision creates information problems—when public goods cross boundaries; Paper B analyzes an analogous trade-off between relying on informal relational sanctions (where deterrence and execution costs are tightly linked) and formal legal sanctions (where deterrence can be decoupled from execution cost) and when each is preferable.

shared_topics.topic: institutions (constitutions or contracts) as relational governance that structure long‑run relationships and manage conflict
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly compares federalism to a contract governing long-run intergovernmental relations (even a contract written for bankruptcy), arguing federal structure prescribes terms of cooperation/conflict; Paper B treats formal contracts and dispute-resolution clauses as devices that structure ongoing buyer–seller relationships and help manage opportunism and conflict over time.

shared_topics.topic: information, monitoring, and the role of adjudication or centralized decisionmakers in improving signals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights information problems arising from centralization (and the informational limits of federal or centralized decisionmaking); Paper B shows how formal adjudication and monetary remedies can generate information (judicial findings, evidence) that improve the reliability of informal sanctions and reduce misfires.

shared_topics.topic: instrumental/consequentialist evaluation of legal structures by their effects on behavior and welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates evaluating federalism primarily by its effects on people rather than doctrinal purity and uses social‑science reasoning about likely behavioral outcomes; Paper B evaluates contractual design choices instrumentally—by their deterrence, informational, and cost consequences for parties in long-term relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49indlrev621!!ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS

papers.node_id: 109columlrev431!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION
papers.authors: Ronald J. Gilson; Charles F. Sabel; Robert E. Scott
papers.abstract:
Rapidly innovating industries are not behaving the way theory expects. Conventional industrial organization theory predicts that when parties in a supply chain have to make transaction-specific investments, the heightened risk of opportunistic behavior by their counterparties will drive them away from contractual relationships and toward vertical integration.The pressure toward vertical integration will be especially powerful in rapidly innovating industries where swift technological change produces uncertainty in supply-chain relationships - that is, where the future states of those relationships cannot be predicted probabilistically.In the presence of uncertainty, contemporary contract theory offers no general solution to the problem of assuring both efficient levels of transaction-specific investment ex ante and adjustment to an efficient outcome ex post, after uncertainty is resolved.When contract cannot address opportunism successfully, firms should dominate markets as a means to organize supply relationships.
Despite conventional industrial organization theory, however, contemporary practice is moving away from vertical integration. Producers today recognize that they cannot themselves maintain cutting-edge technology in every field required for the success of their products. Accordingly, companies are increasingly electing to acquire by contract components that in the past they would have made themselves. Put otherwise, instead of vertical integration, we observe vertical disintegration in a significant number of industries. Moreover, in the process of vertically disintegrating, firms are developing forms of contracting beyond the reach of existing contract theory models.
To explain the incursions of contract on the domain of the vertically integrated firm, some theorists have emphasized "modularity." Their claim is that new production tools permit parties to more or less standardize the interface between separate stages (or modules) of production.Each module can serve many purposes and therefore fit a variety of different products. The result is a moderation in the intensity of firm-specific investments and corresponding reductions in the risk of opportunism and thus in the need for vertical integration.
But the modularity hypothesis does not fit many of the new supply-chain relationships. Despite its apparent benefits, modularity is a double-edged sword: It may trap a firm in a no-longer-competitive technology.To avoid the "modularity trap," firms instead are engaging each other in a process of iterative collaboration and co-design of both the interface and the components it joins.
Other theorists have suggested, therefore, that the collaborative process that replaces vertical integration is governed by relational contractingrather than modularity.Here, the focus is on the dominance of noncontractual social and network bonds and informal cooperation as the mechanisms that support collaboration by constraining opportunism. Pure relational contracting, however, does not explain the complex contracting forms that disintegrated firms have devised to cope with the continuing uncertainty caused by rapid technological change.
What we see instead is a rich braiding of explicit (i.e., legally enforceable) obligations and implicit (i.e., legally unenforceable) obligations. The explicit and implicit obligations interact within a formal governance structure that regulates the exchange of highly revealing information but does not necessarily impose legally enforceable obligations to buy or sell anything. This braiding creates an interactive process that constrains opportunism as the parties' investments in detailed knowledge of each other's character and capabilities raise switching costs - the costs one party to a contract must incur in order to replace the other party to the contract.
In this Article, we connect this emerging contract practice to theory, learning from what has happened in the real world to frame a theoretical explanation of this cross-organizational innovation and to reconceptualize the boundaries of the firm accordingly. We argue that the vertical disintegration of the supply chain observed in many industries is mediated neither by fully specified explicit contracts that allow suppliers to produce a modular component of the ultimate product nor by entirely implicit relational contracts supported only by norms of reciprocity and the expectation of future dealings. Rather, we suggest that the changes in firm boundaries are mediated by a new form of contracting - what we call "contracting for innovation."Contracting for innovation supports iterative collaboration between firms by interweaving explicit and implicit terms that respond to the uncertainty inherent in the innovation process: The inability of the parties to specify ex ante the nature of the product to be produced or its performance characteristics means that the terms of performance will be determined by the very governance process the contract creates.
As with the conventional account of the forces pushing toward vertical integration, opportunism plays a central role in explaining the organization of disintegrated innovation in the supply chain. However, here the opportunism is of a character somewhat different than that discussed in the conventional vertical integration literature. Moreover, it is addressed in a radically different fashion - the process of collaboration itself erects a barrier to taking advantage of the other party's specific investments. More precisely, as the parties invest in developing information about their respective capabilities, the cost of switching partners, and therefore the constraint on opportunism, goes up in tandem.
This Article proceeds in five Parts. We begin our discussion in Part I with an account of the ongoing vertical disintegration of the supply chain in innovative industries and consider various theoretical accounts of the process before offering our own assessment. Part II moves to a review of contract theory and its inability to offer a general solution to the canonical contracting problem of ensuring both the efficient level of specific investment in the face of uncertainty and efficient production once the uncertainty is resolved. Part III then describes three real world exemplars illustrating a continuum of contracts that support collaborative innovation. We use these transactional exemplars in Part IV to frame, but not to prove, our theoretical account of contracting for innovation. In Part V, we return to the theory of the firm and suggest that there is no theory of the firm. Following Bengt Holmstrom and John Roberts,we argue that the organizational boundaries of production, and the techniques that govern conduct within and across those boundaries, represent a variety of mechanisms that evolve in response to changes in the firm's real activities and the problems the firm must address. We conclude that future work investigating parties' efforts to contract for innovation requires both qualitative and quantitative data sufficient either to give confidence that our account captures current practice or to instruct us on what we have missed.
. Vertical Disintegration and Collaboration Among Firms: Industrial Organization in an Uncertain World
In the last two decades, the organization of firms in the United States and other advanced economies has changed in two fundamental ways. First, many transactions that used to take place within firms - for example, research and development, the manufacture of key components, and the assembly of final products - are now organized by agreements between firms. There is thus a decrease in the proportion of economic activity coordinated within firms and a corresponding increase in the proportionof economic activity conducted through contract in the market.Second, market transactions between firms increasingly involve novel forms of collaboration - particularly rich and carefully organized exchanges of information designed to identify and utilize possibilities for innovation. This novel collaborative form constitutes contracting for innovation.
Collaborative innovation is not just a shift from hierarchy - the organization of transactions within firms - to contract. Rather, the unavoidable mutual vulnerabilities among collaborators motivate corresponding innovations in contractual governance to support the new transactional structure. In this part, we briefly canvass the most salient evidence for the shift from hierarchically organized transactions to interfirm collaborative innovation; speculate on the reasons for it; and present two contrary, but similarly incomplete, accounts of current economic organization to underscore the novelty of the simultaneously formal and informal mechanisms by which firms learn to innovate together.

questions.question: Do firms in rapidly innovating industries rely on hybrid contractual governance-an interweaving of explicit (legal) and implicit (relational) obligations-to support iterative interfirm collaboration and thereby substitute for vertical integration (i.e., promote vertical disintegration)?

Can such hybrid contracting mechanisms (contracting for innovation) secure efficient levels of transaction-specific investment ex ante and efficient adaptation ex post under deep uncertainty, or does uncertainty still push firms toward vertical integration?

Does the collaborative process itself (through investments in detailed knowledge of partners and governance that facilitates information exchange) raise switching costs enough to constrain opportunism between firms?

papers.node_id: 59emorylj649!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS
papers.abstract:
It is likely true that marriages are types of contracts.But contracts are not generally like marriages. Friendships are also, in part, types of contracts. Yet many contracts are also like friendships. At the least, it is more illuminating to think of contracts as friendships than as marriages. Let me explain.
For some time, so-called "relational" contract theorists- theorists who urge us to focus on "relational" elements in contracts in order to devise a theory and law of contracts- have sought to convince us that the majority of contracts, particularly the most relational ones, are types of marriages.Moremodestly, perhaps, they suggest that marriage is a good analogy for relational contracting. Even those sympathetic to the law and economics movement have suggested the equivalence between relational contracts and marriages.
The core idea of "relational contract as marriage" is that most contracts, like marriages, share the following properties: (1) they ensnare parties into - and control party compliance through - a thick set of social norms; (2) they generally give parties autonomy in resolving internal disputes through those social norms; (3) they are very costly to exit; (4) they leave many terms open; (5) they tend to be incomplete in specifying obligations, especially on the issue of how the parties will cooperate over time; (6) parties tend to presume good faith and best efforts in performance and tend to allow for easy modifications for changed circumstances; and (7) they establish interdependence, partiality, and solidarity. Indeed, some have even examined the equivalence between marriages and relational contracts to determine what the content of marital law ought to be.The purchase of the analogy for relationalists, however, is tied up with their most general point - that discrete, one-shot transactions between strangers have occupied the center of "classical" contract law and contract theory to its detriment. In reality, as relationalists have demonstrated since the 1960s, contracts involve thicker relationships than those among strangers. Indeed, we cannot understand the social or legal practice of contracting as a practice among strangers; this insight alone has dramatic implications for our entire market economy and our effort to regulate it through contract law and otherwise.
This Article makes an effort to replace the marriage analogy in relational contract thinking with a story that ties contracts and friendships closer together. Part I is a brief overview of relational contract theory (as it is conceptualized by contracts scholars in law schools). Part II highlights how friendships are very much like relational contracts and how friendship can be illuminated by exposing its morphological similarity to relational contracts. Part III argues that friendship rather than marriage should be viewed as the paradigmatic relational contract. And Part IV explores some of the legal and theoretical ramifications for contract law and theory in light of the view that friendships are types of relational contracts and relational contracts are types of friendships. Ultimately, this window into relational contracts and friendships furnishes a few important lessons. First, it supports the legal enforceability ofsome contracts, both explicit and implicit, between friends. Second, it supports and revises certain prescriptions of relational contract theory. Third, it helps us better understand the relationship between social norms and legal norms. Finally, understanding relational contracts as friendships helps us make better sense of the under-compensatory nature of contractual remedies.
Let me not overstate the thesis here: I am not building a general theory of friendship or contract. This Article only suggests that putting these social practices side-by-side and exposing their morphological similarities can help illuminate each practice. Certainly, if pressed, some relationalists might concede that the place of marriage in relational contract theory is only as a suggestive analogy. This Article proposes that friendship offers a better and more illuminating analogy that can do some modest work in advancing our understanding of contract doctrine and theory.

questions.question: Whether friendships provide a better and more accurate analogy or model than marriages for understanding the structure and operation of relational contracts.
Whether and to what extent explicit and implicit agreements formed within friendships should be legally enforceable.
How reframing relational contracts as friendships changes legal theory and policy-particularly the role of social norms in shaping obligations and the appropriate design of contractual remedies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a market-based certification mark (the "Fair Employment" mark) to induce and bind employers to ENDA-like non‑discrimination duties when legislation fails, and Paper B emphasizes how many contractual obligations are governed by relational, privately enforced norms (friendship/relational contracts) that operate alongside or instead of formal legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms in filling gaps left by formal law or incomplete agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on reputation, market signaling, and voluntary employer commitments to fill enforcement deficits from lack of federal antidiscrimination law, while Paper B analyzes how social norms underpin relational contracts and perform the gap‑filling, cooperative functions that formal contract terms often omit.

shared_topics.topic: the legal enforceability of informal or nontraditional commitments and mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether and how a certification mark/IP device can create legally meaningful obligations and incentives for employers, and Paper B examines the enforceability and normative legitimacy of implicit or friendship‑based contractual obligations under contract law.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal innovation outside traditional legislative routes to address perceived legal deficiencies
