shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between rules and standards (formalism versus contextualism) in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique the proliferation of vague standards and debate interpretive methodology — Paper A warns that standards are cheap for the state to produce and may poorly complete markets, advocating formalism to protect designed mechanisms, while Paper B contrasts the 'hypothetical bargain' and 'new formalist' approaches and examines when courts should modestly apply plain meaning versus supply context‑dependent terms.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design questions about adjudication (who should decide, specialized courts/arbitration and the costs of judicial intervention)
shared_topics.justification: Both consider institutional constraints on courts as critical to whether and how intervention should occur — Paper A highlights adjudication systems and the potential role for specialized courts or arbitrators to reduce communication/trial costs for implementing mechanisms, while Paper B emphasizes institutional costs, counter‑opportunism risks and the need to assess whether courts are the right actors to supply terms or deter opportunism.

papers.node_id: 104columlrev1428!!ARTICLE: EMBEDDED OPTIONS AND THE CASE AGAINST COMPENSATION IN CONTRACT LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE: EMBEDDED OPTIONS AND THE CASE AGAINST COMPENSATION IN CONTRACT LAW
papers.authors: Robert E. Scott; George G. Triantis
papers.abstract:
Compensation is the governing principle in contract law remedies. This principle shapes the key doctrines that specify the consequences of breach. Expectation, the default measure of damages that derives from the compensation principle, aims to put the promisee in the position shewould have occupied had the promisor performed. Alternatively, specific performance is available at the option of the promisee only when the court believes money damages are inadequate compensation for her loss. Although parties may agree to liquidated damages, contract doctrine instructs them to abide by the compensation norm. But despite its profound influence on contemporary contract law doctrine, the compensation principle has tenuous historical, economic, and empirical support. Its evolution in the common law resulted primarily from ill-conceived path dependence; compensation is virtually ignored in the theoretical analysis of efficient contract design; and compensation plays little role in the contracts actually negotiated by commercial parties and agreed to by consumers. As a result of an unfortunate turn in history, lawmakers view contract damages as compensation for wrongs. This has impeded both the efficient evolution of default remedies and the efficient regulation of liquidated damages.
Rather than conceiving of damages as compensation, the right to breach and pay damages is better understood as a valuable option sold by the promisee to the promisor. Indeed, the right to breach is only a subset of a broader category of termination rights that gives one party an option to walk away from the contemplated exchange.A firm offer or unilateral promise, for example, grants the promisee such an option. Broad warranties, such as satisfaction-or-your-money-back provisions, give buyers similar options. Requirements, output, or installment contracts grant one party substantial discretion to determine the contract quantity. Anda contract may provide that one party has the right to terminate, cancel, renew, return, or redeem goods.
Either or both parties to a contract, therefore, commonly enjoy the right to terminate at some cost. For the purposes of analysis and argument, we focus on the option held by a buyer of goods or services.The buyer holding an option has the right to avoid the exchange by paying either a termination fee or damages. The price of an embedded option is determined just as the price of any other product: It is a function of the option's value to the option holder, the cost to the option writer, and the competitiveness of the market in which they transact. Options are essentially insurance contracts that divide risks according to their respective exercise prices.For any given exercise price, the option price divides between the parties the surplus created by the option - namely, the difference between the option's value to the buyer and its cost to the seller. The parties should choose a pairing of option price and exercise price that maximizes this surplus. Sometimes the option price is fixed by the contract (e.g., in the form of a nonrefundable deposit or termination fee), and at other times it is left to be judicially determined as damages for breach of contract. Given the great variety of conditions under which parties contract for this option, it should not be surprising that commercial and consumer contracts contain a wide range of option prices. We explain the heterogeneity in option prices and argue that they are rarely equivalent to the measure of the seller's expectation in a completed sale.
Consider an electronics store that sells television sets for $ 400 and offers full refunds for any returns made within thirty days. This contract gives the buyer a free thirty-day option to purchase the television set for $ 400. A buyer who does not know whether her family needs a television set or will like this particular model values the opportunity to return it free of charge. Thus, the option is valuable to her because she is uncertain as to the value of the television set to her family. The retailer in this case bears significant costs in accepting returns, including the cost of receiving,inspecting, and reselling the returned goods, often through a discount outlet or internet sale. Yet, the retailer often does not charge for the option.Such "free" options are particularly interesting for our purposes because these contracts make no attempt to compensate the seller for losses it suffers when the buyer walks away from the contemplated exchange.
Under many other termination provisions, buyers pay positive option prices in the form of fees or damages. These fees sometimes exceed the compensatory amount - for example, the seller's foregone profit. Consumers are familiar with instances of such overcompensation in a variety of transactions. For example, economy fares on airlines are typically conditioned on a penalty of $ 100 if the passenger chooses to cancel and apply the ticket price against the fare of another flight. The penalty applies even on flights that are overbooked and almost certain to be full. Thus, the penalty is not simply compensation for the airlines' losses.
Indeed, casual observation reveals that termination fees in both commercial and consumer contracts regularly depart from the compensatory amount in both directions. Retailers often have the right to return unsold merchandise to the wholesaler or distributor. Rights of return are common, for example, in the retailing of books, journals, newspapers, musical compact discs, jewelry, and cigarettes.Aircraft manufacturers permit purchasers to cancel orders or to change the type of aircraft at no charge even after the manufacturer has made a significant investment in production.
In this Article, we offer an explanation for these contracting patterns based on the insurance (or risk management) function of embedded options.It is well known that compensatory remedies insure the buyer against the seller's breach and thereby against the risk of fluctuations in the seller's cost of performance that lead it to breach. The buyer, however, still bears the risk of fluctuations in the value of the seller's performance. Options created by termination rights insure buyers against this risk and thereby may promote the risk management objectives of business contractors.
When the buyer's option comes in the form of the right to breach and pay expectation damages, the buyer's liability on termination is a function of the profit that the seller would gain from the exchange. Under an expectation damages rule, therefore, the buyer shrugs off some of the risk of fluctuations in performance value, but assumes some of the risk in fluctuations in the seller's profit. If the buyer contracts for the right to terminate and pay a fixed amount rather than expectation damages, the buyer can also avoid the risk associated with the seller's cost. The buyer may be prepared to pay a premium to be able to shift both the risk in the value of performance and the risk in the seller's costs. In these cases, the parties may agree to pay fixed liquidated damages that are greater than the (ex ante) expected amount of the seller's loss from breach. Under the current penalty rule, however, courts will refuse to enforce this term.Our analysis suggests a benign explanation for this supercompensatory damages term: It is the product of a negotiated sale of insurance from the seller to the buyer in the form of an embedded option.
Given the close link between options and insurance, it should not be surprising that the optimal terms of embedded options are a function of considerations that determine insurance contracts - namely, risk-bearing capacity, adverse selection, and moral hazard. Although we discuss the role of these considerations in the structuring of embedded options, our principal contribution is to show that many contracts contain embedded options and that the optimal terms and prices of these options are heterogeneous. This analysis is consistent with our observation of a wide variety of termination provisions in practice.
Our analysis has important normative implications for the default rules of contract damages and for the freedom of parties to contract away from the defaults. Termination provisions serve valuable risk management objectives when they depart from the compensation principle. Thecharacterization of breach damages as the price of an option that yields value to the buyer reinforces the criticisms of the penalty rule that have been raised by contracts scholars.The recent litigation concerning late fees charged by Blockbuster video stores is illustrative.There, the plaintiffs argued that the fees were unenforceable penalties.But the court recognized that the right to extend the rental period was valuable, that a rational consumer would pay a price for this right that might be higher than the cost to Blockbuster, and that courts should not engage in regulation of this price.We argue that courts similarly should enforce all termination provisions, regardless of their form.
Courts are not well suited to set default contract damages either. It is unlikely that any given damages default will reflect the option price that most parties would adopt in their contracts. In most contract relationships, an expectancy default rule is no more appropriate with respect to damages than with respect to the price of any other good, service, or contract term for which there is no established market price. We suggest, moreover, that the particular salience of a damages default - particularly one founded on an entrenched compensation principle - discourages parties from writing explicit termination provisions and deters the courts from specifically enforcing them. Thus, we argue in favor of a bargain-facilitating, instead of a majoritarian, approach. Where commercial parties have failed to provide expressly for termination rights, we propose that the courts specifically enforce the exchange. In the context of consumer transactions, where merchant sellers typically draft the contracts, the default should give the consumer a free option if the parties fail to make an express provision regarding termination rights.
This Article proceeds as follows. In Part I, we contrast the contemporary dominance of the compensation principle of contract damages against its tenuous historical roots, its marginal relevance in contract economics, and its limited use in commercial and consumer contracts. Part II characterizes the termination provisions available to a buyer - including the right to breach and pay damages - as call options that serve an important risk management function. We demonstrate that optionprices, including breach damages, might take a wide range of values. We specify factors that explain the variations in the prices paid for these options and show that these prices may appear either undercompensatory or overcompensatory to a court. Part III develops the implications for optimal default rules for breach of contract summarized above. We conclude that contracting parties should be free to set the prices for embedded options, and that the law should not provide default damages rules that effectively establish prices for the parties when they fail to do so for themselves.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CANONS OF CONSTRUCTION FOR CHOICE-OF-LAW CLAUSES

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts versus contracting parties in setting default rules and enforcing contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts are poorly suited to set damages defaults and should generally enforce parties' negotiated termination provisions, while Paper B evaluates a proposed doctrinal reform (limiting inquiry into subjective intent) and questions whether judicial intervention or deference is the right response to indeterminate boilerplate clauses.

shared_topics.topic: problems posed by standardized or boilerplate contract terms in commercial and consumer markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents widespread, heterogeneous termination clauses (returns, liquidated damages, penalties) and their practical divergence from compensation norms in consumer and commercial contracts, while Paper B studies 'black hole' boilerplate (the pari passu clause) and its potential to create market-wide inefficiencies when left indeterminate.

shared_topics.topic: how contract terms allocate risk (insurance/option value) and the consequences of ambiguity for risk distribution and market efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theoretical framework treating termination rights and breach damages as embedded options/insurance that allocate risk between buyer and seller, and Paper B shows how ambiguous boilerplate clauses can unexpectedly reallocate risk across market participants and thereby disrupt restructuring or pricing, prompting calls for doctrinal or market fixes.

shared_topics.topic: the effectiveness of market processes versus doctrinal reform in correcting problematic standard terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties and markets typically negotiate a wide range of option prices and that defaults can discourage explicit contracting, while Paper B analyzes whether private-market standard-setting (and its collective-action dynamics) or judicial/doctrinal change is the feasible solution to problematic boilerplate like the pari passu issue.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98texlrev439!!ARTICLE: Designing and Enforcing Preliminary Agreements
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Designing and Enforcing Preliminary Agreements

shared_topics.topic: the appropriateness and role of expectation/compensatory damages as a default remedy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critically engage the default of expectation (compensatory) damages: Paper A examines when courts should award expectation versus reliance damages for breaches of preliminary agreements (including negotiating-in-good-faith breaches), while Paper B critiques the compensation principle more broadly and reconceptualizes damages as the price of an embedded option, arguing parties should be free to set non‑compensatory termination prices.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as risk‑allocation devices (insurance function of contract terms)
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how contract terms allocate exogenous risk between parties: Paper A shows preliminary agreements are used to allocate risks (e.g., interest‑rate changes) during staged bargaining, and Paper B models termination rights/embedded options as insurance that reallocates risk over performance value and cost.

shared_topics.topic: how parties design staged or multi‑stage contracting to manage investment and surplus division
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study incentives in multi‑stage contracting: Paper A focuses on preliminary agreements' role in encouraging specific investment while deterring opportunistic value‑claiming during later negotiation stages, whereas Paper B explains how parties negotiate option prices and exercise terms to divide the surplus and manage strategic termination incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts and default rules in enforcing flexible standards or nonstandard contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Both address judicial intervention and defaults: Paper A defends judicial enforcement of open‑ended standards (good faith/best efforts) in certain preliminary agreements and justifies expectation remedies despite vagueness, while Paper B criticizes courts imposing compensatory defaults, urging enforcement of parties' chosen termination terms and cautioning against courts setting option prices by default.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 106nwulrev1153!!Article: BROADCAST CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: Article: BROADCAST CONTRACTING

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of contract default rules and proposals for reform
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue that prevailing default doctrines in contract law are poorly suited to actual contracting practice — Paper A criticizes the vague common-law treatment of third‑party‑beneficiary rights and urges a clearer, rule‑based requirement for express grants of third‑party rights, while Paper B challenges the dominance of the compensation/expectation default for breach damages and advocates defaults that better accommodate negotiated termination rights and option pricing.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering to allocate rights and risks to outsiders or non‑parties
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze how contracting parties deliberately craft terms that create legally consequential rights outside the bilateral exchange — Paper A examines 'broadcast contracting' by which parties confer enforceable entitlements on a defined class of third parties, and Paper B analyzes embedded termination options and liquidated damages as contractual tools for allocating risk and creating rights to walk away.

shared_topics.topic: critique of judicial discretion and the call for clearer, enforceable contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Each paper expresses concern that courts currently rely on vague standards or ad hoc judgments that generate uncertainty and litigation — Paper A faults judicial conjecture in identifying intended vs incidental beneficiaries and recommends clearer evidentiary rules, while Paper B argues courts are ill‑suited to set damages prices and should instead enforce explicit termination provisions (and adopt sensible defaults when parties omit them).

shared_topics.topic: use of economic theory to explain contractual forms and inform legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works deploy economic analysis to explain why particular contractual devices arise and how the law should treat them — Paper A provides an economic account of broadcast contracting and its transaction‑cost and welfare implications, and Paper B develops an options/insurance model to explain heterogeneous termination provisions and to justify different default rules for damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18geomasonlrev245!!ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY

shared_topics.topic: design of default rules for commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the entrenched expectation/compensation default for breach damages and argues for defaults that facilitate bargaining (including enforcing parties' termination choices), while Paper B examines how statutory drafting and evolving codes (e.g., UCC revisions) produce numerous default rules and considers how alternative default structures (bright-line rules vs standards) affect legal complexity and predictability.

shared_topics.topic: suitability of courts and legislators to set detailed contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts are poorly suited to set damages defaults (they cannot price embedded options well) and should defer to parties' negotiated terms, whereas Paper B documents how legislative and judicial efforts to micromanage commercial transactions (through detailed code provisions) produce interpretive disputes and suggests rethinking the extent to which law should prescribe fine-grained commercial rules.

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between legal rules and commercial practice/expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that the compensation principle diverges from how commercial and consumer contracts actually allocate termination rights and option prices, and Paper B documents that the proliferation and complexity of commercial statutes (and overlapping regimes like UCC/CISG/UCITA) create rules that often misalign with transactors' expectations and practices.

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of contractual arrangements and the resulting transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the wide variety of embedded termination options and liquidated-damage terms across commercial and consumer contracts and the normative need for legal rules that accommodate that heterogeneity, while Paper B emphasizes that numerous, internally complex provisions and competing legal regimes increase transaction costs and produce inconsistent judicial outcomes for commercial actors.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83nyulrev1726!!ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE

shared_topics.topic: legal characterization and role of termination/exit rights (including the 'right to breach')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconceptualizes the buyer's right to breach or terminate as a tradable embedded option and analyzes its pricing and insurance function; Paper B investigates whether contract law is a power-conferring system that enables parties to create or modify obligations (including exit rights) and develops the 'compound rule' category to explain doctrines that anticipate and facilitate purposive use of such rights.

shared_topics.topic: default remedies and damages rules (expectation damages versus alternative default regimes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the entrenched expectation/compensation default for breach and argues for treating damages as an option price or for alternative defaults (e.g., consumer free option), while Paper B analyzes how the structure of contract doctrines (validity conditions, parol evidence, etc.) functions as defaults that determine when and how legal consequences attach, affecting whether law looks duty-imposing or power-conferring.

shared_topics.topic: functional analysis of contract doctrines as mechanisms for risk allocation and enabling legal change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reads termination provisions and liquidated damages through the lens of insurance and risk-management functions, explaining heterogeneity in contractual terms; Paper B adopts a functionalist 'design stance' to explain why contract rules are structured to impose duties, create powers, or operate as 'compound rules'—i.e., as instruments serving identifiable functions like enabling purposive legal change.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy versus judicial intervention in enforcing negotiated terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that parties should generally be free to set prices for embedded options and that courts should enforce termination provisions rather than policing liquidated-damages clauses, while Paper B examines doctrinal features that either facilitate parties' purposive use of contract law or impose duties, drawing out implications for how much deference courts should give to parties' bargaining and how to justify enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69minnlrev471!!ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and losses when performance fails (breach or impracticability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconceptualizes breach damages and termination rights as priced options that allocate risk between buyer and seller, while Paper B traces the doctrine of commercial impracticability from an all-or-nothing rule toward explicit loss-sharing solutions for redistributing losses when performance becomes impracticable.

shared_topics.topic: parties' ability to use contract terms to allocate risk (and the desirability of enforcing those terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that parties routinely buy and sell embedded termination options (including liquidated fees) and should be free to set those prices, and Paper B's primary loss-allocation alternative places responsibility on contracting parties to allocate losses and encourages judicial facilitation of out‑of‑court settlements.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and default remedial rules in adjusting or setting loss-allocation outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the entrenched expectancy/compensation default and urges courts to avoid imposing a one-size damages default, favoring enforcement of negotiated termination terms, while Paper B criticizes historical judicial refusal to spread burdens and proposes concrete judicial methodologies for allocating losses when private arrangements fail.

shared_topics.topic: the need for flexible doctrines that reflect commercial heterogeneity in contracting and risk-management practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents widespread, heterogeneous termination provisions and explains them as insurance/risk-management choices, concluding that defaults should accommodate diversity; Paper B likewise emphasizes the absence of a consistent judicial methodology and proposes a flexible framework to incorporate loss‑sharing tailored to commercial circumstances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54ambuslj519!!ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: normative goals of contract doctrine (party autonomy, efficiency, and equitable considerations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes competing normative goals by mapping interpretive approaches (authorial/textual, linguistic/purposive, interpreter-as-author) and links them to neoformalist versus relational contract theories; Paper B challenges the compensation-centered normative default in remedies and reframes breach rights as privately priced options that better serve parties' risk‑allocation and efficiency interests.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate judicial role in filling gaps and setting defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether judges should prioritize textual constraints or incorporate external circumstances and equitable considerations when construing contracts; Paper B argues courts are poorly suited to set damages defaults (the compensation norm) and should generally enforce parties' expressly or implicitly bargained termination terms rather than impose judicially determined prices.

shared_topics.topic: context-sensitive rules that vary with contract characteristics and relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a context-dependent interpretive model that calibrates weight to textual versus extrinsic evidence based on contract features and relational context; Paper B likewise recommends different default treatments for termination rights (e.g., enforcing explicit commercial bargains but granting consumers a free option) depending on whether contracts are negotiated commercially or drafted by merchants.

shared_topics.topic: critique of entrenched doctrinal defaults and proposals for alternative conceptual frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the simplistic textualist/contextualist binary and offers a hermeneutic taxonomy to reconceptualize interpretation; Paper B critiques the historical path‑dependence of the compensation principle and proposes an alternatives framework treating termination rights as market‑priced embedded options (an insurance/option paradigm).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83texlrev1581!!ARTICLE:The Law and Economics of Contract Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Law and Economics of Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between upfront drafting (negotiation) costs and later litigation/interpretation costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the social transaction-cost tradeoff (x vs. p(x)[...]) and argues interpretation doctrine should minimize total drafting plus adjudication costs; Paper B shows parties often choose contract terms (including termination/option prices) that reflect bargaining over ex ante costs and the costliness of specifying contingencies, implying similar tradeoffs between detailed drafting and relying on post‑contract remedies or dispute resolution.

shared_topics.topic: how default legal doctrines (interpretation rules or default damages) shape contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how textualist/formalist interpretation raises drafting burdens by refusing extrinsic information and thus alters parties' incentives to invest in clarity, while Paper B argues that an entrenched compensation default deters parties from specifying termination prices and steers contracting outcomes, advocating different default rules to facilitate bargains.

shared_topics.topic: strategic use of incompleteness or deliberate ambiguity (including embedded termination options) to allocate risk under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties may deliberately leave contracts ambiguous or incomplete to economize on negotiation costs and delegate gap‑filling to courts, and Paper B treats termination provisions and breach‑for‑damages as embedded options parties buy/sell to manage risk, explaining why contracts often leave contingent risk‑allocation to priced options rather than exhaustive clauses.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in assigning meaning or value to contractual choices (interpretation versus pricing of remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how judicial interpretation methods and the risk of judicial error affect social costs and contracting incentives, while Paper B critiques courts’ default pricing of breach (compensation) and argues courts are poorly suited to set option prices or second‑guess negotiated termination terms, raising common questions about the appropriate judicial function in valuing contract terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73califlrev261!!ARTICLE: The Limits of Expanded Choice: An Analysis of the Interactions Between Express and Implied Contract Terms.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Expanded Choice: An Analysis of the Interactions Between Express and Implied Contract Terms.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of default (state‑supplied) contract terms on private contracting choices and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the default expectation‑damages rule and argues that judicially imposed damages defaults effectively set prices for embedded termination options, shaping parties' incentives to draft termination provisions; Paper B analyzes how implied and standardized state‑supplied terms (the ‘‘Expanded Choice’’ postulate) function as default preformulations that shape bargaining, signal content, and constrain the ways parties can vary or opt out of those defaults.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial interpretation and enforcement doctrines shape contract design and market behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts are poorly suited to set damages defaults and should defer to parties' negotiated termination terms (including liquidated damages), while Paper B examines the doctrinal struggle between textualist and contextualist interpretation, parol evidence rules, and how ex post judicial methods feed back into ex ante contracting choices and error‑reduction signaling.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk via contract terms (including termination rights viewed as insurance/options)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models termination rights and the right to breach as embedded options/insurance that allocate risks (and thus have prices reflecting risk‑bearing capacity, adverse selection, moral hazard); Paper B engages with how implied and express terms allocate risks between parties through standardized clauses and how those allocations affect formulation errors and the choice to accept or renegotiate risk allocations.

shared_topics.topic: the costs and barriers to contractual innovation arising from standardized or entrenched doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that an entrenched compensation principle and damages defaults deter parties from writing explicit termination provisions and distort option pricing, while Paper B argues that expanding and refining implied standard terms raises the opting‑out burden and retards the evolution of new, emergent contractual formulations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should respect and enforce negotiated termination provisions and allow parties to price embedded options rather than impose compensatory damages defaults; Paper B compares New York's formalist enforcement (preferred by commercial parties) with California's contextualist approach and treats parties' forum choices as evidence favoring formalist rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role and design of default rules (especially damages/termination defaults) versus party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the entrenched compensatory default for breach and urges default rules that facilitate parties' negotiated termination rights, while Paper B analyzes how ex ante choice-of-law and forum-selection clauses reflect parties' attempts to select legal defaults that best support their transactions.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency of private ordering and market-driven contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses observed heterogeneity in termination fees and embedded options to argue that private contracting (risk allocation via options) is economically efficient, and Paper B treats the marketplace's selection of New York law and arbitration rules as empirical evidence that private ordering and bright-line rules improve commercial efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: using contracting parties' actual practices as empirical evidence to inform normative doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A points to common commercial and consumer practices (returns, liquidated damages, cancellation rights) to challenge historical and theoretical reliance on compensation, and Paper B relies on empirical patterns in choice-of-law/forum clauses and industry dispute-resolution practices to support claims about which legal regimes better serve commercial parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70stjohnslrev239!!ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of the compensation (expectation) principle as the default remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly criticizes the dominance of expectation/compensation as the governing remedial default and argues for treating breach liability as a priced option instead; Paper B engages this theme indirectly by discussing restitution and the limited use of doctrines (like frustration) that would alter ordinary compensatory outcomes, highlighting courts' reliance on traditional remedial concepts.

shared_topics.topic: termination/discharge doctrines as mechanisms for reallocating risk from supervening events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes termination rights and the right to breach as embedded options that reallocate risk between parties, while Paper B examines the doctrine of frustration of purpose—whether and when a party may be discharged when supervening events destroy the bargain—and the practical limits on relief that reallocation would entail.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the proper role of courts in enforcing or supplying default contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts are ill‑suited to set default damages and should enforce parties' negotiated termination provisions or provide bargain‑facilitating defaults, whereas Paper B documents how courts identify frustration as a doctrine but rarely apply it, raising questions about the courts' gap‑filling practices and doctrinal clarity.

shared_topics.topic: contract terms as tools of risk management/insurance and the normative implications for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames embedded termination rights and liquidated damages as insurance-like products whose prices allocate risk and should be respected, and Paper B treats the allocation of the risk of unanticipated events (the 'unshared risk of doing business') as central to whether courts should excuse performance, thereby engaging a similar risk‑management lens.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE REGULATORY FUNCTIONS OF TRANSNATIONAL COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: NEW ARCHITECTURES

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how regulatory provisions, certification requirements, and contractual clauses reallocate process-compliance burdens and monitoring duties along multi-tier supply chains. shared_topics.topic: the structure and enforcement of remedial provisions and the proper role of courts/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the coexistence of multiple remedial systems (sale contract remedies, certification sanctions, regulatory penalties) and the challenges of monitoring and reacting to overlapping breaches. shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of contractual terms driven by market bargaining, certification requirements, and risk preferences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that certification schemes and incorporated regulatory provisions change contract content (e.g., minimum prices, duration) and produce varied contractual architectures across chains. compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55wmmarylrev1869!!ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties privately negotiate embedded options, liquidated damages, and termination fees as market-priced risk-shifting devices; Paper B documents widespread use of ex tempore private institutions—dispute boards, ISDA committees—that specify obligations in real time and thereby complete otherwise incomplete contracts without judicial intervention.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents diverse commercial and consumer termination provisions and argues against a one-size-fits-all expectancy default in favor of defaults that respect bargains or context (e.g., a consumer free option); Paper B documents industry-specific ex tempore practices in construction and derivatives and argues that doctrinal defaults and judicial rules must account for such sectoral variation rather than assume uniform ex ante/ex post choices.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Lesson on Some Limits of Economic Analysis: Schwartz and Scott on Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should refrain from imposing an expectancy damages default and instead enforce parties' negotiated termination prices (or supply bargain-facilitating defaults), while Paper B examines when courts should supply meanings or defaults through interpretation and how economic prescriptions affect the boundary between judicially imposed rules and private ordering.

papers.node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
papers.title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
papers.abstract:
Is the domain of contract waxing or waning? Lawrence Friedman's pathbreaking 1965 book,Contract Law in America, characterized contract law as covering a residual category of relatively unimportant transactions. He argued that whenever particular types of transaction became sufficiently salient -- such as those concerning employment or insurance -- specialized regulation was promulgated that "robbed contract [law] of its subject-matter."Nine years later, Grant Gilmore expressed this idea similarly inThe Death of Contract, where he regarded "the general law of contract as a residual category -- what is left over after all the 'specialized' bodies of law have been added up."
In stark contrast to this residual conception, many scholars have trumpeted a much more imperialist conception of contract's domain. John Langbein, for example, recently opined:Contract has become the dominant doctrinal current in modern American law. In fields ranging from corporations and partnership, to landlord and tenant, to servitudes, to the law of marriage, scholars have come to understand our legal rules as resting mainly on imputed bargains that are susceptible to alteration by actual bargains.Under this view, the bedrock principles of contract inform (or should inform) an ever increasing range of legal relationships.
Contract has become the dominant doctrinal current in modern American law. In fields ranging from corporations and partnership, to landlord and tenant, to servitudes, to the law of marriage, scholars have come to understand our legal rules as resting mainly on imputed bargains that are susceptible to alteration by actual bargains.
What gives? The easiest way to reconcile these radically different claims about the domain of contract is to recognize that authors employ varying definitions about what makes a particular area of law "contractual." A residualist might only consider an area contractual if disputes are decided by common law courts using common law principles such as the consideration requirement.Imperialists on the other hand might consider any field to be contractual if the parties have substantial freedom to reorder their legal relationship privately.
Arthur Corbin long ago cautioned against scholars being diverted by such definitional misunderstandings:Definitions [of contract] have been constructed by almost all writers on law and in many thousands of judicial opinions . . . . It is a very common error to suppose that legal terms, such as contract, have one absolute and eternally correct definition. The fact is that all such terms have many usages, among which every one is free to select. One usage is to be preferred over another only in so far as it serves our necessity and convenience.Corbin wisely warned that we should not particularly care whether a field is characterized as contractual -- unless something turns on the characterization. Our first response to someone's impassioned suggestion that a particular area is or is not contractual should be "Who cares?" or perhaps more precisely "Whyshould we care?"
Definitions [of contract] have been constructed by almost all writers on law and in many thousands of judicial opinions . . . . It is a very common error to suppose that legal terms, such as contract, have one absolute and eternally correct definition. The fact is that all such terms have many usages, among which every one is free to select. One usage is to be preferred over another only in so far as it serves our necessity and convenience.
We should be quite skeptical of any canon definitions that are divorced from consequentialist considerations. Essentialist debates about what is contract are not only semantic in the most pejorative sense of the word, but may divert attention from what is really at stake. Common law decision making is prone to error when judges divorce the meaning of words from their legal consequences.Take, for example, a rent-to-own transaction whereby a consumer rents atelevision with an option to buy. In struggling to determine whether such a transaction is appropriately characterized a "credit sale," courts often lose sight of the fact that what turns on this designation is whether the seller needs to disclose an implicit interest rate.Even nonactivist judges who want only to be faithful to the legislature's intent should ask whether the legislature in using this term intended to force rent-to-own businesses to disclose this type of information. But in the most egregious examples of this type of reifying interpretation, the standards for characterizing behavior are wholly divorced from the legal consequences of the characterization.
Given my extreme skepticism about the utility of defining a contractual canon, I now will argue cautiously for the following definition: an area of law should be considered contractual if parties can privately reorder a substantial portion of their legal relations.While I have no stake in maintaining that this is the only valid definition, I hope to show that the definition, in Corbin's terms, might prove to be convenient because it might lead policymakers and scholars, when speaking of contract, to focus on a central aspect of contract -- whether and how parties contract around default rules.
This definition puts me squarely within the imperialist camp, but in three senses, I claim only to be a "wimpy imperialist." First, the focus on rules that are susceptible to private reordering does not necessarily include areas of law in which the rules conform to the "hypothetical contract" that parties would enter into if they could costlessly contract.Thomas Jackson, for example, has claimed that bankruptcy rules conform to the hypothetical bargain that creditorswould strike amongst themselves.But as Jules Coleman has acutely observed, these theories are really arguments that particular rules are efficient.The hypothetical bargain approach is used routinely to describe areas of law that are not contractual because the rules are largely mandatory or not susceptible to private reordering, such as bankruptcy or professional ethics. Describing such areas as being contractual is not useful. Because hypothetical bargaining theories routinely assume monolithic preferences (i.e., every contracting pair is assumed to want the same contract), these theories divert policymakers from making the difficult but important assessments about whether particular rules should be susceptible to private reordering or not.
, my definition of contract is wimpy because it does not incorporate a presumption that contractual rules should be defaults (susceptible to private reordering) or a presumption that majoritarian defaults should be chosen. In contrast, Fred McChesney represents what I would call a strong-form imperialist. To his credit, he clearly states what hinges on calling corporate law contractual: "Since the firm is best explained in the contractarian paradigm as a set of contractual rules that reduce transaction costs, mandatory law overriding contracts is the exception. Those advocating legal coercion thus must bear the burden of showing why coercion should trump contracts."But the fact that a substantial number or even a majority of rulesaresusceptible to private reordering does not create a presumption that other rules in the areashouldbe. Here, McChesney is leaping from "is" to "ought" without sufficient justification. My wimpy brand of contractarianism more modestly hopes to focus policymakers and scholars on the consequences of making particular rules mandatory. In addition, a conclusion that particular rules should be susceptible to private reordering does not lead me to presume that these defaults should be set at what the majority of contractual parties favor. Indeed, Rob Gertner and I have shown that "penalty" or "information-forcing" defaults might produce more efficientcontractual equilibria than so-called majoritarian defaults.My wimpier conception of contract intends to induce a more explicit consideration of how parties would bargain in the shadow of a variety of possible defaults.
Finally, by demanding that a substantial number of rules be susceptible to private reordering, the definition does not include areas where parties make all-or-nothing decisions to consent to a whole set of legal rules. The definition thereby excludes vast areas of tort and regulatory law that individuals opt into by consenting to undertake particular activities, such as driving cars. While there are interesting positive and normative issues about how particular sets of mandatory rules affect individuals' decisions to participate in particular activities, characterizing such areas as contractual might divert the policymakers' focus away from the core issues that should be in the foreground of policymakers' and scholars' minds.
In particular, my thesis is that defining the contractual canon as I have will help illuminate three normative issues: (1) Should particular rules be mandatory or merely defaults (which may be privately changed)? And if defaults, (2) Which default should be chosen?; and (3) What should be the necessary and sufficient conditions for contracting around the default? The impulse of too many scholars is to analyze legal rules as though, like much of tort law, they were not or could not be susceptible to private reordering. But a host of related normative questions arises in contexts where parties have or should have the freedom to reorder substantial parts of their legal relationship.

questions.question: Is the domain of contract law expanding or contracting - i.e., to what extent are various legal relationships governed mainly by rules that parties can privately reorder?
Should rules that structure interpersonal legal relationships be set as defaults that parties may modify by agreement, or as mandatory rules that cannot be contracted around?
Which designs of default rules and what conditions or constraints on contracting around those defaults produce more efficient and normatively desirable outcomes?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether international dispute mechanisms (notably the WTO) should be seen as self-enforcing or coercive and how coercive enforcement can crowd out self-enforcement; Paper B examines when legal rules should be defaults (subject to private re‑ordering) versus mandatory, which is the same normative distinction between private/self‑enforcement and legally coercive rules.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of definitional choices about what counts as 'contractual' or 'self‑enforcing' for legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how classifying the WTO process as self‑enforcing drives different policy conclusions and cautions about misclassification, while Paper B argues that definitional disputes over what is 'contract' matter only to the extent they affect consequential policy choices about defaults and mandatory rules.

shared_topics.topic: role and impact of third‑party adjudication and enforcement agents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes features of the WTO dispute settlement (independent adjudicators, limits on third‑party initiation) and how those institutional features affect enforcement dynamics, and Paper B interrogates the role of courts and doctrinal classification (e.g., what triggers disclosure obligations) in shaping contracting space and the practical consequences of judicial characterization.

shared_topics.topic: limits of applying contract theory across different institutional contexts and skepticism about universal contractarian assumptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns against transplanting lessons from international agreements to commercial contracts because of contextual differences (e.g., non‑signatory harms, managerial incentives), and Paper B warns against blanket hypothetical‑bargain or contractarian claims (e.g., treating many areas as contractual) without examining institutional particulars and normative consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 164upalrev1403!!ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS

shared_topics.topic: boundaries of what counts as the ‘deal’ or the contractual domain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that complex M&A transactions are ‘unbundled bargains’ whose boundaries extend beyond the acquisition agreement into ancillary contracts, and Paper B interrogates when an area of law (or a set of relations) should be characterized as contractual, both probing where and why the scope of contract law should be drawn.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and the use of modular/ancillary contracts to tailor defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties deliberately use multiple ancillary agreements to modularize and precisely allocate rights and risks around a central deal, while Paper B focuses on the normative and descriptive significance of rules that are susceptible to private reordering and how defaults should be set or contracted around.

shared_topics.topic: judicial characterization and contract interpretation with consequential legal effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how courts’ interpretation of peripheral agreements (e.g., treating confidentiality clauses as implied standstills) can determine whether deals proceed, and Paper B criticizes reifying characterizations divorced from consequences, stressing that how judges label transactions has important legal and policy effects.

shared_topics.topic: transaction-cost and efficiency rationales for contract design (centralized vs unbundled structures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a transaction-cost account of why parties unbundle deals—modularity and precision increase ex ante efficiency and reduce ex post enforcement costs—while Paper B locates contractarian arguments (including transaction-cost explanations for firm and rule design) at the center of debates over when private ordering should be permitted.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis397!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT

shared_topics.topic: whether default rules should be set to match majority expectations (majoritarian defaults)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether the UCC warranty default corresponds to consumer expectations by comparing prices for explicit, disclaimed, and silent warranty terms on eBay; Paper B directly addresses the normative debate over whether defaults ought to track majority preferences, criticizing strong presumptions in favor of majoritarian defaults and urging more explicit justificatory standards.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretation and legal significance of contractual silence/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how consumers interpret a silent warranty clause (i.e., the default UCC rule) and measures market responses to silence versus explicit terms; Paper B treats defaults (including the practical effect of silence) as central to whether a domain is 'contractual' and emphasizes that characterizations should turn on the legal consequences of leaving terms unset.

shared_topics.topic: parties' ability and conditions to contract around defaults (private reordering)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A operationalizes the idea that parties can alter default rules by drafting explicit warranty language and tests whether consumers price those alterations differently; Paper B defines the contractual domain by the extent to which parties can privately reorder legal relations and raises normative questions about when and how rules should be susceptible to such reordering.

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical evidence and consequences in choosing and evaluating default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contributes experimental evidence about consumer expectations to evaluate the quality of a statutory default (the UCC warranty), highlighting empirical limits and interpretation; Paper B argues that debates about contract's scope should be tied to consequentialist considerations (including how defaults affect behavior) and cites empirical or bargaining-based theories (e.g., penalty defaults) as relevant to selecting defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71ucololrev541!!ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE

shared_topics.topic: designing statutes and doctrines to guide judicial discretion (Legal Realism influence)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes essentialist definitional debates and urges that legal categories and rules be structured with an eye toward their legal consequences and how judges will apply them; Paper B traces how Karl Llewellyn, a Legal Realist, intentionally shaped the U.C.C. to guide judicial decisionmaking rather than eliminate judicial discretion.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default rules and parties' ability to privately reorder commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defines the contractual domain by the extent parties can privately reorder legal relations and emphasizes focusing on defaults that parties can contract around; Paper B (on the U.C.C.) engages with commercial-law design choices that enable private ordering and flexible gap‑filling in commercial transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the normative question of when rules should be mandatory versus default (contractarian vs mandatory regulation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames as central the normative inquiry whether particular rules should be mandatory or merely default and how to choose defaults; Paper B discusses U.C.C. provisions influenced by Llewellyn that reflect deliberate choices about which commercial rules are flexible standards versus binding mandates.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal labels and classifications affect legal consequences and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows concern that characterizing transactions (e.g., 'credit sale' or 'rent‑to‑own') can divert courts from the consequences that should follow and affect disclosure/rights; Paper B examines how Llewellyn's drafting of U.C.C. language and concepts sought to shape the legal significance of commercial classifications and thereby influence outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: what counts as 'contract' / the proper definition of the contractual domain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly debates rival canonical definitions (residualist vs imperialist) and proposes a working definition based on whether parties can privately reorder a substantial portion of their legal relations; Paper B likewise takes up the definitional question by rejecting individualistic accounts and offering a substantive, relational account of what contract is (a form of collaboration), thereby reshaping which practices should be treated as contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal significance of doctrines like consideration and expectation remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes traditional doctrinal markers (e.g., the consideration requirement) as part of discussions about whether an area is 'contractual' and how courts deploy such tests; Paper B directly analyzes the consideration doctrine and the expectation remedy, arguing these doctrines are best understood in light of the contract relation and its moral values.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for enforcing and structuring contract law (why and how to justify defaults or mandatory rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds consequentialist and policy questions—asking which rules should be mandatory vs. defaults, which defaults to choose, and when parties should be allowed to contract around rules; Paper B develops a moral-philosophical foundation (contract as recognition/collaboration) that bears on when promises and agreements ought to be enforceable and how law should treat contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between private ordering/autonomy and limits on contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its definition on parties' capacity to privately reorder legal relations and stresses evaluating the consequences of allowing such reordering; Paper B treats contracts as products of self-interested parties forming collaborative relations and addresses the justificatory limits of legal enforcement of those private bargains, engaging the same issue of how much freedom contracting parties should have.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: defaults as information‑forcing mechanisms revealing asymmetric private information

shared_topics.topic: efficiency trade‑offs between alternative default settings given preference distributions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques assuming majoritarian defaults and emphasizes that different default choices can improve efficiency depending on parties' preferences; Paper B models how the distribution of buyer valuations determines whether the Hadley default or a full‑damages default yields higher efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: bargaining around defaults and transaction costs of private reordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on when and how parties can privately reorder legal relations and the transaction‑cost consequences of contracting around defaults; Paper B shows that a Hadley default can reduce bargaining/transaction costs and influence parties' incentives to contract or take precautions in the shadow of the default.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes that legislative and doctrinal shifts toward formalism should depend on empirical evidence about commercial preferences and practices and finds that such evidence is lacking for neoformalism; Paper A argues against purely definitional or hypothetical-bargain approaches and urges attention to consequentialist, empirically-informed questions about how parties actually bargain in the shadow of different defaults.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal classifications and interpretive rules produce substantive legal consequences for parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A illustrates that labels (e.g., 'credit sale' versus rent-to-own) determine duties like disclosure and emphasizes that characterizations must be tied to consequences; Paper B shows that shifting interpretive rules (plain meaning vs. allowance for trade usage/course of performance) will change what evidence courts consider and thereby materially affect contractual outcomes and commercial practices.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its normative theory in welfare-maximization for business-to-business contracts and rejects other norms (fairness, distribution) in that domain, and Paper B urges that definitional and doctrinal choices about what counts as contract should be guided by consequentialist considerations (including efficiency) rather than essentialist semantics.

shared_topics.topic: the desirability of defaults versus mandatory rules and the extent of private reordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when default rules are useful and contends many statutory defaults are unnecessary or should be contractible around, and Paper B centers its definition of 'contractual' on whether parties can privately reorder legal relations and focuses on the normative questions of which rules should be defaults and how parties can contract around them.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of party sophistication and heterogeneity for crafting contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a sharp distinction between sophisticated commercial firms and other parties, arguing different rules (e.g., textualist defaults, liberty to contract) should apply to firms, while Paper B criticizes monolithic 'hypothetical bargain' assumptions and emphasizes that heterogeneity of preferences matters for whether and how legal defaults should be set or made mandatory.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how internal industry norms, standard contract models, and other private-ordering mechanisms often dominate ordering in construction transactions; Paper B centers on the extent to which parties can 'privately reorder' their relations and treats private reordering capacity as the core criterion for calling an area contractual.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and policy question of mandatory rules versus defaults (and which defaults to choose) in transactional law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats external public law as a potential 'safety net' and evaluates how statutory backstops or codification might supplement or constrain private contracts in construction; Paper B explicitly frames a research and policy agenda around whether specific rules should be mandatory or left as defaults, which defaults to adopt, and the conditions for contracting around them.

shared_topics.topic: the practical consequences of definitional choices about what counts as 'contractual' (i.e., why characterization matters for regulation, disclosure, and enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how classifying construction transactions (hybrids, sales, services) shapes regulatory exposure, drafting practices, and dispute management, motivating reform; Paper B argues that debates over whether an area is 'contractual' should be evaluated by their legal consequences, showing that labeling affects disclosure duties, enforcement regimes, and legislative or judicial responses.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates competing 'pictures' of contract law (duty‑imposing, power‑conferring, and its proposed third category, 'compound rules') to identify which concept best renders our contract law intelligible; Paper B debates rival definitions of the 'contractual canon' (residualist vs imperialist) and proposes a working definition based on the extent to which parties can privately reorder their legal relations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' purposive autonomy/private ordering in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the idea that some contract rules function to enable parties to purposively create legal obligations (power‑conferring and compound rules); Paper B likewise treats private reordering—parties' ability to reshape defaults and bargain around rules—as the core criterion for deeming areas 'contractual' and as the focal normative problem.

shared_topics.topic: how legal structure (formalities, validity conditions, and defaults) sorts for or against purposive contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes validity conditions (e.g., seals) and the absence thereof to explain when the law sorts for actors' legal purpose and introduces 'compound rules' that anticipate purposive use without formalities; Paper B focuses on whether rules should be mandatory or left as defaults susceptible to contracting around, and on what conditions should govern parties' ability to contract around defaults.

shared_topics.topic: normative and policy consequences of choosing one conceptual picture or canon over another
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications from its functional/compound‑rule account (arguing it supports pluralist justificatory theories and affects how we should justify contract rules); Paper B emphasizes that definitional choices about what is 'contractual' have direct normative consequences for whether rules should be default or mandatory and for how policymakers should set defaults and design conditions for contracting around them.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contracts as Organizations

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes legal scholars' expertise in contract language, drafting norms, and judicial interpretation as essential to understanding contracts; Paper B criticizes semantic or formal characterizations by courts (e.g., labeling transactions) and urges attention to the practical legal consequences of those characterizations.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally focuses on whether areas of law are 'contractual' by virtue of parties' ability to privately reorder defaults and asks normative questions about which rules should be mandatory or default; Paper A examines contracts as governance devices within organizations, implicating questions about contractual autonomy and how parties structure rights and obligations rather than relying on ex post interventions.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of theoretical frameworks on framing empirical and normative questions about contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the dominance of economic theories in empirical contract research and proposes organizational theories to broaden inquiry; Paper B demonstrates how adopting different conceptual frameworks (residualist vs imperialist/contractarian) changes which policy and normative questions scholars and judges consider relevant.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that judges should ground characterizations and doctrinal choices in legal consequences and policy (not mere semantics), while Paper B develops a theory of judicial 'decision procedures' and practical reason by which courts weigh plural values when determining contract formation and content.

shared_topics.topic: when contractual rules should be default (susceptible to private reordering) versus mandatory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its definition of the contractual domain on whether parties can privately reorder legal relations and poses normative questions about which rules should be defaults and the conditions for contracting around them; Paper B addresses the same issue indirectly by explaining how plural values (liberty, equality, etc.) and contextual adjudication should guide when autonomy should be honored versus when protections should be imposed.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes essentialist definitions and reliance on hypothetical-bargain efficiency arguments for generating misleading characterizations of 'contractual' areas, and Paper B explicitly rejects monist approaches that subordinate all contract issues to a single super-value, arguing instead for pluralist, context-sensitive reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: balancing competing values (liberty, equality, efficiency, community) in contract formation and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the normative tension between allowing parties to reorder defaults (liberty/autonomy) and protecting other social goods through mandatory rules, while Paper B provides a framework for courts to identify and rank values like liberty, equality, and communal duties and to integrate those rankings into doctrinal decisions about formation and enforcement.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts moral promises with legally enforceable contracts and emphasizes that contract law uniquely enables individuals to alter their legal positions and rely on others' ability to enforce those private orders; Paper B explicitly defines the 'contractual' domain in terms of whether parties can privately reorder substantial portions of their legal relations and uses that criterion to map the scope of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: tension between commitment (stability) and revision (fickleness) and how law should accommodate changes of mind
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally explores the normative problem of 'fickle' agents, arguing that contract law (unlike moral promise) can and should accommodate persistent agency and the ability to revise commitments; Paper B engages the related practical question of when legal rules should be flexible enough to permit parties to change the default allocation of rights and obligations, implicating how law treats evolving preferences.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for permitting or limiting contractual freedom (agency, autonomy, liberal values)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its analysis in concepts of moral agency and autonomy, debating why we should recognize normative powers to bind oneself and when those powers ought to be constrained to preserve persistent agency; Paper B interrogates why it matters to label an area 'contractual,' urging that such labels should turn on consequentialist and normative considerations about the desirability of private ordering and the proper limits on contractual freedom.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default vs mandatory rules and doctrines that enable contracting around defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes that contract law contains doctrines that are more permissive than moral practice and discusses legal accommodations for regret and reversal (i.e., mechanisms that allow revisions); Paper B develops a framework focused on which rules should be defaults susceptible to private reordering, which should be mandatory, and what conditions should govern contracting around those defaults.

shared_topics.topic: capacity for private ordering (ability to contract around default rules) as a defining feature of the contractual domain

shared_topics.topic: concerns about doctrinal vagueness, judicial discretion, and the value of predictability

compared_to.partner_node_id: 7jsmallemergingbusl283!!ARTICLE:I MEAN WHAT I SAY, I THINK: THE DANGER TO SMALL BUSINESSES OF ENTERING INTO LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE AGREEMENTS THAT MAY NOT REFLECT THEIR INTENTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:I MEAN WHAT I SAY, I THINK: THE DANGER TO SMALL BUSINESSES OF ENTERING INTO LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE AGREEMENTS THAT MAY NOT REFLECT THEIR INTENTIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how reliance on form contracts and limited attorney access can lock small businesses into terms that do not reflect their intentions, and Paper B examines how standardized regimes and defaults interact with private ordering and disclosure regimes, highlighting how doctrinal choices affect parties subject to standard-form transactions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.

papers.title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
papers.abstract:
Hadley v. Baxendale,one of the most celebrated cases in contract law,sets forth the default rule that unforeseeable consequentialdamages are unrecoverable.The case has come to represent an important limit to the general rule awarding full expectation damages for breach.And over time, Hadley has taken on even greater significance as an archetype for contract default rules that efficiently expose asymmetric information.
A sophisticated line of literature examines the Hadley rule from an economic point of view,building theoretical models to determine whether it is efficient.While many variables matter, one key con-cern is the distribution of buyer valuations for contract performance.Economic theory suggests that if many buyers place a low value on performance while few buyers place a high value on performance (see Figure 1a)-and if a buyer's valuation is private, unobservable information-then the Hadley rule may be preferable to a rule that awards full expectation damages.Under these circumstances, a Hadley default may force private information to be revealed in a way that encourages efficient precautions against breach and minimizes transaction costs from bargaining around the default.If the valuation distributions are reversed (Figure 1b), the Hadley rule may be inefficient, and a full-damages default might be better.

questions.question: Whether a default contract damages rule that disallows recovery for unforeseeable consequential losses is more efficient than a full-expectation-damages default when buyers' valuations for performance are private information.

How the distribution of buyer valuations (e.g., many low-value buyers and few high-value buyers versus the reverse) affects which damages default (limiting consequential losses versus full expectation damages) yields greater overall efficiency.

Whether a damages default that limits recovery can induce buyers to reveal private valuation information and thereby generate more efficient precaution incentives and lower transaction/bargaining costs.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Hadley rule as a default damages rule that can reveal private buyer valuations and induce efficient precautions when valuations are asymmetric; Paper B analyzes UCC integration and parol/extrinsic-evidence rules as default doctrines that determine what written terms govern and thus shape parties' incentives when contracting under private information.

shared_topics.topic: the role of evidentiary and interpretive doctrines (foreseeability, parol evidence, extrinsic evidence) in revealing parties' private information and fixing obligations

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules affect transaction costs and bargaining around written contracts
