papers.node_id: 55wmmarylrev1869!!ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING
papers.title: ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING
papers.abstract:
This Article argues that the dominant view of contract design and interpretation is fundamentally limited and misleading. This view is that parties have precisely two options with respect to any given future circumstance: clearly specify their responsibilities to one another at contract formation or leave their responsibilities vague, relying on a court to determine them after performance.For example, a construction contract could specify the use of Reading brand pipe in exchange for $ 77,000.This ex ante contracting approach involves thorough negotiation and drafting. Alternatively, ex post contracting enlists a court to later specify an incomplete contract by calling for "merchantable" pipe in exchange for a "reasonable" fee, and then litigating whether the tendered pipe or payment met the contractual requirement. Concerning interpretation, scholars generally advise courts to interpret in whatever way helps parties to lower the sum of those two costs.
Though intuitive and widely accepted, the ex ante / ex post dichotomy leaves out a third, "real-time" approach to contracting, in which a third-party agent specifies the contract for the parties. Following the language of ex ante, which means "before the fact," and ex post, which means "after the fact," this Article introduces "ex tempore," which means "in the moment."
Parties utilize ex tempore contracting techniques when they draft largely incomplete agreements at contract formation but provide a means for ongoing completion in the course of performance. Forexample, parties might include a vague term, such as "merchantable" or "reasonable," but then stipulate that a certain individual shall define that term as the need may arise. This approach allows the parties to have clarity of obligation at or around performance, avoiding costly disputes while economizing on front-end costs.
Though largely unnoticed, ex tempore contracting is extremely widespread in some industries. The construction industry, which employed 6 percent of all Americans (12 percent if production, hauling, and distribution of equipment and materials are included) prior to the recent economic downturn and contributed 8 percent to GDP,stands at the forefront of ex tempore contracting. It is now common practice for construction contractors to draft incomplete contracts and entrust a cadre of neutral experts, thedispute board, to make decisions whenever a given issue becomes salient. Such boards answer questions the parties have not specified, such as: "Is there a duty to help the contractor find qualified employees?"or "Does the contract require the owner to audit and review the subcontractor's costs before disputing them?"Dispute boards are becoming the norm in construction contracts because of their startling effectiveness in improving projects; in an industry in which 25 percent of projects lead to disputes,dispute boards resolve 98 percent of claims brought before them.
Likewise, the credit derivatives market, constituting a titanic $ 27 trillion in notional value,has turned to ex tempore contracting to allow agile and effective contracting in a time of economic and regulatory change. Complex derivatives routinely include seemingly vague terms combined with techniques for achieving instantaneousclarification. For example, many owners of Greek bonds had protected themselves against the risk of nonpayment by entering into credit default swaps (CDS).These insurance-like derivatives offered payment to the bondholders if Greece were to renege on its obligations.As Greece grew increasingly reluctant to pay its debts, bondholders did not look to the contract text nor to a court to determine whether they were entitled to payment under the CDS. Instead, a committee of the dominant trade association, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), had authority to rapidly clarify entitlements and define the word "default."Few have noticed the quasi-adjudicative role played by ISDA, which has proven invaluable in facilitating the use of credit default swaps and, at times, reducing systemic risk. Fewer still have noticed that one can best understand this function as an expression of ex tempore contracting.
Despite the prevalence of ex tempore contracting, courts, parties, and scholars have been slow to recognize its significance. As a result, courts misunderstand and frustrate parties' contractual choices and disrupt the usefulness of ex tempore contracting. For example, courts sometimes mistakenly characterize ex tempore contracting as mere mediationand thereby permit parties to frustrate the ex tempore determination process, say, by refusing to select board membersor even to attend at all.
At a more abstract level, the failure to notice ex tempore contracting has led scholars to overestimate their understanding of contract design and judges' ability to improve it with simple changes ininterpretation techniques. For example, courts sometimes apply penalty defaults in cases of contractual silence in order to cause parties to contract more explicitly and thereby disclose important information to one another.In one such case,Hadley v. Baxendale, a court denied recovery of unforeseeable consequential damages for a broken crankshaft,even though most parties would probably prefer the defendant to be liable for all such damages.Scholars have defendedHadleyas encouraging parties to communicate and negotiate.Yet opportunistic parties can circumvent information-forcing defaults if they can instead furtively opt for ex tempore contracting.
In offering a challenge to the dominant contract design paradigm, this Article takes up a call for research extending the existing literature.Oliver Williamson identifies a type of "trilateral governance," in which third-party agents are used to update or modify incomplete contracts on an ongoing basis.He even mentions architects' preliminary adjudicatory role at construction sites, a precursor to the dispute board discussed in Part II.A, as an example of trilateral governance.This foreshadowing of ex tempore contracting allows it to be considered within the family of the relational contracting and transaction costs economics literature. Byproviding a detailed discussion of ex tempore contracting in construction and financial derivatives, this Article explores Williamson's insight for its deep potential.
The Article will proceed as follows: Part I reviews recent literature on contractual completeness and the ex ante / ex post dichotomy in order to situate ex tempore contracting. It then introduces ex tempore contracting and analyzes the main drivers of its usefulness. Ex tempore contracting is attractive when interim determination of responsibilities is preferable to doing so at contract formation or after performance and when agent determination of responsibilities is preferred to party or court determination. The former requirement will correspond to circumstances in which uncertainty is high but coordinating is costly for parties. The latter will occur when uncertainty is high and the parties value clarity at the time of performance, post-transaction relief is unlikely to be complete, or it is difficult for the many parties to coordinate a settlement. This analysis is of great importance in continuing to analyze important contracting realities and the forces that drive them. It also guides discussion of subsequent examples of ex tempore contracting.
Part II applies this theory to examples of ex tempore contracting. Section A looks at the use of ex tempore contracting in construction through dispute boards. In addition to its role in advancing this Article's theoretical contribution, the discussion of dispute boards constitutes a significant contribution in its own right as the first extended academic treatment of this fascinating innovation in dispute management. Despite their revolutionary potential, dispute boards are almost unknown to scholars of contracts and dispute resolutionand barely examined even by those scholars who care about construction law.This Section explores diverse uses ofdisputes boards, their advantages, and their risks, utilizing a cache of dispute board decisions that the State of Florida recently made public. Section B describes the role of ex tempore contracting in credit derivatives transactions, in which complicated financial relations are governed by apparently incomplete agreements whose clarity and specification come in the course of performance.
Having established the pervasiveness of ex tempore contracting, Part III then draws out the implications of ex tempore contracting. Section A examines the judicial treatment of ex tempore institutions, showing how courts can better support parties informed choice of ex tempore contracting by allowing its use even when a court may find it otherwise futile or unconscionable. Section B problematizes the judicial and scholarly treatment of penalty defaults. Section C then speculates as to how parties might choose to better use ex tempore contracting in the future, such as including it alongside earnout agreements in M&A contracts.

questions.question: When and why do contracting parties choose to delegate real-time specification of contractual obligations to a third-party agent instead of fully specifying terms at formation or relying on courts after performance?

Does delegating ongoing contract specification to third-party decisionmakers reduce disputes, transaction costs, and systemic risk compared with traditional ex ante (fully specified) or ex post (court-resolved) contracting approaches?

How should legal institutions and judicial practice treat and support parties' use of third-party, real-time decisionmakers for completing contracts to preserve the parties' choices and the effectiveness of such mechanisms?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43iowajcorpl1!!ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts

shared_topics.topic: real-time completion of contractual terms by external agents (human or automated)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze contracts that deliberately leave terms open to be specified during performance by an external decision-maker — Paper A describes human third-party decisionmakers like construction dispute boards and ISDA committees, while Paper B describes algorithmic or machine-driven systems that translate broad objectives into specific directives at the time of performance.

shared_topics.topic: challenge to the ex ante / ex post dichotomy and related doctrinal categories (rules vs. standards, complete vs. incomplete contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue that these contracting forms blur traditional contract-theory categories: Paper A introduces the 'ex tempore' (in-the-moment) alternative to ex ante/ex post contracting, and Paper B shows how self-driving contracts confound distinctions between rules and standards and between completeness and incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: who supplies and how to govern third-party decision-makers/providers
shared_topics.justification: Both works identify the provider of the real-time mechanism as legally and economically central — Paper A focuses on institutional providers (dispute boards, ISDA committees) and their roles, and Paper B examines markets for third‑party or platform vendors, arbitration/insurance providers, and the governance and certification challenges they pose.

shared_topics.topic: implications for judicial treatment, interpretation, and enforcement doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider how courts and existing doctrines should treat contracts that defer specification to others: Paper A critiques judicial misunderstandings of ex tempore institutions and the misapplication of defaults, while Paper B surveys how doctrines like definiteness, assent, unconscionability, and enforcement must be reevaluated for self-driving contracts.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑costs, strategic incentives, and the conditions under which parties prefer in‑performance specification
shared_topics.justification: Both analyses explain why parties opt to defer specification — weighing front‑end drafting costs, uncertainty, need for clarity at performance, and coordination costs — with Paper A applying this to construction and credit derivatives and Paper B applying it to self‑pricing and monitoring-enabled markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38yalejonreg678!!ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for completing incomplete contracts (ex ante, ex post, ex tempore)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A introduces and develops 'ex tempore' contracting as a distinct mode of completing incomplete contracts in real time (alongside ex ante drafting and ex post judicial specification), while Paper B situates contract law as a planning device whose mandatory rules, defaults, and standards function to complete markets and thereby fill out incomplete state-contingent contracts.

shared_topics.topic: delegation to third-party agents or private institutions to specify or adjudicate terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and analyzes widespread private delegation (dispute boards in construction, ISDA committees in derivatives) that authoritatively specifies obligations during performance; Paper B similarly examines decentralized implementation and the delegation to parties and private mechanisms (auctions, platforms, specialized arbitrators/courts) as central to realizing efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the design and consequences of default rules versus standards and interpretive doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how courts' use of penalty defaults and interpretive doctrines can misunderstand or frustrate parties' choices to employ ex tempore devices, while Paper B analyzes default rules versus standards under GET, warns of overreliance on indeterminate standards, and argues that interpretive formalism and carefully chosen defaults affect market completion and parties' ability to implement mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, asymmetric information, and mechanism-design solutions embedded in contracting institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that ex tempore contracting economizes on front-end negotiation costs and helps resolve uncertainty and coordination problems during performance, whereas Paper B calls for integrating mechanism design and GET insights to address asymmetric information, communication costs, and the practical implementation constraints of incentive-compatible contractual mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: the role and capacity of adjudicatory institutions (courts, specialized tribunals, arbitrators) in supporting or undermining contractual innovations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how ordinary courts sometimes mischaracterize or obstruct ex tempore institutions and recommends judicial approaches that respect parties' chosen real-time adjudicators, while Paper B interrogates the adjudication system's ability to implement planning and mechanism-design goals, proposes specialized tribunals/arbitrators to reduce communication costs, and questions courts' capacity to perform complex mechanism roles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev451!!Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for filling gaps in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A introduces and analyzes 'ex tempore' contracting—delegating real-time gap-filling to third‑party agents during performance—while Paper B analyzes how trade usages, course of dealing, and course of performance operate as background gap‑filling rules that supply terms when parties leave contracts incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation choices and deference to private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how courts treat ex tempore institutions and urges judicial recognition of parties' choices to use third‑party decisionmakers, whereas Paper B debates plain‑meaning versus incorporationist judicial strategies for deciding whether to treat business norms as part of the contract.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, specification costs, and opportunism as drivers of institutional choice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers use a cost/benefit framework—Paper A frames ex tempore contracting as a response to high uncertainty and costly front‑end coordination, and Paper B evaluates incorporation versus plain meaning in terms of specification costs, error costs, and the ability of norms to deter opportunistic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role and legal status of industry-developed private norms and third‑party institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents industry practices (dispute boards, ISDA committees) that create quasi‑adjudicative, real‑time norms, while Paper B examines the legal recognition and enforcement of privately developed trade usages and business norms under Article 2, asking when courts should give them contractual effect.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68tennlrev73!!ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

shared_topics.topic: contractual ambiguity and vague terms (e.g., “merchantable,” “reasonable”)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes parties' deliberate use of vague or incomplete language and how such terms are later specified in performance, while Paper B systematically treats how courts should resolve ambiguous contractual language and the interpretive challenges that arise from imprecise drafting.

shared_topics.topic: who resolves gaps and ambiguities — courts versus third‑party decisionmakers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds ex tempore mechanisms (dispute boards, ISDA committees) as alternatives to court resolution of incompleteness, and Paper B addresses the judicial role and rules for resolving ambiguity, thereby engaging with the comparative allocation of gap‑filling authority.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal default rules and their effects on drafting incentives (e.g., contra proferentem, penalty defaults)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and situates penalty defaults in the literature on contract design and notes how parties can circumvent information‑forcing defaults by delegating resolution, while Paper B examines contra proferentem and other interpretive doctrines that function as defaults shaping parties' drafting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract design and dispute resolution practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative and empirical implications for when parties should use ex ante, ex post, or ex tempore techniques (with industry examples), and Paper B offers a practical, systematic approach for courts in Tennessee that has direct consequences for how parties should draft and litigate ambiguous contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62dukelj707!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW

shared_topics.topic: private ordering as a source of binding norms outside formal statute
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how private institutions (dispute boards, ISDA committees) create and enforce obligations within contractual relations, and Paper B theorizes how customs and social practices—also nonstate or private—generate legally significant norms, treating both as forms of nonstate normative governance that interact with formal law.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for filling gaps in formal rules or contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies 'ex tempore' contracting as a way parties deliberately leave contracts incomplete and rely on ongoing mechanisms to supply content at performance, while Paper B argues that customs/normative practices operate to supply normative content where formal legal rules are silent or indeterminate.

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment and evidentiary standards for nonstatutory norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts' misunderstandings of ex tempore institutions and the use of default rules that can undermine parties' chosen mechanisms, and Paper B critiques the dominant evidentiary/additive approach to proving custom (usus + opinio juris), arguing for a different framework that better captures how law should recognize customary practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of ongoing discursive interaction and reciprocal practices in making norms authoritative
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes real-time, interactive processes (boards, committees, in-performance determinations) that produce binding specifications, and Paper B centers 'discursive normative practices'—reciprocally oriented, communicative interactions—as the site where customs and legal norms are formed and sustained.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52hastingslj645!!SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC

shared_topics.topic: use of third‑party adjudicators (dispute boards, ISDA committees) to fill contractual gaps

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy and the design of default rules (limits on contracting and choice‑of‑law)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the tension between protecting parties (especially consumers) and respecting freedom to contract, including choice‑of‑law and default rules in the UCC; Paper B shows how parties deliberately choose incomplete contracts plus procedural mechanisms (ex tempore) to avoid costly front‑loaded specification and to circumvent information‑forcing defaults.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a longstanding debate about statute versus common law and the ALI/NCCUSL role in making commercial rules versus leaving matters to judges or markets; Paper B documents how courts currently misread or undermine parties' use of ex tempore institutions and argues courts should better defer to or accommodate private contracting arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial law should adapt to complex or novel transactions (software, electronic goods, complex derivatives, construction practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the difficulty of drawing doctrinal boundaries (e.g., Article 2 vs software/electronic goods) as technology and hybrid goods evolve, while Paper B studies contracting innovations in complex settings (construction projects, credit derivatives) that respond to uncertainty and rapid change, illustrating pressures on traditional contract rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1615!!ARTICLE: Reconsidering Contractual Liability and the Incentive to Reveal Information
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reconsidering Contractual Liability and the Incentive to Reveal Information

shared_topics.topic: how contractual rules affect parties' incentives to reveal private information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how limits on contractual liability change high-valuation buyers' incentives to disclose their valuation, while Paper B discusses how doctrines like penalty defaults are intended to force information revelation and how parties can instead choose alternative contracting forms that change those revelation incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the welfare and efficiency implications of designing contract liability/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when limitations on liability are socially desirable given their informational effects, and Paper B assesses how judicial default rules (and courts' treatment of them) interact with party choices like ex tempore contracting to affect project efficiency and dispute rates.

shared_topics.topic: who (parties, courts, or third-party agents) determines contractual obligations when contracts are incomplete
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how legal rules governing liability influence information transfer and the resulting allocation of obligations, while Paper B explicitly develops the ex ante / ex post / ex tempore taxonomy comparing party-specified terms, court-filled obligations, and third‑party (e.g., dispute boards or ISDA committees) determination.

shared_topics.topic: strategic contracting choices used to circumvent or exploit legal informational mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties may respond strategically to liability rules (e.g., revealing valuations under certain limits), and Paper B documents how parties can evade information-forcing defaults or litigation by opting into ex tempore mechanisms that achieve real-time specification instead of court-determined terms.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS:IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION THE LIMITS OF EMPIRICISM: WHAT FACTS TELL US: COMMENTS ON DANIEL KEATING'S 'EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION'

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation of incomplete or conflicting contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how courts treat incomplete contracts and urges recognition of ex tempore mechanisms instead of forcing ex ante specificity or ex post adjudication; Paper B analyzes how courts apply U.C.C. §2-207 (the 'battle of the forms') in practice and questions what empirical patterns tell us about doctrinal choices for resolving conflicting terms.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical evidence to inform contract doctrine and reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals industry facts (e.g., dispute board success rates, CDS market practices) to argue for a doctrinal shift recognizing ex tempore contracting, while Paper B directly interrogates the role and limits of empirical research (citing Keating's study) in shaping how scholars and courts should treat §2-207 and related commercial rules.

shared_topics.topic: private or industry-based mechanisms for filling contractual gaps (third‑party decisionmakers and trade bodies)

papers.node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTIONOn the Golden Gate [University School of Law] campus recently, a group of first-year students at risk of losing their [merit] scholarships were trying to make sense of the system … [T]he phrase "bait and switch" came up a lot. Several assumed that they were given what is essentially a discount to get them in the door."I had a friend once who told me that hunting is a sport," said one Golden Gate merit grant winner who anticipated coming up shy of a 3.0 average. "I said, 'Hunting is not a sport.' He said: 'Sure it's a sport. It's just that the animals don't know they're in a game.' That's what it feels like to be a law student these days. You have no idea you're in a game."
On the Golden Gate [University School of Law] campus recently, a group of first-year students at risk of losing their [merit] scholarships were trying to make sense of the system … [T]he phrase "bait and switch" came up a lot. Several assumed that they were given what is essentially a discount to get them in the door."I had a friend once who told me that hunting is a sport," said one Golden Gate merit grant winner who anticipated coming up shy of a 3.0 average. "I said, 'Hunting is not a sport.' He said: 'Sure it's a sport. It's just that the animals don't know they're in a game.' That's what it feels like to be a law student these days. You have no idea you're in a game."
When do bait-and-switch tactics cross the line from "fair sport" to "turkey shoot"? A range of bait-and-switch tactics emerge in the marketplace. Some have been deemedlawfulfair sport, and others have been deemedunlawful"turkey shoots." Extending the metaphor, the formal hunting rules appear to reflect a sense of norms and imbued marketplace customs. Just as real hunting rules are driven by custom, norms, and formal regulation, so are rules about sales tactics. In this Article, I find that custom and normsdrive the approach toward formal regulation of bait-and-switch tactics more than welfare advancement.The cultural explanation of commercial regulation can be identified in the history of commercial regulationand, I will argue, can be used to explain current regulation and to predict and guide its future. I use bait and switch to illustrate these dynamics.
Though custom and norms tend to explain our regulatory regime more closely than the construct of welfare advancement,this phenomenon might not always lead to the most desirable social result. Reinforcement of norms may correspond with notions of fairness, which may diverge from welfare advancement.This is not to say that reinforcing custom comes without benefits. A triumph of custom may vindicate the idea that certain rules are worth the welfare price because they elevate the morality and the fairness of the marketplace.
In the consumer environment, persuasive and creative sales tactics are perpetually invented and deployed, and regulators are left to discern whichtactics are deceptive. Choosing where and when to regulate common market activities can have a large impact. Consumer transactions are the fundamental lifeblood of the economy and, in aggregate, advance welfare.Government claims the responsibility of promoting the flow of accurate information "without unduly burdening legitimate business activity."Bait and switch plays a significant role in the market, but the legal literature ignores not just the tactic, but what can be learned from examining it.
Of course, with bait and switch, definition of the tactic presents a critical starting point. Bait and switch is frequently used to describe a range of commercial behaviors, only some of which meet the legal criteria for deception under section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act (FTC Act).For the purposes of this Article, I expand the scope of the term "bait and switch" beyond the legal definition to include scenarios where consumers are lured in with a low-price introductory offer and are later locked in to paying a potentially higher price for the same offer.Some of these tactics are omnipresent and lawful, but others have been designated unlawful by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC),by federal statute,by state regulation,and are also held in disfavor by common law doctrines.
The aforementioned "hunted" scholarship students at Golden Gate embraced "bait-and-switch" terminology.They felt like they had bought anoffering at a low price only to be switched to a higher price, but they were not really alleging the deployment of atraditionalbait-and-switch tactic. The FTC defines "bait" asan alluring but insincere offer to sell a product or service which the advertiser in truth does not intend or want to sell. Its purpose is to switch consumers from buying the advertised merchandise, in order to sell something else, usually at a higher price or on a basis more advantageous to the advertiser.These students,as I will discuss, may have been "allured," but they were not "switched."
an alluring but insincere offer to sell a product or service which the advertiser in truth does not intend or want to sell. Its purpose is to switch consumers from buying the advertised merchandise, in order to sell something else, usually at a higher price or on a basis more advantageous to the advertiser.
My definition of bait and switch includes the FTC definition, but expands it to apply to a range of tactics that offend general marketplace sensibilities. I discuss a number of these tactics, including a hypothetical of an auto dealer advertising a car just to lure customers to the lot,the real case of a retailer that frequently promoted a special offering to drive store traffic but rarely actually sold it on those terms,and the company that required in-home salespersons to disparage big-ticket promoted goods to encourage the sale of higher-margin goods.
Although they may not be explicitly labeled as such in a legal context, other forms of bait and switch exist, are regulated differently, and evoke different market customs. For example, "free offers" lure the attention of consumers to a packaged promotion. The FTC requires a free offeror to disclose conspicuously why an offer is not truly "free."That is, after luring attention to an advertisement, the offeror presents the entirety of the sales story. This presents the market with a different sort of "switch," a lawful switch, but a bait and switch nonetheless. Despite constituting a form of bait and switch, courts and regulators have been unwilling to eschew this old and established custom, though a plain look at free offers reveals that they interfere with consumer cognition. Stronger regulation that departs from the custom might conceivably advance welfare.
Also outside the formal bait-and-switch definition, but perhaps within its popular definition, are "teasers"--low-price introductory offers that can be used to lure consumers into arrangements where the terms can turn dramatically against their favor once they are locked in. The history of credit card rate regulation provides a high-profile example. The Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009(CARD Act) applied the brakes on well-established customary tactics. Historically, banks would dangle low rates to acquire customers and later raise the rate on their balances.The CARD Act embodiment of bait-and-switch-like regulation provides further opportunity to explore how underlying economic and political forces can suddenly change the deep customs and culture associated with a set of business practices.
If one accepts the factual basis of the law students' 2011 allegations,Golden Gate could have been offering a "teaser," but could not be said to be engaging in unlawful bait-and-switch behavior. The school sincerely intended to offer the students additional educational services, and did not intend to use the initial offering to "switch" the students to purchase something different. The students cried foul about a change in price that they felt resulted from a misleading initial offer. The argument about law school merit scholarships mirrorssome of the problems addressed by the CARD Act. Understanding the cultural dynamics that drove Congress to regulate bait-and-switch practices with sudden severity might prove instructive for understanding how students may have effected a modest change in law school merit scholarship practices.If custom and culture drive regulationmore so than welfare advancement, the roadmap to change, including the obstacles, is clearer.
Each flavor of bait-and-switch regulation provides an opportunity to explore the ways we have permitted custom to prevail over welfare advancement. In Part I, to provide grounding, I describe the current regulatory approach toward bait and switch. In Part II, I provide an overview of the theory undergirding the role norms and customs play in commercial regulation. In Part III, I examine three distinct categories of bait-and-switch behavior and regulation to assess whether they reinforce norms or customs and whether the regulatory approach promotes welfare advancement. In Part III.A, I examine "traditional" bait-and-switch regulation, as the FTC defines it, including special rules for retail grocers. In Part III.B, I analyze "free offer regulation," and in Part III.C, "teaser" regulation via the CARD Act and first-year law school merit scholarships, respectively. I also discuss "lawful" forms of bait and switch and the role of custom in Part III.D. In Part IV, I globally assess the interplay between custom, norms, and welfare advancement in the regulation of broader bait-and-switch practices, and describe why this approach endures.
Below, I will outline the role of bait-and-switch regulation in our consumer economy. I then follow with a discussion of how the role of custom in commercial regulation informs discussion about the social welfare cost of custom in bait-and-switch regulation. Ultimately, I conclude that the primacy of custom and norms should compel policymakers to carefully consider the welfare impact of commercial regulations--and should inform advocates about how to influence regulatory change.

questions.question: Whether commercial regulation of bait-and-switch tactics is driven primarily by prevailing marketplace customs and norms rather than by deliberate assessments of consumer welfare.

What welfare costs and benefits arise when regulators enforce or tolerate different forms of bait-and-switch (e.g., low-price teasers, free offers), and how does privileging custom affect overall social welfare?
How do cultural and political dynamics shape when and how regulators intervene against various bait-and-switch practices, producing variation in regulatory responses across contexts?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication
