papers.node_id: 65casewres297!!ARTICLE: FACILITATING INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: FACILITATING INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
Legal certainty is a central principle for the rule of law. Contract doctrine illustrates the centrality of that principle perhaps more than any other legal field.In the ideal depiction of contracting, two parties negotiate an agreement prior to undertaking performance obligations. Once both parties have consented to the terms of an agreement and have entered into a contract, then the parties perform their obligations because it is in their rational self-interest to do so; otherwise, no contract would have been signed in the first place. If one party absconds and does not meet his contractual obligation, a court can easily determine breach and damages because the terms of the parties' deal were clear and certain.
In this contracting ideal, compliance is the goal. Parties want to be certain that they will get what they contracted for, or at least thatthey will be otherwise compensated for a breach. Certainty is the reason parties formally contract rather than informally agree. And it is easy to understand why "[o]ne of the core principles of contract law is the requirement of definiteness."In this model, incomplete contracts that fail to give adequate guidance to the parties about their duties and obligations are more likely to result in opportunistic behavior and litigation and make litigation more time consuming and costly if it does result. Thus, lawyers are taught to avoid these drafting pitfalls.
Even more importantly, courts punish parties who either carelessly or purposefully draft incomplete contracts.These parties cause systemic costs in litigation that, in the traditional view, could have and should have been easily avoided by better drafting.A simple sales contract illustrates. Consider a buyer who agrees to purchase one hundred widgets for five dollars per widget in a one-time transaction. The parties negotiate these terms before any obligations accrue and detail the terms in a written contract. If the buyer receives the widgets but does not pay the seller $ 500, the questions of breach and damages are entirely straightforward.
But now consider a second contract. Here, one firm partners with another to co-develop new technology, utilizing the strengths of bothentities to build a product that is not yet fully conceived. After development, the parties intend for the product to be jointly marketed and sold worldwide. In this second contract, compliance still matters--a party that makes a relationship-specific investment does not want the other pulling out of the deal--but so do coordination, collaboration, and innovation. By contracting, the parties need to mitigate riskandfacilitate coordination, all against a backdrop of complexity and uncertainty.
Perhaps the parties could accomplish these goals by drafting a highly detailed contract with extensive control provisions to try to prevent opportunistic behavior.This is the strategy the law prefers.But it is not only difficult and costly to accomplish, it may also not be the best or most efficient strategy in certain contexts. Recent interdisciplinary scholarship in economics, psychology, and the law has found that specificity, financial incentives, and control provisions, in general, can signal mistrust and crowd out parties' intrinsic motivation to perform.Control-based contracting can give the impression that the principal is trying to constrain the agent and does not trust the agent to implicitly deliver skillful or consummate performance.Agents respond reciprocally to this sort of treatment. An agent who perceives being treated unfairly will in turn react negatively.
In addition, contracts that are highly specified can create cognitive problems. Agents will often adhere to the strict requirements specified in the contract at the sacrifice of furthering the main objective of the deal.Agents do not think for themselves; they merely do what is required.
On the flip side, more flexible contracting has been shown to mitigate these problems. Less-complete contracts that rely on trust and reciprocity rather than control can induce higher effort levels and a more cooperative principal-agent relationship than the traditional approach. They also mitigate the cognitive problems identified inhighly detailed contracts. For both behavioral and cognitive reasons, detailed, highly certain contracts may actually lead to greater inefficiency and an increased likelihood of litigation than more incomplete ones.
Despite much scholarship now suggesting a more flexible contracting approach, however, lengthy and complicated contracts filled with boilerplate and specific financial incentives continue to be commonplace in commercial transactions. This Article explores why incomplete contracting has not taken hold more widely despite its promise. It suggests that the theory is sound. But the law does not embrace the theory. Contract law assumes that incomplete contracts are always undesirable and should always be deterred. Contract doctrine actively disincentivizes parties from writing incomplete, flexible contracts, even when they might be efficiently employed.
This is most obvious in contract law's (renewed) preference for formalist interpretation in contracts between sophisticated entities. Formalist courts prioritize the four corners of the written agreement when confronted with interpretation questions, incentivizing parties to draft more complete contractsex ante. Even contextualist interpretation is somewhat unfriendly to incomplete contracts. Contextualist courts look to evidence outside the contract in an attempt to discern the intent of the partiesat contract execution. For the most part, though, they ignore the evolution of the relationship post signing--an integral aspect to the success of flexible contracting.
If the normative goal of contract doctrine is to incentivize commercial activity and efficient dealmaking, the doctrinal approach deriding incompleteness is out of step with the goal. This Article suggests instead an approach to contract interpretation that borrows from principles of constitutional interpretation: dynamic contextualist interpretation. Given that less-specified contracts may be efficient, particularly in a variety of commercial contexts, courts reviewing such contracts should treat them more flexibly and liberally. Courts should account for the nature of flexible contracting--that not all decisions will be madebeforecontract execution. Deals may evolve over time. Indeed, this may be the most efficient approach. The law assumesthat contracts are static and focuses on the agreement between the parties at execution. But many contracts are not static. They are dynamic, and their meaning evolves as the parties' relationship evolves. Contract doctrine should match this reality. This Article begins to explore how and when that could be accomplished.
The Article proceeds in four parts. Part I rejects the traditional assumption that "good" contracts arenecessarilydetailed and specific. It reviews the growing interdisciplinary body of work suggesting that for both economic and behavioral reasons, commercial parties writing less-specified contractsex antemight engender better contracting resultsex post. Part II describes why few parties nonetheless take advantage of more flexible contracting forms that might be more efficient. It describes how lawyers are actively disincentivized from writing incomplete contracts by exploring both the doctrinal and sociolegal deterrents to these cooperative methods of contracting. Part III sets out the normative argument. It suggests that contract doctrine creates drafting incentives for transacting parties and that the current matrix is creating the wrong incentives. The right incentives should support commercial activity and generate efficient outcomes. Thus, doctrine should be reformed to better reflect and support these new models of contracting. Finally, Part IV begins to discuss how contract doctrine might be reformed for a particular class of contracts. Courts reviewing purposely relational contracts should not only treat them more flexibly and liberally but should take a dynamic and contextual approach to matters of interpretation. Contracts may have been static and unchanging in the traditional model, but these new forms of purposefully incomplete contracts are dynamic and evolving, and the law should follow suit.

questions.question: Whether less-specified (purposefully incomplete or relational) contracts produce more efficient commercial outcomes (e.g., greater cooperation, innovation, and lower costly litigation) than highly specified contracts.

Why commercial parties and their lawyers do not more widely adopt incomplete, flexible contracting practices despite evidence of their potential benefits-specifically, whether legal doctrines and sociolegal incentives systematically discourage the use of incomplete contracts.

Whether courts should interpret and enforce incomplete, evolving contracts more dynamically (allowing post-signing evolution and context to inform meaning) and, if so, whether such a shift in interpretive approach would promote efficient dealmaking.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113yalelj541!!ARTICLE:Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract law in facilitating efficient commercial transactions between firms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract doctrine should incentivize flexible, incompletely specified deals when those contracts yield better coordination and joint value, and Paper B develops a welfare-maximization normative theory holding that contract law for firm-to-firm transactions should be confined to rules that facilitate efficient trade and investment (i.e., maximizing contractual surplus).

shared_topics.topic: interpretive regimes (textualist/formalist vs contextualist/dynamic interpretation) and their effects on contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes formalist, four-corners approaches and proposes a 'dynamic contextualist' interpretive method to accommodate evolving relational contracts, while Paper B defends a textualist/default hard-parol approach as the optimal baseline for business-to-business contracts and discusses when parties should be able to alter interpretive rules.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete/relational contracting, defaults, and when the law should accommodate versus deter incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on why purposefully incomplete (relational) contracts can be efficient yet are doctrinally disfavored, advocating doctrinal reform to support them; Paper B analyzes the limited domain in which defaults and standards are useful for firms, argues many statutory defaults are unnecessary, and examines when the state should provide default rules versus allow parties to contract around them.

shared_topics.topic: relation-specific investments and the need for enforcement versus self-enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights relationship-specific investments as a reason parties prefer flexible contracting and stresses how law should account for evolving post-signing decisions, and Paper B identifies protection of relation-specific investments (and the limits of self-enforcement) as a core justification for legal enforcement in volatile markets and long-term firm relationships.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules create drafting incentives and shape contracting strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that current doctrine and litigation incentives push lawyers toward highly specified, control-based drafting even when that is inefficient, and Paper B emphasizes that default and mandatory rules alter firms' contracting costs and contends the law should minimize distortive mandatory interventions so that firms can choose efficient contractual arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41seattleulrev209!!ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today

shared_topics.topic: role of reciprocity, trust, and social norms (relational contracting) in commercial behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both papers draw on empirical and behavioral research showing that commercial parties often act from mutual expectations of flexibility, reciprocity, and fairness (Paper A's mutualism/dualism and Paper B's trust-and-reciprocity account), and argue that contract doctrine should account for these relational motives rather than assuming purely self-interested, efficiency-driven actors.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal mismatch between traditional contract law and modern contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Each article critiques how current doctrine (formalist certainty, focus on single questions like intent or efficiency) is ill-suited to contemporary contracting — Paper A calls contract law 'uni-faceted' and unable to process mutualism/dualism, while Paper B shows doctrine disincentivizes incomplete/flexible contracting and preserves an outdated preference for completeness.

shared_topics.topic: need for interpretive approaches that accommodate dynamic, post-signing evolution of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both propose rethinking judicial interpretation to capture evolving expectations: Paper A advocates an Aristotelian means-ends analysis that considers both means and ends of exchange, and Paper B proposes 'dynamic contextualist' interpretation so courts can treat relational/incomplete contracts more flexibly as relationships evolve.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how courts should enforce non‑standard contractual forms (terms‑in‑a‑box, boilerplate, or purposely incomplete terms)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper confronts enforceability questions about modern contract forms — Paper A analyzes the legitimacy of surprise 'terms-in-a-box' (e.g., mandatory arbitration) under an Aristotelian just-exchange framework, while Paper B examines how doctrine currently punishes incompleteness and how the law could better facilitate intentionally less-specified contracts.

shared_topics.topic: use of interdisciplinary empirical evidence (behavioral/experimental economics) to justify doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Both rely on interdisciplinary studies showing predictable non‑standard behavior (e.g., fairness motivations, crowding-out from controls, cognitive effects of specificity) and use that evidence to argue that contract doctrine should be reformed to reflect how parties actually behave.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20ncjltechon267!!ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS

shared_topics.topic: how private ordering through contract terms/privacy policies interacts with law and whether legal intervention is needed
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract doctrine shapes drafting incentives—arguing courts currently deter efficient, purposely incomplete contracts—and calls for doctrinal reform to enable flexible private ordering; Paper B shows firms use privacy policies to contract away genetic-property and data rights in the absence of federal regulation and argues for statutory intervention to constrain private ordering in the DTC genetics market.

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between static legal interpretation and evolving relationships or data uses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the law's static, four-corners approach and advocates a dynamic contextualist interpretation for relational, evolving contracts; Paper B highlights that genetic data collection and subsequent uses evolve over time and that existing legal frameworks and static privacy policies fail to address those evolving downstream data uses.

shared_topics.topic: how disparities in bargaining power and party sophistication affect contractual outcomes and the need for protective rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the incentives and doctrinal presumptions governing sophisticated commercial parties and how doctrine can misalign drafting incentives, while Paper B emphasizes consumer vulnerability and the imbalance between individual consumers and large DTC companies using boilerplate privacy contracts—both raise concerns about how legal rules should account for asymmetries in bargaining position and sophistication.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of consent and informational disclosure in contractual exchanges under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses incomplete contracting as a deliberate response to uncertainty and the role of trust, information exchange, and post-signing coordination, questioning whether formalistic requirements capture actual consent; Paper B documents that consumers routinely accept complex privacy policies without informed understanding, raising doubts about whether contractual consent legitimately authorizes broad future uses of genetic information.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46ukanlrev115!!ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unforeseen contingencies in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats uncertainty and unforeseeable future contingencies as a central justification for intentionally incomplete, flexible contracting and argues courts should interpret such contracts dynamically; Paper B analyzes the allocation of risk for unforeseen subsurface and latent site conditions in construction contracts (and the role of differing site condition clauses), asking how law and contract terms should assign those risks and who should bear cost overruns.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine and judicial interpretation shape drafting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prevailing doctrinal approaches (formalist and contextualist interpretation) incentivize parties to over-specify contracts and deter flexible contracting; Paper B examines whether statutory clauses and common-law doctrines regarding site conditions and change orders influence bidders' and owners' drafting and procurement choices—and whether the common law has room to alter those incentives.

shared_topics.topic: contract design's impact on opportunism and post-signing behaviour
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how detailed control provisions can crowd out trust and provoke opportunistic or mechanically narrow performance, whereas less-specified relational contracts can foster cooperation; Paper B documents how fixed-price bidding plus clauses like differing site conditions can lead to opportunistic change orders and cost-shifting after contract award, and how legal rules can mitigate or exacerbate that behaviour.

shared_topics.topic: the normative aim of contract law to promote efficient commercial outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A makes an explicit normative claim that contract doctrine should be reformed to support efficient, relational, and evolving deals; Paper B evaluates whether existing contract terms and the interplay with common law produce efficient allocations of risk in construction procurement or instead routinely generate costly overruns and inefficiencies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj103!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Desperately Seeking Consideration: The Unfortunate Impact of U.C.C. Section 2-306 on Contract Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Desperately Seeking Consideration: The Unfortunate Impact of U.C.C. Section 2-306 on Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: Impact of implied 'good faith'/'best efforts' duties on parties' discretion and contractual efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes UCC §2-306 and courts' use of 'good faith' or 'best efforts' to limit the quantity-setting party's discretion and thereby distort the parties' negotiated allocation, while Paper B locates implied duties within a broader critique that doctrinally imposed terms discourage efficient flexible contracting and can harm ex ante incentives.

shared_topics.topic: Judicial interpretive doctrines and their effect on the viability of incomplete/relational contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents courts' post hoc invocation of vague standards to reinterpret ostensibly discretionary contracts, and Paper B argues that formalist/contextualist interpretive approaches disincentivize deliberately incomplete relational contracts and proposes a dynamic contextualist alternative.

shared_topics.topic: Protection of reliance and relation-specific investments: contractual devices versus judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys contractual mechanisms (take-or-pay, minimums, performance bonds, pricing formulas) parties can use to protect reliance and criticizes courts for substituting judicially imposed protections, while Paper B examines how contract law's treatment of reliance and uncertainty shapes parties' drafting choices and may undermine efficient reliance-protection strategies.

shared_topics.topic: Trade-offs between contract specificity and flexibility in long-term/adaptive agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that granting discretion in long-term variable-quantity contracts can be the most efficient way to adapt to changing circumstances and that courts' interventions disrupt that calibration, while Paper B reviews economic and behavioral research showing that less-specified, flexible contracts can improve cooperation and adaptation and argues doctrine should accommodate such trade-offs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67emorylj1!!ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE

shared_topics.topic: normative framework for when contracts should be complete versus intentionally incomplete
shared_topics.justification: Both papers develop and deploy criteria for assessing the desirability of contractual completeness — Paper A synthesizes law-and-economics and behavioral literatures to argue when price terms should be required (notably in healthcare), while Paper B identifies commercial contexts (relational, innovative deals) where purposeful incompleteness is efficient and argues doctrine should accommodate that reality.

shared_topics.topic: behavioral and cognitive consequences of contract specificity
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantive interdisciplinary evidence showing that highly specified contracts can crowd out intrinsic motivation, signal mistrust, and produce cognitive fixation on enumerated terms, whereas less-specified (relational) contracts can foster cooperation and better performance.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law/doctrine creates drafting incentives and should be reformed
shared_topics.justification: Each paper critiques existing contract doctrine for producing the wrong incentives — Paper A argues courts currently enforce open price-term contracts and should deter that through a penalty default, while Paper B argues formalist and current interpretive practices deter efficient incompleteness and should be replaced with doctrines that support flexible relational contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and default rules in filling gaps in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both centrally discuss judicial responses to contract gaps: Paper A proposes an information-forcing penalty default (fill omitted price with $0) to induce ex ante price disclosure, while Paper B recommends a more permissive, dynamic contextualist interpretive approach so courts fill or interpret gaps in ways that preserve evolving relational agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 19upajbusl809!!ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: treatment of incomplete contracts and judicial gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the implied incorporation doctrine functions as a form of judicial gap‑filling for unexpressed terms and assesses its fit given the problem of incomplete contracts (especially under Article 2 of the UCC), while Paper B focuses on the efficiency and desirability of deliberately incomplete (relational) contracts and argues contract law currently deters such gap‑filling approaches that would enable flexible post‑execution governance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation versus legal construction in shaping contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a doctrinal distinction between contract interpretation and contract construction and argues the implied incorporation rule operates as construction (operation of law) rather than mere interpretive default, and Paper B debates interpretive styles (formalist vs contextualist) and proposes a ‘dynamic contextualist’ approach so courts better accommodate evolving, incomplete agreements.

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual rules should be default (opt‑out) or mandatory (non‑waivable)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether implied statutory incorporation is a mandatory rule or a defeasible interpretive default and concludes it generally operates as an immutable rule unless the lawmaker permits waiver, while Paper B critiques doctrinal constraints that effectively force parties into fully specified contracts and advocates reforms to allow parties to choose (opt into) flexible, incomplete contracting regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how legal doctrine and statutory law shape private ordering and transactional incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the interplay between statutes, public policy, and private contracting (including when statutes should give rise to private contractual rights or defenses), and Paper B analyzes how prevailing judicial doctrines and doctrinal incentives influence lawyers and parties to prefer complete, control‑based contracts over potentially more efficient flexible or relational forms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84ucinlrev217!!ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*

shared_topics.topic: critique of idealized contract theory versus real-world contracting
shared_topics.justification: Both papers question the canonical economic and moral theories that assume complete, coherent, and static bargains—Paper A argues that the traditional model privileging highly specified contracts is mistaken in many commercial contexts, while Paper B argues that academic contract theory wrongly abstracts from the messy realities of complex deals and litigation.

shared_topics.topic: problems created by under-specified or boilerplate drafting
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with how vague, boilerplate, or otherwise under-specified contract language generates downstream problems—Paper A studies the normative case for deliberately incomplete (relational) contracts and why doctrine discourages them, while Paper B diagnoses how thoughtless or boilerplate drafting enables 'lexical opportunism' and disproportionate liability.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation doctrines and the judicial role in resolving ambiguity
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how courts interpret ambiguous or incomplete agreements—Paper A proposes a 'dynamic contextualist' interpretive approach to accommodate evolving relational contracts, and Paper B analyzes how post hoc textual interpretation and linguistic indeterminacy shape litigation outcomes and undermine theoretical justifications for enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and strategic behavior around contract text and relationships
shared_topics.justification: Both address opportunistic conduct tied to contract form and enforcement—Paper A treats opportunism as the traditional rationale for detailed drafting but also argues flexible contracting can reduce opportunism via trust and reciprocity, while Paper B centers on adversaries exploiting textual ambiguity (lexical opportunism) as a pervasive strategic problem in disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44lawsocyrev299!!ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the role of social and market norms in structuring contract terms and impeding deviation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses sociolegal deterrents and market expectations that push parties toward highly specified, boilerplate contracts rather than flexible forms; Paper B documents the Israeli dollarization norm as a pervasive social default pricing term and analyzes why individual parties conform rather than contract around it.

shared_topics.topic: how law, doctrine, and regulation shape incentives for contract drafting and can fail to produce efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract doctrine (formalist and contextualist interpretation) actively disincentivizes purposeful incompleteness and calls for doctrinal reform to support relational contracting, while Paper B evaluates Israeli legislative attempts to counter dollarization and shows how legal intervention interacted with — and sometimes failed to change — entrenched contracting practices.

shared_topics.topic: behavioral and cognitive drivers of contracting choices (trust, reciprocity, cognitive biases)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on behavioral economics and psychology to show how control-heavy, highly specified contracts can crowd out intrinsic motivation and create cognitive lock-in, and Paper B invokes cognitive-psychology literature to explain why parties continue using sticky contract terms like dollar-indexing despite changing incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the dynamic nature of contractual relationships and the stickiness or change of contract terms over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that many contracts are relational and evolve post-signing, advocating dynamic contextualist interpretation to accommodate that evolution, while Paper B traces the historical persistence of dollar-indexed terms and their sudden unraveling, using that history to study how contract terms change (or remain stable) over time.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52drakelrev235!!ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303

shared_topics.topic: role of post-formation conduct in interpreting and giving effect to contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes traditional contract doctrine for largely ignoring how parties' relationships and conduct after signing should inform interpretation and enforcement, advocating a dynamic contextualist approach; Paper B analyzes the UCC's use of course-of-performance evidence (post-formation conduct) to interpret agreements, argues this use is analytically and policy-wise problematic, and contrasts it with waiver as an alternative means of giving effect to post-contractual behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules create incentives that shape contracting practices (completeness vs flexibility)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that current contract doctrine and judicial formalism incentivize overly detailed drafting and deter efficient incomplete, relational contracts; Paper B considers how the UCC's course-of-performance rules (and their expansion under revised Article 1) embed commercial norms into law and therefore influence commercial behavior and drafting choices across transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretive tension between strict/formalist textualism and contextual or dynamic approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts formalist four‑corners interpretation with contextual and proposes a dynamic contextualist framework for relational contracts, while Paper B critiques the UCC's interpretive construct for course of performance as inconsistent with basic contract theory and other provisions, thereby engaging the same debate over when and how courts should rely on text versus context/post-formation evidence.

shared_topics.topic: governing ongoing/commercial relational transactions rather than one-off sales
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contracts that are relational, evolving, and require coordination and trust (e.g., joint development), arguing doctrine should accommodate ongoing decisionmaking; Paper B likewise addresses evidence and rules (course of performance, waiver) that apply to repeated or continuing commercial relationships under the UCC and the implications of extending those rules across long-term commercial transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24chaplrev89!!ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism as competing interpretive doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts' preference for formalist/textualist interpretation (four-corners) versus contextualist approaches and argues for a dynamic contextualism suited to relational contracts; Paper B analyzes the conceptual differences and practical operation of textualism and contextualism, showing how they pull courts in opposing directions and cause doctrinal confusion.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretation doctrine influences drafting incentives and the prevalence of incomplete/relational contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that existing interpretive doctrines disincentivize parties and lawyers from drafting intentionally incomplete, flexible contracts and thus distort efficient contracting, while Paper B links interpretive incoherence (including ambiguity rulings and the parol evidence rule) to increased drafting and litigation costs, thereby affecting how parties negotiate and write contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of extrinsic/parol evidence and post‑execution contextual evidence in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contextualist courts look to evidence outside the four corners but often ignore post‑signing evolution and urges courts to account for post‑execution dynamics; Paper B focuses on the parol evidence rule and clarifies how extrinsic evidence is defined and used under different interpretive regimes, including whether contextualism eliminates or preserves parol evidence limitations.

shared_topics.topic: the ambiguity determination stage and its consequences for resolving incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises problems arising when courts treat incomplete, relational agreements as ambiguously drafted and therefore penalize parties, advocating a different approach to ambiguity in evolving deals; Paper B provides a detailed conceptual analysis of the ambiguity determination (including latent ambiguity distinctions) and how different treatments of ambiguity (or its elimination under contextualism) affect adjudication and allocation between judge and jury.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84tullrev1437!!ARTICLE: The Origins of Sale: Some Lessons from the Romans
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Origins of Sale: Some Lessons from the Romans

shared_topics.topic: the role of formality versus informality in creating binding obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Roman distinction between formal promises (stipulatio) and informal consensual sales, showing how absence or presence of ceremony determined enforceability; Paper B critiques modern formalist doctrines that privilege the written, fully specified contract over informal or relational agreements and discusses how that affects parties' willingness to rely on less formal arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: how legal doctrine and classification shape commercial practices and what transactions become enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks why Roman jurists recognized sale (and later some consensual contracts) but left other transaction types like barter legally blind, arguing doctrinal choices directed what market practices were viable; Paper B shows how contemporary contract doctrine (interpretive rules and enforcement norms) creates incentives or deterrents for parties to adopt flexible, incomplete contracting forms, thereby shaping commercial behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the trade-off between certainty and flexibility in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies Roman law's limits (e.g., no generic sales, consent-based binding only for certain contracts) as possibly deliberate trade-offs between transactional certainty and practical flexibility; Paper B directly evaluates the economic and behavioral trade-offs between highly specified, certain contracts and purposefully incomplete, flexible contracts and calls for doctrinal adjustment to better balance those goals.

shared_topics.topic: the emergence and legal recognition of new contract types (and resistance to them)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical emergence of the sale as a new contract species and investigates why other transaction forms (barter, generic sale) were slow or resisted in Roman law; Paper B addresses the contemporary emergence of relational/incomplete contracts and analyzes why established legal doctrines resist treating them as legitimate or enforceable forms deserving of different interpretive rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104harvlrev375!!ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.

shared_topics.topic: role of nonlegal sanctions (reputation, trust, reciprocity) as an enforcement alternative to formal contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how parties rely on trust, reciprocity, and relational norms rather than detailed legal terms to induce performance in cooperative, innovation-focused deals; Paper B systematically analyzes reputation, shame, and other extra-legal sanctions as the mechanisms that sustain commitments outside formal enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: why parties choose incomplete or informal commitments (drafting costs, cognitive and behavioral effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals interdisciplinary evidence that detailed, control-based drafting can crowd out intrinsic motivation and produce cognitive lock-in, making less-specified agreements sometimes more efficient; Paper B explains how high drafting/information costs and parties' rational (or mistaken) judgments lead transactors to rely on oral, informal, or expressly nonbinding commitments.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine and interpretation shape drafting incentives and commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prevailing doctrinal regimes (formalist or even contextualist interpretation) discourage purposeful incompleteness and push parties toward over-specified contracts; Paper B shows that existing legal rules governing enforceability often leave nonlegal commitments outside the law and proposes that legal standards affect whether parties use legal versus nonlegal sanctioning systems.

shared_topics.topic: normative reform: when courts should tolerate, enforce, or adapt to relational/incomplete commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes 'dynamic contextualist' interpretation and doctrinal reforms to accommodate evolving, purposely incomplete relational contracts; Paper B recommends deferring to parties' choices about enforceability but intervening when parties misassess the adequacy of nonlegal sanctions, and suggests specific doctrinal and regulatory adjustments (e.g., promissory estoppel) to better account for nonlegal sanctions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43bclrev819!!ARTICLE: The Rhetoric of Legal Backfire
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Rhetoric of Legal Backfire

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and rhetoric create incentives that shape private behavior and lawmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that contract doctrine (formalist vs contextualist interpretation, remedial rules) creates drafting incentives that push parties toward highly specified contracts even when relational incompleteness would be efficient; Paper B shows that pervasive 'legal backfire' rhetoric creates political and public incentives that deter regulators and legislators from adopting or maintaining laws, skewing lawmaking toward anti-regulatory responses.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of empirical and interdisciplinary evidence (vs rhetorical claims) in evaluating legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on interdisciplinary empirical work from economics and psychology to argue that behavioral effects of specificity favor incomplete relational contracts and that doctrine ignores this evidence; Paper B criticizes many backfire allegations as empirically weak and urges that policymakers subject such claims to careful empirical review rather than accept rhetorical assertions.

shared_topics.topic: unintended negative consequences of legal design and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents behavioral and cognitive unintended harms of highly specified contracts (crowding out intrinsic motivation, cognitive fixation) that can worsen outcomes; Paper B catalogues alleged 'legal backfires'—laws producing results contrary to their aims—and warns that purported unintended consequences are often invoked rhetorically to oppose regulation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of interpretive approaches by courts and policymakers in determining whether law achieves its purposes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts' interpretive doctrines (formalism vs contextualism) and refusal to account for post-signing relational evolution undermine the effectiveness of flexible contracting; Paper B analyzes how policymakers' and commentators' interpretive framing of evidence (via backfire rhetoric) can foreclose debate and mislead decisions about whether laws are achieving their intended goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev535!!SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD: A COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: PROMISSORY FRAUD: A COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules create ex ante incentives for parties when drafting and making promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how expanding or narrowing promissory fraud liability would change parties' incentives to promise, deceive, or disclose (weighing benefits and costs of deterrence and over-deterrence), and Paper B shows how contract interpretation and doctrinal penalties for incompleteness incentivize parties to draft highly specified contracts rather than use flexible, relational forms.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts in assessing promisor intent and the meaning of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on liability contingent on a promisor's state of mind—how courts should determine and treat deceptive intention to perform—and Paper B calls for a more dynamic, contextualist judicial approach to interpret evolving promises and relationships rather than rigid, four-corners readings.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when contract disputes should be treated through traditional contract doctrines versus tort-like responses to deception
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly questions whether deliberate misrepresentations of intent should be handled as promissory fraud (with tort remedies like punitive damages) rather than mere breach with expectation damages, and Paper B engages the related question of when doctrinal responses (e.g., strict enforcement and formalist interpretation) are appropriate versus when the law should allow nontraditional, relational solutions to govern performance and disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between formal certainty (complete, specific contracts) and flexibility/relational governance in achieving efficient contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights tensions between established contract principles (certainty, strict breach liability, expectation damages) and doctrines that intrude on those principles when promises are deceptive, while Paper B develops the behavioral and institutional case that less-complete, trust-based contracting can be more efficient and that doctrine currently biases toward formal certainty.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reconsidering Contractual Liability and the Incentive to Reveal Information

shared_topics.topic: how contractual rules affect parties' incentives to reveal private information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how limitations on contractual liability change buyers' incentives to disclose valuations and analyzes when such disclosure is socially desirable; Paper B examines how contract specificity and control provisions act as signals (of mistrust) and affect parties' willingness to cooperate and share information in relational settings.

shared_topics.topic: how legal doctrine and rule design shape ex ante drafting incentives and the prevalence of incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how liability regimes (legal rules governing contractual liability) influence parties' behavior and the information they transmit, while Paper B argues that doctrinal interpretations and enforcement incentives push parties toward highly detailed contracts and deter purposeful incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency tradeoffs of limiting liability versus promoting flexible/incomplete contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks when limitations on contractual liability (a form of rule design) produce socially desirable informational outcomes, and Paper B evaluates when less-specified, flexible contracts yield better economic and behavioral outcomes and should be favored by the law.

shared_topics.topic: strategic and opportunistic behavior in contracting and governance mechanisms to address it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes strategic revelation and how liability rules can alter opportunistic incentives, whereas Paper B considers the risks of opportunism from incomplete contracts but also how relational governance, trust, and dynamic interpretation can mitigate opportunism and improve performance.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal incentives created by contract interpretation rules on parties' choice of contract completeness

shared_topics.topic: the trade-off between predictability/certainty and relational/flexible (dynamic) contracting

papers.node_id: 105valrev1025!!ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
In contexts ranging from the mundane to the momentous, parties turn to documents that look like enforceable formal contracts, but that fall short of being legally binding - and also seem unmoored from formalorinformal enforcement. In business transactions, this is particularly odd: parties have the means and sophistication to use binding, formal contracts,but appear to elect not to use them. Why do parties go through the trouble of drafting formal-looking agreements that they do not enforce? And if there is no formal or informal enforcement, what motivates parties to abide by contractual terms?
This Article shows how these "faux contracts" - formal-looking documents that explicitly exclude enforcement of any kind - add value in ways that real contracts cannot. Non-binding term sheets in mergers and acquisitions ("M&A") are the driving example, but non-binding documents like term sheets are found in many complex business transactions. These faux contracts allow parties to harness the organizational and clarification benefits of creating a contract, while excluding most consequences of breach. This Article also explains how and why non-binding term sheets motivate M&A parties to play by the rules, even though the parties are not part of a tightly knit community.
Non-binding or unenforceable agreements can be found in many contexts. Non-competition clauses in California employment agreements are good examples. These agreements restrict an employee's ability to work for a competitor for some time after leaving the original employer. Non-competition clauses are valid and enforceable legal contracts in most states.In 2008, however, the California Supreme Court reaffirmed, in asplashy and well-publicized case, the state's long-standing position that non-competition clauses are unenforceable.Nonetheless, California employers and employees continued to sign them - even though an employer cannot take the issue to court if an employee breaches the clause.Surrogacy contracts where they are outlawed,contracts for illegal activity,Internet click-wrap agreements with unconscionableterms,and certain prenuptial agreement provisionsoffer just a few more examples of parties entering into non-binding or unenforceable agreements.
Non-binding or unenforceable agreements in these situations, however, are unsurprising. In these contexts, unequal bargaining power between the parties, lack of knowledge about the contract's unenforceable nature, or lack of viable binding alternatives can often explain why parties turn to non-binding agreements.
In M&A deals, the situation is different: parties are business-savvy, and have both the technical sophistication and financial means to negotiate and enter into binding contracts. They are also often advised by sophisticated counsel and experienced bankers who can help them make contracts that are binding and enforceable. Yet, prior to signing a definitive contract, M&A parties often negotiate, agree to, and even sign a non-binding term sheet outlining critical deal terms.
While term sheets have many formal-looking bells and whistles - they are written in legal language, often with the advice of counsel, and signed by parties - parties agree that the "business terms" are legally non-binding and unenforceable.In other words, parties can breach those business terms - terms about price, what is sold, and how - without being taken to court. Why do sophisticated parties enter into non-binding agreements? And if enforcement is off the table, what accounts for the fact that once a term sheet is signed, parties proceed to act as though they have signed a binding document, usually later entering into a definitive formal document on terms that closely resemble the term sheet's?
Much of contract law assumes that enforcement is an important way to motivate behavior.This assumption also underlies much of legal scholarship and theory: jail time for committing crimes,fines imposed for infringing intellectual property rights,and sanctions for violating regulations and treatiesare all examples of formal enforcement mechanisms that are believed to motivate behavior.
Where formal enforcement is unavailable, inadequate, or not preferred, informal enforcement, such as reputational sanctions, can fill the gap or provide support for formal enforcement.The importance of informal enforcement is especially well-documented in tightly knit communities,such as those of rural ranchers,whalers,high-seas pirates,and diamond merchants,among others. In these communities, individuals are repeat players, so poor behavior in one transaction will sully their future transactions - a result that many individuals wish to avoid. Robust relational contracting relationships also exist in a variety of businesses on the West Coast,in the Midwest,and in Hollywood filmmaking.Because M&A parties can be one-off players in the M&A market (and therefore do not have the same reputational concerns as a repeat player in a tightly knit community), the non-binding and unenforceable nature of these business terms is particularly surprising. Moreover, like the formal contracting scholarship, the relational contracting scholarship also relies on enforcement (although of the extralegal variety) as an important motivator.
This Article takes a different route. Existing literature largely focuses on enforcement - the back end of contracting - but some contracts have no "back end." For one thing, contracting parties often simply abide by the terms to which they agreed. For another, even when disputes arise,many contracts are not formally enforced through litigation - parties simply renegotiate or settle.In modern contracts between corporate and commercial parties, formal enforcement is perhaps even rarer, as parties have become leerier of high litigation costs and the disclosure of sensitive information during the discovery process.Even the cheaper, faster, and more private arbitration processes have become very expensive.Without dispute, there is no documented enforcement, no opinion, and no evidence that a scholar can examine to draw conclusions about contracting, breach, or enforcement - so studying contract law from the back end necessarily gives insight into only a small sliver of contracting practice.
Because studying ex post enforcement paints an incomplete picture, studying ex ante contract design has become an important way to understand some of the basic questions of contract law and theory: How do parties enter into contracts?This Article adds to the contract designliterature. In particular, this Article takes a close look at a particularly odd type of contract - the formal-looking but non-binding and unenforced "faux contract" - and asks why sophisticated business parties willingly choose to enter into them and adhere to them.
This Article builds on my own previous work, which asks a related question: Why do parties usepreliminaryagreements in mergers and acquisitions?There, interviews with deal lawyers revealed that parties use preliminary agreements after most material deal uncertainty and complexity have been resolved, rather than very early in the deal's lifecycle. This time proximity accounts for why preliminary agreements are often followed up with full, binding acquisition agreements on substantially similar terms. That Article also noted that parties use preliminary agreements not because they want to enforce them, but for a variety of organizational and signposting functions. Left under-explored, however, are many questions surrounding the preliminary agreements'non-bindingnature. This Article picks up where that one left off and tries to tease out the meaningfulness, if any, of usingnon-binding,unenforcedcontract-like devices in complex business transactions. In theory, the ideas here could extend to non-binding contract-like devices used outside of the preliminary context: for example, M&A lawyers have mentioned, at various times, the stickiness of jointly-prepared issues lists, shared checklists, and funds flow memoranda, which are not preliminary, but are also formal-looking and non-binding.
The remainder of this Article proceeds as follows. Part I considers a puzzle: other scholars have focused on contracts as tools for enforcement - and enforcement, in turn, is understood to mitigate economic transaction costs, such as incentive misalignment and information asymmetry. Relatedly, some minor enforcement of these contracts - perhaps through the award of reliance damages for breach - is meant to mitigate opportunism and holdups in the early dealmaking process.But this focus on enforcement does not explain why parties enter into non-binding agreements that attach no enforcement. This Part investigates the shortcomings of the conventional focus on enforcement and asks: Why do parties incur the costs of drafting an agreement, if not to make a contracting relationship enforceable? Part II uses interviews with practicing lawyers to tease out several reasons parties use and adhere to non-binding agreements. Interview participants highlighted the multi-stage nature of complex dealmaking and reported that good-faith performance of early non-binding terms played a role in building a long-term relationship of trust within the ecosystem of a particular deal. Trust is necessary because complex deals are incompletely contracted, and trust fills the gaps left by contract provisions. Individual contract negotiators are also motivated to behave reasonably throughout the early deal process, even without a binding document, because they expend social capital within their own institutions to shepherd the deal through to completion. Interview participants also emphasized the collaborative process of dealmaking and described non-binding agreements as useful tools for facilitating collaboration. Ordinary frictions of trade, such as organization and coordination costs - what others have termed "mundane" transaction costs - present significant hurdles to dealmaking, and the process of drafting a shared document helps parties collaborate. Finally, interview participants described the process of bundling binding and non-binding terms in term sheets as substantively or formally nudging deal parties toward abiding by non-binding terms. Part III considers implications of faux contracting for contract theory, enforcement, and design.

questions.question: Why do sophisticated parties in complex transactions choose to draft and sign formal-looking but legally non-binding agreements instead of (or prior to) binding contracts?
When formal and informal enforcement are unavailable or limited, what mechanisms motivate parties to comply with the terms of non-binding contract-like documents?
What specific functions or value (e.g., organizational, informational, relational) do non-binding, formal-looking agreements provide that binding contracts cannot replicate?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20utahlrev1121!!ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication

shared_topics.topic: the role of enforcement (formal and informal) in producing contractual compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates adjudication strategies by considering how judicial enforcement (and predictable application of law) influences parties' behavior, and Paper B investigates why parties comply with non‑binding 'faux contracts' by relying on alternative motivators like reputational pressure, trust, and deal‑process incentives when formal enforcement is absent.

shared_topics.topic: instrumentalist/efficiency justifications for contract law and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A adopts an instrumentalist starting point and argues that formalist adjudication best advances contract law's social and efficiency goals, while Paper B analyzes non‑binding agreements through a transaction‑cost/efficiency lens, asking how such design choices facilitate dealmaking and lower coordination costs.

shared_topics.topic: how ex ante contractual forms and drafting choices shape parties' expectations and subsequent behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that predictable doctrines and clear adjudicative rules protect parties' legitimate expectations and reduce legal mistakes, whereas Paper B studies how term sheets and other preliminary, formal‑looking documents (even when non‑enforceable) create expectations, 'nudge' behavior, and structure the subsequent formation of binding deals.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional limits and costs of litigation or adjudication and their implications for legal practice and contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its advocacy for a formalist approach partly in courts' institutional competence and the costs of legal error, and Paper B documents how high litigation/discovery costs and arbitration expenses lead sophisticated parties to design non‑enforceable mechanisms and rely on non‑judicial means to govern transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj335!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity

shared_topics.topic: how drafting clarity or ambiguity of legal texts shapes commercial predictability and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses how an imprecise statutory provision (UCC §2-209) creates judicial and advisory confusion that corrodes predictable commercial decision‑making, while Paper B shows how parties and their lawyers deliberately use formally drafted but non‑binding documents (term sheets, checklists) whose precise wording or disclaimers shape how parties coordinate and behave in deals.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal enforcement and the role of alternative mechanisms in securing deal performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that unclear rules about modification and waiver undermine expectations about enforceability and can produce unintended consequences in commerce, and Paper B investigates situations where formal enforcement is absent by design and explains how trust, reputational incentives, organizational norms, and document design nonetheless motivate parties to comply.

shared_topics.topic: contract/instrument design as a tool to reduce transaction and coordination costs in complex commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that poor legislative drafting increases transactional friction and creates a 'commercial calamity,' whereas Paper B shows that drafting preliminary, bundled, or partial documents serves organizational, collaborative, and coordination functions that lower transaction costs during multi‑stage deals.

shared_topics.topic: the consequential impact of drafters' choices (legislative committees vs. deal practitioners) on commercial law and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how lawmakers' indecision and drafting committee choices produced a lasting problematic rule in the UCC, and Paper B analyzes how practitioners' conscious drafting choices—whether to make documents non‑binding, to bundle terms, or to use formal‑looking instruments—produce predictable behavioral outcomes in dealmaking.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51arizlrev1!!Article: Contracts as Organizations
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contracts as Organizations

shared_topics.topic: non-enforcement functions of contracts (organizational, symbolic, and coordination roles)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how formal-looking but non-binding ‘faux contracts’ (especially M&A term sheets) deliver organizational, clarifying, and coordination value despite lacking enforceability; Paper B develops the idea that contracts serve as organizational and symbolic artifacts that structure collective action and governance beyond mere legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: limits of enforcement-centric economic theories of contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the conventional focus on enforcement as the primary motivator of contractual performance and asks why parties adhere to non-enforceable agreements, while Paper B argues that mainstream economic theories (which center on ex post advantage-taking and enforcement) are insufficient and should be supplemented by organizational perspectives.

shared_topics.topic: empirical and qualitative study of real-world contract drafting and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs interviews with deal lawyers to examine how draft term sheets and preliminary agreements function in practice, and Paper B surveys and advocates for empirical work on contracts that attends to drafting norms, contract language, and the actual uses of contract texts.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as tools for facilitating complex, multi-stage transactions (e.g., M&A) and collaboration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on multi-stage dealmaking in M&A and how non-binding documents enable collaboration, trust-building, and bundling of terms across stages; Paper B emphasizes that contracts create and sustain organizing efforts and can be analyzed to understand how parties coordinate and govern complex contractual relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78valrev821!!ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for filling gaps in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes default rules as a legal mechanism that occupies a middle ground between expressly agreed terms and immutable background norms to fill unavoidable contractual gaps, while Paper B studies how parties use formal-looking but non-binding documents (term sheets, preliminary agreements) and other ex ante devices to manage incompleteness in complex deals without relying on litigation.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of silence or non-explicit assent as a form of indirect consent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues silence can count as an inchoate or indirect expression of consent that justifies enforcing certain default rules, and Paper B examines how signing non‑binding or unenforceable documents nevertheless produces commitments and predictable behavior despite the absence of formal legal assent.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-legal or informal mechanisms (trust, reputation, social capital) versus formal enforceability in ensuring performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends choosing conventionalist default rules that reflect community understandings to reduce disagreement and reliance costs, and Paper B documents how trust, institutional social capital, collaborative norms, and reputational incentives cause sophisticated parties to honor faux contracts even when formal enforcement is excluded.

shared_topics.topic: contract design as choice architecture—using defaults, bundling, and document form to steer behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how default rules should be designed to reflect parties' expectations and facilitate consent, while Paper B shows how bundling binding and non-binding terms, drafting formal-looking term sheets, and other preliminary documents function as design tools that nudge parties toward later performance or definitive agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65uclalrev376!!ARTICLE: Deal Momentum
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Momentum

shared_topics.topic: why sophisticated M&A parties use non-binding preliminary agreements (term sheets/LOIs) instead of binding contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers investigate the puzzle that deal-savvy M&A parties routinely draft and sign formal-looking but explicitly non-binding preliminary agreements, asking why they choose non-enforceable devices even though they could create binding contracts.

shared_topics.topic: preliminary agreements as organizational/signaling devices that create deal momentum
shared_topics.justification: Both articles argue (based on interviews) that preliminary agreements function as signposts—adding formality, clarifying resolved issues, coordinating parties, and marking the point in a transaction when momentum makes a deal likely to close—rather than primarily serving as enforceable promises.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms that motivate parties to honor non-binding terms absent formal legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine non-legal motivators for compliance—such as trust-building, social capital within organizations, collaborative negotiation processes, bundling of binding and non-binding terms, and the reduction of transaction/coordination costs—that explain why parties follow term-sheet terms despite a lack of judicial remedies.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract theory and judicial enforcement (reframing focus from enforcement to contract design)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique enforcement-centered scholarship, advocate studying ex ante contract design and practice, and draw out implications for how courts and scholars should treat preliminary agreements (including whether courts need to impose legal remedies).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54fordhamlrev35!!ARTICLE: THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE AND IMPLIED TERMS: THE SOUNDS OF SILENCE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE AND IMPLIED TERMS: THE SOUNDS OF SILENCE.

shared_topics.topic: the role of preliminary or non-final documents (term sheets/negotiations) in creating obligations beyond the written contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why parties sign formal-looking but non-binding term sheets and how those preliminary documents shape later behavior and the final deal; Paper B examines whether and when evidence of prior or contemporaneous negotiations can be used to add, vary, or supply contractual terms under the parol evidence rule.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual obligations can arise from sources other than the final integrated writing (implied terms, in-fact or in-law)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how parties adhere to non-binding commitments and how bundling or customs in deal practice effectively creates obligations outside formal enforcement, while Paper B doctrinally analyzes courts' power to imply terms (implied-in-fact or implied-in-law) and the interaction of that implication with the parol evidence rule.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of reliance on a written document as the sole measure of parties' duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the assumption that drafting a formal document is primarily about enforceability and shows actors rely on non-legal mechanisms to implement deal terms, and Paper B interrogates the legal assumption that a written integrated agreement exhausts parties' obligations by considering when extrinsic evidence or implied duties supplement or displace the writing.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and doctrinal treatment of prior negotiations and their ability to define, negate, or supplement contractual duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses interviews to show that negotiated understandings and the process of drafting (even if labeled non-binding) influence conduct and later contract terms, while Paper B analyzes whether the parol evidence rule permits proof of negotiations to establish, define, or negate obligations and how courts distinguish implied terms from proven negotiated terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42geojintll639!!ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA

shared_topics.topic: how legal and regulatory design shapes firms' organizational choices and cross-border transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties design (non‑binding) contractual documents as a deliberate legal choice that shapes deal structure and behavior, while Paper B examines how treaty and domestic nationality rules constrain airline ownership and argues for a redesigned 'lex aviatica' to enable different organizational forms and cross‑border consolidation.

shared_topics.topic: use of intermediate or alternative governance devices when full legal integration is infeasible or costly

papers.node_id: 45arizstlj925!!ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years
papers.title: ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years
papers.authors: David G. Epstein; Adam L. Tate; William Yaris
papers.abstract:
Many commercial disputes arise from disagreements regarding the terms of a written contract for the sale of goods.Perhaps the most notorious case involving such a disagreement is Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.There, Judge Friendlyfirst stated that "the word "chicken' standing alone is ambiguous," and then looked to parol evidence - "an exchange of cablegrams" - and extrinsic evidence - "a definite trade usage that "chicken' meant "young chicken'" - to determine whether the seller breached a written contract for the sale of "US Fresh Frozen Chicken" by delivering stewing chickens.
While Frigaliment involved a dispute over interpreting a term in a written sale of goods contract, Frigaliment was a pre-UCC case.Accordingly, Judge Friendly's opinion does not use the language of Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code ("UCC").
Too often, the reported opinions in post-UCC cases that involve a dispute over interpreting a term in or adding terms to a written contract for the sale of goods do not use the language of the UCC. Instead, attorneys andjudges use (and misuse) the terms "extrinsic evidence," "parol evidence," and the "parol evidence rule," rather than the language of Article 2.
Consider the following argument from Shell Oil Co. v. AmPm Enterprises, Inc.,a United States district court case involving a 1994 written contract for AmPm's sale of Shell petroleum products.AmPm's position was that a 1993 oral agreement that Shell would finance AmPm's construction of a car wash was a part of the deal.More specifically,
Defendants argue that a prerequisite to application of the parole [sic] evidence rule is a finding by the court that the parties intended the written instrument to be the complete expression of their agreement. Defendants contend that extrinsic evidence of prior or contemporaneous agreements or negotiations is admissible as it bears on the threshold question of whether the written instrument is in fact an "integrated" agreement.
Or, consider the statement by a New York Appellate Division Court in Kolmar Americas, Inc. v. Bioversal, Inc.:
Article 2 of the UCC does not authorize the introduction of parole [sic] evidence to vary the plain meaning of the GTC tax clause. Extrinsic evidence does not merely "explain" or "supplement" a contractual term within the meaning of UCC 2-202 when the purported explanation or supplement actually contradicts the unambiguous contractual terms.
To state the obvious, both Shell and Kolmar misspell "parol evidence."More importantly, both Shell and Kolmar are sale of goods cases governed by the Uniform Commercial Code.This is important because the UCC provisions on extrinsic evidence and parol evidence are different from the common law of some states.More specifically, the UCC distinguishesbetween extrinsic evidence and parol evidence to a greater extent than the common law of some states.
The lawyer in Shell and the judges in Kolmar confuse "extrinsic evidence" with "parol evidence" by using the terms erroneously or interchangeably. Under the structure of UCC § 2-202, the Shell evidence of "prior or contemporaneous agreements or negotiations" is "parol evidence," not "extrinsic evidence." And, unlike UCC § 2-202, the New York court in Kolmar is using the terms "parole [sic] evidence" and "extrinsic evidence" interchangeably.
In this essay, we will compare (1) the common law parol evidence rule with UCC § 2-202, (2) UCC § 2-202(a)'s treatment of extrinsic evidence with UCC § 2-202(b)'s treatment of parol evidence, and (3)UCC § 1-303's provisions relating to extrinsic evidence with UCC § 2-202(a) provisions relating to extrinsic evidence.

questions.question: Whether and how a modern commercial statutory framework differentiates between (a) evidence offered to explain or supplement the meaning of written contract terms and (b) prior or contemporaneous oral agreements offered to vary or contradict a written contract, and what effect that distinction has on admissibility and interpretation in sale-of-goods disputes.

To what extent do judges and lawyers conflate or misuse these categories of evidence in litigation over written sale-of-goods contracts, and how does that confusion influence judicial reasoning and case outcomes.

How does the treatment of explanatory/supplementary evidence versus evidence of prior/contemporaneous agreements under modern commercial statutes compare to traditional common-law approaches, and what are the practical implications for contract drafting and dispute resolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67dukeljonline102!!ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS

shared_topics.topic: meaning and treatment of boilerplate / standardized contract language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A deals with interpreting contested terms and trade usages in sale-of-goods contracts (often arising from standardized forms), and Paper B focuses on 'contractual black holes'—standard-form boilerplate that lacks a clear recordable meaning—and how doctrine should treat such clauses.

shared_topics.topic: calls for doctrinal clarification or reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for correct application and clearer use of UCC provisions to prevent misuse of parol/extrinsic-evidence concepts, and Paper B evaluates and proposes doctrinal reforms (and alternatives) to address the problems caused when boilerplate clauses become legally indeterminate.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between market practice/trade usage and legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how trade usage and industry practice function as forms of extrinsic evidence under the UCC to supply or clarify meaning, and Paper B studies how market actors and standard-setting in response to judicial interpretations (e.g., drafting new clauses) shape and respond to judicial meaning-making of boilerplate.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE MITIGATION PRINCIPLE: TOWARD A GENERAL THEORY OF CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION

shared_topics.topic: how market and commercial context (trade usage, substitute markets) should shape contract rules and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the availability of substitute performances and the transactional environment as the major variable determining how mitigation duties should be specified, while Paper B focuses on sale‑of‑goods contexts—trade usage, course of dealing, and UCC provisions—to show how commercial practices influence admissible evidence and contract interpretation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conceptualizing Contractual Interpretation

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DEAL STRUCTURE

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
