papers.node_id: 39connlrev923!!ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
papers.title: ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
papers.abstract:
Judicial decisions, legal analysis and theories of justice often depend on when a decision is made, ex ante or ex post. Does justice depend on when we decide? If so, what is at stake?
Recently, these questions became particularly important against the background of the issue of torture under the ticking bomb circumstances.Many people oppose any form of torture, whether under terms of necessity or not.They point out that allowing torture in one specific case will lead to moral rootlessness toward human dignity and human rights.However, if asked whether torture should be employed if it will prevent a ticking bomb from exploding and killing 1000 innocent people, few will nonetheless also agree to create an exception. Some suggest that this"ticking bomb" exception should be allowed ex ante through regulation.Others suggest that law should prohibit torture ex ante, but if the particular case arises then we should consider whether it was permissible to use torture after it was already employed, either through a necessity defense or a public debate held afterwards.This debate repeats itself also with respect to coercive methods of interrogation, which are not formally considered "torture."As we decide what type of interrogation methods should be allowed, it becomes increasingly important to examine the merits and challenges presented by ex ante and ex post approaches toward the issue of torture and coercive interrogations methods more generally. What are the stakes in following ex ante and ex post perspectives on these issues? Who should decide between the two perspectives? What tools can law offer decisionmakers in making this choice?
The issue of torture is only one example for the potential choice between ex ante and ex post perspectives toward legal issues. Once this choice is realized in torture, it becomes visible in many other areas of law, from contracts to civil procedure and legal transitions.While the ex ante and ex post distinction has already been addressed by legal theory sporadically in these different areas of law, this Article offers the first attempt to connect the different examples and theoretical approaches under one framework in order to examine the ex ante and ex post distinction in torture.
Fortunately, much has already been written on the ex ante and ex post distinction in various areas of law.Legal theory usually takes one of twoapproaches toward the ex ante and ex post distinction. The first approach addresses the two perspectives as reflecting a choice between following policy considerations premised on the economic model of rational choice versus considerations of just outcomes, often associated with fairness.While following an ex ante perspective is important for making individuals act optimally ex ante, following an ex post perspective is important because of the limits of the rational choice model in directing behavior in uncertain environments. Accordingly other considerations need to be taken into account ex post in order to set the appropriate policy for diverse legal issues. Another approach views the choice between the two perspectives as based on whether legal directives should be cast as rules or standards.Rules are associated with ex ante analysis because they receive their content before individuals act, whereas standards enable decisionmakers to consider the particular circumstances of cases as they arise ex post. The choice between ex ante and ex post perspectives is therefore a choice made in advance by devising legal directives as either rules or standards. This Article seeks to avoid the partisan and polarized debate in legal scholarship over which of the two perspectives is superior for different contexts by examining the potential availability of both perspectives for both good and disturbing effects in different legal settings and particularly in torture.
The Article's thesis is that both perspectives are available and important for decisionmakers and legal actors, whether they are legislatures, judges or administrators. Legal instances are a slice of time and time is always flowing. While the ex ante perspective offers a way to solve particular cases looking forward based on rational choices, it is nonetheless stable because it is limited to the set of cases captured before the fact. The ex post perspective provides the opportunity to engage in reexamination in light of particular cases and the experiences they offer after the fact. At the same time, the ex post perspective might rely on cases which are not representative and may reflect arbitrary decisions.
argue that the dual availability of both perspectives in different legal contexts suggests three dilemmas-normative, institutional and personal-all of which are important for addressing the choice between the perspectives. At the normative level, in each legal field we should determine whether ex ante or ex post analysis is preferable for the legal issue at hand. Are ex ante incentive arrangements more appropriate in the issue of torture compared to the fields of contract law or civil procedure?At the institutional level, law has to consider which institution is suitable or even capable of considering which perspectives. Are courts more suitable than legislatures or other administrative officials for considering whether to excuse torture after the fact rather than allow it before the fact? The third dilemma concerns the actors acting within institutions. Each legal actor-whether it is an officer in charge of interrogations or a court reviewing the officer's decision-has to determine whether to follow the ex ante determination of the law or to follow an ex post perspective toward the issue. Suppose law prohibits torture ex ante, should the officer in charge of an interrogation ignore this rule if the use of torture will lead to information that will save the lives of 1000 people? Should a court reviewing the officer's decision excuse the officer's actions ex post based on a necessity defense?
In Part II, the Article traces the recent debate over whether torture should be regulated ex ante or ex post and analyzes the benefits of following ex ante and ex post perspectives in the ticking bomb circumstances. Once these stakes and benefits are realized in the issue of torture they become visible in other areas of law. Accordingly, the Article briefly contrasts the choice between ex ante and ex post perspectives in torture with similar problems in contracts and civil procedure in order to offer a more general viewpoint from which to consider the dual availability of the ex ante and ex post perspectives in the issue of torture.
In Part III, the Article turns to examine the suitability of theoretical approaches previously offered for the choice between ex ante and ex post perspectives for the issue of torture. Is ex ante policy analysis more suitable for the issue of torture or should law prefer an ex post perspective? Are rules or standards more suitable for regulating torture? Do these theoretical approaches resolve the choice between the two perspectives in the issue of torture and also in other settings? I argue that the current theoretical approaches fall short of offering a satisfying resolution of the ex ante and ex post distinction, because they focus on an exclusive choice between the perspectives in every legal setting. However, both perspectives are important for the normative analysis of legal fields, from contract law to constitutional law. Both perspectives are important for institutional analysis and for actors acting within these institutions, whether they are administrative officials or judges. We should avoid the pretense that it is possible to choose between the perspectives, entirely exclusively of the other. If we do choose only one perspective, we should be aware of the cost of binding ourselves for the future, even under catastrophic cases. Accordingly, in Part IV, I offer a framework to address the choice between the two perspectives, by discussing the normative, institutional, and personal dilemmas arising out of the dual availability of the ex ante and ex post perspectives in torture.

questions.question: Does choosing ex ante regulation (pre-authorized rules) versus ex post adjudication (after-the-fact justification or excuse) produce different moral, legal, and practical outcomes for the permissibility and restraint of coercive interrogation or torture in emergency (e.g., 'ticking bomb') scenarios?

Which institutional actors (legislatures, courts, or administrative officials) are more suitable or capable of deciding whether to adopt an ex ante or ex post approach to authorizing or excusing coercive interrogation practices?

How do ex ante versus ex post legal frameworks shape the incentives, decisionmaking behavior, and responsibility of individual actors (e.g., interrogators or reviewers) faced with high-stakes emergency situations where prohibited actions might save lives?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107geolj1277!!ARTICLE: Contract Creep
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Creep

shared_topics.topic: designing distinct doctrinal tracks versus unified legal regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the wisdom of a tracked contract law (separate regimes for 'sophisticated parties' and 'consumers') and the risks when those tracks blur; Paper B treats the ex ante/ex post distinction (and associated rules vs standards) as an analogous choice between different legal regimes and examines the consequences of selecting one framework over another across domains including contracts.

shared_topics.topic: defining boundaries and categorical criteria for triggering a doctrinal regime
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the practical difficulty of identifying who counts as a 'consumer' versus a 'sophisticated party' and how fuzzy categories enable doctrinal creep; Paper B likewise addresses how and when to apply ex ante versus ex post perspectives, raising normative and institutional questions about which cases or actors should fall into each perspective.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between predictability (rules/ex ante) and flexibility/justice (standards/ex post)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights tensions between modular standardized clauses (predictable, portable rules) and the need for bespoke doctrine sensitive to particular transactional goals; Paper B explicitly articulates the rules (ex ante, predictive) versus standards (ex post, case-sensitive) tradeoff and analyzes their respective virtues for incentives and fairness.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of decisionmaking authority (courts, legislatures, administrators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls on judges, lawmakers, drafters and scholars to devise clearer criteria and institutional responses to contain or manage creep; Paper B develops an 'institutional dilemma' asking which institutions are best suited to make ex ante or ex post determinations and to apply exceptions after the fact.

shared_topics.topic: evaluating downstream effects and doing cost–benefit analysis of doctrinal design choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges attention to the unintended costs of doctrinal migration and recommends weighing the benefits of experimentation against the harms of creep; Paper B cautions about the costs of binding the future (or excusing acts ex post) and proposes a framework for weighing normative, institutional, and personal dilemmas when choosing perspectives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52drakelrev235!!ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante versus ex post choice in legal regulation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the distinction between making legal determinations before events occur (ex ante) and assessing them after the fact (ex post): Paper A develops a general framework and dilemmas (normative, institutional, personal) about choosing ex ante or ex post approaches (using torture/ticking‑bomb as the focal example), while Paper B critiques the Uniform Commercial Code's practice of letting postcontractual conduct (course of performance) re‑interpret preexisting agreements and therefore represents an ex post interpretive move in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal rules or post hoc standards should govern behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the ex ante/ex post choice as manifesting in the rules‑versus‑standards debate and examines the costs of binding rulemaking versus case‑by‑case standards, and Paper B engages the same tension by questioning whether fixed contractual terms should yield to flexible interpretive devices (course of performance) or instead be managed through doctrines like waiver.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of authority to decide ex ante vs ex post questions
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider which institutions are appropriate for making or revising ex ante rules or for applying ex post assessments: Paper A asks whether legislatures, courts or administrators should set or revisit prohibitions (e.g., torture), and Paper B analyzes the statutory placement of course‑of‑performance in Article 1 and the consequences for courts, drafters, and state legislatures in shaping postformation interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of post‑event conduct and its corrective role vis‑à‑vis formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats ex post reexamination of concrete cases (and actors’ conduct) as a tool that can override or excuse ex ante prohibitions in extreme situations, while Paper B focuses on how parties’ postformation conduct (course of performance or waiver) should or should not be allowed to alter the meaning or application of preexisting contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: policy trade‑offs between predictability/stability and flexibility/adaptive justice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers assess the normative and behavioral consequences of preferring precommitment versus hindsight adjustment: Paper A emphasizes how exclusive reliance on one perspective sacrifices either ex ante incentives or ex post responsiveness, and Paper B argues that admitting course‑of‑performance interpretation undermines contractual predictability and commercial norms compared with alternatives like waiver.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67emorylj1!!ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS IN HEALTH CARE

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante versus ex post timing of legal decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract doctrine (and judicial gap-filling) affects behavior by focusing on whether price terms are set before transactions occur, while Paper B develops a general framework comparing ex ante and ex post approaches (using torture and other domains as examples) and the normative stakes of when law decides.

shared_topics.topic: which institutions should set legal rules (courts versus legislatures/administrators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should adopt a penalty-default gap-filling rule to force ex ante price disclosure, and Paper B directly interrogates the institutional question of which bodies (courts, legislatures, or administrators) are suitable to adopt ex ante or ex post rules and to excuse conduct after the fact.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between rules and standards (including use of defaults) and their incentive effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a bright-line penalty default (a rule that fills omitted price terms with $0) to create incentives for providers to disclose prices, while Paper B frames the rules-vs-standards debate as the rules/ex ante approach versus standards/ex post approach and analyzes how those forms shape behavior and decisionmaking.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between law-and-economics incentive reasoning and alternative normative/behavioral concerns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law-and-economics arguments about transaction costs with behavioral findings about relational benefits of incompleteness to decide when contracts should be complete, and Paper B contrasts ex ante policy/incentive analysis rooted in rational-choice models with ex post concerns about fairness, uncertainty, and just outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the application of ex ante/ex post reasoning to contract law and contractual gap-filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on incomplete patient-provider contracts and proposes a doctrinal remedy for omitted price terms, and Paper B explicitly uses contract law as one of the domains where the ex ante/ex post distinction matters, discussing how the choice of timing affects contract enforcement and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev1437!!ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the choice between rule-based (ex ante) regulation and standards-based (ex post) adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central debate as an ex ante/ex post distinction and links it to the rules-versus-standards literature when deciding whether to permit or prohibit practices (e.g., torture) before or after they occur; Paper B treats enforcement defaults and all-things-considered interpretive tests as alternative interpretive devices that functionally map onto rule-like defaults versus case-by-case (standards-like) determinations of contractual intent.

shared_topics.topic: design and effects of legal defaults on behavior and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how ex ante rules shape incentives under a rational-choice model and how ex post review responds to informational limits and experience, while Paper B develops an analytic framework for enforcement/nonenforcement defaults (including "sticky" defaults and opt-out costs) to show how interpretive defaults influence parties' expectations and conduct.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of decisionmaking (who should decide: legislatures, courts, administrators, or actors)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises an institutional dilemma about which institutions are suitable to adopt ex ante prohibitions or ex post excuses (legislatures, judges, administrative officers) in contexts like interrogation, and Paper B analyzes the role of courts' interpretive function, doctrinal presumptions, and different transaction types in assigning who determines whether parties intended legal liability.

shared_topics.topic: balancing law's duty-imposing and power-conferring functions when setting legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the normative trade-offs between ex ante incentive-oriented policy and ex post concerns about fairness and representativeness when legal directives constrain or permit action, and Paper B explicitly frames rules for interpreting contractual intent as tools to balance contract law's simultaneous functions of imposing duties and empowering parties to create enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: treatment of exceptional or context-specific cases where ordinary rules may misfit
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses extreme cases (the "ticking bomb") to explore whether exceptions should be pre-authorized or excused after the fact and how atypical cases reveal limits of ex ante rules, while Paper B examines special transaction contexts (gratuitous promises, spousal agreements, reporters' promises, preliminary agreements) where ordinary presumptions about intent and enforceability may be inapplicable and demand tailored interpretive rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nyulrev1023!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante versus ex post choice in legal decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the normative consequences of preferring ex ante rules versus ex post reassessment: Paper A develops a general framework contrasting ex ante regulation and ex post excuses (illustrated by torture and other fields), while Paper B applies the same distinction to contract adjudication, arguing for honoring parties' ex ante choices over ex post judicial realignment.

shared_topics.topic: rules versus standards (precise terms versus vague/delegated standards)
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat the rules/standards tradeoff as a mechanism for allocating decision authority: Paper A links rules to ex ante directives and standards to ex post case-specific judgments, and Paper B discusses parties' selection of precise (rule-like) vs vague (standard-like) contract terms and the consequences of courts converting rules into standards.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of authority (who decides — courts, legislatures, administrators, or parties)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine which actor should hold decision power: Paper A raises institutional questions about whether legislatures, courts, or administrators should choose ex ante or ex post approaches, and Paper B argues that commercial parties (not courts) should control whether to permit ex post equitable intervention, restricting judicial override unless expressly delegated.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs under uncertainty and the role of incentives/costs in choosing legal design
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how uncertainty and incentive structure shape legal design choices: Paper A highlights limits of rational-choice ex ante analysis and the need for ex post correction under uncertain environments, while Paper B models front-end (drafting) versus back-end (enforcement) costs, and the incentive effects of legal versus relational enforcement in contract design.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of judicial/equitable override (hindsight correction) on future behavior and doctrinal reliability
shared_topics.justification: Both critique or explore the consequences of permitting ex post judicial correction: Paper A worries that ex post exceptions (e.g., necessity defenses for torture) change normative expectations and institutional behavior, and Paper B shows how equitable override of formal contract terms undermines parties' ability to rely on ex ante design choices and affects future contracting strategies.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Index Theory: The Law, Promise and Failure of Financial Indices

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between ex ante regulation and ex post review/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central question as whether to permit or prohibit practices (like torture) through ex ante rules or to assess conduct ex post (necessity defenses, after-the-fact review), while Paper B evaluates responses to index dysfunction (market contracting, litigation, government control) in terms of ex ante versus ex post solutions and their limits.

shared_topics.topic: which institutions should set, monitor, and enforce rules for socially important practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether legislatures, courts, or administrators are better suited to adopt ex ante or ex post perspectives (and to implement rules or standards), and Paper B examines the roles of private index producers, regulators, and courts (and proposes intellectual property law) as alternative institutional arrangements for governing indices.

shared_topics.topic: how incentives and human discretion shape the production and potential abuse of critical social goods
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how ex ante incentive structures and limits of rational-choice models affect behavior in high-stakes settings (e.g., interrogation), while Paper B documents how discretionary reporting and incentive structures faced by banks and index providers enable manipulation and shape index quality and risk.

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs of committing to rigid rules versus allowing case-by-case flexibility (rules vs standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly treats the rules-versus-standards framing as a core theoretical way to think about ex ante/ex post choices, and Paper B repeatedly emphasizes that indices involve subjective methodological choices and that no single regulatory solution fits all cases, highlighting tradeoffs between fixed methodologies and flexible oversight.

shared_topics.topic: post-failure accountability and legal remedies for institutional breakdowns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises whether actors should be excused or punished ex post (e.g., necessity defenses for torture) and explores institutional accountability, while Paper B surveys litigation, regulatory penalties, and other legal mechanisms (including restoring property rights) as remedies to index manipulation and institutional failures.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante vs ex post distinction as a foundational analytic
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center the ex ante/ex post distinction as the key lens for evaluating legal rules: Paper A uses it to diagnose contract doctrines (ex ante personal-sovereignty rules vs ex post equitable doctrines), while Paper B develops a general framework for when and how ex ante and ex post perspectives should guide legal decisionmaking across domains (torture, contracts, procedure).

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs between forward‑looking incentives and backward‑looking fairness
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between using ex ante rules to secure incentives and respect parties' autonomous choices (Paper A's personal sovereignty account) versus relying on ex post fairness or justice to correct harsh or disproportionate outcomes (Paper B's discussion of just outcomes and the limits of the rational choice model).

shared_topics.topic: which institutions and actors should apply ex ante or ex post perspectives
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss allocation of authority—Paper A criticizes judges (e.g., Posner in Lake River) for importing ex post equity into contract adjudication, while Paper B explicitly poses an institutional dilemma about whether legislatures, courts, or administrators are better suited to adopt ex ante rules or to assess cases ex post.

shared_topics.topic: the rules vs standards framing of ex ante/ex post doctrines and doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers map the distinction onto doctrinal form: Paper A contrasts black‑letter, rule‑like ex ante contract doctrines with legacy equitable standards (penalty/forfeiture/excuse), and Paper B analyzes whether legal directives should be rules (ex ante) or standards (ex post) and the implications of that choice.

shared_topics.topic: practical harms and risks of privileging ex post reasoning (opportunism, unpredictability, undermining consent)
shared_topics.justification: Both identify concrete costs from ex post intervention: Paper A argues ex post doctrines enable opportunistic litigation and erode contracting autonomy (undermine personal sovereignty), while Paper B warns that ex post case‑by‑case adjudication can be arbitrary, unrepresentative, and impose institutional and personal dilemmas in high‑stakes contexts (e.g., torture).

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS BILATERAL COMMITMENTS: A NEW PERSPECTIVE ON CONTRACT MODIFICATION

shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes institutional and personal dilemmas about whether legislatures, courts, or administrators should decide ex ante prohibitions versus ex post excuses, and Paper A similarly considers the roles of parties, courts, and contractual terms in creating or enforcing limits on modification and when judges should be cautious in enforcing ex post changes.

shared_topics.topic: normative trade‑offs beyond simple efficiency, including fairness, dignity, and signaling effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs efficiency gains from bilateral commitment against signaling and other normative concerns and briefly considers non‑efficiency values, while Paper B juxtaposes ex ante policy incentives with ex post concerns about just outcomes, human dignity (in torture debates), and the risk that ex post decisions may reflect arbitrary or non‑representative cases.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC

papers.node_id: 57syracuselrev227!!ARTICLE: K.I.S.S. THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE GOODBYE: SIMPLIFYING THE CONCEPT OF PROTECTING THE PARTIES' WRITTEN AGREEMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: K.I.S.S. THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE GOODBYE: SIMPLIFYING THE CONCEPT OF PROTECTING THE PARTIES' WRITTEN AGREEMENT
papers.abstract:
Ask any person of average intelligence whether a party to a contract should be allowed to introduce alleged oral promises and assurances made before and during the creation of a written contract for the purpose of proving that the parties actually agreed to matters other than that reflected by the writing.Odds are he or she will tell you no.Our intuition tells us this must not be allowed. Refined legal reasoning affirms our intuition by questioning whether reasonable people who take the time to reduce components of their agreement to writing would leave out important details to which they allegedly agreed or write down something other than that to which they actually agreed. However, introduce that same concept to first year law students; throw in reverberations of integration; give it a legalistic-sounding title like "The Parol Evidence Rule." Now, the learned law professor has perplexed virtually every budding lawyer by cloaking a simple concept with a shroud of complexity and assuring her students that one will only gain true understanding of this rule by ritualistically performing the sacred three-step analysisdesigned to decode the rule. Accordingly, it stands to reason that the parol evidence rule is billed as the most litigated doctrine in contract law.
For centuries, the mysteries of the parol evidence rule have plagued American contract jurisprudence. Law professors have capitalized on this mystique by parading in front of first-year students while spewing hypotheticals and explanations of how the court approaches a parol evidence rule issue by inquiring whether the parties intended for theproffered writing to be integrated, i.e., to reflect their final expression of agreement, at least as to the terms contained therein.Only if this inquiry is answered in the affirmative does the court proceed to a determination of the degree of integration intended by the parties.By this time, most of the first-year law students, still reeling from the near-fatal effect of the damages formulas with which they were previously bombarded, are on information-overload.Thus, any seemingly-plausible explanation as to how to go about analyzing a parol evidence rule issue is readily accepted by the weary students without question. It is no wonder that law students have a great deal of difficulty with the parol evidence rule. Many court opinions, to which the students turn in desperate attempts to make sense of the complex web of rules, tests and exceptions, seem to reflect the same confusion among jurists, from incorrect references to the rule as "parole evidence,"to the inherently redundant analysis used to separately determine contractual intent and integration.There is no secret that courts find application of the parol evidence rule to be problematic.
Generally speaking, the parol evidence rule prevents the parties to a contract from using matters extrinsic to their written agreement to vary the terms of the writing.Thus, the parol evidence rule is premised on the existence of a written agreement.The prevailing approach to determining whether a written agreement can be supplemented or contradicted by matters allegedly occurring prior to or contemporaneously with the creation of that written agreement is to first ask whether the parties intended for the written agreement to reflect the final expression of the terms included.If that question is answered in the affirmative, then inquiry is made into whether the parties intended for the written agreement to cover the full universe of their understandings and agreements on the subject matters of the written agreement or just those specifics of their agreement actually mentioned in the writing, leaving other agreed-upon aspects of thetransaction unwritten.The second question delves into the degree of integration to be accorded the written agreement.In either case, the written agreement undoubtedly already exists. The fact that few, if any, courts accord due significance to the objective manifestation of the parties in reducing their agreement to writing is puzzling. More troubling is the fact that there is a plethora of conflicting case law containing different statements of and various approaches to the parol evidence rule, although purporting to explain the same concept.As one court concedes:
We, … no different than the courts in most other jurisdictions, have used a variety of principles, chosen randomly with no consistency, from the common law, the treatises of Professor Williston and Corbin, and the First and Second Restatement of the Law of Contracts … . thus, the random selection of principles … has made the parol evidence rule … no different than in most other jurisdictions, a deceptive maze rather than a workable rule.
Hence, the majority of cases discussing the parol evidence rule do not offer much assistance to understanding the issue.
The uncertainty produced by inconsistent application of the parol evidence rule and exceptions has the added effect of preventing attorneys from properly advising clients on the pros and cons of litigation, which in turn creates an increased burden on the judicial system.It has been referred to as "a maze of conflicting tests, subrules, and exceptions adversely affecting both the counseling of clients and the litigation process."The lengthy and costly litigation stemming from efforts to navigate the murky waters of parol evidence, not to mention the appeals that are sure to follow the confusing decisions rendered by the trial courts, all are byproducts of a wayward rule.Undoubtedly, the current state of the rule has wide-reaching adverse ramifications.
That being said, the parol evidence rule as we now know it is in need of a major overhaul. Certainly, a rule that is easier to understand and apply will go a long way in producing more consistent outcomes, well-reasoned court opinions, and more efficient use of judicial resources.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, it is perfectly understandable that an unconventional attempt such as this to clarify the parol evidence rule may be met with a great deal of reluctance. After all, it cannot be said that lawmakers, courts, and attorneys alike have wasted countless hours marching through the rubric of rules designed to determine whether a prior oral or written agreement can be used to supplement or contradict a writing purporting to reflect the parties' final agreement. At some time in our legal careers, we all have been caught up in the frenzy to understand the parol evidence rule. Accordingly, we committed valuable time to reading the applicable statutes, understanding the cases, and memorizing the sacred approach to a parol evidence rule issue. However, if one dares to extract herself from the tangled mess of rhetoric in order to examine the policies underlying the parol evidence rule from a holistic approach, it suddenly becomes clear that we have been duped. We are all guilty of making much to-do about nothing. It is time to honor the ageless adage, "keep it simple, stupid," or K.I.S.S. for short, and in doing so K.I.S.S. the parol evidence rule good-bye.
Contrary to the suggestions of the title of this article, I do not suggest the total obliteration of what we refer to as the parol evidence rule.While the rationale for the creation of the rulemay have lost its luster, the underlying tenet that a written agreement deserves some degree of protection from oral impeachment is well-respected in modern times. Admittedly, the rule has honorable intentions of avoiding the unilateral alteration of contracts.However, it has been criticized for its rigid dictateas well as for its amorphous nature.In the words of one legal scholar, "[It] may have done more harm than good."Instead of throwing the baby out with the bathwater, the frailties presented by the current application may be cured by rudimentary adjustments that preserve the mission while removing the cloud of confusion currently surrounding theparol evidence rule.
This Article attempts to demystify the parol evidence rule by suggesting a simplified approach to the inquiry of when a party is allowed to vary the terms of a written agreement by introducing prior or contemporaneous evidence of matters relating to the subject matter of the writing.Part I begins with a historical account of the origins of the parol evidence rule, the policies underlying such a rule, and the modern-day rule as we know it.Part II suggests that the very name, "parol evidence rule," must be the first thing to go in light of the confusion spurred by this misnomer.Part III explores the commonly-accepted modern approach to a parol evidence rule issue and questions the needs for such a complex approach.Part IV reviews some of the common exceptions to the parol evidence rule and highlights the redundancies and pitfalls inherent to such exceptions.Part V suggests a simplified rule and an analysis of the issue that achieves a desired and predictable result.Finally, this Article concludes with a few thoughts deserving of further exploration.

questions.question: When should parties be allowed to introduce prior or contemporaneous oral or other extrinsic evidence to contradict or supplement the terms of a written agreement?

Would replacing the current complex set of rules with a simplified, clearer rule about admitting extrinsic evidence produce more predictable adjudication, reduce litigation costs, and improve the quality of judicial outcomes?

papers.title: ARTICLE: LACKING SWISS PRECISION: THE FIRST-SALE DOCTRINE IN COSTCO V. OMEGA
papers.abstract: Copyright law seeks to achieve its constitutional mandate "to promote the progress of Science"in part by providing copyright owners with the exclusive right to control the distribution of their copyrighted works.The first-sale doctrine,which provides that "[o]nce [a] copyright owner consents to the sale of particular copies of his work, he may not thereafter exercise the distribution right with respect to those copies,"limits the exclusive distribution right. InCostco Wholesale Corp. v. Omega, S.A.,the Supreme Court granted certiorari to clarify whether the first-sale doctrine applies to imported goods manufactured abroad.U.S. retailers often import foreign-made goods previously sold to third parties by the goods' manufacturers.Whether the first-sale doctrine applies determines whether U.S. retailers must obtain a manufacturer's permission before importing goods the manufacturer has already sold abroad. Nevertheless, theequally divided Supreme Court's one-line per curiam decision leaves this important question without an authoritative answer.

questions.question: Whether an authorized sale of a copy made and first sold abroad prevents the copyright owner from controlling that copy's subsequent importation or resale in the United States.
Whether U.S. retailers must obtain a manufacturer's permission before importing goods that the manufacturer has already sold to third parties outside the United States.

papers.node_id: 84ucinlrev217!!ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*
papers.title: ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*
papers.abstract:
This is a reflection on the gap between the real-life practice of contract law and the academic theory that tries to explain it. As someone who used to do mergers and acquisitions as a lawyer and corporate executive, I occasionally get a call to comment on pending litigation. I also happen to be an academic theorist who has written about contract theory, and a teacher who guides first-year law students through the standard fare of casebook law. These interludes in which I leave the ivory tower and revisit contract disputes in the real world cause me to shake my head sadly, as they generally confirm my intuition that trying to connect before-the-fact contracting intentions and behaviors with colorable after-the-fact interpretation disputes misses the point.
My skepticism about academic theories of contract law most recently flared up in connection with an eight-year-old dispute, the result of a contested public company takeover, between Johnson & Johnson, the frustrated suitor, and medical device maker Guidant Corporation, now a subsidiary of the winning bidder, Boston Scientific Corporation. The contract issues are straightforward despite having arisen out of the documentation of a deal worth more than $ 20 billion. I will tell the story of the case and explain the context of relatively standard M&A contract practice.Then I will reflect on the implications of the case forthe prevailing economic and moral theories justifying state intervention in the enforcement of private agreements, at least when we put aside the abstractions and get down to cases.
With the disclaimer that I had no stake in the outcome of the case and no particular sympathy for Boston Scientific's uncomfortable situation, digging into J&J's claim caused me to have flashbacks to my most frustrating experiences as a general counsel: contending with a phenomenon I am here calling "lexical opportunism," an aspect of contract practice having three elements. First, the parties must have reduced a complex business arrangement to contractual text, portions of which text are as devoid of thoughtful drafting or close negotiation as the boilerplate in a consumer contract. Second, an adversary cleverly develops a legal theory based upon a colorable interpretation of that text. Third, this interpretation creates a potential for staggering liability beyond all common sense.
have long harbored two bugaboos about contract theory, at least when thinking about the complex deals I did versus the "Dick and Jane"contracts that are the necessary fodder for broad theory. The first is the fantasy that contract law actually does much to limit opportunism except in the arid laboratories where law professors conduct their thought-experiments. The second is the illusion of mutual consent against which to measure the putative opportunism or the moral force of the promise as a rational process in either contract formation or interpretation.Most business agreements worth litigating over were, atthe time of their creation, a complex synergy of individual intentions and motivations, more or less complete communications, drafting practices, pressures, and deadlines, many of which propelled the contract to its execution as a thing, a deed, or an event, and not necessarily as a logical and coherent text. In contrast, merely focusing after-the-fact on the logic and coherence of the text is, as often as not, an economist's simplification, a moralist's ideal, or a lawyer's delusion.
My purpose here is to use the dispute between J&J and Boston Scientific as a case study in lexical opportunism. In Part II, I describe the interpretation issue that led to litigation with as much as $ 7 billion in damages and interest at stake. In Part III, I discuss (a) what it means to engage in theoretical assessments and justifications of social institutions like contract law; (b) how the justification of contract law by way of inhibiting economic opportunism is based on the simplest of "Dick and Jane" examples, rather than the kind of contract discourse found in any real-world contract worth spending millions to litigate; and (c) how normative theory based on upholding the moral sanctity of promise keeping evaporates when the parties disagree about the meaning of their promises. In Part IV, I take account of a recent study by Mitu Gulati and Robert Scott of a particular instance, like the contract provision at issue in Johnson & Johnson v. Guidant, of a surprising mismatch between the deal and the contract, and argue that both economic and moral theories about contract law (a) fail to take account of the nature of the very language in which any contract of any complexity is drafted, and (b) depend on the naive adoption of the correspondence theory of truth. The nature of language permits opportunism, and the only check on it is the desire, from whatever motivation, not to be opportunistic. I conclude with what I hope are some constructive thoughts about the appropriate use of theory in lawyering, and thereby mitigate my skepticism whether any single theory or discipline is capable of meaningful explanation or prediction about lexical opportunism.

Whether the ideal of mutual consent or a close correspondence between parties' intentions and contract text is a reliable basis for interpreting and enforcing complex, high-value business agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: limits of economic contract theory to explain real-world contracting and bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prevailing economic models and moral theories simplify contracts into coherent texts and therefore fail to capture how complex business deals actually get made and litigated; Paper B shows that standard economic accounts of default rules (e.g., the Coasean/information‑forcing story for Hadley) omit key strategic bargaining incentives and so mischaracterize how parties will behave around legal defaults.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract language, drafting practices, and the deal–contract mismatch
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the phenomenon of 'lexical opportunism,' emphasizing how boilerplate or carelessly drafted text can be exploited and how the written instrument often mismatches the negotiated deal; Paper B examines how default doctrines, liquidated damages rules, and foreseeability doctrines interact with what parties actually write and negotiate, stressing how textual defaults affect and are affected by drafting choices.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and strategic incentives in contracting (interpretive opportunism vs bargaining strategy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes opportunistic post‑hoc interpretations of contractual language that can create outsized liabilities, while Paper B analyzes strategic incentives during bargaining—showing that parties may have incentives not to reveal or to misrepresent private information—so both diagnose different forms of opportunism that undermine simple theoretical accounts.

shared_topics.topic: bridging theory and empirical/case evidence to assess doctrinal claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the Johnson & Johnson v. Guidant takeover dispute and practitioner experience to test the relevance of theory, and Paper B surveys centuries of consequential‑damages cases and doctrinal practice to evaluate whether the information‑forcing/default theory aligns with actual contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: critiques of normative justifications for contract rules (promise‑keeping vs efficiency/Coasean claims)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates moral (promise‑keeping) and economic justifications for enforcing contractual interpretations, arguing they evaporate in complex settings; Paper B questions the Coasean/efficiency rationale for penalty/default rules like Hadley, arguing that normative efficiency claims rest on unrealistic assumptions about bargaining and disclosure.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.topic: the deal–text gap in complex commercial transactions

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques economic and moral justifications of contract law as rooted in simplified 'Dick and Jane' examples that do not explain real-world contracting, while Paper B argues that top‑down codification (e.g., UCC-style synthesis) and abstract models misread the transactional ecology of the construction industry and calls for a more realistic, bottom‑up approach.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that boilerplate clauses and poorly negotiated text create opportunities for adversarial reinterpretation and massive liability, and Paper B examines the widespread use of standard industry contract models in construction, their structural limits, and how they contribute to conflict and the need for reform.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering, industry practices, and non-judicial conflict-management as alternatives or complements to public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that the real check on opportunism is parties' motives and practices rather than doctrinal rules, and Paper B analyzes private ordering (industry norms, internal implementing structures, and conflict‑management mechanisms) as central to how construction transactions are governed, with public law functioning more as a safety net.

shared_topics.topic: practical reform strategies sensitive to transactional realities rather than doctrinal abstraction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A ends with constructive suggestions about using theory in lawyering to address lexical opportunism pragmatically, and Paper B develops an action strategy (including facilitated planning, possible codification calibrated to industry realities, and institutional reforms) aimed at realistic improvement of construction transactional law.

papers.node_id: 49akronlrev1!!ARTICLE: Liberty at the Borders of Private Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: Liberty at the Borders of Private Law
papers.abstract:
Most people place great value on their liberty. In fact, some would rather die than live without it.The quest for liberty has been one of the strongest currents in modern political and intellectual history and has been a driving force in the founding of the United States as well as economic and political developments in Europe and around the world.This Article takes the advancement of liberty seriously, both as an important part of American and European culture, history, and politicsand as an objective in the ongoing work of reforming and restructuring the law and legal systems across the globe. The examples focus on United States law,but the same issues and problems pervade other legal systems as well. The analysis does not presume that liberty is the only social value of importance, but it focuses on the relationship between law and liberty to put the connections between the two in the clearest light possible. The great advantage of focusing the analysis on liberty for its own sake is that the reader does not have to accept idiosyncratic value judgments. Almost everyone values liberty and cares about the ways in which the law may advance or impede it.
In spite of the importance that most people attach to liberty, it is not always clear what we mean when we refer to it. Scholars have debated the relative importance of different kinds of liberty and have drawn useful distinctions, for example, between the freedom from evils, such asphysical force or coercion exerted by others, and the freedom to act, such as the freedom to speak one's mind or worship the religion of one's choice.Nonetheless, there is no consensus about the freedoms that are essential to liberty, and so its meaning remains nebulous and elusive. To focus the analysis, therefore, liberty is defined to require 1) that individualsbe as free as possible from the exercise of coercionby others, including the State,except to the extent that they have truly and voluntarily assented to the coercion, and 2) that individuals have a sphere of personal autonomy and privacy within which they are free from intrusions by the State or others to think what they will, say what they want, associate with whomever they like, and be whoever they are.While the appropriate scope of autonomy and privacy rights may be debatable, few, if any, would dispute that they are integral to liberty.
There is a wide range of literature on the relationship between law and liberty, but most of it focuses specifically on the relationship between public law and liberty.Public law is usually defined as the branch of the law that addresses relationships between levels ofgovernment and relationships between governments and individuals.Scholars have no doubt focused on public law and liberty because there are so many important public law questions that bear on the liberties of individuals - for example, the powers of governments to regulate speech, engage in searches and seizures of persons and property incidental to an arrest, or to regulate the right to bear arms.
This Article, on the other hand, focuses on the relationship between private law and liberty. Private law is usually defined as the branch of law that addresses the relationships between individuals, rather than between individuals and their governments.There is already a significant amount of literature addressing the relationships between private law and liberty, but much of it focuses on the justifications for private law and the role of the government in facilitating and regulating private legal transactions.Most of it has very little to say about specific private law doctrines.In contrast, this Article explores the ways in which specific private law doctrines may advance or impede liberty.
One of the lynchpins in the analysis is the simple and noncontroversial observation that when courts enforce private legal rights they exercise the powers of State coercion against the parties subject to their enforcements.Courts' decisions about whether to enforce claims under private laws therefore have direct consequences for liberty. The courts thus play an important role in advancing liberty through their enforcement or non-enforcement of private legal claims under well-known contract and property doctrines. Unfortunately, there are some important ways in which courts may also undermine liberty through their enforcement or non-enforcement of some private legalclaims under some other well-known contract and property doctrines.
Another one of the lynchpins of the analysis is the equally simple and noncontroversial observation that corporate persons are created under state laws for the benefit of their owners and/or other interested parties and, presumably, for the good of society. Both for-profit and non-profit corporations enjoy rights and privileges under the law, including, for example, the right to sue and be sued, limited liability, and preferential tax treatment; they are, in that sense, State-sponsored entities.In return for the rights and privileges they enjoy, they are often subjected to restrictions and regulations that do not apply to natural persons - for example, a for-profit corporation may have reporting obligations under securities regulations and a non-profit corporation may not be allowed to participate in political campaigns. Although they are private legal entities, because of the rights and privileges they enjoy under state and federal law, the State is complicit whenever a corporation impinges upon the liberties of natural persons. In particular, the State is complicit whenever a corporation impinges upon an individual's liberty by intruding into her sphere of personal autonomy and privacy. The concern may be mitigated when the corporation is for-profit, subject to the discipline of the market, but it is exacerbated when the corporation is non-profit that receives significant tax exemptions as a public charity.
This Article argues that private laws are no less important to liberty than public laws and that if private laws are constructed and applied appropriately they will advance liberty, but if not, they may actually facilitate the exercise of coercion and, therefore, undermine liberty. To that end, this Article illustrates some of the ways in which certain well-known private law doctrines may advance liberty.But it also expresses concerns about the application of some other private law doctrines. One of the concerns lies in the fear that private laws may sometimes allow some individuals and corporations to use the courts, and implicitly, therefore, the power of State coercion, to impinge upon the liberty of other individuals. This concern is explicated using private land use restrictions as an example. Another concern is that private laws may allow corporations to use their rights and privileges to intrude into thespheres of personal autonomy and privacy that are essential to the liberty of natural persons. This concern is explicated using lifestyle covenants and morals clauses as an example.
Part II of this Article discusses the relationships between liberty, the State, and private law and elaborates on some of the presumptions of the analysis. Part III focuses on the relationships between liberty and specific property law doctrines. It uses examples from human rights, the first in time, first in right rule, findings and adverse possession, and eminent domain to illustrate some of the ways in which property doctrines may advance or undermine liberty, depending on whether the doctrines are appropriately constructed and applied. It also raises concerns about the ways in which property law may systematically undermine liberty, using courts' enforcements of some private land-use restrictions as an example. Part IV focuses on the relationships between liberty and specific contract law doctrines. It uses examples from the parol evidence rule, the unconscionability doctrine, and the impracticability doctrine to illustrate the ways in which contract doctrines may advance or undermine liberty, depending on whether the doctrines are appropriately constructed and applied. It also raises concerns about the ways in which contract law may systematically undermine liberty, using, as an example, the practices of some State-sponsored, non-profit corporations that use lifestyle covenants and morals clauses in their employment contracts to intrude into their employees' spheres of personal autonomy and privacy. Part V offers some conclusions.

questions.question: Whether courts' enforcement or non-enforcement of private legal claims increases or decreases individuals' liberty by enabling state coercion or by protecting personal autonomy and privacy.

Whether state-created legal privileges for corporate entities allow those entities to intrude into individuals' spheres of autonomy and privacy, making the State complicit in such intrusions and thereby affecting liberty.

Whether the structure and application of private law systematically advances individual liberty or instead facilitates private actors' use of the courts and state power to restrict others' behavior and autonomy.

papers.node_id: 51stanlrev1591!!ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults
papers.title: ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults
papers.abstract:
Recent theoretical analysis of contract default rules has devoted significant attention to the use of penalty default rules as a way to induce a contractor to reveal private information. Penalty default rules demonstrate how efficient rules cannot be derived by simply asking what most parties would have contracted for had they written a complete contract. Such "majoritarian" default rules derive from an implicit assumption about the reason why a particular contract is incomplete. A fuller efficiency analysis tries to understand the reasons why contracts are incomplete and how different default rules affect the efficiency of the contracting process and the contracts themselves. Our goal here is to show how an understanding of the underlying causes of contractual incompleteness informs the optimal choice of default rules.
Barry Adler's fine articlecorrectly identifies a new reason why it may be difficult to use "penalty" or "information-forcing" defaults to induce contractors to reveal private information about their personal attributes (what game-theorists tend to call their "type"). In an earlier article,we had shown that, when one side to a contract has private information and the other side has market power, the privately informed party may be reluctant to contract around a penalty default (and thereby reveal information) if doing so would allow the other side to extract more of the gains from trade.But Adler has shown that even when the private information and the market power are on the same side of the contract - as when a privately informed buyer contracts in a market with competitive sellers - the privately informed party may still be reluctant to contract around a penalty default.In our earlier model, theinformed buyer was reluctant to contract around the penalty defaults because doing so would subject her to a supracompetitive price; in Adler's model, the informed party is reluctant to contract around penalty defaults because doing so would destroy the subsidized pricing that the privately informed party receives by hiding out in the undifferentiated pool.
Adler should be credited for identifying this additional reason why privately informed parties may be reluctant to contract around default rules. But showing that it may be harder to induce information revelation with a particular type of penalty default is not an argument in favor of setting "hypothetical" or "majoritarian" defaults. Efficiency gap filling should grow out of one's substantive theory of why particular contracts are incomplete. Adler's insight actually strengthens an implication of our earlier articles: The effect of a particular default rule on information revelation, and thus on efficiency, depends on numerous characteristics of the contracting environment that are independent of the "hypothetical contracting" inquiry - that is, merely assessing what the parties would have contracted for if there were no private information. Other factors, including the distribution of types, the magnitude of transaction costs, and the distribution of bargaining power, will all affect the likelihood that a particular penalty default will induce separation and enhance efficiency. Adler adds another factor to this list - the possibility that revealing information might eliminate an informed party's subsidy from pooling. Even these results underestimate the problem of predicting outcomes since they were derived in overly simplistic and unrealistic models of contract negotiations whose purpose was merely to show the possibility that penalty defaults could be efficient.
Majoritarian theories of default choice are implicitly derived from a transaction cost based theory of incomplete contracts. But when contracts are strategically incomplete because of one side's private information, then there is no reason to think that majoritarian or hypothetical default setting will conduce to efficiency. When transaction costs are low and contracts are incomplete because of private information, the potential welfare losses from choosing an inefficient default are largely independent of transaction costs and, as we have previously shown, can dwarf the mere out-of-pocket costs of contracting around.
The normative implication of Adler's analysis is not that policymakers should reflexively retreat to majoritarian defaults, but instead the message is that "life is hard." When contracts are incomplete because of a contractor's private information about her "type," it will be difficult for efficiency-minded lawmakers to identify the efficient default.Penalty defaults at timeswill still be efficient,but Adler shows there is a narrower range of circumstances where information-forcing rules will produce efficient separation making it difficult for lawmakers to determine when they will be effective.
Adler's analysis, however, is only about one type of minoritarian rule - a penalty default set to cause information about contractor's type.In this comment, we develop a simple model that identifies four other rationales for minoritarian rules based on

questions.question: Whether and under what conditions penalty (information-forcing) default rules improve contracting efficiency by inducing parties with private information to reveal their type, compared with setting defaults based on what most parties would have chosen (majoritarian defaults).

How the underlying reasons for contractual incompleteness (e.g., private information, transaction costs, market power, pooling/subsidies) and features of the contracting environment (distribution of types, bargaining power, magnitude of transaction costs) affect the optimal choice of default rules and the welfare consequences of those defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: how the reasons contracts are incomplete should guide default-rule choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theoretical argument that the optimal choice between majoritarian and minoritarian (including penalty) defaults depends on why contracts are incomplete (private information, transaction costs, etc.), while Paper B empirically examines why parties often leave terms unresolved in exchange-of-forms sales and how that reality bears on how section 2-207 and gap-fillers should operate.

shared_topics.topic: the role and effects of statutory or judicial gap-fillers/default terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different default rules (majoritarian, penalty/minoritarian) affect efficiency and information revelation, and Paper B focuses on the U.C.C. gap-fillers under section 2-207, how they become the fallback terms in battles of the forms, and practitioners' views about relying on those defaults.

shared_topics.topic: strategic behavior around disclosure and form-exchange tactics (separation/pooling, 'magic language', last-shot dynamics)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how defaults can induce or deter information revelation (separating vs pooling equilibria) and how parties respond strategically to penalty defaults, while Paper B documents firms' strategic drafting and use of conditional acceptance language, last-shot/mirror-image dynamics, and the common practice of not reading opposing boilerplate.

shared_topics.topic: how transaction costs and bargaining power shape whether parties negotiate or accept defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that transaction costs and the distribution of bargaining power alter the welfare consequences of default choices and the feasibility of contracting around defaults, and Paper B reports that negotiation costs, deal size, technological factors, and market power (e.g., mega-retailers) determine when parties accept form-exchange outcomes versus negotiating terms.

shared_topics.topic: normative and doctrinal implications for reforming default rules and statutory design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications about the limits of one-size-fits-all (majoritarian) defaults and cautions policymakers about contexts where penalty defaults may or may not work, while Paper B provides empirical input and practitioner preferences aimed at guiding Article 2/section 2-207 reform and simplification of default doctrines.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how contracts cope with incompleteness and uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that relational (intentionally relational) contracts offer a flexible governance mechanism that lets parties determine key terms through ongoing interaction to cope with project uncertainty, while Paper B analyzes why contracts are incomplete (transaction costs, private information) and how default rules (majoritarian or penalty) should be chosen to fill those gaps efficiently.

shared_topics.topic: the role of incentives and information asymmetry in shaping contractual form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes designing contractual regimes and relational norms (reciprocity, deterrence of opportunism) to align incentives in highly interdependent, technology-enabled collaborations, and Paper B studies how default rules create incentives (or fail to) for parties to reveal private information and avoid opportunistic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: static written terms versus dynamic, relationship-based governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts conventional, discrete contracts that try to pre-specify contingencies with relational contracts that evolve through performance, while Paper B contrasts hypothetical/majoritarian default-setting (which presumes a static bargain) with minoritarian/penalty defaults that interact with dynamic bargaining incentives and strategic incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: how bargaining power and asymmetric positions affect optimal contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses industry examples (e.g., Pixar–Disney, suppliers–manufacturers) to show how power asymmetries and evolving relationships shape the move toward relational arrangements, and Paper B explicitly shows that the distribution of bargaining power and type distributions influence whether penalty or majoritarian defaults will induce efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that modern contract law selects for reciprocal, bargained-for exchanges and shared forward-looking commitments because enforcing those commitments facilitates complex joint projects, while Paper B treats default rules as a mechanism that determines which terms (and thus which bargains) survive in incomplete contracts and shows how those rules affect the kinds of transactions that are effectively enforced and the resulting welfare.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages doctrinally with the enforcement of purely executory promises and the rejection of nominal consideration as part of the evolution of consideration doctrine, while Paper B builds a theory of why contracts are incomplete (transaction costs, private information, strategic incompleteness) and analyzes how default rules should respond to those reasons.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' motivations, information, or types in shaping enforceability and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers a debate over whether enforcement should track promisor motivation (reciprocal inducement) versus remuneration, and Paper B models how private information and parties' incentives to hide or reveal their type influence whether penalty or majoritarian defaults will induce efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for designing contract doctrine (efficiency versus protecting relationships or distributional effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a normative account that contrasts enforcing commercially valuable shared commitments with exempting intimate or social agreements from enforcement, whereas Paper B assesses the normative consequences of majoritarian versus minoritarian/penalty defaults through an efficiency lens and highlights distributional and informational reasons why particular defaults may be preferable or problematic.

papers.title: Article: MARK(ET)ING NONDISCRIMINATION: PRIVATIZING ENDA WITH A CERTIFICATION MARK
papers.abstract:
People in the United States strongly support the simple idea that employers should not discriminate against gays and lesbians. In a 2003 Gallup poll, eighty-eight percent of respondents said that "homosexuals should … have equal rights in terms of job opportunities."Even prominent social conservatives - such as George W. Bush - give lip service to the idea that employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is wrong.
But gay rights advocates have achieved only modest legal reform on this issue. Seventeen states have prohibited employment discrimination against gays and lesbians.A seemingly modest bill, the Employment Non-Discrimination Act (ENDA), which only prohibits disparate treatment on the basis of sexual orientation, has been introduced several times in Congress, always without success.ENDA has little chance of passing during the Bush administration unless midterm elections in 2006 radically change the face of Congress.Civil rights advocates may even abandon ENDA andinstead promote a broader, omnibus civil rights improvement act, in which employment rights for gays would presumably play a part.
This Article attempts to extend ENDA rights to individual employees by another means. The certification mark, a little-known piece of intellectual property, provides a mechanism for employers to commit to the exact substantive duties of ENDA. We have created a symbol, an FE inside a circle, that we call the "Fair Employment" mark.

questions.question: Whether and how a certification mark can serve as a private-law mechanism for employers to commit to and be held to nondiscrimination obligations regarding sexual orientation.
Whether use of a certification mark would effectively change employer behavior and deter discriminatory hiring, firing, or promotion practices compared with relying on public statutory protections.

Whether the market-consumers, employees, and other stakeholders-would recognize, value, and enforce a 'fair employment' certification mark as a credible signal of nondiscriminatory employment practices.
