papers.node_id: 108columlrev1610!!ARTICLE: MARKET DAMAGES, EFFICIENT CONTRACTING, AND THE ECONOMIC WASTE FALLACY
papers.title: ARTICLE: MARKET DAMAGES, EFFICIENT CONTRACTING, AND THE ECONOMIC WASTE FALLACY
papers.abstract:
Contract theory identifies three central goals that the law should pursue in facilitating efficient contracting. Initially, the law should maximize the probability that parties will contract when contracting would create gains in excess of costs. For example, when parties contract to perform services, the buyer expects to earn the difference between the value he will realize from performance and the contract price, and the seller expects to earn the difference between the price and her costs.Protecting these expectations at the contracting stage maximizes the probability that the parties will contract when each of their gains exceeds contracting costs. Thereafter, the law should create an incentive for the parties to invest in the relationship in order to maximize the joint expected surplus. Here, the law should select a damage measure that does not induce the buyer to invest excessively in reliance in order to increase his litigation return. Finally, the law should create an incentive for the parties to tradewhen the buyer values performance in excess of the seller's costs.To achieve these goals, contract law commonly selects the "market damage" measure whenever there is a market for substitutes. This measure specifies damages as the difference between the market price for goods or services at the time of breach and the contract price. In certain service contexts, however, courts believe that full market damages would overcompensate the buyer. Courts equate overcompensation with "economic waste" and reduce the buyer's damages accordingly. This Article argues that market damages are always the preferable damage measure when a market for substitutes exists, even in circumstances where courts today believe that these damages would constitute economic waste.
It is tempting to argue that direct measures of the buyer's expectation are preferable to market damages because these measures precisely implement the law's goal. Thus, for example, direct expectation damages award the buyer the exact difference between his value and the contract price. Direct damage measures have two undesirable properties, however. First, it is often difficult to verify the value that a buyer would have realized had the seller performed.Courts cannot award direct expectation damages when they cannot measure the expectation. Second, direct expectation damages protect the buyer's expectation given the investment the buyer made in the contract. As a consequence, they create an incentive for the buyer to invest excessively when, as is often the case, the seller cannot observe the buyer's reliance actions.These two difficulties create incentives for parties to contract out of direct expectation damages; and indeed, consequential damage exclusions are ubiquitous.
The difficulties with direct expectation damages may be avoided by protecting the buyer's expectation with specific performance. This remedy gives the buyer what he expects at the price he agreed to pay. Specific performance also makes low informational demands on the trier of fact because she need not recover the buyer's valuation.Specific performance,however, also has two undesirable properties. First, circumstances may change materially between the time of contracting and the time of performance. If the parties at performance time are not symmetrically informed about values and costs, they may be unable to agree on a modification of their contract that directs the efficient outcome. If renegotiation fails, a court may compel the seller to perform under the original, inefficient contract.Second, and of greater significance, specific performance requires a court order and is discretionary.Court orders commonly take a long time to obtain and, when granted, may require the court to police performance by the seller. Specific performance thus is not a realistic option for buyers who require either a prompt or a difficult-to-supervise performance.Since many buyers prefer prompt performance or prefer not to deal with reluctant sellers, specific performance is sought no more frequently in jurisdictions where the remedy is available as of right than it is sought in the United States, where the remedy is discretionary with the court.
Market damages protect the buyer's expectation interest indirectly, but without the undesirable properties that accompany the other remedies.A buyer who purchases a substitute for the breaching seller's performance and then recovers as damages the difference between the price he paid and the contract price obtains the performance he wanted at the contract price. Market damages also make relatively low information demands on the trier of fact. A court must know only the contract price and the cover or repurchase price, both of which are commonly verifiable. The seller also knows these values. Hence, under market damages she can make an efficient decision regarding whether or not to perform. In addition, market damages do not require courts to supervise complex performances, nor do they confront buyers with the difficult choice either of waiting too long for a remedy or of having no remedy at all (when their valuations are unverifiable). The buyer can purchase a substitute performance promptly and recover from the seller later. Finally, market damages do not create moral hazard: The buyer cannot increase his legal award by the reliance actions he takes after the contract is made.As real world evidence of these virtues, parties seldom contract out of the market damages rule when they can purchase substitute performances.
Market damages, however, are widely believed to have a serious defect when the seller is providing a service. In service cases, buyers commonly sue for the "cost of completion" - the cost of purchasing a substitute performance in the market. But sometimes the cost of completion greatly exceeds the gain in the market value of the buyer's property that the seller's performance would have produced. Since other sellers will have similar costs to those of the contract seller, awarding cost-of-completion damages in these cases was once thought to subsidize "economic waste."The buyer could use the damages to purchase a performance whose cost greatly exceeded its value. This putative danger is primarily present in construction contexts.In a typical case, such as Jacob &Youngs, Inc. v. Kent,a contractor has deviated from the agreed upon performance in an apparently minor way, but the costs of remedying that defect would be much higher than the reduction in property value that the deviation produces. Alternatively, in cases such as Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.,a lessee has agreed to restore the lessor's property after the lessee has used it, but the costs of restoration turn out to be much higher than the increase in property value that restoration would have created. Courts commonly reject market damages in these cases in favor of awarding the buyer the "market delta" - the difference between the market value of the buyer's property had the seller performed and the property's actual market value.
The economic waste rationale for awarding market delta damages is unsatisfactory, however, because a rational buyer will not use the cost-of-completion damage award to purchase a performance that is worth less to him than its price. The buyer will spend the legal award, but he will not waste it.Modern courts realize that buyers will not use the money toundertake repairs that require substantial and inefficient demolition or that have little economic benefit, but they continue to reject damages measured by the ex post market price of the contract performance.Since the cost-of-completion award is meant to enable the buyer to purchase a substitute, and since the buyer will purchase something else, the contemporary rationale holds that cost-of-completion damages would only redistribute wealth from sellers to buyers.Thus, modern courts restrict buyers to the market delta in order to avoid a "windfall."
The consequences of denying market damages in these contexts have been poorly understood, however. The desirability of awarding these damages whenever the buyer can purchase a substitute performance on the market becomes clear only when those consequences are exposed. Our analysis of the choice between a market delta award and full market damages supports the following claims. First, restricting buyers to the market delta misallocates resources. When a party contracts, she can sue her partner if he breaches but is similarly exposed to liability if she breaches. Under market damages, these effects exactly offset, so that parties make contracts when their expected gain exceeds contracting costs. The market delta measure, however, distorts the parties' incentives to contract. The measure functions as a subsidy to sellers by reducing the damages for which a breaching seller would otherwise be liable. Sellers pay less than full market damages when they breach but recover full market damages when buyers breach. As a consequence, sellers realize positive expected profits: They expect to gain more when they perform than they expect to lose when they fail to perform. The market delta measure also functions as a tax on buyers, who are liable for full damages when they breach but cannot collect full damages when the seller breaches.The subsidy encourages new sellers to enter the market to compete the excess profits away while the tax discourages buyers from entering because they may incur losses in expectation. The tax and subsidy effects do not exactly offset, however. Hence, the market delta rule distorts both seller and buyer decisions to enter the market. We show below that the subsidy effect is more significant than the tax effect, so that the market will have an inefficiently large number of firms in equilibrium.
Although the market delta damage measure misallocates resources, some courts may believe nonetheless that the more important concern is distributional. It appears unjust to impose a large windfall loss on the seller, which is the apparent result of awarding cost-of-completion damages when they greatly exceed the market delta.This concern prompts our second claim: The seller's windfall loss is smaller than is generally realized in the common case where the buyer prepays for the contract service. A buyer who has prepaid is entitled both to restitution of the price paid for the service and to damages for the breach of contract.Cost-of-completion damages incorporate this restitutionary component. The cost of completion is the ex post market price for the contract service. This price, in turn, is the sum of (a) the ex ante market price and (b) the difference, if any, between the ex post market price and the ex ante market price.Hence, if the initial contract and the replacement contract were both made at current market prices, awarding the buyer the cost of completion satisfies both his restitutionary claim to recover the price and his expectation interest claim for market damages. Sincethe buyer has an independent right to restitution when the seller takes the money but fails to perform the contract service, courts that wish to avoid windfall losses should compare the market delta not to the full cost of completion but only to the market damages portion. The difference between market damages and the market delta necessarily is smaller than the difference between full cost-of-completion damages and the market delta. Since prepayment is common, an implication of our second claim is that courts that prefer the market delta measure should still award market damages in more cases than they now do.
Courts and most commentators have overlooked this implication because they have not recognized that buyers prepay for the services that commonly appear in the cases.This omission probably occurs because the services are bundled together and are not separately priced. As an example, the royalty on a mineral lease is smaller if the lessee agrees to restore the land after mining, but there seldom is an explicit "subprice" for restoration.The cost of constructing a building seldom is disaggregated into separate prices for the promise to install the plumbing and the promise to correct defective work. But to deny that the buyer in such cases has prepaid is to assert, implausibly, that the mining lessee had agreed to restore for nothing or that the contractor did not charge for the service of correcting nonconforming plumbing.
The bundling problem would sometimes make it infeasible for a court to retain the economic waste rule but apply it only when the market delta is well below the market damages component. This version of the economic waste rule is hard to implement in the prepayment case becausethe court must disaggregate a cost-of-completion award into its constituent elements of restitution (i.e., the ex ante contract price of the service) and market damages.If the contract has one price for a bundled set of tasks (i.e., mining plus restoration), identifying which portion of the price is for the service at issue can be difficult. A court's realistic choices will often reduce either to continuing the current practice of comparing the full cost of completion to the market delta or to awarding cost-of-completion damages in all cases.
Despite the fact that current practice vitiates the buyer's right to restitution, a court concerned with avoiding large windfall losses may still be more willing to apply the market delta rule in the prepayment case. This is because windfall losses are larger when the buyer prepays. Parties bundle services such as construction or restoration because the original seller is the lowest-cost provider (e.g., a mining lessee may more cheaply restore than a stranger to the already-mined property). Because bundling is efficient, the contract price for a bundled service is less than the price for that service if it were purchased separately: The lower the contract price, the larger are market damages and the larger is the gap between these damages and the market delta.
This analysis leads to our third claim: The market delta rule creates two additional inefficiencies when buyers prepay. First, the tax that the market delta rule imposes on buyers becomes large when sellers can retain prepayments but not perform the contract service satisfactorily. In this circumstance, many buyers would expect to lose money. These buyers will avoid contracting for the service in its efficient bundled form in favor of contracting for the service separately at a higher price. Second, restricting buyers to the market delta in the prepayment case creates a moral hazard. The market delta rule is applied against buyers who sue for money damages but will not cover because the cost of purchasing the service after the seller has completed her other tasks exceeds its value. Sellers, however, sometimes can reduce the cost of performing the contract service below the buyer's value by taking precautions in the interim between the time of contract and the time when the seller is to complete the entire performance. But a prepaid seller's incentive to invest efficiently in cost reduction is materially reduced if her damage exposure for failing to invest is capped by the market delta. Cost-of-completion damages in these cases thus function as an efficient deterrent against this moral hazard.
Finally, parties contract in market contexts when material movements in market prices would otherwise disrupt their plans. Market damages eliminate the disruption risk because they insure parties against price movements. We show that market damages uniquely induce parties to contract when contracting costs are less than the disruption that a contract can avoid. Our initial three claims demonstrate the superiority of market damages at protecting the expectation interest of parties who make contracts. Our final claim holds that parties will make ex ante efficient contracts if they expect always to receive market damages when their promisors breach.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part I examines a sample of cases concerning the award of damages for a seller's breach in order to recover the law in action under the economic waste doctrine. When the cost of completion significantly exceeds the market delta, most contemporary courts apply the economic waste rule and limit the buyer to the diminution in market value. This Part also shows that, in effect if not in law, the market delta measure is a mandatory rule. Part II shows that awarding market damages to sellers but selectively denying them to buyers misallocates resources, that market damages cannot adversely affect investment incentives, and that protecting the expectation interest with market damages uniquely maximizes the probability that parties will make efficient contracts. In Part III, we develop the additional inefficiencies that the market delta rule produces when buyers prepay. Part IV applies the prior arguments to show that cost-of-completion damages should be the universal default regardless of the extent to which this award would exceed the market delta. In the conclusion, we generalize the analysis by commenting briefly on the courts' regrettable tendency to enact mandatory rules that displace standard commercial practice.
. Recovering the Law on Buyers' Damages in Service Contracts

papers.node_id: 46sandiegolrev595!!Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment
papers.title: Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment
papers.abstract:
As the title of this Article suggests, I will argue that Dick Speidel may have been correct in asserting that court adjustment makes sense in limited circumstances. But years ago, I allied myself with Speidel and I will only briefly review my reasons why here.My main goal in this Article is to argue that nothing courts have decided or writers have analyzed since Aluminum Co. of America v. Essex Group, Inc. (ALCOA), a somewhat infamous case in which the court adjusted a long-term contract, proves that court adjustment is always wrongheaded. In fact, as with so many policy issues, we may never identify the best judicial approach to disrupted long-term contracts because resolution depends on too many variables and unknowns.So Speidel may have been right. Of course, he also may have been wrong.
will focus on recent literature and cases to enumerate the unresolved questions about court adjustment. Part II briefly reviews Speidel's approach to court adjustment. Part III outlines the judicial and scholarly reaction to court adjustment, focusing on the more recent treatments. Part IV claims that too many questions remain unanswered to know whether Speidel was right or wrong.

questions.question: Whether courts should modify long-term contracts when unforeseen events disrupt performance (i.e., whether judicial modification is an appropriate remedy versus alternatives).
Whether judicial modification of long-term contracts produces better economic or social outcomes than leaving parties to damages, termination, or private renegotiation.
Under what factual, economic, or institutional conditions judicial modification of long-term contracts is likely to be beneficial versus harmful.

papers.node_id: 116pennstlrev987!!Article: Metaphors, Models, and Meaning in Contract Law
papers.title: Article: Metaphors, Models, and Meaning in Contract Law
papers.abstract:
There is probably no better example of the frustrating gap between academic law and the practice than the indoctrination first-year students receive in contract law. Although the casebooks vary in their approaches, by early December, the typical student has been bamboozled by elements of doctrine that experienced practitioners know almost never come up. The practitioner might ask why we study consideration and offer-and-acceptance when those are rarely issues in the real world. Indeed, it is a fair observation that only a tiny portion of the first-year contracts course involves the issue of contract interpretation. Yet practitioners know that the real world of contracts is almost exclusively about negotiating and writing documents and perhaps interpreting them later (whether or not they get litigated), and almost never about the vast majority of doctrinal issues - consideration, offer and acceptance, defenses, impossibility - covered by the course.
The classical scholars who sought to organize the study of contract law scientifically over one hundred years ago created a powerful theoretical paradigm that lives on in the traditional first year contract law course.There is nothing either unusual or wrong with powerful theoretical paradigms; raw experience only becomes meaningful and useful when minds process it.The downside of these paradigms of legal theory and pedagogy, however, is the power to channel thought in what Elizabeth Mertz describes as "language forms."The focus on the formsof argumentation as the core of pedagogy "creates a closed linguistic system that is capable of devouring all manner of social detail, but without budging in its core assumptions."These language forms and the classification system designed to make sense of them were immensely powerful,developed by those working inside the legal institutionand based upon legal propositions developed through the lens of after-the-fact litigation.
Above all, the categories and classifications of legal propositions within the system were contingent, reflecting the minds of the brilliant theorists who shaped the modern contracts curriculum more than any necessary reason the propositions needed to be organized in the categories they created.For example, my contracts class reads Judge Skelly Wright's landmark 1965 opinion in Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture Co.,in which the court deemed a cumulative financing scheme directed at low-income buyers to be unconscionable and unenforceable. A student asked whether Batsakis v. Demotsis,which we had studied earlier, was relevant to the discussion. In Batsakis, a case decided sixteen years prior to Williams, the court declined to inquire into the unfairness of the consideration, even though it was clear that the contract was grossly unfair and the result of wartime profiteering. Why, asked the student, had Batsakis not been considered as an "unconscionability" case? The student's observation was profound: there was no logical reason that the lawyers could not have arguedunconscionability in Batsakis, but either they did not or the court declined to consider it. Nonetheless, Batsakis regularly appears in casebook chapters on consideration because the basis of the decision is a legal proposition about consideration, even though the sense of unfairness that caused the litigation is equally relevant to legal propositions about unconscionability.
A closed system of language and classification is another way of expressing what legal sociologist Gunther Teubner calls law's "epistemic trap."Law as a social institution develops its own models and constructs of reality. Its "cognitive operations … construct idiosyncratic images of reality and move them away from the world constructions of everyday life and from those of scientific discourse."This is particularly true in contract law. Much of the standard pedagogy is the presentation of classical formalism as the straw man to be knocked down by the theoretical responses that developed over the course of the 20th century.Those alternative conceptions of the law did not eliminate the trap; even Legal Realism is still legal in the sense that it is a vision from within the community of lawyers about how its closed linguistic system should best reflect the outside world.
The epistemic trap is particularly pronounced in the law of contracts (and hence in the first-year contracts class) because the subject matter demands dealing with legal truth in an exceptional way and applies particular conceptual structures to arrive at such truth. As in all other areas of the law, theorists and students need to come to terms with what makes legal propositions true or correct as applied in particular cases. That process is not markedly different in litigation over contracts and property on one hand, versus, say, torts or criminal law on the other. Indeed, to the extent that the coherence of the propositions is an indication of their truth or correctness, as Karl Llewellyn observed eighty years ago, the work of a lawyer or judge in determining the law in the case method proceeds on the assumption "that all the cases everywhere can stand together. It is unquestionably the assumption you must make, at first. If they can be brought together, you must bring them."
Contract law demands not just truth as normative coherence - a system of rules that do not contradict one another - but also truth as descriptive correspondence to the independent reality that was the underlying transaction.The received wisdom among most academic theorists and "lawyers' lawyers" is that rational actors will shape their voluntary agreements before the fact in light of their expectation of how the system will resolve disputes after the fact. The body of contract law propositions thus provides a default reconstruction of the entire transactional lifecycle, but it does so only through the lens of the after-the-fact adjudication that sets the normative rules. The theoretical debates in contract law over the last one hundred years have revolved around the relationship of after-the-fact normativity to before-the-fact description. Ironically, the most vigorous modern academic defense of classical contract law formalism comes from contract theorists using rational actor welfare economics to posit an ideal (but admittedly unachievable) "complete contract"that wholly eliminates thepossibility of opportunismamong otherwise "boundedly rational" contracting parties.The modern defense of the contending school of legal realism in contract law is no less rational in the effort to reconstruct what the parties supposedly intended (maximizing their joint economic surplus) from the totality of the circumstances, including the formal document they created.
In either case, the prevailing (and powerful) metaphor for the contract is either as a model of the ideal transaction or some notional "meeting of the minds." Is that metaphor appropriate? My answer is: often yes, but perhaps not as often as the "rationalists" of contract law would like to think.Does the contract "map" either the ideal or the actuality of a transaction? Sometimes it does map, particularly in the provisions that are constitutive of the deal structure itself, like the price, the structure of merger or stock transfer, or the mechanics of the post-closing adjustment in acquisition agreements. Sometimes it does not map, as in the provisions negotiated in the wee hours of the morning, allocating the perceived risk of some remote contingency that seems to loom heavily and which requires some agreement to satisfy the parties, even if they are not quite sure what the agreement means. Sometimes it does map the transaction, in the price and description on the front side of the break-apart triplicate form; sometimes it does not map it, as in most of the boilerplate (even between sophisticated purchasers and sellers) on the back. Moreover, the rational conception of a contract as a check onafter-the-fact opportunism is one more honored in academic theory than in practice. Why do law-and-economics scholars insist that contracts are a necessary safeguard against opportunism (which would otherwise reduce the incentive to invest)when clients regularly ask their lawyers how to "break" a contract, and lawyers manage regularly to come up with an interpretation of the language and events colorable enough to take a good swing at it?
The million-dollar question is: just what are the litigating parties and courts reconstructing? The usual dialectics in contract theory - formalism versus realism, textualism versus contextualism, moral versus welfare-based theoretical justifications, and so on - arise out of the same metaphoric image of contracts as rationally created models of before-the-fact inter-subjective events and understandings from which models after-the-fact observers ought to be able to reconstruct some version of the before-the-fact transaction. I want to challenge how we think about theoretical and doctrinal classifications in contract law, and I want to propose alternative metaphors to deal with the after-the-fact litigation reconstructions and the before-the-fact transactional realities.
Part I provides a brief primer on the metaphor theory I use throughout this analysis, particularly the concept of physical analogs in which categories are metaphoric containers, ideas are metaphoric objects, and the transactional lifecycle is a journey. The lesson to be taken from Part I is that metaphoric thinking is pre-logical and pre-propositional; it is the best explanation of the source of the "aha" moment of inspiration or understanding in which we hypothesize the possibility of an answer. In law, it is the essence of issue spotting - a metaphoric leap that precedes the articulation of a result by way of legal propositions.
In Part II, I propose escaping the epistemic trap of legal propositions and classifications by confronting the standard approaches to contract theory and doctrine, almost all of which employ the "contract as rational model of the transaction" metaphor. The alternative metaphor is of a journey that begins with wholly internal and subjective wants of individual parties. The parties engage in inter-subjective transactions that have objective manifestations. Sometimes those manifestations include objectified documentation of the parties' inter-subjective transactions: the contract, which is the object or thing that the parties have created. Sometimes an arbiter must resolve a dispute arisingbetween the parties because they do not agree about the consequences of their inter-subjective transaction or the objective document they created.
Part II also addresses an implication of the alternative metaphor. Seen as a part of the entire transactional lifecycle, the traditional debates in contract theory - whether courts adopt Langdellian textualism or Corbinian contextualism, or justify their after-the-fact adjudication of contract disputes on moral or efficiency grounds - are of less consequence than one would think. The metaphor of "contract as linguistic model" suggests not only coherent legal truth in the adjudicative process, but correspondent truth as well; that the mutual intention of the parties is something discoverable as though we were scientists seeking explanations of the physical world. That is an overstatement. The point of seeing the transactional lifecycle as a process or journey from individual and subjective desires to a written document is to understand that the objectification is an end in itself. Each observer of or participant in the transactional lifecycle has a stake in the outcome and a view from somewhere. The metaphor of process or journey allows theorists and students to take account of those divergent incentives and perspectives for both the before-the-fact transaction and the after-the-fact dispute resolution.
Part III addresses the use of pre-propositional metaphors as the source of intuitive judgments among competing algorithms of contract law. If the language of the law in doctrinal analysis creates the epistemic trap, then we break free of the trap when we identify the conceptual frames, models, and metaphors with which the participants in and observers of the transactional journey perceive and make use of the rules. The metaphoric approach to cognition suggests that our ability to perceive concepts, categories, and classifications, and thus to judge whether a particular circumstance fits within a general rule, precedes the ability to express the reasons for that judgment. The participants and observers in the contract dispute resolution process apply the language of legal reasoning in a motivated way, framed by prototypes within competing concepts and categories. Legal argument about whether a promise is enforceable as a contract, for example, occurs by way of the application of propositions setting forth conditions of enforceability, such as the definiteness of the promise, the existence of consideration or reliance, and so on. Here too the rule-based argument is the tail of the dog; what precedes it are competing prototypical images of a gift and an arm's-length negotiated bargain. The real question is the extent to whichthose prototypes exert a metaphoric pull on the facts of the case under adjudication.

questions.question: Whether and how the dominant metaphor of contracts as rational, model-like representations of pre-transactional intent shapes doctrinal classification, pedagogy, and the reconstruction of disputes in contract adjudication.

Whether conceptualizing contracting as a transactional journey from subjective desires to an objectified document offers a more accurate or useful framework for interpreting contracts and resolving post-transaction disputes.

To what extent pre-propositional metaphors and prototypical images (mental models) held by judges, lawyers, and parties drive intuitive judgments and legal reasoning in contract interpretation, compared with explicit, rule-based argumentation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the epistemic project of adjudication—asking whether courts can or should reconstruct a parties' ‘meeting of the minds’ and how doctrinal categories map (or fail to map) the transactional reality; Paper B frames the same issue methodologically, asking when courts should supply terms or liability rules because parties did not or could not complete a bargain and what reconstructed or court-supplied terms would accomplish.

shared_topics.topic: methodological debates over judicial intervention versus deference to parties (textualism/formalism vs contextualism/hypothetical bargain/new formalists)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the rival paradigms (formalism, realism, textualism, contextualism) as competing metaphoric and doctrinal frameworks that channel legal reasoning; Paper B directly evaluates competing methodological approaches—hypothetical bargain proponents versus new formalists—about when courts should intervene to fill incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of theoretical models and metaphors/frameworks on doctrinal outcomes and decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that metaphors and cognitive frames (contract as model vs contract as journey) prefigure issue-spotting and doctrinal application; Paper B deploys and critiques conceptual models (e.g., hypothetical bargain, information-based models, behavioral uncertainty) to justify or oppose different forms of court-supplied terms, showing how model choice shapes intervention rules.

shared_topics.topic: uncertainty, bounded rationality, and opportunism as limits on contract completeness and as drivers of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses boundedly rational actors and the limits of the ‘complete contract’ metaphor used in law-and-economics defenses of formalism; Paper B develops a behavioral-uncertainty account focused on opportunism and sunk costs to explain why parties fail to craft complete contingent contracts and when law should step in.

shared_topics.topic: welfare-oriented instrumental justifications for supplying or refraining from supplying contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights law-and-economics justifications (efficiency, preventing opportunism) as central modern defenses of contract formalism and questions their fit with practice; Paper B explicitly assesses whether court intervention increases gains from trade and social welfare, weighing instrumental benefits against institutional and informational costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75molrev493!!Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract Law, Party Sophistication and the New Formalism

shared_topics.topic: theoretical divide between formalism and realism in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the continuing debate between formalist and realist approaches: Paper A critiques century-old classical formalism and later realist responses as competing metaphoric frameworks for understanding contracts, while Paper B diagnoses a contemporary 'new formalism' and situates party sophistication as the mechanism courts use to reconcile formalist literalism with residual realist concerns.

shared_topics.topic: how courts reconstruct parties' intentions and the meaning of contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine post‑hoc reconstruction of agreements — Paper A by questioning whether adjudicators can or should reconstruct a 'before‑the‑fact' transaction from documents and events, and Paper B by showing that courts treat sophistication as a proxy for whether parties' stated terms should be taken at face value when inferring intent.

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism as competing interpretive methods
shared_topics.justification: Each article engages the textualism/contextualism divide: Paper A explicitly contrasts Langdellian textualism and Corbinian contextualism and attributes those choices to underlying metaphors, while Paper B demonstrates that new formalist courts prefer literal content for 'sophisticated' parties and retain contextual inquiry for others.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between before‑the‑fact bargaining and after‑the‑fact adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Both papers foreground lifecycle dynamics of contracting: Paper A frames contracting as a journey from subjective wants to objectified documents and criticizes reliance on after‑the‑fact norms to explain beforehand behavior, and Paper B emphasizes how ex post doctrines (and labels like sophistication) affect parties' ex ante expectations, certainty, and predictability.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of party attributes (information, resources, sophistication) for doctrinal treatment
shared_topics.justification: Each article treats party characteristics as doctrinally consequential: Paper A discusses divergent incentives, boilerplate use, and differences between sophisticated and unsophisticated actors as shaping whether the contract 'maps' the transaction, while Paper B centers on defining 'sophistication' and argues courts must assess information and resource asymmetries when choosing interpretive and remedial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90umkclrev253!!ARTICLE: FORMALISM VERSUS ANTI-FORMALISM IN CONTRACT LAW: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FORMALISM VERSUS ANTI-FORMALISM IN CONTRACT LAW: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY

shared_topics.topic: textualism/formalism versus contextualism/anti-formalism in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the long-standing doctrinal debate between formalist/textualist and realist/contextualist approaches as competing metaphoric and epistemic frameworks for understanding contracts, while Paper B directly pits formalistic and anti-formalistic theories against one another and empirically examines which approach governs term-identification in commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of written versus extrinsic evidence in identifying contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the assumption that contracts reliably 'map' transactions and questions over-reliance on after-the-fact textual reconstruction, and Paper B operationalizes that tension by contrasting reliance on written communications with consideration of non-written (oral or behavioral) evidence in identifying contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between before-the-fact transactional/drafting practices and after-the-fact adjudicative reconstruction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the transactional lifecycle—negotiation, drafting, objectification, and later dispute resolution—and how different metaphors affect reconstruction, while Paper B studies how market drafting choices (and courts' identification rules) align with or diverge from parties' ex ante practices and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of standard-form/model contracts and boilerplate in commercial contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes that boilerplate and standardized provisions often do not 'map' the underlying transaction and shape litigation dynamics, and Paper B empirically analyzes model commercial contracts (from a major supplier) to assess which interpretive clauses are included and how standard forms reflect market incentives.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for interpretive doctrines (efficiency/welfare versus moral/coherence claims)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates interpretive doctrines within competing normative frameworks—welfare economics, moral realism, coherence—and critiques their metaphoric assumptions, while Paper B explicitly evaluates the economic efficiency (joint-surplus maximizing) implications of adopting formalistic versus anti-formalistic identification rules in commercial settings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 109pennstlrev397!!ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*

shared_topics.topic: textualism/formalism versus contextualism/realism as competing interpretive frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the clash between classical/formal (textualist) approaches and contextual/legal-realist approaches to contract interpretation — Paper A traces this divide historically through Llewellyn and the UCC, while Paper B critiques the persistence of formalist pedagogy and explores the realist response in doctrinal practice.

shared_topics.topic: the use of extrinsic evidence and the project of reconstructing parties' intent (before-the-fact vs after-the-fact)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how courts and parties use context and extrinsic materials to reconstruct what the contracting parties meant or intended, with Paper A emphasizing the admission of extrinsic evidence under contextualism and Paper B framing this reconstruction as part of the transactional lifecycle and the limits of after-the-fact reconstruction.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive methodology shapes doctrinal outcomes (e.g., implied terms, unconscionability, reliance)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers link interpretive theory to concrete doctrinal results — Paper A shows how contextualism influenced areas like reliance recovery, pre-contractual liability, and implied-in-fact contracts, and Paper B shows how interpretive frames affect when and how doctrines like consideration and unconscionability are applied.

shared_topics.topic: the intellectual influence of Karl Llewellyn and Legal Realism on contract interpretation and pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with Llewellyn's role and realist ideas: Paper A centers on Llewellyn's authorship of the UCC and his ‘full contextualism,’ while Paper B invokes Llewellyn's observations about coherence and the case method to critique prevailing metaphors and teaching in contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100cornelllrev23!!ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly engage the doctrinal debate over whether courts should prioritize a contract's plain text or consider extrinsic context: Paper A analyzes that debate through competing interpretive regimes and doctrinal rules (parol evidence, plain meaning, U.C.C.), while Paper B situates the dispute within broader theoretical metaphors and shows how textualist and contextualist frames guide adjudicative reconstruction.

shared_topics.topic: who decides the mix of ex ante contracting versus ex post adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Both works probe the tension between party autonomy in designing contracts and the role of courts in resolving ambiguities: Paper A maps institutional choices (parties, trade associations, agencies, courts) that determine the textual/contextual mix, and Paper B examines how after-the-fact adjudication reconstructs or departs from the parties' before-the-fact transaction and the limits of relying on post-hoc legal propositions.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of prototypes and metaphors on doctrinal reasoning
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that cognitive frames—prototypical images or metaphors of what a contract is—structure legal argument: Paper A critiques the overreliance on a few contract prototypes (e.g., bargained executory contracts, mass-market adhesion) and shows their misfit across contracting environments, while Paper B theorizes how metaphors (contract-as-model, contract-as-journey) and prototypical images drive issue-spotting and legal interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' sophistication (sophisticated vs unsophisticated actors) shapes contracting and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both articles treat the distinction between legally sophisticated and unsophisticated parties as central: Paper A classifies interpretive regimes and protections based on whether parties are capable of bespoke drafting or rely on courts/collective regimes, and Paper B highlights the practical gulf between practitioner drafting (including boilerplate and negotiated bespoke terms) and doctrinal categories taught in law schools, showing how sophistication affects what matters in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: the gap between doctrinal contract law and the law-in-action/transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the first-year contracts curriculum and the discipline's 'epistemic trap,' arguing doctrinal categories often misrepresent how contracts function in real transactions; Paper B develops a 'new legal realism' account showing how remedies rules and commercial norms produce renegotiation and settlement practices that differ from doctrinal expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules and doctrines (mitigation, Hadley foreseeability, certainty) shape incentives to renegotiate, settle, or 'efficiently' breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the rational-actor/economic metaphors that justify after-the-fact normativity and the claim that contracts constrain opportunism, while Paper B empirically and doctrinally analyzes mitigation, Hadley, damages certainty, and limitation clauses to show how those rules induce loss‑sharing, settlements, and adjustments rather than strict performance.

shared_topics.topic: the problem of reconstructing parties' intentions and the limits of adjudication (textualism vs contextualism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the metaphors and models courts use to reconstruct a 'before-the-fact' transaction (textualist vs contextualist frames) and the limits of correspondent truth, while Paper B considers how foreseeability, proof requirements, and evidentiary/doctrinal limits constrain what courts can or will reconstruct about losses and expectations, thereby affecting dispute outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of metaphors, prototypes, and folk/relational norms on legal reasoning and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes that pre-propositional metaphors and prototype images (e.g., contract as model vs contract as journey) drive issue-spotting and doctrinal application, and Paper B documents business folk norms (e.g., 'a deal is a deal' vs mutual help in relations) and shows how those informal norms interact with law to produce settlements and renegotiations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38sandiegolrev13!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Placid, Clear-Seeming Words: Some Realism About the New Formalism (with Particular Reference to Promissory Estoppel)

shared_topics.topic: the role and legitimacy of reliance/promissory estoppel as a doctrinal response
shared_topics.justification: Paper A signals a focused treatment of promissory estoppel and the reliance interest in the context of the new formalism, and Paper B addresses reliance as one of the core doctrinal tests (alongside consideration) that courts use to decide enforceability and reconstruct parties' obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between doctrinal categories taught or asserted and the realities of contracting practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges formalist labels and how doctrine is presented (implied by its realist corrective to 'new formalism'), while Paper B diagnoses the contracts curriculum and doctrinal taxonomy as an 'epistemic trap' that channels thought away from transactional practice and the lifecycle of deals.

shared_topics.topic: after-the-fact reconstruction of parties' intentions and the interpretive work of courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates doctrines (like promissory estoppel) that function in adjudicative reconstruction of parties' expectations, and Paper B analyzes how courts and theorists attempt to reconstruct 'before-the-fact' transactions from documents and events, contrasting textualist and contextualist approaches.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77chikentlrev87!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:THE WRITTEN CONTRACT AS SAFE HARBOR FOR DISHONEST CONDUCT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:THE WRITTEN CONTRACT AS SAFE HARBOR FOR DISHONEST CONDUCT

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal doctrinal rules and the realities of transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the traditional contract-law pedagogy and doctrinal categories for privileging after-the-fact formalism over the transactional lifecycle, arguing that doctrinal classifications can be an 'epistemic trap'; Paper B analyzes how bright‑line doctrines like the parol evidence rule trade off certainty and exclusion of context and thus can misfit the messy realities of business transactions, producing unjust outcomes or perverse incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of the written contract as an accurate record of parties' intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether contracts reliably 'map' pre‑contractual inter‑subjective transactions and emphasizes objectification and loss of subjective meaning in documentation; Paper B examines the privileged status of written agreements (statute of frauds, parol evidence rule) and shows how reliance on written texts can conceal or enable misleading precontractual representations.

shared_topics.topic: cognitive and linguistic foundations of contract interpretation and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a metaphors-and-prototypes account, arguing that pre‑propositional metaphors and cognitive frames shape issue spotting and adjudicative judgments; Paper B draws on linguistics and psychology to evaluate the parol evidence rule, focusing on memory, perception, and the indistinct line between forgetting and self‑serving testimony.

shared_topics.topic: incentives for opportunism or dishonest conduct and doctrinal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes the law-and-economics story that contracts curb opportunism, noting that parties and lawyers routinely seek ways to 'break' or reinterpret contracts; Paper B documents how privileging written terms can create a 'safe harbor' for sharp precontractual practices and proposes stronger sanctions and consumer protections to counteract opportunistic behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev429!!SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the debate between formalism (textualism) and realism (contextualism) in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies a contemporary movement of scholars advocating formalist constraints on courts (labeling it a 'fear of contract') and critiques that formalist posture; Paper B likewise traces the historical dominance of classical formalism, critiques its 'epistemic trap,' and situates legal realism and alternative approaches in direct opposition to textualist/formalist models.

shared_topics.topic: the proper grounding of contractual obligation — explicit consent versus an objective reconstruction of intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on critics anxious about imposing obligations not rooted in explicit, voluntary consent and defends an objective theory that sometimes imposes obligations beyond actual consent; Paper B interrogates the 'meeting of the minds' metaphor and the project of after-the-fact reconstruction, questioning how and when courts should treat contractual meaning as corresponding to parties' subjective intentions versus objective manifestations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contextual evidence, relational norms, and extrinsic factors in contract interpretation and adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A lists as central the contested claims that courts should avoid contextual interpretation, redressing unaddressed mistakes, and incorporating relational norms; Paper B engages the same dispute over textualist versus contextualist interpretation, arguing that metaphors and prototypes shape when judges look beyond text and how they use extrinsic circumstances to resolve meaning.

shared_topics.topic: understanding contract law as part of a transactional lifecycle or social infrastructure rather than a self-contained doctrinal system
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract law as societal infrastructure that must regulate cooperative activity beyond written consent to function reliably; Paper B similarly emphasizes the transactional lifecycle—negotiation, drafting, objectification, and adjudication—highlighting the gap between doctrinal classifications taught in the academy and the practices of contracting in the real world.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87nclrev1699!!ARTICLE: NORTH CAROLINA COMMON LAW PAROL EVIDENCE RULE*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: NORTH CAROLINA COMMON LAW PAROL EVIDENCE RULE*

shared_topics.topic: the Williston v. Corbin divide in interpretive approach and its doctrinal influence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the historical and ongoing Williston–Corbin split as the fundamental cleavage shaping the parol evidence rule in North Carolina, while Paper B situates that same split within broader debates (textualism/Langdellian formalism versus Corbinian contextualism) about how courts should reconstruct contractual meaning.

shared_topics.topic: when and how courts may consider extrinsic (parol) evidence to ascertain parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the parol evidence rule’s prohibitions and exceptions—criticizing presumptions that exclude extrinsic evidence—whereas Paper B examines the epistemic and metaphoric foundations that drive decisions to rely on the written text versus contextual, after‑the‑fact evidence of intent.

shared_topics.topic: the presumptions of finality/completeness of written contracts and their practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the legal presumption that a written document is final and complete as both doctrinally flawed and harmful in application, and Paper B interrogates the notion of the written contract as an objectified ‘model’ of the transaction, showing how treating the document as definitive obscures the transactional lifecycle and produces misaligned adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between contract doctrine (as taught or doctrinally framed) and real-world transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the parol evidence rule’s mystical faith in the written word misreads ordinary commercial practice and can produce unjust results, while Paper B criticizes contract pedagogy and theoretical paradigms for channeling thought away from the actual practices of negotiating, drafting, and interpreting commercial documents.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71ucololrev541!!ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE

shared_topics.topic: Legal Realism's influence on contract and commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how Karl Llewellyn and the Legal Realist movement shaped the Uniform Commercial Code's substantive provisions and interpretive approach, while Paper B situates Legal Realism as one of the central theoretical responses to classical formalism and discusses its continuing role and limits in contract theory and pedagogy.

shared_topics.topic: The formalism vs. contextualism/textualism debate in contract law and statutory interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows the U.C.C. was drafted to embody Llewellyn's push away from rigid formalism toward rules that invite context-sensitive interpretation, and Paper B analyzes the same doctrinal fault line—textualist/formalist approaches versus Corbinian/contextualist and realist approaches—and its effects on teaching and adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: Judicial discretion and the after-the-fact reconstruction of transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes Llewellyn's conviction that statutes like the U.C.C. should recognize and guide inevitable judicial discretion, and Paper B explores how courts and litigants reconstruct parties' intentions after the fact, questioning how doctrinal categories shape that discretionary reconstruction.

shared_topics.topic: Correspondence between legal rules/models and real-world commercial/transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the U.C.C. was designed to better reflect and regulate commercial realities as practiced by merchants, whereas Paper B critiques dominant metaphors (contracts as ideal models) and proposes alternative process-oriented metaphors to improve how legal doctrine maps onto the transactional lifecycle.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65uclalrev376!!ARTICLE: Deal Momentum
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Momentum

shared_topics.topic: the transactional lifecycle and the timing of when agreements crystallize
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the transactional lifecycle by contrasting before-the-fact bargaining and the after-the-fact adjudicative reconstruction of deals, arguing that doctrine often misreads where meaning is created; Paper B empirically locates preliminary agreements at a late stage of the lifecycle and argues they mark a moment when deal uncertainty has been largely resolved and the transaction is likely to proceed.

shared_topics.topic: the role of written documents as objectifications or markers of inter-subjective deal understandings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contracts as objects that sometimes do and sometimes do not ‘map’ the underlying inter-subjective transaction and emphasizes the limits of treating contract text as a complete model; Paper B treats non-binding term sheets and letters of intent as formal markers that objectify and signal accumulated deal momentum rather than as fully descriptive, binding reconstructions of parties' intentions.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contract design and enforcement (when and why law should enforce agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates doctrinal frameworks (formalism vs realism) that assume after-the-fact enforcement reconstructs and secures ex ante transactions, questioning that presumption; Paper B shifts focus from enforcement to design, arguing that preliminary agreements often function without legal bite and that their utility arises from signaling and formality rather than from enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: how observers (courts, lawyers, parties) infer meaning and intent from pre-propositional cues, metaphors, or signals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes pre-propositional metaphors, prototypes, and epistemic traps that shape how judges and lawyers categorize facts and infer parties' intentions; Paper B explains how parties and lawyers use non-binding documents and the concept of 'deal momentum' as signals that create expectations and guide behavior even in the absence of formal adjudicative reconstruction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev1002!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Justice Traynor and the Summer of Love: Misunderstanding the Parole Evidence Rule in Pacific Gas
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Justice Traynor and the Summer of Love: Misunderstanding the Parole Evidence Rule in Pacific Gas

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Pacific Gas and the parol evidence rule, debating when courts may admit extrinsic evidence to construe ambiguous terms; Paper B treats the textualism-versus-contextualism debate more broadly, analyzing how and why courts and practitioners rely on or reject extrinsic materials when reconstructing parties' understandings.

shared_topics.topic: textualism versus contextualism and the discoverability of contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes Chief Justice Traynor's linguistic theory and defends the functional limits of the four-corners/parol framework, while Paper B interrogates the metaphors (contract as model vs journey) that underlie textualist and contextualist approaches and how they shape beliefs about whether meaning is encoded in words or must be reconstructed from the transaction.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between interpretive rules, litigation costs, and parties' drafting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames the parol evidence rule as a cost-benefit device that restricts evidence to lower litigation costs and create drafting incentives, and Paper B similarly emphasizes how doctrinal rules and metaphors influence real-world negotiating, boilerplate practices, and how parties draft to achieve predictable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: critique of doctrinal categories and the mismatch between doctrinal pedagogy and transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents doctrinal confusion and the practical consequences of judicial misframing in Pacific Gas (and later corrective rulings), while Paper B diagnoses an 'epistemic trap' in contract law pedagogy and argues that entrenched classifications (e.g., consideration vs unconscionability, textualism vs realism) misrepresent how transactions are actually created and litigated.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97columlrev1710!!ARTICLE: THE INVERTED HIERARCHY OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AND SUPPLEMENTATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INVERTED HIERARCHY OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AND SUPPLEMENTATION

shared_topics.topic: how courts and decisionmakers reconstruct parties' intent and the ‘transaction in fact’ after the fact
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the gap between the before-the-fact transactional reality and after-the-fact adjudicative reconstructions, arguing that metaphors and prototypes shape how interpreters perceive what the parties meant; Paper B evaluates competing theories about whether interpreters should reconstruct the bargain in fact (Llewellyn-style) or instead rely more heavily on legal standards, showing both are competing accounts of that same reconstructive task.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role and hierarchy of interpretive sources (express terms, course of performance/dealing, trade usage, default rules, and standards like reasonableness/good faith)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly argues for an 'inverted hierarchy' that privileges standards of reasonableness, good faith, default rules and trade usages over a strict sequential primacy of express terms, while Paper A engages this same issue indirectly in its critique of textualism versus contextualism and in discussing which parts of a written contract actually 'map' the transaction versus which are supplemented or interpreted by external norms.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for choosing interpretive methods (efficiency, fairness, realizations of parties' intentions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law-and-economics rationalist justifications with realist and moral accounts for why courts should interpret contracts one way or another, and Paper B defends its inverted hierarchy on ethical grounds (fairness, redistributive justice, paternalism) as well as on efficiency and on better realizing parties' actual intentions.

shared_topics.topic: the divergence between doctrinal pedagogy/classification and actual judicial or commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses an 'epistemic trap' in doctrinal categories and metaphors built into contract pedagogy that may misdescribe how contracts function in practice, while Paper B marshals doctrinal analysis and empirical/behavioral evidence to show that courts and contracting behavior conform more to an inverted interpretive order than to the conventional doctrinal story taught in many sources.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67sclrev535!!ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates redesigning contract clauses (e.g., costs-of-cover provisions), using in-house playbooks and escalation strategies to negotiate data‑security terms; Paper B criticizes doctrinal pedagogy and emphasizes that real contract law practice centers on negotiating and writing documents, boilerplate, and deal‑closing techniques.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents cases where companies' posted privacy/security promises diverged from practice (FTC scrutiny) and stresses drafting to manage that divergence; Paper B theorizes how contracts often fail to 'map' the actual transaction, explores why boilerplate and rushed clauses may not reflect parties' true dealings, and considers how courts reconstruct meaning after the fact.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of external normative frameworks (regulatory decisions, industry standards, doctrinal rules) on contract design and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how FTC decisions and evolving industry security norms affect what contractual security provisions should require and may be used as evidence of reasonable practices; Paper B analyzes how doctrinal theories and metaphors (formalism, realism, textualism/contextualism) shape the expectations parties bring to contract design and how adjudicators reconstruct contractual meaning.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: how default legal rules and judicial gap-filling affect parties' contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how courts’ default damage rules and the practice of filling obligational gaps change parties’ incentives to write state-contingent contracts and can produce large strategic inefficiencies; Paper B analyzes how the prospect of after‑the‑fact adjudication and doctrinal gap‑filling (textualist vs contextualist approaches) shapes what parties write and expect from contract documents.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between before‑the‑fact contracting (drafting) and after‑the‑fact adjudication (interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how the availability and common knowledge of defaults influence ex ante contracting and whether parties will contract around defaults, while Paper B critiques the dominant theoretical metaphors that assume adjudicative norms map cleanly back to parties’ ex ante intentions and proposes reframing the transaction lifecycle to account for both drafting and later interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: strategic behavior, opportunism, and renegotiation in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines strategic bargaining, market power, and the incentives to breach or renegotiate when contracts are contingently incomplete and how defaults can exacerbate inefficiencies, and Paper B interrogates the assumption (common in law‑and‑economics) that contracts primarily serve to guard against opportunism, showing how practice often reflects deliberate strategies to ‘manage’ or exploit interpretive gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of theoretical models/metaphors in explaining and prescribing contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs and extends economic 'second‑generation' incomplete‑contract models to analyze default rule design and its normative implications, while Paper B critiques prevailing legal metaphors (e.g., contract as complete model or meeting of minds), urging more realistic conceptual frames for both doctrinal analysis and the use of models in legal pedagogy and policy.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Designing and Enforcing Preliminary Agreements

shared_topics.topic: the gap between doctrinal contract rules and real-world negotiation practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques scholarship that frames preliminary agreements only in terms of formal doctrines like reliance, arguing preliminary agreements are tools for regulating staged negotiations; Paper B critiques the traditional contracts curriculum and doctrinal paradigms for failing to capture the actual transactional lifecycle and everyday bargaining practices, urging metaphors that connect doctrine to real-world dealmaking.

shared_topics.topic: the role and defensibility of legal standards (e.g., good faith / best efforts) versus bright‑line rules or textualism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contextual standards like good faith or best efforts can be well-suited to govern multistage negotiations and justifies judicial enforcement (including expectation damages) in some contexts; Paper B analyzes the textualism/contextualism divide and how pre‑propositional metaphors and models shape whether courts rely on standards or strict rules in adjudicating contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret and reconstruct parties' intentions and negotiated documents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts determine whether parties intended to assume binding negotiation duties and what such duties require, emphasizing fidelity to settled preliminary terms; Paper B studies the processes and metaphors by which tribunals and advocates reconstruct 'what the parties meant,' arguing that interpretation is driven by competing prototypes and metaphoric frames as much as by formal propositions.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between commitment and flexibility in multistage contracting and the design of preliminary agreements to allocate risk and deter opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames preliminary agreements as mechanisms to balance commitment and flexibility—protecting reliance, discouraging value‑claiming investments, and allocating exogenous risks during staged negotiations; Paper B offers an alternative 'journey' metaphor that foregrounds the transactional lifecycle and divergent stakeholder perspectives, which similarly illuminates why parties and courts must reconcile the need for durable commitments with ongoing flexibility.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Designing and Enforcing Preliminary Agreements

shared_topics.topic: the gap between the negotiated transaction and after-the-fact judicial reconstruction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes the epistemic gap between the parties' transactional lifecycle and the court's after-the-fact reconstruction, criticizing doctrinal classifications that privilege adjudicative models; Paper B grapples with courts' role in determining whether parties actually bound themselves in preliminary agreements and the evidentiary and remedial problems that arise when reconstructing incomplete deals.

shared_topics.topic: contracts (and preliminary agreements) as instruments to regulate staged bargaining — allocating risk and locking in aspects of a deal

shared_topics.topic: the role and choice of interpretive standards (textualism vs contextualism, good‑faith/best‑efforts standards) in policing negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how metaphors and doctrinal frames (textualist vs contextualist approaches) shape adjudicative outcomes and pre-propositional judgments about meaning; Paper B defends the use of contextual standards like good faith or best efforts in preliminary agreements, addresses concerns about vagueness and judicial error, and explains when courts should enforce such open‑ended norms.

shared_topics.topic: parties' strategic behavior (opportunism, holdup, value‑claiming) and legal mechanisms to deter or remediate it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the standard law-and-economics narrative that contracts simply guard against opportunism, noting frequent lawyer strategies to 'break' deals and the limits of formalist models; Paper B centrally models preliminary agreements as devices to deter value‑claiming, prevent holdup, protect specific investments, and shape remedies when bargaining breaks down.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LACKING SWISS PRECISION: THE FIRST-SALE DOCTRINE IN COSTCO V. OMEGA

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between doctrinal pedagogy/theory and real-world transactional practice (negotiation, drafting, boilerplate)
