papers.node_id: 2016byulrev1!!ARTICLE: Mind the Gap
papers.title: ARTICLE: Mind the Gap
papers.abstract:
Any discussion regarding the gap-filling powers of arbitrators must begin by identifying (1) the situations involving genuine gaps, and (2) the common reasons for the presence of such gaps in commercial agreements. Starting with the definition of genuine gaps, a recent paper by Alan Rau illustrates the potential for confusion, and the extent to which even this basic question remains a source of controversy. In his paper, Rau leads with the theoretical possibilities that gaps could mean everything (in the sense that all contracts are incompletely specified) or nothing at all (in the sense that the latticework of contract law provides an answer to all questions that arise among the parties).
Ultimately, Rau settles on the proposition that gaps represent nothing in particular. To the contrary, he asserts that gap-filling lies on the same continuum as contractual interpretation;thatinterpretation and gap-filling both aim to specify the obligations of the parties;that they differ only in degree;and that any doctrinal separation between the two lacks coherence, stability, and utility.Viewed from this set of assumptions, Rau implies that Supreme Court's recent treatment of interpretation and gap-filling in Green Tree Financial Corporation v. Bazzle,Stolt-Nielsen,and Oxford Health Plansshould have reflected the linear exposition of a single theme.Instead, the Court broadly defined the interpretive powers of arbitral tribunals in Bazzle, recognized the existence of strict limits on their gap-filling powers in Stolt-Nielsen, and returned to embrace an almost limitless interpretive power in Oxford Health Plans, a sequence that Rau describes as encompassing a "dizzying series of twists and turns."
On the one hand, Rau's points seem incontestable. One can describe interpretation and gap-filling as involving a common effort to specify the obligations of the parties. On the other hand, differences in degree matter. For example, a series of tasks may all involve the splitting of wood, but the process and the tools may change dramatically depending on whether one splits twigs, branches, or logs. Even focusing on logs, it makes a huge difference whether one splits southern yellow pine (which weighs roughly fifty-two pounds per cubic foot),or quebracho (which weighs over seventy-seven pounds per cubic foot and takes its name from the Spanish words for "axe-breaker").
The fact is that interpretation and gap-filling involve distinct undertakings.Interpretation requires an examination of the parties' intent based on express terms,testimony regarding their intentions,implied terms drawn from the overall structure of the agreement,course of performance,course of dealing,and usageof trade.In rare cases, even this broad range of tools does not permit discernment of the parties' intent.This marks the place where interpretation ends and gap-filling begins. According to, which the Supreme Court quoted in Stolt-Nielsen,gap-filling has virtually nothing to do with intent.Gap-filling aims neither to identify the parties' intent, which cannot be discerned by any of the usual sources, nor even to speculate what the parties would have intended in a hypothetical bargain.To the contrary, when gap-filling, courts take the wheel from the parties and supply reasonable terms based on "community standards of fairness and policy."
The point is that gap-filling turns its face from the emphasis on intent and towards the imposition of standards based on externalyardsticks. It should be obvious that the divergence in perspectives is significant, entrenched in doctrine, involves different tasks, and will produce different outcomes.
As suggested above, genuine gaps on material terms may not occur frequently.But they do occur, and perhaps with greater frequency in the modern economy.According to leading sources, three reasons lie at the heart of the gaps that do arise. First, parties may foresee a situation, but resolve to deal with it in a subsequent agreement.This represents the paradigmatic "agreement to agree." Second, the parties may foresee a situation, but fail to address it in their agreement,because the issue seems insignificant,discussion of the topic seems unpleasant,or negotiations may delay implementation of the transaction.Third, the parties simply may not foresee a situation.For transactions characterized by complex, long-term relationships among parties who operate in increasingly global and unstable markets, the probabilities of such lapses increase.
This last observation holds particular relevance for international commercial arbitration, because that mechanism represents the leading means of dispute-settlement for the complex, cross-border transactions that seem likely to produce gaps.The question then becomes whether arbitrators possess the tools to perform the task of gap-filling in ways that protect the legal interests of contracting parties. As a corollary, it also seems relevant to determine whether arbitrators possess the same, better, or worse tools than national courts. To begin that inquiry, Part II surveys the evolution of U.S. judicial doctrine with respect to omitted material terms, as well as international developments regarding the powers of arbitrators to deal with problems caused by the omission of material terms.

questions.question: What are the common causes and types of genuine gaps in commercial contracts (how and why do material terms get omitted)?
Are contractual interpretation and judicial gap-filling distinct tasks with different aims and methods, or are they points on a single continuum?

Can arbitrators effectively fill genuine contractual gaps in commercial disputes in a way that protects the parties' legal interests, and do arbitrators have institutional tools that are better, worse, or equivalent to those of national courts for that task?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev128!!ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing contractual interpretation from gap-filling/tacit agreement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with when adjudicators should seek the parties' intent versus impose supplemental terms: Paper A debates the doctrinal boundary between interpretation and gap‑filling by arbitrators, while Paper B analyzes the tacit‑agreement test versus the 'reason to know' foreseeability standard as modes of inferring or denying that parties accepted liability for consequential losses.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and desirability of default rules that supply contract terms or allocate risk
shared_topics.justification: Both examine whether legal defaults reflect commercial parties' preferences and when courts/arbitrators should supply terms—Paper A questions whether gap‑filling by tribunals produces appropriate default terms for omitted material provisions, and Paper B questions the default rule permitting recovery of foreseeable consequential damages and whether parties typically would opt into or out of that rule.

shared_topics.topic: the role and comparative competence of tribunals (courts vs arbitrators) in resolving incomplete-contract problems
shared_topics.justification: Both investigate which decision‑maker is best suited to supply missing terms or determine liability: Paper A surveys U.S. and international doctrine on arbitrators' powers to fill gaps relative to national courts, while Paper B studies how courts apply standards (tacit agreement vs reason to know) and the implications of those doctrines for commercial parties.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracting in complex, long‑term, relationship‑specific transactions and mechanisms to address holdup
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how complex, cross‑border or long‑term commercial relationships produce omitted terms and strategic problems—Paper A emphasizes that modern, global transactions increase the incidence of genuine gaps for arbitrators to address, and Paper B shows that relationship‑specific investments create holdup risks that influence whether parties tacitly or expressly accept consequential‑damage liability as a protective mechanism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev128!!ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal gap‑filling and default terms when contracts are silent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Restatement/UCC defaults (and the tacit‑agreement test) operate when parties are silent about consequential damages, while Paper B analyzes the broader question of when and how tribunals should supply omitted material terms and fill genuine contract gaps.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation focused on parties' intent versus imposition of external standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the tacit‑agreement (intent‑oriented) approach with the objective 'reason to know' foreseeability standard for consequential damages, and Paper B explicitly distinguishes interpretation (drawing on intent, course of dealing, usage) from gap‑filling that applies community fairness and policy yardsticks.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness in long‑term/commercial relationships and its causes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how incomplete specification of remedies (consequential damages) affects relationship‑specific investment and creates holdup risks in long‑term commercial deals, while Paper B documents why complex, long‑term, and international transactions produce material gaps that necessitate gap‑filling.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of authority to supply missing terms (courts vs arbitrators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how courts have applied different standards (tacit agreement vs reason‑to‑know) in supplying or denying consequential damages, and Paper B evaluates arbitrators' gap‑filling powers relative to national courts and the implications for protecting contracting parties' interests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev527!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: PRICE ADJUSTMENT IN LONG-TERM CONTRACTS.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: PRICE ADJUSTMENT IN LONG-TERM CONTRACTS.

shared_topics.topic: filling gaps in long‑term commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address situations where contracts omit material terms (especially in complex, long‑term transactions) and examine how those omissions should be remedied—Paper A as a general inquiry into the nature and frequency of genuine gaps and gap‑filling doctrine, and Paper B through the concrete example of price adjustment clauses and litigation over omitted or imperfect price terms.

shared_topics.topic: authority and competence of arbitrators versus courts to supply or change contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate whether arbitrators (and arbitration tribunals) possess the tools or legal authority to resolve omitted terms or renegotiate outcomes and compare that capacity to national courts—Paper A surveys doctrinal and international developments on arbitrators' gap‑filling powers, while Paper B discusses assigning price‑revision decisions to courts or third parties (including arbitrators) and the practical problems that arise.

shared_topics.topic: responses to changed or unforeseen circumstances (price adjustment, force majeure, renegotiation)
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how the law should handle changed circumstances that render agreed terms unsatisfactory—Paper B focuses on price swings, force majeure, and doctrines like contract revision or a duty to renegotiate, while Paper A lists unforeseeability and changing markets as core sources of gaps that demand judicial or arbitral responses.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal line between interpretation and gap‑filling (when to ascertain intent versus rewrite terms)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the distinction between interpreting parties' intent and imposing externally sourced terms: Paper A explicitly analyzes the interpretation vs gap‑filling divide in doctrine and case law, and Paper B confronts the related question in practice when courts or tribunals must decide whether to construe ambiguous/open‑ended price clauses or to effectively revise the contract.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev631!!SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM

shared_topics.topic: the nature and authority of third‑party dispute resolution in international and commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether the WTO dispute‑settlement system should be treated as coercive adjudication or a form of self‑enforcement, while Paper B examines the scope of arbitral tribunals' powers (versus courts) to resolve disputes in international commercial contracts, so both probe how third‑party adjudication functions and is characterized across contexts.

shared_topics.topic: how legal enforcement regimes interact with self‑enforcement and parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that introducing coercive enforcement can crowd out reliance on self‑enforcing remedies in international agreements, and Paper B analyzes how arbitrators or courts fill contract gaps — both address how different enforcement modalities affect contracting parties' reliance on private enforcement and strategic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: contract incompleteness (gaps) and the appropriate response by legal institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on when genuine gaps arise in commercial agreements and whether arbitrators should supply terms, while Paper A is concerned with parties' deliberate avoidance of formal enforcement in light of incomplete agreements; together they engage the problem of incomplete contracting and institutional gap‑management.

shared_topics.topic: comparability and limits of transferring doctrines between international agreements and private commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cautions against directly applying lessons from international treaty enforcement to private contracts because of contextual differences (e.g., third‑party beneficiaries, political incentives), and Paper B considers whether doctrines governing national courts and arbitrators should be applied or adapted in international commercial arbitration, so both interrogate how legal rules travel between international and private spheres.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105valrev1025!!ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracting and materially omitted terms (gaps)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat contracts as often incompletely specified: Paper A analyzes when and why material gaps arise and how doctrine distinguishes interpretation from gap-filling, while Paper B treats complex M&A term sheets as responses to incomplete contracting and examines why parties accept and work within those incompletenesses.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms that fill contractual gaps outside formal court enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both works study non-judicial gap-resolution: Paper A interrogates arbitrators' power to supply terms and how arbitration compares to national courts, and Paper B analyzes informal or extralegal mechanisms (trust, reputational pressures, organizational practices) that lead parties to abide by non-binding documents in lieu of formal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design choices (form, bindingness, and interpretation) manage uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on how contracting parties and decisionmakers design or interpret contractual instruments to manage uncertainty: Paper A asks when courts/arbitrators should interpret versus supply terms, while Paper B examines the deliberate use of formal-looking but non-binding 'faux' documents and bundling of binding and non-binding terms as a design strategy.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction complexity and multi-stage/deal processes in producing gaps and shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both authors link complex, long-term, or multi-stage commercial transactions to greater likelihood of gaps and special contracting practices: Paper A highlights modern global transactions as prone to omitted terms and raises arbitration's relevance, and Paper B shows how multi-stage M&A processes and deal complexity encourage use of non-binding term sheets and reliance on relationship-based gap-filling.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42sandiegolrev533!!EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts

shared_topics.topic: distinction between interpretation and gap-filling in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze where interpretive inquiry ends and gap-filling begins: Paper A contrasts single-inquiry (author's intent) interpretation with pluralist, multi-factor approaches to discerning meaning in wills and contracts, while Paper B draws a doctrinal line between interpretation (ascertaining intent from terms, course of performance, usages) and judicial/arbitral gap-filling when intent cannot be discerned.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' intent versus imposition of external standards/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between privileging the parties' subjective or objective intent and resorting to externally imposed norms: Paper A debates privileging author/speaker intent versus multiple practical factors, and Paper B contrasts intent-based interpretation with gap-filling that supplies reasonable terms based on community standards, fairness, or policy.

shared_topics.topic: institutional authority to alter, displace, or supplement contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Both examine who may legitimately change a text's meaning or supply omitted terms — Paper A asks whether judges may (or should) displace a text's meaning under pluralist practice versus single-inquiry restraint, and Paper B queries whether arbitrators (versus courts) possess appropriate powers and tools to fill gaps and supply terms in commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how contextual change, complexity, or omission creates indeterminacy in private agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat how temporal change, complexity of transactions, and unstated assumptions produce interpretive indeterminacy: Paper A shows how evolving social/practical contexts can alter a statute or contract's modern meaning, and Paper B catalogs why material gaps arise in complex, long-term, cross-border commercial agreements and how that increases demand for gap-filling.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms and industry customs in shaping legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that custom and marketplace norms, more than welfare-maximizing analysis, drive how bait-and-switch practices are regulated; Paper B shows that gap-filling by courts and arbitrators often relies on community standards of fairness and trade usage rather than pure intent, highlighting the normative weight of customs in resolving disputes.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules respond when formal doctrine is silent or indeterminate (gap‑filling)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines commercial behaviors that fall outside or beyond the FTC's formal bait‑and‑switch definition and asks how regulators decide when to intervene, while Paper B analyzes when contracts contain genuine gaps and whether courts or arbitrators should supply terms, treating both as questions about filling legal or regulatory voids.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction and boundary between doctrinal categories and practical commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A expands and problematizes the doctrinal category of 'bait‑and‑switch' to capture practices market actors perceive as deceptive, and Paper B draws a line between contractual interpretation (party intent) and gap‑filling (external imposition), with both papers interrogating where legal categories stop matching commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: the normative choice between fairness/community standards and welfare/efficiency in resolving commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts regulation that reinforces fairness and market morality with regulation aimed at welfare advancement, arguing regulators often favor the former; Paper B explains that gap‑filling substitutes party intent with standards of fairness and policy, reflecting the same normative tradeoff in contract and arbitration contexts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43iowajcorpl1!!ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for filling contractual gaps (AI-driven algorithms vs arbitrators/courts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contracts that use machine-driven analytics to generate and update terms after execution, while Paper B examines how arbitrators and courts supply omitted material terms—both grapple with who or what legitimately supplies post-execution terms and the consequences of those different mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: distinction between contractual interpretation and gap-filling (intent-based interpretation vs externally imposed standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that self-driving contracts blur traditional distinctions between rules and standards and between ex ante agreement and ex post resolution, and Paper B digs into the doctrinal split between interpretation (seeking parties' intent) and gap-filling (imposing community standards), with both questioning where interpretation ends and gap-filling begins.

shared_topics.topic: who should provide and regulate post-execution term determination (third-party vendors, platforms, arbitrators, government)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the emergence of markets for third-party providers (e.g., certified code vendors, platform operators, arbitration services) that will supply self-driving contract logic and asks how they should be governed; Paper B focuses on the role and powers of arbitrators to fill gaps and whether they have appropriate tools, so both engage with the institutional question of which actors may lawfully and effectively determine missing terms.

papers.node_id: 73molrev667!!Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs
papers.title: Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs
papers.abstract:
This paper will examine some theoretical aspects of contractual non-disclosure and the related doctrine of unilateral mistake. These two legalrubrics are conceptually similar;each is concerned with the degree to which parties must communicate their understandings about the nature of the contract into which they are about to enter. If one party fails to reveal enough information, the other party may enter into the agreement under a misunderstanding and consequently may attempt to avoid contractual liability on the basis of mistake or on a theory of nondisclosure. The law of contracts clearly attaches a great deal of importance to ensuring that contracting parties have a mutual understanding about their agreement - a meeting of the minds- for that is the cornerstone of mutual assent. Indeed, one of the foundational theoretical goals of contract doctrine is to establish rules of law that will induce parties to reveal information that will reduce the cost of contracting and minimize the negative effects of breach. This "information forcing" concept has received substantial attention by many leading scholars as the animating principle behind the rule of Hadley v. Baxendale,which limits consequential damages to those that are foreseeable (i.e., those that have been communicated by the party seeking damages).
Yet there are, naturally, times when forcing parties to reveal their private information is not desirable. The very nature of market transactions dictates that trade is on one level the result of a seller who values his goods less highly than the buyer. While in cases where both parties enjoy full information, this disparity in valuation is often caused by circumstances affecting the relative need of the parties for the good - a pharmacist would not sell his last bottle of aspirin if he were suffering a migraine. In many other cases, the disparity can be explained by the fact that one party knows something the other doesn't know - the seller of a used car may know that the oil had never been changed for the first 50,000 miles. The buyer of a parcel of swamp land may know that the local government is in the early planning stages of a drainage and development project that will greatly enhance the land's value. Sometimes the law requires full disclosure, while at other times it does not.This ambivalence about disclosure results in a tension which occasionally expresses itself in disputes over whether or not a party to a contract had lived up to his disclosure obligations, and whether, as a result of incomplete information, the less well-informed party is entitled to relief in the form of rescission.
This article focuses on the commentary the law of buyer nondisclosure has generated in the last 30 years,in particular a 1978 article by ProfessorAnthony Kronmanand a 1982 article by Professor Saul Levmore.Kronman argued that, when a buyer of a good has discovered heretofore unknown information about that good as a result of a deliberate search, the law should not impose a duty to disclose that information lest the buyer forfeit to the seller the profit of his search and be stripped of his incentive to generate the socially beneficial information.Levmore took Kronman's analysis as a starting point and concluded that the protection buyers with specialized information needed could not be provided by the "silence-is-golden" rule Kronman proposed.Levmore argued that in order to protect such a buyer's ability to capitalize on his private information, and thus preserve future parties' incentive to develop socially beneficial information, a rule of "optimal dishonesty" was required; such a rule would permit the buyer to lie during negotiations, an action that would otherwise constitute fraud.In Part II, I will describe the doctrinal backdrop against which Kronman and others were working and will explain their arguments in greater detail.
Kronman's analysis formed the bedrock of what has become a fairly settled area of contracts scholarship, at least among law and economics scholars.I do not intend to challenge the insights he and Levmore have contributed.Instead, I will demonstrate in Part III that the model upon which these and other modern scholars have based their discussions of buyer nondisclosure is structurally limited, and I will attempt to extend their analysis by introducing and examining a richer model.I will then address the questionof which legal rule is the most appropriate to govern the enriched model. I will conclude that in my model, preserving the buyer's incentive to invest in information does not necessarily require the rule Levmore suggested (Optimal Dishonesty) - a rule that, to some extent, offends traditional contract doctrine and theories of contract that are rooted in morality.Further, by emphasizing the communicative or signaling effects of silence, I will suggest that in many contexts, the Silence is Golden rule is conceptually unstable and should not be addressed as a distinct rule in my analysis.
In Part IV, I will compare the efficiency of Levmore's rule to a rule requiring minimal truthful disclosure (which I term a "Word to the Wise" rule) in the context of my model. I will argue that in this model, a Word to the Wise rule is just as efficient as, or only slightly less efficient than a rule of Optimal Dishonesty. But I will not limit my analysis of the appropriate disclosure rule to considerations of efficiency. This article departs from the theoretical monism inherent in economic analysis and often adhered to in autonomy-based contract theory. Instead, I offer a pluralistic approach to the problem this article explores.Thus, in Part V, I discuss whether any compelling reason outside the realm of efficiency militates in favor of a Word to the Wise rule. Finally, I will offer my conclusion that in a model of two-sided informational inputs, a Word to the Wise rule is the better rule, given a multitude of considerations, including efficiency, longstanding contract doctrine, fairness and a perspective from intellectual property theory.

questions.question: In bilateral contracting where both parties can acquire private information, is it necessary to allow a party to mislead or remain silent (thereby forgoing a duty to disclose) in order to preserve incentives to invest in information and maximize contractual efficiency?

Can a rule requiring minimal truthful disclosure by an informed party achieve the same (or nearly the same) efficiency and incentive effects as a rule that permits deception, while also better satisfying fairness and other non-efficiency considerations?

Should strategic silence be treated as a distinct communicative signal in models of two-sided informational inputs, or is the concept of 'silence as a separate rule' conceptually unstable in such settings?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016wislrev981!!ARTICLE: CAFFOLDING: USING FORMAL CONTRACTS TO SUPPORT INFORMAL RELATIONS IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAFFOLDING: USING FORMAL CONTRACTS TO SUPPORT INFORMAL RELATIONS IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION

shared_topics.topic: contracting under uncertainty and incomplete information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a two-sided informational-input model to analyze how parties with private information form contracts and when nondisclosure leads to relief for mistake, while Paper B studies innovation-oriented relationships where pervasive uncertainty makes contracts necessarily incomplete and examines how parties manage adaptation and gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the role of disclosure, silence, and communicative signaling in shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes doctrines governing buyer nondisclosure, the signaling effects of silence, and competing rules (e.g., Silence-is-Golden vs Word-to-the-Wise vs Optimal Dishonesty), while Paper B highlights how formal contract language and legal classification function as communicative scaffolding that coordinates parties' beliefs about performance and breach.

shared_topics.topic: incentives to acquire, preserve, and exploit private information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how different legal rules affect a buyer's incentive to invest in search-generated information and the social value of that information, and Paper B considers how parties in innovation relationships design contractual and informal structures to preserve incentives to invest effort and specialized knowledge when future contingencies are unknown.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal legal rules/documents and informal enforcement or relational mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates doctrinal rules (mistake, nondisclosure, fraud) within their incentive and communicative effects on parties, and Paper B empirically and theoretically examines how formal contracts (and legal advice) are used not primarily for litigation but to scaffold and support informal enforcement (reputation, termination) in long-term innovative collaborations.

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of contract doctrine beyond pure litigation enforcement (efficiency, fairness, and doctrinal fit)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares efficiency, doctrinal tradition, fairness, and intellectual property perspectives to recommend disclosure rules, whereas Paper B questions enforcement-centered accounts and offers a normative/functional account of why formal contracting is valuable even absent credible litigation threats.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1994wislrev331!!ARTICLE: STRUGGLING WITH QUICKSAND: THE INs AND OUTs OF COTENANT POSSESSION VALUE LIABILITY AND A CALL FOR DEFAULT RULE REFORM Copyright 1994, Evelyn Alicia Lewis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STRUGGLING WITH QUICKSAND: THE INs AND OUTs OF COTENANT POSSESSION VALUE LIABILITY AND A CALL FOR DEFAULT RULE REFORM Copyright 1994, Evelyn Alicia Lewis.

shared_topics.topic: design and normative evaluation of default rules in private law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how default legal rules should be designed and evaluated: Paper A examines the competing default-rule systems that allocate rental liability among cotenants and proposes a reformed default rule, while Paper B critiques prevailing models of disclosure defaults in contract law and proposes alternative rules (e.g., 'Word to the Wise') for two-sided informational settings.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of entitlements and liabilities among co-parties in the absence of agreement
shared_topics.justification: Both works focus on how the law allocates rights and burdens when parties have not contracted: Paper A studies how cotenants are assigned rental rights and liability by default, and Paper B studies how buyer/seller informational asymmetries are treated by default doctrines (nondisclosure, mistake, rescission).

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of legal rules on party behavior and information investment
shared_topics.justification: Each paper is concerned with the behavioral incentives created by legal rules: Paper B analyzes how disclosure or silence rules affect incentives to search for and produce private information (and whether rules should protect those incentives), while Paper A examines how default rental-liability rules shape cotenants' incentives to rent, share benefits, or litigate.

shared_topics.topic: tension between domain-specific doctrines and general default/contract theory and non-efficiency values
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with conflicts between specialized substantive doctrines and general theoretical accounts: Paper A tests property-based cotenancy rules against general default-rule theory and recognizes doctrinal tensions, and Paper B evaluates disclosure rules not only for efficiency but against longstanding contract doctrine, morality, and fairness.

shared_topics.topic: judicial application and doctrinal backdrop of the rules
shared_topics.justification: Each paper pays close attention to how courts apply doctrinal rules and the existing doctrinal landscape: Paper A compares how judiciaries actually apply competing cotenancy default systems, and Paper B reviews doctrinal precedents (e.g., Hadley v. Baxendale, mistake/nondisclosure doctrines) as the backdrop for its theoretical model.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT

shared_topics.topic: legal treatment of mistake and nondisclosure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a formal model of buyer nondisclosure and analyzes competing doctrinal proposals (Kronman's silence-is-golden, Levmore's optimal dishonesty) and their fit with unilateral mistake rules; Paper B explicitly analyzes the mistake and excuse doctrines as examples of equitable interventions that courts use to realign formal terms with perceived contractual intent.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape incentives to acquire, reveal, or exploit private information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on buyers' incentives to search for and monetize private information and whether disclosure or lying rules will preserve those information‑production incentives; Paper B frames contracting choices (legal vs relational enforcement, precise vs vague terms) in terms of front‑end and back‑end information and verification costs that determine parties' incentives to gather and rely on information.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between enforcing formal contract terms and permitting equitable/judicial correction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts doctrinally permissive rules (allowing deception) with minimal truthful‑disclosure rules and assesses their coherence with traditional contract doctrine; Paper B critiques the modern two‑stage regime that lets courts override formal terms via equity and argues for stricter enforcement of formal terms unless parties expressly delegate corrective authority.

shared_topics.topic: balancing efficiency with doctrinal, moral, and fairness considerations in choosing rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares efficiency outcomes of Alternative rules (Optimal Dishonesty vs Word to the Wise) but also weighs fairness, doctrinal pedigree, and IP perspectives in recommending a rule; Paper B grounds its defense of formalist enforcement in a contract‑design efficiency argument while acknowledging doctrinal history and the normative implications of equitable intervention.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design choices (precision vs vagueness; ex ante allocation of enforcement) interact with doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's enriched model of two‑sided informational inputs leads to recommendations about disclosure rules that affect how parties will structure bargains and share information; Paper B develops a detailed theory of contract design—precise vs vague terms, legal vs relational means—and shows how doctrinal enforcement regimes either enable or frustrate those ex ante design strategies.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL PRODUCTS: ISSUES PERTAINING TO DERIVATIVE MARKET PARTICIPANTS AND THEIR RELATIONSHIPS

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE TEXAS RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION LIABILITY ACT: FRAMEWORK FOR CHANGE

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules about interpretation and disclosure shape parties' incentives to create, reveal, or withhold information when contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights economic, institutional, and behavioral advantages motivating textualist or contextualist stances and proposes context-dependent rules that will affect contracting behavior; Paper B explicitly models the incentives to search for information, to disclose or conceal it, and how different legal doctrines alter those incentives and socially optimal information production.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev681!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats silence and other non-verbal or non-textual information as communicative (examining when silence must be disclosed or can signal private information), and Paper B addresses whether arbitrators may or should admit extrinsic evidence (past practice, negotiations) when the contract text appears plain.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules allocate incentives to generate, reveal, or rely on information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly models how disclosure rules (Silence-is-Golden, Optimal Dishonesty, Word-to-the-Wise) affect a buyer's incentive to search for and exploit private information, while Paper B shows how interpretive rules (plain meaning versus contextual approaches) shape parties' drafting, bargaining, and reliance incentives in collective bargaining and arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: conflict between formalist/textualist rules and contextual/intent-focused approaches in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques treating silence as a unitary formal rule and favors a richer account of signaling and context, and Paper B critiques the plain meaning textualist rule and argues for alternatives that incorporate context and parties' intentions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2texwesleyanlrev467!!ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Texas law's requirements for proving lost profits—competent, objective evidence and reasonable certainty—and argues regression can satisfy that evidentiary burden; Paper B analyzes contract doctrines of nondisclosure and mistake, asking when one party must reveal private information and thus what level of disclosed information is legally sufficient to support or avoid contractual liability.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes admissible competent evidence (routinely kept business records and objective data) from speculative, subjective opinion and explains when first‑hand testimony suffices; Paper B interrogates the normative and doctrinal treatment of private informational advantages (buyers' specialized information), weighing incentives to generate information against doctrines that might obligate or protect disclosure.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

papers.node_id: 43hastingslj1!!ARTICLE: Mistake, Frustration, and the Windfall Principle of Contract Remedies.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Mistake, Frustration, and the Windfall Principle of Contract Remedies.
papers.abstract:
The problems we call "mistake" and "frustration" are described in contract doctrine as if they were exceptional conditions, when in fact they are endemic to the bargain transaction.They are ordinarily treated as separate topics, when in fact they represent aspects of the same phenomenon.  And while mistake and frustration are traditionally thought to constitute grounds for relief from contractual obligation, a more accurate generalization is that a court finding mistake or frustration willdenyrelief, whether it is being asked to force a transaction ahead or to undo one that has been wholly or partially performed.
A substantial body of case law supports an important but unacknowledged rule of contract doctrine: that the proper legal response to certain problems resulting from contracts that are "incomplete" or "not fully specified" is to leave the parties alone.  Such a rule stands in sharp contrast to the usual prescription of modern commentary, which recommendsthat "gaps" in contracts be "filled" by judicial intervention to serve a variety of social ends.  The question thus arises whether the traditional rule may not serve the same or equally valuable ends with equal or greater efficiency.
This Article proposes (1) a unified conceptual model for describing the problem of mistake and frustration; (2) a hypothesis about the case law; (3) a review of the case law to defend the hypothesis; and (4) an argument against the prevailing academic conception that sees a mistaken or frustrated contract as an occasion for judicial intervention in the form of "gap-filling."

questions.question: Whether the problems labeled as mistake and frustration are manifestations of the same underlying phenomenon of contractual incompleteness (i.e., whether they should be understood and analyzed as a unified concept).
Whether courts in practice follow a rule of non-intervention-denying remedial relief and leaving the parties to their bargain-when contracts are incomplete or go awry.

Whether leaving parties alone (denying relief) in cases of contractual incompleteness produces equal or greater efficiency or social welfare than judicial intervention to fill gaps or provide remedial relief.

papers.node_id: 56clevstlrev613!!ARTICLE: MODELS AND GAMES: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EXPLANATION AND UNDERSTANDING FOR LAWYERS AND ETHICISTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: MODELS AND GAMES: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EXPLANATION AND UNDERSTANDING FOR LAWYERS AND ETHICISTS
papers.abstract:
Mine is an unusual pragmatic agenda, because I am not as interested in the particular problems lawyers face as much as I am in how they think about the problems. With all due respect to Edward Levi's classic tome,I have never been quite sure what it means to reason (or think) like a lawyer.Langdellian legal formalism, or legal realist contextualism, critical legal theory, and the variants of law and economics that currently dominate the legal academy are all ways of making sense of what is going on around us. They are the "theories" we use to organize thedata. In those cases, the theory (we hope) has academic rigor, but we have colloquial "theories" all the time in everyday life. "Here's my theory why so-and-so got denied tenure" is not a statement of scientific theory, but it is an attempt at explanation of human behavior in a causal sense--we are amateur historians trying to make sense why something happened.
propose to organize "thinking like a lawyer" in terms of our approach to complex constructs of rules that appear to us in some instances to be games and in other instances to be models. A lawyer can be modeler, game creator, or game player. A lawyer writing the provision of a business acquisition agreement that describes the business being sold is amodeler.A lawyer writing the procedural rules in the agreement for resolving the post-closing price adjustment, or for determining whose counsel will have primary responsibility for defending a third party claim under the indemnification provision is agame creator.The lawyer litigating these issues in arbitration or in court is agame player.To engage in any of those acts is to use the legally trained mind to make sense of what is going on, and to act on it. But there are different ways of making sense, and it is not common in legal education to undertake the exercise of thinking about thinking, or theorizing about theory. That is what I intend to do here.
There is certainly nothing wrong with modeling--legal formalism, or law and economics, being examples--as a way of making sense of human behavior. But lawyers, it seems to me, need to recognize that "thinking like a lawyer" (at least in the formal or economic way) is very much a cultural phenomenon of the last 150 years or so. Indeed, thinking of the law as a science, as Langdell did when he developed the case method, means that the lawyer thinks as objectively about human affairs as a physicist might about atomic particles. The French philosopher Gabriel Marceau described this mindset, and it strikes me as one we might well want in our legal advisor:[T]he scientist, in his conception of the external world, is and must be completely a realist; he is concerned with an order of truths which he must consider as wholly outside of, and completely distinct from, his own self. . . . With the scientist, the self has, in so far as it possibly can, vanished away. His task is to bring order into a world which is as little as possiblehis ownparticular world, which is as much as possibletheworld in general; and from his own point of view, it is certainly not up to him to ask whether this notion of "the world in general" is a fiction.But what if the world of the lawyer as scientist turns out to be a fiction? If the lawyer has bought into the notion that the world really is governed by the assumptions of rational actor economics, or that the business is in reality nothing more than a particular arithmetic result one gets by pushing revenue and cost data into the model created by generally accepted accounting principles, can something go wrong?
[T]he scientist, in his conception of the external world, is and must be completely a realist; he is concerned with an order of truths which he must consider as wholly outside of, and completely distinct from, his own self. . . . With the scientist, the self has, in so far as it possibly can, vanished away. His task is to bring order into a world which is as little as possiblehis ownparticular world, which is as much as possibletheworld in general; and from his own point of view, it is certainly not up to him to ask whether this notion of "the world in general" is a fiction.
My answer is "yes." There are games we can play that are not a fiction. Trying a case or playing football is real. Negotiating a business acquisition is real. There are models we can create (including using games as models) that are fictions in the sense that we understand, generally, that they mimic or illuminate, but are not the real thing. If we are being responsible in public company disclosure practice, we understand that generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP") create just such a model. But what if we lose that sense of objectivity about GAAP, and itbecomesthe game? That is, we attribute thingness to the financial statements. What if we lose sight of the places in which the business acquisitionmodelsan understanding, and begin to believe itcreatesan understanding?
The business ethics literature is replete with evidence that unethical behavior often has less to do with conscious moral choice than with the perceptual frames in which people make decisions. Professors Tenbrunsel and Messick argue, for example, that "ethical fading" is the "process by which the moral colors of an ethical decision fade into bleached hues that are void of moral implications."What many businesses call "ethics training" is useless because "individuals do not 'see' the moral components of an ethical decision"; instead "psychological processes fade the 'ethics' from an ethical dilemma."
Like other observers of ethical behavior, I see no route to ethics other than theorizing how our minds frame and rationalize moral decisions.My contribution is that the lawyer's or the ethicist's skill in identifying legal constructs as games or models is one route to effective ethical, moral, and legal counseling in the business and transactional environment. In psychological terms, it questions the decision-making frames. In philosophical terms, it poses the ontological question, What is real? Practicing lawyers (or law professors) need to think aboutthinking itselfor face the possibility of being misled by precisely the same context facing their clients.In short, lawyers need to be pragmatic ontologists.
There are two polarities that lead me to games and models as one way of thinking about thinking. The first is a first person-third person polarity. This is another way of stating H.L.A. Hart's seminal treatment of the internal versus external point of view. Hart contended that rules are something more than mere habits that an external observer could record; rules are matters of obligation and not merelypatterns of regularity. It is not merely an observable habit that chess players move particularly pieces in particular ways; the players themselves "have a reflective critical attitude to this pattern of behavior: they regard it as a standard for all who play the game."The rules of conduct in chess, for example, have ameaningfor the game players that might not be readily apparent to the external observer.Take the example of a traffic light. The external point of view observes the regularities of behavior, and begins to make predictions about whether conduct will meet with hostile reaction or punishment. We begin to observe that cars facing red lights stop, and those that do not stop cause accidents, or get tickets, or are honked at by other drivers. To the internal point of view, the red light or green light is more than prediction of behavior; it means something (red = stop or green = go) with regard to their own behavior.Michael Moore distinguishes explanation (in Hart's external sense) from non-natural meaning (in Hart's internal sense), even though we can say, externally, red lightsmeanthat cars will stop, in the same way we can use the phrase "cloudsmeanrain" to suggest a predictive natural relationship.
The second polarity has to do with how some constructs of rules differ from others in their relative "thingness" or "aboutness." There have been occasional references to this in the academic literature. June Carbone quoted an unidentified Stanford professor to the effect that what distinguishes the law of property is the "thingness of it."Another commentator coined the concept of "aboutness" with regard to contracts.In his classic essay, Arthur Leff observed that the "paper with words" that accompanies a consumer product really is athingin the nature of a label or a warning, rather than a contract to which the ill-fitting precepts of contract law apply.Leff as well saw something different about property; he observed that Hohfeld's vocabulary of claims, privileges, powers, and immunities in property failed to take hold not because of any failure in the analysis, "but more of the fact that a farm, for instance, bundle of powers, privileges, rights, etc. or not, persists in the consciousness as 'dirt with boundaries.'"Perhaps the most extensive treatment of "thingness" is Michael Madison's consideration of the ways in which the lawshould treat intangible things that come into being as the result of design, contract, practice or policy.
Neither polarity, it seems to me, fully accounts for the way lawyers in practice interact with rules. My thesis is that the two polarities--first person-third person and aboutness-thingness--come together if we think about constructs of rules as games versus models. Games and models, including legal games and models, are both constructs of rules. Games are real in a way that models are not. Games have thingness--an independent reality, and models have aboutness--they map onto something else that is real. But models and games are not dichotomous as the preceding claim makes them out to be. Sometimes models look just like games, and sometimes games can serve as models. Because models look like games, we may come to believe they are real--that the models have thingness rather than aboutness. People are prone to think some of the models they deal in all the time are real, like games, and perhaps even more real than the reality the models are supposed to represent. When that happens unreflectively in business, ethical and legal problems can ensue.
While I believe the distinction between games and models ultimately comports with our common intuitions, and is helpful in making sense of what lawyers do, I also acknowledge this is an ambitious recasting of the philosophy of rules, and thus need to provide some concrete examples in law and business.In Part II, I explorethe idea of contrasting legal constructs as games and legal constructs as models in more depth. First, what do I mean by "game" and what do I mean by "model"? Second, what does it mean to claim that a game is real and has "thingness" or that a model is not real and has "aboutness"? How does the complexity of games and models contribute to confusion between the two? Finally, what kinds of legal constructs have more "thingness" than other areas of the law that have model-like "aboutness"? I use examples from commercial law (Article 2 is model-like; Article 9 is game-like), business association law (corporations are somewhat more game-like and partnerships are somewhat more model-like), and contracts (those elements of a business acquisition agreement, like the description of the business being sold, that are model-like, and those, like the post-closing price adjustment or the indemnification rules, that are game-like).
In Part III, I explore the consequence of confusing games and models in two contexts, and consider the co-optation from models into games and vice versa. The first context is financial accounting. Language itself is a kind of game (so the philosophers of language teach us) reflecting shared understandings of linguistic communities. The language of accounting is complex and nuanced, but, I contend, ultimately intended to assist business managers in creating financial models of their businesses. But the power of the language game is such that participants in the financial reporting process can be co-opting into the game of accounting rather than using accounting to model, as accurately as possible, the reality of an underlying business. The second context is contract interpretation. I consider how a law-and-economics approach to contract interpretation uses a model versus a game approach, and hence fails to appreciate that modelers and game players often view differently what constitutes a satisfactory statement why something happened the way it did.
In Part IV, I explore the consequences for lawyers of failing to distinguish between legal games and legal models, or more positively, the benefits they bring as compliance officers and transaction counselors when they are able to assess the patterns--game or model--they and other participants in the bigger game of business are using to organize their sensory data. I address this in two different aspects: effectiveness as a transactional lawyer, and the possibility of the tainting of ethical or compliance judgment. In Part V, I attempt to reconcile my game-model distinction, and its attendant concerns about scientific explanation and attributive cause-and-effect, into the intellectual history of the social sciences of the last hundred years.
. LEGAL CONSTRUCTS AS GAMES AND MODELSSomeone says to me: "Shew the children a game." I teach them gaming with dice, and the other says "That sort of game isn't what I meant."

questions.question: Does confusing legal constructs that are models (representations) with constructs that are games (real rule-governed practices) lead lawyers to make flawed explanatory, normative, or ethical judgments in transactional and compliance settings?
How do lawyers' roles as modelers, game creators, and game players influence their reasoning, advice, and decision-making when interacting with complex rule systems?
Which kinds of rule-constructs tend to be more model-like versus more game-like, and how does that ontological difference affect behavior, interpretation, negotiation, and dispute resolution?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2020michstlrev643!!ARTICLE: THE PROTEAN CONCEPT OF MATERIALITY IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PROTEAN CONCEPT OF MATERIALITY IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether a contractual term is 'material' or 'essential' to the agreement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes how courts decide whether a term or matter is 'material' across multiple contract doctrines; Paper A treats certain contract components (e.g., price or the description of the business vs indemnification or post-closing adjustment rules) as differing in centrality by characterizing some terms as model-like (aboutness) and others as game-like (thingness), affecting whether they will be treated as core to the deal.

shared_topics.topic: the context- and doctrine-specific nature of contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that materiality is protean and must be determined with attention to the specific doctrinal purpose and facts of each dispute; Paper A likewise emphasizes that whether to treat a contractual construct as a model or a game depends on the transactional and adjudicative context, so interpretation is situation-dependent rather than uniform.

shared_topics.topic: the ontological status of contractual and accounting representations (thingness versus aboutness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an explicit distinction between constructs that have 'thingness' (games, durable realities) and those that have 'aboutness' (models, representations) and warns of harms when models are reified; Paper B's inquiry into materiality similarly turns on whether a term is treated as fundamentally real/essential to the parties' bargain or as a peripheral representational detail, making ontological status central to legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive or theoretical frameworks (law-and-economics, formalism, fairness/policy) shape contract outcomes and compliance risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how adopting model-driven frameworks (e.g., law-and-economics, accounting models) can reframe lawyers' judgments and produce ethical or compliance blind spots; Paper B shows that materiality determinations are malleable in light of the policies, goals, and equities of each doctrinal inquiry, so differing theoretical commitments change who wins and what remedies follow.

shared_topics.topic: the allocation between subjective/internal perspectives and objective/external ones (and the fact-versus-law question) in contract disputes

papers.node_id: 104harvlrev375!!ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.
papers.title: ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.
papers.abstract:
"If he doesn't pull this off, he's got to live with the shame."So one investment adviser explained Henry Kravis' efforts to refinanceRJR Nabisco's faltering junk bonds.The notion that Kravis has a highly developed sense of shame may strike observers of the financial markets as anomalous.But the skeptical view would underestimates the extra-legal forces that help maintain the functioning of markets.  Kravis' concern for the plight of bondholders was induced not by fear of legal liability -- it is reasonably clear that the bonds imposed no legally enforceable duty to refinance-- but rather by an array ofnonlegalpressures.  For example, Kravis clearly desired to maintain his, and RJR Nabisco's, reputation among potential bond purchasers.
Kravis' transactions with the bondholders are typical.  Virtually all commercial transactions involve nonlegal commitments -- commitments enforced only or predominantly by nonlegal sanctions such as concern for reputation.  Although transactors regularly rely upon these commitments, they are not enforceable under the standard rules of contract formation and interpretation.
The phenomenon appears in two aspects.  First, transactors frequently fail to place their commitments in a form that satisfies the criteria for legal enforceability.  For example, banks extend loans and lines of credit on the basis of oral understandings that are not embodied in a loan document or that vary the document's terms.Consumers are bombarded by a welter of competing product claims that may be too vague or too informal to support legal enforceability under standard contract doctrine.Farmers make, and buyers rely upon,oral promises to sell crops, although the promises are unenforceable under the Uniform Commercial Code's statute-of-frauds provision.Employers make, and workers rely upon, oral commitments to pay pensions, even though these commitments are often held to be unenforceable under federal pension law.
, transactors often place their commitments in legally enforceable form but then attach disclaimers of legal liability.  For example, corporate managers execute elaborate but explicitly nonbinding "agreements in principle" for corporate mergers.For millions of workers, handbooks or other documents that specify the norms of theworkplace -- including provisions governing wages, promotions, benefits and pensions, and grounds for dismissal -- clearly disclaim the creation of any legal obligation.
The pervasiveness of these nonlegal commitments is evident.  Much less apparent is why transactors -- even sophisticated transactors in complex markets -- rely on these legally unenforceable promises.  The phenomenon cannot be convincingly explained without an understanding of the role of nonlegal sanctions as an alternative mechanism for enforcing commitments.
This Article attempts to provide that understanding of nonlegal sanctions and to lay the foundation for the proper regulation of nonlegal commitments by the legal system.  Part II begins that task by exploring the theoretical backdrop for the analysis.  It explains how a better understanding of nonlegal sanctions can fill conceptual gaps in liberal, communitarian, and instrumentalist theories of contract law.  The Article then undertakes a three-stage analysis of the role of nonlegal sanctions.
Part III explains how rational transactors decide between legal and nonlegal "sanctioning systems." After describing the different forms of nonlegal sanctions and the circumstances in which legal and nonlegal sanctions are equivalent, this Part analyzes conditions under which parties would find it less costly to use nonlegal sanctions exclusively, rather than structuring commitments so that they are legally enforceable as well.
Part IV then argues that, when transactors have not acted rationally, legal decisionmakers may be able to improve transactors' welfare by enforcing commitments that the parties left to nonlegal sanctions.  Legal intervention can, in theory, correct information deficiencies that lead parties to rely mistakenly on nonlegal sanctions.In particular, high information and drafting costs, or poor judgment by naive or improvident transactors, may justify legal intervention.
Part V contends that the previous analysis commends a significant reformulation of current contract and commercial law doctrines governing the enforceability of nonlegal commitments.  In general, legal decisionmakers should defer to the parties' decision about whether their commitments may be legally enforced.  Legal decisionmakers should, however, evaluate that decision in light of the parties' rational assessment, at the time of contracting, of the availability of nonlegal sanctions and the effectiveness of those sanctions in ensuring compliance.  Legal decisionmakers should intervene sparingly, only when the parties' assessment was significantly mistaken.  To illustrate this approach, Part V proposes a revision of:for the legal system to improve the welfare of transactors, promissory estoppel, like the other extracontractual doctrines currently used to regulate nonlegal commitments, must explicitly acknowledge and analyze nonlegal sanctions.  Part V also recommends new approaches to contract interpretation and administrative regulation of commercial transactions.

papers.node_id: 98iowalrev535!!ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing
papers.title: ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing
papers.abstract:
Normative legal theories aim to say what the law should be. They make proposals for changing the law and provide standards for evaluating existing laws and other proposals. They currently dominate the leading legal scholarship. It is important to understand what successful such theories would look like. By making it possible to justify and criticize laws soundly, normative legal theories undergird the legal system's legitimacy.
On one dimension, there are only two kinds of theories - "pluralist" and "monist." Robust pluralist theories take all relevant values into account and balance them when they compete.A pluralist theory of contract law, for example, might consider freedom of and freedom from contract, contractual security, fairness, and Rule of Law values, including administrability.The only relevant alternative type of theory is a monist theory. A monist theory takes one and only one value into account and, consequently, hopes to avoid balancing competing values. A monist theory of contract law, for example, might rest on economic efficiency, autonomy, promise, consent, transfer, Aristotelian ethics, or reliance.
Over the last four decades, monist theories have proliferated, notably those based on efficiency.Monists object to pluralist theories' need tobalance values when they compete.Monists, however, have not adequately justified this objection. Pluralists have done little to defend their turf. No one has thoroughly considered the clash between them in the legal context.
This clash matters. In the United States, much intractable ideological conflict currently threatens social cohesion, political functionality, and respect for the law. Factions square off in large part because each takes a monist value seriously. It would be unfortunate for this kind of conflict to infect the law, though it has done so already to some extent, at least in the legal academy.
This Article presents the case for pluralism and balancing in normative legal theories. It argues that both pluralist and monist theories pursue the same normative goal - to justify final recommendations about what the law should be, all things considered, insofar as the state of the art permits. At any stage of development, a theory fails if it is not capable of achieving this goal. In two crucial respects (finality and inclusiveness), pluralist theories are capable of success. Monist theories are not. Because no other kinds of theories are relevant, it follows logically that all normative legal theories should be pluralist.
Part I introduces and explains the ultimate goal of all normative legal theories. Part II distinguishes pluralism and monism, and it illustrates a pluralist theory with a recent theory of contract interpretation. Part III advances the normative case for pluralism and balancing, showing that pluralist theories are capable of achieving the normative goal. Part IV turns to the monist alternative, illustrates it with a competing theory of contract interpretation, and demonstrates that monist theories are not capable of achieving the goal. Together, Parts I through IV make the normative case for pluralism and balancing. Part V raises the question: Why would anyone be a monist? It suggests that monists probably think that monism has non-normative advantages over pluralism due to coherence, epistemic, and Rule of Law concerns. Pluralism and monism, however, both fall short of these ideals. Consequently, the choice between them should turn on their comparative normative virtues. On that score, this Article concludes, pluralism is clearly superior.

questions.question: Should normative legal theories adopt a pluralist approach-balancing multiple relevant values-instead of a monist, single-value approach in order to produce justified, all-things-considered recommendations about what the law should be?

Are monist (single-value) normative legal theories capable of achieving the core normative goal of providing final, inclusive, and justifiable legal recommendations, or do they systematically fail compared with pluralist theories?
Do the non-normative advantages claimed for monism (e.g., greater coherence, epistemic clarity, or Rule of Law benefits) justify preferring monist theories over pluralist, balancing approaches?

papers.node_id: 87nclrev1699!!ARTICLE: NORTH CAROLINA COMMON LAW PAROL EVIDENCE RULE*
papers.title: ARTICLE: NORTH CAROLINA COMMON LAW PAROL EVIDENCE RULE*
papers.abstract:
The thrust of the parol evidence rule ("PER") is to make written terms effective as the terms of a contract as a matter of law. That sounds like a relatively simple and unobjectionable function. In reality, the rule has so eluded reason as to inspire a whole catalog of dark metaphor and phantasmagorical description for which it is famous.Such is its associated uncertainty and confusion that Eric Posner recently observed that "in virtually every jurisdiction, one finds … cries of despair."Despite the odds, much has been written in an attempt to bring a measure of predictability and uniformity to the case law. Such efforts might have been more successful but for a fundamental split between the two greatest authorities of the past century, Samuel Williston and Arthur L. Corbin.The fervency of their disagreement about the PER diluted whatever potential their work might otherwise have had in clarifying the law; arguably it merely fed the prevalent confusion and hysteria, resulting in a kind ofjudicial hopelessness. So great has been their influence that it is nearly impossible to talk about what the courts do with the PER without characterizing it by reference to Williston or Corbin.
In North Carolina, the exploration of the PER was conducted by giants in the law. In 1932, a seminal articlewas co-authored by Dean Charles T. McCormickand James H. Chadbourn,who was then editor-in-chief of the North Carolina Law Review. In 1955, John P. Dalzell brought their work up to date in a second piece.Their work provides a secure foundation for this Article. Because the subject is timeless, the recommendations of these luminaries remain sterling even after so many years, and it is with a heightened sense of responsibility to their legacy and to the practitioners and judges of this state who have benefited from it that this reassessment of the rule is undertaken.
Part I of this Article demonstrates the confusion and complexity of the PER. Its origins are examined, highlighting an irrational mystical belief in the talismanic quality of the written word that has little to do with real transactions. Part II provides a simple Discussion Model to serve as a convenient point of reference, so that the reader may follow the discussion in the outline of the rule. The very heated controversy between Corbin and Williston is described in Part III. These preliminary parts of this Article provide important background for Part IV, which explicates the case law in North Carolina. Part IV has a number of divisions, which either mirror or extend the organization of the rule shown in the Discussion Model of Part II and are typical of most, if not all, PERs. The issue of finality is emphasized and the application of a poorly crafted presumption of finality and completeness is criticized. Because the law pertaining to interpretation has influenced PER analysis in North Carolina, attention is given to an array of tests for ambiguity. Part V undertakes a more sophisticated look at the rule, pulling together the prior text and offering some suggestions for practice in North Carolina and in other states with similar rules. The conclusion begs the courts to avoid the great potential for harm that the PERthreatens, urging them to fashion a coherent rule with more predictable and humane results.

questions.question: How do courts in North Carolina interpret and apply the parol evidence rule to decide when extrinsic (prior or contemporaneous) statements may be used to alter, explain, or supplement written agreements, and how consistent and predictable are those applications?
Does treating written agreements as presumptively final and complete (a presumption of finality) lead to distorted, unjust, or otherwise harmful outcomes in contract disputes?
How do competing doctrinal frameworks for admitting or excluding prior negotiations and understandings affect judicial decisionmaking under the parol evidence rule?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty and the need for coherent, predictable rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers diagnose confusion and inconsistent judicial application in core contract doctrines — Paper A criticizes the chaotic case law and calls for a coherent parol evidence rule in North Carolina, while Paper B documents that frustration of purpose is often acknowledged in theory but rarely applied, raising concerns about doctrinal incoherence and predictability.

shared_topics.justification: Both articles wrestle with boundary problems among doctrines — Paper A analyzes how tests for ambiguity and rules about finality affect parol evidence inquiries, and Paper B closely distinguishes frustration of purpose from impossibility, impracticability, and related concepts and critiques courts' tendency to conflate them.

shared_topics.topic: the role of policy considerations in judicial willingness to excuse or enforce bargains
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines how non‑doctrinal policy choices shape outcomes — Paper A urges courts to avoid harm and fashion humane, predictable PER outcomes, and Paper B catalogs policy reasons courts have refused to grant relief for frustrated purposes even while recognizing the doctrine abstractly.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of treatises, major authorities, and the Restatements on doctrinal development
shared_topics.justification: Both works trace how prominent authorities have shaped courts' approaches — Paper A emphasizes the Williston/Corbin divide and its impact on PER jurisprudence, while Paper B discusses treatise and Restatement endorsement of frustration and how that contrasts with actual case law application.

shared_topics.topic: the idea of doctrines as 'gap-fillers' or implied conditions affecting finality and contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Each article addresses whether certain doctrines should operate as implied legal conditions or default gap-fillers — Paper A critiques presumptions of finality and completeness under the PER, and Paper B evaluates whether frustration of purpose functions (or fails to function) as a true gap-filling basis for discharge of obligations.
