papers.node_id: 67buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts
papers.authors: Gaston De Los Reyes; Kirsten Martin
papers.abstract:
Today's leading theories of economic governance converge on the premise that humans frequently interact with each other strategically,as game theory would suggest, and also opportunistically, bending or breaking rules to their advantage.The seminal rendering of the concept is given by Nobel LaureateOliver Williamson. The opportunism that grounds his theory of transaction cost economics is defined as "self-interest seeking with guile," where guile refers to "incomplete or distorted disclosure of information, [and] especially to calculated efforts to mislead, distort, disguise, obfuscate, or otherwise confuse."
Few concepts have been more pivotal to contract law scholarship over the last forty years than the opportunism attributed ex ante and ex post to contracting parties.The observed and presumed tendency to act opportunistically through "calculated efforts … to mislead, renege, cheat or otherwise take advantage of the vulnerabilities of … trading partners,"has been invoked to make sense of the entire warp and woof of the subject. Parties are said to make contracts to forestall opportunism,and contracts are said to break down for failing to do so.Courts of law and, especially, equity are seen to have evolved the doctrines they did to counteract opportunism,and decade after decade scholars have called on courts to mitigate opportunism in contracting.
Self-interest seeking with guile comes in many flavors; every one presupposes a covertness without which the opportunistic gambit would go nowhere. Consider the following anecdotes:
Anecdote 1. A bank has an agreement with a client to provide checking account services in exchange for a fee and/or minimum deposits. The bank adds additional services to the client account without notice or permission, and deducts the corresponding fees from the client's checking account.
Anecdote 2. A customer pays a down payment to a builder. The builder skips town with the down payment.
Anecdote 1 is modeled on the recent Wells Fargo scandal. This "too big to fail" bank,between 2009 and 2016, drew funds from the millions of fake accounts its agents opened, without the request of its unsuspecting customers, because the customers were unsuspecting.By the same token, the builder in Anecdote 2 who converts the down payment gets to take the cash because the client did not suspect the scheme afoot.These two examples epitomize the forward-lookingdissembling which is the hallmark of the blatant form of opportunism that Williamson's first book, Markets and Hierarchies: Analysis and Antitrust Implications,helped make central to theorizing in contract law.
In the voluminous literature that has ensued - not only in lawbut also in economics,management,and organization theory- scholars have plumbed the many-sided depths of opportunism conceptualized as self-interestseeking with guile (henceforth, "blatant" opportunism).What theorists (of all fields) have nevertheless overlooked, and contract law scholarship has yet to expressly incorporate into its conceptual canon, is the novel species of "lawful" opportunism that Williamson identified as part of his 1991 revamping of transaction cost economics.
Lawful opportunism is the chief transaction cost concern that Williamson highlights in accounting for a third "mode" of governance to complement the markets and hierarchies that titled his first book."Hybrid" governance, as termedby Williamson, comprises the off-the-market, customized, negotiated, and yet arms-length transactions that organizations and people pursue jointly without the advantages of a price mechanismto standardize terms over large numbers of participants.This is the realm of freely negotiated relations and dealings, and the contract law that provides its institutional foundation is the common law of contracts from a typical first-year Contracts course. These deals are not the sales contracts governed by the UniformCommercial Code,the contractual relations covered by employment law,or the boilerplate that causes so many conceptual difficulties in consumer law.Rather, this is the domain of free contract, where "the principle of private autonomy"continues to hold sway.
In Williamson's treatment, contracts become susceptible to lawful opportunism "as disturbances become highly consequential … [and] the "lawful' gains to be had by insistence upon literal enforcement exceed the discounted value of continuing the exchange relationship."Beyond this cost-benefit tipping point, the worry - for Williamson as a theorist and for entrepreneurs and managers as contracting parties - is that "strict enforcement would have truly punitive consequences … resulting [in] "injustice' … supported by (lawful) opportunism."
To appreciate the difference between guileful opportunism (Anecdotes 1 and 2) and its lawful kin,consider the following anecdotes featuring strict enforcement with arguably punishing judgments of enforcement:
Anecdote 3. A tenant leases land from a landlord for four years, without addressing obligations if the tenant cannot occupy the land. After the first annual payment, the tenant is driven from the land by an occupying army during a civil war and ceases payments. Thelandlord sues the tenant for the missing lease payments.
Anecdote 4. A concert promoter and a theater owner agree that the promoter will pay $ 100 per night to rent the venue for four nights, without addressing what happens if the owner cannot provide the theater. The theater burns down, and both parties suffer economic losses. The promoter sues to recover its specific investments (promotional expenses), claiming breach of contract.
Anecdote 5. A-Corp is building a power plant and requires environmental emissions credits. A-Corp enters into a deal to purchase the required credits from B-Corp, without addressing what happens if B-Corp cannot deliver the credits. B-Corp's credits are revoked by the regulator, and the trading price for the needed credits more than doubles. A-Corp sues B-Corp for the increase in price.
The actions taken by the plaintiff-parties to realize damage awards in these examples are not defined by (and do not require) trickery or deception, as with the first set of anecdotes. On the contrary, since the conduct amounts to the pressing of legal entitlements to recover a damage award - whether through oral demands or the filing of a complaint - the counterparty's express awareness is a precondition to the efficacy of the exercise.
What drives parties to act in lawfully opportunistic ways?Williamson's high-level sketch demarcates theeconomic cost-benefit tipping point that makes legal enforcement attractive next to relationship-preserving alternatives in a specific context: contractual calamity beyond the bounds of the bargain.In addition, the account specifies the institutional fault line at the root of lawful opportunism to be the willingness of courts to hear claims for "the "lawful' gains to be had by insistence upon literal enforcement" where a highly consequential disturbance has undercut the spirit of the deal that was bargained.
Beyond this economic and institutional analysis, Williamson does not explore the individual characteristics that tend to give rise to lawful opportunism, his focus being the institutional (macro-level) implications for governance.If the willingness to act with guile stokes blatant forms of opportunism (like Wells Fargo's swindling), what characteristic animates lawful opportunism? Absent a micro-level conceptualization (like the character of guile provides blatant opportunism), organizational theorists and behavioral legal scholars have little foothold to break ground with empirical research that elucidates when and why parties experience lawful opportunism and, consequently, how to forestall its costs.
To fill this conceptual gap, this Article develops and extends Williamson's diagnosis that literal enforcement provokes the institutional fault line that foments lawful opportunism in Part I.This Article's further contributionin Part II is to build upon the analysis set forth in Part I with an empirical study designed to examine factors that predict variance in the propensity to press one's legal entitlements in conditions ripe for lawful opportunism. Participants were presented with a vignette that put them in the position of a contracting party who has to respond to a highly consequential disturbance that made the counterparty's performance as per the terms of the agreement impossible. Participants then selected among a range of options that were alternatively cooperative (hence tending to preserve the relationship), blatantly opportunistic (i.e., actions to appropriate value guilefully), or lawfully opportunistic in character (i.e., actions to appropriate value by enforcing, or threatening to enforce, legal entitlements). The findings concerning the propensity of participants to select lawfully opportunistic responses reinforce the conceptual conclusion that entitlement is to lawful opportunism as guile is to the blatant opportunism so well understood by scholars.
Why does all this matter for public policy and law? The fear of becoming victim to lawful opportunism - for entrepreneurs, for managers of business organizations, and for citizens at large - presents a transaction costthat dampens the potential for arms-length contracting to serve as a vehicle for ingenuity and productivity. Responding to this challenge and potential, the overarching aim of this Article is to promote the mitigation of the transaction costs of lawful opportunism through theoretical and empirical extensions of Williamson's sparse sketch of the concept.
The discussion of results is presented in Part III, and Part IV concludes.

questions.question: Whether contracting parties, when faced with a highly consequential unforeseen disruption that makes performance impossible, prefer to press their legal entitlements (seek damages or literal enforcement) rather than cooperate to preserve the relationship or resort to deceptive (guileful) opportunism.

Whether the expectation that legal authorities will strictly enforce contractual terms (literal enforcement) increases the incentive for parties to pursue lawful opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of losses after contractual disruption or excuse (impossibility/frustration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses concrete vignettes (e.g., war, fire, revoked credits) and an experiment to study how parties respond—by suing to enforce entitlements—when performance is rendered impossible or highly consequentially disturbed; Paper B directly analyzes the legal problem of who should bear reliance losses when performance is excused for impossibility/frustration and proposes a loss‑sharing rule.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tradeoff between efficiency (risk allocation/wealth maximization) and fairness in designing remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames the debate explicitly as efficiency versus fairness and argues for equal sharing of reliance losses on moral and partnership grounds; Paper A engages the same tradeoff by showing how strict, literal enforcement (efficiency‑like entitlements) can produce punitive, unjust outcomes and transaction costs, motivating normative calls to mitigate enforcement rules.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law doctrines and court enforcement shape parties' incentives and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes and empirically investigates how willingness of courts to enforce literal entitlements creates 'lawful opportunism' and raises transaction costs for arm's‑length contracting; Paper B analyzes how judicial allocation of reliance losses (the doctrinal choice) determines who bears risk, thereby affecting parties' incentives to invest, insure, or litigate and motivating doctrinal reform toward loss sharing.

papers.node_id: 121columlrev1659!!ARTICLE: OBSOLESCENCE: THE INTRACTABLE PRODUCTION PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE: OBSOLESCENCE: THE INTRACTABLE PRODUCTION PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW
papers.abstract:
Contract law has a production problem. Commercial parties require a contract law that is both efficient when it is created and also adapts efficiently when commercial circumstances change. But currently no legal institution exists that can satisfy both of these criteria. Three legal institutions produce commercial contract law today: courts, statutes that regulate discrete areas, and private lawmaking bodies that create general contract law rules.As we will show, each has limitations. Common law courts develop default rules that are efficient when they are created and are updated as economic conditions change. But lawmaking through the judicial process only produces a restricted set of general contract law rules, and updating is slow: These constraints reflect the limited capacity ofcourts to address more particular commercial practices adequately.In response, both public and private lawmaking institutions have created specialized statutes that specify rules for discrete legal areas such as secured debt, commercial paper, financial transactions, and bankruptcy.These specialized statutes are useful complements to the general law of contracts. Yet, the rules were enacted at the instance of cohesive interest groups: The public interest was poorly represented in the enactment process.The felt need for more and better rules governing the general law of contracts led the private lawmaking groups to produce the law of sales in Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) and the two Restatements of Contracts. These private lawmaking efforts developed new default rules that covered a wider range of contract law issues than the common law, but history has shown that the rules do not adapt to changing circumstances.
The source of the difficulties that plague the commercial law production process is the singular fact of obsolescence.A commercial law rule, whether a default rule or a mandatory rule, is obsolete when it is no longer "apt." An apt rule efficiently solves a "contracting problem" in the current state of the world and also solves the problem in future states of the worldthat are "relevantly similar" to the current state.But if in a future state the contracting problem takes a different form, the apt solution to the problem can change as well. An obsolescence concern exists, therefore, when a legal rule becomes inapt: That is, the rule does not solve the contracting problem in its current form.
Obsolescence is a significant concern because the commercial world of today is dissimilar in significant ways from the world that existed when our leading commercial laws were created.UCC Article 2 took its current form by 1952, and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts was completedby 1979.Neither body of law has been materially amended since then.The obsolescence concern is also present in discrete legal areas like bankruptcy that enact specific statutory solutions. The reorganization chapters of the Bankruptcy Code were last comprehensively redone in 1978.But today many insolvent firms are directly sold to the market through an ill-defined process rather than reorganized under the Code's elaborate rules.
An obsolete term in a restatement, statute, or even a private contract is not innocuous.There are two concerns. First, suppose that a UCC sales law default rule efficiently solved a contracting problem when enacted, but the world has evolved to a different state in which the problem takes a different form. The private lawmaking groups created the UCC default rule because it was too costly for contracting parties to solve the problem themselves.If it remains too costly for private agents to solve the problemefficiently in its current form, obsolescence causes parties to treat the problem with second-best solutions.The second concern with obsolescence is that a vestigial default could transition from being harmless but unhelpful to being dangerous. Such transitions can occur when a defaultapplies linguistically, but not substantively, to the current version of the parties' contracting problem. A party behaving strategically may then attempt to exploit the linguistic fit to generate an unfair or inefficient judicial interpretation in its favor.
The persistence and significant costs of obsolescence demand a critical reexamination of the institutional features of the commercial law production process. This Article focuses specifically on the comparative institutional question: How have private markets and the three legal institutions governing commercial contract law--courts, public and private rules for managing specialized areas, and general contract law codifications--fared in their responses to the obsolescence concern?
We begin that inquiry by briefly reviewing how the developments over the past one hundred years have produced our modern commercial law. For around 700 years, from 1200 to 1900,only oneinstitution--common law courts--functioned in England and America to produce commercial law.Courts could function unaided for so many years because intrinsic to common law adjudication is a mechanism for generating a particular subset of efficient contract law rules. Consider, for example, a case of firstimpression in which the parties' contract lacks a term to resolve their dispute, so the court has to fill the gap.The court's decision may become a rule when future parties recognize that the initial court's resolution of the case faces them with a choice: to respond to the first case with an express term that regulates the same dispute or to leave a gap in the contract. If a subsequent contracting dyad leaves a gap, the first case becomes a precedent in the sense that the court will resolve the later dyad's dispute with the rule that it used to resolve the initial dispute. Rules in cases thus become default terms in contracts that are written later unless parties contract out.
A court's decision can function as an efficient precedent, however, only if four conditions are satisfied: (1) Parties in other commercial contexts face the same contracting problem as the parties in the first case; (2) The solution to the problem conditions on verifiable information;(3) The later parties left a contract gap: Their agreements did not otherwise regulate the problem, thereby creating the opportunity for later courts to rule on the issue; and (4) The initial court's ruling solved the problem as the parties would have solved it had they contracted over it. But condition (4) implies condition (3): The future parties will have left a contract gap only because the rule in the first case efficiently solved their problem.
This sketch of the common law adjudication mechanism shows that a common law contract rule has two key properties. First, the rule is "transcontextual": The rule efficiently solves a contracting problem for parties functioning in diverse contexts.If the rule in the first case lacked this property, the rule would be a historical curiosity only. Future parties inother areas would not have left a contract gap, but rather would have contracted about the problem for themselves.The second property is that the rule roughly tracks changing commercial patterns. When commerce materially changes, parties do different deals under new contracts. If the future parties' contracts nevertheless also leave a gap where a solution to the problem could be found, the rule in the first case continues to function as a precedent: The rule has been "updated." But if parties functioning in new commercial situations create contracts that expressly govern the issue, the rule in the first case becomes vestigial: It has no current function. However, the common law mechanism, triggered by current disputes, will then create new rules when the four conditions specified above are satisfied.
The updating feature of the common law mechanism has an inherent limitation, however. Parties in different commercial contexts often require solutions that are specific to their circumstances. But generalist courts are ill-equipped to supply specific solutions to particular industries. The solution they suggest for a specific problem will likely not be the outcome that the parties would have specified had they contracted over the issue. That failure, in turn, implies that future parties in the industry would not leave a gap in their contract, and no default rule would be formed. Private lawmakers responded to this regulatory gap by creating discrete bodies of commercial law, including secured credit to regulate transactions between creditors and their debtors, and commercial paper and bank deposits to regulate short-term financing transactions.Many of these discrete lawmaking efforts have been regularly updated as focused interest group pressures stimulate reform proposals.Yet, this focused response to the risk of obsolescence raises a further concern: Interest group pressure producesspecialized commercial rules that are privately efficient but not necessarily socially efficient.This disregard for the public interest justifies a continuing role for general contract law rules that take broader social interests into account.
The American legal establishment long recognized, therefore, that a modern economy benefits from a law that applies to contracts generally, but for several reasons, American lawyers were unsatisfied with the common law mechanism. The first reason follows from our earlier analysis: Default rules are slow to form.Litigation must proceed over time in different contexts before a default rule is fully formed. Consequently, most of the common law default rules were developed in the nineteenth century following the Industrial Revolution, and the process of rule development slowed considerably thereafter.Because the process of developing default rules had slowed, courts had relatively few general rules with which to fill gaps in incomplete contracts.This stasis in common law rule development followed from the second reason: Courts are poor regulators of a modern economy. Courts cannot find facts, apart from case records, and so they cannot hold accurate views of the context in which a possible rule will function and the effects of current rules. In addition, judges are generalist lawyers. The typical judge has little commercial expertise and cannot effectively resolve the economic issues that a possible rule may pose. Another rule-generating mechanism was required.
Widespread dissatisfaction with the common law process produced the two major interventions that sought to change contract law itself. The first effort at a codification of contract law occurred at the turn of the twentieth century when the Uniform Law Commission (ULC) produced theUniform Sales Act.That effort soon proved obsolete, however, and throughout the interwar period only the courts were able to keep sales law current with changing commercial practice.This led to the second effort by the American Law Institute (ALI) and the ULC in the mid-twentieth century to codify the general law of contracts.Article 2 of the UCC governing sales transactions has since been enacted in every state (except Louisiana), and it was followed by the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, which usefully summarized important contract doctrines for common law courts.The Restatement also had a distinct policy focus, identifying some contract rules as better solutions to a given contracting problem than others.
The justification for the codification of general contract law rules follows from the dissatisfaction with the common law process. UCC drafters and the ALI members responsible for particular restatements are thought to be more expert and to have more real-world knowledge than the typical common law judge.Moreover, the felt need for more default rules is genuine: Private parties will not solve every contracting problem that they face.Contracting parties seldom can internalize the full gain from creating a useful solution to a common contracting problem--others can copy their innovation--but nonetheless they bear the full cost.When the cost exceeds a contracting dyad's share of the gain, the problem will not be solved efficiently without outside help. Private lawmakers can use their expertise and knowledge to solve these common problems and supply contracting parties with the solutions in the form of UCC or Restatement sections. In prior work we have criticized the rationale for this method of supplying contract terms on the ground that the ALI and ULC are alsoinstitutionally limited.The focus here, however, is on the deeper institutional problem. As discussed above, a public program of supplying contract law rules must satisfy two conditions: The rules must first solve contracting problems as the parties would have solved them; and second, the rules must update promptly as economic conditions change. In this Article, we show that even if the ALI and ULC once supplied rules that parties themselves would have chosen, these private groups no longer do so: Their rules remain but the problems have changed.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I describes the dramatic changes in contemporary contracting practices that have rendered state-supplied default rules, as well as those we designate as "quasi-mandatory" rules, obsolete.We develop an economic theory that shows parties will reject an obsolete state-supplied default because the term cannot solve the current version of their contracting problem and bad faith parties could exploit the term strategically.But parties are unlikely to create a new term equivalent to an apt state-supplied default because of its excessive cost.The theory predicts that parties instead will replace the obsolete default term with second-best solutions.Yet, the obsolete default lives on. Similarly, parties can only escape the constraints imposed by an obsolete quasi-mandatory rule by costly contracting around the rule. Finally, Part I analyzes the coordination problems that may prevent private parties from revising obsolete terms in standardized interdependent contracts.
Part II provides evidence of the persistence and costs of obsolete terms.Here we show how the theory developed in Part I explains many of the contracting patterns we observe as parties attempt to adjust to the constraints imposed by obsolete default and quasi-mandatory rules.Consistent with the theory, parties avoid obsolete terms by settling on less efficient alternatives.This Part also presents evidence that parties in large, multilateral markets often fail to revise standardized obsolete terms notwithstanding the heightened level of litigation risk that they face as a result.
Part III considers the several systemic reasons that explain why UCC Article 2, the Restatement, and the Bankruptcy Code remain rocks in theriver of changing commercial practice.Obsolescence persists when coordination on an efficient replacement fails because individual parties would bear too much of the cost and internalize too few of the gains to reward efforts to initiate legal change.The private lawmaking bodies that created today's obsolete contract law rules also are poorly equipped institutionally to create current ones.These institutions meet episodically: They have little incentive to update the rules by adopting controversial reforms, and interest group competition can instantiate a status quo bias.And when the rulemaking process is captured by insiders, as in the case of bankruptcy, specialized rules also can become "sticky."
Part IV revisits commercial law's production problem by asking how other institutions that supply commercial law rules have responded to the obsolescence concern. Some private interests have created specialized contract terms that parties are then invited to adopt in their contracts,but this solution to updating is still underproduced.The two public institutions that are largely free from persistent obsolescence are specialized lawmaking bodies and common law courts. Organized interest groups that supply rules for specialized fields can update their rules but at the cost of promoting private interests over the public interest.What remains are common law courts, the institution with which we began. Courts' rules are efficient and update over time, but at first blush do not appear to cover much of the ground. We show, however, that once artificial institutional boundaries are set aside, the activity of common law courts is more vibrant than is commonly assumed.
Part V concludes that the splintering of our general contract law into contract laws for specialized fields--such as corporate, bankruptcy, and financial contracting--points to an emerging institutional response to the externalities that the specialized laws create.
We have two closing observations. First, the common view is that general contract law is created by two institutions: common law courts and "private legislatures" such as the ALI and the ULC that produce UCC Article 2 and the Restatements. This view is incorrect because the contractlaw products of the ALI and the ULC are largely obsolete.Today, there are courts and episodic, specialized interventions. The question we raise is whether this is the best American law can do.
Second, we note the novelty of our analysis. There are two significant prior contributions. Grant Gilmore observed that early twentieth-century codification efforts became obsolete, but for reasons that differ from ours. According to Gilmore, these uniform law codifications were intended to "embalm[] the past"--that is, to solve yesterday's doctrinal problems and enact the solutions into law.A codification that does this will inevitably become obsolete because the future poses different doctrinal problems.But the UCC and Restatement were not so much meant to solve old legal problems as to solve, in the form of default and quasi-mandatory rules,currenteconomic problems. In contrast to Gilmore, we show that such laws become obsolete only when the economic problems either disappear or take new forms.
Guido Calabresi wrote an important book about obsolete statutes and judicial responses.Calabresi's subject was the statute that had outlived its animating purpose but that continued to affect behavior because it was a statute.He then asked howcourtsrespond to an obsolete law by analyzing the strengths courts exhibit and the constraints they function under when attempting to make such laws current.We also observe that obsolescence occurs for statutes that are difficult to update. But, in contrast to Calabresi, we analyze the case of an obsolete commercial law that no longer affects behavior because parties contract out of the law's terms. As a consequence,our subject concerns howpartiesrespond when a law that was supposed to solve the parties' contracting problems no longer does so. Thus, the comparative question this Article asks--which legal institution can best create an efficient law to regulate commercial contracting--is entirely novel. Nor has any prior work analyzed contract obsolescence as a discrete problem to ask why and where such obsolescence exists and how it can persist. We recognize, however, that our more important contribution may be to introduce the subject of comparative institutional analysis to private law fields.

questions.question: Which legal institutions (courts, specialized public regulators, or private lawmaking bodies) are most effective at producing and updating commercial contract law so that legal rules remain apt as commercial practices change?

How does the obsolescence of longstanding state-supplied contract rules affect private contracting behavior and economic efficiency - specifically, do parties adopt second-best arrangements or become vulnerable to strategic exploitation when rules no longer solve current contracting problems?
What institutional factors (e.g., coordination problems, interest-group influence, episodic rulemaking) explain why obsolete contract rules persist and resist efficient revision?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: how remedies and default rules shape renegotiation and settlements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines (mitigation, expectation damages, Hadley foreseeability, certainty) limit remedies and thereby induce loss-sharing, renegotiation, and informal settlements in relational contracts; Paper B shows that state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory rules (UCC, Restatement, statutes) function as defaults parties respond to or contract around, and when obsolete produce second‑best private renegotiation and alternative settlement practices.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between formal doctrine and law-in-action (negotiated process rationality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds 'new legal realism' and negotiated process rationality to show that formal contract doctrines operate within informal networks and practices that drive settlements and behavior; Paper B documents how courts, private lawmakers, and parties in practice create, ignore, or circumvent written rules, emphasizing contracting-around and institutional limits that produce a divergence between doctrinal texts and commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: adaptation (updating) of contract law to changing commercial and relational contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on relational, long-term contracts and asks how remedial rules affect parties' ability to adjust obligations over time; Paper B analyzes obsolescence of general contract rules (UCC, Restatements, bankruptcy) and the failure of legal institutions to update defaults to match changed commercial practices, especially where relational or specialized contracting has become dominant.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, litigation costs, and asymmetric power shaping outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes litigation expense, speed, reputational concerns, and bargaining asymmetries that push businesses toward settlements and informal accommodation; Paper B emphasizes coordination costs, the expense of revising defaults, and interest‑group capture that prevent parties or institutions from efficiently replacing obsolete rules, leading to persistent second‑best practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic 'efficiency' as a justificatory standard for rules and breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with the idea of 'efficient breach' and debates whether remedial rules properly allocate risk to promote economically sensible breaches or merely cheapen performance; Paper B treats default and codified rules as justified by efficiency at creation and interrogates how those efficiency justifications fail when rules become inapt as circumstances change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81uchilrev151!!SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Renegotiation Design by Contract
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Renegotiation Design by Contract

shared_topics.topic: renegotiation, hold-up, and incentives for relationship-specific investment
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center on the problem that parties who make relationship-specific investments face post-contractual renegotiation risk (holdup) that distorts ex ante investment incentives: Paper A analyzes mechanism-design contract solutions (RD contracts, TIOLI offers) to prevent holdup, while Paper B studies how static or obsolete legal rules produce second-best private responses to renegotiation risks and thereby shape contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracts and the role of default terms
shared_topics.justification: Both treat contracting as intrinsically incomplete and focus on default rules as the gap-filling device: Paper A builds on incomplete-contracts theory to motivate renegotiation-design clauses and asset allocation, and Paper B analyzes how state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory rules arise, become obsolete, and affect parties’ incentives to contract around or rely on them.

shared_topics.topic: legal remedies and enforceability (specific performance, injunctions, damages) as mechanisms to support efficient contracting
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the importance of enforceable remedies for making contractual designs credible — Paper A emphasizes specific performance, injunctions, and asymmetric penalties as necessary to implement RD contracts and protect investment returns, while Paper B examines courts and statutory regimes as the institutional means by which default rules and remedies are produced, enforced, and updated (or persist as obsolete).

shared_topics.topic: allocation of bargaining power and the use of asset-ownership or contractual devices to influence renegotiation outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both explore how allocation of bargaining power affects ex ante incentives: Paper A examines contractual allocations (TIOLI offers, leasebacks, exclusive-dealing, late fees) and how asset ownership can be combined with contracts to shape outside options, while Paper B considers how statutory regimes (secured transactions, corporate and bankruptcy rules) and court-made defaults allocate rights and power across contracting parties and thereby influence bargaining outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the interface between contract-theory solutions and real-world legal/institutional constraints (implementation and obsolescence)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers are concerned with whether theoretical fixes to contracting problems can be implemented in practice: Paper A documents real-world contractual forms that instantiate theoretical RD mechanisms, and Paper B investigates how institutional features (courts, specialized statutes, private lawmaking bodies) produce, update, or leave obsolete the legal backdrop that enables or frustrates efficient contractual innovation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev451!!Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem

shared_topics.topic: The role of UCC Article 2's incorporation of commercial norms (trade usages, course of dealing/performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the UCC Article 2 strategy of treating trade usages and related business norms as part of the parties' agreement and analyzes when incorporation is functionally desirable; Paper B treats Article 2 as a central example of private-law codification whose default rules can become obsolete and whose institutional origins shape their ongoing fit with commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: Default rules versus express specification and the costs of specification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the incorporation/plain-meaning debate in terms of specification costs (what parties must write explicitly) versus interpretive/error costs, arguing specification burdens justify some incorporation; Paper B develops an economic theory showing why parties may not replace or write around obsolete default terms because specification or coordination costs are too high, leading to second-best solutions.

shared_topics.topic: The judicial role, interpretive error costs, and courts' capacity to update commercial norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on judicial incorporation and how courts can functionally identify and enforce trade usages while minimizing judicial error; Paper B analyzes courts as one of the three institutions that produce contract law, emphasizing courts' updating role, evidentiary/competence limits, and how precedent formation interacts with changing commercial contexts.

shared_topics.topic: Opportunism and strategic exploitation of norms or obsolete rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that trade usages serve a functional role in controlling opportunistic behavior and that enforcement should be sensitive to that deterrence function; Paper B shows how obsolete defaults or quasi-mandatory rules can be strategically exploited by bad-faith parties and how such exploitation shapes parties' contracting responses.

shared_topics.topic: Comparative institutional analysis of how commercial contract norms are produced and updated (private lawmaking, statutes, courts, and private ordering)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques formalist rejection of judicially incorporated norms and advocates evaluating interpretive regimes by their functional effects on contracting problems; Paper B offers a broader institutional diagnosis—the production problem and obsolescence—comparing courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies (like the ULC/ALI/UCC) in their ability to produce and update efficient commercial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1621!!ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: how parties and institutions fill gaps in incomplete contracts (default rules and gap‑filling)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how common law courts, statutes, and private lawmaking supply default rules to fill contractual gaps and how those defaults become obsolete; Paper B starts from the premise that LTAs and framework contracts are necessarily incomplete and examines how formal provisions and other mechanisms are used to fill gaps in practice.

shared_topics.topic: private versus public production of contract rules (who supplies standardized terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies (ALI/ULC/UCC) and private market actors as sources of contract rules and critiques their ability to update; Paper B examines how firms (OEMs, suppliers) create LTAs and standard form Ks as privately produced, centralized rule-sets and when parties rely instead on alternatives or legal intervention.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑cost and bargaining dynamics as explanations for contract form choice and persistence of alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers an economic theory showing why parties avoid or fail to replace obsolete state‑supplied terms because of the costs and coordination problems involved; Paper B advances a bargaining/dynamic transaction‑cost account explaining why firms choose LTAs, purchase orders, or other arrangements and why alternative forms persist as cost‑minimizing strategies.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between informal enforcement (relational norms) and formal legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how parties may contract around or exploit obsolete rules and how courts play a role in updating and enforcement, implying reliance on informal practices when law is mismatched; Paper B studies the ‘braiding’ of formal information‑sharing provisions with informal enforcement, asks when low‑powered or legal remedies are appropriate, and analyzes the law’s role where norms already govern behavior.

shared_topics.topic: standard‑form contracting, centralization, and coordination problems in multilateral markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights coordination failures that prevent revision of standardized, interdependent contract terms and the stickiness of such standards in large markets; Paper B focuses on SFK LTAs drafted by OEMs that centralize decision‑making and standardize terms across many suppliers, and explores when that centralization succeeds or when coordination leads parties to choose alternatives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 47alalrev387!!ARTICLE: Development of Reform of the Preexisting Duty Rule and Its Persistent Survival
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Development of Reform of the Preexisting Duty Rule and Its Persistent Survival

shared_topics.topic: persistence of entrenched contract doctrines despite changing commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses widespread 'obsolescence' in major contract law sources (UCC Article 2, Restatements, Bankruptcy Code) that no longer fit modern contracting, while Paper B documents the 400-year survival of the preexisting duty rule and explains why that particular doctrine remains resistant to change despite market shifts and sustained criticism.

shared_topics.topic: institutional capacity and comparative responses to doctrinal obsolescence (courts, legislatures, private bodies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A undertakes a comparative institutional analysis of courts, specialized statutory law, and private lawmaking bodies (ALI/ULC) in producing and updating contract rules, and Paper B analyzes how judicial reluctance, limited judicial reforms, and legislative 'intrusion' have shaped the evolution and partial reform of the preexisting duty/consideration doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: constraints on contractual modification and the resulting inefficiencies or second‑best private solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that obsolete default or quasi‑mandatory rules constrain parties from efficient self‑help, producing costly second‑best contractual workarounds or coordination failures, and Paper B focuses specifically on how the preexisting duty rule bars enforcement of many consensual modifications, creating market friction and prompting calls for reform or statutory fixes.

shared_topics.topic: risk of strategic exploitation or coercion arising from doctrinal misfits and the need for policing mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that vestigial defaults can be linguistically but not substantively applicable and thus exploitable by opportunistic parties, while Paper B surveys judicial and statutory developments that seek to police coercive or unfair modifications so as to mitigate the rule's harsh or exploitable effects.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2727!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS:IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION COMMERCIAL NORMS AND THE FINE ART OF THE SMALL CON: COMMENTS ON DANIEL KEATING'S 'EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION'
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS:IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION COMMERCIAL NORMS AND THE FINE ART OF THE SMALL CON: COMMENTS ON DANIEL KEATING'S 'EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION'

shared_topics.topic: use of standardized or master agreements to avoid 'battle of the forms' and doctrinal mismatches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the business practice of executing pre‑existing master agreements to govern a series of transactions and thereby avoid the technical problems of mismatched invoices/forms; Paper B treats the private creation of standardized contract terms as a systematic market response to obsolete or costly state‑supplied defaults and identifies such standardized terms as an underproduced solution to updating problems.

shared_topics.topic: how private contracting interacts with and attempts to circumvent default legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how master agreements can displace the typical document‑by‑document determination that triggers default rules in 'battle of the forms' disputes, while Paper B develops the broader theory of parties contracting around obsolete default or quasi‑mandatory rules and the efficiency and strategic implications of doing so.

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment and enforceability risk of privately produced contractual solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises doubts about when courts will uphold master agreements and notes potential doctrinal objections, and Paper B analyzes courts' capacities and limits in updating or accommodating private ordering, including the litigation risks and strategic exploitation that arise when defaults become obsolete.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems in standardized, multilateral contracting and the persistence of inefficient terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents firms coordinating via master agreements across repeated deals to standardize terms, and Paper B studies why coordination failures prevent marketwide revision of obsolete standardized terms in large multilateral markets, causing parties to persist with second‑best solutions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev631!!SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RELATIONAL CONTRACTS AND THE NEW FORMALISM

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between self-enforcement and coercive (legal) enforcement in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties respond to state-supplied rules by contracting around obsolete defaults and relying on private ordering or second-best private solutions instead of coercive legal enforcement; Paper B directly debates when international agreements should rely on self-enforcing remedies versus coercive adjudication (e.g., WTO mechanisms) and whether lessons about self-enforcement transfer to commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of adjudication/courts (or adjudicatory processes) in governing and updating contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines common-law adjudication as a mechanism for generating and updating default contract rules and its epistemic and institutional limits; Paper B interrogates whether WTO dispute-resolution functions as adjudication or self-enforcement and discusses the practical and symbolic limits of adjudicatory processes in international (and by analogy private) contracting.

shared_topics.topic: comparative institutional questions about which institutions best produce and update contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a comparative institutional analysis of courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies (ALI/ULC) and their ability to create timely, socially efficient contract rules; Paper B raises comparative concerns about applying institutional lessons from international regimes to private commercial contracting and highlights contextual differences in institutional design and incentives.

shared_topics.topic: strategic incentives of parties (or agents/states) in exploiting legal rules or invoking legal compulsion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how bad-faith actors can exploit obsolete default or quasi-mandatory rules and how parties strategically avoid or work around state-supplied terms; Paper B discusses strategic behavior as well, noting that governments may avoid appearing submissive to law and corporate agents may prefer invoking legal compulsion to deflect blame, affecting reliance on legal enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94tullrev961!!SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of UCC Article 2 and general contract codifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes UCC Article 2 and Restatements as central state- and private-produced bodies of general contract law that have become institutionally sticky and increasingly obsolete for modern commercial practices; Paper B engages Article 2 and codified remedial doctrines when evaluating how expectancy damages operate under the U.C.C. and common-law frameworks and the practical limits of those codifications in compensating parties.

shared_topics.topic: whether default legal rules and remedial doctrines provide the correct incentives for contracting and reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats default rules (and quasi-mandatory rules) as instruments designed to supply efficient contract terms and incentives, but shows obsolescence can distort those incentives and push parties to second-best solutions; Paper B treats expectation damages as the remedial 'default' that is supposed to secure reliance and incentive to perform, but demonstrates empirically and doctrinally that expectancy often fails as a fully restorative or reliable incentive.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and the costs of contracting around ill‑fitting legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops theory and evidence that parties often face prohibitive costs to create new, apt terms and therefore either accept obsolete defaults or adopt costly second‑best arrangements, especially in standardized multilateral markets; Paper B's examples (e.g., hiring a replacement service, litigation expenses, lost profits) illustrate the real-world transaction and reliance costs that arise when remedial doctrines and contractual performance do not align.

shared_topics.topic: the insufficiency of traditional contract doctrines to address contemporary commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that longstanding common-law and codified contract rules have become misaligned with modern contracting forms and practices (obsolescence), while Paper B argues that traditional remedial doctrine—expectation damages—functions more as a guidepost than a complete solution, leaving important contemporary harms and allocation questions unresolved.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev707!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.topic: the function and effects of default rules in contract law (including parties contracting around them)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a theory of default and quasi-mandatory rules, showing how obsolete state-supplied defaults persist, induce second‑best private solutions, and are costly to contract around; Paper B explicitly invokes the default/penalty‑default literature (Ayres & Gertner) and discusses contract law as a default regime that parties negotiate around in practice.

shared_topics.topic: comparative institutional production of contract law — courts versus codification/private lawmakers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a comparative institutional analysis of who produces and updates commercial contract law (common‑law courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies like the ALI/ULC) and the limits of each; Paper B compares common‑law adjudication to civil‑law codes and international instruments (e.g., CISG), debating how different institutions (judges, codes, international drafters) create and import contract doctrines like foreseeability.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion, vagueness of doctrinal rules, and the tradeoff between predictability and adaptability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes courts' role in generating and updating default rules but highlights limits from generalist judges and slow rule formation; Paper B focuses on the vagueness of the Hadley foreseeability rule, the discretionary space it gives judges, and concerns about predictability versus judicial adaptability.

shared_topics.topic: historical contingency, persistence, and obsolescence of contract doctrines (how past choices shape present rules and whether they update)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on obsolescence — how rules (UCC Article 2, Restatements, Bankruptcy Code) persist after commercial conditions change and why updating fails; Paper B traces the historical adoption and diffusion of the foreseeability rule (Hadley → CISG), queries whether that historical choice matters today, and explores why some doctrines persist or are interpreted differently across time and systems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71indlj45!!ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: judicial adaptation and reconstruction of contracts in response to changing circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends courts' power to reconstruct or excuse contractual terms (via doctrines like impracticability, mistake, and good faith) when contracts malfunction, and Paper B analyzes courts as one of the central institutions that must update and adapt contract law over time and their limits in producing apt rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role and justification of default rules and contract doctrines that allocate risk or excuse performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines specific doctrines (impracticability, mistake, penalties, forfeiture, good faith) as tools that override or modify agreed terms to allocate losses or prevent opportunism, while Paper B focuses on state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory rules (UCC Article 2, Restatements) and how those defaults can become obsolete or be strategically exploited.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency versus fairness/public-interest rationales for intervening in private contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs economic efficiency objections against fairness-based defenses (unselfish performance, loss alignment) for judicial intervention, and Paper B evaluates when institutional rulemaking (courts, statutes, private bodies) produces socially efficient versus privately captured or inefficient contract rules and the public-interest implications of obsolescence.

shared_topics.topic: responding to unforeseen events and changed commercial realities in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how doctrines should operate in the 'twilight zone' of unexpected events and proposes principles for when to excuse or realign losses, while Paper B studies obsolescence — how rules that once fit contracting problems become inapt as commercial practices change and what institutions can (or cannot) correct that mismatch.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49indlrev621!!ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: contractual governance of multi‑party/collective initiatives and coordination failures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how coordination problems among many contracting parties prevent revision of obsolete standard terms and lead to second‑best arrangements; Paper B proposes collective impact agreements as written contractual governance to solve authority, accountability, and capacity gaps in multi‑actor social coalitions.

shared_topics.topic: institutional adequacy for producing and updating contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies (ALI/ULC/UCC) in their ability to produce and timely update commercially apt contract rules; Paper B argues existing legal practice lacks frameworks for sustaining collective initiatives and proposes new transactional lawyering tools and standard agreement forms to fill that institutional gap.

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting versus default/formal rules in dynamic contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how static default or quasi‑mandatory rules become obsolete and how parties resort to contracting around them or to second‑best solutions; Paper B explicitly grounds collective impact practice in relational contract theory and offers drafting principles to capture evolving relationships and goals rather than relying on rigid, one‑off terms.

shared_topics.topic: how incentives, interest groups, and public‑interest considerations shape contract formation and content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how specialized statutes and private lawmaking can be captured by cohesive interest groups producing privately efficient but socially suboptimal rules; Paper B addresses cross‑sector power dynamics and stresses agreements should protect community/public interests when diverse private, nonprofit, and public actors collaborate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58buffalolrev1031!!ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: courts as primary decision agents in forming and updating contract law/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats judges as the central decision agents who must apply plural values and practical reason to determine contract formation rules; Paper B analyzes the common law adjudicative mechanism and the limits and updating role of courts in producing default contract rules over time.

shared_topics.topic: tension between general/default rules and context-sensitive adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues judges should move along a spectrum from subjective to objective theories and apply plural values contextually rather than a single 'super' value, while Paper B examines how one-size-fits-all codifications (UCC/Restatement) become obsolete and how courts and specialized bodies struggle to supply context-specific solutions.

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs among efficiency, liberty, equality, and the public interest in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds competing values (liberty to contract, equality, moral and cultural duties) and proposes pluralist balancing, and Paper B repeatedly evaluates rules through an efficiency lens while critiquing private lawmaking capture and the neglect of broader public-interest or equality considerations in specialized rulemaking.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design and decision procedures for producing and revising contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes that judges use explicit decision procedures and practical reason to integrate multiple theories horizontally and vertically when forming contracts; Paper B conducts a comparative institutional analysis of courts, statutes, and private-law bodies—identifying coordination problems, capture, and stickiness—and asks which institutional arrangements best produce and update apt contract rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100geolj5!!ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?

shared_topics.topic: instrumental versus non‑instrumental motivations for complying with contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A experimentally tests whether compliance with contracts is driven solely by instrumental cost‑benefit calculations or also by expressive/moral commitments (showing noninstrumental ‘expressive power’ of obligations), while Paper B analyzes contracting parties' strategic, instrumental responses to obsolete legal defaults and how those incentives (and potential exploitation) shape whether parties comply with, contract around, or update legal terms.

shared_topics.topic: effects of vagueness, ambiguity, and uncertainty in contract terms on parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts 'legal uncertainty' (vagueness about an obligation's content) with 'enforcement uncertainty' (probability of detection) and measures their distinct behavioral effects, and Paper B examines how linguistic fit, contract gaps, and inapt (obsolete) rules — forms of ambiguity or mismatch — influence parties' decisions to leave gaps, contract around defaults, or exploit ambiguous defaults.

shared_topics.topic: differences between negotiated (bilateral) and standardized (take‑it‑or‑leave‑it) contracts and their legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows negotiated contracts elicit stronger expressive commitment to performance than standard‑form contracts, whereas Paper B studies the prevalence and stickiness of standardized, interdependent terms (e.g., UCC/Restatement defaults), the coordination problems that prevent revising standardized terms, and the distinct regulatory challenges posed by standardization.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contracting choices and public/private legal institutions (courts, statutes, private restatements) in shaping contract rules and compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates contractual obligations relative to state‑created norms (comparing prior regulatory/criminal findings to private contracts) and considers implications for doctrines like contract interpretation, while Paper B undertakes a comparative institutional analysis of how courts, statutes, and private lawmaking bodies produce, update, and interact with parties' contracting behavior (including when parties contract around or rely on those institutions' defaults).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59emorylj649!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AND FRIENDSHIPS

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and default terms address incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the production and persistence of state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory terms, and how parties respond to contractual gaps when defaults become obsolete; Paper B treats relational contracts as typically leaving many terms open and examines the legal significance and enforceability of those gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between social norms/good‑faith expectations and formal legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how parties rely on, contract around, or exploit legal defaults and how strategic behavior and informal practices interact with obsolete statutory or Restatement terms; Paper B foregrounds the role of social norms and presumptions of good faith in relational contracts and explores how legal norms should incorporate or supplement those informal norms.

shared_topics.topic: whether existing legal institutions and doctrines adequately regulate evolving or relational contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates courts, specialized statutes, and private lawmaking bodies for their capacity to produce and update commercially apt contract rules in a changing economy; Paper B questions whether traditional contract doctrines (often modeled on discrete transactions) sufficiently capture relational contracting and proposes doctrinal revisions to better accommodate friendship‑like contractual relations.

shared_topics.topic: the design and limits of judicial enforcement and remedies for nonstandard/relational contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how obsolete defaults and coordination failures shape litigation risk and the practical effects of state terms on parties' behavior; Paper B analyzes the under‑compensatory nature of remedies in relational contexts and argues for tailored enforcement approaches to preserve ongoing cooperative relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85brooklynlrev393!!ARTICLE: The Impossibility Doctrine in Commercial Contracts: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Impossibility Doctrine in Commercial Contracts: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: tension between economically optimal risk-allocation and existing contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory contract rules can become inefficient or inapt as commercial conditions change, while Paper B empirically tests whether the economically optimal ‘superior risk-bearer’ allocation for impossibility aligns with contracting parties' choices versus the traditional impossibility doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: parties' tendency to contract around or adopt legal defaults and what that reveals about doctrinal adequacy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models and documents how sophisticated parties avoid or replace obsolete default terms with second-best solutions, and Paper B measures the extent to which sophisticated commercial parties include or reject the economic model in their contracts, evidencing real-world contracting behavior vis-à-vis legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: institutional question of who should set or update default rules—courts, statutes, or private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with which institutions (courts, public statutes, private lawmaking) can best produce and update efficient contract law, and Paper B engages this question indirectly by contrasting the legal doctrine courts apply with the contractual allocations parties actually prefer, bearing on whether courts or parties should bear risk-assignment roles.

shared_topics.topic: empirical study of commercial contracting practices to evaluate doctrinal prescriptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence that obsolete statutory/restatement terms persist and distort contracting patterns in large markets, and Paper B conducts an empirical analysis of commercial contracts to determine how frequently parties adopt the economic model for impossibility, using observed contractual language to test normative claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 102valrev1523!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT

shared_topics.topic: limits of private drafters (ALI/UCC/Restatements) to produce effective, up-to-date default rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers criticize private lawmaking bodies (the ALI, ULC/NCCUSL, and the UCC/Restatements) for failing to supply a body of default contract rules that (a) efficiently fill gaps across contemporary commercial contexts and (b) update as commerce changes, with Paper A emphasizing the resulting obsolescence and Paper B documenting the drafters' empirical and conceptual failures.

shared_topics.topic: comparative institutional question: courts versus statutes and private lawmaking for creating defaults and adapting law
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze which institutions are best suited to generate and revise contract defaults—arguing courts have updating advantages and produce acceptable transcontextual rules, while specialized statutes and private bodies either capture narrow interests or produce sticky, outdated rules (Paper A frames this as a production/obsolescence problem; Paper B frames it as the common law's comparative advantage).

shared_topics.topic: the rules-versus-standards problem and the transcontextual/contextual distinction for defaults
shared_topics.justification: Both engage deeply with whether law should provide rule-like defaults or broad standards, arguing that many contract terms are contextual so standards (and transcontextual defaults) are ill-fitting; Paper B elaborates the rules/standards and transcontextual distinction, and Paper A links that distinction to why codified defaults become obsolete or are avoided by parties.

shared_topics.topic: obsolescence, parties' contracting responses (contracting around, second‑best solutions), and coordination failures
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how commercial change renders statutory or restated defaults inapt—leading parties to contract around, adopt second-best solutions, or fail to coordinate on replacements—Paper A develops economic theory and evidence of persistent obsolete terms, while Paper B explains why drafters' choices (standards or insufficient contextual rules) drive the same practical avoidance by parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105valrev1025!!ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: how parties manage incomplete contracts using non-enforceable defaults or instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how parties respond when state-supplied default or quasi-mandatory rules become obsolete and therefore resort to second‑best private solutions; Paper B analyzes why sophisticated parties intentionally use formally non‑binding documents (term sheets/faux contracts) to fill gaps and govern multi‑stage deals without relying on formal enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering as a substitute for or complement to formal legal institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the capacity of private lawmaking bodies (UCC, Restatements) and market actors to produce and update contract rules and shows private solutions emerging where public rules are stale; Paper B shows how contracting parties themselves create private-order devices (non‑binding agreements, shared checklists) to coordinate transactions and achieve functions that courts or statutes do not provide.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems and the stickiness of standardized contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why coordination failures among market participants and costs of initiating change leave standardized default terms obsolete and persistent; Paper B shows that shared, formal‑looking but nonbinding documents serve as coordination and collaboration tools that help move complex deals forward despite frictions, highlighting both the power and limits of document standardization.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and incentives when formal enforcement is absent or inadequate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how obsolete legal rules can be exploited strategically and how parties adopt protective, second‑best arrangements to deter bad faith; Paper B investigates how, in the absence of formal enforcement of term sheets, parties nonetheless deter opportunism through reputational, organizational, and collaborative incentives and by structuring ex‑ante documents to nudge compliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29urichlrev1471!!ARTICLE: QUANTIFYING LIABILITY UNDER THE ARCHITECT'S STANDARD OF CARE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: QUANTIFYING LIABILITY UNDER THE ARCHITECT'S STANDARD OF CARE

shared_topics.topic: misalignment between legal standards and current commercial practice producing inefficiencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how default and quasi-mandatory contract rules become obsolete and force parties into second‑best, costly workarounds; Paper B argues that the prevailing professional standard of care for architects is distorted relative to the contractual and economic realities of modern construction projects, producing inefficient outcomes for design professionals and projects.

shared_topics.topic: tension between contractually allocated liability and externally imposed legal standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how state‑supplied defaults and mandatory rules constrain parties' ability to allocate risk and may be costly to contract around, while Paper B highlights the conflict between the liability architects assume under contracts and the legal/professional standard of care imposed by courts or regulators that can reallocate or amplify that liability.

shared_topics.topic: the role of litigation and courts in shaping obligations and their costs for parties in commercial settings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats courts as a primary mechanism that creates and updates default contract rules (with attendant litigation costs and slow updating), and Paper B emphasizes the rise in claims against architects, the cost of defending those claims, and the judicial enforcement of the professional standard of care that affects industry behavior.

shared_topics.topic: transactional and coordination problems in multi‑party, standardized commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how coordination failures and interdependent standardized contracts prevent parties from revising obsolete terms, while Paper B describes how complex construction projects and dispersed design errors lead to insurers or individual parties absorbing liability and difficulty in apportioning or contracting around risk.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 37jlegalstud503!!ARTICLE: Completing Contracts in the Shadow of Costly Verification
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Completing Contracts in the Shadow of Costly Verification

shared_topics.topic: how costly verification and litigation shape contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper B builds a formal model showing that costly court verification and litigation expenses affect whether parties include noisy or costly signals and standards in contracts; Paper A empirically and institutionally argues that litigation costs and the limited capacity of courts to update rules cause parties to adopt second-best contractual solutions and avoid or contract around obsolete statutory or default terms.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracts, defaults and standards (e.g., 'best efforts') as responses to enforcement limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes why parties use standards and imperfect, hard-to-verify measures (like 'best efforts') instead of fully specifying contingent duties due to verification tradeoffs; Paper A studies why parties leave gaps or rely on state-supplied default and quasi-mandatory rules (or contract around them), emphasizing the persistence of incomplete/default terms when updating or full specification is costly.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of courts and legal institutions in producing and enforcing contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper B treats the court as a costly fact-finder whose judgments (and the prospect of litigation) provide signals that influence incentive provision and settlement dynamics; Paper A compares courts, statutes, and private lawmaking bodies, emphasizing courts' updating mechanism and their practical limitations in developing and enforcing apt commercial default rules.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior and strategic exploitation of ambiguous or obsolete contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B shows how hard-to-prove breaches (e.g., confidentiality or effort standards) create opportunities for opportunistic termination and settlement leverage, altering contract design; Paper A documents how obsolete or linguistically fitting defaults can be exploited by parties acting strategically to obtain favorable judicial interpretations, leading to inefficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84tullrev1437!!ARTICLE: The Origins of Sale: Some Lessons from the Romans
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Origins of Sale: Some Lessons from the Romans

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of contract doctrines and their fit to commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how twentieth-century general contract codifications (UCC Article 2, Restatement) have become obsolete as commercial practices changed, while Paper B traces the Roman jurists' historical recognition of sale and explains how those ancient doctrinal choices reflected and fit the commercial realities of their time.

shared_topics.topic: institutional sources and limits in producing contract law
