shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on why parties' unclear or ambiguous language leads to interpretation disputes and the normative question of how meaning at formation should be ascertained; Paper B investigates the emergence and persistence of a standardized pricing provision (dollar‑indexation) as a social default term and the difficulties parties face in contracting around or changing that provision.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71ucololrev541!!ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE

shared_topics.topic: how statutory drafting and legal reform interact with entrenched commercial contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Llewellyn intentionally drafted the U.C.C. to translate a jurisprudential vision into statutory form that would shape commercial practice, while Paper B empirically studies how Israeli legislation tried (with limited success) to alter the entrenched dollar-indexing norm in real estate contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-formal behavioral forces (judicial discretion, social norms, cognitive biases) in shaping commercial law and contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages Legal Realist claims that judges exercise discretion and that statutes should be crafted to guide that behavior; Paper B documents how social conformity and cognitive biases — not only standard economic incentives — drive contracting choices like dollarization.

shared_topics.topic: the formation, persistence, and change of default commercial terms or standards (standardization and uniformity in commercial practice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces efforts to create uniform default rules and standards through the U.C.C. to promote consistent commercial outcomes, and Paper B traces the emergence, stickiness, and eventual breakdown of a market-wide default pricing term (dollarization) in Israeli real estate contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2005uilllrev303!!SYMPOSIUM: UNCORPORATION: A NEW AGE?: THE EXIT STRUCTURE OF STRATEGIC ALLIANCES
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: UNCORPORATION: A NEW AGE?: THE EXIT STRUCTURE OF STRATEGIC ALLIANCES

shared_topics.topic: contractual mechanisms to mitigate opportunism and hold-up in long-term contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how alliance agreements use detailed termination provisions, contractual (management) boards, and deadlock procedures to deter opportunism among partners; Paper B examines indexing and pricing provisions (and draws on hold-up/opportunism literature) as mechanisms parties use in long-term real-estate contracts to allocate risk and limit opportunistic behavior over the contract term.

shared_topics.topic: governance of long-term relational contracts and choice of provisions to manage intertemporal risk and investment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats strategic alliances as long-term relational contracts and studies how governance and exit provisions shape incentives for nonfinancial investments; Paper B studies long-term rental/sale contracts and focuses on the pricing/indexing clause as a core governance device that allocates risk and affects contracting behavior over time.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal legal structures and social/institutional norms in shaping contract design and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A brings corporate law insights to bear on how contractual governance devices (e.g., management committees, deadlock rules) are structured and enforced within alliances; Paper B empirically examines how social default terms (the dollarization norm) persist or change and how legislative interventions and legal rules interact with prevailing contracting norms.

papers.node_id: 2016uilllrev487!!ARTICLE: OPPORTUNISTIC RESALES AND THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
papers.title: ARTICLE: OPPORTUNISTIC RESALES AND THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
papers.abstract:
It is well understood that the Uniform Commercial Code (the "Code" or the "U.C.C."), through its provisions on remedies, seeks to compensate an aggrieved seller through a construct that takes into account actual or substituted transactions based upon market-based considerations.More particularly, the provisions of section 2-706permit a seller to recover the value of a replacement transaction in certain circumstances,whereas section 2-708(1)attempts to protect the seller in terms of the substituted transaction by allowing a market-based recovery. In an observation more than fifty years ago, then Professor Ellen Peters - now Connecticut Supreme Court Chief Justice, retired - posited:
Does the existence of the substitute preclude reliance on the market-contract standard, or does the complainant have a free option to choose whichever measure turns out to be the more favorable? To permit the option is to allow speculation at the expense of the party in breach; forbidding it allows the party in breach to profit from a substitute transaction which he can neither compel nor control.
Even with the passage of more than fifty years, no single, conclusive response to this question has emerged with respect to whether a seller who resells advantageously can increase the damages award through recourse to market-based damages. In their treatise, Professors James J. White and Robert S. Summers observe that the answer is "not clear," but that "a seller should not be permitted to recover more under 2-708(1) than under 2-706."Professor Henry Gabriel argues the "seller should be allowed to elect between the two remedies regardless of the seller's good faith post-breach activities concerning the non-accepted goods."Like the commentators, courts have been divided as to the answer of the recovery of market-based damages in advantageous resales.This Article seeks to bring greater perspective to the interplay of seller resales under section 2-706 and the recovery of market-based remedies under section 2-708(1), by examining the basic tenets of both the common law of contracts and the Code alike: that the expectation measure of damages allows the aggrieved seller only to be "put in as good a position as if the other party had fully performed."
An example of this problem is in order. Suppose a seller and buyer make a contract for the sale of grass seed at $ 0.72 per pound.The buyer repudiates the contract due to a falling market for the seed at a time when the market price at tender is at $ 0.64 per pound. The seller later resells the seed at $ 0.75 per pound when the market recovers. The seller, having come ahead $ 0.03 over the contract price on the resale, nevertheless brings suit against the buyer, and the seller claims market-priced damages under section 2-708(1), rather than damages under section 2-706.
In examination of this problem, this Article does not question seller recourse to either the resale remedy or the market-based remedy under these provisions in a wide variety of cases, or suggest a rewriting of these provisions at a time when such efforts are not likely to be availing.This Article also does not quibble with the application of section 2-708(2) in the cases of so called "lost-volume sellers."Rather, this Article proposes a more careful and extensive look at the application of sections 2-706 and 2-708 in this specific context of advantageous resales. Moreover, although other scholars might at times conclude that Code provisions would benefit from substantial revision, rewording, and perhaps even deletion of provisions, this Article does not take that path.
, section 2-708(1) itself has been described as "among the least novel and least remarkable of the Code's damages provisions."Ordinarily, the operation of this section's market-based remedy simply placesan aggrieved seller in the same situation as performance would yield, at least hypothetically.Said another way, section 2-708(1) in most cases is consistent with the basic principles of the expectation theory, and we should not seek to disturb that function.It even operates consistently with expectation principles in most resales that fail under section 2-706, often because it is not "commercially reasonable" to provide the seller a measure of damages that affords the standard market-based recovery.It is sometimes said that section 2-708 operates as a sort of "statutory liquidated damages" clause and, as such, occupies a key role in the provision of seller remedies.
, we are not likely to have a revision, or even a drafting project, to Article 2 in the near future. The unsuccessful, lengthy battle to amend Article 2 failed soundly with the withdrawal of the proposed amendments in 2011.As such, despite any perceived benefits of tinkering with the provisions of Article 2 - many of which are arguably more in need of statutory revision than section 2-708(1) - such an undertaking is not the most likely successful strategy at this time for tackling troublesome provisions.Rather, strategies for keeping the Code relevant to commercial parties and helpful to courts are more likely to focus on interpretive measures that reflect changing practices and examine more closely any unresolved applications.
This Article will attempt to guide those endeavoring to apply section 2-708(1) when a seller has made some resale, regardless of whether or not complying with section 2-706. Part II of this Article surveys the basic provisions of the Code relevant to seller resales and market-based recovery, including the relevant historical framework.Part III begins with a discussion of the generally accepted principle of both common law and the Code alike that an aggrieved party can recover a remedy that is ordinarily non-punitive and based on and limited to an expectationmeasure of damages.While not fully compensating an aggrieved party for all losses suffered, expectation damages are considered the most appropriate measure of damages in most cases. This Part then demonstrates why, in general, it should not be expected that contractual damages provide any type of windfall to an aggrieved party and that some of the theories that surround a seller's resale are based on the misplaced understanding that the law should not relieve a breaching buyer of market price damages due to the seller's advantageous resale. Part IV examines the decision of the Oregon Supreme Court in Peace River Seed Co-Operative, Ltd. v. Proseeds Marketing, Inc.,and other courts and commentators that have expressed a position on these resales.This Part offers a critique of the decision and the commentators, while providing an analysis of section 2-708 that takes into account, to a greater degree, the broader considerations of remedies theory under the Code and contract law as a whole. Finally, in Part V, this Article argues that a seller who resells at a price higher than the contract price is limited to recovery of only incidental damages because it is consistent with other provisions of the Code and the expectation principle.In doing so, Part V explains the consequences of this limitation on a seller's damages, whereby the seller cannot speculate at the expense of the buyer, and as such, there is no windfall to the buyer. Part VI concludes that a better balanced application of section 2-708(2) should preserve a seller's right to elect a remedy in most cases, but be subject to a limitation on the seller achieving the position equivalent to full contractual performance.

questions.question: Whether a seller who resells goods at a price above the original contract price can recover market-based damages (or otherwise increase recovery) beyond the damages measured by the resale itself.

Whether remedial rules should allow an aggrieved seller to elect between alternative damage measures after a buyer's breach, or instead be limited so as to prevent the seller from obtaining a windfall through advantageous post-breach transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1987dukelj1!!ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: remedial responses to contract breach in commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the menu of judicial remedies for long-term supply-contract disruption (specific performance, damages, excuse, restitution, or court adjustment), while Paper B scrutinizes the remedial options available to an aggrieved seller under the U.C.C. (resale damages under §2-706 versus market-based recovery under §2-708), with both papers debating which remedy best accords with commercial realities.

shared_topics.topic: tension between expectation, reliance, and restitution interests
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts reliance and restitution interests with expectation remedies when arguing for limited court adjustment (e.g., shortening duration to protect reliance investments), and Paper B grounds its critique of advantageous resales in the expectation principle, arguing damages should not give a breaching party or aggrieved seller a windfall beyond putative expectation.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion and the proper scope/limits of courts in shaping contractual remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A responds to criticisms that courts lack expertise or guidance to adjust complex long-term contracts and proposes doctrinal limits on when and how adjustment should occur, while Paper B addresses divergent court approaches to applying §§2-706/2-708 and advocates interpretive strategies (rather than statutory overhaul) to guide judicial application of market-based remedies.

shared_topics.topic: fair allocation of unforeseen losses and preventing windfalls
shared_topics.justification: Paper A’s 'gap model' recommends court adjustment to share unallocated calamitous losses fairly between parties, and Paper B argues that allowing sellers to recover market-based damages after profitable resales would create impermissible windfalls, so damages rules should prevent speculative gain at the nonbreaching party’s expense.

shared_topics.topic: filling contractual gaps and interpreting implied expectations in commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an 'agreement model' based on parties' implicit expectations and relational risk allocation, and Paper B confronts situations where the Code and courts must interpret what remedies the parties implicitly agreed to or should be limited to when contracts and statutes are silent or ambiguous about advantageous resales.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69valrev967!!ARTICLE:THE MITIGATION PRINCIPLE: TOWARD A GENERAL THEORY OF CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE MITIGATION PRINCIPLE: TOWARD A GENERAL THEORY OF CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION

shared_topics.topic: how the availability and character of substitute markets should affect damages and mitigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a well-functioning market for resale influences whether sellers recover market-based damages under U.C.C. §§2-706/2-708 and whether resales create windfalls; Paper B models how the market for substitute performances governs the content of the duty to mitigate and which categorical mitigation rules are appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the expectation-damages principle as a limit on recoverable gains (preventing windfalls/speculation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the resale vs. market-recovery dispute around the expectation measure—arguing sellers should not be put in a better position than full performance—while Paper B grounds its mitigation principle in minimizing joint performance costs so that remedies do not produce inefficient or speculative gains.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when the injured party must pursue substitute transactions and how that choice affects remedy available
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses whether a seller who resells (sometimes advantageously) may elect market-based damages or be limited because of the resale, and Paper B examines the timing and scope of the duty to mitigate—specifically when an injured party must seek substitutes and whether obligations to deal with breachers or take alternatives mature.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between substantive performance obligations and remedial rules (how performance doctrines should inform damages and mitigation doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates U.C.C. remedial provisions in light of broader contractual performance and expectation theory, while Paper B develops a general theory tying parties' performance duties to a consistent set of mitigation/remedial rules and suggesting tailored contractual regimes where standard rules misfit.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1983uilllrev811!!ARTICLE: THE WEED AND THE WEB: SECTION 2-201'S CORRUPTION OF THE U.C.C.'S SUBSTANTIVE PROVISIONS -- THE QUANTITY PROBLEM
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE WEED AND THE WEB: SECTION 2-201'S CORRUPTION OF THE U.C.C.'S SUBSTANTIVE PROVISIONS -- THE QUANTITY PROBLEM

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalistic Statute of Frauds requirements and Article 2's flexible policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that section 2-201's mechanical quantity requirement (Statute of Frauds) undermines Article 2's flexible, policy-driven framework and calls for a commercially sensitive reading; Paper B similarly worries that literal application of remedy provisions can produce results at odds with commercial expectations and urges interpretive restraint rather than formalistic outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation as the primary tool to reconcile competing UCC provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for using narrow constructions of 2-201 that disable other Code provisions and proposes interpretive techniques short of repeal; Paper B likewise emphasizes interpretive approaches to harmonize sections 2-706 and 2-708(1) instead of seeking statutory rewriting.

shared_topics.topic: protecting expectation principles and avoiding windfalls in enforcement/remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that enforcement should reflect the parties' substantive bargains and not permit parties to escape obligations through technical Statute of Frauds constructions; Paper B analyzes whether sellers may obtain a windfall by electing market-based damages after an advantageous resale and argues remedies should be limited to preserve expectation-based relief.

shared_topics.topic: intra-Code conflicts and the need to harmonize specific UCC sections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the conflict between section 2-201 and other Article 2 provisions (e.g., 2-204, 2-306) that govern formation and quantity, showing how one provision can cripple others; Paper B examines the interplay between remedy provisions (2-706 and 2-708) and how they should be applied together to produce coherent results consistent with the Code's remedial scheme.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36geojintll1145!!ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China

shared_topics.topic: the choice between expectation damages and specific performance as the appropriate remedy for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how UCC provisions (particularly §§2-706 and 2-708) align with the expectation measure of damages and when sellers may recover market-based sums, while Paper B examines the tension between expectation damages and specific performance in China and how those remedies shape incentives for breach or performance.

shared_topics.topic: whether the law should allow or constrain opportunistic/advantageous breaches or resales (avoiding windfalls)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses whether a seller who resells at a price above the contract should be limited to incidental damages to prevent a windfall at the buyer's expense, and Paper B considers the doctrine of efficient breach—whether law should permit breaches that are privately profitable but socially efficient, and the moral and legal resistance to such utilitarian breaches in China.

shared_topics.topic: the predictability and administrability of contract remedies in judicial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for interpretive approaches to apply Article 2 consistently and to limit speculative recoveries by sellers, while Paper B emphasizes how Chinese courts' flexible remedies, judicial discretion, and uneven compensation practices undermine parties' ability to predict litigation outcomes and thus affect the viability of doctrines like efficient breach.

shared_topics.topic: the role of market conditions and market-based metrics in shaping remedies and breach decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on market-price recovery under §2-708(1) and how market movements interact with resale remedies, and Paper B uses market examples (e.g., a second buyer offering a higher price) and statutory language about market availability to assess how market realities influence decisions to breach and the formulation of legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev31!!ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior by contracting parties and legal responses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze specific forms of opportunism in commercial transactions — Paper A examines lawyers inserting latent contractual 'hostages' that can advantage one party, while Paper B examines sellers who resell advantageously — and both consider how legal rules and remedies should respond to curb or accommodate that opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and the expectation-recovery norm as the evaluative standard
shared_topics.justification: Each article evaluates disputed practices against an economic or expectation-based benchmark: Paper A asks whether hidden contractual rights can be efficient (drawing on Williamsonian hostage theory), and Paper B assesses resale and market-based damages against the expectation measure to avoid windfalls.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract construction, statutory interpretation, and remedies in shaping incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how interpretive doctrines and remedial rules affect behavior — Paper A critiques contract-construction principles and defenses that limit creation/enforcement of hidden rights, while Paper B critiques judicial and U.C.C. interpretations of §§2-706/2-708 that determine whether sellers can profit from advantageous resales.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, reputational constraints, and private-ordering mechanisms to limit opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines non-judicial mechanisms and costs that influence opportunistic strategies — Paper A emphasizes reputational effects, negotiation costs, and hidden hostages as credible commitments, and Paper B discusses how legal interpretation and predictable remedies preserve commercial practices and limit speculative conduct that raises transaction costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev645!!SYMPOSIUM: THE INCOMPLETENESS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF RELATIONAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE INCOMPLETENESS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF RELATIONAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract law in supporting commercial parties' expectations (expectation damages theory)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the background conception about how law should support competent commercial parties who draft incomplete or relational agreements, while Paper B grounds its analysis of U.C.C. remedies in the expectation measure of damages and argues damages should put an aggrieved seller in the position of full performance without producing windfalls.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling and the interpretation of incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on problems that arise when courts fill gaps in deliberately incomplete relational contracts and whether that captures parties' intentions, and Paper B examines how courts should interpret and apply U.C.C. provisions (2-706 and 2-708) to address gaps created by breaches and subsequent resales.

shared_topics.topic: application and limits of law-and-economics reasoning in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages directly with the use of sophisticated law-and-economics tools to propose reforms for relational contracting, and Paper B employs market-based and expectation-focused economic reasoning to evaluate remedies under the Code and to critique doctrinal responses to advantageous resales.

shared_topics.topic: reform versus interpretive adjudication as responses to doctrinal problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses proposed legal reforms to better accommodate relational/incomplete contracting and questions that reformist conception, while Paper B explicitly rejects near-term statutory rewriting of Article 2 and advocates interpretive strategies to keep the Code relevant to contemporary commercial practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58alalrev765!!ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and application of the Uniform Commercial Code (especially Article 2)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts a close doctrinal analysis of UCC Article 2 remedies (sections 2-706 and 2-708(1)) and how courts should apply them in resale cases; Paper B examines recent revisions and drafting choices for Articles 1 and 2 and analyzes how changes to those Code provisions should be applied (including whether and how they should operate retroactively).

shared_topics.topic: the proper remedial norm: expectation-based damages versus incentive/fairness considerations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its argument in the expectation measure of contract damages and argues against allowing sellers windfalls from advantageous resales; Paper B contrasts incentive-based (pro-retroactivity) approaches with reliance/expectations-based fairness, arguing that commercial-law transition policy must weigh both incentives and parties' expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation and transitional/interpretive strategies when the Code is ambiguous or evolving
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for interpretive approaches by courts to resolve the split over resale and market-based remedies and critiques specific judicial decisions; Paper B addresses how courts have filled legislative silence on transition issues and the interpretive uncertainty that follows commercial-law reforms, urging tailored 'rational retroactivity' doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: how post-contract or post-rule changes in circumstances (party conduct, resales, or legal reform) should affect parties' rights and liabilities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether a seller's post-breach resale (especially an advantageous one) should alter the seller's recoverable damages under the Code; Paper B analyzes how parties' reliance or ability to anticipate legal change (and their post-enactment conduct) should influence whether commercial-law revisions are applied retroactively or with transition relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 109pennstlrev397!!ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*

shared_topics.topic: interpretive methodology for applying the Uniform Commercial Code (Article 2)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends a 'full contextualism' / dual-track theory for interpreting the Code, arguing for a contextualist hermeneutic; Paper B confronts interpretive choices courts make under Article 2 (esp. §§2-706, 2-708) and urges interpretive measures that resolve ambiguities in light of commercial practice and remedial theory.

shared_topics.topic: remedies under the UCC and the expectation measure of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how the contextual turn reshaped remedial doctrines (reliance recovery, implied-in-fact contracts) under contract law and the Code; Paper B directly analyzes seller remedies under §§2-706 and 2-708, debating whether market-based recoveries fit the expectation principle and arguing for limits to prevent windfalls.

shared_topics.topic: commercial reasonableness, merchant practices, and 'open terms' versus formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes Llewellyn's project of embedding merchant rules, open terms, and commercial reasonableness into the Code as a corrective to abstract formalism; Paper B repeatedly invokes commercial reasonableness and the realities of merchant resales when assessing whether and how sellers may recover under the Code.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judges and doctrinal development in applying the Code
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Llewellyn within Legal Realism to critique judicial formalism and promote contextual judicial decision-making under the Code; Paper B surveys divergent court decisions on opportunistic resales and calls for more coherent judicial application of Article 2 provisions consistent with remedies theory.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57uchilrev1155!!ARTICLE: The Case for Market Damages: Revisiting the Lost Profits Puzzle.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Case for Market Damages: Revisiting the Lost Profits Puzzle.

shared_topics.topic: proper measure of seller damages in breached goods contracts (market damages vs resale/lost profits)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether sellers should recover market-based damages or be limited to resale or lost-profits measures: Paper A focuses on the tension between UCC resale under §2-706 and market recovery under §2-708(1) in cases of advantageous resales, while Paper B debates the merits of market damages versus lost profits more broadly and defends market damages as the appropriate default in market contracts.

shared_topics.topic: whether awarding market damages can create windfalls or overcompensation
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the concern that market damages may overcompensate an aggrieved seller (creating a windfall), with Paper A arguing sellers who resell above contract price should be limited to incidental damages to avoid speculation, and Paper B examining cases where market damages exceed the seller's ex ante expected profits and critiquing lost-profits remedies that arose in response.

shared_topics.topic: expectation/full-performance principle and the ex ante vs ex post valuation of expectancy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers invoke the expectation (full-performance) principle and analyze whether damages should be measured ex ante or ex post: Paper A emphasizes that damages should put the aggrieved seller in the position of full performance without speculatory gains, while Paper B draws a distinction between ex ante (market-based) and ex post (lost-profits) perspectives and argues damages reflect which perspective on risk allocation the contract embodies.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and harmonization of UCC Article 2 remedies (sections 2-706 and 2-708) with contract remedies theory
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage in doctrinal interpretation of Article 2 remedies, critiquing courts and commentators and proposing how §§2-706 and 2-708 should be applied or harmonized with broader remedies theory—Paper A by proposing limits on market recovery after advantageous resales, and Paper B by arguing the UCC should presumptively favor market damages as reflecting parties' likely risk allocation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules on damages shape bargaining incentives between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Hadley-based foreseeability as a default limitation on consequential damages and argues that existing models ignore strategic bargaining incentives; Paper B considers how UCC remedies (sections 2-706 and 2-708) affect sellers' choices post-breach and whether allowing certain recoveries alters pre- and post-contract incentives.

shared_topics.topic: strategic post‑breach behavior (opportunism, resale, and information transmission) driven by remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how promisees and promisors strategically (mis)represent values and breach probabilities when default liability rules are in place, while Paper B studies sellers' opportunistic resales and whether the availability of market‑based damages induces speculation or good‑faith conduct after breach.

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of expectation damages and limits on recovery in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the information‑forcing justification for limiting consequential damages and explores alternative default rule designs, whereas Paper B grounds its analysis explicitly in the expectation principle, arguing that sellers should not obtain windfall recoveries beyond putting parties in the position of full performance.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal and empirical case‑law to evaluate the efficiency and application of remedial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys historical cases on consequential damages, Laidlaw nondisclosure, and liquidated damages to test theoretical claims about Hadley and defaults, and Paper B reviews judicial decisions (including Peace River Seed) and commentators to assess how courts apply UCC remedial provisions and the practical consequences for commercial parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 109columlrev431!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING FOR INNOVATION: VERTICAL DISINTEGRATION AND INTERFIRM COLLABORATION

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior and mechanisms to constrain it
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center opportunism as a core problem: Paper A examines opportunistic resales and whether a seller who benefits from post-breach market moves may unfairly profit at the buyer's expense under UCC remedies, while Paper B analyzes how firms design contractual and relational governance to prevent opportunistic exploitation of transaction-specific investments in disintegrated supply chains.

shared_topics.topic: contractual governance and remedial rules as tools to shape ex post behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how statutory remedies (UCC §§2-706 and 2-708) and judicial interpretation allocate gains and losses after breach, effectively governing parties' incentives; Paper B investigates a spectrum of governance devices—braided explicit and implicit contract terms, information exchanges, and switching costs—that functionally regulate post-contractual conduct in innovation collaborations.

shared_topics.topic: limits of contracting under uncertainty and handling unforeseen post-contract events
shared_topics.justification: Both articles grapple with incomplete contracting: Paper A addresses unforeseen market recoveries after breach and whether existing UCC provisions properly accommodate those events, while Paper B addresses the inability to specify future product/performance under rapid technological change and how contracts (and governance processes) adapt ex post.

shared_topics.topic: how allocation of remedies or contractual terms affects parties' incentives to invest and the risk of creating windfalls
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes expectation damages doctrine and argues limits on seller recovery to avoid windfalls that distort incentives, whereas Paper B links contractual form and governance to ensuring efficient levels of transaction-specific investment and preventing opportunism that would deter such investment.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51arizlrev1!!Article: Contracts as Organizations
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contracts as Organizations

shared_topics.topic: the limits of economic/market-based theories for interpreting contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the appropriateness of relying on a market-based measure (U.C.C. §2-708(1)) to award damages when a seller's advantageous resale could produce a windfall, while Paper B critiques the dominance of neoclassical and agency economic models in empirical contract scholarship and argues they do not fully capture contracting practices or doctrinal nuance.

papers.node_id: 1996wislrev75!!ARTICLE: ORGANIC TRANSACTIONS: CONTRACT, FRANK LLOYD WRIGHT AND THE JOHNSON BUILDING
papers.title: ARTICLE: ORGANIC TRANSACTIONS: CONTRACT, FRANK LLOYD WRIGHT AND THE JOHNSON BUILDING
papers.abstract:
International agencies and reformers call for the nations of the former Soviet bloc, China and developing countries to embrace the rule of law.  Often this call includes or focuses on western contract law and its remedies.However, empirical research suggests that contract law, atbest, plays a small role in capitalist economies.These studies show that business people often do not plan with contract law in mind, they deal in ways that preclude the formation of a legally binding contract, and they do not assert contract rights to settle disputes. Several writers have argued that this research is far too instrumental--too focused on a direct relationship between means-to-reach-ends.The research, they say, focuses on drafting contracts to gain rights, performing in light of the parties' formal agreement, and litigating to resolve disputes. Contract law, these writers argue, plays a crucial part in establishing the trust necessary for business dealings even when parties do not use it directly.Business people expect contracts to be performed, in part, because they assume that they could counter default by using legal remedies. Written contracts provide the needed structure for complex transactions. Both contract law and formal written contract documents reinforce the cultural norm that commands us to perform our promises.
It would be difficult to test directly these assertions about the tacit assumptions held by business people. Perhaps contract law plays an important symbolic role in modern economies. Perhaps it provides the needed normative structure that can be just assumed without discussion.  However, I am skeptical for a number of reasons: we know, for example, that people engage in economic transactions in many situations where they should understand that contract law could play but little role in reinforcing their commitments. Trust can rest on many norms and structures reinforcing obligations other than contract law. In many Asian societies, for example, long-term continuing relations based on extended family ties offer powerful incentives to perform promises.
This paper looks at how people can perform complex commitments without formal planning and even implicit threats to use legal sanctions.  It is a case study of an on-going relationship between Frank Lloyd Wright, the internationally famous architect, and S.C.Johnson & Son, Inc., as Wright designed and supervised construction of the Johnson Administration Building. The building featured an unusual design, seeking both utility and artistic excellence. It represented a major investment made by the Company in the middle of the Depression of the 1930s. Wright's design produced an architectural triumph. In 1986, members of the American Institute of Architect's College of Fellows were polled about the "most successful" examples of architectural design in the United States. The Johnson Administration Building ranked ninth on their list.Nonetheless, the process of creating this masterpiece was not a smooth one.
Materials in the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation Archivesas wellas reports of those who witnessed the process show how the parties conducted the relationship that created this great building. We have letters from Mr. Wright and from Hibbard Johnson, the President, and Jack Ramsey, the General Manager of the Johnson company. Many who remember the construction of the building have been interviewed or have written accounts of the events of almost sixty years ago.
First, I will put the negotiations in context. I will describe S. C.Johnson & Son, the two officials who negotiated for the firm, Frank Lloyd Wright, and the building itself as it was finally constructed. I will review the transaction by which Wright won the commission to design the Johnson building and the uncertain contract created to govern the relationship. Then I will turn to the many problems faced by the parties as the building was being constructed. I will offer explanations for why the parties dealt with these problems as they did and why they did not use contract law. Finally, I will look at the claims for contract law, considering the Johnson Administration Building experience.

questions.question: Whether parties can successfully complete complex, high-value collaborative projects without formal written agreements or the expectation that legal remedies will be used to enforce performance.

What alternative mechanisms (for example, trust, reputation, ongoing relationships, managerial practices or cultural norms) enable parties to perform and resolve disputes when they do not rely on formal legal enforcement.
Whether the mere existence or symbolic presence of legal remedies shapes parties' expectations and supports performance even when the law is not directly invoked.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:WHY CONTRACTS SCHOLARS SHOULD READ LEGAL PHILOSOPHY: POSITIVISM, FORMALISM, AND THE SPECIFICATION OF RULES IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract law as a background norm or symbolic structure versus as an enforcement tool
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically probes whether contract law served mainly as a tacit, symbolic reassurance that enabled performance in the Wright–Johnson relationship (and finds alternative norms often did the work); Paper B debates whether norm-laden legal rules (good faith, reasonableness) actually function as law that guides behavior or merely as normative language, drawing on legal philosophy to ask when law should be treated as binding guidance versus symbolic content.

shared_topics.topic: how parties manage complex, partially specified transactions without invoking formal legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a case study of an unusually complex architectural commission governed by an uncertain/implicit contract and shows how the parties resolved disputes and sustained performance without recourse to litigation; Paper B theorizes incompleteness in contract rules as a form of ‘partial planning,’ examining when vague rules can be specified over time and whether legal systems should rely on such open-ended instruments rather than strict specifications.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal, rule‑based contract doctrines and context‑sensitive, flexible approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that business actors often do not structure deals around formal contract doctrines and instead operate through practices and expectations, raising questions about limits of rigid rules; Paper B explicitly analyzes the formalism vs. anti‑formalism debate, arguing that overly context‑sensitive rules undermine predictability and that some return to formal rules may be warranted.

shared_topics.topic: the sources of trust and non‑legal enforcement (social norms, ongoing relationships) versus reliance on legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how trust, long‑term relationships, and organizational norms enabled performance in lieu of asserting contractual rights in the Johnson building project; Paper B engages with the idea that law incorporates or references social norms (promise theory, good faith) and asks whether embedding such norms in legal rules effectively substitutes for or complements non‑legal enforcement mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: predictability, specification of obligations, and the litigation/transaction‑cost consequences of vague contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents parties' avoidance of contract litigation and the practical methods they used to cope with uncertainty in obligations; Paper B argues that vagueness and context‑dependence in modern contract law increase uncertainty and litigation costs and examines whether clearer, more specified/formal rules would better serve contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: the reliance on long‑term relationships, reputation, and repeated interactions to sustain complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the ongoing Wright–Johnson relationship and alternative norms (continuing relations, trust) that ensured performance, and Paper B centers on reputational governance, repeat‑player effects, and the long‑term costs of default that underpin sovereign lending markets.

shared_topics.topic: use of qualitative case‑study evidence (archives, interviews, litigation documents) to challenge prevailing theoretical assumptions about contracts and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses archival materials and interviews from the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation to question assumptions about the centrality of contract law, and Paper B uses interviews, court records, media, and case examples to revise theories about the role courts and law in sovereign debt enforcement.

papers.title: ARTICLE: Outsourcing, Modularity, and the Theory of the Firm
papers.authors: Margaret M. Blair; Erin O'Hara O'Connor; Gregg Kirchhoefer
papers.abstract:
In recent years the practice of "outsourcing" and "offshoring" of production and services by firms in a wide range of industries has become quite common.This represents a change in the organization of production in many firms, from inside to outside the firm. As such, it challenges theorists in management, economics, and the law to rethink some of the accepted explanations that theorists have offered about the boundaries of the firm. Why is it that some productive activity is organized entirely within the boundaries of individual firms, while other activities are organized through contracts, either via arms-length market exchanges or by longer-term formal contracts?
Theories that attempt to explain why business organizers choose one structure rather than another - governance by contractual agreement, for example, rather than governance within a firm - are called "theories of the firm." Among the most well-accepted ideas in the "theory of the firm" literature is that productive activities will tend to be carried out within a single firm, governed by hierarchical decision-making, when the "transactions costs" associated with using markets or contracts are higher than the costs of using internal hierarchy.If this is correct, then the widespread shift amongmultinational companies toward outsourcing - in which production activities that had previously been carried out within vertically integrated firms are arranged through one or more contracts across "supply chains" of different firms - suggests that either the cost of contracting has fallen in a variety of settings, or the cost of internal governance has risen (or both).
Yet we understand little about what has happened to change the relative costs of contracting and internal governance. Some observers have off-handedly noted that transportation and communications costs have declined dramatically with the advent of the Internet,but it is not obvious that declines in the cost of these inputs have been greater for travel and communication across firm boundaries than they have for travel and exchanges among participants within the same firm.
Another common explanation for increased outsourcing is that outsourcing makes it possible for western companies to take advantage of lower-cost labor in Asia, Latin America, and Eastern Europe.But here again, a firm need not outsource to take advantage of cheaper labor; it can often lower its labor costs simply by relocating its own operations to where the labor is cheaper.
In fact, outsourcing to service providers in low wage countries might entail substantial increases in writing and enforcing contractsgiven that, in many cases, rule of law institutions in these countries are significantly weaker than those in the United States.Thus, it is not obvious to us that either lower transportation and communications costs, or lower labor costs in developing countries, would by themselves necessarily encourage outsourcing to offshore companies.
We do not here offer a completely satisfactory answer to the puzzle of the recent growth in outsourcing, but we believe that outsourcing contracts can help to inform both the "why" and the "how" of business arrangements moved outside the firm. Put differently, we believe that the parties' contracting arrangements could reveal something about any such new contracting mechanisms tailored to outsourcing, and help us understand the residual concerns of the firms involved.
Thus, we examine the structure and content of a small number of contracts that corporations have entered into to govern outsourcing relationships. Such contracts constitute written evidence of an effort by the outsourcing or "customer" firm to separate out production activities along new lines, or in some new dimension, so that an outside firm can perform those activities. If the activities were previously performed in-house, what are the problems associated with separating them out that the customer and supplier firms must anticipate and provide for in the contracts? What are the new governance arrangements that the parties hope will enable them to carry out the work successfully across firm boundaries? And how are these arrangements expected to work?
Specifically, we examine seven outsourcing contracts and some associated documents provided to us by Kirkland & Ellis LLP's Chicago office, which has a sizeable practice in the negotiation and drafting of outsourcing contracts. Each contract provided to us wasredacted to conceal the identities of the parties,and each involves a U.S.-based corporation arranging to have a substantial activity such as business services, data management, or manufacturing performed outside the United States by another firm. In each case, employees within the outsourcing firm previously had performed the activities. And in each case, the contracts were intended to govern a relationship that the parties expected to last for a substantial number of years.
We evaluate provisions of these contracts through the lens of a theory of production in firms articulated recently by Harvard Business School Professor Carliss Baldwin.Professor Baldwin builds on the notion of "modularity" in production - which is a way of thinking about the degree to which activities at one stage of production are interconnected with, and dependent upon, activities at other stages - to develop a theory to explain where we should expect to find activities carried out within the same firm, rather than across boundaries between firms. We believe modularity theory helps to illuminate how contract structure and terms help both to facilitate and to manage the outsourcing relationship. This framework also suggests where contracting party tensions may arise in the new business arrangements.
In Part II, we briefly review the theory-of-the-firm literature and explain the concept of modularity as it applies to this literature. Then we consider how modularization of a production process might make it easier to govern the process by contract rather than by internal hierarchy, and what characteristics of a production process help to make it modular. We further suggest that the contracts themselves may help to modularize production - indeed, that sufficiently sophisticated contracts may help to offset or overcome interconnectedness that arises from purely physical production attributes.
In Part III, we describe some of the relevant terms of seven outsourcing contracts. We also describe how various features of thesecontracts appear to us to be designed to help "modularize" aspects of production, so that they can more easily be governed across firms rather than by fiat within a single firm.
In Part IV, we offer some tentative observations about how these contractual governance arrangements help to reduce the transactions costs of outsourcing relative to hierarchical governance. We also compare our seven contracts to a larger sample of outsourcing contracts assembled by Professor George Geisto see whether the clauses that we believe help facilitate these outsourcing arrangements are also found in the contracts Geis studied. And we compare our contracts and observations based on them to an extensive analysis of three contracts studied by Professors Ronald Gilson, Charles Sabel, and Robert Scott.
In addition, we briefly discuss a few outsourcing relationship disputes that have resulted in litigation for insight into unresolved problems that some novel contract provisions might present.
We conclude with the observation that outsourcing contracts offer a potentially productive source of insights into the theory of the firm, especially theories about the location of the boundaries of firms. They also provide insight into the economy-wide factors that have been driving outsourcing, and into the effects of outsourcing over time on the firms and industries that reorganize in this way.
. Hierarchy and Modularity in the Theory of the Firm
Although economists have been studying the theory of the firm for nearly a century,neither theorists nor empirical researchers havereached agreement about the primary factors that cause business organizers to buy some inputs in spot markets, while forming long-term contracts for other inputs, and generating still other inputs from within their firm. Most economists agree with Coase that the choice of whether to "make" or "buy" an input probably has something to do with the relative transactions costs associated with each approach.But they disagree over what factors cause transactions costs to be higher in markets than in internal production (or vice versa).
Some economists essentially assume away the question by regarding the governance of relationships within a firm as no different from governing relationships by contract - a firm is just a "nexus" of contracts, they say.Others stress that the important difference between within-firm governance and contractual governance has to do with differences in the incentives created by these two forms. In particular, they argue that relationships governed through markets and contracts generally involve more "high-powered" incentives for the parties to maximize the productivity and profitability of each step in the productive process.Under someconditions, high-powered incentives may lead to greater overall efficiencies. But where the steps in the production process, or in different aspects of the enterprise, are interdependent, high-powered incentives can lead parties to engage in wasteful attempts to shift costs or risks onto other parties to the enterprise. In such a situation, theorists have argued, it might be better to organize within a single firm, where managers can use a variety of different organizational and reward schemes to try to elicit cooperation.
But what factors cause production stages to be interdependent? Interdependence can occur when a party to the enterprise makes investments in assets that are specific to that enterprise. In that case, others participating in the enterprise can take advantage of this firm-specific investment by demanding a larger share of the profits generated by the enterprise or by forcing greater liabilities and risks onto the investing party than the investor thought she would bear when she made the decision to invest. The party making the investment would be vulnerable to this "hold up" by the others because those assets will not produce the hoped-for return without full cooperation from all parties.Thus, Oliver Williamson and others have argued that where such investments are important, it may often be cheaper to carry out the various steps within a singlefirm.Within-firm production, in which all of the highly specific assets are owned by a single entity, is thought to work better in such cases. If specific assets are owned by a single entity that is carrying out the entire enterprise itself, then the firm's managers might be able to maximize the efficiency of the joint enterprise, and participants will have fewer opportunities and incentives to try to push costs or risks onto another party within the entity.Implicit in this theory is that the potential for costly disputes among participants in an enterprise can be mitigated if the participants are all subject to the authority of a hierarchical decision-making process within a single firm.
Management theorists have recently explored a contributor to interdependence that stresses technological differences between production activities performed within firms and activities carried out across firms. Specifically, if the work of an enterprise can be organized into "modular" units, then interdependence between units is greatly reduced. Indeed, modularity is defined as a measure of the interdependence of steps in the production process.A"module" is a component or a step in production that can be carried out separately from other steps or components, but is linked to those other steps through a common interface that allows it to link in multiple ways to more than one other type of component or step.The more "modular" different steps of production are, then, the less interdependent, and the easier it should be to govern the relationships among parties carrying out the steps by contracts rather than by within-firm hierarchical arrangements. For example, enterprise-specific investments at related or sequential stages of production tend to reduce modularity, while the use of standardized equipment, parts, metrics, and processes tends to increase modularity. The literature on modularity in production offers a useful framework for understanding and explaining the rapid growth in outsourcing by large firms. In this Part we briefly review the literature on the role of hierarchy in firms, especially firms where knowledge is an essential asset (Subpart A), and then we review the literature on the problem of modularity and interconnectivity between steps in the production process (Subpart B). Subpart B also identifies some implications of modularity for outsourcing contracts.

questions.question: Whether greater modularity of production stages increases the likelihood that firms will outsource those stages rather than perform them within the firm.

Whether and how contractual governance provisions can substitute for internal hierarchy by modularizing interdependent production activities and thereby reducing the transaction costs of long-term outsourcing relationships.

What kinds of contractual tensions and unresolved problems arise when formerly in-house activities are moved outside firm boundaries, and how those issues affect the durability and performance of outsourcing arrangements.
