papers.node_id: 129yalelj690!!ARTICLE: Paid on Both Sides: Quid Pro Quo Exchange and the Doctrine of Consideration
papers.title: ARTICLE: Paid on Both Sides: Quid Pro Quo Exchange and the Doctrine of Consideration
papers.abstract:
Under the common law, contractual liability attaches to commitments made to others. Unlike the law of property, which lays down not only the legal consequences of the various forms of ownership but also the conditions of ownership itself, the common law of contract piggybacks on an independent social practice that it does not purport to create or define--namely, the practice of committing to courses of conduct by making promises or entering into agreements.Since interpersonal commitments are pervasive features of social life--they are made in all contexts in which humans interact cooperatively and in every medium in which they communicate--the most basic task confronting this body of law is to demarcate the sphere of legally enforceable commitments and thereby to determine the domain of the contractual. In the common-law tradition, the broadest and most visible line separating enforceable and unenforceable commitments is drawn by the doctrine of consideration, a fact that explains the doctrine's enduring position in the law-school curriculum. Like the doctrines of first possession in property, assault in tort, and nondelegation in administrative law, consideration's prominence is due not to the frequency with which it arises in litigation but to the fundamental position it purports to occupy in the structure of a major area of law.
Notwithstanding these pretensions, it cannot be said that the doctrine of consideration, in its modern form, has performed this basic demarcating function in a consistent or principled manner. At least since the late nineteenth century, and quite likely since its origins in the sixteenth, the doctrine of consideration in contract law has been understood to rest on a distinction between exchange transactions (i.e., bargains) and gratuitous transactions, and to limit the legal enforcement of promises and agreements, unless under seal, to those belonging to the former category.This general conception of consideration--whatis known as the bargain theory of consideration--has been reduced in modern times to a more specific rule, which can be traced to Christopher Columbus Langdell's textbook definition of consideration as "the thing given or done by the promiseein exchange forthe promise."This modern consideration rule, requiring as a condition of contractual validity that the promisor receive something in exchange for her promise, has been handed down to at least four generations of students together with a number of well-known problems that continue to hamper the doctrine, both in theory and in practice.These problems include certain undesirable or counterintuitive applications of the rule (in areas such as conditional gift promises, contract modifications, option contracts, guarantee agreements, and social and domestic agreements) as well as a failure to identify a plausible rationale that can be used to make sense of it. As a result of these problems, many have called for the wholesale eradication of the bargain requirement.The principal aim of this Article is to open up space between the general conception and the specific rule and to show that many of the familiar difficulties with consideration result from the specific rule rather than from the general conception. My purpose is not so much to defend the bargain requirement as it is to render it intelligible; only then will we be able to ask whether consideration is a doctrine worth keeping and what, if anything, might take its place.
By claiming that the modern rule badly implements the bargain requirement, I mean more than that the rule emphasizes the wrong aspects of a bargain, or takes too narrow a view of the range of objects whose exchange would satisfy the requirement. Rather, my claim is that the modern rule implicitly relies on a seductive but altogether mistaken conception of what a bargain or exchange is.While this conception was implicit in Langdell's definition, it was rendered explicit the following year by Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., and later codified (and slightly modified) in the Second Restatement of Contracts.Thus, in its boldest formulation, my claim is that two giants of the common law, Langdell and Holmes, mangled a central doctrine of contract law by severing the link between the doctrine of consideration and the proper conception of a bargain. This error, in my view, spawned confusion that has impeded contract law to this day. Given a better understanding of the notion of bargain or exchange and a doctrine of consideration refashioned so as to make contact with it, many of the problems associated with the modern rule can be resolved.
Quite apart from consideration, there is ample independent reason to want an adequate account of quid pro quo exchange, and it is another central aim of this Article to use the doctrine of consideration to develop and anchor such an account. Quid pro quo exchange is one of the basic modes of giving and receiving benefits, and it is both broader and narrower than is sometimes supposed. On the one hand, the category includes more than narrowly economic activity (such as the sale and barter of the marketplace or wage labor arrangements in the workplace), and embraces transactions as varied as plea bargains, prisoner exchanges, and bribes. On the other hand, while quid pro quo is a species of reciprocity (that is, of "returning kindness with kindness"), it should not be conflated with the more general category. There are many ways in which two individuals can confer benefits upon one another without carrying out a quid pro quo. For example, when, without any discussion of reward, an individual in distress receives help from a sympathetic passerby, the recipient may later be moved to send a gift (for instance, chocolate or wine) to the helper in a gesture of gratitude. Although each person has given something to the other, in the form of goods or services, no quid pro quo has occurred, and it would be incorrect (and not merely cynical) to say that the help was given in exchange for the gift, and vice versa.
The theoretical challenge, then, is to identify the species of reciprocity that constitutes an exchange. This is a task well worth pursuing, as it is difficult to overstate the practical and theoretical significance of the exchange form. In thelaw alone, quid pro quo figures prominently in a wide range of legal contexts--civil as well as criminal, public as well as private--and lies at the heart of a variety of raging legal controversies concerning official corruption, insider trading, and other matters. Although quid pro quo is a transsubstantive concept in the law, we find the law's most developed and influential account of it in the context of the doctrine of consideration. Indeed, one finds in the legal literature surrounding this doctrine two fundamentally different conceptions of quid pro quo. Developing these accounts and subjecting them to critical scrutiny will allow us to produce an adequate theory that captures the essential elements of the exchange form.
In keeping with the norms of the law-review genre, the remainder of the introduction summarizes, in broad outline, the arguments that follow. As we have seen, Langdell's definition of consideration insists on an exchange relation between the consideration and the promisor'spromise(rather than the promised performance). But this exclusive focus on the commitment itself as the object of exchange places it in tension with the traditional common-law conception of bargain or exchange, according to which the objects of an exchange are given in payment, or remuneration, for each other. For, on the one hand, the modern consideration rule is satisfied only if the parties' acts of assent themselves stand in an exchange relation to one another.And yet, on the other hand, there are many valid contracts--for example, ordinary sales contracts contemplating the transfer of goods for money--where neither the parties themselves nor outside observers would regard the parties' acts of assent (in contrast with their ensuing performances) as constituting payment or remuneration for anything. The modern consideration rule thus required the development of a new conception of exchange, which was rendered explicit first by Holmes and then in the Second Restatement. According to this account, classifying two performances as a quid pro quo is a way of characterizing the apparent motives of the parties rendering those performances. Specifically, to subsume two acts (promissory or otherwise) under the exchange concept is to describe each one as rendered with the apparentaim of inducing the other.Combining Langdell's definition with this account of exchange, which I will call the reciprocal-inducement account, allows us to reformulate the modern consideration rule: for an agreement to satisfy the rule, the offer must be made with the apparent aim of inducing the acceptance (whether counterpromise or performance) and the acceptance must be extended with the apparent aim of binding the offeror to her terms.
Although there is evidently some connection betweendoingAin exchange forB anddoingAin order to getB, this motivational account of exchange is both overinclusive and underinclusive. Counterexamples to the theory will be discussed in Part II, but we may observe at the outset that its conditions are frequently satisfied by plans to coordinate activities between friends and familymembers (indeed, between members of preexisting cooperative units more generally) even when neither the parties themselves nor outside observers would regard such plans, or their execution, as constituting a quid pro quo. This is worth highlighting since it bears considerably on the challenge of identifying a plausible rationale for the consideration rule. As I will argue in Part III, its most plausible justifications regard its distinction between the bargained-for and the gratuitous as a legally tractable (albeit rough and ready) way of capturing an important distinction between social contexts or spheres. Consideration, according to this family of views, serves chiefly to exempt promises and agreements formed in certain social contexts from legal enforcement. Such explanations are not available to proponents of the modern rule, however, since its conditions are satisfied pervasively by agreements lying on both sides of any relevant social divide (such as that between personal and impersonal domains). By obscuring these explanations, the modern rule fairly exposes the doctrine to the charge, frequently made, that it is a senseless historical anachronism.
The philosophical mistake at the heart of the modern consideration rule is also the source of many of the well-known problems concerning concrete cases. Some of these difficulties relate to counterintuitive results: given that it embodies a mistaken conception of bargain, the modern rule unsurprisingly treats transactions that are patently gratuitous as though they were bargains, and vice versa. For example, if a genuine bargain requirement rules out anything at all, it surely rules out informal donative promises--that is, commitments to give someone a gift or do someone a favor without expectation of payment--as candidates for legal enforcement.However, as I will show, the modern rule is satisfied by many genuinely donative promises, namely, those involving conditions imposed by a donor who is eager to donate (for instance, a parent, eager to help a child pursue some project, promises to gift a thousand dollars provided the child agrees not to spend any of it on wine). Another perennial problem for the doctrine concerns "fair and equitable" modifications of contractual terms, such as a promise to pay more for a service than the price originally agreed upon due to an unanticipated rise in the cost of providing that service. In such cases ofpreexisting duties, a strict application of the modern rule often fails to find consideration. Courts have reasoned, for example, that the promise to pay a higher price could not be made in exchange for the promise to perform the service because the latter promise had already been bargained for and secured in the initial contract.This outcome is both a counterintuitive application of a bargain requirement--after all, the transaction clearly remains a quid pro quo exchange of money for a service after the modification of the terms--and a target of heavy criticism on policy grounds.Other well-known problem cases include gardenvariety commercial agreements that would not qualify as bargains on any characterization, such as firm offers (that is, commitments not to rescind a particular offer) or guarantee agreements (that is, commitments to another's creditor to serve as the debtor's guarantor). The Second Restatement makes an exception of these cases, but cannot explain the special treatment on principled grounds.Gestures are made in the direction of Lon Fuller's functional explanation--appealing to the alleged evidentiary, cautionary, and channeling functions of the bargain requirement--with the intimation that, bargains or not, these functions are anyway served by the agreements in question.However, as I demonstrate in Part III, Fuller's functional explanation is not only unconvincing, but also unavailable to proponents of the modern rule. For, although it is not immediately apparent, Fuller's account also relies on the idea that the distinction between the bargained-for and the gratuitous tracks an important divide between social contexts, a view that cannot be accommodated by a motivational account--such as the modern reciprocal-inducement account--whose conditions lack any sensitivity to social distinctions. Accordingly, in the absence of any plausible rationale, the Restatement's exceptional treatment can only be viewed as ad hoc.
The defects of the modern consideration rule can be traced to the defective conception or bargain lying at its core. Formulating a better rule is possible, but doing so requires a better grasp of the concept of bargain or exchange. The venerable common-law definition of bargain or exchange as reciprocal payment or remuneration, according to which two performances constitute a quid pro quo exchange if each performance serves as payment or remuneration for the other, provides the basis of this better account. The traditional authorities left the crucial notion ofpaymentundefined, however, which has allowed the law to lose its handle on the exchange concept. Accordingly, Part II provides an original theory of quid pro quo exchange that doubles as a theory of reciprocal payment. On this reciprocal-remuneration account, classifying performances as an exchange is a way of characterizing the normative significance of the performances, and not the motives of the parties. More precisely, according to this view, two performances constitute a quid pro quo when the parties regard those performances as satisfying two conditions: first, that each performance satisfies the debt incurred by the other, and second, that after the sequence of performances neither party shall owe the other anything on account of the other's performance. Together, these conditions imply that, in the wake of the sequence of performances, the parties will be "all paid up" as far as the performances are concerned.
The first condition makes reference to the notion of debt, a species of obligation. While the English language distinguishes between debt and nondebt obligations (one's obligation to repay a loan is a debt, while one's obligation to ensure that one's child has lunch money before leaving the house is not), there has been, as far as I am aware, no substantial effort by theorists to identify debt'sdistinctive features.Without a proper understanding of debt, however, it is not possible to differentiate quid pro quo exchanges from the broader class of "I will if you will" agreements or mutually beneficial collaboration more generally. Part II, accordingly, provides an account of debt in service of its account of exchange. According to this account, the mark of a debt is that performance--for example, paying a creditor the sum of money owed on account of a particular loan--does not guarantee satisfaction. For example, one may pay a creditor the exact sum that one owes without discharging one's debt, as when one's payment is for the purchase of additional merchandise sold by the same creditor. What is needed to satisfy a particular debt is not merely a rendition of the required performance, but a rendition in satisfaction ofthat specific debt(and not some other one). This, in turn, raises the question of how one succeeds in matching particular performances with particular obligations, and the answer may lie in either conventional rules or the mutual understanding of the parties. This distinguishing feature of debt explains both the possibility of accumulating multiple debts (each calling for its own rendition of the same type of performance) and widely observed strictures against "double counting."
The second condition adds to the first that following the performances each party emerges with no lingering obligations arising from the other's performance. In particular, this condition rules out lingering debts of gratitude and duties to reciprocate, unless these arise from aspects of the transaction that are distinct from the required performance.
This account of exchange can be used as the basis of a bargain requirement that avoids many of the well-known defects that plague the prevailing account. According to the remuneration theory of consideration, a promise satisfies the consideration requirement if it can be inferred that the parties regard either the promised performance, or the promise itself, as standing in a relation of reciprocal payment (that is, in an exchange relation) to either the performance, or the promise, of the promisee.This formulation, while registering that a promisecanbe exchanged--as it arguably is when an insurance policy, or a bond, is issued for value--also reflects that it is often the contemplated performances, rather than the promises themselves, that lend the transaction the character of an exchange.This version of the consideration rule does not result in treating bargains as though they were gratuitous transactions or vice versa. Conditional donative promises (when genuinely donative) do not satisfy the consideration test, since the donee's fulfillment of the condition does not stand in a (reciprocal) payment relation to the donor's gift (or commitment to give it). Likewise, the doctrine of consideration poses no obstacle for contract modifications: when two parties agree to alter the price of a particular service, they do not thereby dislodge its status as an exchange. What is contemplated, before and after the modification, is a quid pro quo exchange--money for a service.
The remuneration theory of consideration also has an intelligible rationale--one that enjoys substantial historical corroboration and that provides a principled basis for the traditional exceptions in cases such as firm offers and guarantee agreements. As many have observed, friends and family members tend to shy away from the quid pro quo form in favor of other modes of reciprocity when conferring and receiving benefits among themselves.This empirical observation receives support from the remuneration theory of exchange, which exposes thereasonsfriends and family sometimes have to avoid the exchange form.This observed tendency, together with the contestable, but plausible, normative assumption that the law ought not to enforce promises between intimates unless those intimates expressly enlist the law, typically by invoking legal formalities at the time of formation, provides a rationale for the bargain requirement. On thisinterpretation, the consideration rule does not identify conditions that give the lawreasonto enforce a promise. That is, the rule does not rest on the normative position that a promise ought to be enforcedbecause ofits relation to a bargain. Rather, the point of the bargain requirement is to identify (however roughly) a class of promises--informal promises in social and domestic contexts--that the law has reasonnotto enforce, either because the law's general reasons for enforcing agreements do not apply in these contexts or because features of these contexts override the law's general reasons in favor of enforcement. This rationale not only renders the rule intelligible, but also explains why the law draws (and should draw) exceptions for forms of commercial commitment that, while not belonging to an exchange, tend not to be used by intimates. As I have said, the rationale also receives significant historical corroboration. I have already observed that the modern rule of consideration is not sensitive to social context, and so not up to the task of screening for informal social and domestic agreements. Accordingly, if the rationale is correct, one would expect that the adoption of the modern rule by legal authorities would lead to the introduction or invocation of some other doctrinal mechanism to perform this function. When we consult the historical record, this is indeed what we find. In particular, the legal-intent requirement (requiring an intent to establish legal relations as a condition of liability), or some variation of it, has been consistently wheeled in by legal authorities in both England and America to avoid enforcement of informal social and domestic agreements as soon as the modern consideration rule was adopted.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I addresses in more detail the relation between the textbook definition of consideration and the textbook specification of that definition in the motivational terms of reciprocal inducement. It demonstrates that by insisting, in all cases, upon an exchange relation between the consideration and the promisor's promise (rather than his or her performance), the textbook definition of consideration commits the theorist to rejecting this traditional definition of bargain or exchange and to embracing instead the motivational alternative (in terms of reciprocal inducement). Part II criticizes the motivational theory of quid pro quo exchange and provides in its place an original philosophical account that doubles as a theory of reciprocal payment. Analyzing quid pro quo exchange requires analyzing in turn the notion ofdebt, which, like quid pro quo exchange, is as socially important as it has been philosophically neglected. Finally, Part III shows that the conception of exchange as reciprocal payment can be used to fashion an alternative consideration rule, one that avoids many of the well-known difficulties associated with the prevailing rule, and that can be rendered intelligible by a plausible, historically compelling rationale.

questions.question: What conception of quid pro quo exchange should underlie the legal distinction between enforceable contractual commitments and nonenforceable gratuitous promises?

Does characterizing exchange in motivational terms (i.e., as acts done to induce reciprocal promises or performances) accurately identify bargains, or does this account produce counterintuitive and unprincipled results in routine transactional contexts?

Can an alternative, debt- or payment-based account of exchange-where each performance discharges a specific obligation and leaves the parties 'all paid up'-better explain, justify, and organize the law's rules for when promises should be legally enforced and when informal social/domestic commitments should be exempt?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly examines how contract doctrine (consideration, legal-intent, formalities) is used to draw the line between promises the law will enforce and those it will not, while Paper B analyzes how authoritarian regimes rely on informal self-censorship norms (rather than constant legal policing) to regulate speech online, treating the boundary between formal prohibition and social practice as central to control.

shared_topics.topic: limits of formal enforcement when social or informational practices govern behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law necessarily 'piggybacks' on preexisting social practices and that formal rules can misfire when they fail to track those practices; Paper B shows that formal censorship is practically limited by information volume and thus must rely on social enforcement (self-censorship), exposing a similar tension between formal authority and the realities of social/informational behavior.

shared_topics.topic: strategic use of ambiguity or doctrinal devices by authorities to shape compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how legal authorities resort to doctrines and formalities (e.g., seals, legal-intent requirements) to signal which promises will be enforceable, whereas Paper B describes how regimes deliberately leave speech boundaries unclear so that fear and uncertainty induce self-censorship, both treating ambiguity as a tool to manage conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the role of perceptions, reputational incentives, and sequential social learning in sustaining or breaking norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes parties' mutual understandings, debts, and social context (including how reputational and interpersonal considerations influence whether exchanges are treated as bargains), while Paper B models how individual acts and reputational concerns produce informational and norm cascades online that can either sustain self-censorship or trigger rapid norm collapse.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether collaborative technologies (like BIM) are producing contracting practices that the existing legal architecture should treat differently, and Paper B argues the prevailing consideration rule mischaracterizes what counts as an exchange and thus fails to capture many real‑world bargaining practices, so both evaluate the adequacy of established doctrines for novel commercial forms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' intentions, norms, and social context in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes parties deliberately adopting relational norms (reciprocity, adaptability, shared risk) in digitally mediated projects and asks how law should support that intentionality, while Paper B contrasts motivational (reciprocal‑inducement) versus normative (reciprocal‑remuneration) accounts of exchange and stresses how social context (intimates vs commercial actors) and perceived intentions affect whether promises should be legally enforced.

shared_topics.topic: contractual mechanisms for coping with uncertainty and interdependence in multi‑party projects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that intentionally relational contracts and BIM foster interdependence and allow contractual terms to be set or adapted over the life of complex projects to manage uncertainty, and Paper B develops a theory of quid pro quo and debt that bears on when legal rules should recognize or withhold enforcement to manage expectations and obligations in ongoing reciprocal arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW

shared_topics.topic: how law relies on independent social practices to delineate legal obligations

shared_topics.topic: the proper characterization of reciprocity versus quid pro quo exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a critique of the prevailing motivational account of exchange and proposes a reciprocal-remuneration account distinguishing quid pro quo from broader forms of reciprocity; Paper B centers reciprocally oriented conduct as a core feature of the normative practices through which customs form, engaging the same problem of distinguishing exchange-like reciprocal structures from other social coordination.

shared_topics.topic: the role of doctrinal or evidentiary devices in identifying when social norms become legally operative
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how doctrines (consideration, legal-intent requirement, formalities) function to screen informal social/domestic promises from legal enforcement and to supply evidentiary/cautionary roles; Paper B argues that the dominant 'outside/inside' conception often functions as an evidentiary frame and that legal systems may adopt evidentiary standards to prove that a custom has legal force.

shared_topics.topic: philosophical analysis and redefinition of foundational normative concepts (debt, obligation, custom) to ground legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides an original conceptual account of debt and reciprocal payment to reframe the doctrine of consideration, while Paper B offers an integrated philosophical account of custom as a discursive normative practice challenging the additive 'usus/opinio' model, with both papers reconstructing core normative concepts to better fit legal theory.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: contract modification and renegotiation (how doctrines affect enforceability and settlement)

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between formal doctrine and law-in-action in relational contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a new-legal-realism account showing that formal rules interact with industry norms, negotiated-process bargaining, and long-term relationships in ways courts do not capture; Paper B argues the modern consideration rule mischaracterizes ordinary social and commercial practices and fails to track the social contexts in which promises are actually made, urging a conception that aligns doctrine with real-world exchange.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law doctrines allocate risk and induce loss-sharing or 'efficient' breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how damages rules and limited remedies create incentives to share losses, permit breach as a loss-allocation device, and influence parties' willingness to adjust deals; Paper B addresses how the bargain/consideration requirement demarcates which commitments the law will enforce—thereby shaping which promises (and attendant risks) are subject to legal remediation versus informal, nonenforced arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: the normative purpose and justification of core contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates competing rationales for remedies (preventing breach vs facilitating economically sensible adjustments) and defends attention to empirical consequences as part of doctrinal justification; Paper B critiques the historical and philosophical bases of the modern consideration rule and offers an alternative rationale (reciprocal-remuneration) to make the doctrine intelligible and normatively defensible.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the doctrine of consideration (and related doctrines like legal-intent) functions as a screen that exempts social and domestic promises from enforcement and proposes a revised test tuned to those boundaries; Paper B interrogates whether and how the law should treat 'relational' or deliberately incomplete commercial agreements, i.e., where norms and ongoing relations (rather than discrete formal terms) govern behavior, and whether current doctrine properly draws the line between enforceable bargains and relational practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and law in implementing parties' intentions versus imposing formal exchange structures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether doctrines like consideration should identify contexts the law ought not enforce (sensitivity to social context) rather than mechanically enforcing exchanges, emphasizing when legal intervention is appropriate; Paper B critiques the background law‑and‑economics assumption that courts should reliably support commercial parties' drafted but incomplete bargains, raising doubts about whether judicial gap‑filling captures parties' intentions or imposes external structures.

shared_topics.topic: conceptual foundations of 'exchange' and reliance on motives versus normative relations (quid pro quo, debt, and expectations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a philosophical account of quid pro quo as reciprocal remuneration and a theory of debt that distinguishes motive‑based (reciprocal inducement) from normative/payment‑based conceptions of exchange; Paper B engages with law‑and‑economics models of relational contracting that presuppose particular conceptions of exchange, enforcement incentives, and parties' expectations, and it criticizes the adequacy of those conceptual foundations for guiding legal reform.

shared_topics.topic: whether doctrinal rules accurately track parties' actual intent and commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the modern motivational account of consideration mischaracterizes parties' exchange relations and obscures plausible rationales for the doctrine, and Paper B tests the same normative claim empirically by asking whether sophisticated parties' inclusion of anti-course-of-performance clauses reveals their true intentions about modification rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of formalities and written requirements in delimiting enforceable promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses legal formalities (seals, the legal‑intent inquiry) as mechanisms the law uses to distinguish enforceable bargains from informal social promises, whereas Paper B focuses on the prevalence and function of written no‑oral‑modification (NOM) and related clauses as formal devices that parties use to restrict oral or conduct‑based modifications.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between contract doctrine and commercial contracting practices of sophisticated parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses doctrinal analysis and historical practice to explain why certain commercial exceptions to consideration make sense, while Paper B analyzes 1,550 SEC‑filed commercial contracts to show how sophisticated commercial actors actually draft clauses (NOM, anti‑waiver, anti‑assignment) that reflect or push back on existing contract doctrines.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Origins of Sale: Some Lessons from the Romans

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal explanation of foundational contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical emergence and internal logic of Roman sale law and asks why development stopped at certain points, while Paper B traces the historical evolution of consideration (from traditional bargain notions through Langdell and Holmes) to diagnose conceptual errors and propose an alternative doctrinal rationale.

papers.node_id: 96kylj43!!ARTICLE: Plain Meaning vs. Broad Interpretation: How the Risk of Opportunism Defeats a Unitary Default Rule For Interpretation This article was selected by the Program Committee of the American Law and Economics Association for presentation at the annual meeting of the American Law and Economics Association that was held May 5 and 6, 2007 at Harvard Law School and presented on May 6, 2007.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Plain Meaning vs. Broad Interpretation: How the Risk of Opportunism Defeats a Unitary Default Rule For Interpretation This article was selected by the Program Committee of the American Law and Economics Association for presentation at the annual meeting of the American Law and Economics Association that was held May 5 and 6, 2007 at Harvard Law School and presented on May 6, 2007.
papers.abstract:
Without interpretation many contracts would remain uncertain of meaning and incapable of enforcement. Courts interpreting contracts must grapple with what the words of a contract mean as well as how to make that determination.These questions are likely to be troubling when the plaintiff and defendant have dueling interpretations of the meaning of a contract's terms.
The problem of contract interpretation presents courts with significant questions about the nature and methodology of judicial intervention into private arrangements. The court often assumes an active role in interpreting the words of a written contractin part because words have more than one meaning or because a contract is incomplete.When a court chooses amongst variable meanings, or interprets contracts to craft limitations on parties' behavior when express limits do not exist, its choice must be justified using a justificative framework explored below.
Traditionally, commentators have advocated one of two general approaches to supply the methodology to govern judicial choices of contract meaning.The first restricts interpretation to the words used inthe contract and the other accepts extrinsic evidence about what one or both of the parties to the contract intended that the words would mean or objective evidence of the meaning supplied by contextor evidence of how ordinary commercial parties in a trade used the term or behaved in the current contract.
This article argues that it is wrong to think that courts must make a dichotomous choice always to prefer extrinsic evidence or always to exclude it.Sometimes the appropriate interpretive methodology should explicitly forego extrinsic evidence while at other times it should embrace extrinsic evidence. The choice between the two methodologies should depend upon an assessment in each case about which interpretive methodology is most likely to (1) curb opportunistic behavior; and (2) implement the parties' actual intentions and overall goals,in a cost-effective way to maximize gains from trade.
The drive to curb opportunism under conditions of bounded rationality has been the focus of much of the work in new institutional economicson rationalizing governance structures.These works seek to explain the "organizational imperative" to control opportunism in a cost-effective way, particularly where specific asset investment makes a simple exit from a contract relationship costly.This paper presents an analytical framework for choosing an interpretive methodology that can curb opportunism and implement the parties' goals to maximize joint gains. It is associated with the law and economics branch of contract theory and thus seeks interpretive rules that will maximizeex ante efficiency. However, it posits that to achieve those goals and efficiency, courts must do more than promote standardization through giving judicial approval of a predefined set of "contractual signals for future parties"through law-supplied default terms and interpret terms to recognize private efforts to trump the state-supplied terms "when necessary to avoid an ill-fitting [state] formulation."Courts must be willing to actively interpret contracts to curb opportunism even if it does not result in a stock of standardized terms that all parties can use in future contracts.
Of course, the parties are always free to choose the interpretive methodology that a court should use to interpret the contract.That choice might seem to obviate the need for a methodology to guide courts. Parties could, for example, control the interpretive process in part by limiting interpretation to the actual words of the contract, including a merger clause that would theoretically restrict the court's role to the written document.This does not solve the interpretive problem, however. The parties often do not so specify, in which case courts must adopt an interpretive methodology that not only supplies that term but also appreciates the fact that the parties failed to do so. Moreover, even when the parties supply an interpretive methodology, perhaps by including a merger clause that restricts extrinsic evidence,that provision must itself be interpreted andthere are often exceptions that are crafted by courts, providing an occasion for judicial interpretation.
Whether a court is interpreting the words of the contract or the interpretive directions of the parties or filling a gap in a contract, the methodology the court uses should not be artificially separated from a normative theory that will identify interpretations that will be value maximizing for the parties. Nor can a court isolate the interpretive question from the context of the problems that the contractual language was crafted to solve or the transaction costs associated with crafting solutions to those problems.The interpretive process must therefore start by understanding the normative justification for any judicial intervention in private arrangements, paying attention to the bargaining problems that parties face, including the costs of anticipating future contingencies and future behaviors, the potential gains from effectively controlling opportunism (and the deadweight loss from failing to control it),while minimizing the costs of doing so, including the likely error and litigation costs from particular interpretive approaches in particular types of contexts dealing with parties' various problems.
The role of courts in contract cases is to preserve the autonomy of the parties by preserving the bargain they negotiated and maximizing the returns from the bargain. If, however, a contract is incomplete in ways that will be explored in this article, the court will have to judge, using an appropriate interpretive methodology, how to minimize occasions for opportunism by the partieswhile simultaneously minimizing drafting costs for the parties and enforcement costs.Opportunism is a threat ex ante to the bargainers' ability (and the ability of other potential contracting parties) to maximize their gains from trade. Opportunism is the enemy of bargains and of efforts to achieve the maximum benefits of bargains.
Alternative goals of contract interpretation that vie with curbing opportunistic behavior include: "uniformly [i.e., predictably] interpreting the contract terms chosen by contracting parties" and "standardization"of terms.To achieve standardization, courts interpret express terms in such a way as to permit deviations and that deviation then becomes a new default rule.These new defaults can be invoked by parties in future contracts.
This article posits that the function of the courts in interpreting contracts should include a third goal of discouraging opportunistic behavior as a means of maximizing gains from trade and controlling deadweight losses.
In some ways these different goals of commercial law courts may seem inherently contradictory. How can terms have any predictable meaning if the court "interprets" fixed quantity to mean flexible quantity and thereby creates a new default? However, if courts are sensitive to how the goals can be achieved in each case and when one goal should be trumped by another goal, courts can continue to promote the values that are important to the parties. For example, in some cases discouraging opportunism will require a court to hew carefully to the textual language, simultaneously fostering predictability. In other cases discouraging opportunism, especially in incomplete contracts, will require courts to interpret the contract broadly. Although that approach might arguably impair predictability and autonomy, since the express terms constitute an empty shell and leave certain matters unresolved, the courts cannot simply enforce the express terms as a way of promoting autonomy. Instead, the court has to address whether broad interpretation and law- supplied terms should be embraced as a means of increasing the autonomy by increasing the range of outcomes that the parties can achieve in the face of contracting difficulties. Insistence on adherence to express language should give way to controlling opportunism. Otherwise, textualism would simply be a vehicle for promoting unbargained-for gains for the opportunistic party.
Opportunism arises because parties lack foresight about the future, and because bargaining over possible future contingencies and adding language to contracts is expensive.As the context for contractual performance changes, the costs and benefits of the original bargain change and one party or the other may have an incentive to seek to change the nature of the bargain to take advantage of those circumstances by interpreting its obligations in a certain way. Opportunism also arises when one party has the discretion (whether or not made explicit) due to incompleteness that allows that party to make choices in an opportunistic fashion.

questions.question: Whether courts should adopt a single default interpretive rule (always confine interpretation to the contract's words or always admit extrinsic/contextual evidence) when resolving ambiguous or incomplete contracts.

Whether courts should select an interpretive methodology on a case-by-case basis-choosing the approach that best deters opportunistic behavior and minimizes transaction and enforcement costs-to better implement the parties' intentions and maximize joint gains.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54depaullrev1077!!ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: managing contractual contingency and incompleteness in complex commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contracts as one human response to contingency and examines how lawyers cope with uncertain future events in dealings like M&A and venture capital; Paper B analyzes how courts should interpret incomplete contracts and choose interpretive methodologies to supply meaning where parties left contingencies unresolved.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the rational‑actor/economic model and the need for broader perspectives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the dominance of economic models (homo economicus) and urges philosophical and moral perspectives to understand dealmaking behavior; Paper B likewise invokes bounded rationality and opportunism as departures from idealized economic actors and builds interpretation rules that account for these limitations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of lawyers and courts in resolving uncertainty and curbing opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates a practical, leadership role for lawyers in completing deals beyond strict adjudicative frameworks; Paper B focuses on the courts' interpretive choices (textual vs. extrinsic) as tools to curb opportunistic behavior and implement parties' intentions when private ordering is incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: trade‑offs between predictability/standardization and flexibility to address contingency or opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes doctrinaire adherence to single models and calls for pragmatic idealism that balances measurable and incommensurable values in transactions; Paper B explicitly analyzes when textualist predictability should give way to broader interpretation to prevent opportunism, weighing standardization against case‑specific flexibility.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016wislrev981!!ARTICLE: CAFFOLDING: USING FORMAL CONTRACTS TO SUPPORT INFORMAL RELATIONS IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAFFOLDING: USING FORMAL CONTRACTS TO SUPPORT INFORMAL RELATIONS IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION

shared_topics.topic: managing incomplete contracts and unforeseen contingencies in uncertain/innovation contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines innovation-oriented relationships where pervasive uncertainty makes detailed, court-enforceable terms infeasible and documents how parties still use formal contracts as adaptive scaffolding; Paper B develops an interpretive framework for courts to supply or refrain from supplying meaning in incomplete contracts so as to resolve gaps and implement parties' goals.

shared_topics.topic: the role of formal law (contracts and judicial interpretation) in coordinating parties' expectations to enable informal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that formal contract drafting and legal advice function as 'scaffolding' to coordinate beliefs and make reputation and termination threats effective in the absence of industry norms, while Paper B treats judicial interpretation as a law-supplied mechanism that can supply terms or limit them to coordinate behavior and curb opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between predictability/standardization and flexibility/adaptation in contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Macaulay-style reliance on fixed industry norms with innovation contexts where formal contracts are used to create shared classifications for flexible adaptation, and Paper B analyzes when courts should prioritize textual predictability versus broad, context-sensitive interpretation to achieve efficient outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism risk and legal/institutional design choices to deter it under bounded rationality
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the problem as parties needing mechanisms (formal contracts, legal reasoning) to prevent opportunistic reinterpretation in novel collaborations, and Paper B explicitly models how courts should choose interpretive methodologies to minimize opportunism and maximize ex ante gains from trade given bounded foresight and transaction costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43bclrev819!!ARTICLE: The Rhetoric of Legal Backfire
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Rhetoric of Legal Backfire

shared_topics.topic: assessing unintended consequences of legal rules through empirical and contextual analysis rather than rhetorical or doctrinal defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should choose interpretive methodologies case-by-case—weighing transaction costs, litigation error costs, and the likelihood of opportunism—to avoid interpretations that produce bad outcomes; Paper B argues that allegations of 'legal backfire' are often rhetorical and urges lawmakers to investigate empirical evidence and context rather than accept backfire claims at face value.

shared_topics.topic: balancing predictability/standardization against flexibility and context-specific interpretation in legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a tradeoff between predictable, standardized (textualist) interpretations and broader, context-sensitive readings that curb opportunism in incomplete contracts; Paper B similarly discusses how fear of backfire and over‑reliance on crude objections can produce overly conservative or quick‑fix laws and calls for lawmaking that balances stable rules with adaptability.

shared_topics.topic: strategic or opportunistic behavior by stakeholders and how legal institutions should deter or respond to it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines opportunism by contracting parties who exploit ambiguity and recommends interpretive rules to limit such gaming; Paper B documents how interest groups, advocates, and others strategically deploy 'backfire' rhetoric to influence policy outcomes and urges institutions to recognize and guard against such strategic argumentation.

shared_topics.topic: developing normative frameworks for legal decision‑making under uncertainty to maximize social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a normative, law‑and‑economics framework for courts to select interpretations that maximize ex ante gains from trade given bounded rationality and incomplete contracts; Paper B recommends normative safeguards—careful review and evidentiary standards—so policymakers do not let rhetorical backfire claims distort decisions under uncertainty.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Impracticability as Risk Allocation: The Effect of Changed Circumstances Upon Contract Obligations for the Sale of Goods

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between predictability/formalism and flexible, reality‑sensitive adjudication

shared_topics.topic: maximizing commercial efficiency and protecting parties' gains from trade
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats resolution of changed circumstances as an economic problem of risk allocation that should reflect commercial realities to preserve bargains; Paper B situates interpretive methodology in a law-and-economics framework, advocating approaches that minimize opportunism and transaction costs to maximize joint gains from contracting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46ukanlrev115!!ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unforeseen/latent site conditions in contracts

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and the role of courts/common law in filling gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether common law has a role in redistributing costs and filling gaps left by standard contract clauses in construction procurement; Paper B analyzes when courts should supply interpretive methodologies or law‑supplied default rules to fill gaps in incomplete contracts and thereby shape outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior (low-bid/change-order strategies) arising from hidden contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and critiques patterns in which contractors low-bid fixed-price contracts and later seek change orders when unforeseen conditions appear; Paper B centers interpretation choices on curbing opportunism generated by bounded rationality and incomplete contracting, arguing courts should choose interpretive methods that minimize opportunistic gains.

shared_topics.topic: transaction, drafting and enforcement cost considerations in choosing contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the budgetary and administrative costs (change orders, overruns) associated with how contracts allocate unforeseen risks; Paper B explicitly balances drafting costs, enforcement and litigation costs, and error risks in selecting interpretive approaches or default rules that maximize joint gains from trade.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE CONCEPT OF CHANGE: PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ATTEMPTS TO REGULATE MODIFICATION, WAIVER, AND ESTOPPEL

shared_topics.topic: how courts should fill gaps in incomplete contracts to curb opportunism while preserving party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an interpretive framework arguing courts should sometimes favor textualism and sometimes admit extrinsic evidence depending on which approach best restrains opportunistic behavior in incomplete contracts; Paper B analyzes doctrines of modification, waiver, and estoppel (and proposes a coercion test) to determine when courts should allow or resist changes to agreed deals, likewise wrestling with gap-filling versus locking in bargains.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of private ordering and when judicial or statutory intervention is justified
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses when courts should override or supply interpretive rules despite parties' choices (or silence) to maximize ex ante efficiency and curb opportunism; Paper B assesses private attempts to constrain change (NOM/NOW clauses) and offers statutory and doctrinal reforms recognizing both parties' contractual choices and the institutional constraints on courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 3texamlrev91!!ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: opportunism in contracting and legal responses

shared_topics.topic: role of social and relational context in contract law and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that social context and relational norms matter for legal doctrine: Paper A calls for operationalizing relational contract concepts (solidarity, reciprocity, background social norms) into empirical and doctrinal work, and Paper B contends that courts should sometimes embrace extrinsic/contextual evidence about trade usage and parties' relationships rather than rely solely on text.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracting and mechanisms for filling gaps (defaults, interpretation, design)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage substantively with incompleteness in contracts and how to address it: Paper A discusses the interaction of formal contract design with relational commitments and how relational expectations affect responses to incompleteness, while Paper B analyzes when judicial interpretation and law-supplied default terms should be used to fill gaps to maximize joint gains and limit opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: application of transaction-cost / new institutional economic frameworks to doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Each article grounds its analysis in transaction-cost or new institutional economics: Paper A points to transaction cost economics and business-social-science empirical work as ways to operationalize relational contracting for legal scholarship, and Paper B explicitly uses transaction-cost and bounded-rationality reasoning to choose interpretive methodologies that minimize costs of opportunism and error.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70stjohnslrev239!!ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FRUSTRATION OF CONTRACTUAL PURPOSE - DOCTRINE OR MYTH?

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling and implied terms/default rules for incomplete contracts

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for supervening events and unforeseeable contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether supervening events that destroy a party's bargain motive should excuse performance under the frustration doctrine, and Paper B addresses how courts should interpret contracts (textually or with extrinsic evidence) to allocate risk and deter opportunistic reinterpretation when unexpected contingencies arise.

shared_topics.topic: why courts recognize doctrines in the abstract but narrowly apply them in practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the pattern that courts 'pay lip service' to frustration of purpose yet rarely grant relief, and Paper B likewise rejects a unitary interpretive rule—arguing courts should vary methodology case-by-case—thereby engaging the same puzzle about judicial behavior versus doctrinal pronouncements and the policy reasons behind narrow application.

shared_topics.topic: need for doctrinal clarity and conceptual distinctions among contract doctrines/methods
shared_topics.justification: Paper A insists on distinguishing frustration of purpose from impossibility, impracticability, and price‑adjustment claims and criticizes doctrinal conflation, while Paper B distinguishes textualist versus extrinsic interpretive methodologies and emphasizes precise normative criteria for choosing among them to avoid error and opportunism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: strategic bargaining incentives and opportunism affecting parties' willingness and ability to bargain around defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops game-theoretic critiques showing that promisees and promisors have strategic incentives that typically undermine the idea that a penalty default will induce truthful revelation or bargaining around the default; Paper B centers on opportunism and bounded rationality, explaining how parties may exploit interpretive gaps and why courts should choose interpretive rules that curb opportunistic re-interpretation in post-contractual bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and transaction/drafting costs as determinants of whether courts should supply terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes the limits of the Coasean assumption that parties can costlessly bargain around defaults and emphasizes how strategic frictions and transaction costs affect whether defaults should be imposed, while Paper B explicitly models incomplete contracting and drafting costs to argue that courts sometimes must fill gaps via interpretation or law-supplied defaults to maximize joint gains.

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs in legal doctrine between maximizing ex ante efficiency/gains-from-trade and preserving predictability/autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the efficiency rationale for traditional default rules and assesses empirical and theoretical welfare implications of expansive versus penalty defaults, and Paper B proposes an interpretive framework that weighs curbing opportunism and maximizing ex ante efficiency against goals like predictability and contractual autonomy when choosing between plain-meaning and broad interpretation.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and governance within contractual relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes relational norms and governance mechanisms that constrain opportunistic behavior in long‑term exchanges, and Paper B centers its analysis on choosing interpretive rules that curb opportunism and thereby protect the parties' ability to realize joint gains.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates how formal law and judicial intervention interact with relational norms (especially as contracting evolves), and Paper B develops a law‑and‑economics framework for when courts should rely on text versus extrinsic evidence to interpret contracts and effectuate parties' goals.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between predictability/standardization and flexibility/adaptation in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how relational contracting may resist or supplement standardized legal rules in favor of flexible, relationship‑specific obligations, while Paper B analyzes the tension between predictable textual interpretation and broader, context‑sensitive interpretation aimed at adapting to changed circumstances and preventing opportunism.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE WEED AND THE WEB: SECTION 2-201'S CORRUPTION OF THE U.C.C.'S SUBSTANTIVE PROVISIONS -- THE QUANTITY PROBLEM

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that courts and parties use §2-201 as a mechanical escape route that can encourage opportunistic behavior and frustrate legitimate bargains; Paper B explicitly proposes that courts choose interpretive methods aimed at curbing opportunism (even at the cost of predictability) to protect contracting parties and preserve joint gains.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2019wislrev1109!!ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes doctrinal and practical limits on courts (damages, specific performance) that constrain the enforceability and thus the real-world effect of KSR terms; Paper B focuses on how courts' choice between plain-meaning and extrinsic-evidence approaches determines whether parties' agreements are enforced as written or supplemented, and how that choice affects opportunism and contractual outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: Controlling opportunism and transaction costs through contractual design and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames KSR as part of a relational mix—enforceable and unenforceable terms braided to induce compliance and allow adaptation—addressing governance gaps created by market structure; Paper B develops an economic framework where courts choose interpretive methods case-by-case to minimize opportunism and drafting/enforcement costs, showing how design and interpretation jointly control strategic behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies legislative efforts to alter the dollarization norm and their limited immediate effects, and Paper B examines how courts' interpretive choices create or override norms, weighing predictability/standardization against preventing opportunism to maximize ex ante efficiency.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Case for Market Damages: Revisiting the Lost Profits Puzzle.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should choose interpretive approaches that minimize opportunism and maximize ex ante gains from trade, and Paper B analyzes how a court decision interpreting a boilerplate clause (e.g., pari passu in sovereign debt) can produce large market-wide costs and incentives to re-draft standard contracts.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how doctrinal reform is justified and practicable to address interpretive failures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes that interpretive rules should be sensitive to transaction costs and opportunism rather than rely on a unitary rule, and Paper B evaluates a specific reform proposal (eliminating subjective intent inquiries for black holes), questioning its feasibility and whether doctrinal change is warranted given alternative market solutions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes curbing opportunistic behavior as a central normative goal that can justify broad or restrictive interpretation; Paper B gives special attention to contra proferentem (construing ambiguities against the drafter), a doctrinal mechanism courts use to limit drafter opportunism when resolving ambiguities.

shared_topics.topic: proposing a principled, case-sensitive framework for interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers an analytical, cost-benefit framework for selecting interpretive methodology based on transaction costs, bounded rationality, and likelihood of opportunism; Paper B likewise develops a systematic approach for resolving contractual ambiguity, recommending consistent principles and precedents for courts to apply.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Questionable Ascent of Hadley v. Baxendale

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry, concealment, and opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on opportunism caused by bounded rationality and incompleteness and recommends interpretive choices that minimize opportunistic exploitation; Paper B studies how default rules (especially penalty‑defaults) aim to force disclosure but may fail when parties can conceal information or pool, especially under stochastic outcomes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes bargaining/drafting costs and enforcement costs as central to deciding when courts should apply textual or contextual interpretation, since costly contracting makes some judicial intervention desirable; Paper B models how transaction costs (and expected costs of opting out) affect whether parties will defect from a default rule or remain pooled under it, altering the default's desirability.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that complexity (or simplicity) can signal opportunistic bargaining, asymmetric information, or reliance on reputation and thus should affect enforcement to prevent advantage-taking; Paper B centers opportunism as the key normative goal, arguing interpretive methodology should be selected to minimize opportunistic exploitation and maximize joint gains from trade.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT
