papers.node_id: 1998wislrev463!!ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM
papers.title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM
papers.abstract:
Meaningful law reform … must be sensitive to the concept of law as an organic entity with a past, present and future; an entity which evolves in often unpredictable and inexplicable ways.
The largest production sector in the United States economy is the construction industry.It accounts for annual expenditures of half a trillion dollars per year and directly employs one of every twenty workers, represents as much as thirteen percent of the gross national product,and touches the lives of every citizen. The realm of the built environment comprehends an extraordinarily rich spectrum of law and legal relations. The building process involves the efforts of contractors, professionals, analysts, artisans and laborers as well as manufacturers and suppliers, associating in all sorts of ways: service contracts, sales contracts, contracts involving land, and every conceivable hybrid; product- or result-oriented transactions and effort-focused transactions; discrete "one-shot" deals, and most often, extended long-term relationships.The hoped-for result is the production of a unique prototype performing varied functions over a life span of many years. This transactional system represents a veritable minefield of conflict which is a fertile source of recurring, often unique legal issues.
At a time when much attention in the United States is focused on reform of the Uniform Commercial Code,it is natural to ponder application of the UCC model to other commercial venues. Paeans to commercial codification enshrine the values of realism, modernization, uniformity and clarity, and extol the potentialities of a system of laws animated by the principles of the marketplace. The vision of a cohesive body of principle facilitating commercial exchange by bridging jurisdictional boundaries, clarifying legal standards, and supplementing the agreement in fact - a conceptual ocean upon which float a myriad of diverse transactions - is truly compelling.Although the reality of the"unified" commercial law falls well short of the vision (just as historical reality differs in many respects from the romantic ideal) many who seek a systematic nexus between law and commercial practice still find the prospect of codification alluring.In addition to serving as the vehicle for significant commercial reform inside and outside their boundaries, codification and code reform are attended by intense critical interplay among scholars and practitioners. The commercial code continues to serve as a platform for ongoing debate and a wellspring of legal scholarship.
The transactional law of building design and construction stands in sharp contrast to the UCC approach to commercial transactions within its scope. In the private arena, there is no overarching codification or synthesis of public law defining and limiting this spectrum of transactions.Nor, until relatively recently, was there significantprofessional or academic emphasis on construction law.Given the consequences for practice, teaching and scholarship, a critical assessment of this arena is long overdue.
As diverse theorists have recognized, meaningful study of a legal system requires an investigation of its ordering principles, as well as the complex structures that develop and implement those principles.These principles and structures include not only positive public laws and public law-giving and law-enforcing mechanisms, but a wide array of "private orderings" which overlap and interact with the public law framework in various, often complex ways.Part II's study of the relationalenvironment of construction contracting will show that ordering principles in the form of public (or external) law are often of secondary importance to discrete relationships and rules of provenance internal to the industry, especially extensively integrated agreements based on standard industry models.The existence of substantive principles undergirding the legalorder presumes the existence of mechanisms to develop, identify, and apply those principles.In addition to judicial and legislative functions, implementing structures perform a variety of other critical functions - social, cultural, informational, planning, and mediative.Such structures include the legal profession and supporting academic institutions,internal industry organizations,and mechanisms aimed at managing conflict with minimal interference from public courts or public law.
In the crucible of conflict that is the construction process, numerous "cases of trouble" - from payment controversies, to conflicting security interests, to mushrooming third-party liability - tax the ingenuity of contract drafters and build a case for legislative reform.The case is strengthened by the advent of new project delivery systems, the revolutionin communications,and the special concerns of residential owners.Part III will examine the prospects of systemic reform, beginning with the possibilities and limitations of standard contract models and, ultimately, the potentialities of external law as a backdrop and "safety net" for private transactions, including a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts. It will closely consider the structural, practical and political questions raised by codification, and assay less ambitious public law initiatives. Part III will conclude by discussing the potential contributions of implementing structures - conflict management approaches, the legal profession, and educational and research institutions - to positive change by addressing the root causes of conflict and encouraging more enlightened lawmaking on all levels. Part IV sets forth a possible "action strategy" for systemic reform, beginning with an "intensive, facilitated planning program" involving key actors in the transactional system.
The intent of this treatment is to offer a broader, more realistic perspective for consideration of the form and function of contract law; to enhance academic and professional appreciation of the much-overlooked body of law governing design and construction contracts; and to augment the small but growing body of scholarship critically assessing the advantages and disadvantages of further commercial law synthesis - but working "from the bottom up" rather than "from the top down."

questions.question: Whether creating an overarching, uniform set of legal rules for design and construction transactions would improve clarity, uniformity, and dispute outcomes compared with the current fragmented, private-ordering system.

Whether private-ordering mechanisms internal to the construction industry (for example, standardized contract models, industry organizations, and alternative conflict-management practices) are more determinative of transactional behavior and outcomes than public law interventions.

Which reform strategy-top-down codification of transactional rules versus bottom-up, industry-led institutional and conflict-management changes-more effectively reduces recurring disputes and addresses the root causes of conflict in construction projects.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 12wmmarybuslrev329!!ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: private regulation / private ordering embedded in commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how private regulation and self-regulatory standards (by trade associations, firms, and NGOs) are being incorporated into sales and service contracts, changing the substantive obligations of parties; Paper B examines the construction industry's reliance on internal industry organizations, standard-form agreements, and other private-ordering mechanisms that shape conduct independently of public law.

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting and long‑term supply/build relationships that favor broad standards and off‑contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that long-term supplier relationships lead parties to draft flexible, process‑oriented regulatory provisions and to rely on reputational or informal sanctions rather than formal damages; Paper B similarly emphasizes extended design and construction relationships, the prevalence of integrated standard contracts, and industry practices that resolve problems informally to preserve ongoing collaborations.

shared_topics.topic: limits of traditional legal frameworks and the need to adapt/ reform doctrinal tests or codification to new transactional realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that traditional tax accrual rules (the all events tests) struggle to account for regulatory obligations embedded in contracts and proposes doctrinal adjustments (an implied acceptance requirement); Paper B critiques the mismatch between the UCC-style codification model and the transactional realities of construction law and explores possibilities for systemic reform or tailored codification.

shared_topics.topic: private enforcement and alternative dispute‑resolution and monitoring mechanisms (audits, arbitration, industry conflict management)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses monitoring, third‑party audits, and arbitration as tools parties use to enforce contractual regulatory provisions and to avoid local courts; Paper B surveys conflict‑management structures within the construction transactional system, including industry dispute resolution, mediation, and other non‑judicial implementating structures that limit reliance on public courts.

shared_topics.topic: uncertainty about the existence, timing, and character of rights and liabilities and its practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how conditional obligations, uncertain satisfaction of performance standards, and information asymmetries complicate the timing and recognition of income/expenses under the all events tests; Paper B addresses similar uncertainty in the construction context—about who bears what obligations, project outcomes, and liability allocations—and how that uncertainty shapes contractual design and calls for legal or institutional responses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53santaclaralrev73!!ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: the role of standardized contract forms and industry model clauses in governing commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how extensively integrated standard contract models function as the internal ordering mechanism of the construction industry and shape dispute patterns, and Paper B discusses the distinct interpretive issues that arise with standardized versus negotiated contracts (and warns about abuses in adhesion/standard-form contexts).

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and evidentiary role of extrinsic materials (trade usage, course of performance, course of dealing) in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on when courts should admit extrinsic evidence such as trade usage and course of performance and proposes limiting subjective evidence in favor of public meaning, while Paper A repeatedly points to industry practices, trade norms, and extrinsic private-ordering mechanisms as de facto sources of meaning and governance in construction contracting.

shared_topics.topic: codification or statutory synthesis versus private ordering as mechanisms of commercial law reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly evaluates the prospects and limits of creating a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts and contrasts codification with private industry orderings, and Paper B engages this theme normatively by assessing whether courts (and uniform regimes like the UCC) should treat language and external usage as part of a single interpretive framework.

shared_topics.topic: how to treat unequal bargaining power (adhesion/residential contexts) compared with negotiated commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the special concerns of residential owners and different dynamics in less-negotiated construction relationships, and Paper B explicitly distinguishes negotiated commercial contracts from consumer/adhesion contracts and argues for different interpretive and evidentiary rules (and greater reliance on equity) in the latter.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between predictability/certainty and fairness/ad hoc resolution in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames the interpretive debate as a tradeoff between predictability (public meaning/objective rules) and fairness (contextual equity), and Paper A considers how reform, conflict-management structures, and external law might balance predictable transactional rules against equitable dispute-resolution needs in the construction industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1621!!ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the role of standard-form and industry model contracts in governing repeated commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how construction relies on extensively integrated, standard industry contract models and asks whether those models should be supplemented or replaced by codification; Paper B studies why firms adopt standard-form LTAs or bespoke agreements (SFKs) and how SFKs drafted by OEMs centralize terms and reduce costs across repeated supply-chain transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between formal legal rules and private ordering/informal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes private orderings (industry norms, internal organizations, mediated conflict management) operating alongside public law and asks when external law should act as a safety net; Paper B examines how LTAs braid formal provisions with informal norms, when low-powered (informal) sanctions suffice, and when legal enforcement is warranted to backstop informal mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form functions as a planning and transaction-cost minimizing tool
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames construction contracting as a transactional system where contract form and reform can reduce recurring conflicts and transaction frictions; Paper B develops a bargaining/transaction-cost account showing that parties choose LTAs, purchase orders, or other forms to minimize opportunism, uncertainty, and other transaction costs while serving planning needs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry governance structures and professional institutions in managing conflict and shaping contractual behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights implementing structures — the legal profession, industry organizations, educational and research institutions, and conflict-management mechanisms — as central to improving practice and lawmaking; Paper B considers network governance, relational contracting, and supplier-buyer practices (information sharing, benchmarking, training) as institutional alternatives or complements that govern behavior and resolve disputes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of codification and the prospects for legal reform versus private solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically assesses the possibility and limits of codifying construction transactions (even proposing a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts) while stressing bottom-up reform; Paper B questions whether formal LTA provisions or legal remedies should be expanded or restrained given informal enforcement and suggests when legal enforcement is cost-minimizing versus when private arrangements suffice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84ucinlrev217!!ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*

shared_topics.topic: the deal–text gap in complex commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how complex M&A bargains often become compressed into incoherent or boilerplate text that diverges from the parties' negotiated deal, producing 'lexical opportunism'; Paper B similarly documents how construction projects produce unique, multifaceted bargains that standard or fragmented contracts frequently fail to capture, generating recurrent ‘cases of trouble.’

shared_topics.topic: limits of abstract contract theory when applied to transactional practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques economic and moral justifications of contract law as rooted in simplified 'Dick and Jane' examples that do not explain real-world contracting, while Paper B argues that top‑down codification (e.g., UCC-style synthesis) and abstract models misread the transactional ecology of the construction industry and calls for a more realistic, bottom‑up approach.

shared_topics.topic: the role and problems of boilerplate / standard-form drafting in producing opportunism and dispute
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that boilerplate clauses and poorly negotiated text create opportunities for adversarial reinterpretation and massive liability, and Paper B examines the widespread use of standard industry contract models in construction, their structural limits, and how they contribute to conflict and the need for reform.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering, industry practices, and non-judicial conflict-management as alternatives or complements to public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that the real check on opportunism is parties' motives and practices rather than doctrinal rules, and Paper B analyzes private ordering (industry norms, internal implementing structures, and conflict‑management mechanisms) as central to how construction transactions are governed, with public law functioning more as a safety net.

shared_topics.topic: practical reform strategies sensitive to transactional realities rather than doctrinal abstraction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A ends with constructive suggestions about using theory in lawyering to address lexical opportunism pragmatically, and Paper B develops an action strategy (including facilitated planning, possible codification calibrated to industry realities, and institutional reforms) aimed at realistic improvement of construction transactional law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 144upalrev1765!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS

shared_topics.topic: tension between codification (uniform commercial law) and existing industry-specific private orderings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the UCC's aim to discover and impose 'immanent business norms' and studies how that interacts with a private industry tribunal (NGFA), while Paper B evaluates the prospects and limits of applying a UCC-style codification to the construction transactional system and emphasizes the importance of existing private orderings.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry norms/usages in shaping contractual interpretation and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Code's reliance on course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade and questions their suitability for judicial decisionmaking, and Paper B studies substantive principles internal to the construction industry—customs, standard models, and provenance rules—and how they function as ordering principles.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between written contracts and parties' extralegal or relationship-preserving practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that parties may intentionally act in ways that contradict written terms for relational reasons and that treating performance as the best indicator of intent is misguided, while Paper B documents how construction transactions rely on integrated standard contracts and informal relational rules that often diverge from or supplement formal agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the design and effects of alternative dispute-resolution and implementing structures on commercial behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence from the NGFA adjudicative system showing how industry tribunals adopt formalistic or relationship-preserving approaches, and Paper B examines implementing structures—internal industry organizations, conflict-management mechanisms, and tribunals—as central to managing construction disputes and shaping legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how public-law interventions (court definitions or codification) alter incentives for cooperation, renegotiation, and the evolution of commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that applying Code-based norms can prevent parties from choosing optimal mixes of legal and extralegal terms and can inhibit flexible adjustment and expansion of practices, while Paper B explores how a Uniform Code or other external legal reforms would interact with private transactional incentives and the potential consequences for long-term relationships and dispute incidence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83texlrev1581!!ARTICLE:The Law and Economics of Contract Interpretation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The Law and Economics of Contract Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between drafting (negotiation) costs and litigation/interpretation costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A formalizes this tradeoff (C = x + p(x)[y+z+e]) and argues interpretation doctrine should minimize the sum of drafting and adjudication costs; Paper B repeatedly emphasizes the transaction-cost consequences of complex construction deals and the need to design rules and practices (including potential codification) that reduce the overall cost of transacting in the construction industry.

shared_topics.topic: deliberate contractual incompleteness and delegation of unresolved contingencies to adjudicators or later processes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why parties may rationally leave contracts ambiguous or incomplete (to economize on negotiation costs or as compromise) and the implication that courts will be called on to fill gaps; Paper B documents how construction contracts routinely leave unresolved allocation problems across long projects and examines how the system relies on subsequent dispute-resolution, industry practices, or law to resolve those contingencies.

shared_topics.topic: role of private ordering and industry standard forms versus public law or codification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that interpretive doctrines (e.g., textualism) affect parties' incentives to invest in clear drafting and hence interact with reliance on private ordering, while Paper B studies how the construction transactional system depends heavily on standard industry models and internal governance, and evaluates the potential and limits of external codification (e.g., a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts).

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for managing conflict outside public courts (arbitration, industry dispute management, implementing institutions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes arbitration and the costs/benefits of submitting interpretive disputes to adjudication as part of the transaction-cost calculus; Paper B analyzes a wide array of implementing structures—private conflict management, professional norms, and institutional arrangements—that handle disputes with minimal public-court intervention and can serve as complements or alternatives to judicial resolution.

shared_topics.topic: contracts for long-term, uncertain performance and allocation of future risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contracts regulate the future, that unforeseeable contingencies make interpretation central, and that perfect foresight is prohibitively costly; Paper B emphasizes the distinctive long-duration, uniquely specified projects in construction, the prevalence of uncertainty across project lifecycles, and the resulting legal and transactional problems of allocating and managing future risk.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26jlegalstud203!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS BILATERAL COMMITMENTS: A NEW PERSPECTIVE ON CONTRACT MODIFICATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS BILATERAL COMMITMENTS: A NEW PERSPECTIVE ON CONTRACT MODIFICATION

shared_topics.topic: whether parties should be able to contractually preclude later modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the welfare consequences of enforcing contractual clauses that limit or preclude ex post modification and argues some parties would benefit from being able to 'tie their hands'; Paper B examines the prevalence and function of standard form and bespoke clauses in construction contracts and assesses whether private ordering or external law should validate industry-specific contractual regimes that constrain post‑award change.

shared_topics.topic: how anticipation of renegotiation (ex post modification) affects ex ante incentive design in long‑term transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the prospect of mutually beneficial post‑contract modifications can undermine incentive structures (e.g., moral hazard, adverse selection) and reduce ex ante welfare; Paper B treats construction as a prolonged, relational transactional system where the expectation of change and dispute influences contract drafting, allocation of risk, and project delivery choices.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate balance between private ordering (party‑crafted contractual rules) and public legal standards or codification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs allowing parties to design their own modification rules against default legal doctrines and suggests legal rules could better facilitate bilateral commitment; Paper B surveys the limits of industry self‑regulation in construction, explores the potential of a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts, and asks when external law should supplement or override internal industry practices.

shared_topics.topic: use of contractual design and standard form contracts to manage risk, conflict, and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes enforcing contractual terms that constrain renegotiation as a tool to manage incentive problems and reduce welfare losses from opportunistic modification; Paper B analyzes standard industry contract models and integrated agreements as instruments to allocate risk, reduce transaction costs, and manage the frequent 'cases of trouble' in construction projects.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrinal rules (e.g., reliance, unforeseen circumstances) in policing modifications and protecting transactional stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends judicial caution in enforcing modifications based on reliance and suggests doctrines like unforeseeability could be recalibrated to preserve bilateral commitment; Paper B discusses the judiciary and public law as part of the implementing structures—a legal 'safety net'—and evaluates how courts and legal doctrines interact with private dispute‑management in construction transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 164upalrev1403!!ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS

shared_topics.topic: the boundaries of a deal and the legal significance of multi-agreement transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the construction sector's transactional system of layered, hybrid and long-term agreements and asks how those multiple linked contracts function as a whole; Paper B develops the concept of "unbundled bargains," showing how ancillary agreements (e.g., NDAs) interact with acquisition agreements to define the boundaries of M&A deals and affect enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role and risks of standard-form templates and boilerplate in complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques reliance on industry standard models and integrated form contracts in construction and their consequences for disputes and governance; Paper B documents how template confidentiality agreements and boilerplate language produced unanticipated, case-determinative consequences in M&A and urges more careful drafting and design.

shared_topics.topic: how contract interpretation by courts shapes transaction design and party behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how legal doctrines and public law (and their unpredictability) influence contracting practice in the construction industry and motivates calls for reform or codification; Paper B shows concretely how Delaware courts' interpretation of a confidentiality clause in Martin Marietta altered parties' incentives and will affect future deal structuring.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between private ordering mechanisms and public law as a background governance framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates industry-internal governance (private orderings, standard contracts, conflict-management institutions) and assesses the need for external legal backstops or a uniform code; Paper B explores how privately negotiated ancillary agreements operate within the public-law context (court review) and how that interaction informs whether parties choose to unbundle or consolidate contractual arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: conflict management, dispute risk, and the transaction-costs implications of contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats payment disputes, third-party liability, and other recurring conflicts as drivers for structural reform and for adopting mechanisms that reduce costly litigation; Paper B analyzes how unbundling increases modularity and precision to lower ex ante transaction costs and ex post enforcement costs, and how mis-specified ancillary clauses can precipitate expensive injunctions and litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 74oklalrev127!!ARTICLE: IMPLIED WARRANTIES V. EXPRESS SPECIFICATIONS UNDER THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPLIED WARRANTIES V. EXPRESS SPECIFICATIONS UNDER THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE

shared_topics.topic: limits and applicability of the UCC (codified commercial law) to complex, industry-specific transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes tensions within the UCC—how its implied-warranty gap-fillers interact with express technical specifications in real-world sale-of-goods disputes—while Paper B critically examines whether the UCC model can be meaningfully applied to the construction transactional system and whether a similar codification would work for design and construction contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of express specifications and standard-form agreements in allocating risk and displacing statutory default protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when parties' express specifications should control over (or displace) UCC implied warranties, and Paper B examines extensively integrated, industry-standard contract models and how private contractual terms allocate responsibility and reduce reliance on public-law default rules in construction projects.

shared_topics.topic: need for doctrinal clarity and legal reform to achieve uniformity and predictability in commercial contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies conflicting judicial frameworks and recommends a single analytical approach (precision and completeness) to guide courts, and Paper B surveys structural, practical and political options for systemic reform—including a possible uniform code for design and construction—aimed at greater clarity and uniformity.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between default (gap-filling) public law rules and private ordering/autonomy in transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on implied warranties as statutory gap-fillers and how parties can disclaim or modify them through contracts, while Paper B foregrounds how private ordering, industry norms, and internal dispute-management structures often supersede public law, treating external law as a safety net rather than the primary regulator.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 30yalejonreg1!!Article: Index Theory: The Law, Promise and Failure of Financial Indices
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Index Theory: The Law, Promise and Failure of Financial Indices

shared_topics.topic: private ordering of market infrastructure with broad public effects
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how privately produced artifacts — construction-standard contracts and industry contract models in Paper A, and financial benchmarks/indices like Libor in Paper B — function as de facto market infrastructure that governs millions of transactions and produces effects far beyond the immediate parties, raising questions about accountability and the appropriate role of public law.

shared_topics.topic: standardized industry models as governance mechanisms and their limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the centrality of standard-form and industry model construction contracts in organizing relationships and resolving disputes, while Paper B treats indices and their methodologies as standardizing devices for markets; both probe how reliance on such standardized models can create systemic risks and legal gaps.

shared_topics.topic: human discretion, subjectivity, and vulnerability to manipulation or conflicts of interest in producing reference points
shared_topics.justification: Both articles emphasize that important market referents are produced through discretionary human processes — contract drafting and industry practices in construction (Paper A) and banks' judgment-driven rate submissions for Libor (Paper B) — and that this subjectivity creates opportunities for manipulation, capture, and recurring conflict.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between public legal reform (codification/regulation) and private/institutional solutions for risk management
shared_topics.justification: Each paper weighs the limits of top-down legal fixes — Paper A on the prospects and limits of a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts and other statutory solutions, Paper B on why conventional regulation or litigation is insufficient for indices — and discusses alternative institutional fixes (industry governance, professional norms, property-right allocations, or conflict-management structures) to address root causes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26jlegalstud203!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS BILATERAL COMMITMENTS: A NEW PERSPECTIVE ON CONTRACT MODIFICATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS BILATERAL COMMITMENTS: A NEW PERSPECTIVE ON CONTRACT MODIFICATION

shared_topics.topic: use of contract design/clauses to manage relational contracting and prevent opportunistic ex post modification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties may want to 'tie their hands' by drafting and enforcing terms that limit later, ex post profitable modifications to preserve incentives and maximize ex ante welfare; Paper B examines how standard form contracts, integrated agreements and drafting practices in the construction industry function as private-ordering tools to allocate risk and control opportunism (including change orders and mid-project modifications) in long-term project relationships.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private ordering and public law as mechanisms for governing contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts existing legal doctrine (which favors voluntary modification) with private contractual devices and recommends legal changes to facilitate bilateral commitment; Paper B similarly studies how industry-internal private orderings (standard contracts, dispute-management institutions) interact with public law and investigates the potential role of external legal reform or a construction-specific code as a 'safety net' for private transactional systems.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for legal reform to better serve specialized transactional contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal adjustments (e.g., enforcing anti-modification clauses, imposing requirements on acceptable modifications, judicial caution) to address welfare losses from modification opportunities; Paper B develops and assesses systemic reform proposals for construction contracting (including a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts and other public-law initiatives) to reduce conflict and better align law with industry practice.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency/welfare implications of contract rules and their effects on incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its argument in welfare economics, showing that allowing ex post profitable modification can harm ex ante incentives (moral hazard, adverse selection) and reduce contractor welfare; Paper B assesses how the current transactional law and possible reforms affect project performance, conflict costs, and the efficiency of relationships within the construction industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68tennlrev73!!ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

shared_topics.topic: contractual ambiguity and the drafter's responsibility (including contra proferentem)

papers.node_id: 44ambuslj639!!ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts
papers.abstract:
Suppose that a contract between two parties,AandB, provides for two alternative modes of performance. More specifically,A, the promisor, promises to perform one ofXorYin return forB, the promise, agreeing to pay some fixed price.Suppose that the choice of performingXorYis entirely at the election ofA, the promisor, and, further, thatAbreaches the contract by categorically refusing to perform eitherXorYIt is obvious thatB, the nonbreaching promise, is entitled to some kind of remedy vis-a-visA. The question this article addresses is "To what remedy shouldBbe entitled?"
The question is both important and timely. It is important because alternative contracts are in widespread use, arising in circumstancesincluding employment contracts, rent-to-own contracts, contracts with liquidated damages clauses, take-or-pay contracts, and requirements contracts. It is timely because, as demonstrated by the Supreme Court of Canada's recent judgment inHamilton v. Open Window Bakery,the common law continues to experience uncharacteristic difficulty in articulating consistent principles governing remedies in breach of alternative contracts cases. In the United Kingdom, courts have enunciated at least three (arguably four) different rules regarding remedies in breaches of alternative contracts. In the United States, the majority of jurisdictions select that mode of performance which would result in the lowest recovery forB, the plaintiff promise. This majority rule systematically disadvantages promises by facilitating Pareto inferior opportunistic breaches of contract in certain circumstances.
The problems with remedies for breach of alternative contracts stand in stark contrast to the settled approach for remedies for breach of conventional contracts. Throughout common law jurisdictions, courts award money damages in an amount designed to compensate a disappointed plaintiff promise for the loss of the defendant promisor's performance.As has long been known, the common law compensatory principle is consistent with an effort to dissuade opportunistic breaches of contract.Courts attempting to proceed on this compensatory basis, confronted with assessing damages for the breach of an alternative contractbyA, will attempt to determine the amount of damages that will adequately compensateBfor the loss ofA'sperformance. In determining damages, the natural focus will be on the valueBexpected to derive from the performance ofA'spromise. But how should courts assess and compute the valueBplaced onA'spromise to perform eitherXorY?
One approach would be to valueA'spromise by making reference solely toB'svaluation of eitherXorY. This approach might be supported on the basis that the only practicable way to evaluate the value ofA'spromise toBis to adopt just one of the bargained-for modes of performance as the basis for compensation. If this approach is accepted, then just one alternative must be selected as the basis for computing the damagesAowes toB. But how is this choice to be made? What criteria are relevant to guiding the choice? And, moreover, at what point does the choice we will deem the breaching party to have made crystallize? For example, should it be based on the information that would have been known at the time of contract, at the time of breach, at the time of adjudication, or some other time? As we will see, courts give varying answers to these questions.
Another approach would be to average the value of the performance ofXandYto the promise. This averaging approach, however, is artificial and overly simplistic in that it ignores the fact that the promisor has the ability under the contract to control the mode of performance. Because the promisor has the advantage of the election, the averaging approach would lead to erratic results, sometimes overcompensating and sometimes undercompensating promises. One would expect typically that the averaging approach would lead to overcompensation forB, the promise, because the cost of performance toA, the promisor, is apt to be correlated with the value of performance byB.If this is the case, thenAwill tend to select the least costly mode of performance, indicating that an average of the various options will lead to overcompensation. Nevertheless, where there is not a close relationship (or no relationship) between the cost of performance toAand the value of performance toB, the averaging approach might well result in undercompensation.For these reasons, an averaging approach is apt to be unsatisfactory.
The literature surrounding contractual remedies suggests that option theory is highly relevant when analyzing remedies for breach of contract.We do not disagree. In general, analyzing contractual obligations as options to "perform or breach and pay damages" is illuminating. Indeed, in a recent article, Robert Scott and George Triantis analyze contract remedies for breach, using option theory, arguing that damages for contractual breach should be regarded as the exercise price of the option held by the promisor to escape from the promisor's performance obligations, rather than as compensation for a wrong done by the promisor to the promisee.Scott and Triantis argue that damages for breach of contract should thus be entirely rethought and that courts should allow (indeed, encourage) parties to negotiate explicitly regarding termination rights ex ante and then enforce the bargain on the terms struck by the parties.The thrust ofScott and Triantis's argument is that the common law rule of compensatory damages is an unfortunate historical development and that it would be better for parties to explicitly negotiate, and courts to enforce, contractual termination rights, rather than retain the status quo of a quasi-mandatory rule of compensatory expectation damages.
We find the option analysis compelling, but assume that courts cannot and will not so readily abandon the compensation principle as suggested by Scott and Triantis.In our view, however, courts may be receptive to approaching remedies in alternative contracts consistently with the compensation principle, but in a manner different than has heretofore prevailed. The alternative contracts we analyze are contracts in which the parties already have explicitly provided for various modes of performance in the agreement, though none of the agreed-upon alternatives has been performed by the promisor.Indeed, even taking as given the compensation principle (as we do), the courts have not been uniformly up to the task of appropriately assessing damages.
The central challenge of settling upon an appropriate remedy in cases involving alternative contracts is thatA'sdecision to performXorYwill turn on his or her own benefit when performance is contemplated, but will turn on the magnitude ofB'sforgone gains fromXorY, at a later, more remote point in time, when breach is contemplated. This leads to a discontinuity inA'sdecision rule that has proven to be quite difficult for common law courts to address satisfactorily. More specifically, theperplexing question is whether a court should uncritically accept a claim by the promisor that the mode of performance which results in the lowest recovery by a disappointed promise would have been selected. If courts decline to adopt this approach, as we argue they should, is there a superior remedial rule to guide them in determining the appropriate remedy in cases involving alternative contracts?
This article demonstrates that there is potentially a superior remedial rule available. Surprisingly, however, no jurisdiction has articulated and adopted this remedial approach. Part II of this article adopts a positive perspective, canvasing the rules governing remedies in breaches of alternative contracts in a number of common law and civil law jurisdictions, finding in the process that, although the civil law approach is more or less consistent across jurisdictions, the prevailing common law is mixed across jurisdictions and in some instances contradictory within jurisdictions. Part III adopts a normative approach and demonstrates that the most desirable remedial rule for breaches of alternative contracts is one that has not yet been adopted in any of the leading common law or civil law jurisdictions. In addition, Part III explains how the conventional common law remedy for breach of contract is actually just a special case of the desirable remedial rule applicable to contracts with multiple modes of performance. Part IV interrogates the mismatch between the positive law and the ostensibly desirable remedial rule, analyzing the robustness of the appropriateness of this rule in the presence of informational asymmetries, strategic behavior, and the challenges of adjudication in an attempt to determine whether there are sound reasons that no jurisdiction has yet adopted the rule identified as best in Part III. Thus, Part IV seeks to determine whether any of the rules currently used is a second-best response in light of considerations not incorporated into the normative analysis of Part III. Part V concludes with the suggestion that common law courts (and legislatures in civil law jurisdictions) adopt the principle that the mode of performance that would be selected if specific performance were ordered be used for the purposes of assessing compensatory damages.

questions.question: When a promisor breaches a contract that gave the promisor the unilateral choice between two alternative performances, what monetary remedy should the non-breaching party receive?

Which method should courts use to pick which alternative counts for computing compensatory damages - e.g., the alternative the promisor would likely have chosen, the alternative that best reflects the promisee's valuation, an average of the alternatives, or the alternative a court would have required?
Do informational asymmetries, strategic incentives, or adjudication costs justify adopting a remedial rule different from the rule that would maximize compensation or efficiency?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: whether judicial doctrines produce consistent, desirable outcomes in complex contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses inconsistent common-law rules for remedies in contracts with multiple modes of performance and argues for a superior remedial principle courts should adopt; Paper B similarly interrogates whether modern interpretive doctrines (neoformalism versus standards) will produce predictable, welfare-improving results when applied to the messy realities of commercial contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between formal rules and flexible standards in contract interpretation and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly debates neoformalism (sharper rules) versus standards (open-textured U.C.C. approach) for contract interpretation, while Paper A evaluates competing remedial rules (majority rule, averaging, proposed new rule) and implicitly asks whether a bright-line remedial rule or a more flexible, case-sensitive measure better serves compensation and deterrence.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' ex ante expectations, information timing, and choice points in deciding remedies or interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether damages should be assessed based on information at formation, breach, or adjudication and how the promisor's ex ante election affects incentives; Paper B emphasizes that model-based normative recommendations must reflect real-world timing, industry practices, and empirical evidence about what contracting parties expect and rely upon.

shared_topics.topic: how standardized or widespread commercial contract forms affect the suitability of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on the prevalence of form contracts and the operation of U.C.C. article 2 across varied commercial contexts, arguing that changes toward formalism may have adverse practical effects; Paper A studies alternative-form contracts that are commonly used in commerce (employment, take-or-pay, rent-to-own) and evaluates how remedial rules operate given those standard contractual structures.

shared_topics.topic: the use of economic analysis to evaluate and justify doctrinal choices (efficiency, option-theory, opportunistic breach)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs option theory and efficiency reasoning to analyze promisor incentives and to critique existing remedial rules that allow opportunistic, Pareto-inferior breaches; Paper B surveys and critiques recent neoformalist arguments grounded in economic efficiency and calls for empirical validation of such efficiency-based doctrinal shifts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules and remedial measures shape parties' ex ante contracting and choice of contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how obligational default rules (including damage rules) influence whether parties contract around defaults and which contracts are written, while Paper B examines how the choice of remedy for breach (which effectively functions as a default allocation of losses) affects promisor and promisee incentives and thus the desirability of alternative contract forms.

shared_topics.topic: incentives for opportunistic breach or renegotiation created by legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies strategic bargaining and how particular defaults can exacerbate inefficiencies from opportunistic behavior or strategic reluctance to form contingent contracts, and Paper B analyzes how remedial doctrines (and the promisor's option to perform or pay damages) can systematically facilitate or deter opportunistic breaches of alternative contracts.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling of incomplete contracts through damages and doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes obligational vs. contingency incompleteness and focuses on how courts fill obligational gaps (e.g., by setting damages or applying excuse doctrines) to address state‑contingent failures, while Paper B focuses on how courts should compute damages when contracts provide multiple but unexercised modes of performance—i.e., how remedies fill specification gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the role of asymmetric information, transaction costs, and adjudication difficulties in rule choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that even small transaction costs and informational asymmetries make the choice of default rules outcome‑sensitive and can multiply equilibria, and Paper B explicitly tests remedial rules for robustness in the presence of informational asymmetries, strategic behavior, and difficulties of proof in adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: modeling contracts as an option to 'perform or pay damages' to assess optimal remedies/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the perform‑or‑pay framing to explain how damage rules operate as obligational defaults, and Paper B draws on option theory (the promisor's option to escape performance by paying damages) to recommend how damages should be set in alternative‑performance contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY ALMOST EVERYTHING THAT I DID WANT TO KNOW ABOUT CONTRACT LITIGATION: A COMMENT ON GALANTER

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses uphill/downhill litigation and repeat-player vs one-shotter dynamics that create unequal bargaining and litigation outcomes; Paper B explicitly models informational asymmetries and strategic selection of performance modes by the promisor as central problems that any remedial rule must address.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents variation in what gets litigated, courts' doctrinal complexities, and the growth of arbitration and private governance as alternatives to litigation; Paper B surveys divergent common-law (and civil-law) remedial rules across jurisdictions, critiques courts' inconsistent handling of alternative-contract cases, and assesses whether courts can or should adopt a uniform remedial principle.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates remedial rules for alternative contracts in light of how parties actually bargain and select modes of performance, arguing courts should choose damages consistent with the parties' likely expectations; Paper B empirically and methodologically examines how businesses actually use writings and norms in contracting and considers whether doctrines like the Statute of Frauds (UCC 2-201) should be defended on that basis.

shared_topics.topic: combination of positive description and normative prescription in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly conducts a positive survey of existing remedial rules across jurisdictions and then advances a normative proposal for the best remedial rule; Paper B likewise offers positive claims about business practices and hints at a normative defense of the UCC provision, alongside methodological remarks on using case reports to infer norms.

shared_topics.topic: use of legal rules to deter opportunistic conduct and manage strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different remedial rules (and compensatory damages) either discourage or enable opportunistic breaches and examines informational asymmetries and strategic incentives; Paper B addresses the role of formalities and the Statute of Frauds in shaping contracting practices, implicitly concerned with reducing opportunism and evidentiary games between parties.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrines shape ex ante bargaining and incentives (law as an incentive mechanism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses option-theoretic reasoning to show how remedy rules alter promisor choices to perform or breach and influence negotiated allocations of termination rights; Paper B assesses whether formal requirement rules (e.g., written memorialization under UCC 2-201) reflect and should shape commercial bargaining and the allocation of risk in transactions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: limits of generalist courts (adjudication capacity) in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts lack the institutional knowledge and empirical capacity to combine text and context across diverse commercial environments and so commercial parties increasingly rely on specialized regimes; Paper B documents pervasive judicial inconsistency in awarding remedies for alternative-performance contracts and analyzes how adjudication difficulties have prevented adoption of a superior remedial rule.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties use drafting tools (integration, anti‑waiver, modification clauses and bespoke regimes) to specify the mix of text and context courts should apply, while Paper B examines contracts that explicitly grant the promisor a choice of X or Y and asks how those drafting choices should determine the proper remedy when the promisor breaches.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "AGREEING TO DISAGREE": FILLING GAPS IN DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and critiques existing gap-filling doctrines and proposes a new 'pro-defendant' default for deliberately incomplete agreements; Paper B likewise analyzes how courts should treat contractual alternatives and which rule to apply when the contract does not pin down a single outcome, comparing existing remedial rules and proposing a superior rule for selection.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that a pro-defendant gap-filling rule affects parties' incentives to invest and negotiate by reducing unilateral retraction risks, while Paper B explicitly evaluates how different remedial rules encourage or allow opportunistic breaches and considers incentive-compatible rules consistent with compensation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies agreements where parties deliberately preserve veto or future approval rights over certain terms, explaining how that reserved election should shape enforcement; Paper B analyzes contracts in which the promisor has the contractual election between alternative performances and how the law should respond when that election is not exercised or is breached.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77chikentlrev87!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:THE WRITTEN CONTRACT AS SAFE HARBOR FOR DISHONEST CONDUCT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:THE WRITTEN CONTRACT AS SAFE HARBOR FOR DISHONEST CONDUCT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that privileging written, integrated contracts (parol evidence rule, statute of frauds, shrink-wrap) can create 'safe harbors' that incentivize dishonest precontractual conduct and strategic testimony; Paper B analyzes how the promisor's election in alternative-performance contracts enables opportunistic breaches and how remedial rules can either facilitate or deter that behavior.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates hard versus soft versions of the parol evidence rule and the tradeoff between evidentiary certainty and contextual justice; Paper B assesses competing remedial rules for alternative contracts and the tension between a mechanically administrable damages rule and one that yields substantively correct, deterrence-consistent outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: informational asymmetries, adjudication difficulties, and the reliability of facts or valuations in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on psychology and linguistics to show memory failure and dishonest testimony complicate fact-finding about precontractual promises; Paper B addresses informational asymmetries and evidentiary/adjudicative challenges in determining which mode of performance should set compensatory damages.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic and behavioral analysis to critique and reform contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes economic literature and behavioral insights (psychology, linguistics) to argue for regulatory and evidentiary reforms around the parol evidence rule; Paper B applies option-theory and economic reasoning to diagnose the insufficiencies of existing remedial rules and to propose a welfare-improving damages principle for alternative contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100cornelllrev23!!ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a typology showing how legally sophisticated versus unsophisticated parties choose different contract designs and interpretive regimes (textualist vs contextualist) and argues that party design often should displace generalist judicial inquiry; Paper B examines contracts in which parties have explicitly allocated alternative modes of performance or termination rights and asks whether courts should enforce those ex ante allocations or substitute their own remedial judgments.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the fit of expectation damages for collaborative, information‑exchange or highly uncertain contracting contexts where future gains are indeterminate, and shows how different contracting forms call for different remedial logics; Paper B analyzes breaches of alternative contracts and whether the ordinary compensatory principle yields the right damages, proposing a different measure tied to the mode of performance a court would order under specific performance.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that levels of uncertainty and market thickness drive parties toward different contracting and interpretive regimes (bespoke clauses, trade‑association codes, or court reliance), altering what remedies and context are appropriate; Paper B explicitly evaluates how informational asymmetries and strategic behavior influence which remedial rule for alternative contracts is implementable and robust in practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Corporations and Autonomy Theories of Contract: A Critique of the New Lex Mercatoria

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses law-and-economics conceptions of the corporation and how those models bear on contract-theory debates, while Paper B employs option-theoretic and economic efficiency arguments to evaluate existing remedial rules for alternative contracts and to derive a superior damages principle.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes doctrinal moves that try to dismiss certain theories and urges more integrative theoretical foundations for contract law, and Paper B surveys divergent judicial rules across jurisdictions, identifies doctrinal shortcomings, and proposes a concrete remedial rule to better align doctrine with normative theory.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Maybe Dick Speidel Was Right About Court Adjustment
