papers.node_id: 66casewres111!!ARTICLE: RETHINKING JACOB & YOUNGS V. KENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: RETHINKING JACOB & YOUNGS V. KENT
papers.abstract:
Most living lawyers have run intoJacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kentin their legal education. It has long been a staple in Contracts casebooks.While the result has been widely applauded, in recent years there has been some push-back. Professor Kenneth Ching has recently criticized both Cardozo's argument and the result.Professor Robert Scott in a number of papers, some coauthored, has also concluded that the result was wrong.Yet given the state of New York law at the timeCardozo's result was correct. Moreover, I will argue, the outcome is one that parties would adopt today. Ironically, despite the usual characterization of New York as being formalistic and having "hard" rules, its "soft" position on one question played a significant role.
The core facts are simple. Kent, a very wealthy lawyer, hired Jacob & Youngs to build a mansion. The contract price was about $ 77,000.The contract required that Kent make the final payment of $ 3,483.46 upon the architect providing a certificate acknowledging completion.The architect refused to award the certificate because the contract required that all the pipes be Reading Pipe, but a substantial amount of pipes installed were of other brands. The architect ordered that Jacob & Youngs replace the nonconforming pipe even though that would have required tearing down significant portions of the structure at a great cost. The contractor refused to do so, Kent refused to make the final payment, and Jacob & Youngs sued.
In a 4-3 decision, Cardozo held that the contractor had substantially performed and that the mistake was inadvertent. He stated:We think the evidence, if admitted, would have supplied some basis for the inference that the defect was insignificant in its relation to the project. The courts never say that one who makes a contract fills the measure of his duty by less than full performance. They do say, however, that an omission, both trivial and innocent, will sometimes be atoned for by allowance of the resulting damage, and will not always be the breach of a condition to be followed by a forfeiture.Cardozo continued: "The willful transgressor must accept the penalty of his transgression. For him there is no occasion to mitigate the rigor of implied conditions. The transgressor whose default is unintentionaland trivial may hope for mercy if he will offer atonement for his wrong."A finding of substantial performance meant that the contractor would receive the final payment less an allowance: "In the circumstances of this case, we think the measure of the allowance is not the cost of replacement, which would be great, but the difference in value, which would be either nominal or nothing."
We think the evidence, if admitted, would have supplied some basis for the inference that the defect was insignificant in its relation to the project. The courts never say that one who makes a contract fills the measure of his duty by less than full performance. They do say, however, that an omission, both trivial and innocent, will sometimes be atoned for by allowance of the resulting damage, and will not always be the breach of a condition to be followed by a forfeiture.
McLaughlin, in dissent, painted a very different picture: "The plaintiff did not perform its contract. Its failure to do so was either intentional or due to gross neglect which, under the uncontradicted facts, amounted to the same thing, nor did it make any proof of the cost of compliance, where compliance was possible."If the error were minor and inadvertent, he would have found that there had been substantial performance, but the deviation was neither. He rejected the contractor's claim that the difference in value between Reading pipe and other pipe was either nominal or nothing.The contractor could not substitute something just as good. The dissent quoted at length an 1858 decision,Smith v. Brady:suppose it will be conceded that every one has a right to build his house, his cottage or his store after such a model and in such style as shall best accord with his notions of utility or be most agreeable to his fancy. The specifications of the contract become the law between the parties until voluntarily changed. If the owner prefers a plain and simple Doric column, and has so provided in the agreement, the contractor has no right to put in its place the more costly and elegant Corinthian. If the owner, having regard to strength and durability, has contracted for walls of specified materials to be laid in a particular manner, or for a given number of joists and beams, the builder has no right to substitute his own judgment or that of others. Having departed from the agreement, if performance has not been waived by the other party, the law will not allow him to allege that he has made as good a building as the one he engaged to erect. He can demand payment only upon and according to the terms of his contract, and if the conditions on which payment is due have not been performed, then the right to demand it does not exist. To hold a different doctrine would be simply to make another contract, andwould be giving to parties an encouragement to violate their engagements, which the just policy of the law does not permit.McLaughlin's reference to the uncontradicted facts is misleading. The record contained almost no facts since the trial judge had not allowed any proof. The rejection of those facts was precisely the reason for the Appellate Division's reversal.
suppose it will be conceded that every one has a right to build his house, his cottage or his store after such a model and in such style as shall best accord with his notions of utility or be most agreeable to his fancy. The specifications of the contract become the law between the parties until voluntarily changed. If the owner prefers a plain and simple Doric column, and has so provided in the agreement, the contractor has no right to put in its place the more costly and elegant Corinthian. If the owner, having regard to strength and durability, has contracted for walls of specified materials to be laid in a particular manner, or for a given number of joists and beams, the builder has no right to substitute his own judgment or that of others. Having departed from the agreement, if performance has not been waived by the other party, the law will not allow him to allege that he has made as good a building as the one he engaged to erect. He can demand payment only upon and according to the terms of his contract, and if the conditions on which payment is due have not been performed, then the right to demand it does not exist. To hold a different doctrine would be simply to make another contract, andwould be giving to parties an encouragement to violate their engagements, which the just policy of the law does not permit.
The lack of facts was not for want of trying. Plaintiff's counsel would ask: "Do you know X?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "What is X?" Objection. Sustained.This pattern was repeated twenty times. So it is not surprising that the facts were uncontradicted. But the appeal was based on the Appellate Court's finding that the facts (all 20 X's) were wrongly excluded. The reversal was upon a question of law, not facts. McLaughlin just ignored the legal question and was content to rely on his characterization of the limited facts that had made it into the record.
Of course, Cardozo did not have the facts either. Yet unlike the Appellate Division, his decision did not simply remand for retrial. Professor Ching writes:Cardozo took the extremely aggressive approach of not merely remanding for a new trial, but of directing a verdict in favor of Jacob & Youngs, largely on the grounds that substantial performance had occurred. But how could Cardozo know substantial performance occurred? There was virtually no evidence on this very issue!Actually, there was a factual basis, albeit not in the record. There had been a previous trial. In that trial the judge let the facts in and the jury found for Jacob & Youngs.The trial judge, however, held that "[i]t was error to submit the case to the jury, and for that reason the verdict should be set aside, and also for the reason that it was against the weight of evidence."There is no indication as to why a second trial was necessary.Perhaps the existence of that factual record was the basis for Kent's decision to stipulate that a finding for the plaintiff would be dispositive: "[D]efendant hereby stipulates and agrees that if the said order of the Appellate Division be affirmed, judgment absolute shall be rendered against him in favor of the above-named plaintiff."Cardozo was not being aggressive; he was merely doing what the parties had agreed to.
Cardozo took the extremely aggressive approach of not merely remanding for a new trial, but of directing a verdict in favor of Jacob & Youngs, largely on the grounds that substantial performance had occurred. But how could Cardozo know substantial performance occurred? There was virtually no evidence on this very issue!
That only explains why Cardozo could render a final judgment in the case. It does not justify that judgment. The decision raised a number of issues. Why should the plaintiff's willfulness matter? Why settle for substantial performance? If the law is to find substantial performance, what should be subtracted from the contract price--the value of completed performance, the cost of completion, or something else? Finally, there is the dog that didn't bark. The contract made the final payment conditional on the architect's certificate. No certificate, no payment it would seem. Neither Cardozo nor McLaughlin even raised that argument; what happened?
Before moving on to these questions, I should make four observations. First, there was an easier way to get to the result. The specifications included the following: "Where any particular brand of manufactured article is specified, it is to be considered as a standard. Contractors desiring to use another shall first make application in writing to the Architect, stating the difference in cost, and obtain their written approval of the change."Plaintiff's brief noted: "Under this provision of the contract, pipe of Reading Manufacture was to be regarded simply as 'standard'. Plaintiff, having furnished pipe equal in all respects thereto complied with this provision of the contract. Itsonly failure was in inadvertently omitting to get the approval of the architect."If Jacob & Youngs could prove that the non-Reading pipe met the standard, then its breach was only the failure to get the architect's written approval. Damages for this failure would be nominal since there would have been no basis for the architect to withhold approval.
, in discussing the Restatement (Second) of Contracts illustration in § 229, which is based onJacob & Youngs, Scott & Kraus make this argument:It is, of course, possible that the drafting was careless or made in ignorance of the legal implications of making a contractual obligation a condition rather than a promise. But such a conclusion would require some objective evidence to override the strong presumption that commercially sophisticated parties such as . . . the contractor, exercise reasonable care in executing their agreements and know or should know the legal implications of the express contractual language to which they agree.The legal implications depend on both the contract language and the law of the relevant jurisdiction. If, in fact, the pre-existing New York law imposed constraints on the contractual language, the parties should be presumed to have the knowledge of both the contract language and the law.
It is, of course, possible that the drafting was careless or made in ignorance of the legal implications of making a contractual obligation a condition rather than a promise. But such a conclusion would require some objective evidence to override the strong presumption that commercially sophisticated parties such as . . . the contractor, exercise reasonable care in executing their agreements and know or should know the legal implications of the express contractual language to which they agree.
That leads to the third point. The contract was a standard form contract for the entire country.If the language was inconsistent with New York law, then it had to be interpreted accordingly. That is pretty obvious. It matters, particularly in resolving the nonbarking dog problem. It turns out that New York gave less weight than most other jurisdictions to the architect's certificate.
,, and (I suspect) most contracts professors, had been under the impression that the prominence of Cardozo's decision was due to its innovative nature and that much of this--the emphasis on willfulness, the substantial performance, the value of performance--was a sharp break from the past. In fact, it was not. As we shall see, the notion of substantial performance of building contracts and the role of willfulness was over fifty years old.New York precedent on the costversus value of completion was skimpier, but it did exist, even though it was not cited in plaintiff's brief.
The legal background will be described in Part I. I begin with the development of the doctrine of substantial performance and the role of willfulness. If the contractor's compensation were conditional on the architect providing a certificate of completion, what happens if the architect refused to provide the certificate? If a court concludes that the work had been substantially performed, how should the contractor's award be modified? In Part II, I revisitJacob & Youngsto show how the result followed from the pre-existing law. That, of course, does not mean that it was a sensible outcome. In Part III, I show that theJacob & Youngsresult has, in essence, been incorporated into the standard form building contracts.

papers.node_id: 82lawcontempprob1!!ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
papers.abstract:
What kind of contract is boilerplate? Is it typical - because it literally describes most actual contracts? Is it anomalous - because it departs from standard ideas about contract formation, which apply to most other contracts? Is it not contract at all - because it lacks meaningful assent on one side? How courts should deal with boilerplate seems to turn on these prior questions regarding its basic character: If it is not contractual at all, then it should not be enforceable. If it is normal contract, then it requires no special treatment. If it is anomalous, though legitimate and enforceable, it would call for its own interpretive regime.
It turns out, though, that how we interpret boilerplate has repercussions for what it is, or how we conceive its legal status. That is, only if our interpretive methodology makes good sense of boilerplate - if it renders boilerplate the recognizable product of the kind of consent we are looking for in contract, and delivers outcomes that serve autonomy and efficiently govern transactions - only then can we justify applying the apparatus of contract to boilerplate and thereby accept it as the means by which the terms of innumerable transactions are set.
In this Article, I argue that boilerplate is properly regarded as normal contract. We can treat it "normally" for two reasons. First, contract interpretation should always take into account factors that scholars deem especially important in the context of boilerplate. Thus, if we understand general contract interpretation in that way, boilerplate does not require its own interpretive regime. More specifically, boilerplate only functions if we take into account the standard market terms that it ordinarily accompanies. I argue, however, that courts should always take standard market terms into account as a benchmark for interpreting ambiguous contract language. More generally, contract interpretation should always incorporate external references of reasonable meaning. Properly applied, such an externally-sensitive methodology would operate to account for third-party effects of boilerplate interpretation without requiring a specialized procedure.
The second grounds for treating boilerplate normally is that some kinds of contextual considerations regarding the process of formation are self-effacing with respect to boilerplate. Because it is appropriate for courts to take into account communications between the parties regarding ambiguous contract terms when interpreting those terms, we might worry that courts will assign meaning to meaningless variation among boilerplate or retroactively imbue communications between contracting parties with significance they did not have. But the general rule works fine for boilerplate as long as courts recognize boilerplate as such. That is, if a given text is standardized, that just means that the parties did not in fact negotiate the language of that term and that evidence pertaining to their negotiations is therefore not relevant to its meaning. This news is not hard to swallow for courts that understand contract as no less than the product of markets than the work product of attorneys.
The interpretive method recommended here is normative triangulation, under which courts interpret ambiguous contract terms in light of the parties' background duties.Normative triangulation seems at first blush orthogonal to standard postures in the debate on contract interpretation. The primary debate is between formalism and contextualism, and the contested question is how much inquiry courts should make into the circumstances of contract. Formalists would defer to party choice, and at least sharply limit judicial inquiry into facts outside the text of an agreement where it records a transaction between sophisticated parties.Contextualists would have courts more easily incorporate a variety of contextual considerations, including communications between the parties, their prior course of dealing, course of performance, and trade usage.
This debate is misguided in two important respects. First, participants in the debate, but especially contextualists, tend to assume that the relevant context is largely specific to the parties, such that contextualization is substantially the same as tailored gap-filling. But the relevant contextual facts are usually not specific to the parties, rather they describe the market in which they operate.
The second mistake is committed mostly by formalists. One of their compelling arguments sounds in judicial humility - or, in its more snarky form, a charge of judicial incompetence. That is, some formalists argue that parties will generally be risk-averse and prefer that judges undertake a more minimal inquiry.Contextual evidence, on this view, actually makes it easier to manipulate the judicial process and renders its outputs more unpredictable.Others argue that because more information is more expensive, at least sophisticated parties would not wish to pay more to reduce the odds that courts will get the right answer. Their ambitions are more limited; they just want courts to get it right "on average."
In this Article, I argue that, while some parties are more risk-averse than others, risk aversion is indeed the appropriate stanceof courtsin selecting their interpretative methodology. Courts should avoid assigning meaning to contract language that is surprising; contract interpretation should not be creative. This risk aversion argues in favor of judges discounting both their own untethered understanding of contract languageandtheir judgments about the particular intentions of contracting parties in favor of the third, often overlooked leg of interpretation - social determinants of contract terms. The interpretive preferences of courts need not merely mirror those of parties because contract is a regulatory tool of the state whose purposes include, but are not limited to, actualizing the preferences of various contracting pairs. From the perspective of the state, the external bases for private agreement are doubly significant: they are both predictive of contracting parties' intentions, and therefore indirect evidence of those intentions; and also independently indicative of what a reasonable contract under those circumstances would be.
Non-particularized, contextual information is generally appropriate in normative triangulation, which charitably reads the terms of a contract as compliant with background duties - which, in most commercial contexts, willturn on market norms.While we do not have reliable information about exactly what courts do well,market norms should be relatively cheap for courts to discern. Just as courts are better at filling in price than quantity, courts are better at ascertaining market norms and reading contract terms in that context than they are at attempting to reconstruct the particular bargain that any two contracting parties may have struck. Risk aversion thus cuts in favor of assuming contracts are market-conforming unless there is a clear indication that the parties chose to meaningfully depart from the market standard.
Normative interpretation delivers especially important benefits in the context of boilerplate. Where terms are used en masse, they have consequences that no single private user has reason to assign substantial weight. However, a court that interprets a term in a fashion that ordinarily takes into account that it governs many similarly - even if not identically worded - deals cannot but take into account the reasonableness of the interpretation across the market. The court will naturally avoid the distortions that arise from interpreting a single agreement in isolation. In particular, a court interpreting boilerplate should favor the interpretation that minimizes externalities both to other users of the given boilerplate and to other concentrated groups with a stake in the boilerplate. Systematically interpreting boilerplate in this way will make it more costly for bilateral sets of contracting parties to transact on anti-social terms.
In this Article, I proceed as follows. Part II briefly describes the debate between contextualists and formalists. It summarizes and advocates normative triangulation as an intermediate position that prioritizes "market-general" contextual considerations over "party-tailored" kinds of considerations. Similarly, because normative triangulation justifies external reference on the public availability of background conditions, I argue that some kinds of market-general considerations are more appropriate than others. For example, the theory would favor published prices, formal trade association guidance, and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)-filed agreements over information available only via witness testimony.The interpretive methodology here is not specific to boilerplate.
Part III applies normative triangulation to boilerplate and argues that doing so ameliorates many concerns about present treatment of boilerplate withoutrequiring any special doctrinal edifice. This Part also defends the application of a general contract law to apparently distinct species of contract like boilerplate.
In Part IV, I consider the implications of my recommended interpretive approach for how we understand boilerplate. In particular, I address those who argue that we are better off dismissing boilerplate as unilateral and therefore non-contractual. I argue that recognizing boilerplate as socially situated actually redeems it as no more or less bilateral than many other forms of contract about which we are sanguine in a market-based society. Like most private agreements, boilerplate is embedded in public markets and reflects the virtues and vices of a market economy. Finally, Part V concludes.

questions.question: Whether standardized/boilerplate contract terms should be treated as ordinary contractual terms (and thus governed by general contract law) or regarded as requiring a distinct interpretive regime or being non-contractual

Whether courts should interpret ambiguous contract language by prioritizing market-wide/contextual evidence (background duties and market norms) over party-specific negotiations or subjective intentions
Whether interpreting boilerplate with a market-general, risk-averse methodology reduces harmful externalities and improves predictability and alignment with contracting parties' likely intentions

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1547!!ARTICLE: The Questionable Ascent of Hadley v. Baxendale
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Questionable Ascent of Hadley v. Baxendale

shared_topics.topic: designing/filling contractual gaps through defaults or interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues about how courts should interpret ambiguous boilerplate terms and proposes an externally-sensitive interpretive methodology (normative triangulation) as the proper way to fill gaps; Paper B analyzes Hadley-derived penalty-defaults and models how default rules should be chosen to fill incomplete contracts and induce desirable behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate weight of market-general norms versus party-specific intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends courts should prioritize market norms and external references over idiosyncratic party-tailored evidence when construing boilerplate; Paper B similarly evaluates default rules by reference to market consequences (pooling, pricing) and the informational role defaults play across parties rather than only the bilateral bargain.

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the role of courts versus lawmakers in setting contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A prescribes a judicial interpretive stance (risk-averse, market-aware) for courts deciding boilerplate disputes, while Paper B questions whether judges or legislatures can reliably set optimal penalty-default rules and stresses the difficulty of that institutional task.

shared_topics.topic: accounting for social or market-wide externalities when choosing doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes interpreting boilerplate to minimize third‑party externalities and to avoid imposing anti‑social terms across many transactions; Paper B studies how default regimes can create cross‑party subsidies or pools (and associated welfare effects), complicating assessments of a rule's social desirability.

shared_topics.topic: the role of uncertainty and risk (risk aversion, stochastic damages) in selecting doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for judicial risk aversion in interpretation—courts should avoid surprising, creative assignments of meaning—while Paper B demonstrates that damages are stochastic and that uncertainty about damages/probabilities materially alters the incentives and effectiveness of penalty-default rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95nwulrev91!!Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS

shared_topics.topic: how courts should choose interpretive methodology (formalism vs contextualism)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the debate over textual/formalist versus contextualist interpretation: Paper A proposes 'normative triangulation' as a middle path that privileges market-general context, while Paper B argues that courts should let features like contractual complexity or simplicity inform whether to fill gaps or apply literal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: using market norms and external, non-party-specific context as interpretive benchmarks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should read ambiguous terms against standard market terms and publicly observable benchmarks; Paper B similarly treats conventions, reputational norms, and environmental features as background that explain why parties draft simple or complex contracts and thus should inform interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form (boilerplate, simplicity, or complexity) should affect enforcement and gap-filling
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the legal significance of a contract's structural features: Paper A focuses on boilerplate/standardized terms and whether they require special doctrinal treatment, while Paper B analyzes how the degree of complexity or simplicity signals the parties' contracting environment and therefore should affect how aggressively courts supply terms or enforce literal language.

shared_topics.topic: inferring bargaining process, opportunism, and incentives from contract structure to guide judicial responses
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat observable contract characteristics (standardized clauses, low complexity, high complexity) as evidence about negotiation costs, asymmetric information, reputation, or advantage-taking; they argue courts should use those inferences to choose doctrines that deter opportunism and produce predictable, welfare-relevant outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64dukelj605!!Article: HOLLYWOOD DEALS: SOFT CONTRACTS FOR HARD MARKETS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: HOLLYWOOD DEALS: SOFT CONTRACTS FOR HARD MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: contractual formalization as a strategic deal term that calibrates enforceability and flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes the degree of formalization (soft vs hard contracts) as an explicit bargaining choice that trades off legal enforceability for flexibility and lower transaction costs; Paper B treats standardization/boilerplate as a form of contractual form that should be interpreted in light of its market role, effectively recognizing how formality and standard language shape what commitments courts will enforce.

shared_topics.topic: use of market norms and standardized terms as the appropriate benchmark for understanding and interpreting contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties rely on industry practices and reputational expectations in Hollywood to govern behavior when written detail is limited, and Paper B argues courts should use market-general norms and published standards as the primary external reference when interpreting ambiguous or boilerplate contract language.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between legal enforcement and extra-legal mechanisms (reputation, market discipline) in sustaining transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that soft contracts are sustained by a mix of tentative legal threats and reputational liability, and Paper B highlights how social determinants and market conformity function as extrajudicial constraints that interpretation should respect, so that contractual governance relies on both law and market-based discipline.

shared_topics.topic: transaction/specification costs and holdup risk as drivers of contract design and judicial approach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links high specification and enforcement costs and holdup risk to the adoption of soft, less formalized instruments (and to the decline of vertical integration), while Paper B foregrounds information and enforcement costs (judicial informational limits and parties' risk aversion) in justifying an interpretation method that relies on cheaper, market-level information rather than costly party-specific reconstruction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58alalrev765!!ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context

shared_topics.topic: when and how contracting parties (or regulated actors) can reasonably rely on existing rules and anticipate changes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should be risk‑averse in assigning meanings to contract language so as not to surprise parties and undermine reasonable expectations; Paper B devotes extensive analysis to transition policy and asks when parties could or should have anticipated legal changes (and therefore when retroactive application is fair or efficient).

shared_topics.topic: the use of market‑level/default norms versus party‑specific intentions in interpreting or applying commercial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes 'normative triangulation' that privileges market‑general contextual facts and external benchmarks when interpreting ambiguous boilerplate; Paper B analyzes the prevalence and function of default rules in the U.C.C. and how those defaults (as hypothetical bargains) interact with the prospect of law changes and retroactivity.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and incentives — whether to expose private actors to interpretive or governmental change for social welfare reasons
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes judicial risk‑aversion and recommends discounting creative or idiosyncratic interpretations in favor of market‑conforming readings to minimize negative externalities; Paper B evaluates the consequentialist case for pro‑retroactivity (exposing actors to government risk to produce efficient incentives) and explains why that incentive story may misfit many commercial contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of institutional competence, information costs, and transaction costs in doctrinal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims courts are relatively well‑suited to identify market norms and should therefore rely on external, publicly available information rather than reconstructing bespoke bargains; Paper B stresses cognitive limits, negotiation costs, and informational uncertainty that make anticipation or insurance against legal change costly, arguing these institutional and transaction costs must shape retroactivity and commercial rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1994wislrev331!!ARTICLE: STRUGGLING WITH QUICKSAND: THE INs AND OUTs OF COTENANT POSSESSION VALUE LIABILITY AND A CALL FOR DEFAULT RULE REFORM Copyright 1994, Evelyn Alicia Lewis.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STRUGGLING WITH QUICKSAND: THE INs AND OUTs OF COTENANT POSSESSION VALUE LIABILITY AND A CALL FOR DEFAULT RULE REFORM Copyright 1994, Evelyn Alicia Lewis.

shared_topics.topic: designing default rules to govern relationships when parties have not reached an agreement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes competing default-rule regimes that allocate rental liability among cotenants when there is no agreement and proposes a redesigned default to better fit default-rule theory; Paper B treats how courts should interpret boilerplate as a question of what default interpretive regime should apply when parties have not negotiated terms, arguing for an externally-sensitive methodology rather than special-case treatment.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in gap‑filling and applying default doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how judiciary practice implements the two state approaches to cotenancy liability and critiques application gaps, while Paper B focuses on judicial interpretive methodology for ambiguous or non-negotiated boilerplate and prescribes how judges should fill interpretive gaps.

shared_topics.topic: using market norms or external benchmarks to inform legal defaults and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests cotenancy default rules against general default‑rule theory (which relies on contract/market-based premises) and seeks a rule that respects market-relevant commonalities, and Paper B explicitly endorses interpreting ambiguous terms by reference to market norms and other external, publicly-available benchmarks.

shared_topics.topic: balancing party-specific intent/autonomy against systemic/regulatory considerations (risk aversion and efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs property-specific cotenancy doctrines against broader contract default theory—trading off individualized agreements and state policy—and proposes a default that respects those tensions; Paper B argues that courts should be risk‑averse and favor market‑conforming, systemically reasonable readings of boilerplate over reconstructing particular parties' intentions to promote predictable, efficient outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 144upalrev1765!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS

shared_topics.topic: the role of market norms / usage of trade as external reference points in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should routinely interpret ambiguous terms by reference to market-standard terms and other market-general background duties (normative triangulation); Paper B examines and critiques the UCC's directive that judges discover and apply 'immanent business norms' (usage, course of dealing, course of performance), showing empirically that merchant adjudicators often reject that approach and analyzing its consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the formalism versus contextualism debate about how far courts should inquire beyond the text (course of dealing, course of performance, trade usage)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates boilerplate within the formalism/contextualism debate and proposes a middle path that privileges market-general contextual facts over party-specific tailoring; Paper B directly challenges the Code's contextualist impulse to treat performance and trade usage as controlling, arguing this can misread parties' intentions and produce perverse effects.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive/adjudicative methodology alters contracting behavior and market outcomes (including externalities from standardized terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that interpretive choices (e.g., favoring market-conforming readings) shape whether boilerplate produces negative externalities and how markets self-regulate; Paper B shows that the Code's insistence on importing business norms into adjudication changes parties' incentives, can constrain extralegal cooperative norms, and thereby alters commercial relationships and practices.

shared_topics.topic: differences between public courts and private merchant tribunals in applying norms and the implications for commercial ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts should and can use publicly observable market information to interpret standardized terms, while Paper B compares courts to a private NGFA merchant tribunal that adopts a more formalistic approach, using that contrast to draw implications about which adjudicative forum better preserves merchant practices and relationship norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis397!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT

shared_topics.topic: alignment of default rules/contractual silence with market expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether the UCC default warranty that applies when contract language is silent matches consumer expectations by comparing prices across explicit, disclaimed, and silent eBay listings; Paper B argues normatively that courts should assume contracts conform to market norms and therefore adopt interpretive defaults that track ordinary market expectations rather than imaginative judicial reconstructions.

shared_topics.topic: use of market norms and standard terms as benchmarks for interpreting ambiguous language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how consumers read and price explicit warranty language versus silence—showing that market actors treat standard warranty statements meaningfully—while Paper B develops an interpretive methodology (normative triangulation) that prioritizes published market norms and trade usage as primary external references when courts resolve ambiguity in contract language.

shared_topics.topic: legal treatment and consequences of boilerplate/standardized terms (including externalities)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies standardized warranty formulations ('as is', 'satisfaction guaranteed', UCC text, or silence) and their effects on transaction prices and consumer expectations, and Paper B analyzes how boilerplate functions en masse, emphasizing that interpretation should account for the broader externalities boilerplate imposes across market participants and minimize anti-social term selection.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal rules and interpretive doctrines should be grounded in actual contracting behavior (empirical vs. normative justification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A supplies field-experimental evidence assessing whether an existing statutory default conforms to consumer behavior, and Paper B provides a normative argument that courts should rely on market-general signals and predictable social determinants—effectively grounding interpretive doctrine in observable market patterns and practical predictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 74califlrev1123!!ARTICLE: Of Expectations, Incomplete Contracting, and the Bargain Principle.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Of Expectations, Incomplete Contracting, and the Bargain Principle.

shared_topics.topic: using market benchmarks (price or market norms) as the baseline for interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes modeling parties' expectations in terms of price and an agreed-upon range of contract values (market price at enforcement) rather than event-by-event allocations; Paper B argues courts should interpret ambiguous terms by reference to market norms and external, market-general benchmarks when reading boilerplate and other contracts.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling for ambiguity or unallocated risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats excuse, modification, and enforcement as mechanisms for addressing unallocated risks and outlines a theory for how courts should determine what risks parties actually consented to and how to allocate unallocated excess; Paper B defends an interpretive methodology (normative triangulation) by which courts fill gaps or ambiguities using background duties and market context rather than speculative reconstructions of particular parties' intents.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal design tradeoffs between certainty/stability and responsiveness to incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how classical complete-contract doctrines provide bright-line certainty but misalign with realistic incomplete bargaining and how liberalizing modification/excuse doctrines undermines contractual stability; Paper B emphasizes judicial risk aversion and the need for interpretive rules that reduce unpredictability and externalities, arguing for approaches that balance predictability with accurate, market-informed outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: what counts as meaningful consent in standardized or unnegotiated terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether contracts reflect real consent when parties cannot foresee or allocate risks and recommends focusing on what parties actually consented to (e.g., price ranges); Paper B directly addresses whether boilerplate manifests sufficient bilateral assent and argues that treating standardized terms as embedded in market practices can legitimize their enforceability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nyulrev487!!ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between party autonomy and mandatory default rules (enforceability of contract modifications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates whether parties should be permitted to contract around the law's refusal to enforce anti-modification clauses and whether alternative private devices can achieve immutability; Paper B analyzes the limits of deference to party choice in interpretation (formalism vs contextualism) and defends an interpretive stance that sometimes restrains pure party autonomy in favor of predictable, market-conforming outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of market norms and third‑party/background duties for contractual meaning and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B builds a theory of 'normative triangulation' that anchors ambiguous terms in market norms and background duties, arguing courts should use external market references; Paper A treats how multi‑party market arrangements and trust/organizational structures interact with default contract law, showing parties and courts both rely on external legal and market frameworks to determine what agreements mean and bind.

shared_topics.topic: the use and legal effects of standardized or collective contractual devices (boilerplate, collective agreements, MFNs, trust techniques)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on boilerplate as a standardized form that must be interpreted with attention to market-wide effects; Paper A examines collective agreements, MFN clauses, and a representative trustee technique as collective or structural devices parties employ to influence modification rights and third‑party consequences, assessing their enforceability and market role.

shared_topics.topic: transaction, coordination, and information costs shaping drafting strategies and judicial approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the transaction costs and strategic incentives that make various anti‑modification devices (single third parties, multi‑party schemes, MFNs, representative trustees) more or less practical; Paper B emphasizes courts' risk aversion and the informational costs of contextual inquiry, arguing judges should rely on relatively cheap, publicly available market signals rather than costly party‑specific reconstruction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: appropriate scope and power of judicial intervention in contracting (tempered enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts should calibrate their involvement in private ordering — Paper A argues courts should be risk-averse in interpretation, discounting creative or party-tailored readings in favor of market‑anchored meanings, while Paper B urges 'low-powered' judicial enforcement that protects verifiable formal elements without imposing heavy sanctions that would crowd out informal cooperation.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation of market norms and third‑party/external effects into contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that contract law should look beyond the bilateral text to market‑wide information — Paper A argues ambiguous boilerplate should be read against standard market terms and publicly available industry data, and Paper B shows how braiding and courts' light-touch remedies must account for market practices and externalities to preserve cooperative interfirm relations.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction and blending of formal (textual/legal) and informal (reputational/practical) mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Each paper develops a middle ground between pure formalism and pure contextualism: Paper A's 'normative triangulation' integrates non‑particularized contextual benchmarks with textual interpretation, while Paper B describes 'braiding' as an intentional design that interweaves formal contractual provisions with informal, reputation‑based enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how to handle standardized, underspecified, or incomplete contractual arrangements using external information and governance procedures
shared_topics.justification: Both articles confront contracts that lack individualized, fully‑specified bargains — Paper A treats boilerplate as standardized language requiring external, market‑based gap‑filling, and Paper B studies contracts for innovation where parties rely on formal information‑sharing and governance processes to fill substantive gaps and create enforceable cooperation norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 12wmmarybuslrev329!!ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: contracts as vehicles for private or regulatory governance (private/self-regulation embedded in contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how boilerplate terms are embedded in market practices and can carry regulatory effects beyond bilateral bargains, while Paper B analyzes how modern contracts incorporate private and self-regulatory provisions (e.g., supplier codes, audits, standards) and the legal challenges that creates for governing those arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretive role of market-wide standards and norms in assessing contractual meaning and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should interpret ambiguous boilerplate against market norms and other external references (normative triangulation), and Paper B shows that many contractual regulatory provisions arise from industry standards and self-regulation, requiring legal tests (like the all events tests) to account for those market-driven standards when determining rights and liabilities.

shared_topics.topic: third‑party effects and externalities of widely used contractual terms and the need for legal doctrines to account for them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that interpreting boilerplate must take account of cross-market externalities and minimize harms to other users and affected groups, while Paper B highlights that contractual regulatory clauses address social and environmental externalities (and that noncompliance produces harms beyond the contracting parties), creating consequences for legal recognition and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty about contractual obligations and the need to adapt legal tests or interpretive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses uncertainty about assent, meaning, and negotiation of standardized terms and proposes a risk‑averse, market‑sensitive interpretive method, whereas Paper B identifies uncertainty in applying the tax ‘all events’ accrual tests when agreements include regulatory/self‑regulatory obligations and proposes modifying those tests (an implied acceptance requirement) to accommodate such arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DEAL STRUCTURE

shared_topics.topic: how drafters' design choices (rule-like vs standard-like language; modular vs integrated structure; use of boilerplate) affect enforcement and interpretation

shared_topics.topic: the importance of market norms and external, non-party-specific context as interpretive benchmarks

shared_topics.topic: concerns about systemic effects and third-party externalities from particular interpretive outcomes or structural designs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that interpreting boilerplate must account for externalities to other users and market actors to avoid socially costly distortions, and Paper B shows that the way agreements interlock across provisions and contracts can produce cascade effects (e.g., closing conditions), raising similar worries about systemic consequences of interpretation and design.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW

shared_topics.topic: the formative role of law in constructing market relations and moral demands

shared_topics.topic: use of market norms and social context as the proper benchmark for legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A disputes the idea that market interactions are purely impersonal and highlights how social and legal context inflects market behavior; Paper B insists courts should interpret ambiguous contract terms against market-general norms and publicly observable benchmarks rather than purely party-specific facts.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between legal permissions and moral responsibility in market transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the gap between what law permits and what morality may require, arguing market participation does not excuse moral duties; Paper B likewise brings moralized background duties into interpretation, arguing courts should favor readings of boilerplate that minimize externalities and reflect background responsibilities beyond narrow contractual consent.

shared_topics.topic: whether standard market practices/instruments (impersonal relations, boilerplate) are 'normal' and should be governed by ordinary legal/moral regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the view that market relations are characteristically impersonal and insulated from ordinary moral critique, defending the idea that market practices are subject to moral assessment; Paper B argues that boilerplate is properly treated as normal contract (not anomalous or non-contractual) and should be addressed through the ordinary interpretive apparatus informed by market context.

shared_topics.topic: deference to market norms versus party‑specific bargaining evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should prioritize market‑general contextual information (published prices, trade usage, SEC filings) over party‑tailored evidence when reading boilerplate; Paper B emphasizes that parties can and do fine‑tune contractual allocations (pricing mechanisms, minimums, take‑or‑pay) and criticizes courts for substituting their own protections rather than respecting market‑based bargains.

shared_topics.topic: when courts should impose or infer duties limiting contractual discretion (e.g., good faith / best efforts)

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of market norms and external, non‑party‑specific information in reading and enforcing contracts

papers.node_id: 21upajbusl142!!ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW
papers.abstract:
Much of the literature on transnational law indulges in a technocratic utopianism, hailing the dawn of a new era of globally-harmonized, efficient contract law that evolves at the speed of business.Henceforth, we have been promised, national borders will no longer be arbitrary speed bumps along the forward path of international commerce. Implicit in this account is the assumption that legal globalization means legal unification. But, in reality, the future of contract law will be as fragmented as the past; it will just be fragmented differently. This Article argues that a specific and previously-unidentified type of legal differentiation is gaining momentum within contract law: even as the law governing commercial contracts increasingly harmonizes across territorial boundaries, it will increasingly fragment along boundaries between industry sectors. In other words, the old distinctions are indeed breaking down, but they are changing rather than disappearing.
Adapting a term coined in the public international law context, I call this phenomenon "sectoral fragmentation." Distinctions between different kinds of contractual relationships (sales of goods, leases, franchises, joint ventures, etc.) will matter less, as will the nationalities of the contracting parties and the place(s) where the contract was formed and performed. The industry context within which the contract is concluded will matter more. Or to put it differently:what typeof contract is implicated in a dispute will gradually become less significant in determining the applicable rules, while thesubject matterof the contract will become more significant. In a sectorally fragmented legal regime, contracts for the purchase of crude oil by a refiner and for the purchase of office paper by the same refiner may have identically written terms(mutatis mutandis), but will be interpreted differently, will have different terms implied into them (including their dispute resolution provisions), and will have different rules for determining the remedies available and how damages are to be calculated.
Contracting practices have always varied from industry to industry, so to the extent that private governance prevails over public governance, the law will necessarily become differentiated along sectoral lines. The rise of private, contractual governance, already documented in the legal and political science literature, is part of the sectoral fragmentation picture.What is new is that the structures of private governance are now recapitulated in formal contract law, including in laws promulgated by states.Sectoral fragmentation of law is thus evidence corroborating the proposition that the balance of regulatory power has shifted from public to private governance, and is also an example of the more subtle incorporation of private perspectives into public governance. Public regulation of contracts is not withering away, but state lawmaking processes are increasingly relegated to validating, incorporating, and supplementing privately-generated standards.
Scholars of transnational law have argued that the positive law is being "suffocated" in the era of globalized commerce, as commercial relationships are increasingly conducted beyond the reach of national laws and courts.This Article argues that no such suffocation is occurring; instead, in a reverse of the traditional conception, formal contract law is being remade in the shadow of private contracts.
Whatever one's scholarly or political agenda, it is important to understand sectoral fragmentation. Most academic writing on transnational law focuses on three issues: thenatureof transnational law as law (its legality), thesourcesof transnational law, and theprocessesby which transnational laws are promulgated.Largely missing from this theorizing is thecontentof transnational legal rules, which is seldom considered outside of studies of specific industries or supply chains. By identifying thephenomenon of sectoral fragmentation, this Article shows why what appears to be a gap in the literature is actually a reflection of the changing structure of contract law. There will not beanysingle, global set of rules that will constitute transnational contract law. Instead, much of the law will be structured as a set of distinct but overlapping parallel bodies of law, each applicable to a different industry sector.
The phenomenon of sectoral fragmentation is a specific example of the broader trend toward greater complexity and specialization in contract law. Although it is impossible to predict the consequences of these developments with certainty, there will inevitably be winners and losers. In general, commercial parties prefer to be governed by specialized law applied by specialists. Particularism in law increases efficiency by better aligning legal outcomes with commercially reasonable ones; it permits parties to rely more on standard terms and usages (and thereby reduce transaction costs on individual contracts), while minimizing the risk that their intentions will be misinterpretedex postby a court or arbitral tribunal.Different industry sectors involve different types of contractual relationships and are subject to different risk profiles; it would be surprising if a single set of rules for contractual interpretation, say, or for damages calculation yielded efficient results for all sectors. These benefits should not be underestimated.
But there are potential drawbacks as well. Complexity in law, especially when doctrinally complex law is applied by diverse specialist tribunals, inhibits the ability of public authorities to regulate commercial activity. Sectoral fragmentation is also likely to privilege incumbent firms by increasing the barriers to entry into an industry sector, which may create harmful disincentives to innovation. The normative divisions thataccompany legal specialization contribute to a breakdown in common standards as a general matter; this conceptual phenomenon, accompanying a shift in the balance of power from public to private governance, threatens the rule of law.
Sectoral fragmentation plays out as a theme running through various phenomena related to globalization and the development of transnational law. It is largely a self-sustaining phenomenon, and it may not be possible for any group of policymakers to change its course. It is therefore all the more important to come to grips with its trajectory. "A richer understanding of transnational legal ordering facilitates both critique and reform. otherwise scholars are blind to how law operates, and they replicate that blindness in their teaching, their scholarly work, and their normative prescriptions."In other words, there is no way back to a world without globalization, so we had best set about understanding the world with it.
This Article explores the phenomenon of sectoral fragmentation: its causes, its characteristics, and its consequences. Part II describes the concept of fragmentation as developed in public international law, and argues for its relevance to the evolution of private law. Part III sets out the four main mechanisms or processes through which legal fragmentation has occurred in the public international law context, and shows that these processes are all operative in transnational contract law. Part IV argues that sectoral fragmentation is an inevitable consequence of the rise of transnational commercial communities as the key drivers of transnational legal rule-making; it then explains how the mechanisms set out in Part III lead specifically to sectoral fragmentation. Finally, Part V, the Conclusion, briefly speculates as to the broader political and normative consequences of a sectorally fragmented transnational contract law.

questions.question: Whether transnational contract law is evolving to fragment along industry-sector boundaries (so that legal rules increasingly differ by industry) even as it harmonizes across national borders.
Whether and to what extent private, industry-specific contracting practices and private governance drive the content of formal public contract law and become incorporated into state-made rules.

What the economic and regulatory consequences of such sectoral fragmentation are for efficiency, barriers to entry and innovation, and for the enforceability and coherence of legal authority (rule of law).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 3texamlrev91!!ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: private contractual governance shaping formal contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that empirical findings about relational norms from business disciplines show how private contracting behavior produces economically significant expectations that law should recognize and operationalize; Paper B shows that private, sector-specific contractual governance is being recapitulated into state law, so formal contract rules increasingly validate and incorporate privately-generated standards.

shared_topics.topic: use of interdisciplinary empirical methods (e.g., transaction cost economics and business social science) to inform contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for partnering with management and marketing scholars and using frameworks like transaction cost economics to operationalize relational expectations for legal analysis; Paper B similarly relies on empirically-grounded accounts of transnational commercial communities and supply‑chain practices to explain mechanisms driving sectoral differentiation of contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: industry/sector specificity as a determinant of contract rules and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that relational norms and background social context vary across exchange relationships and can and should shape contract design and incentives; Paper B argues that the applicable law and doctrinal outcomes will increasingly depend on the industry context—leading to different implied terms, remedies, and interpretive rules by sector.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial practice and relational norms influence judicial/doctrinal interpretation (implied terms, evidence, and remedies)

papers.node_id: 43iowajcorpl1!!ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
papers.title: ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
papers.abstract:
This Article: explores the theoretical implications of self-driving contracts. We define a self-driving contract as a contract that writes its own terms or fills its own gaps. To be more precise, a self-driving contract has three key features. It is an agreement where (1) the parties set only broad ex ante objectives; but (2) the contract uses machine-driven analytics and artificial intelligence to translate the general ex ante objective into a specific term or directive at the time of performance; where (3) those terms are based on information gathered after the parties execute the initial agreement.We draw an analogy to self-driving or autonomous cars. Just as a passenger in a self-driving car relies on the car to determine the optimal means (direction, speed, lane choice) to travel between twolocations and to update its determination to account for real-time contingencies (traffic, weather, construction), the parties to a self-driving contract agree to a shared goal and trust in the contract to direct them on precisely how to achieve that goal in light of real-time contingencies.
Stated in the abstract, this idea may sound like radical science fiction. But the first generation of these contracts already exists, primarily in the form of self-pricing contracts. The most familiar example can be found in the auto-insurance industry, where parties agree to price terms that adjust automatically based on computer-driven analytics.Similar pricing terms can be found in dental insurance, in short-term rental agreements,and in transportation services.
As technologies that allow for predictive accuracy and ubiquitous monitoring and communication advance, self-driving contracts will proliferate. Predictive technologies will provide increased information that allows parties to more precisely choose the actions that will benefit their mutual interests. Parties will have the ability to predict with high confidence that, given scenario X, action Y is the optimal course of action to achieve their agreed upon goal. Monitoring technologies will provide access to the information necessary to determine whether scenario X has in fact occurred. And communication technologies will transmit the directives resulting from the analysis to the relevant actors.These technologies pave the way for self-driving contracts.
The emergence of this form of contracting will have a significant impact on the way we think and talk about contracts. First, it will reveal that the existing language of contract theory is deficient. Self-driving contracts blur the distinctions between rules and standards, between ex ante agreements and ex post dispute resolutions, and even between complete and incomplete contracts. For example, while some will view self-driving and related contracts as hopelessly incomplete, the opposite view - that they are among the most complete contracts - equally consistent with existing literature. This indeterminacy in the language of contract theory and law has led scholars (and will lead courts) to struggle in interpreting and enforcing these contracts.Notions of assent, definiteness, agreements to agree, unconscionability, mutual mistake, renegotiation, and even efficient breach cannot be cleanly transported to the world of self-driving contracts. Analyzing these questions through the language of self-driving contracts may provide important clarity that is currently missing.
Similarly, some recent proposals for resolving contractual ambiguities (such as using survey technologies) can be understood more clearly once one recognizes that they are just particular forms of self-driving contracts.Thinking about those proposals through the lens and language of self-driving contacts will reveal their costs and benefits - and how the law should treat them - in ways that traditional contract theory does not.
Most importantly, we identify the questions of who provides the self-driving contract and how to govern the providers as the central challenges for the law. In that context, we will explore first-party providers, third-party providers, and government providers. We draw distinctions between how the law views these alternative providers in sophisticated-party transactions, on the one hand, and consumer transactions, on the other.
This Article: , thus, has two primary aims. First, we begin developing a new language of contract theory, so scholars and lawyers can fully grasp what is at stake when disputes about self-driving contracts arise. Second, we explore some fundamental implications of the emergence of self-driving contracts.
We proceed in three parts. In Part II, we describe self-driving contracts and the technology behind them. In Part III, we explore the challenges that self-driving contracts pose for the language and theory of contract law. We briefly lay out some doctrinal and policy implications related to those challenges.
In Part IV, we show that the most important challenge for the law of self-driving contracts relates to the markets that will provide these self-driving contracts. We discuss the likely rise of a market for third-party vendors providing certified computer code to govern contractual relationships. We predict that arbitration services and insurance providers will evolve and likely fill the space as the providers of self-driving contracts. Other platform providers like Uber or Airbnb are also likely candidates to fill this market. Here, we also discuss the important distinctions between the markets for self-driving contracts in consumer transactions, on the one hand, and for self-driving contracts in sophisticated business and finance transactions on the other hand.
Before we proceed, a quick word on what this Article: is not. This Article: does not address self-enforcing contracts and similar technologies like blockchain.These contracts - often referred to as "smart contracts" - innovate on a different plane than self-driving contracts. They contain automated provisions that allow for enforcement of specific provisions without resort to adjudication. In this way, they are extensions of escrow technologies like the letter of credit. The innovation, however, is that the self-executing contracts can trigger automated enforcement without a third-party intermediary - that is, without the escrow agent or the bank which issues the letter of credit.
Self-driving contracts are a completely different category of contracts. Self-driving contracts require judicial enforcement.But they automate the creation and interpretation of the terms that are to be enforced. The key is that the contract uses technologies like artificial intelligence and learning algorithms to update the terms governing the parties' relationships based on contingencies as they arise.

questions.question: How should legal systems interpret, assess, and enforce agreements in which the parties set only broad objectives but rely on machine-driven analytics and AI to generate specific contractual terms after formation?

What governance, regulatory, and market arrangements are appropriate for providers of algorithmic 'self-driving' contract services (whether provided by the parties themselves, third-party vendors, or the state), and how should those arrangements differ between consumer transactions and sophisticated commercial transactions?

Do self-driving contracts improve contractual outcomes-such as efficiency, alignment with parties' goals, reduction in disputes, and lower transaction costs-relative to traditional contracting methods, and under what conditions?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55wmmarylrev1869!!ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EX TEMPORE CONTRACTING

shared_topics.topic: real-time completion of contractual terms by external agents (human or automated)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze contracts that deliberately leave terms open to be specified during performance by an external decision-maker — Paper A describes human third-party decisionmakers like construction dispute boards and ISDA committees, while Paper B describes algorithmic or machine-driven systems that translate broad objectives into specific directives at the time of performance.

shared_topics.topic: challenge to the ex ante / ex post dichotomy and related doctrinal categories (rules vs. standards, complete vs. incomplete contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue that these contracting forms blur traditional contract-theory categories: Paper A introduces the 'ex tempore' (in-the-moment) alternative to ex ante/ex post contracting, and Paper B shows how self-driving contracts confound distinctions between rules and standards and between completeness and incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: who supplies and how to govern third-party decision-makers/providers
shared_topics.justification: Both works identify the provider of the real-time mechanism as legally and economically central — Paper A focuses on institutional providers (dispute boards, ISDA committees) and their roles, and Paper B examines markets for third‑party or platform vendors, arbitration/insurance providers, and the governance and certification challenges they pose.

shared_topics.topic: implications for judicial treatment, interpretation, and enforcement doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider how courts and existing doctrines should treat contracts that defer specification to others: Paper A critiques judicial misunderstandings of ex tempore institutions and the misapplication of defaults, while Paper B surveys how doctrines like definiteness, assent, unconscionability, and enforcement must be reevaluated for self-driving contracts.

shared_topics.topic: transaction‑costs, strategic incentives, and the conditions under which parties prefer in‑performance specification
shared_topics.justification: Both analyses explain why parties opt to defer specification — weighing front‑end drafting costs, uncertainty, need for clarity at performance, and coordination costs — with Paper A applying this to construction and credit derivatives and Paper B applying it to self‑pricing and monitoring-enabled markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107geolj1277!!ARTICLE: Contract Creep
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Creep

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal significance of the consumer vs. sophisticated‑party distinction

shared_topics.topic: how contracting and drafting technologies blur doctrinal boundaries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that drafting technologies, cut‑and‑paste portability of clauses, and searchable model forms enable ‘creep’ of doctrines between transaction types; Paper B centers on AI, monitoring, and predictive technologies that generate terms ex post and thereby collapse traditional lines (rules vs standards, ex ante vs ex post, complete vs incomplete contracts).

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and interpretive challenges for novel contractual forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how analogical reasoning and migration of specialized doctrines create uncertainty about which rules should apply across contexts; Paper B argues that self‑driving contracts expose gaps in existing concepts (assent, definiteness, unconscionability, mistake) and will force courts to reinterpret or extend doctrines to fit new automated term‑generation practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of third‑party providers, standardized modules, and market governance of contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A points to modular contract design and the portability of standardized clauses as mechanisms that spread doctrine across tracks; Paper B predicts a rising market for third‑party vendors and platform providers who will supply certified code or algorithms that effectively write contract terms, raising governance and regulatory questions for those providers.

shared_topics.topic: arbitration and dispute‑resolution markets as both a doctrinal and market response
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses arbitration‑clause enforceability as a case study of doctrinal creep between sophistication tracks; Paper B identifies arbitration services (and insurers) as likely entrants into markets that supply or certify self‑driving contract code, linking doctrinal treatment of arbitration to the practical market architecture for novel contracting.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal challenges to traditional contract concepts (rules vs. standards, completeness, interpretation, implied terms)

shared_topics.topic: shifts in dispute‑resolution institutions toward specialization and private fora
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that sectoral fragmentation will produce specialized tribunals and doctrinal complexity that constrain public regulation; Paper B predicts arbitration services, insurance and platform providers will play central roles in enforcing and certifying self‑driving contracts, raising similar questions about privatized, specialized dispute resolution.

shared_topics.topic: implications for enforcement, litigation strategy, and doctrinal interpretation

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Private Order of Innovation Networks

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes predictive analytics, ubiquitous monitoring, and communications as the technological basis enabling contracts to determine terms and direct performance, and Paper B studies information‑sharing routines, transparency mechanisms (e.g., management committees), and how those informational flows enable informal and formal governance of alliances.

shared_topics.topic: multidimensional exchange hazards beyond simple opportunism (tradeoffs among hazards)

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.
