papers.node_id: 20ncjltechon267!!ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS
papers.title: ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS
papers.abstract:
The twenty-first century has witnessed an expansion of societal interest from safekeeping tangible assets--such as the home, cash, and family--to protecting intangible assets as well, such as online bank accounts, social media, and even individual genetic identifiers. Americans often secure their Facebook profiles with case-sensitive passwords that require a numberanda symbol to prevent unauthorized users from gaining access.Most online accounts even require that users answer highly intrusive and personal security questions as a secondary method of access to the account in the case the user in question forgets their login information.While Twitterand electronic banking sites have ramped up their defenses, deoxyribonucleic acid ("DNA") testing kits with limited data security have swept the nation, leaving some test kit users' personal genetic information accessible to others.
Direct-to-consumer ("DTC") genetic testing kits are marketed--often through the internet--directly to the consumer, who sends a DNA sample back to the testing kit company for analysis.The company processes the DNA sample and sends the consumer the results, which can include information about a person's ancestry, potential health issues, and more.Ancestry (or genealogical) testing is considered a form of DTC genetic testing.The quality of these at-home test kits varies,but some of the more well-known brands perform an intricate analysis of the consumer's DNA sample. For example, AncestryDNA("Ancestry") analyzes all 22 pairs of non-sex chromosomes, providing a broad look at the consumer's entire family tree.
The popularity of these DTC genetic testing kits has exploded in recent years, and the trend is expected to continue.By the end of2017, over twelve million consumers had submitted a DNA sample through an at-home genetic testing kit.Ancestry, the leading genealogy company, processed the DNA of more than seven million people in that year.The runner-up in the competitive DTC genetic testing market, 23andME, analyzed over three million DNA samples.The concentrated market of DTC genetic testing requires heavy promotion to stand out. Ancestry spent approximately $ 109 million on television and other ads in the United States in 2016.23andME totaled $ 21 million on advertisements that same year.As advertising and technology advance, the DTC genetic testing industry is expected to soar in value--with an estimated net worth of over $ 2.5 billion by 2024.
Ancestryprides itself on providing a comprehensive report of a consumer's recent genetic and ancestral history.But sales of AncestryDTC genetic testing kits are driven by many other factors, such as the desire to know risks for certain genetic diseasesand the desire to connect with long-lost relatives.Even when seriousmotives such as these are involved, the privacy policy is likely an afterthought for a consumer.But this privacy policy isn't just any other run-of-the-mill privacy policy.Ancestry's privacy policy is contracting away consumers' rights to arguably the most personal asset a human has--their genetic information. As of this article's publication, there is no federal law regulating the storage, disclosure, and use of this genetic information.
The need for a uniform, all-encompassing federal law that regulates collection, storage, and use of genetic information is urgent. DTC genetic testing kits continue to rise in popularity while collecting, storing, and using Americans' DNA without federal limitation. In Section II, this Recent Development covers Ancestry's privacy policy and the limits the company places on itself when using consumers' genetic information. Section III discusses governmental use of DTC genetic test results. Section IV reflects on the current legal landscape regulating use of genetic information. Lastly, Section V describes the features of a viable federal statute which would place external limits on DTC genetic testing companies' use of their consumers' information.

questions.question: Whether direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies' privacy policies and business practices permit the collection, storage, and use of consumers' genetic information in ways that undermine individual privacy and control over that data.
Whether current legal protections adequately limit government and third-party access to and use of genetic data obtained through direct-to-consumer testing.
What statutory design features would effectively regulate how genetic information collected by direct-to-consumer testing may be collected, stored, shared, and used.

papers.node_id: 2texwesleyanlrev467!!ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS
papers.title: ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS
papers.authors: Kevin Scott Marshall; Kurt J. Beron
papers.abstract:
The existence and amount of a firm's lost profits are key elements in most commercial damage cases. Practitioners must be able to demonstrate to the trier of fact the appropriateness and effectiveness of the methodology employed to calculate lost profits.While practitioners generally employ experts to perform a lost profits analysis, it is essential that practitioners understand the conceptual relationship between the legal standard and the methodology employed. In Texas, the legal standard requires the use of a methodology that goes beyond the mere assertion that the plaintiff has sustained a loss. Given that standard of proof, the purpose of this article is to demonstrate that there is one superior methodology for determining lost profits: multivariate regression analysis. I. The Legal Standard
Historically, courts have recognized that a plaintiff is entitled to recover lost profits when it is proven that the loss of profits is caused by a defendant's act or omission and the amount of loss is shown with sufficient certainty.Generally, anticipated profits are not recoverable when "they are dependent on uncertain and changing conditions,such as market fluctuations, or the chances or changes of business, or where there is no evidence from which they may be intelligently estimated."
Although Texas law does not require lost profits be susceptible to exact calculation, it does demand such loss be ascertained with a reasonable degree of certainty.In Texas, it has long been established that before a plaintiff may recover lost profits, "the amount of the loss must be shown by competent evidence with reasonable certainty."Thus, there are three related conceptual requirements for recovery of lost profits: 1) competent evidence; 2) reasonable certainty; and 3) causation. Each element must be established prior to recovery. Therefore, it is critical that practitioners fully understand these requirements. A. Competent Evidence
The terms relevancy, competency, and materiality are frequently used as synonyms when in fact their meanings are distinguishable.Generally, all evidence relevant to a plaintiff's claim for lost profits is admissible. Relevant evidence is evidence having a tendency to make the existence of any fact of consequence to the determination of the action more or less probable than it would be without the evidence.However, relevant evidence may be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice.
While evidence may be relevant, material, and probative on the issue, it may nonetheless be inadmissible because it is not competent.Competent evidence is evidence that is fit and appropriate given the nature of the matter to be proved.Further, evidence is competent evidence if it is of a nature, sort, or type that is acceptable to the court either under the applicable rules of evidence or case law.Con-versely, incompetent evidence is inadmissible in court on any issue regardless of its materiality or relevancy.
In Texas, courts have uniformly held that competent lost profit evidence must be predicated upon objective, factual data surrounding the previous operation of the business claiming the loss.Such data may include, but is not limited to, the previous profits and expenses of the business,fluctuations in market conditions,business risks,operational duration,profitability of comparable businesses,the owner/operator's business experience,and any other relevant economic facts and circumstances impacting profits.Therefore, when seeking to recover lost profits, a plaintiff should introduce the business' records and other objective data on market conditions and risks associated with the business. Failure to use such objective, factual data may preclude recovery of lost profits.
For example, in Automark of Texas v. Discount Trophies,the Dallas Court of Appeals reversed and reformed the trial court's judgment awarding lost profits, given "the complete absence from the record of objective facts, figures and data" regarding the plaintiff's profits.The court noted:
The distinguishing feature between the line of Texas cases permitting recovery for lost profits and the line of cases denying recovery is a reliance upon routinely kept business records which have been produced in court - that is, upon an evaluation of a business's decreased profitability based upon objective facts, figures, and data and not upon the subjective opinions of interested parties.
It merits noting that where lost profits testimony is based on "first-hand knowledge of financial data,"Texas law does not strictly require the introduction of supplemental objective data such as financial records. In fact, there is common law authority to the contrary.For instance, testimony based upon first-hand knowledge of the business records or data in question may have probative value even though it is not supplemented by underlying business records.However, most courts have held that opinion testimony must be supplemented by underlying business records.B. Reasonable Certainty
While a plaintiff's proof of lost profits must be based on competent evidence, the loss must be shown with a reasonable degree of certainty.Texas courts have long recognized that proving lost profits is "inherently speculative."Further, Texas courts draw a distinction between uncertainty as to the amount of lost profits and uncertainty as to the fact of lost profits.Uncertainty of the amount of lost profits will not necessarily defeat recovery for lost profits,however, uncertainty as to the fact of lost profits is fatal to recovery.It is imperative to keep this distinction in mind.
It is well established that opinion evidence based on speculation or conjecture lacks probative value and is inadmissible. Further, opinion evidence will not support a jury finding even when admitted without objection.As a result, certain general rules regarding the recoverability of lost profits have evolved from this judicial perspective. For instance, in Texas, prospective profits are generally not recoverable for new or unestablished businesses because such profits are not "susceptible of being established by proof to that degree of certainty which the law demands."Generally, new or unestablished businesses have no profit history from which to reasonably anticipate future profits, and "therefore any proof [regarding the expectation] of future profits would be entirely too speculative and conjectural as to allow a recovery for such profits."Moreover, evidence that the plaintiff's business "lost money from the very beginning,"""neverturned a profit,'… [or] "never got out of the red ink,'""will preclude recovery for lost profits."
However, the general reluctance to allow lost profits recovery for new or unestablished businesses has been incorrectly interpreted to mean that new or unestablished businesses may never recover lost profits. In fact, courts deny recovery of lost profits for new or unestablished businesses because there is simply no profit history from which to estimate reasonably anticipated future profits. Thus, an owner of a new or unestablished business may prevail where he is seeking recovery of lost profits provided he produces sufficient, competent evidence from which a trier of fact can find a reasonable expectation of profits existed but for the defendant's acts or omissions. For example, lost profits may be recoverable by a new enterprise owner if factual data is otherwise available to furnish a sound basis for computing the probable loss.
In Texas Instruments, Inc. v. Teletron Energy Management, Inc.,the Texas Supreme Court held that when presented with proper documentation, a court should not prohibit a business - whether old or new - from recovering lost profits.The Teletron court explained that the finder of fact must not focus on the newness of the business entity, but rather on the newness of the allegedly damaged activity.For example, consideration of the experience of the persons involved in the activity, the nature of the business activity itself, and the relevant market conditions should be central to the determination of lost profits, irrespective of the newness of the business entity.
Uncertainty in measuring the amount of lost profits will not necessarily defeat recovery.Texas courts have found it impossible to announce with exact certainty any rule measuring lost profits,andproof to a mathematical exactness is not required.In fact, courts have held that questions concerning the methodology used to predict lost profits, or the factual basis for an opinion regarding the amount of lost profits, goes to the weight and not to the admissibility of evidence.However, if the methodology or the underlying factual basis used to determine the extent of lost profits is overly speculative, its admissibility as opinion evidence may be challenged under Rule 403 of the Texas Rules of Civil Evidence.Rule 403 states, "Although relevant, evidence may be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, confusion of the issues, or misleading the jury, or by considerations of undue delay, or needless presentation of cumulative evidence."C. Causation
Proving causation is critical to any plaintiff seeking lost profits damages. "Lost profits may be recoverable if they are the natural and probable consequences of wrongful conduct and their amount is shown by competent evidence with reasonable certainty."Consequently, lost profits are recoverable only if there is sufficient, competent evidence in the record from which "to make a meaningful correlation" between the business' loss of profitability and the defendant's act or omission.The terms causation and correlation are often misused by courts and practitioners when discussing the effects of a defendant's acts on a plaintiff's profits.
This misapplication of these terms often arises because the terms have both legal and scientific meanings. Legally, the loss of profit must have been proximately caused by a defendant's act or omission to be recoverable.When discussing legal causation, we are generally concerned with the concept of proximate cause. Proximate cause is defined as a "cause which in a natural and continued sequence, pro-duces an event, and without which the event would not have occurred ...."
Although use of the term correlation is rare in the practice of law, its meaning is especially significant within the realm of the social sciences. Correlation generally means that two or more events (or values) are related. "Two variables are said to be correlated if knowing the value of one helps us to predict the value of the other."For example, in proving a lost profits case, the finder of fact is concerned with whether there is a correlation between the defendant's act or omission and the plaintiff's loss of profits. Although establishing a positive correlation between the plaintiff's loss and the defendant's acts or omissions does not necessarily prove causation, the relationship does provide a foundation on which to build a lost profits case.
The concept of causation within the realm of the sciences has been the subject of much academic and philosophical debate.There are essentially three criteria for inferring cause.To infer cause, the sciences and the law require that: (1) the cause precedes the effect; (2) covariation exists between the cause and the effect; and (3) potentially influencing forces are controlled and ruled out as alternative explanations for the effect.
Therefore, it logically follows that in a lost profits case, the law requires the defendant's act or omission precede the plaintiff's loss; the plaintiff to establish a covariation between the defendant's act or omission and the plaintiff's loss of profits; and that other economic forces, which may also affect the plaintiff's profits, such as recent market fluctuations and developments, be controlled to rule out alternative explanations for the plaintiff's loss. Once a plaintiff demonstrates the general criteria for inferring cause, he can assert the defendant's acts or omissions proximately caused his loss of profits.II. The Methodology - Multivariate Regression Analysis
The Texas Supreme Court does not sanction any one method for determining lost profits.The court acknowledges that "what constitutes reasonably certain evidence of lost profits is a fact intensive determination."Further, the Texas Supreme Court has held "once a party has chosen a particular method for measuring their lost profits, they must provide a complete calculation."Regression analysis, sometimes called multivariate or multiple regression analysis, provides this calculation. It is a tool capable of estimating and measuring a correlation between a plaintiff's profitability and the defendant's acts and omissions while controlling external factors such as market and regional economic conditions.
"Regression analysis is a method for examining the relationships among large numbers of variables."This methodology allows an individual to summarize the degree to which variations in the values of a number of variables correspond to variations in the value of a single variable.The practical use of regression analysis has grown markedly over the past twenty-five years due to the development of statistical methodology, computer technology, and the availability of statistical data.Moreover, using regression analysis for the purpose of proving both the existence and amount of damages is not new to the law.
As confirmed in Southwest Battery Corp. v. Owen,the recovery of lost profits may be impacted by a number of "uncertain and changing" variables.The strength of regression analysis for measuring lost profits is its ability to assess the impact, if any, of a number of vari-ables on a single variable such as lost profits.When a number of variables influence the existence and amount of lost profits, regression analysis provides a method for assessing the individual influence each variable has on the existence of lost profits. If properly modeled, regression analysis may assist the trier of fact in evaluating large quantities of objective, financial, and institutional data to determine both the existence and amount of lost profits with a known degree of certainty.
Most regression models are set up in the following form: The behavior of the dependent variable is assumed to be a function of a set of independent variables. Regression analysis provides summary statistics that may be helpful in describing the relationship between each of the independent variables and the dependent variable.Regression analysis begins with the specification of the major variables that affect the dependent variable. In a lost profits case, this involves the identification of important independent variables that reflect important and systematic influences on profits (the dependent variable). Since profits are equal to the difference between revenues and costs, the analytical variables should be the variables affecting revenues and costs. For example, a plaintiff's revenues are directly related to sales. If the plaintiff can prove the defendant's conduct caused the plaintiff to lose sales, the plaintiff may be entitled to recover any corresponding loss in profits.
To properly use regression analysis, this information must be modeled into a mathematical equation.Assuming that a linear relationship exists between the variables,the equation will take the following form:
PROFITS = constant + b<1>(SALES) + b<2>(COSTS) + b<3>(MARKET FACTORS) + etc.
Each of the capitalized terms are variables that will differ from case to case. PROFITS is the dependent variable, that is, the variable predicted by the equation. Each of the other variables influences the plaintiff's profits. The other variables are known as independent variables, that is the variables that predict the plaintiff's profits. For ex-ample, PROFITS might be the profits earned in a particular quarter; SALES might be the number of units sold in that quarter; COSTS might be the costs of production and distribution for that quarter; and MARKET FACTORS might be indicators of what competitors are doing. The term constant, also called the intercept, is an important part of the mechanics of performing regression analysis and in making predictions.Since its construction and use is entirely by the econometrician, further discussion of the constant is beyond the scope of this article.
Beginning with empirical data on the applicable variables, regression analysis results in an equation describing the functional relationship between each independent variable and the dependent variable.The value of the multipliers (b<1>, b<2>, b<3> … , etc.) in the equation, commonly called regression coefficients or slopes, reflects the relationship between the specific independent variable and the dependent variable (profit).
If properly performed, regression analysis predicts how increasing or decreasing any of the independent variables has affected or will affect profits.Substituting different values for the independent variables and solving the equation allows the econometrician to predict a value of the plaintiff's profit at different points in time. Comparing the calculated profits from two different values for sales shows the impact of the change in sales on profit. Thus, if an individual can establish that sales are lower by a certain amount due to the actions of the defendant, the econometrician can show its impact on profits. Moreover, this technique allows the econometrician to state his conclusion with statistical confidence in terms of the probability of error.
This approach might well have satisfied the Texas Supreme Court in Holt Atherton Industries, Inc. v. Heine.In Holt Atherton, the trial court found lost profits existed for the plaintiff's company when the company could not operate at full capacity because one of its two bulldozers was in the repair shop for an extended period of time.However, the Texas Supreme Court reversed the trial court, holding the trier of fact had no basis for determining whether the plaintiff's damages were established with reasonable certainty or were based on pure speculation because the evidence offered was legally insufficient to prove lost profits.Specifically, the court determined evidence was lacking to show that (a) the bulldozer would have been actually em-ployed had it not been in the shop; and (b) the time period sought for lost profits matched the time the bulldozer was in the shop.
In Holt Atherton, regression analysis could have estimated the demand for bulldozer services based on monthly inquiries and requisitions from customers. Including the demand for bulldozer services as a variable would have produced an estimation of the potential revenue over the time period in question. Coupling this variable with operational costs would have provided a complete estimation of lost profits within a reasonable degree of certainty that may have survived the Texas Supreme Court's scrutiny. III. Illustration
The following illustration demonstrates the need to employ regression analysis in a lost profits case. In this example, the plaintiff seeks to recover lost profits allegedly caused by the defendant's failure to correctly publish the plaintiff's advertisement. The plaintiff's address and telephone number were printed incorrectly and remained in print and in circulation for a one-year period. Obviously, the defendant's incorrect publication of the plaintiff's address or telephone number could prove detrimental to the plaintiff's profits. However, changes in market conditions could also affect the plaintiff's sales and thus impact his profits. To establish a case for lost profits, the plaintiff must be able to isolate and measure with a reasonable degree of certainty the effect the misprinting of the advertisement had on his profits. Regression analysis allows the plaintiff to explain the effect of the defendant's actions, while accounting for other factors that may have impacted the plaintiff's profits.
Factors that may be relevant include the size and composition of the plaintiff's management staff; the type and number of employees; the plaintiff's salary and employment expenses; the amount of the plaintiff's advertising appearing at any given time; the plaintiff's operating expenses during a given time, the economic market conditions in which the plaintiff does business, the degree of competition in the plaintiff's market; and general business trends of the plaintiff's industry. Since all these factors may impact the plaintiff's profit, it is critical to isolate their effects because the plaintiff is only entitled to recover for the loss of profits that resulted from factors attributable to the defendant. The analyst, in this case, should collect relevant data over a representative number of quarters and specify the following model:
PROFITS PER QUARTER = constant + b<1>(SALES PER QUARTER) + b<2>(CORRECT ADVERTISEMENTS IN THE PREVIOUS QUARTER) + b<3>(INCORRECT ADVERTISEMENTS IN THE PREVIOUS QUARTER) + b<4>(# OF EMPLOYEES PERQUARTER) + b<5>(MARKET CONDITIONS DURING THAT QUARTER) + etc.
In this particular case, it is not the current advertising that is important, but rather the period of incorrect advertising. Once the model has been properly specified, regression analysis allows the analyst to isolate and measure the impact of the defendant's publication errors in the plaintiff's advertisements. Conclusion
Given the multidimensional legal standard for proving a case of lost profits in Texas, the practitioner is advised to use a multidimensional methodology for proving and measuring profit loss. The common practice of looking at the plaintiff's accounting books to determine the existence and extent of lost profits ignores a myriad of other factors that influence profits over time. For instance, the actions of competitors and economic circumstances surrounding buyers in the market place may have a tremendous effect on profits. An expert who predicts future levels of a plaintiff's profits by merely comparing profits before and after a defendant's conduct unrealistically assumes all factors that influence profits are constant. This uni-dimensional methodology is suspect because of its speculative nature. Moreover, in the event the data obtained using this methodology is admitted, it may fail on cross-examination.
Multivariate regression techniques are superior to most other methodologies for demonstrating lost profits. Factors impacting business profits are multivariate and are not equal in their respective effects on a particular business. Accordingly, the methodology employed should be capable of analyzing and isolating the multivariate effects on a particular plaintiff's profits so that the trier of fact may isolate and ascertain the effect of a defendant's conduct alone. Further, multivariate regression's ability to analyze large quantities of objective, factual data satisfies the competency requirement of the law. Properly modeled, it also estimates the degree of certainty in its quantified prediction of a plaintiff's lost profits. Therefore, it addresses concerns that lost profits be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty. Finally, it provides scientific evidence linking a defendant's conduct and a plaintiff's loss, thereby satisfying the law's requirement of proving causation. Understanding the utility of this technique is a necessary prerequisite for competent and strategic investigation, preparation, and discovery. The utilization of this technique is recommended not only because it accommodates the requirements of the law, but because it is extremely persuasive.

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty and the need for clarity in commercial rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how vague or internally inconsistent statutory language (UCC §2-209) produces confusion for judges and practitioners, and Paper B confronts the legal requirement that lost-profits claims be proved with a "reasonable degree of certainty," showing how vague proof or methodology can doom commercial claims.

shared_topics.topic: how courts apply standards to commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how judges struggle to apply an obfuscated statutory rule on contract modification and waiver, while Paper B surveys Texas courts' evidentiary and doctrinal standards (competent evidence, reasonable certainty, causation, Rule 403) governing the admissibility and evaluation of lost-profits claims.

shared_topics.topic: importance of precise, objective methodology/evidence for commercial litigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that unclear statutory drafting leaves judges and lawyers without usable rules, and Paper B argues that objective, well-specified techniques (multivariate regression and business records) are required to meet legal standards and avoid speculative findings.

shared_topics.topic: how poor rules or methods increase commercial unpredictability and litigation risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that waffled or half-reformed statutory drafting creates regulatory chaos and commercial calamities, and Paper B shows that speculative or uni-dimensional proof of damages invites exclusion, reversal, and undermines predictability of commercial remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46ukanlrev115!!ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?

shared_topics.topic: proving causation — isolating the defendant act or the unforeseen condition as the cause of loss
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address the legal and evidentiary need to link a specific cause to economic harm: Paper B systematically analyzes legal and scientific criteria for proving that a defendant's act caused lost profits (including temporal precedence, covariation, and ruling out alternatives), while Paper A discusses disputes over whether unforeseen subsurface/latent site conditions (versus contractor error or predictable risk) are the causal basis for change-order costs.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary standard and need for objective, expert-supported proof of monetary claims
shared_topics.justification: Both articles emphasize that recovery turns on competent, objective proof rather than speculation: Paper B requires objective financial data and recommends multivariate regression and expert analysis to satisfy 'reasonable certainty,' and Paper A likewise implicates the necessity of factual site investigations, documentation and expert assessments to substantiate claims for additional contract payments under differing-site-condition disputes.

shared_topics.topic: who bears financial responsibility for unforeseen events and the legal mechanisms for compensating cost increases
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with allocation of risk and remedies for unexpected economic consequences: Paper A examines contract clauses (the differing site condition provision) and the role of common law in assigning unforeseen subsurface risk and triggering change orders, while Paper B analyzes when courts will award monetary relief (lost profits) so that injured parties are compensated for economic harms caused by another's conduct, thereby reallocating losses through legal remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 144upalrev1765!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS

shared_topics.topic: use of business practices and empirical data as admissible evidence in commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that objective business records and multivariate regression analysis are necessary and admissible to establish lost profits, while Paper B examines the Uniform Commercial Code's expectation that courts discover and apply 'usage of trade' and 'course of dealing'—i.e., actual commercial practices—as authoritative evidence when deciding contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: role and evaluation of domain expertise and experts in adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the crucial role of econometric experts and the courts' gatekeeping function in assessing the competence and methodology of expert lost‑profits testimony, and Paper B compares industry‑expert NGFA arbitrators with courts, interrogating when and how adjudicators' commercial expertise should influence legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: inferential problems in drawing legal conclusions from observed business behavior and the need to control for alternative explanations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on isolating a defendant's effect on profits by statistically controlling for market and operational factors to establish causation with reasonable certainty, and Paper B critiques the Code's tendency to treat parties' actual performance as definitive evidence of intent, arguing that observed behavior may reflect relationship‑preserving norms or extralegal arrangements rather than the parties' intended legal bargain.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20ncjltechon267!!ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS

shared_topics.topic: treatment of scientific or technical data as legal evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that multivariate regression analysis should be accepted and properly applied as expert scientific evidence to prove lost profits under evidentiary and certainty standards, while Paper B examines how direct-to-consumer genetic test results (scientific/technical data) are collected, used, and disclosed with few legal limits, raising questions about how such data ought to be handled in legal and governmental contexts.

shared_topics.topic: legal significance and control of privately held data
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes reliance on objective, firm-held business records and empirical data as competent evidence to establish damages, and Paper B focuses on companies' control over consumers' genetic data via privacy policies and the consequences of that private control for individuals and third parties, so both engage with how corporate data holdings function within legal rights and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: whether existing law adequately adapts to novel empirical/technological developments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques traditional, uni-dimensional approaches to proving lost profits and argues courts should accommodate modern econometric methods to meet legal standards, while Paper B argues the current federal regulatory framework is inadequate for DTC genetic testing and advocates statutory reform, with both papers assessing whether existing legal rules properly address new empirical methods or technologies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.

shared_topics.topic: the relative influence of legal enforcement versus market, moral, and social forces on parties' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges that market conditions, competitor actions, and other economic forces affect profits and stresses that legal proof must isolate the defendant's effect from those nonlegal influences; Paper B explicitly theorizes market, moral, and social 'glues' as the primary determinants of promise-keeping and treats law as an additional, often secondary, enforcement mechanism—both papers grapple with how much law itself versus nonlegal forces drive outcomes and how that should inform legal treatment.

shared_topics.topic: attributing causation and ruling out alternative explanations when awarding remedies or enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the legal requirement of causation in lost-profits claims and argues for multivariate regression to control for confounders and demonstrate that a defendant's act proximately caused losses; Paper B emphasizes that observable performance may be explained by multiple motives (market, moral, social) and that the state should consider and distinguish these alternative explanations before claiming law-based causation—both engage with the evidentiary and analytic problem of correctly attributing observed outcomes to the right causes for legal decisions.

shared_topics.topic: bringing social-scientific and economic analysis into legal doctrine and adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates using econometric techniques (multivariate regression) and objective financial data as the proper method to satisfy courts' evidentiary standards; Paper B draws on economic and social-science concepts (market incentives, social sanctions, behavioral motives) to evaluate and critique contract-law paradigms—both papers integrate empirical/economic reasoning into arguments about how law should operate.

papers.node_id: 19upajbusl809!!ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION
papers.title: ARTICLE: STATUTES AND RULES OF LAW AS IMPLIED CONTRACT TERMS: THE DIVERGENT APPROACHES AND A PROPOSED SOLUTION
papers.abstract:
The great majority of state and federal courts accept the general common law rule that courts in construing contracts shall incorporate relevant, unmentioned laws as implied contract terms.A common formulation is "the laws which subsist at the time and place of the making of a contract, and where it is to be performed, enter into and form a part of it, as if they were expressly referred to or incorporated in its terms."Dating back to the early nineteenth century,this principle of contract construction is a "basic legal concept of longstanding and accepted use."
Despite the doctrine's pervasive theoretical and practical importance asa "silent factor in every contract,"courts have failed to articulate a consistent, convincing policy and doctrinal rationale. Most courts also have overlooked numerous doctrinal deficiencies, gaps, and contradictions and, further, have not acknowledged the decisions restricting or even rejecting the precept. Similarly, no commentator has provided an in-depth treatment even though a Westlaw search reveals nearly 1,200 decisions on this topic.
This Article is the first effort in the literature to undertake a comprehensive descriptive and normative analysis of what will be called the "implied incorporation doctrine." Replete with presumptions and legal fictions, the principle is an uneasy merger of the rules of statutory and contract construction. This problematic melding of statutory and contractual principles is the main reason for the divergent approaches and doctrinal contradictions. After canvassing the key issues surrounding the principle, I will propose a uniform formulation that better maintains the legal and logical differences between laws and contract.
The Article proceeds as follows: Part II poses some possible justifications for the implied incorporation doctrine and discusses some basic doctrinal concepts. After exploring the connection between the impliedincorporation precept and the nature of contract, and considering the enduring problem of incomplete contracts, this Part concludes that the doctrine is best suited under Article Two of the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.) in contracts for the sale of goods. Otherwise, the precept is very much flawed on doctrinal and normative grounds.
In assessing the policies often stated as supporting the doctrine, Part III rejects the courts' undue reliance on the legal fictions that every person knows the law and parties naturally intend to include applicable law as implied contract terms. The Article criticizes courts' heavy reliance on the parties' uncommunicated intent as a basis for relief. This part shows how these presumptions are actually mandatory rules of law that rest upon dubious public policy reasoning and shaky hypothetical bargains. This part further analyzes where the doctrine runs counter to the generally disfavored nature of implied contract terms and it questions whether the doctrine is even a true implied term. This part also explores the relationship between the doctrine and contract as a form of private ordering. Next, this part addresses whether the doctrine can be explained by the common law view that private parties may not abrogate existing laws by way of contract.
Part IV compares the implied incorporation doctrine to other principles of statutory and contractual construction. First, it describes the differing roles and functions of statutes and contracts. Second, it shows how the doctrine contradicts the principles for when a law may be deemed to support a private right of action. To implement a rational policy against the excessive implied incorporation of laws, courts should not routinely construe relevant or applicable laws to provide a free standing contractual right of action or defense. Third, this part shows how courts inappropriately pile one fiction upon another when they reason that a party knows and intends the law to be an implied part of the contract.
After it explores whether parties may properly opt out of the implied incorporation doctrine, Part IV explains why the doctrine is actually an immutable (mandatory) rule under current law and not an interpretive default rule (gap filler) as a number of courts and commentators have concluded. The reason is that default principles pertain to contract interpretation and the implied incorporation doctrine pertains to the different concept of contract construction. The difference is contract "construction" addresses the unexpressed implications of the contract by operation of law whereas "interpretation" assesses the meaning of the words in the contract.The contract interpretation versus contract construction divide is crucial for a proper understanding of this doctrine and the Article addresses this distinction at length. Lastly, Part IV covers the ramifications of parallelcontractual and statutory enforcement of applicable laws as well as other canons of contractual construction.
Part V documents a number of cases that push back on the implied incorporation doctrine or reject the precept (even as other cases from these same jurisdictions endorse it). The most problematic jurisdiction is the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which has three or four case law versions of the doctrine ranging from full acceptance to almost full rejection.
The last part of the Article (Part VI) offers a major overhaul of the current implied incorporation doctrine. The Article proposes that as a normative matter, courts and lawmakers should simply support the limited policy basis underlying the rule. Unless the parties have sufficiently included the law as an express contract term, the true principle should be that implied incorporation of a law is proper only as dictated by the law maker's intent for the enactment. As under the better view, this view of the precept is a matter of contract construction and not contract interpretation.
Reconciling the disparate strands of the implied incorporation doctrine, a fuller description of my proposed reform is that a law can form the basis for an implied contract right or a contract defense only where: (1) the law in question is for either the joint benefit of the parties or exists for the sole benefit of the moving party,and(2) the contract expressly incorporates the particular laws (or parts of laws) as term(s) of the agreement,or(3) the law maker's intent for the law (inclusive of laws stemming from the state's police power) requires that a contract contain the law as conveying both a contractual rightandremedy. A party may waive the protection of a law unless the lawmaker has precluded waiver of such a right.
This scaled-back version of the common law doctrine is a consistent, fully-supported solution commensurate with the true scope and effect of the implied incorporation doctrine. It also comports with the U.S. Supreme Court's and many state high courts' increasingly narrow approach toward distilling private rights from public laws. Therefore, this Article should attract the interest of courts and legislatures willing to reconsider the doctrine.

questions.question: Should courts treat relevant, unmentioned laws or public rules as implied terms of private contracts that can create contractual rights or defenses?

If laws may be implied into contracts, what criteria (for example, legislative intent or whether the law benefits the parties) should determine when a law gives rise to an implied contractual right or remedy?
Is the principle that unmentioned laws become part of a contract a mandatory rule that parties cannot waive, or is it a default gap-filling rule that contracting parties may opt out of?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev561!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation of external norms into contractual obligations (laws, norms, or relational practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the written contract often omits governing practices and relational norms that effectively function as contract terms and must be studied outside the document; Paper B analyzes the judicial practice of treating statutes and rules as implied contract terms and proposes doctrinal limits on when external laws should be read into agreements.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracts and gap‑filling mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that long‑term agreements are necessarily incomplete and rely on relational adaptation, renegotiation, or private governance to fill gaps; Paper B treats the implied incorporation doctrine as a contested form of gap‑filling (construction vs interpretation) and assesses where legal rules should supply missing terms, especially under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and parties' ability to craft bespoke governance instead of relying on formal legal terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how parties create private ordering (procedures, hostage exchanges, tailored governance) to manage idiosyncratic transactions outside the written instrument; Paper B examines contract as a form of private ordering, whether parties can contract around statutory defaults, and the circumstances under which courts should respect or override such private arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' intent and judicial presumptions about knowledge of law in construing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns against inferring parties' expectations solely from the document and highlights strategic incentives to misstate terms or rely on unstated expectations; Paper B criticizes judicial fictions that parties know and intended applicable law to be part of their bargain and scrutinizes reliance on uncommunicated intent as the basis for implied terms.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of enforcement, remedies, and protections against opportunism for transaction‑specific investments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties protect idiosyncratic investments (price design, hostages, governance) and why enforcement or renegotiation can fail when relational safeguards are weak; Paper B evaluates when statutes should supply contractual rights or remedies (versus being inapplicable) and how parallel statutory/contractual enforcement affects parties' protection against opportunistic conduct.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105califlrev1725!!SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: use of the contract metaphor to analyze public-law relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats statutes and regulatory rules as potential implied terms of private contracts and analyzes doctrine in terms of contract construction; Paper B analyzes federalism by explicitly likening intergovernmental arrangements to contracts that prescribe the terms of cooperation or conflict.

shared_topics.topic: when and whether public laws should bind private agreements (mandatory rules vs opt-out/default rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether statutes operate as mandatory implied contract terms or merely interpretive/default gap-fillers and whether parties can waive those statutory protections; Paper B engages the parallel question at the constitutional level by asking whether federal structures and sovereignty doctrines impose binding constraints on states and citizens or leave room for decentralized choice.

shared_topics.topic: critical assessment of existing doctrine and proposals for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents doctrinal confusion about the implied incorporation doctrine and proposes a narrower, intent-focused reform; Paper B critiques Gerken's Federalism 3.0, measures its claims against social‑scientific theory, and proposes an alternate theoretical account to guide evaluation of federalism.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between centralization and decentralization and their effects on rights, remedies, and private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the implied incorporation principle is most defensible in the uniform, centralized context of UCC Article Two and is problematic elsewhere, implicating how central legal rules interact with private ordering; Paper B analyzes the substantive trade-offs of decentralized versus centralized governance—how decentralization can be progressive or regressive and creates collective action versus information problems that shape outcomes for people.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev429!!SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FEAR OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling and courts imposing obligations beyond explicit consent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends an objective theory of contract that requires courts to enforce obligations and contextual practices beyond explicit assent, while Paper B analyzes the 'implied incorporation' doctrine as a form of judicially imposed term (incorporating statutes into contracts) and questions when courts may properly supply such unexpressed obligations.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation vs formalism — whether courts should use contextual/purposive methods or rigid formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques a resurgence of formalist arguments that reject contextual interpretation and relational norms, and Paper B critiques doctrinal fictions and divergent judicial approaches, proposing a reform that distinguishes construction from interpretation and better aligns methods with legal purpose.

shared_topics.topic: boundaries between contract obligations and other legal regimes (statutory/private rights, tort, precontractual liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines precontractual liability and the debate over treating non-consensual obligations as contract or tort, while Paper B focuses on when statutes and rules should create contractual rights or defenses (i.e., when public laws become part of private contracts) and the doctrinal limits on hybrid statutory-contractual enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: default (opt-out) rules versus mandatory rules in contract law and parties' ability to exclude rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the critique that courts should not design default or extra-consensual obligations and discusses the necessity of some default frameworks, whereas Paper B centrally analyzes whether implied incorporation is an opt-out-able interpretive default or an immutable/mandatory constructional rule and proposes limits on waiver.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56clevstlrev767!!ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS

shared_topics.topic: whether courts may rely on uncommunicated party intent to supply contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly criticizes courts' heavy reliance on hypothetical or uncommunicated intent as a basis for treating statutes as implied contractual terms, while Paper B challenges the view that contractual meaning depends on private mental states and argues meaning is grounded in public linguistic practice rather than speakers' hidden intentions.

shared_topics.topic: the normative choice between textual/plain-meaning rules and alternative interpretive doctrines (construction, gap-filling, implied terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes contract interpretation from contract construction and debates when courts should fill gaps or imply statutory terms, proposing a narrowed doctrine; Paper B defends the possibility of plain meaning and stresses that selecting among interpretive rules is a matter of legal policy rather than linguistic impossibility.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy of legal fictions and epistemic assumptions underlying contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques fictions such as 'everyone knows the law' and other presumptions that sustain implied incorporation, and Paper B rejects philosophical premises (e.g., words having inherent or absolute referents) that underlie judicial claims that plain meaning is impossible, with both papers examining how such assumptions affect doctrinal validity.

shared_topics.topic: the circumstances under which external legal norms or extrinsic evidence may be incorporated into contractual rights and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on when statutes or public laws can be treated as forming part of a contract (and when waiver is possible), while Paper B addresses when courts may properly rely on textual plain meaning versus looking to extrinsic context or evidence to ascertain contractual language, so both probe limits on importing external material into contract interpretation/construction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev1012!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: How Did We End Up in a World Where Browsewraps Are Enforced Even When They Waive All Consumer Rights?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: How Did We End Up in a World Where Browsewraps Are Enforced Even When They Waive All Consumer Rights?

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract and judicial protection against abusive terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes a judicial turn toward a Lochnerian freedom-of-contract posture that enforces adhesive browsewraps and waives consumer protections, while Paper B assesses limits on private ordering by questioning whether and when courts should treat laws as implied contractual limits to prevent parties from abrogating statutory protections.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when contractual language (including online boilerplate) can waive statutory protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how online retailers' clickwrap/browsewrap terms effectively waive UCC defaults and other consumer rights, and Paper B analyzes the doctrine of implied incorporation and the conditions under which parties may or may not opt out (i.e., waive) statutory protections, proposing rules about when waiver should be permitted.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrinal frameworks for treating unexpressed contract terms (construction vs interpretation; default vs mandatory rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes doctrines like unconscionability, good faith, and the Restatement to criticize courts' declining policing of form contracts, while Paper B gives an extended doctrinal critique—distinguishing contract construction from interpretation, exposing legal fictions, and proposing a coherent rule-set for when laws should be treated as implied terms.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction of statutory regimes (particularly UCC Article 2) with private contractual ordering in sales transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A laments that UCC default protections for buyers are being overridden by modern contract enforcement of boilerplate terms, and Paper B specifically situates the implied-incorporation principle within Article Two of the UCC, arguing the doctrine is most defensible in sale-of-goods contexts and proposing a narrowed, statute-sensitive application.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev31!!ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and normative justification of unexpressed contract terms (implied statutes vs hidden/latent rights)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrine that statutes and rules of law are incorporated into contracts as implied terms and critiques its doctrinal and policy foundations; Paper B analyzes how lawyers create and rely on latent or hidden contractual rights (hostages) and evaluates when courts should enforce such uncommunicated dispositions as part of the bargain.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal distinction between contract construction and contract interpretation (and its consequences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the construction versus interpretation divide to show why implied incorporation operates as construction (with mandatory effects) rather than as a default gap-filler; Paper B examines how principles of contract construction and defenses determine whether hidden contractual hostages can be created and thus shapes transactional design.

shared_topics.topic: how mandatory rules, default rules, and contractual defenses shape transactional incentives and bargaining strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether implied incorporation is an immutable (mandatory) rule or an opt-outtable default and the resulting effects on parties' private ordering; Paper B shows that contract doctrines and defenses that limit hidden rights alter lawyers' incentives to identify and allocate contingent risks and thus affect negotiation strategies and transaction costs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of presumptions about parties' knowledge/intent and public-policy limits on private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques legal fictions (e.g., that everyone knows the law or intends its inclusion) and explores when public laws should be allowed to create private contractual rights, while Paper B investigates how covert contractual devices and signaling (and reputational costs) interact with norms of cooperation and public-policy constraints on enforceability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36houslrev1!!ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and scope of the UCC (Article 2) and proposed Article 2B for modern transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses the implied incorporation doctrine's proper operation under UCC Article Two (sales of goods) and limits the doctrine largely to that Article, while Paper B directly addresses the need for a new or revised UCC regime (proposed Article 2B) to govern information and digital-service transactions that do not fit traditional goods-based rules.

shared_topics.topic: how statutory and public-law norms interact with private contracts (when statutes or public rights become contractual terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrine that statutes and unmentioned laws may be treated as implied contract terms and critiques when courts convert public laws into private contractual rights or defenses, and Paper B engages the overlap between contract rules and other legal regimes (notably intellectual property and regulatory norms) in defining the rights and duties surrounding information transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between mandatory rules and default (waivable) contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that implied incorporation is treated as a construction-based, often immutable (mandatory) rule rather than a waivable default and explores when parties can opt out, while Paper B repeatedly emphasizes freedom of contract and the need for contract-law background rules that function as defaults appropriate to commercial practice in the information economy.

shared_topics.topic: the need to adapt doctrinal frameworks and interpretive concepts (images, construction vs interpretation) to new commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the courts conflate statutory and contractual construction and insists on distinguishing contract 'construction' from 'interpretation' to correct doctrinal errors, whereas Paper B argues that prevailing 'images' and categories from a goods-based era mislead courts and scholars and calls for reconceptualizing contract doctrine to fit information- and service-oriented transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65casewres297!!ARTICLE: FACILITATING INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FACILITATING INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: treatment of incomplete contracts and judicial gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the implied incorporation doctrine functions as a form of judicial gap‑filling for unexpressed terms and assesses its fit given the problem of incomplete contracts (especially under Article 2 of the UCC), while Paper B focuses on the efficiency and desirability of deliberately incomplete (relational) contracts and argues contract law currently deters such gap‑filling approaches that would enable flexible post‑execution governance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation versus legal construction in shaping contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a doctrinal distinction between contract interpretation and contract construction and argues the implied incorporation rule operates as construction (operation of law) rather than mere interpretive default, and Paper B debates interpretive styles (formalist vs contextualist) and proposes a ‘dynamic contextualist’ approach so courts better accommodate evolving, incomplete agreements.

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual rules should be default (opt‑out) or mandatory (non‑waivable)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether implied statutory incorporation is a mandatory rule or a defeasible interpretive default and concludes it generally operates as an immutable rule unless the lawmaker permits waiver, while Paper B critiques doctrinal constraints that effectively force parties into fully specified contracts and advocates reforms to allow parties to choose (opt into) flexible, incomplete contracting regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how legal doctrine and statutory law shape private ordering and transactional incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the interplay between statutes, public policy, and private contracting (including when statutes should give rise to private contractual rights or defenses), and Paper B analyzes how prevailing judicial doctrines and doctrinal incentives influence lawyers and parties to prefer complete, control‑based contracts over potentially more efficient flexible or relational forms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres151!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling of incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrine that courts incorporate unmentioned laws as implied contract terms as a form of gap-filling in contracts, assessing its doctrinal fit and limits; Paper B situates itself in the incomplete-contracts literature and examines when and how courts (or legal frameworks) fill contractual gaps and the implications of those judicial responses.

shared_topics.topic: limits of courts' fact-finding and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes the economic literature's assumption that courts are often unable to evaluate key factual claims and shows how that shapes models of contract law, while Paper A critiques courts' doctrinal reasoning in invoking legal fictions (e.g., that parties know the law) and assesses how courts' limitations produce inconsistent approaches to implied incorporation.

shared_topics.topic: mandatory rules versus default (interpretive) rules and parties' ability to opt out
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly confronts whether implied incorporation operates as an immutable, mandatory rule or a gap-filling interpretive/default rule and discusses waiver/opt-out, and Paper B examines assumptions (like ease of renegotiation and the role of legal rules) that bear on whether contractual provisions should be treated as mandatory or adjustable by the parties.
