papers.node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
papers.abstract:
In the economic analysis of law, famous cases are often famous not so much because of how courts have actually interpreted and applied them, but because they suggest potentially efficient legal rules.  In this way, the rule of a famous case comes to represent a particular set of efficiency arguments, and these arguments become as foundational to the economic analysis of law as are the cases to doctrine.  But economic explanations of doctrinal efficiency are themselves grounded in certain assumptions and conventions.  Indeed, one of the valuable things about the economic approach to law is its straightforward statement of the assumptions from which analysis proceeds.To treat a particular efficiency argument as an established "rule" is therefore to treat argument as myth and to lose what is perhaps most valuable about the economic approach: the potential to progressively enrich our understanding of legal rules and institutions by examining their efficiency under progressively more realistic, if more complex, behavioral and environmental assumptions.
This Article attempts to further the progressive research program of law and economics by questioning the established economic analysis of one of the foundational contract law cases,Hadley v. Baxendale.By limiting the extent of promissory liability for consequential damages to those which are "foreseeable,"Hadleyexemplifies a "default" contract rule: an implicit term of acontract unless the contracting parties explicitly agree to vary it.BecauseHadleyrepresents a default rule on contractual liability, the economic analysis ofHadleyis an analysis of both a particular legal rule -- the foreseeability limitation on consequential loss liability -- and a general rule of contract construction -- the implied default term.  Here, I draw on insights about strategic bargaining from contemporary game theory to argue against the grain of the established understanding of both theHadleyforeseeability test and default rules generally.  In so doing, I hope to expand the economic understanding of default rules, and, at the same time, to contribute to the nascent relationship between law and game theory.
In the established economic understanding,Hadleyillustrates a "penalty" default rule: a rule which "forces" the revelation of information which the revealing party might generally wish not to reveal.In theHadleysituation, the default rule is takento provide only limited promisor liability for promisee consequential loss.  This rule penalizes a promisee who will suffer high consequential loss -- such as large lost profits -- by denying her recovery of much of her loss.  Faced with the prospect of large uncompensated damages in the event of breach, the promisee will have an incentive to tell the promisor that she will suffer large lost profits.  The promisor may then agree to be liable for the full extent of such a promisee's loss, but only if the promisee agrees to pay a higher price for the contract.  The promisee and society must be better off with such a rule, because the information which the promisee is "forced" to reveal allows the promisor to take the optimal, fully informed level of precaution against breach.
For some years, my intuition has been that this story fails to account for strategic incentives in bargaining.  Again, according to the established view a promisee who will suffer loss of exceptionally large profits if the promisor breaches is supposed to tell the promisor that performance is especially important and valuable, and then agree to some price increase in exchange for the promisor's agreement to accept liability for these exceptional losses.  But if weare talking aboutbargainingover the contract, then we are talking about a process of strategic information transmission, a process in which the promisee tries to persuade the promisor that she cannot pay a high price, and the promisor tries to persuade the promisee that she should.  In this process, the promisee would generally want to convince the promisor that her value from performance is low -- that is, that she will not make especially large profits from successful lerformance.  And the promisor would want to persuade the promisee -- especially one who will not be fully covered against all consequential loss -- that performance is virtually a sure thing, so that the contract is very valuable to the promisee, and also that performance is very costly, so that the promisee must pay a relatively high price or else the promisor will walk away.
But then the general strategic incentives in this bargaining situation are directly at odds with the established information-forcing justification for the rule inHadley:the promisee is supposed to reveal her crucial item of private information -- her value from performance -- and thus do what is generally completely contrary to her strategic interest in the bargaining game.  The promisee is, moreover, supposed to do this even though there is no incentive for the promisor to reveal his key item of private information -- the actual probability of breach.  Generally, the higher the initial probability of breach under the limited liability default rule, the more the promisee benefits from getting the promisor to agree to increase his liability above this default.  So bargaining around theHadleydefault is more likely, the higher the promisee's estimation of the probability of breach under this default.  But then we have a final strategic problem with bargaining around theHadleydefault: to get the contract in the first place, the promisor generally wants to persuade the promisee that the breach probability is low.  So to bargainaroundthis default, the promisor must convey information which is generally directly contrary to his strategic interest in bargainingwiththe default.  Put somewhat more simply, the promisor wants a profitable contract, but risks not getting any contract at all by seeking to extract a high price from the promisee in exchange for insuring the promisee against losses above what the default provides.  Thus, the promisor will not have an interest in bargaining around the default.
At virtually every stage in this story, strategic incentives in bargaining seem to cut against the idea that the penalty default rule inHadleycan force promisees to reveal information.  The story shows, moreover, how the established understanding neglects entirely the promisor's incentive to reveal information.  But just asHadleyqua case stands as a fixed point in the common law, so too doesHadleyas theory stand as a pillar in the economic analysis of contract law.  How can it be thatHadleyas a theory about bargaining around the law is so at odds with my simple intuitive story?
My goal in the remainder of this Article is to answer this question.  The answer has, I think, at least two, related parts.  First, existing formal (mathematical) economic models of the rule inHadleyhave simply not been formulatedto capture the kind of strategic incentives which my story identifies.  The models therefore are actually special and correspond poorly to what the nontechnical person imagines when he thinks of "bargaining" around the law.  Second, because, as I mentioned earlier,Hadleyrepresents a general type of legal rule -- the default rule -- the validity of the established understanding ofHadleyhas tended to follow from the more general, established economic understanding of default rules.  This general understanding -- which I call the "Coasean Contractual Theory" -- rests on an enormously powerful and influential insight, the Coase Theorem.But this insight and the theory constructed upon it also fail to account for strategic incentives, and instead simply assume that there is no impediment to bargaining other than direct transaction costs.
In Part I of this Article, I explain in detail how the absence of explicit consideration of bargaining incentives limits both the specific established understanding ofHadleyand the general Coasean Contractual Theory.  In Part II, I sketch some stylized stories depicting the strategic difficulties that are likely to arise when parties try to bargain around an information-forcing or penalty default such as theHadleyrule.  My goal in Part II is to persuade the reader that even in admittedly simple models, strategic bargaining considerations tend to favor what I call "expansive" default rules, such as the "foreseeability" limitation whichHadleyhas actually become.  I do not claim to have presented a general theory, and indeed I think that a truly general treatment of the bargaining problem inHadleyin fact would require more modeling horsepower than the game theoretic analysis of bargaining has yet developed.Still, my series of vignettes argues that expansive default rules often eliminate strategic impediments to bargaining around the default.
Having made these points about bargaining incentives, it remains possible that I will have said little about the actual efficiency of expansive default rules, for it may be that even though it is easy to bargain around such rules, almost everyone prefers the "penalty" default.  That is, it may be that theHadleyrule really is no penalty at all, but rather simply what the majority would have contracted for anyway.  By imposing an expansive default, we would then simply force people to incur needless transaction costs in bargaining around the law.  Professor Richard Epstein has in fact recently mounted just this sortof empirical attack on expansive default rules,and empirical observations about the terms contained in "most" contracts of a given class are more generally an important part of the Coasean approach to default terms.
In Part III of this Article, I meet the empiricist challenge to my theoretical results.  I argue that an extensive (although admittedly incomplete and methodologically informal) survey of hundreds of cases on consequential damages over the last 120 years (which includes a period whenHadleywas more stringently interpreted than it now is, as under Holmes' tacit agreement view)finds few cases where the promisee claimed to have done what the information-forcing theory says she should have done: nobody seems to have claimed that they told the promisor that they would suffer unusually large consequential damages.  At the same time, there are scores of recent cases in which the parties apparently accepted the more expansive "foreseeability" version ofHadley.I do not contend that any of this constitutes conclusive empirical proof that most people like the "foreseeability" limitation and that those who do not are able to bargain around it.  Rather, I contend merely that there is no conclusive evidence one way or the other.  And I make the general point, made also by Ayres and Gertner,that just as people sometimes fail to bargain around a default rule not because the default is efficient for them but because there are strategic impediments to bargaining around it, the observation that lots of people bargain around a default rule does not imply that the rule they bargain to is the optimal default rule.  It may be that the bargained-to rule would, for strategic reasons, not be bargained around were it the default rule.
Part III also points out the trouble the information-forcing theory ofHadleyhas in harmonizingHadleywith other, related contract doctrines such as the nondisclosure rule inLaidlaw v. Organand the law's reluctance to enforce liquidated damage provisions.The law's reluctance to enforce liquidated damage provisions makes it very difficult for bargainers to do the very thing that the information-forcing theory says they should do.Laidlaw'saccepted meaning within the economic analysis of law (which it must be stressed is, likeHadley'smeaning, quite different than its meaning as actual contract doctrine) that it is undesirable to force the revelation of at least some kinds of information is also problematic for the information-forcing theory.  Both of these related doctrines, however, are consistent with my theory.
Finally, in Part IV, I conclude with some limited remarks on the problems of positivism in the economic analysis of law that are raised byHadleyandHadley'splace in the larger attempt to "explain" the common law from an economic point of view.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?

papers.node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
papers.abstract:
Two separate groups of academics have brought about a renaissance of sorts in the analysis of incomplete contracts.  Law and economics scholars -- writing in law reviews -- have shown renewed interest in how efficiency-minded lawmakers should fill gaps in incomplete contracts.Yet even before this, a group of economists -- writing in economics journals -- began developing new theories of "incomplete contracting" that are still largely unincorporated in the legal literature.These two strands of analysis have remained largelyindependent, in part because they focus on two different forms of contractual incompleteness.
Legal scholars use the term "incomplete contracting" to refer to contracts in which the obligations are not fully specified.  A contract to sell a good would be "obligationally" incomplete, for example, if it failed to specify the price, quantity, or date of delivery.  In contrast, a contract is obligationally complete if the obligations of the parties are fully specified for all future states of the world.  A contract that failed to specify the seller's obligations in the event of a flood or the buyer's breach would thus be obligationally incomplete.  Default rules respond to obligational incompleteness by filling these obligational gaps.
Economics scholars, on the other hand, use the term "incomplete contracting" to refer to contracts that fail to fully realize the potential gains from trade in all states of the world.  These contracts are considered "contingently" incomplete or "insufficiently state contingent." For example, a contract to deliver certain goods to a house tomorrow for $ 100 may be obligationally complete in the sense that obligations are fully specified for all future states of the world.  However, the contract may be insufficiently state contingent in that the contractual obligations fail to fully realize the potential gains from trade in all states of the world.Contracts that are "insufficiently state contingent" (contingently incomplete) give private parties incentives -- in at least some states of the world -- to either renegotiate or breach the original contract to realize these additional gains from trade.
Setting damages for breach of contract can cause courts to respond to both types of contractual incompleteness -- obligational and contingency.  Since a contractual promise is a promise "to perform or to pay damages,"contracts that do not set the amount of breach damages for each party fail to fully specify the parties' obligations under all future states of the world; hence, these contracts are "obligationally incomplete." Most contracts are obligationally incomplete in this sense, because most contracts do not have liquidated damages clauses.  Courts, in determining the amount of damages for breach of contract, are often called upon to fill this obligational gap.
This form of gap filling, however, has at times been used to respond to contracts that are "insufficiently state contingent." For example, imagine a contract which, because of an unanticipated state of the world, cannot be carried out or can only be carried out with great losses.  This contract is obligationally incomplete, since it does not specify the damages for breach in the unanticipated state of the world, and it is contingently incomplete because it does not make the parties' contractual duties dependent upon the unanticipated state of the world.  When faced with such contracts, courts use the excuse doctrines of impossibilityand impracticabilityto fill the damages gap with zero damages.
By filling obligational gaps with provisions that are state contingent, courts can respond to both types of contractual incompleteness.  Awarding zero damages when there is excused performance is one way to use obligational incompleteness regarding damages to correct the flaws of contingently incomplete contracts.As such, the judicious use of obligational gap filling can reduce the cost of writing contracts that are contingently incomplete.
Filling the damages gap with state contingent damage measures, however, does not collapse the difference between obligational and contingency incompleteness.  Contracts with liquidated damages clauses may be obligationally complete (because obligations are fully specified in all states of the world)but not contingently complete (because obligations do not exploit gains from trade in all states of the world).  Moreover, making default damage obligations more state contingent may not fully exploit all gains from trade.Thus, courts may be unable to respond efficiently to contingency incompleteness by filling obligational gaps -- because the contract may not have any obligational gaps or may not have the right gaps to allow a court to efficiently reallocate the parties' obligations.  Efficient contract law needs to be responsive to both forms of incompleteness.This Article shows how the choice of obligational default rules affects the strategic reluctance of parties to enter into sufficiently state contingent contracts and thereby maximize gains from trade.
We examine how transaction costs and market power affect the strategic incentives to contract around different default rules.  In a recent article, we argued that strategic bargaining could impede parties from contracting around inefficient default rules.Last year, Jason Johnston went beyond our arguments to show how the incidence of market power could impact the inefficiency of strategic bargaining.  Johnston's article could be read to imply that even in a world without transaction costs, the choice of contractual defaults could impact the types of contracts made and the social benefits of contracting.
In contrast to the implications of Johnston's article, we explicitly propose that default rules do not affect the contractual equilibrium when it is costless to contract and when both parties know the default rule.  This is what we characterize as our "irrelevance conjecture" -- the choice of default becomes irrelevant when it is costless to contract and when the default rule is common knowledge.Without these transaction costs (and when the default rule is common knowledge), strategic bargaining can still cause inefficient contracting, but the same contractual equilibrium will be reached by private parties, regardless of the default rule.
When even slight costs in contracting around a default rule are introduced, however, the choice of default rule can affect both the contractual equilibrium and the net social benefits of contracting, i.e., efficiency.  Whereas costless contracting produces a relatively simple contractual equilibrium (which is independent of the default rule), the introduction of transaction costs producesa proliferation of equilibrium contracts that depend on both the choice of default rule and a variety of underlying structural variables.
In fact, the introduction of transaction costs can actually exacerbate the inefficiencies of strategic bargaining -- so the gains from contracting can fall by more than the size of the transaction costs.  We show that the inefficiencies of strategic bargaining, therefore, are not necessarily limited by the size of transaction costs.  The choice of an inefficient default rule can generate inefficiencies that, because of strategic bargaining, are much greater than the cost of contracting around the inefficiency.
In short, the introduction of even slight transaction costs will make the determination of efficient legal rules dramatically more difficult.  We demonstrate that the behavior of contracting parties can change significantly in response to extremely small changes in other, more subtle underlying variables -- such as the valuations of particular buyers.
A main thesis of this Article is that relatively simple contractual settings can give rise to enormous complexity.  While we can show that different default rules -- and in certain circumstances, immutable rules -- would be theoretically efficient, our model suggests that there is small hope that lawmakers will be able to divine the efficient rule in practice.
These results strengthen the growing consensus among contract scholars that default rules should not simply be the hypothetical contract that parties would choose in a world without transaction costs.The hypothetical contract standard fails to account for the inefficiencies that can be caused by strategic bargaining under conditions of asymmetric information and how these inefficiencies depend upon, and can be exacerbated by, the costs of contracting around a given default rule.  When the parties have symmetric information, the hypothetical contract standard yields efficient results.  When the parties have asymmetric information, however, the hypothetical contract standard fails to provide an effective framework for choosing efficient rules.
This Article uses some of the new modeling techniques that economists have been using to model contingency incompleteness to analyze legal responses to obligational incompleteness.Methodologically, the law and economicsof default rules has entered a "second generation" of analysis that begins by explicitly recognizing private preference for different types of contracts.Typically, these models assume either two types of buyers or two types of sellers.  The two types are defined so that different contractual provisions will maximize the gains of trade between the buyers and sellers.  Though the assumption that two types of buyers deal with one type of seller seems crude, it represents an important advance over earlier economic analysis of contractual gap filling.The "first generation" analysis often discovered the single contractual rule that would maximize the gains from trade for all contracting parties.  In an important sense, however, this mode of analysis proved too much: if a rule enhances efficiency for all contracting types, then one should be agnostic about whether to make the rule mandatory or merely a default around which parties can contract.
The decision to use default rules, however, grows out of a realization that contracting parties will often prefer different contractual provisions -- and that contractual flexibility can therefore increase the total gains from trade.  To analyze the choice of default rules in a context where contractual flexibility is important, contracting models need to allow the possibility that some parties might want different contracts.  By allowing for two different types of contracts, these "second generation" models are better suited to analyze whether a particular default rule maximizes the total gains from trade -- because these models can assess whether parties are likely to contract for the different obligations and at what cost.
Though our model of default rules is part of this "second generation" analysis, it retains the traditional factual scenario used to study default rules -- the case ofHadley v. Baxendale.Hadleycontinues to be one of themost analyzed contract cases in law and economics literature.ThoughHadleyprovides our starting point, we show that our analysis has relevance to a wide range of contractual defaults.
In Part I, we extend the recent insights of Johnston to show that the inefficiencies of strategic bargaining depend on the incidence of market power and that these inefficiencies can persist even when it is costless to contract around a given default.  A central result is that the choice of a default rule will not affect how people contract when it is costless to contract for alternative obligations and when both parties are aware of the prevailing default.
In Parts II and III, we relax both of these prerequisites to examine how the contractual equilibrium can be affected either by the presence of transaction costs or by uncertain or mistaken beliefs about the prevailing default rule.  In particular, we show that the presence of even slight transaction costs can dramatically change both the types of contracts that people write and the net gains from trade.  Finally, in Part IV, we explore the sources of and relation between contractual failure and contractual incompleteness with an eye towards structuring efficient default and immutable rules.

questions.question: Does the choice of obligational default rules affect the contractual equilibrium and allocation of obligations when parties can costlessly contract around defaults and the default rule is common knowledge?

Do small transaction costs or uncertainty/mistaken beliefs about the prevailing default cause the choice of default rule to materially change the contracts parties write and the overall efficiency (net gains from trade), potentially amplifying inefficiencies from strategic bargaining beyond the size of the transaction costs?

How do transaction costs, market power, and informational asymmetries interact to shape parties' strategic incentives to contract around defaults and thereby influence which legal rules (defaults or immutable rules) are socially optimal?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: APPLICATION OF THE DOCTRINE OF COMMERCIAL IMPRACTICABILITY: SEARCHING FOR "THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON".

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment of impossibility/impracticability (excuse doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively engage with the doctrines of impossibility and commercial impracticability: Paper A analyzes how courts have applied and reshaped excuse doctrines (and critiques ALCOA's expansive approach), while Paper B treats impossibility/impracticability as a legal mechanism courts use to fill obligational gaps (e.g., awarding zero damages) and thereby influence contracting outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: courts as gap-fillers/default-rule makers versus strict enforcers
shared_topics.justification: Both works examine the role of courts in filling contractual gaps — Paper A discusses judicial implication of terms, modification, and loss‑sharing as alternatives to strict enforcement, and Paper B models how default rules and judicially-imposed damage measures fill obligational incompleteness and alter parties' incentives.

shared_topics.topic: state-contingent obligations and the desirability of contractual flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on whether and how contracts (or judicial responses) should be made contingent on unforeseen states of the world: Paper A argues for a pragmatic, relationship‑oriented duty to adjust and flexible tools to handle supervening events, while Paper B analyzes how making default rules more state‑contingent can (or cannot) correct contingency incompleteness and affect efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: judicial modification/allocation of losses and risk-sharing
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of when courts should reallocate losses or impose risk‑sharing: Paper A critiques judicial interpolation of new pricing and loss‑sharing in ALCOA, and Paper B shows how default damage rules and court gap‑filling can reallocate obligations and influence whether parties renegotiate or breach.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between doctrinal choice and commercial/efficiency consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers link doctrinal choices to commercial realities and efficiency: Paper A argues that excuse doctrine must be grounded in an agreed vision of contract to be practically useful for commerce, while Paper B models how the choice of defaults, transaction costs, and market structure affect contractual efficiency and the feasibility of contracting around rules.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: distinction between obligational incompleteness and contingency (state‑contingent) incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Both papers explicitly engage the difference between contracts that fail to specify obligations (the lawyers' 'obligational' gaps) and contracts that are insufficiently state‑contingent (the economists' notion of incompleteness), using that distinction to frame how and when legal or private responses should operate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and default rules in filling contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how judicial gap‑filling (including default damage rules, excuse doctrines, and interpretive regimes) can correct or distort outcomes arising from incomplete contracts and consider when courts should intervene versus defer to private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: verifiability, asymmetric information, and enforcement/litigation costs
shared_topics.justification: Each paper treats unverifiability and asymmetric information as central constraints—examining how limits on courts' ability to verify facts and the costs of enforcement shape contract design, the desirability of certain terms, and the choice of legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, renegotiation, and strategic bargaining affecting efficiency and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Both articles study how transaction costs and the prospect of ex post renegotiation or strategic bargaining change parties' incentives to invest, to include contingent terms, and to rely on default rules, altering which legal rules are efficient in practice.

shared_topics.topic: private/transactional strategies for managing incompleteness (contracting around defaults, delegation, litigation/settlement strategies)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that parties adopt private strategies—liquidated damages, delegation, settlement, litigation tactics, or contracting around defaults—to manage incompleteness, and analyze how the costs and feasibility of those strategies interact with the choice of legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: design and role of default rules to address contract incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises whether new theoretical conceptions should reshape doctrine and defaults; Paper B provides a detailed economic model of how different default rules (and their state-contingency) respond to obligational and contingency incompleteness.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the economic analysis critique that contract doctrine should prioritize wealth maximization and predictability; Paper B evaluates default rules and doctrines through a law-and-economics lens, showing when and how rules promote or undermine efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: effects of transaction costs, asymmetric information, and strategic behavior on contracting and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights relational and empirical critiques that doctrine must account for real-world behavioral complexity; Paper B models how transaction costs, market power, asymmetric information, and strategic bargaining change which contracts are written and whether default rules are efficient.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between academic contract theory and judicial/statutory practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that many new theoretical literatures have not been incorporated into case law or statute and worries about a neoformal judicial reaction; Paper B emphasizes the practical difficulty lawmakers face in selecting efficient rules and how theoretical prescriptions may fail to map onto real-world contracting.

shared_topics.topic: contract governance and enforcement mechanisms for incomplete contracts

shared_topics.topic: role of transaction costs and enforcement costs in shaping contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that even slight transaction costs of contracting around defaults can dramatically alter equilibrium contracts and efficiency, and Paper B explains how costs or frictions in using public legal institutions make private, network-based enforcement (and avoidance of formal litigation costs) a viable alternative to support long-distance trade.

shared_topics.topic: interaction and complementarities between formal legal rules and private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how the choice of legal default rules affects parties' incentives to contract and the potential for strategic bargaining, while Paper B investigates how private-order mechanisms can substitute for or complement public legal institutions and legal formalities in sustaining exchange.

shared_topics.topic: information, reputation, and strategic incentives under asymmetric information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how asymmetric information and strategic bargaining can frustrate efficient contracting around defaults, and Paper B analyzes how information flow in small-world networks and reputational sanctions create incentives for truthful behavior and cooperation among traders.

shared_topics.topic: how underlying market or organizational structure affects contract efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how the incidence of market power and the structure of valuations affect the inefficiencies produced by strategic bargaining and default rules, and Paper B shows that the small-world pattern of ties and presence of key information nodes in trading networks shape the effectiveness of reputation-based contract governance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 102valrev1523!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT

shared_topics.topic: the choice between default rules and standards (rules vs standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how different obligational default rules (including state-contingent damages) can be used to fill gaps and respond to contingency incompleteness, while Paper B analyzes the drafters' turn to transcontextual standards in the UCC/Restatement and criticizes that choice as ill-suited for many contracting problems.

shared_topics.topic: how default terms shape parties' incentives to contract around them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the selection of a default rule can alter private parties' strategic bargaining and their willingness to contract around inefficient defaults (or to renegotiate/breach), and Paper B documents that commercial parties routinely contract away from undesirable defaults or standards, so default design affects actual contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction costs, asymmetric information, and market power in default-rule efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models how even slight transaction costs, asymmetric information, and the incidence of market power can magnify inefficiencies from strategic bargaining and make default choice consequential, while Paper B appeals to transaction-cost and informational limits on drafters (and the acceptability constraint) to explain why many legislated defaults fail.

shared_topics.topic: institutions for gap-filling: courts/common law versus private drafters
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts' use of doctrines (e.g., impossibility, damages) to fill obligational and contingency gaps and how judicial gap-filling can be state-contingent, and Paper B argues that the common law process is better suited than private drafting projects to produce acceptable, transcontextual defaults.

shared_topics.topic: context-specificity of efficient defaults and limits of one-size-fits-all rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that making obligational defaults more state-contingent does not necessarily capture all gains from trade and that simple settings can yield complex context-sensitive equilibria, while Paper B develops the contextual vs transcontextual distinction and argues most efficient defaults must be context-specific, limiting the feasibility of universal defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 97columlrev1710!!ARTICLE: THE INVERTED HIERARCHY OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AND SUPPLEMENTATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INVERTED HIERARCHY OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AND SUPPLEMENTATION

shared_topics.topic: the role and design of default rules as gap-fillers in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that default rules (and general standards) should occupy a primary place in the hierarchy of interpretive/supplementary sources, while Paper B analyzes how obligational default rules functionally fill gaps in contracts and how different default choices affect the legal response to incomplete bargains.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and interpretive standards shape parties' contracting behavior and strategic responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals empirical, economic, and psychological evidence that parties' actual behavior aligns with an inverted interpretive hierarchy and that rules influence realized intentions, and Paper B models how parties strategically bargain or contract around defaults (and how transaction costs and market power alter those incentives).

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrines in supplementing contracts with state‑contingent measures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines courts' practice and doctrinal patterns in contract interpretation and supplementation (emphasizing standards like reasonableness and good faith), and Paper B studies how courts use doctrines (e.g., impossibility, impracticability, damages awards) to impose state‑contingent obligations or zero damages to address both obligational and contingency incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between legal rules (defaults/standards) and economic efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims the inverted hierarchy better realizes parties' intentions and enhances economic efficiency, while Paper B investigates how the choice of default rules, transaction costs, asymmetric information, and strategic bargaining can increase or reduce the gains from trade and thus affect overall efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of market practices, trade usages, and private preferences on optimal interpretive and default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes trade usages and parties' customary practices as central interpretive inputs that support an inverted hierarchy, and Paper B's ‘second‑generation’ models explicitly incorporate private preferences, differing contractual types, and market power to assess how defaults should be set in light of prevailing market norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44ambuslj639!!ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how obligational default rules (including damage rules) influence whether parties contract around defaults and which contracts are written, while Paper B examines how the choice of remedy for breach (which effectively functions as a default allocation of losses) affects promisor and promisee incentives and thus the desirability of alternative contract forms.

shared_topics.topic: incentives for opportunistic breach or renegotiation created by legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies strategic bargaining and how particular defaults can exacerbate inefficiencies from opportunistic behavior or strategic reluctance to form contingent contracts, and Paper B analyzes how remedial doctrines (and the promisor's option to perform or pay damages) can systematically facilitate or deter opportunistic breaches of alternative contracts.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling of incomplete contracts through damages and doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes obligational vs. contingency incompleteness and focuses on how courts fill obligational gaps (e.g., by setting damages or applying excuse doctrines) to address state‑contingent failures, while Paper B focuses on how courts should compute damages when contracts provide multiple but unexercised modes of performance—i.e., how remedies fill specification gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the role of asymmetric information, transaction costs, and adjudication difficulties in rule choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that even small transaction costs and informational asymmetries make the choice of default rules outcome‑sensitive and can multiply equilibria, and Paper B explicitly tests remedial rules for robustness in the presence of informational asymmetries, strategic behavior, and difficulties of proof in adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: modeling contracts as an option to 'perform or pay damages' to assess optimal remedies/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the perform‑or‑pay framing to explain how damage rules operate as obligational defaults, and Paper B draws on option theory (the promisor's option to escape performance by paying damages) to recommend how damages should be set in alternative‑performance contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between obligational incompleteness and contingency (state-contingent) incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and centers its analysis on the two meanings of 'incomplete contract'—obligational gaps (missing specified obligations/remedies) versus contingently incomplete contracts (insufficient state-contingency that leaves gains unrealized)—and shows how legal rules differently address each. Paper B likewise interrogates the ambiguity of 'incompleteness,' cataloguing missing terms, unanticipated contingencies, and parties' reasons for omission, and stresses that these different senses have different implications for intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the choice and design of default/background legal rules versus after‑the‑fact judicial implication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how the selection of obligational default rules (and when rules are immutable) shapes parties' incentives to contract around defaults and affects efficiency. Paper B distinguishes background statutory/common‑law rules from ad hoc terms implied at litigation, analyzing how justificatory standards and effects differ when the legal rule is a pre‑existing background rule versus a post‑hoc intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the role of strategic/opportunistic behavior, asymmetric information, and transaction costs in shaping contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models strategic bargaining, asymmetric information, market power, and even slight transaction costs to show how these factors can generate inefficiencies and multiple equilibria that depend on the default rule. Paper B focuses on opportunistic behavior combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs as central problems motivating (or cautioning against) judicial intervention and default rule design.

shared_topics.topic: remedial doctrines and state‑contingent remedies as mechanisms to fill contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts set breach damages, use liquidated damages, and deploy excuse doctrines (impossibility/impracticability) or zero damages to create state‑contingent obligations that address both obligational and contingency incompleteness. Paper B engages with remedial doctrines (promissory estoppel, the irrevocability of unilateral offers, Code remedies) and examines how these background remedial rules affect parties' exposure and contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between promoting efficient contracting via defaults and protecting parties' freedom/notice (freedom from contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that defaults chosen to mimic the hypothetical frictionless contract can fail under asymmetric information and transaction costs, making selection of efficient defaults fraught. Paper B raises 'freedom from contract' and notice concerns, warning that uncertain or after‑the‑fact standards can impose unanticipated liabilities and thus that interference must be weighed against consent and the parties' ability to contract around rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses Hadley as the canonical setting for analyzing how default rules on damages fill obligational gaps and interact with contingency incompleteness; Paper B centers Hadley and its foreseeability/certainty requirements to explain why many aggrieved buyers settle or renegotiate rather than litigate for consequential losses.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how asymmetric information and the incidence of market power influence whether parties can or will contract around inefficient defaults and how strategic bargaining can worsen welfare; Paper B describes empirically and doctrinally how disparities in legal resources, bargaining leverage, and incentives shape settlement offers and the practical realization of contract remedies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that simple default rules can enhance predictability but may produce large inefficiencies when parties face transaction costs or asymmetric information, and Paper B examines the parol evidence rule's certainty-promoting effects versus the need to admit context to avoid unfair outcomes—highlighting the same tension between certainty and flexibility.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on judicial gap‑filling (e.g., damages, excuse doctrines) as a response to obligational and contingency incompleteness, and Paper B considers judicial treatment of extrinsic evidence (parol evidence) and when courts should relax or enforce formal written terms to resolve ambiguities and disputes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A finds market shifts (e.g., mega-retailers) change bargaining leverage and effectively let large buyers set purchase-order terms, influencing how §2-207 plays out in practice; Paper B analyzes how the incidence of market power and informational asymmetries interact with default rules to determine the extent of strategic inefficiencies and the contracts parties end up making.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE REGULATORY FUNCTIONS OF TRANSNATIONAL COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: NEW ARCHITECTURES

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the effects of even small transaction costs and the incidence of market power on parties' ability to contract around defaults and on equilibrium inefficiencies; Paper B documents how asymmetries in supply-chain bargaining (e.g., retailers vs. suppliers) and the costs of implementing certification/regulation influence which regulatory clauses are included and the overall contract structure.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the choice of damage rules and excuse doctrines as means of filling obligational gaps and influencing breach/renegotiation incentives, whereas Paper B analyzes the coexistence and interaction of multiple remedial systems (contract damages, certification sanctions, regulatory penalties) when the same factual violation triggers simultaneous contractual and regulatory consequences.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration

shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how the choice of default rules and the costs of contracting around them affect what contracts parties actually form and the resulting social welfare, and Paper B treats doctrines (like consideration requirements and remedies) as legal structures that instantiate and shape the contract relation; both analyze the law’s role in structuring the parties’ agreements rather than treating contracts as purely private.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats contracts as tools to realize gains from trade and studies how contingent completeness and state‑contingent terms affect renegotiation and efficiency, while Paper B characterizes contracts as relations of collaboration and joint endeavor that create and sustain social coordination; both therefore analyze contracts’ role in enabling cooperative interaction among parties.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing

shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses how Cardozo's refusal to fill gaps affected business certainty and contracting practice in the newsprint industry; Paper B models how different default rules and courts' gap-filling can alter incentives to contract around defaults and materially affect the gains from trade and efficiency.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that Cardozo's opinion may have unintentionally facilitated anticompetitive behavior in the paper industry by increasing uncertainty; Paper B explicitly studies how the incidence of market power and strategic bargaining interact with default rules to produce inefficiencies that can magnify the costs of contracting.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Cardozo's apparent preference for certainty in Sun Printing and the tension with his other flexible, justice-driven contract decisions; Paper B examines when defaults versus tailored contracts are socially desirable, showing how transaction costs and asymmetric information make the choice between certainty and flexibility consequential.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how courts and default legal rules fill obligational gaps and how those defaults interact with private bargaining, while Paper B examines how parties use self‑regulation, audits, informal sanctions, and contractual monitoring as alternative gap‑filling and enforcement mechanisms and asks how tax rules should treat such private enforcement.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how uncertainty (including mistaken beliefs about the prevailing default) and asymmetric information alter contracting equilibria and efficiency, and Paper B documents how self‑regulation amplifies uncertainty about when rights/liabilities are fixed for tax accrual purposes and proposes doctrinal responses to that uncertainty.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that even slight costs of contracting around a default or of bargaining can dramatically change equilibrium contracts and welfare, and Paper B emphasizes switching costs, monitoring/enforcement costs, and long‑term relationship considerations that lead parties to use broad standards, informal enforcement, or conditioned payments rather than precise contractual terms.

papers.title: ARTICLE: STRUGGLING WITH QUICKSAND: THE INs AND OUTs OF COTENANT POSSESSION VALUE LIABILITY AND A CALL FOR DEFAULT RULE REFORM Copyright 1994, Evelyn Alicia Lewis.
papers.abstract:
This Article undertakes two related, but separate, analyses of the "default" rules governing rental liability between co-owners of real property when cotenants have no agreement respecting this matter. A large majority of states take one approach to this problem, while a small minority of states take a completely opposite approach.
Part One of this Article compares and analyzes the basic designs of these two default rule systems relative to how they are actually applied by the judiciary. This analysis reveals a need for redesign of the systems. Part Two of this Article then undertakes an independent analysis of the designs of the two systems, testing their compliance with the premises of general default rule theory. This testing necessitates examination of both the commonalities and tensions between the specific, property law foundations of the cotenancy rental liability rules and the more general, contract law foundations of default rule theory. Based on the results of this testing, this Article proposes a modified version of the minority default rule system which recognizes these commonalities while respecting the tensions. Further, a real-life story of a troubled cotenancy, presented in segments throughout this Article, focuses the diverse issues addressed by this Article.$ SE
Louise was still laughing hard when she moved to answer the ringing telephone. A friend, one of eight to ten friends and family members crammed around the huge kitchen table, had just told a joke. It ranked only about a four on a joke scale of ten, but Louise's laughter was easily evoked that Thanksgiving eve. All five of her children, then young adults, were home for the holiday with their spouses and her grandchildren, returned from those faraway places they'd foolishly chosen to live. Also, the kitchen had returned to being the center of household and neighborhood activity reminiscent of its daily hum before the children moved away. Displaying her remarkable talents at informal Black, southern hospitality, Louise was effortlessly preparing a perfect meal while engaging in conversation from the silly to the profound and keeping the kitchen table stocked with tasty nibbles for the never-ending stream of friends stopping by for "just a minute." The present jokester had been there for three hours.
Reaching for the phone, Louise stifled her laugh, turned away slightly to block the noise from the group, and cheerily said "hello." Meanwhile, the kitchen occupants, seasoned in the ways of the household, continued their conversation at the same decibel level--Louise would let them know if she couldn't hear.
But she heard all too well. The slight tensing in her back gave the only indication that her happiness of moments before had been rudely halted. The call ended after only a few moments and Louise quickly moved to stir something on the stove, searching among the pots to find her lost composure before anyone noticed her change in mood. But I already had.  Being able to detect my mother's (or my father's) slightest discomfort or pleasure has always been something of a mixedblessing. I call it the "curse of the eldest daughter," but I suspect my siblings share it.

papers.title: ARTICLE: SUBSTANCE AND PROCEDURE IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION: THE DEVELOPMENT OF A NEW LEGAL ORDER.
papers.abstract:
International commercial arbitration is growing by leaps and bounds.  Both institutional and ad hoc arbitrations are proliferating.  In these arbitrations, the tribunals are most frequently composed of arbitrators from different countries with different legal training, background, and experience.  The lawyers handling the cases before these international tribunals are also different from those appearing before domestic tribunals.  They not only practice before the courts of their own countries, but, increasingly, they are likely to possess experience in processing cases before international, arbitral tribunals.
Indeed, arbitrators are likely to be selected from a rather limited group, especially in the more important cases.  The institutions appoint them because, quite properly and understandably, they wish to appoint persons with proven track records.  Similarly, the parties prefer to appoint arbitrators about whose performance information can be gained.  The usual selection process, under which each party appoints an arbitrator and thetwo party-appointed arbitrators or an institution select the chairman,permits the institutions and the parties to take these factors into account.
These developments have had a marked effect on the law practiced in international arbitral tribunals, both on the procedural and the substantive law level.  Unfortunately, since most proceedings before, and awards rendered by, international arbitral tribunals remain unreported, much of what has been happening is neither generally known nor accessible to the legal profession at large.As a consequence, this Article reflects in large measure my personal experiences as an international arbitrator.

How does the limited reporting and transparency of arbitral proceedings and awards affect the development, dissemination, and predictability of legal norms in international arbitration?

papers.node_id: 34emorylj93!!ARTICLE: SUPPLEMENTING WRITTEN AGREEMENTS: RESTATING THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE IN TERMS OF CREDIBILITY AND RELATIVE FAULT
papers.title: ARTICLE: SUPPLEMENTING WRITTEN AGREEMENTS: RESTATING THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE IN TERMS OF CREDIBILITY AND RELATIVE FAULT
papers.abstract:
In 1928 the New York Court of Appeals stated the facts of a relatively straightforward transaction and framed an issue involving the Parol Evidence Rule as follows:
In the fall of 1923 the Laths owned a farm.  This they wished to sell.  Across the road, on land belonging to Lieutenant-Governor Lunn, they had an ice house which they might remove.  Mrs.  Mitchill looked over the land with a view to its purchase.  She found the ice house objectionable.  Thereupon "the defendants orally promised and agreed, for and in consideration of the purchase of their farm by the plaintiff, to remove the said ice house in the spring of 1924." Relying upon this promise she made a written contract to buy the property for $ 8,400, for cash and a mortgage and containing various provisions usual in such papers.  Later receiving a deed, she entered into possession and has spent considerable sums in improving the property for use as a summer residence.  The defendants have not fulfilled their promise as to the ice house and do not intend to do so.  We are not dealing, however, with their moral delinquencies.  The question before us is whether their oral agreement may be enforced in a court of equity.
Mitchill v. Lathis still referred to as "the leading collateral agreement case."Its majority and dissenting opinions,dealt with inthe discussion that follows, demonstrate that many eminent and capable judges, in accord on proper formulation of the Parol Evidence Rule, still reach opposite results in applying it.
The substantive concept underlying the Parol Evidence Rule is sometimes characterized as one of discharge-- that participants in negotiations typically intend, consciously or subliminally, to have a resulting written agreement, an "integration," evidence terms finally agreed to in discharge of those proposed, discussed, or tentatively assented to in the dickering process.The Parol Evidence Rule formulations of both Restatements, finalized almost fifty years apart,are stated in terms of discharge of prior and contemporaneous agreements through integration,leading to specified evidentiary consequences.
A procedural justification commonly advanced in support of the Parol Evidence Rule is jury control.  Unless the judge has opportunity for a threshold determination whether to exclude proffered proof of agreement not set forth in the writing for lack of relevancy because of discharge, the proof might unjustly influence an undisciplined jury in favor of its proponent, typically the "little guy," in the transaction at hand.The judge still makes the critical determination of extent of discharge manifested by integration -- the "circle of assent" manifested by the writingwithin which the alleged collateral agreement cannot be permitted to intrude.  Both Restatements categorize this determination as one of party intent, but the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, embracing the so-called modern approach advocated by Corbinand Wigmoreand largely popularized by the Supreme Court of California led by Justice Traynor,is far more receptive than its predecessor to use of extrinsic evidence for this critical purpose.
There should be little surprise that the Restatement (Second) invites full consideration by the court of evidence extrinsic to the writing before determining breadth of integration.  The Restatement (Second) parts company with the Restatement (First) and rejects the notion that an integration serves as the only competentevidence of party intent.  The writing no longer speaks for itself but is only evidence of the intended agreement.  As such, it must be viewed in full context to effectuate the parties' true intent.Once the writing is no longer the exclusive source of intended meaning, it cannot be the exclusive determinant of its own completeness.  Experience tells us that selected words of obligation are no better suited for the latter purpose than the former.
A basis premise developed in this Article is that the Restatement (Second)'s treatment of the Parol Evidence Rule suffers from an attempt to breathe recognition of the evidentiary inconclusiveness of the writing into a Restatement (First) Parol Evidence Rule construct better suited to treat the writing, wherever possible, as the exclusive manifestation of party intent.  In its rules governing determination of the intended meaning of an integration, the Restatement (Second) eschews application of a plain meaning rule to a writing unambiguous on its face, and adopts in its stead in section 201 a "relative fault" calculus to be employed irrespective of whether the writing has an ostensibly plain meaning.  In the absence of shared actual intent, section 201 focuses on what the parties knew or should have known of each others' intentions, given the totality of surrounding circumstances.  Subsections (1) and (2) of section 201 provide:
(1) Where the parties have attached the same meaning to a promise or agreement or a term thereof, it is interpreted in accordance with that meaning.
(2) Where the parties have attached different meanings to a promise or agreement or a term thereof, it is interpreted in accordance with the meaning attached by one of them if at the time the agreement was made
(a) that party did not know of any different meaning attached by the other, and the other knew the meaning attached by the first party; or
(b) that party had no reason to know of any different meaning attached by the other, and the other had reason toknow the meaning attached by the first party.
This Article argues that courts should adopt a "relative fault" approach in determining intended scope of integration and concomitant discharge.  Before concluding with a proposed reformulation of the Parol Evidence Rule designed to achieve full conceptual consistency between the intrinsically linked determinations of intended meaning and intended scope of integration,this Article illustrates, using Mitchill as backdrop, perceived shortcomings of the respective Parol Evidence Rule formulations of the two Restatements.

questions.question: Should courts admit and weigh extrinsic evidence to supplement or vary the terms of a written agreement based on the parties' relative credibility and comparative fault/knowledge, rather than presuming the writing alone is the final and exclusive expression of their intent?

What method should courts use to determine the intended scope of a written agreement (i.e., how much prior or contemporaneous negotiations are discharged by the writing): a plain-meaning/integration presumption or a contextual inquiry that considers surrounding circumstances and parties' relative knowledge?
How can the rules governing admission of extrinsic evidence be reformulated to make determinations of intended meaning and scope of integration conceptually consistent, fair, and predictable?
