papers.node_id: 88nyulrev128!!ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
papers.abstract:
Introduction: Consequential Damages and Their Disclaimer
Contract law traditionally limits recovery for consequential damages to losses foreseeable at the time of contracting. Traditional contract doctrine gauges "foreseeability" by what "may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it."Contemporary compilations of contract law equate "contemplation" with an objective standard, and thus include within the realm of foreseeability that which a reasonable person would understand to be a "natural" consequence of the breach. The Restatement (Second) of Contracts denies recovery of a loss "that the party in breach did not have reason to foresee as a probable result of the breach when the contract was made,"and defines as foreseeable a loss that follows from the breach "in the ordinary course of events," or "as a result of special circumstances … that the party in breach had reason to know."The Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.) permits buyers to recover consequential damages for any loss resulting from unavoidable "general or particular requirements and needs of which the seller at the time of contracting had reason to know."
Contemporary law-and-economics discussions of consequential damages tend to accept this default rule as a given and focus on the information-forcing qualities of the foreseeability restriction.Yet thesame literature takes as its operating assumption the proposition that contractual default rules should reflect the preferences that most commercial parties would share in similar circumstances.Failure to draft such rules will induce parties to expend resources transacting around the defaults in a way that does not alter the substance of the ultimate bargain, and may cause parties to assign the contract a lower value than if their preferred term had been available for silent incorporation into the bargain.
On this understanding, the default rules of the Restatement and the U.C.C. that permit recovery of foreseeable consequential damages make sense only if they reflect the terms to which most parties would have agreed. But most contracts literature assumes that commercial parties systematically contract out of consequential damages entirely. Commentators suggest that "consequential damage exclusions are ubiquitous" among sophisticated commercial actors, notwithstanding that the foreseeability doctrine already limits the scope of liability.Brief reflection indicates why this would be the case. Foreseeability, defined in terms of "reason to know," is a notoriously indefinite doctrine, particularly where a third-party arbiter must determine from hindsight what was foreseeable at the time of contracting. To the extent that foreseeability relates only to type of damages rather than to amount, even a party aware that its breach will cause consequential damages of a particular type, such as lost profits, could be uncertain about the extent of its exposure and thus be unable to calculate optimal investments in precautions against breach.
Moreover, the extent to which consequential damages will materialize typically lies within the control of the aggrieved party. That party controls the degree to which it will rely on the contract to make investments that might founder in the event of breach and has better information about the benefits it anticipates receiving from full performance. Full compensation for breach thus induces overinvestment in the contract in a manner that a weapon as blunt as the mitigation doctrine may not sufficiently constrain.If the aggrieved party can protect against these losses more easily than the breaching party, then rational parties would allocate the risk to the former.
But if the Restatement and U.C.C. default rules that permit recovery of foreseeable consequential damages are so inconsistent with the preferences of commercial parties that they are willing to contract around them, then it is the general default of awarding consequential damages, rather than the foreseeability limitation, that begs for explanation. Perhaps some rationale can be found in those few cases in which sophisticated commercial actors do not exclude consequential damages. Notwithstanding the claims of ubiquitous exclusion, some sophisticated commercial parties do not disclaim consequential damages. Contracts without disclaimers fall into two categories: (1) those in which the parties are silent about consequential damages and (2) those in which the parties restate the default. Silence may indicate intent to incorporate the defaults of the Restatement and the U.C.C. But some of these contracts may represent exceptions to "ubiquitous" exclusion only in a formal sense, since failure to bargain away from consequential damages may reflect the stickiness of the default rather than a preference for it.Given the low probability of breach, and judicial discretion over the award of lost profits as consequential damages, even sophisticated parties may retain the default.
The acceptance of consequential damages as a matter of contract design is clearer in a second category of non-exclusion cases, in which parties not only fail to opt out of the default, they explicitly providefor it, including lost profits. By restating the default, these parties arguably signal courts to impose liability for consequential damages even when judicial discretion might otherwise limit their recovery. The open-ended exposure created by such clauses indicates that parties who agree to them are not treating the clause as a simple option, such as a termination fee or liquidated-damage clause. Rather, because the breaching party's liability is not finally determinable at the time of breach, including an express consequential-damages clause appears to invite both the overreliance and inefficient risk allocation that excluding consequential damages purports to avoid. Nevertheless, the explicit nature of these clauses implies that some parties believe that the promise to pay consequential damages in the event of breach maximizes the value of the contract. That possibility suggests that cases in the first category - parties that fail to opt out of the default - may reflect a similar preference, though embodied in tacit rather than explicit agreement. That is, the absence of exclusion may signify not inattention or the stickiness of the default, but instead an affirmative desire to permit recovery of consequential damages in the event of breach.
In this Article, I explore the circumstances under which sophisticated parties commit to payment of lost profits as consequential damages in the event of breach. I claim that both the contracts in which parties expressly allow lost-profit recoveries and the cases that interpret the scope of what the parties "contemplated" reveal that a promise to pay consequential damages can solve a holdup problem that might otherwise frustrate mutually beneficial exchange. I infer that parties and, perhaps more controversially, courts have perceived that a commitment to pay lost profits can diminish the threat inherent in transactions that require one party to make a relationship-specific investment - an investment that, once made, cannot readily be utilized in an alternative transaction - before the other party is obligated to invest in the same transaction.In transactions with those characteristics, the investing party risks exploitation by its counterparty after the initial investment is made. I suggest that a pledge to pay consequential lost profits in the event of breach reduces the threat of holdup. As a result, in a discrete set of circumstances the promise has value in excess of its cost, including the cost otherwise inherent in assigningconsequential damages to the party less able to avoid them. While a pledge of lost profits in the event of breach is not the exclusive response to this holdup problem, it is a plausible, and perhaps superior, means of avoiding it.
Moreover, if relationship-specific investment is sufficiently salient, then it may be possible to fashion a default rule for consequential damages that is more consistent with majoritarian preferences. Salience would permit courts more accurately to distinguish between situations in which the parties had reason to allocate the risk of consequential damages to a breaching party - who had tacitly agreed to their payment - and situations in which there seems little commercial reason for parties to have adopted the default rule. Under the latter circumstances, courts attentive to the majority practice of opting out and to the negative effects of the minority default might exercise greater discretion to exclude consequential damages under the nebulous standard of foreseeability or under other restrictions on the recovery of lost profits, such as the need to demonstrate them with reasonable certainty. But recognition of the limited circumstances in which parties would allocate the risk of lost profits to the breaching party also suggests a different rule when those circumstances materialize. Indeed, such a rule lurks in the history of consequential damages in the guise of the much-maligned "tacit agreement test," which allows recovery only of consequential damages for which the breaching party has accepted liability.
In the next part of this Article, I examine the move away from the tacit agreement test and toward the "reason to know" standard for recovery of lost profits as consequential damages.In Part III, I discuss the relationship between optimal investment and holdup, and contractual mechanisms for overcoming the latter. Part IV reviews contracts in which the parties expressly assign responsibility for lost profits to the breaching party. I find that those contractssystematically allow recovery of lost profits by a party who is required to make relationship-specific investments.
In Part V, I return to the case law. Cases from New York, which has stubbornly resisted the broad "reason to know" interpretation of consequential damages in favor of the tacit agreement test, suggest that courts infer tacit agreement from contracts that are silent with respect to consequential damages only where the non-breaching party is required to make a relationship-specific investment. Of course, it is plausible that courts in "reason to know" jurisdictions arrive at similar results. They might conclude that parties had "reason to know" of consequential damages only where the transaction required unique investment. If that is the case, then the "reason to know" standard would not necessarily be less hospitable to relationship-specific investment than the tacit agreement test. I therefore examine cases from a "reason to know" jurisdiction to see whether there exists a pattern of awarding lost profits only where such investments are present.

questions.question: Whether a contractual promise to pay lost profits (consequential damages) encourages optimal relationship-specific investment by reducing the threat of post-contractual holdup.
Whether sophisticated parties deliberately include or omit liability for consequential damages (explicitly or tacitly) depending on whether the transaction requires relationship-specific investments.
Whether courts should (or do) infer that silent contracts allocate the risk of consequential damages to the breaching party when the transaction involves relationship-specific investments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016byulrev1!!ARTICLE: Mind the Gap
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mind the Gap

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing contractual interpretation from gap-filling/tacit agreement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with when adjudicators should seek the parties' intent versus impose supplemental terms: Paper A debates the doctrinal boundary between interpretation and gap‑filling by arbitrators, while Paper B analyzes the tacit‑agreement test versus the 'reason to know' foreseeability standard as modes of inferring or denying that parties accepted liability for consequential losses.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and desirability of default rules that supply contract terms or allocate risk
shared_topics.justification: Both examine whether legal defaults reflect commercial parties' preferences and when courts/arbitrators should supply terms—Paper A questions whether gap‑filling by tribunals produces appropriate default terms for omitted material provisions, and Paper B questions the default rule permitting recovery of foreseeable consequential damages and whether parties typically would opt into or out of that rule.

shared_topics.topic: the role and comparative competence of tribunals (courts vs arbitrators) in resolving incomplete-contract problems
shared_topics.justification: Both investigate which decision‑maker is best suited to supply missing terms or determine liability: Paper A surveys U.S. and international doctrine on arbitrators' powers to fill gaps relative to national courts, while Paper B studies how courts apply standards (tacit agreement vs reason to know) and the implications of those doctrines for commercial parties.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete contracting in complex, long‑term, relationship‑specific transactions and mechanisms to address holdup
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how complex, cross‑border or long‑term commercial relationships produce omitted terms and strategic problems—Paper A emphasizes that modern, global transactions increase the incidence of genuine gaps for arbitrators to address, and Paper B shows that relationship‑specific investments create holdup risks that influence whether parties tacitly or expressly accept consequential‑damage liability as a protective mechanism.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34tourolrev83!!SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and enforcement of incomplete or indefinite contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Cardozo's Sun Printing refusal to enforce a contract for lack of definite price/duration and the broader indefiniteness doctrine, while Paper B examines how courts treat silence or gaps (tacit agreement vs reason‑to‑know) when awarding consequential damages, both focusing on when judges should or should not supply missing terms.

shared_topics.topic: why parties leave contract terms open or remain silent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates the historical and commercial reasons parties in the newsprint industry left price and duration open, and Paper B interrogates the strategic or tacit reasons parties omit exclusion clauses for consequential damages, treating silence as potentially deliberate rather than accidental.

shared_topics.topic: effect of contract doctrines on commercial behavior, investments, and market outcomes (holdup and anticompetitive consequences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that Cardozo's decision increased uncertainty and may have enabled anticompetitive behavior in the paper industry, while Paper B uses law‑and‑economics to show how default rules on consequential damages affect relationship‑specific investment, holdup risk, and parties' contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal critique of contract law rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers situate doctrinal disputes in historical and institutional context — Paper A reconstructs the facts and economic background of Sun Printing to critique Cardozo's reasoning, and Paper B traces the shift from the tacit‑agreement test to the 'reason to know' standard and evaluates the costs and benefits of that evolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016byulrev1!!ARTICLE: Mind the Gap
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mind the Gap

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal gap‑filling and default terms when contracts are silent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Restatement/UCC defaults (and the tacit‑agreement test) operate when parties are silent about consequential damages, while Paper B analyzes the broader question of when and how tribunals should supply omitted material terms and fill genuine contract gaps.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation focused on parties' intent versus imposition of external standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the tacit‑agreement (intent‑oriented) approach with the objective 'reason to know' foreseeability standard for consequential damages, and Paper B explicitly distinguishes interpretation (drawing on intent, course of dealing, usage) from gap‑filling that applies community fairness and policy yardsticks.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness in long‑term/commercial relationships and its causes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how incomplete specification of remedies (consequential damages) affects relationship‑specific investment and creates holdup risks in long‑term commercial deals, while Paper B documents why complex, long‑term, and international transactions produce material gaps that necessitate gap‑filling.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of authority to supply missing terms (courts vs arbitrators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how courts have applied different standards (tacit agreement vs reason‑to‑know) in supplying or denying consequential damages, and Paper B evaluates arbitrators' gap‑filling powers relative to national courts and the implications for protecting contracting parties' interests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16tourolrev1037!!COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?
compared_to.partner_title: COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?

shared_topics.topic: courts inferring assent / tacit agreement from silence or conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the 'tacit agreement' test and how courts infer that silent contracts incorporate consequential-damages liability (or not) based on the transaction's context; Paper B examines Hill v. Gateway and ProCD, criticizing courts that infer assent to undisclosed terms from consumer conduct or silence.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/efficiency reasoning to justify doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates consequential-damages defaults within law-and-economics accounts (majoritarian preferences, transaction-costs, holdup) to explain when parties would accept or opt out of liability; Paper B critiques courts' appeals to 'common sense' grounded in neoclassical economic efficiency as a basis for enforcing terms and imputing expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules and silence affect parties' incentives to invest and contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how default liability for consequential damages influences relationship-specific investments and can mitigate or worsen holdup, producing incentives to contract around defaults; Paper B discusses how imposing or implying terms (through accept-or-return rules) changes consumer and vendor behavior by shifting disclosure costs and transactional incentives.

shared_topics.topic: standards of notice/foreseeability ('reason to know') and uncertainty in adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the 'reason to know' / foreseeability standard and its indeterminacy when courts retrospectively assess what parties contemplated; Paper B analyzes judicial standards for what a reasonable buyer should have known or inferred, showing similar concerns about uncertainty and the legitimacy of imputing knowledge or notice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: whether sophisticated parties accept or contract around statutory/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses contracting parties' choice of governing law and forum (notably the market preference for New York law) to show that sophisticated actors prefer formal default rules, while Paper B studies the ubiquity (and exceptions) of consequential-damages disclaimers to analyze when commercial parties opt out of or retain default damage rules.

shared_topics.topic: the substantive effects of jurisdictional/doctrinal variation (formalism v. contextualism), especially New York doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts New York's formalist contract interpretation with California's contextualist approach and links that contrast to parties' forum choices; Paper B contrasts New York's tacit-agreement test with the broader 'reason to know' standard and examines how those doctrinal differences affect awards of consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: how contract rules influence ex ante investment incentives and the holdup problem for relationship-specific investments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that predictable, formal rules facilitate efficient contracting and thus commercial activity, while Paper B shows that promises (or defaults) about consequential damages can be used to mitigate holdup and encourage relationship-specific investments that would otherwise be underprovided.

shared_topics.topic: using observed market behavior, industry dispute practices, and case law as evidence for designing or justifying contract default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on empirical studies of forum/choice-of-law selection and industry arbitration practices to infer which doctrinal regimes commercial parties prefer, and Paper B analyzes contract clauses and judicial decisions (including patterns across jurisdictions) to infer when parties tacitly accept or reject default damage allocations and how defaults might be calibrated.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33jlegalstud157!!ARTICLE: Decreasing-Liability Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Decreasing-Liability Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how breach-liability rules affect parties' investment incentives and holdup
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how constant liability through phased performance gives poor incentives and argues liability should decrease (e.g., by deducting past expenditures) to improve behavior across phases; Paper B studies how allowing or disclaiming consequential damages (especially lost profits) alters the incentives for relationship-specific investment and can mitigate holdup or induce overreliance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of relationship-specific or sunk expenditures in optimal contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models performance as phased spending that becomes sunk over time and recommends liability adjustments to account for those sunk costs; Paper B focuses on relationship-specific investments that are non‑transferable and argues that remedial rules (or explicit clauses) for lost profits can be justified to protect such investments.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of default legal rules versus tailored contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the positive-law default of constant liability in phased contracts and proposes a different default (decreasing liability) that improves incentives; Paper B examines the Restatement/U.C.C. default on foreseeable consequential damages versus parties' widespread contracting-out and when courts should infer tacit agreement to the default, probing when defaults reflect majoritarian preferences.

shared_topics.topic: design of damages and liability allocation to internalize prevention ability and reduce inefficiencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that deducting past expenditures from liability can better align promisor incentives across contract phases; Paper B analyzes how allocating consequential damages (or excluding them) assigns risk to the party better able to avoid the loss and thereby affects optimal precaution and investment decisions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68minnlrev117!!ARTICLE: Consideration in Exclusive and Nonexclusive Open Quantity Contracts Under the U.C.C.: a Proposal for a New System of Validation.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Consideration in Exclusive and Nonexclusive Open Quantity Contracts Under the U.C.C.: a Proposal for a New System of Validation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the Uniform Commercial Code in shaping contractual enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how U.C.C. formulations of foreseeability and consequential-damages rules affect liability and party expectations, while Paper B analyzes U.C.C. provisions (especially §§2-204 and 2-306) as the vehicle for validating otherwise indefinite open-quantity agreements.

shared_topics.topic: judicial standards for inferring parties' obligations (e.g., 'reason to know', 'tacit agreement', 'good faith')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and contrasts the 'tacit agreement' and 'reason to know' standards for awarding consequential damages, and Paper B treats the U.C.C.'s implied duty of good faith as the operative judicial standard to validate and police open-quantity commitments.

shared_topics.topic: when courts will enforce or validate open-ended/indefinite contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when courts will permit recovery for open-ended consequential lost profits (effectively enforcing an indefinite liability), and Paper B develops a framework under the Code to validate open-quantity contracts that lack definite numeric terms.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal legal doctrines and commercial practice/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the discrepancy between default legal rules on consequential damages and commercial parties' tendency to contract around them (or to tacitly accept them), while Paper B addresses the mismatch between common-law invalidation of open contracts and commercial reliance on ongoing open-ended supply commitments, arguing the Code should better reflect business practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100marqlrev997!!ARTICLE: WHO NEEDS CONTRACTS? GENERALIZED EXCHANGE WITHIN INVESTMENT ACCELERATORS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHO NEEDS CONTRACTS? GENERALIZED EXCHANGE WITHIN INVESTMENT ACCELERATORS

shared_topics.topic: the role of tacit or implicit norms as substitutes for explicit contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how MDIA mentors rely on informal norms and a 'veil of altruism' — generalized exchange — rather than formal agreements; Paper B analyzes the tacit agreement doctrine and how courts or parties treat silence or implicit commitments as allocating liability for consequential damages.

shared_topics.topic: why parties eschew explicit contractual terms and rely on informal exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates mentors' motivations (indirect benefits, reputational learning, reduced transaction costs) for not demanding pay or equity, while Paper B probes why sophisticated commercial actors sometimes retain or restate default consequential-damages rules rather than contracting them away, suggesting strategic reasons for foregoing explicit disclaimers.

shared_topics.topic: relationship-specific (or non-redeployable) investments and the risk of holdup and opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on how promises to pay lost profits can mitigate holdup when one party must make relationship-specific investments; Paper A treats mentors' time, expertise, and social capital as investments vulnerable to opportunism and analyzes how MDIA institutions try to reduce that risk without contracts.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and doctrinal design to sustain exchanges absent complete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes how MDIAs structure interactions, norms, and reputation mechanisms to promote generalized exchange and its sustainability; Paper B considers tailoring default doctrinal rules (e.g., tacit agreement vs. 'reason to know') or explicit contract clauses to permit efficient reliance and preserve transactions when formal contracting is incomplete.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres151!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions

shared_topics.topic: holdup risk from relationship-specific investments
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how transactions that require one party to make investments specific to the relationship create a risk of opportunistic exploitation (holdup), with Paper A arguing that consequential-damages commitments can mitigate holdup and Paper B situating holdup within the incomplete-contracts literature as a central problem that shapes parties' ex ante decisions.

shared_topics.topic: incentives to rely, invest, and take precautions under contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how legal rules and contract design affect parties' incentives to rely on promised performance and to make (or refrain from) precautionary or relationship-specific investments: Paper A links availability of lost-profit recovery to over- and under-investment and reliance choices, while Paper B highlights that the incomplete-contracts literature has paid insufficient attention to incentives to take precautions and invest to avoid accidental breach.

shared_topics.topic: default rules, explicit allocation of risk, and contracting-out
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how default legal rules versus explicit contractual terms shape the allocation of risk for consequential losses — Paper A analyzes the Restatement/U.C.C. foreseeability default and why parties opt out or expressly adopt consequential-damage clauses, and Paper B discusses how reliance on judicial defaults and the limits of contract specification influence transactional planning and parties' choices to contract around defaults.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling, tacit agreement, and courts' role in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address the role of courts in filling gaps when contracts are silent: Paper A contrasts the 'tacit agreement' test with the 'reason to know' foreseeability standard and shows how courts infer parties' tacit allocation of consequential damages, while Paper B emphasizes courts' informational limits and examines judicial responses to incomplete contracts and how those responses affect parties' behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2014uilllrev1795!!LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
compared_to.partner_title: LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?

shared_topics.topic: how default legal rules versus private contracting shape parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether default corporate rules (versus the flexibility of uncorporate forms) meaningfully alter how parties allocate control and constrain agency costs, while Paper B analyzes the default rule permitting recovery of foreseeable consequential damages and whether sophisticated parties contract around that default, showing how default doctrines influence ex ante investment and risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of relationship-specific investment and holdup in structuring legal remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly examines how relationship-specific investments create holdup risk and how a promise to pay consequential damages can mitigate that problem; Paper A situates similar concerns (agency costs and the need for governance structures) within the choice of business form, arguing organizational design matters for controlling post-contract opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between formal legal rules and informal relational norms (trust/tacit agreement)

papers.node_id: 100cornelllrev23!!ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
papers.title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
papers.authors: Ronald J. Gilson; Charles F. Sabel; Robert E. Scott
papers.abstract:
Contract interpretation remains the most important source of commercial litigationand the least settled, most contentious area of contemporary contract doctrine and scholarship.Framed by the battle between the titans of contract, Samuel Williston and Arthur Corbin, and continuing to the present, two polar positions have competed for dominance in contract interpretation. In a textualist regime, generalist courts cannot choose to consider context; in acontextualist regime, these courts must consider it. Thus, text or context.
Underlying this dispute are contrary assumptions about the prototypical contract each interpretive style addresses. For the nineteenth-century forerunners of the modern textualists, the key prototype was a contract for commodity futures, a bargained-for, voluntary agreement between fully informed and competent parties, embodying crossed promises, at least one of which is to be executed in the future, and establishing the idea of expectation damages derived from plausible calculations about the gains of a forgone transaction.Their twentieth-century intellectual heirs broadened the prototypical transaction to include all bespoke or state-contingent contracts in which the parties, aided by counsel, are legally sophisticated--capable of designing ex ante contracts that will put them in the best available position to respond to whatever eventuates.Because they are able to embed as much or as little of the contractual context as they wish in a written, integrated contract, legally sophisticated parties are more likely to resent than to welcome a court's efforts to supplement or circumvent their original design by its own contextual investigation. Hence, these sophisticated parties prefer textualist interpretation, as embodied in the parol evidence and plain meaning rules and the effect of integration, anti-waiver, and modification clauses.These doctrines direct courts to look to a contract's formal language and disregard claims, unless anchored in the text, that the parties intended to assign contract terms a special meaning revealed by the course of dealings or other feature of the context of their relation, or otherwise intended to supplement the formal contract by unwritten understandings and undertakings.
Contextualist interpretation, in contrast, directs courts to determine whether extrinsic evidence of the circumstances surrounding the contract or its performance improves understanding of what parties intended regardless of the contractual text. For contextualists, the prototypical contractual transaction is one in which one or both parties are, or for that contract choose to be, legally unsophisticated: unable or unwilling to incur the expense to express their undertakings in contract language, and therefore reliant on the equitable judgments of courts in case of disputes. Contextualists argue that the court's untrammeled authority to consider context is important in two core prototypical settings. The first is the mass-market, standardized contract between sophisticated sellers and unsophisticated consumers, who do not or cannot bargain over contractual terms. Extending the court's inquiry beyond the contract's four corners is necessary to prevent such necessarily passive parties from exploitation through adhesion to formal contract terms that do not reflect their real intentions.
The second core contextualist prototype involves commercial rather than consumer contracting. As stressed by Karl Llewellyn and partially reflected in the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.), many commercial parties do business in a deeply nuanced world where formal and informal understandings mix in a melange of explicit terms and underlying practice whose joint application to the particular contract can be illuminated by the parties' course of dealings.In this setting parties who are sophisticated about their business choose to be legally unsophisticated in the sense of avoiding ex ante design: the stakes in any given transaction are generally insufficient to justify bespoke contracting aided by legal counsel. Instead, the parties prefer to entrust adjudication, including determination of the details of the contractual context, to generalist courts. For the contextualist, willfully restricting a court's access to the trove of information bearing on the parties' real relationship degrades judicial interpretation and frustrates these parties' efforts to govern their transactions efficiently.
And so the debate has continued: either the parties are empowered to write their contracts to create desired incentives and predictable results without courts later assessing whether the words mean what they say at the instance of a disappointed party, or the courts are presumed to have been delegated the task of assessing the parties' real intentions in light of relevant facts that are not in the contract's text. Viewed in this way, the debate is not about the stark choice between text or context but rather about who decides the appropriate mix of text and context to use in resolving a dispute over the meaning of the parties' contractual rights and obligations. The problem, however, is that the artificially narrow focus over which of these class prototypes should apply universally has erroneously framed the choice of the best decision maker as either the parties themselves exercising their freedom to contract as they please or a common law court protecting vulnerable parties from erroneously imposed contractual obligations. This is a false choice and thus the debate is inconclusive. In fact, the range of options for allocating decision rights in the world inhabited both by parties designing their contracts and generalist courts interpreting them is much more diverse and variegated - more highly contextualized as it were - than the assumption that the law must choose between ex ante party autonomy and ex post adjudication. Properly conceived, the mix of text and context in the particular case is best chosen by a wide range of interpretive regimes (both public and private)that function as complements to common law adjudication rather than as antagonists.
Our goal in this Article, therefore, is to shift the focus of discussion from the potential generalization of (competing) contractual prototypes to what we call the design space for contracting: various features in the transactional setting that dispose contracting parties to choose a particular regime and a complementary form of adjudication to govern their relation, rather than another. More precisely, we present a typology of these relations sufficiently rich to capture the breadth of current contractual experience but also sufficiently parsimonious to serve as the basis for an understanding of the central relationshipbetween the factors that shape the design of any given contract and the role of courts in interpreting that design.
The starting point of our analysis is the recognition that how contracting parties deal with interpretation issues in designing their contracts, and how courts optimally respond to the parties' efforts, depends on two critical characteristics of the particular contracting environment. The first is the level of uncertainty- whether commercial practices are stable and predictable, or disrupted by unforeseeable changes in technical possibilities and market conditions. The second is the scope, thickness, or scale of the market - whether there are many traders or few engaged in a particular class of transaction using similar contracting strategies.All else equal, the higher the level of uncertainty, the more difficult it is for parties to write and courts to interpret complete, state-contingent contracts. Rather, when the level of uncertainty is high, collaborating parties develop interpretive mechanisms based on rich and regular exchange of information on a project's progress that allow each party to ascertain the other's capacity jointly to define and produce a product. All else equal, the greater the number of traders engaged in a transaction, the more likely that the interpretive regime - terms adapted to current need and a mechanism for adjusting terms as needs change - will be provided by a collective entity, such as a trade association, that can provide to a court the necessary context for interpretation.
The interplay of these two forces - uncertainty and scale - draws attention to new forms of contracting among legally sophisticated parties unanticipated in earlier discussions of textualist prototypes, andhelps clarify the (often overwhelming) institutional demands that contextualist prototypes place on generalist courts. Most of the commercial contracting practices that have evolved in response to varying levels of uncertainty and scale do not map onto any of the traditional prototypes that have been the foundation of the current disputes between textualists and contextualists.Thus, for example, the design of sophisticated information-exchange regimes to cope with high levels of uncertainty, where parties explore the capacities of their counterparts and the viability of joint projects, in effect abandons the probabilistic world at the foundation of the executory contract and its regime of expectation damages. Here collaboration becomes the precondition for determining the probabilities of success, and for this reason expectation of future gain cannot be the measure of breaches of the obligation to collaborate.
The design space for contracting marked out by increasing levels of uncertainty and market thickness highlights new forms of legally sophisticated contracting, but it also recasts the contextualist prototypes as special cases that demand novel institutional responses. Placed in our typology, mass-market contracts with consumers - one of the two traditional prototypes involving legally unsophisticated parties - stands as a special case of contracting in thick markets under low uncertainty. While large and well-endowed sellers either have no need to cooperate with others or can collude with their peers when they do, consumers are fragmented and infrequent buyers of many goods, and must resolve nearly insurmountable collective action problems to secure economies of scale in contracting. Whatever protection the state wishes to provide these isolated and legally unsophisticated parties must occur, therefore, at the initial stage in the form of interpretive limits on the design of consumer contracts. The lessons of scale that have motivated commercial parties to create specialized interpretive regimes argue for a similar response to the regulation of consumer contracts: agencies and courts working in tandem can best assess the fairness and efficiency of non-negotiated contract terms.
Similarly, the second prototype of legally unsophisticated parties - smaller firms such as machine shops supplying numerous firms in various industries with parts produced using the same set of flexible machines - is in our typology a special case that straddles two categories. On the one hand, these sellers engage in repeated dealings in fairly thick markets: the parts are made by the same processes, often tosimilar tolerances, even if the uses vary greatly. But transactions of the same type with the same kind of party are too infrequent and irregular as to warrant investments in creating and updating an industry-wide code with precise contract terms. On the other hand, no single transaction or set of transactions with a single buyer is large enough to warrant investment in legal sophistication and an elaborate, bespoke contract. Hence, legally unsophisticated commercial parties in this betwixt and between situation use standard-form documents; they typically elect to leave their agreements unintegrated and to ignore conflicts between forms proffered by each.The result is an interpretive default that delegates to courts the decision on how best to flesh out unwritten understandings on a case-by-case basis.
But there is virtually no evidence that courts, even those operating under the U.C.C.'s invitation to broadly examine context, actually undertake such empirical investigations, and hence little reason to imagine they could succeed if they did.Long-term, reciprocal relations always reflect the idiosyncrasies of the histories of each party with the others, and these idiosyncrasies prevent the community's practice from settling into a determinate rule.Thus, even if generalist courts were better equipped for empirical investigation than they normally are, there will typically be no custom-based, context-embedded rule for them to discover.Nonetheless, under certain circumstances - most often when judges and parties share a common background, and meet in the resolution of broadly similar cases over many years - courts historically, and in special cases today, have developedexpertise in particular domains of commerce, and by entering the parties' epistemic community can create an interpretive regime that effectively accommodates ex post review of their practices.
The only one of the traditional prototypes that does, in contrast, fit securely in our typology concerns commercial transactions in thin markets at medium levels of uncertainty. In this case, legally sophisticated parties act in conformity with textualist expectations: they specify ex ante, in bespoke contracts, the mix of text and context a generalist court should apply in its after-the-fact determination of their respective obligations, and they rely on adherence to their instructions.But increase the level of uncertainty and the contract becomes an interpretive framework that limits the court to sanctioning defections from broad, mutual commitments to collaborate.Decrease, perhaps only slightly, the level of uncertainty, and increase the number of transactors, and the contract becomes a collection of precise terms, defined and frequently updated by a trade association, and disputes arising under it are likely to be resolved by a specialized, arbitral body.
More generally, our typology of the different interpretive regimes that choose between text and context not only strips the traditional contractual prototypes of general significance, but shows that generalist courts are, and under current conditions should be, less central to adjudication of contract disputes than assumed by both sides in the ongoing debate. Our analysis strongly suggests that courts need to acknowledge in doctrine, and contract scholars must acknowledge in theory, what commercial parties have long recognized in practice: generalist judges applying general, mandatory legal doctrine cannot effectively determine the environments in which context matters.The evolution of the history of contract doctrine shows that the common law has lost the general capacity to successfully combine text and context through the adjudicatory process as a substitute for a regime of contract design.In contrast to early courts of equity, where the courts were close to the actors in a largely homogenous economy, generalist courts today are removed from the enormously varied commercial contracting context in modern economies and therefore critically impaired in their ability to divine how and when parties would braid both text and context in their contracts. Given the variety of situations, the limits of the generalist judiciary, and the doctrinallogjam courts have created, it is perhaps unsurprising that sophisticated commercial parties turn to specialized interpretive regimes to accommodate text and context and to resolve their disputes reliably at acceptable cost.
The Article proceeds as follows. In Part I we survey in more detail the existing landscape of contract interpretation doctrine and scholarship. Here we show how and why the current debate came to be framed as a contest among proponents of contrasting contractual prototypes, each represented as of nearly universal significance. We argue that the focus on the traditional text versus context prototypes masks the way that differences in levels of uncertainty and scale shape contemporary contracting practices.
In Part II we address history to show that generalist courts in pre-industrial England, in contrast to today, were capable of supporting the two contract functions at odds in current doctrinal disputes - adhering to ex ante rules and updating those rules over time by combining text with context - especially when the two functions were divided between law and equity. With the merger of law and equity and the embodiment of the merged doctrine in the prototype of the executory contract, the difficulty of such "unified" and universally applicable modes of interpretation became apparent.
In Part III we focus on the critical roles of uncertainty and scale in determining how legally sophisticated parties, both individually and collectively, create interpretive regimes that determine the mix of text and context in commercial contracting. Here we generally endorse the textualist claim that these commercial parties are better able than generalist courts to decide how best to take context into account in different environments, but we qualify that assertion by specifying the various situations in which the resulting interpretive arrangement deviates from the classical image of the bargained-for, state-contingent contract.
Finally, in Part IV we focus on the unique issues raised when legally unsophisticated parties contract. With respect to consumer transactions, we address the analytic and policy confusion that has resulted from courts deploying general contract principles to address the problems of consumer protection. We argue that deterring rent-seeking and exploitation requires an interpretive regime such as that in the European Union that authorizes protection of certain interests in particular domains and prohibits practices antithetical to those interests and an orderly market generally. With respect to legally unsophisticated commercial parties, we then show that the core problem is the assumption that generalist courts are capable of both divining underlyingcustom and practice and applying that knowledge to the case at hand. We argue that the institutional knowledge that developed in traditional courts of equity can be replicated if courts can acquire an expertise in the relevant transactional prototypes. However, legally unsophisticated commercial parties who rely on generalist courts to unpack context are subject to a measurably higher risk of judicial error: these parties inevitably trade off lower front-end contracting costs for higher enforcement costs on the back end.

questions.question: How do levels of uncertainty and the scale (thickness) of a market determine whether contracting parties should set the mix of textual versus contextual rules themselves ex ante or instead delegate interpretive authority to adjudicators ex post?

Under what transactional conditions do specialized private or public interpretive regimes (e.g., trade associations, arbitral bodies, agencies) produce more efficient, predictable, or lower-cost contract interpretation than generalist courts?
What forms of interpretive regime best protect legally unsophisticated parties in mass-market or small-firm transactions while minimizing enforcement costs, exploitation, and rent-seeking?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71indlj45!!ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Defense of Judicial Reconstruction of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: who should decide the appropriate mix of text and context in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central debate as a question of which decision maker (parties via contract design, generalist courts, or specialized/private regimes) should choose the mix of textual and contextual interpretation; Paper B likewise grapples with whether judges may or should override bargained terms (reconstruct contracts) when terms no longer serve their intended purpose, i.e., who gets the authority to reshape contractual meaning after formation.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between interpretation and judicial reconstruction of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts should be limited to interpreting written terms versus allowed to supplement or override them based on context and contractual design choices; Paper B probes the line between ordinary interpretive rules (including good-faith interpretation) and more intrusive judicial reconstruction (e.g., under impracticability, mistake, or penalty doctrines), arguing for principled limits on reconstruction.

shared_topics.topic: doctrines that excuse, modify, or police contractual terms in response to unexpected events
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on specific doctrines (impracticability, mistake, good faith, penalties, forfeiture) that permit courts to excuse or modify terms when events frustrate contractual expectations; Paper A likewise examines how high uncertainty and unforeseen contingencies undermine expectation-based remedies and create situations where courts or alternative regimes must fill gaps or reframe remedies (including when expectation damages are inappropriate).

shared_topics.topic: institutional competence and the role of specialized interpretive regimes versus generalist courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts are often institutionaly ill-suited to combine text and context and shows why contracting parties create specialized or private interpretive regimes; Paper B engages the competence of judges and juries to determine whether parties anticipated events and whether judicial reconstruction will produce better or fairer outcomes, weighing judicial capacity and incentives.

shared_topics.topic: economic and fairness justifications for limiting freedom of contract through judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses efficiency and protection rationales (especially for unsophisticated parties and thick markets) for limiting pure textualist enforcement and for deploying regulatory or collective interpretive responses; Paper B explicitly defends judicial modification doctrines against freedom-of-contract and economic-efficiency objections, invoking fairness (unselfish performance, loss alignment) and possible efficiency benefits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: the text-versus-context debate (formalism vs contextualism) in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central doctrinal dispute between textualist and contextualist approaches, arguing parties and institutions choose mixes of text and context; Paper B critiques recent 'Neoformalist' calls for sharper formal rules and defends the continued need for contextual inquiry in many settings.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretive role and structure of the Uniform Commercial Code (Article 2)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the U.C.C. as emblematic of contextualist practices and discusses how it invites courts to consider commercial context; Paper B focuses on Article 2's open, standards-based structure and analyzes the consequences of legislatively pushing the U.C.C. toward greater formalism.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and weight of trade usages, course of dealing/performance, and other extrinsic evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how doctrines like parol evidence, trade usage, and course of dealings fit into parties' contract-design choices and when courts should use them; Paper B discusses Neoformalists' proposals to curtail trade-usage and course-of-performance evidence and the potential costs of doing so in practice.

shared_topics.topic: how contracting environment (form contracts, market scale, and uncertainty) should determine interpretive regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a typology showing that uncertainty and market thickness drive whether parties prefer bespoke textual rules, industry codes, or court-based context inquiry; Paper B emphasizes the 'real world' predominance of form contracts and asks how increased formalism would operate in those varied commercial environments.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical grounding and attention to real-world practices when proposing doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its typology and institutional recommendations in historical and commercial practice and critiques assumptions about courts' empirical capacities; Paper B argues that empirical evidence is required before adopting Neoformalist reforms and warns that theoretical proposals may misfit actual business practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: how uncertainty shapes contract form and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that heightened uncertainty in innovation drives parties to create 'braided' contracts that mix formal governance and informal performance terms; Paper B identifies uncertainty as a primary axis determining whether parties write bespoke text, rely on interpretive regimes, or build information-exchange mechanisms to guide adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how formal legal enforcement 'crowds out' informal governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages explicitly with the crowding‑out literature and proposes braiding as a way to endogenize trust and avoid displacement of informal sanctions, while Paper B situates that tension within the text-versus-context debate, showing how contractual design and institutional choice affect when court intervention will undermine private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: the role of structured information‑exchange regimes in creating trust and enabling collaboration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on formalized information-exchange obligations as the mechanism that 'braids' formal and informal enforcement and builds knowledge of counterparties' capabilities; Paper B likewise highlights sophisticated information‑exchange and ongoing disclosure regimes as interpretive devices parties adopt under high uncertainty so courts or specialists can understand their collaborative intent.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of generalist courts and the turn to low‑powered enforcement or specialized interpretive regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents courts' emerging use of 'low‑powered' remedies (e.g., duty to negotiate) and warns against over‑formalization that would undermine braiding; Paper B argues generalist judges lack the institutional knowledge to mix text and context effectively and shows why contracting parties instead create specialized adjudicative or collective interpretive regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design allocates decision and interpretive rights between parties and adjudicators
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties deliberately design formal governance (timed disclosures, governance processes) to allocate decision rights and make informal enforcement feasible; Paper B develops a 'design space' framework explaining how parties choose the mix of text and context and delegate interpretive authority (ex ante to parties or ex post to courts/specialists) depending on uncertainty and market scale.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18geomasonlrev245!!ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of the UCC and other uniform commercial statutes for governing novel commercial transactions (software, electronic payments, paperless transfers)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents repeated legislative efforts (revisions to Article 9, Article 4A, UETA, UCITA, and the interplay with CISG) and questions whether the UCC's structure can accommodate new transaction forms; Paper B cites the U.C.C. as a focal point in the text-versus-context debate and examines how codified commercial doctrine shapes parties' ability to design contracts in changed transactional environments.

shared_topics.topic: whether bright-line textual rules or flexible contextual standards better reduce complexity and produce predictable outcomes in commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the policy debate as one between proponents of bright-line rules and advocates for standards, arguing that standards can sometimes reduce complexity and proposing 'minimalist' simplification strategies; Paper B analyzes the text-versus-context interpretive divide (textualist vs contextualist), showing how different mixes of rules and standards affect dispute resolution and parties' contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: how law should respond to technological change and high uncertainty in markets (legislative codification versus market/common-law evolution or private ordering)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys legislative reactions to technological developments (e.g., payment systems, electronic transactions, software contracting) and contrasts statutory intervention with leaving issues to common law; Paper B studies contracting under high uncertainty and argues that parties develop information-sharing, private or collective interpretive regimes when ex ante drafting is infeasible, raising similar questions about the appropriate legal response to novel, uncertain transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the allocation of interpretive and lawmaking authority among legislatures, courts, agencies, and private entities (specialized regimes vs generalist courts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates legislative initiatives (ULC, ALI, statutes) as tools to simplify or preempt divergent common-law development, while Paper B examines who—parties, courts, specialized bodies, trade associations, or agencies—should choose the appropriate mix of text and context and argues for complementary specialized interpretive regimes rather than reliance on generalist courts alone.

shared_topics.topic: regulation and interpretive protection for unsophisticated parties and controversies over statutes that affect consumers (e.g., UCITA)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts consumer and governmental backlash against UCITA and concerns about statutes that disadvantage consumers in software and electronic transactions; Paper B separately addresses mass-market, standardized consumer contracts as a core contextualist prototype, arguing that interpretive limits and agency/court oversight are required to protect legally unsophisticated parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103columlrev1641!!ARTICLE:A THEORY OF SELF-ENFORCING INDEFINITE AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A THEORY OF SELF-ENFORCING INDEFINITE AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: when courts should enforce incomplete or indefinite agreements versus leaving disputes to private enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the indefiniteness doctrine and argues that courts' refusal to enforce deliberately incomplete agreements can be normatively justified because parties often rely on reciprocal self-enforcement; Paper B analyzes the limits of generalist courts and argues that the appropriate mix of judicial (textualist/contextualist) intervention depends on contractual design and institutional context.

shared_topics.topic: why parties deliberately leave terms unspecified (deliberate incompleteness) and rely on self‑enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory that parties intentionally write indefinite agreements to exploit reciprocity and avoid legal enforcement, while Paper B explains that parties may choose not to specify terms ex ante because uncertainty, transaction costs, or market scale make bespoke specification inefficient and they instead design interpretive regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how transactional environment features (uncertainty, market thickness, repeated interaction) determine contract design and enforcement mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers factors like one‑shot transactions, repeated dealings, and experimental evidence on reciprocity to explain when self‑enforcement works, and Paper B offers a typology where uncertainty and market thickness drive whether parties use precise text, contextual regimes, or collective interpretive institutions.

shared_topics.topic: use of contracts and informal agreements as screening, information‑exchange, or signaling devices to select and coordinate partners
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes 'comfort agreements' as screening tools to reveal reciprocity preferences and select cooperative partners, while Paper B discusses information‑exchange regimes, collective codes, and other design features parties use to coordinate expectations and provide context for interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of legal doctrines and adjudicatory regimes on private contracting behavior (including crowding out or displacement of private mechanisms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that imposing legal liability can crowd out reciprocal self‑enforcement and worsen incentives, and Paper B shows how textualist/contextualist doctrines and the limits of generalist courts shape parties' incentives to develop private, specialized interpretive regimes instead of relying on ex post judicial supplementation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44ambuslj639!!ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts

shared_topics.topic: limits of generalist courts (adjudication capacity) in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that generalist courts lack the institutional knowledge and empirical capacity to combine text and context across diverse commercial environments and so commercial parties increasingly rely on specialized regimes; Paper B documents pervasive judicial inconsistency in awarding remedies for alternative-performance contracts and analyzes how adjudication difficulties have prevented adoption of a superior remedial rule.

shared_topics.topic: how explicit contract design (clauses and alternative-performance terms) should govern post‑breach outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties use drafting tools (integration, anti‑waiver, modification clauses and bespoke regimes) to specify the mix of text and context courts should apply, while Paper B examines contracts that explicitly grant the promisor a choice of X or Y and asks how those drafting choices should determine the proper remedy when the promisor breaches.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of information, uncertainty, and parties' sophistication on optimal interpretive and remedial regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a typology showing how market uncertainty, scale, and legal sophistication shape whether parties favor textualist or contextualist interpretive regimes, and Paper B studies informational asymmetries and strategic incentives that make certain remedial rules (including the one the authors propose) more or less robust in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of expectation damages and alternative remedial doctrines (specific performance, option‑theoretic approaches) for nonstandard contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights cases (e.g., collaborative, high‑uncertainty transactions) where expectation damages and standard measures fail and the court's role should differ, while Paper B critiques conventional compensatory damages in alternative‑performance contracts, considers option‑theoretic perspectives, and proposes using the mode of performance that would be chosen under specific performance to compute damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69alalrev469!!ARTICLE: THE INTERPRETATION OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INTERPRETATION OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY

shared_topics.topic: whether sophisticated commercial parties prefer textualist (integration/merger) interpretation rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests this claim by analyzing 1,521 SEC-disclosed commercial contracts and finds a clear majority include textualist 'merger' clauses; Paper B develops the theoretical claim that legally sophisticated parties often (though not always) prefer textualist regimes and explains the conditions that make that preference sensible.

shared_topics.topic: use of specific contractual devices (merger/integration, no-oral-modification, notices, anti-waiver) to lock in interpretive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A measures the prevalence of merger clauses and shows statistical correlation between merger clauses and other textualist devices (no-oral-modification, notices), while Paper B analyzes how such clauses function as part of contract design to instruct courts and constrain ex post contextual inquiry.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive authority between parties' contract design and courts (generalist vs specialized adjudication)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications from observed clause choices about how interpretation rules should treat party autonomy, and Paper B argues at length that the mix of text and context is a matter of contract design, that generalist courts are often ill-equipped to supply context, and that parties or specialized regimes may better provide interpretive rules.

shared_topics.topic: empirical evidence versus doctrinal/theoretical claims about interpretation and how that should inform contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A supplies empirical evidence about what sophisticated parties actually write into contracts and uses those findings to inform normative debate, while Paper B supplies a doctrinal and institutional theory (uncertainty and market thickness) about when various interpretive doctrines make sense and recommends doctrinal and institutional responses accordingly.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2012uilllrev89!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S CONSTITUTIVE CORE: SOLVING PROBLEMS BY MAKING DEALS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT'S CONSTITUTIVE CORE: SOLVING PROBLEMS BY MAKING DEALS

shared_topics.topic: limits of generalist courts in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the institutional limits of judicial adjudication: Paper A argues that generalist courts lack the epistemic capacity to combine text and context across varied commercial settings and thus cannot reliably determine when context matters, while Paper B treats courts as limited problem-solving actors that implement parties' solutions rather than create them, stressing the constraints of adjudication as an institutional means of resolving contractual problems.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive or decision rights between parties and courts (contract design vs adjudication)
shared_topics.justification: Both works focus on who should choose the mix of textual and contextual rules — Paper A frames this as an allocation problem in contract design (parties choosing interpretive regimes vs courts imposing context), and Paper B explains contract law as enabling parties to structure solutions and examines when the law (courts) should step in to implement or enforce those privately designed solutions.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as problem‑solving devices to enable cooperation under uncertainty and scale
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat contracting as a mechanism for coordinating action: Paper B develops a general problem‑solving account of why deals matter, and Paper A analyzes how different levels of uncertainty and market thickness produce distinct contracting practices and interpretive regimes that facilitate collaborative problem solving (e.g., information‑exchange regimes, trade association codes).

shared_topics.topic: role of party sophistication, trust, and need for legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both address how characteristics of parties shape reliance on private ordering versus legal protection: Paper A distinguishes legally sophisticated and unsophisticated actors (and the consequences for textualist versus contextualist regimes), while Paper B emphasizes how preexisting common objectives and mutual trust reduce the role of law, and lack of trust or divergent objectives makes contract law necessary to solve coordination problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between ex‑ante contract design and ex‑post adjudication as modes of governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes parties' choice to enforce literal legal entitlements (lawful opportunism) versus preserving exchange relationships after a disturbance, framing it as a governance choice in Williamson's hybrid domain; Paper B develops a 'design space' showing when parties should decide the mix of text and context ex ante (through contract design or specialized regimes) versus delegate meaning‑making to courts ex post.

shared_topics.topic: how transaction costs, uncertainty, and market scale shape contracting and enforcement incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A locates lawful opportunism at a transaction‑cost tipping point where disturbances are highly consequential and literal enforcement becomes attractive; Paper B shows that levels of uncertainty and the thickness of the market determine whether parties write bespoke state‑contingent contracts, rely on collective codes, or accept courts' contextual inquiry.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of party characteristics (legal sophistication, sense of entitlement) on choosing literal enforcement versus cooperative responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports empirically that a party's sense of entitlement predicts propensity to press legal entitlements (lawful opportunism) rather than cooperate; Paper B distinguishes legally sophisticated and unsophisticated parties and explains how those traits drive preferences for textualist (literal enforcement) versus contextualist interpretive regimes.

shared_topics.topic: institutional responses to mitigate opportunism and interpretive costs (specialized regimes, regulatory limits, organizational design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for doctrinal and policy measures to reduce the transaction costs and harms of lawful opportunism, while Paper B catalogues institutional solutions—trade associations, specialized arbitral bodies, agencies, and consumer‑protection regimes—that parties and policymakers deploy to limit exploitative literal enforcement and improve interpretive outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36houslrev1!!ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law developed for sales of physical goods poorly fits transactions in digital information, licenses, and services and calls for retailored rules (e.g., Article 2B). shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates how applying goods-based categories (title, risk-of-loss) to information transactions produces irrelevant or incoherent results. Paper B critiques the dominant textualist/contextualist prototypes rooted in the executory-goods model and shows they fail to capture contemporary contracts marked by collaboration, uncertainty, or standard-form trade practices.

shared_topics.topic: who decides the mix of text and context: party autonomy versus judicial/regulatory intervention (including consumer protection)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the tension between longstanding freedom-of-contract principles and regulatory projects (UCC revisions, EU Directive, FTC) prompted by electronic markets. Paper B analyzes that tension through the textualist/contextualist debate, distinguishing legally sophisticated parties who prefer ex ante design from unsophisticated/consumer cases that may require courts or agencies to limit contractual design.

shared_topics.topic: the need for specialized institutional or private interpretive regimes instead of reliance on generalist courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A points to legislative and regulatory initiatives (UCC Article 2B, EU and FTC projects) as institutional adaptations for information transactions. Paper B documents how market actors create trade associations, arbitration bodies, or other specialized interpretive regimes because generalist courts lack the institutional capacity to combine text and context across varied commercial settings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44ambuslj639!!ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how parties' legal sophistication and contract design should determine courts' interpretive and remedial role
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a typology showing how legally sophisticated versus unsophisticated parties choose different contract designs and interpretive regimes (textualist vs contextualist) and argues that party design often should displace generalist judicial inquiry; Paper B examines contracts in which parties have explicitly allocated alternative modes of performance or termination rights and asks whether courts should enforce those ex ante allocations or substitute their own remedial judgments.
