papers.node_id: 68depaullrev1!!ARTICLE: THE COURSE OF PERFORMANCE DOCTRINE IN COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE COURSE OF PERFORMANCE DOCTRINE IN COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
papers.abstract:
The course of performance doctrine - under which a contract can be modified by the post-contractual conduct of the parties- is a basic building block of U.S. contract law.The desirability of the doctrine, however, has been a source of intense theoretical debate and controversy among legal scholars.The central theoretical argument that proponents of the doctrine present is that its application reflects the actual intention of the parties.Interestingly enough, the major theoretical argument presented by opponents of the doctrine is quite the opposite: the doctrine stands contrary to the intention of the parties.
While the theoretical debate over the course of performance doctrine is profound, extensive, and ongoing, there are no systematic empirical studies aimed at directly exposing the parties' true intention about the doctrine. Specifically, there are no studies concentrating on the frequency with which anti-course of performance clauses, which aim to prevent the application of the doctrine, are included by the parties in real-world contracts. The study contained in this Article aims to fill this research void.
Focusing on the preferences of sophisticated parties to commercial contracts, this Article analyzes 1,550 commercial contracts disclosed to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The results of the study reveal that the majority of contracts (80.06%) include an anti-course of performance clause, known as a "no-oral-modificationclause" (NOM clause).This clause stipulates that all modifications of the contract be made only in writing. The results also indicate that NOM clauses are not mere boilerplates that are inadvertently added to the contracts. Particularly, the study found a significant statistical association between the existence of a NOM clause and the existence of other related clauses - such as anti-waiver, anti-assignment, and notices clauses - which require the post-contractual actions of the parties to be made only in writing.
This Article is structured as follows: Parts I and II will provide context by briefly reviewing the course of performance doctrine and the context underlining the theoretical debate over the desirability of the doctrine. Part III will present the empirical test of this study. It will review the data and discuss the methodology used for empirically testing the frequency with which a NOM clause is included in commercial contracts between sophisticated parties. It will also examine the statistical association between the NOM clause and related clauses. Part IV will discuss the normative implications of the empirical results.

questions.question: How often do sophisticated commercial contracting parties include clauses that require any contract modifications or waivers to be made in writing (thereby excluding post-contractual oral modifications)?

Do clauses requiring written modifications tend to co-occur with other related contractual provisions (e.g., anti-waiver, anti-assignment, notice requirements), indicating that such clauses are deliberately chosen rather than inert boilerplate?

papers.node_id: 81nyulrev487!!ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
papers.abstract:
The common law of contracts has always paid lip service to, but never fully embraced, the concept of freedom of contract. By contrast, the general thrust of many contemporary economic analyses of contract law is towards promoting a brand of contract law that provides almost complete freedom of contract to sophisticated commercial actors.Scholars working in this tradition generally take the view that contract law should consist almost exclusively of "default" rules rather than "mandatory" or "immutable" rules,terms of art that refer to the distinction between rules that can and cannot be ousted by agreement of the parties.The rules that provide the basic structure of the contracting game by discouraging fraud and duress are usually presumed to be immune from scrutiny by proponents of the freedomof contract paradigm.But even those rules no longer appear to be entirely safe.
The laissez-faire approach to contract law has recently been taken to the ultimate extreme with an attack upon the rules governing the scope of freedom of contract itself. Prominent law and economics scholars have argued that contracting parties should be free to determine whether or not the courts give effect to subsequent attempts to modify their agreements.In other words, it has been argued that the rules concerning the enforceability of contract modifications should be default rather than mandatory rules.
The most straightforward way to implement this recommendation would be to provide for the enforcement of anti-modification clauses, meaning contractual provisions that purport to prohibit enforcement of modifications. Interestingly, there does not appear to be a single reported case in which an English or American court has been asked to enforce an anti-modification clause contained in a bilateral agreement.However, there are a number of cases in which courts have been called upon to enforce clauses that purport to regulate the form of contract modifications by prohibiting oral modifications.In thosecases, Anglo-American courts have established a general principle that any contractual provision that purports to limit the enforceability of a subsequent modification is unenforceable.This feature of Anglo-American law has been characterized as an inefficient mandatory rule.
However, it is misleading to focus exclusively upon the question of whether or not anti-modification clauses are enforceable because there may be other devices that can be used to forestall contract modifications ("anti-modification devices"). Although legal academics often ignore this fact, even moderately sophisticated commercial actors routinely and strategically tap the benefits of an array of legal principles that lie outside the domain of "contract law" as it is conventionally understood in order to avoid inconvenient legal norms.Forinstance, multi-party contracts can be used to create a normative framework for subsequent bilateral contracting that differs significantly from the default legal framework.Several professional sports leagues have exploited this fact by drafting collective agreements that restrict the ability of individual athletes and teams to renegotiate bilateral player contracts governed by the collective agreement.
Contracting parties can also exploit the tremendous degree of flexibility offered by the modern law of business organizations (corporations, trusts, partnerships, etc.). This allows them to filter their contractual rights and duties through legal entities whose internal governing norms override the effects of external norms imposed by contract law.A significant portion of the Article is devoted to defending the proposition that, contrary to popular belief, Anglo-American law permits contracting parties to use a type of anti-modification device that exploits principles of trust law to effectively override the prohibition upon enforcement of anti-modification clauses. For convenience, I will refer to the device as the "representative trustee technique."
The essence of the representative trustee technique is that it raises the cost of modifying a contract by providing that, in the event of modification, one of the principal parties to the contract will become subject to costly obligations to a large number of other parties.Using a single third party is widely recognized to be a flawed approach, because the third party has an incentive to release the principal parties from their obligations in exchange for a share of thepotential benefits from modification.The possibility of using multiple third parties and thereby increasing the costs of negotiating such a release has also been discussed,but the transaction costs of implementing such a scheme will often be prohibitive.Finally, in an interesting paper Charles Knoeber has suggested that a particular type of agreement involving multiple third parties, namely a most favored nation ("MFN") agreement, can be and is used as an anti-modification device.However, as will be discussed at greater length below, MFN clauses do not necessarily preclude contract modifications.Furthermore, they impose more substantial restrictions upon a firm's future dealings than does a simple anti-modification device. For both these reasons MFN clauses do not seem like particularly attractive anti-modification devices. The representative trustee technique appears likely to be substantially more effective and less costly than any of these other anti-modification devices.
The existence of an (apparently) enforceable yet unused method of discouraging contract modifications casts doubt upon claims that there is significant pent-up demand for enforceable anti-modification clauses. Alternatively, it suggests that any such demand can be satisfied without altering the legal treatment of anti-modification clauses. Either way, the principal normative implication of this analysis is that there is little need to remove the current limitations on parties' freedom to contract over the scope of freedom of contract itself.
This Article is organized as follows. Part I describes the reasons why actors may be interested in adopting enforceable anti-modification clauses. Part II discusses a range of factors that might limit the demand for enforceable anti-modification clauses. Part III briefly summarizes the ambiguous state of the available evidence concerning the demand for enforceable anti-modification clauses and discusses the way in which an alternative anti-modification device might be used to estimate that demand. Part IV describes the representative trustee technique and its potential ability to serve as an anti-modification device. It begins by outlining the technique, then discusses potential legal objections to its enforcement, and then finally outlines its advantages over other potential anti-modification devices that have been discussed in the literature. In light of this discussion, Part V argues that it is worth exploring the question why there is no evidence of contracting parties making use of the representative trustee technique as an anti-modification device. One step in this direction is to consider the possibility that contracting parties are simply ignorant of the representative trustee technique's potential. This Part, however, argues that widely used financial contracts incorporate the key elements of the representative trustee technique, thus casting doubt on claims that either ignorance or lack of ingenuity can explain the technique's apparent disuse. This Part concludes by arguing that the most plausible explanation for the representative trustee technique's lack of popularity is the fact that only a negligible number of contracting parties would actually derive any significant benefits from using an anti-modification device to render their contracts immutable. Part VI explores the normative implications of this conjecture, focusing specifically upon whether and to what extent it undermines the arguments that have been made in favor of enforcing anti-modification clauses. Part VII concludes.

questions.question: Is there substantial demand among contracting parties for contract terms that make agreements effectively immutable by preventing courts from enforcing subsequent modifications?

Can contracting parties achieve effective immutability through alternative legal or organizational devices (for example, multi-party arrangements or third-party structures) instead of relying on courts to enforce anti-modification provisions?

If such alternative anti-modification devices are legally available, why are they apparently unused-because of ignorance, prohibitive costs or legal obstacles, or because most parties gain little benefit from rendering contracts immutable?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how firms braid explicit and implicit obligations and raise switching costs through collaborative governance to prevent opportunistic reneging in innovative supply chains; Paper B investigates legal and organizational devices (anti‑modification clauses, the representative trustee technique, multi‑party contracts) that parties might use to block or deter opportunistic contract modifications and hold‑up.

shared_topics.topic: use of multi‑party or organizational structuring beyond simple bilateral contracts to achieve commitment and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents governance forms that go beyond simple bilateral contracts—formal structures that regulate information exchange and create interdependencies—while Paper B explores how parties exploit multi‑party agreements, trusts, and entity design to render agreements effectively immutable or to shape the normative framework for future bilateral modifications.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal contract law and the role of extra‑legal or noncontractual mechanisms in securing agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the complementary role of relational contracting, social norms, and implicit obligations when formal contracts cannot fully specify outcomes amid innovation, and Paper B highlights how parties turn to other areas of law (trust law, corporate forms) or normative devices to achieve contractual ends when the common law restricts enforcement of certain clauses.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between flexibility for ex post adaptation and the demand for commitment/immutability in contracts under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how contracting for innovation must balance the need for iterative, adaptive collaboration with protections for specific investments, while Paper B debates the desirability and mechanisms of making contracts immutable (preventing modifications) versus preserving parties' flexibility to renegotiate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105califlrev1725!!SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: allocation of authority between private ordering and external legal mandates
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the tension between parties' freedom to contract (default rules) and mandatory limits on that freedom (unenforceability of anti-modification clauses), while Paper B analyzes the tension between state-level autonomy and national legal doctrines (decentralization versus centralized federal rules) and when authority should be reallocated upward or left to subunits.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design for managing future cooperation and conflict
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how contracting parties use multi-party arrangements, trusts, and organizational forms (e.g., the representative trustee technique or MFN clauses) to structure and constrain future contract modifications, and Paper B frames federalism as a mechanism that prescribes the terms of intergovernmental cooperation or conflict—both examine how institutional form governs subsequent relationships.

shared_topics.topic: consequentialist evaluation of legal rules versus doctrinal/formal approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses the normative need to change doctrinal rules about enforceability of anti-modification clauses by looking at practical demand and available workarounds, and Paper B explicitly urges evaluating federalism by its effects on people rather than by sovereignty doctrine, so both favor outcome-focused assessment over formalistic rules.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs and collective-action constraints on governance mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how transaction costs and incentives (e.g., costs of assembling multiple trustees, third-party incentives to release obligations) limit the feasibility of anti-modification devices, while Paper B highlights collective action problems and information frictions that constrain decentralized provision of public goods—both treat such costs as central limits on legal and institutional solutions.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:Language and Formalities in Commercial Contracts: A Defense of Custom and Conduct

shared_topics.topic: the role and enforceability of non‑written practices and devices (custom, conduct, trusts/organizational arrangements) in shaping contractual obligations and preventing modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes so‑called anti‑modification devices (e.g., the representative trustee technique, multi‑party arrangements, organizational filtering) as ways parties can make contracts effectively immutable; Paper B defends usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance as nonverbal, customary components of the parties' language that determine contractual content and should be admissible to show assent.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between written formalities and extrinsic evidence in contract interpretation and modification
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues against neoformalists who would confine judges to written words and urges that performance and industry usage function as legal formalities and admissible interpretive evidence; Paper A examines whether formal contractual provisions (anti‑modification or form‑of‑amendment clauses) should be enforced or treated as unenforceable regardless of parties' written expressions.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy (freedom to contract) and judicially imposed mandatory rules that limit contracting out
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly criticizes proposals to convert rules governing contract modifications into defaults and interrogates the demand for enforceable anti‑modification clauses; Paper B confronts reforms that would strip courts of inquiry into custom and conduct, an intervention that likewise limits parties' ability to have their chosen practices and manifestations of assent recognized by law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56scallrev573!!ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.

shared_topics.topic: default versus mandatory rules in contract law and the normative criteria (efficiency vs fairness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether rules about contract modifications (e.g., enforceability of anti‑modification clauses) should be default or mandatory and critiques a laissez‑faire, efficiency‑oriented approach; Paper B contrasts a wealth‑maximizing (efficiency) allocation of reliance losses with a fairness‑based rule (equal loss sharing) and argues normatively for the latter.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms to deter opportunistic renegotiation and to allocate unforeseen risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes legal and contractual devices (anti‑modification clauses, MFN, the representative trustee technique, multi‑party arrangements) designed to raise the cost of or prevent post‑contract modifications and opportunism; Paper B proposes equal loss‑sharing and a partial‑ignorance model as institutional solutions to prevent one party exploiting excused performance and to allocate unforeseen reliance losses.

shared_topics.topic: use of multi‑party or relational/institutional frameworks and partnership analogies to shape bilateral contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how multi‑party contracts, collective agreements, and organizational forms (trusts, trustees) can be used to create a broader normative framework that constrains bilateral modifications; Paper B treats contracts as moral partnerships or 'common enterprises,' using partnership analogies to justify sharing losses and to inform how bilateral obligations should be governed.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Rhetoric of Legal Backfire

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical evidence in assessing claims about legal rules' effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the ambiguous and limited empirical evidence regarding contracting parties' demand for enforceable anti-modification clauses and uses doctrinal/transaction-cost analysis to test that claim, while Paper B argues that allegations of 'legal backfire' are frequently rhetorical and unsupported by persuasive empirical or factual proof and should be treated with skepticism.

shared_topics.topic: strategic responses by private actors and interest groups to legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how sophisticated contracting parties exploit organizational forms, multi-party arrangements, and a 'representative trustee' device to bypass or alter the effects of default contract-modification rules, and Paper B examines how interest groups, critics, and policymakers strategically deploy 'backfire' rhetoric to influence the adoption, repeal, or interpretation of laws.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when law should be reformed in response to alleged harms or unintended consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications about whether courts or legislatures should change the enforceability of anti-modification clauses given the limited demand and available private workarounds, while Paper B addresses the normative problem of when lawmakers should heed or resist claims that a law 'backfires,' urging careful review rather than rhetorical capitulation.

papers.node_id: 95nwulrev91!!Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS
papers.title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS
papers.abstract:
Recent work in the law and economics of contracts suggests that contracts ought to be highly complex and "fine-tuned." They should have many terms describing the obligations of parties across alternative future states of the world; these terms should provide for highly variable rewards for desired behavior and penalties for undesired behavior; and these rewards and penalties should bear a complex mathematical relationship to the value of the benefits produced by the different kinds of behavior. In practice, however, many contracts are quite simple. They divide the future into very crude partitions; they provide for constant or close to constant payments across different outcomes; and the terms are easy to understand. This divergence between theory and practice suggests that the assumptions underlying the economic models of contracts should be revised, and it raises basic questions of public policy of interest to lawyers. What are the advantages and disadvantages of complexity in contracts? How should courts think about the complexity of contracts? Should courts enforce complex contracts more strictly than they enforce simple contracts?
To understand why these questions are important, one might compare the idea of contractual complexity with the better developed idea of contractual completeness. Courts and contracts scholars now understand that a contract might be more or less "complete," in the sense of describing the obligations of parties in different future states of the world. A more complete contract takes account of many future contingencies that would change the value of performance - increases in the cost of inputs, decline in demand for the product, and so on. A less complete contract might simply state the price and performance - deliver the widget on January 1, for $ X - without saying what happens if the product is destroyed in transit or similarevents occur. Courts seem to be more willing to aggressively interpret incomplete contracts than complete contracts. Thus, completeness matters. The question is whether contractual complexity matters as well.
We argue that it does, and that the current tendency of scholars to focus on completeness and neglect complexity has resulted in an inadequate understanding of contracts and contract law.
One of our major themes is that complexity is predicted by models that make unrealistic assumptions about human behavior and the environment. The basic point of these models is that contracts should be complex because of pervasive uncertainty about the future. Because any of an indefinitely large set of events could influence the cost or value of the performance, a desirable contract would condition performance on all of these events. As is well understood, one reason that parties would not draft such a contract is that the drafting would be extremely costly. But there are many other reasons why parties may avoid complexity when drafting contracts, including: asymmetric information, monitoring dynamics, evolutionary pressures, conventions, reliance on trust and reputation, enforcement costs, bounded rationality, and renegotiation.To take one example, when a firm cares about its reputation, and its customers know this, they may enter into a simple contract that does not describe the firm's obligations in detail, because both sides expect the firm to act in the customer's interests when it is time to perform. Our positive arguments about contractual complexity are in principle susceptible to empirical testing and should be of interest to lawyers who draft contracts and are concerned about the appropriate level of detail.
Our other major theme is that the complexity of a contract is a relevant consideration for courts when they decide how to interpret a contract. We do not argue that simple contracts are good and complex contracts are bad, or vice versa; nor do we argue that courts should always interpret simple contracts and complex contracts differently. Our argument is more modest and subtle. It is that the relative complexity of a contract can tell a court something about the contractual goals of the parties, the process of negotiation, and the environment that the parties faced when they negotiated the contract. Under certain conditions, the degree of complexity reveals whether one party took advantage of the other party, whether negotiations were hampered by asymmetric information, whether the parties anticipated that trust or reputational concerns would resolve disputes, or whether other factors influenced the contract. Because courts care about preventing advantage-taking, overcoming problems of asymmetric information, encouraging trust, and so on, they should take account of the complexity of the contract when deciding how to interpret the contract and whether to enforce it.
A word about the methodological background of this article. There are two economic literatures on contracting. One is "law and economics;" theother is the "economics of contracts."Both focus on people's incentives to enter, invest in, breach, and renegotiate contracts, or broadly to engage in "contract-related behavior." The two literatures share an underlying purpose: to describe the conditions under which the value of contractual exchange is maximized. However, the law and economics literature focuses on the effects of legal rules, whereas the economics of contracts literature takes legal rules as given and examines the optimal design of contracts. Law and economics has a public orientation; it gives advice to courts and legislatures about the design of legal rules. Economics of contracts has a private orientation; it gives advice to parties entering exchange relationships about how to design their contracts.
As some authors have pointed out, the distinction between these literatures is artificial; a rapprochement is needed.Although the two literatures have different focuses, their origins and methods are quite similar, and their divergence has created two problems. First, the economics of contracts literature has made a number of methodological advances that have not yet spread to the law and economics literature. Unfortunately, these advances are often quite technical, and this has hampered the transport across disciplinary boundaries. Second, there is no reason why law and economics should ignore problems of contract design,and why economics of contracts should ignore problems of legal design. Indeed, the two subjects cannot be separated; lawyers, judges, and legislatures cannot evaluate contract rules without understanding the contracts that these rules are supposed to regulate.Yet the law review literature on contracts is almost completely devoid of the positive analysis of contracts.
This article uses insights from the economics of contracts literature to discuss both legal rules and contract design. The ideas of contractual simplicity and complexity are used to organize the discussion. The degree of complexity of a contract is one of its central features, and it is a source of concern to those who design contracts. The positive regularity that we seek to explain is the apparent use of highly simple contracts despite the complexity of the environments in which people use contracts. This is the subjectof Parts I and II, which together discuss examples and terminology, and Part III, which explores reasons for contractual simplicity.
We also make several normative arguments in Part IV. There is a traditional law and economics approach to contract interpretation, which holds that courts should fill gaps in contracts by either supplying terms that maximize the value of the contract (the terms that the parties themselves would have chosen if transaction costs were zero) or providing correct incentives for parties to reveal information to each other. There are also more recent attempts, relying on the economics of contracts literature, to defend more formal or literal interpretation of contracts. Our focus on complexity reveals defects in both approaches. We argue that the proper interpretative strategy depends on the cause of the gap in the contract, and that the complexity or simplicity of the contract provides clues about what that cause is in any given case.

questions.question: Why do contracting parties often draft simple contracts even though economic theory predicts they should draft complex, highly state-contingent contracts?

Does the observable complexity of a contract provide reliable evidence about the parties' contracting environment (for example, asymmetric information, reputation concerns, bargaining power, or renegotiation incentives)?

Should courts use the degree of a contract's complexity to guide interpretation and enforcement, and if so, under what conditions should simple and complex contracts be interpreted or enforced differently?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51arizlrev1!!Article: Contracts as Organizations
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contracts as Organizations

shared_topics.topic: contract complexity and its implications for contract design and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage substantively with how the internal structure of contracts — especially their degree of complexity (many contingent terms) versus simplicity — affects contracting outcomes; Paper B develops the theory that complexity (or its absence) matters for interpretation and enforcement, while Paper A treats contract form as an organizational artifact whose structure should be analyzed by alternative theories and empirically evaluated.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard economic contracting models and the need for alternative theoretical perspectives
shared_topics.justification: Both articles criticize the dominance of neoclassical/agency/incomplete-contract economic models in explaining contracting behavior and call for supplementation — Paper A explicitly proposes four organizational theories to enrich the account, and Paper B shows that economic models that predict highly complex contracts rely on unrealistic behavioral/environmental assumptions and thus need modification.

shared_topics.topic: explanations for why many real-world contracts are simple despite uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider why parties often draft crude or simple contracts instead of the fine‑tuned contingent agreements predicted by some economic models, invoking causes such as drafting costs, asymmetric information, monitoring and enforcement costs, reputation/trust, bounded rationality, and incentives to renegotiate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract language, drafting norms, and courts in shaping contract meaning and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that the actual wording and drafting conventions of contracts — and how courts interpret them — are central to understanding contract governance; Paper B argues courts should use contract complexity as a clue to parties' goals and drafting context, while Paper A stresses legal scholars' expertise in language and judicial interpretation as essential to empirical and theoretical study of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the need for broader empirical and methodological approaches to studying contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers call for expanding empirical inquiry beyond the narrow set of questions motivated by standard economic theories (primarily advantage‑taking and ex post opportunism): Paper A surveys and critiques the current empirical literature and urges organizational perspectives, and Paper B highlights testable positive predictions about simplicity/complexity that invite empirical validation and better integration between contract design and legal analysis.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis383!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT

shared_topics.topic: the significance of tacit or implied assumptions/terms in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends a 'shared-assumption' test that treats unstated, tacit assumptions as part of the contract and grounds judicial relief, while Paper B treats implied terms and gaps as central interpretive problems and links contract complexity to when courts should imply or supply terms.

shared_topics.topic: how uncertainty and foreseeability of future events affect enforcement or excuse of performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether foreseeability or the parties' tacit beliefs about low-probability events should determine excuses for nonperformance (impossibility/frustration), and Paper B analyzes pervasive uncertainty as the reason parties might or might not draft complex contingencies and how that shapes contract design and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of party sophistication, bargaining context, and asymmetric information on contract content and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes differences between sophisticated and unsophisticated parties in holding tacit assumptions (and thus in the appropriateness of relief), while Paper B identifies asymmetric information, negotiation dynamics, reputation, and related factors as drivers of contractual simplicity or complexity and as indicators courts can use about the parties' bargaining context.

shared_topics.topic: the proper judicial role in gap-filling and interpreting contracts based on contract features (complexity/simplicity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts routinely can and should infer parties' tacit assumptions and provide relief in unexpected-circumstance cases, whereas Paper B argues that the degree of contractual complexity should inform judicial interpretive strategies and when courts should supply or resist supplying terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82lawcontempprob1!!ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: how courts should choose interpretive methodology (formalism vs contextualism)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the debate over textual/formalist versus contextualist interpretation: Paper A proposes 'normative triangulation' as a middle path that privileges market-general context, while Paper B argues that courts should let features like contractual complexity or simplicity inform whether to fill gaps or apply literal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: using market norms and external, non-party-specific context as interpretive benchmarks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should read ambiguous terms against standard market terms and publicly observable benchmarks; Paper B similarly treats conventions, reputational norms, and environmental features as background that explain why parties draft simple or complex contracts and thus should inform interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form (boilerplate, simplicity, or complexity) should affect enforcement and gap-filling
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the legal significance of a contract's structural features: Paper A focuses on boilerplate/standardized terms and whether they require special doctrinal treatment, while Paper B analyzes how the degree of complexity or simplicity signals the parties' contracting environment and therefore should affect how aggressively courts supply terms or enforce literal language.

shared_topics.topic: inferring bargaining process, opportunism, and incentives from contract structure to guide judicial responses
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat observable contract characteristics (standardized clauses, low complexity, high complexity) as evidence about negotiation costs, asymmetric information, reputation, or advantage-taking; they argue courts should use those inferences to choose doctrines that deter opportunism and produce predictable, welfare-relevant outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107geolj1277!!ARTICLE: Contract Creep
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Creep

shared_topics.topic: observable contract features (complexity vs simplicity) as evidence about bargaining context and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the degree of contractual complexity or simplicity reveals information about negotiation, asymmetric information, reputation, and renegotiation incentives and therefore should guide courts' interpretive choices; Paper B likewise treats observable drafting choices (e.g., bespoke vs boilerplate clauses) as central to whether a doctrinal track or interpretation is appropriate and warns that misreading those signals contributes to doctrinal creep.

shared_topics.topic: party heterogeneity (sophisticated parties vs consumers) and its doctrinal implications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how differences in parties' incentives, information, and reputational constraints can explain why parties choose simple or complex contracts and thus justify different legal treatment; Paper B focuses on the two-track idea (sophisticated parties vs consumers), the difficulty of drawing that boundary, and how failure to account for party heterogeneity produces problematic migration of doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: standard-form, modular, or portable clauses and their effects on governance and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights conventions, drafting costs, and reliance on standard terms as reasons parties use simple or modular contracts and explains how these practices affect enforcement and interpretation; Paper B analyzes how modular drafting and the portability of clauses enable rules developed in one transactional context to be cut-and-pasted into another, producing 'creep' across doctrinal regimes.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate judicial interpretive strategies for gap-filling and enforcement given contract design and transactional context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques one-size-fits-all interpretive prescriptions and argues courts should tailor gap-filling or literal enforcement to the causes of simplicity or complexity in the deal; Paper B critiques judicial and scholarly approaches that assume doctrinal containment, urging more deliberate interpretive and doctrinal choice to prevent undesirable spillovers between contract regimes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92columlrev997!!ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: why parties use open or simple contracts under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why, despite uncertainty about future states, parties often use open-ended or simple contracts (e.g., open terms, crude partitions) — attributing this to drafting and enforcement costs, reduced incentives to test or haggle, renegotiation, and other frictions that make complexity impractical.

shared_topics.topic: incentive alignment and principal–agent problems in discretionary performance
shared_topics.justification: Both works study contracts that give one party substantial discretion (agency or sharing arrangements) and consider how contractual features (gain‑sharing, negligence‑like terms, rewards/penalties) are used to induce performance and align the agent’s incentives with the parties' joint interests.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret and enforce incomplete/complex/open‑term contracts
shared_topics.justification: Each paper develops normative guidance for judicial review — Paper A proposing a joint‑maximization/negligence benchmark and attention to structural alignment, and Paper B arguing that a contract’s complexity provides evidentiary clues about parties’ goals and thus should influence interpretive and enforcement choices.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between contractual complexity/completeness and practical simplicity/open terms
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tradeoff between theoretically fine‑tuned, complete contracts and the observed prevalence of simpler or open contracts, exploring costs and benefits of complexity (drafting, monitoring, bounded rationality, reputation) and the implications for contract design and legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev379!!SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

shared_topics.topic: reasons parties leave contracts simple or incomplete (bounded rationality, transaction costs, asymmetric information, reputation, sunk costs)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why real-world contracts are often simple or omit contingencies, citing bounded rationality, drafting and enforcement costs, asymmetric information, reliance on reputation or extralegal enforcement, and sunk-cost considerations as central explanatory mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: when courts should imply terms or otherwise intervene (background/default rules versus case-by-case gap-filling)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of judicial or legislative intervention—distinguishing background/default rules from ad hoc judicial implication—and evaluate the normative and practical justifications for imposing terms versus leaving gaps to private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior and the role of legal/default rules in deterring or accommodating it
shared_topics.justification: Each paper treats opportunism as a key problem that interacts with incompleteness and bounded rationality, considering whether default rules, good-faith doctrines, or implied terms are appropriate tools to prevent advantage-taking and facilitate efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form (complexity or simplicity) should affect judicial interpretation and concerns about consent/freedom from contract
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that features of the contract — its degree of complexity or simplicity — convey information about parties' expectations and bargaining context, and thus bear on interpretive choices; they also share concern that uncertain or retroactive interventions can undermine parties' consent and 'freedom from contract.'

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1joflegalanalysis207!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and gap‑filling of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the degree of contractual complexity or simplicity provides courts with evidence about parties' goals and the appropriate interpretive approach, while Paper B develops concrete doctrinal tests (the shared‑assumption and bounded‑risk tests) for when courts should grant relief and how to treat tacit or missing terms, so both engage with how judges should interpret and supplement incomplete or ambiguous contracts.

shared_topics.topic: role of tacit assumptions and parties' expectations at formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that observed contractual simplicity or complexity reveals what parties anticipated and thus should influence interpretation, and Paper B centers its analysis on parties' tacit incorrect assumptions (the shared‑assumption test), using those expectations to determine when relief from enforcement is warranted.

shared_topics.topic: constraints on contracting (bounded rationality, information asymmetry, reputation, transaction costs) shaping contract form and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A catalogues reasons—bounded rationality, asymmetric information, monitoring costs, reputation, renegotiation—that produce simple contracts despite uncertainty, and Paper B incorporates behavioral and informational constraints (loss aversion, reasonable risk allocation, methodological reliance on norms of similarly situated parties) when deciding when courts should adjust enforcement in unexpected‑circumstances cases.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and appropriate remedies when unforeseen events occur
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links contractual detail and complexity to how parties allocate incentives and risks and argues courts should account for that in enforcement, while Paper B provides a framework for reallocating risk via different remedial regimes (reliance damages, modified expectation damages) under its shared‑assumption and bounded‑risk tests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104columlrev1428!!ARTICLE: EMBEDDED OPTIONS AND THE CASE AGAINST COMPENSATION IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMBEDDED OPTIONS AND THE CASE AGAINST COMPENSATION IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: default remedies and judicial gap-filling in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique one-size-fits-all defaults and discuss how courts should fill gaps: Paper A argues that the default expectancy/compensation rule is historically weak and poorly suited to price embedded termination options, urging courts to enforce parties' negotiated termination terms (or supply consumer-favoring defaults); Paper B analyzes how courts should supply or respect terms depending on contract complexity, arguing interpretation and gap-filling should account for why parties left gaps.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as devices for risk allocation (options/insurance) and the pricing of termination rights
shared_topics.justification: Both treat contract clauses as tools for allocating risk rather than merely allocating liability: Paper A models rights to breach, returns, and liquidated damages as embedded call options/insurance whose price depends on risk-bearing, market competition, and surplus division; Paper B situates contractual form (simplicity vs complexity) in part in terms of how parties manage uncertainty and risk through contractual design.

shared_topics.topic: informational and behavioral frictions (asymmetric information, moral hazard, bounded rationality, reputation, renegotiation) shaping contract design
shared_topics.justification: Both papers identify non‑ideal behavioral and informational factors that influence why parties draft particular terms: Paper A emphasizes adverse selection, moral hazard, and risk-bearing capacity in structuring embedded options and liquidated-damage clauses; Paper B catalogs asymmetric information, monitoring costs, bounded rationality, reputation, and renegotiation as central explanations for why contracts are simple rather than 'fine-tuned.'

shared_topics.topic: heterogeneity of contractual terms and normative implication that courts should account for contract-specific context
shared_topics.justification: Both emphasize that real-world contracts display wide variation and that doctrine should respect that heterogeneity: Paper A documents diverse termination provisions and argues for allowing a broad range of option prices (even supercompensatory ones); Paper B documents variation in complexity and argues courts should use contractual complexity as a signal about parties' objectives and negotiation environment when deciding interpretation and enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 24chaplrev89!!ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Interpretation and the Parol Evidence Rule: Toward Conceptual Clarification

shared_topics.topic: the textualist versus contextualist approaches to contractual interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides an in-depth conceptual analysis of textualism and contextualism, including their stages and how they treat ambiguity; Paper B engages the same divide by contrasting literal/formal interpretation with more contextual or gap‑filling approaches and arguing that contract complexity affects which approach is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling, enforcement rigor, and who decides contractual meaning (judge v. jury)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when interpretive disputes should be resolved by judges versus juries and how the parol evidence rule interacts with gap‑filling; Paper B examines whether courts should strictly enforce contracts or supply terms, arguing the answer should depend on the causes of gaps and the contract's complexity.

shared_topics.topic: the role of extrinsic/parol/contextual evidence in inferring parties' intent and resolving ambiguity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A scrutinizes different definitions of 'parol evidence,' types of latent ambiguity, and how courts weigh interpretive evidence; Paper B treats features like contractual complexity as contextual evidence about negotiation, asymmetric information, or reliance that courts should consider when interpreting agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the economic and drafting consequences of interpretive doctrines (transaction costs, litigation, and efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how doctrinal incoherence in interpretation raises drafting costs, increases litigation, and undermines economic efficiency; Paper B analyzes how transaction costs, bounded rationality, reputation, and legal rules shape parties' choices about contract complexity and the social welfare implications of different interpretive policies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57syracuselrev227!!ARTICLE: K.I.S.S. THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE GOODBYE: SIMPLIFYING THE CONCEPT OF PROTECTING THE PARTIES' WRITTEN AGREEMENT

papers.node_id: 42geojintll639!!ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA
papers.abstract:
After finding that they have survived long enough to make it through the first decade of their "21st Century," members of the cosmopolitan speciesHomo sapienshave also realized they can enjoy a cup of Starbucks coffee in Moscow; devour a McDonald's hamburger in Beijing; and demand face-to-face technical support for an iPad in Sydney. But if they want to board a Lufthansa flight originating in Los Angeles, aiming to deplane in Tokyo or Seoul, they will find that such an opportunity (and thousands of similar opportunities to use airlines of other countries for overseas travel) is foreclosed by the rules of international aviation law. Why that is so, and how an emerginglex aviaticacould lead to an end of that unsettling anomaly, is the subject of this Article.
Transnational corporations are the norm in this 21st Century world. Yet, ever since international commercial air travel became possible at the close of World War II, airlines have been straitjacketed by treaty-based restrictions that require them to be owned and controlled by a specific state (or by the citizens of that state). Only through that state/airline bond (typically based on legal incorporation, principal place of business, and like factors) does the airline receive permission to access the air transport markets of other states.The mandate of citizenship purity means that no airline can be designated by more than one state to serve its international air routes.The purity rules explain why only United Airlines or American Airlines, but not Lufthansa, can serve the Los Angeles/Tokyo or Los Angeles/Seoul markets directly from a permanent hub at L.A. International. They also explain why Lufthansa cannot merge with or acquire United Airlines, itslongtime Star Alliance partner, to secure access to United's U.S. international aviation markets. Without a commercial airspace equivalent of themare liberum,on the one hand, and burdened by the citizenship rules on the other, airlines depend on government-to-government aerodiplomacy--a complex web of bilateral treaties--to secure the traffic rights that enable them to build their international air networks.
The treaty limitations on ownership and control are backed up by national laws that impose similar (and often much more specific) constraints on foreign ownership. These national limits, which serve to uphold the treaty-based restrictions, are beholden to them as well. States that might otherwise remove their national foreign investment restrictions have little incentive to do so if their liberal approach jeopardizes market access rights under treaties with other states that are not similarly inclined.
The citizenship rules essentially confine airlines to their national capital markets. Recent events have exposed the economic deadweight of such a limited horizon. As well as costs associated with protecting air transport from terrorist threats after 9/11,airlines were hit by oscillating kerosene pricesand the demand effects of the "Great Recession."Other events, from labor disputes to natural disasters such as Europe's "Volcanic Ash Crisis,"battered the industry's stability. And structural factors exacerbate these fiscal strains: major international aviation markets, notably the U.S./EU Atlantic corridor, face overcapacity from multiple (in many cases state-sponsored) air carriers and an inability, dictated by the citizenship regime, to consolidate in order to rationalize market imbalances.
An emerging normative shift, one that we propose to characterizeusing the undeniably showy but pleasingly resonant term "lex aviatica,"holds potential for unseating the citizenship regime in international aviation. The shift is one that we detected in an earlier writing:it derives from an evolving consensus among airlines and sympathetic government officials that the time has come to dismantle the citizenship purity rules.To set the stage for this discussion, we provide first a concise survey of the astonishingly complex bilateral trade system that has governed the world's airlines for over 60 years. The citizenship or nationality rulesare embedded in that system and their removal will necessarily unwind a substantial part of it.To understand the consequences of removing these rules, it is necessary to understand what they do.We go on to evaluate two initiatives--twin beachheads of an incominglex aviatica--which could allow states to suppress the citizenship rules without risking serious disruption of their aviation trade relationships.The Article closes with a glimpse of the kinds of broader state-sponsored reforms, further elements of a newlex aviatica,that could allow the industry that has created our globally connected world to become global itself.
