papers.node_id: 46amjcompl485!!ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law
papers.abstract:
In his Note outlining our Bristol Conference topic,our General Reporter afforded us considerable latitude in the preparation of our National Reports. We were invited to address the general nature of the UNIDROIT Principles,their content (with a view to comparing it to national/domestic law),as well as the purposes to which the Principles might properly be put.
In the first, more general part of my Report, I discuss the Principles as a kind of Restatement and their use as a source of international commercial law. In the second part, I seek to compare the limits of commercial contract freedom (contract validity): under the Principles and under Danish domestic law.
1. The Principles as a Restatement and a Source of ContractLaw
As I wish to emphasize what I see as a significant relationship between the nature of the UNIDROIT Principles and their purposes, I take the liberty of combining my response to these questions under a single heading.
certainly agree with the General Reporter's assessment that the essential nature of the Principles is "a sort of international Restatement of contract law." Indeed, since my colleagues and I on the University of Copenhagen Law Faculty consider the Principles to be a most significant and persuasive international Restatement, we now make sure that all our studentsare introduced to the UNIDROIT Principles, inter alia, as part their required courses in Contracts andSales.In this way, we openly acknowledge that the greatest influence on our domestic law of contract now comes from outside.
But if this Restatement-aspect rightly expresses the essential nature of the Principles, it would seem to follow that an important purpose of the Principles should be to serve as just such a Restatement, i.e., as a persuasive source of internationally accepted principles of contract law, lex mercatoria and the like.In this, I suspect, our General Reporter would agree.
And yet, it seems to me that the Preamble to the Principles, as presently drafted, fails to acknowledge this significant source-of-law function.Though the Preamble rightly suggests that e.g., Danishrules of private international law would permit parties to "contract in" to the Principles,that the Principles might provide solutions to certain, otherwise "insoluble" problems,that they could be used by Danish courts to interpret international instruments,and that at least some Principles might serve as a model for Danish legislators,nothing is said about the fact that e.g., Danish commentators, courts and arbitrators can make good use of the Principles as a Restatement, that is, as a convenient source of general principles of law and/or as a source of the usages and customs of international trade, lex mercatoria and the like.
This source-of-law function (purpose) of the Principles seems particularly important in systems where great reliance is placed on uncodified, essentially judge-made rules of law. In Denmark, for example, where the bulk of our existing contract law is not to be found in statutes, it seems unlikely that our Parliament would make much use of the Principles as a model for future legislation: our Contracts Act (Aftaleloven: which deals only with questions of contract formation, validity and agency) is not currently up for revision,and - in the absence of any European commandment- Denmark would hardly elect to codify the rest of its Contract law, let alone enact an even broader Civil Code.
What does, however, seem very likely is that some UNIDROIT Principles will rub off on, and thus become part of our own judge- made contract law. We in Denmark predict, for example, that our domestic rules on liability will drift towards the international formulations in UNIDROIT and CISG.And indeed, as we academics writeabout the Principles (and require our students, the future Danish judges, to absorb the message),our prophesy begins to fulfill itself!
Should such internationalism surprise observers from outside? Denmark's initial "no" to Europe's Union was a shot heard far and wide,but that general expression of reluctance to yield national sovereignty might also reflect a preference for voluntary internationalism in the field of private and commercial law.As early as 1892, Julius Lassen (the father of our modern law of Obligations), could make the following observations regarding the impact in Denmark of foreign private and commercial law:
Although the Danish Law of Obligations is essentially national in character, its main principles correspond in large measure to those of European and American law… In the presentation of the Danish Law of Obligations, it therefore becomes natural and necessary to take due account .. of foreign legislation and legal literature… But just as a certain degree of unanimity in European law will provide important support for the results which Danish legal science has derived from our law's basic principles, so will our results be challenged when foreign practice and science … reach conclusions which differ from ours …
Lassen's logic still rings true in our own day and age, particularly in internationally oriented commercial contexts, where Danish doctrine and jurisprudence often make reference to foreign and international sources of law.Therefore, if a given UNIDROIT Principle is perceived to express an internationally accepted - and persuasively reasoned - general principle of law, then a Danish court confronted with an international dispute might well be expected to draw inspiration from that particular Principle as (part of) an appropriate solution in the concrete case. Once applied by our courts, the UNIDROIT solution becomes an integral part of the Danish solution, part of our own judge-made law, our applicable rule of law (gaeldende ret). In this way, that which previously might have represented a domestic,perhaps even a parochial solution, becomes internationalized and thus better suited to the modern needs of trade.
To take a concrete example: the next time a Danish court is asked to test the effectiveness (validity) of a peculiarly Danish standard term, i.e., a burdensome term which the foreign contracting party might not expect or understand, then - if due account is taken of the UNIDROIT Principle persuasively formulated in Article 2.20 - that surprising term should not be held effective, i.e., it should not be enforced by the court. (Later, I will provide a fuller explanation of this particular prophesy and the existing Danish case law on point.)
In making these arguments and predictions, I fully recognize that the Principles do not simply purport to restate the law. Just as with the highly successful (Second) American Restatement of Contracts,some UNIDROIT Principles are clearly innovative, designed to better meet the needs of international trade.
Yet this innovative aspect of some UNIDROIT Principles will not disqualify the Principles as a source of Danish law. Quite the contrary: just as the various American Restatements are considered persuasive and authoritative by reason of their source,the Principles will be similarly regarded by reason of theirs.Applying the Principles as a non-mandatory source, Danish judges will make use of those innovative and other UNIDROIT articles which they consider persuasive and helpful in the concrete case. In our largely un-codified private and commercial law environment,a Danish judge, basking in the democratic climate of Scandinavian Realism,may sometimes even start with the result, i.e., that solution which seems reasonableand fair in the concrete case, and then proceed to reason "backwards" to the ratio, using legal logic and all persuasive sources of law to test the correctness of the decision first intuitively reached.
Now, to the extent that the UNIDROIT Principles reflect - not just general principles of law, but also - the usages and customs of international trade,my suggested source-of-law function would seem even more clear-cut. For in Denmark, as elsewhere,the relevant usages and customs of the trade rank even higher on the source- of-law scale than the otherwise applicable gap-filling rule, and that is true irrespective of whether the gap-filling rule is expressed in a statute or not.And since the relevant trade usage for a Danish court in an international context is the international one,the UNIDROIT Principles qualify as a convenient and reliable source, not only for our national courts, but also for international arbitrators applying Danish law, i.e., even when it proves possible "to establish the relevant [gap-filling] rule of the applicable law."
shall not dwell here on the sometimes elusive, even confusing nature of the lex mercatoria conception. Suffice it to state that the phrase is sometimes used to cover both general principles of law and the conceptually distinct category of general usages and customs of the trade.In any event, I do not feel that the force of the arguments made here is diminished by the fact that the UNIDROIT Principles might be considered to contain elements of lex mercatoria in both these respects.
To sum up: if the Principles represent a codification of general principles of law, lex mercatoria and the like, they may rightly be applied by courts and arbitrators - not only when the parties have agreed that their contract be governed by the (UNIDROIT) Principles,or when they have agreed that their contract be governed by general principles of law, etc.- but also when the parties have notso agreed.The American Restatement was designed to serve courts and arbitrators as a source of the applicable (American) law; shouldn't this function of the new international Restatement at least be mentioned on the UNIDROIT list?
Ultimately, if the source-of-law function suggested here were to be specified in the Principles' Preamble, this would, in my view, also advance the larger harmonization process, the globalization of private law. It would provide a country like Denmark, proud of its own traditions and unique legal heritage, with an additional justification for progressive (rule-improving) harmonization by consent, a clearly stated alternative to the more wooden, lowest-common-denominator kind of unification sometimes imposed upon us "from above."
would therefore most respectfully propose that an additional Purpose be added to the Principles' Preamble, one which might be worded something like this:
They [the Principles] may be applied, even absent the parties' agreement, as a source of general principles of contract law and/or as a source of the usages and customs of international trade (lex mercatoria).
Although my colleagues and I at the University of Copenhagen have already begun to make use of the Principles as a source of general contract principles,and though we are already prepared to recommend that Danish courts do likewise, it would, in my view, represent a positive contribution to the internationalization process if the UNIDROIT drafters deemed it appropriate to expressly authorize this use of the Principles, as a Restatement of the law.
2. The Content of the Principles: the Limits of ContractualFreedom
Moving on from nature and purpose to substance, we National Reporters were asked to focus on the content of the UNIDROIT Principles with a view to comparing it to our national legal systems.
Those Reporters who choose to focus on specific topics were asked to make a general introductory statement regarding the degree of compatibility of the Principles as a whole with domestic law. So I start my content-discussion by stating that I find the UNIDROITPrinciples to be highly compatible with the Danish law of contracts. Indeed, the great majority of the individual UNIDROIT Principles are already recognized in Danish judge-made or statutory law.
Granted, we might name a few Danish innovations more boldly formulated than the corresponding UNIDROIT Principles,just as we might cite other Danish rules too bold (as yet) for any world-wide Restatement of private law.Conversely, the application of some internationally oriented UNIDROIT Principles might sometimes help our judges avoid the pitfalls of an excessively provincial point of view.
And yet, such individual distinctions hardly disturb the overall picture: that of the compatibility between the Principles and Danish law. Thus, both the remedial matrix of the Principles (specific performance, termination, damages) and the conception of force majeure as an excuse from liability (as opposed to discharge of obligation) are quite compatible with Danish and other Scandinavian law.The fact that UNIDROIT liability does not require proof of fault (culpa)hardly represents a significant practical difference, in that Danish law, as regards generic obligations, provides a most significant exception to our fault-based liability rule.
Having made these general observations, I shall now focus on the principles of contractual freedom and pacta sunt servanda, as theserelate to contract validity under the UNIDROIT Principles and Danish domestic law.
The thing worth examining here is not so much the very general (contractual freedom and binding contract) rules as such, but rather the limitations and exceptions which each system tacks on to its general rules. As the Principles are intended only for commercial use, I will exclude from my comparison Danish rules of law which are restricted to consumer transactions and the like.
We can, of course, start our discussion with the general rules. And when it comes to contractual freedom, Article 1.1 lays down the UNIDROIT black letter law:
The parties are free to enter into a contract and to determine its content.
The parties' freedom to enter an agreement and to determine its content is significant, because the parties become bound by the content of their contract, i.e., their self-made rules of inter-partes law.Or, as Article 1.3 puts it:
A contract validly entered into is binding upon the parties.
Binding in this (legal) context means that a court or arbitral tribunal will enforce the contract thus entered - i.e., the parties' own piece of private legislation - by providing an injured contracting party with a set of remedies in the event of the other party's breach.
Now these very general maxims of party-autonomy and pacta sunt servanda, made applicable to international commercial contracts governed by the UNIDROIT Principles, have also long been recognized under Danish and other Scandinavian law.This is, at least, the starting point (udgangspunktet), as we in Denmark sometimes say. Indeed, as if to underline the point in a number of specific applications, the UNIDROIT Principles even provide us with numerous ex tuto re-affirmations of the general rule.
Of course, no modern legal system has been so reckless as to grant the parties total autonomy or to enforce all promises as binding between them.Therefore, neither the UNIDROIT Principles nor Danish domestic law requires the enforcement a promise made at gunpoint,or promise procured by fraud:contracts induced by these and similar means can be avoided - in whole or at least in part.None of us wants to reward the extortionist or the swindler with the "benefit of the bargain" - or anything else.
But the list of UNIDROIT exceptions to party autonomy and binding contracts is much longer than this. As regards contractual freedom (Article 1.1), the Principles not only contains its own list of exceptions from which the parties may not derogate (so-called mandatory rules);it is further acknowledged that mandatory rules of national (i.e., domestic)law may sometimes prevail.By its own terms, the pacta sunt servanda rule in Article 1.3 applies only to contracts validly entered into, and - as already noted - we find various rules of invalidity defined in the Principles themselves. Grouping the individual UNIDROIT exceptions for present comparative purposes within two larger pigeonholes which I have labeled (a) and (b) below,and putting aside the ever-present "good faith" caveat,we find that, under the Principles, a contract (or clause) will not bind:
(a) if induced by fraudulent representation,threat,or mistake,or
(b) in the case of a surprising standard term,a grossly unfair exemption,a grossly excessive penalty,(other cases of) gross disparity,or hardship.
Granted, virtually all the UNIDROIT exceptions - those in group (a) as well as those in group (b) - are also recognized (in one form or another) as limitations upon contractual freedom under Danish domestic law. But the UNIDROIT exceptions still seem rather different, as regards both substance and form.
For one thing, although the three rather traditional defenses to contractual freedom collected here as group (a) are also grouped together in the Principles (under the general heading of Validity),there is no obvious common denominator as regards the five items which I group together here in group (b). Indeed, we find the five group-(b) items spread across four separate UNIDROIT chapters,although I would expect most Danish jurists to view all these as variations on the same basic theme.
Taking first a brief look at the items collected here as group (a), we see the UNIDROIT codification of three traditional - and thus hardly controversial - defenses to contract validity. Also the original (1917) version of the Danish Contracts Act contains separate statutory provisions for fraud, threat and mistake, and these - at least as regards the clear-cut cases - all seem more or less compatible with the UNIDROIT view.
Though courts and arbitrators should be equipped with rules for these extreme situations, we see relatively few Danish decisions involving commercial contracts induced by intentionally misleading or coercive conduct, i.e., by fraudulent misrepresentations or threats(duress).Also uncommon are the cases we in Denmark put under the heading of (mutual) mistake.
Of somewhat greater practical significance are those cases which Danish theorists categorize as "induced error" (fremkaldt vildfarelse),i.e., the cases Common law jurists label innocent or negligent misrepresentations.For some reason, the drafters of the Principles chose to put these cases - not alongside the "fraud" category (as in the corresponding judge-made Danish and Common law rules), but rather in the "mistake" pigeonhole (Article 3.5). My own preference would have been to set up a separate category for non- fraudulent (i.e., innocent/negligent) misrepresentation,as I feel this would put sharper focus on the key considerations when a contact is allegedly induced by one party's clearly erroneous statement: the factors being the degree of culpability exhibited by the representor and the materiality of the misrepresentation made.(I would expect, incidentally, that a party led to contract by the other party's negligent misrepresentation could claim reliance/negative interest damages even if liability for expectation damages were effectively disclaimed.)
Moving along to the mixed bag of UNIDROIT exceptions collected in this paper as group (b), we find much more innovative - and, for some systems, surely more controversial - exceptions to the UNIDROIT (contract-freedom) rule. For it seems clear that all five of these exceptions provide courts and arbitrators with the power to police the content of commercial contracts, i.e., to deny enforcementof a "surprising" (burdensome) standard term,a grossly "unfair" liability exemption,a grossly "excessive" penalty,a term (or contract) which (otherwise) gives one party an "excessive advantage,"or where the initial "equilibrium" of the contract has been fundamentally altered by the course of subsequent events.
The common denominator here, at least from a Danish perspective, would seem to be judicial censorship based on a qualified "reasonableness" test.Whereas UNIDROIT treats cases of gross disparity and hardship as separate categories (depending upon the point in time at which the disparity occurs), the Danish Contracts Act combines these under a single, much simpler head: 36 of the Contracts Act, our so-called General Clause.For the same reason, we find no direct Danish statutory analogues for the more specific UNIDROIT provisions on unfair exemption and penalty clauses or as regards surprising (and thus, for the surprised party unreasonable) standard terms. Also these validity sub-sets are considered adequately dealt with by our General Clause, which (in unofficial translation)provides:
1. A contract can be amended or held unenforceable, in whole or in part, if enforcement would be unreasonable or contrary to accepted standards of fair dealing. …
2. In making the determination referred to in paragraph 1, consideration shall be given to the circumstances at the time of contracting, the content of the contract and circumstances which have later occurred.
Because 36 of the Danish Contracts Act is a truly general clause, applicable to virtually all instances of unreasonableness, in consumer and commercial contracts alike, all five of the separate situations covered by individual UNIDROIT Principles in group (b)above would surely fall within the broad contours of our General Clause.
Granted, 36 was designed, inter alia, to provide consumers with the protection of a broad mandatory rule. And if we compare the number of judicial applications in consumer contexts, we might well conclude that Danish courts have applied 36 in commercial cases with considerable restraint. And yet, the General Clause is properly characterized as a significant and distinctive feature of our general law. The legislative history of the provision clearly indicates that also parties in commercial relationships deserve protection against unfair terms,and Danish courts have acted accordingly: the General Clause has been used in various commercial contexts to police both procedural and substantive unfairness in contracts between merchants.
Introduced in Denmark in 1975, the General Clause rendered irrelevant (and therefore replaced) a number of more specific statutory provisions, inter alia, rules which permitted Danish courts to police a clearly unreasonable "penalty" (liquidated damages)clause or a "default" clause which would deny the party in breach restitution in the event of termination.A key function of the General Clause is indeed to authorize judicial "censorship" of clauses like these, i.e., clauses which - in one way or another - unreasonably upset the contractual balance between breach and remedy.And given the 1995 amendment to the original 1975 statute,which empowers courts and arbitrators to amend (as well as set aside) unreasonable contracts, the Danish assault on the traditional citadel, the "idol" of freedom of contract, now seems complete.
In sum, as regards commercial contracts, it seems fair to say that the total substantive content of the Danish General Clause seems at least equal to the sum of what I might label the "5 UNIDROIT parts."Thus, a Danish court is authorized to apply 36 to deal with (serious) cases of commercial contract imbalance, i.e., where the content of the contract gives one party an excessive advantage, irrespective of whether this is due to the status of the contracting parties (so-called disparity in bargaining power) or not. And the result according to UNIDROIT Article 3.10 is precisely the same, the somewhat misleading Gross disparity-label notwithstanding:if one party has misused its superior bargaining power, then that factor (among others) will be relevant in the concrete case, but the main focus of both the Danish and the UNIDROIT rules is the content of the objectional contract or term.For similar reasons, the more narrowly drafted UNIDROIT provisions designed to regulate surprising (standard) terms,(unreasonable) exemption clauses and (excessive) penalty provisions all fall within the purview of our much broader General Clause.
In Denmark, as already noted, we see an increasing interaction, a kind of symbiosis between international and domestic rules of law.As an important example, the more specific UNIDROIT (in)validity Principles, designed to police international commercial contracts, have recently been cited in Danish doctrine as providing new outside support for the commercial application of our General Clause.Indeed, the relevant UNIDROIT Principles may not only provide us with concrete guidelines for the commercial application of our own - very general and overt - validity rule,but also with important guidelines for the commercial application of our traditional covert censorship techniques (discussed below).
In making these essentially superstructural observations concerning the regulation of private contractual freedom under the UNIDROIT Principles and Danish law, I am not here suggesting that the overall validity-solution provided by one rule-set is necessarily superior to that of the other. The more general Danish approach is better-suited to its broader purpose: the policing of consumer and commercial contracts alike. The more specific UNIDROIT limitations have the advantage of highlighting instances of commercial contract unfairness, in that (even Danish) courts and arbitrators may be more willing to use these kinds of tools than to brandish the far more general Danish clause, that seemingly uninhibited limitation on the freedom-of-contract rule.
(Since even the more specific UNIDROIT approach to contract regulation does not necessarily preclude all risk of too-frequent application (censorship), I am tempted to express, at least parenthetically, some reservations as regards the UNIDROIT validity-Principle relating to contract termination and adaption by reason of Hardship.The risk, as I see it, is that this particular UNIDROIT innovationmay provide arbitrators - and ultimately, perhaps even courts - with convenient grounds to "split the baby" or rewrite the parties' contract in cases where this would not advance the cause of economic efficiency (or fairness) in international trade.In other words, I fear that this specific UNIDROIT validity-formulation poses a greater threat to rightfully binding contracts than does e.g., the much more abstract and elastic authority of the Danish General Clause.The fact that some parties, in some cases, voluntarily draft hardship- clauses or re-negotiate their international contracts and grant eachother hardship concessions does not necessarily provide support for a gap-filling Hardship rule.The custom among those merchants who seek to preserve their contractual relationships ought not be generalized into a rule applicable even in situations where one contracting party has lost the other party's trust. I would therefore respectfully suggest that the UNIDROIT drafters re-think the hardship problem in light of Lisa Bernstein's helpful distinction between relationship- preserving norms and end-game norms.)
Finally, to add a touch of "real life" and specificity to my National Report, I wish to comment upon two commercial cases previously decided by the Danish Supreme Court. The first example (Beauty Box) is intended to demonstrate that - quite apart from the black-letter validity-solutions provided by the UNIDROIT Principles, judge-made law will continue to play a significant role on the complex commercial contract stage. The second example (Warehouse Fire) should show how an arguably provincial Danish solution might benefit from a dose of lex mercatoria, the codified solution which the Principles now provide.
Beauty Box.With a view to producing a new model beauty box for sale in England, Danish Buyer (B) places an order in September, 1977 with Danish Seller/manufacturer (S) for 3 spray-casting tools, to be delivered "latest January 4, 1978, guaranteed."S's confirmation form refers to certain standard Nordic terms for the delivery of plant and machinery (NL);these provide that S must cure any defects, but they disclaim all liability for "lost profits." The goods delivered in January are defective, and, after the failure of S's repeated attempts to cure, B cancels the contract and claims damages for expected profits (beauty box sales in England) lost.
The question in Beauty Box is a familiar one: whether the seller's standard liability disclaimer should take precedence over the applicable gap-filling liability rule.
(Note that though the sales contract - and thus the applicable sales law - in Beauty Box is domestic,the same domestic principles available to police the terms of that contract in 1986 would also be available in an international context, e.g., in a CISG-sale today.Note also that, in harmony with the UNIDROIT and CISG gap-filling solutions,the Danish SGA would hold S liable without fault, for profits foreseeably lost,whereas in the other Scandinavian countries,the domestic Sales Acts now differentiate between fault and no-fault liability, depending on whether compensation for "direct" or "indirect" loss is claimed.)
In Denmark, even a commercial contract can be policed for fairness, if need be by using our General Clause.But in commercial cases, our courts continue to give preference to more traditional, judge-made rules of law. Preferring covert techniques to overt (General Clause) policing in a commercial context, courts and arbitrators in Denmark are likely to employ a series of tests.The first of these asks whether the (standard) clause in question has been incorporated (vedtaget) into the overall contract between the parties. If this hurdle is passed, courts employ an interpretation test to determine whether the term applies to the dispute at hand. Finally, as regards incorporated terms held applicable, i.e., if all else fails, courts can resort to validity conceptions, the 36 reasonableness-test.
As regards the first stage of this 3-stage rocket, our incorporation-standard remains essentially uncodified and therefore highly flexible.Interpreting Danish cases, commentators re-state the law like this: the more burdensome the (standard) clause, the greater therequirements for incorporation.Though some standard terms might - by virtue of their recognition and use within a given context - be more readily incorporated, courts and arbitrators should be reluctant to hold parties to provisions not negotiated on their behalf or otherwise unfamiliar to them.
Assuming a Danish court holds a given clause to be incorporated in the parties' overall agreement, the next step (hurdle) is to consider how that clause should be construed, e.g., whether a repair-or-replace clause remains the buyer's exclusive remedy if the seller later proves unable to repair or replace. We can get some help here from the contra proferentem idea,but our courts seem driven (not just by syllogistic reasoning and legal logic, but also) by a desire to reach a commercially reasonable result. Given the general premise that a merchant-promisor ought not be permitted to speak with a forked tongue, a strong promissory commitment (in Beauty Box: "delivery latest January 4, 1978, guaranteed") made by S at the start of the contracting process ought not be easily obliterated by disclaimers laid down later, in fine-print standard terms.
So in this case, the standard remedy and disclaimer, even if held incorporated, will be interpreted within the total contractual context. This seller's strong promissory commitment is backed up by a single, limited method of enforcement: the promise to repair or replace. Where, as here, S cannot seasonably cure, the agreed remedy fails to achieve its essential purpose.Because we cannot turn back the clock, enforcement of the disclaimer (the letter of the private agreement) would deny B a minimum adequate remedy.Indeed, in this kind of situation, an award of consequential damages may provide the only fair means of contract enforcement.
And so, in the real Beauty Box case (UfR 1986.654 H) the Danish Supreme Court found S liable, upholding the High Court's award of 300,000 Dkr. in damages, 200,000 of this compensation for estimated profits lost. The High Court decision emphasized the interrelationship between the clear nature of Seller's commitment and the degree of Buyer's (justifiable) reliance.Like the High Court, the Supreme Court emphasized the Seller's failure to cureand rejected Seller's claim regarding an allegedly agreed remedy pursuant to the NL standard terms.
All this, I think, tends to confirm that black-letter rules of validity (like our 36) are potentially helpful, but also that they do not provide a totally self-sufficient matrix for policing each and every commercial contract/clause. At least in our Danish contract climate, no restatement or statutory codification can wholly supplant the need for judge-made rules of law.
Looking now at the flip-side of the codification-coin, I would like to illustrate how Danish courts might use the new, black-letter UNIDROIT Restatement to supplement and further develop the existing judge-made Danish law. Once again, I build my discussion around a concrete paradigm inspired by a Danish Supreme Court case:
Warehouse Fire.Swiss owner (O) contracts to store his goods, worth millions, in W's warehouse in Denmark. The contract consists of W's standard order-confirmation which contains a fine-print footnote in Danish referring to the "NSAB" standard terms (the General Conditions of the Nordic Freight Forwarders, also mentioned in fine-print English footnotes in W's previous writings to O).Later, W's entire warehouse is destroyed by a fire attributed to "causes unknown." When sued by O's property-insurer, W (who isunder-insured)denies all liability, contending that the NSAB terms put the burden of proving W's alleged negligence on O.
Now, before considering the applicability of the NSAB terms to this specific bailment, a word should be said about the general gap- filling rule. Although liability in Denmark is ordinarily predicated on culpable breach,the bailee (depositaren) in a bailment (depositum) contract will usually bear the burden of proving that he is not at fault.Therefore, if the cause of the Warehouse Fire cannot be established, Danish law says that, absent contrary agreement, the bailee (or his insurer) should shoulder that "risk." And this is, I suppose, the same sort of risk-allocation which merchants elsewhere would be likely to expect.
But let the bailor - i.e., O in Switzerland - beware! For if the Nordic NSAB terms are deemed incorporated into this bailment contract, they may well be interpreted as (re)reversing the usual (default) burden of proof, with the result that bailor O in Switzerland would then bear the Warehouse Fire risk.
As previously indicated, Danish courts often resolve the "incorporation" issue by a flexible, multi-factor kind of test:Are the standard terms actually enclosed with the contract or merely mentioned by reference (as here)? Is the reference to the standard terms conspicuous or, as in this case, in fine-print? Is the contract language understandable to both parties, or is it (as here) in a foreign legal tongue? Last, but not least, the content of the contract should be considered, along a sliding scale: the more burdensome or unexpected the standard term in question, the greater the requirements for incorporation.And note that whereas the NSAB would qualify as an "agreed document" as between Nordic suppliers,that need not imply that the NSAB should be held incorporated with equal ease, by mere reference, vis-a-vis the Swiss party here.In fact, if the NSAB is read (interpreted) to mean that the bailor must bear the Warehouse Fire kind of risk, then O (or O's insurer) can only recover damages if the NSAB is held not to have been "agreed to" by him.
Now, although most of the incorporation factors just listed would seem to work in favor of the Swiss bailor (O), the real Warehouse Fire case (UfR 1995.856 H) was resolved in favor of the Danish bailee (W). In its brief ratio, the Supreme Court emphasized one particular fact: in connection with previous transactions between the parties, O had received communications from W containing (very fine print) English-language footnotes referring to the NSAB standard terms. Against this background, the Supreme Court reversed the court below (Landsretten), holding that the Danish-language footnote in the form used to confirm O's Warehouse Fire bailment was sufficient to incorporate the entire NSAB "agreed document" as part of the contract concerned. Then, in a seemingly distinct piece of reasoning, the Supreme Court proceeded to interpret the relevant NSAB terms as placing the burden of proving fault on the bailor O (and thus O's insurer).So in the end, O's insurer was left with the risk of the "unexplained" fire and O's Warehouse-Fire loss.
A surprising result? Perhaps for some. But it should be noted that some Danish commentators had previously criticized the Supreme Court for scrutinizing the (however burdensome) content of an "agreed" document like the NSAB.In any case, the Danish concept of precedent is flexible, in that great importance is placed on the specific controversy between the parties in question. And recalling that Danish judges are sometimes said to reason "backwards" (to justify the "right" result),we might view the decision in Warehouse Fire - not so much in terms of prior case law regarding standard terms- but rather as a decision between these particular parties, in their concrete situation, a decision perhaps in part influenced by altruistic concerns. By holding the entire NSAB - including the rule which alters the usual burden of proving fault - "incorporated" as part of the contract between these parties, the Court has decided to let this loss "lie where it falls". Rather than render a hard-nosed judgment against the not-proven-negligent and under-insured warehouseman (W), the court leaves the parties in this arguably "close case" where it found them, with O's deep-pocket insurer now holding the bag.
The real reason(s) behind the decision to hold the NSAB terms "incorporated" in Warehouse Fire? We commentators should be cautious, since we can but speculate and guess. And yet, given the advent of the UNIDROIT Principles in 1994, we cannot help but wonder what might have happened if this new international Restatement had been available as a relevant source.Might the advancement of the international black-letter codification of the Surprising terms principle (Article 2.20) have made a difference, perhaps even persuaded the Supreme Court to deny enforcement of the - arguably surprising and burdensome - NSAB term?

questions.question: Whether an international, non-binding restatement of commercial contract principles can be used by domestic courts and arbitrators as a persuasive source of law even when the parties have not chosen it as their governing law.

How the permissible limits on party autonomy set out in an international restatement compare to those applied by a domestic legal system, and what this means for when courts should refuse to enforce or should adapt contractual terms that produce an unfair or materially imbalanced outcome.

Whether expressly recognizing the restatement's role as a source of general principles and trade usages in its prefatory material would promote its uptake by domestic institutions and advance harmonization of commercial contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1987dukelj1!!ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: court-ordered contract adjustment and adaptation in response to unforeseen events (hardship)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends limited court adjustment (e.g., modifying duration or terms) under an 'agreement' and 'gap' model for long-term supply contracts facing dramatic cost shifts; Paper B analyzes the UNIDROIT hardship/adaptation provisions and how Danish courts might permit or resist judicial termination or adaptation in commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and allocation of unforeseen risks in long-term/commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's 'gap model' addresses situations where parties failed to allocate catastrophic risk and advocates judicially fashioned sharing of losses; Paper B treats the UNIDROIT Principles (and Denmark's General Clause) as gap-filling tools and examines how international principles or judge-made rules reallocate risks when contracts are silent.

shared_topics.topic: policing unfair standard terms and limits on contractual freedom (surprising clauses, exemption and penalty clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the policy objection that judicial adjustment undermines freedom of contract and prompts drafting around rules, while Paper B directly compares UNIDROIT provisions and Danish law on surprising standard terms, unfair exemptions and excessive penalties and their enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts and policy trade-offs between certainty and flexibility in commercial contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines objections that courts lack expertise and that adjustment would reduce certainty and planning, and argues targeted judicial remedies are practicable; Paper B debates whether Danish courts should adopt UNIDROIT as persuasive law, weighing harmonization and flexibility against respect for pacta sunt servanda and legal predictability.

shared_topics.topic: available judicial remedies for changed circumstances (specific performance, termination, damages, restitution, modification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys possible court responses—specific performance conditioned on adjustments, excusal, restitution, bargaining orders—and recommends limiting adjustment to duration in many cases; Paper B catalogs the UNIDROIT remedial matrix (specific performance, termination, damages) and describes Danish statutory and judge-made remedial powers to amend or set aside unreasonable contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42geojintll639!!ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA

shared_topics.topic: tension between national regulatory sovereignty and market-driven international integration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how UNIDROIT Principles interact with Danish domestic law and how states resist or accommodate transnational restatements of contract law, while Paper B analyzes how treaty-based nationality rules constrain airlines and why states and industry actors are considering dismantling those sovereign constraints to enable cross-border airline integration.

shared_topics.topic: the emergence of transnational, industry-driven legal norms as alternatives or supplements to treaty/national law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the UNIDROIT Principles and lex mercatoria as a potential international 'Restatement' that courts and arbitrators may apply absent party agreement, and Paper B theorizes an emergent 'lex aviatica' — normative practices among airlines and sympathetic officials — that could supplant or reshape treaty controls.

shared_topics.topic: proposals and mechanisms for reforming international legal frameworks to better fit modern commerce
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes amendments to the UNIDROIT preamble and rethinking specific doctrines (e.g., hardship) to improve harmonization and gap-filling, while Paper B evaluates concrete initiatives and broader state-sponsored reforms aimed at unwinding nationality rules and redesigning the aviation treaty regime.

shared_topics.topic: legal constraints on commercial freedom and market structure imposed by mandatory rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes specific UNIDROIT and Danish limits on party autonomy (e.g., surprisal clauses, unfair exemptions, hardship, general clause) that police contractual content, whereas Paper B analyzes how citizenship/ownership mandates and treaty traffic-rights rules restrict airlines' ability to consolidate and operate across borders.

shared_topics.topic: the role of gap-filling, adjudication, and adaptive mechanisms in cross-border disputes and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on gap-filling principles, judicial/adjudicative discretion and arbitration when contracts are silent or disrupted (e.g., hardship, standard terms), and Paper B discusses institutional and procedural initiatives that would be needed to manage traffic-rights, state relations, and market disruption if nationality rules are relaxed.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres169!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Contractual Incompleteness: A Transactional Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Contractual Incompleteness: A Transactional Perspective

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and default rules for incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles and Danish law supply gap-filling rules (and argues the Principles can operate as a source of law to fill gaps), while Paper B surveys the literature on default rules and asks what courts should supply when contracts are silent, treating gap-filling as central to responses to contractual incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing of unfair or 'surprising' standard terms (limits on freedom of contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares UNIDROIT's specific invalidity doctrines and Denmark's broad General Clause as tools for courts to police surprising terms, unfair exemptions, penalties and gross disparity; Paper B treats doctrines like unconscionability and judicial intervention as the legal limits that shape how parties and lawyers design contracts under incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation and interpretation of standard form terms (battle of the forms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A details multi-factor tests Danish courts use to determine whether fine-print standard terms (e.g., NSAB) have been incorporated and how they are construed, and Paper B explicitly cites the 'battle of the forms' and interpretation literatures as central problems when parties' writings conflict or omit details.

shared_topics.topic: transactional drafting and private-law strategies to manage incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how parties draft standard terms, incorporation practices, and use of international instruments (UNIDROIT) to structure risk and expectations, while Paper B argues scholars should focus on transactional planners and catalogs strategies lawyers and parties use to minimize dispute costs and manage incomplete contracting.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and remedial regimes (liability, hardship, damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how UNIDROIT and Danish law allocate liability (fault vs. no-fault), police penalty/exemption clauses, and treat hardship/adaptation and remedies like specific performance or damages; Paper B highlights allocation of contractual risks, investments, renegotiation costs and remedial incentives as key variables that private parties must manage when contracts are incomplete.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2011utahlrev1461!!ARTICLE: Confronting the Certainty Imperative in Corporate Finance Jurisprudence
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Confronting the Certainty Imperative in Corporate Finance Jurisprudence

shared_topics.topic: the judicial role in shaping commercial law versus judicial restraint
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses a longstanding pattern of judicial deference in corporate finance (the 'Certainty Imperative') and calls for courts to play a more active law‑making and remedial role; Paper B analyzes how Danish judges and arbitrators actually craft results in commercial contract disputes (through incorporation tests, interpretation and the General Clause), showing courts as pivotal actors in developing contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the use of restatements or external doctrinal sources to fill gaps and harmonize commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates courts as potential agents of legal reform in finance and suggests a doctrinal shift to better reflect economic substance; Paper B treats the UNIDROIT Principles as an international 'Restatement' that domestic courts and scholars can (and do) use to fill gaps, guide interpretation, and promote harmonization with domestic contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret, police, and allocate remedies for private financing/contractual arrangements (standard terms, disclaimers, hardship, allocation of loss)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes narrow, strict construction in finance cases and argues for allocation of rights and remedies aligned with the parties' economic arrangements to promote market stability; Paper B gives detailed, practical analysis of doctrine used to police surprising standard terms, unfair exemptions, penalty clauses and hardship, and how courts allocate remedies when agreed contractual remedies fail.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between legal certainty/formalism and substantive economic efficiency or market stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames this as the central conflict—legal certainty enforced via judicial restraint has been justified as preserving market stability but may instead undermine it—urging a new paradigm; Paper B engages the same tradeoff in practice by weighing predictability (incorporation tests, black‑letter UNIDROIT rules) against substantive control of unfair terms and flexibility (Danish General Clause, hardship), and considers the implications for international commercial stability.

shared_topics.topic: trade usages / lex mercatoria as a source of contractual content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the UNIDROIT Principles and lex mercatoria as persuasive external sources that courts and arbitrators may apply or adopt into domestic adjudication, while Paper B argues that trade usage can supply missing or controlling terms (such as disclaimers) in commercial sale contracts, particularly for JIT supply relationships.

papers.node_id: 73califlrev261!!ARTICLE: The Limits of Expanded Choice: An Analysis of the Interactions Between Express and Implied Contract Terms.
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Expanded Choice: An Analysis of the Interactions Between Express and Implied Contract Terms.
papers.authors: Charles J. Goetz; Robert E. Scott
papers.abstract:
Although trade and its defining terms lie at the very core of contract law, perceptions of the state's involvement in the exchange process remain peculiarly incomplete.  Everyone understands that the state supplies the fundamental property-defining rules for pre-trade endowments.  For instance, governmentally provided rules of tort, nuisance, and civil rights establish basic boundaries of what initially belongs to an individual and, hence, what he has to offer in exchange.  When an exchange subsequently takes place, however, the parties themselves assume an important part of the burden of communicating what rights are being given and received.  Although the state's general rules of contract provide a set of standard gap-filling assumptions or implied terms, almost every agreement requires the parties to provide some additional individualized content.  At one level, the private and state-supplied terms of an executory contract represent an attempted interpartycommunicationof the substantive entitlements intended to be exchanged.  Since, however, theterms communicate evidence of the exchange's content to the state as well, they also constitute the principal legaldefinitionof the rights reallocation.  Unfortunately, this definitional process requires parties to employ inherently error-prone signals -- the "formulations" or their agreement.If the chosen combination of privately and publicly supplied terms results in an inappropriate formulation, a party may suffer a costly surprise when the contract is legally enforced.  The disappointed party will frequently contend that the content of the contract, as ultimately interpreted, does not accurately describe the original intent or expectation.
Many such complaints about the misformulation or misinterpretation of an agreement are rooted in tensions between implied and express terms and between standard and unconventional forms of expression.  To the extent that these tensions have been understood at all, the major attempt to harmonize them relies on what we term the Expanded Choice postulate.The postulate maintains that implied terms expand contractors' choices by providing standardized and widely suitable "preformulations"thus eliminating the cost of negotiating every detail of the proposed arrangement.  This Expanded Choice thesis implicitly presumes a neutral policy toward individualized agreements: atypical parties lose nothing, since they remain unrestrained from designing customized provisions to replace the state-supplied terms.
Despite the seductive persuasiveness of the Expanded Choice postulate, its reassurances are marred by unacknowledged incongruities.  For example, the courts' tendency to treat state-created rules as presumptively fair often leads to judicial disapproval of efforts to vary standard implied terms by agreement.Indeed, as the system for implying terms into contracts becomes more highly refined, the opting-out burden of those who prefer a different allocation of risks grows weightier.Furthermore, conflicting applications of the parol evidence and plain-meaning rules betray widespread judicial uncertainty over the proper method of interpreting agreements that intermingle express and implied terms.These and other related problems have exposed a central question that remains unresolved: To what extent do implied and express terms, and standardized and individualized forms of agreement, function in antagonistic rather than complementary ways?  This issue can be illuminated by focusing attention on the environment in which contractual formulations evolve.
Part I of this Article develops a conceptual analysis of the interaction between private and state-supplied contractual formulations.  Our framework departs from the conventional view that state-supplied contract clauses are means merely of reducing negotiating and other resource costs; it focuses instead on the value of implied terms as widely useful, predefined signals that reduce the incidence of certain identifiable types of formulation errors.  From this perspective, privately provided express terms constitute more refined attempts to reduce the definitional errors resulting from inappropriate formulations.  We show how such express signals are, paradoxically, so vulnerable to misinterpretation that they may actually increase error.  Contracting parties, therefore, must rely on the state's standardization of express and implied terms in order more safely to combine implied and express terms in their agreements.  This error-reduction conceptualization clarifies the ways in which formulation errors occur, how private parties and courts react to them, and how the state can and does influence the formulation of private contract terms.
Part II examines the theoretical implications of this analysis for the Expanded Choice postulate.  We argue that the very benefits of the state's efforts to imply and standardize widely useful terms create hithertooverlooked barriers to innovative forms of contractual agreement.  As more complex and refined terms are implied from the patterned behavior of contracting parties, variation by express agreement becomes more difficult and costly than is commonly realized.  Similarly, expanding the set of standard terms and clauses retards the evolution of new, "emergent" formulations.  These barriers to innovation restrain the development of alternative contractual formulations and favor highly reliable but possibly ill-fitting language, thereby imposing added costs on innovative relationships.
We consider the normative implications of our analysis for contractual interpretation in Part III.  The error-reduction framework demonstrates that the prevailing judicial approach to ex post interpretation has far-reaching feedback effects on the operation of the ex ante contractual signalling system.  Moreover, an examination of recent cases challenges the conventional premise that methods of contractual interpretation have evolved over the past half-century from an extreme focus on narrow "plain meaning" to the opposite pole of liberal contextual construction.  Surprisingly, the cases reveal a continuing struggle between "textualist" and "contextualist" interpretive methodologies.  Depending upon which methodology they favor, courts and commentators view the purpose of contract interpretation as a determination either of what the contracting parties subjectively intended or of what the contract itself objectively means.  We argue that this struggle between methodological extremes reflects a failure to understand and accommodate the respective roles of implied and express terms in contractual formulations.  Properly understood, the tensions between these competing methodologies can be alleviated through interpretive principles designed explicitly to facilitate improvements in contractual formulation.  Finally, we suggest modifications in the interpretive process to better accommodate the complex and demanding formulations required by specialized modern contractual relationships.

questions.question: Whether the state's provision of standardized implied contract terms expands parties' effective contractual choice by lowering transaction costs or instead constrains choice and innovation by making variation and opting-out more difficult and costly.
Whether privately drafted express terms reduce formulation errors (misinterpretation of contractual meaning) or paradoxically increase such errors when combined with state-supplied implied terms.
Whether courts' interpretive methodologies create feedback effects that promote or impede accurate contractual signaling and the evolution of new, customized contractual formulations.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the justification for imposing non‑express obligations: Paper A critiques Kostritsky's utilitarian standard for courts to imply terms and distinguishes between ad hoc judicial implication and pre‑announced background rules, while Paper B theorizes the role of state‑supplied implied clauses as gap‑fillers and considers the normative limits and feedback effects of expanding those standard terms.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between express terms and implied/default/background rules and the costs of contracting around them
shared_topics.justification: Both papers investigate how default and background rules interact with private drafting: Paper B develops the 'Expanded Choice' critique showing that standardized implied terms can make opting out costly and retard innovation, and Paper A discusses how default rules (and the costs of individual contracting) influence parties' choices and the appropriateness of letting courts insert terms versus permitting express modifications.

shared_topics.topic: interpretive uncertainty, notice, and the effects on contractual signaling and 'freedom from contract'
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with the consequences of uncertain interpretive standards: Paper B examines textualist versus contextualist methods and how ex post interpretation feeds back into ex ante signalling and formulation errors, while Paper A worries that vague all‑things‑considered or promissory‑estoppel standards create notice problems that undermine parties' ability to avoid unwanted obligations (the 'freedom from contract' concern).

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, transaction costs, sunk costs, and the role of defaults in mitigating strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat opportunistic behavior and transaction costs as central to why the legal system supplies defaults: Paper A emphasizes opportunism combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs as a primary rationale for court or statutory interventions, and Paper B shows how state‑supplied implied terms reduce certain error/transaction costs (and thereby limit opportunism) while also creating frictions for atypical arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE TEXAS RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION LIABILITY ACT: FRAMEWORK FOR CHANGE

shared_topics.topic: normative reform to improve doctrinal or statutory operation

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Formalist Theory of Contract Law Adjudication

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances an instrumentalist argument that formalist adjudication best serves contract law's market-promoting goals, and Paper B draws normative implications from its error-reduction analysis, arguing that interpretive principles should be shaped to improve ex ante contractual signaling and overall contractual performance.

papers.node_id: 2joflegalanalysis397!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF CONTRACTUAL SILENCE: A FIELD EXPERIMENT
papers.abstract:
Much of contract law concerns the formulation of default rules--rules that apply when contract documents are silent. Parties are free to change these rules by contract. For example, the Uniform Commercial Code Section 2-314 states the warranty of merchantability as a default rule that applies when a contract for the sale of goods is silent on warranties. Section 2-316 explains that the warranty of merchantability can be altered by explicit terms in a sales contract.
Most default rules aim to be majoritarian; the rulemakers intend the default rules to be the rules that would be included in the agreement if the parties had considered the issue (Scott & Kraus 2007, 89-93). If rulemakers can intuit people's expectations when making an agreement, then they save contracting parties the cost of formalizing those expectations in writing. There are many obstacles to the formulation of majoritarian default rules. Perhaps the greatest obstacle is that rulemakers do not know what most parties implicitly intend when they form an agreement and instead are forced to guess the majoritarian rule (Schwartz and Scott 2003).
This paper provides evidence about consumers' implicit understanding of contractual silence through the use of a field experiment. This empirical evidence is used to evaluate the quality of lawmakers' guesses regarding consumer expectations.
UsedApple iPod Nanoswere sold via auction to consumers on the eBay marketplace. The eBay format includes an item description section that frequently includes important contractual terms, such as the warranty of goods. Some randomly selected iPod auctions explicitly stated the warranty of merchantability in the warranty, taken from the UCC ("UCC iPods"). Other iPods were sold with all warranties disclaimed ("as is"), or with satisfaction guaranteed ("satisfaction guaranteed").
A fourth set of iPods were sold with the warranty section silent. Legally, this silence means that the default UCC warranty applies. If consumers interpret contractual silence appropriately (from a legal perspective), then "silent" term iPods should sell for similar prices to explicit UCC warranty iPods. If consumer interpretations of silence are more favorable than the default rule, then silent iPods should sell for more than iPods with explicit UCC warranties, while if silence is interpreted as having a worse meaning than the UCC, then silent iPods should sell for less than explicit UCC warranty iPods. In other words, substantial differences between prices for silent iPods and explicit UCC warranty iPods would suggest that the framers of the UCC have chosen a default rule that does not comport with most consumers' intuitive understanding of silence.
Unfortunately, the results of the field experiment are quite imprecise, precluding confident statements about relative prices. (The price of iPods fluctuates a surprising degree from day to day.) Ninety-five percent confidence bounds for the estimates presented in this paper include impact estimates that would alter the conclusions presented here. Nevertheless, the field experiment provides suggestive evidence that consumers interpret contractual silence appropriately. The UCC framers' best guess regarding consumer expectations is surprisingly accurate. Silent iPods sold for roughly the same price as legally identical iPods with the explicit UCC warranty sold during the same period. Silent iPods sell for over $ 3 less than otherwise identical satisfaction guaranteed iPods and for over $ 12 more than "as is" iPods. The field experiment results therefore suggest that the default rule for warranties roughly corresponds to the expectations of consumers; that is, the UCC rule is empirically majoritarian.
This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses existing literature on the selection of default rules. Section 3 describes the design of the field experiment. Section 4.1 presents summary statistics from the field experiment and demonstrates that consumers read and price different warranty terms on eBay. Section 4.2 examines how consumers interpret contractual silence and discusses whether the UCC warranty rule constitutes a majoritarian default rule. Section 5 concludes.

questions.question: Whether consumers interpret contractual silence about product warranties as conveying the same protections as an explicit default warranty, as revealed by similar willingness to pay.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Momentum

shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests whether consumers interpret contractual silence as conveying the UCC default warranty (i.e., whether silence functions like an implicit term), while Paper B analyzes why sophisticated parties use non-binding preliminary agreements to signal that a deal is likely to proceed, showing that form itself communicates expectations and coordinates behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private ordering and informal norms in producing compliance without formal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides evidence that consumers price and act as if default legal rules fill silent gaps, implying reliance on shared expectations rather than litigation; Paper B argues preliminary agreements function as signposts that generate momentum and adherence through norms and organizational practices rather than judicial enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract design and the choice of default rules or doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the UCC's default warranty aligns with consumer expectations (testing the majoritarian quality of defaults), and Paper B considers how the law should treat preliminary, non-binding agreements given their design role in dealmaking, both drawing normative lessons for how legal rules should be set or enforced.

shared_topics.topic: how ambiguity or incompleteness in pre-contractual stages affects downstream bargaining and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the economic effect of leaving warranty terms silent (incomplete specification) on prices and consumer behavior, while Paper B studies how parties deliberately leave preliminary agreements non-binding or brief (incompleteness) and how that incompleteness coincides with a stage of resolved uncertainty that shapes the final deal.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts

shared_topics.topic: alignment between legal default rules/doctrines and real contracting expectations

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames default rules as a cost-saving device to govern issues parties do not draft, using experimental evidence to assess their adequacy, while Paper B analyzes intentionally relational contracts (and integrated project delivery) as contractual designs that manage uncertainty, reduce renegotiation costs, and allocate risk dynamically over time.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of technological and marketplace contexts on contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies contracts and consumer behavior in an online marketplace (eBay) to see how listing formats and silence affect prices and expectations, whereas Paper B examines how collaborative digital technologies (e.g., BIM, data interchange) reshape incentives and make relational contracting more feasible and attractive in industry practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ORGANIC TRANSACTIONS: CONTRACT, FRANK LLOYD WRIGHT AND THE JOHNSON BUILDING

shared_topics.topic: reliance on informal governance, norms, and ongoing relationships instead of formal legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how consumers price and behave when contracts are silent (implying reliance on market norms and expectations rather than negotiated legal clauses), while Paper B documents how S.C. shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a field experiment on eBay to measure actual market responses to different warranty language, and Paper B uses archival materials and interviews as a case study of a real-world contractual relationship to assess how contracts function in practice.

shared_topics.topic: consequences for legal rulemaking and policy about contract law's practical role
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws implications for whether default rules chosen by drafters (the UCC) are majoritarian and therefore appropriate, whereas Paper B questions policy prescriptions (such as transplanting Western contract law) by showing that formal legal rules may play a limited or symbolic role in governing commercial behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INTERPRETATION OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACTS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY

shared_topics.topic: empirical assessment of parties' expectations/preferences about contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a field experiment on eBay to infer how consumer buyers interpret warranty silence versus explicit warranty language, while Paper B analyzes 1,521 SEC-disclosed commercial contracts to infer sophisticated parties' revealed preferences for textualist interpretation clauses.

shared_topics.topic: alignment between legal default or interpretive doctrines and contracting parties' expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the UCC warranty-of-merchantability default corresponds to consumer expectations as revealed by prices, and Paper B evaluates whether the textualist interpretation regime (as implemented by merger clauses) corresponds to the preferences of contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: meaning and signaling of explicit versus omitted contractual language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how silence in the warranty section functions (whether it is interpreted like an explicit default, or differently), while Paper B studies the inclusion of explicit textualist clauses (merger, no-oral-modification) as signals about interpretation rules and their non-random co-occurrence with other clauses.

shared_topics.topic: using empirical data to inform doctrinal and normative debates in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers bring empirical methods to bear on longstanding theoretical disputes in contract doctrine—Paper A via a field experiment testing defaults and consumer behavior, and Paper B via systematic contract-document analysis testing the prevalence and associations of interpretive clauses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82lawcontempprob1!!ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: alignment of default rules/contractual silence with market expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether the UCC default warranty that applies when contract language is silent matches consumer expectations by comparing prices across explicit, disclaimed, and silent eBay listings; Paper B argues normatively that courts should assume contracts conform to market norms and therefore adopt interpretive defaults that track ordinary market expectations rather than imaginative judicial reconstructions.

shared_topics.topic: use of market norms and standard terms as benchmarks for interpreting ambiguous language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how consumers read and price explicit warranty language versus silence—showing that market actors treat standard warranty statements meaningfully—while Paper B develops an interpretive methodology (normative triangulation) that prioritizes published market norms and trade usage as primary external references when courts resolve ambiguity in contract language.

shared_topics.topic: legal treatment and consequences of boilerplate/standardized terms (including externalities)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies standardized warranty formulations ('as is', 'satisfaction guaranteed', UCC text, or silence) and their effects on transaction prices and consumer expectations, and Paper B analyzes how boilerplate functions en masse, emphasizing that interpretation should account for the broader externalities boilerplate imposes across market participants and minimize anti-social term selection.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal rules and interpretive doctrines should be grounded in actual contracting behavior (empirical vs. normative justification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A supplies field-experimental evidence assessing whether an existing statutory default conforms to consumer behavior, and Paper B provides a normative argument that courts should rely on market-general signals and predictable social determinants—effectively grounding interpretive doctrine in observable market patterns and practical predictability.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical evidence and consequences in choosing and evaluating default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contributes experimental evidence about consumer expectations to evaluate the quality of a statutory default (the UCC warranty), highlighting empirical limits and interpretation; Paper B argues that debates about contract's scope should be tied to consequentialist considerations (including how defaults affect behavior) and cites empirical or bargaining-based theories (e.g., penalty defaults) as relevant to selecting defaults.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SPACE BETWEEN MARKETS AND HIERARCHIES

shared_topics.topic: the role of default rules and the costs/benefits of leaving contract terms silent versus specifying them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether the UCC warranty default matches consumer expectations when contracts are silent, exploring the drafting-cost rationale for defaults; Paper B discusses why firms choose particular contractual arrangements (vs vertical integration) in light of transaction costs and the tradeoffs of specifying detailed contractual rights.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on warranties and disclaimers as contractual allocations of liability that affect ex post outcomes for buyers and sellers, while Paper B explicitly argues that hybrid contracts (carving out control rights, long-term contracts) can guard against hold-up problems arising from relation-specific investments.

shared_topics.topic: evidence-driven inquiry into how real-world parties respond to contractual arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a field experiment on eBay to measure consumer pricing responses to different warranty language (including silence), and Paper B marshals industry examples, case discussion, and empirical trends in offshoring to assess how firms actually structure hybrid governance contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOMEONE ELSE MAY OWN A PIECE OF YOU: LACK OF FEDERAL REGULATION OVER DIRECT-TO-CONSUMER DNA TEST KITS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the current legal landscape as insufficient to protect genetic privacy and proposes legislative reforms, and Paper B investigates whether existing UCC defaults accurately reflect and protect consumer expectations in the market for used goods, thereby testing the protective fit of current legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: contractual allocation of ownership/risks over personal assets (goods or data)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how privacy policies allocate rights and potential ownership/uses of consumers' genetic data, effectively assigning risk and control to firms, whereas Paper B examines how warranty clauses and contractual silence allocate risk and implied ownership interests in the sale of goods.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE AMBIGUITY: IP LICENSES AS A CASE STUDY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the UCC's default warranty rule aligns with consumer expectations and thus justifies that default, whereas Paper B proposes normative guidelines for judicial tolerance or supplementation of ambiguous provisions depending on transaction traits.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides field-experimental data from eBay to assess how market actors interpret silence, and Paper B draws on multidisciplinary social-science and complex-systems research to justify when ambiguity is socially and economically desirable for shaping legal treatment.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Impracticability as Risk Allocation: The Effect of Changed Circumstances Upon Contract Obligations for the Sale of Goods

shared_topics.topic: how courts or law supply terms when contracts are silent or incomplete
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses judicial allocation of risk and excuse doctrines when contracts lack provisions for changed circumstances, while Paper B experimentally investigates how contractual silence is interpreted in practice and whether statutory defaults fill those gaps in the way parties expect.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS
