shared_topics.topic: the role of formality versus consent in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how contemporary commercial actors use master agreements to fix terms in advance and thereby reduce reliance on competing transactional forms (invoices, confirmations), raising questions about whether consent embodied in non-standard or pre-exchanged documents will be treated as dispositive; Paper B analyzes the Roman distinction between formal contracts (stipulatio) and consensual sales, emphasizing that sale was binding by consent without special formalities and contrasting that with other contracts that required delivery, thus engaging the same substantive issue of when mere agreement suffices to create obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial practice interacts with and drives doctrinal development
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses empirical data on business contracting practices (battle of the forms, master agreements) to ask whether legal doctrine and courts will adapt to those practices; Paper B provides a historical argument that Roman jurists recognized sale because of prevailing transactional practices and that tradition then constrained further doctrinal development, likewise studying law as responsive to (and bounded by) practice.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal limits on recognizing and enforcing non‑standard or pre‑packaged transaction devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether courts and scholars will accept master agreements and thereby effectively eliminate 'the battle of the forms,' highlighting possible doctrinal objections despite commercial utility; Paper B examines Roman law's refusal to recognize certain transaction types (e.g., generic sale, fully developed barter) and treats those absences as deliberate doctrinal limits that reflect, and sometimes frustrate, commercial needs.

papers.node_id: 83lawcontempprob71!!ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS
papers.abstract:
Traditional economic analysis distinguishes economic organization along three dimensions: firm, contract, and market. This categorization is misleading in any number of respects, but none more so than the assumption that contract and market are separate modes of exchange. In fact, other than barter, which is almost unknown in contemporary commercial transactions, every market transaction is implemented by contract. Thus, in markets the two modes of exchange are inextricably combined.Moreover, the vast majority of contract activity occurs in some form of market, so it does not require much loss of generalization to say that not only are contracts in all markets, but markets are also in all contracts. This implies that as markets change in character so too will the contracts that are embedded in them. Economists have failed to appreciate the implications of this integration of contract and market because of their naive and parsimonious conception of contract. But lawyers, too, have failed to appreciate the tension between the fact that markets change the shape of contract and the state's commitment to a unitary regime of contract law. This failure to understand the relationship between contract law and the central institutions of economic organization has significant consequences. Among them is the failure to recognize what I call the fundamental paradox of contracting in markets, the topic that I take up in this Article.
To explain the paradox, I begin by distinguishing two quite different economic objectives. The first objective is the goal of efficient market exchange through contract - the process of designing contracts that motivate parties to maximize the joint gains from transactions.The second quite distinct objectiveis the efficient production of contracts - the process of creating widely useful terms and conditions that implement enforceable legal obligations. Much of law and economics scholarship has been devoted to the first efficiency objective but, until recently, the second has been virtually unexplored.Thus, we know a great deal about how to design contracts to motivate parties to invest optimally in their relationship, but very little about the shape-shifting process by which widely-used contract terms that motivate investment are produced. Yet, that production process is the source of the paradox of contracting in markets: as markets thicken (more and more parties participate in the same or similar transactions), the factors that generate efficiencies in the production of contracts - standardization and economies of scale - are the same factors that produce inefficiencies in the very contract terms that parties rely on to motivate performance. And, as with any paradox, the reverse is true: the factors that produce more efficient contract design - bespoke efforts to motivate investment and trade - are the same factors that generate the loss of scale and the resulting inefficiencies in the production of contracts.
Recognizing this paradox is the first step toward answering a central question that remains unresolved: how can (and do) contracting parties in thick, multilateral markets optimize between efficient production of contracts and efficient contract design?The challenge is to exploit production efficiencies without at the same time degrading the contract terms that motivate performance. My claim is that the key to optimizing the activity of contracting in thick markets requires overcoming a fundamental collective action problem endemic to the production process: the private interests of the parties in these markets diverge from their collective interests. Understanding how effective coordination can create a functioning network to address the obsolescence that is a byproduct of standardization has important normative implications. In particular, it suggests that current approaches to consumer transactions that focuson the regulation of exploitative terms inbilateralcontractual relations misconceive the problem. Consumer contracts are made in large,multilateralmarkets. Understanding the inherent inefficiencies of contracts in those markets is the key to reframing the regulation of consumer transactions. State assistance in overcoming collective action impediments in these markets is likely to be far more efficacious than either unconscionability constraints on adhesion contractsor traditional command and control regulation of patently abusive terms.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part II sets out the paradox of contracting in markets in some detail. I first explain how parties in thin orbilateralcontracting markets optimize contracting costs by shifting resources between the transaction costs of negotiating and drafting ex ante agreements and the expected litigation costs of enforcing those contracts. This bespoke balancing of ex ante and ex post contracting costs produces the most efficient transaction for the contracting cost.But as markets thicken, traders can exploit economies of scale inmultilateralcontracting markets by standardizing the production of the contracts that govern the exchange transaction.However, this standardization leads to inefficiencies endemic to boilerplate: boilerplate terms are sticky, resistant to adaptation to changed conditions, and subject to "black holes" that remain in the contract even in the face of adverse legal consequences.I examine the ways in which obsolete design has led to costly litigation in thick markets, particularly the markets for sovereign and corporate bonds, where agency costs have impaired efforts to revise obsolete contracts terms.
In Part III, I trace the different ways that some parties who trade in multilateral markets have overcome the collective action problems that impede more efficient contract design by creating a governance structure - or "spider" - to organize their loose web of relationships. This focus on coordination and cooperation conceives of the contracting parties in multilateral markets as potential members of a commercial network with the capacity to shareinformation in important ways.I explore the different forms of network organization from trade associations that function in low uncertainty environments to supply chain networks that share information in more uncertain settings.In some cases, however, high uncertainty renders parties incapable of coordinating their network activities. The leafy green industry illustrates how in this environment the state can facilitate coordination by helping to create a spider for the network.
In Part IV, I turn to the normative question of how best to deal with the problems of bad contract design in consumer markets. Consumer transactions have long been a fraught subject for scholarly analysis. Many scholars continue to view the regulation of consumer contracts through the lens of the bilateral contracting market.Even when the focus properly shifts to multilateral markets, few solutions to perceived inefficiencies have gained traction. Early efforts to motivate disclosure have foundered on the multiplicity of terms in consumer contracts, a form of information overload that prevents market forces from eliminating inefficient terms. I argue that conceiving of consumers and their sellers as a network without any spider offers a fresh perspective on why conventional solutions to reducing the costs of inefficient (and exploitative) contract terms have been unsuccessful. I conclude that a regulatory solution that aids in organizing the network of buyers and sellers may better address the problem of obsolete and encrusted contract terms in multilateral consumer markets.

questions.question: How do parties in thick, multilateral markets trade off the efficiencies of standardized, mass-produced contract terms against the need for bespoke contract design that motivates optimal investment and performance?

How and under what conditions can decentralized market participants organize (via private network governance) to overcome collective action problems and revise or update obsolete boilerplate in multilateral contracting markets?

Can state-facilitated coordination of market participants more effectively address inefficient or exploitative standardized contract terms in consumer markets than traditional bilateral-focused regulatory tools?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 89michlrev1815!!ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL BARGAINS: THE NORMATIVE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL BARGAINS: THE NORMATIVE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: tension between standardized (boilerplate) contracts and bespoke contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how thick markets drive standardization and economies of scale in contract production that can undermine the bespoke terms needed to motivate performance, while Paper B treats how interpretive conventions and default rules should account for the prevalence of standard terms versus individualized bargains when construing parties' obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of market custom and collective practices in shaping contractual content and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that multilateral markets produce widely used terms and that parties may need collective governance (trade associations, networks) to update them, while Paper B examines how courts should use custom and typical practices (or the behavior of parties of a given 'type') when constructing hypothetical bargains and interpretive rules.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when courts or law should supply terms not explicitly agreed to (implied duties / hypothetical bargains)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly debates the justification and method for enforcing hypothetical bargains and implying duties such as good faith, and Paper A raises the related normative question of how contract law should respond to inefficient or obsolete terms in mass-market contracts where explicit negotiation is rare.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between instrumental efficiency (transaction-cost minimization) and party autonomy/consent in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a dual efficiency problem—efficient market exchange versus efficient production of contracts—and argues for collective solutions, while Paper B analyzes justificatory principles (autonomy, fair allocation, minimizing transaction costs) to determine when interpretive conventions should override literal assent.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and enforcement problems arising from obsolete or ambiguous standardized terms in thick markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents costly litigation and 'sticky' boilerplate that resists adaptation in markets (e.g., bond and consumer markets), and Paper B develops a framework for how interpreters should resolve ambiguity and supply terms—addressing exactly the doctrinal problems that obsolete standardized language creates for courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45iowajcorpl885!!ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal (written/legal) and informal (relational/norms-based) contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the 'braiding' thesis that many modern collaborations combine enforceable contract provisions with informal governance to manage opportunism, while Paper B analyzes how market-embedded contracts (including standardized boilerplate) coexist with informal market practices and how that mix shapes incentives and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: effect of market thickness/scale on contract form and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats market 'thickness' as a determinant of when parties choose braided or other contractual tools, and Paper B centers the paradox that as markets thicken standardization and scale efficiencies arise but can degrade contract quality and adaptability.

shared_topics.topic: organizational governance solutions for multilateral contracting problems (committees, networks, 'spiders')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies institutional innovations like DoD 'alpha contracting' with joint committee structures to manage preliminary, collaborative negotiations, while Paper B studies how actors in thick markets create governance architectures (trade associations, supply-chain networks, or a coordinating 'spider') to overcome collective-action barriers in contract production.

shared_topics.topic: contracting under uncertainty and incentives for relationship-specific investment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes joint learning, information-sharing, and locking-in investments as functions of braided agreements in uncertain, innovative projects, and Paper B examines how bespoke contract design vs boilerplate affects parties' ability to motivate investment and adapt under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: normative role for state and courts in shaping or assisting contractual networks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how judicial intervention can complement or crowd out informal governance and situates braiding within a non-unitary theory of contract law, while Paper B argues for targeted state facilitation (rather than only bilateral consumer protections) to help organize networks and address obsolete or exploitative standard terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev379!!SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior as a justification for legal intervention or contractual design limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how opportunism (especially combined with sunk costs and bounded rationality) motivates courts or legislatures to imply terms or adopt default rules to curb strategic behavior, while Paper B identifies agency costs and opportunistic dynamics in thick markets as drivers of boilerplate stickiness and the need for collective or state remedies to prevent exploitative or inefficient contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between standardized background/default rules and bespoke contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the distinction between background/default legal rules and after-the-fact judicially-implied terms, arguing that defaults can be justified when individual contracting is too costly, and Paper B develops the paradox that standardization (boilerplate) yields production efficiencies but can degrade the quality of contract design, forcing a choice between scale and tailored incentives.

shared_topics.topic: collective action and coordination problems in producing and updating widely used contract terms, and the role of governance or the state
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses why default rules or statutory regimes (e.g., the UCC) may be imposed because individual parties face high contracting costs, and Paper B diagnoses a collective action problem in multilateral markets—arguing that private networks or state-facilitated 'spiders' are needed to coordinate revision and production of efficient contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: information problems (bounded rationality, asymmetry, and information overload) that undermine contractual completeness and effective consent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes bounded rationality and information asymmetries as sources of contract incompleteness and as limits on parties' ability to bargain around defaults, while Paper B highlights information overload in consumer markets and the inability of market forces to eliminate inefficient terms, showing how informational constraints shape both contract form and legal responses.

shared_topics.topic: standard-form/adhesion contracts, consent, notice, and the limits of private contracting for consumer protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about freedom from contract, consent under long form and click-through agreements, and the uncertainty of standards like promissory estoppel, whereas Paper B focuses on consumer boilerplate in multilateral markets and argues that regulatory or network-level interventions may be more effective than bilateral unconscionability doctrines at addressing exploitative standardized terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev99!!ARTICLE: THE SPACE BETWEEN MARKETS AND HIERARCHIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SPACE BETWEEN MARKETS AND HIERARCHIES

shared_topics.topic: contractual governance as an alternative between markets and firms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze contracting as a governance mechanism that sits between spot markets and firm hierarchies: Paper A shows how hybrid outsourcing arrangements (partial ownership plus retained control rights) serve as a middle ground for locating production, while Paper B theorizes that contracts are embedded in markets and that market change reshapes contractual forms, blurring the firm/market divide.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of control rights to mitigate hold‑up and agency problems
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how contract design allocates control, residual rights, and commitments to manage relation‑specific investments and agency risks: Paper A emphasizes carving out control rights in hybrids to prevent hold‑up and reduce agency distortions in offshore outsourcing, and Paper B emphasizes contract terms as the primary tool to motivate investments and avoid opportunism, especially in multilateral settings.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between standardized (scale) contracts and bespoke incentive alignment
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between using standardized, scalable contract forms and bespoke, transaction‑specific drafting: Paper A discusses how different organizational choices (captives, competitive vendors, hybrids) balance cost pressures and bespoke control, while Paper B develops the paradox that standardization yields production efficiencies but can degrade the incentive‑architectures that bespoke contracts provide.

shared_topics.topic: the need for network or collective governance to produce and sustain contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider governance beyond bilateral deals—how multi‑party coordination or network structures shape contract production and enforcement: Paper A explores industry‑level outsourcing arrangements and evolving contractual innovations that enable complex vendor relationships, and Paper B analyzes how ‘spiders’ or supply‑chain networks overcome collective‑action problems to coordinate standard terms and update obsolete contract boilerplate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38yalejonreg707!!ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal institutions/doctrine and economic analysis of contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a unitary regime of contract law interacts (and sometimes mismatches) with market-driven, embedded contracts and their standardization, while Paper B examines how lawyers' deep knowledge of statutes, doctrines, and institutional processes is indispensable to rigorous economic analysis of law.

shared_topics.topic: coordination and governance mechanisms to resolve collective-action problems in multilateral contracting markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how market participants create governance structures (trade associations, supply‑chain networks, or a state‑facilitated 'spider') to overcome collective‑action barriers to revising standardized contracts, and Paper B highlights law schools and legal scholars as institutional coordinators who synthesize multidisciplinary perspectives and structure scholarly and policy collaboration.

shared_topics.topic: normative implications for legal policy and regulation of contracts and markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes reframing consumer‑contract regulation toward state assistance in organizing buyer‑seller networks rather than bilateral unconscionability rules, while Paper B addresses how legal academics influence the normative framing of law‑and‑economics and the policy goals that guide legal reform.

shared_topics.topic: limits of abstract economic modeling and the need for contextual, analogical, and multidisciplinary reasoning in understanding contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes economists' parsimonious conception of contract and emphasizes context, standardization effects, and market dynamics, whereas Paper B argues that lawyers' analogical reasoning and cross‑disciplinary training supplement and correct the simplifying assumptions of economic models when analyzing legal problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between market forces and contract law as complementary mechanisms for ensuring performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that market transactions are always implemented by contracts and that markets shape contract terms, advocating state facilitation where market-produced contracts become inefficient; Paper B analyzes 'law glue' alongside market, moral, and social sanctions, treating state enforcement as one of several complementary mechanisms that sustain contractual performance.

shared_topics.topic: tension between transactional (bespoke) contracting and standardized/relational contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a paradox where bespoke contract design produces better incentives but standardization produces production efficiencies (boilerplate problems), while Paper B contrasts the Contract-as-Transaction paradigm with Contract-as-Relation, debating whether doctrine should treat contracts as isolated transactions or as ongoing relational arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: collective action and coordination problems in multilateral or continuing relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies a collective action problem in thick markets that prevents parties from updating or improving standardized contract terms and proposes network governance or state-aided 'spiders' to coordinate; Paper B emphasizes social and market 'glues' (including reputational and relational pressures) that coordinate behavior in ongoing relationships and supports the idea that non-legal coordination mechanisms matter to contract performance.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between ex ante contracting (drafting/standardization) and ex post enforcement (litigation/enforcement system design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties in thin markets balance negotiating/drafting costs against expected litigation costs and how thick markets shift that balance toward standardized production; Paper B focuses on the relevance of enforcement-system characteristics, noting that people have preferences over enforcement costs and that the state's design of enforcement influences contracting behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev707!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.topic: how remedies (damages vs specific performance) and the concept of efficient breach shape contracting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the German preference for specific performance and fault-based liability with common-law reliance on damages and the efficient-breach idea, showing how remedial regimes alter parties' incentives; Paper B analyzes how contract design and enforcement (including the tradeoff between ex ante drafting and ex post litigation/remedies) affect parties' investment incentives and the optimal shape of contracts in markets.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the state and legal rules in structuring contract markets and overcoming collective-action problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how statutory regimes (e.g., CISG, EC consumer sales directive) and judge-made doctrines (Hadley) influence commercial behavior and cross-border contracting, while Paper B argues that state intervention or facilitation may be necessary to organize market actors (create a "spider") to address coordination failures and reform obsolete standardized contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of predictability, certainty, and rule clarity for transactional efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the vagueness of the foreseeability rule and emphasizes German law's premium on predictable, rule-based outcomes to reduce judicial discretion; Paper B shows that predictable, standardized contract terms generate production efficiencies in thick markets but can become obsolete and create inefficiencies if not governed, linking legal certainty to transactional costs.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between private market practices (standardization, trade customs) and formal contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how merchants' practices, commercial attitudes, and international drafters (e.g., Ernst Rabel, merchants opposing foreseeability) shaped substantive rules and their application; Paper B analyzes how market participants produce boilerplate and governance networks to standardize contracts, and how those private-production processes interact with and sometimes frustrate formal legal regulation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis383!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT

shared_topics.topic: how contracts deal with unforeseen contingencies and tacit assumptions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with the fact that contracts are often silent about many future contingencies — Paper B develops and defends a 'shared‑assumption' test for when tacit, unstated assumptions justify judicial relief for unexpected events, while Paper A analyzes how thick markets and standardized boilerplate leave many contingencies unaddressed and generate inefficiencies when conditions change.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and default legal rules in filling contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is centrally concerned with when courts should excuse performance or imply terms (defending a judicial shared‑assumption approach), and Paper A critiques the limits of a unitary contract law regime while arguing for state or institutional interventions (beyond simple policing of bilateral adhesion) to address obsolescent or exploitative standardized terms in multilateral markets.

shared_topics.topic: how party sophistication and market context shape contractual expectations and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both authors emphasize that contracting parties’ sophistication and the market environment matter — Paper B distinguishes sophisticated commercial actors from unsophisticated parties when assessing tacit assumptions and foreseeability, and Paper A shows how thick multilateral markets (and differences among participants) drive standardization, collective‑action problems, and differing capacities to revise contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the costs of standardization/boilerplate and the tension between bespoke contract design and scalable production
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how standard form contracts achieve production efficiencies yet create 'sticky' or obsolete terms that impair performance and provoke litigation; Paper B complements this by showing that many contracts are necessarily silent (tacit assumptions) and that silence creates doctrinal issues about when legal excuse or gap‑filling is appropriate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev1012!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: How Did We End Up in a World Where Browsewraps Are Enforced Even When They Waive All Consumer Rights?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: How Did We End Up in a World Where Browsewraps Are Enforced Even When They Waive All Consumer Rights?

shared_topics.topic: enforcement and harms of standardized/boilerplate/adhesive contracts in consumer markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how market thickening leads to standardized boilerplate that is sticky, obsolete, and generates inefficiencies in multilateral consumer markets; Paper B documents the practical harms when courts enforce standardized online form contracts (clickwraps/browsewraps) that waive consumer rights and function as adhesive terms.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries between repeat players and consumers and their impact on contract fairness

papers.node_id: 54fordhamlrev35!!ARTICLE: THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE AND IMPLIED TERMS: THE SOUNDS OF SILENCE.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE AND IMPLIED TERMS: THE SOUNDS OF SILENCE.
papers.abstract:
WHEN a client asks his lawyer what his duties are under a particular written contract, the lawyer's first words of response are usually: "Show me the contract." Yet a party's contractual obligations cannot be determined solely from a literal reading of a contractual document.  The obvious first step is to interpret the document's language in light of all relevant circumstances, including any prior dealings between the parties and usages of the trade.  Assuming that interpretation reveals no provision in the writing covering a particular issue, should the lawyer advise the client that he has no obligations other than those listed in the contract?  Definitely not.
A seller of goods, for example, may have made no express warranties, yet be liable for breach of implied warranties arising from the circumstances of the sale.Furthermore, an obligation of good faith and fair dealing, which exists in all contracts,requires in some cases only absence of interference in the other party's performance, but in others, affirmative conduct to cooperate in enhancing the other party's profitsunder the contract.Assuming that the parties intend a contract, terms absent from the agreement of the partiesbut necessary for the resolution of the parties' contractual rights and obligations may be supplied by the court.The purpose of this Articleis to explore the relationship between the implication of terms, sometimes called "the process of implication,"and the parol evidence rule.  Although each topic has been the subject of considerable scholarly examination,the relationship between the two has received scant attention.
The parol evidence rule states that if the parties assent to a writing as the final and complete expression of the terms of their agreement, evidence of prior or contemporaneous agreements may not be admitted to contradict, vary, or add to the terms of the writing.Although the courts traditionally assumed such assent from the mere fact that an apparently complete writing was entered into,the Uniform Commercial Code and the Second Restatement of Contracts (Second Restatement) no longer make that assumption.The increased willingness of courts to supply terms to fill gaps in parties' agreements and the liberalization of the parol evidence rule mean that one who enters into an apparently complete written contract has no assurance that his only obligations are those expressed in the writing.  A court might "imply" a term, or permit the other party to prove a term agreed to during negotiations but not included in the final written agreement.  This Article explores the dynamic between the two possibilities.
Part I of this Article considers whether a rule of law that applies to the agreement as written is protected by the parol evidence rule.  This issue arises when a party seeks to introduce proof of an oral agreement displacing a rule of law that would apply to the agreement as written.  Parts II through V pose the opposite question: Does the parol evidence rule exclude a term implied by law?  Whereas the issue addressed in Part I assumes that the court has already decided that a legal obligation exists, Parts II through V do not.  Part II considers whether the parol evidence rule applies to obligations imposed by law.  In other words, does the fact that the parties have entered into a written agreement effect the court's ability (or willingness) to supply a term?  Parts III through V consider whether the parol evidence rule bars proof of the negotiations of the partiesto establish a legal obligation (Part III), to give definition to a legal obligation (Part IV) or to negate a legal obligation (Part V).
The inquiry into the relationship between the parol evidence rule and implied terms is complicated by the lack of uniformity of scholarly and judicial opinion as to the scope of the rule.This lack of uniformity in turn reflects divergent opinions on the theoretical bases of the rule.Although most authorities agree that the parol evidence rule is not a rule of evidence,there is no agreement as to whether it is a rule of substantive law based on the intention of the parties,a rule of form which operates to limit freedom of contract,a rule of estoppel,a rule of procedureor a rule of judicial convenience.
A second complication arises because this inquiry requires careful identification of the basis on which the particular obligation is implied.  An obligation may be implied as an inference of the intention of the parties, i.e., implied in fact, or as a duty imposed by law to fill a gap in the parties' agreement, i.e., implied in law.The courts, though, are seldomclear as to whether "implied" terms are imposed by law or implied in fact.The distinction, however, may have certain consequences on the operation of the parol evidence rule.This Article will generally adopt the Second Restatement approach that "implied" terms are usually imposed by law,but will also consider the consequences of treating those terms as implications of fact.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how implied terms and the liberalization of the parol evidence rule can defeat parties' expectations that a written instrument captures all obligations; Paper B critiques the fragility of a system that seeks to protect private ordering for sophisticated parties while imposing different constraints (e.g., consumer protection doctrines), highlighting similar limits on autonomy occasioned by doctrinal intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the role of drafting practices, standardized clauses, and 'boilerplate' in shaping legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how trade usages, prior dealings, and the circumstances of bargaining can create implied warranties or obligations not memorialized in the writing; Paper B analyzes how modular drafting, portability of clauses, and cut-and-paste practices cause doctrinal rules and clauses to migrate across contexts and produce unintended legal effects.

shared_topics.topic: importance of doctrinal classification (e.g., implied-in-fact vs implied-in-law; consumer vs sophisticated parties) for rule application and consequences of category instability

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52hastingslj645!!SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of trade usage, prior dealings, and 'merchant reality' to interpreting and implying contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes interpreting writings in light of prior dealings and trade usages and how those facts can give rise to implied warranties or duties, and Paper B recounts Llewellyn's conception of the UCC as reflecting empirical 'merchant reality' and raises the empirical and normative question of how far law should ratify commercial practice.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames implied terms versus parol evidence in light of differing theoretical bases (substantive law, estoppel, form) and notes consequences of treating implied terms as law-imposed or fact-based, while Paper B directly debates statute versus common law, the ALI vs NCCUSL roles, and how those institutional choices determine whether gaps are filled by courts or by legislatures.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy (freedom of contract) and courts/statutes supplying default or mandatory terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether parties who execute an apparently complete writing can avoid legal obligations supplied by courts (implied-in-law) or proved from negotiations, and Paper B raises whether commercial law should prioritize default rules that honor party choice or protect weaker parties and when to limit parties' ability to select governing law or contract around defaults.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary status of trade usage, course of dealing, and course of performance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the evidentiary role of commercial customs and prior dealings: Paper A cites prior dealings and trade usages as context for interpretation and potential bases for implied obligations, and Paper B specifically treats trade usage/public conventional meaning as admissible interpretive evidence while warning against admitting course-of-performance or subjective-intent evidence.

shared_topics.justification: Both works address when a contract is treated as ambiguous and whether courts may fill gaps or supply terms—Paper A explores whether the parol evidence rule blocks proof of terms the court might supply, and Paper B discusses using public meaning to preserve predictability while reserving extrinsic, intent-based evidence for equitable claims where fairness, not textual meaning, justifies supplementation.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Judicial Incorporation of Trade Usages: A Functional Solution to the Opportunism Problem

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames judicial incorporation of norms as a form of gap-filling that can supply terms parties did not expressly write to prevent opportunism; Paper B systematically examines courts' power to imply terms—distinguishing implied-in-fact from implied-in-law—and whether the law may supply missing contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between a plain-meaning/parol-evidence approach and admission of extrinsic norms or negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a plain-meaning (anti-incorporation) stance with an incorporationist approach and critiques cost/benefit claims of plain-meaning advocates; Paper B directly analyzes the parol evidence rule and whether it bars (or permits) evidence of prior negotiations, usages, or implied obligations that would vary or supplement a writing.

shared_topics.topic: normative/functional justifications for supplying or refusing extrinsic obligations (including controlling opportunism and effectuating parties' expectations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a functional, goal-oriented defense of incorporating trade usages to deter opportunistic behavior and achieve contracting goals; Paper B links the implication of terms to resolving parties' contractual rights, supplying duties like good faith, and assesses theoretical bases for when courts should impose such obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105valrev1025!!ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FAUX CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: how contractual obligations can arise from sources other than the final integrated writing (implied terms, in-fact or in-law)

shared_topics.topic: the limits of reliance on a written document as the sole measure of parties' duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the assumption that drafting a formal document is primarily about enforceability and shows actors rely on non-legal mechanisms to implement deal terms, and Paper B interrogates the legal assumption that a written integrated agreement exhausts parties' obligations by considering when extrinsic evidence or implied duties supplement or displace the writing.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and doctrinal treatment of prior negotiations and their ability to define, negate, or supplement contractual duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses interviews to show that negotiated understandings and the process of drafting (even if labeled non-binding) influence conduct and later contract terms, while Paper B analyzes whether the parol evidence rule permits proof of negotiations to establish, define, or negate obligations and how courts distinguish implied terms from proven negotiated terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether the parol evidence rule should exclude proof of negotiations used to create, define, or negate implied contractual duties, and Paper B examines how advertising claims, promotional offers, and seller intent (pre-contractual representations) factor into liability under deception doctrines like the FTC Act and statutory regulation.

shared_topics.topic: the definitional boundary problems that determine the scope of legal enforcement (what counts as an 'implied term' or a 'bait-and-switch')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes conceptual distinctions (implied in fact vs implied in law) and how those labels affect application of the parol evidence rule, while Paper B critiques competing definitions of bait-and-switch (FTC narrow definition vs broader popular usages like 'teasers' and 'free offers') and shows how definitional choices shape regulatory outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMBEDDED OPTIONS AND THE CASE AGAINST COMPENSATION IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts may imply terms or admit parol evidence to fill gaps in an apparently complete writing and asks when judicially supplied obligations should bind the parties; Paper B similarly debates the proper judicial role, arguing courts should not impose a compensatory damages default but instead enforce parties' negotiated termination/option terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how extrinsic evidence—prior dealings, trade usages, and negotiations—may be used or barred under the parol evidence rule to define or add terms, and Paper B likewise grounds its account of heterogeneous option prices in the parties' negotiated bargains and market practices, implicating the significance of negotiation-history and commercial context for what obligations actually exist.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether assent to a written integration prevents admission of prior or contemporaneous negotiations to displace or define legal obligations and whether courts can imply terms despite integration; Paper B contrasts doctrines (hard/Williston vs soft/Corbin) and describes the spectrum of how courts treat integration and admit evidence of prior agreements, oral conditions, or collateral terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks what caused apparent recent changes in contract doctrine and surveys possible drivers of legal change, and Paper B attributes and examines doctrinal shifts (e.g., influence of the UCC and the Second Restatement) and links those instruments and judicial reasoning to evolving treatment of implied terms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the broader debate over conservative/formalist versus interventionist approaches to private law, and Paper B analyzes the specific conflict between treating a writing as the complete expression (parol evidence/formal rule) and judicial interventions that supply implied-in-law or implied-in-fact terms.

shared_topics.topic: effects of doctrinal change on private ordering, predictability, and parties' expectations

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: TAXONOMY FOR JUSTIFYING LEGAL INTERVENTION IN AN IMPERFECT WORLD: WHAT TO DO WHEN PARTIES HAVE NOT ACHIEVED BARGAINS OR HAVE DRAFTED INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the circumstances under which courts imply terms (implied in law vs in fact) and how such implied terms interact with the parol evidence rule, while Paper B develops a welfare-oriented taxonomy for when judicial intervention to fill gaps or supply liability rules in incomplete contracts is justified (focusing on opportunism, sunk costs, and behavioral uncertainty).

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores obligations like the duty of good faith and when such duties can be supplied or evidenced despite an apparently complete writing, and Paper B treats the good-faith doctrine and law-imposed performance obligations as examples of court-supplied solutions to control opportunism and increase gains from trade.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the parol evidence rule and doctrines about admissible proof affect whether extrinsic agreements or implied obligations can be enforced; Paper B critiques the simplistic treatment of enforcement in economic models and emphasizes verifiability and litigation realities as constraints that influence what terms will be written and enforced.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrines and limits under which courts imply terms (in fact or in law) to fill gaps in written agreements, while Paper B treats incomplete contracting as a central problem and examines how parties (and courts indirectly) must fill gaps in long‑term relations through renegotiation or governance arrangements.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the parol evidence rule and whether it bars admission of prior negotiations or proof of legal obligations, and Paper B argues empirically and doctrinally that understanding contractual disputes requires looking beyond the formal instrument to relational evidence and private ordering.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the obligation of good faith and fair dealing and how its content can vary with context, while Paper B focuses on long‑term relational contracts where parties are expected to adapt cooperatively, consider hostage strategies, and make commitments that amount to implied duties supporting the relationship.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether legal rules or judge‑supplied obligations are displaced or protected by the written agreement and parol evidence limits, and Paper B examines private ordering and governance mechanisms parties create to govern adaptation and enforcement of relations and why such private structures sometimes fail, implicating the role of law.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the Uniform Commercial Code and the Restatement have changed assumptions about completeness and the operation of the parol evidence rule, while Paper B evaluates the promise and problems of applying a UCC‑style codification to design and construction contracts (including prospects for a Uniform Code for Design and Construction Contracts).

shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes doctrinal justifications (intention, estoppel, form, judicial convenience) for limiting or admitting extra‑textual evidence and for imposing legal duties, while Paper B emphasizes private ordering (standard contract models, implementing structures, conflict management) and the interplay with public law as a safety net or supplement to manage recurring construction disputes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS

shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the tension between honoring parties' ex ante intentions and judicial supplementation: Paper A contrasts choosing defaults that reflect parties' probable intentions with defaults chosen for other reasons, while Paper B distinguishes terms implied in fact (inference of the parties' intent) from terms imposed by law and studies how the parol evidence rule affects proof of those intentions.

shared_topics.justification: Both articles treat background legal rules as more than neutral scaffolding: Paper A argues default rules instantiate distributive choices that parties contract against, while Paper B probes whether and how a writing displaces obligations imposed by law or background norms (implied terms), affecting how much freedom parties actually have to define their own obligations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes when and how courts imply terms (implied in fact vs implied in law) and whether parol evidence allows proof of omitted obligations, and Paper B engages the complementary question in the construction context—how agreements are supplemented or 'filled in' by standard forms, industry practices, or external legal rules when contracts are incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: tension between private ordering/standard-form agreements and external/public legal norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes whether legal obligations imposed by law are displaced or obscured by an apparently complete writing under the parol evidence rule, while Paper B studies how private orderings, standard industry contract models, and implementing institutions interact with (and sometimes supplant or depend upon) public law as a regulatory backdrop or safety net.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry practices, prior dealings, and contextual interpretation in defining contractual duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes interpreting written contracts in light of prior dealings, trade usage, and surrounding circumstances when identifying express or implied obligations, and Paper B foregrounds industry-specific norms, standard contract models, and relational practices as central determinants of parties' rights and the substantive content of construction contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the shift from presuming integration to the U.C.C. and Second Restatement's less rigid approach and explores consequences for implication and parol evidence; Paper B invokes Llewellyn, the U.C.C., and doctrinal history to explain how modern rules have expanded courts' ability (and the institutional limits of doing so) to consider trade usages, course of dealing, and other context.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how private information and strategic withholding affect the desirability and effectiveness of penalty defaults that try to induce revelation, and Paper B studies how proof of prior negotiations (or its exclusion by the parol evidence rule) influences the court's willingness to imply terms—both engage with the evidentiary/ informational role of negotiations in shaping contractual gap-filling.

papers.node_id: 62amjcompl687!!ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+
papers.abstract:
Clarity and reasonableness are both ideals in contract, as in other relations. States favor contracts whose terms are unambiguous to those they bind, as well as to third parties. States also prefer contracts that are "reasonable" in the sense that terms are consistent with what most parties expect and regard as fair. Policymakers thus have both substantive preferences regarding the terms on which exchange will occur, and also meta-preferences regarding the formal properties of those terms, which speak to the process by which agreements are entered and adjudicated.
Contract scholars often debate how best to achieve clarity and reasonableness. More specifically, they debate the relative merits of default rules that preserve "freedom of contract," on the one hand, and mandatory terms, on the other.
On the whole, American policymakers and legal scholars tend to favor default rules because they are reluctant to forego the benefits of private ordering.
, the Article deconstructs the consequences of mobility - mobility of consumers, workers and firms. Mobility too is conceived here as a property of a jurisdiction rather than individual contracting parties. As discussed infra Part III, its effects are complex. On the one hand, mobility is likely to mean that the contracting preferences of the population are in flux, which makes it difficult to institute a mandatory term that is optimal over time. On the other hand, mobility increases the information costs for consumers and employees as they attempt to match themselves to firms offering products, services or employment on suitable terms. Even if mobility makes mandatory terms more valuable, however, it makes them improbable. Even efficient mandatory terms may be unappealing to firms; if mobile, these firms have a credible threat of exit that will cause them to exercise disproportionate influence on the policymaking process. Second, diffuse interest groups like consumers and employees usually require the cooperation of a powerful firm or firm-type in order to push through mandatory regulation. In a market characterized by high mobility, they are less likely to find a willing and stable coalition partner. The result is that we should expect to see fewer mandatory terms in jurisdictions with high mobility.
The third factor explored here is the sectoral composition of the domestic economy. The significance of this factor turns on the information problems associated with cross-border contracting. Consumers and employees face high informational hurdles in contracting with foreign-based firms. States can adopt mandatory terms in order to facilitate national branding. The value of this strategy turns on what proportion of the economy is devoted to manufacturing exports, and whether manufacturing takes place in sectors that would benefit from standardized terms.
Finally, the Article studies the respective capacities of courts to develop binding interpretive rules, legislatures to pass mandatory legislation and executives to monitor and enforce mandatory legislation (together, "institutional capacity"). Common law courts may be better at developing ex post interpretative defaults that operates asflexible substitutes for mandatory legislation. Some common law countries, like the United States, also have veto-ridden legislative processes that make it difficult to pass mandatory regulation, as well as administrative agencies ill-equipped to enforce it. The optimal regulatory strategy of a country depends on its comparative institutional advantages in the development and enforcement of rules.
These four factors do not exhaust the ways in which political economy shapes regulatory choices. But they collectively demonstrate that a regime's regulatory choice should and does depend on contingent features of its politics and economy.
The immediate payoff of the political economy approach recommended here is to understand differences between jurisdictions. But a second payoff is to gain insight into the dynamics of transnational regulation. Although we might be tempted to treat transnational regimes as an opportunity to generalize the 'best' national model, the significance of political economic factors warns against such aspirations. Just as we cannot transplant a national model from one domestic jurisdiction to another,

questions.question: Whether jurisdictions with high population, worker, and firm mobility are less likely to adopt mandatory contractual terms and more likely to rely on default rules for governing contracts.

Whether an economy's sectoral composition-particularly a large share of export-oriented manufacturing-increases the likelihood that policymakers will adopt mandatory, standardized contract terms to facilitate cross-border contracting and national branding.

Whether a country's comparative institutional capacities (the relative strengths of courts, legislatures, and executive agencies) determine whether it relies on courts' interpretive defaults or on mandatory legislation and enforcement to regulate contractual terms.

compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW

papers.node_id: 56clevstlrev767!!ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS
papers.abstract:
The fashion in American law schools is to teach that contractual language cannot have a plain meaning. Some of this teaching may be inadvertent. Most of it occurs when students study the "plain meaning rule." This rule allows a judge, after finding unambiguous language (plain meaning) in a written contract, to refuse to look at other evidence of that language's meaning.
The rule is heavily criticized, but claims against it have been exaggerated. One of these exaggerated claims is that plain meaning is impossible. This claim is found in the caselaw opinions that students are made to read. It appears most clearly inPacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.("PG&E"),decided in 1968 by JusticeRoger Traynor of the California Supreme Court. Traynor's opinion appears in nearly every Contracts casebook.BecausePG&E'sfacts actually do not put the plain meaning rule in issue, that case is often supplemented by another case more on point, such asIn re Soper's Estate.I describe both of these opinions in Part I.
Both opinions claim that plain meaning is impossible. There are two premises to this claim. First, the judges assert that plain meaning could only be found by reading a document if words had inherent meaning, or absolute and constant referents. But they do not, the argument goes. Second, the opinions claim that the meaning of words is actually the thoughts and intentions of the speaker, or perhaps the speaker and hearer. No written contract could ever adequately reveal these. Plain meaning is therefore impossible. This claim is left irrefuted in the casebooks and contract law literature, Part I notes, and in most teaching of contract law. The consequence is that students are taught that plain meaning is impossible. A startling implication of this conclusion, as Part I explains, is that the majority of U.S. courts, which hold to the plain meaning rule, are relying on a fiction.
But the claim that plain meaning is impossible is false, as are its premises. Part II explains why. Drawing on the philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, Part II.A shows why the meaning of words cannot be the thoughts and intentions of the speaker, hearer, or anyone else. Part II.B demonstrates that plain meaning does not require that words have "inherent meaning" or "absolute and constant referents." Plain meaning is possible and occurs quite apart from reference or another theory of inherent meaning. Plain meaning rests instead on our unreflective, public, conventional practice of language use. Most meaning is plain.
Part III explains that, though plain meaning is immune from attack on grounds of impossibility, whether the plain meaning rule is the best legal rule is another matter. Actually, all of the legal rules currently available for determining the meaning of contractual language are possible. Which rule one chooses is not a matter of possibility at all, or of language philosophy, but of legal reasoning and social policy.

questions.question: Whether written contractual language can have a determinate, objective plain meaning (i.e., whether plain meaning is possible).
Whether the meaning of words in contracts is constituted by the parties' subjective intentions or by public, conventional practices of language use.
Whether privileging the text's ordinary meaning over extrinsic evidence is justified as a legal rule given considerations of legal reasoning and social policy.
