papers.node_id: 27textechlrev1!!ARTICLE: THE TEXAS RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION LIABILITY ACT: FRAMEWORK FOR CHANGE
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE TEXAS RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION LIABILITY ACT: FRAMEWORK FOR CHANGE
papers.abstract:
The Texas Legislature enacted the Residential Construction Liability Act (RCLA) in 1989 and subsequently amended it in 1993.The RCLA was enacted "to provide a fair and appropriate balance [with respect] to the resolution of construction disputes between a residential contractor and owner."Although the Act amended the Property Code, it was designed to address characteristic problems that arose when a homeowner asserted claims against a homebuilder under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act (DTPA).For example, the DTPA does not provide a homebuilder an opportunity to inspect alleged construction defects and arrange for necessary repairs even though prompt inspection and repair can often mitigate damages.
This Article considers whether, in practice, the RCLA has achieved its drafters' original intent. Furthermore, this Article focuses on problems that have arisen with respect to the practical application of the RCLA and suggests a framework for change. Part II reviews the legislative history of the RCLA and discusses how it grew out of abuses of the DTPA. Part III analyzes selected provisions of the RCLA that have proved problematic and suggests appropriate revisions. Part IV suggests a revision to the RCLA to make mandatory abatement of an RCLA lawsuit an appropriate remedy under certain circumstances. Finally, Part V discusses problems that have arisen with respect to contribution and indemnity and that, arguably, cause the greatest difficulty in the practical application of the RCLA. Following the Article's conclusion is Appendix A, which codifies all of the proposed revisions and additions suggested in this Article. It is the authors' hope that legislation similar to that proposed in Appendix A will be enacted in 1997 by the Texas Legislature.

questions.question: Whether the enacted statutory framework for resolving residential construction disputes has, in practice, achieved its drafters' intended balance between homeowners and builders.

Whether the statutory scheme's remedies and procedures should be revised-including making temporary suspension (abatement) of lawsuits mandatory in some circumstances-to better allow inspection and repair and thereby mitigate damages.
How rules governing contribution and indemnity among parties in residential construction claims should be structured to reduce practical difficulties and improve the scheme's operation.

papers.node_id: 67sclrev535!!ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?
papers.abstract:
I. DATA BREACH INTRODUCTORY CONCEPTS
Describing a data breach is like describing a party. Certain people have been invited, but there are always a few uninvited guests. Some of these guests have entered with invited guests, who used their keys. Some guests heard the noise, smelled the delicious food, or just knocked on the door out of curiosity. Regardless, there is a point at which the host realizes that one of the uninvited guests has eaten the food, or even packed a portion to go, and it is time to decide whether to oust the guest, call it a night for the entire party, or even call the cops. Like an actual data breach, it is hard to tell exactly what has been taken out at this point, on day zero. Nevertheless, the host knows that the unauthorized guest has accessed valuable information, which may be sensitive or personal information, and may later view it, process it, or sell it to a third party.
Information has become, in many cases, primarily or exclusively electronic. Digitization of information has shifted the source of value in society to databases.Correspondingly, the concentration of this information into big data storage in databases renders the data more vulnerable to single point of entry, single point of attack, and single point of breach. The number of data breaches has grown in recently years,but more significantly, the scope, magnitude,and social impact of the breaches has expanded. As a result, the total cost to society of data breaches has risen dramatically.
Consumers have not been left to their own devices, and the government has stepped in to examine the causes of data breaches.The FTC has investigated several companies' data security practices and found them lacking.In FTC v.Wyndham WorldWide Corp.,the district court agreed that not only did the FTC have the authority to ferret out substandard data practices in the corporate world, but that companies should read FTC decisions and act accordingly. The FTC did indeed have some say in setting a baseline for industry security practices.In August of 2015, the Third Circuit court affirmed the district court's holding, leading with the facts of Wyndam's multiple data breach events and enumerating the myriad security hazards present in the company's processes and systems.Though it was not part of the core holding on appeal, the court noted that the company's security plans did not meet the standard in its posted security policy.It's not difficult to imagine an FTC investigation or court case in the near future in which the parties offer their data breach contract clauses as evidence of reasonable, industry standard level practices that demonstrate an effort to maintain effective security practices.
Snapchat and TRENDnet, Inc. also failed to survive the FTC's scrutiny of their security measures, each by a fair measure.In re Snapchatled to a settlement in which the FTC explained, rather patiently, that it is not permissible to design an app with a core service of limited photo display and then keep the photos, ostensibly forever.In the Matter of TRENDnet, Inc.also centered upon a patently offensive use of personal data in the form of unauthorized access to insufficiently secured home security camera video.In the TRENDnet matter, however, the security system was at issue and a third party captured the personal data in a clear data breach scenario. In both situations, customer expectations regarding privacy and security were not met.
These cases reflect a growing awareness at the FTC as well as in the public consciousness of privacy and security issues in mobile app and Internet of Things ecosystems.In each case, not only did the FTC opine on the proper level of privacy and security protocols for companies holding and processing data, but also noted in particular the gap between what was promised contractually and what was delivered to the contracting party.These casescapped several years of the FTC's consolidation of power in dictating data security principles,but the battle is not yet over. As technology changes, going deeper into specifics in the mobile ecosystems and Internet of Things security protocols will be necessary to satisfy regulators, contracting parties, vendors, and customers.
As a consequence, corporate and in-house legal have stepped up their knowledge on these issues and have had to respond almost in real time to developing industry standards and customer demands. Initially, legal resources were devoted to remedying the immediate dangers by stemming the flow of data, catching the perpetrators of intentional breach, and pursuing or defending their companies against class action lawsuits and fines.Next, attorneys began to collect and analyze the consequences of fifty states worth of data breach legislation,and the myriad requirements associated with data breach, primarily notification of customers, media, government, and/or law enforcement. While all of these concerns remain, the impetus of the privacy and security movement now must be towards ascertaining the longer-term consequences of an actual or threatened data breach for companies.
The need for long-term planning for inevitable breaches requires the redesign not only of security procedures for corporate data, but of the contractual provisions designed to protect data, protect the network, and protect each company in the transaction from extreme liability in the event of a data breach. There are several junctures in the contract negotiation timeline at which tointroduce data protection provisions,but the earlier the better in order to avoid unpleasant surprises.
The methodology for addressing this need is the holistic enhancement of security provisions in corporate contracts, specifically, the redesign of costs of cover provisions in these contracts. From an internal governance perspective, corporate legal departments may develop contract playbooks for each template agreement. These playbooks may include provisions, for internal use only, indicating fallback negotiating strategies and fallback contract or clause language that the negotiating in-house counsel may use to close the deal. In addition, the fallback provisions may include a note that in order for the parties to go beyond standard fallbacks, the negotiating deal attorney will need to escalate the ask up their chain of authority. In this context, provisions related to costs of cover for data breach may reach the general counsel of a corporation, even for a smaller deal, as the expense of each breach may exceed the value of the deal to the company. The ultimate goal in this contract re-boot is to avoid not the contingency of a data breach, but the contingency that a data breach swallows the value of the deal described in the contract, or even the value of the transacting company as a whole. As a result of this reconsideration, parties will be better able to bear their existing risks, as well as shoulder the risks posed by new technologies.
There are social values associated with drafting contracts in the right way. One of these values is a reconfiguration of legal efforts in contract drafting towards cost saving, company saving, and economy saving effects.In order to find the right path, there is a careful balance between the competing forces ofwhat works for that deal, and what is effective for the greater good, incorporating stakeholder values. Stakeholders should include affected shareholders, but also consumers, third party companies and individuals, and society as a whole. Using contract drafting as a methodology to affect change or improve society is not new.The theoretical framework for contract negotiation must acknowledge the vast legal literature on contract economicsassociated with the allocation of costs,but then go beyond this history to tell a new story about how this theory will work to advance under the auspices of new technologies.

questions.question: Who should be contractually responsible for paying the costs of a data breach (investigation, notification, remediation, defense, settlements and related cover) between parties to a commercial contract?

How should contracting parties design and allocate "costs of cover" clauses so that the allocation of breach-related costs minimizes the risk that a data breach will destroy the value of the deal or the company?
What are the trade-offs and social implications of different contractual allocations of data-breach response costs for firms, customers, third parties, and society?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49indlrev621!!ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPACT TRANSACTION: LAWYERING FOR THE PUBLIC GOOD THROUGH COLLECTIVE IMPACT AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: contract drafting as a mechanism to advance public or social objectives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of 'impact transaction' and advocates drafting collective-impact agreements to achieve large-scale social change, while Paper B argues that redesigning contract clauses (e.g., costs-of-cover and security provisions) can promote consumer protection, corporate resilience, and broader social values in the face of data breaches.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk, responsibility, and costs by contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates how collective-impact initiatives should allocate authority, duties, and accountability among collaborating parties and proposes contractual solutions, and Paper B analyzes who should bear the financial and remediation burdens after a data breach and how contract language can allocate those costs.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as governance tools for long‑running, relational collaborations and contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds collective-impact initiatives in relational contract theory to govern ongoing cross-sector collaboration, and Paper B emphasizes long-term planning through contract playbooks, fallback clauses, and provisions that govern responses to future breach contingencies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transactional lawyers and in‑house counsel in shaping outcomes through agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for transactional lawyers to partner with collective-impact actors to draft agreements that sustain social initiatives, while Paper B describes how corporate legal departments and general counsel must craft and negotiate security and allocation clauses to protect deal and corporate value and influence industry practices.

shared_topics.topic: inclusion of multi‑stakeholder accountability and participation rules in agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines who gets to participate in collective impact and how initiatives are held accountable (proposing contractual mechanisms), and Paper B highlights that contract design must consider multiple stakeholders (shareholders, consumers, third parties, and society) when apportioning responsibilities and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90texlrev1153!!ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract drafting and private ordering in allocating commercial risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on redesigning contract clauses (e.g., costs-of-cover, playbooks, fallback language) to allocate and limit liability for data breaches, and Paper B shows that medieval commercial practice relied on explicit contracts (and statutes) rather than amorphous custom to allocate risks in trade, treating contracting as a primary private-ordering mechanism.

shared_topics.topic: standardization and spread of contractual forms as a mechanism for governing transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends corporate standard clauses and contract playbooks to create predictable industry practices for handling breaches, while Paper B analyzes how recurring contract forms (bills of exchange, insurance, partnership agreements) spread across regions and functioned as the closest thing to a transnational commercial norm.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contractual norms and public regulation or judicial standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how regulators (FTC) and courts may treat contractual promises and data-security clauses as evidence of industry standards and legal obligations, and Paper B documents that many widely used commercial rules in medieval Europe ultimately arose from statute and judicial decision rather than diffuse custom, showing the interplay between private agreements and public law.

shared_topics.topic: contracts and customs as gap-filling/default rules where formal law is incomplete
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates explicit fallback and gap-filling provisions in contracts to handle unforeseen data-breach consequences, and Paper B interrogates the extent to which custom (versus contract or statute) functioned as local gap-filling in commerce and why such customs failed to produce uniform default rules across jurisdictions.

shared_topics.topic: alternative governance mechanisms (intermediaries, in-house processes) that substitute for uniform legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes internal governance—corporate legal departments, escalation to general counsel, and contractual negotiation processes—as means to manage breach risk absent uniform rules, while Paper B highlights external intermediaries (brokers, notaries, hostellers) that enabled merchants to transact successfully without a single transnational law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56amjcompl703!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Actors: The State's Private Law and the Economy - Commercial Law as an Amalgam of Public and Private Rule-Making
compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Actors: The State's Private Law and the Economy - Commercial Law as an Amalgam of Public and Private Rule-Making

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and the interaction between private rules/contracts and state regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the overlap and interdependence between private law and state law in commercial life and when private rules arise or give way to state regulation; Paper B examines how contractual data-breach clauses function within a regulatory context (e.g., FTC scrutiny) and how contracts may be used as evidence or instruments that interact with public enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: private governance/ordering in commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces historical and functional varieties of non‑state law governing trade and commerce, while Paper B treats contractual clauses and corporate playbooks as forms of private governance that structure how firms prevent and respond to data breaches.

shared_topics.topic: how industry standards and private norms emerge and shape behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses conditions that favor the emergence of non‑state rules and customary commercial practices; Paper B considers how contract language and negotiated clauses can crystallize industry security practices and be cited to demonstrate reasonable standards to regulators and courts.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and costs through private legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the functions of legal rules in commerce (including allocation of rights, obligations and risk) and factors influencing whether such allocations are made privately or publicly, while Paper B focuses concretely on how contracts allocate the 'costs of cover' for data breaches and redesigning clauses to distribute financial exposure.

shared_topics.topic: economic reasoning (efficiency and cost considerations) as a driver of legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds economic thinking—efficient use of scarce resources—as central to why private rules develop and how law functions in economic subsystems, and Paper B frames contract drafting and clause design in terms of cost‑saving, preserving transactional value, and allocating economic consequences of breaches.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72oklalrev797!!ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: ex ante contract design to manage future disputes and contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory of procedural customization showing how parties draft dispute-resolution processes before disputes arise to limit litigation opportunism; Paper B argues that parties must redesign substantive contract clauses (especially for data breaches) ex ante to allocate responsibilities and avoid catastrophic post-breach consequences.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of costs and risks through contractual clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explains how parties can bargain over procedural advantages and trade procedural terms for substantive rights to manage adjudicatory risk, while Paper B focuses on how contracts should allocate the "costs of cover" and other financial burdens following a data breach.

shared_topics.topic: how transaction attributes (uncertainty, scale, frequency) shape contract drafting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a framework linking environmental and behavioral uncertainty and deal scale to the desirability of procedural tailoring, and Paper B emphasizes that technological context (e.g., big data, IoT), deal size, and evolving breach risk should drive more or less aggressive contractual protections.

shared_topics.topic: the role of lawyers and in-house playbooks in standardizing contract responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames business lawyers as transaction-cost engineers who design multivalent contracts and procedural portfolios, and Paper B describes corporate legal departments creating contract playbooks and fallback clause language for negotiating data-breach allocations.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contracting and public/regulatory norms or fora
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines parties' choices among private and public dispute-resolution mechanisms (arbitration, courts, specialized tribunals) and how standards/rules affect contract design, while Paper B discusses how FTC enforcement, industry standards, and regulator expectations influence how parties draft and justify data-security and breach-liability clauses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81uchilrev151!!SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Renegotiation Design by Contract
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Renegotiation Design by Contract

shared_topics.topic: contractual allocation of liability and costs for adverse contingencies (e.g., data breaches, hold-up events)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contracts should allocate the costs of cover and liability when a data breach occurs, proposing clause language and playbooks to determine who pays; Paper B analyzes how contract terms (default options, penalties, exclusive-dealing, etc.) allocate economic consequences across parties when unforeseen states occur or renegotiation threatens investment returns.

shared_topics.topic: designing contract terms to shape renegotiation and bargaining power and thereby preserve investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops the renegotiation-design (RD) approach—TIOLI offers, default trades, asymmetric penalties—to give parties predictable bargaining power and encourage bilateral investment; Paper A discusses drafting fallback provisions, escalation rules, and allocation clauses so that parties know ex ante how breach-related disputes and remediation negotiations will be handled, thereby affecting incentives to invest in security and mitigation.

shared_topics.topic: using contract design to preserve transactional or firm value against catastrophic contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames clause redesign as necessary to prevent a data breach from swallowing the value of a deal or the firm and recommends contractual safeguards to protect corporate value; Paper B explains how RD contracts and asset-control devices can prevent holdup that would destroy ex ante investment value and thus affects the boundary and value of firms.

shared_topics.topic: dependence of contractual solutions on the legal/regulatory enforcement environment and remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper B examines how access to specific performance, injunctions, and the permissibility of certain remedies determine whether RD mechanisms can be implemented; Paper A shows how FTC actions, litigation risk, and evolving regulatory expectations shape what contractual privacy/security promises mean in practice and how courts or regulators may treat contract clauses as evidence of standards.

shared_topics.topic: translation of theoretical contract mechanisms into practical drafting practices and real-world clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper B surveys real-world contract forms (output/requirements contracts, leasebacks, exclusive-dealing, late-fee asymmetries) that instantiate theoretical RD solutions; Paper A translates contract-theory and cost-allocation ideas into prescriptive clause language, playbooks, and negotiation strategies for data-security and breach-response contracting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38yalejonreg678!!ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Economic Challenges for the Law of Contract

shared_topics.topic: allocation of contractual costs and risk (including 'costs of cover' clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract law's default and mandatory rules function to allocate risks and complete markets, while Paper B focuses on drafting and negotiating contract provisions (especially 'costs of cover' and indemnity clauses) that allocate the financial burdens of data breaches between parties.

shared_topics.topic: use of default rules versus negotiated/party-specified terms and the limits of standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts default rules, mandatory rules, and vague standards and warns that standards may poorly complete markets, and Paper B engages the same tradeoff in practice by debating template fallback language, industry security standards, and the sufficiency of contractual promises versus more specific, negotiated obligations.

shared_topics.topic: contracting as a tool to manage externalities and broader social harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract law as a planning institution that can (and should) remedy market incompleteness and pecuniary externalities, and Paper B treats contract drafting for data security as a means to mitigate the societal costs of breaches and to protect stakeholders beyond immediate contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contract design and enforcement institutions (courts and regulators)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines adjudication mechanisms, the role of courts (including formalist versus contextualist interpretation) and specialized tribunals in enabling efficient contracting mechanisms, while Paper B documents regulatory enforcement (FTC scrutiny) and how contract clauses may be used as evidence of industry practices, affecting how parties draft and enforce security obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1999wislrev607!!ARTICLE:THE LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE CONCEPT OF CHANGE: PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ATTEMPTS TO REGULATE MODIFICATION, WAIVER, AND ESTOPPEL
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE CONCEPT OF CHANGE: PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ATTEMPTS TO REGULATE MODIFICATION, WAIVER, AND ESTOPPEL

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and costs through contractual clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines (modification, waiver, estoppel) and contractual devices (NOM/NOW clauses) affect the parties' ability to reallocate or lock in risk, while Paper B focuses on contract clauses (costs-of-cover, indemnities, fallback language) that allocate the financial burden of data breaches between contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contract terms and public/regulatory law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how statutory reform (proposed UCC revisions) and judicial doctrine will shape enforceability of private agreements about modification and waiver, and Paper B examines how regulatory enforcement (FTC decisions, state breach laws) and public expectations influence what contractual security and liability provisions are considered acceptable or effective.

shared_topics.topic: limits on enforceability of contractual provisions and doctrinal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes the doctrinal limits on enforcing clauses that bar modification or waiver (and proposes a coercion test), while Paper B grapples with how far contract clauses can shield parties from liability or be used as evidence of reasonable practices in regulatory or litigation contexts, raising questions about when such clauses will be honored or overridden.

shared_topics.topic: designing contracts to manage change, contingencies, and institutional needs (certainty vs. flexibility)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract law as mediating the tension between locking in bargains and accommodating change, proposing rules and legislative compromises to balance certainty, flexibility, and reliance; Paper B treats data breaches as an inevitable contingency and advocates proactive drafting (playbooks, clause design) to preserve deal value while balancing party, stakeholder, and societal interests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78valrev821!!ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SOUND OF SILENCE: DEFAULT RULES AND CONTRACTUAL CONSENT.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of financial responsibility for contingent harms through contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on who should bear the costs of data-breach remediation and insurance ('costs of cover') and argues for redesigning contract clauses to allocate that financial risk; Paper B analyzes how default rules and gap-fillers operate to allocate rights and obligations when parties do not specify terms, which directly affects who bears contingent costs in incomplete contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the consequences of silence or omitted clauses and the use of gap-filling/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly highlights the risks that arise when contracting parties fail to address data-protection contingencies (and recommends proactive clause drafting and playbooks), while Paper B theorizes how silence should be treated—through default rules or conventionalist gap-fillers—and when silence can be taken as (indirect) consent, thereby determining contractual outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between background legal/industry norms and private contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how regulatory decisions (e.g., FTC cases) and emerging industry standards inform what provisions parties include in data-security contracts and may be used as evidence of reasonable practices, whereas Paper B examines how statutory and judicial default rules (like provisions of the U.C.C.) function as background norms that shape or fill parties' agreements.

shared_topics.topic: contract drafting practices and governance mechanisms to manage uncertainty and risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates internal governance tools—contract playbooks, fallback language, escalation procedures—to manage bargaining over data-breach clauses and preserve firm value, and Paper B treats default rules as a legal governance mechanism that parties can rely on or contract around, addressing how parties and legal systems allocate transaction costs of specifying contingencies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100geolj5!!ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Are All Contractual Obligations Created Equal?

shared_topics.topic: effect of contractual ambiguity (content vagueness) versus enforcement uncertainty on compliance

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INVERTED HIERARCHY OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AND SUPPLEMENTATION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for an 'inverted hierarchy' that gives legal standards like reasonableness and good faith priority over literal express terms and factual bargaining, while Paper B treats regulatory and industry expectations (e.g., FTC standards and posted security policies) and contractual promises as baseline standards that shape parties' obligations and liability in data-breach contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry customs, trade usages, and regulatory norms in shaping and proving contractual duties

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and costs through contractual drafting and default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how default contract rules and supplementation promote efficient and fair allocation of risks and realization of parties' intentions, while Paper B focuses on how data-breach clauses and 'costs of cover' provisions (and corporate contract playbooks) are drafted and negotiated to allocate breach costs and protect deal/company value.

papers.node_id: 92columlrev997!!ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.
papers.abstract:
This Article offers a general account of contracts that give a party substantial discretion in performance through open terms.  Open terms often are used when the owner of an asset of uncertain value employs an agent to develop the asset or when two parties work together under uncertain conditions.  Many contracts use open terms, and these contracts represent a disproportionate share of litigated contracts.  This Article uses an oil and gas lease and a long-term requirements contract between a buyer and seller with interdependent operations to illustrate some basic features of many open term contracts.
People enter into these contracts because of the benefits they derive from open-ended sharing relationships.  These contracts give one party discretion in performance while attempting to induce him to exercise that discretion to maximize the parties' joint return.  Often, the necessary inducement is provided by requiring that the party having discretion share the return on his performance and perform under a negligence-like term.  In practice, however, these contracts are not likely to induce optimal performance, since costs and returns are divided and because of defects in the terms regulating performance.
Yet contracts with open terms are attractive despite their defects, because they align individual risk and joint risk at the time of contracting better than do contracts with fixed performance terms.  That is, the terms better align individual outcome with joint outcome, so one party may not suffer a loss in excess of the parties' joint loss.  This alignment of risks may greatly reduce the cost of entering into a contract under conditions of uncertainty.  The use of open terms reduces the parties' incentive to test to determine more accurately the probability or value, or to haggle over contingencies that might result in a loss to one party under a fixed term, but that do not make the contract jointly less attractive than alternative investments.
There is much scholarly work on open term contracts, especially in the field of economics, but previous commentators have not given a complete account of these contracts or provided guidelines for their enforcement.  Part I of this Article gives an overview of my argumentand places it within the context of the existing scholarly literature and other relevant work in economics.  This Part also defends the claim that the goal of contract should be to maximize the parties' joint expected return.
Parts II through IV explain the characteristics and reasons for the use of sharing arrangements and negligence-like terms in contracts under which a principal employs an agent to develop an asset of uncertain value.  Part II shows how an agent may be induced to develop an asset for a principal through a gain-sharing arrangement and a negligence-like performance term.  The Part demonstrates, however, that an agent's performance under such a contract is not likely to maximize the parties' joint return.  Part III suggests that despite this performance defect, gain-sharing and negligence-like performance terms are used because they reduce the parties' incentive to test or to haggle over the division of an uncertain expected gainwhen contracting.  Part IV discusses several additional defects in a contract with a sharing arrangement and a negligence-like performance term, defects that arise when a principal relies on an agent's performance by investing in contract resources that might be used in better ways.
Part V shows that a requirements contract in which price is adjusted to equal the seller's cost has properties similar to an agency contract with a sharing arrangement and a negligence term.  It suggests that parties may accept the defects inherent in such a contract because it provides an inexpensive way to deal with risks that are expected to have an offsetting impact on them.
Part VI proposes some basic guidelines for enforcing contracts with open terms.  It suggests that a rule of joint maximization, which is similar to Learned Hand's standard of negligence, ought to be the benchmark in reviewing performance under open terms.Further, courts ought to look for structural factors that align or divide one party's interest in performing and the parties' joint interest, and ought to impose a higher standard of scrutiny when those interests diverge significantly.  Part VI proposes important incremental reforms in the rules governing output and requirements contracts, best efforts contracts, and mineral leases.

questions.question: Whether contracts that give one party substantial discretion through open terms (e.g., profit-sharing and flexible performance obligations) induce that party to behave in ways that maximize the parties' joint expected return.

Whether parties choose open-term contracts despite their incentive defects because such contracts better align individual and joint risk under uncertainty and reduce the costs of testing and bargaining compared with fixed-performance contracts.
What enforcement or review standard for performance under open-term contracts best promotes joint maximization and mitigates the incentive and structural problems these contracts create.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60ucinlrev405!!SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/game-theoretic analysis to evaluate and design legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is explicitly about applying game theory to corporate law and practice to predict strategic outcomes and inform rule design, and Paper B uses economic analysis (principal-agent and incentive theory) to explain when open-term contracts arise and how legal doctrines should treat them.

shared_topics.topic: incentive design and principal–agent problems in legal arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores strategic interactions among corporate actors (e.g., managers, directors, shareholders) through game-theoretic lenses, while Paper B analyzes how contracts with open terms and gain-sharing allocate incentives between principals and agents and the resulting performance implications.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and the use of sharing arrangements under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper B shows that open terms and sharing arrangements align individual and joint risk under uncertainty, and Paper A, via game-theoretic perspectives on corporate behavior, addresses how legal and contractual structures distribute risk and shape parties' choices under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: how legal standards and enforcement should respond to strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper B proposes a 'joint maximization' benchmark (akin to negligence) for reviewing performance under open terms, and Paper A discusses how game-theoretic reasoning can guide courts and regulators in crafting enforcement rules that account for strategic responses by corporate actors.

shared_topics.topic: the role of bargaining, testing, and strategic withholding of information in contractual and corporate settings
shared_topics.justification: Paper B examines how open terms reduce incentives to test or haggle over contingencies, and Paper A applies game theory to analyze bargaining, information revelation, and strategic withholding among corporate parties and counterparties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35ucdavislrev319!!ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith

shared_topics.topic: allocation of discretion in long-term/open-quantity contracts (requirements and output clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze contracts that leave quantity or performance open (e.g., requirements and output clauses) and examine how and why one party is granted discretion to vary quantity over the life of a long-term deal and the consequences of that allocation for the counterparty and the transaction as a whole.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate legal standard to constrain discretionary performance (good faith vs. negligence/joint‑maximization)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of what doctrinal benchmark courts should apply to review performance under open terms—Paper A advocating a negligence-like or joint‑maximization standard and Paper B critiquing broad invocations of 'good faith' and proposing narrower, transaction‑sensitive limits.

shared_topics.topic: courts' role in interpreting and enforcing open terms versus deference to parties' contractual allocations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers debate how actively courts should interpret open terms—Paper A proposes enforcement guidelines and scrutiny tied to structural alignment of incentives, while Paper B argues for greater deference to the parties' negotiated allocation of discretion and only limited judicial intervention.

shared_topics.topic: risk allocation, incentives, and joint versus individual returns under open contractual arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Both works explore how open terms change the allocation of risk and incentives (e.g., sharing arrangements, gain‑sharing, price adjustments to costs) and how those allocations affect parties' incentives to invest, test information, or bargain, with an eye toward maximizing joint expected returns or protecting reliance interests.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism and manipulation of quantity or performance (reliance, asset transfers, and underproduction)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront problems of opportunistic behavior—Paper A in terms of agents shirking or misallocating contract resources and Paper B in terms of buyers reducing requirements, selling plants, or otherwise manipulating quantity—and discuss doctrinal responses to such manipulation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: contracting under uncertainty using open-ended or indeterminate terms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why parties adopt non‑fixed, open-ended contractual arrangements when future states are uncertain — Paper A focuses on open terms, requirements and mineral leases that leave performance discretionary, while Paper B examines contracts for innovation that deliberately leave substantive outcomes unspecified to cope with technological and market uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: design of incentives to align individual discretion with joint returns
shared_topics.justification: Both works study mechanisms that try to induce a party with performance discretion to act in the parties' joint interest — Paper A by examining gain‑sharing and negligence‑like terms in principal–agent settings, and Paper B by showing how braided formal/informal mechanisms and staged switching costs build incentives for cooperative behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information, observability, and the costs of testing or bargaining in shaping contract form
shared_topics.justification: Each paper emphasizes information problems — Paper A discusses how open terms reduce incentives to test or haggle over uncertain values and how informational asymmetries affect performance, while Paper B centers on formalized information exchanges that reveal capabilities and character to create trust and enable informal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of courts and enforcement regimes for nonstandard or hybrid contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both offer normative and doctrinal guidance about judicial review of indeterminate contracts — Paper A proposes a joint‑maximization (negligence‑like) benchmark and tailored scrutiny, whereas Paper B argues for low‑powered judicial enforcement of verifiable elements to protect braided contracts without crowding out informal sanctions.

shared_topics.topic: contracts that leave substantive obligations to be developed through ongoing collaboration or agent discretion
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study contractual forms that intentionally defer specification of performance to the relationship itself — Paper A via agent‑developed assets under sharing arrangements, and Paper B via collaborative innovation agreements where substantive performance terms are generated through the contract's governance and information processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 106nwulrev1153!!Article: BROADCAST CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: Article: BROADCAST CONTRACTING

shared_topics.topic: economic rationale for using nonstandard contract forms to manage uncertainty and reduce transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes 'broadcast contracting' as a one-stop multilateral commitment that can reduce transaction costs and coordinate behavior across many actors under uncertainty, while Paper B explains why parties adopt open-term and gain-sharing contracts (e.g., mineral leases, requirements contracts) to better align risks and avoid costly testing or bargaining over uncertain contingencies.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as devices to allocate risk and align incentives between parties (and with outsiders)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study how contract structure redistributes risk and shapes incentives—Paper A shows how promissory commitments to a class of third parties can create enforceable obligations that alter incentives, and Paper B shows how sharing arrangements and negligence-like performance terms allocate returns and motivate an agent's actions relative to the parties' joint interest.

shared_topics.topic: normative arguments about how courts should review and enforce unconventional contractual arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for moving from vague, judge-made standards toward a rule requiring explicit grants of third-party rights for 'broadcast' contracts, while Paper B develops enforcement guidelines favoring a joint-maximization (negligence-like) benchmark and recommends heightened judicial scrutiny when private and joint interests diverge.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing doctrinal vagueness and advocacy for clearer legal rules to limit speculative litigation
shared_topics.justification: Both articles diagnose current common-law approaches as underinclusive or amorphous—Paper A highlights the difficulties courts face distinguishing intended from incidental beneficiaries under current third-party-beneficiary doctrine, and Paper B points to defects and enforcement uncertainty under open-term doctrines—and each urges clearer, more structured doctrines to reduce litigation costs and unpredictable outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95nwulrev91!!Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS

shared_topics.topic: why parties use open or simple contracts under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why, despite uncertainty about future states, parties often use open-ended or simple contracts (e.g., open terms, crude partitions) — attributing this to drafting and enforcement costs, reduced incentives to test or haggle, renegotiation, and other frictions that make complexity impractical.

shared_topics.topic: incentive alignment and principal–agent problems in discretionary performance
shared_topics.justification: Both works study contracts that give one party substantial discretion (agency or sharing arrangements) and consider how contractual features (gain‑sharing, negligence‑like terms, rewards/penalties) are used to induce performance and align the agent’s incentives with the parties' joint interests.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret and enforce incomplete/complex/open‑term contracts
shared_topics.justification: Each paper develops normative guidance for judicial review — Paper A proposing a joint‑maximization/negligence benchmark and attention to structural alignment, and Paper B arguing that a contract’s complexity provides evidentiary clues about parties’ goals and thus should influence interpretive and enforcement choices.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between contractual complexity/completeness and practical simplicity/open terms
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tradeoff between theoretically fine‑tuned, complete contracts and the observed prevalence of simpler or open contracts, exploring costs and benefits of complexity (drafting, monitoring, bounded rationality, reputation) and the implications for contract design and legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27cornelljlpubpoly553!!ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW

shared_topics.topic: the formative role of law in constructing market relations and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law does not merely enforce transactions but helps form the moral landscape and the very shape of market relations; Paper B treats contract law and judicial enforcement rules (e.g., negligence-like standards, joint-maximization review) as structuring parties' choices and the practical meaning of open-term agreements.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules allocate and constrain discretion in market transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the idea that market interactions are necessarily impersonal and insulated from moral demands, implicating the need to regulate actors' discretion; Paper B analyzes contracts that deliberately vest one party with substantial discretion (open terms) and studies how contract design and legal standards (sharing arrangements, negligence-like terms) govern and discipline that discretion.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship and potential gap between legal obligations and moral responsibility of market participants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally examines how legal permissions in the market can diverge from moral duties and argues that market participants retain moral responsibility despite legal allowances; Paper B addresses similar tensions by proposing enforcement benchmarks (joint maximization, negligence analogues) to hold parties to performance expectations that may extend beyond simple legalistic permissions.

shared_topics.topic: design of legal/institutional mechanisms to align individual incentives with joint or social outcomes under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with whether market structures and law should allow actors to 'bracket out' moral demands or be held responsible for impacts on others, implicating institutional alignment of incentives with justice; Paper B shows how open-term contracts, sharing rules, and judicial standards are used to align individual performance incentives with the parties' joint expected return when value is uncertain.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 115yalelj814!!ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design

shared_topics.topic: choice between precise rules and vague standards (open terms) in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why parties elect precise, specified contractual terms versus vague or open-ended terms: Paper A models the rule/standard tradeoff as a front-end (proxy specification) versus back-end (court choice) decision, while Paper B analyzes why parties use open terms and negligence-like standards (e.g., 'best efforts') to govern performance under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: how courts and evidentiary processes supply meaning to vague terms (proxy selection and negligence review)
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat adjudication as the mechanism that fills out vague obligations: Paper A describes litigation as an evidentiary proxy-selection process that supplies ex post content to standards, and Paper B proposes that courts apply a Learned-Hand-style negligence/joint-maximization review and look to structural factors when enforcing open terms.

shared_topics.topic: use of sharing arrangements and principal–agent incentives under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the problem of inducing optimal performance when one party (an agent) has discretion over an asset or action under uncertainty: Paper B examines gain-sharing plus negligence terms to align agent behavior with joint returns, and Paper A explains how parties choose term precision to produce incentives given informational advantages and enforcement costs.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between front-end transaction/drafting costs and back-end enforcement/litigation costs in contract design
shared_topics.justification: Both articles argue that contract form reflects a tradeoff between the costs of specifying obligations up front and the costs of resolving disputes later: Paper A explicitly models front-end versus back-end cost allocation driving the use of precise or vague terms, while Paper B emphasizes that open terms reduce bargaining, testing, and drafting costs despite enforcement defects.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113nwulrev1009!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS

shared_topics.topic: when and how private (network- or reputation-based) ordering can substitute for or complement public legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether Maghribi traders relied primarily on private-order institutions (multilateral reputation, small-world network ties, and market practices) versus formal legal mechanisms and argues private ordering can complement or substitute law; Paper B similarly explores when parties accept informal/open contractual arrangements (sharing rules, negligence-like terms) instead of rigid legal terms and how those arrangements interact with judicial enforcement, treating private governance as an alternative or supplement to formal remedies.

shared_topics.topic: incentive design for delegated performance under uncertainty (gain‑sharing, negligence standards, and reputational sanctions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops how gain‑sharing and negligence‑like contractual terms attempt to induce an agent to develop uncertain assets but typically fall short of joint‑value maximization; Paper A examines how reputational incentives and coalition/network structures could induce cooperative performance among agents/traders across distances, treating reputational sanctions as a mechanism analogous to contractual incentive devices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information flows and network structure in enabling or constraining contract governance under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that small‑world network patterns and informational hubs can circulate reputation information widely enough to sustain multilateral private ordering; Paper B emphasizes how open terms change parties' incentives to test or bargain over uncertain information and how information asymmetries affect the efficiency of sharing rules and the need for institutional safeguards.

shared_topics.topic: standards for adjudication and institutional responses to flexible or informal arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper B proposes a 'joint maximization' (Learned Hand–style) benchmark and tailored rules for reviewing performance under open terms and specific contract types (requirements, best‑efforts, leases); Paper A engages with how legal formalities observed by Maghribi merchants relate to private ordering and suggests how courts and formal institutions can interact with or support network‑based private governance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16cardozojconflictresol395!!ARTICLE: "COMMERCIAL PEACEMAKING"-- THE NEW ROLE OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION LEGAL ORDER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "COMMERCIAL PEACEMAKING"-- THE NEW ROLE OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION LEGAL ORDER

shared_topics.topic: use of legal and institutional mechanisms to facilitate cross-border trade and commercial cooperation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that bespoke international commercial arbitration institutions can remove informal trade barriers between rival states and thereby promote bilateral commerce; Paper B argues that contract structures (open terms, sharing arrangements) and their enforcement rules function as legal mechanisms that enable parties to form commercial relationships under uncertainty and so facilitate trade and investment.

shared_topics.topic: managing uncertainty and commercial risk through legal arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames arbitration institutions as tools to manage political and legal uncertainty that deters cross-border dealings between parties from rival states, while Paper B analyzes how open-term contracts allocate and align risks between parties and reduce the costs of contracting under uncertain values and probabilities.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering versus state-backed enforcement in sustaining commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats international commercial arbitration as an autonomous, transnational legal order distinct from state jurisdiction that can govern cross-border disputes, and Paper B examines the interplay between private contractual arrangements and public enforcement (courts applying negligence-like or joint-maximization standards) when open terms require judicial oversight.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and doctrinal design to align incentives and reduce transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores designing local arbitration institutions (e.g., Jerusalem Arbitration Center, Kaesong Committee) tailored to rival-state contexts to overcome barriers to cooperation, while Paper B proposes doctrinal reforms and enforcement guidelines (e.g., joint maximization standard, scrutiny based on structural factors) to better align parties' incentives and lower contracting and enforcement costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev170!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND INNOVATION: THE LIMITED ROLE OF GENERALIST COURTS IN THE EVOLUTION OF NOVEL CONTRACTUAL FORMS

shared_topics.topic: use of open or flexible contract terms to manage uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how open terms (e.g., gain-sharing, negligence-like, requirements and best-efforts clauses) are used to allocate risk and reduce bargaining/testing costs under uncertainty; Paper B treats contractual innovation—such as collaborative contracting and preliminary agreements—as parties' responses to uncertain environments that produce flexible, non‑standard terms requiring contextual interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of discretion and incentives within contracts (sharing arrangements vs party autonomy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how contracts grant one party substantial discretion and use sharing arrangements and negligence-like standards to try to induce joint-value‑maximizing behavior (while noting defects), and Paper B examines who should shape that discretion—arguing that sophisticated parties create regimes to allocate decision rights and that courts should generally respect those party‑crafted allocations.

shared_topics.topic: judicial standards and the appropriate role of courts in enforcing nonstandard/novel contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a judicial benchmark (a rule of joint maximization similar to negligence) and recommends varying scrutiny based on structural alignment of incentives, while Paper B argues for a limited, deferential role for generalist courts (the 'passive virtues') that gives effect to contextualizing regimes but still polices opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: influence of market/contextual institutions and structural factors on contract form and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges courts to examine structural factors that align or divide parties' interests and recommends reforms for specific contract types (e.g., requirements contracts, mineral leases), and Paper B develops a taxonomy showing how market thickness and uncertainty and external contextualizing regimes (trade associations, specialized tribunals) shape both the formation of novel contracts and the appropriate interpretive role of courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53wakeforestlrev1!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE

shared_topics.topic: how contract law should accommodate parties' changes of mind and future preference shifts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes open-term contracts as a way parties deliberately leave performance unspecified to cope with future uncertainty and changing circumstances, while Paper B directly addresses 'fickleness' and argues contract doctrine should accommodate agents' legitimate revisions of commitments over time.

shared_topics.topic: how to treat and review discretionary performance by a contracting party
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines contracts that grant one party substantial discretion (e.g., gain‑sharing, best‑efforts, requirements contracts) and proposes negligence‑like or joint‑maximization benchmarks for review, and Paper B wrestles with the normative limits of binding commitments and how legal doctrine should respond when parties exercise or later revise discretionary promises.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and incentives under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that open terms and sharing arrangements are used to align individual and joint risk and to reduce costly precontractual testing or bargaining under uncertainty, and Paper B discusses how contractual allocations of risk are designed to handle factual uncertainty and regret arising from changes in information or values.

shared_topics.topic: normative standards and purposes of contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for an enforcement ideal grounded in maximizing the parties' joint expected return (a Learned‑Hand‑style negligence/joint‑maximization standard) to police open terms, while Paper B explores the normative purposes of contract law (as distinct from morality of promise), arguing that contract doctrine should balance promoting self‑authorship with allowing revision and protecting agency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62villlrev603!!Article: INTERPRETING STALE PREFERENTIAL RIGHTS TO ACQUIRE REAL ESTATE: BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT OF PROPERTY
compared_to.partner_title: Article: INTERPRETING STALE PREFERENTIAL RIGHTS TO ACQUIRE REAL ESTATE: BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT OF PROPERTY

shared_topics.topic: judicial standards for interpreting and enforcing long‑term or open‑ended contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a benchmark for reviewing performance under open terms (a joint‑maximization/negligence‑like standard and heightened scrutiny where private and joint interests diverge), and Paper B argues for a more contextual, flexible judicial gap‑filling/interpretive model beyond the Restatement to govern stale preferential purchase rights.

shared_topics.topic: contracting under uncertainty and incomplete specification of future contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why parties adopt open terms to cope with uncertain asset values and to avoid costly testing or haggling over contingencies, while Paper B documents how long‑lived ROFRs/options become incomplete as unforeseen circumstances arise and parties fail to anticipate future states.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and incentives when one party holds discretionary rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies gain‑sharing and negligence‑style terms that give an agent discretion and examines how those terms split returns and affect incentives to maximize joint return, and Paper B examines how preferential purchase rights (ROFRs/ROFOs/options) allocate future control and economic upside—affecting incentives to develop, preserve, or sell land over long horizons.

shared_topics.topic: practical reforms and drafting guidance to mitigate problems with long‑duration contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes concrete enforcement guidelines and incremental rule changes for output/requirements/best‑efforts contracts and mineral leases, and Paper B recommends drafting practices and a court interpretive framework to resolve disputes and manage risks created by aging preferential purchase rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98iowalrev535!!ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Normative Legal Theories: The Case for Pluralism and Balancing

shared_topics.topic: the normative goal(s) of contract law (what the law should aim to achieve)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central project of normative legal theory as delivering justified, all-things-considered recommendations about what the law should be and uses contract law to illustrate that task; Paper B explicitly defends a substantive normative goal for contracts — maximizing the parties' joint expected return — and places its doctrinal proposals in service of that goal.

shared_topics.topic: the debate between single-value (monist) and multi-value (pluralist) approaches in contract doctrine, especially concerning efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly contrasts monist (e.g., efficiency-centered) theories with pluralist balancing and argues for pluralism; Paper B operates from an efficiency/joint‑maximization perspective but recognizes tradeoffs and practical limits that create the need to weigh other values (risk allocation, administrability), thus engaging the same mono- vs. plural-value tension in the contractual context.

shared_topics.topic: standards for interpreting and enforcing contracts with discretionary or 'open' terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses theories of contract interpretation as an arena where normative theory must deliver final recommendations (illustrating pluralist vs monist implications); Paper B develops concrete enforcement and interpretive rules for open‑term contracts (a negligence-like/joint‑maximization standard and scrutiny based on structural incentives), thereby addressing how judges should interpret and police contractual discretion.

shared_topics.topic: how incentive alignment, risk allocation, and transaction costs should inform contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A lists administrability, fairness, and similar pragmatic values as considerations pluralist theories must balance in crafting and evaluating contract law; Paper B analyzes how open terms allocate risk, shape incentives to test or invest, and reduce bargaining costs, and argues these practical considerations should guide enforcement and doctrinal design.

papers.node_id: 1983uilllrev811!!ARTICLE: THE WEED AND THE WEB: SECTION 2-201'S CORRUPTION OF THE U.C.C.'S SUBSTANTIVE PROVISIONS -- THE QUANTITY PROBLEM
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE WEED AND THE WEB: SECTION 2-201'S CORRUPTION OF THE U.C.C.'S SUBSTANTIVE PROVISIONS -- THE QUANTITY PROBLEM
papers.abstract:
Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Codecreates a flexible, policy-sensitiveframework for the interpretation and enforcement of sales contracts.  This system was intentionally drafted to be responsive to developing commercial practice.The Statute of Frauds,on the other hand, as interpreted by most courts, represents a rigid, policy-free,free, mechanical threshold test for enforceability.Because this test is manifestly alien to the dynamic character of Article 2, to accommodate the Statute of Frauds within its framework requires some effort.  This article begins that effort, proposing a resolution of the problems generated by the provision that lies at the center of dissonance between the Statute of Frauds and the rest of Article 2: section 2-201(1)'s quantity provision.
One might expect the growing judicial understanding of general Code methodology and policy to influence the construction of section 2-201.What is actually happening, however, is that a number of U.C.C. provisions are being crippled by the Statute of Frauds.  These endangered provisions are central to the Code's fluid and pragmatic scheme governing the formation and substantive content of enforceable agreements.Like kudzu,section 2-201 is choking the new growthproduced by Article 2's substantive sections.  The effect is to hamper courts' efforts to monitor complex and important commercial relationships in rapidly changing and often unpredictable markets; this serves neither justice nor efficiency.  Needless to say, this pattern often frustrates the parties' legitimate intentions while fostering illegitimate purposes.Promising legal developments are being effectively reversed. For example, open quantity contracts finally and painfully won legal approval under sections 2-204 and 2-306,only to fall victim to section 2-201.  The complicated issues presented by these critically important contracts are being subsumed within the popular simplistic and mechanical construction of the Statute of Frauds.
Decisions utilizing such a construction damage not only individual transactions, but also invade cases which present no Statute of Frauds issue.  Each time a complex issue is avoided by cursory disposition under section 2-201, the courts lose an opportunity to become more proficient in utilizing Code machinery to deal effectively with the merits. This may help to preserve judicial suspicion and hostility toward evolving forms of commercial relationships potentially cognizable under the Code,especially when the contract lacks the old certaintiesof a definite moment of formation and definite terms of agreement.
Perhaps the most easily illustrable and most clearly deplorable example of the Statute of Frauds' subtle crippling of substantive law occurs in open quantity contracts.  These contracts provide the clearest and most compelling argument for a new recognition of the statute's destructive potential, and thus for a newly sensitive approach to the statute's terms and their application.  A great deal of litigation under section 2-201 involves open quantity contracts and the results are generally unsatisfactory.  The issue is important commercially because open quantity contracts are widely used in critical economic transactions.The common construction of section 2-201, however, has encouraged recourse to the Statute of Frauds as a method of escape for parties whose bargains prove disappointing.
It is doubly appropriate, then, that the quantity problem serves as the focus of this article's effort to illustrate and resolve the disturbing implications of the statute's orthodox construction.  Because section 2-201(1)'s quantity provision poses the most common difficulties, this article focuses primarily on the necessity for and sufficiency of a quantity term in a written memorandum under that subsection.  The discussion, however, carries obvious implications as to the proper interpretation of the statutory exceptions to section 2-201(1) as well.
To appreciate the strength of the argument for the construction of section 2-201(1) proposed in this article, one should understand the nature and scope of the section 2-201(1) problem.  Accordingly, part II of this article details representative cases and indicates typical errors in section 2-201's application.  These errors defeat the substantive Code provisions which otherwise would allow enforcement of the agreements. The cases reveal a tendency to disassociate the inquiry regarding the quantity termshownin the writings from the quantity agreed to by the parties andreflectedin the writings.  In their analysis under section 2-201, for example, courts generally refuse to allow parol evidence or even simple inference to influence their determination of the meaning of quantity language shown in the writings.  Thus, even contractsthat fully represent the agreed quantity in writing fail under the Statute of Frauds.
Such a result is inappropriate because these quantity provisions would readily survive challenge on the merits raising such issues as indefiniteness, illusoriness, or mutuality of obligation.  Thus, legitimate contracts for which the Code promises substantive enforceability fail under the Statute of Frauds.  These contracts fail not because of any real danger of perjury, for the existence of the transaction is usually well established or admitted; they fail solely on a technicality -- a mechanical construction of the quantity language of section 2-201(1).
The inescapable conclusion of the argument set forth in this article is that repeal of section 2-201 is the best and wisest course to deal with the problems the Statute of Frauds poses.Because repeal appears unlikely in the near future,several suggestions are proposed for a sensible and commercially sensitive reading of the statute.  These suggestions can be followed without drafting changes.  The proposed construction of the Statute of Frauds quantity provision is detailed in Part IV.  It suggests and justifies a reading that eliminates any requirement that a writing state or even indicate quantity to allow enforceability under section 2-201(1).  To support the conclusion that such a reading is mandated by the ascertainable policies and purposes of the Code generally and of Article 2's Statute of Frauds in particular, the proposed construction of section 2-201(1) follows a discussion in Part III of the purposes of prior Statutes of Frauds, the intentions of the Article's drafters and the guidance found in general Code policy.  As an interim measure for courts which still adhere to the present rule that requires quantity be stated in the writing, this article suggests means of reducing the destructive potential of the rule upon the Code sections affecting enforceability on the merits, especially of open quantity agreements. These suggestions are made in the second part of the article, in which the cases are discussed.  All the proposals are designed to servesection 2-201's underlying purposes better and bring the statute's effect more in line with general Code policy.

questions.question: Does a formal written-quantity requirement for enforceability of sales agreements undermine the substantive policies of a flexible commercial code and lead courts to refuse enforcement of commercially valid bargains?

Should courts be allowed to use extrinsic evidence, inference, or other interpretive methods to supply or confirm quantity when a writing does not explicitly state it, rather than mechanically denying enforcement?
Do rigid formal Statute-of-Frauds-type rules impede judicial development and enforcement of evolving commercial arrangements (such as open-quantity contracts) in modern markets?
