papers.node_id: 83nyulrev1726!!ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE
papers.title: ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE
papers.abstract:
Theorists commonly adopt one of two pictures of contract law. On the first picture, entering into a contract is an act of self-legislation in which the parties create new legal obligations for themselves. In Lon Fuller's words: "When a court enforces a promise it is merely arming with legal sanction a rule or lex previously established by the party himself. This power of the individual to effect changes in his legal relations with others is comparable to the power of a legislature."On this picture, contract law is what H.L.A. Hart calls a "power-conferring" rule. It enables persons to create and modify their legal obligations to one another. The other picture depicts contract law as concerned with extralegal wrongs, such as breaking a promise, causing reliance harms, or unjustly enriching oneself at the expense of another. Consider, for example, Charles Fried's claim that "since a contract is first of all a promise, the contract must be kept because a promise must be kept."This suggests that the purpose of contract law is to enforce the moral obligation to perform one's promises. On this picture, contract law is what Hart calls a "duty-imposing" rule: It is designed to require promisors to perform or to compensate promisees for the harms caused when they fail to do so.
call these two conceptions "pictures" because, like a picture, each organizes our understanding of its subject matter. Each is a way of seeing contract law as a unified whole. And, like a picture, it is legitimate to inquire into the descriptive accuracy of each, though descriptive accuracy need not be the only criterion by which we judge them.
Many contract theorists adopt a power-conferring or duty-imposing picture not because they believe that it best describes the contract law we have, but because it follows from more general political or moral principles that justify the imposition of contractual liability.Thus Randy Barnett's libertarian theory of legal entitlements leads him to conclude that the state is justified in enforcing promises only when the promisor manifestly intended to be legally bound in a quasi-legislative act.This leads naturally to a view of contract law as power conferring. By contrast, Patrick Atiyah's view that contract law ought to serve remedial principles--correcting for the harms unfulfilled promises cause and preventing the promisor's unjust enrichment--underwrites his picture of contract law as imposing tort-like duties on those who induce reliance in others.Similarly, Fried's commitment to the principle that "respect for others as free and rational requires taking seriously their capacity to determine their own values" explains his account of contract law as enforcing the moral obligation to perform one's promises.
This Article approaches the question from a different direction. Rather than starting from above and asking whether one or another normative principle recommends a contract law that is power conferring or duty imposing, it starts from below and asks what picture bestdescribes the contract law we have.Such an inquiry is what Jodi Kraus calls "conceptual explanation," as distinguished from justificatory legal theory.The aim is "to identify a concept, or set of concepts that render the phenomena sought to be explained maximally 'coherent'" so as to capture the "immanent, inherent, intrinsic, or internal rationality or intelligibility, deep structure, animating or underwriting principles, logical consistency, or theoretical or conceptual unity" of contract law.The question is whether the duty-imposing, the power-conferring, or some other picture best captures the underlying logic of our contract law.
Answering that question requires a deeper understanding of the concepts of power-conferring and duty-imposing rules. Hart describes the distinction in The Concept of Law as follows:
Under rules of the one type, which may well be considered the basic or primary type, human beings are required to do or abstain from certain actions, whether they wish to or not. Rules of the other type are in a sense parasitic upon or secondary to the first; for they provide that human beings may by doing or saying certain things introduce new rules of the primary type, extinguish or modify old ones, or in various ways determine their incidence or control their operations. Rules of the first type impose duties; rules of the second type confer powers, public or private. Rules of the first type concern actions involving physical movement or changes; rules of the second type provide for operations which lead not merely to physical movement or change, but to the creation or variation of duties or obligations.
This passage is representative of Hart's treatment of the power-duty distinction, which consists mainly of examples and appeals to his readers' intuitions rather than a detailed analysis of the concepts. Among other things, Hart does not discuss how to tell whether a given rule is duty imposing or power conferring. Nor have subsequent theorists examined the distinctive marks of power-conferring or duty-imposing rules. Most theorists who discuss the power-duty distinction have a different agenda: They are concerned with structural features of law as such, rather than the best description of this or that area of law.And it is typically easy to tell whether a law is power conferring or duty imposing. For example, it is fairly obvious that laws against murder or theft are duty imposing, while laws assigning authority to legislatures or judges are power conferring.
It is not obvious, however, in the case of contract law. If we want to understand whether the contract law we have is duty imposing, power conferring, or something else, we need a theory of how to tell whether a law belongs to one or another of these categories. I find the beginnings of such a theory in Joseph Raz's account of power-conferring norms as rules whose function is to enable persons to effect normative change when they so desire. It follows from this definition, I argue, that a characteristic mark of a power-creating body of law is that it includes rules that anticipate and enable its purposive use. Using contract law as an example, I describe various forms such rules might take. Differentiating between them allows me to introduce a novel distinction between two types of legal powers and to thereby describe a third picture of contract law that is neither purely power conferring nor purely duty imposing.
suggest reserving the term "power conferring" for laws designed to ensure that a person's acts result in legal change only when it is her purpose to achieve such a change. That is, power-conferring rules include conditions of validity that sort for the actor's legal purpose. The most familiar examples of such validity conditions are legal formalities. By requiring legal actors to perform an otherwise meaningless act, such as affixing a seal to an agreement, the law ensures that they expect and want the legal consequences. The presence of such validity conditions indicates that the law's sole function is to give persons the power to effect legal change.
It is possible, however, for a law to anticipate and enable its purposive use without employing such validity conditions. I coin the term "compound rule" for laws that do not condition the legal consequences of an act on evidence of the actor's legal purpose but are structured in a way that both ensures that a significant proportion of actors subject to them are likely to have such a purpose and recognizes and facilitates that purposive use. I argue that the structure ofcompound rules suggests that they function both to impose duties and to create powers.
This analysis explains why the power-duty distinction should be a site of disagreement in contract theory. It is undeniable that many contracting parties expect and want contractual liability. That is, many parties treat contract law like a legal power. The law has taken cognizance of this fact in a variety of doctrines--such as the statute of frauds, the contra proferentem rule, and the parol evidence rule--that anticipate and encourage parties' instrumental use of the law.Yet unlike most legal powers, the common law of contracts does not include validity conditions that clearly sort for a contractual purpose. Since the decline of the seal, parties need not adhere to a special legal form. In fact, the rules governing implied-in-fact contracts, unilateral contracts, and implied modification by postformation behavior mean that the parties need not even express their agreement in so many words. The attempt to introduce a generic intent-to-contract requirement in England has largely failed, while courts in the United States generally conform to the Restatement rule that "neither real nor apparent intention that a promise be legally binding is essential to the formation of a contract."Taken together, these doctrinal facts make the contract law we have look more like a set of rules that imposes duties than one that confers powers. The category of compound laws provides an attractive alternative to both pictures, one that integrates insights of each without supposing that either explains all aspects of contract law.
While compound rules share characteristics of both duties and powers, they are not a simple mix of the two. Rather, they are a distinctive category of rules with a structure all their own.The categoryis defined by four conditions. First, because compound laws do not include conditions of validity that sort for legal purpose, we can expect that people will sometimes commit legally relevant acts--such as entering into an agreement for consideration--for reasons other than to achieve their legal consequences. Second, it must be possible to tell a story about why the law would want to attach those legal consequences to acts of that sort, a story that does not involve empowering persons to purposively effect legal change. In the case of contract law, this will be a story about why we would want to hold parties legally liable for the nonperformance of exchange agreements. Third, while the law does not sort for legal purpose, the legal consequences must be such that a significant proportion of legal actors want to bring them about. In the case of contract law, this condition is satisfied since many parties enter into contracts expecting and wanting legal enforcement. Finally, the law must include rules that anticipate and enable its purposive use. I identify a number of contract doctrines that fit this description.
The concept of compound laws is not tailored to the law of contract. It would also seem to describe, for example, marriage, which in many jurisdictions can be entered into either formally or informally.It is interesting that marriage and contract both involve voluntary directed obligations--what we owe others as a consequence of our chosen relationships with them.The significance of that fact, and whether there exist other examples of compound laws or rules, are good questions that I leave for another day.
As I have said, this Article is an exercise in conceptual explanation: The goal is to render contract law intelligible. The analysis adopts what Daniel Dennett calls the "design stance," which itselfworks both from above and from below.First, a law's function has consequences for how it must be structured. Just as an automobile's transportation function means that it must have an energy source, so the function of legal powers requires that the laws that establish them anticipate and enable their purposive use. Working from above, one can ask whether a law has those features and thereby determine whether it serves that function. Second, the design stance is also a strategy for explaining individual rules by seeking out their purpose or raison d'etre. Starting from the premise that every legal rule serves some function, and taking into account general truths about the law and human nature, one can abduce a rule's likely purpose. This analysis from below is akin to determining the use of an unfamiliar tool: The structure of the artifact provides information about its intended use.
Because I begin with the law we have and ask what concepts render it intelligible, my approach is comparable to the pragmatic method that Jules Coleman employs in his theory of tort law.But where Coleman "seeks to identify the normatively significant elements of the practice and to explain them as embodiments of principle,"I seek to explain those elements as embodying functions. Functions occupy the space between practices and the principles that justify them.A principle is a broadly applicable moral or political commitment capable of justifying our legal practices; a function is a law's more immediate use or point. To say that a law serves a certain function is not yet to say what principle or principles might justify it, for a given function can be compatible with any number of principled justifications. The final Part of this Article makes a few suggestions about the implications of my functionalist account of contract law as a compound rule for the principled justification of contract law.
The Article is structured as follows. Part I describes Raz's functionalist account of legal powers and argues that the distinctive marks of power-creating laws are rules that expect and enable persons toeffect legal change purposively. Parts II and III then investigate, by way of a close examination of contract law, the different mechanisms or rules that can serve those functions. Contract law is an especially rich source for thinking about the structure of legal powers because, while it is clear that persons often treat contract as if it were a legal power, using it to purposely create legal obligations for themselves, contemporary contract law does not include rules obviously designed to sort for such a purpose. The result of this analysis is my distinction between power-conferring and compound rules, which expands our understanding of legal powers in general. Part IV draws some general conclusions for the theory of contract law. The plausibility of the compound picture of contract is evidence of the empirical strength of pluralist justificatory theories. While others have argued for pluralism from the premise that no unitary theory has yet to succeed, I show that pluralism is indicated by the very structure of contract law. Part IV also describes in some detail an example of such a pluralist theory, which I find in Raz's scattered comments on the relationship between contract and promise.

questions.question: Does the existing law of contract primarily function as a power-conferring regime (enabling parties to purposively create legal obligations), as a duty-imposing regime (imposing obligations akin to moral duties), or as a hybrid/compound form that combines features of both?
What conceptual markers or structural features distinguish power-conferring rules from duty-imposing rules, and to what extent does contract law exhibit those markers?

If contract law is best characterized as a compound or hybrid form, what follows for the appropriate normative justification(s) of contract law (e.g., whether a pluralist set of principles is required rather than a single justificatory theory)?

papers.node_id: 46ambuslj179!!ARTICLE: Trade Usage and Disclaiming Consequential Damages: The Implications for Just-in-Time Purchasing
papers.title: ARTICLE: Trade Usage and Disclaiming Consequential Damages: The Implications for Just-in-Time Purchasing
papers.abstract:
Although Japan has recently suffered its own economic setbacks, its dramatic emergence as an industrial power in the last three decades prompted a revolution in supply chain management.Practitioners as well as scholars in the areas of production management,marketing,purchasing,logistics,human resource management,and even accountinghave been diligently investigating and promoting Japanese manufacturing techniques as a model for American and European production.The Japanese, led by the pioneer TaiichiOhnoat the Toyota Motor Company, have emphasized limited production runs, short setup times, relentless quality control, inventory reduction, and waste elimination.These Japanese production management techniques have been referred to collectively as Just-in-Time (JIT) managementor kanban.In contrast, an early 1980s vintage U.S. operations management text declared confidently, "A firm cannot exist without inventory, and how well a firm controls its inventory affects how well the firm controls its mission."
Because of the success demonstrated by Japanese companies as a result of implementing these manufacturing techniques,many American and European businesses have embraced certain aspects of JIT management.Although Japan and the United States differculturallyand in their legal environment in respects that may affect the Implementation of JIT management principles in the United States,todate the legal literature has barely explored the issues arising out of JIT management.Indeed, references to various aspects of JIT management principles appear in a variety of contexts in the reported cases in the United States.This article reviews some of JIT's criticalelements,concentrating on the possible effect of trade usage on the allocation of consequential damages resulting from the breach of the contract of sale by a supplier to a JIT production facility and concluding that the parties to a JIT supply contract often rely on trade usage to supply missing terms to an incomplete or ambiguous contract of sale, including disclaimers of consequential damages resulting from a late delivery by the JIT supplier. This article argues that courts should recognize and effectuate a disclaimer of consequential damages arising out of trade usage in the appropriate circumstances.

questions.question: Whether parties to just-in-time supply contracts rely on industry trade usage to supply missing terms that disclaim or reallocate consequential damages when a supplier breaches (for example, by late delivery).
Whether courts should recognize and enforce disclaimers of consequential damages that arise from trade usage in the context of just-in-time purchasing relationships.

shared_topics.topic: Policy and doctrinal critique of formalistic common-law rules in favor of commercially realistic interpretation

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for changed circumstances or performance burdens in sale-of-goods contracts

shared_topics.topic: allocation and limitation of consequential damages for supplier breaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on how trade usage in JIT markets can operate to disclaim or limit consequential damages from late deliveries, and Paper A frames the broader choice between excusing performance and imposing damages as central to how courts allocate the burdens of changed circumstances in sales contracts.

shared_topics.topic: role of commercial practice and trade usage in supplying or modifying contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that trade usage in JIT supply chains can fill gaps and create disclaimers in otherwise incomplete sale contracts, and Paper A repeatedly emphasizes that courts should interpret impracticability and UCC provisions in light of commercial realities and merchant practices.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and application of UCC/common-law doctrines to reflect commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys UCC provisions and case law on impracticability and critiques courts for failing to implement the Code drafters' commercial aims, while Paper B urges courts to recognize and effectuate trade-usage-based disclaimers in the sale-of-goods context to reflect contemporary JIT commercial practices.

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: role of trade usage in filling gaps and supplying contract terms under UCC Article 2

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should recognize disclaimers of consequential damages arising from commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts ought to recognize and effectuate disclaimers of consequential damages based on trade usage in JIT contexts, and Paper B considers how shifts toward interpretive formalism (reducing reliance on trade usage/course of performance) would change courts' approaches to contractual risk allocation including disclaimers.

shared_topics.topic: standards-based (flexible) versus rule-based (formal) interpretation in commercial contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A operates within and invokes the U.C.C.'s standards (e.g., trade usage) to justify outcomes in JIT contracts, while Paper B is centrally concerned with the normative and practical debate between maintaining standards-based doctrines in Article 2 and adopting sharper, rule-like neoformalist approaches.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contract doctrine and real-world commercial practices (form contracts, JIT purchasing)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how legal doctrines (trade usage, disclaimers) affect the feasibility and risk allocation of the JIT production/supply model, and Paper B evaluates how proposed doctrinal changes (neoformalism) would operate in the actual marketplace dominated by form contracts and varied commercial practices.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering (non‑state rules) versus state law in commerce
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows firms and suppliers relying on private commercial practices (trade usage) to allocate risk in JIT arrangements and urges courts to give effect to those practices, while Paper B systematically investigates the emergence, forms, and conditions for private rule‑making and its interaction with state law in the commercial sphere.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling and allocation of contractual risk through informal norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how JIT contracts rely on trade usage to fill contractual gaps—particularly disclaimers of consequential damages for late deliveries—whereas Paper B examines how non‑state rules and customs function to regulate transactions and fill regulatory or contractual voids in commerce.

shared_topics.topic: judicial recognition and incorporation of private commercial norms into formal law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should recognize and effectuate disclaimers arising from trade usage in appropriate cases, and Paper B analyzes the role of state law in relation to private rules, including when and why state institutions adopt, enforce, or override commercial customs.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*

shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces Llewellyn's influence on the UCC and how the Code institutionalized contextual interpretive methods, and Paper B applies those commercial sale doctrines (e.g., trade usage and gap‑filling in sales contracts) in arguing how courts should treat disclaimers and remedies in JIT supply relationships.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation's impact on allocation of remedies (reliance, consequential damages, pre‑contractual liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the contextual methodology to doctrinal developments in reliance recovery and pre‑contractual liability, and Paper B examines how recognizing trade usage and disclaimers affects who bears consequential damages in breaches of sale contracts under JIT arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory

shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how non-written governance — whether informal relational norms in braided agreements (Paper A) or industry trade usages in JIT supply contracts (Paper B) — operate to supply terms and manage behavior when formal contracts are silent or incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and limits on consequential damages in interfirm supply relationships
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront how contracting parties allocate downstream risk in complex production settings: Paper B focuses on disclaimers of consequential damages in JIT supply contracts, while Paper A examines how braided formal/informal mechanisms manage opportunism and investment risk across collaborative innovation projects.

shared_topics.topic: formalized collaborative contracting to manage complex, uncertain production processes
shared_topics.justification: Each paper studies departures from classic arm's-length transactions toward collaborative processes for designing production and sourcing — Paper A through 'alpha contracting' and braided preliminary agreements, and Paper B through the contractual and customary adjustments that arise in Just‑in‑Time supplier relationships.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in recognizing and enforcing nonstandard governance practices
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss judicial response to modern contracting forms: Paper A evaluates whether and how courts should treat braided mixes of formal and informal governance, and Paper B argues courts ought to recognize and give effect to trade‑usage-based disclaimers in JIT contexts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE MITIGATION PRINCIPLE: TOWARD A GENERAL THEORY OF CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and design of contractual remedies (liquidated damages, disclaimers of consequential damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how traditional rules and judicial uncertainty about liquidated damages and bonus clauses limit parties' ability to allocate remedies, while Paper B focuses on whether trade usage in JIT supply chains can supply and justify disclaimers of consequential damages for late delivery.

shared_topics.topic: how transactional environment (well‑developed markets vs specialized/JIT relationships) should shape contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that standard categorical mitigation rules fit environments with robust markets for substitute performance but fail in specialized/relational settings, and Paper B studies JIT supply as a specialized transactional environment with limited substitutes that calls for different allocation norms.

shared_topics.topic: use of extrinsic norms or customized clauses to fill gaps in incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends allowing parties wide latitude and preformulated clause menus so bespoke contractual mechanisms can govern complex situations, whereas Paper B shows how parties rely on trade usage to supply missing contract terms (including liability disclaimers) in JIT arrangements and urges courts to honor those norms.

shared_topics.topic: obligations to reduce losses through cooperation, information sharing, and mitigation in relational supply contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A formulates a mitigation principle requiring parties to discover, share, and act on relevant information to minimize joint costs, and Paper B implicates parallel duties in JIT supply relationships where timely information and cooperation affect whether consequential losses arise and should be allocated by contract or usage.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83nyulrev1726!!ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THREE PICTURES OF CONTRACT: DUTY, POWER, AND COMPOUND RULE

shared_topics.topic: whether and how trade usage and commercial practices supply missing contractual terms and disclaimers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how parties to Just‑in‑Time supply contracts rely on trade usage to supply missing terms—most prominently disclaimers of consequential damages for late delivery—and argues courts should enforce such disclaimers when grounded in usage; Paper B treats doctrines (like contra proferentem and parol evidence) that recognize and enable parties' instrumental use of law and explicitly discusses how contract law takes cognizance of commercial practices that shape parties' expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the extent to which contract law enables private ordering (power‑conferring) versus imposing default duties, and the doctrinal mechanisms that anticipate purposive use
shared_topics.justification: Paper B offers a theoretical taxonomy (duty‑imposing, power‑conferring, and compound rules) and identifies doctrines that anticipate purposive use of contract law; Paper A provides an applied instance—commercial actors using trade usage to disclaim consequences—illustrating how contract law can function as a tool of private ordering and raising questions about which doctrinal responses courts should adopt.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling and interpretive doctrines for incomplete or ambiguous agreements (implied terms, parol evidence, implied‑in‑fact contracts, trade usage)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on trade usage as a mechanism for supplying missing terms in incomplete JIT supply contracts, while Paper B analyzes a range of gap‑filling and interpretive doctrines (implied‑in‑fact contracts, implied modification, parol evidence) and asks how such rules reveal the underlying function of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of liability and remedies for breach, especially disclaimers of consequential damages and the justificatory story for imposing or denying remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concentrates on the allocation of consequential damages in supply contracts and argues that trade usage often operates to disclaim such damages for late deliveries; Paper B investigates why contract law attaches legal consequences to exchange agreements, contrasting remedial (duty‑imposing) and permissive (power‑creating) accounts and thereby engaging with the normative bases for allocating liability and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev923!!ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?

shared_topics.topic: the choice between ex ante rules and ex post adjudication for regulating behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes whether sensitive practices (e.g., torture or interrogation) should be governed by ex ante prohibitions or left to ex post assessment (necessity defenses, after‑the‑fact review); Paper B addresses the parallel in commercial settings where parties may leave terms open and courts must decide after the breach whether trade usage or disclaimers supply the missing obligations.

shared_topics.topic: which institutions should supply or apply legal norms (courts vs legislatures vs private ordering)

shared_topics.topic: the rule versus standard tension and the role of customary practices as gap-fillers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the ex ante/ex post divide as roughly a choice between rules and standards and explores limits of each approach; Paper B treats trade usage (custom) as a nonformal standard that can fill contract gaps or operate instead of explicit contractual rules, and urges courts to give effect to that customary standard.

shared_topics.topic: how legal allocations of liability or exceptions shape actor incentives and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how ex ante prohibitions versus ex post excuses (and the availability of exceptions like necessity) affect actors' incentives in high‑stakes contexts such as interrogations; Paper B analyzes how disclaimed consequential damages or trade‑usage allocations alter supplier and buyer incentives in just‑in‑time supply relationships.

papers.node_id: 129yaleljf535!!ARTICLE: Twenty-First-Century Contract Law Is a Law of Agreements, Not Debts: A Response to Lewinsohn
papers.title: ARTICLE: Twenty-First-Century Contract Law Is a Law of Agreements, Not Debts: A Response to Lewinsohn
papers.abstract:
In recent decades, much of the scholarship exploring the theoretical foundations of contract law has focused on promising, as a moral concept and social practice. The last decade or so, in particular, has given rise to explorations of the correspondence between our legal rules and our moral and societal norms ofpromising.By contrast, Jed Lewinsohn barely mentions promising in his excellent article on the consideration doctrine,Paid on Both Sides: Quid Pro Quo Exchange and the Doctrine of Consideration.Instead, he focuses on another prelegal concept: exchange.
It is beyond debate, and has been for well over one hundred years now, that the consideration doctrine deems a promise eligible for enforcement when the promise has, in some sense, been given in exchange for something else.By contrast, promises that have been given merely as gifts are (largely) unenforceable. Yet despite its central place in the law of contract, the concept of exchange, unlike promise, has received very little close analysis in either contract theory or philosophical literature. Exactly what is an exchange? And to what degree does, and should, the consideration doctrine track our prelegal concept of exchange? Because consideration is the principal dividing line between the promises we enforce and those we do not, answers to these questions may tell us much about the very purpose of contract law itself. Lewinsohn's philosophical treatment of exchange fills this important gap.
Lewinsohn points out a shift in the definition of consideration that occurred almost without notice in the late nineteenth century.Writers of that period, most notably Oliver Wendell Holmes and Christopher Columbus Langdell, began to define the consideration doctrine in terms of bargained-for exchanges, by which they (eventually) meant promises that had been given in order to induce a return promise or performance.In Lewinsohn's view, this is a different conception of exchange from the one that had informed the consideration doctrine prior to Holmes and Langdell.Previously, the concept of exchange had included remuneration--one's promised performance was to pay off a debt in somesense--but did not require that a given promise be motivated by a desire for a return promise or performance.
Having described this shift, Lewinsohn takes on three primary tasks. First, he argues that the motivational conception of exchange is at odds with many details of our consideration doctrine, leading to several doctrinal problems.Second, he seeks to explain the concept of exchange without reference to the idea of reciprocal inducement or any other motivation of the promisor.Finally, he gives a brief normative defense of the consideration doctrine based on this thinner conception of exchange.For Lewinsohn, the consideration doctrine is justified not by the promises to which it applies, but rather by the ones it screens out, namely the vast majority of agreements among intimates.Society has an interest, he argues, in exempting these latter agreements from legal enforcement. The consideration doctrine, then, is justified by protecting agreements among loved ones from being treated like payments for services.
In what follows, I will briefly address Lewinsohn's work on each of these three fronts, leaving aside his historical account of the shift to the motivational conception. I will argue that Lewinsohn's account of exchange does indeed better fit with the hundreds of years of English common law that preceded Holmes and Langdell, but that the newer concept of a bargained-for exchange is better suited to modern contract law, which has catered more to the commercial context (whether business-to-business or consumer-to-business) than to agreements between intimates (like family members) or near-intimates (like neighboring farmers in the eighteenth century). Both contract law and theory have moved on, and rightly so. The idea of reciprocal inducement picks out a certain subset of exchanges, the kind of agreements that we as a society have found worthy of enforcement. These exchanges include not only the payment of debts, but also shared plans and forward-looking agreements, the enforcement of which enhances our ability to embark on complicated, coordinated projects over time. Lewinsohn's definition of and justification for the consideration doctrine do not account for modern contract law's focus on enforcing the plans to which contracting parties commit (as opposed to merely the debts they have accrued).
This Essay proceeds as follows. In Part I, I will briefly explain Lewinsohn's conception of exchange and suggest that it might have even more to offer than he has yet shown. In Part II, I will critique Lewinsohn's doctrinal objections to the motivational account of exchange and argue that his account of exchangefails to explain modern developments, such as the rejection of nominal consideration and the enforcement of purely executory contracts. Finally, in Part III, I will conclude by making a broad case for a law of contract that does care about motivations as indicators of the kind of exchanges worth enforcing. I will contrast this approach with contract theories that, like Lewinsohn's, explain and justify contract law in terms of its impact on individual interpersonal relationships. The best explanation for the consideration doctrine lies not in the agreements it screens out, but rather in the ones it selects for enforcement. By enforcing shared commitments, not just payments for obligations owed, contract law empowers individuals and organizations to accomplish together what they would likely struggle to accomplish alone.

questions.question: Should the enforceability of a promise turn on whether it was made as part of a bargained-for, reciprocal exchange intended to induce a return promise or performance, versus whether it merely remunerates a past obligation or is a gratuitous gift?

Which normative rationale best justifies limiting or permitting judicial enforcement of promises: protecting intimate/relational agreements from legal intervention, or enabling and enforcing forward-looking coordinated commitments that facilitate cooperation (especially in commercial contexts)?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1591!!ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults

shared_topics.topic: how contract law selects which promises or exchanges to enforce to enable socially valuable coordination
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that modern contract law selects for reciprocal, bargained-for exchanges and shared forward-looking commitments because enforcing those commitments facilitates complex joint projects, while Paper B treats default rules as a mechanism that determines which terms (and thus which bargains) survive in incomplete contracts and shows how those rules affect the kinds of transactions that are effectively enforced and the resulting welfare.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal and theoretical treatment of incomplete and executory contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages doctrinally with the enforcement of purely executory promises and the rejection of nominal consideration as part of the evolution of consideration doctrine, while Paper B builds a theory of why contracts are incomplete (transaction costs, private information, strategic incompleteness) and analyzes how default rules should respond to those reasons.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' motivations, information, or types in shaping enforceability and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers a debate over whether enforcement should track promisor motivation (reciprocal inducement) versus remuneration, and Paper B models how private information and parties' incentives to hide or reveal their type influence whether penalty or majoritarian defaults will induce efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for designing contract doctrine (efficiency versus protecting relationships or distributional effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a normative account that contrasts enforcing commercially valuable shared commitments with exempting intimate or social agreements from enforcement, whereas Paper B assesses the normative consequences of majoritarian versus minoritarian/penalty defaults through an efficiency lens and highlights distributional and informational reasons why particular defaults may be preferable or problematic.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83denvulrev101!!ARTICLE: Corporations and Autonomy Theories of Contract: A Critique of the New Lex Mercatoria
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Corporations and Autonomy Theories of Contract: A Critique of the New Lex Mercatoria

shared_topics.topic: applicability of promise/autonomy theories to modern commercial and corporate contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether promise-based or motivational (bargained-for) conceptions of exchange best justify enforcement in modern, commercial contract law, while Paper B asks whether autonomy-based theories (grounded in individual promise and consent) can plausibly be applied to contracts formed by corporations and in firm-to-firm commerce.

shared_topics.topic: whether motivations/intent (reciprocal inducement) should determine enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends attention to reciprocal inducement and the promisor's motivations as central to which exchanges contract law enforces, and Paper B interrogates autonomy-focused accounts that rely on individual motives by exploring how corporate actors (and their institutional motives) complicate such motivation-based justifications.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling autonomy/promise theories with economic/welfare approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts promise-focused and exchange-focused justifications for consideration and argues for a theory that explains enforcement of shared commitments, while Paper B explicitly addresses the divide between autonomy and efficiency/welfare theories and urges integrating the two rather than dismissing one for commercial contracting.

shared_topics.topic: contract law's adaptation to commercialization and historical doctrinal shifts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes a historical shift (Holmes/Langdell) toward a bargained-for conception of consideration reflecting commercial needs and critiques how different conceptions track modern developments, and Paper B evaluates the 'new lex mercatoria' tendency to narrow theory to commercial firm-to-firm transactions and considers how conceptions of the corporation interact with that commercial focus.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 74califlrev1123!!ARTICLE: Of Expectations, Incomplete Contracting, and the Bargain Principle.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Of Expectations, Incomplete Contracting, and the Bargain Principle.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of the bargained‑for exchange (bargain) conception of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the rise of a motivational, bargained‑for conception of consideration and defends reciprocal inducement as the better fit for modern commercial contracting; Paper B takes the bargain theory as its starting premise and critiques its behavioral assumptions and implications for doctrine, arguing the model needs reform to reflect real bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: what contract law should enforce — promises/debts versus shared forward‑looking commitments/expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues modern contract law enforces forward‑looking shared plans and commitments (not merely payments of debts), while Paper B focuses on expectation enforcement (the expectation measure) and how doctrines should track the parties' actual expectations and agreed‑upon range of values.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal treatment of executory contracts, modification, and excuse in the face of incomplete contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses modern developments such as enforcement of purely executory contracts and the rejection of nominal consideration that a thinner conception of exchange cannot explain; Paper B analyzes incomplete contracting and the expanding doctrines of excuse and modification, arguing current approaches create incoherence with classical enforcement rules.

shared_topics.topic: the normative justification and function of the consideration/enforcement doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques alternative justifications (e.g., protecting intimate gift agreements) and defends consideration as selecting the kinds of exchanges whose enforcement enables coordinated projects, while Paper B interrogates whether enforcement premised on complete allocation serves the bargain principle and proposes a justificatory shift toward doctrines that reflect realistic, truncated risk allocations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of forward‑looking, executory commitments (plans) versus mere debts or gifts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how small-world network structures and prominent information nodes allowed multilateral reputational sanctions to govern long‑distance trade among Maghribi merchants; Paper B treats social expectations and interpersonal contexts (e.g., promises among intimates versus commercial bargains) as nonlegal mechanisms that the law deliberately screens in or out of enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: when formal legal enforcement substitutes for or complements private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether private network governance could replace or work alongside courts and legal formalities in sustaining exchange, showing ways legal forms might bolster private ordering; Paper B evaluates why contract law enforces some kinds of exchanges (bargained‑for promises) but exempts others, effectively delineating the boundary where law intervenes versus leaves norms to govern behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how enforcement rules shape the ability to coordinate complex economic activity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that network‑based private enforcement enabled multilateral trade over distance and thereby supported broader commercial integration, while Paper B argues that modern contract law's enforcement of reciprocal, bargained commitments is justified because it enables parties to make and rely on forward‑looking coordinated plans.

shared_topics.topic: normative and doctrinal criteria for which promises or agreements deserve legal protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the empirical and normative question of whether the historical record supports treating certain merchant practices as enforceable private-order institutions rather than legal claims, and Paper B interrogates doctrinal foundations (consideration, promise versus exchange) to justify why the law selects some promises for enforcement and excludes others.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should enforce expectation-based, forward-looking commitments versus historical debts or other moral duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the expectation measure—how damages should put the promisee in the position of performance—and analyzes competing formulas for computing expectation damages; Paper B debates whether the consideration doctrine should track remuneration/debt or instead enforce bargained-for, forward-looking reciprocal commitments, defending enforcement of shared plans over merely recognizing past debts.

shared_topics.topic: principles for choosing among competing doctrinal formulas or conceptions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that multiple expectation-based formulas often conflict and develops principles to determine which formula should apply in particular breach scenarios; Paper B critiques rival conceptions of exchange (motivational vs remuneration) and offers doctrinal and normative criteria for choosing the conception that should ground the consideration doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: how core doctrines operate across different contract categories (goods vs services, executory contracts, and atypical breaches)

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52hastingslj645!!SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC
