papers.node_id: 164upalrev1403!!ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS
papers.abstract:
In 2012, Delaware courts enjoined a $ 5.5 billion hostile takeover bid based on their interpretation of the word "between" in a confidentiality agreement.The courts' decisions inMartin Mariettahighlighted the important role that ancillary agreements can play in shaping major business transactions.
Most mergers and acquisitions (M&A) scholarship has focused on the acquisition agreement--the heavily negotiated central agreement in any M&A deal. But all M&A deals are also governed by dozens of ancillary agreements--smaller agreements entered in conjunction with or around the time of the acquisition agreement--without which deals cannot go forward. This Article investigates why deals are memorialized with constellations of agreements, rather than with just one. Through a study of complex M&A deals, this Article begins to probe why these "unbundled bargains" exist, how they add value in business transactions, and what they imply for contract interpretation and deal design.
The facts ofMartin Mariettaare typical of the early stages of any friendly M&A deal. In 2010, the country's two largest construction aggregates companies, Martin Marietta Materials and Vulcan Materials, entered into two routine confidentiality agreements while discussing a potential deal.Confidentiality agreements are among the most common ancillary agreements in M&A transactions: parties enter into these short, simple agreements to protect nonpublic information exchanged during initial evaluation and negotiation.Because deal lawyers often consider confidentiality agreements straightforward and boilerplate, junior attorneys or in-house counsel usually draft them.
Martin Marietta's general counsel drafted the agreements, using a confidentiality agreement template that the parties had used before.In the agreements, the parties agreed not to use information shared in confidence for any purpose other than "a possible business combination transaction . . .between[the parties]."This meant, for instance, that they would not use proprietary information learned during due diligence to compete against each other. This is a common provision when the deal parties are competitors. Martin Marietta and Vulcan negotiated on and off over the next year and a half, exchanging nonpublic information in the process.Friendly talks fizzled around the time changes in Vulcan's stock price made the deal particularly attractive to Martin Marietta.
On December 12, 2011, Martin Marietta launched an unsolicited exchange offer for Vulcan's shares, preparing the offer using nonpublic information Vulcan had shared with Martin Marietta.In its unsolicited exchange offer-- a type of hostile takeover--Martin Marietta publicly offered to acquire Vulcan shares from any and all of Vulcan's stockholders.Vulcan stockholders could exchange each Vulcan share for half a share of Martin Marietta's more valuable stock.That same day, Martin Marietta filed suit in the Delaware Chancery Court, seeking a declaration that nothing in the confidentiality agreements barred Martin Marietta's hostile takeover.Vulcan countersued, seeking to enjoin Martin Marietta's exchange offer.
Ultimately, both the Delaware Chancery Court and the Delaware Supreme Court agreed with Vulcan, granting a four-month injunction against Martin Marietta's hostile takeover.The opinions turned in part on the courts' interpretations of the word "between" in one of the confidentiality agreements. The parties had disputed the meaning of the provision that barred the parties from using information for purposes other than "a possible business combination transaction . . .between[the parties]."The courts found that the parties meant to limit use of the information to pursuit of a transactionbetweenthe two parties--Martin Marietta and Vulcan.Because the hostile takeover was an attempt by Martin Marietta to buy shares from Vulcan's stockholders on the public market, rather than from Vulcan, it was not a transaction between the two parties.Therefore, Martin Marietta violated the provision when it used nonpublic information in the hostile transaction.
TheMartin Mariettadecisions caused a stir among deal lawyers. Companies seeking to sell themselves often require potential buyers to sign confidentiality agreements that have explicit "standstill provisions."These provisions prevent potential buyers from announcing a bid (including a hostile bid) for the target for a period of a year or two from the conclusion of the sale process.TheMartin Mariettaconfidentiality agreements did not contain explicit standstill provisions, but the courts nonetheless enjoined Martin Marietta's bid as though the agreements contained standstill provisions.
Many deal lawyers lambasted the decisions for finding an "implied standstill provision."One law firm noted that "the court . . . gave very little, if any, weight to . . . [the fact] that two sophisticated parties (with sophisticated counsel) did not discuss or include a standstill provision in [the agreement]."Others called the decisions "a wakeup call . . . that confidentiality agreements negotiated in the early stages of a deal can have significant consequences down the road."A year after the decisions, one lawyer wrote that "[Martin Marietta] reminded people that these are real agreements. These are not boilerplate, and they'renot something you just sign to move on . . . . People are spending a lot more time and being much more careful in constructing and negotiating them."
For deal lawyers,Martin Mariettareveals the importance of small agreements in major deals. It shows that ancillary agreements like confidentiality agreements-- drafted quickly by busy in-house lawyers or inexperienced first-year associates at law firms--must be taken seriously, and can significantly affect major deals. InMartin Marietta, a confidentiality agreement--an agreement so peripheral to the heart of the deal that it barely qualifies as part of the deal at all--nonetheless determined the most important part of the deal: whether it could go forward at all.
If deal lawyers are just beginning to appreciate the importance of ancillary agreements in practice, legal scholars have an even more rudimentary understanding of the role these agreements play in shaping deals. To date, there has been no comprehensive account of why ancillary agreements exist.Specifically, legal scholars have not tackled the issue of why M&A deals are governed by a constellation of agreements--the much-studied acquisition agreement and dozens of under-studied ancillary agreements--rather than by a single comprehensivedeal document. This Article provides a comprehensive account of the dynamic interactions between ancillary agreements and acquisition agreements in M&A dealmaking. In doing so, it begins to develop a new theory of the deal and posits that a deal's boundaries extend beyond the acquisition agreement and into the corners of unbundled bargains. Reframing complex deals as unbundled bargains has important implications for contract theory and transactional practice: it suggests new ways for courts to interpret complex deal disputes and for parties to design better deals.
Both courts and parties routinely underestimate the boundaries of deals. This underestimation affects both the way that courts interpret deal disputes and whether parties choose to unbundle their deals into separate contracts. For example, although deal lawyers were aghast at the courts' decisions inMartin Marietta, reframing theMartin Mariettadeal as an unbundled bargain sheds new light on the courts' decisions. The decisions actually suggest that those courts understood unbundling--they interpreted a confidentiality agreement as part of the M&A deal, allowing it to determine whether the deal could go forward at all. If courts regularly view M&A deals as unbundled bargains, parties should, in the future, feel more comfortable unbundling their bargains into multiple contracts, because no matter how many agreements memorialize a deal, those parts will be interpreted together should a dispute arise. There is another benefit to courts understanding unbundled bargains, and interpreting the parts of unbundled bargains together: because parties know that deal parts will be interpreted together in a dispute, they have less incentive to obfuscate parts of the deal by burying them in undisclosed or less-scrutinized ancillary agreements.
This Article proceeds in three Parts. Part I introduces the concept of unbundled bargains. It illustrates the dynamic relationship between ancillary agreements and acquisition agreements in M&A deals. Part II introduces a new theory of the deal, and shows how and why M&A deals are unbundled bargains. Unbundled bargains add value to M&A deals by increasing modularity and precision, which increases dealmaking efficiency ex ante and reduces deal enforcement costs ex post. Part III considers the implications of unbundled bargains for contract interpretation and deal design.
The principles developed in this Article can be applied beyond M&A to help illuminate when and why bargaining parties strike bargains through single contracts and when and why they use many interconnected agreements.

questions.question: Why do parties in complex transactions memorialize their agreements as multiple interconnected ancillary contracts rather than a single comprehensive agreement?
Do these 'unbundled' constellations of agreements increase modularity and precision in deals, thereby improving ex ante dealmaking efficiency and reducing ex post enforcement costs?
How does treating multiple interconnected agreements as parts of the same deal affect how adjudicators interpret contractual disputes and how parties design and disclose deal terms?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35ucdavislrev319!!ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation shaping contractual allocation of rights and duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts for using the vague good-faith standard to supplant parties' negotiated allocation of quantity discretion in long-term contracts, while Paper B analyzes Delaware courts’ interpretive choices (e.g., construing confidentiality clauses to imply standstills) that effectively reframe the bargain in M&A disputes.

shared_topics.topic: contract design and drafting choices as tools for allocating risk and control
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how parties can and should tailor contractual terms (minimums, pricing regimes, linked requirements) to calibrate discretion and reliance, and Paper B shows why parties unbundle deals into multiple, targeted agreements (confidentiality, ancillary contracts) to achieve modularity and precision in deal design.

shared_topics.topic: the power of implied or default terms to alter parties' expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the UCC/’good faith’ default can impose protections sellers may not have bargained for, and Paper B explores how courts can treat ancillary clauses as implying standstills or other obligations that materially change what sophisticated parties thought they agreed to.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms to prevent opportunism and protect reliance investments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on sellers’ concern about buyer opportunism in requirements/output contracts and how contractual mechanisms (or judicial intervention) can protect reliance, while Paper B studies confidentiality and related ancillary agreements as tools to prevent opportunistic use of nonpublic information in M&A processes.

shared_topics.topic: responding to contractual incompleteness and transaction complexity through structure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses incompleteness in long-term contracts by allocating decision-making discretion and proposing default rules to respect parties’ bargains, and Paper B explains how complex M&A deals manage incompleteness and reduce enforcement costs by unbundling transactions into multiple interconnected agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 3texamlrev91!!ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: contractual architecture and contract design (single comprehensive contract versus multiple ancillary agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how relational expectations and social context should inform the design of contractual arrangements, arguing that law should account for relational as well as formal commitments; Paper B analyzes why M&A deals are structured as constellations of ancillary agreements (unbundled bargains), how that modular architecture adds value, and what it implies for designing deals.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal contracts and relational/social context in commercial exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that relational norms (reciprocity, solidarity, background social context) are economic behaviors that interact with formal contract law; Paper B shows how apparently peripheral agreements and parties' implicit expectations (e.g., implied standstills) can function as part of the broader deal context and change substantive outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of transaction-costs and organizational theory to explain contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights transaction cost economics and related business-school literature as vehicles for operationalizing relational contract concepts, while Paper B deploys transaction-cost concepts (modularity, precision, ex ante efficiency, ex post enforcement costs) to explain why parties unbundle deals into multiple agreements.

shared_topics.topic: implications for judicial interpretation and doctrine when contracts are embedded in wider deal structures or social practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses challenges and possibilities of turning empirical relational-contract findings into admissible evidence and doctrinal guidance for courts, and Paper B analyzes how courts treated ancillary agreements in Martin Marietta and argues that viewing deals as unbundled bargains should inform judicial interpretation and litigation strategy.

shared_topics.topic: value of interdisciplinary and empirical study of contracting to inform legal scholarship and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for partnering with organizational, marketing, and management scholars to empirically operationalize relational expectations and influence doctrine, and Paper B bases its account on a systematic study of complex M&A transactions to develop a theory of unbundled bargains with practical implications for dealmakers and courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev495!!SYMPOSIUM: "PRODUCTIVE DISINTEGRATION" See Hugh Collins, Regulating Contracts 55, 360-61 (1999). AND THE LAW OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "PRODUCTIVE DISINTEGRATION" See Hugh Collins, Regulating Contracts 55, 360-61 (1999). AND THE LAW OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: interpretive consequences of boilerplate and ancillary agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how standard-form consumer clauses (e.g., Gateway) and implied terms function in practice and can produce significant redistributions of risk, while Paper B shows how routine ancillary documents like confidentiality agreements (treated as boilerplate) can carry dispositive effects in M&A (e.g., implied standstill in Martin Marietta).

shared_topics.topic: role of judges and doctrinal choice between formalism and contextualism in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates new formalism versus contextualized, realist adjudication and the competency of judges to apply contextual norms of fairness, and Paper B documents courts interpreting peripheral agreements in light of the entire deal (treating unbundled documents together), illustrating a contextual approach to resolving disputes.

shared_topics.topic: categorization of transactions and the boundaries of a 'deal'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes transaction types and the need to 'narrow categories' to map normative responses across different contracting spheres, and Paper B develops the 'unbundled bargains' concept showing that M&A deals are composed of interrelated agreement-types and that a deal's boundaries extend beyond the central acquisition agreement.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design (structure, modularity, and unbundling) affects parties’ bargaining power and autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines freedom of contract (freedom to/ freedom from) and how doctrinal rules and consumer protections shape parties' autonomy, while Paper B argues that unbundling into multiple modular agreements changes ex ante efficiency and ex post enforcement incentives, with direct effects on what parties can and cannot do.

shared_topics.topic: the prevalence and legal significance of implied or sub rosa norms and terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts' use of implied terms and sub rosa adoption of fairness/cooperation norms when formalist rules are insufficient, and Paper B shows courts imputing an implied standstill or treating ancillary clauses as integral to the overall deal even when parties did not expressly negotiate those limits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1998wislrev463!!ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.topic: the boundaries of a deal and the legal significance of multi-agreement transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the construction sector's transactional system of layered, hybrid and long-term agreements and asks how those multiple linked contracts function as a whole; Paper B develops the concept of "unbundled bargains," showing how ancillary agreements (e.g., NDAs) interact with acquisition agreements to define the boundaries of M&A deals and affect enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role and risks of standard-form templates and boilerplate in complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques reliance on industry standard models and integrated form contracts in construction and their consequences for disputes and governance; Paper B documents how template confidentiality agreements and boilerplate language produced unanticipated, case-determinative consequences in M&A and urges more careful drafting and design.

shared_topics.topic: how contract interpretation by courts shapes transaction design and party behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how legal doctrines and public law (and their unpredictability) influence contracting practice in the construction industry and motivates calls for reform or codification; Paper B shows concretely how Delaware courts' interpretation of a confidentiality clause in Martin Marietta altered parties' incentives and will affect future deal structuring.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between private ordering mechanisms and public law as a background governance framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates industry-internal governance (private orderings, standard contracts, conflict-management institutions) and assesses the need for external legal backstops or a uniform code; Paper B explores how privately negotiated ancillary agreements operate within the public-law context (court review) and how that interaction informs whether parties choose to unbundle or consolidate contractual arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: conflict management, dispute risk, and the transaction-costs implications of contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats payment disputes, third-party liability, and other recurring conflicts as drivers for structural reform and for adopting mechanisms that reduce costly litigation; Paper B analyzes how unbundling increases modularity and precision to lower ex ante transaction costs and ex post enforcement costs, and how mis-specified ancillary clauses can precipitate expensive injunctions and litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how transaction costs shape contract structure and governance choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes M&A deals through a transaction-costs lens, arguing that unbundled bargains (multiple ancillary agreements) increase modularity and reduce ex ante bargaining and ex post enforcement costs; Paper B situates lawful opportunism inside Williamson's transaction-costs framework and studies when parties choose literal enforcement (raising transaction costs) versus relationship-preserving alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of judicial enforcement and contract interpretation on contracting behavior and deal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how courts' interpretation of ancillary agreements (e.g., implying a standstill) alters the boundaries of deals and thus parties' incentives to unbundle or disclose terms; Paper B focuses on how courts' willingness to enforce literal contractual entitlements creates conditions for lawful opportunism and thereby influences parties' enforcement choices and contracting strategies.

shared_topics.topic: contractual design choices (unbundling, modularity, completeness) as tools to allocate risk and mitigate dispute costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that using multiple, specialized ancillary agreements increases precision and efficiency and can lower enforcement costs; Paper B examines how features of contract design and incomplete contingent terms make agreements susceptible to lawful opportunism and discusses design- and policy-based mitigation.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior enabled by contractual gaps, ambiguity, or ancillary terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how parties might hide consequential deal terms in ancillary agreements and how courts' joint interpretation reduces incentives to obfuscate, while Paper B differentiates blatant (deceptive) opportunism from lawful opportunism that exploits literal entitlements and contractual gaps, and empirically investigates factors predicting such behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: legal significance of peripheral or ancillary terms (low‑scrutiny documents) in generating substantive legal constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how seemingly peripheral ancillary agreements (e.g., confidentiality clauses) can be interpreted as integral deal terms that bar hostile bids, while Paper B analyzes how peripheral marketing tactics and introductory offers (e.g., teasers, free offers) can trigger bait‑and‑switch regulation despite appearing minor or routine.

shared_topics.topic: how narrow wording or customary phrasing is interpreted to create implied obligations or liabilities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on courts parsing a single word (“between”) in a confidentiality agreement to impose an implied standstill effect, and Paper B studies how definitional boundaries of “bait‑and‑switch” and related phrases determine when regulators treat marketing conduct as deceptive or unlawful.

shared_topics.topic: the role of customs, norms, and market practices in shaping enforcement and judicial/regulatory responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents deal‑lawyers’ customary treatment of boilerplate ancillary documents and how courts’ willingness to treat those documents as part of the deal changes enforcement expectations, while Paper B argues that custom and norms—rather than pure welfare calculus—drive which bait‑and‑switch practices are formally regulated or tolerated.

shared_topics.topic: practical implications for drafting, deal design, and regulatory strategy to avoid unintended legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws out implications for how parties should unbundle and draft multiple agreements knowing courts may read them together, and Paper B advises how firms and advocates should design offers and regulatory arguments (or seek legislative change) in light of how regulators and courts treat teasers, free offers, and other sales tactics.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113pennstlrev1031!!Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: how private agreements interact with and are enforced by public courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts treating ancillary agreements (e.g., confidentiality provisions) as integral parts of M&A deals and enforcing them—sometimes implying standstill effects—while Paper B emphasizes that international commercial arbitration is often a hybrid system in which parties routinely rely on national courts to enforce or supplement arbitral outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: why parties choose particular contractual architectures (single comprehensive contract vs multiple linked agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory of 'unbundled bargains,' explaining why parties deliberately split complex M&A deals into modular ancillary agreements, and Paper B analyzes how parties select dispute-resolution mechanisms (private arbitration, trade association systems, or litigation) as part of transaction design based on expected enforcement and governance tradeoffs.

shared_topics.topic: use of ancillary or private-ordering mechanisms to constrain counterparty opportunism and manage risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how ancillary clauses (confidentiality, implied standstills) function to limit parties' conduct and preserve bargaining value during deals, while Paper B studies private-ordering institutions (industry arbitrations, reputational sanctions, arbitration clauses) as tools that parties use to discipline behavior and secure contract performance outside or alongside public law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction attributes (complexity, distance, clarity, urgency) in shaping governance and enforcement choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that modularity and precision from unbundling add value in complex transactions and reduce enforcement costs, and Paper B identifies attributes—distance, complexity of the good, clarity of law, need for speed—that explain when parties prefer private arbitration, trade association mechanisms, or court litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9wmmarybuslrev435!!SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?

shared_topics.topic: the purpose of contract law in supporting market transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a Market Theory arguing contract law should be structured to support morally desirable, well-functioning markets; Paper A shows empirically how contract rules (and courts' treatment of agreements) shape the functioning of M&A markets by enabling or foreclosing particular transactions.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret the boundaries of deals and which agreements count as part of a transaction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether ancillary contracts (e.g., confidentiality agreements) are properly read as part of an M&A deal, while Paper B addresses, from a normative perspective, how the law should decide which promises/contracts deserve enforcement—both concern delimiting enforceable deal terms.

shared_topics.topic: how enforcement choices affect private ordering and contract design (including use of multiple, modular agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues parties unbundle bargains into ancillary agreements for modularity and precision and that court treatment will influence that practice; Paper B contends that the normative structure of contract law will shape which markets and contracting practices are supported or discouraged, thus affecting how parties design contracts.

shared_topics.topic: which specific promises or clauses should be enforceable given their market effects (e.g., confidentiality/standstill implications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A’s Martin Marietta example shows enforcement of a confidentiality clause operated like an implied standstill with major market consequences, and Paper B directly interrogates which promises contract law ought to enforce or reject based on their moral and market repercussions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev1437!!ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: how courts interpret parties' intent to be legally bound
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a taxonomy and normative framework for when and how courts should find that parties intended their agreements to be legally enforceable, and Paper B analyzes Delaware courts' interpretive choices (e.g., reading a confidentiality clause to restrict hostile bids) that effectively determine whether parties were bound by a contested provision.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability and legal significance of preliminary/ancillary agreements (e.g., confidentiality agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A specifically examines preliminary agreements and recommends rules for when they should be treated as binding, while Paper B studies confidentiality and other ancillary agreements in M&A (the Martin Marietta case) to show how such peripheral documents can control major transactions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default rules versus express opt-outs in contract design and drafting strategy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes enforcement versus nonenforcement defaults and the costs of requiring express statements to opt out, and Paper B shows the practical consequences for dealmakers of leaving terms implicit or using boilerplate ancillary documents—illustrating why parties might (or might not) expressly draft opt-outs or standstill language.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial interpretation affects parties' incentives, relational trust, and deal-structuring choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how interpretive rules and sticky defaults interact with relational costs and extralegal trust, and Paper B shows empirically that courts' willingness to read ancillary agreements into the deal (e.g., implying a standstill) changes parties' incentives to unbundle, disclose, or bury terms and thus affects deal design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42sandiegolrev533!!EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how judges should interpret contract clauses in light of contextual and extrinsic factors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a pluralist theory arguing that contract interpretation legitimately draws on multiple factors (authorial intent, reader understanding, background practices) rather than a single inquiry, and Paper B empirically shows courts interpreting a confidentiality clause by reference to surrounding deal context and related agreements in Martin Marietta.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when multiple interconnected agreements should be read together as one 'deal' (the boundaries of a deal)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether meaning is fixed within a single text or shaped by broader practical purposes and related materials, and Paper B introduces the concept of 'unbundled bargains' and demonstrates that ancillary agreements are often construed as part of the same deal.

shared_topics.topic: judicial recognition or imposition of implied obligations through interpretation (e.g., implied standstills)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the tension between discerning fixed textual meaning and judges' displacement or adaptation of meaning in order to reach practical results, and Paper B documents courts effectively finding an implied standstill via interpretation of a confidentiality agreement, with major transactional consequences.

shared_topics.topic: implications of interpretive approaches for drafting, deal design, and legal practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links interpretive theory (pluralist vs single-inquiry) to desirable judicial practice and how texts should be approached, while Paper B draws direct lessons for deal lawyers—showing that ancillary drafting choices matter because courts will treat related agreements together and that parties should therefore design and draft with interpretive aggregation in mind.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2019wislrev1109!!ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY

shared_topics.topic: contract as a tool of governance beyond pure exchange
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how contracts are used to regulate conduct and produce social or organizational outcomes beyond the delivery of goods or payment — Paper A examines 'contract social responsibility' (e.g., inclusion riders and supplier sustainability clauses) as a means to advance social norms, and Paper B shows how ancillary agreements in M&A shape the governance and possible outcomes of complex deals beyond the acquisition agreement itself.

shared_topics.topic: the design choice to allocate rights and obligations across multiple, granular contractual provisions
shared_topics.justification: Both works investigate why parties draft detailed, modular terms rather than a single comprehensive promise — Paper A describes KSR's 'braiding' of enforceable and non‑enforceable clauses to create granularity and flexibility, while Paper B theorizes 'unbundled bargains' and the use of ancillary agreements to increase modularity and precision in deal design.

shared_topics.topic: limits of formal enforceability and the role of non‑legal/relational mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Each paper grapples with the fact that many important contractual provisions may be weakly enforceable or unenforceable and yet still have effect through relational, expressive, or reputational channels — Paper A situates KSR in relational contract theory and emphasizes expressive/instrumental effects, and Paper B emphasizes how unbundling and deal practice rely on shared expectations and ex‑post interpretation to reduce enforcement costs.

shared_topics.topic: how courts and interpretation determine deal boundaries and the practical force of peripheral clauses
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider how judicial interpretation can expand or constrain the practical scope of a transaction by treating peripheral or ancillary clauses as part of the core deal — Paper A discusses doctrinal limits on enforcing socially oriented clauses, and Paper B analyzes Martin Marietta to show how a confidentiality clause was interpreted as effectively imposing standstill‑like limits on a takeover.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: boundaries of what counts as the ‘deal’ or the contractual domain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that complex M&A transactions are ‘unbundled bargains’ whose boundaries extend beyond the acquisition agreement into ancillary contracts, and Paper B interrogates when an area of law (or a set of relations) should be characterized as contractual, both probing where and why the scope of contract law should be drawn.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and the use of modular/ancillary contracts to tailor defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows parties deliberately use multiple ancillary agreements to modularize and precisely allocate rights and risks around a central deal, while Paper B focuses on the normative and descriptive significance of rules that are susceptible to private reordering and how defaults should be set or contracted around.

shared_topics.topic: judicial characterization and contract interpretation with consequential legal effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how courts’ interpretation of peripheral agreements (e.g., treating confidentiality clauses as implied standstills) can determine whether deals proceed, and Paper B criticizes reifying characterizations divorced from consequences, stressing that how judges label transactions has important legal and policy effects.

shared_topics.topic: transaction-cost and efficiency rationales for contract design (centralized vs unbundled structures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a transaction-cost account of why parties unbundle deals—modularity and precision increase ex ante efficiency and reduce ex post enforcement costs—while Paper B locates contractarian arguments (including transaction-cost explanations for firm and rule design) at the center of debates over when private ordering should be permitted.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54smulrev867!!SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:The Statute of Frauds and the Parol Evidence Rule Under the NCCUSL 2000 Annual Meeting Proposed Revision of U.C.C. Article 2
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ON REVISED ARTICLE 1 AND PROPOSED REVISED ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE:The Statute of Frauds and the Parol Evidence Rule Under the NCCUSL 2000 Annual Meeting Proposed Revision of U.C.C. Article 2

shared_topics.topic: how courts admit and interpret extrinsic or ancillary writings to determine contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes proposed revisions to the UCC parol evidence rule and how extrinsic records may be used to prove contract terms, and Paper B shows how courts treated a confidentiality agreement (an ancillary writing) as determinative of deal scope, spotlighting judicial interpretation of documents outside a central acquisition agreement.

shared_topics.topic: the legal status and enforceability of peripheral or ancillary agreements (including boilerplate templates) in major commercial deals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when formal requirements and exceptions render records enforceable under the statute of frauds (affecting peripheral writings), while Paper B studies how short ancillary agreements like confidentiality or standstill-type provisions—often drafted as boilerplate—can bind parties and shape whether an M&A transaction can proceed.

shared_topics.topic: whether multiple documents or unbundled bargains should be treated together as one integrated deal
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's discussion of record formalities and how contract evidence is aggregated bears on when separate writings can constitute an enforceable contract, and Paper B directly theorizes unbundled bargains where acquisition and ancillary agreements function as a constellation to be interpreted together in disputes.

shared_topics.topic: implications of doctrinal rules for transactional practice and deal design (including transaction and enforcement costs)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses how changes to the statute of frauds and parol evidence rule would affect parties' incentives, formality burdens, and litigation outcomes, and Paper B argues that unbundling affects modularity, precision, ex ante efficiency, and ex post enforcement costs, proposing doctrinal and design responses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113nwulrev1009!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS

shared_topics.topic: private ordering as a substitute or complement to public enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Maghribi traders used network-based private ordering (reputation, selective hiring) to sustain long‑distance exchange with little reliance on courts, while Paper B shows how parties use ancillary contracts and deal design as private ordering tools that shape and sometimes preclude recourse to public remedies in M&A.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information regimes and confidentiality in enabling or constraining transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how small‑world ties and prominent information nodes circulated reputational information that deterred cheating and supported trade; Paper B shows how confidentiality provisions and other ancillary agreements govern information use and can decisively enable, constrain, or block transactions.

shared_topics.topic: contractual architecture/structure as a governance mechanism to manage opportunism and reduce enforcement costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how particular network structures (small‑world patterns, subnetworks, hubs) create pathways for multilateral reputational enforcement, and Paper B develops the idea of 'unbundled bargains'—modular ancillary agreements—that increase precision and lower ex ante negotiation and ex post enforcement costs.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between private practices and judicial/legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the historians' critique about legal formalities and explores how private network governance can operate alongside or be supported by legal institutions, while Paper B analyzes how court interpretation of peripheral agreements (e.g., implied standstills) affects deal outcomes and incentivizes different contract design choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev675!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE

shared_topics.topic: whether a contract (or deal) is best understood as a discrete document or as part of a broader constellation/relationship
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances relational contract theory, arguing that contracts are embedded in ongoing relationships and cannot be understood in isolation, while Paper B reframes complex M&A transactions as 'unbundled bargains,' showing that a deal consists of multiple interconnected agreements rather than a single standalone acquisition contract.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of ancillary or 'boilerplate' agreements and off‑paper relational practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contractual meaning and obligations often arise from the surrounding relationship and practices beyond the written text, and Paper B demonstrates empirically that ancillary documents like confidentiality agreements—often treated as boilerplate—can control major deal outcomes and must be treated as integral parts of the deal.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret contracts in light of surrounding deal context and relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the idea that interpretation should account for relational norms and the relational setting of contracting, and Paper B analyzes Delaware decisions (e.g., Martin Marietta) to show courts already interpret ancillary agreements together with core deal documents, effectively treating the broader deal context as relevant to interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract/deal design and drafting (modularity, precision, and governance over time)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative and theoretical consequences from relational contracting about how parties should structure obligations and governance across ongoing relationships, while Paper B offers a theory of unbundled bargains showing that modular, multi‑agreement design increases precision and efficiency and affects ex ante bargaining and ex post enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56scallrev573!!ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CASE FOR LOSS SHARING.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and losses through contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties use multiple ancillary agreements (e.g., confidentiality clauses, standstill-like terms) to allocate rights, duties, and risks across a constellation of documents in M&A deals; Paper B addresses how reliance losses should be allocated when performance is excused and evaluates contract design and remedial rules as mechanisms for assigning such losses.

shared_topics.topic: contract interpretation and the boundaries of a deal
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts treating ancillary agreements as part of the overall deal—interpreting a confidentiality clause to determine whether a merger could proceed—while Paper B engages with doctrines (impossibility, frustration, impracticability) and remedial allocation, which likewise require judicial interpretation of when contractual obligations continue or are excused and how consequences attach.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency versus fairness tradeoffs in structuring contractual relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that unbundling into modular ancillary agreements improves ex ante efficiency and reduces ex post enforcement costs, whereas Paper B contrasts a wealth-maximizing (efficiency) allocation of reliance losses with a fairness-based, loss-sharing approach and defends equal sharing on moral/justice grounds.

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing contracts as multi-participant or relational enterprises rather than single, self-contained documents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reframes complex deals as 'unbundled bargains'—a network of interrelated contracts that together form the deal—while Paper B conceptualizes contract as a moral partnership or 'common enterprise,' using that relational view to justify sharing unforeseen losses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45arizstlj369!!ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages

shared_topics.topic: principles for resolving conflicts among contractual norms or formulas
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops principles for choosing among competing expectation-damages formulas when multiple expectation-based measures yield conflicting results; Paper B analyzes how courts reconcile and interpret multiple interconnected agreements (e.g., reading a confidentiality clause as effectively limiting deal conduct) and thus deploy interpretive principles to resolve conflicts across deal documents.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual form and modular structure affect legal outcomes and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the particular damages formula used (and whether standard formulas apply) can drastically change a promisee's remedy; Paper B shows that unbundling a transaction into an acquisition agreement plus ancillary contracts alters what obligations exist and how disputes are enforced, sometimes producing significant transactional consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the risks and consequences of relying on standardized or boilerplate provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques commonly used, standard expectation-damages formulas and highlights puzzles and inappropriate applications of those standard rules; Paper B documents how template confidentiality clauses and other boilerplate ancillary agreements can produce unforeseen and dispositive results (e.g., implied standstills) in major deals.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts/doctrine in shaping remedy and deal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal principles courts should use to select and apply expectation-damages formulas in recurring breach scenarios; Paper B studies judicial decisions (Martin Marietta) to show how courts' interpretations of ancillary agreements concretely shape the available remedies and the scope of deals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: ex ante versus ex post meaning of contractual language and when ‘meaning’ fixes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes that many terms acquire their operative meaning only when a disputed circumstance arises and that a true ex ante mutual intention often does not exist, while Paper B empirically shows how short, early-stage contract text (e.g., confidentiality clauses) gets interpreted later in M&A disputes and can determine deal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the substantive role of ancillary or 'boilerplate' agreements in shaping major transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper B studies why deals are structured as constellations of ancillary agreements and how those peripheral contracts can control core outcomes, and Paper A engages with how specific negotiated language (or seemingly peripheral text) can be decisive in later disputes and yet may not reflect settled ex ante intent.

shared_topics.topic: how courts interpret contractual texts and the implications of judicial interpretive methods for deal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory linking judicial rule-induction and private contract interpretation, arguing courts should focus on pragmatic resolution rather than uncovering ex ante intent, while Paper B documents how Delaware courts’ interpretive choices (e.g., reading an implied standstill into a confidentiality clause) affect how parties draft and unbundle deals.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, strategic use of information, and the constraining (or illusory) role of contract language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the premiss that ex post opportunism can be deterred by seeking ex ante intent and treats opportunistic reinterpretation as largely inevitable, and Paper B shows a concrete instance—use of nonpublic information in a hostile bid—where contractual language and judicial interpretation operate as mechanisms that enable or constrain opportunistic deal behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34tourolrev83!!SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling versus refusing to enforce indefinite contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts treated ancillary confidentiality language as part of the overall M&A deal (effectively interpreting interrelated documents together), while Paper B studies Sun Printing where Cardozo refused to enforce a contract for indefiniteness and contrasts that refusal with modern gap‑filling approaches in the UCC and Restatement.

shared_topics.topic: why contracting parties leave terms open or split transactions across multiple instruments (contract design choices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory of 'unbundled bargains' explaining why parties use multiple ancillary agreements to achieve modularity and precision, and Paper B investigates the economic and historical reasons parties leave material terms (price, duration) open for later agreement.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial contract interpretation shapes commercial and competitive outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that courts' reading of an ancillary confidentiality clause produced an effective 'implied standstill' that altered takeover strategy, and Paper B argues that Cardozo's interpretation in Sun Printing increased uncertainty and may have affected competitive behavior in the newsprint industry.

shared_topics.topic: the decisive role of precise wording and boilerplate drafting in commercial contract enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how a single word in a boilerplate confidentiality clause ('between') determined whether a hostile bid was enjoined, while Paper B focuses on how the phrasing and omission of material terms in the agreement led Cardozo to a disputed characterization and outcome.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing inter-party or intergovernmental relationships as contracts/agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes M&A transactions as 'unbundled bargains' made up of many interconnected contracts rather than a single document; Paper B repeatedly treats federalism as if it 'prescribes terms' like a contract for intergovernmental cooperation or conflict, explicitly using the contract metaphor to analyze state–federal relationships.

shared_topics.topic: design trade-offs in structuring multi-actor arrangements (modularity/bundling versus integration/centralization)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why parties choose multiple ancillary agreements—arguing unbundling raises modularity and precision but creates enforcement considerations—while Paper B analyzes the centralization/decentralization trade-off (collective-action problems under decentralization versus information problems under centralization) in designing federal structures.

shared_topics.topic: how legal boundaries and allocation of rights/powers shape practical outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that where deal boundaries are drawn (which agreements are treated as part of the deal) can determine whether a transaction can proceed (e.g., implied standstills), and Paper B focuses on how the allocation of authority between national and state governments (the federal–state boundary) affects policy outcomes and who benefits politically.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial or doctrinal interpretation versus consequential evaluation in legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts’ willingness to treat ancillary agreements as part of the deal influences parties’ contract design and incentives, while Paper B debates whether federalism should be judged by doctrinal coherence or by its empirical effects on people, endorsing a consequentialist perspective while noting doctrinal implications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36geojintll1145!!ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study of Legal Transplant: The Possibility of Efficient Breach in China

shared_topics.topic: contract and deal design to manage incentives and enforce performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how remedy rules (specific performance vs expectation damages) shape parties' incentives to perform or breach and how legal rules influence contract behavior in China; Paper B explains why parties unbundle transactions into multiple agreements and how that modular deal design allocates risks, precision, and enforcement across contracts to improve ex ante efficiency and ex post enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and the predictability of contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the flexible, uncertain way Chinese courts award remedies undermines predictability for breaching parties considering an efficient breach; Paper B shows that courts’ treatment of ancillary agreements (e.g., reading confidentiality clauses together with the acquisition agreement) can decisively determine whether a deal can proceed, so judicial interpretation crucially shapes deal boundaries and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: information problems and transaction costs shaping contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the high information demands and informational frictions that complicate efficient-breach decisions—especially in transitional markets and close-knit communities; Paper B grounds the value of unbundled bargains in reduced transaction and enforcement costs and increased precision, arguing that informational modularity drives parties to use multiple, targeted agreements.

shared_topics.topic: litigation incentives and parties' willingness to resort to courts as part of deal strategy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats willingness to litigate as a precondition for efficient breach to work, noting Chinese parties are less inclined to go to court which affects legal transplant viability; Paper B highlights that because courts will interpret ancillary agreements as part of the deal, parties must account for potential litigation and remedial consequences when drafting or signing even peripheral agreements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS

shared_topics.topic: whether and when separate documents should be read together as a single deal (deal-boundaries and integration across instruments)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of 'unbundled bargains' and shows courts may treat ancillary agreements as part of an overarching deal, affecting enforceability; Paper B's analysis of interpretive rules (and the admissibility of extrinsic evidence) bears directly on the legal question of when multiple documents should be interpreted together rather than as isolated contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the practical importance of drafting and boilerplate language in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the Martin Marietta confidentiality template to show how seemingly boilerplate ancillary clauses can determine major transaction outcomes; Paper B’s account of meaning as public, conventional language use and of doctrinal choices about plain meaning highlights how textual formulation and drafting practices materially shape legal interpretation and litigation risk.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive doctrines influence contracting behavior and deal design (normative/policy implications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that selection among interpretive rules is a matter of legal policy and will have social consequences; Paper A shows empirically that judicial interpretation of ancillary clauses feeds back into parties' incentives to unbundle or consolidate agreements, illustrating the policy effects of interpretive doctrines on transactional practice.

papers.node_id: 38yalejonreg707!!ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?
papers.title: ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?
papers.authors: Robert E. Scott; George G. Triantis
papers.abstract:
The law-and-economics movement has transformed the analysis of private law in the United States and, increasingly, around the world. Starting with just a few adherents fifty years ago, it is now a fixture in fields of scholarship such as business law, contracts, torts, and property. Scholars in these and other fields of law are, without exception, familiar with the basic tools of marginalist analysis, game theory, problems of private information and rational choice under scarcity and uncertainty. As the interdisciplinary enterprise developed from 1970 to the early 2000s, legal scholars drew on methods from economics to develop countless insights about the operation and effects of law and legal institutions, thereby permitting policy makers to better understand the legal and social order. Within the past 20 years, a new generation of lawyer-economists have applied economic methods to derive testable hypotheses subject to increasingly rigorous empirical analysis. Throughout this period, the discipline of law-and-economics has benefited from a partnership among trained economists and academic lawyers. Yet one cannot help noticing that the tools just described derive primarily from theoretical and empirical economics and not law. A logical question thus demands attention: what role do academic lawyers play in law-and-economics scholarship? We take the opportunity presented by this Symposium on future challenges to law-and-economics to address that question.
We can best frame our inquiry by beginning with a few uncontroversial assumptions. First, academic lawyers know the law (whether statutes, regulations or common law doctrines) and the process by which courts and other legal institutions operate. Thus, lawyers are, at a minimum, an invaluable resource for anyone doing economic analysis of law.The more challenging question is whether lawyers have methodological skills beyond their knowledge of the law that add value to the scholarly project. Second, law is not an autonomous academic discipline.Law is to the social sciences and the humanities what engineering is to the natural sciences: like engineering, law is an applied or translational discipline, in both its normative and positive modes of analysis. Many of the analytic methods used by a prototypical academic lawyer are borrowed from other disciplines, including psychology, history, sociology, philosophy, and economics.
While several leading law-and-economics scholars have written that the field is simply the trade of applying economic methods to legal knowledge,we offer an alternative claim that legal academics make significant methodological contributions to law and economics scholarship. On its face, that may not seem like a very controversial claim. Many would agree that academic lawyers contribute more to this enterprise than their deep knowledge of law and the institutions within which law functions. In doing so, these observers may remark, for example, that lawyers "ask the right questions," or "solve difficult problems," "better understand policy goals," or "add complexity to the economist's simplifying assumptions."But the conclusory nature of these observations suggests that identifying the distinctive skills of the academic lawyer is a difficult task, in large part because legal skills have so much of the character of tacit knowledge.We set out in this Essay to unpack this tacit knowledge. We offer an interpretive theory of law and economics scholarship over the past 50 years that incorporates the specific methodological skills of the academic lawyer.Our central claim is that, in addition to the legal resources they provide to the economic analyst, academic lawyers also contribute cognizable analytical skills developed both through their involvement in law as an applied discipline and their mastery of the analogical method of argument used in common-law analysis.Whether used in isolation or combined with economic methods, these skills add value to our understanding of the world that a talented economist per se could not provide herself.
Law schools have long been the primary home in universities for multidisciplinary analysis. Legal academics, particularly those trained in the legal realist tradition, have long adapted tools to analyze legal issues from a number of social sciences--economics, political science, psychology, and sociology, to name four--and the humanities--history, philosophy, and literary analysis. When legal academics have applied economics to law, they have done so against a backdrop that is much more ecumenical than that of their economist counterparts. In law schools, the norms of economic analysis are constantly challenged from the perspectives of other disciplines, and exposure to this tension often distinguishes the law-and-economics works authored by legal academics.
In addition, law-and-economics scholarship is influenced by the common law training of legal academics, at least in the Anglo-American jurisdictions. The common-law method is essentially inductive in extracting from legal cases and opinions the set of factors that are essential to a legal result. This process of generalizing from the particular in order to find similarity across cases requires a sophisticated form of analogical reasoning in order to determine which similarities are relevant and which are not. As generations of legal realists have noted, however, there is a looseness to such analogical reasoning, often driven by normative goals. Importantly, lawyers use analogy in a particular way--as part of an adversarial process in which one analogy is always contrasted with another in opposition. This contestation refines the skill of using analogies as tools to harness different perspectives and policy goals. We conjecture that this type of analogical reasoning works synergistically with the logical rigor of economic analysis, whether in the framing of theoretical models or in strict causal inference in econometrics.
In sum, the legal academics' methodological contribution to law-and-economics is a toolbox that combines analogical argument with the perspectives gained from the range of social sciences and humanities. These tools are used to enrich the explanatory and normative theories of observed legal phenomena provided by economists. We begin in Part I of theEssay with a brief descriptive account of the differences between the disciplines of economics and academic law, and then outline how one might expect these comparative advantages to meld in collaborations between the disciplines. In Part II we set out the essence of our claim: the academic lawyer's contribution is to take insights from multiple disciplines and, by using the skills of analogical argument, apply them in ways that expand the boundaries of economic thinking. Part III sets out several examples of past law-and-economics scholarship that support our claim. We speculate in the Conclusion that lawyers may not continue play as significant a role in the next generation of law-and-economics scholarship. Whether this is seen as a loss or as the healthy maturation of the field turns on the question we pose: are lawyers more than a resource for economists studying the law? While we cannot prove the affirmative--either by legal burdens of proof or by statistical significance--we do hope to shift the intellectual burden of proof going forward.

questions.question: Do academic lawyers contribute distinct methodological skills-beyond supplying knowledge of statutes, cases, and institutions-that add independent value to law-and-economics scholarship?

What specific methodological contributions (for example, analogical reasoning and multidisciplinary perspectives) do academic lawyers bring, and how do those skills interact with economic methods to change the framing, modeling, or interpretation of legal-economic research?
Will the role of academic lawyers in law-and-economics scholarship remain significant in future generations of the field, or will their contribution decline as the discipline matures?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62dukelj707!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW

shared_topics.topic: the methodological basis for identifying legal norms (behavioral regularities vs discursive practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the standard additive account that treats custom as observable behavior plus interior belief and proposes an integrated 'discursive normative practice' account for how customs become legally relevant; Paper B interrogates the methodological contribution of lawyers to law-and-economics, emphasizing distinct legal methods (analogical, inductive, and practice-sensitive reasoning) that shape how legal norms are identified and theorized.

shared_topics.topic: the role of discursive interaction/argumentation in law formation and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that legally significant customs arise in rich contexts of discursive normative practices and intermeshing social anticipations; Paper B highlights how lawyers use adversarial analogical argument and cross-disciplinary discourse to refine legal concepts and shape theoretical and empirical economic analyses of law.

shared_topics.topic: interplay between normative commitments and descriptive/empirical inquiry in legal scholarship
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that customs are normative practices not reducible to mere behavioral description and challenges descriptive-additive accounts; Paper B frames law as an applied discipline combining positive and normative analysis and examines how lawyers' normative goals influence the framing and interpretation of empirical and theoretical work in law-and-economics.

shared_topics.topic: the use and limits of evidentiary standards or proofs to establish the existence or validity of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concedes the additive conception may survive as an evidentiary standard used by legal systems to prove a custom's standing, questioning its adequacy as an account of normativity; Paper B discusses how economists and lawyers generate testable hypotheses and empirical evidence about legal effects and questions who supplies the methods and standards for such proof in law-and-economics.

shared_topics.topic: interdisciplinarity: how law draws on and integrates methods from other social sciences and humanities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates custom within social interaction and implicitly calls for approaches attentive to social-philosophical and sociological context; Paper B explicitly examines how legal academics import and synthesize tools from economics, sociology, philosophy and history and how that ecumenical stance shapes legal theorizing and empirical work.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob71!!ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal institutions/doctrine and economic analysis of contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a unitary regime of contract law interacts (and sometimes mismatches) with market-driven, embedded contracts and their standardization, while Paper B examines how lawyers' deep knowledge of statutes, doctrines, and institutional processes is indispensable to rigorous economic analysis of law.

shared_topics.topic: coordination and governance mechanisms to resolve collective-action problems in multilateral contracting markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how market participants create governance structures (trade associations, supply‑chain networks, or a state‑facilitated 'spider') to overcome collective‑action barriers to revising standardized contracts, and Paper B highlights law schools and legal scholars as institutional coordinators who synthesize multidisciplinary perspectives and structure scholarly and policy collaboration.

shared_topics.topic: normative implications for legal policy and regulation of contracts and markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes reframing consumer‑contract regulation toward state assistance in organizing buyer‑seller networks rather than bilateral unconscionability rules, while Paper B addresses how legal academics influence the normative framing of law‑and‑economics and the policy goals that guide legal reform.

shared_topics.topic: limits of abstract economic modeling and the need for contextual, analogical, and multidisciplinary reasoning in understanding contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes economists' parsimonious conception of contract and emphasizes context, standardization effects, and market dynamics, whereas Paper B argues that lawyers' analogical reasoning and cross‑disciplinary training supplement and correct the simplifying assumptions of economic models when analyzing legal problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev465!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: AN EMPIRICAL VIEW OF CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: AN EMPIRICAL VIEW OF CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: empirical/descriptive analysis of law versus doctrinal or theoretical accounts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers contrast empirical, descriptive studies of legal institutions with more formal doctrinal or theoretical accounts: Paper A documents a turn toward testable, empirical law-and-economics and asks what lawyers contribute methodologically, while Paper B presents an empirical account of contracting practice and argues that academic contract doctrine poorly describes how contracting actually operates.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal legal rules and the importance of private ordering/continuing relationships
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the idea that much of legal life is governed outside formal adjudication—Paper B explicitly documents private governance and long-term business relationships that supplant doctrinal contract law, and Paper A emphasizes that law operates as an applied discipline where understanding institutional practice and nonlegal modes of ordering is essential to law-and-economics analysis.

shared_topics.topic: interdisciplinarity in legal scholarship (economics, sociology, history, etc.)
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces foreground interdisciplinary methods: Paper A argues law-and-economics draws on and is enriched by multiple social sciences and humanities, and Paper B situates its empirical study of contract within law-and-society/sociological research traditions and the broader cross-disciplinary discussion about how contracts function in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the distinctive methodological role of legal academics (tacit knowledge, analogical reasoning, empirical description)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers debate what scholarly skills lawyers bring to legal inquiry: Paper A claims legal academics contribute tacit skills like analogical reasoning and multi-disciplinary synthesis to law-and-economics, while Paper B illustrates how legal scholars' empirical descriptions challenge doctrinal assumptions and reshape theoretical debates about contract.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that academic lawyers contribute an empirical, law-in-action perspective (legal realism) that complements economic models, and Paper B explicitly adopts 'new legal realism' to show how contractual doctrines and business practices shape renegotiation and settlement outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical and interdisciplinary methods (law-and-society and economics) to study legal phenomena
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the turn in law-and-economics toward testable, empirical work and the multidisciplinary stance lawyers bring, while Paper B draws on law-and-society research, empirical anecdotes, and institutional observation to explain how contracts are actually renegotiated and enforced.

shared_topics.topic: common‑law analogical reasoning and doctrinal indeterminacy affecting predictability and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights analogical (case-based) reasoning as a distinctive methodological contribution of legal academics that complicates economic simplifications, and Paper B demonstrates how common-law doctrines' vagueness and analogical application (e.g., mistake, impracticability) generate uncertainty that shapes litigation strategies and settlements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: APPLICATION OF THE DOCTRINE OF COMMERCIAL IMPRACTICABILITY: SEARCHING FOR "THE WISDOM OF SOLOMON".

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that lawyers’ analogical and interdisciplinary methods inject normative perspectives and policy goals into economic analysis of law, while Paper B repeatedly frames doctrines of excuse and contract modification in terms of fairness, relationship‑preservation, and policy choices underlying judicial decisions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the substantive role lawyers play in shaping law through methods that can expand economic models, and Paper B critiques and assesses judicial efforts (e.g., ALCOA) to interpolate price/risk‑sharing terms or otherwise modify contracts rather than strictly enforcing original promises.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation of economic or commercial reality considerations (risk‑/loss‑sharing) into legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the marriage of economic methods with legal analysis and how lawyers contextualize economic models, and Paper B focuses on attempts (and resistance) to import loss‑ and risk‑sharing (commercial/efficiency) concepts into excuse/impracticability doctrine to reflect commercial realities.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on Kant, Wittgenstein, and Habermas to reconceptualize contract meaning and dispute, arguing philosophical insights are necessary to understand non‑cognitive uses of language; Paper B emphasizes that legal scholars routinely integrate psychology, sociology, history, and humanities alongside economics to generate more nuanced accounts of legal phenomena.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that trained lawyers and legal academics contribute distinctive methodological skills (analogical reasoning, applied discipline expertise) to law-and-economics scholarship; Paper B documents how industry-specific legal actors (merchant tribunals, drafters of trade rules) and their expertise actually create and interpret a private commercial legal system in the cotton trade.

shared_topics.topic: integration of economic analysis with legal methods to explain private law and institutions

shared_topics.topic: how non-judicial norms, reputational mechanisms, and extra-legal sanctions support contracting and compliance
