shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the conditions under which promises will be kept without state coercion and when the state must supply 'law glue' — Paper A catalogs market, moral, and social sanctions that sustain performance and cautions against overstating doctrine's role, while Paper B models when contracts are self‑enforcing (reputation, repeated play) and identifies enforcement as necessary only outside that range.

shared_topics.topic: Role of relation‑specific investments and repeated dealings in justifying contract law intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat relation‑specific investment and the prospect of ongoing relationships as central reasons for legal intervention: Paper A emphasizes the discounted future benefits of relations that can motivate performance, and Paper B identifies protection of relation‑specific investments as a primary justification for enforcement rules in commercial contracts.

shared_topics.justification: Each paper questions which legal rules the state should provide versus leave to parties: Paper A argues the state's enforcement system must be calibrated to the social and market context and to parties' preferences, while Paper B develops criteria limiting when defaults or mandatory rules are desirable for business contracts and advocates a narrower, efficiency‑focused set of statutory/default rules.

shared_topics.topic: Competing doctrinal paradigms for interpreting and organizing contract law (transactional/textualist vs relational/contextual approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the debate over doctrinal frameworks — Paper A critiques the move from a Contract‑as‑Transaction paradigm to Contract‑as‑Relation and defends reasons to retain transactional doctrine, while Paper B similarly defends a Willistonian/textualist approach for contracts between firms and argues against broad relational interpretive methods as defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev645!!SYMPOSIUM: THE INCOMPLETENESS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF RELATIONAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE INCOMPLETENESS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF RELATIONAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: law-and-economics analysis of relational or incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage substantively with the problem of incomplete (relational) contracts and how law and economics frameworks should understand and respond to agreements that intentionally leave terms open; Paper A critiques the existing law-and-economics conception applied to relational contracts, while Paper B develops an efficiency-based theory for how contract law should treat incomplete commercial bargains, especially where relation-specific investment matters.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts in interpreting and gap‑filling commercial agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both works address whether and how judges should fill gaps or interpret ambiguous commercial contracts; Paper A criticizes judicial gap‑filling that may misstate parties' intentions, and Paper B argues for a default textualist interpretive regime with limited gap‑filling and party-controllable evidentiary scope.

shared_topics.topic: the normative question of what contract law should provide for sophisticated commercial parties
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the normative role of contract law in relation to competent business actors — Paper A questions the background conception that law should adapt to support deliberately incomplete commercial drafting, while Paper B proposes that law for firms should be narrowly tailored to facilitate efficiency (enforcement and interpretation) and defer to party sovereignty.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and design of defaults and mandatory rules for business contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with whether statutory defaults and mandatory rules appropriately serve commercial contracting — Paper A highlights risks of doctrinal responses (e.g., indefiniteness doctrine, judicial supplementation) to incomplete drafting, and Paper B analyzes when defaults are justified, criticizes many existing defaults/mandatory rules as misdirected, and recommends limiting mandatory interventions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope and boundaries of contract law (residual vs imperial views)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends narrowing the domain of contract law to transactions between sophisticated firms (Category 1) and argues many existing doctrines are category mistakes, while Paper B directly debates whether contract is a residual leftover or an expanding 'imperial' canon and proposes a consequentialist test for when an area should be treated as contractual.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract rules should be chosen by consequentialist/efficiency criteria
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its normative theory in welfare-maximization for business-to-business contracts and rejects other norms (fairness, distribution) in that domain, and Paper B urges that definitional and doctrinal choices about what counts as contract should be guided by consequentialist considerations (including efficiency) rather than essentialist semantics.

shared_topics.topic: the desirability of defaults versus mandatory rules and the extent of private reordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when default rules are useful and contends many statutory defaults are unnecessary or should be contractible around, and Paper B centers its definition of 'contractual' on whether parties can privately reorder legal relations and focuses on the normative questions of which rules should be defaults and how parties can contract around them.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of party sophistication and heterogeneity for crafting contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a sharp distinction between sophisticated commercial firms and other parties, arguing different rules (e.g., textualist defaults, liberty to contract) should apply to firms, while Paper B criticizes monolithic 'hypothetical bargain' assumptions and emphasizes that heterogeneity of preferences matters for whether and how legal defaults should be set or made mandatory.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56clevstlrev767!!ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS

shared_topics.topic: textualist/plain-meaning interpretation as the default for commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that for Category 1 (firm-to-firm) contracts courts should adopt a textualist default—honoring ordinary meanings, hard parol evidence rules, and merger clauses—because firms prefer and are best served by predictable texts; Paper B defends the possibility and legitimacy of plain meaning, showing it is not philosophically impossible and can serve as a valid interpretive approach in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: parol evidence, merger clauses, and limits on extrinsic evidence in interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A endorses narrow evidentiary bases for interpreting business agreements while allowing parties to expand those bases by contract, explicitly discussing parol evidence and merger clauses; Paper B analyzes and critiques the plain meaning rule (which permits courts to refuse extrinsic evidence), engaging with the same doctrinal debate over when judges may consider outside evidence of meaning.

shared_topics.topic: rejection of subjective intent in favor of public linguistic practices as the basis for meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper B draws on Wittgenstein to deny that contractual meaning reduces to the speaker's private intentions and instead grounds meaning in public, conventional language use; Paper A likewise treats courts' role as mapping ordinary semantic content of writings to legal effects rather than attempting to reconstruct parties' inner states, thereby favoring an objective/textual approach.

shared_topics.topic: choosing interpretive doctrines as a matter of legal policy and commercial efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the selection of interpretive rules as a normative, welfare-maximizing question—courts should adopt rules that facilitate firms' surplus-maximizing contracting; Paper B emphasizes that the choice among available interpretive rules (including plain meaning) is not a linguistic impossibility issue but a legal-policy question about which doctrine best serves legal and social goals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob71!!ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: efficiency (maximizing contractual surplus) as the central normative aim of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a tension between two efficiency objectives — designing contracts to maximize joint gains and producing contracts efficiently at scale — and argues legal responses should account for that tradeoff; Paper B develops and defends an efficiency-only normative theory for business contracts, arguing contract law should facilitate maximization of joint gains and restrict other aims in that domain.

shared_topics.topic: how market structure and party sophistication (thin/bilateral vs thick/multilateral; firm vs consumer) should shape legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes differences between thin/bilateral and thick/multilateral markets and the resulting implications for contract design and law (e.g., standardization in thick markets), while Paper B draws a taxonomy of transaction categories (especially firm-to-firm contracts) and argues different legal rules and doctrines should apply depending on the contracting context and party sophistication.

shared_topics.topic: the problems and consequences of standard-form/boilerplate contracts, defaults, and the production of widely used terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how standardization and boilerplate in thick markets generate ‘sticky’ or obsolete terms and collective-action barriers to updating them, and recommends institutional fixes; Paper B analyzes the limits of default rules and standards for business contracts, arguing many defaults are inappropriate for sophisticated parties because parties will contract around bad defaults.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of the state versus private coordination in solving coordination/collective-action problems in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes collective-action failures in the production and revision of contract terms in multilateral markets and advocates state facilitation of network governance to overcome them, especially in consumer markets; Paper B similarly interrogates what functions the state should perform (enforcement, interpretation, limited defaults) versus leaving choices to firms, thereby debating when public intervention is justified versus private ordering.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65tullrev1309!!ARTICLE: SUBSTANCE AND PROCEDURE IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION: THE DEVELOPMENT OF A NEW LEGAL ORDER.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SUBSTANCE AND PROCEDURE IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION: THE DEVELOPMENT OF A NEW LEGAL ORDER.

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of private ordering and party autonomy in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how international arbitration functions as a form of private ordering in which parties and arbitral institutions shape procedural and substantive law; Paper B argues normatively that contract law for sophisticated firms should defer to parties' preferences and allow contracting parties wide autonomy, limiting state intervention to enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: when and how legal enforcement should supplement self-enforcing commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses enforcement through private arbitration tribunals as a mechanism to resolve commercial disputes that parties do not resolve privately, while Paper B analyzes when legal enforcement (courts, damages, rules) is needed to protect relation-specific investments or prevent disruptive breaches and thus is the central function the state should provide for business contracts.

shared_topics.topic: interpretive rules and decisionmaker practices in commercial dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how arbitrators from diverse legal backgrounds and institutional practices affect the substantive and procedural interpretation of rules in international commercial disputes; Paper B develops a normative claim that courts (and by extension adjudicators) should use a textualist default interpretation for contracts between firms and that interpretation doctrines are a central design choice of commercial law.

shared_topics.topic: the emergence of commercial legal norms through non‑legislative institutions and market practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the development of a new transnational legal order driven by arbitral institutions, repeat players, and unreported awards; Paper B similarly focuses on how commercial law should reflect firms' contracting practices and market-created expectations (a modern law merchant), stressing that norms often originate from market actors rather than comprehensive statutory design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113nwulrev1009!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS

shared_topics.topic: when and how reputation creates self‑enforcing contracts that reduce the need for legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory that many commercial (firm‑to‑firm) contracts are or can be self‑enforcing through repeated interaction and market reputation, limiting when courts must intervene; Paper B analyzes how multilateral reputation in small‑world merchant networks could sustain long‑distance trade without recourse to public courts, identifying the network conditions that make reputational enforcement effective.

shared_topics.topic: the proper boundary between private ordering and public contract law (substitution vs complementarity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law for sophisticated firms should be narrowly tailored because firms and markets can choose contract terms and enforce them privately, while Paper B debates whether private order institutions (like traders' coalitions or network reputational regimes) substitute for or instead complement formal legal institutions in supporting exchange.

shared_topics.topic: the informational prerequisites for effective non‑legal governance of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that reputational and market mechanisms require relevant information and that courts/statutory drafters cannot replicate all private information, motivating limited mandatory rules and defaults; Paper B shows how the small‑world structure of ties and central information nodes among Maghribi traders generated the information flows necessary for multilateral reputation to govern contracts across distances.

shared_topics.topic: limits on mandatory defaults and the allocation of enforcement responsibilities given variation in transaction types and governance structures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends many default and mandatory contract rules are unnecessary or harmful for transactions between sophisticated firms because parties can contract around them or rely on market governance; Paper B provides a historical case showing that when private governance structures (networked reputational mechanisms) exist, the practical need for formal legal defaults or mandatory protections is similarly reduced, highlighting how governance context should shape the role of formal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72oklalrev797!!ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy to customize substantive and procedural contract rules (limits of defaults and mandatory rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that sophisticated firms should be free to contract around many statutory defaults and that many mandatory rules are unjustified for Category 1 (firm-to-firm) contracts; Paper B analyzes the extent to which parties actually exercise autonomy over the backend process, treating procedural rules as potential defaults or bargained terms and explaining when parties tailor procedure ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: when formal legal enforcement is necessary versus reliance on self-enforcement and market norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies self-enforcing contracts and market reputation as substitutes for legal enforcement and pinpoints when courts are needed (volatile markets, relation-specific investments); Paper B similarly shows how frequency and scale (and industry norms or trade associations) reduce reliance on formal adjudication and explain when parties adopt formal procedural safeguards instead.

shared_topics.topic: contract design to manage transaction-specific risks under incomplete contracting (relation‑specific investment, hold-up, and litigation opportunism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its normative theory in the need to facilitate efficient trade and ex ante investment, stressing enforcement to protect relation-specific investments and prevent hold-up; Paper B situates procedural customization as a tool to address shading and litigation opportunism arising from incomplete contracts and uncertain future states, and analyzes how parties trade off ex ante and ex post governance.

shared_topics.topic: choice of interpretation and adjudication regimes (who decides, evidentiary scope, standards) as part of contract governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a textualist default, narrow evidentiary rules, and party-tailorable interpretation regimes for business contracts; Paper B treats selection of decision‑makers, adjudicative fora, evidentiary and decision standards (e.g., arbitral authority, standards of decision) as deliberate procedural design choices that parties use to shape dispute outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53santaclaralrev73!!ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PUBLIC MEANING RULE: RECONCILING MEANING, INTENT, AND CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: appropriate interpretive default for negotiated commercial contracts (textualism vs contextualism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a textualist default for Category 1 (firm-to-firm) contracts while allowing parties to expand the interpretive evidentiary base by agreement; Paper B proposes the 'public meaning' rule as the correct interpretive default for negotiated commercial contracts and rejects subjective-contextualist interpretation except in cases of true ambiguity.

shared_topics.topic: which categories of extrinsic evidence courts should admit (trade usage vs course of performance/dealing or subjective intent)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats evidentiary scope as something courts should keep narrow for business contracts (but permit party-specified broadening) and identifies trade usage/interpretation rules as important; Paper B draws a sharp distinction admitting public/conventional evidence such as trade usage while excluding evidence tied to subjective intent (course of performance/dealing) except when a contract is intractably ambiguous.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between judicial intervention (equity/mandatory rules) and party autonomy/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues many default and mandatory rules are unnecessary or harmful for sophisticated commercial parties and that party sovereignty should govern absent externalities; Paper B likewise urges that fairness interventions should be handled explicitly through equity rather than by expanding interpretive inquiry, preserving predictability and the parties' written allocations.

shared_topics.topic: limits of applying rules for consumer/adhesion contexts to negotiated commercial transactions (tailoring rules to sophisticated parties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A confines its efficiency/textualist theory to contracts between sophisticated firms and rejects applying rules appropriate for individual or consumer contracts to commercial contracts; Paper B similarly confines its public-meaning proposal to negotiated commercial contracts and warns against applying it to consumer adhesion contexts where public-meaning evidence is less protective of weaker parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45iowajcorpl885!!ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory

shared_topics.topic: interaction of formal contractual provisions and informal governance ("braiding")
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how formal legal rules (defaults, interpretation, enforcement) interact with market-based informal enforcement (reputation, self-enforcement) and argues firms prefer legal frameworks that support efficient private ordering; Paper B develops and tests the braiding thesis that formal contract provisions can be designed to generate and complement informal norms, showing how formal clauses foster transparency, mutual monitoring, and informal sanctions in collaborative deals.

shared_topics.topic: scope conditions determining when parties choose formal, informal, or braided governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A sharply limits its normative account to transactions between sophisticated firms and identifies market features (absence of externalities, firm sophistication, volatility) that justify certain legal defaults and enforcement roles; Paper B asks when braiding is used versus other governance tools, proposing determinants such as uncertainty, market thickness, exchange hazards, and network topology that shape parties' choice of governance mode.

shared_topics.topic: relation-specific investments and the need for enforcement or locking mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the principal justification for legal enforcement in commercial contracts is to protect relation-specific investments and to secure efficient ex ante investment when self-enforcement is insufficient; Paper B shows braided agreements and processes like alpha contracting function to 'lock in' partners and support joint learning and investments that would otherwise be underprovided absent formal structures.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate role of courts/state in contract interpretation, defaults, and mandatory rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a prescriptive view that the state should focus on enforcement, adopt textualist interpretation defaults, and minimize mandatory rules to respect party sovereignty; Paper B engages the normative question of judicial intervention's effects on private governance—whether courts will crowd out or support informal institutions—and considers implications for doctrine and contract design.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94tullrev961!!SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of expectation damages and other remedies as the primary enforcement tool to incentivize performance and reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats enforcement (including damages rules) as the core thing contract law must supply for commercial deals and links remedies to protecting relation‑specific investments and efficient ex ante investment; Paper B analyzes the expectation measure directly, arguing that expectation damages are neither fully restorative nor absolute but nonetheless function as the principal remedial instrument to incentivize reliance and performance, and maps the practical limits of that instrument.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules should be designed (mandatory rules vs party‑contractible defaults) to serve commercial parties' incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues many remedial and related contract rules (interpretation defaults, modification rules, liquidated damages, etc.) should be non‑mandatory and tailored to firms' preferences because firms can better choose efficient terms, while Paper B shows empirically and doctrinally how limits and exceptions to expectation damages affect parties' losses and bargaining, implicating whether the law should leave remedial allocations to contracting parties or impose defaults.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of deference to parties' stated intentions/textualist interpretation as a governance mechanism for commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a textualist default interpretation for Category 1 (firm‑to‑firm) contracts and stresses allowing parties to broaden evidentiary bases if they wish, while Paper B engages (via Professor Hillman's 'lore') with the belief that parties' intentions should govern formation and interpretation and examines how perceptions of intention and context influence remedial outcomes and doctrinal expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.

shared_topics.topic: when courts and statutory rules are necessary versus when market, reputational, or moral forces will secure performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes which commercial bargains are self-enforcing (via repeated dealings and reputational sanctions) and identifies the narrow conditions (volatile markets, relation-specific investments) where legal enforcement is required; Paper B articulates 'market,' 'moral,' and 'social' glue that often sustains performance and treats state 'law glue' as a backstop, arguing law's role is often modest and contingent on these other forces.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of continuing relationships and relation-specific investments for legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that protection of relation-specific investments and the preservation of ongoing commercial relations justify state enforcement in some firm-to-firm contracts; Paper B likewise foregrounds the relational paradigm—the discounted value of future cooperative gains—as a key explanation for why parties perform and as a central consideration for assessing the need and design of legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: how contracting context and party characteristics should shape the scope and design of contract law (party autonomy, defaults, and institutional design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for limiting contract law for sophisticated firms, endorsing party sovereignty, narrow defaults, textualist interpretation, and fewer mandatory rules tailored to firms' preferences; Paper B questions the extent to which legal doctrine should structure contracting, stresses that people have preferences about enforcement institutions, and suggests that doctrinal design should account for differences in motives and relational contexts rather than applying a one-size-fits-all transactional model.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69minnlrev471!!ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.

shared_topics.topic: allocation_of_losses_and_remedies_for_failed_performance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with how contract law should distribute economic consequences when performance fails: Paper A analyzes the role of damages and enforcement rules as the principal state function to secure efficient trade and investment, while Paper B traces the evolution of commercial impracticability remedies and develops methodologies for judicial or negotiated loss-sharing when strict performance would be uneconomical or unfair.

shared_topics.topic: private_party_autonomy_vs_judicial_adjustment_of_contract_risks
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether risk allocation should be left to commercial parties or second-guessed by courts: Paper A argues that sophisticated firms should be free to choose terms and that courts should generally honor party sovereignty (with limited mandatory rules), whereas Paper B’s primary proposal gives parties the first opportunity to allocate losses (including facilitated settlements) and only then contemplates judicial reallocation when private agreement fails.

shared_topics.topic: design_and_limits_of_default_rules_and_doctrines_in_commercial_contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address what kinds of default rules or judicial doctrines are appropriate for commercial transactions: Paper A develops criteria limiting when the state should supply defaults or mandatory rules for firm-to-firm contracts, and Paper B proposes a structured methodology for incorporating loss-sharing into the doctrine of commercial impracticability (i.e., how a commercial doctrine should be shaped to function as an effective default or fallback).

papers.node_id: 52drakelrev235!!ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
papers.title: ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
papers.abstract:
Karl Llewellyn's broad vision for the Uniform Commercial Code was to incorporate normative commercial practices into the commercial body of law - or turn immanent commercial norms into immanent law.The overall effectiveness of the Code's broad incorporation strategy in promoting and preserving commercial norms is subject to substantial scholarly critique.However, this Article focuses specifically on a singleelement of Llewellyn's incorporation strategy: the use of "course of performance"evidence to interpret agreements under the Uniform Commercial Code.
Course of performance evidence is the only evidence used to interpret an agreement's original terms that does not come into existence until after formation of the agreement in question.As such, it is unquestionably unique. In this Article, I suggest that the use of course of performance evidence to interpret prior agreements is also of questionable wisdom because: (1) it is analytically flawed in light of basic contract theory; and (2) it is poor policy in light of the commercial norms the Code seeks to promote. I further suggest that the doctrine of waiver presents a superior alternative for giving effect to parties' postformation conduct, inasmuch as it avoids the analytical flaws and provides for a more balanced set of commercial effects than those likely to arise from the use of course of performance to interpret the parties' prior agreement. I then move on to discuss new challenges in the application of course of performance evidence under revised Article 1 of the Code.
Until quite recently, the statutory use of course of performanceevidence to interpret agreements was, at least arguably, limited to Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code.However, with the 2001 revisions, course of performance evidence is now addressed in Article 1,and is, therefore, applicable throughout the Code.Thus, any challenges presented by the use and application of course of performance evidence now implicate other portions of the Code, such as negotiable instruments under Article 3, banking law under Article 4, letters of credit under Article 5, and security interests under Article 9.While the drafters of revised Article 1 appear to have recognized at least one potential problem with the application of course of performance evidence to negotiable instruments under Article 3,this Article discusses the potential for additional challenges under Article 3 and throughout the Code. With its broadened applicability under revised section 1-303, the use and application of course of performance evidence takes on additional importance under the uniform version of the Code, and the issue is particularly pertinent today, as state legislatures consider whether to adopt the various new revisions to Article 1.
Part II of this Article explores the historical development and analytical underpinnings of the use of postcontractual conduct, as ultimately addressed as course of performance evidence under section 2-208. I discuss the new analytical construct introduced by the Code, and compare this construct with the treatment of subsequent conduct under earlier domestic law and under current international law, as codified in the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. Part III explains why the use of course of performance evidence, as provided for in the Code, is analytically inconsistent with both basic contract theory and other Code provisions. These analytical inconsistencies are further developed in the context of a classic contracts interpretation case decided under the Code. Part IV discusses the policy issues that cut against using course of performance evidence to interpret parties' prior agreements. I explain why these policy issues call into question using course of performance evidence for interpretation, even if such evidence may have some limited logical relevance with respect to interpretation of the parties' agreement. Part V explains why the application of the doctrine of waiver to postformation conduct represents a preferable alternative to the use of a course of performance as an aid in interpretation of the parties' prior agreement. Finally, Part VI looks at previous Code decisions discussing the potential use of course of performance evidence outside the scope of Article 2 and the potential implications of these decisions on the newly broadened use of course of performance evidence under section 1-303. I then discuss a few of the specific new problems likely to arise from using course of performance evidence in combination with other Code Articles.

questions.question: Whether parties' conduct after a contract is formed should be used to interpret the original meaning of the parties' agreement (i.e., as evidence of what the contract terms meant at formation).

Whether post-formation conduct is better treated as evidence that parties have relinquished rights or effectively modified their deal, rather than as interpretive evidence of the prior agreement's original terms.
Whether expanding the use of post-formation conduct as evidence across many types of commercial transactions creates problematic legal or policy consequences for other areas of commercial law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev923!!ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante versus ex post choice in legal regulation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze the distinction between making legal determinations before events occur (ex ante) and assessing them after the fact (ex post): Paper A develops a general framework and dilemmas (normative, institutional, personal) about choosing ex ante or ex post approaches (using torture/ticking‑bomb as the focal example), while Paper B critiques the Uniform Commercial Code's practice of letting postcontractual conduct (course of performance) re‑interpret preexisting agreements and therefore represents an ex post interpretive move in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal rules or post hoc standards should govern behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the ex ante/ex post choice as manifesting in the rules‑versus‑standards debate and examines the costs of binding rulemaking versus case‑by‑case standards, and Paper B engages the same tension by questioning whether fixed contractual terms should yield to flexible interpretive devices (course of performance) or instead be managed through doctrines like waiver.

shared_topics.topic: institutional allocation of authority to decide ex ante vs ex post questions
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider which institutions are appropriate for making or revising ex ante rules or for applying ex post assessments: Paper A asks whether legislatures, courts or administrators should set or revisit prohibitions (e.g., torture), and Paper B analyzes the statutory placement of course‑of‑performance in Article 1 and the consequences for courts, drafters, and state legislatures in shaping postformation interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of post‑event conduct and its corrective role vis‑à‑vis formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats ex post reexamination of concrete cases (and actors’ conduct) as a tool that can override or excuse ex ante prohibitions in extreme situations, while Paper B focuses on how parties’ postformation conduct (course of performance or waiver) should or should not be allowed to alter the meaning or application of preexisting contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: policy trade‑offs between predictability/stability and flexibility/adaptive justice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers assess the normative and behavioral consequences of preferring precommitment versus hindsight adjustment: Paper A emphasizes how exclusive reliance on one perspective sacrifices either ex ante incentives or ex post responsiveness, and Paper B argues that admitting course‑of‑performance interpretation undermines contractual predictability and commercial norms compared with alternatives like waiver.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104harvlrev375!!ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: NONLEGAL SANCTIONS IN COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIPS.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and normative role of post-formation conduct in defining parties' obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties' post‑contractual reliance on nonlegal sanctions and informal commitments (reputation, oral promises, disclaimers) affects whether obligations are treated as legally enforceable, while Paper B focuses on 'course of performance' — a species of post‑formation conduct — debating whether it should be used to interpret or be supplanted by waiver doctrine under the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial norms and extra‑legal sanctions should be incorporated into formal commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for legal doctrines that acknowledge and evaluate the effectiveness of nonlegal sanctions when deciding enforceability, and Paper B critiques the UCC's incorporation of commercial practice (via course of performance) and examines whether the Code properly translates immanent commercial norms into statutory law.

shared_topics.topic: limits of judicial intervention and deference to parties' contracting choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends substantial judicial deference to parties' decisions to rely on nonlegal enforcement, intervening only when parties' assessments were significantly mistaken, whereas Paper B argues for doctrinal limits on using post‑formation conduct to rewrite prior agreements and proposes waiver as a more restrained response than treating performance as reinterpretation.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal critique and proposals for reforming commercial/contract doctrines (including UCC provisions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes reformulating doctrines like promissory estoppel and contract interpretation to account for nonlegal sanctions, and Paper B proposes rethinking the application of course of performance under revised UCC §1‑303 and advocates greater use of waiver, identifying specific problems and suggesting doctrinal alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: tension between contract theory and commercial practice in interpreting agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates reliance on nonlegal sanctions within liberal, communitarian, and instrumentalist contract theories and analyzes rational choice between legal and nonlegal sanctioning systems, while Paper B argues that the Code's use of course of performance is analytically inconsistent with basic contract theory and other UCC provisions.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SUBSTANCE AND PROCEDURE IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION: THE DEVELOPMENT OF A NEW LEGAL ORDER.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes how arbitrators and repeat commercial practice among international parties shape both procedural and substantive norms in arbitral tribunals, while Paper B analyzes the UCC’s deliberate incorporation of post‑contractual practice (course of performance) into statutory interpretation and critiques that mechanism as a way of turning commercial habits into law.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ALL EVENTS TESTS IN AN ERA OF SELF-REGULATION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how self‑regulatory clauses, third‑party audits, and informal sanctions interact with contractual promises and recognition of rights/liabilities, while Paper B examines whether postcontractual practices should be used to interpret or waive written terms and how that shifts contractual allocation of risk and expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY
