shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the analytical consistency of course-of-performance interpretation with basic contract theory and other Code provisions, while Paper B traces the historical development of core contract doctrines (e.g., consideration) and reflects on the intellectual foundations and coherence of the common law of contract.

papers.node_id: 7jsmallemergingbusl283!!ARTICLE:I MEAN WHAT I SAY, I THINK: THE DANGER TO SMALL BUSINESSES OF ENTERING INTO LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE AGREEMENTS THAT MAY NOT REFLECT THEIR INTENTIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE:I MEAN WHAT I SAY, I THINK: THE DANGER TO SMALL BUSINESSES OF ENTERING INTO LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE AGREEMENTS THAT MAY NOT REFLECT THEIR INTENTIONS
papers.abstract:
A number of commentators have written on the subject of the relevance of contracts, and in particular contract law, to businesses.For the most part, however, these articles focus upon big and medium sized businesses. Very little has been written concerning the relevance of contracts and contract law to small and emerging businesses. Yet small businesses, in the aggregate, are an integral part of our economy.Indeed, as President George Bush stated in his 1999-2000 report to Congress on the state of small business, "small businesses have always been the backbone of our economy."Small businesses"account for most innovation and job creation,"which helps the economy when it is strong, but also helps to put the economy "back on the tract to long-term growth"when the economy is weak.In addition, like larger businesses, small businesses utilize contracts in their daily transactions. Thus, they warrant greater study.
In spite of this need for study, the author is unaware of any existing empirical survey that focuses primarily on small businesses and contract law. The author intends to conduct such a survey. This study, however, is currently still in its preliminary stages. As a result, this Article cannot provide a definitive answer to the question of how relevant contracts and contract law are to small businesses. It will, however, posit ideas and, thus, begin the discourse on the subject.
In particular, this Article will demonstrate that, in order to effectively run its affairs, a small business will want and need legally enforceable agreements for a variety of different transactions. It needs both the detailed written agreement and the less detailed, perhaps oral, agreement in order to sufficiently protect its interests. However, while a small business may have little or no difficulty in entering into legally binding agreements, it may experience greater difficulty in entering into agreements that will effectuate its intended purpose. That is, if a case goes to court, the court may not interpret the agreement as the small business intended. Such an eventuality will hurt the small business if it feels the need to resort to suit; perhaps even more importantly, however, it will impede the ability of the small business to negotiate concerning performance.
The difficulty that a small business will encounter in effectuating its interest is due, in part, to the fact that many small businesses simply cannot afford to hire attorneys as often as is necessary to help draft adequate agreements or contract forms.Thus, the small business is left to rely upon its business experience to protect its interest via contract. Unfortunately, this experience may prove inadequate to the task.
Although there are many rules of contract law that may cause problems for the unwary businessperson, this Article will focus upon the parol evidence rule and the rules of contract interpretation as being of particular concern to a small business. This concern arises from the fact that a small business will often seek to memorialize important or risky agreements in a writing. In addition, for similar reasons, larger businesses may insist upon memorializing these same agreements in a writing. Further, form contracts are often utilized to avoid or reduce attorney's fees. These forms may contain terms that do not reflect the intentions of the small business or they may not contain the parties' entire agreement. In spite of this, our unwary businessperson may discover that, according to the law, she is bound to perform according to the precise terms of the form contract. She may also discover that she is only entitled to performance from the party according to the precise terms of the contract. Yet,enforcing the intentions of the contracting parties is necessary if contracts truly are private legislation.Thus, to the extent that it is clear that a party intended to enter into an agreement that is different from the one that was written and the other party knew of that intention, contract law should accommodate the one party's intention.
As a result, this Article suggests that, in attempting to interpret a contract or to apply the parol evidence rule, a court should not limit itself to looking at the written agreement in a vacuum. Rather, it should also examine the context in which the agreement was made. In examining this context, the court should not assume that a small business is a sophisticated business. Rather, it should consider the extent of the small business's experience and the availability of attorney assistance.

questions.question: Whether small businesses frequently enter into written agreements that do not reflect their actual intentions and thereby face greater risk of unfavorable enforcement or impaired bargaining when disputes arise.

Whether courts, when resolving contract disputes, should take into account the transactional context-including a small business's experience and access to legal counsel-to better effectuate the parties' true intentions.
To what extent reliance on standardized form contracts and limited access to legal assistance leads small businesses to be bound by terms they did not intend.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62amjcompl687!!ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Political Economy of Regulating Contract+

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between private ordering (default rules) and mandatory regulation to protect less‑sophisticated parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how small businesses rely on private ordering and written forms and argues courts should interpret contracts to reflect parties' intentions when counsel is absent, while Paper B analyzes when policymakers adopt default rules versus mandatory terms given political‑economic constraints, with both probing whether and how the law should intervene to protect weaker or less informed contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and courts as providers of interpretive defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges courts to examine contextual evidence (parol evidence, sophistication, access to counsel) when construing contracts for small businesses, and Paper B treats common‑law courts' capacity to develop ex post interpretive defaults as an institutional substitute for mandatory legislation, so both focus on the role of judicial interpretation in shaping contract outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries and transaction costs affecting contracting outcomes for vulnerable parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights small firms' limited access to attorneys and business inexperience as information constraints that cause misaligned written agreements, while Paper B analyzes how mobility and cross‑border contracting raise information costs for consumers, employees and firms, with both papers linking informational disadvantages to the need for legal or regulatory responses.

shared_topics.topic: risks and effects of standardized/form contract terms that may not reflect parties' intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the dangers small businesses face when form contracts contain terms inconsistent with their intentions, and Paper B discusses clarity, standardized terms and national branding as regulatory concerns, so both engage with how boilerplate or standardized terms can produce unfair or unanticipated results and challenge existing legal responses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58alalrev765!!ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rational Retroactivity in a Commercial Context

shared_topics.topic: the role of default rules versus bargained/immutable contract terms in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the U.C.C.'s reliance on default rules (versus immutable rules) affects the desirability of pro‑retroactivity and parties' ability to contract around statutory defaults; Paper B examines how standardized/form writings can misstate parties' actual bargains and argues courts must account for parties' real intentions when enforcing written agreements, implicating the same tensions between defaults, bespoke terms, and contractual freedom.

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty and retroactive or post‑adoption change as a risk to transactional parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with transition policy and how retroactive statutory or judicial changes (e.g., revisions to Articles 1, 2, 9) create uncertainty that alters incentives and transactional behavior; Paper B addresses uncertainty in how contracts will be interpreted (parol evidence rule, judicial construction) and how that interpretive uncertainty can frustrate small businesses' expectations and negotiation strategies.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries and party sophistication in contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights informational asymmetries and the cognitive/coordination limits when two commercial parties must anticipate legal change (and when one party has more information), undermining a blanket pro‑retroactivity rule; Paper B focuses on how small businesses' lack of resources and legal sophistication leaves them vulnerable to entering agreements that do not reflect their intentions, the same structural imbalance that affects contractual risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation/doctrine in shaping commercial expectations and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the retroactive effect of judicial lawmaking (e.g., unconscionability doctrines) and how courts' post‑enactment interpretations create transition problems in commerce; Paper B urges courts to use contextual, sophistication‑sensitive interpretive approaches (parol evidence, contract construction) so that judicial interpretation better aligns outcomes with parties' expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72oklalrev797!!ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: how ex ante drafting and written/form contracts determine ex post enforcement and whether courts should consider context and intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that written and form contracts often bind small businesses in ways that diverge from their intentions and urges courts to interpret agreements in light of the transaction context and parties' sophistication; Paper B likewise treats ex ante contract design (including choice of interpretation regimes and back-end rules) as central to how disputes will be resolved and emphasizes that parties can and should anticipate adjudicatory processes when drafting.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of party sophistication, scale, and access to legal counsel on contract design and enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on small businesses' limited resources and legal sophistication as a reason they enter inadequate contracts and suffer from unfavorable judicial interpretation, while Paper B analyzes how attributes like scale, frequency, and behavioral uncertainty (and implied differences in sophistication/resources) predict whether parties customize procedural rules or rely on industry norms.

shared_topics.topic: use of standardized/module clauses versus tailored contractual solutions and the risks of mismatch with parties' real intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that reliance on form contracts and boilerplate to save attorney fees can produce terms that do not reflect the parties' actual agreement, and Paper B documents that parties often choose modular procedural bundles (forum selection, arbitration, waivers) but sometimes need or devise more tailored procedural arrangements when bespoke governance is valuable.

shared_topics.topic: contractual mechanisms to mitigate litigation opportunism and transaction costs through front‑end design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns that poor drafting and rigid interpretation increase the costs and strategic disadvantages small businesses face in litigation and negotiation, while Paper B develops a theory of procedural customization showing how parties use ex ante procedural rules and tradeoffs between front‑end and back‑end specification to reduce litigation opportunism and overall contracting costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60ucinlrev405!!SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape strategic behavior in contracting and corporate transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A applies game theory to corporate law to analyze how legal rules and institutional design create strategic incentives for firms and managers, while Paper B shows how contract doctrines (form contracts, parol evidence, rules of interpretation) alter small businesses' negotiation choices and expose them to strategic risks when they cannot afford tailored counsel.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and party sophistication in bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats information asymmetries and differences in player sophistication as core game-theoretic issues that affect outcomes in corporate settings, and Paper B focuses on the practical consequences of limited sophistication and asymmetric access to legal advice for small businesses in contract formation and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal rules producing winners and losers in disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's symposium theme—'just winners and losers'—uses game-theoretic lenses to study how legal rules allocate gains and losses among corporate actors, and Paper B documents how contract interpretation and evidentiary rules can systematically advantage one contracting party (often the better-resourced party) and disadvantage small businesses.

shared_topics.topic: importance of context and interpretation for predictable outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that game-theoretic analysis can inform how courts and regulators design rules to produce predictable strategic responses, while Paper B argues that courts should consider the contextual facts (parties' intent, sophistication, access to counsel) when interpreting contracts so that enforcement better reflects parties' expectations and negotiated outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 129yaleljf535!!ARTICLE: Twenty-First-Century Contract Law Is a Law of Agreements, Not Debts: A Response to Lewinsohn
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Twenty-First-Century Contract Law Is a Law of Agreements, Not Debts: A Response to Lewinsohn

shared_topics.topic: the role of party intent/motivation in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether the consideration doctrine should track the promisor's motivations (bargained-for inducement vs remuneration) and whether motivations indicate which promises merit enforcement; Paper B examines how courts' failure to give weight to a small business's actual intentions (as opposed to the literal written terms) can produce outcomes that do not reflect the parties' intended bargains.

shared_topics.topic: suitability of contract doctrines for commercial actors (including small businesses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the modern doctrine of consideration evolved to serve commercial, forward-looking agreements and coordinated plans rather than intimate gifts, while Paper B focuses on small commercial actors and whether existing rules (and practical constraints like lack of counsel) leave them vulnerable when using form contracts or writings.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of judicial doctrinal rules on which agreements are enforced
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the consideration doctrine functions as a gatekeeper that selects certain agreements for enforcement and screens out others, and Paper B critiques doctrines such as the parol evidence rule and interpretive rules for causing courts to enforce written terms that may misstate the parties' agreement.

shared_topics.topic: formalism versus contextualism in contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts older, thinner/conceptual accounts of exchange with a motivational, bargained-for conception that better captures enforced commercial commitments, while Paper B argues courts should look beyond formal written texts to the surrounding context and the parties' sophistication to effectuate true intentions rather than mechanical enforcement of form language.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43flastulrev1265!!ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the court's role in supplying or interpreting contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts inevitably interpret written agreements (invoking the parol evidence rule and rules of interpretation) and should examine context rather than reading writings in a vacuum; Paper B treats the judicial selection of default rules as the core mechanism by which courts fill gaps in incomplete contracts and shows that such selection is unavoidable and normatively consequential.

shared_topics.topic: the prominence and limits of party intent as a guide for resolving contractual indeterminacy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes enforcing the parties' actual intentions (and using contextual evidence to do so) so small businesses are bound only by what they intended; Paper B analyzes the common judicial method of choosing default rules that reflect parties' ex ante intentions and contrasts that approach with alternative rationales (efficiency, distributive aims).

shared_topics.topic: the significance and consequences of default/form contract terms for contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how standardized/form contracts and memorializing agreements in writing can bind small businesses to terms that do not reflect their intentions (often because they cannot afford counsel); Paper B focuses on default rules (including penalty defaults) and how the choice of defaults alters parties' entitlements and incentives, i.e., the material effects of non‑party‑supplied terms.

shared_topics.topic: how differences in bargaining power, sophistication, or access to counsel shape contractual outcomes and distributional effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on small businesses' relative lack of sophistication and attorney access and urges courts to account for that when interpreting contracts; Paper B situates default rules within a framework of distributive justice, showing that legal rule‑selection systematically advantages some parties over others and cannot be distributionally neutral.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: doctrines of contract interpretation (including the parol evidence rule and plain-meaning approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how the parol evidence rule and interpretive doctrines can prevent small businesses from having courts enforce their true intentions, while Paper B debates neoformalist calls to revive plain-meaning/formal interpretive rules and reduce reliance on trade usage and contextual evidence.

shared_topics.topic: effects of form contracts on contracting parties' rights and expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how standardized/form contracts can bind small businesses to terms that do not reflect their intentions or protect their interests, and Paper B analyzes how the U.C.C.-governed, form-contract-dominated commercial world would be affected by a shift toward greater formalism.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between legal rules and real-world contracting practices and party sophistication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should consider the context, business experience, and limited attorney access of small firms when interpreting agreements, and Paper B critiques abstract normative models by emphasizing the complexity of real-world contracting, industry practices, and the limits of applying simplistic formal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical evidence in shaping contract doctrine and statutory reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the lack of empirical research on small businesses' experiences with contract law and proposes empirical study, while Paper B insists legislative or doctrinal moves toward greater formalism should be grounded in empirical evidence and finds that such evidence is lacking for the proposed shift.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110nwulrev63!!Article: CUSTOM IN THE COURTS
compared_to.partner_title: Article: CUSTOM IN THE COURTS

shared_topics.topic: formalist (agreement‑centric) versus contextual (usage/surrounding circumstances) approaches to contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically critiques the UCC's incorporation strategy that injects trade usages and other contextual standards into contract meaning and argues for shifting toward a more formalist, agreement‑centric approach for business‑to‑business transactions; Paper B argues courts should examine the transaction context (not read writings in a vacuum) to give effect to parties' actual intentions, emphasizing a contextual interpretive stance for protecting small businesses.

shared_topics.topic: the role and consequences of the parol evidence rule in enforcing written agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Code's permissive parol evidence rule interacts with trade‑usage incorporation and may influence litigation and specification costs; Paper B focuses on how the parol evidence rule can harm small businesses by locking them into written terms that may not reflect their intent and urges courts to consider extrinsic context.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary standards and reliability for proving trade usages or parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical findings that courts often accept weak evidence (party testimony/affidavits) to establish trade usages and flags risks of interpretive error; Paper B highlights small businesses' limited access to counsel and resources, implying similar evidentiary and proof problems when trying to show that agreements diverge from written forms or reflect particular intentions.

shared_topics.topic: practical impact of interpretive doctrines on business bargaining, transaction costs, and risk allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how the incorporation approach affects specification costs, summary judgment, and strategic litigation behavior among firms (especially large multi‑agent firms), while Paper B examines how interpretive rules can expose small businesses to unintended obligations, impede negotiation, and increase the costs and risks of contracting without sophisticated counsel.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj11!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Clouds of Mystery: Dispelling the Realist Rhetoric of the Uniform Commercial Code
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Clouds of Mystery: Dispelling the Realist Rhetoric of the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: whether commercial law should track actual merchant practices or reshape them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the UCC's claim that Article 2 was derived from and intended to reflect merchant practices, showing Llewellyn selectively adopted or rejected market behavior; Paper B similarly questions whether contract doctrines (e.g., written/form contracts) actually reflect parties' commercial intentions and urges attention to the real practices of small businesses.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formalist rules and contextual/pragmatic interpretation in commercial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the myth that the UCC is a pure product of Legal Realism and highlights Llewellyn's pragmatic, situational use of doctrine versus theory; Paper B argues against mechanically applying rules like the parol evidence rule and calls for contextual, pragmatic contract interpretation sensitive to parties' circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate scope of judicial discretion in shaping commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Llewellyn's normative stance that law should sometimes 'control' marketplace practices and that drafters/judges can choose doctrine to produce preferred outcomes; Paper B urges courts to exercise discretion by examining contextual evidence and the parties' sophistication when interpreting agreements rather than enforcing texts in a vacuum.

shared_topics.topic: how commercial law should treat less-sophisticated or vulnerable market participants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the normative question that the law must not simply abdicate to business practices and sometimes should regulate or correct market behavior; Paper B focuses on small businesses' vulnerabilities (limited counsel, reliance on form contracts) and recommends interpretive rules that account for their inexperience and protection needs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev681!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION: THE PLAIN MEANING RULE IN LABOR ARBITRATION.

shared_topics.topic: the exclusionary effect of formal rules (parol evidence / plain meaning) on use of extrinsic evidence
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze doctrines that bar or limit consideration of extrinsic evidence—Paper A focuses on the parol evidence rule and Paper B on the plain meaning rule—and show how those doctrines operate to exclude contextual or extrinsic proof of the parties' agreement.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract interpretation should prioritize parties' actual intent over literal textualism
shared_topics.justification: Both articles criticize strictly text‑based interpretation and argue that adjudicators should seek to effectuate the contracting parties' intentions rather than mechanically enforcing the written words alone.

shared_topics.topic: the adverse consequences of rigid textual interpretation for certain classes of parties (form users, unsophisticated actors, or parties relying on past practice)
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces demonstrate that strict application of textual rules can produce results contrary to the parties' expectations—Paper A emphasizes small businesses using form contracts or lacking counsel, and Paper B shows how reliance on plain meaning can disregard prior practices or negotiated understandings in labor agreements.

shared_topics.topic: advocacy for contextualist or alternative interpretive frameworks that admit extrinsic evidence and past practices
shared_topics.justification: Each article surveys the limits of the prevailing textual rule and proposes or endorses alternative approaches (contextual inquiry, consideration of bargaining context, past practice, and parties' experience) to better align outcomes with the parties' objective intentions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16cardozojconflictresol395!!ARTICLE: "COMMERCIAL PEACEMAKING"-- THE NEW ROLE OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION LEGAL ORDER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "COMMERCIAL PEACEMAKING"-- THE NEW ROLE OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMERCIAL ARBITRATION LEGAL ORDER

shared_topics.topic: how dispute-resolution mechanisms shape commercial actors' willingness and ability to transact
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that how contracts will be interpreted and enforced (and the availability of remedies) affects small businesses' ability and willingness to enter and perform commercial transactions, while Paper B shows that developing effective international commercial arbitration institutions removes barriers to cross-border trade between rival states and encourages private-sector commerce.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private ordering and non‑state adjudicative systems versus state courts in commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on private contracts and the risks that state court doctrines (e.g., parol evidence, interpretive rules) can frustrate parties' private ordering, whereas Paper B treats international commercial arbitration as an autonomous, non‑state legal order that parties can use instead of national courts to resolve commercial disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of parties' relative sophistication and access to legal resources on contractual outcomes and institutional design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that small businesses' limited access to attorneys and lower sophistication can lead to contracts that do not reflect their intentions and adverse court outcomes, while Paper B motivates the creation of tailored local arbitration institutions to meet the needs and capacities of parties (including businesses operating between rival states) who lack confidence in or access to traditional legal fora.

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between written/form terms and parties' intentions and the need for contextualized dispute-resolution rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes strict application of doctrines like the parol evidence rule that can bind parties to form or written terms contrary to their intentions and urges courts to consider context, and Paper B promotes bespoke arbitration mechanisms that can better accommodate the commercial context and expectations of disputing parties (e.g., Israel/Palestine, Korea) than default national rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35wmmarylrev1509!!SYMPOSIUM: THE REVISION OF ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE: STANDARDS FOR REVISING ARTICLE 2 OF THE U.C.C.: THE NOM CLAUSE MODEL
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE REVISION OF ARTICLE 2 OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE: STANDARDS FOR REVISING ARTICLE 2 OF THE U.C.C.: THE NOM CLAUSE MODEL

shared_topics.topic: parol evidence rule and no-oral-modification (NOM) clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the parol evidence rule and how it can prevent small businesses from proving agreements that differ from a written form, while Paper B directly examines the treatment and enforceability of NOM clauses in the proposed revision of UCC Article 2.

shared_topics.topic: judicial consideration of contracting context and party sophistication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should look beyond a written document to the parties' context, experience, and access to counsel when interpreting contracts, and Paper B addresses whether Article 2 (and its NOM-clause rules) should incorporate contextual standards or bright-line rules when governing commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: effects of standardized/form contract terms on parties' intentions and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how use of form contracts to avoid attorney fees can produce terms that do not reflect a small business's intentions, and Paper B treats standardized clauses (like NOM clauses) as core examples of terms whose regulation or revision raises costs, uncertainty, and fairness concerns for commercial actors.

shared_topics.topic: balancing legal certainty (enforceability of written terms) versus flexibility to honor actual agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the harm to small businesses when courts rigidly enforce written terms that diverge from parties' intentions, and Paper B weighs the policy trade-offs of enforcing or modifying doctrinal rules (e.g., NOM clauses) in Article 2 to preserve predictability without unduly frustrating legitimate commercial modifications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: the merits and dangers of interpretive formalism (plain meaning rule) versus contextual approaches to contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques recent 'Neoformalist' calls for sharper, more formal interpretive rules (including renewed support for the plain meaning rule) and assesses their suitability for Article 2; Paper B argues that strict formal interpretation can harm small businesses and urges courts to consider parties' intentions and contextual factors instead of applying formal meaning mechanically.

shared_topics.topic: the prevalence and effects of standardized/form contracts in real-world commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that modern sales practice is dominated by form contracts and analyzes how increased formalism would operate in that environment under the U.C.C.; Paper B focuses on how small businesses rely on form contracts (often without counsel), which can produce written terms that do not reflect their intentions and create legal risk.

shared_topics.topic: the role and admissibility of extrinsic evidence (parol evidence, trade usage, course of performance) in discerning parties' agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys scholarship advocating reduced roles for trade usage and course of performance and questions empirical support for that shift; Paper B centers on the parol evidence rule and interpretive doctrines, arguing courts should permit contextual evidence to vindicate parties' true agreements—especially for unsophisticated small firms.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical study of contracting practices to guide normative and statutory reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A insists legislative or doctrinal moves toward greater formalism should be grounded in empirical evidence of contracting behavior and warns the evidence is lacking; Paper B notes the absence of empirical surveys focused on small businesses and proposes studying their contracting practices to understand how contract law affects them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should interpret written agreements in light of surrounding context and party sophistication rather than applying formalistic rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should not treat a written agreement in a vacuum (invoking the parol evidence rule and interpretation doctrines) and should consider a small business's sophistication and access to counsel; Paper B similarly criticizes semantic and formalistic characterizations of transactions and urges judges to attend to the legal consequences and contextual realities when construing whether something is ‘contractual.'

shared_topics.topic: the limits of private reordering (freedom to contract) and when default rules should be mandatory versus waivable
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally analyzes which rules should be defaults susceptible to private reordering and which should be mandatory, while Paper A illustrates a practical limit on private reordering—small businesses constrained by form contracts, lack of counsel, and interpretive rules that may prevent their intended bargains from governing.

shared_topics.topic: the legal and policy consequences of labeling a transaction as 'contractual' (or characterizing its form)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B stresses that characterizations matter because labels determine disclosure obligations and regulatory treatment (e.g., rent-to-own as credit sale), and Paper A shows that calling a written form the binding contract (or not) has direct consequences for small businesses' duties and entitlements when courts enforce or construe those labels.

shared_topics.topic: risks posed by standardized/form contracts and information asymmetries in effectuating parties' actual intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how reliance on form contracts and limited attorney access can lock small businesses into terms that do not reflect their intentions, and Paper B examines how standardized regimes and defaults interact with private ordering and disclosure regimes, highlighting how doctrinal choices affect parties subject to standard-form transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41seattleulrev209!!ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of standardized/form/boilerplate terms (e.g., terms‑in‑a‑box, arbitration clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses the problem of ‘terms‑in‑a‑box’ and whether mandatory arbitration and other boilerplate survive absent explicit assent, while Paper B focuses on the risks that small businesses face when form contracts contain terms that may not reflect their intentions, raising the same question of when standardized terms should be treated as binding.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' intentions, expectations, and relational norms in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contract law should account for mutualism and dualism — the actual expectations and reciprocal norms parties bring to transactions — and Paper B argues courts should look beyond the written text (parol evidence and context) to ascertain what the parties intended, especially for less sophisticated actors.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of traditional contract doctrines to capture real-world contracting practices and the need for doctrinal adaptation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques contract law’s uni‑faceted approaches and proposes an Aristotelian means‑ends analysis to align doctrine with contemporary relational behaviors, while Paper B criticizes rigid application of rules like the parol evidence rule and calls for contextualized interpretation to better serve how small businesses actually contract.

shared_topics.topic: effects of informational/sophistication asymmetries on contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights scenarios where purchasers or individual actors encounter surprise legal‑ware in shipped terms and where empirical behavior departs from standard rational models, and Paper B documents how small businesses’ limited access to counsel and relative unsophistication can lead them to be bound by written terms that do not reflect their intent, both raising concerns about fairness and enforceability in asymmetric settings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27cornelljlpubpoly553!!ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AGAINST MARKET INSULARITY: MARKET, RESPONSIBILITY, AND LAW

shared_topics.topic: the formative role of law (especially contract and property forms) in constructing market relations and moral expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law does not merely enforce market transactions but helps constitute market relations and the moral demands that attach to them via legal forms like contract and property; Paper B shows how contract doctrines and written forms concretely shape small businesses' transactional expectations and practices, illustrating law's constitutive effect.

shared_topics.topic: the gap and tension between legal enforceability and parties' moral or factual intentions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that legal permissions can diverge from moral duties and that law may leave moral responsibilities unmet, while Paper B documents how written agreements and formal contract rules (e.g., parol evidence) can bind parties in ways that fail to reflect their actual intentions, arguing courts should examine context to bridge that gap.

shared_topics.topic: how legal formalism can disadvantage less powerful or less sophisticated market participants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes presumptions that market relations are impersonal and thereby can absolve actors of moral responsibility, implicating how legal forms may shield conduct; Paper B highlights small businesses' particular vulnerability to adverse outcomes from rigid contract doctrines because they often lack counsel and sophistication, calling attention to power and capacity asymmetries produced or amplified by law.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of strict contract interpretation doctrines (e.g., parol evidence rule) for realizing the parties' true agreement and facilitating fair market transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how legal forms of contract influence what market participation demands morally and socially, while Paper B analyzes specific doctrinal rules—especially the parol evidence rule and interpretive canons—and argues courts should incorporate contextual evidence and the parties' sophistication to ensure contracts effectuate intended transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: formalist versus contextual approaches to contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally contrasts New York's formalist emphasis on the written text with California's contextual, equity-oriented approach and links party choice to these regimes; Paper B directly critiques strict formalist treatment and argues courts should examine contextual evidence (especially for small businesses) rather than treating the writing in isolation.

shared_topics.topic: the parol evidence rule and the primacy of written agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that formalist courts treat the written contract as the definitive source of meaning, influencing forum choice by sophisticated parties; Paper B focuses on the parol evidence rule and warns that rigid application of written-document primacy can bind small businesses to terms that do not reflect their intentions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party sophistication and resource asymmetries in shaping contractual outcomes and preferred rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that sophisticated commercial parties choose jurisdictions (e.g., New York) that enforce bright-line, formal rules to maximize transaction value, while Paper B emphasizes that small or unsophisticated businesses lack legal resources and therefore may be disadvantaged by formalist doctrines unless courts account for their limited experience and access to counsel.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52drakelrev235!!ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of extrinsic/post-formation evidence (course of performance, parol evidence) in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the UCC's use of course of performance evidence (especially after its expansion in revised Article 1) and argues it is analytically and policy-wise problematic; Paper B focuses on the parol evidence rule and urges courts to look beyond a writing to contextual or extrinsic evidence so that agreements reflect parties' actual understanding.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between textual/formal enforcement of written contracts and giving effect to parties' actual intentions and commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the use of course of performance as potentially distortive of contract doctrine and commercial norms, while Paper B documents how strict, text-focused enforcement of form contracts can bind small businesses contrary to their intentions and impede bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: whether existing doctrinal tools should be adjusted (e.g., preferring waiver over course of performance; flexible application of parol evidence) to better protect contracting parties and commercial expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes the doctrine of waiver as a preferable means to give effect to post-formation conduct and examines problems from the UCC revisions, whereas Paper B advocates for courts to apply interpretation and parol evidence rules with sensitivity to parties' sophistication and context to avoid unfair outcomes for small businesses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj11!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Clouds of Mystery: Dispelling the Realist Rhetoric of the Uniform Commercial Code
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Clouds of Mystery: Dispelling the Realist Rhetoric of the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: whether commercial contract law should prioritize formal written terms or the parties' actual intentions/context (realism vs formalism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should not treat writings in a vacuum and should consider the context and parties' intentions when applying rules like the parol evidence doctrine; Paper B interrogates the claim that the UCC (especially Article 2) is a product of Legal Realism and shows how drafters like Llewellyn selectively relied on or ignored market practices, thus engaging the same debate over formalist doctrine versus context-sensitive, practice-based interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrines and codes (parol evidence rule, UCC Article 2) shape commercial practice and should be applied
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how the parol evidence rule and contract interpretation rules can bind parties to written terms that may not reflect their intended deal, while Paper B analyzes Article 2 of the UCC and its jurisprudential claims about reflecting or controlling merchant practice, with both papers examining the practical effects of doctrinal choices on commercial transactions.

shared_topics.topic: treatment of differing party sophistication and the law's accommodation of small/merchant actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes small businesses' limited access to counsel and lesser sophistication, urging courts to account for those realities in contract interpretation; Paper B contrasts how the UCC and its drafters treated 'men of commerce' and merchants, debating whether the law should defer to merchant practices or regulate them, thus both papers engage the question of how legal rules should respond to differences in commercial experience and bargaining power.

papers.node_id: 36houslrev1!!ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
papers.title: ARTICLE:IMAGES AND CONTRACT LAW - WHAT LAW APPLIES TO TRANSACTIONS IN INFORMATION
papers.abstract:
This is an era of turmoil in contract law, entailing the most pronounced changes since the 1960's. In the United States, the Uniform Commercial Code ("UCC") is being redrafted; two newarticles have been added and a third is proposed.Numerous states and several countries have redefined the concepts of signature and writing, and have also enacted new theories for determining when or whether a person is responsible in contract.A proposed European Union ("EU") Directive on Electronic Commerce calls for the EU countries to reconsider fundamentals of contract law.A White House white paper lays out a commitment to long-standing U.S. adherence to concepts of contractual freedom updated to a newly emerging electronicmarketplace.A Federal Trade Commission ("FTC") project calls for a fundamental reconsideration of consumer protection rules applying to e-mail, CD-ROMs, and the Internet.
While there are other factors at work, the core explanation for this widespread activity lies in the emergence of a new market (actually a new economy) that does not fit old patterns. This new economy calls for renewed attention to how contract law interacts with commercial contract practices. Transactions in this new environment differ from transactions in the old in both technique and subject matter. The differences demand retailored contract concepts.
We have experienced a fundamental shift from a goods-based economy to one a substantial part of which entails distribution of digital information and services. The contract law developed in the 1940's and 1950's to accommodate sales of toasters, automobiles, and other wares, while adequate for those purposes, does not correspond to the commercial premises relevant to contracts for licensed access to a digital database, for multi-location use of network or communications software, or for access to, or use of, other information assets. The images that legislators, judges, lawyers, and academics tend to employ in understanding these information transactions, however, referback to the other type of commerce, causing dislocation, misunderstanding, and uncertainty.
The idea that "information" can be the subject matter of a commercial exchange is not new, but the extent to which such transactions permeate the marketplace is new. The motion picture, broadcast, and print publishing industries seem to have been with us for a long time but this is true only for the print publishing industry. The motion picture industry is approximately one hundred years old, while other information and entertainment industries are far newer, dating only to the 1970's or 1990's. This growth resonates from the emergence of an information-based economy fueled by the interactive and communications capabilities of software and digital systems. The commercial issues in creating, compiling, distributing, and enabling use of the output of these information-sector industries entail, overall, a vastly different enterprise than does manufacturing and distributing hard goods ("wares" as Karl Llewellyn described them). The subject matter is intangible; the rights and duties associated with them are defined not by the old law of personal property, but by technological control of systems or property rights under intellectual property law, such as copyright.The contractual relationships differ dramatically from those of the goods or "real" estate sectors. The dominant types of contracts for intangible property are licenses, or other limited grants, in which the transferor retains the right to control not only the information, but also the uses of the information given to the transferee.This is a far different model than a sale of goods, which gives the buyer full rights in the subject matter (i.e., the item sold).
This Article discusses these differences and their consequences for contract law, especially for commercial contract law. Part I deals generally with the question of how contract law should relate to contract and commercial practice, and with the role of the images used to develop appropriate contract law rules. In the United States, that relationship has always been one of seeking to foster freedom of contract and to facilitate the creation of, and reliance upon, commercial contractual relationships.Although this focus has been muddied by the tendency toward regulation in consumer relationships and other selected areas ofcommerce (e.g., securities law), the basic principles remain strikingly resilient in fundamental contract law. Those principles argue for a legal regime in which contract rules serve a background function, providing rules appropriate to the commercial relationship. The rules, however, are routinely and comprehensively subject to the dominant effect of the parties' agreement.
In the 1930's, Llewellyn used a seemingly simple insight to support development of what eventually became UCC Article 2 - he emphasized that the labels and images we use as reference points do matter in making decisions about appropriate contract law.In a time following basic change in the economy, the images we deploy are likely to be throwbacks to an older era that may serve poorly in the new. In the 1930's, Llewellyn was talking about the change from an agrarian to an industrial economy. Today, we face the same issue caused by the change from a goods-based economy to an information and services economy. The images that we bring from the world of goods differ fundamentally from the reality and expectations in the world of information and services transactions.
Part II of this Article explores some of the differences between goods and digital information as commercial subject matter. It then asks what should be a simple question in an information economy: "If I give information, rights in information, or services to you, what obligations of accuracy, quality, or utility do I have?" In answering this question, we see a sharp distinction between this field and the application of existing contract law to sales of goods. The obligations established in reference to sales differ from the obligations anticipated regarding services and information. We also see a direct illustration of the disorientation created by mismatched images, for here the distinction between the subject matter of traditional commerce (goods) and the subject matter of the new economy (information and services) is most clear. By relying on categories and images that do not sensibly relate to the commercial context with which we currently deal, current contract law provides little coherent guidance for modern transactions in the information economy. A comparison to the misuse of the concept of title to resolve risk-of-loss in the pre-Llewellyn era is apposite and explicit because in both contexts the result inreported cases is not always an incorrect outcome, but a failure of relevance. The law fails to provide relevant standards for parties and courts to plan transactions or resolve disputes.
Today, the question of obligation in information-based transactions is resolved by a process of categorization that is not only inexact, it is incomprehensible. The categories range from labeling an information deal as a transaction in goods, to describing it as a services contract. Courts lack a coherent language of obligation for these transactions and, thus, draw on concepts and labels from law geared to another era and a different transactional framework. One primary contribution that we can make to the new economic environment is to begin to provide a lexicon and framework derived from a focus on these types of transactions themselves. This, of course, is exactly what is proposed in proposed Article 2B of the UCC.

questions.question: How should contract law allocate rights, duties, and remedies in commercial transactions that transfer or license digital information and information-based services?
What obligations of accuracy, quality, or utility should apply when one party provides information, rights in information, or information-based services to another?
How do legacy conceptual images and categorical frames drawn from goods-based commerce distort or impede the development of coherent contract rules for the information economy?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68amulrev1621!!ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A BARGAINING DYNAMIC TRANSACTION COST APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: need to adapt contract law and doctrine to new economic forms (innovation/information economies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates long-term agreements and supply‑chain contracting within a deverticalized, innovation‑driven economy and argues for analyzing contract form through transaction costs and bargaining in that new context; Paper B argues the shift from a goods‑based to an information/services economy requires retooling contract law (and the UCC) because old categories and images misfit modern information transactions.

shared_topics.topic: information as distinct contract subject matter and the role of information‑sharing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes LTAs' formal information‑sharing provisions (and their role in monitoring, learning, and protecting sunk investments), while Paper B focuses on transactions where the commodity is digital information or access and asks what accuracy, quality, and control obligations should govern those exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: incompleteness, uncertainty, and how contracts respond to them (bargaining and planning under uncertainty)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats LTAs as necessarily incomplete in innovation and manufacturing settings and explains contract forms as bargains that allocate risks and planning needs under uncertainty; Paper B highlights how information transactions resist neat categorization under existing doctrines, producing uncertainty about parties' obligations that the law must better accommodate.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal legal rules and informal enforcement/norms (appropriate level of legal enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly examines when informal enforcement and 'low‑powered' sanctions suffice versus when legal remedies are warranted in supply‑chain LTAs, drawing on law‑and‑norms literature; Paper B similarly emphasizes that contract rules should serve as a background to commercial practice and facilitate party reliance, implicating choices about how much law should govern information transactions.

shared_topics.topic: use of standardized contractual forms (SFKs, licenses) as governance and control devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes OEM‑drafted standard form LTAs as tools to centralize terms, planning, and control opportunism across repeated transactions; Paper B identifies licenses and limited grants as the dominant contractual form in information markets and examines how those forms differ functionally from goods sales and how doctrine should treat them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95indlj485!!ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Law's Transferability Bias

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of the UCC and statutory frameworks for governing modern commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Article 9 of the UCC and related doctrines compel assignability (e.g., voiding nonassignment clauses) and thereby shape market practices; Paper B analyzes ongoing UCC revision efforts (including proposed Article 2B) and broader statutory initiatives as necessary responses to transactions in digital information and services.

shared_topics.topic: tension between freedom of contract (party autonomy) and mandatory legal rules that override private agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how assignability doctrines and mandatory rules subvert parties' negotiated choices about transferability of rights; Paper B similarly interrogates the role of background legal rules versus party agreements in the information economy and whether existing or new laws should limit or support contractual freedom in digital transactions.

shared_topics.topic: commodification and marketability of contractual rights across different subject matters
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the economic and legal forces that treat debts and rights to sue as tradable assets and collateral (financialization of contract rights); Paper B addresses the emergence of information and service rights as commercial assets (licenses, controlled access) and the need to reconceive contract rules for intangible, marketable information.

shared_topics.topic: how underlying legal images, classifications, and conceptual frameworks (e.g., property vs. promise, goods vs. information) shape doctrine and policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques circular conceptual arguments that treat contractual rights as property to justify transferability, while Paper B stresses that using goods-based images to understand information transactions produces misfit and calls for new conceptual vocabularies tailored to information commerce.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between legal rules and commercial practices/expectations (including reliance, reputation, and relational governance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties rely on reputational and relational mechanisms and that identity-of-counterparty matters when assignments occur; Paper B highlights that information transactions have different commercial premises and expectations, so contract law must align background rules with prevailing market practices and reliance interests.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1987dukelj1!!ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COURT ADJUSTMENT OF LONG-TERM CONTRACTS: AN ANALYSIS UNDER MODERN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law should adapt to changing commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that traditional contract doctrines (developed for goods) are ill-suited to transactions in information and services and calls for new, tailored rules (e.g., Article 2B); Paper B likewise argues existing doctrines (impracticability, specific performance) misfit many long-term commercial relationships and proposes jurisprudential adjustments to better fit commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for unforeseen or disruptive events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that the move from goods to information changes how risk (e.g., quality, accuracy, loss) should be allocated and that old categories (title/risk-of-loss) are often irrelevant; Paper B directly analyzes how long-term contracts should allocate risk when unanticipated cost shocks occur and proposes models (agreement and gap) for when courts should reallocate losses.

shared_topics.topic: the balance between party autonomy (express agreements) and background legal rules/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contract law should serve as a background regime that respects parties' agreements while providing relevant default standards for information transactions; Paper B examines when courts should honor explicit bargains versus supply judicially-fashioned adjustments where agreements are silent or implicitly assume renegotiation.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of relational/implicit expectations and the judiciary's role in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that images and categories must reflect the relational and licensing nature of information commerce (implicit controls and duties), suggesting doctrinal reform to capture those realities; Paper B formulates an 'agreement model' based on parties' implicit expectations of cooperation and evaluates the propriety and form of judicially-crafted adjustments as a remedy in relational long-term contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100marqlrev997!!ARTICLE: WHO NEEDS CONTRACTS? GENERALIZED EXCHANGE WITHIN INVESTMENT ACCELERATORS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHO NEEDS CONTRACTS? GENERALIZED EXCHANGE WITHIN INVESTMENT ACCELERATORS

shared_topics.topic: the limits of traditional contract law for information or knowledge exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that doctrines developed for sales of goods (title, risk-of-loss, warranties) poorly fit transactions in digital information and services and calls for new contract frameworks (e.g., Article 2B); Paper B shows that mentor–startup exchanges in accelerators routinely operate without formal contracts, revealing practical and doctrinal gaps when applying traditional contract rules to information/knowledge transfers.

shared_topics.topic: when informal norms, reputational sanctions, or generalized exchange substitute for formal contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties' agreements and commercial practices should shape contract rules and that mismatched legal images produce uncertainty in information markets; Paper B documents how accelerators institutionalize generalized exchange—unilateral giving and indirect returns—so norms and reputational mechanisms sustain pro‑social information sharing without legal instruments.

shared_topics.topic: how rights, consideration, and obligations are allocated in transactions involving intangible assets or expertise
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how licenses and limited grants (not sales) change the nature of obligations (accuracy, quality, utility) in information transactions; Paper B analyzes why mentors provide valuable expertise absent direct consideration, identifying indirect reputational, learning, and network benefits that function as consideration surrogates.

shared_topics.topic: multi‑party or networked exchange structures that defy bilateral contract models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights commercial arrangements like multi‑location software licenses and licensed access that do not map to bilateral goods-sale models; Paper B analyzes MDIA mentor–startup networks where benefits are circulated indirectly across a group (three or more parties), showing the insufficiency of bilateral contracting theories for such networked exchanges.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100cornelllrev23!!ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: reforming contract doctrine to accommodate information- and service-based transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law developed for sales of physical goods poorly fits transactions in digital information, licenses, and services and calls for retailored rules (e.g., Article 2B). Paper B likewise shows that many modern contracting practices (including sophisticated information‑exchange regimes) do not map onto traditional interpretive prototypes, requiring different doctrinal responses.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of traditional contract categories/prototypes (goods, executory contracts, plain textualism) for modern commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates how applying goods-based categories (title, risk-of-loss) to information transactions produces irrelevant or incoherent results. papers.node_id: 71ucololrev541!!ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
papers.title: ARTICLE:KARL LLEWELLYN'S FADING IMPRINT ON THE JURISPRUDENCE OF THE UNIFORM COMMERCIAL CODE
papers.abstract:
The Uniform Commercial Code ("U.C.C.") at one time indisputably owed more to Professor Karl N. Llewellyn than to anyone else. Although Llewellyn did not initiate the plan to combine various uniform state laws on business subjects into a coherent code,he played a pivotal role in translating this objective into the U.C.C. Llewellyn led the U.C.C.'s drafting as the "Chief Reporter" from 1942 until his death in 1962.He and his wife, Professor Soia Mentschikoff, also served as reporters for three of the nine "articles" - or principal parts - of the U.C.C.Throughout this process, Llewellyn consistently strived to make the U.C.C. distinct from other statutes and laws by imbuing it with features that reflected his deeply held juridical beliefs.For these reasons, the U.C.C. has acquirednicknames like "Karl's Kode"and "Lex Llewellyn."
Llewellyn was a leader of the Legal Realist movement that emerged in this country during the 1920s and 1930s.Scholars associated with this school of jurisprudence did not agree on everything, but they all held an intense interest in understanding what actually influences judges when they decide cases.As discussed more fully within, some of the Legal Realists, including Llewellyn, shared a prescriptive vision for crafting legislation. They believed that statutes should seek to improve judicial decisions by recognizing that judges inevitably act with considerable discretion, and by seeking to guide this discretion rather than futilely attempting to eliminate it.
When Llewellyn set to work on the U.C.C. project, he naturally wanted to implement his jurisprudential ideas.As the following in-depth discussion will show, Llewellyn succeeded in giving the U.C.C. at least five important features inspired byLegal Realism. In particular, as a result of his influence, the U.C.C.:

questions.question: Whether the principal drafter's Legal Realist jurisprudential ideas shaped the substantive design of the commercial code and continue to guide how courts interpret and apply that code.
To what extent features of the commercial code originally inspired by Legal Realism have persisted, evolved, or faded in subsequent judicial and doctrinal development.

papers.node_id: 99michlrev1724!!ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS
papers.abstract:
The cotton industry has almost entirely opted out of the public legal system, replacing it with one of the oldest and most complex systems of private commercial law.Most contracts for the purchase and sale of domestic cotton, between merchants or between merchants and mills, are neither consummated under the Uniform Commercial Code ("Code") nor interpreted and enforced in court when disputes arise. Rather, most such contracts are concluded under one of several privately drafted sets of contract default rules and are subject to arbitration in one of several merchant tribunals. Similarly, most international sales of cotton are governed neither by state-supplied legal rules norby the Convention on the International Sale of Goods, but rather by the rules of the Liverpool Cotton Association.
The institutions that create and administer the industry's private legal system work extraordinarily well. The trade rules are periodically revised to respond to technological advancements, market changes, and ambiguities revealed during disputes. Their content is known and understood by most market participants. The arbitration tribunals that resolve disputes do so expeditiously and inexpensively. Their decisions, which are recorded in written opinions, reveal a distinctive and coherent jurisprudential approach. Within the industry, arbitration awards are widely respected and complied with promptly. In short, the industry has succeeded in creating and maintaining a private legal system ("PLS") in which transactions costs, error costs, legal system costs, and collection costs are low. This system has endured since the mid-1800s, surviving widespread social change, years of extreme price volatility, and substantial changes in the background public legal regime.
This Article draws on a detailed case study of contractual relations in the cotton industry to examine the ways that the rules, norms, and institutions that constitute the industry's PLS create value for transactors. Part I describes the formal operation of the PLS and discusses the ways that its substantive rules, adjudicative approaches, and arbitral procedures improve on those provided by the Code and the public legal system. Part II describes the many steps taken by cotton industry institutions to strengthen the social and informational infrastructures of trade. It discusses how these efforts combine to make reputation-based nonlegal sanctions a powerful force in the industry and explores how the availability of these sanctions makes important features of the PLS work better than they would in their absence. It also suggests that the availability of such sanctions may enable transactors to create value-enhancing contract governance structures that might be either unavailable or prohibitively expensive if their transactions were governed by the public legal system. Part III takes a step back and explores how the industry's efforts to support the legal and extralegal aspects of contracting relationships, together with certain other features of cotton institutions, have succeeded in creating conditions that are conducive to the creation, maintenance, and restoration of cooperative contracting relationships. Part IV concludes by suggesting that understanding how the cotton industry's institutions create value for transactors may help identify other industries and other contexts in which private institutions can play a positive role in supporting trade.

questions.question: Whether and how an industry's privately created rules, arbitration tribunals, and trade institutions can effectively substitute for the public legal system in governing contracts and resolving disputes, while lowering transaction, error, legal, and collection costs for market participants.

Whether the availability of industry institutions and reputational (nonlegal) sanctions enables transactors to design and maintain contract governance structures that would be infeasible or prohibitively expensive under public-law adjudication.

How private trade institutions (through rule revision, information sharing, and adjudicative practices) create, maintain, and restore cooperative contracting relationships in a market over long periods despite technological change, price volatility, and shifts in the background legal regime.
