papers.node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
papers.title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
papers.abstract:
Lawyers who negotiate and litigate over complex deals have an intuitive notion of the value of what they do in connection with the contract: the arguments around technical contract language are often a lawyers' game; in most cases, what is clear would have been clear on a handshake; and what is tightly negotiated bears only a random relationship to the areas of future dispute. In short, if the lawyers happen to have drafted tight and clear language around the particular matter in dispute, it is as much luck as foresight.Reading most academic analyses of contracts is something like watching a single episode of the currently popular "arrest and trial" television shows. The parties negotiate andsign a contract, a dispute arises, and is adjudicated in just several moments of thought.
Real-life commercial relationships cannot be so easily encapsulated. Long-term supply agreements can run for years; a shareholders' agreement or LLC operating agreement will span the entire life of a business; a typical acquisition agreement may take weeks to negotiate, additional months to close, and thereafter its warranties, covenants, and indemnification provisions will govern the buyer-seller relationship for years. The contract does not embody the relationship but reflects an aspect of it that was, at one time, dealt with in language meant to anticipate future events. Most of the relationship occurs without explicit reference to the contract. When there is a disagreement (and even then perhaps not), someone reaches for the file or the closing book to see what, if anything, was agreed on that particular subject.
Only then does the problem arise to which much of contract scholarship is directed. If the parties do not resolve the commercial issue by non-legal means, and if the contract is not sufficiently clear on the subject so the parties agree on the outcome, or if a court has an easy case, how do courts go about filling gaps that the parties simply did not address, or providing meaning in the present circumstance to words that do not unambiguously resolve the problem? The academic literature on that subject is represented by formalists and contextualists,moralistsand economists,those advocating complexity and those advocating simplicity,those seeking the intention of the parties and those seeking to impose a more objective market or societal intention,those presuming intention would be economically efficient and those believing an economically efficient result should simply be imposed.
There is a common thread, however, in any of the approaches to the resolution of hard cases of contract language interpretation. Whether inherent in the words of the agreement or in the context of its formation, mutually intended meaning is presumed to have affixed as of the time of the agreement's making.But by the time the dispute arises, the making of the agreement isancient history, and, as often as not, the contract is mere text. The disputing parties are ascribing meaning to the words as of the time of their disagreement, and now looking for connections to the past by which they may persuade each other or a court of the erroneous interpretation proposed by the other.
The normative implication of the common understanding that meaning affixed when the contract was executed is opportunism, the gaining of an advantage (or avoidance of disadvantage) when later circumstances make the agreement less favorable than expected.Advocates of the sanctity of promise would decry opportunism on moral grounds;welfare maximization theorists worry that opportunism undercuts the value of a system of contract that encourages investment.
want to suggest an alternative answer, which I believe is intuitive to practitioners but may be provocative in the academy. In a complex commercial relationship, when there is an ex post dispute over interpretation, particularly long after the parties negotiated the agreement, I question whether a mutual intention ever existed that is capable of determination either by the parties or a court. To the contrary, I contend the words of the agreement take on meaning only when a circumstance arises to which the words must be applied, and which is capable of becoming a dispute. What follows from that conclusion is a rejection of the idea that opportunism is a problem of any import to be addressed.
The argument goes as follows. The creation of the complex contract and its later interpretation are distinct events in a difficult case of ambiguity. If there is mutual intention at the time of a dispute over terms capable of a truly difficult case of disambiguation, it will be apparent at the time of the application of those terms to the relevant circumstance, but in that instance there will be no dispute and no jurisprudence. But, in that case, there is no going back to a mutually intended meaning as of the time the contract was made.
What the parties are then doing, whether individually or together, by applying the rule of a contract to the present facts, is no different than a judge's application of a Rule of Law to a new case, a matter on which philosophers have written extensively.Is there a rule inherent in previous cases which can be divined by induction and applied to the next case? The formalists say "yes."The skeptics say "no," relying on twentieth-century advances in the philosophyof language.Language (not just that which appears in a contract) is the means by which we structure our very interaction with the world and each other.Before we use it cognitively and reflectively, we use it reactively and responsively, obeying rules in a way that is not necessarily rational or cognitive.Moreover, analysis of language and judgment teaches us one cannot apply a scientific inductive rule to the use and meaning of words. Indeed, there is no rule for the application of a rule. So the rule-skeptics conclude there is no Rule of Law - there is no principle that can be induced scientifically from the prior case, and judges are largely unconstrained in the matters before them.
Strangely, the same debate has not transposed to questions of ex ante agreement and ex post interpretation of agreements. Whatever the approach, the current contract scholarship, even when it brushes up against this same problem of rule-induction, passes quickly to filling gaps and resolving ambiguities, without much further thought.I want to argue that rule of law and contract interpretation are the same. The process is an induction applied at the time of a dispute to a previously existing text (albeit one produced by the parties themselves and not a judge or legislature).
How then do we explain the process by which we seem to be agreeing ex ante and disputing ex post? I contend the process of creating the contract ex ante is simultaneously an instance of non-cognitive and cognitive communication. We do think deeply about some of the specific words of our agreements at the outset, and sometimes we are lucky enough actually to anticipate a future circumstance. The pragmatic reality of much of the complex contracting that is later disputed suggests, however, there may be as much possibility as not that there was no ex ante cognition around the words, and hence no ex ante meaning.
What happens later? Because there never was full cognition and intentionality in the creation of contracts (even where undertaken by sophisticated lawyers with relatively unlimited budgets), the potential dispute ripens only when the later circumstance arises. It is possible that the words will have a shared meaning and there will be no dispute. But it is also possible the two parties, having differing beliefs or self-interest, will first induce different statements of the rule from the contractual text, and then engage in competing hindsight analyses of the language, after the events have occurred to which the contract language is applied, and where there is some color to the positions of each side. Based on years of experience in dealing with these kinds of cases in practice, I contend the better insights derive not from traditional legal doctrines or economic theory looking to divine mutual intention and deter opportunism, but from philosophies around rule-induction (Kant),the use of words in language games (Wittgenstein),and the circumstances by which our use of language turns from non-cognitive communicative interaction to a cognitive discourse of argumentation and justification (Habermas).
The Langdellian science of law, as well as the cross-disciplinary social sciences brought to bear on law (primarily the insights of economic theory, whether based in welfare-maximizing rational actor assumptions or in more complex behavioral or institutional economics) all operate on the assumption of a reflective use of language: a cognitive process in which the parties do something intentional to secure legal rights or economic or strategic advantage in the future.In assuming that the process of creating agreement is cognitive and intentional, and in failing to consider the possibility it is not, all theories of contract interpretation err.
It is a pragmatic reality that the parties assess language, risk, and cost at the time of the dispute, and almost every calculus of the possible result of a dispute is opportunistic in the sense of maximizing the present value of the past words. There are a number of conclusions we may begin to draw from this insight, the most significant of which is this: in a colorable dispute over the meaning of a contract term, it is futile to attempt to determine the ex ante intention of the parties, and the notion of opportunism as a legal issue is an illusion. Whether one acts opportunistically is a function of extra-legal morals and norms, and not controllable by disputable language, if the parties choose to dispute it. The proper focus of courts, therefore, is a pragmatic resolution of disputes, and not a search for mutual intention.
In Part II, I set the context of commonly understood doctrines of intentionin the context of a complex and long-term contract relationship.In Part III, I review the relationship of prior decisions to present rulings in the jurisprudence of judge-made law.I explore three different assessments of judicial decision-making, all of which express skepticism as to the ability to induce a rule from prior cases: (a) the legal pragmatism first articulated by Justice Holmes;(b) Linda Meyer's analysis of the creative process of judicial decision-making (applying Kant's Critique of Judgments);and (c) rule-skepticism based on Wittgenstein's philosophy of language.In Part IV, I make the leap from judicial rule-induction to private rule induction in order to understand what it really means to have agreed or disagreed about the terms of an agreement.I conclude that the disagreement arises only in the context of the present dispute.First, I show that the making of the contract is both a cognitive and non-cognitive process that goes beyond mere "bounded rationality."Second, I argue that the parties' conflicting interpretations of the agreement are attempts to derive, on an ex post basis, inductive rules from the words of the contract that should have, had we been focusing on them at the time we contracted, dictated the result in a particular circumstance.Because this is precisely what we cannot do, by the very nature of words and language, then a meeting of the minds is a self-fulfilling conclusion. If the mutual intention is clear enough, there is no dispute to come before a judge (or the case is ridiculously easy and arises out of some motivation other than a real dispute over interpretation). If a dispute exists and the case is not easy, then there never was an ex ante meeting of the minds to divine. I then review contemporary contract theory, from the philosophy of promising to application of law and economics, in order to show that all of it is based on the same form of impossible rule-induction.
Finally, in Part V, I speculate on some of the implications if my theory is correct.I suggest, even where there are agreed words, there is less ex ante meeting of the minds than one would expect, and even less agreement on the rule established by the ex ante words when ex post circumstances create theincentive for dispute.In short, all disputes are opportunistic, and controlling opportunism would mean controlling disputes, something I contend is beyond the power of human beings, much less the law they create.

questions.question: Whether parties to complex, long-term contracts form a determinate, recoverable mutual intention about ambiguous terms at the time of contracting, such that that intention can be reliably ascertained and applied in later disputes.

Whether ex-post opportunistic reinterpretation of contractual language (seeking advantage by recharacterizing past words after events occur) is a meaningful problem that legal rules can control, or whether it is largely an illusion arising from the indeterminacy of language and the fact that contractual meaning is constructed only when disputes arise.

When contractual terms are ambiguous and mutual intent is indeterminate, whether the appropriate judicial approach is to seek an asserted ex-ante intent or to adopt a pragmatic, forward-looking resolution focused on resolving the present dispute.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNBUNDLED BARGAINS: MULTI-AGREEMENT DEALMAKING IN COMPLEX MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS

shared_topics.topic: ex ante versus ex post meaning of contractual language and when ‘meaning’ fixes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes that many terms acquire their operative meaning only when a disputed circumstance arises and that a true ex ante mutual intention often does not exist, while Paper B empirically shows how short, early-stage contract text (e.g., confidentiality clauses) gets interpreted later in M&A disputes and can determine deal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the substantive role of ancillary or 'boilerplate' agreements in shaping major transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper B studies why deals are structured as constellations of ancillary agreements and how those peripheral contracts can control core outcomes, and Paper A engages with how specific negotiated language (or seemingly peripheral text) can be decisive in later disputes and yet may not reflect settled ex ante intent.

shared_topics.topic: how courts interpret contractual texts and the implications of judicial interpretive methods for deal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory linking judicial rule-induction and private contract interpretation, arguing courts should focus on pragmatic resolution rather than uncovering ex ante intent, while Paper B documents how Delaware courts’ interpretive choices (e.g., reading an implied standstill into a confidentiality clause) affect how parties draft and unbundle deals.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, strategic use of information, and the constraining (or illusory) role of contract language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the premiss that ex post opportunism can be deterred by seeking ex ante intent and treats opportunistic reinterpretation as largely inevitable, and Paper B shows a concrete instance—use of nonpublic information in a hostile bid—where contractual language and judicial interpretation operate as mechanisms that enable or constrain opportunistic deal behavior.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68tennlrev73!!ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

shared_topics.topic: challenges in ascertaining parties' mutual intent when interpreting contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center on the difficulty courts face in identifying the parties' mutual intent—Paper A argues that a determinate ex ante mutual intention often does not exist in complex, long‑term deals and is reconstructed ex post, while Paper B treats failures of draftsmanship, imprecision, and memory frailties as practical obstacles to effectuate mutual intent and develops a doctrinal approach to address them.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and resolution of ambiguous contract language
shared_topics.justification: Both works substantively engage with contractual ambiguity and doctrines for resolving it—Paper A critiques the assumption that gaps/ambiguities can reliably be filled by uncovering ex ante intent and reframes interpretation as inductive rule application, while Paper B surveys interpretive principles (including contra proferentem) and proposes a systematic method for resolving ambiguous terms in Tennessee courts.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of judicial doctrines and precedent (rule‑induction) in filling gaps and deciding hard cases
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how judges use prior rules and interpretive canons to resolve disputes—Paper A questions the possibility of inducing stable interpretive rules from past cases and links rule‑skepticism to contract interpretation, whereas Paper B treats the existing rule‑laden doctrine as the framework to be navigated and leverages federal precedents as persuasive authority in forming a coherent approach.

shared_topics.topic: ex post opportunism and how parties exploit ambiguity in disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the theme that parties, after events occur, will frame past words to maximize advantage—Paper A argues that ex post reinterpretation is inevitable and that 'opportunism' is an illusory legal problem, while Paper B addresses how courts confront potentially strategic or inadvertent ambiguity (e.g., via contra proferentem) and seeks doctrinal solutions to limit unfair exploitation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev561!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.

shared_topics.topic: whether the written contract document captures the parties' full agreement or must be supplemented by the relational context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the written instrument often omits crucial understandings and that researchers and courts must look to the ongoing contractual relation to see what the parties actually agreed to; Paper B similarly contends the contract text does not embody a fixed meaning and that much of the relationship and its understandings exist outside (or only emerge after) the written words.

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual meaning is fixed at formation (ex ante mutual intention) or is created/applied ex post through rule-induction
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally argues that meaning typically arises only when a dispute triggers application of the words and that ex ante mutual intention is often indeterminate; Paper A engages the same issue descriptively by showing how parties rely on adaptive understandings rather than fixed clauses, so interpretation and expectations are shaped by later interactions, not only the original drafting.

shared_topics.topic: how parties manage adaptation, renegotiation and gap-filling in long-term exchanges (private governance vs formal legal remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines private ordering, governance structures, hostage exchanges, and other relational mechanisms parties use to monitor, adapt and enforce long-term contracts instead of relying on formal clauses; Paper B analyzes private rule-induction and urges courts (and scholars) to see contract interpretation as a pragmatic, context-driven exercise akin to parties' own ex post rule-making, emphasizing non-judicial processes of resolving gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the conception and legal relevance of opportunism in long-term contracting and dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats opportunism as a central hazard of transactions with idiosyncratic investments and discusses pricing, hostages and governance as responses to opportunistic risk; Paper B questions the salience of opportunism as a legal category by arguing that ex post reinterpretation is often an inevitable, language-driven process and that treating later claims as merely opportunistic misreads how meaning and disputes actually arise.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should prioritize ex ante mutual intent or apply bright-line/formal rules in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that genuine ex ante mutual intention is often nonexistent for difficult ambiguities and urges pragmatic, ex post resolution rather than searching for a historical meeting of the minds; Paper B critiques recent neoformalist calls for sharper, more formal interpretive rules (e.g., plain-meaning approaches) and examines the costs of privileging formalism over contextual methods in real-world contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the possibility and legitimacy of rule‑induction from prior cases or contract text
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its critique on rule‑induction, arguing that neither judges nor parties can reliably induce determinate rules from past language or precedent for novel disputes; Paper B engages the same worry from the opposite direction, questioning whether a legal move toward stricter, inductively applied formal rules (statutory or judicial) fits the heterogeneous realities of Article 2 practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical/real‑world contracting practices versus abstract theoretical models in shaping doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses practitioners' pragmatic experience and contends that theoretical models (including many law-and-economics accounts) mischaracterize how meaning is created and disputes arise; Paper B similarly insists that neoformalist recommendations rest on models that may be ‘off’ and that legislative or doctrinal shifts should be grounded in empirical evidence about how contracts operate in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tradeoff between predictability/efficiency and flexibility/pragmatism in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes that attempts to control opportunism via ex ante attribution of meaning are futile and that courts should focus on pragmatic dispute resolution rather than formalistic enforcement of intent, challenging efficiency-based doctrinal prescriptions; Paper B directly weighs neoformalists’ claims that increased predictability and efficiency justify stricter rules against the real‑world costs of losing flexible, standards‑based interpretation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior and the limits of legal control
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that apparent opportunism in contract disputes is often an ex post reinterpretation of text and that controlling opportunism via searching for ex ante intent is futile; Paper B analyzes bait-and-switch as a class of opportunistic commercial tactics and asks when and how regulation can or should prevent such practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms and customs versus formal legal or welfare-based rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes formalist and welfare-maximizing approaches to contract interpretation and points to language-games and pragmatic norms as central to meaning; Paper B shows that regulators often defer to marketplace customs and norms in policing bait-and-switch conduct and contrasts that deference with welfare-advancing regulation.

shared_topics.topic: the problem of defining and interpreting legal language ex post
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how contractual words acquire disputed meaning only when applied to concrete circumstances and argues mutual ex ante intention is often indeterminate; Paper B wrestles with the legal definition of 'bait-and-switch' versus its broader popular usage and examines how regulators and courts interpret advertising and sales-language in practice.

shared_topics.topic: pragmatic enforcement and regulatory design versus searching for subjective intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes courts should prioritize pragmatic dispute resolution over attempts to recover parties' original intentions; Paper B evaluates regulatory responses (FTC, statutes, statutes like the CARD Act) and advocates policy approaches that account for pragmatic effects, customs, and the welfare consequences of different enforcement choices.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Clouds of Mystery: Dispelling the Realist Rhetoric of the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: whether commercial rules (the UCC / contract terms) are genuinely grounded in actual merchant practices or instead reflect doctrinal/theoretical choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the 'Realist' origin story of the UCC, arguing Article 2 selectively used or ignored merchant practice and was shaped by Llewellyn's doctrinal choices; Paper B similarly questions the assumption that contract language embodies a clear ex ante mutual intention grounded in parties' practices, arguing meaning often arises only ex post and is not reliably traceable to preexisting commercial behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the proper relationship between legal theory and doctrine in commercial law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Llewellyn's pragmatic, sometimes opportunistic, use of theory versus doctrine in drafting the Code and the resulting social vision of doctrine/theory relations; Paper B interrogates core theoretical frameworks (formalism, contextualism, law & economics) that underlie contract interpretation and argues these theories rest on flawed assumptions about rule-induction and intentionality.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts versus market actors/parties in producing and applying commercial rules and meanings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether the law should 'conform to' or 'control' marketplace practices and highlights the drafters' willingness to use law to shape commerce; Paper B argues that in hard interpretive cases meaning is produced at the time of dispute, so courts must pragmatically resolve issues rather than reconstruct an unverifiable ex ante intention of the parties.

shared_topics.topic: debunking dominant narratives or 'myths' about commercial law (origins, intention, and opportunism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A exposes the mythologized account that the UCC is the 'ultimate Realist statute' rooted in merchant practice; Paper B exposes the 'ex post illusion' that mutual intention existed and treats the common worry about opportunism as founded on a misleading narrative about how contracts are created and later interpreted.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of strategic behavior and opportunism in contracting, disclosure, and dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats claims of opportunism in ex post interpretation as largely a product of hindsight and parties’ present incentives when disputes arise, and Paper B focuses on strategic bargaining incentives (who reveals information, who benefits from defaults) to show how opportunism and strategic signaling affect whether and how parties bargain around legal defaults.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges doctrinal and economic theories that presume cognitive, intentional contracting and reliable rule‑induction by judges, while Paper B critiques standard law‑and‑economics/Coasean models and formal economic accounts of default rules for failing to capture realistic strategic incentives and empirical patterns in contract practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LACKING SWISS PRECISION: THE FIRST-SALE DOCTRINE IN COSTCO V. OMEGA

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Lesson on Some Limits of Economic Analysis: Schwartz and Scott on Contract Interpretation

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Trade Usage and Disclaiming Consequential Damages: The Implications for Just-in-Time Purchasing

papers.node_id: 69fordhamlrev31!!ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
papers.title: ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
papers.abstract:
Lawyers have garnered a reputation for being unreasonable and excessively contentious.This popular sentiment is embedded in our culture. If lawyers cannot change that perception, a second-best outcome (from the perspective of lawyers) would be the formation of an understanding that there is a reason why they appear to act unreasonably, that it can be desirable for lawyers to act in a way that initially appears to be unreasonable. This Article attempts to build a basis for that understanding in the context of lawyers participating in large commercial transactions.
To provide a specific context for the discussion, consider a negotiation strategy occasionally adopted by counselin a leveraged lease of an aircraft to a large airline.Typically in such a transaction,an airline's contractual right to purchase an aircraft is assigned to a trustee. The trustee acquires the funds to purchase the aircraft by issuing debt interests to "debt participants" and equity interests to "equity participants." Financial institutions, such as banks and insurance companies, purchase these interests.The trustee enters into a long-term lease of the aircraft with the airline. The terms of the lease are of crucial importance to both the debt and equity participants, because the lessor's rights under that lease circumscribe their rights.
One important issue addressed by the lease will be the locations to which the aircraft may be flown,because the return to the debt and equity participants may be substantially and adversely affected if the aircraft is located in certain countries. For example, the presence of the aircraft in some countries may increase the likelihood of a casualty to the aircraft. Alternatively, its location in other countries,or the registration of the aircraft in another country,may restrict the ability of the trustee to obtain possession of the aircraft after a default. Consequently, the debt and equity participants will seek to include in the lease restrictions on the locations to which the aircraft may be flown.
Paradigmatic of the type of "unreasonable" action giving rise to the popular perception of lawyers would be the insertion, by counsel for the airline, of the following facially innocuous lease provision: "The lessee may re-register the aircraft only in a "permitted country.' For this purpose, "permitted country' means a country that has signed the Convention on the International Recognition of Rights in Aircraft."This provision, on its face, appears appropriate. A lessor would appear to have a "right" in an aircraft under the lease. A superficial understanding of the proposal would lull counsel to the debt or equity participants into eliding the full import of the provision. However, the value of rights under a convention is ephemeral if the rights cannot be practicably realized in the country in question. For example, acountry, such as Iraq,could be a signatory, but the convention may not afford the lessor the rights that it anticipated. Additionally, the existence of the rights does not ameliorate any risk of destruction of the aircraft.
Of course, the parties could expressly and knowingly agree that the airline would be permitted to relocate and re-register the aircraft in Iraq. But one suspects such an agreement would not be reached were the parties to negotiate explicitly about the matter.
For U.S. carriers and debt and equity participants, it seems highly likely that the "direct" benefit to the airline of having the right to take these acts would be small, relative to the cost to the debt and equity participants of agreeing to a lease that gives the airline that right.The proposal of a contract term that appears innocuous but has a latent impact that would not have been agreed upon had the negotiations addressed the issue more directly, is a form of negotiation that provides one basis on which lawyers can be categorized as unreasonable. This type of negotiation tactic - providing the latent allocation of rights and duties - is common and persistent,and one reason patterns of commercial behavior persist is that they are efficient. The persistence of this type of negotiation may indicate that it provides benefits that are not obvious.Perhaps this manner of negotiation increases the aggregate value to the parties of the transaction being negotiated in some indirect fashion.
This type of negotiation strategy could also persist merely becauseit results in the allocation to one party of a greater share of the transaction's aggregate value, an amount sufficient to compensate that party for a decrease in the aggregate value of the transaction as a whole. Or, more colloquially, the portion of the pie (representing the aggregate transaction value) taken by the party who benefits from that negotiation strategy increases, even if the total size of the pie is diminished.
A third possible rationale for the persistence of this negotiation strategy could be the presence of unreasonable lawyers as an artifact of path dependence.That is, even if the use of unreasonable lawyers would not be efficient if one could unilaterally impose an alternative on the relevant community, the manner in which transactional practice has developed could prevent a transition to a more efficient alternative.
If this type of negotiation were always inefficient, one would expect reputational factors to permit the achievement of a more efficient outcome. This outcome should occur particularly in the largest commercial transactions involving the best known law firms in large cities. In these transactions, the frequency of interaction should facilitate dissemination of reputations. Of course, it is not obvious that reputational factors could eliminate all substantially inefficient bargaining strategies. Opportunism may persist if there is an insufficient number of interactions to permit reputations to be adequately formed or if mechanisms to propagate reputations are inadequate.
In summary, although the persistence of a negotiation strategy that proposes latent contractual terms that would not necessarily have been agreed upon otherwise raises the question of whether it is efficient, its persistence does not conclusively demonstrate that it is. This Article argues that contractual relationships created by this negotiation strategy can be efficient based on the concept of a"hostage" developed by Oliver E. Williamson.Williamson argues that opportunistic behavior by one party to a contractual relationship can be reduced through a "credible commitment" effected by the delivery of a hostage.Part I briefly outlines the use of hostages in contractual relationships. This Part reviews the value provided by hostages and presents alternative solutions to opportunism, such as the use of vague contractual undertakings.
One limitation of the use of hostages to restrain opportunism is that the context of a transaction may not provide an obvious hostage. Part II examines how lawyers create hostages in the form of unreasonable contractual rights that limit future opportunistic behavior. One criterion a hostage must meet, if it is to be efficacious, is the hostage must have little value to the hostage-holder other than deterrence of the other party's opportunism.If the holder of a hostage can gain value by diverting the hostage to its own use, the delivery of that hostage may reduce opportunism by the delivering party, only to increase opportunism by the party taking the hostage. Ultimately, that resolution would not provide a solution to potential opportunism, thereby eliminating the benefit derived from such an exchange. This Part argues that contract provisions that may appear to be unreasonable are, in fact, well suited to performing the function of a hostage.
Part II additionally reviews the mechanics by which commercial transactions are negotiated, noting that there are costs arising from the negotiation of hostages. These costs can arise where the taking of a hostage sends a false signal to the other party, indicating uncooperative behavior or mistrust. These signals may prevent contract formation or may otherwise increase the costs of contracting. This Part proposes taking a "hidden" contractual right (or hostage) - taking a hostage from a party who is not aware that it has provided a hostage.Such actions may avoid the increased negotiation costs that result from the negotiation of hostages.
Parts III, IV and V examine implications of this negotiation strategy. Part III reviews the impact of this strategy on lawyers' reputations. This Part argues that one consequence of the adoption ofnegotiation strategies involving the acquisition of hidden contractual hostages is a negative accretion in lawyers' reputations.
Part IV reviews selected principles of contract law and their impact on the ability to create hidden contractual rights.If the creation of hidden contractual hostages can increase transaction value, that fact has implications on the selection of contract construction rules.
As discussed in Part IV, certain principles of contract construction, and certain defenses to the enforcement of a contract, limit the ability of lawyers to seize hidden contractual hostages. These principles and defenses not only limit the ability of transactional lawyers who identify risks to allocate these risks by contract but also decrease the incentive for a lawyer to identify contingent risks during contract negotiations. Part V examines the implications of this decreased incentive on lawyer conduct.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent lawyers' insertion of latent or hidden contractual rights (so-called 'hostages') can credibly deter opportunistic behavior and thereby increase the aggregate efficiency or value of commercial transactions.
Whether the use of hidden contractual hostages generates reputational and negotiation costs (for lawyers and parties) that offset any efficiency gains from reduced opportunism.

How rules and doctrines governing contract interpretation and enforceability affect the ability of parties to create and rely on hidden contractual hostages, and how those rules in turn shape lawyers' incentives to identify and allocate contingent risks in transaction drafting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45iowajcorpl885!!ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Braided Agreements and New Frontiers for Relational Contract Theory

shared_topics.topic: use of formal contractual provisions as commitment devices to restrain opportunism in complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how explicit formal provisions (as part of 'braided' agreements) create information routines and lock parties into relationships to mitigate cheating and support joint investment; Paper B argues that lawyers draft seemingly unreasonable or hidden contractual ‘hostages’ to credibly commit parties, reduce opportunism, and thereby affect the allocation of transactional value.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal contracts and informal governance (complements vs substitutes)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the braiding thesis that formal and informal governance can complement one another in collaborative production, while Paper B examines how parties and counsel strategically choose concealed formal terms to avoid the costs of bargaining over informal signals, suggesting a strategic substitution or complementarity between formal clauses and reputational/relational mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: reputation, repeated interaction, and path dependence as limits on or substitutes for formal mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly invokes ongoing relationships and future-deal threats as informal sanctions relevant to whether parties rely on braiding, and explores when markets use alternative governance tools; Paper B analyzes how reputational dynamics and path dependence shape the persistence or elimination of aggressive negotiation tactics and the incentives lawyers have to surface contingent risks.

shared_topics.topic: negotiation process and institutional design as determinants of transactional governance and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies procedural innovations like DoD 'alpha contracting'—joint preliminary negotiation structures and committee oversight—as governance choices that foster trust and joint learning, while Paper B focuses on micro-level negotiation strategies (hidden hostages) and the signaling/transaction-cost consequences of how lawyers design and negotiate terms.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law doctrines and judicial intervention shape parties' incentives to design governance structures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the normative stakes of whether courts should intervene (crowding out or supporting informal institutions) and situates braiding within contract interpretation theory, while Paper B examines how principles of contract construction and enforceability limits affect the feasibility of hidden hostages and alter lawyer incentives to identify and allocate contingent risks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95valrev1437!!ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INTENT TO CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: interpretive/default rules that determine whether parties are legally bound
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an analytic framework comparing enforcement vs nonenforcement defaults and express-opt-out rules for assessing parties' intent to be legally bound; Paper B examines how contract-construction principles and defenses affect the ability of lawyers to create latent rights or 'hostages,' i.e., how judicial interpretive rules shape which written provisions become enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: economic/transaction-cost analysis of contract doctrines (efficiency, incentives, reputations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates intent-to-contract rules using economic ideas about incentives, sticky defaults, and the tradeoffs between duty-imposing and power-conferring functions; Paper B uses Williamsonian transaction-cost reasoning to justify otherwise 'unreasonable' drafting tactics, and analyzes reputational and incentive consequences for lawyers and parties.

shared_topics.topic: negotiation strategies, signaling, and relational costs of making obligations explicit
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the relational and informational costs of requiring parties to expressly opt out or opt in to legal enforcement and how those costs affect default stickiness; Paper B studies negotiation tactics that hide or obscure rights (hidden hostages) to avoid costly signaling and shows how those tactics alter bargaining dynamics and relational trust.

shared_topics.topic: latent/hidden contractual terms (hostages) and the enforceability of preliminary or unspoken allocations of risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses enforcement of preliminary agreements and when parties must say they intend to be bound, criticizing tests that allow latent obligations; Paper B analyzes how lawyers create and exploit latent contractual rights as hostages, and how doctrines of contract construction and defenses either enable or restrict such hidden allocations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nyulrev1023!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT

shared_topics.topic: the use of hidden or latent contractual provisions ("hostages") as a tool of contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of lawyers inserting facially innocuous but substantively latent rights as ‘hostages’ that deter opportunism and can increase (or redistribute) transaction value; Paper B treats parties' choice of precise rules versus standards and the deliberate selection of enforcement means as a way to design contracts ex ante, including reliance on formal terms that may operate as deliberate commitments rather than expressions of ends.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicative doctrines and contract interpretation affect parties' drafting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract construction rules and defenses limit the ability to create and enforce hidden hostages and thus shape lawyers' incentives to identify and allocate contingent risks; Paper B argues that equitable override of formal doctrine undermines parties' ability to choose precise contractual means and thus distorts contract design incentives.
