shared_topics.topic: whether and how contract law should incorporate moral or normative content (e.g., good faith, promise theory) that governs personal conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrines and contractual clauses (like morals clauses and lifestyle covenants) that let private agreements intrude on personal autonomy and privacy, and Paper B directly addresses the inclusion of normative concepts in contract law (promise theory, good faith, reasonableness), questioning whether norm-laden rules help or hinder law's ability to guide conduct.

papers.node_id: 16tourolrev1037!!COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?
papers.title: COMMON SENSE AND CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM: Common Sense and Contract Law: Fear of a Normative Planet?
papers.abstract:
I.HILL V. GATEWAYAND COMMON SENSE
The topic of this symposium, the role of "common sense" in contract law, was inspired by a rhetorical question posed by the Seventh Circuit inHill v. Gateway 2000:"Where's the sense in that?" The argument that contract law should follow "common sense" seems rather innocuous, but it often provides rhetorical cover for unspoken normative assumptions. This observation is not meant to imply that contract law should, or can, be free of normative baggage. Rather, I would simply suggest we pay more attention to the role that normative assumptions play in contract law.
Gatewaywas a class action suit customers brought against a personal computer seller. According to the court, the nominal plaintiffs, Rich and Enza Hill,responded to a printed advertisement by ordering a home computer by telephone from Gateway 2000. When they received the computer, the shipping box also contained a form stating additional terms not discussedover the phone. These terms included a clause requiring disputes regarding the purchase to be submitted to arbitration. According to the form, buyers were bound by these terms unless they returned the computer within 30 days. The Hills stated that they noticed the form, but did not read it carefully enough to notice the arbitration clause.
The Hills did not return the computer. After more than 30 days had passed, they complained to Gateway about the computer's performance and alleged that its components did not match those advertised. When Gateway did not respond to their satisfaction, the Hills filed suit. Gateway sought, and ultimately obtained, enforcement of the arbitration clause. According to the Seventh Circuit,the Hills became bound by the arbitration clause by failing to return the computer within 30 days.
The Seventh Circuit'sGatewayopinion relies on the idea of "common sense" in at least two different ways. First, it suggests that the Hills lacked common sense if they failed to understand that their telephone conversation did not embody all the terms of their contract with Gateway. A standard, traditional application of contract law would characterize the phone call as the formation of a sales contract, and the shipment of the computer as performance of that contract. Under this view, when the phone conversation ended, it was too late for either party to unilaterally add or change the terms of the contract.According to the court, however, "Although this is one way a contract could be formed, it is not the only way."Following an earlier Seventh Circuit case,ProCD v. Zeidenberg,the court argued that in a consumer purchase, the vendor is the offeror, who makes an offer by tendering the product. As "master of the offer," Gateway could impose any conditions of acceptance, including the accept-or-return condition.
Of course, this theory would fail if a contract of sale had already been formed over the phone.The court attempts to show that the Hills knew that the telephone conversation did not constitute a contract. Of course, it does not argue that the Hills were familiar with theProCDrule. Nonetheless, according to the court, "the Hillsknewbefore they ordered the computer that the carton would contain some important terms, and they did not seek to discover these in advance."The court apparently does not mean that the Hillsactuallyknew this, but rather that theyshould haveinferred it from Gateway's advertisement. Why, according to the court, should the Hills have inferred this? Because, according to the court, "Gateway's ads state that their products come withlimited warranties and lifetime support."Apparently, however, the ads, like the telephone agent, did notmention arbitration. The court seems to suggest that because Gateway's ads mention warranties and product support, the Hills should have surmised that their purchase could be subject to any number of other additional terms not mentioned in the ads or by the telephone agent. It was up to the Hills to ask the agent about undisclosed terms.
, the court argues that the law must make "sense," by which it means something very specific: legal rules must maximize wealth. The Hills argued thatProCDshould be restricted to contracts involving software, but the court scoffed, "where's the sense in that?"According to the court, disclosing the terms over the phone would be costly to vendors and would bore and discourage customers, thus harming both classes.The court implies that contract formation and terms are based on whether they make "sense" and not on whether they are actually assented to; and, further, that the Hills, as reasonable buyers, should have known this. There is no finding that the Hills actually knew that efficiency required the telephone clerks to omit important terms, that they knew that a judicial analysis of contract formation would rely on a principle of wealth maximization rather than on the Hills' own manifestations of assent, or that the Hills based their contracting choices on long-term wealth maximization rather than on short-term rent-seeking considerations.
TheGatewaycourt posits a model of "sensible" human behavior. The court evaluates the reasonableness of both the conduct and contractual expectations of the parties against this model.Gateway's expectations accorded with common sense, while the Hills harbored deviant expectations; thus it is only natural that Gateway wins and the Hills lose. That is, according to the court, the law's presumptions about contractual expectations reflect not only the result favored by the law, but also the natural tendency of most people.
One problem with this approach is that judges' models of baseline human behavior are colored by their personal experience and ideological leanings. Doesn't everyone know that a vendor taking phone orders can't be bothered to disclose all the terms of sale? On the other hand, doesn't everyone know that when I agree to buy something over the phone, I agree only to the terms discussed in the phone call? Legal doctrine has no methods of its own for describing and modeling human behavior and expectations.
Hill v. Gateway, of course, follows the influential Seventh Circuit practice of importing the model of the "rational person" from neoclassical economics. The neoclassical law and economics approach assumes as a descriptive matter that the process of self-interested bargaining yields efficient outcomes.Hence, it suggests that the efficiency of terms is itself evidence that most parties would have assented to them. One reason theHills "knew" that additional terms would be in the box was that, according to the court, such was the more efficient practice. Thus it is unnecessary to examine assent directly. Because freedom of contract results in efficient terms, efficiency and assent are effectively collapsed into a single inquiry.
The rational behavior hypothesis is often criticized for being overly simplistic, and for lacking empirical basis. In this symposium, Professor Ledwon argues that in application, the description of the "rational person" suffers from a "failure of imagination" -- that the describer tends to describe him or herself. Professor Ghosh claims that the rational behavior hypothesis suffers, rather, from an overabundance of imagination, in that it describes a world too unlike the one in which we actually live. The participants in this symposium suggest (among other things) that other nonlegal disciplines can assist the law in building more nuanced and empirically accurate models of human behavior.

questions.question: Whether courts' appeal to "common sense" in contract disputes substitutes unspoken normative assumptions (such as efficiency or rational-actor models) for actual evidence of parties' assent when determining contract formation and terms.
Whether treating economically efficient terms or the rational-actor model as proxies for mutual assent yields outcomes that accurately predict parties' real expectations and behavior in contracting.

Whether judges' personal experiences and ideological perspectives shape the baseline models of human behavior they apply in contract adjudication, and whether those judicial models empirically match how consumers and sellers actually form expectations and consent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: when and how courts may infer assent from conduct or silence (formation by performance/omission)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Hill v. Gateway and ProCD, critiquing courts that infer assent (e.g., accept-or-return or failure-to-return) from a buyer's silence or conduct; Paper B analyzes U.C.C. §2-207 and §2-207(3) formation-by-performance rules, exploring when performance counts as acceptance and how courts treat conduct as assent.

shared_topics.topic: the enforcement and normative implications of boilerplate/standard-form terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on vendor-drafted boilerplate (e.g., arbitration clauses shipped in a box) and how invoking 'common sense' rationalizes enforcing such terms, while Paper B studies the battle-of-the-forms problem—how conflicting boilerplate between merchants is resolved—and empirically examines parties' behavior toward standard terms.

shared_topics.topic: the fit between doctrinal default rules and actual commercial behavior (doctrine vs practice)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes judicial reliance on doctrinal presumptions tied to efficiency and a rational-agent model that may not reflect real consumers, and Paper B empirically tests common scholarly assumptions about §2-207 by interviewing practitioners to see how the statute operates in practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of economic/efficiency reasoning and behavioral assumptions in shaping contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the Seventh Circuit's law-and-economics justifications (wealth-maximization, rational person) for treating certain practices as 'common sense,' and Paper B considers how legal rules like §2-207 interact with market incentives and practitioners' expectations, assessing whether legal incentives align with commercial realities.

shared_topics.topic: effects of market practices and technology on contract formation and term allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes the court's efficiency rationale about disclosure costs and customers' attention as drivers of doctrinal outcomes, while Paper B explicitly studies technological change and market consolidation (e.g., mega-retailers) to determine how such shifts alter the prevalence and resolution of form-exchange disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between doctrinal rules and real contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts that invoke a vague notion of 'common sense' to treat consumer behavior as conforming to doctrinal presumptions (e.g., inferring assent from failure to return goods), while Paper B documents how real-world parties routinely combine formal and informal practices (braiding) that doctrinal categories fail to describe or predict.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of economic or rational-actor models to justify contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Seventh Circuit's use of a neoclassical, efficiency-based 'rational person' model to justify enforcing undisclosed terms, and Paper B interrogates how contract theory and experiments adopt rational/informational assumptions when modeling when formal enforcement will crowd out or complement informal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of information flows and notice to formation, governance, and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on notice (the buyer seeing but not reading terms in the box) and questions whether courts can impute constructive knowledge, whereas Paper B treats structured information exchanges as the core mechanism by which formal contract terms 'braid' with informal sanctions to build trust and enable cooperation under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial enforcement choices shape contracting practices (including risks of over- or under-enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how a court's doctrinal framing (treating efficiency as dispositive) changes which practices are treated as legitimate and hence encourages vendor strategies, and Paper B analyzes how courts' willingness to impose 'low-powered' versus strong formal remedies can either support braided contracting or inadvertently crowd out informal governance.

shared_topics.topic: what counts as assent, commitment, or enforceable obligation in environments of uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether inferred expectations of 'reasonable' buyers can substitute for manifested assent to contract terms, while Paper B explores how parties create enforceable commitment regimes through partially formalized information duties that sustain informal obligations despite uncertainty about substantive outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113nwulrev1009!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT GOVERNANCE IN SMALL-WORLD NETWORKS: THE CASE OF THE MAGHRIBI TRADERS

shared_topics.topic: private ordering versus public legal enforcement as primary contract governance mechanism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether Maghribi traders relied primarily on private-order institutions (network-based reputation and implicit contracts) rather than courts to sustain long-distance trade, while Paper B examines how courts treat vendor-drafted private terms (and whether judicial enforcement should defer to such private ordering), engaging the tension between private contracting practices and public legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: information transmission, notice, and reputation in contract formation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how small-world network structures and information nodes could circulate reputational information widely enough to make multilateral reputation-based enforcement feasible, and Paper B focuses on notice and informational dynamics (whether buyers knew or should have known about undisclosed terms), with courts inferring knowledge or relying on presumed information costs.

shared_topics.topic: use of behavioral and normative models (rational actor / 'common sense') to justify contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on behavioral implications of network ties and cooperative equilibria to explain how private ordering can work, whereas Paper B critiques courts' invocation of 'common sense' and the neoclassical rational-actor model as normative/descriptive bases for resolving contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency as a justificatory principle for contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes economic forces (efficiency, innovation incentives) that give rise to small-world trading ties and argues private ordering can complement legal institutions for efficient exchange, while Paper B documents and criticizes courts' explicit reliance on wealth-maximization or efficiency arguments to validate enforcement of vendor-imposed contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: role of social norms, identity, and cultural practices in shaping contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes culture, collective identity, and implicit norms (e.g., coalition membership rules) as foundations for contract governance among Maghribi merchants, and Paper B explores how judges' appeals to shared expectations or 'common sense' social norms affect findings about assent, reasonableness, and the content of contractual obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44lawsocyrev299!!ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the role of social norms and 'common sense' in shaping contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a widespread social default (dollarization) that structured real estate pricing regardless of individual pecuniary incentives, while Paper B analyzes how courts invoke 'common sense' to justify doctrinal rules and thereby import prevailing social expectations into contract law.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the neoclassical/rational‑actor model for explaining contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that traditional economic indexing and efficiency models fail to fully explain why parties used dollar pricing, and Paper B critiques courts' reliance on a neoclassical 'rational person' model as descriptively and normatively inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between law (statute/judicial doctrine) and contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how Israeli legislation attempted (with limited immediate effect) to change the dollarization norm in real estate contracts, and Paper B shows how judicial doctrines (invoking common sense) actively shape which contractual expectations are enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of behavioral science and cognitive biases to contract formation and design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on cognitive psychology to explain inertia and biased decision‑making in contracting around dollar clauses, while Paper B calls for incorporating insights from nonlegal disciplines to build more accurate models of how real people form and understand contracts.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical and qualitative methods to study real‑world contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a qualitative case study of microlevel contracting behavior in Israel, and Paper B emphasizes the need for empirical, interdisciplinary methods (beyond doctrinal reasoning) to ground assumptions about human behavior in contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44lawsocyrev299!!ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Old Habits Are Hard to Change: A Case Study of Israeli Real Estate Contracts

shared_topics.topic: role of social norms/common‑sense practices in shaping contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a long‑standing Israeli norm of pricing real estate in US dollars and analyzes how that social practice structured contracting choices; Paper B critiques courts' reliance on a nebulous notion of 'common sense' about what contracting parties should expect and shows how those shared expectations influence doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the neoclassical/rational‑actor account of contracting and the need for behavioral explanations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that traditional economic indexing and risk‑allocation models cannot fully explain dollarization and invokes cognitive psychology to account for sticky contract terms; Paper B challenges the law‑and‑economics assumption that efficiency equals assent, arguing judges rely on an idealized rational actor and urging more realistic behavioral models.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between law (judicial or legislative) and prevailing contracting norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Israeli legislation attempted to unseat the dollarization norm and how legal intervention interacted with entrenched market practices; Paper B analyzes how judicial decisions (e.g., Hill v. Gateway) actively shape contract doctrine by embedding normative presumptions about ordinary contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: value of interdisciplinary empirical and qualitative methods to study contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs a qualitative case study and draws on sociology and cognitive psychology to explain microlevel contracting choices; Paper B calls for empirical realism and insights from nonlegal disciplines to correct judges' and scholars' simplistic assumptions about how people form and understand contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85neblrev875!!ARTICLE: Avoiding Economic Waste in Contract Damages: Myths, Misunderstanding, and Malcontent
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Avoiding Economic Waste in Contract Damages: Myths, Misunderstanding, and Malcontent

shared_topics.topic: critique of law-and-economics reasoning in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers scrutinize courts' reliance on economic reasoning—Paper A critiques the Seventh Circuit's use of a neoclassical 'rational person'/efficiency model to infer assent in Hill v. Gateway, while Paper B criticizes judges' theoretical ignorance and misapplication of microeconomic concepts in the 'economic waste' doctrine governing contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: conflict between actual party assent/intent and judicially imposed economic norms
shared_topics.justification: Both works address situations where courts substitute efficiency-driven norms for the parties' manifested bargains—Paper A shows courts treating efficiency as evidence of assent (rather than relying on actual manifestations), and Paper B shows courts upsetting contracted-for expectation interests by refusing cost-of-performance damages to avoid perceived economic waste.

shared_topics.topic: need for richer behavioral and economic models to guide doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both call for better modeling of contracting behavior—Paper A urges incorporation of empirical, interdisciplinary (behavioral) insights beyond simplistic rational-agent assumptions, and Paper B applies microeconomic and game-theoretic analysis to demonstrate how courts should more accurately predict parties' strategic behavior and remedial incentives.

shared_topics.topic: judicial application of doctrine producing perverse or inefficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers document that current judicial doctrines can generate undesirable results—Paper A argues that invoking 'common sense'/efficiency can legitimise normative biases and misallocate risks, while Paper B argues that using diminution-in-value to avoid 'economic waste' often creates the very inefficiency and windfall the courts seek to prevent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev128!!ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TACIT AGREEMENT AND RELATIONSHIP-SPECIFIC INVESTMENT

shared_topics.topic: courts inferring assent / tacit agreement from silence or conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the 'tacit agreement' test and how courts infer that silent contracts incorporate consequential-damages liability (or not) based on the transaction's context; Paper B examines Hill v. Gateway and ProCD, criticizing courts that infer assent to undisclosed terms from consumer conduct or silence.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/efficiency reasoning to justify doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates consequential-damages defaults within law-and-economics accounts (majoritarian preferences, transaction-costs, holdup) to explain when parties would accept or opt out of liability; Paper B critiques courts' appeals to 'common sense' grounded in neoclassical economic efficiency as a basis for enforcing terms and imputing expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules and silence affect parties' incentives to invest and contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how default liability for consequential damages influences relationship-specific investments and can mitigate or worsen holdup, producing incentives to contract around defaults; Paper B discusses how imposing or implying terms (through accept-or-return rules) changes consumer and vendor behavior by shifting disclosure costs and transactional incentives.

shared_topics.topic: standards of notice/foreseeability ('reason to know') and uncertainty in adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the 'reason to know' / foreseeability standard and its indeterminacy when courts retrospectively assess what parties contemplated; Paper B analyzes judicial standards for what a reasonable buyer should have known or inferred, showing similar concerns about uncertainty and the legitimacy of imputing knowledge or notice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev1475!!ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BARGAINS BICOASTAL: NEW LIGHT ON CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: formalist (rule-based) versus contextual (equity- or fairness-based) approaches to contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques judicial reliance on a single, supposedly 'common sense' model (as in Hill v. Gateway) that treats efficient, rule-like outcomes as dispositive, while Paper B directly contrasts New York's formalist contract jurisprudence with California's more contextual, equity‑oriented approach and analyzes consequences of that divide.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic efficiency / rational‑actor assumptions to justify doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the Seventh Circuit's importation of neoclassical 'rational person' and wealth‑maximization assumptions into contract formation questions, and Paper B builds on contract theory (and empirical contracting choices) that treats efficiency and rational assessment by sophisticated parties as the basis for preferring formal rules.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should treat assent, boilerplate, and standard‑form/post‑formation terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether consumers actually assented to arbitration and other terms found only in shipped boilerplate (accept‑or‑return clauses), questioning doctrinal moves that infer assent; Paper B considers how different interpretive regimes (formalist enforcement of written bargains vs contextual re‑writing) affect the enforcement of negotiated terms and parties' ex ante contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: the informational role of private ordering and market choices in identifying optimal contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts' normative models should be informed by empirical and interdisciplinary descriptions of behavior rather than judges' intuitions, while Paper B uses market evidence (choice‑of‑law/forum clauses and industry dispute practices) to show that private actors' selections reveal a preference for certain doctrinal regimes, treating marketplace behavior as a test of optimal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60ucinlrev405!!SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.topic: application of formal economic models (game theory / law-and-economics) to legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a symposium explicitly about applying game theory to corporate law and practice, and Paper B documents and critiques the Seventh Circuit's reliance on law-and-economics (neoclassical/efficiency) models in contract law (e.g., Gateway), so both engage the project of importing formal economic models into legal analysis.

shared_topics.topic: the descriptive vs. normative role of economic models in judicial decision‑making
shared_topics.justification: Paper A (by focusing on game theory's application to corporate law) and Paper B (by showing how courts invoke 'common sense' that masks normative/efficiency claims) both address how models are used not only to describe behavior but to justify or prescribe legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of the rational‑actor/strategic behavior assumption
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concerns game‑theoretic (strategic, often rational‑actor) accounts of corporate behavior, while Paper B directly interrogates the 'rational person' hypothesis in contract law, critiquing its empirical plausibility and ideological bias—both papers therefore engage the question of whether standard behavioral assumptions fit legal contexts.

shared_topics.topic: how theoretical models influence winners and losers in litigation and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's title/theme ('Just Winners and Losers') foregrounds how game‑theoretic analysis identifies strategic advantage in corporate disputes, and Paper B shows concretely how courts' efficiency/rationality models (as in Hill v. Gateway) determine which parties prevail, so both examine the downstream distributive effects of using such models in law.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE POSSIBILITY OF PLAIN MEANING: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE CONTRACT PRECEDENTS

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of interpretive theories to decide contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts deploy particular theories of interpretation (Paper A: the 'plain meaning' rule and its philosophical premises; Paper B: appeals to 'common sense' and ProCD-style vendor-offer models) to determine contractual terms and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on normative models (e.g., 'common sense' or the rational actor) rather than direct evidence of assent
shared_topics.justification: Paper B criticizes courts for inferring assent from a normative efficiency model and invoking 'common sense' to justify outcomes; Paper A challenges judicial claims that linguistic philosophy makes plain meaning impossible, showing that such normative or philosophical premises can improperly drive doctrinal conclusions.

shared_topics.topic: the relation between textual meaning and parties' intentions/assent
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question whether contract meaning should be equated with the subjective intentions of parties (Paper A rejects the idea that words mean only speakers' thoughts and defends public, conventional meaning; Paper B confronts courts that treat silence or failure to read as evidence of assent and debates whether actual assent or inferred norms should control).

shared_topics.topic: grounding interpretation in social practice or empirical models of behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that plain meaning rests on unreflective, public, conventional language practices rather than abstract referential theories, while Paper B calls for more nuanced, empirically informed models of human behavior (beyond judges' intuitions or neoclassical assumptions) to undergird contract doctrines.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AND THE PROBLEM OF FICKLE PEOPLE

shared_topics.topic: how contract law infers or imputes assent when parties' actual intentions are unobserved or changing

shared_topics.topic: the normative values that justify enforcing contracts (agency/autonomy versus efficiency/wealth maximization)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract and promise doctrines in terms of competing values—supporting agency, revision, and autonomy—whereas Paper B shows how courts rely on 'common sense' and economic efficiency as covert normative assumptions shaping contractual rules.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how the law should accommodate post-formation change of mind, regret, or consumer ignorance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally defends accommodating 'fickleness' and revision across time in contractual relations, and Paper B examines doctrinal outcomes (e.g., accept-or-return, arbitration-in-a-box) that enforce terms despite buyer ignorance or later regret, raising the same question of permissive versus strict enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal doctrines and institutions in mediating private commitments and public enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the moral practice of promising with the institutional role of contract law and surveys doctrines that can accommodate persistent agency, while Paper B analyzes how judicial doctrines and rhetorical invocations of 'common sense' operationalize particular models of contracting within the court system.

shared_topics.topic: use of efficiency (wealth‑maximization) as a justificatory rationale for contract rules

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev629!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY ALMOST EVERYTHING THAT I DID WANT TO KNOW ABOUT CONTRACT LITIGATION: A COMMENT ON GALANTER
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY ALMOST EVERYTHING THAT I DID WANT TO KNOW ABOUT CONTRACT LITIGATION: A COMMENT ON GALANTER
papers.abstract:
Marc Galanter offers an empirical answer to the nasty question: what is contracts about? Those of us who have devoted years to trying to understand the subject should be glad that he finds that there still is some "there" there. Nonetheless, Galanter's story isn't a simple celebration of the virtues of a basic subject. Twenty-seven years ago, he pointed out that parties to litigation are "repeat players" or "one-shotters," and the configuration of the parties mattered.Repeat players have great advantages. Now he divides parties into those litigating "downhill" and those attempting to fight "uphill."Again, the configuration of parties matters.
There is a story about contract law that paints it as a once proud legal area that has fallen on hard times. Grant Gilmore once called me the "Lord High Executioner of the Contract is Dead" movement.He read my 1963 articleas saying that the norms and sanctions inherent in long-term continuing relations left no role for contract law to play. Lawrence Friedman saw contract as the law of leftovers, areas too new or too unimportant to have their own specialized statutes.Those who count cases found contract drying up and becoming less and less of the business of trial and appellate courts.
The serious illness, if not the death, of contract makes sense. Contract law is a flawed product that would seem to breach the warranty of merchantability. It is supposed to put the aggrieved party in position that he or she would have been in had the contract been performed.However, a skeptical survey of contracts remedies should give anyone pause. Specific performance is an exceptional remedy. Damages are limited by doctrines such as mitigation, the contemplation of the parties rule of Hadley v. Baxendale,and proof of damages with reasonable certainty. Liability turns on a bewildering array of qualitative rules: Would a reasonable person have thought that the other party was making an offer?Were the goods such as pass without objection in the trade?A buyer can revoke its acceptance if a defect "substantially impairs its [the goods] value to him."A seller who fails to deliver is excused "if performance as agreed has been made impracticable by the occurrence of a contingency the nonoccurrence of which was a basic assumption on which the contract was made."As is true of all qualitative rules, we can think of clear cases at the extremes but we are left with a wide center filled with neatly matched arguments for both sides. Add to this, the costs of litigation. Under the American rule, each party pays its own lawyers' fees.Suing a firm with which you do business, often means that you will lose your long term relationship with them.One doesn't live amarriage by running to the divorce court to settle disputes. Businesses can solve many contract disputes by negotiated settlements at much less cost. At the very least, the situations left where contract law seems an appropriate tool to resolve business problems are a limited subset of all business disputes.
Yet Galanter finds that after a trough running from about 1930 to 1960, contract made an important comeback. Those of us who read appellate reports in this area can offer a few speculations backed by a little empirical grounding.More and more during the last half of the twentieth century accepted business patterns have been disrupted and provoked contract litigation: War closed the Suez Canal.The Vietnam conflict strained the ability of firms that supplied the military to perform their civilian contracts.The oil producing states formed OPEC to raise prices, and they succeeded in provoking a drastic sudden increase, and this upset the assumptions about costs of those who had made long term bargains.Globalization caused some firms to downsize in the United States, and employees who assumed that they had tenure during good behavior found that they were but employees at will.Technological change produced disruption too. Computers were sold as the solution to all kinds of business and manufacturing problems before the computer manufacturers could make reliable machines.The peaceful atom wasgoing to solve both the problems of energy and environmental protection. The actual construction and operation of nuclear power plants provoked disputes involving large sums of money.These disruptions may have caused the relational glue holding bargains together to come unstuck. Plaintiffs may find contract law flawed, but they had few, if any, other tools. I once analogized attempting to deal with these problems of disrupted contracts through classic contract law as trying to drive nails with a wrench. My colleague Mark Galanter responded: "But it is better than trying to drive nails with a banana." Or to draw another metaphor from the 1960s, when you are left with lemons, make lemonade. Business lawyers went into the lemonade business.
What of Friedman's view of contract as the law of leftovers, areas too new or unimportant to have their own statute?As an account of history, Friedman was right. However, years after he wrote his book, contract law became a powerful tool in the hands of business lawyers for gutting many statutes.During the 1960s and 1970s, Congress and the state legislatures passed many statutes attempting to empower employees who might be the victims of discrimination, consumers who faced conduct on the borders, if not in the middle, of fraud, and franchisees subject to the power of franchisers. The business lawyers' solution? Sneak an arbitration clause into something you could call a contract, create a Kangaroo Court as an arbitration panel located in places as inconvenient as possible, and find sympathetic judges who will sing the praises of ADR while applying the Federal Arbitration Act while ignoring any requirement of communication.The law of leftovers that we saw as a dead rattlesnake turned out to be a very alive one that was only sitting very still while sunning itself.
Despite Gilmore's colorful turn of phrase, my 1963 article never claimed that contract was dead. I noted there: "one uses or threatens to use legal sanctions to settle disputes when other devices will not work and when the gains are thought to outweigh the costs."Situations where legal sanctions seem to make sense are a limited subset of all contract disputes. Writing about contracts that assumes that litigation is the major, usual or typical way to resolve disputes rests on a false assumption. As Galanter has stressed elsewhere, litigation is the form of dispute resolution alternative to the typical ways of dealing with nonperformance.Once we recognize this, we can ask what there is about the cases that go to trial and that are appealed that distinguishes them from the more usual contract problems. My own guess is that if we were able to compare a sample of these cases to those that are handled apart from the formal legal system, we would find those that come to court are close calls. In some, there are plausible doctrinal arguments for both sides. In others, application of the doctrine fights what many would see as common sense. Even cases involving close calls are likely to be settled unless something stands in the way.
Those commenting on papers based on empirical findings have a few conventional tricks. Because all data are flawed, statistics give us only probabilities and are based on assumptions hard to satisfy in dealing with things legal, and findings always can be interpreted several ways, we must brace ourselves for an essay on method.I will try to limit my comments in this area to a simple but important question: When the studies that Galanter assembles and reports talk about "contract," what do they mean? There are indications that some of these studies are talking about something other than the subject of Professor Williston's classic course. Galanter's discussion of punitive damages rests on cases of employment discrimination and consumer protection against fraud and conduct on the borders of fraud. The borders of contract and tort are not fixed and certain.We can only hope that all of the tables comparing therise and fall of contracts and torts classified the cases as one or the other in the same way. It is at least possible that those compiling the data might reach different conclusions. For example, fraud or misrepresentation cases usually involve attempts to overturn contracts. Does the one doing the coding reason that the underlying dispute involves the validity of a contract or does that person decide that fraud is a tort? As I look at all the tables, this doesn't concern me too much. The story is plausible and consistent with what I know from other sources. I view this kind of data as calling for judgment rather than producing results that are clearly and undeniably true.
Galanter's look at the data prompted him to offer concepts with which to interpret it. He divides contract litigation into the "downhill" and the "uphill" sectors, and he finds that it matters which we have. He says:
Cases in the uphill cluster are typically brought by individuals against organizations, are more frequently contested, take considerably longer, and end with fewer plaintiff victories. In contrast, in the much larger downhill cluster, the typical plaintiff is an organization but defendants are split, with a slight preponderance of organizational defendants, defaults are frequent, settlements are somewhat less frequent, disposition comes sooner, trials are quite rare, and plaintiffs have a very high win rate.
I suppose that we would have to add cross-country skiing cases too if we want to stay with the metaphor. Appellate cases teach us that there are atleast a few where firms of roughly equivalent size and skill sue each other.
How does this all fit with Galanter's famous "Haves" article?What is the difference between classifying parties as involved in uphill or downhill litigation or as repeat-players and one-shotters? Certainly the ideas overlap. The employee suing a corporation that formerly employed her is involved in uphill litigation, and the game is very likely to involve a one-shotter suing an institution that has all the advantages of a repeat player. GMAC suing to repossess a Chevrolet is engaged in downhill litigation, and it is a repeat player chasing a one-shotter. While I do not see anything in the data that Galanter presents about the point, my guess is that even if we gave an employee the advantages of a skilled and experienced lawyer and made her more of a repeat player, the downhill nature of the litigation would still mean that it would be risky to bet that she would win.
Galanter compares his empirical picture with that offered by two contracts casebooks.He finds that the casebooks present an unrepresentative sample of the real world of contracts in courts. In the casebooks, emphasis is placed on the uphill sector, and plaintiffs win more often than they do in the courts. Galanter comments: "Thus the student is presented with contracts as an arena in which more often than not David vanquishes Goliath … This is an irresistible scenario."He suggests that a function of the casebook is to reassure students that law embodies a benign balance and create false consciousness.
one of the editors of Galanter's Casebook A, but so is Galanter himself.There is something to his charge. As I once put it: "we want to believe that a lawyer, armed only with reason, can champion the weak and overcome the powerful. This myth drew many of us to law school, and it is hard to give up."I love to teach Steiner v. Mobil Oil,where two solo practitioners beat what was at the time a large law firm, and a retail gasoline dealer bests a major multinational. Contracts: Law in Action (Casebook A) points this out in a footnote at the beginning of the case. Furthermore, we do reprint victories of consumers, smallfranchisees, and employees at will. Nonetheless, I doubt whether any student reading the casebook with any care would conclude that there is a benign balance. For example, employment at will is an important contracts problem. We offer the history of the change from an employer's right to fire for good, bad, or no reason to the limitations imposed by the California courts in the 1970s.Those California decisions would be counted as uphill cases where the plaintiff won. But we emphasize the counterrevolution that began when Chief Justice Rose Bird and two of her colleagues were voted off the California court.We stress that the hill is steeper and harder to climb. Much the same can be said about the consumer protection cases that we offer. Those from the era of Ralph Nader and the consumer movement find plaintiffs successfully climbing the mountain.More recent decisions that we give students in a supplement involve plaintiffs attacking rent-to-own with hidden high interest rates.These plaintiffs tend to lose. The book over and over stresses cost barriers to litigation.Nonetheless, a new edition of the book will offer a much more qualified view of the possibilities of individuals confronting power in the contracts area.
Galanter tells us that contract is far more written about in academic journals than litigated in courts. After a relatively dry period, it is now difficult to keep up with all the writing relating to contracts.Have the courts turned to a more conservative kind of new formalism and retreated from the sort of judging in the grand style advocated by Llewellyn?Can courts do what Llewellyn in article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code directed them to do or do we face a capability problem?Candefault rules encourage contracting parties to do the right thing?To what extent can we claim that contract still rests on choice? To what extent is contract but a set of symbols to legitimate the statutes of a private government imposed on those that buy from them?As has been true for almost the entire second half of the twentieth century, most of this literature rests on assumptions about contracts and contracting parties rather than data. For example, there seems to be no end to articles about efficient breach. Yet the writers seldom, if ever, ask whether one wanting to get out of a contract will offer the sum that would make the breach efficient. When Juan Ignacio Lopez became the purchasing agent for General Motors, he demanded that all suppliers cut their prices by 20%.This may have breached many contracts; it certainly violated the expectations of the suppliers. Lopez did not offer to pay these suppliers for their lost anticipated profits. He gave them the choice of remaining as GM suppliers or tangling with GM's lawyers in protracted litigation. His goal was not an efficient breach. Had any of the suppliers sued, they would be engaged in trying to climb uphill, and the assault on this summit would not have been easy.I find little concern with this reality in the scholarly literature.It is messy and complicates elegant theories.
Galanter concludes: "In spite of the demise of classical contract doctrine, the decline of debt litigation, the spinoffs of specialized fields, and the proliferation of non-litigative controls contract remains one of themainstays of the litigation area."By making this case so clearly, he has done a real service for those who study contracts. At the same time, his article should provoke a reexamination of what is being litigated in this area and by whom. Moreover, his data supports our sense that the area is extremely political in a number of senses of that term. Seldom will those who must battle uphill find it a fair fight.If they were to win too often, something would change to ward off their claims.And all this benefits some and disadvantages others. The impact is not random.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev379!!SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior interacting with bounded rationality and sunk costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how opportunism combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs can justify courts implying terms or creating defaults to deter strategic behavior; Paper B documents how strategic advantage (e.g., repeat players, downhill plaintiffs) and opportunistic tactics shape which contract disputes reach litigation and their outcomes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between background/default rules (e.g., UCC defaults, irrevocability of unilateral offers) and after-the-fact implication of terms and asks when each form of intervention is justified; Paper B likewise interrogates whether courts and doctrine (including default frameworks) or private ordering best resolve contract problems, observing how doctrinal shifts affect real-world contracting and litigation patterns.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries between parties (repeat-players, one-shotters, uphill/downhill dynamics)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses information asymmetries and enforcement capacity that make some parties vulnerable to opportunism and thus potentially justify intervention; Paper B empirically analyzes repeat-player vs one-shotter and uphill vs downhill configurations, showing how relative power and experience predict litigation success and access to remedies.

shared_topics.topic: indeterminacy of doctrinal standards and the consequences for consent and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about vague all-things-considered utilitarian standards and doctrines like promissory estoppel producing uncertain liability that may impinge on 'freedom from contract'; Paper B emphasizes the prevalence of qualitative, hard-to-predict rules in contract law and how that uncertainty shapes which disputes are litigated and how they resolve.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, litigation costs, and reliance on private ordering instead of courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that high individual contracting costs and shared problems of opportunism can make law-imposed defaults more efficient than bespoke contracting; Paper B highlights the high costs of litigation and the tendency of parties to resolve most contract disputes through negotiation, settlement, or other nonlitigious mechanisms rather than in court.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:The ALI and the UCC

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the growing role of statutes and regulatory schemes (and how contracts and arbitration clauses have been used to displace statutory protections), while Paper B directly frames the debate over whether commercial law should be statutory (the UCC/Articles) or left to common-law evolution and the ALI's Restatement-style approach.

shared_topics.topic: institutional power, participation, and how access shapes outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes asymmetries in litigation (repeat players vs one‑shotters; uphill vs downhill plaintiffs) and how costs and institutional advantages bias outcomes, while Paper B examines who participates in shaping commercial law (ALI vs NCCUSL, consumer representation, elite membership) and how participation and resource barriers affect law reform decisions.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy, default rules, and the use of contracts to sidestep protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how business actors use contract drafting (e.g., arbitration clauses) and default rules to circumvent statutory protections and how default rules influence bargaining, while Paper B raises the normative and doctrinal questions of how much freedom parties should have (choice‑of‑law clauses, limits on contracting away protections) and whether default rules should be more protective.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Remedies and Alternative Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that specific performance is an exceptional remedy and that damages doctrines (mitigation, Hadley, certainty) significantly limit relief in contract litigation; Paper B centers on which remedial rule (damages valuation or specific performance baseline) courts should use when a promisor breaches an alternative-performance contract and ultimately proposes using the mode that would be chosen under specific performance to set compensatory damages.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic or "efficient" breach and promisor incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes scholarly reliance on efficient-breach models and highlights real-world cases where powerful parties opportunistically force renegotiation without paying compensation; Paper B analyzes how prevailing remedial rules can facilitate Pareto-inferior opportunistic breaches and develops a remedial rule intended to deter such opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries, strategic behavior, and information asymmetries between parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses uphill/downhill litigation and repeat-player vs one-shotter dynamics that create unequal bargaining and litigation outcomes; Paper B explicitly models informational asymmetries and strategic selection of performance modes by the promisor as central problems that any remedial rule must address.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal fragmentation and the role of courts versus private ordering/alternative dispute mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents variation in what gets litigated, courts' doctrinal complexities, and the growth of arbitration and private governance as alternatives to litigation; Paper B surveys divergent common-law (and civil-law) remedial rules across jurisdictions, critiques courts' inconsistent handling of alternative-contract cases, and assesses whether courts can or should adopt a uniform remedial principle.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Corporations and Autonomy Theories of Contract: A Critique of the New Lex Mercatoria

shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges using empirical data to reexamine what is actually litigated and criticizes reliance on elegant but unrealistic theoretical assumptions; Paper B argues for integrating autonomy and welfare/efficiency theories rather than dismissing one, insisting theory-building must be sensitive to the empirical/legal conception of the corporation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Lexical Opportunism and the Limits of Contract Theory*

shared_topics.topic: expectation damages as an incentive device versus their practical efficacy

shared_topics.topic: the gap between doctrinal 'lore' and empirical/practical reality of contract litigation

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights doctrines (Hadley v. papers.node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
papers.abstract:
"Reality-based" television is the latest fad to have worked its way into our national consciousness. It began with the "Real World," a successful show on MTV, and has been followed by newer versions such as "Big Brother," "Survivor," "Survivor 2," and (inevitably) "Temptation Island." These shows purport to show "real" human beings solving the kinds of real problems that confront all of us. But "Real World" is an ironic title: while these shows are marketed to be more "real" than a sitcom or movie, they are anything but "real." They involve strangers carefully selected and brought together by a producer to live with one another in an unnatural (or unusual) environment surrounded by TV cameras. Can we learn anything truly reflective of the human condition from these little dramas? Given the artificial and unnatural setting into which the individuals have been dropped, one must be extremely skeptical.
We encounter a similar problem when we attempt to project normative recommendations about the shape of the law using man-made models of citizen behavior. Such efforts usually involve an author's construct of the contracting environment and projection from that model the rules she contends would improve the "real world" of contract law. Inevitably the models will be "off" to one degree or another and the contended-for rules will thus be "off" as well. Since modeling is probably an essential tool for making useful comments about law, the question is not whether the model is "off" - it always is; rather the question is how far off is the model from the phenomena it is supposed to model.
In contracts, the focus of this Symposium, the theorist's job is harder today than it used to be because the modern, real world of contracting is understood to be far more complex than it was in earlier years. Beginning in the late 1950s, empirical studies have hinted at this complexity and confirmed a serious mismatch between our relatively simple rules of contract law and the complex environment within which it must operate. There has been a scholarly agenda for many years whose object has been to study and better understand the complex environment so that the rules might be better fitted to work within it.
One of our oldest and most successful commercial statutes, article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.), is a statute that does not come close to mirroring the complexity of real world contracting. Indeed, its textual simplicity seems to stand in stark contrast with what we know about business contracting. Still, the Code seems to have accommodated business complexity very well. Its drafting began in the 1940s and it has remained largely unchanged since first widely adopted in the early 1960s. Its stability over time may well be due to its open structure which tends to use "standards" instead of "rules"and, perhaps for that reason, tends to hide the very complex demands it makes of those who use it.To the extent article 2 of the U.C.C. has influenced the development of business practice at all,the Code does not seem to have restricted its growth and development.
Recently, there has been a burst of scholarly activity that begins with now-familiar observations of real world complexity, moves in the direction of comparably simple rules, but tentatively advocates far sharper rules for contract law generally and article 2 of the Code in particular. These "Neoformalists"claim that predictability, certainty, and economic efficiency require a simple and more formal approach, not one that masks its complexity through the use of "standards" instead of "rules." Much of the most interesting work focuses on the article 2 rules governing interpretation of contracts.
The normative theories coming from this recent work are complex; some are based on valuable new empirical observations suggesting thatwhole industries prefer a formal interpretive approach to one that is more nuanced. Yet the normative recommendations have a "Back to the Future" quality to them. For example, some have advocated much-reduced roles for trade usageand course of performance evidence in commercial contracts governed by the U.C.C.,and new life for the "plain meaning rule."Most of the approaches have been driven by economic models and an economic-type of analysis asserting that, ultimately, it is better - because it is more efficient - for courts to interpret contracts using a more formal approach and it would be better if our governing law would prompt or compel them to do so.
It seemed useful to review some of this recent literature and its critiques and then consider the implications of bringing these ideas into the "real world" of sales, which tends to be dominated by form contracts, rather than contracts that are actually negotiated, and which is governed by a U.C.C. sales law that functions across an extraordinarily wide range of contract settings. In short, I want to consider how "Neoformalism" might operate in the complex, real world populated by busy lawyers and real business people, and governed by article 2 of the U.C.C.
The discussion will proceed in two Parts. The first will abstractly consider formalism in contract interpretation in an attempt to see why a legislature might wish to increase interpretive formalism through a statute such as the U.C.C. It concludes that, ultimately, legislative decisions should depend on empirical evidence and that the empirical evidence for a move toward more formalism in contract interpretation is lacking. The second Part will consider the implications of bringing a more formal interpretive approach into the U.C.C. regardless of the quality of the reasons for doing so. It will conclude that, however theoretically justified it might be, such a change in the context of the actual operation of the U.C.C. will produce undesirable consequences that outweigh whatever benefits the change might bring.

questions.question: Does adopting a more formal, rule-based approach to contract interpretation (versus a standards-based, context-sensitive approach) produce greater predictability, certainty, and economic efficiency in commercial contracting?
Is there empirical evidence that supports legislative action to increase interpretive formalism in contract law?

What practical effects - including costs and unintended consequences - would imposing more formal interpretive rules have on real-world commercial transactions, particularly those dominated by standardized form contracts and diverse contracting settings?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TEXT AND CONTEXT: CONTRACT INTERPRETATION AS CONTRACT DESIGN

shared_topics.topic: how contracting environment (form contracts, market scale, and uncertainty) should determine interpretive regimes

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical grounding and attention to real-world practices when proposing doctrinal reform

papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
Over the years there has been a great deal of writing about the interpretation of contracts, and appropriately so. What aspect of interpretation is fashionable varies over time. Only a few years ago, gap filling was clearly the fashionable subject. Today interpretation of the words used in a written contract is more fashionable, and that is my topic.
My special focus will be on the role of the jury in the interpretation of written contracts.When writing in an area about which so much has been written over the past century, it is hard to be original. Others have pointed out, as will I, that fear of the jury has helped shape the law in the area of interpretation, with the result that the law often seems confused and inconsistent with some basic contract values.I will point out, as few have, that juries nonetheless decide a great number of contracts cases. I will raise questions about whether shaping legal rules to avoid letting the jury interpret written contracts is essentially futile. If it is futile, then perhaps we should consider abandoning the civil jury. This is the nearly uniform course elsewhere in the world but it is probably not politically feasible here. If not feasible, then I will suggest that perhaps we should learn to live with the jury and give up the confusing and distorting efforts to keep contract interpretation issues from the jury. This, too, I will conclude is not likely to happen. I will then examine some less radical alternatives to improving the confused state of the law, concluding that it is questionable whether they will work. My overall conclusion will be tempered despair - the law is confusing and inconsistent and likely toremain so, but we have survived that way for a long time so maybe the problems generated by confusion and inconsistency are not as great as they might appear.
As with all articles about the interpretation of written contracts, this article will be importantly about the parol evidence rule, and its companion, the plain meaning "rule." But I want to begin at a more general level. A basic principle for distinguishing which issues are appropriate for the jury is the distinction between questions of fact and law. And because the fact/law distinction is also used in defining the scope of appellate review, that issue will be discussed as well.

questions.question: Whether efforts to structure legal rules can effectively prevent juries from resolving the meaning of written contracts, or whether those efforts are futile

Whether the fact/law distinction appropriately allocates interpretive tasks between juries and judges (and thereby shapes appellate review), and how that allocation affects the consistency and outcomes of contract interpretation
