papers.node_id: 42sandiegolrev533!!EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts
papers.title: EDITOR'S SYMPOSIUM:WHAT IS LEGAL INTERPRETATION?A Pluralist Approach to Interpretation: Wills and Contracts
papers.abstract:
. Introduction: Single-Inquiry and Pluralist Accounts of Interpretation
This account of legal interpretation focuses mainly on wills and contracts. It adopts a pluralist approach, one that treats a number of factors as potentially relevant and does not assume that all relevant factors necessarily reduce to one overarching inquiry that is the same whatever legal text is being interpreted.
The major controversy among the participants at the illuminating conference which gave rise to this issue's essays was whether this kind of pluralist approach is defensible or, instead, interpretation of textual meaning in law (and indeed more broadly) reduces itself to a single inquiry. Although this article is primarily designed to explicate particular theoretical questions about the interpretation of wills and contracts, it is also intended to be a defense of a pluralist approach.
Getting a handle on the exact disagreement between single-inquiry theorists and pluralists is not simple; doing so constitutes a crucial first step for evaluating what follows. Proponents of a single-inquiry view typically claim that interpretation of the meaning of a communication reduces to a factual determination about the circumstances of the communication's origin. Larry Alexander, a convener of the conference, has consistentlyadopted a writer's (or speaker's) intent approach,and that was the version of the single-inquiry view that attracted the widest support at the conference from other legal scholars and from literary critics. According to this view, if I mean "shut the door," but I slip and say "shut the window," my communication means "shut the door," however much I mislead listeners. Put differently, the true meaning of what I have said is "shut the door." "Author's intent" theorists do not deny that sentence meaning often diverges from speaker meaning, but they privilege the latter as the real meaning of the communication and the object of interpretation in a strict sense. We can easily imagine a more textualist, listener-reader centered version of the single-inquiry view. The objections I shall suggest to a single-minded author's intent account of meaning apply to a single-minded reader's understanding approach as well.
"Pluralists," among whom I count myself, believe "meaning" is a practical concept, that interpretation to discern meaning is not reducible to a single inquiry. Pluralists believe that the best account of meaning will vary among disciplines and among subfields within disciplines.Exactly how to interpret a writing, exactly how to assign it meaning, will depend on the purposes of engaging in that endeavor, and these purposes may render many factors relevant. When they look at law, pluralists note that judges and scholars consult multiple factors in discerning the meaning of legal texts.
Were this consideration totally decisive, the pluralists would definitely win the day, because no one doubts that judges and other actors ascribe meaning to legal texts on the basis of many factors. But the single-inquiry theorists mount a twofold response. First, judges and lawyers may engage in a plurality of inquiries to decide how a text will apply to a situation,but these efforts can be partly understood as their relying on the answer to one inquiry (say, sentence meaning) as evidence for the answer to another, controlling, inquiry (writer meaning). In practice, the "controlling" inquiry (writer's meaning) might even fade into the background if bars on evidence preclude most of the ways of discerning that meaning apart from sentence meaning.
, insofar as interpreters self-consciously accord independent weight to the results of inquiries other than the focal one, to that degree they are not, whatever they may say, asking about the text's meaning; they are surveying reasons that might incline them to displace that meaning with some alternative. This aspect of their overall evaluation is a different exercise from interpretation in a strict sense (which is to discern meaning). It may be that judges appropriately undertake this different exercise. The single-inquiry theorists do not claim that their conceptualization of meaning and interpretation yields a direct answer to the practical question about how judges should decide legal cases; and these theorists do not even mind if we call this different exercise a form of interpretation. But we must understand that interpretation in the true or strict sense it is not. One way in which this idea was offered at the conference was that interpretation in the strict sense bears no interesting theoretical relation to other exercises in practical decision that are sometimes loosely included within "interpretation" in a broader sense.
Let me say straight out that I think the conceptualization favored by single-inquiry theorists can work. These theorists can provide a strict account of meaning and interpretation that does not do violence to social facts and relevant values. I believe that, without doubt, a pluralist account can also work - a point that most of the single-inquiry theorists at the conference did not concede.
How then should we choose between the two kinds of accounts? Conceptual clarity, present understanding within the discipline, and relation to desirable practice are three obvious criteria.
The single-inquiry approach may seem to have a conceptual advantage over its competitor in sharply delineating various questions of fact and evaluation. But pluralists do not blindly suppose that all aspects of interpretation are the same; they see as clearly as do the single-inquiry theorists that writer's intent is not the same thing as modern reader understanding or coherence with other texts. It is conceivable that the same single-inquiry approach works best for other fields of interpretation, such as literary criticism and religious hermeneutics, and that the desirability of a unifying theory should lead us to adopt that conceptual approach for law. Without undertaking the effort here, I shall simply assert my strong skepticism that across diverse disciplines, the same single inquiry is best understood as the key to interpretation of meanings.
In regard to present understanding within the law of common law systems, the pluralists win hands down. Relatively few judges and scholars talk as if the meaning of legal texts reduces to a single inquiry.
The question about desirable practice is more subtle. The single-inquiry theory contemplates a two (or multi) step approach: figure out meaning and then decide whether to displace it. But what if much judging never undertakes step one, that is, never tries to determine exactly what is a text's meaning according to the crucial single inquiry? That, in fact, is the reality, whatever one takes as the favored single inquiry. (To be more precise, I do not deny that likely writer's intent will often play a role and will sometimes be decisive. I claim only (1) that judges will sometimes resolve what counts as a text's meaning without settling the question of writer's intent, and (2) that proceeding in this manner is desirable.) The single-inquiry theorist has the resources to accommodate this reality about practice, acknowledging that in some legal cases judges may desirably reach a practical resolution without discerning meaning. But, along with present understanding in law, this feature of desirable practice strongly favors the pluralist account as yielding less confusion and greater clarity.
The disagreement over the better conceptualization very likely reflects underlying convictions, agendas, or tastes that are ideological. Although the single-inquiry approach to meaning and (strict) interpretation does not rule out other bases for practical decisions in legal cases, it does seem to cast them in a suspicious light. Who could doubt that judges should interpret statutes to discern meaning? If they displace meaning, are they not indulging themselves in creative disregard of legislative authority? On the other hand, if, as the pluralist account supposes, judges possess a stock of standards of interpretation to determine meaning, when they employ these they seem naturally to be doing what they should. An example I raised during discussion illustrates the rhetorical connection between conceptual theories of meaning and practicalappraisals of judging.
Arizona treats as confidential "any confession made to [a clergyman] in his character as clergyman or priest in the course of discipline enjoined by the church to which he belongs."I assumed (hypothetically) that the law was adopted early in the twentieth century when a number of states had priest-penitent privileges that were quite limited; but that the overwhelming modern view is that the privilege should extend to communications to clergy made in ordinary counseling sessions. For years, let us imagine, Arizona prosecutors have not sought testimony from clerics about what they have learned in counseling; but now a divorce lawyer seeks to require testimony from a minister of the United Church of Christ about what a parishioner-husband said to her in counseling.
The judge first looks at the natural language of the law. "Confession" made in the "course of discipline enjoined" by the church does not seem to cover a husband's admission in marital counseling that he struck his wife, given to a minister of denomination that has no discipline of confession to individual clerics. But, if the church encourages couples with marital difficulties to seek counseling, privileging such an admission is not an extreme stretch of the language. Reflecting both on the fact that the population of Arizona in the early twentieth century was substantially Roman Catholic, and on the narrowness of the priest-penitent privilege as it was then conceived, the judge concludes that the relevant legislators (probably) meant to privilege only formal Roman Catholic confession and perhaps confession in the few other churches (such as the Episcopal Church) that retain individual confession but do not make it mandatory or encourage it strongly.
asserted that many judges in this position, influenced by modern conceptions of clerical privilege and concerned about favoring some religions over others,would now conclude that the language should be taken in a broader, more inclusive (though somewhat strained) sense.
On a pluralist, multifactor understanding, this example shows how the meaning of a law can change over time; the judge's interpretive question is what ingredients should figure in a modern interpretation of the language. For the single-inquiry (author's intent) theorist, meaning was fixed at enactment. The judge who reaches the conclusion that the authors most probably intended a restricted meaning is left only with thequestion whether to displace that meaning. Now, as far as logic is concerned, a pluralist could well contend, "Leave a change like this to the legislature," and a single-inquiry theorist might say, "Let the judge go ahead and displace this meaning instead of imposing a tiresome task on legislators." But readers will not be surprised that most single-inquiry theorists did not look favorably on this exercise in judicial creativity; most pluralists thought that such an interpretation (in their sense) could well be within the bounds of judicial authority. Thus, the conceptual rhetoric connected to practical conclusions in a predictable fashion.
What follows in this essay, excerpts from an introduction and chapters on wills and contracts in a book on legal interpretation on which I am now working, represents a pluralist approach. Most of us who write about legal interpretation think mainly about statutory and constitutional texts and common law principles. Wills and contracts are also legally authoritative texts, ones serving mainly private objectives. Because they do not present the same issues of multiple authorship and continuity over long periods of time as do statutes and constitutions, their analysis yields sharp insight into interpretive issues that arise even when the connections of author and text are comparatively simple.
My examination is limited in two important respects. Although most of the basic questions about textual interpretation that we shall examine are also raised within civil-law countries, I focus on common-law systems. I do not consider how much guidance we might glean from forms of nonlegal interpretation; these might provide helpful analogies or provide reasons to think some approaches are more promising than others.
Although the body of this essay does not directly contest single-inquiry theories, it demonstrates how extremely awkwardly such theories apply to wills and contracts.

questions.question: Whether the meaning of a legal text (especially wills and contracts) is best determined by a single controlling inquiry (e.g., the creator's intent or a single notion of sentence meaning) or by a pluralist, multi-factor approach that treats many considerations as potentially relevant.

Whether judges should ordinarily first determine a text's strict meaning and then decide whether to displace it, or whether resolving cases pragmatically without settling that strict meaning is an appropriate and desirable mode of judicial decisionmaking.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of contractual clauses to allocate liability and costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how contract language (especially 'costs of cover' clauses) should allocate responsibility for data-breach expenses, while Paper B develops a theory of how contracts are interpreted by judges and scholars to determine parties' obligations and liabilities.

shared_topics.topic: use of external standards and regulatory decisions as evidence in construing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses using FTC findings and industry security practices as benchmarks or evidence bearing on contractual reasonableness and promise-fulfillment, and Paper B treats judges' reliance on social facts, background norms, and other external considerations as part of a pluralist approach to contract interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: how evolving facts, technology, and expectations affect the meaning and enforcement of contractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that rapid technological change and shifting privacy/security expectations require rethinking and redrafting contract provisions, while Paper B analyzes how meaning can change over time and how interpreters may legitimately give different weight to temporal context when construing contracts.

shared_topics.topic: practical consequences of interpretive theories for drafting and adjudication of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for proactive contractual drafting (playbooks, fallback language) to manage future disputes over breaches and costs, and Paper B connects theoretical interpretive choices (single-inquiry vs. pluralist) to desirable judicial practice and the guidance those choices provide to lawyers and judges in resolving contract disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 3texamlrev91!!ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RELATIONAL ECONOMICS OF COMMERCIAL CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: role of social and relational context in interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that relational norms and background social context are economically consequential and should be operationalized in contract law and doctrine; Paper B defends a pluralist interpretive approach that counts social facts and changing communal practices among the relevant factors when construing wills and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal doctrine and theory adequately reflect actual commercial contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends mainstream contract scholarship has largely ignored relational contracting findings from business social sciences and urges doctrinal adjustment, while Paper B critiques single-inquiry theories as failing to capture how judges actually decide contract cases and argues for a theory that matches practice.

shared_topics.topic: incorporating empirical and interdisciplinary social‑science evidence into contract scholarship and adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly calls for partnerships with organizational theory, marketing, and management scholars to gather empirical data on relational expectations; Paper B likewise emphasizes attention to present social understandings and factual contexts (historical practice, changing norms) as essential inputs to legal interpretation of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal textual/authorial approaches and pragmatic/contextual decision‑making in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the interaction of formal contractual commitments with background relational expectations and the limits of narrow economic models, and Paper B contrasts single‑inquiry (author's intent/textual) accounts with a pluralist approach that permits judges to weigh pragmatic considerations alongside—or sometimes instead of—strict textual meaning.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016byulrev1!!ARTICLE: Mind the Gap
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mind the Gap

shared_topics.topic: distinction between interpretation and gap-filling in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze where interpretive inquiry ends and gap-filling begins: Paper A contrasts single-inquiry (author's intent) interpretation with pluralist, multi-factor approaches to discerning meaning in wills and contracts, while Paper B draws a doctrinal line between interpretation (ascertaining intent from terms, course of performance, usages) and judicial/arbitral gap-filling when intent cannot be discerned.

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' intent versus imposition of external standards/defaults
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between privileging the parties' subjective or objective intent and resorting to externally imposed norms: Paper A debates privileging author/speaker intent versus multiple practical factors, and Paper B contrasts intent-based interpretation with gap-filling that supplies reasonable terms based on community standards, fairness, or policy.

shared_topics.topic: institutional authority to alter, displace, or supplement contractual meaning
shared_topics.justification: Both examine who may legitimately change a text's meaning or supply omitted terms — Paper A asks whether judges may (or should) displace a text's meaning under pluralist practice versus single-inquiry restraint, and Paper B queries whether arbitrators (versus courts) possess appropriate powers and tools to fill gaps and supply terms in commercial contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how contextual change, complexity, or omission creates indeterminacy in private agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat how temporal change, complexity of transactions, and unstated assumptions produce interpretive indeterminacy: Paper A shows how evolving social/practical contexts can alter a statute or contract's modern meaning, and Paper B catalogs why material gaps arise in complex, long-term, cross-border commercial agreements and how that increases demand for gap-filling.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83lawcontempprob71!!ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: how courts should treat evolving meanings of contractual terms and legal texts over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether judges should fix meaning at enactment (single-inquiry/author's intent) or allow multifactor, purposive reinterpretation as social practices change (pluralism), using wills and statutes; Paper B documents how contract terms (especially boilerplate) become obsolete as markets thicken and asks whether and how legal or regulatory actors should enable updating of those terms.

shared_topics.topic: tension between standardized (boilerplate) contracts and bespoke interpretive or drafting approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that interpretation may need to account for context, purpose, and multiple factors rather than a single authorial intent—an account that matters when texts are generic or indeterminate; Paper B shows that standardization and boilerplate generate scale efficiencies but also stickiness and inefficiencies that bespoke contracting would avoid, creating a substantive tradeoff both papers address.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of courts and the state versus private ordering in fixing contract defects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers whether judges should displace textual meaning or leave changes to legislatures and how interpretive doctrines legitimize judicial action; Paper B argues that market actors face collective-action barriers to revising inefficient terms and contends that state-facilitated coordination or governance structures may be necessary to overcome those barriers.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between market practices/private governance and doctrinal rules of contract interpretation/production
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that judges and scholars draw on multiple social facts and practices when assigning meaning to legal texts (including contracts), while Paper B emphasizes that market structure and private networks shape the production and content of contracts, raising questions about how doctrinally unitary contract law should respond to heterogeneous market-embedded contracting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100yalelj615!!ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Bargaining and the Economic Theory of Contract Default Rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default or implied contract terms in contract construction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on Hadley v. Baxendale as exemplifying an implied default term (the foreseeability limitation) and critiques the economic story justifying penalty versus expansive defaults; Paper B treats contracts as legal texts whose meaning must be ascertained and shows how interpretive theory (pluralist vs single-inquiry) bears on how courts identify and apply implied or default terms.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' private information and intentions should affect interpretation and contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how private information (promisee's value from performance, promisor's breach probability) and strategic incentives affect bargaining around defaults; Paper B examines the status of author/speaker intent versus other contextual evidence in discerning meaning and how that information should be weighed by interpreters.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of strategic behavior on the desirability and operation of legal rules governing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly models strategic bargaining and argues that strategic incentives can undermine traditional Coasean/penalty-default justifications, favoring expansive defaults; Paper B considers how judges' interpretive choices respond to strategic or practical pressures (e.g., evolving practices, judicial incentives) and how interpretive approaches affect the behavior of contracting parties and adjudicators.

shared_topics.topic: the use of real-world judicial practice and empirical observation to evaluate interpretive or economic theories of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts an empirical survey of consequential-damages cases to challenge the information-forcing account and to assess which default actually operates in practice; Paper B emphasizes how prevailing judicial practice and the ways judges actually interpret wills and contracts inform and support a pluralist interpretive account.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35ucdavislrev319!!ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Discretion in Long-Term Open Quantity Contracts: Reining in Good Faith

shared_topics.topic: whether contract interpretation should prioritize the parties' contemporaneous allocation of discretion/intent versus a multifactor contextual inquiry
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should defer to the parties' negotiated allocation of quantity-discretion and not read in broad external limits, while Paper B contrasts single‑inquiry (author's intent) and pluralist approaches and defends a multifactor interpretive framework for wills and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper judicial role in modifying or displacing the parties' bargain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for using the good‑faith norm to rewrite long‑term open‑quantity contracts and urges restraint, and Paper B analyzes when judges may permissibly 'displace' a text's meaning versus strictly discerning it, debating the legitimacy of judicial reinterpretation in contract cases.

shared_topics.topic: the use and limits of commercial background and contextual evidence when construing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses courts' invocation of commercial background (and the UCC Official Comment) in construing 2‑306 quantity terms and finds that courts often supplant parties' bargains with uninformed readings, while Paper B defends a pluralist account in which background facts, social practices, and other contextual ingredients legitimately figure into interpreting contracts.

shared_topics.topic: balancing protection of reliance/expectations against negotiated risk allocation and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how courts use good faith to protect a seller's reliance interest—arguing sellers should instead signal reliance by contract (e.g., minimums/pricing)—and Paper B treats interpretation as a tool for realizing private expectations and purposes, questioning when interpretive choices should alter parties' anticipated entitlements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 4wmmarybuslrev575!!ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EXPLAINING "BAIT-AND-SWITCH" REGULATION

shared_topics.topic: the influence of social norms and custom on legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that judges and interpreters routinely rely on a variety of social facts, practices, and contemporary understandings (customs) when assigning meaning to wills and contracts, while Paper B shows that commercial regulation of bait-and-switch tactics is driven more by marketplace norms and customs than by welfare-maximizing analysis.

shared_topics.topic: whether legal meaning should be fixed at origin (authorial intent) or can evolve with practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a debate between single-inquiry (author's intent) accounts and pluralist accounts that allow meaning to change based on purposes and changing contexts, and Paper B treats the scope of 'bait-and-switch' (and related doctrines like teaser and free-offer rules) as expanding or contracting over time in response to evolving market practices and regulatory responses.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-textual, policy-oriented considerations (fairness/welfare) in shaping doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether and when interpreters should treat policy and other evaluative reasons as part of interpretation versus as separate exercises of displacement, and Paper B explicitly contrasts welfare-advancement justifications for regulating bait-and-switch tactics with decisions that instead reinforce fairness-oriented norms.

shared_topics.topic: which institutional actors and routes should produce doctrinal change (judicial interpretation vs legislative/regulatory action)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether changes in meaning or departures from textual meaning should be left to legislatures or can be made through judicial interpretation, while Paper B analyzes how regulatory agencies and Congress (e.g., the FTC and the CARD Act) have altered the law governing bait-and-switch practices and how cultural forces affect the prospects for such institutional change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nyulrev487!!ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DEMAND FOR IMMUTABLE CONTRACTS: ANOTHER LOOK AT THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF CONTRACT MODIFICATIONS

shared_topics.topic: how courts determine whether contractual clauses (e.g., anti-modification provisions) are enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Anglo‑American case law and doctrinal rules that render anti‑modification and form‑of‑modification clauses unenforceable, asking when courts will give effect to such provisions; Paper B treats contracts as legal texts and examines interpretive practices judges use to determine a contract's meaning and when to accept or displace textual indications, which directly bears on enforcing particular contractual clauses.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how judges should privilege textual/writer intent versus other factors when resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B defends a pluralist interpretive approach that treats writer intent, sentence meaning, social practice, and other factors as potentially relevant to contract interpretation; Paper A engages this issue practically by showing that courts sometimes refuse to enforce certain contractual terms (like anti‑modification clauses) despite parties' expressed intent, raising the question of which interpretive or normative grounds justify displacing textual party choices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background legal norms and non‑contractual doctrines in shaping contractual rights and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how actors exploit trust law, corporate forms, multi‑party agreements, and other non‑contractual devices to alter the practical effect of contract rules; Paper B emphasizes that interpretation of wills and contracts is influenced by broader legal practices and norms, showing that background legal context and evolving social understandings inform how contractual language is read and applied.

shared_topics.topic: the normative allocation of authority among parties, judges, and legislatures over the scope of freedom of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly debates whether the law should permit parties near‑complete freedom to structure the modifiability of their agreements or retain mandatory protections, with implications for judicial enforcement; Paper B addresses the related normative question of when judges may or should 'displace' a text's meaning rather than defer to authorial intent or leave changes to the legislature, thus tackling who appropriately shapes binding legal content.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 40bclrev879!!ARTICLE: The "New Conservatism" in Contract Law and the Process of Legal Change
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The "New Conservatism" in Contract Law and the Process of Legal Change

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual interpretation should prioritize authorial intent versus a multifactor (pluralist) approach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends a pluralist interpretive theory for wills and contracts against single-inquiry (author's intent or reader-centered) accounts; Paper B interrogates recent shifts in contract law doctrine (the so-called "new conservatism") that implicate how judges construe and apply contractual terms, engaging the same dispute about what interpretive methods courts actually use and should use.

shared_topics.topic: the process of legal change in contract law (how and why doctrines evolve over time)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses examples (e.g., changing scope of clerical-privilege language) to show how judges can reconceive textual meaning over time and debates about whether change should come from judges or legislatures; Paper B explicitly asks whether contract law has recently changed, what caused that change, and what such change reveals about the mechanisms of doctrinal evolution in private law.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of judges versus legislatures in shaping contractual meaning and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses the normative choice between judges displacing textual meaning and leaving changes to legislatures, illustrating practical tensions in contractual and statutory interpretation; Paper B's examination of a "new conservatism" in contract law similarly engages whether courts are being more or less interventionist and what institutional actors should drive doctrinal development.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of ideological or normative commitments on contract law adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the single-inquiry vs pluralist dispute to underlying convictions and rhetorical agendas that shape judges' practical conclusions; Paper B frames the observed shift as a conservative movement in contract law and seeks to explain the political/ideological forces that may have produced doctrinal change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of contractual texts — textual meaning versus parties' intentions and practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes theories (single-inquiry author's intent vs pluralist approaches) about what counts as the meaning of wills and contracts; Paper B repeatedly confronts how contract clauses, form language, and doctrines (force majeure, limitation clauses) are read in practice and how parties’ intentions and practical commercial consequences shape how contractual texts are treated.

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal rules and law-in-action (judicial doctrine versus negotiated/relational practices)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that judges often deploy multiple interpretive considerations beyond a single theoretical inquiry and questions how that relates to desirable judicial practice; Paper B documents how remedies rules, mitigation, and foreseeability interact with renegotiation, settlements, and commercial norms, showing a gap between formal doctrine and how contract law operates in practice.

shared_topics.topic: role of extrinsic social facts and policy in reaching outcomes (use of context, norms, and consequences in interpretation/enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a pluralist account that treats social facts, background practices, and purposive concerns as relevant to interpreting texts; Paper B marshals empirical law-in-action evidence—business norms, litigation costs, bankruptcy risk, market conditions—to explain why courts and parties interpret and enforce contractual obligations in particular ways.

shared_topics.topic: judicial adaptation of legal meaning or rules over time versus stability (when to reinterpret versus leaving changes to other actors)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses whether judges should update meanings of statutes or stick to original authors' intent (illustrated by the clerical-confession example); Paper B addresses whether doctrines (e.g., mistake, impracticability, damages rules) should be applied or adapted in response to economic shocks and relational contracting, and whether courts or parties should drive adjustments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 47alalrev387!!ARTICLE: Development of Reform of the Preexisting Duty Rule and Its Persistent Survival
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Development of Reform of the Preexisting Duty Rule and Its Persistent Survival

shared_topics.topic: judicial adaptation and reinterpretation of contract doctrines over time
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how courts have repeatedly tried (and largely failed) to reform or finesse the preexisting duty rule through judicial decisions, while Paper B analyzes competing theories (single-inquiry vs pluralist) about when and how judges may reinterpret contractual language or doctrinal texts as circumstances change.

shared_topics.topic: judicial versus legislative roles in reforming contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents statutory intrusions that partially abrogated the common-law preexisting duty rule and discusses why legislatures stepped in where courts would not, and Paper B directly interrogates whether changes in meaning or application of legal texts (including contracts) should be left to judges or to legislative bodies.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of historical origins and authorial intent for applying contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the preexisting duty rule's historical roots in assumpsit and how that pedigree affects its continued application, while Paper B examines the extent to which interpretation should privilege original/author intent versus contemporary purposes when construing wills and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: tension between rigid doctrinal rules (consideration) and practical commercial/equitable needs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the conflict between the formal consideration doctrine (and the preexisting duty rule) and the need for fair, consensual contractual modifications in a fluid market, and Paper B's pluralist approach defends weighing multiple practical and purposive factors—not just strict textualist metrics—when resolving contract interpretation problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev389!!SYMPOSIUM: "AGREEING TO DISAGREE": FILLING GAPS IN DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "AGREEING TO DISAGREE": FILLING GAPS IN DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: how to determine the meaning of contract terms left open or ambiguous
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a new regime (pro-defendant gap fillers) for contracts where parties deliberately left terms 'to be agreed,' rejecting both the traditional no-contract rule and simple reasonable-market gap fillers; Paper B treats contracts as a central example in its defense of a pluralist theory of legal interpretation, showing that determining a contract's meaning cannot be reduced to a single inquiry and must draw on multiple interpretive factors.

shared_topics.topic: judicial supplementation (gap‑filling) versus leaving meaning to the parties or legislature and the legitimacy of judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts should supplement incomplete contracts and proposes selectively pro-defendant supplementation as a legitimate judicial technique, while Paper B examines the broader question of when judges may permissibly displace or expand textual meaning (including in contracts) and debates the legitimacy of judges updating or supplementing meanings versus deferring to the drafter/legislature.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' intent (subjective/hypothetical consent) versus objective or default standards in interpreting contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the presumption of hypothetical consent/mimicking defaults for deliberately incomplete bargains and grounds its proposal in a different reading of the parties' intent, and Paper B directly engages the dispute between author-intent (single-inquiry) accounts and pluralist approaches that treat intent as one among multiple relevant factors in construing contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive choices affect practical policy outcomes (incentives, transaction security, and doctrinal consequences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links different gap-filling rules to incentive effects—precontractual investment, negotiation dynamics, and the likelihood of reaching full agreement—and argues that pro-defendant rules improve transactional security; Paper B evaluates interpretive theories partly by their fit with desirable legal practice and consequences, illustrating how different interpretive paradigms produce distinct practical and doctrinal outcomes (e.g., judicial creativity, deference to legislatures, and evolving meanings).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99michlrev1724!!ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates single-inquiry (author/reader intent or sentence meaning) versus pluralist, multifactor methods for interpreting wills and contracts; Paper B shows how the cotton industry's arbitration tribunals and private default rules interpret contract terms in practice, relying on trade usages and tailored substantive rules rather than only public-code text.

shared_topics.topic: the role of extrinsic norms, practices, and institutional context in shaping contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's pluralist account emphasizes that social practices, purposes, and disciplinary aims should figure into assigning meaning to legal texts; Paper B documents how industry norms, reputation, and institutional practices (trade rules, repeated dealings, and arbitration norms) actively shape how contracts are read and enforced in the cotton trade.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and functioning of private or nontextual legal mechanisms as substitutes or complements to public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when judges may displace textual meaning and how interpretive methods relate to desirable practice and legal authority; Paper B analyzes the cotton trade's private legal system (private default rules and merchant tribunals) as an alternative to state law, exploring its legitimacy, efficiency, and interaction with public legal regimes.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of adjudicators' procedural and jurisprudential practices on the development of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on judges' interpretive decisionmaking and how differing exercises (strict interpretation vs practical decision) produce legal outcomes; Paper B emphasizes how merchant arbitration tribunals produce written opinions, coherent jurisprudential approaches, and revisions to trade rules that shape contractual expectations and legal doctrines within the industry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev931!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: pluralist versus single-inquiry theories of contract meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly debates pluralist (many relevant factors) against single-inquiry (writer's intent or sentence meaning) accounts of interpretation and applies that debate to contracts and wills; Paper A engages the same theoretical divide in practice by contrasting recent emphases (gap-filling vs textual interpretation) and treating competing bases (text, intent, context) for construing written contracts.

shared_topics.topic: fact vs law distinction and who decides interpretive questions (judge vs jury)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the role of the jury and treats the fact/law distinction as the basic principle for allocating interpretive issues and appellate review; Paper B repeatedly frames interpretation as involving factual determinations (e.g., circumstances of communication/writer's intent) versus legal/conceptual questions and considers the implications for who should resolve meaning.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of evidentiary rules (parol evidence/plain-meaning) on what interpretive inquiries are possible or privileged
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the parol evidence rule and the plain-meaning rule as central doctrinal mechanisms that shape contract interpretation; Paper B discusses how evidentiary bars and admissibility constrain judges’ ability to discover writer's intent and thus push interpreters toward sentence/text-based answers, treating rules of evidence as shaping interpretive practice.

shared_topics.topic: practical judicial choice about displacing textual/authorial meaning versus updating or interpreting for current purposes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explores when judges should treat a text's historical authorial meaning as fixed or instead use other considerations to revise or ‘displace’ that meaning (with examples showing changing statutory understanding over time); Paper A likewise interrogates whether courts (and the law) should structure rules to steer interpretation away from juries (or otherwise shape outcomes) and considers pragmatic alternatives and the normative acceptability of judicially altering or constraining interpretive outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67arklrev873!!ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Case Study in Collaborative Technology and the Intentionally Relational Contract: Building Information Modeling and Construction Industry Contracts

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of traditional contract doctrine to accommodate collaborative, adaptive contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that collaborative technologies like BIM are pushing commercial parties toward intentionally relational contracts that traditional, discrete risk‑allocation contracts may not adequately govern; Paper B contends that conventional single‑inquiry interpretive theories poorly fit many contract situations and defends a pluralist approach that better accommodates evolving contractual practices.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of parties' intent versus evolving relational norms in defining contractual meaning and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that relational norms and ongoing cooperation often come to govern projects more than initial written terms as relationships and technology use evolve; Paper B analyzes the tension between privileging original author/speaker intent and allowing multiple contextual factors to determine the meaning of wills and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how legal actors (courts, lawyers) should respond to changing commercial practices and technologies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how lawyers can draft or translate business concepts into intentionally relational contractual terms and how contract law might adapt to technologically enabled collaboration; Paper B examines whether judges should stick to a fixed interpretive inquiry or use a pluralist set of standards to adapt meanings in light of contemporary practices and values.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as mechanisms for managing uncertainty, interdependence, and ongoing decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents relational contracts as flexible, negotiated frameworks that allow critical terms to be resolved during an ongoing interdependent relationship to cope with uncertainty; Paper B shows how interpretive methods for contracts and wills must account for purposes, changing circumstances, and multiple factors when assigning meaning to texts governing future contingencies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90texlrev1153!!ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant

shared_topics.topic: the extent to which contract and statute, rather than custom, generate binding legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats wills and contracts as legally authoritative private texts and examines how meaning and legal force are derived from those texts, while Paper B argues historically that the most widespread aspects of medieval commercial law emerged from contract and statute rather than from transnational custom.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and interpretive discretion when texts or customs are indeterminate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how judges often consult multiple factors and sometimes resolve cases without settling a single authoritative meaning (displacing or supplementing textual meaning), and Paper B documents how medieval courts and later statutes were invoked to create clearer commercial rules when local custom proved indeterminate or nonuniform.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of private ordering as a substitute for state law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether pluralist interpretive practices appropriately treat private documents (wills, contracts) and the standards judges use to enforce them, and Paper B critiques the romanticized view that medieval private ordering (the law merchant) was sufficient to provide a uniform transnational legal system.

shared_topics.topic: historical change in legal meanings and the relevance of origin versus contemporary practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses examples (e.g., clergy privilege) to show how meanings attributed to texts can shift over time and how origin intent may conflict with modern practices, while Paper B analyzes how historians and merchants dealt with evolving commercial practices and demonstrates that historical claims about uniform medieval customs are often mistaken.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 110columlrev1377!!ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRAIDING: THE INTERACTION OF FORMAL AND INFORMAL CONTRACTING IN THEORY, PRACTICE, AND DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in shaping the enforceability of contracts (how courts should intervene)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts currently apply 'low-powered' enforcement (e.g., duties to negotiate in good faith) to braided contracts and warns that overzealous formal enforcement can crowd out informal cooperative mechanisms; Paper B examines the judicial function in interpreting wills and contracts and defends a pluralist view in which judges legitimately use multiple tools (and sometimes displace literal meaning) to reach practically desirable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of strict textualist/ single-inquiry approaches for incomplete or evolving contractual arrangements

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of factual context, parties' practices, and information exchanges in resolving contractual meaning and facilitating cooperation

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING PROCEDURAL INNOVATION: HOW AND WHEN PARTIES CALIBRATE PROCEDURE THROUGH CONTRACT
