papers.node_id: 2014uilllrev1795!!LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
papers.title: LARRY RIBSTEIN MEMORIAL SYMPOSIUM: TRUST V. LAW (IN A BOX): DO ORGANIZATIONAL FORMS REALLY MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
papers.abstract:
One need not delve far into Larry Ribstein's 2009 masterwork, The Rise of the Uncorporation,to appreciate his commitment to a coherent theoretical defense of the proposition that business forms matter. Not surprisingly, the analytical framework he employed was transaction cost economics.Among other things, this approach to economic analysis assumes economic actors (1) are rational (though boundedly so) and opportunistic, and (2) may choose to self-regulate their relationships through contract.He argued that business association forms are special long-term contracts meant to deal rationally with an unknowable and contingent future. Not only do the parties need to set up decision making structures to deal with future events, but those structures also need to embody coherent sets of rules to deal efficiently with them.Larry was passionate that uncorporations - business forms like partnerships (particularly those with some measure of limited liability) and LLCs - are not only different from the traditional corporate model in this respect but significantly better, as they do a better job of letting owners and managers specify in advance the means by which they will control agency costs (i.e., the costs that arise when managers act in their own best interest rather than that of the owners). That strikes me as fairly noncontroversial and within the disciplinary bounds of transaction cost economics.
What I take issue with here is Larry's attempt to go beyond Oliver Williamson's explicit resistance to incorporating something as incommensurable as noncalculative trust into the economic model. Larry was too much a lawyer and therefore too rooted in the real world to think that incommensurable things like trust did not matter. So in his 2001 article, Law V. Trust,Larry went where Williamson declined to tread. He argued that arrangements more situated in private contract than regulation - the distinction he would later make as between the uncorporate form and the traditional corporation - had an impact on trust among the participants in the business venture.In short, as far as Larry was concerned,mandatory regulation, including standard form corporate law, was oil to the water of what Oliver Williamson called "personal trust" or what Larry called "strong-form trust." That is, regulation cannot produce personal trust; even more importantly, the presence of regulation can "crowd out" otherwise salutary personal trust.
In Larry's conception, default fiduciary obligations - the kind that seem to embody relationships based in personal trust - would exist only where there has been "contractual delegation of broad power over one's property."Fiduciary duties so conceived would only oblige one to refrain from self-dealing.As for other duties that might encompass personal trust, they would need to be set forth in a contract, the essence of which would be articulating, before the fact, the terms of a relationship so as to minimize the transaction costs, agency and otherwise, that may arise after the fact.Whatever personal trust may be, it ought to be the law between the parties only if they expressly make it so.Hence, if one chooses contract as the means of regulating a relationship, one should not expect legal relief for a failure of personal trust or other personal characteristic unless the parties established a duty relating to such characteristic in the contract. Conversely, if one chooses personal trust as the means of regulating a relationship, one should expect only to have nonlegal avenues of recourse. Yet having said all that, Larry concluded that the process of private contracting (as one finds in unincorporated business entities) is still more conducive than the mandatory impositions of the corporate form to the retention of traditional trust in a business relationship - i.e., traditional trust is less likely to be "crowded out" by the increasing complexity of external regulation.
resist that last move. Taking a page from a physical scientist, Lee Smolin, I want to suggest here - and this is not meant to be denigrating - that a wholly economic approach to understanding the significance of standard business forms is doing social science in a box.Notwithstanding the algorithms of transaction cost economics as applied in this context, people still operate with human virtues and vices, not the least of which are trust, fear, greed, and panic. Notwithstanding its ambition togo beyond the abstractions of the neoclassical theory, transaction cost theory still aspires to scientific precision, and deals with these virtues and vices as well as the unwieldy complexities, paradoxes, and inconsistencies of real world business transactions in the same way that theory in physics deals with the gap between the models and the reality. It stays inside the box and simply ignores them. That was what Williamson did with noncalculative trust, and what Larry tried to overcome while still remaining within the disciplinary boundary.
less inclined to see the world through the lens of an economic model, so I have a somewhat different way of making sense of law and trust, and how that relates to the importance of business association forms. Larry and I would have agreed that law (at least business association law) is law and trust is trust and they are significantly different creatures. Where I am pretty sure we would have parted company (and do in this regretfully one-sided debate) is in the extent to which economic models and business association forms map onto those motivations that really make a difference in how people interact, whether as partners, limited partners, LLC members, or corporate shareholders. My thesis is that virtues and vices like trust, greed, fear, and panic pretty much span the entirety of human history, but conceptions about business law and economics are relatively modern inventions. There is a certain amount of rational hubris in thinking there was a quantum leap in human evolution when Bentham and Mill first conceived of happiness as measurable by units of utility or when we modern folks started reflecting our abstract conceptions of subjective rights in contracts. Virtues like trust and their counterpart vices - greed, fear, panic - seem to me as likely to kick in after the fact whether we are talking about partnerships, limited partnerships, LLCs, corporations, or - heaven forbid - nonprofits and benefit corporations. The rational and the affective reside in all of us, to a greater or lesser extent, side by side.
Larry pulled no punches in telling me when he thought I was wrong, which was frequent. I think he would find some humor in the thesis of my contribution to a symposium in his memory: not that he was wrong, but that he was trying to force trust into a model that really has no way of handling it. In Part II, I suggest Larry's work was in fact a struggle against "law and economics in a box." The modifier "in a box" meansthat the incommensurable parts of business relationships are hard to model; hence, like physicists dealing with their own disciplinary paradoxes and contradictions, one puts them aside to make some theoretical headway. What we will see is that Larry was more in touch with the real world and thus doing his science less in the box than, say, Williamson, but his effort to reconcile law and trust by translating them both into a common denominator of economic jargon simply did not work.Larry was right in thinking trust was important as a factor in business relationships, but it was a mistake to try to measure law and trust on a utilitarian "sliding scale" under which increasing complexity of law and regulation in the commercial arena purportedly "crowds out" trust.
In Part III, I react to the "crowding out" metaphor and propose an alternative - the metaphor of the machine - for thinking about the relationship of, on one hand, the use of economic theory and legal constructs as a means of prediction and control of an unknowable future and, on the other, those aspects of human nature that resist reduction to predictable regularities. Business organizations are complex yet intangible modern systems under which people and property are supposed to operate with something approaching machine-like efficiency. Rules and law, as a subset of rules generally, are the rational machine parts we use in constructing the system. But the system is still populated by human beings whose emotions, urges, desires, greed, and altruism defy reduction to machine-like algorithms. I am not sure exactly what something like "traditional trust" is. Nevertheless, if we (1) focus solely on the machine-like parts of the system or (2) try to analyze trust as though it were a machine part, we are missing something important. At the risk of metaphor overload, those incommensurables are to the science of business association forms as dark matter or dark energy is to the current state of physics.That is, we know something exists, but we cannot account for it in our models. I reconcile the orderliness of the law - the modern machine - and the unpredictability of human nature with a different metaphor about traditional trust as system-regulating liquid. In other words, it is something like trust that keeps either corporations or uncorporations (if not whole economies) from melting down.

questions.question: Whether more contractually flexible organizational forms (as opposed to standardized, regulation-heavy forms) lead to higher levels of interpersonal trust among business participants.
Whether the imposition of mandatory regulatory rules for business relationships crowds out or undermines personal, nonlegal trust-based governance.
Whether economic/transaction-cost models adequately capture the role of noncalculative trust and other human virtues and vices in shaping behavior within business organizations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27jlegalstud67!!ARTICLE: Profit-Sharing Contracts in Hollywood: Evolution and Analysis
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Profit-Sharing Contracts in Hollywood: Evolution and Analysis

shared_topics.topic: contracts and organizational forms as mechanisms to control agency costs and monitoring problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how Hollywood profit-sharing contracts convert fixed salaries into contingent pay and reduce monitoring costs or budgetary agency problems for studio executives; Paper B treats business association forms (corporations, partnerships, LLCs) as long-term contractual devices that parties use to structure decision rights and control agency costs and delegated authority.

shared_topics.topic: how legal regulation and court decisions shape private contracting and fiduciary/delegation rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the Buchwald litigation and how contractual definitions (e.g., 'net profits') and audit provisions interact with legal review and industry practice, showing law affects how contracts are written and enforced; Paper B examines default fiduciary duties, the contractual delegation of powers, and the claim that mandatory corporate rules can 'crowd out' or interact with private-ordering and trust.

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of contractual and organizational forms in response to changing economic and regulatory environments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the historical development of profit- and revenue-sharing contracts in the motion-picture industry and links changes in contract form to shifts in industry economics and regulation; Paper B traces the rise of 'uncorporations' (partnerships, LLCs) and argues organizational form choices evolved as responses to transaction costs, agency concerns, and regulatory contexts.

shared_topics.topic: use of contingent compensation or contractual delegation to allocate risk and manage asymmetric information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes that net‑profit and other sharing contracts function as risk‑sharing devices and as mechanisms to mitigate asymmetric information between studios and talent; Paper B emphasizes that parties use contractual delegation and choice of entity to allocate decision rights and incentives under uncertainty, thereby managing informational and incentive problems inherent in business relationships.

shared_topics.topic: limits of standard economic (principal-agent/transaction-cost) models and the role of non‑economic factors like trust in governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A expresses skepticism about applying a standard principal‑agent framework alone to movie contracts and suggests alternative hypotheses involving behavioral and organizational motives; Paper B explicitly critiques 'law and economics in a box,' arguing that transaction‑cost models inadequately capture trust, emotions, and other incommensurable factors that influence how organizational forms function in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: limits of economic modeling for prescribing legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique reliance on simplified economic models to prescribe law: Paper A argues transaction-cost economics cannot capture noncalculative trust and other affective human factors, while Paper B warns that formalist/economic models of contracting are inevitably 'off' from the complex real-world and cautions against overreliance on such models when reforming contract law.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal legal rules/mandatory regulation and informal/private-ordering norms like trust
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how formal legal frameworks interact with informal social mechanisms: Paper A debates whether standard corporate regulation 'crowds out' personal trust and contrasts mandatory corporate law with contractual private ordering, and Paper B contrasts statutory/formal interpretive rules with reliance on contextual standards (trade usage, course of performance) that better reflect industry practice.

shared_topics.topic: how legal form or interpretive doctrine shapes real-world contracting and governance
shared_topics.justification: Both ask whether doctrinal choices meaningfully affect behavior: Paper A considers whether business association forms (corporations vs uncorporations/LLCs) materially influence trust and agency-cost control, while Paper B analyzes whether greater interpretive formalism (e.g., a revived plain-meaning approach) would improve or harm actual sales contracting under the U.C.C., especially in a world of form contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical evidence and attention to real-world complexity when changing law
shared_topics.justification: Both argue that normative or legislative changes should be empirically grounded: Paper A stresses that human virtues/vices complicate model-driven prescriptions, and Paper B explicitly contends that moves toward neoformal interpretive rules lack sufficient empirical support and may produce undesirable practical consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 109pennstlrev397!!ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reason and Context: A Dual Track Theory of Interpretation*

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal rules and social/contextual norms (how context and trust shape legal meaning and operation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces Llewellyn's 'full contextualism' showing that extrinsic social and commercial context must inform contract interpretation; Paper B examines how interpersonal trust and other nonlegal social forces interact with (and can be crowded out by) legal forms and regulation in business associations.

shared_topics.topic: role of default/open terms versus standardized/hierarchical rules in private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the UCC embodied 'non-fixed rules' and promoted open merchant terms that allow context-driven interpretation, while Paper B contrasts mandatory corporate law with uncorporate forms that rely on private contracting and default rules (or expressly drafted duties) to govern relationships.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of competing theoretical frameworks for explaining legal practice (legal realism/contextualism versus law-and-economics models)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates and defends Llewellyn's Legal Realist/contextual jurisprudence against abstract conceptualism, and Paper B critiques transaction-cost/law-and-economics models as 'in a box,' arguing they cannot fully capture trust and other human factors in organizational life.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive methodologies or organizational form choices affect allocation of obligations, remedies, and agency problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links interpretive method (contextualism versus hierarchical rules) to doctrinal outcomes in reliance recovery, precontractual liability, and implied contracts, while Paper B analyzes how choice of business form and default fiduciary rules (or contractual specification) shapes agency costs, duties, and available recourse for failures of trust.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: limits of ex ante contracting/business forms to govern future contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine whether legal instruments created before the fact—whether business organizational forms or detailed contract language—can meaningfully anticipate and manage an unknowable future; Paper A questions the capacity of organizational form and transaction-cost models to account for post-formation human behavior, while Paper B argues that meaning and control often only arise ex post, undermining the idea that ex ante drafting secures outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role and control of opportunism/agency costs by law versus informal norms
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the issue of opportunism and agency costs—Paper A centers opportunism as a core assumption of transaction-cost analysis and debates whether law or private contracting better controls self-dealing, while Paper B interrogates the legal salience of opportunism in interpretation disputes, arguing that opportunistic behavior is largely an ex post phenomenon not readily constrained by contractual language.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal legal/economic models and non-cognitive human factors (trust, language, emotions)
shared_topics.justification: Both criticize the reductionism of formal models: Paper A critiques law-and-economics approaches for ignoring incommensurable human virtues and vices like trust and panic, and Paper B draws on philosophy of language and non-cognitive communicative theory to show that contract formation and interpretation involve reactive, non-cognitive elements ordinary economic/legal models miss.

shared_topics.topic: how rules/texts are applied to unforeseen events (rule-induction and gap-filling)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the problem of applying pre-existing legal rules or contractual texts to novel circumstances: Paper A frames organizational rules as machine parts that may fail to account for human unpredictability, while Paper B analyzes contract interpretation as an act of rule-induction at the time of dispute, explaining why gap-filling and meaning assignment are essentially ex post processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 29cardozolrev261!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATIONS AND SETTLEMENTS: DR. PANGLOSS'S NOTES ON THE MARGINS OF DAVID CAMPBELL'S PAPERS

shared_topics.topic: how formal legal rules interact with and affect interpersonal trust and norms in commercial relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally debates whether statutory corporate rules and mandatory regulation 'crowd out' or substitute for personal trust in business associations, while Paper B examines how doctrinal rules (mitigation, foreseeability, limits on consequential damages) shape parties' willingness to cooperate, share losses, and rely on informal norms in long-term dealings.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract design and organizational form in allocating risk and controlling agency costs in ongoing transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats business association forms (partnerships, LLCs, corporations) as distinct long-term contracts that can be designed to specify decision-making and limit agency costs, and Paper B analyzes how explicit contractual terms and default remedial rules allocate loss-bearing and induce renegotiation in relational contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the incentives created by legal remedies and defaults for breach, renegotiation, and settlement in relational contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly analyzes how limited remedies and doctrines like mitigation/ Hadley foster efficient breach, loss-sharing, and settlements; Paper A similarly considers how legal defaults versus private contracting affect parties' incentives to rely on law or trust when facing contingent future events.

shared_topics.topic: emphasizing 'law in action' and skepticism of purely formal economic models for explaining commercial behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes transaction-cost economics for staying 'in a box' and downplaying human virtues/vices, advocating attention to noncalculative factors; Paper B advances a 'new legal realism' perspective, stressing empirical law-in-action, negotiated processes, and how practical constraints and informal networks shape outcomes beyond formal doctrinal predictions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21upajbusl142!!ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contracting and public regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether private contracting (uncorporate forms, explicit contracts) should displace or coexist with mandatory corporate law and whether regulation 'crowds out' personal trust; Paper B argues that public contract law is increasingly remade in the shadow of privately-generated standards, with states validating and incorporating private governance structures.

shared_topics.topic: role of trust and informal commercial norms versus formal legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally examines how personal trust, virtues and vices operate alongside or outside legal rules and whether law can or should capture trust; Paper B documents the rise of private commercial communities, standard terms, and sectoral practices—informal norms that shape contracting and are increasingly reflected in formal law.

shared_topics.topic: transaction-cost / efficiency justifications for legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Ribstein's defense of particular business association forms in transaction-cost economics (owners choose forms to minimize agency and transaction costs); Paper B explains sectoral fragmentation as providing efficiency gains—specialized rules and standard terms that reduce transaction costs and better align legal outcomes with commercial expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how legal form or specialization affects economic outcomes and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that different organizational forms (partnerships, LLCs, corporations) structure decisionmaking and agency costs with consequences for behavior and trust; Paper B shows that sectoral legal specialization alters dispute resolution, remedies, barriers to entry, and the balance of public vs private regulatory power, producing winners and losers in markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113pennstlrev1031!!Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: the balance between private ordering (contractual governance) and public/state law in resolving commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes international commercial arbitration as a hybrid choice between private adjudication and recourse to public law, showing parties often select public substantive law and court assistance; Paper B similarly examines how business association forms let parties rely on private contractual governance (uncorporations) as an alternative to mandatory corporate law and questions how law and private ordering interact.

shared_topics.topic: how transactional attributes and party preferences determine opting for arbitration, courts, or particular organizational forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically theorizes that attributes like geographic/cultural distance, complexity of the good, clarity of applicable law, and need for speed drive parties toward arbitration or court litigation; Paper B addresses how parties choose organizational forms (partnerships, LLCs, corporations) and contractual arrangements to manage future uncertainty, agency costs, and human motivations, linking institutional choice to the underlying transaction and relational context.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay of private enforcement mechanisms (reputation, contractual remedies) with public enforcement (judicial enforcement, fiduciary duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts trade‑association arbitration—enforced via extralegal sanctions like expulsion—with international arbitration’s frequent reliance on courts to enforce awards; Paper B discusses fiduciary obligations, contractual delegation of duties, and when parties should expect legal versus nonlegal remedies, exploring when private sanctions suffice and when legal enforcement is required.

shared_topics.topic: the role of trust, reputation, and nonlegal norms as governance tools and their relationship to formal legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights reputational sanctions in trade association arbitration as central private‑ordering tools; Paper B centrally interrogates 'trust' (and the 'crowding out' hypothesis) as a noncalculative, system‑regulating force that interacts with, and may be undermined by, increased legal regulation and formal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: efficiency of contract default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats business association forms and default fiduciary obligations as legally embedded default rules that parties use to allocate rights and control agency costs, while Paper B empirically/theoretically evaluates the Hadley v. Baxendale default on unforeseeable consequential damages and when that default is economically efficient.

shared_topics.topic: designing legal/organizational responses to unforeseeable contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that business forms (corporations, uncorporations, LLCs) are mechanisms for structuring decision-making to handle an unknowable future, and Paper B analyzes how the Hadley rule allocates risk for unforeseeable consequential losses and thereby shapes precaution and bargaining ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: private information, opportunism, and incentives in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A deploys transaction-cost and agency-cost reasoning about opportunistic actors and contractual delegation to limit self-dealing, while Paper B models how asymmetric/private buyer valuations affect whether the Hadley default elicits efficient revelation and precautions.

papers.node_id: 113pennstlrev1031!!Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration
papers.title: Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration
papers.abstract:
The literature on private ordering examines how parties use extralegal means - most commonly reputational sanctions - to enforce contracts. As described by Barak D. Richman, private ordering "compares the efficiencies of private (extralegal) contract enforcement with the more traditional use of public law and state-run courts."A series of studies by Lisa Bernstein illustrates a paradigm case of private ordering - trade associations that use industry arbitrators (private judges) to adjudicate disputes, with the arbitrators' awards typically enforced by the threat of extralegal sanctions such as expulsion from the association.In the trade associations studied by Bernstein, the merchants opted out of the public court system and instead chose to have their disputes resolved by private judges applying industry trade rules.
With its focus on private legal systems, the private ordering literature sets up a seeming dichotomy between public court adjudication of disputes, applying publicly created laws, and private arbitral adjudication of disputes, applying privately developed rules. Trade association arbitrations fit neatly into the latter category;public courts fit almost as neatly into the former. But while the dichotomy highlights the cases of most interest in the private ordering literature, it is too simple. It gives the appearance of an all-or-nothing choice - all public dispute resolution or all private dispute resolution - when in fact hybrid choices are common.
This article seeks to add to the private ordering literature in two ways. First, it argues in Part II that international commercial arbitration, while sometimes cited as an example of private ordering, is in fact - a hybrid case - with important elements of public involvement supplementing the use of a private decision maker. Internationalcommercial arbitration, as distinguished from trade association arbitration, is nonspecialized arbitration between private parties involved in international commercial transactions.In the overwhelming number of cases, parties to international arbitration agreements reject the option of having their dispute resolved under privately developed commercial rules, the so-called new Law Merchant or lex mercatoria. Instead, they choose to have their dispute resolved under publicly created laws.Moreover, unlike parties in trade association arbitrations, parties in international commercial arbitrations often turn to the courts for aid in enforcing awards.Too often, international arbitration is grouped with trade association arbitration in ways that blur the important distinctions between the two. Not all arbitration is alike, and not all parties that agree to arbitrate opt out of the legal system altogether.
, in Part III, this article examines attributes of international transactions that help explain party choice among these different mechanisms of resolving disputes. It considers four attributes: (1) distance - geographic, as well as cultural and political - between the parties; (2) the complexity of the good or service; (3) the clarity of the applicable national law; and (4) the importance of speedy resolution of disputes. Trade association arbitration is most likely to be used for transactions in simple goods, although less likely in international transactions involving greater distances than domestic transactions. International commercial arbitration is the more likely choice for international transactions, except in cases in which the applicable law is clear or emergency relief is likely to be needed. In such cases, parties are more likely to choose litigation in national courts. The attributes thus prove useful in explaining differences in the choice of enforcement mechanism across various types of international transactions. Whether they are as useful in explaining variation among businesses engaged in similar transactions awaits further work.

questions.question: Whether international commercial arbitration operates as a form of pure private ordering or as a hybrid system that substantially relies on public law and court involvement for substantive rules and enforcement.
Whether parties to international commercial disputes prefer that arbitrators apply privately developed commercial rules or publicly created national laws when resolving their disputes.

What transaction attributes (e.g., geographic/cultural distance between parties, complexity of the good or service, clarity of applicable national law, and the need for speedy relief) explain parties' choice among dispute-resolution mechanisms (private arbitration versus public court litigation) in international commerce.

papers.node_id: 56amjcompl703!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Actors: The State's Private Law and the Economy - Commercial Law as an Amalgam of Public and Private Rule-Making
papers.title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Actors: The State's Private Law and the Economy - Commercial Law as an Amalgam of Public and Private Rule-Making
papers.abstract:
Private rule-making has always played a significant role in economic life. This makes it a promising endeavor to trace the particular forms of, and reasons for, this phenomenon and its interaction with state law. Such an enquiry does not amount to merely a narrow look at an insulated sector of society because in sociological perspective, the economy cannot be conceived as distinct from society. Quite to the contrary: it is a subsystem of society, just like religion or education, politics or mobility. Economic thinking, i.e., the quest for an efficient use of scarce resources, permeates all parts of the society. Every individualis affected at least in his or her capacity as a consumer, many also as producers or suppliers of goods and services. Thus, the economy virtually includes everybody to the extent that his or her behavior can be explained by an effort to make an efficient use of scarce resources. Nor is the focus on private law meant to exclude other aspects of the legal framework of economic activities. The classical public/private divide helps to explain the interest involved in, and the regulation of, many legal relations and conflicts; but it neglects the functional character of law and the large grey area of overlap and interdependence between public and private law, which is particularly relevant for trade and commerce and will thus be covered in this paper.
The following remarks investigate which conditions are favorable or unfavorable to the emergence of private rules or state law. Therefore, they will first outline the historical transition from non-state law to state law in the field of trade and commerce (infra part II), before making an inventory of the various types of non-state laws (infra part III), and of the functions of state laws relevant in this area (infra part IV). The inventory will allow an assessment of factors which favor the emergence of non-state rules as well as of others which forestall their evolution (infra part V).
. From Custom to Positivism: A Short History of Business Law

questions.question: Under what economic, social, and institutional conditions do private (non-state) commercial rules emerge, persist, or displace state law in regulating trade and economic activity?
How do private commercial rules and state law interact and overlap in practice, and what distinct functions does state law perform relative to private rule-making in the governance of commerce?
What historical processes and drivers account for the transition from customary or non-state commercial rules to formal state law governing commerce?

papers.node_id: 62dukelj707!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW
papers.title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW
papers.abstract:
Customs, social rules, and conventions are pervasive in our lives. They guide our actions as we navigate complex interactions of social life; they give social significance to the material things that often mediate those relations; and, even more, they define horizons within which actions we conceive and deliberatively entertain actions we undertake. Moreover, for millennia custom has been regarded as an important kind, or source, or ground of law. Although its importance has seemed to decline in modern legal systems, it is often not far below the surface in important parts of municipal law, and it is still thought to play an indispensable role in international law.
An analysis that breaks custom into an external element - regularities of behavior (usus) - and an internal element - convictions of custom followers that behavior conforming to the regularities is legally required (opinio juris) - has been nearly irresistible to theorists of law and of custom generally. What is more natural than to think that custom is a matter of consistent patterns of behavior observable from the outside plus some interior state like belief, attitude, or conviction, which turns patterns of behavior into norms for behavior? Yet, this additive conception of custom, despite its dominance, is deeply flawed, if not incoherent. Many of its problems are frequently rehearsed and recognized, and then almost immediately ignored. The jurisprudence of custom has long been in the grip of a kind of additive addiction, fed by the irresistible naturalness of its approach and the absence of any plausible alternative.
The project of this Essay is to sketch such an alternative, an integrated account that proposes to understand legally relevant customs as embedded in and arising from discursive normative practices. Inspiring this alternative approach is a brief sketch of custom by an ancient sophist turned stoic, which provides a useful foil for a terse characterization of the additive conception. (It also provides evidence that the additive conception is not completely irresistible.) I then seek to break the addiction to this conception in three steps. First, I briefly show how the "outside" versus "inside" trope that dominates thinking about custom beguiles theorists into an uncritical adoption of the additive conception. Second, I argue that this conception is bedeviled by problems deeper than the paradoxes and uncertainties widely, if uncomfortably, acknowledged in the jurisprudence of custom. Finally, I articulate and defend analternative conception, the normative practice account. For this purpose, I focus on three core concepts and the interrelationships between them: normative practice, reciprocally oriented conduct, and discursive interaction. The proposal is that legally significant customs take shape in discursive normative practices in rich contexts of social interaction characterized by intermeshing anticipations and interconnected conduct. I conclude with a brief discussion of the appropriateness of this conception of custom for law, especially international law. First, I argue that international relations are characterized by the kind of social interaction that provides a natural habitat for the essentially discursive practice of international law. But, second, I concede that the additive conception may still play a role in some legal systems, not as a basis for understanding the nature of custom or its normative force, but rather as framing evidentiary standards adopted by those systems for proof of the legal standing or validity of a given custom in them.

questions.question: Whether understanding legally significant customs as an additive combination of observable behavioral regularities and interior convictions accurately captures their normative nature and legal force.

Whether legally significant customs are better explained as arising from discursive normative practices-characterized by reciprocally oriented conduct and discursive interaction-rather than as separable external and internal elements.

Whether the additive conception of custom should be reframed as an evidentiary standard for proving a custom's legal standing, rather than as an account of the nature of custom, and what consequences that reframing has for legal systems (especially international law).

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the dominant additive usus/opinio juris model of custom and proposes a normative-practice account; Paper B critiques the lost-profits trend and advances a risk-allocation (market-damages) framework to replace prevailing approaches to measuring expectancy damages.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of perspective/temporal framing in legal judgment (inside vs outside; ex ante vs ex post)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes the outside/inside dichotomy (observable behavior versus interior conviction) in attributing normative force to custom; Paper B emphasizes the crucial difference between ex ante and ex post perspectives when measuring contractual expectancy and allocating losses.

shared_topics.topic: the role of doctrinal standards and evidentiary rules in identifying and enforcing legal norms or entitlements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the additive conception has been used as an evidentiary frame for proving customs in legal systems; Paper B analyzes how legal default rules and statutory provisions (e.g., the UCC) function as measurement and interpretive standards for awarding damages and thereby determining contractual entitlements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nclrev2239!!ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS

shared_topics.topic: when observable conduct versus internal belief creates legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the dominant 'usus plus opinio juris' model and interrogates how external patterns of behavior and internal convictions combine (or fail to) to produce legally relevant custom, while Paper B grapples with when parties' conduct (promises, course of performance, reliance) can dispense with written terms or constitute waiver/estoppel despite a lack of formal, signed agreement.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal written rules and informal social or commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how modern legal systems purport to marginalize custom yet still rely on embedded social practices to generate norms (especially in international law), and Paper B analyzes the conflict between parties' desire for contractual certainty via no-oral-modification clauses and the practical, informal changes that arise in performance.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary and doctrinal difficulties in recognizing informal norm-formation and proposals for clarification or reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the additive account leaves jurisprudence with paradoxes and calls for an integrated normative-practice account to reconceptualize how law recognizes custom, while Paper B documents inconsistent judicial use of terms like waiver, modification, and estoppel, surveys messy case law, and advocates clearer doctrinal definitions and legislative solutions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of communication, interaction, and reliance in producing normative effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds discursive normative practices and intermeshed anticipations as the loci where customs form, and Paper B shows how communications between parties (sales reps' promises, oral amendments) and the relying party's changed position can generate binding legal consequences despite written prohibitions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRICALLY ASSESSING HADLEY v. BAXENDALE

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and norms coordinate expectations and conduct in social interaction
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that legally relevant customs are practices that shape intermeshing anticipations and reciprocally oriented conduct through discursive interaction, while Paper B shows that the Hadley default rule shapes parties' expectations and precautions by altering incentives and the distribution of foreseeable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of informational asymmetries and evidentiary inference in legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the simple outside/inside (usus/opinio juris) split and highlights how legal systems use evidentiary standards to infer customs from social practices, and Paper B studies how Hadley functions as a default that elicits or exploits private information about buyer valuations and thus depends on inference under information asymmetry.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification of legal rules in light of social and economic effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a normative-practice account justifying when and how customs generate legal force (particularly in international law), while Paper B provides a normative (economic-efficiency) assessment of the Hadley rule, identifying the social and distributional conditions under which that doctrine is justified.

shared_topics.topic: sensitivity of doctrines to social/contextual distributions and empirical conditions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that customs acquire legal significance only within rich social contexts and interactional patterns, and Paper B empirically examines how the efficiency of the Hadley rule depends on the empirical distribution of buyer valuations and real-world bargaining/precaution behaviors.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113yalelj1417!!ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: Critique of individualistic or additive models of legal normativity (e.g., usus/opinio juris; party‑centered contract theories)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers reject dominant reductionist accounts that ground legal norms in separable individual components — Paper A criticizes the 'outside' (behavior) plus 'inside' (belief) additive model of custom, while Paper B rejects individualistic explanations of promises/contracts that locate their moral force in benefits to the separate parties (freedom, expectation, welfare).

shared_topics.topic: Normative practices and social relations as constitutive sources of legal obligation
shared_topics.justification: Each paper advances an account in which law's normative force is generated by social practices and relations rather than by isolated mental states or consequentialist calculations — Paper A emphasizes customs as embedded in discursive normative practices, and Paper B locates the moral and legal core of contract in the relational, communal form of collaboration contracts instantiate.

shared_topics.topic: Reciprocity and discursive interaction as mechanisms for creating obligations
shared_topics.justification: Both works foreground reciprocal, interdependent conduct and communicative/discursive interaction as central mechanisms through which norms and obligations take shape — Paper A focuses on reciprocally oriented conduct and discursive interaction in customs, and Paper B highlights recognition, respect, and collaborative relations produced by promises and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: Implications for legal doctrine and evidentiary recognition of norms
shared_topics.justification: Each paper ties its theoretical account to concrete legal practice: Paper A considers how a practice‑based view of custom affects international law and evidentiary standards for proving custom, while Paper B shows how a relational theory of contract bears on doctrines like consideration and the expectation remedy.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: verifiability and evidentiary standards for normative facts (contract terms or custom)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with how courts or legal systems can or should ascertain contested normative facts: Paper A analyzes the ‘‘verifiability’’ problem in contract enforcement and how litigation strategies, courts' limited competence, and evidentiary regimes affect gap‑filling and enforcement costs; Paper B interrogates the common usus/opinio juris (outside/inside) evidentiary framing for proving custom and how that framing functions as a legal standard for recognizing customary rules.

shared_topics.topic: when to defer to private/social ordering versus judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both works ask when law should step in as opposed to leaving matters to parties or social practice: Paper A evaluates private transactional strategies (delegation, contractual devices, renegotiation) and argues that courts should sometimes refrain or adopt different interpretive regimes depending on causes of incompleteness; Paper B argues that legally significant customs emerge from discursive social practices and that legal systems may appropriately recognize or defer to those practices rather than impose external doctrinal treatments.

shared_topics.topic: the role of normative/social practices in supplying or shaping legal meaning and gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat informal normative practices as sources that shape formal legal outcomes: Paper A shows how parties craft contractual language, signals (parol evidence, liquidated damages), and cooperative practices to manage gaps and influence judicial interpretation; Paper B develops an integrated account of custom as a discursive normative practice that generates the behavioral and justificatory material law draws on, especially in international law.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE UNDERCOVER DETECTIVE LOOKS AT DATA BREACH CONTRACT CLAUSES: WHO SHOULD BE RESPONSIBLE UNDER THE CONTRACT FOR COSTS OF COVER?

shared_topics.topic: the role of discourse, communication, and negotiation in constituting legally operative norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that customs take shape through discursive interaction, reciprocally oriented conduct, and normative practices; Paper B focuses on contract drafting, clause negotiation, and corporate playbooks as communicative practices that create, specify, and operationalize obligations (including who bears post-breach costs).

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for allocating responsibility and costs in response to social harms informed by normative standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how customs and shared normative expectations determine who is bound and what duties follow within legal orders; Paper B analyzes contractual mechanisms (cost-of-cover clauses, risk allocation language) and regulatory influence that assign financial responsibility for the harms of data breaches, situating those allocations against broader social and industry norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42geojintll639!!ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EMERGING LEX AVIATICA

shared_topics.topic: emergence of new international legal norms through state and non‑state practice (e.g., a nascent "lex aviatica")
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses an evolving consensus among airlines and sympathetic government officials that could create a new cross‑border aviation norm that circumvents existing treaty nationality rules; Paper B develops a theory of how legally significant customs arise out of ongoing discursive and reciprocal practices, explaining the social mechanics by which such emergent norms take shape in international law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transnational actors and discursive interaction in shaping international legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the influence of transnational corporations and airlines (and their dialogue with officials) in pressing for regulatory reform across national boundaries; Paper B locates legally relevant custom in 'discursive normative practices' and 'reciprocally oriented conduct,' offering a conceptual account of how sustained interaction among non‑state and state actors produces binding international norms.

papers.node_id: 60ucinlrev405!!SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM -- JUST WINNERS AND LOSERS: THE APPLICATION OF GAME THEORY TO CORPORATE LAW AND PRACTICE: PANEL DISCUSSION
papers.abstract: This panel discussion took place as part of the Fourth Annual Corporate Symposium -- Just Winners and Losers: The Application of Game Theory to Corporate Law and Practice -- at the University of Cincinnati College of Law, Cincinnati, Ohio, on March 1, 1991.

questions.question: Whether and how game-theoretic models can predict the strategic behavior of corporate actors (e.g., managers, shareholders, directors, bidders) and thereby determine which stakeholders are likely to win or lose under different corporate rules and practices.

Whether applying game theory can identify which designs of corporate rules and governance structures produce more efficient or equitable outcomes, and how those rules should be structured to align incentives.

Whether game-theoretic analysis can improve understanding and prediction of strategic dynamics in corporate transactions and disputes (such as negotiations, takeovers, and litigation) and the resulting distributional consequences among parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92columlrev997!!ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE USE OF OPEN TERMS IN CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: incentive design and principal–agent problems in legal arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores strategic interactions among corporate actors (e.g., managers, directors, shareholders) through game-theoretic lenses, while Paper B analyzes how contracts with open terms and gain-sharing allocate incentives between principals and agents and the resulting performance implications.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and the use of sharing arrangements under uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper B shows that open terms and sharing arrangements align individual and joint risk under uncertainty, and Paper A, via game-theoretic perspectives on corporate behavior, addresses how legal and contractual structures distribute risk and shape parties' choices under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: how legal standards and enforcement should respond to strategic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper B proposes a 'joint maximization' benchmark (akin to negligence) for reviewing performance under open terms, and Paper A discusses how game-theoretic reasoning can guide courts and regulators in crafting enforcement rules that account for strategic responses by corporate actors.

shared_topics.topic: the role of bargaining, testing, and strategic withholding of information in contractual and corporate settings
shared_topics.justification: Paper B examines how open terms reduce incentives to test or haggle over contingencies, and Paper A applies game theory to analyze bargaining, information revelation, and strategic withholding among corporate parties and counterparties.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Renegotiation Design by Contract

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts' willingness to grant specific performance, injunctions for output/requirements contracts, and contractual penalty clauses function as mechanism components to guarantee investments; Paper B discusses, using game-theoretic reasoning, how legal remedies and doctrinal choices operate as strategic instruments that alter payoffs and equilibrium behavior in corporate disputes and contracting.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the renegotiation/holdup problem within the incomplete-contracts literature and Property Rights Theory to explain vertical integration and ownership choices; Paper B applies game-theoretic frameworks to corporate law topics, including how transaction costs, incomplete contracts, and strategic interaction influence organizational form, control allocation, and corporate governance outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether particular contract doctrines (like Hadley) materially shape commercial life or are merely one of many forces interacting with larger economic conditions, and Paper B evaluates how corporate-law institutions influence firm behavior and market results through strategic interactions modeled by game theory.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats judges as decision agents who employ practical reason and decision procedures to resolve competing values in contract disputes, and Paper B discusses (via game-theoretic lenses) how courts, regulators, and corporate decisionmakers strategically resolve conflicts and shape institutional outcomes in corporate settings.

shared_topics.topic: how theoretical models influence winners and losers in litigation and doctrine

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative conclusions about how the state should facilitate coordination and reform contract regulation in consumer markets, and Paper B frames corporate-law questions through game theory to evaluate which legal rules produce just or efficient winners and losers, informing policy choices.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Allocating the Risk of the Unforeseen, Subsurface and Latent Conditions in Construction Contracts: Is There Room for the Common Law?
