papers.node_id: 71fordhamlrev799!!SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE
papers.abstract:
I. Neither Holy Nor Roman: Plain Meaning and the Parol Evidence Rule(s)
Underlying the dreaded parol evidence ruleis the notion that words have plain meanings. The list of contracts authorities that havedenied or derided the concept of plain meaning is long, very long,and Professor Margaret Kniffin, in her revision of the chapter of Corbin On Contracts dealing with interpretation, created a twenty-five page section attacking the concept and stating that the judicial trend is to abandon it.Yet Professor Kniffin was too honest a scholar not to admit an important truth. Buried in the midst of this section is one sentence that gives the game away: "the "plain meaning rule' is adhered to by a majority of the jurisdictions in the United States."
Professor Arthur L. Corbin discussed the plain meaning rule in his chapter on interpretation,and argued that the parol evidence rule had nothing to do with interpretation.Corbin's reasoning ran as follows: the parol evidence rule means only that, if the parties agree that a written document will be the exclusive contract between them, they necessarily terminate and supersede any earlier agreements, whether written or oral.While this later "integration" bars evidence of earlier agreements, which are no longer valid, it does not bar extrinsic evidence of its own meaning, even if that interpretation is different from the "plain meaning."Corbin's position is fullysupported by other distinguished writers, including Allan Farnsworthand John Murray,as well as by the more recent editions of Williston's treatise.The only problem with this approach is that stated by Professor Perillo,
The logic of this dichotomy is unassailable, so is its impracticality. The very same words offered as an additional term that are rejected because the court deems the writing to be a total integration, can be offered as an aid to interpretation of an ambiguous written term. Able courts look at both proffers of evidence as governed by the "parol evidence rule."
Thus, the parol evidence rule and the plain meaning rule are conjoined like Siamese twins. Even though many academics and more than a few judges have tried to separate them, the bulk of the legal profession views them as permanently intertwined.
would like to examine these two concepts, and try to understand why courts and lawyers stick to them. Of course, not all their defenders are thoughtless. Recent scholarship, particularly by law and economics types, has shown considerable support for plain meaning and for a rigid parol evidence rule. Again, however, figuring out the reasons for such support can help us to decide if it is time for academics to catch up with practitioners, or vice versa.
The concept of plain meaning, while it has some variations, is pretty straightforward. Most courts that find plain meaning to exist do not spend a lot of time explaining what they mean by it, even in odd situations such as that in the famous Pacific Gas and Electric Co. v. G. W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.,where the trial court and theintermediate appellate court found different - and conflicting - plain meanings.
In contrast, the parol evidence rule has many variations. In fact, like that political anachronism, the Holy Roman Empire, the parol evidence rule fits none of the words in its name: it is not limited to parol - that is, oral - testimony, it is not evidentiary, and it is not really a rule. Even its most basic rationale is strongly disputed: is it an adjunct to the Statute of Frauds, designed to discourage self-serving oral testimony, or does it merely express a presumption that the last statement of the parties' words supersedes what came before, a presumption that may easily be displaced by other evidence, oral or written? There have been extravagances on both sides (assuming there are only two) of the issues. Even assuming that we can figure out how to state the parol evidence rule(s), we then need to ask why we have them and how they fit with the presence or absence of a concept of plain meaning. Perhaps if we knew more about the underlying rationales suggested for various versions of the rule, and, even more interesting, the psychology of those who support one position or another, we might be better able to decide what rules we want, and why.
The inquiry involves psychology, philosophy and politics, as well as the more mundane aspects of contract interpretation. The questions raised by both the parol evidence and plain meaning rules mirror political and social views having nothing to do with contract interpretation. The rationale is intimately connected with an underlying psychology in which certainty and stability battle with party autonomy and intent. On the side of strong reliance on the written document there is a range of emotional and instrumental justifications. A strict parol evidence rule combined with a strong view of plain meaning gives some people psychic comfort as well as predictive stability. It is reassuring to believe that the words on a page provide order, and order is unquestionably comforting.
Writers on semantics, linguistics, philosophy generally, and literary criticism have all spent a lot of time on meaning in general and plain meaning in particular, but the eyes of lawyers and judges glaze over when these discussions are mentioned. While legal writers have oftendebated issues of intent, particularly in matters of constitutional and statutory interpretation, with the exception of H.L.A. Hartand Lon Fuller,few have gone very deeply into the meaning of plain meaning.
In its most rigid form, the plain meaning rule bars extrinsic evidence unless the word is ambiguous on its face. The flaw in plain meaning is, of course, the notion of a latent ambiguity. Everyone concedes that such things exist, and a few piquant examples are often cited, for example, In re Soper's Estate,a Minnesota case in which a man had bought a life insurance policy payable to his "wife." "Wife" is a pretty clear word, and the man had only one wife, but extrinsic evidence showed that he had deserted her and pretended suicide, and was living with another woman when he entered into the insurance contract. The court concluded that he intended to make the second woman his beneficiary, despite the fact that she was not legally his "wife" and another woman was. Similarly, in Raffles v. Wichelhaus,the famous case of the two ships Peerless, the name of the ship on which the cotton was to arrive was clear on the face of the contract, and the existence of another ship also named Peerlessbecame apparent only by extrinsic evidence. Holmes tried to fit Raffles into his objective theory of interpretation because it involved a name,and perhaps he could have fitted Soper in as well, but it is not hard to find similar ambiguities involving ordinary words. Consider a contract providing that a certain act must be done "in the same month" as a demand. The complaint states that a demand was made on June 3 and that the act was performed on June 30, but payment was not made. Extrinsic evidence might show, however, that months of the Islamic or Jewish calendar were intended and that the day corresponding to June 3 was in a different month from the day corresponding to June 30.
A rather homey illustration of latent ambiguity can be found on a cereal box. On the nutrition information panel of the side of Shredded Wheat boxes is a notice reading "Not a low calorie food." This is surprising because all unsweetened dry cereals have about 100 calories per ounce of weight. However, Shredded Wheat is a fairly dense cereal, so a cup of it weighs considerably more than a cup of acereal such as Puffed Wheat, which is mostly air. The densest cereal, Grape Nuts, has about the same number of calories by weight as Puffed Wheat, but a cup of it weighs about ten times as much and has more than ten times as many calories.Is it a higher calorie cereal? Because we do not eat air, we can make a strong argument that the two cereals have the same amount of calories, but since we tend to eat a bowlful at breakfast we can also argue the opposite.Although "not a low calorie food" seems perfectly understandable on its face, the phrase is actually filled with ambiguity, ambiguity that becomes apparent only with the aid of extrinsic evidence of weight, volume and eating habits.
While a rigid plain meaning rule is a poor reason for restrictions on extrinsic evidence, one can add a genuine instrumental justification: strict rules protect against the fear that the more we allow the words of a contract to be challenged in the name of the parties' actual intent, the more we produce disorder or even chaos, waiting to be exploited by unscrupulous litigants who demand a bonus to do what they already promised to do. This, in turn, leads to a different form of comfort. Strict rules satisfy those who feel that, if you learn the rules and follow them, you should be assured that they will be applied firmly and without exception, even if this produces a result that appears unfair in the short run. According to this view, fairness is whatever result the rules produce, because in the long run predictability and invariance usually make for just results.
More "liberal" rules give a different sort of comfort, one in which justice appears to trump formalism,although even among those who dislike a strict parol evidence rule, there are many who still want to protect contract stability. While they reject a rigid exclusion of extrinsic evidence, they would, in fact, admit the evidence only if the judge found it "reasonably susceptible" of the meaning for which it was offered, thus allowing a judge to reject it on the merits with relative ease. Others find this an unacceptable compromise with formalism, because it still prefers the written word to the proffered evidence of the parties' intent. The partisans of various positions areoften uncompromising in their advocacy of a position- evidence, in my view, of the deeply emotional component of the issue.
What we call the parol evidence rule is better thought of as a spectrum. Some courts, old and new, presume that almost all documents, however skimpy or haphazard, represent the final word.Others will not go that far, but still apply Williston's famous "four corners rule" strictly, rejecting extrinsic evidence unless questions of integration and ambiguity of meaning are patent on the face of the writing.Other courts, although they recite the four corners approach, actually require the facial uncertainty to be much less palpable, and admit extrinsic evidence more readily.Still others allow extrinsic evidence to show non-integration and ambiguity themselves,and some even go as far as the Restatement (Second) ofContracts and admit evidence to show meaning without regard to ambiguity.Often lower courts stick to older, more rigid rules and ignore, or at least do not follow, liberalizing cases from their state's supreme court.
The parol evidence rule serves a legitimate end. We enter into written contracts to avoid disputes in the future, and if every contract were simply the beginning point in a testimonial battle, we would gain little by writing things down. But the written word is not as infallible a guide as some think, and people often do not read agreements and often do believe themselves protected when they are told "don't worry about that clause."A detailed survey will reveal countless variations around the country and remarkable gradations of what seem to be fixed rules, even within a given jurisdiction. And even the most rigorous versions of the rule admit many exceptions and allow oral proof of matters such as oral conditions,evidence of fraud or mistake,and collateral agreements.
So, instead of a parol evidence "rule," there is a continuum of many different approaches, all using the same name and often using the same words. In 1967 the young Joe Perillo joined Professor John D. Calamari to complain that
There is no uniform parol evidence rule. Rather, there are at least two rather dissimilar rules which, for convenience, may be denominated the Corbin Rule and the Williston Rule. In view of the confusion engendered by having two contradictory rules expressed in the same terminology, it is remarkable that a few states have shown a degree of consistency. New York, despite some inconsistent cases, generally maintains a rigorously Willistonian approach. Rhode Island seems recently to have adopted the Corbin approach with a Willistonian touch … . Some states, such as Connecticut, reach results consistent with Corbin's test, while utilizing the most varied reasoning. Perhaps most states are consistently erratic. Such is the confusion that in any state a decision may be reached which is ludicrous in result and analysis, or sensible in result but strained in analysis.
More than thirty years later, the even younger Eric Posner, after sketching out what he called the "hard-PER" (roughly the Williston, four-corners, plain meaning approach) and the "soft-PER" (roughly that of Corbin and the Second Restatement of Contracts),cautioned his readers that they
Should, for now, understand that the reality is more complex than the stylized versions of the parol evidence rule developed for the purpose of analysis. Although some jurisdictions use something like the hard-PER, while other jurisdictions use something like the soft-PER, many jurisdictions take different and often conflicting approaches to the treatment of extrinsic evidence. In some jurisdictions, for example, the courts adopt a hard attitude toward the incompleteness exception, while taking a soft attitude toward the ambiguity exception. In other jurisdictions, the courts do the opposite … . In addition, within a single jurisdiction, the parol evidence rule may vary considerably over time… . In virtually every jurisdiction, one finds irreconcilable cases, frequent changes in doctrine, confusion, and cries of despair.
In trying to make sense of these variations we must ask why a given court chooses a particular form of the parol evidence rule. Often the answer appears to be nothing more than ignorance or sloppiness, but at other times the motivation of the courts is discernible and worthdiscussing. I will attempt to make some sense by looking at a number of way-stations along the continuum.

questions.question: Whether judges' and practitioners' reliance on the plain text of written agreements (and exclusion of extrinsic evidence) is primarily driven by a preference for certainty, predictability, and protection against opportunism versus a desire to enforce the parties' actual intent.
What explains cross-jurisdictional and temporal variation in how readily courts admit extrinsic evidence to interpret, supplement, or supplant a written agreement?
How do more rigid versus more liberal rules about admitting extrinsic evidence affect contract stability, fairness, and the likelihood of opportunistic or costly litigation?

papers.node_id: 2004wislrev379!!SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: BACKGROUND RULES, INCOMPLETENESS, AND INTERVENTION
papers.abstract:
In her article, Taxonomy for Justifying Legal Intervention in an Imperfect World,Professor Juliet Kostritsky offers a careful and comprehensive overview of the current contract law literature regarding whether and when courts should intervene to imply a term into an incomplete contract.
Kostritsky's article offers a thorough tour of the usual arguments relating to when courts should (or why courts should not) imply terms into contracts. Her article discusses information deficits regarding the future,asymmetries of information,extralegal means of enforcement,bounded rationality,and the various approaches to default rules (for example, majoritarian, efficient, and information-forcing).As the author properly points out, many of these discussions, particularly recent "new formalist" discussions, too often give insufficient attention to the problem of controlling for strategic and opportunistic behavior.
As the article indicates, opportunistic behavior becomes a significant problem when combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs.Without that combination of factors, parties would either have relatively little to lose, or could respond to the problem of opportunistic behavior by exit on one hand or by detailed contractual terms and litigation on the other.
In this commentary, I will focus on some details on the margin of Kostritsky's analysis. First, I will analyze more closely some of the potentially confusing concepts in the literature. Second, I will consider the possible connections between her discussion and the theme of this Symposium, Freedom from Contract.
In considering the topic of incomplete contracts there is, as Kostritsky observes,some ambiguity regarding the meaning of "incomplete contract," and much of the literature seems to reach one conclusion or another regarding the proper response to "incompleteness" by focusing on only some of the different ways in which a contract might be said to be incomplete.
When a certain potential set of circumstances is not mentioned in a contract (for example, in a service contract, the death or disability of the person who would be providing the service; or in a sale of goods, a war, labor strike, or government regulation that would significantly raise theproducer's costs), there are many reasons why the matter might not be mentioned. One or both parties may have intended the general language of the contract ("X will perform" or "the cost will be $ 1000") to cover all possibilities, including these extreme cases;the extreme possibility may not have occurred to one or both parties; or one or both parties might have calculated that the cost of coming to agreement on the consequences of this low-probability event was greater than any resulting benefit.
One can also speak of "missing terms" in the sense of terms the parties might have included, except for problems about imperfect information, difficulties of proof, or unintended consequences.Thus, it might be better in a sale of goods for the price to reflect the marginal cost of production,but it would be easy to lie about such matters and hard to prove that there was deception;or an employer might want pay to reflect an employee's ability or work habits,
As Kostritsky indicates, the arguments for nonintervention are likely far stronger for some of the above variations of "incompleteness" than for others. For example, courts can refuse to intervene where the parties have made a considered decision not to make price conditioned on market demand because of fear that the buyer might lie about the state of demand.
While this broad meaning of "incompleteness" makes sense in the context of the economic analysis from which it arose, its sometimes sharp contrast to the conventional understanding of the term should be kept in mind. The rhetoric of "incompleteness" seems already to justify intervention: to "fill in" what the parties intended all along but neglected to write down, or what they should have included as a matter of basic fairness. Of course, within the economic literature, as Kostritsky makes clear, the trend or weight of the arguments of late seems to be against such interventions,but one should still note the way that the terminology chosen might sway a judge (or a law student) to a contrary conclusion.
Another important ambiguity in the discussion is the meaning of "intervention." The primary focus of that concept in the context ofcontract law (and, arguably, the primary focus of Kostritsky's discussion) are situations where a court is responding to an individual dispute arising from a single contract, and deciding whether to imply a term into that contract (and that contract alone). However, as Kostritsky has made clear, she is using that term in the broader meaning sometimes found in the law and economics literature, where "intervention" applies to any term or obligation not found in a contract's express language, including terms and obligations (for example, formation and remedial rules) that apply to all contracts and were established or promulgated far in advance of the agreements in which they are said to "intervene."Thus, the mandatory or default rules provided by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (the "Code"), a law codified as a statute in all states other than Louisiana,Indeed, all the rules provided by contract law governing formation, interpretation, performance, and remedies (again, including those terms that the parties can contract around) would be "interventions" in this sense, as these rules are provided by the legal system rather than by the parties themselves. The broader use of "intervention" here has its merits, but one must, of course, keep in mind that the sort of arguments that might justify creating or modifying a general formation, performance, interpretation, or remedial rule (applied only to contracts entered after the new rule has been announced) inevitably will vary from the sort of arguments that would justify inserting a term into an agreement already entered. Kostritsky's article does not always sufficiently distinguish the different kinds of "intervention," and how the justificatory arguments might vary from context to context; this may be a path to consider when the insights of her article are elaborated in future works.
This broader understanding of "intervention" also leads to a different question.At one point, Kostritsky discusses how courts (andthe Restatement (Second) of Contracts) changed prior law to make offers to enter unilateral contracts irrevocable after the offeree had begun performance.In such a situation, the offeree may have substantial sunk costs that have no value outside the potential transaction with the offeror, should the offer be withdrawn.One might raise a question here about the extent to which this example fits Kostritsky's criteria well: there are (frequently) sunk costs, but what of "bounded rationality" or uncertainty about behavior, or the related point of difficulty in responding through detailed contracts? In what sense is the rationality of potential contractors entering unilateral contracts bounded?Entering such contracts, parties may be uncertain about the likelihood that the other party will perform at all or will act opportunistically, and parties may generally be unduly optimistic (that contracts will be fully performed, or, in this case, that offers for contracts will not be withdrawn after performance has begun). However, this view of "bounded rationality" or uncertainty seems to sweep too broadly. Cases of uncertainty or undue optimism would likely apply to nearly all the agreements entered where the parties do not already know one another well from past transactions, or where there is no well-established reputation for performance. With regard to the ability to contract on the matter, there are a number of ways to avoid the problem of withdrawn offers, most of them not terribly complicated: for example, seeking an option contract, keeping the offer open through consideration, or requesting that the offer be of a form acceptable through mere assent rather than only through performance.One mightmake a similar point about the construction subcontracting cases,where general contractors could specify that submission of a bid will be treated as binding assent, with the subcontractor's obligation to perform being conditioned on the general contractor's being awarded the contract.
Kostritsky's primary response appears to be that even if the difficulties here can be circumvented by contractual language, the cost of individual contracting is inefficiently high, especially since nearly all parties in these situations face the same challenge of opportunism and behavioral uncertainty, and the challenge can be faced by a law-imposed (default) term.This, however, raises a different inquiry.
The modern rule for unilateral contracts - making offers irrevocable after performance begins - is an "intervention" only in the broad sense, discussed earlier, that all rules not set by the express terms of the parties' contract are "interventions."From the perspective of parties contracting, the modern rule, like the "classical rule" (offers can be withdrawn until performance is complete) before it, simply is the background law - perhaps immutable, or perhaps a default subject to contracting around, but in any event not an express choice of the parties.This point connects with the basic theme of this Symposium: the freedom from contract. Freedom from contract is the understanding that it is a central aspect of "the freedom of contract" that one is bound to the extent - and only to the extent - that one has voluntarily undertaken such obligations. If one knows that by making an offer for a unilateral contract one may be bound to keep that offer open once an offeree starts performance, then it is a relatively simple matter to avoid that level of contractual obligation: do not make the offer. There is arguably only a problem with the "freedom from contract" if an obligation will be imposed contrary to one's clear choice, or if one is likely unknowingly to "blunder into" contractual (or precontractual) obligation.
One might argue that the precontractual liability created by the rule keeping unilateral contract offers open is a kind of imposition, creating a further limit on the freedom of parties, but it should be noted that whatever constraint is present is not significantly greater than that present for bilateral contracts. In fact, in many ways the constraint andimposition is lesser. When one makes an offer for a bilateral contract and the other party begins performance, in most circumstances that performance would not merely make the offer irrevocable, it would be treated as an acceptance of the offer, creating full contractual liability.
Promissory estoppelmay be a more complicated issue for "freedom from contract." On one hand, the rule of promissory estoppel purports to be objective, and to give parties advance warning that certain actions will make them liable. On the other hand, the test for liability is not set by bright-line rules, but instead involves difficult judgments, for example, about whether reliance on a promise was "reasonable" and whether injustice could only be avoided by enforcement of the promise.A comparable argument might be raised regarding Kostritsky's proposed standard that courts should imply terms into contracts where it would increase welfare, taking into account all relevant concerns (including the prevention of opportunistic behavior).This is a standard that if clearly announced by a legislature or court would give some level of notice to potential contractors, but the uncertainty in its application might mean that even careful parties might have contractual liability imposed upon them that they did not expect and to which they did not consent. This danger need not be dispositive on the merit of Kostritsky's proposal; the proposal might well have significant benefits that clearly outweigh any harms caused through imposed liability, but such potential "freedom from contract" harms should be clearly considered in evaluating the proposal.
"Freedom from contract" (or "freedom not to contract") raises the issue of consent, already a troubling question in a modern era of contracting practice involving long standard-form documents, click-through agreements, and terms sent with the shipment of goods already paid for.However, it is important to recognize that the type of consent issues raised either by contractual rules that transacting parties may not knowor by express contractual terms rarely read, are different in kind from the consent issues raised by contractual terms imposed only after the fact, at the time of litigation. This observation brings the argument back to its earlier point - that the arguments necessary to justify "intervention" standards imposed as default rules that parties can contract around may be quite different from the arguments necessary to justify "intervention" standards imposed after the fact and without giving the parties the opportunity to contract around them.
One final point: while Kostritsky, in discussing her proposal, most often refers to the gains or losses of the parties (or the potential parties) from a contract,she also refers more generally to the issue of "maximizing social wealth"- the gains and losses of the parties combined with those created for the rest of society. It may be, for example, that two potentially contracting parties would gain roughly the same from entering a contract as from using the same resources in some other way, but that the transaction in question might benefit or harm society (third parties) in some significant way. There may even be certain kinds of immoral activityin the formation or performance of an agreement that do not reduce the joint gains from a transaction but that would deter other parties from entering transactions. Economic analysts, of course, have the resources to include all such "externalities" in their analysis. However, as with consequentialist analyses generally, it is one thing to be able to speak in abstract terms about the costs and benefits of an activity, and quite another actually to do the calculations. One has doubts about anyone who claims to know, with even rough confidence, what the long-term social costs and benefits are of, for example, enforcing (or not enforcing) surrogacy agreements, cohabitation agreements, same-sex partner parenting agreements, or divorce-focused premarital agreements, just to name four examples fromfamily law, where the extent of enforceability of certain contracts is highly contested.
In general, it might be useful to hear more about how Kostritsky's formula would work in practice, though this might, understandably, be left for the next article.The author has already mentioned the connection between preventing opportunistic behavior and the constraint of good faith in exclusive dealing contracts (including requirement and output contracts).One might also add that the Code's rules on good faith used to constrain the enforcement of modification agreements likely serve a similar purpose.However, it would be valuable, in due course, to see examples that extend beyond the default rules already imposed by current legislation or established common law.
Kostritsky has shown us how expansive and difficult is the terrain of "incomplete contracts," and how partial - perhaps, inevitably partial - are some of the recent scholarly responses to the problem. In particular, some of the recent discussions have not given sufficient attention to the problems parties have in dealing with possible opportunism.
At the same time, if we are to think clearly about issues of "intervention" and "freedom from contract," we need to differentiate between background rules and rules imposed at the point of litigation, and we need to distinguish standards that give clear notice and those that, even if promulgated in advance, are so uncertain in their application that parties are unable to coordinate their activities in those rules' shadow. When evaluating an all-things-considered utilitarian formula like the one suggested by Kostritsky, we should be cautious because of the uncertainties in the application of such formulas - uncertainties that raise issues both of possible misapplication and also of "freedom from contract."

questions.question: Whether and when courts or the legal system should imply terms into contracts that are silent on certain contingencies in order to increase overall welfare, taking into account opportunistic behavior, information asymmetries, bounded rationality, sunk costs, and transaction costs.

How the form and timing of legal intervention - pre-announced background or default rules versus after-the-fact judicial implication in individual disputes - affect parties' ability to anticipate, avoid, or contract around obligations and thus their freedom to contract.

To what extent standards-based, uncertain interventions (rules whose application is indeterminate) create hidden or imposed contractual liabilities that undermine consent, and how the risk of such harms should be weighed against the potential social-welfare benefits of intervention.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior interacting with bounded rationality and sunk costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how opportunism combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs can justify courts implying terms or creating defaults to deter strategic behavior; Paper B documents how strategic advantage (e.g., repeat players, downhill plaintiffs) and opportunistic tactics shape which contract disputes reach litigation and their outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background/default legal rules versus case-by-case judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes between background/default rules (e.g., UCC defaults, irrevocability of unilateral offers) and after-the-fact implication of terms and asks when each form of intervention is justified; Paper B likewise interrogates whether courts and doctrine (including default frameworks) or private ordering best resolve contract problems, observing how doctrinal shifts affect real-world contracting and litigation patterns.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries between parties (repeat-players, one-shotters, uphill/downhill dynamics)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses information asymmetries and enforcement capacity that make some parties vulnerable to opportunism and thus potentially justify intervention; Paper B empirically analyzes repeat-player vs one-shotter and uphill vs downhill configurations, showing how relative power and experience predict litigation success and access to remedies.

shared_topics.topic: indeterminacy of doctrinal standards and the consequences for consent and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about vague all-things-considered utilitarian standards and doctrines like promissory estoppel producing uncertain liability that may impinge on 'freedom from contract'; Paper B emphasizes the prevalence of qualitative, hard-to-predict rules in contract law and how that uncertainty shapes which disputes are litigated and how they resolve.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, litigation costs, and reliance on private ordering instead of courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that high individual contracting costs and shared problems of opportunism can make law-imposed defaults more efficient than bespoke contracting; Paper B highlights the high costs of litigation and the tendency of parties to resolve most contract disputes through negotiation, settlement, or other nonlitigious mechanisms rather than in court.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93scallrev1323!!ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CASE AGAINST EQUITY IN AMERICAN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: proper scope of judicial intervention versus enforcement of parties' ex ante agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that ex post equitable doctrines (penalty rule, forfeiture, just compensation) improperly let courts override parties' ex ante intentions and thus undermine personal sovereignty; Paper B analyzes when courts should imply terms or intervene in incomplete contracts, weighing the justificatory force of intervention against the value of freedom from contract and the parties' expectations.

shared_topics.topic: default/background rules versus party autonomy (freedom from contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the incorporation of ex post doctrines into black‑letter law as creating background constraints that force parties away from their preferred contracting strategies; Paper B draws a sharp distinction between background/default rules (e.g., UCC rules, irrevocability of unilateral offers) and after‑the‑fact judicial implication, exploring how such background rules affect notice, the ability to contract around terms, and the norm of freedom from contract.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, bounded rationality, and their role in justifying (or rejecting) implied terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how anti‑opportunism rationales have been used to expand ex post doctrines and can conflict with respect for ex ante bargains, producing perverse incentives for strategic litigation; Paper B places opportunistic behavior together with bounded rationality and sunk costs at the center of the argument for when courts or default rules should fill gaps in incomplete contracts.

shared_topics.topic: doctrines that alter remedial expectations (liquidated damages/penalty, forfeiture, promissory estoppel, unilateral‑offer irrevocability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on remedial doctrines (penalty doctrine, just compensation, doctrines avoiding forfeiture) and argues they wrongly restrict parties' remedial choices; Paper B examines remedial and precontractual doctrines (promissory estoppel, the rule making unilateral offers irrevocable after performance begins, and implied remedial terms), assessing their effects on parties' incentives and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: historical origins and doctrinal development as a basis for evaluating contemporary contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces ex post equitable doctrines back to courts of equity and to the replacement of penal bonds by executory contracts as the historical explanation for why such doctrines have outlived their original purpose; Paper B references doctrinal changes (e.g., Restatement and modern unilateral‑contract rules) and cautions about terminological and historical shifts that influence whether interventions are justified today.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between obligational incompleteness and contingency (state-contingent) incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and centers its analysis on the two meanings of 'incomplete contract'—obligational gaps (missing specified obligations/remedies) versus contingently incomplete contracts (insufficient state-contingency that leaves gains unrealized)—and shows how legal rules differently address each. Paper B likewise interrogates the ambiguity of 'incompleteness,' cataloguing missing terms, unanticipated contingencies, and parties' reasons for omission, and stresses that these different senses have different implications for intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the choice and design of default/background legal rules versus after‑the‑fact judicial implication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how the selection of obligational default rules (and when rules are immutable) shapes parties' incentives to contract around defaults and affects efficiency. Paper B distinguishes background statutory/common‑law rules from ad hoc terms implied at litigation, analyzing how justificatory standards and effects differ when the legal rule is a pre‑existing background rule versus a post‑hoc intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the role of strategic/opportunistic behavior, asymmetric information, and transaction costs in shaping contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models strategic bargaining, asymmetric information, market power, and even slight transaction costs to show how these factors can generate inefficiencies and multiple equilibria that depend on the default rule. Paper B focuses on opportunistic behavior combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs as central problems motivating (or cautioning against) judicial intervention and default rule design.

shared_topics.topic: remedial doctrines and state‑contingent remedies as mechanisms to fill contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts set breach damages, use liquidated damages, and deploy excuse doctrines (impossibility/impracticability) or zero damages to create state‑contingent obligations that address both obligational and contingency incompleteness. Paper B engages with remedial doctrines (promissory estoppel, the irrevocability of unilateral offers, Code remedies) and examines how these background remedial rules affect parties' exposure and contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between promoting efficient contracting via defaults and protecting parties' freedom/notice (freedom from contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that defaults chosen to mimic the hypothetical frictionless contract can fail under asymmetric information and transaction costs, making selection of efficient defaults fraught. Paper B raises 'freedom from contract' and notice concerns, warning that uncertain or after‑the‑fact standards can impose unanticipated liabilities and thus that interference must be weighed against consent and the parties' ability to contract around rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT

shared_topics.topic: when courts should excuse performance or imply terms in response to unexpected or omitted contingencies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a shared-assumption test as a ground for judicial relief (impossibility/impracticability/frustration) when parties tacitly assumed a circumstance, while Paper B analyzes the broader criteria and justifications for judicial or statutory 'intervention' to imply terms into incomplete contracts (including default rules like the UCC, promissory estoppel, and unilateral-contract doctrines).

shared_topics.topic: tacit assumptions and implicit (background) terms as part of the contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally treats tacit assumptions as elements of the contract that can justify excuse, and Paper B treats 'missing terms' and background rules as the category of implicit obligations courts or the law may supply, discussing different reasons why terms are omitted and when to fill gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the role of foreseeability versus parties' assumptions in assessing excuse or intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that foreseeability is at best an index and not the determinative test—what matters is the parties' tacit assumption—while Paper B engages with bounded rationality and foreseeability as factors shaping whether courts should impose default terms or intervene.

shared_topics.topic: the epistemic difficulty of courts determining parties' intentions and the verifiability of implied-term tests
shared_topics.justification: Paper A rebuts critiques that courts cannot reliably determine tacit assumptions and compares it to other routine common-law fact-finding, whereas Paper B expresses caution about uncertain, hard-to-apply utilitarian standards and the practical limits of calculating social costs and giving parties clear notice.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' sophistication, opportunism, and sunk costs affect gaps, assumptions, and the need for intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that sophistication affects whether parties tacitly assume low-probability events and thus the appropriateness of excuse, and Paper B focuses on opportunistic behavior combined with bounded rationality and sunk costs as central reasons courts or legislatures might adopt background/default rules to prevent opportunism.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BLACK HOLE APPARITIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts should imply terms or otherwise 'intervene' into agreements and balances that against 'freedom from contract,' while Paper B critiques and proposes doctrinal changes about how courts should interpret (or refrain from interpreting) standardized boilerplate, focusing on the consequences of judicially imposed meanings.

shared_topics.topic: meaning and treatment of standardized or missing terms (boilerplate and incompleteness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a taxonomy of 'incomplete contracts' and explores why terms are missing and when courts should fill gaps, and Paper B studies 'contractual black holes'—boilerplate provisions emptied of meaning—and how doctrine should treat such standardized, potentially meaningless clauses.

shared_topics.topic: role and design of background/default rules in shaping contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes background rules (e.g., UCC defaults, unilateral-offer rules, promissory estoppel) and how they function as interventions parties can contract around, while Paper B considers how judicial interpretation of background boilerplate can effectively become market-wide rules that prompt redrafting and doctrinal reform.

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing genuine gaps or ambiguity from superficially similar phenomena
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses multiple conceptions of 'incompleteness' and the need to distinguish cases where nonintervention is appropriate, and Paper B highlights the problem of 'black hole apparitions'—standardized provisions that resemble true black holes—arguing any remedy must reliably differentiate them.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty, externalities, and market-wide harms from judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that vague utilitarian standards and uncertain application of implied-term doctrines can impose unexpected liabilities and external costs, and Paper B documents how an adverse appellate interpretation (NML) produced large market inefficiencies and debates whether doctrinal reform or market adaptation is the right response.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PARADOX OF CONTRACTING IN MARKETS

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior as a justification for legal intervention or contractual design limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how opportunism (especially combined with sunk costs and bounded rationality) motivates courts or legislatures to imply terms or adopt default rules to curb strategic behavior, while Paper B identifies agency costs and opportunistic dynamics in thick markets as drivers of boilerplate stickiness and the need for collective or state remedies to prevent exploitative or inefficient contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between standardized background/default rules and bespoke contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the distinction between background/default legal rules and after-the-fact judicially-implied terms, arguing that defaults can be justified when individual contracting is too costly, and Paper B develops the paradox that standardization (boilerplate) yields production efficiencies but can degrade the quality of contract design, forcing a choice between scale and tailored incentives.

shared_topics.topic: collective action and coordination problems in producing and updating widely used contract terms, and the role of governance or the state
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses why default rules or statutory regimes (e.g., the UCC) may be imposed because individual parties face high contracting costs, and Paper B diagnoses a collective action problem in multilateral markets—arguing that private networks or state-facilitated 'spiders' are needed to coordinate revision and production of efficient contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: information problems (bounded rationality, asymmetry, and information overload) that undermine contractual completeness and effective consent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes bounded rationality and information asymmetries as sources of contract incompleteness and as limits on parties' ability to bargain around defaults, while Paper B highlights information overload in consumer markets and the inability of market forces to eliminate inefficient terms, showing how informational constraints shape both contract form and legal responses.

shared_topics.topic: standard-form/adhesion contracts, consent, notice, and the limits of private contracting for consumer protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about freedom from contract, consent under long form and click-through agreements, and the uncertainty of standards like promissory estoppel, whereas Paper B focuses on consumer boilerplate in multilateral markets and argues that regulatory or network-level interventions may be more effective than bilateral unconscionability doctrines at addressing exploitative standardized terms.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: THE DESIGN AND INTERPRETATION OF CONTRACTS: WHY COMPLEXITY MATTERS

shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of judicial or legislative intervention—distinguishing background/default rules from ad hoc judicial implication—and evaluate the normative and practical justifications for imposing terms versus leaving gaps to private ordering.

shared_topics.justification: Each paper treats opportunism as a key problem that interacts with incompleteness and bounded rationality, considering whether default rules, good-faith doctrines, or implied terms are appropriate tools to prevent advantage-taking and facilitate efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: how contract form (complexity or simplicity) should affect judicial interpretation and concerns about consent/freedom from contract
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that features of the contract — its degree of complexity or simplicity — convey information about parties' expectations and bargaining context, and thus bear on interpretive choices; they also share concern that uncertain or retroactive interventions can undermine parties' consent and 'freedom from contract.'

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Designing and Enforcing Preliminary Agreements

shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends enforcing contextual standards (good faith/best efforts) in staged negotiations and explains how courts can meaningfully police negotiated-but-incomplete deals; Paper B surveys the normative literature on implying terms, stresses the distinction between preannounced background rules and post‑hoc judicial insertions, and probes when intervention is justified.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques prior scholarship that reduces enforcement of preliminary agreements to protecting reliance investments and argues parties also use such agreements to deter value‑claiming and allocate risk against opportunism; Paper B repeatedly emphasizes opportunistic behavior combined with sunk costs and bounded rationality as a central problem motivating courts or default rules to curb post‑contract opportunism.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.

shared_topics.topic: design and justification of background/default rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on the normative foundations for background or default rules (e.g., UCC defaults) — Paper A analyzes when law-imposed background rules or defaults should substitute for explicit contractual language in light of opportunism and transaction costs, while Paper B interrogates what values (efficiency, fidelity, autonomy) can or cannot legitimately determine the content of those background rules.

shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of legal intervention into incomplete agreements — Paper A develops criteria (bounded rationality, sunk costs, opportunism) for implying terms or creating defaults, and Paper B criticizes attempts to ground post-hoc doctrinal fillings (remedies, implied obligations) in philosophical accounts of promising, arguing that such theories do not by themselves tell courts which terms to imply.

shared_topics.justification: Both express concern that vague or indeterminate legal standards (e.g., all-things-considered utilitarian tests or reasonableness inquiries in estoppel) can impose obligations contrary to parties' expectations; Paper A emphasizes freedom from contract and the need for clear notice of default rules, and Paper B discusses how autonomy/fidelity theories fail to resolve whether rules should be mandatory or opt-outable, thereby implicating consent and predictability.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that collective impact initiatives suffer from a lack of written agreements and advocates proactively memorializing responsibilities in contracts rather than relying on ad hoc practices; Paper B analyzes the distinction between background/default rules and post-hoc judicial implication, emphasizing when law should intervene versus when parties should be left to contract around defaults.
