papers.abstract:
Recent scholarship in the field of contract law has concentrated on contractual incompleteness -- that is, on the fact that except in the simplest and most basic transactions, contracting parties do not work out all of the relevant details and contingencies of their relationship at the outset. The reasons for incomplete contracts are varied. Sometimes parties deliberately leave terms unresolved, trusting future negotiations or social norms to fill in any problems that emerge. Other times, they leave terms unresolved without realizing they have done so, in part because they devote limited attention or resources to their negotiations and in part because contracts are expressed in ordinary language with all its ambiguities. In any event, it is routine for contracting parties not to focus on the fact that their agreements contain interpretative gaps until after a difference of opinion arises.
Most of this recent scholarship has focused on the question of what courts should do when faced with the problem of enforcing an apparently incomplete contract.For example, the literature on default rules addresses the question of what terms courts should apply when the contract is silent on a particular issue,the literature on the battle ofthe forms discusses what courts should do when the parties' writings disagree,and the literature on interpretation discusses how courts should determine whether either of these events has arisen.Focusing on such questions is sensible because when legal disputes arise over an issue of contractual interpretation, courts must decide what to do. On the other hand, focusing exclusively on such questions overlooks the facts that most contractual relationships do not result in disputes and that much of what lawyers do when designing contracts can be understood as managing the problem of incompleteness so that the parties can settle their affairs without resorting to costly litigation.
As I have argued elsewhere, such a court-centered perspective is characteristic of academic legal scholarship in general.Elite legal scholarship, for various historical and sociological reasons, usually tends to address a hypothetical audience of public lawmakers. Scholarship focusing on transactional design, in contrast, tends to be left to practitioner literature or to continuing legal education materials. Tellingly, even scholars coming from a law-and-economics perspective and those who strongly advocate freedom of contract tend largely to address themselves to public lawmakers.
In this Essay, I offer a somewhat different perspective on the topic of incomplete contracts, and in so doing, advocate, more generally, aparticular methodological approach to contracts scholarship and teaching. Specifically, I argue that legal scholars should focus more on addressing the contractual decisions of private lawmakers (that is, transactional lawyers and their clients) and less on the decisions of public lawmakers (that is, courts and legislatures). Stated alternatively, in the language of law-and-economics, scholars should pay greater attention to considerations of private transactional efficiency as opposed to larger issues of social efficiency.
There are two main reasons to advocate such an approach; one reason is pedagogical, and one is substantive. From a pedagogical standpoint, relatively few law students will become judges or legislators, but most will operate as private lawmakers in a contractual setting. Even those who specialize in litigation will regularly create private law in the course of negotiating settlements, which are far more common than litigated trials. To do a good job at private lawmaking, just as in public lawmaking, it is necessary to pay attention to policy considerations, such as efficiency and incentives. But teachers who emphasize policy issues only in the context of social planning fail to deliver this lesson.
There is also a substantive reason -- directly connected to the subject of this Symposium -- for advocating a transactional approach to contracts scholarship. The central lesson of the literature on incomplete contracts stresses that courts are not in a position to effectively supervise many of the things that the parties know and do in negotiating and performing their agreement; rather, the parties have more information than the courts. This informational discrepancy underlies the claim that freedom of contract is desirable from a consequentialist standpoint as opposed to just a libertarian one.
More specifically, from an economic viewpoint, maximizing contractual value requires drawing a proper balance among various decisional margins and trading off reduced efficiency along one margin to achieve enhanced efficiency along another. Richard Craswell's contribution to this Symposium indicates, for instance, that transactional efficiency depends not just on incentives for contractual performance, but also on the parties' investment in ex ante precautions.One should add that it also depends on mitigation behavior, allocation of contractual risks, acquisition and exchange of information, negotiation, as well as the parties' internal organizational arrangements. To make the appropriate tradeoffs among these various dimensions of efficiency, however, one must have detailed information about a variety of factors,such as relative elasticities of demand, expected returns on investment, the discount rates the parties attach to future costs and benefits, relative bargaining power, costs of renegotiation, and the like. But, most of this information is local knowledge; it varies among contracting parties and is much more likely to be accessible to them in the context of planning than to a court in the context of adjudicating a dispute or to a legislature in the context of policy making.
As a result, the economic analysis of contracts is likely to be more useful for private parties than for public officials, especially in a legal regime such as ours that both permits and relies on broad freedom of contract. Despite important limitations on private contracting, such as the doctrine of unconscionability, most contract law is private and there is much that private parties can do to implement their preferred arrangement. In the following Sections, I outline some of the main options and strategies available to private transactional planners in the context of incomplete contracts.

questions.question: How can private parties and their transactional advisors design contracts and related transactional practices to manage contractual incompleteness so as to minimize disputes and maximize joint (transactional) efficiency?

To what extent are private transactional planning and renegotiation strategies more effective than judicial/default-rule intervention at filling interpretive gaps and mitigating information asymmetries in incomplete contracts?

Should legal scholarship and teaching prioritize private transactional efficiency (training transactional lawyers and clients) over a court-centered/public-law focus when addressing the problem of contractual incompleteness, and what are the consequences of such a reorientation?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2019wislrev1109!!ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISING JUSTICE: CONTRACT (AS) SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY

shared_topics.topic: contracts as instruments for pursuing social or normative goals beyond mere exchange
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the concept of 'contract social responsibility' (KSR), showing how parties insert diversity, labor, and environmental norms into contracts; Paper B likewise treats contracts as vehicles of private policymaking, arguing that transactional drafting is a way for private parties to implement policy choices and governance within their relationships.

shared_topics.topic: incomplete or under-enforceable contract terms as a deliberate feature rather than a defect
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds that KSR often relies on a mix of enforceable and unenforceable promises and treats under-enforceability as enabling experimentation and relational governance; Paper B centrally analyzes why contracts are typically incomplete, why parties leave gaps or ambiguity, and how that incompleteness is managed rather than simply remedied by courts.

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting and private ordering versus judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates KSR within relational contract theory (drawing on Macaulay and Gilson) to explain how nonjudicial social enforcement works; Paper B argues that courts lack the information to supervise many contractual relations and therefore emphasizes private ordering, negotiation, and internal governance as the primary means of making contracts work.

shared_topics.topic: transactional drafting strategies and the practical/doctrinal limits of contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the substantive drafting choices, specificity, and doctrinal barriers that shape the efficacy of KSR clauses in practice; Paper B advocates for scholarship and practice that focus on transactional planners, outlining strategies lawyers and parties can use when designing contracts to manage incompleteness and allocate risks.

shared_topics.topic: using contract to fill governance gaps created by decentralized, multi-party production or organizational change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes 'vertical deconstruction' (global supply chains, gig economy, free agency) and presents KSR as a contractual response to governance gaps; Paper B explains that in complex, dispersed transactional settings parties possess localized information and organizational levers that make private contractual arrangements the primary mechanism for resolving governance and incentive problems.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev323!!SYMPOSIUM: TAXONOMY FOR JUSTIFYING LEGAL INTERVENTION IN AN IMPERFECT WORLD: WHAT TO DO WHEN PARTIES HAVE NOT ACHIEVED BARGAINS OR HAVE DRAFTED INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: TAXONOMY FOR JUSTIFYING LEGAL INTERVENTION IN AN IMPERFECT WORLD: WHAT TO DO WHEN PARTIES HAVE NOT ACHIEVED BARGAINS OR HAVE DRAFTED INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: when and how courts should supply terms or default rules for incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the methodological question of judicial intervention in incomplete contracts — Paper A critiques the court-centered focus of much scholarship and calls for attention to private transactional choices, while Paper B develops a model/taxonomy for when court-supplied terms or liability rules will increase welfare and be justified.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information asymmetries and local knowledge in adjudication versus private planning
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that parties often possess local, case-specific information that courts lack; Paper A argues this informational advantage supports private transactional efficiency and freedom of contract, and Paper B contrasts the comparative informational capacities of parties and courts when deciding whether intervention can improve outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: private transactional strategies and nonlegal sanctions as alternatives to judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with the array of private strategies (transactional drafting, organizational arrangements, commercial norms, settlement design) that can manage contractual incompleteness — Paper A urges scholarly focus on these private-lawyering options, and Paper B systematically compares nonlegal sanctions and private solutions to legal intervention.

shared_topics.topic: opportunism, sunk costs, and behavioral uncertainty as drivers of incompleteness and as justification for intervention or planning
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat behavioral uncertainty — especially opportunistic behavior and sunk-cost investments — as central reasons parties fail to write complete contracts and as key factors shaping whether parties should plan contractually or courts should supply protective rules (Paper B builds a behavioral-uncertainty model; Paper A highlights investments, ex ante precautions, and mitigation behavior as transaction-efficiency margins).

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between freedom of contract (private ordering) and welfare-enhancing legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the balance between respecting parties' contractual autonomy and imposing law-supplied terms to increase joint surplus — Paper A defends attention to private-law efficiency and freedom of contract, while Paper B evaluates when reducing the 'freedom not to contract' via judicial rules will or will not improve social and private welfare.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2678!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS: IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and the need for transactional planning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that incompleteness is pervasive and that scholars should focus on how private transactional planners (lawyers and parties) manage interpretive gaps ex ante; Paper B treats the classic ‘battle of the forms’ as a paradigmatic instance of such incompleteness and studies how parties actually behave in light of those gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the battle-of-the-forms (U.C.C. §2-207) as a central doctrinal problem
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly situates the battle-of-the-forms literature within the broader incomplete-contracts debate and cites it as a key doctrinal locus; Paper B is an empirical, doctrinal analysis of §2-207, its formation/terms problems, and its practical consequences.

shared_topics.topic: drafting strategies and form-language as tools to allocate risk and avoid dispute
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the array of private-law strategies transactional lawyers can use to manage incompleteness (allocation of risk, contract design, negotiation, organizational arrangements); Paper B documents and analyzes concrete drafting tactics (e.g., ‘magic’ conditional language, less one-sided boilerplate) firms use to influence which terms will govern.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of default rules/gap-fillers versus private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes a court-centered approach and argues courts lack local information, so private ordering and tailored transactional choices often better achieve efficiency than judicial defaulting; Paper B focuses on how §2-207 interacts with U.C.C. gap-fillers and reports market actors’ reliance on gap-fillers when forms conflict, highlighting both their importance and the uncertainty they create.

shared_topics.topic: empirical attention to how market practices and technology shape contract outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that local knowledge, bargaining power, and organizational choices determine how incompleteness is managed in practice and calls for scholarship attentive to actual private behavior; Paper B provides empirical interview evidence about firms’ real-world practices and the (limited) effects of technology and market shifts on how the battle of the forms operates.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46amjcompl485!!ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Limits of Commercial Contract Freedom: Under the UNIDROIT 'Restatement' and Danish Law

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and default rules for incomplete contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles and Danish law supply gap-filling rules (and argues the Principles can operate as a source of law to fill gaps), while Paper B surveys the literature on default rules and asks what courts should supply when contracts are silent, treating gap-filling as central to responses to contractual incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: judicial policing of unfair or 'surprising' standard terms (limits on freedom of contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares UNIDROIT's specific invalidity doctrines and Denmark's broad General Clause as tools for courts to police surprising terms, unfair exemptions, penalties and gross disparity; Paper B treats doctrines like unconscionability and judicial intervention as the legal limits that shape how parties and lawyers design contracts under incompleteness.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation and interpretation of standard form terms (battle of the forms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A details multi-factor tests Danish courts use to determine whether fine-print standard terms (e.g., NSAB) have been incorporated and how they are construed, and Paper B explicitly cites the 'battle of the forms' and interpretation literatures as central problems when parties' writings conflict or omit details.

shared_topics.topic: transactional drafting and private-law strategies to manage incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how parties draft standard terms, incorporation practices, and use of international instruments (UNIDROIT) to structure risk and expectations, while Paper B argues scholars should focus on transactional planners and catalogs strategies lawyers and parties use to minimize dispute costs and manage incomplete contracting.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and remedial regimes (liability, hardship, damages)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how UNIDROIT and Danish law allocate liability (fault vs. no-fault), police penalty/exemption clauses, and treat hardship/adaptation and remedies like specific performance or damages; Paper B highlights allocation of contractual risks, investments, renegotiation costs and remedial incentives as key variables that private parties must manage when contracts are incomplete.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev931!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: judicial role and limits in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the limits of courts in supervising and filling in the informationally rich, context-specific aspects of incomplete contracts and argues for attention to what courts can and should do; Paper B interrogates how courts (and their interaction with juries) have shaped interpretation doctrines and highlights confusion and inconsistency in judicial approaches to construing written contracts.

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and interpretive doctrines (default rules, parol evidence, plain-meaning)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the literature on default rules, the battle of the forms, and interpretation as mechanisms courts use to fill contractual gaps, while Paper B focuses on the parol evidence rule and the plain-meaning doctrine as central doctrinal tools that determine how gaps and ambiguous language are resolved.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive authority between private parties and public actors (judges, juries, legislatures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for privileging private transactional decisionmaking (contract drafting and bespoke solutions) over reliance on public-law remedies, and Paper B analyzes the consequences of allocating interpretive functions to the jury versus the judge and whether doctrinal efforts to steer issues away from juries are workable.

shared_topics.topic: transactional drafting and litigation-avoidance strategies to manage incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates that transactional lawyers and contracting parties use drafting, relational arrangements, and other ex ante planning to manage incompleteness and reduce costly adjudication; Paper B discusses how procedural and doctrinal choices (e.g., trying to keep interpretation out of juries' hands) reflect efforts to avoid problematic litigation outcomes and shape parties' incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: interpretive formalism versus contextual standards in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques a neoformalist push for sharper, more formal interpretive rules (e.g., reviving plain meaning, reducing trade usage/course of performance) and analyzes their practical consequences; Paper B treats interpretive doctrines (and default rules) as central to the question of what courts should do when contracts are incomplete and stresses how judicial interpretive choices affect transactional behavior.

shared_topics.topic: form contracts, the battle of the forms, and the operation of UCC Article 2 in real-world sales
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how Article 2 has to function across a marketplace dominated by standardized form contracts and warns that greater formalism would distort that practice; Paper B explicitly discusses the battle of the forms and how form-based and incomplete agreements create gaps that parties, transactional planners, and courts must manage.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of empirical/local information in shaping contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that legislative or doctrinal moves toward greater formalism should rest on empirical evidence about actual contracting practices and questions whether that evidence exists; Paper B emphasizes informational asymmetries and local, transaction-specific knowledge—arguing that courts and legislatures lack the detailed information parties possess, which affects how rules should be designed and used.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis and efficiency reasoning to justify rules and private planning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A observes that neoformalist proposals are driven by economic models claiming formal rules improve predictability and efficiency, and interrogates those claims in practice; Paper B adopts a law-and-economics perspective that prioritizes transactional (private) efficiency, detailing the economic tradeoffs parties face when designing contracts and how those tradeoffs inform drafting and planning strategies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev455!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE RELATIONAL CONSTITUTION OF REMEDY: CO-OPERATION AS THE IMPLICIT SECOND PRINCIPLE OF REMEDIES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE RELATIONAL CONSTITUTION OF REMEDY: CO-OPERATION AS THE IMPLICIT SECOND PRINCIPLE OF REMEDIES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role of cooperation and good-faith behavior in managing breaches and contractual performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a normative principle that cooperation is the implicit second principle of remedies—arguing expectation damages should incentivize cooperative responses to breaches—while Paper B emphasizes that parties rely on ex ante norms, renegotiation, and cooperative arrangements (rather than courts) to manage gaps and performance, treating cooperation as central to everyday contracting.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and the limits of judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends the law of contract should enable breach and regulate terms so parties can resolve performance problems without moral condemnation or excessive litigation, and Paper B argues scholarship (and practice) should focus on private transactional planning because courts often lack the information to supervise many contractual choices, privileging private lawmaking over judicially imposed solutions.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness, renegotiation, and gap-filling as routine transactional phenomena
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates breach and remedial rules within ongoing relational contexts where terms and costs change and parties must adapt, while Paper B directly analyzes why contracts are incomplete, how parties anticipate and manage interpretive gaps, and what transactional strategies (including renegotiation) reduce litigation and inefficiency.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and economic incentives shaping remedies, contract design, and mitigation behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation-protecting remedies as facilitating market efficiency by making breach possible but costly and by motivating cooperative cost-minimizing responses, and Paper B foregrounds law-and-economics considerations—tradeoffs among investment, mitigation, risk allocation, and renegotiation—that guide private contractual design and the choice of default rules and remedial expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62villlrev603!!Article: INTERPRETING STALE PREFERENTIAL RIGHTS TO ACQUIRE REAL ESTATE: BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT OF PROPERTY
compared_to.partner_title: Article: INTERPRETING STALE PREFERENTIAL RIGHTS TO ACQUIRE REAL ESTATE: BEYOND THE RESTATEMENT OF PROPERTY

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness in long-term property rights (e.g., ROFRs) and judicial gap-filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how rights of first refusal and similar preferential purchase arrangements frequently leave gaps when they persist for decades and argues courts should fill those gaps contextually; Paper B treats incompleteness as a general contractual phenomenon and surveys how courts decide what to do when terms are missing, grounding the discussion in broader theory of incomplete contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper division of labor between courts and private transactional planning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that parties should better structure long-duration preferential purchase rights but also asks what courts can do when parties fail, advocating greater judicial flexibility; Paper B argues scholars and practitioners should prioritize private-law transactional design because parties have informational advantages and courts are often ill-positioned to supervise detailed bargains.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation doctrines and default rules as responses to silence or ambiguity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes reliance on formal property doctrines (e.g., Restatement rules, RAP, restraints on alienation) and proposes a more contextual interpretive model for stale preferential rights; Paper B surveys literature on default rules, battle of the forms, and interpretation as mechanisms courts use to supply terms when contracts are silent or ambiguous.

shared_topics.topic: managing unforeseeable future changes and the challenges of long-duration contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how the passage of time and changed circumstances make long-lasting ROFRs problematic and recommends contractual design and contextual judicial adjustment; Paper B emphasizes that parties routinely cannot foresee all contingencies, discusses the costs of renegotiation/renegotiation incentives, and outlines transactional strategies to allocate risks and investments over time.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43flastulrev1265!!ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE AND CONTRACT LAW: A HOHFELDIAN ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: default rules as the judicial response to contractual incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts select and apply default rules (including intent‑based, penalty, and distribution‑sensitive defaults) when parties leave contracts incomplete, and Paper B situates default‑rule literature within the broader problem of incomplete contracts and transactional strategies for avoiding judicial gap‑filling.

shared_topics.topic: who should supply missing terms — courts versus private parties (public vs private lawmaking)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that judges inevitably instantiate a particular distributive arrangement when they choose defaults, while Paper B criticizes a court‑centered perspective and urges attention to private transactional planning by parties and their lawyers to fill gaps ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: how to balance party intent and economic considerations when filling gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts intent‑based default rules with economically motivated (including penalty) defaults and argues distributional effects must be balanced with intent and efficiency, and Paper B emphasizes tradeoffs among incentives, investments, and efficiency margins that inform whether courts or parties should set terms.

shared_topics.topic: the normative status and limits of freedom of contract as a constraint on judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates libertarian objections that judicial consideration of distribution violates freedom of contract and argues regulation via defaults is unavoidable, while Paper B distinguishes consequentialist from libertarian defenses of freedom of contract and discusses practical limits (e.g., informational constraints, unconscionability) on judicial replacement of private ordering.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev31!!ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BUSINESS LAWYER AS TERRORIST TRANSACTION COST ENGINEER

shared_topics.topic: transactional strategies for managing contractual incompleteness (e.g., hidden clauses or 'hostages')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how lawyers create latent or hidden contractual rights that function as 'hostages' to manage future opportunism and fill gaps in long-term commercial leases, while Paper B situates that practice within the broader literature on incomplete contracts and emphasizes the variety of private planning techniques parties use to cope with deliberately or inadvertently unresolved terms.

shared_topics.topic: using contract design as a tool to deter opportunism and hold-up (credible commitments)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames hidden contractual provisions as credible commitments or hostages that can reduce opportunistic behavior, and Paper B treats hold-up and opportunism as central inefficiencies of incomplete contracting that transactional planners must address through allocation of risks, incentives, and renegotiation design.

shared_topics.topic: the role and incentives of transactional lawyers as private lawmakers shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how lawyers' negotiation tactics (including insertion of latent rights) affect transaction value and reputations, and Paper B argues for focusing scholarship on the decisions and incentives of transactional lawyers and clients as private lawmakers who design contracts to achieve (private) efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial interpretive doctrines and default rules influence contracting behavior and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract-construction principles and defenses limit the creation or enforceability of hidden hostages and thereby affect lawyers' incentives to identify and allocate risks, while Paper B surveys the literature on default rules, interpretation, and courts' role in filling gaps, arguing that courts' limited information shapes parties' choices in drafting and planning.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80tullrev1109!!AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Experiment in the Optimal Precision of Contract Default Rules
compared_to.partner_title: AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: An Experiment in the Optimal Precision of Contract Default Rules

shared_topics.topic: optimal boundary between judicial/default law and private contracting
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how much detail law should supply versus how much should be left to the parties — Paper A argues scholars should focus on private transactional design because parties possess local knowledge and can tailor arrangements, while Paper B empirically investigates whether default rules should be uniform or differentiated and whether detailed adjustments are better left to contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between simple (one-size-fits-all) and complex (segmented/customized) default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that transactional efficiency requires balancing multiple margins and sometimes tailoring terms to specific contexts, and Paper B directly studies the costs and benefits of simple versus granular default rules and when segmentation of defaults is worthwhile.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and local knowledge as a constraint on legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that parties typically have information courts lack, influencing the desirability of freedom of contract and private tailoring; Paper B likewise recognizes limitations on lawmakers' ability to identify salient characteristics and uses empirical data to evaluate whether heterogeneity across markets justifies more precise defaults.

shared_topics.topic: practical, transactional implications for contract drafting and legal policy
shared_topics.justification: Both works move beyond purely doctrinal or abstract theory toward practical implications for transactional planners and policymakers — Paper A advocates teaching and scholarship oriented to transactional decision-making, and Paper B uses empirical experiments to inform when and how default rules should be designed to serve real market participants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres187!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Incomplete Contracts and the Theory of Contract Design
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Incomplete Contracts and the Theory of Contract Design

shared_topics.topic: limits of judicial supervision over incomplete contracts and its consequences for enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that courts are often ill-equipped to fill interpretive gaps in complex contracts because they lack the parties' local information; Paper A argues this limits courts' ability to supervise performance and supports reliance on private ordering, while Paper B highlights this limitation as a reason to refine economic models of contract enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: importance of private transactional planning and the role of transactional lawyers in managing incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Both essays stress that contractual incompleteness is routinely managed ex ante by private parties and their lawyers — Paper A advocates shifting scholarship and teaching toward private-lawyer decisionmaking and transactional efficiency, and Paper B treats contract design as a domain where economic theory should inform the choices parties make before litigation.

shared_topics.topic: application and limits of economic theory of incomplete contracts to legal practice and scholarship
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage the economic theory of incomplete contracts as a central analytical tool but interrogate its scope — Paper A argues economic analysis is especially useful for private parties given informational asymmetries, while Paper B assesses the theory's strengths and calls out simplifying assumptions that need refinement for legal application.

shared_topics.topic: the need to model legal enforcement (verifiability, litigation) more realistically in contract design
shared_topics.justification: Both papers identify enforcement mechanics as a critical factor for contract design: Paper B directly critiques the stylized verifiability assumption and urges incorporating litigation process into economic models, and Paper A likewise stresses that enforcement realities (courts' limited access to information and default rules) should shape transactional strategies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52drakelrev235!!ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:COURSE OF PERFORMANCE AS EVIDENCE OF INTENT OR WAIVER: A MEANINGFUL PREFERENCE FOR THE LATTER AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NEWLY BROADENED USE UNDER REVISED U.C.C. SECTION 1-303

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary role of post‑formation conduct (course of performance vs waiver) in construing or modifying contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how parties routinely rely on future negotiations, norms, and post‑formation behavior to fill gaps in incomplete contracts and how transactional planners anticipate that conduct; Paper B analyzes the doctrine of course of performance, criticizes its use to interpret prior agreements, and advocates waiver as a preferable legal mechanism for giving effect to post‑formation conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate balance between judicial interpretation and private transactional ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues scholarship should focus on private lawmakers and transactional solutions because parties possess local information courts lack, while Paper B questions statutory and judicial doctrines (expanded course of performance under the UCC) for overstepping or misallocating interpretive authority and proposes doctrinal adjustments that better respect parties' private ordering.

papers.node_id: 56casewres187!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Incomplete Contracts and the Theory of Contract Design
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Incomplete Contracts and the Theory of Contract Design
papers.authors: Robert E. Scott; George G. Triantis
papers.abstract: We are delighted to accept this invitation to write a short essay on the economic theory of incomplete contracts and to illuminate its current and potential impact on the legal analysis of contracts and contract law. Economic contract theory has made significant inroads in legal scholarship over the past fifteen years, and this is a good time to take stock of its strengths and weaknesses. Several recent publications in the Yale Law Journal have offered evaluations of the contributions of contract theory.In this essay, we offer our opinion as to its future path in legal scholarship.In particular, we suggest that economic contract theory should incorporate a more textured understanding of the process for judicial enforcement of contracts. In Part I, we describe briefly the economic theory of incomplete contracts and summarize its most important lessons for lawyers. In Part II, we highlight a limiting feature of economic contract theory: its stylized representation of legal enforcement in the concept of verifiability. We then outline an agenda for research that incorporates a more sophisticated understanding of litigation in the analysis of contract design. We describebriefly the initial steps we have taken in this direction in a forthcoming article.

questions.question: How do the nature and limits of judicial enforcement (including issues of verifiability and litigation processes) affect optimal contract design when contracts are necessarily incomplete?

How should economic models of incomplete contracting be modified to incorporate more realistic litigation dynamics, and how would those modifications change predictions about contracting behavior, transactional planning, and litigation strategies?
