shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that optimal contract design should account for the litigation process and enforcement realities faced by courts and parties; Paper B analyzes why parties intentionally leave terms incomplete (including as a strategy to rely on reciprocity and other self-enforcing mechanisms) and assesses when legal enforcement would be counterproductive for contractual design.

papers.node_id: 56casewres135!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION
papers.abstract:
The three papers in this Symposium address the topic of incomplete contracts.The recognition that parties will often fail to achieve completely contingent contractsthat provide for an optimal outcome in any future state of the world raises the important question of what role courts could or should play in such contracts.
Scholars working in the law-and-economics tradition have suggested that courts should use a hypothetical bargain approach to incompleteness, filling in terms that are optimal (efficient) and thatthe parties themselves would have achieved were it not for the transaction costs.While the authors in this Symposium draw on this traditional economic analysis of contracts, they explore new insights from economics and "economic contract theory"that complicate the analysis of incompleteness in contracts. Relying on economists' theories of incomplete contracts, the Symposium authors identify uncertainty and the cost of and limited access to information as key problems affecting parties both ex ante when contracts are being drafted and ex post when they are being enforced.Uncertainty is a factor that makes it difficult to negotiate contracts that can simultaneously protect specific investments and also promote efficiency ex post.
The Symposium authors sort out what economists and lawyers mean when they reference an "incomplete contract" and identify two key assumptions of the new economic literature. These two assumptions are (1) courts are imperfect and may be unable to verify certain facts and (2) parties can renegotiate the terms of their contracts.Using these insights, the three authors address the implications of the verifiability problem and possibility of renegotiating contractual terms for (1) parties designing complete andcontingent efficient contracts, (2) scholars designing theoretical solutions to the verifiability problem,(3) courts searching for rules that will best promote optimal investment beforehand and ex post efficiency once the future has resolved the prior uncertainty, and (4) contracts scholars attempting to decide what issues should be further explored.
Professors Scott and Triantis illuminate what they view as an unrealistic view of verifiability.That view assumes that matters are either verifiable or not in a static way and that when matters affecting contract enforcement can be classified as nonverifiable, enforcement costs will necessarily be high.Scott and Triantis reject this "stylized" view of verifiability as unrealistic.Rather than accepting unverifiability as an unalterable and insuperable obstacle for parties and courts, they argue that verifiability is a dynamic and nuanced concept. Scott and Triantis view the process as a dynamic one in which parties themselves can affect costs either by investing in litigation strategies in ways that reduce enforcement costs or by trading off between enforcement (what Scott and Triantis call "back-end costs") and drafting costs (what Scott and Triantis call "front-end costs").
Professor Avery Katz also identifies verifiability as a key issue in the literature of incomplete contracts,but he urges a reorientation in contracts scholarship.He urges a "different perspective" that offers advice not only to legal decision-makers but to parties and their lawyers.Katz offers party-based "transactional strategies for managingcontractual incompleteness"problems in ways that will "increase transactional value."
Professor Craswell helps us understand what the economics of incomplete contracts scholarship is and is not about. As Craswell explains, the issue is not about whether a particular contract is or is not complete in the sense that it contains a gap.Rather, what matters in designing optimally complete contracts and deciding on legal strategies to deal with complete and incomplete contracts are the assumptions that certain matters may be unverifiable to a third party and that parties can renegotiate contracts.He uses those assumptions to offer new insights into legal issues that previously had been addressed by the older law-and-economics literature, including how to provide incentives for parties to invest efficiently ex ante and make efficient decisions about breach ex post.Craswell also explores a topic that previously had been addressed by the older literature, but which has not yet been addressed by the "incomplete contracts" literature: whether the law can encourage parties to take efficient precautions that will actually avoid the necessity of breach.
All three authors are concerned with how to improve welfare for the partiesgiven the dual assumptions concerning verifiabilityand renegotiation. Thus, efficiency and incentives remain central to the authors' scholarship on incomplete contracting. However, the papers take different approaches to the issue of achieving optimal outcomes.Craswell accepts the problem of verifiability as a real problem and examines how to design legal rules that will best achieve particular types of efficiencies.In contrast, Katz focuses on guiding parties to design contracts that can overcome or mitigate incompleteness.
Scott and Triantis are also concerned with how to design optimal contracts, but they suggest that to arrive at an answer to that question, economic contract theory must account not only for the possibilities of performance, breach, and renegotiation, but also for litigation or enforcement costs.They stress that scholars who take account of enforcement costs should also conduct a "backward induction" process.In particular, the process would follow a similar pattern to that employed in looking backward at the effects of ex post renegotiation on a variety of matters, including the effects on ex ante efficient investment and ex post efficient breach, to determine the effect ex post litigation costs would have on contract design.In addition, Scott and Triantis explore strategies that parties use in litigation and contract design to demonstrate how the transactors can mitigate verifiability problems themselves.
The idea that contracts are inevitably incomplete is not new to economists or lawyers.What is new is the insight that all contracts are incomplete and that lawyers and economists might approach the idea in different ways.Lawyers emphasize that a contract is incomplete when it contains a gap.Absent a gap, the contract would be considered "obligationally complete."Economists, however, use adifferent approach to determine if a contract is incomplete. They argue that even if a contract contains complete terms, "a contract is incomplete if it fails to provide for the efficient set of obligations in each possible state of the world."A contract does not need to provide an outcome for every state that might materialize. If an optimal contract would differentiate for a particular contingency, then a contract that fails to do so would be incomplete. A judgment has to be made as to whether a contract that looks incomplete is in fact incomplete when measured against an optimal contract.
Traditional approaches to incomplete contracts focused on finding out if and why a contract was incomplete or contained gaps.Some scholars emphasized that incompleteness was often a result of the transaction costs of negotiating for complete contracts given the constraints on the parties' ability to anticipate future states or information.Others argued that incompleteness stemmed from strategic withholding of information and suggested tailored legal strategies tied to the cause of incompleteness.The transaction cost theorists suggested that gaps should be filled to achieve the results that parties would have achieved absent transaction costs using either a hypothetical bargain approachor one that would maximize joint gains for the parties absent such costs.Theorists emphasizing strategic withholding suggested a penalty default rule approach to gap-filling in an attempt to force the disclosure of information ex ante.
The newer economic literature redefines completeness in terms of whether a contract can provide an efficient outcome in all states of the world calling for a distinct outcome.Under this economic definition, it is expected that virtually every contract will be incomplete.Because this incompleteness is accepted as an integral part of contracting,the newer literature focuses on developing a set of rules that will provide optimal incentives for both parties either to perform or breach a contract and to rely efficiently.
The newer literature attempts to develop these rules while recognizing that certain factors make designing such rules very difficult.One is the assumption that courts have limited competence and may be "unable to evaluate key factual claims."The verifiability concept explains why economic theorists think that parties will agree to incomplete contracts even if the parties have complete information.It has also provided a rationale for these theorists to advocate limits on judicial relief under such circumstances.
Scott and Triantis demonstrate that verifiability has a more complex meaning distinct from an all or nothing "binary" conceptand is a component that affects litigation costs. These authors convey the idea that parties can interactively invest in litigation strategies in ways affecting the cost of litigation.Therefore, it may be premature to assume that when matters are "nonverifiable," they will always be so, and that the litigation costs associated with such unverifiable matters will necessarily "outweigh[] the incentive benefits to the parties"from having such terms.
The second assumption of the economic literature on incomplete contracts is the recognition that parties can renegotiate contracts ex post. The Symposium authors use insights and assumptions from economics to explore different facets of the design and enforcement of complete and incomplete contracts.
Using insights from the economic literature, Professor Craswell explores how the law can provide efficient incentives to the partiesin the different stages of a contract. He explains just how easy it would be to advise legal decision-makers on how to "design a legalregime that optimized every incentive"if courts could perfectly ascertain when actions were efficient. The recognition that courts are imperfect and may be unable to discern or verify certain matters (including the efficiency of behaviors) helps to rationalize traditional rules on efficient breach. This recognition also explains the tendency of courts to adopt legal tests that do not rely on a court's direct assessment of the efficiency of certain actions (such as the efficiency of a breach), but that will still provide correct incentives to the parties without putting too many measurement burdens on a court.
Craswell then explores the implications of the second assumption of this newer economic literature -- the possibility that contracts can be renegotiated -- to explore how that factor might complicate the effort to design legal rules encouraging various efficiencies, including efficient breach and efficient reliance.He concludes that the legal rule may not matter all that much once renegotiation as a possibility is recognized when it comes to encouraging efficient breach.However, Craswell explains why designing optimal incentives to rely may be difficult when the renegotiation possibility exists.
Craswell's paper highlights the implications of renegotiation to investigate an incentive that has not been thoroughly explored: the incentive of a party with a performance obligation to take efficient precautions that "reduce[] the probability of an event that would make it harder to perform under a contract" from occurring.This incentive has been neglected because scholars have focused on events that made breaching more likely to occur, but were beyond the parties' control. As a result, the older economic models focused on the decisions parties would make after such an event occurred, ignoring the idea of efficient precautions.
Craswell recognizes there are events that promisors control that may be able to reduce the likelihood of a breach.However, the possibility of renegotiation may dilute a seller's incentive to take efficient precautions, especially when the precautionary steps are of a particular type involving "cooperative" investments whose benefit redounds largely to the noninvesting party.Although not offering a solution, Craswell uses the insights from the economics of incomplete contracting to open up a window onto the hitherto neglected problem of how to design legal rules that will optimize the precautions parties take.
Scott and Triantis also recognize that the perceived problems of verifiability "have driven a large body of the theorists' models."These authors document the accepted theory that parties will be constrained in how they can contract because they will not want their contracts to be conditioned on states that are not verifiable to third parties.That theory also postulates that those constraints on contracting will have negative efficiency effects both ex post and ex ante.Verifiability concerns have also led contract theorists to suggest that courts should take a limited role in intervening in incomplete contracts and to argue that literalist interpretation is the preferred strategy for courts.
Without directly challenging the implications that nonverifiability, in unmitigated form, would pose for both contracting and efficient incentives for parties, Scott and Triantis set out to challenge the conventional wisdom on verifiability in a number of ways and argue for "a more textured understanding of the process for judicial enforcement of contracts."Initially, they create this understanding by assessing the "strengths and weaknesses" of recent economic contract theory and then illuminating these insights for legal scholars.They introduce a new element of the adversarial process as a topic worthy of further research. Contracting parties must account for it when they design their contracts and when they assess strategic choices in litigation.
Next, Scott and Triantis identify the key problem for contract: when contracts are negotiated under conditions of uncertainty, conditions may change that later make it unprofitable for a party to go forward with its contract obligations.There are two conflicting goals that contract law would like to achieve. First, it would like to provide enough security through enforcement to encourage parties to invest ex ante in efficient ways. Second, contract law also wishes to promote ex post efficiency by allowing parties to abandon unprofitable exchanges. If you afford parties the discretion to abandon exchanges, the parties may fail to invest ex ante in these contracts.
Scott and Triantis posit that the traditional solution, which could achieve both types of efficiencies, was for the parties to negotiate a completely contingent contract.They then posit that both transaction costs and verifiability problems will prevent these contracts from being negotiated. They argue that the possible solutions to the verifiability problems suggested by mechanism design theoristsare not likely to provide a solution because the solutions themselves are "unrealistic"and the solutions are not general enough to deal with a wide range of "information problems."
Scott and Triantis identify the contribution of recent economic contract theory in arguing that scholars had to look beyond the decisions as to performance and breachand examine renegotiation. Renegotiationcould affect whether parties would invest efficiently ex ante since parties subject to having part of their specific investments shared with the other party would be reluctant to invest ex ante. At the same time, renegotiation posed a problem for the solutions to the verifiability problem that had been suggested by mechanism design theorists.
Scott and Triantis trace how economic theory has analyzed renegotiation and its likely effect both on incentives and contract design. They suggest that a similar framework of "backward induction" should be applied to litigation, another arena in which parties are likely to act in a strategic manner.Applying their framework, Scott and Triantis assess how the litigation strategy game will affect the parties' design of optimal contracts.
Prior to Scott and Triantis, contract theorists had thought parties were limited to two fairly negative choices (a Hobbesian dilemma): either they could leave gaps in their contract (leading to inefficiencies) or they could complete their contracts, but with terms a court could not verify (subjecting them to another risk of court error). Neither option was palatable, nor were the devices proposed by mechanism design theorists a good way around the problem of unverifiable information.
These authors argue that this picture of verifiability is distorted for several reasons, weakening contract theory in two distinct ways. The distorted view is that matters are really either verifiable or nonverifiable. We know that in cases where the information is nonverifiable, it will not make sense to include such terms. Consequently, scholars have argued that there is a whole "category of contract terms that assumes a priori" that the beneficial effects such terms might have on incentives will not be worth the costs.
Scott and Triantis challenge this view by pointing to the reality of parties' actual contractual practices. If conventional theory were correct, then parties would not include nonverifiable terms, but as Scott and Triantis note, the parties do so anyway.The authors explain that the strange "gap between theory and practice"derives from the failure of economic contract theory to recognize either that front-end andback-end costs should both be considered in assessing the cost of enforcement or that litigation costs can be affected by what the parties themselves do in crafting litigation strategies.
These defects in theory lead the economic contract authors astray. The failure to recognize that parties may decide to contract for terms that are unverifiable and save front-end transacting costs (even if they cause back-end enforcement costs), shows that scholars may have myopically focused on the back-end costs. In doing so, these scholars have neglected the principle that front- and back-end costs must both be weighed in deciding whether aggregate costs (including the possible reduction in transaction costs from postponing decisions that may depend on unverifiable information) justify the beneficial effects on incentives.
Beyond presenting a more nuanced picture of verifiability and a cost/benefit framework that includes both transaction and enforcement costs, Scott and Triantis significantly contribute to the literature by suggesting that parties themselves control litigation costs through their litigation strategies in dealing with the verifiability problem.If courts make errors because they cannot verify events, then parties' incentives for efficiency may be affected because of the uncertainty that the court will reach the correct result.However, Scott and Triantis seek to demonstrate that verifiability concerns with litigation may be mitigated. Even if one accepts that verifiability might pose a problem if all disputes reached a court, parties themselves can take actions that lower those costs. They can settle cases and minimize or eliminate verification costs.
Similarly, renegotiation of contracts would avoid the need for verification. Once the parties had the relevant information, they could simply reach new terms and a court would not be involved. Scott and Triantis link the ways in which other litigation strategies, including "the interacting strategies of the parties to initiate, defend, and present evidence at trial," can contribute to lower litigation costs.
Finally, Scott and Triantis also help persuade the reader that enforcement costs associated with nonverifiable factors may be more "relative," and thus present less of a risk once one recognizes that litigation is not about a "finding of an objective truth" with absolute "certainty."While courts will make some mistakes, the mistakes will be subject to some "risk of error"even though this "risk" is not 100 percent merely because one calls a matter "nonverifiable." This more subtle calculation of risk and associated costs may affect how parties design contracts. By adding litigation strategy to the mix of a promisor's options, Scott and Triantis let us see that the risks of nonverifiability are not as absolute as was once thought and that parties have many options for overcoming verifiability.
The third Symposium author, Avery Katz, shares the view of the other authors that "maximizing contractual value" and "transactional efficiency" should be the central concern in determining how courts and parties should deal with the incompleteness problem in contracts.Like Craswell and Scott and Triantis, Professor Katz stresses that the problem of determining what to do about incompleteness in contracts is a complex problem.Determining whether a judicial response is warranted first requires an understanding of reasons why the contract remains incomplete.
Professor Katz explores both of the problems causing incompleteness in the "ex ante negotiation" of contracts: bounded rationality and strategic nondisclosure.He also highlights "additional and novel explanations"that explain why parties leave contracts incomplete. These explanations emphasize that incompleteness may occur because parties anticipate that the initial contract can be supplemented in subsequent rounds of negotiation. Alternatively, parties may leave a contract incomplete because informational asymmetries between courts and parties will hinder competent judicial decisions interpreting contractual meaning "at a reasonable cost."The ex post enforcement costs of the verifiability problem make it futile to invest efforts in achieving a complete contract since the courts will not be able to ascertain what the parties agreed to.
Katz argues that all of these explanations for incompleteness mean that the decisions on legal intervention must first confront these causes affecting both how parties negotiate contracts ex ante and how or if courts should respond.The complexities in why contracts remain incomplete mean that it is not possible to identify one legal intervention that will enhance efficiency in "all contractual settings."In some instances, courts should be hesitant about intervening with terms if the parties have deliberately failed to cover a contingency deemed of low probability or left a gap in anticipation of the fact that later bargaining could resolve the matter.In other instances, legal intervention may be beneficial in curbing opportunistic behavior by agents."The nature of the substantive issue" is a second factor that should determine whether collective legal intervention is warranted or not.
After addressing the complexity of normative decisions about legal responses to incompleteness in contracts, Katz urges the legal academy to reorient its inquiry away from a comparative institutional assessment limited to hypothetical decision-makers, such as courts and legislatures.Katz stresses that increased intellectual effort should be devoted to the parties themselves who must make difficult decisions about what kind of interpretative regime should apply to their transaction.
Katz suggests several private strategies that the parties themselves can use when they negotiate and draft contracts to "manage" the incompleteness problem in contracts.Some involve investing additional resources to make the ex post contractual gap filling less costly.Others involve delegating authority to one party who can make decisions after the contracting date when uncertainties that ledto the initial incompleteness have been resolved by the passage of time.
Other devices are entered into ex ante but actually operate to discourage ex post filling in of contracts by nonparty actors (parol evidence, liquidated damages clauses, etc.).These devices are a signal to the courts of the parties' preference for literalist and formalistic interpretation rather than a contextualized approach to contract interpretation and gap filling.The assumption is that such devices will lower the costs associated with filling gaps since formalistic regimes will arguably be less costly.The final strategy for dealing with incompleteness is premised on institutional arrangements that promote cooperation between the parties and allow them to complete the contracts ex post, obviating the need for judicial intervention.
Katz concludes by arguing that the relative usefulness of private strategies for dealing with contractual incompleteness depends on a myriad of local factors that can be more easily accessed by private decision-makers than public tribunals.Ultimately, Katz argues that the private decision-makers should be the primary focus of legal scholarship in contracts.

questions.question: How should courts respond to incomplete contracts-i.e., whether to fill contractual gaps or defer to the parties-given courts' limited ability to verify factual claims and the parties' ability to renegotiate, in order to promote ex ante investment incentives and ex post efficiency?
What private transactional strategies can parties and their lawyers use when drafting and structuring agreements to manage contractual incompleteness and thereby increase transactional value?

How do litigation/enforcement costs and the litigation strategies available to parties interact with verifiability constraints to influence whether parties include seemingly nonverifiable terms and what constitutes optimal contract design?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nclrev2239!!ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between contractual certainty (formalism) and ex post flexibility/renegotiation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how parties and courts balance ex ante certainty against the need to renegotiate or abandon unprofitable exchanges (emphasizing incomplete contracting and when judicial intervention is appropriate), and Paper B analyzes the same tension through the lens of no-oral-modification/no-oral-waiver clauses — showing why parties seek to 'lock in' deals and why later informal change may nonetheless occur and be defended.

shared_topics.topic: role of courts and doctrines in gap‑filling, enforcement, and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines what judicial responses (literalist vs contextualist gap‑filling, limits due to verifiability, and optimal legal rules) best promote investment and ex post efficiency; Paper B studies how North Carolina courts treat NOM/NOW clauses and related doctrines (waiver, modification, estoppel), critiquing inconsistent judicial approaches and proposing doctrinal or legislative solutions.

shared_topics.topic: contract drafting and private (transactional) strategies to manage incompleteness or change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A (especially Katz) proposes party-level strategies — delegation, contractual signals, boilerplate choices, and institutional arrangements — to mitigate incompleteness and influence judicial treatment, while Paper B focuses on the drafting, boilerplate use, opinion‑letter practice, and practical ramifications of NOM/NOW clauses as tools transactional lawyers use to control future modification risk.

shared_topics.topic: reliance, waiver, and estoppel as mechanisms that alter formal contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how the possibility of renegotiation and reliance affects incentives to invest and how legal rules should handle reliance (and efficient breach/reliance decisions), and Paper B gives an extended treatment of waiver, modification, and estoppel doctrines that courts use to overcome or enforce against purported oral changes despite formal NOM/NOW provisions.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary/verifiability problems and their effect on litigation costs and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on verifiability (what courts can ascertain), litigation/enforcement costs, and how parties can alter those costs via strategy, while Paper B addresses related evidentiary concerns (Statute of Frauds, need for writing, difficulty proving oral modifications) and how those proof problems influence both judicial rulings and lawyers' drafting practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj729!!ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Strategic Contractual Inefficiency and the Optimal Choice of Legal Rules.

shared_topics.topic: distinction between obligational incompleteness and contingency (state‑contingent) incompleteness
shared_topics.justification: Both papers explicitly engage the difference between contracts that fail to specify obligations (the lawyers' 'obligational' gaps) and contracts that are insufficiently state‑contingent (the economists' notion of incompleteness), using that distinction to frame how and when legal or private responses should operate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and default rules in filling contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how judicial gap‑filling (including default damage rules, excuse doctrines, and interpretive regimes) can correct or distort outcomes arising from incomplete contracts and consider when courts should intervene versus defer to private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: verifiability, asymmetric information, and enforcement/litigation costs
shared_topics.justification: Each paper treats unverifiability and asymmetric information as central constraints—examining how limits on courts' ability to verify facts and the costs of enforcement shape contract design, the desirability of certain terms, and the choice of legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: transaction costs, renegotiation, and strategic bargaining affecting efficiency and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Both articles study how transaction costs and the prospect of ex post renegotiation or strategic bargaining change parties' incentives to invest, to include contingent terms, and to rely on default rules, altering which legal rules are efficient in practice.

shared_topics.topic: private/transactional strategies for managing incompleteness (contracting around defaults, delegation, litigation/settlement strategies)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize that parties adopt private strategies—liquidated damages, delegation, settlement, litigation tactics, or contracting around defaults—to manage incompleteness, and analyze how the costs and feasibility of those strategies interact with the choice of legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43iowajcorpl1!!ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Self-Driving Contracts

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and contract completeness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when and how courts and parties should fill gaps in incomplete contracts and the normative implications of different gap-filling rules; Paper B treats self-driving contracts as a novel mechanism that algorithmically 'fills' or writes terms post‑execution, raising parallel questions about whether such automated gap‑filling should be treated as completing or perpetually leaving contracts incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: use of post‑execution information and verifiability concerns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes verifiability limits and how courts’ inability to check certain facts shapes contract design and enforcement, while Paper B centers on contracts that rely on information gathered after execution (via sensors, analytics), raising analogous issues about what facts are observable, verifiable, and admissible for determining contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: ex‑post adjustment mechanisms: renegotiation versus automated updating
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the implications of ex‑post renegotiation for incentives, investment, and the design of legal rules, and Paper B examines automated, AI‑driven updating of contractual directives as a functional alternative (or complement) to human renegotiation, probing the legal and economic consequences of delegating adjustments to algorithms.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering, third‑party providers, and governance of contractual mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights private transactional strategies parties use (delegation, clauses, institutional arrangements) to manage incompleteness and reduce reliance on courts; Paper B likewise emphasizes the rise of markets and third‑party vendors that supply self‑driving contract code and services, prompting questions about how private providers should be regulated or certified versus relying on judicial intervention.

shared_topics.topic: implications for enforcement, litigation strategy, and doctrinal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops how litigation costs, litigation strategies, and court errors interplay with verifiability and contract design, while Paper B argues that self‑driving contracts will complicate doctrines (assent, definiteness, standards) and enforcement practice, requiring courts to adapt interpretation and remedies to algorithmically produced terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41seattleulrev209!!ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Doing Deals with Aristotle--Today

shared_topics.topic: how courts should treat contract terms given parties' relational expectations and non‑economic motives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should evaluate enforceability through an Aristotelian lens that recognizes mutualism, dualism, and relational norms (flexibility, reciprocity) among contractors; Paper B examines when judicial gap‑filling or deference is warranted versus literalist regimes, emphasizing that parties often leave terms incomplete intentionally because of relational and informational dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: balancing front‑end (drafting/transaction) costs against back‑end (enforcement/litigation) costs in contract design and adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes existing contract doctrine for attending to only one side of exchange and urges means‑and‑ends analysis that would weigh both drafting and enforcement effects; Paper B develops this tradeoff explicitly, arguing verifiability and litigation costs must be weighed against drafting costs and showing parties can strategically shift those costs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of renegotiation and ongoing relational contracting (flexibility, reciprocity) in shaping incentives and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that modern contractors expect and rely on post‑formation cooperative behaviors and that those relational practices should inform enforceability; Paper B treats renegotiation as a central feature of incomplete contracts that alters ex ante investment incentives and the normative case for judicial intervention.

shared_topics.topic: limitations of traditional, single‑axis contract theory and the need to incorporate empirical and behavioral evidence of real contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals empirical studies and behavioral findings to show that actors pursue goals beyond pure efficiency and that law must accommodate mutualism/dualism; Paper B critiques stylized verifiability assumptions in older law‑and‑economics models and incorporates richer economic theory and parties' actual strategies.

shared_topics.topic: competing normative frameworks for resolving contractual gaps (efficiency/hypothetical bargain vs alternative lenses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes an Aristotelian commutative‑justice framework as an alternative to orthodox efficiency or promise‑keeping doctrines when assessing terms‑in‑a‑box and other modern problems; Paper B surveys and critiques law‑and‑economics solutions (hypothetical bargain, penalty defaults) and explores when courts or private ordering should be preferred.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev971!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:NEOFORMALISM IN A REAL WORLD OF FORMS

shared_topics.topic: formalism (literal/plain-meaning) versus contextual/standards-based contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques recent 'neoformalism' proposals that would push courts toward stricter plain-meaning rules and reduced reliance on trade usage/course-of-performance under UCC Article 2, while Paper B analyzes how parties deliberately choose or signal for literalist/formal interpretive regimes (and how courts adopt them) as a tool to manage incomplete contracts and reduce gap‑filling costs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in gap‑filling and the normative limits of judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether legislatures or courts should move toward more formal rules for interpretation given real‑world contracting practices, and Paper B directly addresses when courts should fill contractual gaps (hypothetical bargain, penalty defaults, or nonintervention) given verifiability and renegotiation constraints.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between front‑end drafting (transaction) costs and back‑end enforcement/litigation costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the practical burdens that different interpretive regimes impose on commercial actors using form contracts under the U.C.C., and Paper B develops an explicit framework showing how parties trade off drafting costs against enforcement/litigation costs and can strategically affect litigation costs when contracting under uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: the prevalence and implications of standardized/form contracts in commercial sales
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the dominance of form contracts in sales and examines how interpretive rule changes would affect those transactions under Article 2, and Paper B examines private transactional strategies (standard clauses, delegation, liquidated damages, parol evidence rules) that parties use to manage incompleteness and to shape how standard/commercial terms will be interpreted and enforced.

shared_topics.topic: limits of stylized economic models versus real‑world contracting behavior and evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that legislative or doctrinal shifts toward formalism require empirical support because models are necessarily 'off' from reality, while Paper B critiques the stylized verifiability assumption in economic contract theory and emphasizes a more textured, empirically grounded view of litigation strategies, renegotiation, and parties' actual practices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nclrev2239!!ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS

shared_topics.topic: the tension between contractual certainty and post-contract flexibility (no-oral-modification vs renegotiation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a central tradeoff in incomplete-contract theory between locking in terms to promote ex ante investment and allowing ex post renegotiation to preserve efficiency; Paper B treats NOM/NOW clauses as a transactional technique that embodies the same tension, analyzing how forbidding oral amendments promotes certainty but can frustrate needed informal change during performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrines in gap‑filling and enforcing post‑formation change (interpretation, estoppel, waiver)

papers.node_id: 56casewres151!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: The "Incomplete Contracts" Literature and Efficient Precautions
papers.abstract:
By now, most contracts scholars are familiar with at least some of the conclusions of the economic analysis of contract law. At a minimum, the concept of "efficient breach" is now established in both the literature and the casebooks, with even a cameo appearance in the Second Restatement;and the idea of the most efficient risk-bearer may also be familiar.At present, though, the legal academy has been much less affected by the economic writings whose topic is usually referred to as "incomplete contracts."
Part of my goal, in this Essay, is to present this economic literature in a more easily accessible form. My more important goal, however, is to highlight one shortcoming of that literature, at least as it has developed to date. While that literature has had a good deal to say about some decisions that contracting parties must make -- for example, the decision to perform or breach, or the decision about how heavily to rely on a contract -- it has had little or nothing to say about other decisions, including decisions about precautions that might reduce the likelihood of an accidental breach. In this respect, the recent economic literature has been (if anything) too single-minded in its commitment to one particular mathematical model.
I begin, though, with a discussion of the similarities between the newer literature and the older law-and-economics analysis.Section Ipoints out that, despite its perhaps unfortunate label, the newer literature does not depend, in any interesting way, on the fact that contracts are "incomplete." Instead, the more important features of the newer literature are its assumption that courts are unable to evaluate key factual claims (discussed in Section II below), and its assumption that the parties are almost always in a position to renegotiate their contracts after new information comes to light (discussed in Section III). These assumptions allow the newer literature to say important things about two incentives of interest: the incentive of one party to perform or to breach the contract, and the incentive of the other party to rely on the first party's possible performance. But the newer literature has so far ignored the incentive of either party to take precautions, as I discuss in Section IV.

questions.question: When contracts cannot specify all future contingencies and courts are unable to verify key factual claims (while parties can often renegotiate), do contracting parties have efficient incentives to take precautionary measures that reduce the likelihood of accidental breach?
How should legal rules or judicial responses be structured to induce efficient precaution-taking by parties in situations of contractual incompleteness and likely post-contract renegotiation?

papers.node_id: 21harvjlpubpoly135!!SYMPOSIUM: Law and Economics and the Rule of Law The Sixteenth Annual National Student Federalist Society Symposium on Law and Public Policy -- 1997: PANEL IV: HOW SHOULD JUDGES USE ECONOMICS?: THREE PROPOSALS TO HARNESS PRIVATE INFORMATION IN CONTRACT
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: Law and Economics and the Rule of Law The Sixteenth Annual National Student Federalist Society Symposium on Law and Public Policy -- 1997: PANEL IV: HOW SHOULD JUDGES USE ECONOMICS?: THREE PROPOSALS TO HARNESS PRIVATE INFORMATION IN CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
How should judges decide contract cases when they realize that private parties know more about what is good for them than the judges themselves know? This is a crucial question in structuring contract law, because if judges knew private valuations, we could dispose of contracts altogether and simply let judges order welfare-maximizing trade. Savvy judges, however, realize that they are normally less informed than private litigants and will accordingly be prone to error in deciding cases. The famed "nirvana fallacy"appears when judges or commentators forget that it is difficult for third parties to identify the social optimum. How then should judges operating under conditions of relative ignorance avoid the nirvana fallacy?
My general (but rather uninteresting) answer is that judges deciding contract cases should harness the parties' private information. This is not a new answer. In some ways it is the idea behind the theory of efficient breach. Expectation damages encourage a promisor to breach only when her information tells her that breach is likely to be efficient.
But instead of merely explaining existing rules,I want to apply this idea of harnessing private information to make three proposals about how judges should decide contracts cases. In particular, I favor (1) interpretive safe harbors; (2) extending the rule ofHadley v. Baxendaleto benefit buyers as well as sellers; and (3) giving defendants the option of making injunctions inalienable.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: HYPOTHETICAL BARGAINS: THE NORMATIVE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract Meta-Interpretation

shared_topics.topic: incentive effects of procedural and remedial rules on contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different interpretive regimes and evidentiary rules affect parties' expectations and transactional choices (including concerns about predictability and administrability), while Paper B recommends altering remedial and procedural doctrines (extending Hadley, making injunctions inalienable) to change parties' incentives and the information revealed through litigation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:A THEORY OF SELF-ENFORCING INDEFINITE AGREEMENTS

papers.node_id: 144upalrev1765!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: MERCHANT LAW IN A MERCHANT COURT: RETHINKING THE CODE'S SEARCH FOR IMMANENT BUSINESS NORMS
papers.abstract:
This Article draws on a case study of merchant law in a merchant court to reexamine, and, ultimately, to challenge, the fundamental premise of the Uniform Commercial Code's adjudicative philosophy, the idea that courts should seek to discover "immanent business norms" and use them to decide cases.This philosophy finds expression in specific Code sectionsand Official Comments,judicial opinions,academic commentary,and thewritings of the Code's principal drafter, Karl Llewellyn.Most importantly, it is the basis of the Code's definition of agreement, which includes "the bargain of the parties in fact as found in their language or by implication from other circumstances including course of dealing or usage of trade or course of performance."The Article 2 Editorial Board recently reaffirmed that "reducing the gap between law and practice … in the relevant business community"remains a primary objective of the Code. It is currently considering amendments that would broaden the reach of the Code's course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade provisions.
This Article challenges the idea that courts should seek to discover and apply immanent business norms in deciding cases.It demonstrates that while the drafters of the Code sought to incorporate these norms into the law in an effort to make commercial law more responsive to and reflective of commercial reality, they failed to recognize that this approach would fundamentally alter the very reality they sought to reflect, and would do so in ways that would have undesirable effects on commercial relationships and would undermine the Code's own stated goals of promoting flexibility in commercial transactions and "permitting the continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage and agreement of the parties."
In the spirit of the Code and Karl Llewellyn, this Article begins by looking at merchant practice. It presents a case study of the private legal system created by the National Grain and Feed Association ("NGFA") to resolve contract disputes among its members. The study pays especially close attention to the willingness of NGFA's industry-expert adjudicators to take trade usage,course of dealing, and course of performance into account in deciding cases. It finds that despite their industry expertise, NGFA arbitrators are reluctant to look to these indicia of immanent business norms. Unlike courts, which often permit course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade to trump express written terms, NGFA arbitrators take a formalistic approachto adjudication. They do not permit these considerations to vary either trade rules or written contractual provisions. This Article develops a theory to explain why sophisticated merchant-transactors might find NGFA's approach to adjudication preferable to the Code's approach, and then draws on it to analyze the effects of the Code's adjudicative approach on commercial relationships.
Part I describes NGFA's private legal system and compares its tribunal's adjudicative philosophy to the adjudicative philosophy underlying the Code. Part II discusses the reasons that sophisticated transactors might allocate some aspects of their contracting relationship to the legal realm and some to the extralegal realm, or might include a provision in their written contract while acting or agreeing to act in another, perhaps contradictory, way. It suggests that recognizing the reasons that rational transactors may act or agree to act in ways that may contradict the terms of their contract undermines an important assumption underlying the Code's definition of agreement, namely that "the course of actual performance by the parties is … the best indication of what they intended their writing to mean."It then reconsiders the desirability of the Code's definition of agreement under the more realistic assumption that there is no necessary connection between transactors' actions and their intended meaning of the written provisions in their contract. It concludes that because the Code makes it difficult to enter into purely extralegal self-enforcing agreements, it prevents transactors from selecting the value-maximizing combination of legal and extralegal terms.
Part III is the core of the analysis. It begins by suggesting that transactors do not necessarily want the relationship-preserving normsthey follow in performing contracts and cooperatively resolving disputes among themselves to be used by third-party neutrals to decide cases when they are in an end-game situation.After presenting evidence that merchants implicitly recognize the distinction between relationship-preserving and end-game norms, it suggests that when courts apply the Code's usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance provisions, they will often be using relationship-preserving norms to resolve end-game disputes.It then explores the effects of this aspect of the Code's adjudicative approach on contracting relationships, and demonstrates that this approach both prevents transactors from selecting their preferred mix of legal and extralegal terms and makes them less willing to flexibly adjust their contracting relationships. It also suggests that this approach may undermine transactors' attempts to create the contracting framework that will best promote successful renegotiation and long-term cooperation. Part III concludes by exploring the reasons that the Code's adjudicative approach may inhibit the "expansion of commercial practices."
Part IV returns to the case study and considers the reasons that NGFA's adjudicative approach is particularly well-suited to the private adjudication of grain and feed disputes. Finally, the Article concludes by offering some preliminary thoughts on the implications of the empirical observations and analysis presented in earlier sections for reform of the Code.

questions.question: Whether third-party adjudicators' use of informal industry customs and parties' prior conduct to interpret and decide contract disputes undermines parties' ability to choose between legal and extralegal arrangements and harms flexible, relationship-preserving cooperation and renegotiation.
Whether sophisticated commercial actors and industry-expert tribunals prefer formal enforcement of written contract terms to reliance on implicit business norms, and what explains that preference.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21upajbusl142!!ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SECTORAL FRAGMENTATION IN TRANSNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the growing influence of private governance on formal contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes that private contractual standards and privately-generated governance are being incorporated into state law, producing sectoral fragmentation; Paper B empirically examines a private dispute system (NGFA) and shows how merchant self-governance and private adjudication operate alongside and challenge public-law rules like the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: industry- or sector-specific norms as determinants of contractual rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues transnational contract law will fragment along industry sectors so that subject matter/industry drives applicable rules; Paper B uses the grain-and-feed sector to show how trade usages and sector practices meaningfully shape how disputes are understood and resolved in that industry.

shared_topics.topic: differences between adjudicative forums and their interpretive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A predicts the rise of specialist tribunals and sector-specific application of law; Paper B compares NGFA arbitrators' formalistic approach to courts' tendency to incorporate 'immanent business norms,' analyzing how forum choice and adjudicative philosophy affect outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of usage of trade/course of dealing/course of performance and implied terms in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that implied terms and interpretation will vary by industry and that industry context will determine remedies and dispute resolution norms; Paper B closely examines the UCC's reliance on usage/course/performance to define agreement and contrasts that with NGFA practice, questioning whether such indicia should displace written terms.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs and normative consequences of incorporating commercial customs into law (efficiency vs barriers, rule-of-law concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs efficiency gains from specialization against risks like increased complexity, entry barriers, and erosion of common standards; Paper B argues that judicial incorporation of relationship-preserving commercial norms can undermine parties' ability to choose extralegal mechanisms, reduce flexibility, and produce undesirable effects on commercial relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113yalelj541!!ARTICLE:Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Contract Theory and the Limits of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: interpretive standards for commercial contracts (textualism vs. usage/course of dealing/course of performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically critiques the UCC's encouragement of courts to discover and apply 'immanent business norms' (usage of trade, course of dealing, course of performance) and shows merchant tribunals favor formalistic adherence to written terms; Paper B normatively defends textualist interpretation and a narrow evidentiary base as the appropriate default for contracts between firms, criticizing the UCC/Restatement's broader interpretive practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of extralegal, relationship‑preserving norms versus legal adjudication in merchant disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues merchants follow relationship‑preserving informal norms and often do not want those norms used by third‑party neutrals in end‑game litigation, while Paper B acknowledges self‑enforcement, reputational sanctions, and the limited necessity of legal enforcement except where relation‑specific investments or market volatility make courts necessary.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law should be tailored to sophisticated commercial actors (defining the domain of firm‑to‑firm rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on merchant actors and questions the Code's assumption that immanent business norms can and should govern disputes across commercial contexts; Paper B explicitly limits its normative theory to contracts between firms (Category 1) and develops distinct rules (e.g., enforcement, interpretation, defaults) suited to sophisticated parties.

shared_topics.topic: the desirability and scope of defaults and mandatory rules in commercial contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends the Code's use of usage/course provisions can prevent transactors from selecting an optimal mix of legal and extralegal terms and reduce flexibility, while Paper B argues many contemporary defaults and mandatory rules are ill‑suited to firm contracts and that party autonomy and contractibility should be respected except under narrow conditions.

shared_topics.topic: effects of adjudicative approaches on incentives for investment, renegotiation, and long‑term cooperation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that applying relationship‑preserving norms in court can undermine parties' willingness to flexibly adjust relationships and to structure contracts to promote successful renegotiation; Paper B highlights enforcement as crucial to protect relation‑specific investments and to secure efficient ex ante investment and ex post trade, linking adjudicative design to investment incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1998wislrev463!!ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECONSTRUCTING CONSTRUCTION LAW: REALITY AND REFORM IN A TRANSACTIONAL SYSTEM

shared_topics.topic: tension between codification (uniform commercial law) and existing industry-specific private orderings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the UCC's aim to discover and impose 'immanent business norms' and studies how that interacts with a private industry tribunal (NGFA), while Paper B evaluates the prospects and limits of applying a UCC-style codification to the construction transactional system and emphasizes the importance of existing private orderings.

shared_topics.topic: the role of industry norms/usages in shaping contractual interpretation and legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Code's reliance on course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade and questions their suitability for judicial decisionmaking, and Paper B studies substantive principles internal to the construction industry—customs, standard models, and provenance rules—and how they function as ordering principles.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between written contracts and parties' extralegal or relationship-preserving practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that parties may intentionally act in ways that contradict written terms for relational reasons and that treating performance as the best indicator of intent is misguided, while Paper B documents how construction transactions rely on integrated standard contracts and informal relational rules that often diverge from or supplement formal agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the design and effects of alternative dispute-resolution and implementing structures on commercial behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence from the NGFA adjudicative system showing how industry tribunals adopt formalistic or relationship-preserving approaches, and Paper B examines implementing structures—internal industry organizations, conflict-management mechanisms, and tribunals—as central to managing construction disputes and shaping legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how public-law interventions (court definitions or codification) alter incentives for cooperation, renegotiation, and the evolution of commercial practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that applying Code-based norms can prevent parties from choosing optimal mixes of legal and extralegal terms and can inhibit flexible adjustment and expansion of practices, while Paper B explores how a Uniform Code or other external legal reforms would interact with private transactional incentives and the potential consequences for long-term relationships and dispute incidence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62dukelj707!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: CUSTOM AND LAW: ESSAY: CUSTOM, NORMATIVE PRACTICE, AND THE LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether observable commercial behavior (course of performance/dealing) should be treated as evidence of parties' contractual intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the UCC premise that actual performance is the best indicator of parties' intended meaning, showing merchants may act in ways that contradict written terms; Paper B critiques the additive usus/opinio model by questioning the simple mapping from regularities of behavior to normative belief, arguing for a richer account of how practices generate normative content.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicators should incorporate trade usage/custom into legal decision‑making
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares courts' permissive use of usage of trade and course of dealing with private NGFA tribunals' formalistic refusal to let usage override written terms, arguing about the proper role of such norms in adjudication; Paper B analyzes jurisprudential models for recognizing custom in law and considers how legal systems employ evidentiary or doctrinal standards to decide when customs carry legal weight.

shared_topics.topic: the consequences of legally recognizing customs/usages for the underlying social practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that when courts apply relationship‑preserving business norms to end‑game disputes they change merchant behavior, reduce flexibility, and inhibit the evolution of commercial practices; Paper B examines how conceptualizing custom (additive vs normative practice) affects whether and how law stabilizes, transforms, or merely evidentiary‑recognizes social customs, including in international law.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction and allocation between formal legal rules and extralegal normative practices in commercial relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores why sophisticated transactors deliberately split aspects of their relationship into legal versus extralegal domains and how the Code's approach frustrates that choice; Paper B develops a theory (normative practice account) showing customs arise in discursive interactions outside formal law, bearing on when and whether those practices should be folded into legal regimes.

shared_topics.topic: critique of simplistic two‑part accounts of custom (external regularities + internal belief) and advocacy for a richer, practice‑based understanding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and theoretically undermines the Code's reliance on the idea that external performance reliably signals internal intent, while Paper B explicitly rejects the additive usus/opinio juris model and proposes an integrated, discursive normative practice account of how customs attain legal relevance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2joflegalanalysis383!!ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IMPOSSIBILITY, IMPRACTICABILITY, AND FRUSTRATION--PROFESSOR GOLDBERG CONSTRUCTS AN IMAGINARY ARTICLE, ATTRIBUTES IT TO ME, AND THEN CRITICIZES IT

shared_topics.topic: the proper use of extrinsic, trade, or customary norms in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the UCC's directive that courts discover and apply 'usage of trade,' 'course of dealing,' and 'course of performance' as sources of contractual meaning, while Paper B defends a shared-assumption test that relies on tacit (extrinsic) assumptions underlying contracts — both debate when and how unwritten norms or assumptions should alter the meaning or enforcement of written agreements.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape private ordering and parties' selection of legal versus extralegal enforcement mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the Code's approach constrains parties' ability to choose a preferred mix of legal and extralegal (self-enforcing) terms and thereby affects commercial behavior, and Paper B considers how doctrines (and courts' willingness to grant excuses or allow modification) influence parties' ex ante and ex post contracting choices.
