shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between relationship-preserving practices and 'end‑game' adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that merchants may adopt relationship-preserving norms in performance that they do not want applied by third-party adjudicators in adversarial disputes, and Paper B analyzes when courts should excuse performance based on tacit assumptions (i.e., whether informal, cooperative expectations should be enforceable in litigation).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27jlegalstud67!!ARTICLE: Profit-Sharing Contracts in Hollywood: Evolution and Analysis
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Profit-Sharing Contracts in Hollywood: Evolution and Analysis

shared_topics.topic: how and why contractual forms evolve in response to industry economics and regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical evolution of Hollywood profit- and revenue-sharing contracts and argues that changes in industry structure and regulation drove changes in the contract form; Paper B similarly analyzes how the Uniform Commercial Code and courts' adjudicative philosophy reshape commercial practice and thereby alter the incentives and forms parties choose in merchant contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private industry norms and adjudicative forums versus formal legal rules in shaping contracting practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses industry-understood contractual definitions (e.g., 'net profits') and how internal industry practice and litigation (e.g., Buchwald) affect parties' ability to audit and enforce profit shares; Paper B compares a private merchant tribunal's formalistic adjudication to the Code's norm-driven approach and shows how different adjudicative forums (private tribunals vs courts) influence whether trade usage or written terms govern relationships.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as mechanisms to allocate risk and address asymmetric information and incentive/monitoring problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops explanations for contingent (profit-sharing) pay as risk‑sharing and as responses to asymmetric information and monitoring constraints on studio executives; Paper B examines why sophisticated transactors may separate legal and extralegal terms to manage incentives, preserve relationships, and avoid courts applying relationship-preserving norms in end‑game disputes, i.e., alternative mechanisms for addressing informational and enforcement problems.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of bargaining power and dispute-resolution rules on the content and enforceability of contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts bargaining-power differentials (stars with gross shares vs lesser participants with net‑profit shares) and analyzes how litigation and contract terms affect less powerful parties' payouts and audit rights; Paper B explores how merchants' preferences over legal vs extralegal enforcement and the Code's rules affect parties' ability to craft and rely on contract terms given asymmetric leverage and the choice of adjudicative forum.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Not from Guile but from Entitlement: Lawful Opportunism Capitalizes on the Cracks in Contracts

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicative/enforcement practices shape commercial relationships and incentives to cooperate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the UCC's practice of admitting course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade into adjudication changes parties' incentives and can undermine flexible, relationship-preserving commercial behavior; Paper B shows that literal legal enforcement (what it calls "lawful opportunism") similarly creates incentives for parties to press legal entitlements rather than preserve ongoing exchange relationships.

shared_topics.topic: the conflict between relationship‑preserving informal norms/customs and end‑game judicial enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that merchants distinguish between informal, relationship‑preserving norms used during performance and the norms they would want applied in end‑game disputes, and argues courts applying trade usage can inappropriately import the former into the latter; Paper B conceptualizes and empirically studies how insisting on literal legal rights can exploit the ‘‘spirit’’ of negotiated deals and thereby substitute enforcement for relationship‑preserving responses.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional locus of dispute resolution (private tribunals vs courts) and its effects on normative outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares an industry private adjudicatory forum (NGFA) with courts, finding private tribunals take a more formalistic approach that preserves parties' ability to rely on extralegal practices, while courts' application of trade usage can reshape behavior; Paper B analyzes how the willingness of courts to hear and enforce literal claims creates an institutional fault line that makes lawful opportunism an attractive governance strategy under certain disturbances.

shared_topics.topic: empirical investigation of contracting behavior in response to contract incompleteness or unforeseen disturbances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a case study of NGFA dispute resolution and empirical observations to assess how parties actually behave and how adjudicative rules affect that behavior, especially when written terms and performance diverge; Paper B complements this with an experimental vignette study measuring when individuals choose cooperative, blatantly opportunistic, or lawfully opportunistic responses to consequential contract disturbances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18geomasonlrev245!!ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY

shared_topics.topic: whether adjudicative reliance on trade usage, course of dealing, and course of performance should displace written contractual terms (standards vs bright-line rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the UCC's adjudicative philosophy of discovering and applying immanent business norms (usage, course of dealing/performance) and contrasts that with merchant arbitral formalism that enforces written terms; Paper B engages the related, broader debate over standards versus bright-line rules as a tool for reducing legal complexity and uncertainty in commercial law.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and interpretive doctrines shape transactors' contracting behavior and their mix of legal vs extralegal (relationship-preserving) norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the Code's tendency to treat performance and trade usage as indicia of agreement can prevent parties from selecting an optimal combination of enforceable law and self-enforcing, relationship-preserving practices and can chill flexible cooperation; Paper B analyzes how internal and external legal complexity affects commercial actors' expectations and transaction design and argues simplification can reduce the social and transactional costs caused by current doctrinal complexity.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of private ordering, industry adjudication, and market-developed customs versus public codification and statutory intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the NGFA private tribunal as a case study to argue that industry adjudication operates differently (more formalistic and relationship-protective) than courts applying the Code's norms and may better reflect merchant preferences; Paper B surveys moments when legislatures and uniform-law bodies chose to codify or displace market/common-law developments (e.g., Article 4A, UETA, UCITA) and weighs the tradeoffs of statutory intervention versus letting commercial practices and common law evolve.

shared_topics.topic: reforming the UCC and commercial law (paths and goals of reform, including simplification or doctrinal change)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws implications from empirical observation to suggest preliminary reforms to the Code's interpretive approach to usage and course doctrines; Paper B maps prior reform efforts across the UCC, identifies costs of complexity, and proposes legislative and structural simplification strategies (including a minimalist re-conception) as concrete reform paths.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82lawcontempprob1!!ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RISK-AVERSE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: the role of market norms / usage of trade as external reference points in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts should routinely interpret ambiguous terms by reference to market-standard terms and other market-general background duties (normative triangulation); Paper B examines and critiques the UCC's directive that judges discover and apply 'immanent business norms' (usage, course of dealing, course of performance), showing empirically that merchant adjudicators often reject that approach and analyzing its consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the formalism versus contextualism debate about how far courts should inquire beyond the text (course of dealing, course of performance, trade usage)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates boilerplate within the formalism/contextualism debate and proposes a middle path that privileges market-general contextual facts over party-specific tailoring; Paper B directly challenges the Code's contextualist impulse to treat performance and trade usage as controlling, arguing this can misread parties' intentions and produce perverse effects.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive/adjudicative methodology alters contracting behavior and market outcomes (including externalities from standardized terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that interpretive choices (e.g., favoring market-conforming readings) shape whether boilerplate produces negative externalities and how markets self-regulate; Paper B shows that the Code's insistence on importing business norms into adjudication changes parties' incentives, can constrain extralegal cooperative norms, and thereby alters commercial relationships and practices.

shared_topics.topic: differences between public courts and private merchant tribunals in applying norms and the implications for commercial ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts should and can use publicly observable market information to interpret standardized terms, while Paper B compares courts to a private NGFA merchant tribunal that adopts a more formalistic approach, using that contrast to draw implications about which adjudicative forum better preserves merchant practices and relationship norms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34tourolrev83!!SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: The Uncertainty of Sun Printing

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling versus refusing to enforce indefinite contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when courts (or tribunals) should fill gaps in incomplete commercial agreements: Paper A critiques the UCC-driven practice of treating course of dealing/usage of trade as means to supply or override terms, while Paper B examines Cardozo's Sun Printing refusal to enforce a contract for leaving material terms open and the broader doctrine of indefiniteness.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary role of industry practice, customs, and usage of trade in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage substantively with whether and how adjudicators should rely on trade usages and industry context—Paper A as a direct critique of the UCC's endorsement of 'immanent business norms' (course of performance/dealing/usage), and Paper B by situating the contested contract within the historical and economic practices of the newsprint industry to reassess judicial interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: why contracting parties leave terms open or act inconsistently with written provisions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers ask why sophisticated commercial actors sometimes omit material terms or perform in ways that contradict written agreements: Paper A theorizes strategic allocation between legal and extralegal regimes and the use of relationship‑preserving norms, while Paper B investigates the practical and economic reasons the parties in Sun Printing left price and duration unsettled.

shared_topics.topic: how adjudicative philosophies (formalism vs flexibility/certainty vs justice) affect commercial relationships and market outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Each paper explores the consequences of different adjudicative approaches—Paper A contrasts private arbitrators' formalistic enforcement with the UCC's norm‑seeking flexibility and argues the latter can undermine chosen contracting arrangements, while Paper B critiques Cardozo's decision as increasing uncertainty and possibly enabling harmful industry effects—linking doctrinal choices to the behavior and stability of commercial markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45arizstlj369!!ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conflicting Formulas for Measuring Expectation Damages

shared_topics.topic: adjudicative discretion and doctrinal indeterminacy in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with the problem that contract doctrines leave substantial room for adjudicator choice—Paper A analyzes how courts' invocation of course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade imports uncertainty and judicially-discovered norms into commercial disputes, while Paper B documents that multiple, conflicting formulas for expectation damages exist and there are no universally accepted principles to determine which formula a court should apply.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and remedies influence contracting incentives and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the Code's practice-oriented adjudication changes merchants' ability to allocate legal versus extralegal terms and may deter flexible, relationship-preserving behaviour; Paper B shows that which expectation-damages formula courts apply critically affects parties' incentives to perform, breach, and bargain, and therefore shapes contracting strategy.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between standardized legal doctrines and private or industry-specific ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a uniform Code-oriented approach with a private NGFA tribunal's formalistic, industry-specific adjudication and considers the desirability of allowing bespoke commercial practices to govern; Paper B highlights that one-size-fits-all damages formulas may be ill-suited for recurring breach scenarios and argues for principles that can adapt measures to particular contractual contexts.

shared_topics.topic: determining parties' expectations and the meaning of the bargain as the basis for relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the assumption that course of performance or trade usage reliably reveals parties' intended meaning of their written agreements, while Paper B centers the expectation measure—putting the promisee in the position of performance—raising practical puzzles about how to identify and compute the parties' expectation in different breach scenarios.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: How To Create a Commercial Calamity

shared_topics.topic: tension between legal rules and commercial/relationship-preserving practices

shared_topics.topic: implications for reforming Article 2 and law-drafting lessons
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers reform-oriented observations about how the Code's adjudicative approach could be changed to better align with merchants' needs, and Paper B draws lessons and concrete suggestions for how drafters should (or should not) revise §2-209 to avoid creating a 'commercial calamity.'

shared_topics.topic: the role of adjudicators' interpretive philosophies (formalism vs norm-seeking) in commercial dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts private arbitral tribunals' formalistic enforcement of written terms with courts' norm-seeking use of trade usages, arguing these different philosophies produce different incentives for merchants; Paper B emphasizes how unclear statutory language leaves judges and lawyers without reliable interpretive guidance, exacerbating inconsistent application.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73molrev667!!Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Mistake and Disclosure in a Model of Two-Sided Informational Inputs

shared_topics.topic: whether and when parties' conduct or silence should be treated as evidence of their contractual intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the Code's assumption that actual performance is the best indicator of parties' intended meaning and criticizes using performance-based norms to interpret written agreements. shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal legal doctrines and private/extralegal norms or customs in governing contractual relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts merchant/private adjudication (NGFA) that preserves extralegal, relationship-maintaining norms with the UCC's tendency to fold those norms into formal legal interpretation, arguing this undermines private ordering. shared_topics.topic: efficiency and normative evaluation of competing contract rules (beyond pure legal doctrine)

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The "New Conservatism" in Contract Law and the Process of Legal Change

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly asks what has caused any recent change in contract doctrine and what it implies about legal change generally, while Paper B traces how the UCC's adjudicative philosophy produces behavioral changes among transactors and offers reform suggestions to better align law and commercial needs.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:THE COMFORT OF CERTAINTY: PLAIN MEANING AND THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE CONCEPT OF CHANGE: PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ATTEMPTS TO REGULATE MODIFICATION, WAIVER, AND ESTOPPEL

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CAFFOLDING: USING FORMAL CONTRACTS TO SUPPORT INFORMAL RELATIONS IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Resolving Contractual Ambiguity in Tennessee: A Systematic Approach

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: STATISTICS AND THE LAW: PROVING LOST PROFITS

papers.node_id: 144upalrev1971!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, ECONOMICS, & NORMS: NORMS, FORMALITIES, AND THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A COMMENT
papers.abstract: Jason Johnston's Article makes three contributions to the economics and sociology of contract law.First, it provides a methodological analysis of the use of case reports to discover business norms. Second, it makes a positive argument about the extent to which businesses use writings in contractual relations. Third, it sets the stage for, and hints at, a normative defense of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) section 2-201. Although the first contribution is probably the most interesting and useful, I focus on the second and third, and comment only in passing on the first. I conclude with some observations about the role of formalities in contract law.

questions.question: To what extent do businesses rely on written documents to form, confirm, or modify commercial agreements?
Are legal formalities that require or favor written evidence for certain transactions normatively justified as a way to promote efficient, reliable, or fair contracting?
Can published judicial case reports be used reliably as a method for discovering prevailing business norms about contracting practices?

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: AN EMPIRICAL VIEW OF CONTRACT.
papers.abstract:
When Grant Gilmore called his lectures "The Death of Contract,"he gave a name to a body of work that includes some of mine.  He called me the "Lord High Executioner" of the "Contract is Dead" movement.  However, Gilmore was not very interested in my empirical description of contract.  He said this kind of work lacked theoretical relevance.  I must credit him with an attention catching title.  Nevertheless, he failed to see that the very limited practical role of what professors call contract law poses significant theoretical problems that we are only beginning to confront.
In a way, Gilmore's title is misleading.  Contract as a living institution is very much with us.  In the day-to-day flow of dealings, vast numbers of significant transactions take place to the reasonable satisfaction of all concerned.  People and organizations bargain, they write documents, and they avoid, suppress, and resolve disputes little influenced by academic contract law.  Some cases are taken to court and the formal process begun, although lawyers settle most of them before courts reach final decisions.  There are even opinions by judges relying on traditional contract law, but they are relatively rare.
Furthermore, contract within the academy is still very much alive.  Every morning in law schools all over the United States beginning law students struggle with offer, acceptance, and consideration.  I never argued that contract law died.  Rather, academic contract law is not now and never was a descriptively accurate reflection of the institution in operation.  Moreover, this inaccuracy matters in many ways.
At the end of September in 1984, there was a conference in Madison marking the 21st birthday of the publication in the American Sociological Review of my article on non-contractual relations in business.I am pleased that the article has had a long shelf-life and people still find something in it.  After listening to others at the conference consider long-term continuing relationships, it is a good time for me to reflect on developments over the past two decades.  We must remember that my article reports research done when Dwight Eisenhower was President of the United States, and I wrote it when John Kennedy was in office.  Both the business executives and lawyers interviewed and the author were living in the United States before the decline and fall of the American empire.  Indeed, any article that uses Studebaker taxis as an example was written in the pre-word processor age.  A great deal has happened in 21 years.  We also know much more about the American legal system in operation today than anyone did when I wrote the article.
To reconsider what I wrote, I will summarize the argument of my 1963 article, including some of my later research as well.  Then I will note what I would add were I to write the article today.  Finally, I will consider what difference all of this makes to those interested in contracts and law and society research.  I will talk about developments in the United States, not because I think them more important but only because I know my own society best.

Whether the concepts and doctrines taught as academic contract law accurately describe and explain how contracting actually operates in practice.

How patterns of non-contractual, long-term continuing business relationships and private governance have changed over time (e.g., over the past two decades) and what those changes imply for legal theory and practice.

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between doctrinal contract law and commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Both papers take up the gap between academic/doctrinal pictures of contract and how contracting actually operates: Paper A emphasizes empirically that everyday transactions and continuing relationships are governed largely outside formal contract law, and Paper B documents how judicial doctrines (plain meaning/parol evidence) diverge from both theoretical accounts and commercial realities.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the written instrument (integration) versus extrinsic or relational norms
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how much force courts and parties give to written documents: Paper B analyzes the parol evidence rule and debates over integration and the admissibility of extrinsic evidence, while Paper A discusses how parties rely on documents but often manage expectations and disputes through ongoing, non-legal governance rather than relying solely on the writing.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between certainty/predictability and party intent/flexibility in long‑term relationships
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the normative tension between valuing stable, predictable application of textual rules and allowing flexibility to capture parties' actual intent in continuing relationships: Paper B theorizes the psychological and instrumental attractions of plain meaning and strict parol evidence, and Paper A shows empirically that actors frequently prioritize relational flexibility over formal legal certainty.

shared_topics.topic: variation over time and across forums and the need for empirical/theoretical recalibration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers note doctrinal and practical heterogeneity and argue for adjusting theory in light of observed practice: Paper A surveys decades of changing commercial practice and its theoretical implications, and Paper B documents jurisdictional and temporal variation in parol-evidence/interpretation doctrines and calls for understanding why courts choose particular approaches.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE MITIGATION PRINCIPLE: TOWARD A GENERAL THEORY OF CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of traditional, categorical contract doctrines for long-term or specialized/relational transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that standard categorical rules (e.g., perfect tender, standard mitigation rules) fail to fit specialized or relational contracts and calls for more finely tuned norms; Paper B empirically documents that formal academic contract doctrines rarely describe how long-term continuing relationships operate and thus are poorly suited to the realities of relational contracting.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and party-designed contractual mechanisms versus default legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends permitting parties wide latitude to craft customized mechanisms (and even a menu of preformulated clauses) to govern specialized arrangements; Paper B shows that parties routinely rely on private governance, bargaining, and informal mechanisms rather than default judicial rules, emphasizing the practical dominance of party-driven ordering.

shared_topics.topic: the need to connect theoretical models of contract law with empirical practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an analytic model of optimal mitigation to inform a general theory of contractual obligation and to explain observed doctrinal puzzles; Paper B emphasizes empirical description of contracting behavior and critiques the gap between academic contract doctrine and how contracts actually function, arguing for research that better links theory to practice.

shared_topics.topic: the practical interplay between performance obligations, remedies, and dispute-avoidance in ongoing relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links mitigation duties to the partner's performance obligations and examines how remedial rules should operate in different markets (including reluctance to require dealing with breachers); Paper B documents that most disputes are suppressed, settled, or governed by private practices rather than formal litigation, highlighting how performance, enforcement, and remedies are managed outside traditional doctrinal processes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: What Do Lawyers Contribute to Law and Economics?

shared_topics.justification: Both papers debate what scholarly skills lawyers bring to legal inquiry: Paper A claims legal academics contribute tacit skills like analogical reasoning and multi-disciplinary synthesis to law-and-economics, while Paper B illustrates how legal scholars' empirical descriptions challenge doctrinal assumptions and reshape theoretical debates about contract.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Liberty at the Borders of Private Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that regulatory provisions often use broad standards (e.g., 'reasonable precautions'), creating uncertainty for accrual/accounting recognition and for conditional liabilities when parties adapt conduct over long relationships; Paper B describes how continuing, long‑term business relationships are governed by flexible, imprecise expectations rather than precise legal terms, producing similar indeterminacy and practical consequences for governance.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and empirical significance of silence, tacit consent, and community conventions in shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues silence can be an indirect manifestation of consent and that conventionalist default rules can reflect community expectations; Paper B provides empirical support by describing how continuing commercial relationships depend on shared understandings and conventions rather than express legalistic consent.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Outsourcing, Modularity, and the Theory of the Firm

papers.node_id: 1985wislrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CAVEAT.
papers.abstract:
I.  SETTING THE STAGE
offer the following argument somewhat reluctantly since I am not sure that it is powerful enough to hold the field and I consider myself a friend of the relational contract perspective; I am, however, persuaded that the argument must be reckoned with.  Both the papers in this volume and the tenor of comments at the conference suggest the advantages of replacing the dominant paradigm of contract law, correctly assumed to be Contract-as-Transaction, with the more powerful and meaningful paradigm of Contract-As-Relation. An argument exists, however, which though making major concessions to the relational paradigm, nevertheless preserves the transactional model as the primary source of contract doctrine.
To begin, we should not overestimate the importance of legal doctrine in contracting behavior.  Most who urge the shift to the relational paradigm would readily concede this premise.  Stewart Macaulay's seminalarticlesare the most honored scholarship in support of the assertion but hardly the only evidence of its truth.  If we admit the modest role of contract doctrine and court-law, and ask what holds contracting partners together and causes them to perform their promises, we can quickly identify four varieties of "glue." Three are "natural", and the fourth is an artificial creation legitimated by the first three.  They normally appear in combination, of course, and isolating them completely, one from the other, is usually not possible.
The first on this list, and probably in significance as well, we could call market glue.  The performance of most agreements is, without a doubt, completely consistent with the achievement of goals in the market.  I say "consistent with" and not "caused by" since performance is often consistent with other motives as well.  Given a freely made agreement in which A promises a future exchange of her widgets for B's money, one can assume that the exchange of promises means that A expects to value the money more than the widgets when the time comes for the actual exchange, and B expects to hold the opposite preference.  Most of the time this prediction of preferences turns out to be accurate, and when the time comes it cannot be said that the exchange occurred because of the promise; the exchange would have occurred if A and B were in a position to exchange widgets and money but had never exchanged promises.  Even if the exchange appears not to be in the short-term interest of one of the parties when the time comes to perform, market forces still can explain a willingness to proceed.  Though their preferences as to the relative value of widgets and money may have changed because they now have unexpected alternative opportunities, as the scholars of contract-as-relation so appropriately note, the parties are not strangers, and the discounted value of the potential benefits of the relation may exceed the value of the opportunity which must be forgone in order to perform the promise.  Here, in a sense, the parties have performed because of the promise since that promise may have played an important role in creating or preserving a relationship, but their interest in marketplace success would still be sufficient to explain their behavior; one need not assume they performed because they feared some sanction external to the market.  So even in a society inwhich the state took no interest in promise-keeping we would observe buyers and sellers taking short-term losses on contracts.
The second kind of "glue" is moral glue.  In our society it is generally regarded as virtuous to keep one's promises.  Some people testify, and there is no reason to doubt them, that they keep promises in order to maintain their self-respect, or because they wish to be good people and believe that requires promise-keeping, or because their God commands them to honor their word.  I have no doubt whatever that some promises (who knows how many) are kept simply because people believe it is the right thing to do and they do it.  They may be inconvenienced by performance, but their sense of propriety is strong enough to overcome the temptation to breach.
The third kind of "glue" is the product of social interaction.  People perform their promises because they fear the disapproval of people who are important to them if they do not.  They fear not the loss of self-respect, but the loss of the respect of others.  That is, a person might perform a promise simply to preserve positive social relation with another.  Harvey Leibenstein, in his book Beyond Economic Manhas appropriately pointed out that people within a market maximize things other than money, and persons within marketplace organizations may maximize their own comfort, or power, or pleasure, at the expense of the organization's profitability.  A buyer for a department store who simply enjoys the friendship of a seller may preserve that social relationship, at the expense of the department store's economic goals.  Or a person who knows that fellow members at the country club will sanction him for walking out of a deal may perform to preserve their approval.
Finally, we come to law glue, provided courtesy of the state.  In some situations, the argument runs, state sanctions should be used to encourage persons to perform their promises (or pay if they do not), either because the market, moral, and social sanctions are inadequate to stimulate performance, or because the parties may fail to appreciate their force -- and so law glue is provided to reinforce the effects of the other glues.  The justifications for state intervention are not separate from the reasons people offer to explain why they perform their promises absent state threats; rather the state's justifications are largely derived from those reasons.  The state, in creating contract enforcement rules, takes into account the needs of the market as well as the social and ethical values of its citizens.  Is that all?  Clearly, and significantly, the answer is no.  The state must also take into account values that are related to the enforcement system itself.  People have preferences notonly about promises but also about the appropriate features of a promise-enforcement system, including how much they are willing to spend on it.  The characteristics of any enforcement system have substantial impact on the procedures and principles it applies.  Just how relevant that is will, I hope, become clear in just a few more paragraphs.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent state-provided contract enforcement is necessary to induce parties to perform promises, relative to nonlegal incentives such as market incentives, moral obligations, and social sanctions.
How parties' preferences over the characteristics and costs of an enforcement system shape the design and operation of contract enforcement rules.

papers.node_id: 1985wislrev561!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: A CONTRACT DOES NOT A CONTRACT MAKE.
papers.abstract:
Growing up academically at the University of Pennsylvania during the late '70's exposed me to a wonderful new religion -- relational contracting.  The patriarchs of this decidedly Scottish enlightenment were Stewart Macaulay and Ian Macneil.  Most of us at Penn were introduced to the new scriptures through Oliver Williamson's twice weekly chapel and the writings of Victor Goldberg.  Goldberg, in those days, was something of a missionary whose quest was to bring the one true religion to the heathens -- that is, to the economists.  For that gallant effort he was sometimes chastised as a heretic.  Fortunately, for both lawyers and economists, no one ever burned him at the stake, for his work has contributed enormously to our understanding of relational contracts.Once again Goldberg has written a clear, insightful and provocative article about contracting.  This time he has turned his considerable talents to the task of elucidating Alcoa v. Essexand he has done a marvelous job of it.
But all this praise notwithstanding, Goldberg and I disagree on how to focus an inquiry into Alcoa. He provides a framework for analyzing price adjustments in long-term contracts.  While he focuses on the adjustment clause of the document itself, I believe limiting the analysis to the terms of the contract document is not fully advantageous because it ignores interesting, and often crucial, issues.  Focusing on the contractual relation is a better way to understand what actually transpired between the parties.  I make this assertion for several reasons.
, the written instrument does not always contain the entire agreement.  I witnessed this in the contracting between rail freight carriersand their shippers.The incentives to misstate the actual terms of the Alcoa contract were even stronger because the transaction was surrounded by potential Robinson-Pattman problems which might have led the parties to draft the contract to mask certain features.  This is an empirical question that cannot be answered merely by examining the formal documents.
, looking beyond the contract is important because parties who have, or anticipate, strong relational ties with their contracting opposites are not particularly worried about initial terms of agreement.  They assume that the contract will be adjusted to their mutual advantage as circumstances change.  Since the costs of drafting, monitoring, and enforcing a once-and-for-all agreement outweigh the benefits, it is far more efficient to cross bridges as they are reached.
, the problems Alcoa faced had less to do with the failure of the initial contract terms, than with the failure of the contractual relation.  Any "mistake" was in the development of, or expectations for, the contractual relationship, not in the drafting of the contract document.  This underscores the need to get beyond the document and court record and raises two questions.  Question one is, what type of relationship should Essex and Alcoa have anticipated?  That is, was it the type that should have led the parties to resolve the conflicts that arose?
Numerous types of relationships can develop between contracting parties.  Goldberg recognizes correctly that the contractual relation between Alcoa and Essex was ongoing and long-term.  But the length of the agreement need not determine the form of the relationship.  How parties structure the monitoring, adaptation, and enforcement of the contracts depends upon the characteristics of the underlying transaction and the contracting hazards they portend.  Williamsonargues that three variables determine the characteristics of a governance structure: the degree to which uncertainty is present, the frequency of exchange, and the extent to which the exchanges are supported by idiosyncratic capital.  He suggests that the last is the most important because extensive investments in transaction specific assets can cause competitive conditions to deteriorate after the initial contract is set.  This raises hazards during the contract execution stage.  Parties with idiosyncratic investments are particularly susceptible to opportunistic conduct if and when incomplete terms must be filled in or a problematic issue renegotiated.  This vulnerability gives the parties an incentive to find some wayto protect their investments.  The more idiosyncratic the investment, the more likely the parties will devise unique, privately determined governance structures.
Assuming that the investments in Alcoa were idiosyncratic,question two is, why did not strong relational bonds -- that would have encouraged the parties to give up short-term gains for the benefit of the long-term relationship -- develop between Essex and Alcoa?  That is, why were the parties incapable of adjusting the contract themselves?  Again, the answer lies outside the four corners of the document.  Parties to contracts involving idiosyncratic investments can protect themselves in one of two ways.  First, they can demand a price that compensates them for their marginal costs, and includes an insurance component to protect them from opportunistic behavior that would destroy their investments.  Suppliers making specialized investments require a price premium.  Buyers investing in idiosyncratic capital insist upon a discount.  The price term agreed to by the parties may reflect this last possibility.  That is, perhaps Essex was only willing to make the purchase and locate the plant where it did if the price it paid Alcoa reflected a discount to protect the fabricator from potential opportunistic conduct.  If this were true, Alcoa's present claim is baseless.  But nothing indicates that either party knew the extent demand would change and the price term would benefit Essex.  If they had known the direction and magnitude of the demand shifts, they would have been better off investing in commodities futures.  In any event, the contract reveals neither the reasons for choosing the specific price term used nor for choosing this method of guaranteeing their investments.  Determining these issues requires examining the contractual relation, not just the contract.
Alternatively, the parties could have protected themselves by making a credible commitment to not act opportunistically.  A commitment of this nature can be made in at least two ways.  First, the parties could devise what Marc Galanter refers to as a private orderingby establishing their own set of rules and procedures for negotiating, adapting, monitoring and enforcing the agreement.  I witnessed governance structures of this type in transactions between rail freight carriers and their shippers.  Formal documents did not evidence such a framework.  Finding the governance structure required looking beyond the contract.  Assumingone discovered the existence of a private ordering between Essex and Alcoa, the next question, obviously, is why did it fail to work?  Again, only an understanding of the contractual relation will reveal a sufficient explanation for the failure.
The other method of making a credible commitment is for the parties to make a mutual exchange of hostages.  A modern hostage exchange is similar to those used during medieval times: both parties sacrifice something of value if either acts opportunistically.  Today, rather than exchange first born daughters, or even executive vice presidents, both parties make investments in capital assets that will be destroyed if the contract falls apart.  Alcoa's "hostage" was that portion of the Warwick capacity that was added for, or dedicated to, Essex.  Alcoa might have believed that Essex had posted a similar hostage when it placed its fabricating facility near the Warwick smelter.  The value of the fabricating facility, built specifically to receive aluminum from the Warwick plant, would diminish if the contractual relation failed.  Alternatively, if Essex helped to financeAlcoa's dedicated capacity, the arrangement could have led Alcoa to believe that Essex became tied to the aluminum manufacturer.  After all, Essex could have lost its investment in Warwick if the contract failed.
If these were the hostages Essex posted, imagining why they proved inadequate to force renegotiation of the contract is easy.  Essex could receive aluminum from plenty of other sources if Alcoa were to breach, but any other source would entail additional transportation costs.  This meant that as a hostage the plant was only worth the difference between its use in fabricating Warwick Aluminum and its use in fabricating aluminum that had to be transported from elsewhere.  That is, as a hostage Essex's plant ranked right up there with giving the wicked king your lazy, shiftless third cousin.  Using any of the financing aspects of the agreement as a hostage would be similarly inadequate.  Alcoa's pockets were simply too deep.  Essex would know that Alcoa was never really in danger of defaulting on the "loan."
Thus, under this scenario, Alcoa's problem was not so much a "mistake" concerning the price term, but rather a mistake about the importance that Essex would place on the preservation of the relationship.  Admittedly, many of my observations are little more than speculation -- but they are reasonable hypotheses that require the researcher to look beyond the formal documents for confirmation.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: PRICE ADJUSTMENT IN LONG-TERM CONTRACTS.
papers.abstract:
After parties enter into a contract, changed circumstance might result in one of them being dissatisfied with the price.  Anticipating this, the parties could include a price adjustment mechanism in the agreement.  If the mechanism is imperfect, some dissatisfaction will remain.  This dissatisfaction may result in litigation with the dissatisfied party asking the court either to excuse performance or revise the contractprice.  For example, large changes in fuel prices since 1973 generated considerable litigation.
In this paper, I suggest a framework for analyzing price adjustment in private contracts.  Contrary to most economists and lawyers, I argue that price adjustment problems have little to do with attitudes toward risk.  Rather, the problems are those suggested by the "relational exchange" approach to contracts.This argument will be developed in Part II.
A court faced with a claim of changed circumstance must deal with two questions.  Is the change sufficient to justify relief, and, if so, what relief should be granted?  The court could void the contract and discharge the obligation of the loser, revise the price term as German courts often do,or recognize a duty to renegotiate in good faith, as proposed by my colleague, Richard Speidel.
Contracting parties sometimes invite the courts to rewrite explicit price terms by including open-ended language.  Force majeure clauses, for example, are boiler plate terms which discharge performance under conditions that are not always clearly defined.  More importantly, long-term contracts sometimes provide for price adjustment to prevent a"gross inequity", the nature of which is left undefined.The decisions to discharge or adjust could be left to the courts or assigned to a party other than the courts, and arbitrator, for example.
Part III focuses on Alcoa v. Essex -- the only example of an American court revising the contract price in a long-term supply contract.I am interested in what the parties were trying to accomplish, why the contract worked poorly, and the court's analysis of these issues.  I am not particularly concerned with whether the decision was correct, but for what it is worth, in my opinion the court should not have revised the contract.
Part IV considers general problems confronting courts or arbitrators resolving price adjustment disputes.  Concluding remarks follow in Part V.

questions.question: Are price adjustment problems in long-term private contracts primarily driven by risk allocation concerns or by relational-contracting dynamics between ongoing trading partners?

When changed circumstances make an existing price term unsatisfactory and contractual adjustment mechanisms are imperfect, which institutional response - contract discharge, judicial revision of the price, an enforceable duty to renegotiate, or delegation to a nonjudicial decisionmaker - produces better legal and economic outcomes?

How do open-ended contractual provisions for unforeseen events or equity-based price adjustments affect parties' incentives, the likelihood of litigation, and who should be entrusted to make final adjustments (courts, arbitrators, or contracting parties)?

papers.node_id: 69uchilrev917!!SYMPOSIUM: MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF THE MODERN BUSINESS CORPORATION: EXECUTIVE COMPENSATION & TAKEOVERS: Designing Mechanisms to Govern Takeover Defenses: Private Contracting, Legal Intervention, and Unforeseen Contingencies
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL OF THE MODERN BUSINESS CORPORATION: EXECUTIVE COMPENSATION & TAKEOVERS: Designing Mechanisms to Govern Takeover Defenses: Private Contracting, Legal Intervention, and Unforeseen Contingencies
papers.abstract:
During the takeover wave of the 1980s, managers developed numerous strategies to fend off unwanted bidders and retain control of their firms. These strategies included the poison pill, often used in combination with the effective classified board. Corporate scholars expressed concern over the serious conflict of interest inherent in managerial control over takeovers, arising from the fact that takeovers often presage managerial termination. Many corporate scholars argued that the poison pill should be prohibited.Many also concluded that managers should be required to submit bids to shareholders.
Responding to the fundamental conflict attending boardenacted takeover defenses, the Delaware Supreme Court initially provided for heightened scrutiny of takeover defenses adopted by the board.In Unocal v Mesa Petroleumthe Delaware Supreme Court announced a two-tiered proportionality review of takeover defenses. The first prong entails an assessment of whether the board was responding to a legitimate threat to corporate policy and effectiveness.The second prong asks thecourt to determine whether the defensive measure was proportionate to the threat posed.
The Unocal standard initially appeared to offer the promise of court review of both the purposes for and structure of takeover defenses.It thus appeared to place some effective limitations on the board. This promise largely evaporated with the Delaware Supreme Court's decisions in Unitrin, Inc v American General Corpand Paramount Communications, Inc v TimeWarner, Inc.In these decisions, the Delaware Court effectively removed the teeth from both prongs of the Unocal standard. The court concluded that the board could defend against a noncoercive all-cash, all-shares offer if it determined that the price was too low. Moreover, the court permitted the board to employ any defensive measure it preferred provided the measure was not "preclusive or coercive."Finally, the court also concluded that the board could "just say no" to an acquisition.
Many commentators decried this development in Delaware law. They argued that "just say no" would reduce shareholder welfare by giving the board control over takeovers, a central mechanism for disciplining the board. Leading corporate scholars asserted that shareholder welfare would be maximized by giving shareholders ultimate control over tender offer defenses, thereby wresting from the board managerial authority over this area.
In their contribution to this Symposium, Marcel Kahan and Ed Rock argue that critics of Delaware law may have overstated both the adverse effects of the change in Delaware law and the need for reform. Many proposals for legal intervention presume an essential role for law, largely because they implicitly assume that corporate constituents--shareholders and managers--do not themselves act to redress the problem of board agency costs in adopting takeover defenses. By contrast, Kahan and Rock claim, corporate constituents can, and do, act to reduce agency costs by employing "adaptive devices." This widespread use of private solutions to board agency costs suggests that the development of the poison pill and adoption of "just say no" have not necessarily had a decisive negative impact on corporate welfare, Kahan and Rock assert.This warrants reexamination of the conventional wisdom regarding the need to change Delaware law governing takeovers, they conclude.
Kahan and Rock's recognition of the availability of private solutions to the problem of the board's conflict of interest in responding to tender offers is important, especially since private parties have a range of instruments available to them that are not available to the courts.Nevertheless the possibility of private action does not necessarily lead to the conclusions they reach regarding the significance--or relative lack thereof--of Delaware law governing takeovers. Notwithstanding the possibility of private action, Delaware law may play a vital role because private parties cannot necessarily remedy all agency cost problems associated with tender offers, and courts have instruments available to them that are not available to the parties. Appropriate legal intervention thus may extend beyond adopting optimal default rules parties might adopt to include interventions designed to redress problems the parties cannot solve themselves. Thus optimal legal regimes may operate in concert with private "contracting" by altering the set of feasible private solutions. A suboptimal legal regime can result in suboptimal private agreements. Thus, legal intervention may matter a great deal even when parties can adopt mechanisms to govern a particular issue. An optimal legal regime can enable the parties to adopt arrangements that they otherwise could not (or would not), increasing the parties' joint welfare.
Legal intervention may be particularly important with respect to tender offer defenses because private contracting in this area is adversely affected by many problems, some of which may best be addressed by legal intervention. One important problem, considered here, is that of unforeseen contingencies. This limitation is aggravated by the problem of unverifiability. Corporate constituents' ability to employ private solutions to address the takeover defense problem is limited by the fact that they cannot easily contract to prohibit, or limit the scope of, antitakeover devices. Corporate constituents cannot write contracts that prohibit "antitakeover devices," for example, because it often is difficult to define the term: it is often hard to determine whether a corporate action is an antitakeover device or a legitimate business action. This is particularly true of antitakeover devices employed in advance of a tender offer. Nor can corporate constituents circumvent this problem by identifying and individually prohibiting each potential antitakeover device because they cannot fully anticipate all the measures a board might employ. These other measures might be worse for the firm than the prohibited measures. Thus, absent legal intervention, shareholders who otherwise might wish to limit defensive measures may nevertheless prefer not to restrict the board's power to employ well-known measures, such as the poison pill, for fear that the board will instead use even more destructive devices. By contrast, under a legal regime entailing more careful court scrutiny of board responses to the takeover threat, shareholders might seek to restrict takeover defenses. This regime might thus be welfare-improving.
Accordingly, the conclusion that private parties can respond to the Delaware Court's adoption of "just say no" does not imply that "just say no" did not significantly reduce shareholder welfare. The doctrine leaves shareholders vulnerable to unpredictable strategic board action, in ways the parties cannot adequately redress through private arrangements. Even with private solutions it remains to be considered whether Delaware courts potentially could improve shareholder welfare by altering Delaware antitakeover law to limit the scope of antitakeover defenses. Thus, while private agreements must be taken into account, they do not necessarily replace the need for legal intervention in this area.

papers.node_id: 9wmmarybuslrev435!!SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?
papers.abstract:
InThe Dignity of Commerce, Nathan Oman sets out an ambitious market theory of contract (hereinafter Market Theory), which he argues is a superior normative foundation for contract law than either the moralist or economic justifications that currently dominate contract theory.According to the Market Theory, contract law ought to be structured to support well-functioning markets because such markets are morally desirable.The moral virtues of markets thus mark both the purpose and limits of contract law.If contract law exists to support well-functioning markets because such markets are morally valuable, then it follows that the law should not support immoral or, as termed by Oman, "pernicious" markets.
The significance of this effort should not be understated. A clear normative foundation is essential to the understanding and application of contract law.Only through a theory of why the law enforces contracts can one determine, for example, which promises should be enforced and which should not, how to calculate damages for breach, and the circumstances under which performance will be excused.The Dignity of Commercethus confronts questions that are both theoretically difficult and of practical importance to courts and lawmakers.

questions.question: Should contract law be normatively grounded in the moral value of well-functioning markets, so that its rules are primarily designed to support market structures and outcomes?
Should contract law refuse to enforce agreements that facilitate or constitute markets that are morally pernicious, i.e., do moral limits on markets properly constrain enforceability?
If the purpose of contract law is to support morally valuable markets, how should that purpose shape which promises are enforced, what remedies are awarded, and when performance is excused?

papers.node_id: 94tullrev961!!SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: Perceptions of Contract Remedies
papers.abstract:
Professor Robert Hillman has examined three traditional beliefs, perceptions, or "lore" of contract law: that expectation damages place a party in the position they would have been in had the contract been fully performed;that the reason for breach, including willfulness of breach, is irrelevant to the tenets of performance and breach; and that parties' intentions prevail with respect to formation and interpretation of contracts.Of course, the perception of a recovery upon breach of a full expectancy is one that oversimplifies the reality that aggrieved parties are typically not made whole - they are not put to right. Not surprisingly, Professor Hillman noted that with respect to remedies in particular, "the failure of expectancy damages to make injured parties whole is not the world's best kept secret."Recovery of a full measure of expectation damages is no more than a "myth" that "rarely, if ever, makes the injured party whole"as suggested by Professor Hillman. Yet, it is, nevertheless, central to contract law as a whole that enforcement of a contract necessitates access to remedies and that those remedies are designed to put the aggrieved party in the position they would have occupied had the contract been fully performed in order to provide incentives for parties to rely on contract performance.
Even if our perception of expectancy's recovery is incomplete, the fulfillment of contractual expectations through remedies is the very foundation of contract law,whether such contract is subject to Article2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (the Code or the U.C.C.)or the common law. It is well understood that the flexibility of remedies available in contract law permits its application in an "infinite variety of business [transactions,] customs and practices."An expectation recovery, however, is subject to many exceptions and limitations,such as exclusion of attorney's fees in most cases,difficulty of recovering for emotional distress,or hurdles to recovering consequential damages such as lost profits.These limitations are notwholly due to the natural operation of well-documented exceptions to a basic rule favoring a full expectancy. Ultimately, the expectation doctrine functions more like a guidepost than an absolute, leaving the wholeness of the compensation overlooked.
While there has been consideration of the approaches or formulas for policing contract breach,there has been less discussion of the shortfalls of an expectancy-based formula to provide compensation. More specifically, an aggrieved party is generally entitled to a recovery that places it in the position it would have been if full performance had occurred so long as the recovery is not penal in nature.Yet, it might be questioned, as Professor Hillman has done,whether enforcement of contracts can be quantified in simple terms by this type of measure. Tension exists between the perception of assurance to the nonbreaching party of receiving the "benefit of the bargain" through access to contractual remedies and other remedial objects that place perhaps important limitations on recovery.
An example of the questions raised by a simple breach of contract for the provision of services is in order (Simple Services Hypothetical). Suppose Tom contracts with Sam to watch his dogs, Angus and Porter, on Friday for sixty dollars while he is at a business meeting. Sam is a no-show. Tom spends thirty minutes finding a new dog sitter and ultimately hires Regina to watch the dogs instead, for the price of ninety dollars. Tom is late to his meeting, as well as aggravated. Sam refuses to provide any compensation for the breach, and Tom decides to bring suit for breach of contract to claim his lost expectation. At the minimum, he faces unfavorable responses at work, emotional damages, and the increased cost of hiring Regina. While Sam may possibly have good reasons for breaching the contract, Tom may want to bring a claim for damages.
In examining this problem, this Article does not question the application of the expectation measure as a remedy in principle for most contract breaches, whether under the common law or U.C.C. Moreover, this Article does not suggest a rewriting of applicable Article 2 provisions at a time when such efforts are not likely to be availing.This Article also does not quibble with those that might argue that the expectation measure is insufficient and some remedy might be justified on an expanded basis, such as cases of identity harm to consumers or other harms to third parties.Rather, this Article takes the position that Professor Hillman is correct in asserting that the expectation measure as "lore" is more of a guidepost, rather than an absolute.Any perceptions of contract remedies as being wholly restorative are in err as contract's remedial rules simply fall well below a true expectancy.
My goal is not to convince those who prefer greater remedial options that an expectation measure provides whole or wholly insufficient compensation. Instead, the nature of the expectation measure is the provision of a remedy that incentivizes parties to rely to a degree on contract performance, whether they do or not, with the understanding that contract law will protect their expectation. This Article will attempt to develop and clarify the limits of the expectation measure's remedial application by applying it in select cases to illustrate that any perception that the measure provides full restoration is incorrect. Professor Hillman's assertion that the restorative nature of expectation damages is part of the lore of contracts, but that context has a role to play, is correct.Part II of this Article explores the basic application of expectation damages in a straightforward case of breach of contract in the Simple Services Hypothetical in order to highlight the principles that guide the remedy and how important limitations on recovery undermine any prospect of a full or whole measure of recovery.Part III analyzes the application of the expectancy measure in more complicated cases, using examples involving breaches by buyers and sellers of goods, including the problems of lost profits and litigation expenses.These cases illustrate that expectation does not fully compensate an aggrieved party for all losses suffered, and risk abounds to contracting parties that is not apparent in the foundations of expectation theory. Part IV demonstrates how our perception of restoration inherent in an expectancy only compensates the parties and does not provide a certain remedy to third parties, using corporate human rights policies adopted in supply agreements as an example.Finally, in Part V, this Article argues that standard formula and approaches toward expectancy, while not fully restorative, provide an appropriate measure of recovery in most cases.In doing so, Part V explains the consequences of limiting an expectation measure such that the aggrieved party recovers its expectation, but does not profit from breach, and there is no penalty to seller, and the parties are still willing to contract on the terms offered.

questions.question: Whether monetary expectation damages intended to put a nonbreaching party in the position of full performance actually make injured parties whole in typical contract breaches
Whether the expectation-measure of recovery, even when it falls short of full restoration, nevertheless provides sufficient incentives for parties to rely on and perform contractual promises
How the practical limits and exceptions on recoverable damages affect the allocation of risk, the adequacy of compensation for different types of losses, and the protection of third-party interests
