papers.node_id: 81uchilrev53!!SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: REVELATION MECHANISMS AND THE LAW: Savage Tables and Tort Law: An Alternative to the Precaution Model
papers.authors: Janet M. Currie; W. Bentley Macleod
papers.abstract:
The model of precaution has become a central tool of law and economics, beginning with Judge Learned Hand's brilliant opinion in United States v Carroll Towing Co.In it he argues that a defendant should be found liable for harm if and only if the expected cost of additional care is less than the expected benefit.
The model of precaution relies upon the economics of incentives, a subfield of game theory - the study of how individuals choose actions when these actions affect others.The landmark books of Professor William Landes and Judge Richard Posner, and Professor Steven Shavell illustrate how the precaution model illuminates a wide variety of legal rules.Professor Guido Calabresi and A. Douglas Melamed show how it can be used tointegrate tort and property.Professor Robert Cooter uses the model to provide a unified analysis of tort and contract.
A central result of the model is that the standard for negligence provides incentives for individuals to take socially optimal actions.This perspective is controversial. Professor Richard Epstein argues that the model of precaution cannot explain observed law and does not provide an adequate model of causation as used in court.He suggests that the socially efficient rule should be one of strict liability.Posner responds, providing a number of examples in which Epstein's approach would lead to undesirable results.He describes Epstein's model as being based upon moral rather than economic considerations.
In this Article we show that the model of precaution is a special case of a more general economic model. We develop a simple technique for discussing this more general model that we dub a "Savage Table,"following Professor Leonard Savage.Our more general model based on general equilibrium theory and decision theory encompasses the views of both Posner and Epstein and sheds light on Epstein's observation that the Hand Rule is not consistently used to determine liability.We show that rational choice does not imply the Hand Rule unless one imposes additional restrictions that are not often satisfied in practice.
We show that strict liability can be viewed as a special case of the negligence standard. In addition, the notion of a causal effect can be easily and naturally defined in our framework. The benefit of a clear definition is that it highlights the key evidentiary requirements to determine causation. Recent work in statistics has greatly clarified our understanding of causalinference.There is no way to prove the existence of a causal relationship. The best we can do is to use a credible model of the world and make causal statements within the context of the model.
Once we look at economic phenomena from our more general perspective, we are led to the following legal-impossibility theorem: For every legal rule that is potentially efficient there exists an environment with rational decision makers for which the rule is not efficient. A rational decision maker must make choices conditional upon the information she has. Given incomplete information, there is no guarantee that a rule that encourages good decision making in one context will work in another.
Posner observed that the best way to deal with this problem is to rely upon empirical evidence.Models are still useful. In fact Professor Paul Holland shows that model building is essential to the measurement of causal effects.Theory and evidence must work together to identify those worldviews that are more successful than the alternatives.
The plan for the rest of the Article is as follows. The next Part provides a very brief discussion of the background theory we use. This is followed by a simplified presentation of the main ideas of the economic theory of exchange and rational choice, in particular the key notions of a "commodity," an "act," and a Savage Table, which provides a convenient way to illustrate these concepts. We show that this model leads naturally to a well-defined notion of causality and relate it to the work of Holland.We then illustrate how these ideas can be applied to tort law and discuss some of the empirical work in the area, with particular reference to our own empirical research on tort law.

questions.question: Whether a liability rule that assigns responsibility when the expected cost of additional care is less than the expected benefit reliably induces socially optimal precautionary behavior across different informational environments.
Whether an always-liable (automatic-responsibility) rule can be represented as a special case of such a comparative-liability rule within a more general equilibrium and decision-theoretic framework.

How causal effects relevant to legal responsibility should be defined and what empirical/evidentiary conditions are required to establish causation in economic models, and whether any single legal rule can be guaranteed efficient given rational decision makers with incomplete information.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81nclrev2239!!ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE REGULATION OF CONTRACTUAL CHANGE: A GUIDE TO NO ORAL MODIFICATION CLAUSES FOR NORTH CAROLINA LAWYERS

shared_topics.topic: how parties' information and reliance shape whether legal rules produce efficient or fair outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that rational actors make choices conditional on their information and shows (via a legal-impossibility theorem) that rules which induce good behavior in one information environment can fail in another; Paper B analyzes how parties' reliance on oral modifications or conduct can make rigid enforcement of no-oral-modification clauses produce injustice and argues the law must account for such reliance.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary standards for establishing legal effects (causation in torts vs waiver/modification/estoppel in contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a decision-theoretic framework to clarify the evidentiary requirements for establishing causal effects in tort cases, while Paper B surveys and criticizes the inconsistent evidentiary and doctrinal approaches courts use to find waiver, modification, or estoppel under NOM/NOW clauses.

shared_topics.topic: the desirability of categorical versus qualified legal rules (limits of blanket rules like negligence/strict liability and absolute NOM clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that negligence rules (Hand rule) and strict liability are special cases within a broader model and that no single rule is efficient across all environments, and Paper B argues that treating NOM/NOW clauses as universally binding can produce substantial injustice and advocates statutory or doctrinal qualifications.

shared_topics.topic: incentive and behavioral implications of legal doctrines (precaution/negligence tradeoffs and contractual certainty versus flexibility)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses economic and decision-theory analysis to study how negligence and strict liability create different incentives for precaution, while Paper B examines the practical incentives created by NOM/NOW clauses—how contractual certainty promotes locking in deals but can discourage adaptive, economically sensible informal modifications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90texlrev1153!!ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Myth of the Customary Law Merchant

shared_topics.topic: the limits of private ordering and the role of formal rules (contracts/statutes) versus customs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes reliance on simple precaution-based private ordering by showing (via a more general economic model) that legal standards like negligence do not automatically induce optimal private behavior without additional assumptions, while Paper B shows historically that widespread commercial rules arose mainly from contract and statute rather than a uniform merchant custom, challenging the idea that informal customs alone can reliably govern complex transactions.

shared_topics.topic: context-dependence and transplantability of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proves a legal‑impossibility result that a rule that is efficient in one information environment can be inefficient in another, emphasizing sensitivity to decision-makers' information; Paper B argues that commercial customs typically could not be transplanted intact across medieval localities and therefore could not create a uniform transnational lex mercatoria, highlighting the same problem of context sensitivity.

shared_topics.topic: using empirical or historical evidence to evaluate law-and-economics claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that empirical work is necessary to test and choose among theoretical models (and reports its own empirical tort research), and Paper B uses historical and archival evidence to rebut the economistic/mercatorist narrative that private ordering via a uniform law merchant efficiently governed medieval trade.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of economic models to explain observed legal institutions and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the Hand/precaution model is a special case of a broader decision‑theoretic framework and may fail to predict actual liability doctrines without extra assumptions, while Paper B challenges the explanatory power of the mercatorist account (often advanced by law-and-economics scholars) that private customs naturally produced efficient transnational commercial law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 51stanlrev1591!!ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Majoritarian vs. Minoritarian Defaults

shared_topics.topic: how informational asymmetries and incomplete information affect the efficiency of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a general decision-theoretic model showing that incomplete information can make rules like the Hand negligence standard inefficient in some environments (a legal-impossibility result), while Paper B analyzes how private information about parties' types undermines the effectiveness of default rules and can prevent efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: legal rules as mechanisms to induce behavior or information revelation (negligence/strict liability vs penalty/default rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames negligence and strict liability as incentive devices within an economic model and shows strict liability can be a special case of negligence, whereas Paper B studies penalty default rules and other minoritarian defaults as tools designed to induce information revelation or particular contracting behavior.

shared_topics.topic: context-dependence and limits of one-size-fits-all normative economic models for rule choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that rational choice does not uniquely justify Hand's Rule and proves that any potentially efficient rule can fail in some informational environments, and Paper B emphasizes that whether a default is efficient depends on many environment-specific factors (type distributions, market power, transaction costs), so simple majoritarian prescriptions are often inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical evidence and environment-specific inquiry to inform legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the role of empirical work and credible models to identify causal effects and evaluate legal rules (citing Posner and Holland), while Paper B argues that theoretic examples are often simplistic and that policymakers face empirical uncertainty when deciding between majoritarian and information-forcing defaults.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev923!!ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?

shared_topics.topic: ex ante (incentive-based) versus ex post (case-by-case) legal design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the precaution model (the Hand rule) as an ex ante incentive device for preventing harm and shows its limitations under more general decision models, while Paper B centrally frames legal choice as a tradeoff between ex ante regulation and ex post assessment across contexts (using the ticking-bomb/torture example) and explores when each perspective is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between rules and standards as a normative/instrumental decision
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats negligence, strict liability and the Hand Rule as distinct legal standards/rules and shows how their efficiency properties vary with model assumptions, whereas Paper B explicitly maps the ex ante/ex post distinction onto the rules-versus-standards debate and examines which form of legal directive (rule or standard) better fits different problems.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the rational-choice/efficiency framework under incomplete information and uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proves a legal-impossibility result showing that rules that encourage optimal action for rational agents in some environments fail in others because agents act on their information, and Paper B critiques reliance on rational-choice ex ante policy in uncertain or nonrepresentative cases, arguing that ex post considerations may be needed.

shared_topics.topic: the role of formal models and empirical/causal inference in evaluating legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops Savage Tables and draws on decision theory and modern causal inference to clarify evidentiary requirements and to test models empirically, while Paper B emphasizes that theoretical accounts (ex ante/ex post) are insufficient alone and that policy analysis — implicitly including modeling and empirical assessment — is necessary to decide which perspective to apply.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 115yalelj814!!ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Anticipating Litigation in Contract Design

shared_topics.topic: how evidentiary production and verification costs shape legal incentives and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the evidentiary requirements needed to establish causation and how those evidentiary constraints affect when legal rules (negligence vs strict liability) will induce efficient behavior; Paper B models litigation as an evidentiary process in which parties and courts choose and weigh proxies, showing how the costs of producing and verifying evidence drive the choice between precise and vague contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: using decision‑theoretic / economic models to evaluate legal rules' incentive effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a general decision‑theoretic framework (Savage Tables and general equilibrium notions) to analyze when precaution rules like the Hand formula yield efficient incentives, while Paper B applies economic contract theory to reason about how incomplete contracting and the allocation of front‑ and back‑end costs affect parties' incentive choices in contract design.

shared_topics.topic: the front‑end (ex ante) versus back‑end (ex post) allocation of rule content (rules vs standards) and its efficiency consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts ex ante precaution incentives embodied in negligence/strict liability rules and shows that efficiency depends on the informational environment, and Paper B directly studies the tradeoff of assigning content at contracting (precise terms/rules) versus at enforcement (vague standards), analyzing how that allocation affects overall contracting efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private information and uncertainty in determining whether legal rules are efficient
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates a legal‑impossibility insight that incomplete information can make any potentially efficient rule fail in some environments, and Paper B examines how private information, verification uncertainty, and the parties' informational advantages shape the optimal mix of precise versus vague contract provisions and enforcement mechanisms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev931!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive authority between judges and juries (the fact/law distinction)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes whether contract interpretation questions are factual (for juries) or legal (for judges) and how that distinction shapes appellate review; Paper B engages the related issue in torts by examining who establishes causal facts and how legal standards (negligence vs strict liability) interact with fact-finding and evidentiary determinations.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of extrinsic/evidentiary proof in resolving legal disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the parol evidence rule and the plain-meaning doctrine—limits on using extrinsic evidence to interpret contracts—while Paper B focuses on evidentiary requirements for causal inference in tort law and how models clarify what evidence is needed to support causal claims.

shared_topics.topic: how decision‑makers' information and incentives shape legal rules and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a decision‑theoretic model showing that rational actors with different information can make a rule inefficient (legal‑impossibility theorem); Paper A shows doctrinal rules have been shaped (and distorted) by concern over juries' incentives and behaviors, producing rules designed to steer outcomes given particular decision‑maker tendencies.

shared_topics.topic: the normative limits of doctrinal rules to deliver desired policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that efforts to design contract‐interpretation doctrines to avoid jury influence produce confusion and may fail to achieve core contract values; Paper B proves more generally that any legal rule may fail to be efficient in some informational environments, highlighting limits on doctrinal designs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78templrev99!!ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE BEWITCHMENT OF INTELLIGENCE: LANGUAGE AND EX POST ILLUSIONS OF INTENTION

shared_topics.topic: limits of inferring ex ante intentions or optimal actions from ex post information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows formally that, under incomplete information, legal rules that are efficient in some environments will be inefficient in others and that rational choice does not imply the Hand negligence rule without extra assumptions; Paper B argues that, for complex contracts, a determinate mutual ex ante intention often does not exist or cannot be reconstructed ex post, so courts cannot reliably divine what the parties 'intended.'

shared_topics.topic: epistemic constraints on legal factfinding (causation/meaning) and the role of models or frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a Savage Table decision-theoretic framework and invokes modern statistical work on causal inference to clarify what evidence is required to establish causation; Paper B examines philosophical accounts of language and rule-induction (Wittgenstein, Kant, Habermas) to show the epistemic limits of extracting meaning from contract text at the time of dispute.

shared_topics.topic: normative consequences for legal doctrine given human informational and cognitive limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications about when negligence versus strict liability (or other rules) will produce socially optimal incentives given decision-makers' information, while Paper B concludes that doctrines focused on enforcing an imagined ex ante meeting of the minds misdiagnose opportunism and that courts should adopt pragmatic dispute-resolution rules instead.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between formal theory and practical/empirical adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that theory and empirical evidence must be combined to evaluate which legal rules work across environments and presents empirical tort research, whereas Paper B emphasizes practitioners' experience and pragmatic resolution over abstract doctrinal or purely theoretical accounts of contract interpretation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113yalelj1417!!ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations of legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an account of why promises and contracts give rise to moral and legal obligations (arguing for a relational/communal grounding rather than individualistic accounts), and Paper B asks what normative foundations (efficiency/incentives versus alternatives like strict liability) justify tort rules such as negligence, treating competing justificatory frameworks explicitly.

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectations and information in assigning responsibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically engages with theories that ground promissory and contractual duties in the reasonable expectations of promisees, while Paper B analyzes how parties' information and expectations affect the efficiency and appropriateness of negligence versus strict liability rules and shows that incomplete information can undermine rules that work in other contexts.

shared_topics.topic: using theoretical frameworks to explain and evaluate specific legal doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a philosophical theory of the contract relation to illuminate doctrinal puzzles (e.g., consideration doctrine and expectation remedies), and Paper B develops a formal decision-theoretic/economic framework (Savage Tables and general equilibrium models) to explain and evaluate tort doctrines like the Hand negligence formula, strict liability, and causation.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape interpersonal behavior and coordination
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promises and contracts as practices that create relations of recognition, respect, and collaboration among participants, while Paper B studies how tort and liability rules create incentives that affect individuals' precautionary choices and the broader patterns of social coordination.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 113pennstlrev1031!!Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration
compared_to.partner_title: Penn State Law Review Symposium: Building the Civilization of Arbitration: Private Ordering and International Commercial Arbitration

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and institutional design shape private incentives and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different liability standards (negligence, strict liability) create incentives for precaution and choice under uncertainty; Paper B examines how the choice between private arbitration and public courts (and the rules governing enforcement) affects parties' contracting and dispute-resolution behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information clarity and informational asymmetries in legal choice and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that rational actors make decisions conditional on the information they have and shows that incomplete information can defeat rules like the Hand formula; Paper B treats the clarity of applicable law and distance/complexity between parties as key informational attributes that drive whether parties opt for arbitration or court litigation.

shared_topics.topic: context-dependence of which legal regime or dispute-resolution mechanism is efficient
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proves a legal-impossibility result showing no single liability rule is efficient across all environments and highlights dependence on contextual information; Paper B argues that arbitration versus litigation efficiency depends on transaction attributes (distance, complexity, speed, clarity), asserting there is no one-size-fits-all choice.

shared_topics.topic: the joint use of formal models and empirical evidence to evaluate legal institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a generalized decision-theoretic/economic model (Savage Tables) and stresses the need for empirical work to identify which models fit real-world causation and incentives; Paper B uses a descriptive-analytic framework about transaction attributes and calls for further empirical work to validate how those attributes predict parties' dispute-resolution choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99michlrev1724!!ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:PRIVATE COMMERCIAL LAW IN THE COTTON INDUSTRY: CREATING COOPERATION THROUGH RULES, NORMS, AND INSTITUTIONS

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules function as incentive mechanisms to produce efficient behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes negligence, strict liability, and the Hand Rule through economic models (Savage Tables, decision theory) to show how rules create incentives for precaution; Paper B analyzes the private commercial law of the cotton industry as a set of rules, norms, and arbitration procedures that structure incentives to foster cooperation and efficient exchange.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information and incomplete information in determining whether legal rules work as intended
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that rational actors make choices conditional on their information and proves a legal-impossibility result showing rules may fail under incomplete information; Paper B documents how the cotton industry builds informational infrastructures (reputation systems, recordkeeping, norms) that reduce information problems and make private rules effective.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of alternative legal regimes using theory and empirical/case evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates negligence and strict liability as special cases within a broader theoretical model and calls for empirical work to test models of causation and liability; Paper B uses a detailed empirical case study to compare private commercial law and public law (UCC/courts), showing circumstances under which private regimes outperform public ones.

shared_topics.topic: application of economic/game-theoretic concepts (incentives, transaction costs, reputation) to explain legal institutions' performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames tort standards in terms of incentives and rational-choice/game-theoretic reasoning about precaution and causation; Paper B explains the success of the cotton industry's private legal system via transaction-cost reduction, reputation-based sanctions, and institutional design informed by economic reasoning.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88michlrev489!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT LAW, DEFAULT RULES, AND THE PHILOSOPHY OF PROMISING.

shared_topics.topic: limits of abstract normative theories to determine specific legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that philosophical theories about promising (e.g., fidelity, autonomy) cannot by themselves determine the content of contract law's background or default rules, and Paper B shows that the economic 'precaution' model is only a special-case formalism and that rational-choice theory does not uniquely imply a single tort rule absent further restrictions — both thus critique relying solely on an abstract theory to pick concrete legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: how to choose the form of legal standards or default rules (negligence vs strict liability; waivable vs mandatory contract defaults)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether particular contract rules should be default/waivable or mandatory and criticizes philosophical accounts for failing to guide that choice, while Paper B analyzes the relationship between negligence and strict liability (showing strict liability as a special case) and demonstrates that which liability standard is efficient depends on informational and contextual factors.

shared_topics.topic: economic efficiency versus other justificatory values in shaping law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts arguments that enforce promises on grounds of economic efficiency or relational value with theories grounded in autonomy/fidelity and shows the former can have content implications for background rules, and Paper B explicitly uses law-and-economics models (and engages Posner/Epstein debates) to assess when efficiency-based rules like the Hand Rule or strict liability are appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: need for additional constraints, context, or empirical support beyond formal theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that rejecting efficiency-based justifications still leaves open why certain background rules should be chosen and calls for further argument about competing values, and Paper B emphasizes that models must be paired with empirical evidence and that different informational environments can make a rule efficient in one context but not another.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 102valrev1523!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT AND THE DEFAULT RULE PROJECT

shared_topics.topic: limits of one-size-fits-all legal rules given heterogeneous contexts and information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proves a legal-impossibility result showing that any potentially efficient legal rule can be inefficient in some environments because rational actors act on their private information; Paper B similarly argues that default rules cannot be efficiently specified for the many distinct contracting contexts in an advanced economy, so blanket defaults will fail.

shared_topics.topic: normative and positive evaluation of rules versus standards as mechanisms for default governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes negligence (a standard) versus strict liability (a rule), showing how each arises within a more general decision-theoretic model and when one may be preferable, while Paper B provides a detailed critique of the drafters' turn from rules to standards in contract default design and argues standards are often inappropriate for commercial contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the role of empirical evidence and observed practice in choosing and validating legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that models must be paired with empirical work to identify when legal rules (like the Hand formula) apply and discusses empirical tort research, and Paper B uses observed contracting behavior and market practice to show why many drafted defaults failed and why common-law-created defaults better reflect practice.

shared_topics.topic: decision-making under incomplete information and its implications for institutional design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how agents' choices conditional on their information undermine the universal application of precaution-based liability rules, and Paper B shows that drafters lack the contextual information needed to craft efficient defaults, implying institutional limits on centralized lawmaking versus adaptive common-law processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54ambuslj519!!ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Hermeneutic Perspective on the Interpretation of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: the limits of one-size-fits-all legal rules and the need for context dependence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proves a legal-impossibility result showing that a rule that is potentially efficient in one informational environment can be inefficient in another and argues for empirical/model-based selection; Paper B develops a context-dependent model for contract interpretation that weighs interpretive methods against contract characteristics and relational context.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal theory/models and normative/legal decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the Hand precaution model within a more general Savage-Table decision-theoretic framework and insists that theory must be complemented by empirical evidence when choosing rules; Paper B integrates hermeneutic theory with modern contract theory and emphasizes that hermeneutics supplies analytic possibilities while normative choice among methods depends on contract-theoretic considerations (including economic and institutional arguments).

shared_topics.topic: how latent legal concepts (like causation or intent) should be defined and inferred from evidence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a decision-theoretic notion of causal effect and highlights the evidentiary requirements and limits of causal inference in tort law; Paper B centers the dispute between authorial and textual approaches on how to identify parties' intent and how textual and extra-textual evidence should be weighed in doing so.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of competing legal standards through theoretical frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows negligence and strict liability are special cases of a broader model and compares when each standard is justified under different assumptions; Paper B contrasts neoformalism and relational contract theory, mapping how each theoretical stance supports different interpretive standards and proposing criteria to choose between them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69minnlrev471!!ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Winner Take Some: Loss Sharing and Commercial Impracticability.

shared_topics.topic: using economic analysis (incentives and efficiency) to evaluate legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A generalizes the precaution/negligence model into a broader economic decision-theory framework and assesses when negligence or strict liability produce socially optimal incentives; Paper B evaluates commercial impracticability and loss-allocation through an economic lens, arguing that absolute liability can be inefficient and proposing economically informed loss-sharing remedies.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of losses/liability and risk‑sharing mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how negligence and strict liability allocate the costs of accidents and shows strict liability is a special case of negligence within its model; Paper B develops concrete methodologies for splitting performance losses when contracts become commercially impracticable and asks who should bear residual risk.

shared_topics.topic: limits of doctrinal rules and the need for flexible or alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates a legal‑impossibility result showing that no single legal rule is universally efficient given differing information environments and advocates combining theory with empirical evidence; Paper B critiques the traditional all‑or‑nothing doctrinal approach to impracticability and proposes alternative, more flexible loss‑sharing frameworks (including party-driven solutions) for varied commercial contexts.

shared_topics.topic: handling unforeseen contingencies and uncertainty in allocation and fault
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on decisionmaking under incomplete information and how causation and precaution rules operate when agents have limited information; Paper B addresses allocation of losses caused by unforeseen, commercially impracticable events and how the law should adjust liability and performance expectations under uncertainty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 98michlrev2727!!SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS:IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION COMMERCIAL NORMS AND THE FINE ART OF THE SMALL CON: COMMENTS ON DANIEL KEATING'S 'EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION'
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS:IV. DOCTRINE IN ACTION COMMERCIAL NORMS AND THE FINE ART OF THE SMALL CON: COMMENTS ON DANIEL KEATING'S 'EXPLORING THE BATTLE OF THE FORMS IN ACTION'

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical evidence to evaluate and refine legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that economic models must be tested and supplemented by empirical work (and references the authors' own empirical research on tort law), while Paper B is itself an empirical study of contracting practice and repeatedly discusses what the data does and does not reveal about doctrinal questions.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules interact with private ordering and contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how negligence, strict liability, and legal standards create incentives that shape parties' precautionary behavior, and Paper B studies how commercial parties use master agreements and other contracting practices to structure their transactions and avoid doctrinal frictions like the battle of the forms.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of incomplete information and real-world environments on the effectiveness of legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a legal-impossibility result showing rules that are efficient in some environments can fail under different informational conditions, and Paper B documents real-world contracting workarounds (and remaining problems) that arise because standardized forms and courts' rules do not perfectly resolve informational and coordination gaps.

shared_topics.topic: the central role of judicial interpretation and doctrinal application in producing practical outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates how courts apply standards (e.g., the Hand Rule versus strict liability) and how inconsistent usage affects incentives, while Paper B focuses on how courts might or might not uphold master agreements and the doctrinal hurdles that determine whether private solutions actually resolve disputes.
