shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses price outcomes to infer whether the UCC default reduces transaction costs and accords with consumer expectations (hence potentially improving welfare), while Paper B develops a welfare-oriented model for when judicially supplied terms or liability rules are justified to overcome barriers like opportunism and sunk costs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information costs, uncertainty, and transaction costs in deciding to rely on defaults versus explicit contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A motivates defaults as saving parties the cost of formalizing expectations and uses a field experiment to see if that assumption holds in practice, and Paper B theorizes how information asymmetries, unverifiable contingencies, and the costs of drafting complete contracts affect the desirability of judicial or law-supplied rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9wmmarybuslrev435!!SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: DOES CONTRACT LAW NEED MORALITY?

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations and purpose of contract law (welfare vs moral aims)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers ask what ultimate goal contract law should serve: Paper A develops an instrumental, welfare-driven account—when legal intervention increases gains from trade given opportunism and sunk costs—while Paper B offers a normative Market Theory that grounds contract law in the moral value of well‑functioning markets and uses that moral account to delimit the law's aims.

shared_topics.topic: limits of enforcement and when courts should decline to supply or enforce terms
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of when courts ought not to enforce or should refrain from supplying terms: Paper A debates the ‘freedom from contract’ and new‑formalist cautions against courts imposing unverifiable ex post terms, and Paper B asks which promises or market transactions are morally impermissible ("pernicious") and thus should not be supported by contract law.

shared_topics.topic: translation of normative theory into doctrinal choices (default rules, remedies, and scope of enforceability)
shared_topics.justification: Both link high‑level theory to concrete doctrinal design: Paper A uses its model to recommend when courts should supply default terms or liability rules (including consideration of damages and enforcement incentives), while Paper B argues that a Market Theory yields practical answers about which promises to enforce, how to calculate damages, and when performance should be excused.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private ordering/market norms and legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the boundary between law and private/market-based governance: Paper A compares nonlegal sanctions, commercial norms, and private strategies against judicial intervention as solutions to opportunism, and Paper B evaluates how contract law should support (or refuse to support) market practices based on whether markets are morally valuable or pernicious.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26flastulrev897!!ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: EMPIRE OR RESIDUE: COMPETING VISIONS OF THE CONTRACTUAL CANON

shared_topics.topic: whether particular legal rules should be defaults (susceptible to private reordering) or mandatory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a central normative puzzle as whether rules in a given domain should be mandatory or set as defaults that parties can contract around and which default to choose; Paper B treats the same choice functionally as whether courts (or the law) should supply terms or liability rules when parties have not agreed, i.e., when to impose law-supplied defaults versus respecting nonintervention.

shared_topics.topic: when judicial or legal intervention in incomplete or absent bargains is justified versus respecting party autonomy (freedom to/from contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a methodology for when courts should fill gaps, interpret, or impose liability to increase welfare, weighing intervention against freedom from contract; Paper A similarly insists that debates about what is 'contract' should be driven by consequentialist questions about when the law should permit or impede parties' private ordering rather than by semantic labels.

shared_topics.topic: the role of informational and behavioral uncertainty (opportunism, sunk costs) in motivating law-supplied terms or defaults
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on behavioral uncertainty—opportunism, bounded rationality, and sunk costs—as the key structural barriers justifying legal intervention to control opportunism; Paper A engages these issues by emphasizing information-forcing or penalty defaults, disclosure rules (e.g., rent-to-own implicit interest), and the need to set defaults with attention to information problems that affect parties' bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: capacity for private ordering (ability to contract around default rules) as a defining feature of the contractual domain
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes defining the contractual canon by whether parties can privately reorder a substantial portion of their legal relations; Paper B repeatedly evaluates whether parties can, in practice, achieve bargains or design private solutions (vs needing courts), treating the extent of private ordering capacity as central to whether legal rules should be supplied.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45arizstlj925!!ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Fifty: Shades of Grey - Uncertainty About Extrinsic Evidence and Parol Evidence After All These UCC Years

shared_topics.topic: when courts may legitimately add, supply, or interpret terms in incomplete or ambiguous contracts

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and role of extrinsic/parol evidence and trade usage in resolving contract meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses directly on the doctrinal distinctions in UCC §2-202 and related provisions governing extrinsic and parol evidence and trade usage, and Paper A engages the same functional issue more generally by treating contract interpretation and fact-finding about parties' intentions as a mechanism courts use to fill gaps or resolve ambiguity in agreements.

shared_topics.topic: tension between party autonomy (freedom to/not to contract) and law‑supplied default rules or judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames intervention as a tradeoff between respecting parties' freedom not to have rules imposed and supplying defaults that increase gains from trade; Paper B shows how doctrinal choices about admitting extrinsic evidence or rigid plain-meaning rules affect the degree to which courts impose meanings beyond the parties' written words, implicating the same autonomy-versus-intervention tension.

shared_topics.topic: information and uncertainty problems about parties' intentions or behavior and the courts' institutional capacity to resolve them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a behavioral-uncertainty account (opportunism, sunk costs, bounded rationality) to explain why parties may leave terms unspecified and when courts can improve outcomes, while Paper B documents doctrinal and evidentiary mechanisms (ambiguity determinations, extrinsic evidence, trade usage) courts use to resolve uncertainty about contract meaning and critiques courts' capacity or tendency to misapply those tools.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Corporations and Autonomy Theories of Contract: A Critique of the New Lex Mercatoria

shared_topics.topic: reconciling party autonomy (consent-based) theories with welfare/efficiency theories in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques efforts to exclude autonomy theories from analysis of corporate contracting and argues that autonomy can be reconciled with law-and-economics approaches (e.g., nexus-of-contracts), while Paper B frames the intervention question as a tradeoff between respecting parties' freedom to/from contract and using legal intervention to increase gains from trade, developing conditions under which welfare-augmenting intervention is justified.

shared_topics.topic: how the characteristics and capacities of contracting parties shape doctrinal applicability and normative justification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the consequences of treating corporations (institutional parties) as contracting actors for autonomy-based theories and examines competing conceptions of the corporate actor, whereas Paper B analyzes bounded rationality, informational limits, behavioral uncertainty, sunk costs, and opportunism as party-level features that determine whether parties can complete contracts or require judicially supplied terms.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and methodological basis for courts to interpret contracts, fill gaps, or supply default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses contract interpretation (including corporate-to-corporate cases) to illustrate how autonomy-based arguments operate and to test integration with efficiency models, and Paper B develops a taxonomy and model for when courts should intervene by interpreting contracts, supplying terms, or imposing liability/default rules to control opportunism and improve welfare.

shared_topics.topic: the need for an integrative framework or meta-theory to adjudicate between competing contract-law approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A laments theoretical pluralism in contract scholarship and urges principled integration of autonomy and welfare theories (using corporations as a test case), while Paper B offers a broad, instrumentally oriented framework to guide when legal intervention in incomplete contracts is justified, aiming to unify disparate strands of scholarship on interpretation, default rules, and intervention.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Pragmatic Strategy for the Scope of Sales Law, the Statute of Frauds, and the Global Currency Bazaar

shared_topics.topic: balancing party autonomy (freedom to contract/not to contract) against judicial intervention to promote welfare

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Pragmatic Strategy for the Scope of Sales Law, the Statute of Frauds, and the Global Currency Bazaar

shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises issues about the scope of sales law and enforceability that implicate when informal or nontraditional transactions should be treated as binding, while Paper B develops a methodology for judicial intervention in incomplete or informal bargains (weighing freedom to contract against freedom from contract and when courts should add terms or impose liability).

shared_topics.topic: contract law's instrumental role in facilitating exchange, investment, and gains from trade (addressing transaction costs, sunk costs, and opportunism)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates sales and transactional doctrines (including in global currency markets) within a larger commercial practice that depends on enforceable promises, and Paper B analyzes how enforcement, default rules, and judicial intervention can reduce transaction costs, mitigate sunk-cost risk and opportunism, and thereby increase socially valuable exchanges.

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev455!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE RELATIONAL CONSTITUTION OF REMEDY: CO-OPERATION AS THE IMPLICIT SECOND PRINCIPLE OF REMEDIES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:FORESEEABILITY AND DAMAGES:THE RELATIONAL CONSTITUTION OF REMEDY: CO-OPERATION AS THE IMPLICIT SECOND PRINCIPLE OF REMEDIES FOR BREACH OF CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
I am of the opinion that the main reason the relational theory of contract has encountered such resistance from mainstream thinking on the law of contract thought is that it has been interpreted as a very paternalistic theory opposed to freedom of contract, one which has no or very little place for competition.As I have argued elsewhere, thiscertainly was not Ian Macneil's intention,and, drawing on his work, the relational theory can readily be restated in such a way as to give competition a central place in it.Nevertheless, that the relational theory is associated with general paternalism is undeniable,and in this paper I hope to call this association further into question by giving a general defence of breach of contract from the relational perspective. In a sense I intend to go rather further than in my previous attempts to bring competition into the relational theory, for on this occasion I do intend to argue that, in important ways, Macneil's own views (on breach) are open to radical criticism, as are those of the other principal contributor to the relational theory, Stewart Macaulay.
As I trust will be fully acknowledged in this paper, the defence of breach I will put forward is very substantially indebted to the important contributions to our understanding of the remedies for breach which a number of writers sympathetic to the relational perspective, notably Charles Goetz, Alan Schwartz, and Robert Scott, have made, and continue to make. Nevertheless, the predominant attitude taken towards breach by writers with such sympathies, including Macaulay and Macneil themselves, is that breach represents an amoral or immoral failure by the breaching party to respect, not only the obligations which contracts themselves impose, but, more importantly, those on which contracting rests. It therefore would seem that breach must generally be disapproved from the relational perspective.
will argue that such disapproval is a mistake. Far from it being the function of the law of contract to (so far as possible) prevent breach, the function of that law is to make breach possible, although on terms which the law regulates. This function is so central to the efficient working of the market economy that, in an important sense, there is very little point in passing moral judgement upon it. So long as one is committed to the market economy, one must allow contract to perform this function; and we are all now, of course, committed to that economy. The point I wish to stress, however, is that this is not an instance of having to sacrifice what is "moral" to what is economically "efficient." I will argue that the expectation principle allows breach to work in an efficient way only by giving the parties a strong incentive to co-operate in dealing with the errors the defendant has made whenagreeing the terms of the contract; the manifestation of those errors in increasing costs of performance being the reason the good faith defendant wishes to breach.In order to emphasise the way I am hoping to change the view taken of the expectation principle in the relational theory, I will put my argument in the following way. Whilst protection of the claimant'sexpectation is the first principle of remedies for breach of contract, co-operation in keeping the defendant's costs of furnishing that protection as low as possible is the second principle. One cannot explain the basic structure of the law of remedies using only the first principle. I hope to show one can explain that structure using both principles, which together reveal the co-operative nature of breach.
Whereas the principle of protecting the claimant's expectation is, of course, so well known as to be trite law (until recent developments in the law of restitution in particular have called it into question in England and Wales), the second principle is, to say the least, obscure. Though it is my basic claim that the specific legal rules constituting the second principle do already exist, the principle is not merely not recognised but is denied by those who understand breach as amoral or immoral, and this failure of recognition may be taken to extremes of antagonism in the attitudes and conduct of the parties (and their advisers) to strenuously contested commercial litigation. It is not the least ambitious of my aims that I intend my argument to have the clear implication for those parties that they should eschew this antagonism, which fails to represent, not merely their counterparts', but their own best interest, were they adequately self-conscious of it.

questions.question: Whether, in a market economy, contract law should enable and regulate breaches (rather than primarily seeking to prevent or morally condemn them) as part of efficient contracting practice.
Whether remedies for breach should be structured to both restore the non-breaching party's expected benefit and to incentivize cooperative behavior that minimizes the cost of providing that remedy.
Whether recognizing cooperation as an explicit guiding principle of remedies reduces adversarial conduct (by parties and advisers) and leads to more efficient post-breach outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84nyulrev1023!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT DESIGN AND THE STRUCTURE OF CONTRACTUAL INTENT

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between legal enforcement and relational norms in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a contract-design theory about parties choosing between legal (court-enforced) and relational (reputation, repeat-play) means of performance and argues courts should respect parties' choice; Paper B engages the relational theory of contract and defends remedies (and breach) from a perspective that emphasizes cooperation and the continued role of relational norms alongside legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedies (and judicial intervention) in shaping contractual behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how equitable doctrines and ex post judicial overrides of formal terms alter parties' incentives and undermine certain contract-design strategies; Paper B focuses on remedies for breach (the expectation principle) and argues remedies should enable efficient breach and cooperative error-correction rather than simply punish, thus treating remedies as central to contract function.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules influence ex ante contract design and parties' incentives (precision vs vagueness, rules vs standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes parties' deliberate choice between vague standards and precise rules to shift front-end and back-end contracting costs and shows why faithful formal enforcement matters for those choices; Paper B, from a relational angle, considers how the structure of remedies and allowance for breach create incentives that affect how parties bargain and cooperate when terms prove costly to perform.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between parties' ex ante allocations and courts' ex post use of hindsight
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the two-stage adjudicative regime where courts use hindsight to 'correct' formal terms contrary to parties' chosen means, arguing sophisticated parties often prefer limiting such ex post correction; Paper B addresses the fact that parties err in contracting and defends a remedial framework that permits breach but incentivizes cooperative handling of ex post errors, engaging the same tension between ex ante expectations and ex post adjustments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105califlrev1725!!SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Gerken's Federalism 3.0: Better or Worse Than It Sounds?

shared_topics.topic: cooperation as a central legal principle in sustaining long‑run relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that co‑operation should be treated as an explicit second principle of remedies—structuring damages and incentives so breach is possible but handled cooperatively—while Paper B treats federalism as a constitutional mechanism that prescribes (or fails to prescribe) intergovernmental cooperation for long‑run relationships between governments.

shared_topics.topic: use of contract analogies to model non‑market institutions and constitutional structure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends relational contract theory as a conceptual framework for understanding market transactions and remedies, and Paper B explicitly analyzes federalism through a contract metaphor (e.g., a contract for a smooth or troubled long‑run relationship, or one written for bankruptcy) to explain intergovernmental rules.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between efficiency/instrumental consequences and normative or doctrinal commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts the tension between economic efficiency (making breach possible to preserve market functioning) and moral condemnation of breach, arguing for an expectation‑plus‑cooperation framework; Paper B weighs consequentialist evaluations of federalism (effects on people, collective action vs information problems) against doctrinal doctrines and logical coherence, highlighting inherent policy tradeoffs.

shared_topics.topic: designing legal rules to manage failure, conflict, and the costs of nonperformance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how remedies and the expectation principle are structured to regulate breach, reduce the defendant's costs, and channel responses to nonperformance; Paper B analyzes how federal structures prescribe terms for intergovernmental conflict, allocate responsibility for cross‑border public goods, and effectively write rules that anticipate and manage breakdowns (e.g., 'contract written for bankruptcy').

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58buffalolrev1031!!ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Pluralism in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: balancing economic efficiency and moral or community values in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a core debate as whether contract formation should be grounded in parties' wills, morality, or economic efficiency and argues for pluralist balancing of these values; Paper B directly addresses the tension by defending the role of breach and expectation damages as necessary for market efficiency while arguing that those rules should promote cooperative (and not purely moralistic) responses to breaches.

shared_topics.topic: judicial decision-making as practical reasoning that integrates multiple normative theories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes that judges act as decision agents who rank and apply plural values (liberty, equality, cultural and moral considerations) via practical reason and decision procedures; Paper B likewise is concerned with how the law (and by implication courts and legal doctrine) should recognise both the expectation principle and a cooperative second principle when structuring remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the relational and cooperative dimensions of contracting and performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines cultural and moral pluralism in duties of cooperation (information sharing, audits, good faith) in formation and performance contexts; Paper B develops a relational account of remedies, arguing that cooperation should be treated as an implicit second principle shaping how breach is handled and litigated.

shared_topics.topic: integration of competing contract theories rather than adherence to a single 'super' value
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticises monist theories and advocates pluralist horizontal and vertical integration of autonomy-, community-, rights-, and goods-based contract theories; Paper B criticises readings of relational theory as paternalistic and seeks to assimilate competition, efficiency, and relational insights into a reconciled account of remedies and breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 54depaullrev1077!!ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTINGENCY AND CONTRACTS: A PHILOSOPHY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: contracts as mechanisms to manage contingency and permit breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law (via the expectation remedy) should make breach possible as an efficient way to handle increased performance costs and contingent events, while Paper B treats contracts as one of several normative tools dealmakers use to cope with contingency in complex transactions and analyzes philosophical approaches to that uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: the normatively significant role of cooperation, good faith, and relational practices in commercial contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes cooperation as an implicit second principle of remedies—urging parties and advisers to minimize antagonism and jointly manage the costs of protecting expectations—while Paper B emphasizes trust, honor, and non‑utilitarian relational norms (pragmatic idealism) as essential to getting complex deals done.

shared_topics.topic: limits of purely economic or model-based accounts (homo economicus/Posner-type pragmatism) for explaining real-world dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes readings of relational theory that reduce contracts to paternalistic or purely economic prescriptions and integrates efficiency with relational cooperation, and Paper B directly critiques the dominance of economic/legal models and Posnerian pragmatism, arguing for philosophical and cross-disciplinary complements to economic analysis.

shared_topics.topic: the practical role and responsibilities of lawyers in shaping transactional outcomes and dispute behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how remedies and litigation postures influence party behavior and urges lawyers to promote cooperative resolution when breach occurs, while Paper B analyzes how working lawyers actually address uncertainty in negotiations, recommending a pragmatic‑idealistic stance for deal lawyers to complete transactions and manage contingency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres169!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Contractual Incompleteness: A Transactional Perspective
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: Contractual Incompleteness: A Transactional Perspective

shared_topics.topic: the role of cooperation and good-faith behavior in managing breaches and contractual performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a normative principle that cooperation is the implicit second principle of remedies—arguing expectation damages should incentivize cooperative responses to breaches—while Paper B emphasizes that parties rely on ex ante norms, renegotiation, and cooperative arrangements (rather than courts) to manage gaps and performance, treating cooperation as central to everyday contracting.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and the limits of judicial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends the law of contract should enable breach and regulate terms so parties can resolve performance problems without moral condemnation or excessive litigation, and Paper B argues scholarship (and practice) should focus on private transactional planning because courts often lack the information to supervise many contractual choices, privileging private lawmaking over judicially imposed solutions.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness, renegotiation, and gap-filling as routine transactional phenomena
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates breach and remedial rules within ongoing relational contexts where terms and costs change and parties must adapt, while Paper B directly analyzes why contracts are incomplete, how parties anticipate and manage interpretive gaps, and what transactional strategies (including renegotiation) reduce litigation and inefficiency.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and economic incentives shaping remedies, contract design, and mitigation behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation-protecting remedies as facilitating market efficiency by making breach possible but costly and by motivating cooperative cost-minimizing responses, and Paper B foregrounds law-and-economics considerations—tradeoffs among investment, mitigation, risk allocation, and renegotiation—that guide private contractual design and the choice of default rules and remedial expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev923!!ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Justice: When Do We Decide?

shared_topics.topic: the ex ante vs ex post framing of contract breach and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reframes remedies by treating the law as deliberately enabling breach and regulating the consequences (an implicitly ex post accommodation), while Paper B explicitly develops the ex ante/ex post distinction and cites contracts as a domain where that choice matters for whether rules or after‑the‑fact adjustments govern behavior.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial rules and standards shape incentives to perform and to cooperate after breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the expectation principle combined with a second principle of minimizing defendant costs creates incentives for parties to cooperate once breach is possible, and Paper B links the rules-versus-standards (ex ante rules vs ex post standards) debate to how legal directives structure incentives and allow case‑specific responses.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between moral condemnation and instrumental/efficiency justifications in legal regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the relational critique that breach is morally blameworthy by defending breach as an economically necessary and legally regulated instrument, while Paper B explores similar tensions in the torture/ticking‑bomb context (and in contracts) between categorical moral bans and consequentialist exceptions afforded ex ante or excused ex post.

shared_topics.topic: who (institutions or actors) should decide to follow ex ante rules versus ex post exceptions and how that affects behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the conduct of parties and advisers in litigation and urges cooperative post‑breach behavior within the remedial framework, and Paper B maps institutional and personal dilemmas—legislatures, courts, administrators, or individual officers—in deciding whether to bind actors ex ante or to permit ex post justification.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56casewres135!!SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: INCOMPLETE CONTRACTS: JUDICIAL RESPONSES, TRANSACTIONAL PLANNING, AND LITIGATION STRATEGIES: INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: the normative status and design of remedies for breach (efficient breach/expectation principle)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with how legal rules (including efficient breach doctrines) should be designed given incomplete contracting, renegotiation, and courts' limited verifiability; Paper B explicitly defends the expectation-damages/efficient-breach framework and reframes remedies to incorporate a second principle of cooperation when breach occurs.

shared_topics.topic: how ex post breach/renegotiation interacts with ex ante incentives to invest or perform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the possibility of renegotiation and unverifiability affects parties' ex ante investment and reliance decisions, and how legal rules should account for that; Paper B stresses that allowing breach (and structuring remedies) is crucial to market efficiency and creates incentives for cooperative adjustment after mistakes, affecting parties' contracting choices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' strategic behavior (contract drafting, litigation and settlement strategies) in managing incompleteness and dispute costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how parties deploy front‑end (drafting, delegation, private devices) and back‑end (litigation strategy, settlement) tactics to mitigate verifiability and enforcement costs; Paper B criticizes adversarial litigation and urges cooperative conduct and strategic behavior that keeps the costs of vindicating expectations low when disputes arise.

shared_topics.topic: the proper balance between judicial intervention and private ordering in resolving contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts when courts should fill gaps versus when parties should be left to private transactional strategies (including delegations and explicit signals to courts); Paper B complements this by arguing that the legal regime (protecting expectation) should be calibrated to enable private cooperation and market functioning rather than paternalistically preventing breach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 18geomasonlrev245!!ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMERCIAL LAW'S COMPLEXITY

shared_topics.topic: interaction between common law doctrines and uniform/statutory commercial codes in shaping contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates remedies (expectation principle, restitution developments) within a broader common-law debate about breach and the relational theory; Paper B documents the proliferation and interaction of statutory regimes (UCC Articles, CISG, UETA, UCITA) and how those statutes compete with or supplant common-law contract principles in commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules allocate risk and shape parties' incentives to breach, cooperate, or litigate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the expectation remedy and a proposed second principle of minimizing the defendant's costs create incentives for cooperation and make breach functionally useful in markets; Paper B shows through UCC revisions and the CMCI case how statutory characterizations and complex rules (e.g., perfection, classification of assets) determine who bears transactional risk and thereby influence commercial conduct and litigation decisions.

shared_topics.topic: tension between economic efficiency and moral or doctrinal commitments in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly challenges the moral condemnation of breach by showing breach can serve market efficiency while still supporting cooperative responses; Paper B explores trade-offs in lawmaking (bright-line rules vs indeterminate standards) and how choices intended to regulate commerce in light of technological and economic change affect efficiency and legal certainty.

shared_topics.topic: the need for legal clarity/simplification to reduce transaction and litigation costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A laments the failure to recognize a cooperative second principle in remedies and urges parties to avoid antagonistic litigation that raises costs; Paper B diagnoses 'external' and 'internal' complexity in commercial law and advances legislative and doctrinal strategies for simplification to lower the unacceptable costs of legal complexity.

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev707!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY V. BAXENDALE: STILL CRAZY AFTER ALL THESE YEARS? PANEL DISCUSSION
papers.authors: Joe Spurlock II; Joseph M. Perillo; Allan C. Hutchinson Roy Ryden Anderson; Florian Faust
papers.abstract:
JOE SPURLOCK: This Conference has been quite an eye-opener for me. Most of my life, as a practicing lawyer, politician, and judge, I expected academics and scholars to live in those ivory towers we all hear about. Over the last fifteen years, as a contracts professor, I have learned that this is not true. We don't always live in ivory towers, we sometimes live in hovels, just like everybody else. But to a certain extent scholars are much like judges. You sit in your cloisters or cells, and you do your research and writing, and then it is only on occasions like this that you get a chance to get together and really share ideas.
The only formal speaker we are going to have is Dr. Florian Faust, who is with us from Germany. The rule of Hadley v. Baxendale is found in virtually all common law countries and is, in a somewhat different form, found in the law of many other countries through the influence of Pothier and the French Civil Code.But Dr. Faust comes to us from a land without Hadley v. Baxendale, or as I said to him, the "island of Germany" within the European Union, and is perhaps in contrast to both the civil and common law worlds. I asked him to tell us what would a world without Hadley be like?
FLORIAN FAUST: I think it would be a happy world. First let me come back to the "island" - I do not think that is quite correct. Austria and Switzerland are also part of the island. But even the French are not so far from it as we may think.
We have heard that the rule of Hadley v. Baxendale comes from Pothier,and0 of the French Civil Code,and the French are, of course, very proud of it. If you read the standard French dissertation on the foreseeability rule, by Isabelle Souleau,you get the impression that all countries which don't have this rule are somewhat dubious, but if you actually look at the role the rule plays in French legal practice, it is very small. The French literature even says that courts have classified actions as tortious in order to avoid the foreseeability rule,because they don't like it. My point is that obviously it is in the French code, but it is not considered as something very important. By the way, an interesting point is that you find, in French standard contract literature, a claim that the British have given up that rule. I traced it back. The notion comes from a dissertation where the writer mixed up another casewith contract damages.From this dissertation, it got into two other books,which cited to the first one, and from them it got into one of the standard contracts textbooks without any sources being given- and there it has been now for many years, and they say, "Well, the British have given up that."
The next point to clarify is that the Germans do have the foreseeability rule with regard to international contracts. The rule, as part of the CISG,and before of the Hague Convention,has been in force in Germany for more than 30 years. The law on international commercial contracts of the former German Democratic Republic contained the foreseeability rule as well.
would like to talk a little bit about how it got into the CISG, because I think that is rather interesting. The origins of the CISG go back to the 1920s, and it was an idea of Ernst Rabel, a famous German lawyer. When they started thinking about how to make this international sales law, it was clear from the outset that the foreseeability rule was going to be incorporated. It was especially Ernst Rabel and the other German lawyers who wanted to have that rule included. I think that is partly because of the idea that the grass is always greener on the other side of the fence. The Germans were proud of knowing this English rule, and they wanted to keep it, and of course the English and the French did not disagree. So it was clear from the outset, from 1930, that this rule was going to be part of the international sales law. Whether or not it is a sensible rule was never considered until the late 1950s, when the draft of the Hague Convention was sent out to the different national governments for comments. The Portuguese government wrote back: "Let's cancel that rule out, it does not make any sense." So people suddenly started to think, is it a good rule or not? And it seems that there were, at this time, at least some serious doubts. But everybody said: "Well, now it's too late to think about that. If we cut it out now, we will have to start all over again. So let's just close our eyes and go our way."Before the adoption of CISG, it was not even discussed whether the rule made sense.
However, the issue was thoroughly discussed when the German codes in the 19th century were drafted, not with regard to the German Civil Code but to the commercial code. At that time, both lawyers and merchants who drafted the commercial code opposed this rule very strongly. Perhaps that fits the fact that, as we heard today, at the special jury in the trial of the Hadley v. Baxendale case, the merchants awarded £ 25 of damages. In Germany the opinion of the merchants was that there are not only the Baxendales of this world, but there are also the Hadleys. The question is whether this loss is to be borne by the Hadleys or by the Baxendales? So we have one party at fault(Baxendale), and one innocent party (the Hadleys), and it was common opinion that the innocent party should be made whole. That was the first reason. The second reason, in the 19th century, was that it is not always possible to give notice. There may be cases where the future plaintiff himself does not know of the possible loss, and this should not bar recovery. Also many merchants considered it inappropriate to have to reveal their own business plans and dealings to the other party just in order to get full recovery, so they should be permitted to keep some things secret. The last reason for rejecting the rule was that damages should not be calculable in advance, because that would encourage people to break contracts intentionally, and that is something bad.
think the basis of all of it is perhaps a fundamentally different notion of what a contract is. For a German, the idea of efficient breach is something extremely dubious. For us, contracts are there to keep them, to perform them, and not to decide whether to perform them or to pay damages. Therefore, our standard remedy is specific performance, not damages. So damages really are the last resort, not the first one.
Even more important, we have no strict liability in contract law. So in order to have to pay damages, the defendant must be at fault. In fact, the fault principle and the principle of full recovery are regarded as two sides of the same coin. When in the 1980s people considered a revision of the German Civil Code, one eminent law professor, Ulrich Huber, proposed the foreseeability rule, but explicitly so because he wanted to introduce strict liability in contract law.Ultimately, strict liability was not introduced, and therefore, foreseeability was not introduced either.
The priority of specific performance is nothing specific to German law. If you look at the new EC consumer sales directive,it is more or less the same thing: if the goods are defective, the primary remedy is specific performance. So you have a right to get another TV set without defect, or to have the defective TV set repaired. Only if the seller does not repair or replace the defective goods, you can cancel the contract or get a price deduction. But the whole directive does not say a word about damages, because obviously they are not consideredas a vital remedy. So the different national states are free whether or not to provide a damage award.
think that is the most important ideological basis for the rejection of the foreseeability rule. We think of a contract as something which has to be performed, and if it is not performed, you have to grant full compensation.
In the 19th century Germans considered a sort of substitute rule for the foreseeability rule, which finally made its way into the code, but it is, as a practical matter, not very important. That relates to something we talked about yesterday; the mitigation principle.In fact, if we wanted not to grant full compensation, we would do it under the mitigation principle, and our code explicitly says that the defendant is required to give prior notice to the other party if he risks incurring especially high damages,so to make the other party aware that he or she has to be very careful in performing the contract.
If we look at this kind of rule and compare it with the foreseeability rule, I think it has several advantages. First, you can use it for contract and tort at the same time. Second, the risk of damage which is unforeseeable to both parties is borne by the defendant, not by the plaintiff. Third, because it is a question of mitigation, you have only to give notice if there is a reasonable probability that this notice will alter the other party's behavior. So you do not have to give notice merely to get full compensation afterwards in cases like standard transactions, where it is completely clear that this notice won't have any effect on the level of care the other party observes. Fourth, the notice need not be given at the time the contract is made but only at the time before the breach or the tort. So the other party always has to adjust his or her behavior to his or her present state of knowledge and not to the state of knowledge perhaps of three months ago when the contract was made. So I think that this in fact is the better rule, although it has not been put very much in operation.
To conclude, I would like to make one remark which perhaps also explains why Germany does not have the foreseeability rule. I hope you will forgive me the remark, but something which strikes me about this Conference, as a German lawyer, is that we have heard I think about eighteen talks about and around Hadley v. Baxendale, but none of those talks has dealt with the application of the rule. Nobody has talked about what the foreseeability rule actually says. When is a certain kind of damage foreseeable? What has to be foreseeable, the extent of the damage, the amount, or the kind of damage? What is the level of probability required to make any kind of damage foreseeable?
I have a suspicion that in fact this is considered one of the biggest advantages of this rule in common law: nobody knows what the law actually says and therefore, you can do anything you want with it. As Robert Dunn said in his book on the recovery of damages for lost profits, the rule is merely a "makeweight to a decision based on adequate independent grounds."So I have the impression that the courts can require any kind of probability they want, and if that does not help, they pull the "tacit agreement" test out of the hat and say: "There is a tacit agreement required, and therefore we want to deny that recovery."
That would be an idea very repugnant to a German lawyer, because it means giving the judges lots of discretion. (Of course our judges have some discretion too, but that is something you must not talk about in public.) We have the idea that predictability is of very high value, and that judges are merely the mouth of the law, certainly not an individual person who brings in his or her own conceptions of how the world should be. We don't even know the names of our Supreme Court judges; I think ninety percent of the law students could not name a single Supreme Court judge in Germany. Therefore, we are looking for a rule which gives certainty, and that is certainly not the foreseeability rule.
Also, from an economic viewpoint, I think a rule which gives certainty would be much better. As Ayres and Gertner put it, contract law operates as penalty default rules which simply make the parties contract around and find the rule which is best for their contract.As such a penalty default rule, one should choose a clear rule with which everybody knows where he or she stands, rather than a rule the meaning of which you will only know once the court has decided.
sorry for criticizing heavily the common law, but I guess that is partly what I am here for.
SPURLOCK: Before we respond, let me clear up something for Florian. He says that in Germany they view judges as the mouth of the law. As we know here, in our common law system judges are considered to be the oracles of the law; that is, those people in which all wisdom resides, and therefore, much like the Oracle of Delphi we give you cryptic pronouncements that we expect you somehow to make sense of. Allan?
ALLAN HUTCHINSON: Yogi Berra had a lot of wisdom to say about the law, and one of his reputed lines was: "Prediction is very difficult, especially about the future."[Laughter] This strikes me assaying a lot about law. But as my first line went down well, I will give another, which somehow connects with what Florian said. There was a popular commentator in England, who was asked to explain what football is, or what soccer is. He gave a rather elaborate explanation, but it ended like this: "Football is a simple game where twenty-two players play against each other and in the end Germany wins."[Laughter]
That is one English joke about Germany I am comfortable telling. It is a story where Germany comes out ahead, and Florian thinks that would be the same with the German legal system. I know nothing about Germany, so I speak with no authority on these matters. But I would like to make a couple of comments about what Florian said.
The first is how different really is German law to Anglo-American law in this sense? It is very dangerous, I think, to look at an isolated rule and say: "Well, we don't have that rule. Therefore, our system works differently." It seems to me that one needs to look at the whole of the system. One would need to know more about it. Some of these things have been mentioned. Florian says: "Well, we don't have strict liability, we have fault." But he also says that there is a lot in there that starts to counterweight that. There is the principle of mitigation. There is causation - we might want to look at German causation rules about how one connects events, whether one can claim this or that kind of particular damages that result from the contract. I think that before we can make that assessment of whether German law is truly different in the Hadley v. Baxendale situation, we would have to look at the whole system. That is point number one.
The second point is that if we really wanted to know whether German law was different, we could not just stop by looking at the books. We have a habit of saying "if you look at the books of English law it is this way, if you look at the books of German law it is this way." But what we have to look at is what are the damages actually given out across the board by German courts as compared to American or English courts.
have no answer to that. But I don't think it will be much different at the end of the day, when we assess what is actually going on. It maywell be different, but not significantly different across the board. It seems to me to do this kind of comparative work, which I think is vitally important, we need to do more - dare I say - empirical studies about this kind of material. But these will need to be real empirical studies about what actually happens in the courts. So one needs to look at that.
And one question that Florian flagged - which presumably we could turn around on German law - is not so much what does Hadley v. Baxendale say, but what does Hadley v. Baxendale demand? At this point it is very difficult to say what it demands. To my mind that is why it has been around for 150 years. It can be used by different people for different things.
said, when I presented the other day,that Hadley v. Baxendale is number two in the English common law hit parade, and number one is Donoghue v. Stevenson.Donoghue v. Stevenson is a wonderful case. It says basically nothing about the duty of care relationship.That is part of its appeal; the fact we can't nail down what it says, and it does give rise to lots of different decisions.
Another point, relating to one of the questions Joe asked, and still asks,is what might have happened if there had been no Hadley v. Baxendale. I have been reading a book about a genre of history called "the might have been" - it's probably got another title- but thequestion is "what if this had not happened"? What would things be like? I have not read all the book yet. One of its examples is, what if Margaret Thatcher had been killed by the bomb in Brighton in the late Seventies? What would have been different? What if Hitler had been killed as a child - had stepped off the curb one day and was killed in a road accident. Would history be different?
Well, this is a similar kind of question. What would have happened if the shaft had not broken? If there had been a different group of people on the jury.
My response is that I can't believe that everything turned on those particular events. I understand the idea of the butterfly effect in chaos theory: if you just change the flapping of a butterfly's wing, everything will change throughout the world. But I have difficulty with that. If there had not been Hadley v. Baxendale, there would have been something else. Even the most formalistic lawyer has to believe that material forces have some impact upon the kind of laws we get. It can't just be happenstance that this case came along, and but for this case the rule would have been something different. My view is that if it had not been Hadley v. Baxendale, it would have been another case. The facts or the language might have been slightly different. Even the result in the case might have been different. But we would have ended up in much the same place that we are now. We have to be careful about isolating these decisions. If you realize that Hadley v. Baxendale rule is pretty vague, anyway, another rule may not have led to that many different results.
Finally, the big question to which this speaks is the relationship between law and society. How do we try and understand the relationship between the laws we have and the society of which we are a part? We get easily trapped in our little boxes, whether as German lawyers or English lawyers, into believing that things had to be the way they are. This seems to me rather silly. First, it is even hard to think about law and society as separate in order to even ask the question, "How does one influence the other?" It's hard to imagine what our society would look like if you pulled law out - it's like talking about a body without a skeleton.
To move from the ridiculous to the sublime, we spent this afternoon doing what all lawyers do so well, and which I can do with the best of them, when we were slicing and dicing the Gateway case.I want to go to the other extreme and ask how we answer the question: "Do certain substantive material and social conditions demand certain particular legal forms?" That is a very big and abstract question. It seems to me that this kind of discussion can lead to that. We have a belief, I think, that certain material conditions give rise to and demandcertain legal forms. But if one looks at Germany, England, and the U.S., it is hard to imagine that having or not having Hadley v. Baxendale would have a big effect on the kind of economic or commercial world in which we live.
As lawyers, we seem to think that certain legal forms are important, that they are demanded by the economic realities. When I listen to the kind of presentation that Florian makes, I am persuaded that we need to break away from that kind of thinking. One, we are not really that important as lawyers. Two, contract law is only a kind of default regime which people can negotiate around as much as they want. Three, even if we switch the rules around, things will tend to come out in a similar way because there are larger forces at work.
Now, this does not apply to everything. There is a big argument in Anglo-American law about whether the corporate form was necessary to advance the capitalist agenda, particularly at the end of the nineteenth century. Some people argue that the capitalist economic revolution could not have occurred without the corporate form. I sometimes think that. But I often think that it would have happened some way or another. I can't believe that not having the corporate form would have brought an end to the capitalist advance.
That makes me think there is no necessary connection between the society we have and the laws we have. There are obviously some general connections about contracts and the like, but the particular details of laws we have are not as significant as we, as lawyers, like to think they are. This should chastise us to some extent, that when we do start arguing about Gateway and other such cases - and I am part of that, though I don't really do contract law - sometimes we should think that is an indulgence on our part about details. We should step back and think about the bigger picture, because that is going to have much more of an effect than how exactly we decide particular cases.

papers.node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev243!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:INTRODUCTION: THE HISTORICAL SETTING FOR HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:INTRODUCTION: THE HISTORICAL SETTING FOR HADLEY v. BAXENDALE
papers.abstract:
Joseph and Jonah Hadley ran the City Flour Mills in the docks at Gloucester, England, and in 1853 they had an urgent need to send a broken shaft back to the manufacturer's works. Joseph Baxendale was the managing partner of the carriers Pickford & Co., who did not keep its promise to transport the shaft quickly. This piece describes the historical setting of the City Flour Mills and outlines the events featured in the subsequent legal case that became famous as Hadley v. Baxendale.
The docks at Gloucester developed at the terminus of a ship canal which bypassed a difficult stretch of the River Severn. The canal was completed in 1827 and allowed the largest sailing ships of the day to discharge their cargoes in a basin close to the centre of the city. From here, goods were transferred to smaller craft to continue up the River Severn and through the narrow canal system to supply the growing industrial towns further inland.
The main imports through Gloucester were timber and corn - the latter being a generic term which covered wheat, oats, barley, maize, et cetera. Timber came in the form of squared logs and sawn deals from the Baltic countries, the north of Russia and Canada. To store the wood, extensive yards were established around the terminus basin and down the east side of the canal approaching Gloucester. This trade was particularly stimulated by a boom in the construction of railways. Corn came from Ireland, western Europe and the Black Sea ports around the mouth of the Danube. To store the corn in sacks, five and six storey brick warehouses were built with wooden floors supported by cast-iron columns. This trade benefited from the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, which effectively ended the import duty on foreign corn. Unfortunately, the only convenient export cargo was salt brought down the river from the Droitwich area, and many vessels departed empty to pick up coal from one of the South Wales ports.
One of the pictures shows the bridge at the approach to the terminus basin with some warehouses and the tower of Gloucester cathedralin the background. The bridge was in two halves, each of which was swung open to let a vessel pass. On the extreme right can be seen the bow of a ship that had been towed up the canal by the horse standing on the towpath. This view would have been much like that seen by the crew of the first ship direct from the United States which brought 9,500 barrels of wheat in December 1845.
Trade continued to increase, aided by railway links to the docks, and a second basin was opened in 1849. The good transport facilities attracted the development of local industries, one of the first being the construction of the City Flour Mills by Joseph and Jonah Hadley in 1850. Prior to this, corn imported through Gloucester was sent on to existing mills, but it made sense to build a mill where the corn was being delivered. The two brothers had experience of small water-powered mills, but with no water-power available in the docks area, they set up a steam-powered mill. Initially, the mill was a single building, similar to the nearby warehouses, with a small engine house adjoining supplying power to a few pairs of millstones and some flour dressing machines. The business was immediately successful, and in 1853 the Hadleys added another large building on the site of the engine house and installed more machinery and two new steam engines to double the output of the mill.
During the installation of the new machinery, the crank shaft of one of the steam engines failed, and there was an urgent need to send it back to the manufacturer, Messrs. Joyce & Co. of Greenwich.Pickford's agent in Gloucester said that if it received the shaft before twelve o'clock, it would be delivered in Greenwich the following day.Unfortunately, due to a misunderstanding, the delivery of the shaft was delayed by five working days.
When the Hadley brothers complained about the delay, Pickford's acknowledged responsibility and offered £ 25 in compensation, but the Hadleys demanded an amount closer to £ 125 for their loss of profits during the additional period their mill was idle.The case was heard in the Crown Court at Gloucester's summer assizes before a special jury composed of respected local businessmen.Pickford's barrister argued that the shaft was only worth about £ 10 and their offer of £ 25 damages was more than reasonable.The judge, however, ruled that the value of the object was irrelevant and that the defendants were answerable for the natural consequences of their breach of contract.With this guidance, the jury awarded damages of £ 50.
Pickford's considered that this basis for awarding damages was unreasonable, and in February 1854, they asked the Court of Exchequer to order a new trial.After hearing legal arguments, the judge granted the request and set down the principles which any jury should consider when estimating damages.He said that where a party had entered into and broken a contract, the other party should only receive damages for consequences that might reasonably have been contemplated by both parties at the time that the contract was made.As the Hadley brothers had not made it clear that the profits from their mill were at stake, he considered that it was not reasonable for Pickford's to be expected to make good those profits.
No record has been found of any subsequent retrial before a jury, and it is assumed that the two parties settled out of court. What is certain is that the judge's ruling established the forseeability test for consequential damages that has been followed in virtually every Anglo-American jurisdiction since.
By 1860, the Hadley brothers had transferred their activities to London, and operations at Gloucester were taken over by Joseph Reynolds and Henry Allen, who also had other mills in the area. Their continuing success set a fine example, and six other flour mills were established in Gloucester between 1863 and 1871. All this contributed to a very busy period in the history of the docks, with many vessels bringing in increasing amounts of wheat from all parts of the world.
Reynolds and Allen passed over management of the mill in 1875 to a new partnership formed by their sons, Vincent Reynolds and John Allen, together with Francis Tring Pearce who had married John Allen's sister. They were soon faced with the need for major new investment to meet the threat of growing competition from cheaper foreign flour. A totally new method of milling using rollers instead of the traditional stones had been developed in Hungary, and the partners were obliged to purchase the new equipment or risk getting left behind. Unfortunately, this investment was followed by a period of general economic difficulty, and the partners were forced to pass over the business to new management.
Priday Metford & Co. was formed in 1886 by Charles Priday, who had two other mills in the area, F.K.S. Metford from Bristol and F.T. Pearce from the former partnership. These three quickly got the businessback into profitability, and it was members of these three families that continued to run the mill for the next hundred years.
The general increase in the size of ships in service meant that fewer were able to pass up the canal to Gloucester, and by the early years of the twentieth century, most of the wheat used by the mill arrived at Gloucester in barges towed from larger neighbouring ports. As the size of ships increased still further, Liverpool became the dominant west-coast port for wheat imports, and in the 1970s the delivery of wheat to the mill gradually changed over from the use of barges to lorries coming down the motorway. In later years, a greater proportion of English wheat was used, and considerable deliveries came direct from local farms.
Continuing investment kept the mill machinery up-to-date, but the family business found it increasingly difficult to compete against the big national milling companies. Eventually, the mill was taken over by the Spillers Milling subsidiary of Dalgety plc, and the new management ordered the closure of the mill in March of 1994 because of surplus capacity. This regrettably broke the last link with the corn trade that was once so important in the docks and brought a sad end to the history of one of Gloucester's oldest companies.
By this time, the docks at Gloucester had ceased to be used for commercial traffic and were in the process of being redeveloped for leisure uses. The mill buildings stood empty for a few years, and then they were converted into apartments. This work was virtually complete by June 2004, when a conference was held to mark the 150th anniversary of the historic judgement that has given the City Flour Mills a lasting place in legal history.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RELATIONAL CONTRACTING IN A DIGITAL AGE
papers.authors: Franklin G. Snyder; Ian R. Macneil; John A. Kidwell; David Campbell; Rachel Arnow-Richman
papers.abstract:
Few developments in contracts scholarship in the past half-century have been more influential than relational contract theory.Perhaps no other recent movement has seeped so deeply into the way we think of and discuss contract law than the notion that the things we think of as "contracts" are rooted in larger relationships, and cannot be understood apart from those relationships. But it is also fair to say that no other movement has managed to take so many different forms. Robert Scott and Randy Barnett have both said that "we are all relationists now,"which is almost certainly true - depending on how we define "relationist."
No figure has played a more important role in the development of relational contract theory than Ian Macneil, who has been exploringthe relational aspects of contracting since the early 1960s.For Macneil, the theory involves four basic propositions, no more and no less:

questions.question: Whether and how the common law of contracts operates as a global influence shaping contracting practices and legal thought across different historical or technological revolutions.
Whether relational contract theory's core propositions accurately describe and should guide analysis of contemporary (digital-age) contracting practices.
Whether the relational view of contracting explains contractual behavior and legal outcomes better than traditional transactional models across varied jurisdictions and contexts.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:RULES, PRINCIPLES, OR JUST WORDS?:EXTENDING THE LESSONS OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE 1 156 Eng. Rep. 145 (Ex. 1854).
papers.abstract: I have taught the venerable case of Hadley v. Baxendale more than thirty times to students in Contracts I and an additional thirty or more times to students in a Remedies course. I recently realized that I had underestimated the potential of the case. This Conference, and some conversations with my colleague Bill Whitford led me to realize that Hadley can be used more ambitiously. The trick to doing this is easy. One has simply to ask students to imagine that the notice of special circumstances had been given, and then ask what the victims of the breach would have needed to prove in order to recover significant damages, and whether Baxendale would have had any remaining credible defenses.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent advance notice of special circumstances enables a non-breaching party to recover consequential damages following a contract breach.
What types and standards of proof a non-breaching party must meet to recover significant consequential damages after a breach when special circumstances were disclosed.
Whether disclosure of special circumstances alters the availability or credibility of defenses by the breaching party and thereby shifts the allocation of risk between the contracting parties.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE INCOMPLETENESS OF OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE LAW AND ECONOMICS OF RELATIONAL CONTRACT
papers.abstract: In the articles by Professors Juliet Kostritskyon which I have been privileged to be asked to comment, the resources of sophisticated law and economics as applied to "relational contracts" are used to suggest reforms to the law of contractual agreement. These reforms are intended to make that law of greater use to competent commercial parties who deliberately draft incomplete agreements. Kostritsky and Ben-Shahar tell us that under the current law, such agreements may fall foul of being struck out for indefiniteness, or of being effectively supplanted by judicial gap filling that does not capture the intentions of the parties. Kostritsky and Ben-Shahar have differing opinions about what should be done about this, but, whilst I shall describe their interesting suggestions, I shall not address this Comment to the detail of those suggestions. It is on the background conception of the role of law in supporting commercial parties' contracts which they share that I will principally comment. For I believe this conception is unsatisfactory, but in an interesting way tells us a great deal about the current use of law and economics in contract scholarship and about the current state of relational contract theory.

questions.question: Whether and how the legal system should accommodate and enforce deliberately incomplete relational contracts entered into by sophisticated commercial parties.
Whether the law-and-economics conception of the role of law in supporting commercial parties' relational contracts accurately captures the parties' needs and intentions.
Whether judicial gap-filling practices in the face of contractual incompleteness produce outcomes that align with the parties' intentions or instead warrant legal reform.
